problem: is there a vad system designed with weighted finite state transducers and deep neural networks? how does it work
final_response:
Yes. There are speech activity detection (SAD/VAD) systems that combine weighted finite-state transducers (WFSTs) with deep neural networks (DNNs), typically by using a DNN to produce frame- or segment-level scores and a WFST-based decoder to smooth, constrain, and align those scores into temporally consistent activity labels or segmentation hypotheses.<cite id="d2fca636-0">The output from each DNN in a broadcast-transcription SAD study was explicitly smoothed using a WFST-based decoder, yielding a slight transcription accuracy improvement and a significant reduction in computation time</cite>.<cite id="5937a575-1">This same study reports that DNN-based SAD modules trained on speech and non-speech data, with artificial mixtures at target SNRs, were coupled with WFST smoothing</cite>.

How such a WFST+DNN VAD system works

1) Neural scoring and feature modeling
- A DNN (or deep encoder) computes a high-confidence speech-vs-nonspeech score (or posterior) for each frame or short window. These DNNs are trained on labeled speech/non-speech data (often including noisy mixtures) to predict activity labels or posterior probabilities from acoustic features (e.g., log power spectra and derived dynamics).<cite id="5937a575-0">A DNN-based VAD using time-varying dynamics (first/second-order mel-cepstrum derivatives and subband cues) improved detection in multiple noise types and SNRs compared to spectrum-only baselines</cite>.<cite id="5937a575-2">In that system, subband information around the F0 region was important, and removing it degraded performance</cite>.
- In speech processing pipelines, DNNs are commonly used to model observation likelihoods or posterior probabilities for HMM states (DNN-HMM hybrids), providing strong acoustic modeling while retaining the HMM’s temporal structure for segmentation and decoding.<cite id="014fb0cc-4">In a hybrid HMM/DNN architecture, a DNN is trained to predict posterior probabilities of HMM states from features and can be used to estimate observation likelihoods; TDNNs with sequence-level MMI have been widely used for speech modeling</cite>.

2) WFST-based decoding and smoothing
- The WFST component provides a weighted finite-state graph that enforces temporal smoothness, activity boundary constraints, and other rules (e.g., minimum speech segment lengths, n-gram or linguistic constraints, or domain-specific rules), and it fuses multiple features or hypotheses over time. Conceptually, the WFST maps time-aligned DNN emissions into a globally optimal temporally consistent segmentation by shortest-path decoding (a weighted version of Viterbi/CYK).<cite id="014fb0cc-2">FSTs are a standard tool to represent and manipulate sequence prediction search spaces in speech, with complete HMM-based recognizer examples</cite>.<cite id="014fb0cc-3">Weighted transducers add input/output weights on transitions, enabling probabilistic modeling and shortest-path decoding in speech and related sequence tasks</cite>.
- In practice, the DNN outputs are used as edge weights on an emission graph built by compiling an FST/WFST, and the decoder computes the path with maximum (or minimum) accumulated weight, effectively “smoothing” the DNN decisions across time and enforcing task constraints.<cite id="d2fca636-0">A WFST-based decoder was used to smooth DNN SAD outputs in a broadcast transcription system, improving accuracy and reducing computation time</cite>.<cite id="d2fca636-2">A WFST-based decoder combining a WFSA and WFST has been used to simultaneously transcribe phonemes and detect dysfluencies by constructing an emission graph from encoder posterior frames and finding the shortest path over a topology that encodes allowed edits (e.g., return/skip arcs for repetitions), illustrating how weighted graphs integrate temporal constraints with neural emissions</cite>.

3) End-to-end integration in VAD/diarization systems
- In diarization/recognition workflows, a DNN-based VAD or activity detector can be run first to segment audio into speech and non-speech regions, and a single-pass WFST decoder can then refine the segmentation and feed the speech segments to a DNN-HMM acoustic model (or other ASR components) with minimal insertion errors and low latency.<cite id="d2fca636-4">A production ASR system described uses a DNN-HMM acoustic model with an internally developed single-pass WFST decoder; prior to recognition, DNN-based VAD similar to prior work was applied to minimize insertion errors</cite>.
- WFST decoders can also operate jointly on multiple hypotheses or scores (e.g., activity posterior, phonetic posterior, language-model constraints) to produce aligned activity labels, phoneme sequences, and detected events, depending on how the WFST is constructed and weighted.<cite id="d2fca636-2">By combining a WFST that encodes allowed pronunciation behaviors (e.g., repetitions, insertions) with frame-level neural posterior probabilities, the shortest-path decoder outputs both transcription and event annotations in one pass</cite>.

Training and optimization considerations

- Hybrid DNN–HMM systems are commonly trained with sequence-level objectives (e.g., MMI) using TDNN/DNN emission models, while WFSTs define the search space for decoding rather than the training loss. The same DNN can be trained with large datasets and then deployed with WFST-based search to balance accuracy and efficiency.<cite id="014fb0cc-4">TDNN-based acoustic models trained with maximum mutual information sequence-level objective have been widely adopted for speech recognition, and in hybrid systems the DNN provides state posteriors while the HMM/decoder handles temporal structure</cite>.<cite id="014fb0cc-0">DNN-HMM training and decoding parameters (e.g., max-active) are set in concert with the WFST and lexicon; the DNN-HMM showed performance gains over HMM baselines on impaired speech tasks</cite>.
- The WFST itself may be compiled from decision trees or other finite-state structures to represent feature-space partitions and constraints, enabling efficient weighted transducer composition and shortest-path decoding (Viterbi/CYK variants) at scale.<cite id="014fb0cc-1">Methods for compilation of weighted finite-state transducers from decision trees underpin efficient search and composition in speech processing</cite>.<cite id="014fb0cc-2">FSTs provide a compact representation of the sequence search space with algorithms well-suited to speech recognition tasks</cite>.

What the WFST does in such a VAD system

- Temporal smoothing: The WFST enforces minimum/maximum durations of speech and non-speech segments, preventing choppiness or false alternations caused by noisy DNN scores.<cite id="d2fca636-0">Using a WFST decoder to smooth DNN SAD outputs improved transcription outcomes, indicating that temporal smoothing across frames is beneficial</cite>.
- Constraint enforcement: It can incorporate language-model-like constraints or task-specific rules (e.g., activity alternation, speaker turn structure), aligning VAD decisions with higher-level assumptions about speech behavior.<cite id="d2fca636-2">The WFST topology can encode allowed deviations (e.g., return arcs for repetitions), integrating behavioral constraints into decoding</cite>.
- Multi-hypothesis fusion: Emissions can combine neural activity posteriors with other cues (e.g., energy, voice quality), and the WFST selects the globally optimal path under a unified weighted model.<cite id="d2fca636-2">An emission graph is constructed from log posterior probabilities of phoneme classes over frames, and the WFST topology plus these weights defines the search space over which the shortest path is computed</cite>.

Applications and examples

- Broadcast/transcription SAD: DNN classifiers trained on speech/non-speech mixtures produced per-frame decisions that were then smoothed by a WFST decoder, improving accuracy and reducing computation time for large-volume transcription.<cite id="d2fca636-0">Experiments on mixed-content broadcast data showed that WFST-smoothed DNN SAD yielded both accuracy gains and latency reduction</cite>.<cite id="5937a575-1">The DNNs were trained with speech and non-speech data and artificial mixtures at target SNRs to make the WFST smoothing effective in realistic conditions</cite>.
- Diarization/recognition pipelines: DNN-based VAD pre-segments audio, and a single-pass WFST decoder with a DNN-HMM acoustic model minimizes insertions and supports efficient real-time decoding, demonstrating end-to-end integration of neural scoring with WFST-based search in a diarization-ready system.<cite id="d2fca636-4">A DNN-HMM AM with a single-pass WFST decoder and DNN-based VAD prior to recognition was used to reduce insertion errors in a large-scale system</cite>.
- Beyond VAD: WFST-based decoders have been used to jointly transcribe and detect dysfluencies by combining neural posterior frames with a WFST that encodes allowed phonetic edits, illustrating the same WFST+DNN integration principle across speech behavior analysis tasks.<cite id="d2fca636-2">A WFST combining phoneme posterior emissions with return/skip arcs enabled detection of repetitions and accurate phonetic alignment in a zero-shot setup using upstream encoders</cite>.

Practical considerations and benefits

- Efficiency and latency: WFST decoders operate with weighted Viterbi/CYK algorithms on compiled graphs, often enabling single-pass, low-latency decoding that can incorporate neural scores without per-frame decisions dominating the output.<cite id="d2fca636-0">The WFST-based SAD smoothing reduced computation time for transcription</cite>.<cite id="d2fca636-4">A single-pass WFST decoder was used in a production ASR setup with DNN-based VAD to minimize insertions</cite>.
- Robustness: DNNs provide strong feature-to-activity mapping under noise and reverberation, while WFSTs enforce temporal and task constraints that mitigate noisy DNN fluctuations, yielding more reliable activity segmentations for diarization and downstream ASR.<cite id="5937a575-0">DNN-based VAD with dynamics outperformed spectrum-only baselines across multiple noise types and SNRs</cite>.<cite id="d2fca636-0">Smoothing with a WFST improved accuracy and efficiency in real data</cite>.

Bottom line

- Yes—WFSTs have been combined with DNNs in practical VAD/SAD systems. The approach uses a DNN to generate per-frame or per-segment activity scores and a WFST-based decoder to compute a globally optimal, temporally smooth segmentation under explicit constraints via shortest-path decoding on a weighted FST/WFST graph.<cite id="d2fca636-0">DNN outputs for SAD can be smoothed by a WFST-based decoder with measurable gains in accuracy and efficiency</cite>.<cite id="014fb0cc-4">Hybrid DNN–HMM speech models with WFST-based decoding are standard in speech processing and can be preceded by DNN-based VAD to reduce recognition errors</cite>.<cite id="014fb0cc-2">FSTs/WFSTs provide the compact, weighted search space and algorithms needed to integrate neural scores with temporal and linguistic constraints in sequence prediction tasks like VAD and diarization</cite>.

Title: Enhancement of speech dynamics for voice activity detection using DNN
Snippet: Voice activity detection (VAD) is an important preprocessing step for various speech applications to identify speech and non-speech periods in input signals. In this paper, we propose a deep neural network (DNN)-based VAD method for detecting such periods in noisy signals using speech dynamics, which are time-varying speech signals that may be expressed as the first- and second-order derivatives of mel cepstra, also known as the delta and delta-delta features. Unlike these derivatives, in this paper, the dynamics are highlighted by speech period candidates, which are calculated based on heuristic rules for the patterns of the first and second derivatives of the input signals. These candidates, together with the log power spectra, are input into the DNN to obtain VAD decisions. In this study, experiments are conducted to compare the proposed method with a DNN-based method, which exclusively utilizes log power spectra by using speech signals smeared with five types of noise (white, babble, factory, car, and pink) with signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs) of 10, 5, 0, and − 5 dB. The experimental results show that the proposed method is superior under all the considered noise conditions, indicating that the speech period candidates improve the log power spectra.
</snippet>

Title: Enhancement of speech dynamics for voice activity detection using DNN
Snippet: This study presents a DNN-based VAD method for improving the performance of VAD by introducing dynamics, which may be highlighted by speech period candidates. These candidates are derived from heuristic rules based on the first and second derivatives of the log power spectrum of the RSF output (LPS-RSF). The speech period candidates are calculated for individual subbands and are then input into a DNN together with the log power spectra to generate the VAD decision. To evaluate the performance of the proposed method, we perform experiments using clean and noisy speech signals smeared with five types of noise, namely, white, babble, factory, car, and pink, with SNRs of 10, 5, 0 and − 5 dB. The proposed method effectively detects speech and non-speech periods. The experimental results show that the VAD performance based on log power spectra are improved after combining the log power spectra with the speech period candidates, particularly for noisy speech signals with low SNRs and non-stationary cases. The addition of dynamics expressed by the speech period candidates provides positive information that contributes to the detection of speech periods. 

In this study, we also show that the DNN-based VAD utilizes subbands that may correspond to F0 and its neighbors. The VAD performance degrades when those subbands are eliminated. However, further studies should be performed to analyze other factors that influence the behavior of the employed DNN. Moreover, we intend to make the proposed method work in real time.
</snippet>

Title: MLNET: An Adaptive Multiple Receptive-field Attention Neural Network for Voice Activity Detection
Snippet: The existed DNN-based VAD models only leveraged fixed receptive-field contextual speech information and were unable to handle with speech segments of different lengths adaptively. To overcome this defect, this paper proposed an architecture of MLNET for VAD task. MLNET made use of different gated affined unit to extract different contextual speech information and leveraged the adaptive attention block to select the most focused speech segments. Comparing with the existed models, the experiments demonstrated that MLNET outformed other baseline models and proved that the proposed architecture was helpful to deal with VAD problems.
</snippet>

Title: BACON: Deep-Learning Powered AI for Poetry Generation with Author Linguistic Style Transfer
Snippet: A finite-state transducer (FST) is a type of finite-state automaton whose state transitions are labeled with both and output symbols, and therefore it maps between two sets of symbols. A path through the transducer encodes a mapping from an input symbol sequence to an output symbol sequence. A weighted transducer adds weights on transitions to the input and output symbols of a FST (Vidal et al., 2005). These weights may encode any quantity that accumulates along paths (e.g. probabilities or durations) and allow to compute the overall weight of mapping an input sequence to an output sequence. Weighted transducers are thus a natural choice to represent probabilistic finite-state models, which are commonly used for pattern recognition, or in fields to which pattern recognition is linked, such as computational linguistics, machine learning, time series analysis, computational biology, speech recognition, and machine translation.
</snippet>

Title: Dysfluent WFST: A Framework for Zero-Shot Speech Dysfluency Transcription and Detection
Snippet: Automatic detection of speech dysfluency aids speech-language pathologists in efficient transcription of disordered speech, enhancing diagnostics and treatment planning. Traditional methods, often limited to classification, provide insufficient clinical insight, and text-independent models misclassify dysfluency, especially in context-dependent cases. This work introduces Dysfluent-WFST, a zero-shot decoder that simultaneously transcribes phonemes and detects dysfluency. Unlike previous models, Dysfluent-WFST operates with upstream encoders like WavLM and requires no additional training. It achieves state-of-the-art performance in both phonetic error rate and dysfluency detection on simulated and real speech data. Our approach is lightweight, interpretable, and effective, demonstrating that explicit modeling of pronunciation behavior in decoding, rather than complex architectures, is key to improving dysfluency processing systems.
</snippet>

Yes. There are speech activity detection (SAD/VAD) systems that combine weighted finite-state transducers (WFSTs) with deep neural networks (DNNs), typically by using a DNN to produce frame- or segment-level scores and a WFST-based decoder to smooth, constrain, and align those scores into temporally consistent activity labels or segmentation hypotheses.<cite id="d2fca636-0">The output from each DNN in a broadcast-transcription SAD study was explicitly smoothed using a WFST-based decoder, yielding a slight transcription accuracy improvement and a significant reduction in computation time</cite>.<cite id="5937a575-1">This same study reports that DNN-based SAD modules trained on speech and non-speech data, with artificial mixtures at target SNRs, were coupled with WFST smoothing</cite>.

How such a WFST+DNN VAD system works

1) Neural scoring and feature modeling
- A DNN (or deep encoder) computes a high-confidence speech-vs-nonspeech score (or posterior) for each frame or short window. These DNNs are trained on labeled speech/non-speech data (often including noisy mixtures) to predict activity labels or posterior probabilities from acoustic features (e.g., log power spectra and derived dynamics).<cite id="5937a575-0">A DNN-based VAD using time-varying dynamics (first/second-order mel-cepstrum derivatives and subband cues) improved detection in multiple noise types and SNRs compared to spectrum-only baselines</cite>.<cite id="5937a575-2">In that system, subband information around the F0 region was important, and removing it degraded performance</cite>.
- In speech processing pipelines, DNNs are commonly used to model observation likelihoods or posterior probabilities for HMM states (DNN-HMM hybrids), providing strong acoustic modeling while retaining the HMM’s temporal structure for segmentation and decoding.<cite id="014fb0cc-4">In a hybrid HMM/DNN architecture, a DNN is trained to predict posterior probabilities of HMM states from features and can be used to estimate observation likelihoods; TDNNs with sequence-level MMI have been widely used for speech modeling</cite>.

2) WFST-based decoding and smoothing
- The WFST component provides a weighted finite-state graph that enforces temporal smoothness, activity boundary constraints, and other rules (e.g., minimum speech segment lengths, n-gram or linguistic constraints, or domain-specific rules), and it fuses multiple features or hypotheses over time. Conceptually, the WFST maps time-aligned DNN emissions into a globally optimal temporally consistent segmentation by shortest-path decoding (a weighted version of Viterbi/CYK).<cite id="014fb0cc-2">FSTs are a standard tool to represent and manipulate sequence prediction search spaces in speech, with complete HMM-based recognizer examples</cite>.<cite id="014fb0cc-3">Weighted transducers add input/output weights on transitions, enabling probabilistic modeling and shortest-path decoding in speech and related sequence tasks</cite>.
- In practice, the DNN outputs are used as edge weights on an emission graph built by compiling an FST/WFST, and the decoder computes the path with maximum (or minimum) accumulated weight, effectively “smoothing” the DNN decisions across time and enforcing task constraints.<cite id="d2fca636-0">A WFST-based decoder was used to smooth DNN SAD outputs in a broadcast transcription system, improving accuracy and reducing computation time</cite>.<cite id="d2fca636-2">A WFST-based decoder combining a WFSA and WFST has been used to simultaneously transcribe phonemes and detect dysfluencies by constructing an emission graph from encoder posterior frames and finding the shortest path over a topology that encodes allowed edits (e.g., return/skip arcs for repetitions), illustrating how weighted graphs integrate temporal constraints with neural emissions</cite>.

3) End-to-end integration in VAD/diarization systems
- In diarization/recognition workflows, a DNN-based VAD or activity detector can be run first to segment audio into speech and non-speech regions, and a single-pass WFST decoder can then refine the segmentation and feed the speech segments to a DNN-HMM acoustic model (or other ASR components) with minimal insertion errors and low latency.<cite id="d2fca636-4">A production ASR system described uses a DNN-HMM acoustic model with an internally developed single-pass WFST decoder; prior to recognition, DNN-based VAD similar to prior work was applied to minimize insertion errors</cite>.
- WFST decoders can also operate jointly on multiple hypotheses or scores (e.g., activity posterior, phonetic posterior, language-model constraints) to produce aligned activity labels, phoneme sequences, and detected events, depending on how the WFST is constructed and weighted.<cite id="d2fca636-2">By combining a WFST that encodes allowed pronunciation behaviors (e.g., repetitions, insertions) with frame-level neural posterior probabilities, the shortest-path decoder outputs both transcription and event annotations in one pass</cite>.

Training and optimization considerations

- Hybrid DNN–HMM systems are commonly trained with sequence-level objectives (e.g., MMI) using TDNN/DNN emission models, while WFSTs define the search space for decoding rather than the training loss. The same DNN can be trained with large datasets and then deployed with WFST-based search to balance accuracy and efficiency.<cite id="014fb0cc-4">TDNN-based acoustic models trained with maximum mutual information sequence-level objective have been widely adopted for speech recognition, and in hybrid systems the DNN provides state posteriors while the HMM/decoder handles temporal structure</cite>.<cite id="014fb0cc-0">DNN-HMM training and decoding parameters (e.g., max-active) are set in concert with the WFST and lexicon; the DNN-HMM showed performance gains over HMM baselines on impaired speech tasks</cite>.
- The WFST itself may be compiled from decision trees or other finite-state structures to represent feature-space partitions and constraints, enabling efficient weighted transducer composition and shortest-path decoding (Viterbi/CYK variants) at scale.<cite id="014fb0cc-1">Methods for compilation of weighted finite-state transducers from decision trees underpin efficient search and composition in speech processing</cite>.<cite id="014fb0cc-2">FSTs provide a compact representation of the sequence search space with algorithms well-suited to speech recognition tasks</cite>.

What the WFST does in such a VAD system

- Temporal smoothing: The WFST enforces minimum/maximum durations of speech and non-speech segments, preventing choppiness or false alternations caused by noisy DNN scores.<cite id="d2fca636-0">Using a WFST decoder to smooth DNN SAD outputs improved transcription outcomes, indicating that temporal smoothing across frames is beneficial</cite>.
- Constraint enforcement: It can incorporate language-model-like constraints or task-specific rules (e.g., activity alternation, speaker turn structure), aligning VAD decisions with higher-level assumptions about speech behavior.<cite id="d2fca636-2">The WFST topology can encode allowed deviations (e.g., return arcs for repetitions), integrating behavioral constraints into decoding</cite>.
- Multi-hypothesis fusion: Emissions can combine neural activity posteriors with other cues (e.g., energy, voice quality), and the WFST selects the globally optimal path under a unified weighted model.<cite id="d2fca636-2">An emission graph is constructed from log posterior probabilities of phoneme classes over frames, and the WFST topology plus these weights defines the search space over which the shortest path is computed</cite>.

Applications and examples

- Broadcast/transcription SAD: DNN classifiers trained on speech/non-speech mixtures produced per-frame decisions that were then smoothed by a WFST decoder, improving accuracy and reducing computation time for large-volume transcription.<cite id="d2fca636-0">Experiments on mixed-content broadcast data showed that WFST-smoothed DNN SAD yielded both accuracy gains and latency reduction</cite>.<cite id="5937a575-1">The DNNs were trained with speech and non-speech data and artificial mixtures at target SNRs to make the WFST smoothing effective in realistic conditions</cite>.
- Diarization/recognition pipelines: DNN-based VAD pre-segments audio, and a single-pass WFST decoder with a DNN-HMM acoustic model minimizes insertions and supports efficient real-time decoding, demonstrating end-to-end integration of neural scoring with WFST-based search in a diarization-ready system.<cite id="d2fca636-4">A DNN-HMM AM with a single-pass WFST decoder and DNN-based VAD prior to recognition was used to reduce insertion errors in a large-scale system</cite>.
- Beyond VAD: WFST-based decoders have been used to jointly transcribe and detect dysfluencies by combining neural posterior frames with a WFST that encodes allowed phonetic edits, illustrating the same WFST+DNN integration principle across speech behavior analysis tasks.<cite id="d2fca636-2">A WFST combining phoneme posterior emissions with return/skip arcs enabled detection of repetitions and accurate phonetic alignment in a zero-shot setup using upstream encoders</cite>.

Practical considerations and benefits

- Efficiency and latency: WFST decoders operate with weighted Viterbi/CYK algorithms on compiled graphs, often enabling single-pass, low-latency decoding that can incorporate neural scores without per-frame decisions dominating the output.<cite id="d2fca636-0">The WFST-based SAD smoothing reduced computation time for transcription</cite>.<cite id="d2fca636-4">A single-pass WFST decoder was used in a production ASR setup with DNN-based VAD to minimize insertions</cite>.
- Robustness: DNNs provide strong feature-to-activity mapping under noise and reverberation, while WFSTs enforce temporal and task constraints that mitigate noisy DNN fluctuations, yielding more reliable activity segmentations for diarization and downstream ASR.<cite id="5937a575-0">DNN-based VAD with dynamics outperformed spectrum-only baselines across multiple noise types and SNRs</cite>.<cite id="d2fca636-0">Smoothing with a WFST improved accuracy and efficiency in real data</cite>.

Bottom line

- Yes—WFSTs have been combined with DNNs in practical VAD/SAD systems. The approach uses a DNN to generate per-frame or per-segment activity scores and a WFST-based decoder to compute a globally optimal, temporally smooth segmentation under explicit constraints via shortest-path decoding on a weighted FST/WFST graph.<cite id="d2fca636-0">DNN outputs for SAD can be smoothed by a WFST-based decoder with measurable gains in accuracy and efficiency</cite>.<cite id="014fb0cc-4">Hybrid DNN–HMM speech models with WFST-based decoding are standard in speech processing and can be preceded by DNN-based VAD to reduce recognition errors</cite>.<cite id="014fb0cc-2">FSTs/WFSTs provide the compact, weighted search space and algorithms needed to integrate neural scores with temporal and linguistic constraints in sequence prediction tasks like VAD and diarization</cite>.

Title: Enhancement of speech dynamics for voice activity detection using DNN
Snippet: Voice activity detection (VAD) is an important preprocessing step for various speech applications to identify speech and non-speech periods in input signals. In this paper, we propose a deep neural network (DNN)-based VAD method for detecting such periods in noisy signals using speech dynamics, which are time-varying speech signals that may be expressed as the first- and second-order derivatives of mel cepstra, also known as the delta and delta-delta features. Unlike these derivatives, in this paper, the dynamics are highlighted by speech period candidates, which are calculated based on heuristic rules for the patterns of the first and second derivatives of the input signals. These candidates, together with the log power spectra, are input into the DNN to obtain VAD decisions. In this study, experiments are conducted to compare the proposed method with a DNN-based method, which exclusively utilizes log power spectra by using speech signals smeared with five types of noise (white, babble, factory, car, and pink) with signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs) of 10, 5, 0, and − 5 dB. The experimental results show that the proposed method is superior under all the considered noise conditions, indicating that the speech period candidates improve the log power spectra.

Title: Study on the Use of Deep Neural Networks for Speech Activity Detection in Broadcast Recordings
Snippet: This paper deals with the task of Speech Activity Detection (SAD). Our goal is to develop a SAD module 
 
suitable for a system for broadcast data transcription. Various Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) are evaluated 
 
for this purpose. Training of DNNs is performed using speech and non-speech data as well as artificial data 
 
created by mixing of both these data types at a desired level of Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR). The output 
 
from each DNN is smoothed using a decoder based on Weighted Finite State Transducers (WFSTs). The 
 
presented experimental results show that the use of the resulting SAD module leads to a) a slight improvement 
 
in transcription accuracy and b) a significant reduction in the computation time needed for transcription.

Title: Enhancement of speech dynamics for voice activity detection using DNN
Snippet: This study presents a DNN-based VAD method for improving the performance of VAD by introducing dynamics, which may be highlighted by speech period candidates. These candidates are derived from heuristic rules based on the first and second derivatives of the log power spectrum of the RSF output (LPS-RSF). The speech period candidates are calculated for individual subbands and are then input into a DNN together with the log power spectra to generate the VAD decision. To evaluate the performance of the proposed method, we perform experiments using clean and noisy speech signals smeared with five types of noise, namely, white, babble, factory, car, and pink, with SNRs of 10, 5, 0 and − 5 dB. The proposed method effectively detects speech and non-speech periods. The experimental results show that the VAD performance based on log power spectra are improved after combining the log power spectra with the speech period candidates, particularly for noisy speech signals with low SNRs and non-stationary cases. The addition of dynamics expressed by the speech period candidates provides positive information that contributes to the detection of speech periods. 

In this study, we also show that the DNN-based VAD utilizes subbands that may correspond to F0 and its neighbors. The VAD performance degrades when those subbands are eliminated. However, further studies should be performed to analyze other factors that influence the behavior of the employed DNN. Moreover, we intend to make the proposed method work in real time.

Title: MLNET: An Adaptive Multiple Receptive-field Attention Neural Network for Voice Activity Detection
Snippet: The existed DNN-based VAD models only leveraged fixed receptive-field contextual speech information and were unable to handle with speech segments of different lengths adaptively. To overcome this defect, this paper proposed an architecture of MLNET for VAD task. MLNET made use of different gated affined unit to extract different contextual speech information and leveraged the adaptive attention block to select the most focused speech segments. Comparing with the existed models, the experiments demonstrated that MLNET outformed other baseline models and proved that the proposed architecture was helpful to deal with VAD problems.

Title: Sequence Prediction with Neural Segmental Models
Snippet: This chapter describes finite-state transducers (FST), a useful tool for representing and manipulating the search space of a sequence prediction task. This chapter also includes a complete example of a standard speech recognizer based on hidden Markov models represented as FSTs. See (Mohri, 2009) for a comprehensive review of FSTs and their algorithms, and (Mohri et al., 1996) for their applications to speech recognition.

Title: BACON: Deep-Learning Powered AI for Poetry Generation with Author Linguistic Style Transfer
Snippet: A finite-state transducer (FST) is a type of finite-state automaton whose state transitions are labeled with both and output symbols, and therefore it maps between two sets of symbols. A path through the transducer encodes a mapping from an input symbol sequence to an output symbol sequence. A weighted transducer adds weights on transitions to the input and output symbols of a FST (Vidal et al., 2005). These weights may encode any quantity that accumulates along paths (e.g. probabilities or durations) and allow to compute the overall weight of mapping an input sequence to an output sequence. Weighted transducers are thus a natural choice to represent probabilistic finite-state models, which are commonly used for pattern recognition, or in fields to which pattern recognition is linked, such as computational linguistics, machine learning, time series analysis, computational biology, speech recognition, and machine translation.

snippet.text: A finite-state transducer (FST) is a type of finite-state automaton whose state transitions are labeled with both and output symbols, and therefore it maps between two sets of symbols. A path through the transducer encodes a mapping from an input symbol sequence to an output symbol sequence. A weighted transducer adds weights on transitions to the input and output symbols of a FST (Vidal et al., 2005). These weights may encode any quantity that accumulates along paths (e.g. probabilities or durations) and allow to compute the overall weight of mapping an input sequence to an output sequence. Weighted transducers are thus a natural choice to represent probabilistic finite-state models, which are commonly used for pattern recognition, or in fields to which pattern recognition is linked, such as computational linguistics, machine learning, time series analysis, computational biology, speech recognition, and machine translation.

Title: Study on the Use of Deep Neural Networks for Speech Activity Detection in Broadcast Recordings
Snippet: This paper deals with the task of Speech Activity Detection (SAD). Our goal is to develop a SAD module 
 
suitable for a system for broadcast data transcription. Various Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) are evaluated 
 
for this purpose. Training of DNNs is performed using speech and non-speech data as well as artificial data 
 
created by mixing of both these data types at a desired level of Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR). The output 
 
from each DNN is smoothed using a decoder based on Weighted Finite State Transducers (WFSTs). The

Title: Dysfluent WFST: A Framework for Zero-Shot Speech Dysfluency Transcription and Detection
Snippet: Automatic detection of speech dysfluency aids speech-language pathologists in efficient transcription of disordered speech, enhancing diagnostics and treatment planning. Traditional methods, often limited to classification, provide insufficient clinical insight, and text-independent models misclassify dysfluency, especially in context-dependent cases. This work introduces Dysfluent-WFST, a zero-shot decoder that simultaneously transcribes phonemes and detects dysfluency. Unlike previous models, Dysfluent-WFST operates with upstream encoders like WavLM and requires no additional training. It achieves state-of-the-art performance in both phonetic error rate and dysfluency detection on simulated and real speech data. Our approach is lightweight, interpretable, and effective, demonstrating that explicit modeling of pronunciation behavior in decoding, rather than complex architectures, is key to improving dysfluency processing systems.

Title: Enhancement of speech dynamics for voice activity detection using DNN
Snippet: This study presents a DNN-based VAD method for improving the performance of VAD by introducing dynamics, which may be highlighted by speech period candidates. These candidates are derived from heuristic rules based on the first and second derivatives of the log power spectrum of the RSF output (LPS-RSF). The speech period candidates are calculated for individual subbands and are then input into a DNN together with the log power spectra to generate the VAD decision. To evaluate the performance of the proposed method, we perform experiments using clean and noisy speech signals smeared with five types of noise, namely, white, babble, factory, car, and pink, with SNRs of 10, 5, 0 and − 5 dB. The proposed method effectively detects speech and non-speech periods. The experimental results show that the VAD performance based on log power spectra are improved after combining the log power spectra with the speech period candidates, particularly for noisy speech signals with low SNRs and non-stationary cases. The addition of dynamics expressed by the speech period candidates provides positive information that contributes to the detection of speech periods. 

In this study, we also show that the DNN-based VAD utilizes subbands that may correspond to F0 and its neighbors. The VAD performance degrades when those subbands are eliminated. However, further studies should be performed to analyze other factors that influence the behavior of the employed DNN. Moreover, we intend to make the proposed method work in real time.

problem: Are there any related research that evaluates the utility/effectiveness of retrieved items in RAG?
final_response:
Yes. A growing body of work evaluates how useful the retrieved items are for RAG, both by proposing evidence-centric metrics and by measuring how retrieval impacts downstream task performance and faithfulness. Below, we summarize key directions, representative metrics/benchmarks, and empirical findings.

# Why “utility of retrieved items” matters in RAG
Evaluating RAG requires separating how well the retriever selects helpful evidence from how well the generator uses it; end-to-end metrics alone do not reveal which documents helped or when retrieval harms performance (e.g., via irrelevant or distracting content). <cite id="6b9238d1-3">Traditional end-to-end evaluation lacks transparency about which retrieved document contributed to the generated output and is computationally heavy, making it hard to optimize retrievers for the LLM’s needs</cite>. <cite id="6b9238d1-2">Classical IR metrics (nDCG, MAP, MRR) further misalign with RAG because they assume human-like position discounts and do not account for irrelevant but distracting documents that can degrade generation</cite>.

# Metrics that directly assess retrieved-item utility
Recent work proposes metrics that quantify both the positive contribution of relevant passages and the negative impact of distracting ones, aligning evaluation to the LLM consumer rather than human users.

- eRAG (LLM-as-judge at document-level): <cite id="f316191d-1">eRAG feeds each retrieved document with the query to the LLM and uses downstream task labels (e.g., accuracy, EM, ROUGE) to produce document-level utility scores, which are then aggregated (e.g., MAP, set-based metrics) into a single retriever score</cite>. <cite id="f316191d-1">Experiments across open-domain QA (NQ), fact-checking (FEVER), and dialogue (WoW) show eRAG achieves higher correlation with downstream RAG performance than baselines, with Kendall’s tau improvements of 0.168–0.494, and uses up to 50× less GPU memory than end-to-end evaluation</cite>. <cite id="f316191d-4">eRAG consistently outperforms human-provenance and LLM-annotated relevance baselines as the “LLM, as the primary consumer of retrieved results, is the most reliable judge of retrieval performance”</cite>. <cite id="f316191d-0">Correlation remains strong across varying numbers of retrieved documents, and eRAG maintains higher correlation than common approaches (document-level relevance labels, LLM relevance annotations), confirming its alignment with the generator’s needs</cite>.

Title: Redefining Retrieval Evaluation in the Era of LLMs
Snippet: Traditional Information Retrieval (IR) metrics, such as nDCG, MAP, and MRR, assume that human users sequentially examine documents with diminishing attention to lower ranks. This assumption breaks down in Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) systems, where search results are consumed by Large Language Models (LLMs), which, unlike humans, process all retrieved documents as a whole rather than sequentially. Additionally, traditional IR metrics do not account for related but irrelevant documents that actively degrade generation quality, rather than merely being ignored. Due to these two major misalignments, namely human vs. machine position discount and human relevance vs. machine utility, classical IR metrics do not accurately predict RAG performance. We introduce a utility-based annotation schema that quantifies both the positive contribution of relevant passages and the negative impact of distracting ones. Building on this foundation, we propose UDCG (Utility and Distraction-aware Cumulative Gain), a metric using an LLM-oriented positional discount to directly optimize the correlation with the end-to-end answer accuracy. Experiments on five datasets and six LLMs demonstrate that UDCG improves correlation by up to 36% compared to traditional metrics. Our work provides a critical step toward aligning IR evaluation with LLM consumers and enables more reliable assessment of RAG components

Snippet: In information retrieval, standard metrics such as Mean Average Precision (MAP), Precision, Reciprocal Rank, and Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain (NDCG) [103,110,115] have traditionally been used to evaluate the relevance of retrieved documents to a given query. These metrics are essential in assessing the effectiveness of traditional information retrieval systems, where the primary goal is to measure how well the retrieved documents match the user's query. 

When applied to RAG systems, these retrieval-based metrics extend their focus to consider how the retrieved information contributes to the quality of the generated output. In this context, Accuracy becomes a crucial metric, assessing how precisely the retrieved documents provide correct information for answering queries. Additionally, Rejection Rate [14], which measures the system's ability to decline answering when no relevant information is available, has emerged as a , Vol. 1, No. 1, Article . Publication date: September 2018. key indicator of responsible output generation. Similarly, Error Detection Rate [14] evaluates the model's capability to identify and filter out incorrect or misleading information, ensuring that the generation process is based on trustworthy sources. 

Another important consideration is Context Relevance, which assesses the alignment of retrieved documents with the specific query, emphasizing the need for content directly relevant to the generation task's context. Faithfulness [33] is also critical in determining whether the generated text accurately reflects the information found in the retrieved documents, thereby minimizing the risk of generating misleading or incorrect content. 

The eRAG framework [119] introduces a more refined approach to evaluating retrieval quality in RAG systems by focusing on individual documents rather than the entire retrieval process. It operates by feeding each document in the retrieval list into the LLM alongside the query and evaluating the generated output against downstream task metrics such as Accuracy. The documentlevel scores are then aggregated using ranking metrics like MAP to produce a single evaluation score. This focus on document-level contributions offers a more precise assessment of retrieval quality while being significantly more computationally efficient than traditional end-to-end evaluations. 

Notably, eRAG demonstrates that its document-level evaluation correlates more strongly with downstream RAG performance compared to conventional methods like human annotations or provenance labels.

Title: Alleviating Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models with Active Retrieval Augmentation
Snippet: Recognizing the plurality of retrieval strategies due to the multimodal input, an extensive analysis of different methods is conducted to determine the most optimal retrieving approach. Subsequent to acquiring pertinent text and image pairs from external databases, a reranking strategy is employed to eliminate unreliable outcomes, thereby augmenting LVLMs with the appropriate external information. Particularly, retrieval operations are circumvented when the LVLM exhibits high certainty, to prevent the inclusion of superfluous retrieval that may introduce redundant information. In this context, retrieval is activated using a difficulty metric that relies on the mutual information between multimodal inputs. 

To assess the efficacy of ARA, empirical evaluations are performed using three prevalent LVLMs across four benchmarks related to hallucination challenges. The promising results demonstrate that our framework can effectively mitigate hallucinations. To sum up, our contributions are summarized as follows: 

• Our research thoroughly investigates the three critical dimensions of augmenting LVLMs with external knowledge, including accurately dissecting the retrieval targets, pinpointing the most effective retrieval methods, and the sensible triggering of the retrieval process. • We introduce an Active Retrieval-Augmented large vision-language model (ARA) for mitigating hallucination. Our empirical evidence indicates that, by employing appropriate retrieval mechanisms and carefully timing the retrievals, we can significantly address the issue of hallucination while maintaining a moderate frequency of retrieval. • Through comprehensive experiments, we demonstrate the superior performance of our proposed ARA in alleviating hallucinations using three well-known LVLMs across four hallucinationrelated benchmarks. The results in our paper also suggest that with optimal retrieval settings, the potential of augmenting LVLMs can be more effectively harnessed.

Title: MultiHop-RAG: Benchmarking Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Multi-Hop Queries
Snippet: RAG Evaluation: As RAG systems gain increasing popularity, a variety of RAG benchmarking datasets and evaluation tools have been developed. For instance, RGB (Chen et al., 2023) and RE-CALL (Liu et al., 2023) evaluate the performance of LLMs in generating responses for RAG systems under conditions involving noisy, integrative, and counterfactual queries. However, both datasets primarily focus on evaluating the generation aspect of RAG systems without specifically addressing their retrieval accuracy. In addition, recent advancements have been made in automated RAG evaluation tools, such as ARES (Saad-Falcon et al., 2023) and RAGAS (Es et al., 2023). These tools utilize LLMs to automatically assess the quality of RAG generation, yet they do not introduce benchmarking datasets. Our work introduces one of the first RAG benchmarking datasets, consisting of a knowledge base, a large collection of multi-hop queries, their ground-truth answers, and the associated supporting evidence, thereby complementing existing RAG evaluations. Retrieval datasets: Apart from the context of RAG, several benchmarking datasets exist for information retrieval evaluation. The FEVER (Fact Extraction and VERification) dataset, for instance, contains claims classified as Supported, Refuted, or NotEnoughInfo by the given Wikipedia article (Thorne et al., 2018). Similarly, the SciFact dataset comprises scientific claims paired with evidencecontaining abstracts (Wadden et al., 2020). However, the claims in both datasets are single-hop statements, and the supporting evidence is from one single article, in contrast to the multi-hop queries discussed in this paper. Another dataset, HoVer, involves claims that require extracting and reasoning from multiple Wikipedia articles (Jiang et al., 2020). However, unlike our dataset, HoVer focuses solely on classifying claims as either supported or not supported by the articles without evaluating an LLM generation step. Moreover, in HoVer, the Wikipedia articles from which evidence is drawn are given for claim verification, which is significantly different from our setting, where relevant pieces of evidence need to be extracted from a large knowledge base.
</snippet>

Snippet: From Single-Function to Multi-Dimensional Dynamics In recent years, RAG evaluation has evolved in benchmark design and dataset construction from single-function validation toward multidimensional, systematic assessment. The current evaluation ecosystem has gradually formed a classification framework centered on retrieval quality, generation quality, end-to-end performance, and robustness/timeliness, reflecting the evolution of evaluation priorities and revealing deeper differences across methods in objective setting, data selection, and metric design. 

(1) For retrieval quality, methods such as RAGAs, ARES, and MultiHop-RAG employ standard datasets like WikiEval, NQ, and Hotpot, using traditional IR metrics such as MAP, MRR, and Hit@K. GraphRAG constructs datasets with factual associations and complex reasoning paths to test graph-structured retrieval; CoFE-RAG introduces multidocument formats and diverse query types to improve coverage of real-world document heterogeneity. However, such evaluations still largely rely on static corpora, exhibiting limited capacity to model knowledge updates and dynamic scenarios. BEIR and KILT, as general-purpose evaluation backbones for cross-domain zero-shot retrieval and knowledge-intensive tasks, provide broadly comparable benchmarks for RAG retrieval capabilities [7,41]. Their coverage of diverse tasks and unified Wikipedia snapshots support evaluation of model generalization in unseen domains, serving as foundational platforms for most retrieval module validation. 

(2) For generation quality, methods such as ARES, FeB4RAG, and DomainRAG quantify generation accuracy using F1, ROUGE-L, and Exact-Match, while introducing LLM-as-a-Judge mechanisms to assess semantic consistency and clarity. ReEval leverages datasets like RealTimeQA, containing time-sensitive questions, to test model performance under outdated or missing knowledge. Although automated metrics enhance evaluation efficiency, their alignment with human judgment remains contested: BERGEN's research reveals weak semantic-level correlation in LLM evaluations, exposing current deficiencies in reliability and interpretability.

A growing body of work evaluates how useful the retrieved items are for RAG, both by proposing evidence-centric metrics and by measuring how retrieval impacts downstream task performance and faithfulness. Below, we summarize key directions, representative metrics/benchmarks, and empirical findings.

# Why “utility of retrieved items” matters in RAG
Evaluating RAG requires separating how well the retriever selects helpful evidence from how well the generator uses it; end-to-end metrics alone do not reveal which documents helped or when retrieval harms performance (e.g., via irrelevant or distracting content). <cite id="6b9238d1-3">Traditional end-to-end evaluation lacks transparency about which retrieved document contributed to the generated output and is computationally heavy, making it hard to optimize retrievers for the LLM’s needs</cite>. <cite id="6b9238d1-2">Classical IR metrics (nDCG, MAP, MRR) further misalign with RAG because they assume human-like position discounts and do not account for irrelevant but distracting documents that can degrade generation</cite>.

# Metrics that directly assess retrieved-item utility
Recent work proposes metrics that quantify both the positive contribution of relevant passages and the negative impact of distracting ones, aligning evaluation to the LLM consumer rather than human users.

- eRAG (LLM-as-judge at document-level): <cite id="f316191d-1">eRAG feeds each retrieved document with the query to the LLM and uses downstream task labels (e.g., accuracy, EM, ROUGE) to produce document-level utility scores, which are then aggregated (e.g., MAP, set-based metrics) into a single retriever score</cite>. <cite id="f316191d-1">Experiments across open-domain QA (NQ), fact-checking (FEVER), and dialogue (WoW) show eRAG achieves higher correlation with downstream RAG performance than baselines, with Kendall’s tau improvements of 0.168–0.494, and uses up to 50× less GPU memory than end-to-end evaluation</cite>. <cite id="f316191d-4">eRAG consistently outperforms human-provenance and LLM-annotated relevance baselines as the “LLM, as the primary consumer of retrieved results, is the most reliable judge of retrieval performance”</cite>. <cite id="f316191d-0">Correlation remains strong across varying numbers of retrieved documents, and eRAG maintains higher correlation than common approaches (document-level relevance labels, LLM relevance annotations), confirming its alignment with the generator’s needs</cite>.

- UDCG (utility and distraction-aware IR metric): <cite id="6b9238d1-2">UDCG introduces a utility-based annotation schema and a positional discount optimized for LLM consumption, explicitly modeling positive contributions of relevant passages and the negative impact of distracting but irrelevant items</cite>. <cite id="6b9238d1-2">Across five datasets and six LLMs, UDCG improves correlation with end-to-end answer accuracy by up to 36% compared to traditional IR metrics, supporting the premise that utility-aware evaluation better predicts RAG performance</cite>.

- Surveys and broader frameworks: <cite id="6b9238d1-1">A conversational search survey highlights the gap between IR relevance and RAG utility and notes eRAG’s design to evaluate utilization of each retrieved document via downstream labels</cite>. <cite id="f316191d-2">Surveys of RAG generation summarize evaluation axes that include context relevance, faithfulness, rejection rate, error detection, and accuracy, and position eRAG as a refined, document-level approach that aggregates per-document utility (e.g., with ranking metrics) to measure retrieval quality efficiently</cite>.

# Benchmarks and datasets that probe retrieval and evidence quality
Beyond single-document utility, several benchmarks evaluate how well retrieval supports generation across scenarios like noise, redundancy, and multi-hop reasoning, often with explicit evidence labels.

- Knowledge-grounded and multi-hop: <cite id="adf31751-0">MultiHop-RAG introduces a knowledge base, multi-hop queries, ground-truth answers, and supporting evidence, enabling evaluation of both retrieval accuracy and generation, and addressing gaps in prior datasets that focused mainly on generation under noisy/integrative settings</cite>. <cite id="adf31751-4">CRAG and RAGBench provide cross-domain factual QA and multi-domain evaluations (biomedical, legal, customer support, finance), respectively, with answer accuracy and coverage to assess end-to-end efficacy</cite>.

- Tools and automated evaluation: <cite id="adf31751-0">ARES and RAGAS use LLMs to automatically assess RAG generation quality but do not provide retrieval-only benchmark datasets</cite>. <cite id="adf31751-3">RAGEval proposes scenario-specific generation of evaluation datasets and combines LLM-based and retrieval metrics (e.g., contextual relevance, faithfulness, informativeness) to cover both stages of the pipeline</cite>. <cite id="adf31751-3">RGB introduces task-oriented metrics for noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, and counterfactual robustness</cite>.

- Foundational IR backbones: <cite id="adf31751-2">For retrieval quality, common datasets like WikiEval, NQ, Hotpot support evaluation of IR metrics (MAP, MRR, Hit@K), while BEIR and KILT serve as cross-domain, zero-shot retrieval backbones with unified Wikipedia snapshots to assess generalization</cite>. <cite id="adf31751-2">GraphRAG and CoFE-RAG extend retrieval to graph-structured and multi-document settings with diverse query types to better reflect real-world document heterogeneity</cite>. <cite id="adf31751-4">TRIAD assesses retrieval quality, fidelity, and task-specific utility in a three-dimensional framework</cite>.

- Fine-grained faithfulness and citation analysis: <cite id="adf31751-2">Recent works recommend using tools such as ALCE, QAFactEval, FActScore, FACTS, GaRAGe, and RAGTruth to evaluate interpretability and factual consistency at span and citation levels, moving beyond coarse answer-level metrics to measure span-level alignment and citation quality</cite>.

# Empirical evidence that retrieval improves utility and reduces errors
Foundational and domain-specific studies report that retrieval can reduce hallucinations and improve factuality, and ablations typically show gains when retrieval is enabled and tuned.

- Hallucination reduction and grounding: <cite id="38396069-0">RAG mitigates hallucinations by grounding generation in external knowledge, though it introduces latency and coarse-grained evidence issues</cite>. <cite id="38396069-2">Surveys of hallucination note that RAG has shown promise in reducing language hallucinations by leveraging external knowledge</cite>. <cite id="38396069-4">Active Retrieval Augmentation (ARA) for vision-language models demonstrates that carefully timed and reranked retrieval can significantly mitigate hallucinations across multiple benchmarks while controlling retrieval frequency</cite>.

- Retrieval selection and redundancy: <cite id="38396069-1">RAG pipelines often retrieve semantically redundant passages, which can lead to hallucinations or missed evidence; structured retrieval and compression can improve downstream performance by emphasizing representational coverage</cite>. <cite id="38396069-3">Constraining retrieval to relevant time periods (RAGcutoff) can further improve grounding by avoiding future contexts, illustrating how retrieval constraints affect utility</cite>.

- Retrieval on vs. retrieval off and ablations: While specific numeric deltas vary by setup, multiple works report that with retrieval on and high-quality evidence, downstream systems show reduced hallucinations and improved factual accuracy relative to parametric-only baselines; retrieval latency and coarse granularity remain key trade-offs to manage in production systems <cite id="38396069-0">RAG improves factual accuracy but adds latency and coarse-grained evidence limits</cite>.

# Practical evaluation practices and open challenges
Practitioners increasingly combine retrieval- and generation-focused metrics and leverage LLM-as-a-judge to capture utility that static IR metrics miss.

- Combining IR and generation metrics: <cite id="f316191d-2">Surveys emphasize integrating retrieval metrics (context relevance, coverage) with generation metrics (F1, ROUGE, faithfulness) and rejection/error detection to evaluate responsible and accurate grounding</cite>. <cite id="adf31751-3">Frameworks like RAGAS and ARES use LLMs to assess contextual relevance, faithfulness, and informativeness, reducing dependence on costly human annotations</cite>.

- Alignment and correlation with end-to-end performance: <cite id="f316191d-1">eRAG and related methods show higher correlation with downstream RAG performance than human-provenance or generic relevance labels, supporting LLM-as-judge for utility assessment</cite>. <cite id="6b9238d1-2">Utility-aware IR metrics like UDCG better predict end-to-end answer accuracy than classical IR scores, reinforcing the need to model both helpful and distracting evidence</cite>.

- Open challenges: <cite id="6b9238d1-3">End-to-end evaluations are opaque about per-document contribution and resource-intensive, complicating iterative retriever optimization</cite>. <cite id="6b9238d1-2">Traditional IR rankings assume human-like attention and do not account for the holistic consumption and potential confusion from related but irrelevant content by LLMs</cite>. <cite id="adf31751-4">Benchmarks are expanding to cover dynamic knowledge (timeliness), multi-hop reasoning, and domain-specific constraints, but alignment between automated metrics and human judgment remains an active area of research</cite>.

# Takeaways
- There is substantial research that directly evaluates the utility of retrieved items in RAG. <cite id="f316191d-1">eRAG quantifies per-document usefulness via LLM-based annotations aggregated into ranking/set metrics and shows strong correlation with downstream performance and substantial runtime/memory savings</cite>. <cite id="6b9238d1-2">UDCG provides an IR metric tailored to LLM consumers, improving correlation with answer accuracy up to 36% over traditional metrics</cite>. 
- Benchmarks and evaluation frameworks have emerged across retrieval quality (BEIR, KILT, Wiki/NQ/Hotpot), generation quality (F1/ROUGE, faithfulness), and end-to-end performance (CRAG, RAGBench, MultiHop-RAG, RGB), often with LLM-as-a-judge and fine-grained citation/faithfulness tools <cite id="adf31751-0">MultiHop-RAG</cite><cite id="adf31751-2">BEIR/KILT and specialized retrieval datasets</cite><cite id="adf31751-4">CRAG, RAGBench, RGB, TRIAD</cite><cite id="adf31751-2">ALCE, QAFactEval, FActScore, FACTS, GaRAGe, RAGTruth</cite><cite id="adf31751-3">ARES, RAGAS, RGB</cite>. 
- Empirical studies consistently find that high-quality retrieval improves grounding and reduces hallucinations, while highlighting trade-offs like redundancy, latency, and the need to account for distracting but relevant content <cite id="38396069-0">RAG mitigates hallucinations but introduces latency and coarse-grained evidence limits</cite><cite id="38396069-2">RAG shows promise in reducing language hallucinations</cite><cite id="38396069-1">Redundant retrieval can cause hallucinations or missed evidence</cite><cite id="38396069-4">Active retrieval can mitigate hallucinations with controlled frequency</cite>.

Snippet: Evaluation metrics are crucial for assessing the performance of Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) systems. These metrics help quantify various aspects of the system's effectiveness, including the relevance of retrieved information, the accuracy of generated answers, and the overall quality of the system's output. The following subsections describe key metrics used in the evaluation of the RAG systems.

Title: A Survey of Conversational Search
Snippet: The flexible user-system interaction provides the chance to address complex information needs by multi-turn querying, which means the requirement of the user might not only be a rank list but also a concise answer from the retrieved results. Such a paradigm has become significantly more popular in the era of LLMs, making generation-based evaluation essential. However, conventional metrics such as F1, BLEU score, and exact match (EM) might not fully capture the quality of the generation. On one hand, some reasonable and correctly generated answers might not be annotated as the evaluation gold standard and fail in the traditional token-level metrics. On the other hand, the LLMs can yield accurate responses despite imperfect retrievers or hallucinations with semantic relevant retrieved text [267], raising the issue of evaluating the system by taking into account both retrieval and generation. Aim to combine the top retrieved documents into a comprehensive, pertinent, and concise response, Lajewska et al. [198] collect snippetlevel answer annotations for existing conversational search benchmarks to fill the evaluation gap between retrieval and generation. To improve the correlation of retrieval effectiveness with the performance of the generation procedure, Salemi et al. [197] propose the eRAG metric, which evaluates the utilization of each retrieved document based on the ground truth labels of downstream tasks. Nevertheless, the evaluation gap remains between the aspect of IR and RAG, i.e., an IR-relevant document might not be effective for the downstream RAG task [266]. Thus, how to assess the performance of retrievers within LLM-based generators and better align the retriever-generator with the overall conversational search system is still an open challenge, which requires further exploration [199].

Title: Redefining Retrieval Evaluation in the Era of LLMs
Snippet: Traditional Information Retrieval (IR) metrics, such as nDCG, MAP, and MRR, assume that human users sequentially examine documents with diminishing attention to lower ranks. This assumption breaks down in Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) systems, where search results are consumed by Large Language Models (LLMs), which, unlike humans, process all retrieved documents as a whole rather than sequentially. Additionally, traditional IR metrics do not account for related but irrelevant documents that actively degrade generation quality, rather than merely being ignored. Due to these two major misalignments, namely human vs. machine position discount and human relevance vs. machine utility, classical IR metrics do not accurately predict RAG performance. We introduce a utility-based annotation schema that quantifies both the positive contribution of relevant passages and the negative impact of distracting ones. Building on this foundation, we propose UDCG (Utility and Distraction-aware Cumulative Gain), a metric using an LLM-oriented positional discount to directly optimize the correlation with the end-to-end answer accuracy. Experiments on five datasets and six LLMs demonstrate that UDCG improves correlation by up to 36% compared to traditional metrics. Our work provides a critical step toward aligning IR evaluation with LLM consumers and enables more reliable assessment of RAG components

Title: Evaluating Retrieval Quality in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
Snippet: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) has emerged as a prominent approach in natural language processing, combining the strengths of retrieval and generation models [35], with use cases in decreasing hallucination [1,29], knowledge-grounding [9,16,34], and personalization [25,26].Evaluating RAG systems is important as it ensures the effectiveness of integrating retrieval-based methods with generative models [10,23].Traditionally, RAG evaluation has primarily relied on end-to-end assessment, which entails comparing the generated output with one or more ground truth references [20].While this is crucial, it presents several limitations, especially, for evaluating retrieval models in RAG systems.

First, end-to-end evaluation lacks transparency regarding which retrieved document contributed to the generated output, hindering interpretability of the system's behavior.Secondly, it is resourceintensive, consuming significant time and computational power, particularly when dealing with a large set of retrieval results consumed by the LLM.To process long input sequences resulting from the utilization of all retrieved documents by the LLM, GPUs with substantial memory capacities are essential for end-to-end evaluation.Moreover, many ranking systems rely on interleaving (i.e., replacing one or more documents in the result list) for evaluation and optimization, which further complicates the evaluation, as slight variations in retrieval results necessitate re-computation of the RAG pipeline.Finally, optimizing ranking models often requires document-level feedback, such as user clicks [3,6].However, endto-end evaluation only provides list-level feedback for the retrieval results.That said, this paper studies retrieval evaluation in RAG.

Human annotations can be a potential solution for evaluating retrieval models in RAG, however, accurate annotations are often challenging and costly to obtain.More recently, with the emergence of large language models (LLMs) and their advanced capabilities in reasoning and text comprehension, they have been utilized to annotate documents for retrieval evaluation [10,23].Nevertheless, these approaches predominantly evaluate the retriever in RAG systems based on human preferences, whereas the primary objective of the retrieval model in RAG is to serve the LLM that leverages the retrieved results [35].

Such a paradigm has become significantly more popular in the era of LLMs, making generation-based evaluation essential. On one hand, some reasonable and correctly generated answers might not be annotated as the evaluation gold standard and fail in the traditional token-level metrics. On the other hand, the LLMs can yield accurate responses despite imperfect retrievers or hallucinations with semantic relevant retrieved text [267], raising the issue of evaluating the system by taking into account both retrieval and generation. Aim to combine the top retrieved documents into a comprehensive, pertinent, and concise response, Lajewska et al. [198] collect snippetlevel answer annotations for existing conversational search benchmarks to fill the evaluation gap between retrieval and generation. To improve the correlation of retrieval effectiveness with the performance of the generation procedure, Salemi et al. [197] propose the eRAG metric, which evaluates the utilization of each retrieved document based on the ground truth labels of downstream tasks. Nevertheless, the evaluation gap remains between the aspect of IR and RAG, i.e., an IR-relevant document might not be effective for the downstream RAG task [266]. Thus, how to assess the performance of retrievers within LLM-based generators and better align the retriever-generator with the overall conversational search system is still an open challenge, which requires further exploration [199].

snippet.text: Traditional Information Retrieval (IR) metrics, such as nDCG, MAP, and MRR, assume that human users sequentially examine documents with diminishing attention to lower ranks. This assumption breaks down in Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) systems, where search results are consumed by Large Language Models (LLMs), which, unlike humans, process all retrieved documents as a whole rather than sequentially. Additionally, traditional IR metrics do not account for related but irrelevant documents that actively degrade generation quality, rather than merely being ignored. Due to these two major misalignments, namely human vs. machine position discount and human relevance vs. machine utility, classical IR metrics do not accurately predict RAG performance. We introduce a utility-based annotation schema that quantifies both the positive contribution of relevant passages and the negative impact of distracting ones. Building on this foundation, we propose UDCG (Utility and Distraction-aware Cumulative Gain), a metric using an LLM-oriented positional discount to directly optimize the correlation with the end-to-end answer accuracy. Experiments on five datasets and six LLMs demonstrate that UDCG improves correlation by up to 36% compared to traditional metrics. Our work provides a critical step toward aligning IR evaluation with LLM consumers and enables more reliable assessment of RAG components

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) has emerged as a prominent approach in natural language processing, combining the strengths of retrieval and generation models [35], with use cases in decreasing hallucination [1,29], knowledge-grounding [9,16,34], and personalization [25,26].Evaluating RAG systems is important as it ensures the effectiveness of integrating retrieval-based methods with generative models [10,23].Traditionally, RAG evaluation has primarily relied on end-to-end assessment, which entails comparing the generated output with one or more ground truth references [20].While this is crucial, it presents several limitations, especially, for evaluating retrieval models in RAG systems.

First, end-to-end evaluation lacks transparency regarding which retrieved document contributed to the generated output, hindering interpretability of the system's behavior.Secondly, it is resourceintensive, consuming significant time and computational power, particularly when dealing with a large set of retrieval results consumed by the LLM.To process long input sequences resulting from the utilization of all retrieved documents by the LLM, GPUs with substantial memory capacities are essential for end-to-end evaluation.Moreover, many ranking systems rely on interleaving (i.e., replacing one or more documents in the result list) for evaluation and optimization, which further complicates the evaluation, as slight variations in retrieval results necessitate re-computation of the RAG pipeline.Finally, optimizing ranking models often requires document-level feedback, such as user clicks [3,6].However, endto-end evaluation only provides list-level feedback for the retrieval results.That said, this paper studies retrieval evaluation in RAG.

Human annotations can be a potential solution for evaluating retrieval models in RAG, however, accurate annotations are often challenging and costly to obtain.More recently, with the emergence of large language models (LLMs) and their advanced capabilities in reasoning and text comprehension, they have been utilized to annotate documents for retrieval evaluation [10,23].Nevertheless, these approaches predominantly evaluate the retriever in RAG systems based on human preferences, whereas the primary objective of the retrieval model in RAG is to serve the LLM that leverages the retrieved results [35].

Retrieval Augmented Generation is a natural language processing technique that combines retrieval and generation. The core idea is to augment the output of a generative model by retrieving relevant information from an external knowledge base prior to regenerating the text and then using this information as part of the input. Combined with retrieving the external knowledge base, the model relies on its own knowledge in addition to the RAG to ensure that the generated information content on tourism and historical knowledge contains the most up-to-date information to improve accuracy and contextual relevance. To address knowledge gaps in Large Language Models, TIGMI enhances the generation process by retrieving relevant context from a domain-specific vector database K. The Retrieval-Augmented Generation model integrates knowledge retrieval with generative capabilities, enabling generated outputs to effectively incorporate external knowledge. This integration significantly improves the model's performance on complex tasks. 

First, the document is split into overlapping text segments using LangChain's recursive splitter. This step ensures each text segment retains sufficient contextual information while maintaining smaller computational units by decomposing the document into chunks. These text chunks can be paragraphs, sentences, or smaller units, depending on task requirements. Each text chunk d i is encoded into an embedding vector e i = ChatGLM-6B(d i ) These embedding vectors serve as high-dimensional representations capturing semantic information, enabling comparable vector representations for subsequent similarity calculations. An efficient cosine similarity index is then constructed using FAISS, which enables rapid retrieval of text embeddings and measures document similarity through cosine distance metrics. This architecture allows swift retrieval of the most relevant document segments for any given query from large-scale text corpora.

Given that the user query is a text q, the system computes the cosine similarity between the query vector and all document chunk vectors in the database.
