_**\_**DepthCrafter: Generating Consistent Long Depth Sequences for Open-world Videos**\_**_
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[](https://github.com/Tencent/DepthCrafter#depthcrafter-generating-consistent-long-depth-sequences-for-open-world-videos)

[![Image 1](https://camo.githubusercontent.com/723873ae79dc909233326f4066f6e0599afcd02b900e0444cf13930df91b0115/68747470733a2f2f6465707468637261667465722e6769746875622e696f2f696d672f6c6f676f2e706e67)](https://camo.githubusercontent.com/723873ae79dc909233326f4066f6e0599afcd02b900e0444cf13930df91b0115/68747470733a2f2f6465707468637261667465722e6769746875622e696f2f696d672f6c6f676f2e706e67)

[![Image 2: Version](https://camo.githubusercontent.com/a2842c9918fd6939281a110177266bf79d97ae73318199100be18393a34edd70/68747470733a2f2f696d672e736869656c64732e696f2f62616467652f76657273696f6e2d312e302e312d626c7565)](https://camo.githubusercontent.com/a2842c9918fd6939281a110177266bf79d97ae73318199100be18393a34edd70/68747470733a2f2f696d672e736869656c64732e696f2f62616467652f76657273696f6e2d312e302e312d626c7565)[![Image 3](https://camo.githubusercontent.com/bea07c2b968fd22b2be590dc48fe70a08aa41208459b91c9a7acbff052fd86a8/68747470733a2f2f696d672e736869656c64732e696f2f62616467652f61725869762d323430392e30323039352d6233316231622e737667)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.02095)[![Image 4](https://camo.githubusercontent.com/d95b6841b2a4bc6beed4db2d12b3497d6d5e1759c3dd7c3737535d040f8597e9/68747470733a2f2f696d672e736869656c64732e696f2f62616467652f50726f6a6563742d506167652d477265656e)](https://depthcrafter.github.io/)[![Image 5](https://camo.githubusercontent.com/90791dd325970df153b71dbb65c6f84c148d94d289638cc7a7de16319770ae12/68747470733a2f2f696d672e736869656c64732e696f2f62616467652f25463025394625413425393725323048756767696e67253230466163652d44656d6f2d626c7565)](https://huggingface.co/spaces/tencent/DepthCrafter)

CVPR 2025， **Highlight**

🔆 Notice
---------

[](https://github.com/Tencent/DepthCrafter#-notice)
**DepthCrafter is still under active development!**

We recommend that everyone use English to communicate on issues, as this helps developers from around the world discuss, share experiences, and answer questions together.

For business licensing and other related inquiries, don't hesitate to contact `wbhu@tencent.com`.

🔆 Introduction
---------------

[](https://github.com/Tencent/DepthCrafter#-introduction)
🤗 If you find DepthCrafter useful, **please help ⭐ this repo**, which is important to Open-Source projects. Thanks!

🔥 DepthCrafter can generate temporally consistent long-depth sequences with fine-grained details for open-world videos, without requiring additional information such as camera poses or optical flow.

*   `[25-12-01]` Refactored the codebase for better usability and extensibility.
*   `[25-04-05]` 🔥🔥🔥 Its upgraded work, [GeometryCrafter](https://github.com/TencentARC/GeometryCrafter), is released now, for **video to point cloud**!
*   `[25-04-05]` 🎉🎉🎉 DepthCrafter is selected as **Highlight** in CVPR‘25.
*   `[24-12-10]` 🌟🌟🌟 EXR output format is supported now, with --save_exr option.
*   `[24-11-26]` 🚀🚀🚀 DepthCrafter v1.0.1 is released now, with improved quality and speed
*   `[24-10-19]` 🤗🤗🤗 DepthCrafter now has been integrated into [ComfyUI](https://github.com/akatz-ai/ComfyUI-DepthCrafter-Nodes)!
*   `[24-10-08]` 🤗🤗🤗 DepthCrafter now has been integrated into [Nuke](https://github.com/Theo-SAMINADIN-td/NukeDepthCrafter), have a try!
*   `[24-09-28]` Add full dataset inference and evaluation scripts for better comparison use. :-)
*   `[24-09-25]` 🤗🤗🤗 Add huggingface online demo [DepthCrafter](https://huggingface.co/spaces/tencent/DepthCrafter).
*   `[24-09-19]` Add scripts for preparing benchmark datasets.
*   `[24-09-18]` Add point cloud sequence visualization.
*   `[24-09-14]` 🔥🔥🔥 **DepthCrafter** is released now, have fun!

📦 Release Notes
----------------

[](https://github.com/Tencent/DepthCrafter#-release-notes)
*   **DepthCrafter v1.0.1**: 
    *   Quality and speed improvement 
| Method | ms/frame↓ @1024×576 | Sintel (~50 frames) | Scannet (90 frames) | KITTI (110 frames) | Bonn (110 frames) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | AbsRel↓ | δ₁ ↑ | AbsRel↓ | δ₁ ↑ | AbsRel↓ | δ₁ ↑ | AbsRel↓ | δ₁ ↑ |
| Marigold | 1070.29 | 0.532 | 0.515 | 0.166 | 0.769 | 0.149 | 0.796 | 0.091 | 0.931 |
| Depth-Anything-V2 | **180.46** | 0.367 | 0.554 | 0.135 | 0.822 | 0.140 | 0.804 | 0.106 | 0.921 |
| DepthCrafter previous | 1913.92 | 0.292 | **0.697** | 0.125 | 0.848 | 0.110 | 0.881 | 0.075 | 0.971 |

🎥 Visualization
----------------

[](https://github.com/Tencent/DepthCrafter#-visualization)
We provide demos of unprojected point cloud sequences, with reference RGB and estimated depth videos. For more details, please refer to our [project page](https://depthcrafter.github.io/).

365030500-ff625ffe-93ab-4b58-a62a-50bf75c89a92.mov

🚀 Quick Start
--------------

[](https://github.com/Tencent/DepthCrafter#-quick-start)
### 🤖 Gradio Demo

[](https://github.com/Tencent/DepthCrafter#-gradio-demo)
*   Online demo: [DepthCrafter](https://huggingface.co/spaces/tencent/DepthCrafter)
*   Local demo: gradio app.py 

### 🌟 Community Support

[](https://github.com/Tencent/DepthCrafter#-community-support)
*   [NukeDepthCrafter](https://github.com/Theo-SAMINADIN-td/NukeDepthCrafter): a plugin allows you to generate temporally consistent Depth sequences inside Nuke, which is widely used in the VFX industry.
*   [ComfyUI-Nodes](https://github.com/akatz-ai/ComfyUI-DepthCrafter-Nodes): creating consistent depth maps for your videos using DepthCrafter in ComfyUI.

### 🛠️ Installation

[](https://github.com/Tencent/DepthCrafter#%EF%B8%8F-installation)
1.   Clone this repo:

git clone https://github.com/Tencent/DepthCrafter.git

1.   Install dependencies:

cd DepthCrafter
uv venv
source .venv/bin/activate
uv sync
uv pip list

### 🤗 Model Zoo

[](https://github.com/Tencent/DepthCrafter#-model-zoo)
[DepthCrafter](https://huggingface.co/tencent/DepthCrafter) is available in the Hugging Face Model Hub.

### 🏃‍♂️ Inference

[](https://github.com/Tencent/DepthCrafter#%E2%80%8D%EF%B8%8F-inference)
#### 1. High-resolution inference, requires a GPU with ~26GB memory for 1024x576 resolution:

[](https://github.com/Tencent/DepthCrafter#1-high-resolution-inference-requires-a-gpu-with-26gb-memory-for-1024x576-resolution)
*   ~2.1 fps on A100, recommended for high-quality results:

python run.py  --video-path examples/example_01.mp4 

#### 2. Low-resolution inference requires a GPU with ~9GB memory for 512x256 resolution:

[](https://github.com/Tencent/DepthCrafter#2-low-resolution-inference-requires-a-gpu-with-9gb-memory-for-512x256-resolution)
*   ~8.6 fps on A100:

python run.py  --video-path examples/example_01.mp4 --max-res 512 

🚀 Dataset Evaluation
---------------------

[](https://github.com/Tencent/DepthCrafter#-dataset-evaluation)
Please check the `benchmark` folder.

*   To create the dataset we use in the paper, you need to run `dataset_extract/dataset_extract_${dataset_name}.py`.
*   Then you will get the `csv` files that save the relative root of extracted RGB video and depth npz files. We also provide these csv files.
*   Inference for all datasets scripts: bash benchmark/infer/infer.sh  (Remember to replace the `input_rgb_root` and `saved_root` with your path.)
*   Evaluation for all datasets scripts: bash benchmark/eval/eval.sh  (Remember to replace the `pred_disp_root` and `gt_disp_root` with your wpath.)

🤝🍻 Contributing
-----------------

[](https://github.com/Tencent/DepthCrafter#-contributing)
*   Welcome to open issues and pull requests.

*   Welcome to optimize the inference speed and memory usage, e.g., through model quantization, distillation, or other acceleration techniques.

### Contributors

[](https://github.com/Tencent/DepthCrafter#contributors)[![Image 6](https://camo.githubusercontent.com/64000f0ed45f10397b8ea84cb96d5047937e7e559ce29e056b2a2980cde0ceea/68747470733a2f2f636f6e747269622e726f636b732f696d6167653f7265706f3d54656e63656e742f446570746843726166746572)](https://github.com/Tencent/DepthCrafter/graphs/contributors)

🧪 Testing
----------

[](https://github.com/Tencent/DepthCrafter#-testing)
We provide comprehensive unit tests to ensure code quality and reliability.

### Running Tests

[](https://github.com/Tencent/DepthCrafter#running-tests)
1.   **Run all tests**:

pytest unit_tests/

1.   **Run tests with verbose output**:

pytest unit_tests/ -v

1.   **Run specific test file**:

pytest unit_tests/test_depth_crafter_ppl.py

### Test Structure

[](https://github.com/Tencent/DepthCrafter#test-structure)
*   `unit_tests/test_depth_crafter_ppl.py`: Tests for the main depth estimation pipeline
*   `unit_tests/test_inference.py`: Tests for the inference interface
*   `unit_tests/test_utils.py`: Tests for utility functions
*   `unit_tests/test_unet.py`: Tests for the UNet model

### Requirements

[](https://github.com/Tencent/DepthCrafter#requirements)
*   GPU with CUDA support is required for `test_pipeline_gpu_integration`
*   Tests use small tensor sizes to minimize memory usage
*   All heavy computations are mocked for fast execution

Star History

original_data.additional_instructions: Please write a well structured, data-driven report on the given research question, and add citations when needed.

problem: What are Flow Matching Models?
final_response:
# What Flow Matching Models Are

Flow Matching (FM) is a continuous-time generative modeling framework that learns a velocity field vθ(x, t) which, when integrated as an ODE, transports noise to data samples, while training by directly regressing the vector field rather than by solving costly SDE/ODE simulations at training time.<cite id="2d093dac-0">Flow matching provides a continuous-time framework for generative modeling in which data samples are gradually corrupted by noise and then recovered by learning an instantaneous velocity field</cite><cite id="2d093dac-0">In practice, one approximates the velocity field by a neural network vθ(x, t) and minimizes a mean-squared velocity matching loss</cite><cite id="2d093dac-4">The FM training approach proposes to sidestep the need to differentiate through a costly numerical ODE integration at training time by instead minimizing a local velocity regression loss</cite>. FM unifies score-based and diffusion perspectives through equivalent ODE/SDE forms and enables efficient sampling via standard ODE/SDE solvers.<cite id="2d093dac-0">One may equivalently generate samples via a reverse SDE and the framework unifies score-based and diffusion-based modeling while enabling efficient likelihood evaluation and sampling via ODE/SDE solvers</cite>

Conceptually, FM defines probability paths between a simple prior (e.g., Gaussian noise) and data points, and trains a model to match the instantaneous velocity along those paths; a common choice is a linear interpolation x_t = (1−t)x0 + t x1 with conditional velocity x1 − x0, which yields a simple, widely used objective.<cite id="2d093dac-2">FM provides a simulation-free training objective by directly regressing the velocity vt on a conditional vector field ut(·|x1), with an effective choice ut(xt|x1)=x1−x0 via linear interpolation between data and noise</cite><cite id="2d093dac-4">The loss is formed by sampling noise/data points and a time t and evaluating ||x1 − x0 − vθ(t, xt)||2 where xt is the linear barycenter</cite> FM can be formulated on neural SDEs without sampling noise by directly regressing the drift term (velocity) rather than denoising Gaussian noise at each timestep, which differs from traditional diffusion denoising objectives and avoids stepwise noise-sampling in training.<cite id="a1f1f0a9-0">FM models learn to generate data in a single continuous-time transformation by training a vector field vθ that defines a probability flow ODE</cite><cite id="a1f1f0a9-4">FM introduced a simulation-free method for training CNFs by regressing onto vector fields defining probability paths between noise and data, enabling scalable training without numerical integration</cite>

# Training Objective and Architectures

FM typically minimizes a mean-squared error between the model’s predicted velocity and the true conditional velocity along a chosen path between a noise sample x0 and a data sample x1, with t sampled over [0, 1].<cite id="2d093dac-0">Training proceeds by minimizing the mean-squared velocity matching loss where v*(xt, t)=α′t x0 + β′t ε and t is drawn from [0, 1]</cite><cite id="2d093dac-4">The FM loss regresses ||x1 − x0 − vθ(t, xt)||2 using sampled pairs (x0, x1) and t, with xt = (1−t)x0 + t x1</cite> Architectures can be conditioned on data x1 and on additional guidance cues c; the conditional formulation defines a family of paths pt(·|x1) toward x1, of which linear interpolation is a canonical, effective choice.<cite id="2d093dac-2">FM frames training as regressing vt on a conditional vector field ut(·|x1) that determines pt(·|x1), with u(xt|x1)=x1−x0 for linear interpolation</cite> FM can also be derived from stochastic interpolants that match diffusion forward marginals, yielding equivalent SDE parameters and bridging to score-based generation formulations.<cite id="2d093dac-1">By matching marginal distributions generated by a diffusion forward process to those implied by an interpolant path, one can derive corresponding f_t, g_t and relate generative SDEs, showing equivalences between diffusion and flow-matching formulations</cite>

A critical design choice is the coupling between noise and data when sampling pairs (x0, x1); the default independent coupling is simple but can produce high-curvature ODE paths that are more compute-intensive to integrate at inference, motivating alternative couplings and path designs.<cite id="2d093dac-4">FM’s default independent coupling of noise and data is simple and cheap but known to produce ODE paths with high curvature, increasing compute at inference; sample quality is highly dependent on the number of function evaluations</cite> Extensions include probability paths beyond linear interpolation (e.g., optimal transport-based paths) and rectified/equivariant variants that stabilize training and broaden expressivity.<cite id="2d093dac-2">FM can be flexibly extended to interpolate between distributions other than standard Gaussians</cite><cite id="d2bc9066-1">Variations include OT-CFM, rectified flow, consistent velocity field, and equivariant flow; a line of work also interpolates distributions</cite>

# Relationship to Diffusion and Continuous Normalizing Flows

FM offers a more direct path to probability flow ODEs than diffusion models, which learn to reverse a predefined noising process by denoising Gaussian increments; FM instead learns the drift (velocity) along specified paths between noise and data, often achieving comparable or better sample quality with fewer steps due to direct velocity regression.<cite id="d2bc9066-4">FM offers greater flexibility and interpretability, supporting efficient density modeling and high-quality sample generation, and provides a natural alternative to diffusion when efficiency and theoretical clarity are desired</cite><cite id="a1f1f0a9-4">FM generalizes beyond diffusion methods by accommodating arbitrary probability paths and has shown superior likelihood and sample quality on datasets such as ImageNet compared to diffusion models</cite> The diffusion SDE can be seen as an equivalent stochastic version of the FM PF-ODE, so models can be trained in a deterministic FM objective and sampled via either ODE integration or an associated SDE for stochasticity.<cite id="2d093dac-0">There exists a PF-ODE whose marginals match the interpolation; one can also generate via the reverse SDE with a score-based drift and diffusion coefficient</cite><cite id="a1f1f0a9-0">Any FM ODE has an equivalent SDE with the same marginals; for rectified flow backbones, the SDE can be explicitly constructed with drift and diffusion coefficients</cite>

FM addresses a key computational bottleneck of CNF/ODE-based training and sampling by replacing maximum-likelihood ODE integration with a regression objective, enabling scalable training without numerical solvers; historically, CNFs required expensive ODE simulations for training and sampling, while FMs avoid these costs by directly learning the vector field.<cite id="a1f1f0a9-1">Continuous normalizing flows train by maximum likelihood but require ODE simulations with high computational cost; FM avoids this by using a regression objective to train a CNF without simulations during training</cite><cite id="a1f1f0a9-4">Unlike traditional CNF training, FM directly learns vector fields through a per-sample objective, enabling scalable training without numerical integration</cite> FM also broadens path design beyond diffusion’s fixed noising schedules, including optimal transport-based paths and other couplings, which can improve stability and efficiency.<cite id="d2bc9066-1">FM and its variants refine learning of vector fields and interpolate between distributions in ways distinct from standard diffusion schedules</cite><cite id="2d093dac-4">Choosing different couplings yields different losses and flows; independent coupling can induce high curvature requiring more NFEs</cite>

# Variants and Extensions

FM supports conditioning and guidance beyond unconditional generation. Linear interpolation between x0 and x1 yields a simple baseline, but conditional formulations and rectified flows introduce path corrections and conditioning mechanisms to stabilize training and improve quality.<cite id="2d093dac-2">An effective choice is linear interpolation with u(xt|x1)=x1−x0, but FM’s conditional formulation is general and flexible</cite><cite id="d2bc9066-1">Rectified flow and related methods refine vector-field learning to stabilize image generation and extend to high-resolution text-image generation</cite> Equivariant and structured variants further constrain the velocity field to respect symmetries, improving sample quality and control while retaining FM’s training advantages.<cite id="d2bc9066-1">Equivariant flow and related variants are part of the FM family, broadening applicability while maintaining simulation-free training</cite><cite id="a1f1f0a9-4">FM generalizes with arbitrary probability paths, including optimal transport-based designs, enabling faster training and strong expressiveness</cite>

Guidance methods adapt FM during sampling to control attributes such as class or style. Classifier-free guidance (CFG) combines an unconditional flow model and a conditional flow model via a weighted sum, trading diversity for fidelity as the guidance weight increases; this is a direct analog of CFG in diffusion but operates on flow velocities rather than scores.<cite id="ca7d06f6-0">In classifier-free guided FM, a guided velocity field is obtained by training a guided model and an unconditional model and taking a linear combination scaled by a parameter γ</cite><cite id="ca7d06f6-3">CFG in rectified flow combines unconditional velocity and conditional velocity via a weight w, increasing condition alignment at potential diversity cost</cite> General frameworks for FM guidance derive multiple guidance strategies (e.g., matching-based, Monte Carlo-based, and learned guidance), offering a unified perspective and new design spaces for controllability.<cite id="ca7d06f6-4">A general framework for flow matching guidance derives MC-based, approximate, and learned guidance methods, covering classical cases and providing theoretical derivations</cite> In discrete or structured domains, straight-through guidance and classifier-based strategies adapt FM guidance to handle discrete decisions and sequence structure without retraining the base flow model.<cite id="ca7d06f6-0">For discrete FM, guidance can be classifier-based using scores from a trained noisy classifier at multiple noise levels or training-free via straight-through gradients from a scoring model</cite>

# Efficiency, Sampling, and Guidance

Because FM trains by local velocity regression rather than iterative denoising steps, inference can be highly efficient, with sample quality sensitive primarily to the number of ODE function evaluations; however, path design and coupling choices strongly affect curvature and thus NFE requirements.<cite id="a1f1f0a9-4">FM’s simulation-free training enables scalable models, and CNFs with FM can be sampled without Markov chain steps</cite><cite id="2d093dac-4">Sample quality is highly dependent on the number of function evaluations, and independent coupling can produce high-curvature paths requiring more compute</cite> FM supports both deterministic PF-ODE sampling and stochastic sampling via associated SDEs, allowing flexible control over diversity and enabling compatibility with guidance techniques including classifier-free guidance during sampling.<cite id="2d093dac-0">FM supports PF-ODE and an equivalent reverse SDE for sampling</cite><cite id="a1f1f0a9-3">One can derive families of SDEs with the same marginals as a given flow model to enable flexible stochastic sampling and controllable diversity, and these samplers are compatible with classifier-free guidance</cite>

Compared to diffusion, FM often reduces simulation overhead by avoiding stepwise noise prediction and can yield comparable or better sample quality with fewer steps, while CNF-based approaches historically suffered from expensive ODE integration in both training and sampling; FM mitigates this by regressing the drift directly.<cite id="a1f1f0a9-4">FM enables scalable training without numerical integration and has outperformed diffusion models in likelihood and sample quality on datasets such as ImageNet</cite><cite id="a1f1f0a9-1">FM avoids ODE simulations during training, addressing the high computational cost of CNF maximum-likelihood training</cite>

# Theory and Applications

FM has theoretical underpinnings in flows and continuity equations, with recent work analyzing its statistical behavior and convergence properties and proposing efficiency improvements through specialized path couplings and path designs.<cite id="d2bc9066-1">FM is grounded in flows and continuity equations, and recent studies establish convergence of the FM estimator to the true distribution under some metrics, with ongoing work on convergence rates</cite><cite id="d2bc9066-1">Rectified flow and FM-OT illustrate practical refinements that improve efficiency and generalization</cite> FM has been applied across modalities and domains, including high-resolution image generation, video modeling with pyramidal FM to reduce compute, and even non-image tasks like hyperspectral image reconstruction and trajectory modeling, highlighting its generality and efficiency benefits.<cite id="d2bc9066-1">Rectified flow has been extended to high-resolution text-image generation, and FM variants appear in molecule, text, speech, and motion synthesis</cite><cite id="2d093dac-2">Pyramidal FM specializes in reducing computational cost for video generative modeling by leveraging FM’s flexible path design</cite><cite id="a1f1f0a9-4">FM has been applied beyond generative tasks to trajectory modeling and probabilistic differential equations, demonstrating adaptability across domains with faster inference and explicit path control</cite><cite id="a1f1f0a9-3">On ImageNet, FM-based models demonstrate that flexible stochastic sampling can outperform deterministic samplers, with controllable diversity and compatibility with CFG</cite>

# Limitations and Open Problems

Despite promising results, FM faces training and path-design challenges. Title: Flow-Matching Guided Deep Unfolding for Hyperspectral Image Reconstruction
Snippet: Flow Matching (FM) has recently emerged as a promising paradigm for generative modeling. Its core idea is to directly fit continuous flow paths between probability densities, thereby learning a continuous-time dynamical system. Unlike diffusion models (Ho et al., 2020) that rely on a fixed forward process, flow matching offers greater flexibility and interpretability, supporting efficient density modeling and high-quality sample generation. This makes flow matching a natural alternative to diffusion when both efficiency and theoretical clarity are desired. Lipman et al. (2022) first proposed FM by fitting optimal transport maps along random paths, constructing a path-independent vector field to approximate the target distribution. Subsequent work extended FM to practical applications: Rectified Flow (Liu et al., 2022) introduced path correction for stable image generation, while FM-OT (Kornilov et al., 2024) combined FM with optimal transport to improve efficiency and generalization.These developments demonstrate the versatility of FM in bridging theoretical advances with real-world generative tasks. 

Beyond generative tasks, FM has also been successfully applied to trajectory modeling and probabilistic differential equations, demonstrating strong adaptability across diverse domains. These applications highlight its ability to capture complex temporal dependencies and stochastic behaviors, further broadening its utility beyond image or signal generation. Compared to diffusion models such as DDPM (Ho et al., 2020) and Score-based Models (Song et al., 2020), FM achieves faster inference and provides more explicit control over path evolution. 

Overall, FM pushes generative modeling toward greater efficiency and interpretability. With its flexible path modeling, end-to-end optimization, and strong generative performance, FM shows broad potential in areas including image synthesis, speech, and physical modeling. Yet, CNFs have historically been hindered by their reliance on solving high-dimensional ordinary differential equations (ODEs), making both training and sampling computationally expensive (Ben-Hamu et al., 2022;Rozen et al., 2021;Grathwohl et al., 2019).

Snippet: A key limitation of current discrete flow matching techniques is the lack of training-free guidance strategies. Flow matching guidance [42,43] is performed either with classifier-based or classifier-free guidance. 

Classifier-Free Guidance. In classifier-free guided flow matching [42], the guided velocity field is obtained by training a guided flow model u ϕ t (x|y) and an unconditional flow model u θ t (x) and taking the linear combination of the guided and unconditional velocities scaled by a parameter γ.

Classifier-Based Guidance. In classifier-based guided flow matching [44], a time-dependent classifier p ϕ t (y|x t ) that predicts a classifier score given noisy samples x t separately from the unconditional generator. Then, we sample with a guided velocity field given by 

which requires projection back to the simplex for guided discrete flows. For simplex-based flows, this approach typically involves additional training of noisy classifiers that predict the classifier score given intermediate distributions over the simplex at each time step. Not only are these noisy classifiers less accurate than large pre-trained classifiers on clean sequences, but they also require extensive training as all noise levels need to be included in the training task. 

STGFlow overcomes these limitations by defining a guided flow velocity using the straight-through gradients of the scoring model on discrete sequences sampled with respect to the relaxed Gumbelsoftmax probabilities. # What Flow Matching Models Are

Flow Matching (FM) is a continuous-time generative modeling framework that learns a velocity field vθ(x, t) which, when integrated as an ODE, transports noise to data samples, while training by directly regressing the vector field rather than by solving costly SDE/ODE simulations at training time.<cite id="2d093dac-0">Flow matching provides a continuous-time framework for generative modeling in which data samples are gradually corrupted by noise and then recovered by learning an instantaneous velocity field</cite><cite id="2d093dac-0">In practice, one approximates the velocity field by a neural network vθ(x, t) and minimizes a mean-squared velocity matching loss</cite><cite id="2d093dac-4">The FM training approach proposes to sidestep the need to differentiate through a costly numerical ODE integration at training time by instead minimizing a local velocity regression loss</cite>. FM unifies score-based and diffusion perspectives through equivalent ODE/SDE forms and enables efficient sampling via standard ODE/SDE solvers.<cite id="2d093dac-0">One may equivalently generate samples via a reverse SDE and the framework unifies score-based and diffusion-based modeling while enabling efficient likelihood evaluation and sampling via ODE/SDE solvers</cite>

Conceptually, FM defines probability paths between a simple prior (e.g., Gaussian noise) and data points, and trains a model to match the instantaneous velocity along those paths; a common choice is a linear interpolation x_t = (1−t)x0 + t x1 with conditional velocity x1 − x0, which yields a simple, widely used objective.<cite id="2d093dac-2">FM provides a simulation-free training objective by directly regressing the velocity vt on a conditional vector field ut(·|x1), with an effective choice ut(xt|x1)=x1−x0 via linear interpolation between data and noise</cite><cite id="2d093dac-4">The loss is formed by sampling noise/data points and a time t and evaluating ||x1 − x0 − vθ(t, xt)||2 where xt is the linear barycenter</cite> FM can be formulated on neural SDEs without sampling noise by directly regressing the drift term (velocity) rather than denoising Gaussian noise at each timestep, which differs from traditional diffusion denoising objectives and avoids stepwise noise-sampling in training.<cite id="a1f1f0a9-0">FM models learn to generate data in a single continuous-time transformation by training a vector field vθ that defines a probability flow ODE</cite><cite id="a1f1f0a9-4">FM introduced a simulation-free method for training CNFs by regressing onto vector fields defining probability paths between noise and data, enabling scalable training without numerical integration</cite>

# Training Objective and Architectures

FM typically minimizes a mean-squared error between the model’s predicted velocity and the true conditional velocity along a chosen path between a noise sample x0 and a data sample x1, with t sampled over [0, 1].<cite id="2d093dac-0">Training proceeds by minimizing the mean-squared velocity matching loss where v*(xt, t)=α′t x0 + β′t ε and t is drawn from [0, 1]</cite><cite id="2d093dac-4">The FM loss regresses ||x1 − x0 − vθ(t, xt)||2 using sampled pairs (x0, x1) and t, with xt = (1−t)x0 + t x1</cite> Architectures can be conditioned on data x1 and on additional guidance cues c; the conditional formulation defines a family of paths pt(·|x1) toward x1, of which linear interpolation is a canonical, effective choice.<cite id="2d093dac-2">FM frames training as regressing vt on a conditional vector field ut(·|x1) that determines pt(·|x1), with u(xt|x1)=x1−x0 for linear interpolation</cite> FM can also be derived from stochastic interpolants that match diffusion forward marginals, yielding equivalent SDE parameters and bridging to score-based generation formulations.<cite id="2d093dac-1">By matching marginal distributions generated by a diffusion forward process to those implied by an interpolant path, one can derive corresponding f_t, g_t and relate generative SDEs, showing equivalences between diffusion and flow-matching formulations</cite>

A critical design choice is the coupling between noise and data when sampling pairs (x0, x1); the default independent coupling is simple but can produce high-curvature ODE paths that are more compute-intensive to integrate at inference, motivating alternative couplings and path designs.<cite id="2d093dac-4">FM’s default independent coupling of noise and data is simple and cheap but known to produce ODE paths with high curvature, increasing compute at inference; sample quality is highly dependent on the number of function evaluations</cite> Extensions include probability paths beyond linear interpolation (e.g., optimal transport-based paths) and rectified/equivariant variants that stabilize training and broaden expressivity.<cite id="2d093dac-2">FM can be flexibly extended to interpolate between distributions other than standard Gaussians</cite><cite id="d2bc9066-1">Variations include OT-CFM, rectified flow, consistent velocity field, and equivariant flow; a line of work also interpolates distributions</cite>

# Relationship to Diffusion and Continuous Normalizing Flows

FM offers a more direct path to probability flow ODEs than diffusion models, which learn to reverse a predefined noising process by denoising Gaussian increments; FM instead learns the drift (velocity) along specified paths between noise and data, often achieving comparable or better sample quality with fewer steps due to direct velocity regression.<cite id="d2bc9066-4">FM offers greater flexibility and interpretability, supporting efficient density modeling and high-quality sample generation, and provides a natural alternative to diffusion when efficiency and theoretical clarity are desired</cite><cite id="a1f1f0a9-4">FM generalizes beyond diffusion methods by accommodating arbitrary probability paths and has shown superior likelihood and sample quality on datasets such as ImageNet compared to diffusion models</cite> The diffusion SDE can be seen as an equivalent stochastic version of the FM PF-ODE, so models can be trained in a deterministic FM objective and sampled via either ODE integration or an associated SDE for stochasticity.<cite id="2d093dac-0">There exists a PF-ODE whose marginals match the interpolation; one can also generate via the reverse SDE with a score-based drift and diffusion coefficient</cite><cite id="a1f1f0a9-0">Any FM ODE has an equivalent SDE with the same marginals; for rectified flow backbones, the SDE can be explicitly constructed with drift and diffusion coefficients</cite>

FM addresses a key computational bottleneck of CNF/ODE-based training and sampling by replacing maximum-likelihood ODE integration with a regression objective, enabling scalable training without numerical solvers; historically, CNFs required expensive ODE simulations for training and sampling, while FMs avoid these costs by directly learning the vector field.<cite id="a1f1f0a9-1">Continuous normalizing flows train by maximum likelihood but require ODE simulations with high computational cost; FM avoids this by using a regression objective to train a CNF without simulations during training</cite><cite id="a1f1f0a9-4">Unlike traditional CNF training, FM directly learns vector fields through a per-sample objective, enabling scalable training without numerical integration</cite> FM also broadens path design beyond diffusion’s fixed noising schedules, including optimal transport-based paths and other couplings, which can improve stability and efficiency.<cite id="d2bc9066-1">FM and its variants refine learning of vector fields and interpolate between distributions in ways distinct from standard diffusion schedules</cite><cite id="2d093dac-4">Choosing different couplings yields different losses and flows; independent coupling can induce high curvature requiring more NFEs</cite>

# Variants and Extensions

FM supports conditioning and guidance beyond unconditional generation. Linear interpolation between x0 and x1 yields a simple baseline, but conditional formulations and rectified flows introduce path corrections and conditioning mechanisms to stabilize training and improve quality.<cite id="2d093dac-2">An effective choice is linear interpolation with u(xt|x1)=x1−x0, but FM’s conditional formulation is general and flexible</cite><cite id="d2bc9066-1">Rectified flow and related methods refine vector-field learning to stabilize image generation and extend to high-resolution text-image generation</cite> Equivariant and structured variants further constrain the velocity field to respect symmetries, improving sample quality and control while retaining FM’s training advantages.<cite id="d2bc9066-1">Equivariant flow and related variants are part of the FM family, broadening applicability while maintaining simulation-free training</cite><cite id="a1f1f0a9-4">FM generalizes with arbitrary probability paths, including optimal transport-based designs, enabling faster training and strong expressiveness</cite>

Guidance methods adapt FM during sampling to control attributes such as class or style. Classifier-free guidance (CFG) combines an unconditional flow model and a conditional flow model via a weighted sum, trading diversity for fidelity as the guidance weight increases; this is a direct analog of CFG in diffusion but operates on flow velocities rather than scores.<cite id="ca7d06f6-0">In classifier-free guided FM, a guided velocity field is obtained by training a guided model and an unconditional model and taking a linear combination scaled by a parameter γ</cite><cite id="ca7d06f6-3">CFG in rectified flow combines unconditional velocity and conditional velocity via a weight w, increasing condition alignment at potential diversity cost</cite> General frameworks for FM guidance derive multiple guidance strategies (e.g., matching-based, Monte Carlo-based, and learned guidance), offering a unified perspective and new design spaces for controllability.<cite id="ca7d06f6-4">A general framework for flow matching guidance derives MC-based, approximate, and learned guidance methods, covering classical cases and providing theoretical derivations</cite> In discrete or structured domains, straight-through guidance and classifier-based strategies adapt FM guidance to handle discrete decisions and sequence structure without retraining the base flow model.<cite id="ca7d06f6-0">For discrete FM, guidance can be classifier-based using scores from a trained noisy classifier at multiple noise levels or training-free via straight-through gradients from a scoring model</cite>

# Efficiency, Sampling, and Guidance

Because FM trains by local velocity regression rather than iterative denoising steps, inference can be highly efficient, with sample quality sensitive primarily to the number of ODE function evaluations; however, path design and coupling choices strongly affect curvature and thus NFE requirements.<cite id="a1f1f0a9-4">FM’s simulation-free training enables scalable models, and CNFs with FM can be sampled without Markov chain steps</cite><cite id="2d093dac-4">Sample quality is highly dependent on the number of function evaluations, and independent coupling can produce high-curvature paths requiring more compute</cite> FM supports both deterministic PF-ODE sampling and stochastic sampling via associated SDEs, allowing flexible control over diversity and enabling compatibility with guidance techniques including classifier-free guidance during sampling.<cite id="2d093dac-0">FM supports PF-ODE and an equivalent reverse SDE for sampling</cite><cite id="a1f1f0a9-3">One can derive families of SDEs with the same marginals as a given flow model to enable flexible stochastic sampling and controllable diversity, and these samplers are compatible with classifier-free guidance</cite>

Compared to diffusion, FM often reduces simulation overhead by avoiding stepwise noise prediction and can yield comparable or better sample quality with fewer steps, while CNF-based approaches historically suffered from expensive ODE integration in both training and sampling; FM mitigates this by regressing the drift directly.<cite id="a1f1f0a9-4">FM enables scalable training without numerical integration and has outperformed diffusion models in likelihood and sample quality on datasets such as ImageNet</cite><cite id="a1f1f0a9-1">FM avoids ODE simulations during training, addressing the high computational cost of CNF maximum-likelihood training</cite>

# Theory and Applications

FM has theoretical underpinnings in flows and continuity equations, with recent work analyzing its statistical behavior and convergence properties and proposing efficiency improvements through specialized path couplings and path designs.<cite id="d2bc9066-1">FM is grounded in flows and continuity equations, and recent studies establish convergence of the FM estimator to the true distribution under some metrics, with ongoing work on convergence rates</cite><cite id="d2bc9066-1">Rectified flow and FM-OT illustrate practical refinements that improve efficiency and generalization</cite> FM has been applied across modalities and domains, including high-resolution image generation, video modeling with pyramidal FM to reduce compute, and even non-image tasks like hyperspectral image reconstruction and trajectory modeling, highlighting its generality and efficiency benefits.<cite id="d2bc9066-1">Rectified flow has been extended to high-resolution text-image generation, and FM variants appear in molecule, text, speech, and motion synthesis</cite><cite id="2d093dac-2">Pyramidal FM specializes in reducing computational cost for video generative modeling by leveraging FM’s flexible path design</cite><cite id="a1f1f0a9-4">FM has been applied beyond generative tasks to trajectory modeling and probabilistic differential equations, demonstrating adaptability across domains with faster inference and explicit path control</cite><cite id="a1f1f0a9-3">On ImageNet, FM-based models demonstrate that flexible stochastic sampling can outperform deterministic samplers, with controllable diversity and compatibility with CFG</cite>

# Limitations and Open Problems

Despite promising results, FM faces training and path-design challenges. Independent coupling can induce high-curvature flows that require more NFEs at inference, and stability can depend on the choice of probability path and conditioning strategy.<cite id="2d093dac-4">Independent coupling can produce high-curvature ODE paths, making inference more compute-intensive and sample quality sensitive to NFEs</cite> Conditioning with classifier-free guidance requires training both conditional and unconditional models and can introduce instability if trained solely on the conditional objective, motivating joint optimization strategies that double compute footprint.<cite id="2d093dac-1">Training exclusively on the conditional objective can lead to divergent optimization; joint optimization of conditional and unconditional outputs is needed, effectively doubling VRAM and increasing per-iteration costs</cite> While FM has demonstrated superior likelihood and sample quality on some benchmarks, broader, standardized comparisons across tasks and resolutions remain active areas, and theoretical results on convergence rates and generalization under non-linear paths are still being developed.<cite id="d2bc9066-1">FM has established convergence under some metrics, but convergence rates and detailed statistical behavior remain open questions</cite>

# Practical Takeaways

- FM learns a continuous velocity field by regressing between noise and data along specified probability paths, enabling direct ODE/SDE sampling without iterative denoising steps typical of diffusion, and avoiding expensive ODE integration during training.<cite id="2d093dac-0">FM learns an instantaneous velocity field and supports PF-ODE/SDE sampling</cite><cite id="a1f1f0a9-4">FM’s regression-based training avoids ODE integration and enables fast sampling</cite>

- FM unifies with diffusion via equivalent SDE/ODE formulations and supports both deterministic and stochastic sampling; CFG and other guidance methods adapt FM for controllability without retraining the base model, and general guidance frameworks offer new design space and theoretical grounding.<cite id="2d093dac-0">FM connects to reverse SDE formulations</cite><cite id="a1f1f0a9-3">Flexible SDE families yield stochastic sampling with controllable diversity and CFG compatibility</cite><cite id="ca7d06f6-4">General guidance frameworks unify prior methods and provide theoretical derivations</cite>
- FM has shown strong performance and efficiency across image and non-image domains, with emerging theory on convergence and ongoing work to optimize path couplings and conditioning for robustness and speed.<cite id="a1f1f0a9-4">FM has outperformed diffusion in likelihood and sample quality on ImageNet and applies broadly</cite><cite id="d2bc9066-1">FM’s theoretical and algorithmic developments continue to improve convergence and generalization</cite>

Snippet: Similar to diffusion models (Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015;Song & Ermon, 2019;Ho et al., 2020), flow generative models (Papamakarios et al., 2021;Song et al., 2021;Xu et al., 2022;Lipman et al., 2023;Liu et al., 2023;Albergo & Vanden-Eijnden, 2023) aim to learn a velocity field v t that maps random noise x 0 ∼ N (0, I) to data samples x 1 ∼ q via an ordinary differential equation (ODE): 

Recently, Lipman et al. (2023); Liu et al. (2023); Albergo & Vanden-Eijnden (2023) proposed the flow matching framework, which provides a simple simulation-free training objective for flow generative models by directly regressing the velocity v t on a conditional vector filed u t (•|x 1 ): 

where u t (•|x 1 ) uniquely determines a conditional probability path p t (•|x 1 ) toward data sample x 1 . An effective choice of the conditional probability path is linear interpolation of data and noise: 

and u(x t |x 1 ) = x 1 − x 0 . Notably, flow matching can be flexibly extended to interpolate between distributions other than standard Gaussians. This enables us to devise a new flow matching algorithm that specializes in reducing the computational cost of video generative modeling.

Title: Distilling Two-Timed Flow Models by Separately Matching Initial and Terminal Velocities
Snippet: Diffusion models (Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015;Ho et al., 2020) have demonstrated remarkable effectiveness in generative modeling across diverse domains such as image, audio, and video. Their approach learns the score of a noise-adding process governed by a stochastic differential equation (SDE), which has an equivalent ordinary differential equation (ODE), and reverses the process by simulating one of the differential equations backward in time (Song et al., 2021). Recent advancement like rectified flow (Liu et al., 2023), flow matching (Lipman et al., 2023), and stochastic interpolants (Albergo & Vanden-Eijnden, 2023) extend this framework by introducing different mathematical formulations and more flexibility in the modeling of the noise-adding process. However, the iterative sampling process of diffusion model is computationally intensive. To address this limitation, two main strategies have emerged: 

(1) reducing the simulation cost of ODEs or SDEs (Lu et al., 2022;Shaul et al., 2023), and (2) distillation, which trains a new model (the student) that compresses the sampling process of a diffusion model (the teacher) into fewer steps.

Title: Flow Matching with Semidiscrete Couplings
Snippet: Flow-based generative models (Rezende and Mohamed, 2015;Dinh et al., 2016;Kingma and Dhariwal, 2018;Grathwohl et al., 2018) can gradually transform noise vectors into structured data. Flow models parameterized as time-dependent velocity fields (Chen et al., 2018) v θ (t, x) can be efficiently trained using flow matching (FM) (Lipman et al., 2023;Peluchetti, 2022;Albergo et al., 2023) to yield state-of-the-art performance (Zheng et al., 2024;Esser et al., 2024). The FM training approach proposes to sidestep the need to differentiate through a costly numerical ODE integration at training time by instead minimizing velocity fields locally through a regression loss. In a nutshell, the loss is formed by sampling a pair of noise/data points (x 0 , x 1 ) and a random time t ∈ [0, 1] to evaluate ∥x 1 − x 0 − v θ (t, x t )∥ 2 , where x t := (1 − t)x 0 + t x 1 is a barycenter in the [x 0 , x 1 ] segment. 

Coupling Noise×Data. A crucial ingredient in the FM methodology lies in choosing the coupling of noise/data used to sample pairs. Indeed, given a source and target distribution, there are infinitely many probability paths that can interpolate between them; choosing a different coupling yields a different loss and hence a different flow (Albergo et al., 2023;Liu, 2022). The default formulation of FM (Lipman et al., 2024) relies on the independent coupling, where noise and data are sampled independently. While simple and cheap, this approach is known to produce ODE paths with high curvature, which requires increased compute at inference time. In practice, the quality of samples is highly dependent on the number of function evaluations (NFEs) used to integrate the ODE.

Diffusion models (Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015;Ho et al., 2020) have demonstrated remarkable effectiveness in generative modeling across diverse domains such as image, audio, and video. Their approach learns the score of a noise-adding process governed by a stochastic differential equation (SDE), which has an equivalent ordinary differential equation (ODE), and reverses the process by simulating one of the differential equations backward in time (Song et al., 2021). Recent advancement like rectified flow (Liu et al., 2023), flow matching (Lipman et al., 2023), and stochastic interpolants (Albergo & Vanden-Eijnden, 2023) extend this framework by introducing different mathematical formulations and more flexibility in the modeling of the noise-adding process. However, the iterative sampling process of diffusion model is computationally intensive. To address this limitation, two main strategies have emerged: 

(1) reducing the simulation cost of ODEs or SDEs (Lu et al., 2022;Shaul et al., 2023), and (2) distillation, which trains a new model (the student) that compresses the sampling process of a diffusion model (the teacher) into fewer steps.

Flow-based generative models (Rezende and Mohamed, 2015;Dinh et al., 2016;Kingma and Dhariwal, 2018;Grathwohl et al., 2018) can gradually transform noise vectors into structured data. Flow models parameterized as time-dependent velocity fields (Chen et al., 2018) v θ (t, x) can be efficiently trained using flow matching (FM) (Lipman et al., 2023;Peluchetti, 2022;Albergo et al., 2023) to yield state-of-the-art performance (Zheng et al., 2024;Esser et al., 2024). The FM training approach proposes to sidestep the need to differentiate through a costly numerical ODE integration at training time by instead minimizing velocity fields locally through a regression loss. In a nutshell, the loss is formed by sampling a pair of noise/data points (x 0 , x 1 ) and a random time t ∈ [0, 1] to evaluate ∥x 1 − x 0 − v θ (t, x t )∥ 2 , where x t := (1 − t)x 0 + t x 1 is a barycenter in the [x 0 , x 1 ] segment. 

Coupling Noise×Data. A crucial ingredient in the FM methodology lies in choosing the coupling of noise/data used to sample pairs. Indeed, given a source and target distribution, there are infinitely many probability paths that can interpolate between them; choosing a different coupling yields a different loss and hence a different flow (Albergo et al., 2023;Liu, 2022). The default formulation of FM (Lipman et al., 2024) relies on the independent coupling, where noise and data are sampled independently. While simple and cheap, this approach is known to produce ODE paths with high curvature, which requires increased compute at inference time. In practice, the quality of samples is highly dependent on the number of function evaluations (NFEs) used to integrate the ODE.

Title: Flow matching achieves almost minimax optimal convergence
Snippet: Flow matching (FM) [Lipman et al., 2023, Albergo and Vanden-Eijnden, 2023, Liu et al., 2023b] is a recent simulation-free generative model that produces samples of the target distribution by solving an ordinary differential equation (ODE) initialized with a source normal distribution. The vector field to define the ODE is trained by neural networks with the teaching data of random conditional vectors. This approach bypasses the computationally intensive Monte Carlo sampling required in the diffusion model, which is currently the standard in generative modeling. Various variations have been proposed to refine the learning of vector fields, such as OT-CFM [Tong et al., 2024], rectified flow [Liu et al., 2023b], consistent velocity field [Yang et al., 2024], equivariant flow [Klein et al., 2023], etc. A series of studies also emerge from the viewpoint of interpolating distributions [Albergo et al., 2023c,a]. 

FM has already been applied to various domains with promising performance. Among many others, the rectified flow method has been extended to highresolution text image generation [Esser et al., 2024], and there are also many works on the application of FM to molecule generation [Hoogeboom et al., 2022, Guan et al., 2023, Bose et al., 2023, Dunn and Koes, 2024], text generation [Hu et al., 2024], speech generation [Le et al., 2023], motion synthesis [Hu et al., 2023], etc. 

Although the methods have been developed on the solid theoretical basis of the flows and continuity equation, their statistical behaviors remain less understood. Recent works have established the convergence of the FM estimator to the true distribution under some distributional metrics [Albergo andVanden-Eijnden, 2023, Benton et al., 2023b]. Beyond the convergence, more detailed understandings, such as convergence rates, are still an open question.

Title: Flow-Matching Guided Deep Unfolding for Hyperspectral Image Reconstruction
Snippet: Flow Matching (FM) has recently emerged as a promising paradigm for generative modeling. Its core idea is to directly fit continuous flow paths between probability densities, thereby learning a continuous-time dynamical system. Unlike diffusion models (Ho et al., 2020) that rely on a fixed forward process, flow matching offers greater flexibility and interpretability, supporting efficient density modeling and high-quality sample generation. This makes flow matching a natural alternative to diffusion when both efficiency and theoretical clarity are desired. Lipman et al. (2022) first proposed FM by fitting optimal transport maps along random paths, constructing a path-independent vector field to approximate the target distribution. Subsequent work extended FM to practical applications: Rectified Flow (Liu et al., 2022) introduced path correction for stable image generation, while FM-OT (Kornilov et al., 2024) combined FM with optimal transport to improve efficiency and generalization.These developments demonstrate the versatility of FM in bridging theoretical advances with real-world generative tasks. 

Beyond generative tasks, FM has also been successfully applied to trajectory modeling and probabilistic differential equations, demonstrating strong adaptability across diverse domains. These applications highlight its ability to capture complex temporal dependencies and stochastic behaviors, further broadening its utility beyond image or signal generation. Compared to diffusion models such as DDPM (Ho et al., 2020) and Score-based Models (Song et al., 2020), FM achieves faster inference and provides more explicit control over path evolution. 

Overall, FM pushes generative modeling toward greater efficiency and interpretability. With its flexible path modeling, end-to-end optimization, and strong generative performance, FM shows broad potential in areas including image synthesis, speech, and physical modeling. This broad applicability highlights its promise as a foundation for next-generation generative frameworks.

documents.snippet:
Generative models are designed to learn a complex data distribution p(x) from a simple prior, typically a standard Gaussian distribution N (0, I). Many state-of-the-art approaches are based on learning to reverse a predefined process that maps data to noise. A prominent family of such models is diffusion models. In their foundational formulation (DDPM) (Ho et al., 2020), they utilize a fixed forward process that progressively adds Gaussian noise to a data sample x 0 over discrete timesteps. 

The resulting noisy sample at any time t, denoted x t , can be expressed as 

where ᾱt is a predefined noise schedule and ϵ ∼ N (0, I). A neural network, ϵ θ (x t , t), is then trained to predict the noise component ϵ from the corrupted sample: 

More recent frameworks, such as EDM (Karras et al., 2022), generalize this process by formulating it as solving a continuous-time stochastic differential equation (SDE). EDM provides a principled design methodology, emphasizing crucial choices like network preconditioning. The denoiser network, D θ (x t , σ t ), is scaled to have consistent input and output magnitudes across all noise levels σ t . This network is often trained to predict the clean data x 0 directly, using a weighted loss function that prioritizes different noise levels: 

For the generation part, both approaches start with a sample from the prior, x T ∼ N (0, I), and iteratively apply the learned denoising function to recover a clean sample x 0 . As an alternative to the noise-prediction framework, Flow Matching (FM) (Lipman et al., 2022) models learn to generate data in a single continuous-time transformation. These models learn a vector field v t that transports samples from a prior distribution p 0 (noise) to the target data distribution p 1 (data) by following an ordinary differential equation (ODE): dxt dt = v t (x t ). To make training tractable, FM trains a network v θ to approximate a simple, predefined vector field.

documents.title: Flow matching achieves almost minimax optimal convergence
documents.snippet:
Flow matching (FM) [Lipman et al., 2023, Albergo and Vanden-Eijnden, 2023, Liu et al., 2023b] is a recent simulation-free generative model that produces samples of the target distribution by solving an ordinary differential equation (ODE) initialized with a source normal distribution. The vector field to define the ODE is trained by neural networks with the teaching data of random conditional vectors. This approach bypasses the computationally intensive Monte Carlo sampling required in the diffusion model, which is currently the standard in generative modeling. Various variations have been proposed to refine the learning of vector fields, such as OT-CFM [Tong et al., 2024], rectified flow [Liu et al., 2023b], consistent velocity field [Yang et al., 2024], equivariant flow [Klein et al., 2023], etc. A series of studies also emerge from the viewpoint of interpolating distributions [Albergo et al., 2023c,a]. 

FM has already been applied to various domains with promising performance. Among many others, the rectified flow method has been extended to highresolution text image generation [Esser et al., 2024], and there are also many works on the application of FM to molecule generation [Hoogeboom et al., 2022, Guan et al., 2023, Bose et al., 2023, Dunn and Koes, 2024], text generation [Hu et al., 2024], speech generation [Le et al., 2023], motion synthesis [Hu et al., 2023], etc. 

Although the methods have been developed on the solid theoretical basis of the flows and continuity equation, their statistical behaviors remain less understood. Recent works have established the convergence of the FM estimator to the true distribution under some distributional metrics [Albergo andVanden-Eijnden, 2023, Benton et al., 2023b]. Beyond the convergence, more detailed understandings, such as convergence rates, are still an open question.

This additional degree of freedom allows exploration of stochastic samplers that can help alleviate the issues with the deterministic samplers and outperform them. We demonstrate this empirically on a toy Gaussian setup, as well as on the large scale ImageNet generation task. The stochastic samplers also provide an additional knob for controlling the diversity of generation as we qualitatively demonstrate in our experiments, and are compatible with classifier-free guidance (Ho & Salimans, 2022), as can be seen in Figures 1 and 12. 

Our key contributions are: (1) Specification of a flexible family of SDEs (Theorem 1) that have the same marginal distributions as a given SDE or a flow model, enabling exploration of sampling schemes for a given fixed model, (2) Derivation of new as well as existing special cases directly from Theorem 1 (Corollary 1.1 and Corollary 1.2) demonstrating generality of Theorem 1, (3) Study of a set of SDE families corresponding to Gaussian flow models, derived using Theorem 1, on both a toy as well as a large scale ImageNet setup, demonstrating flexible stochastic sampling and controllable diversity in generation, without requiring retraining (Table 1, Figures 1 and 12).

Generative modeling has seen remarkable advances in recent years, particularly in image generation (Ramesh et al., 2022;Rombach et al., 2022), where diffusion-based approaches based on score matching (Vincent, 2011) have proven highly effective (Ho et al., 2020a;Song et al., 2020b). However, these methods rely on stochastic dynamics that require iterative denoising steps during sampling, leading to significant computational overhead (Song et al., 2020a;Zhang & Chen, 2022). An alternative approach, continuous normalizing Proceedings of the 42 nd International Conference on Machine Learning, Vancouver, Canada. PMLR 267, 2025. Copyright 2025 by the author(s). flows (CNFs) (Chen et al., 2018), models a continuous-time transformation between distributions (Song et al., 2021), enabling direct sampling without Markov chain steps. Yet, CNFs have historically been hindered by their reliance on solving high-dimensional ordinary differential equations (ODEs), making both training and sampling computationally expensive (Ben-Hamu et al., 2022;Rozen et al., 2021;Grathwohl et al., 2019). 

To address these challenges, Lipman et al. (2023) introduced Flow Matching (FM), a simulation-free method for training CNFs by regressing onto vector fields that define probability paths between noise and data distributions. Unlike traditional CNF training, which requires maximum likelihood estimation through ODE solvers, FM directly learns vector fields through a per-sample objective, enabling scalable training without numerical integration. FM generalizes beyond diffusion methods by accommodating arbitrary probability paths, including those based on optimal transport (Chen & Lipman, 2024;Klein et al., 2023), enabling faster training while maintaining expressiveness. Empirically, FM has outperformed diffusion models in likelihood estimation and sample quality on datasets such as ImageNet (Wildberger et al., 2024;Dao et al., 2023;Kohler et al., 2023).

Snippet: A key limitation of current discrete flow matching techniques is the lack of training-free guidance strategies. Flow matching guidance [42,43] is performed either with classifier-based or classifier-free guidance. 

Classifier-Free Guidance. In classifier-free guided flow matching [42], the guided velocity field is obtained by training a guided flow model u ϕ t (x|y) and an unconditional flow model u θ t (x) and taking the linear combination of the guided and unconditional velocities scaled by a parameter γ. 

) This strategy requires training an additional guided flow model on quality-labeled data, which is often scarce. Given that flow models require more training data than simple regression and classification models, classifier-based guidance is preferred for scalability. 

Classifier-Based Guidance. In classifier-based guided flow matching [44], a time-dependent classifier p ϕ t (y|x t ) that predicts a classifier score given noisy samples x t separately from the unconditional generator. Then, we sample with a guided velocity field given by 

which requires projection back to the simplex for guided discrete flows. For simplex-based flows, this approach typically involves additional training of noisy classifiers that predict the classifier score given intermediate distributions over the simplex at each time step. Not only are these noisy classifiers less accurate than large pre-trained classifiers on clean sequences, but they also require extensive training as all noise levels need to be included in the training task. 

STGFlow overcomes these limitations by defining a guided flow velocity using the straight-through gradients of the scoring model on discrete sequences sampled with respect to the relaxed Gumbelsoftmax probabilities. To ensure that the scores of sampled sequences are representative of the relaxed distribution, we sample M sequences and take the aggregate gradient as the guided velocity. This provides a modular training-free strategy for discrete flow matching guidance that conserves the probability mass constraint (Proof in Appendix E).

Title: On the Guidance of Flow Matching
Snippet: In this work, we have proposed the first framework for general flow matching guidance, from which new MC-based guidance g MC , many approximate guidance, and learned guidance g ϕ , are derived, all of them verified by experiments. Many classical guidance methods have been covered as special cases, and we provided a theoretical derivation for each guidance method. We believe this work will facilitate the application of flow matching by opening novel design spaces of its guidance methods.
