documents.snippet:
Generalizable Novel View Synthesis. While Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) [24,30] and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [20] have revolutionized novel view synthesis, they require numerous images with precise camera poses and lengthy per-scene optimization [4,11,25]. Recent methods attempt to jointly optimize camera poses and scene reconstruction [1,5,10,12,16,19,22,33,40], but they still need initial pose estimates. This interdependence can lead to error propagation between pose estimation and scene reconstruction, compromising overall performance. 

To mitigate limitations brought by time-consuming perscene optimization methods, recent learning-based approaches have extended NeRF and 3DGS for generalizable novel view synthesis from sparse images, demonstrating effective generalization to unseen scenes [3,6,6,37,42,44,46]. By scaling up datasets and models, these methods achieve high-quality results without the per-scene optimization traditionally required by NeRF or 3DGS. These approaches incorporate specialized architectures with geometric priors to enhance reconstruction quality. Notable examples include MVSNeRF [3], MuRF [41] and MVSplat [6], which utilize cascade cost volume matching to aggregate multi-view information, while PixelSplat [2] leverages differentiable rendering and epipolar geometry for improved depth estimation. However, despite these advances in generalizable 3D reconstruction, these methods still require calibrated camera poses and sufficient view overlap between input images-conditions rarely met in practical scenarios. Camera poses typically need to be estimated using structure-from-motion (SfM) techniques [29,36], which adds complexity to the inference pipeline. In contrast to these approaches where calibrated camera poses are essential throughout both training and inference, our method enables direct 3D reconstruction from sequences of uncalibrated images. 

Feed-forward Multi-view Stereo Models. Traditional multi-view stereo (MVS) reconstruction typically follows a pipeline of depth map estimation and fusion before surface reconstruction [13,14].

Title: Out-of-Distribution Detection for Monocular Depth Estimation
Snippet: Since epistemic uncertainty results from the lack of knowledge, it is relevant to detecting data not represented by the training distribution, so-called out-ofdistribution (OOD) data. While OOD detection is an active research area in image classification [23,24,37,44], it is rarely explored for complex and high-dimensional tasks like monocular depth estimation. Therefore, we specifically address the detection of OOD samples for depth estimates. Motivated by the image anomaly detection approaches that rely on the reconstruction error [2,7] of autoencoders to detect anomalous data, we propose to detect OOD inputs from depth estimation models also with the reconstruction error. 

In fact, we train a decoder to reconstruct the input image from the features of an already trained and therefore fixed depth estimation model. Since we train the decoder in a post hoc fashion, the depth estimation performance of the underlying model is not affected. More precisely, our image decoder takes the features extracted with the depth encoder of the fixed depth estimation model as input and is trained to predict the original input image. To develop our decoder, we rely on a similar model architecture as the depth decoder. As a result, our method is applicable to various depth estimation models and independent of some specific architecture, i.e., whether the depth estimation model is fully convolutional or transformer-based does not play any role. During inference, the reconstruction error between the predicted and input images serves as the OOD detection score. Our extensive experiments with the OOD detection evaluation protocol show promising results for our method compared to existing uncertainty estimation approaches. 

Our contributions can be summarized as follows: To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to propose an OOD detection method for monocular depth estimation. For this, we do not use OOD examples but rely only on in-distribution training data. In our simple and effective method, we present a second model, represented by an image decoder, to learn image reconstruction post hoc with features extracted by the depth encoder as input. We leverage the reconstruction error as our OOD detection score.

Title: Out-of-Distribution Detection for Monocular Depth Estimation
Snippet: In monocular depth estimation, uncertainty estimation approaches mainly target the data uncertainty introduced by image noise. In contrast to prior work, we address the uncertainty due to lack of knowledge, which is relevant for the detection of data not represented by the training distribution, the so-called out-of-distribution (OOD) data. Motivated by anomaly detection, we propose to detect OOD images from an encoder-decoder depth estimation model based on the reconstruction error. Given the features extracted with the fixed depth encoder, we train an image decoder for image reconstruction using only in-distribution data. Consequently, OOD images result in a high reconstruction error, which we use to distinguish between in- and out-of-distribution samples. We built our experiments on the standard NYU Depth V2 and KITTI benchmarks as in-distribution data. Our post hoc method performs astonishingly well on different models and outperforms existing uncertainty estimation approaches without modifying the trained encoder-decoder depth estimation model.

Title: RoboDepth: Robust Out-of-Distribution Depth Estimation under Corruptions
Snippet: Depth estimation from monocular images is pivotal for real-world visual perception systems. While current learning-based depth estimation models train and test on meticulously curated data, they often overlook out-of-distribution (OoD) situations. Yet, in practical settings -- especially safety-critical ones like autonomous driving -- common corruptions can arise. Addressing this oversight, we introduce a comprehensive robustness test suite, RoboDepth, encompassing 18 corruptions spanning three categories: i) weather and lighting conditions; ii) sensor failures and movement; and iii) data processing anomalies. We subsequently benchmark 42 depth estimation models across indoor and outdoor scenes to assess their resilience to these corruptions. Our findings underscore that, in the absence of a dedicated robustness evaluation framework, many leading depth estimation models may be susceptible to typical corruptions. We delve into design considerations for crafting more robust depth estimation models, touching upon pre-training, augmentation, modality, model capacity, and learning paradigms. We anticipate our benchmark will establish a foundational platform for advancing robust OoD depth estimation.

Title: Out-of-Distribution Detection for Monocular Depth Estimation
Snippet: Motivated by anomaly detection, we present a simple and effective OOD detection approach for monocular depth estimation. Starting from an already trained encoderdecoder depth estimation model, we train an image decoder post hoc for input reconstruction using features extracted by the fixed depth encoder. Designing our image decoder architecture similar to the depth decoder makes our approach applicable to different models regardless of their model architecture, i.e., whether they are fully convolutional or transformer-based. Compared to existing uncertainty estimation approaches, our method, which relies on the reconstruction error as the OOD detection score, shows impressive performance on the epistemic uncertainty evaluation protocol with the benchmarks NYU Depth V2 and KITTI as the in-distribution data and different OOD datasets.

Title: Conditional Generative Adversarial Network for Monocular Image Depth Map Prediction
Snippet: Bhutani et al. [18] proposed a Bayesian inference-based method for monocular image depth estimation and confidence prediction. This method estimates the posterior distribution of each pixel's depth and confidence through a combination of a neural network that estimates the prior distribution of pixel depth and a noise model, and the pixel values of the input image. Almalioglu et al. [19] proposed a monocular visual odometry (VO) and depth estimation algorithm based on depth learning. This method trains an unsupervised monocular VO and depth estimation model using geometric constraints from binocular vision, allowing for motion estimation and scene depth estimation even in extreme environments. The method introduces a new "Persistent" loss function which enables the network to learn persistent estimation of optical flow and scene depth, while reverse depth estimation and optical flow prediction increase the loss function's robustness. The method also employs a pyramid depth network, designed to extract depth information from various scale feature maps, resulting in more accurate and robust depth estimation. 

Although the results may not always be outstanding, these methods and their practical applications are still worth exploring.

problem: give me the best pretrained model for temporal action detection and video understanding
final_response:
# What “best pretrained model” means in temporal action detection (TAD) and video understanding

Temporal action detection requires localizing and classifying all action instances in untrimmed videos, often evaluated with mAP across tIoU thresholds and long-duration, dense, and overlapping instances; Epic-Kitchens-100 is a canonical benchmark because it combines long videos, many per-video instances, and overlapping actions under heavy camera motion, making it a stringent testbed for TAD and video understanding methods.<cite id="be42d413-0">Epic-Kitchens-100 presents the largest challenge for temporal action detection/segmentation when considering average video length, instances per video, and overlapping instances; Table 6 reports mAP results for temporal action detection</cite> “Best” depends on task (dense TAD vs. video QA/understanding), supervision (frame-level vs. video-level), and deployment (compute, openness). Below are evidence-backed recommendations and why.

# Strong pretrained backbones and pretraining strategies for TAD

- SlowFast (and inflated 3D ResNets) remain a robust default backbone for TAD due to their ability to model both appearance and motion; they are widely used on Epic-Kitchens and other TAD benchmarks and can be pretrained on large-scale action datasets (e.g., Kinetics) for transfer.<cite id="9568f81b-2">For THUMOS14, ActivityNet, and UnAV-100, two-stream I3D (inflated 3D CNN) is used for visual features; for Epic-Kitchens-100, SlowFast pretrained on Epic-Kitchens is employed</cite> <cite id="8218573e-0">Features extracted from Kinetics-400 pretrained SlowOnly improved downstream action localization and segmentation, indicating better temporal sensitivity from temporal variations</cite>

- Long-term temporal context helps in egocentric and dense TAD. Larger temporal spans and memory-augmented or long-window models improve performance on Epic-Kitchens; MeMViT demonstrates gains by extending temporal receptive fields, and ablations show egocentric settings prefer longer spans.<cite id="be42d413-2">For EPIC-Kitchens, a longer-term model with M=4 (32×longer-term, 70.4 s receptive field) worked best; recognition in egocentric videos is challenging due to motion blur</cite> <cite id="be42d413-3">An OADT one-stage TAD pipeline fine-tunes on Epic-Kitchens after Kinetics pretraining and uses dense sliding windows for segment proposals</cite> <cite id="8218573e-3">In Ego-Only, a simple blob detector with frozen MAE features achieved 8.2% mAP and longer spans (16–32 s) were preferred; finetuned SlowFast with VSGN and ActionFormer also show sensitivity to span and architecture</cite>

- Self-supervised/MAE-style pretraining is generally beneficial for video understanding, but care is needed for egocentric data. Image MAE pretraining transfers well to many recognition tasks, yet frozen MAE features can underperform on egocentric action detection unless adapted, and long-term temporal pretraining or finetuning is crucial in this domain.<cite id="8218573e-3">Frozen MAE features perform poorly on egocentric action detection (mean mAP drop), and finetuning on Kinetics helps but remains worse than end-to-end Ego-Only; longer temporal spans improve performance</cite> <cite id="8218573e-0">Temporal dynamic augmentation and pretraining improve downstream temporal sensitivity for action localization and segmentation</cite>

- Temporally-adaptive convolutions and improved temporal modeling can further boost recognition features used for TAD. Adapter modules like TAdaConv consistently improve SlowFast, R(2+1)D, and R3D baselines, suggesting a practical way to upgrade pretrained backbones before TAD heads.<cite id="be42d413-1">Adding TAdaConv improves recognition accuracy over SlowFast, R(2+1)D, and R3D baselines on Epic-Kitchens-100</cite>

Practical takeaway: Start with a SlowFast backbone pretrained on a large-scale action dataset (e.g., Kinetics-400/700) and adapt with temporal modeling upgrades (e.g., TAdaConv, longer temporal context) and sufficient pretraining duration. If using MAE-style encoders, validate on your domain: egocentric or long-duration tasks may require domain finetuning and longer temporal spans rather than relying solely on frozen features.<cite id="8218573e-3">Egocentric settings benefit from longer temporal spans and finetuning; frozen MAE features alone are weak for egocentric detection</cite> <cite id="be42d413-2">Longer-term SlowFast variants perform better on Epic-Kitchens</cite>

# State-of-the-art TAD detectors and when to use them

- ActionFormer (transformer-based one-stage): On Epic-Kitchens-100, ActionFormer substantially outperforms strong BMN/G-TAD baselines with SlowFast features, achieving 23.5% average mAP for verb and 21.9% for noun using mAP@[0.1:0.1:0.5], indicating robust localization under dense, overlapping actions.<cite id="84a715cb-3">ActionFormer achieves 23.5% verb and 21.9% noun average mAP on EPIC-Kitchens-100, outperforming BMN and G-TAD by >13.5% absolute points using SlowFast features</cite> It is a strong default for egocentric, dense TAD when you can afford transformer inference and have a good backbone.

- TriDet (one-stage with boundary modeling): TriDet reports state-of-the-art on THUMOS14, HACS, and EPIC-KITCHENS-100 with lower latency than two-stage baselines, by modeling relative boundary distributions and multi-granularity perception; this is attractive for real-time or latency-sensitive pipelines.<cite id="84a715cb-4">TriDet achieves SOTA on THUMOS14, HACS, and EPIC-KITCHENS-100 with lower latency; e.g., 69.3% mAP on THUMOS14 vs. a prior baseline with 74.6% latency</cite>

- Two-stage/graph and proposal-based detectors remain competitive and are commonly used as strong baselines on TAD tasks; many SOTA systems build on SlowFast features or other pretrained video encoders. For very long videos, efficient proposal strategies and segment aggregation are key.<cite id="8218573e-3">VSGN is used as a TAD detector with Video Swin-L pretrained on Kinetics; training and inference settings are described, showing a common two-stage pattern atop strong backbones</cite> <cite id="be42d413-3">G-TAD and BMN were strong baselines on Epic-Kitchens-100 prior to ActionFormer</cite>

Practical takeaway: If high mAP is priority and latency acceptable, ActionFormer or TriDet atop a strong SlowFast or Swin-based backbone is a top choice. For long-duration, overlapping actions in egocentric videos, prefer backbones and pretraining that support long temporal context and consider egocentric-specific finetuning.<cite id="be42d413-2">Longer-term SlowFast improves Epic-Kitchens performance</cite> <cite id="8218573e-3">Egocentric TAD benefits from longer spans and finetuning</cite>

# Video-language models for video understanding and TAD-like grounding

Video-language models (VLMs) support video understanding through dense captioning, temporal grounding, and QA, and can be adapted for TAD by training detection or grounding heads. Pipelines often extract visual features from pretrained video encoders (SlowFast/I3D) and fuse audio (e.g., VGGish) and language for event localization and dense retrieval.<cite id="9568f81b-2">DEL uses I3D (two-stream) for THUMOS/ActivityNet/UnAV-100 and SlowFast pretrained on EPIC-Kitchens; audio features from VGGish (pretrained on AudioSet) are fused for dense event localization</cite> <cite id="9568f81b-4">For EPIC-Kitchens-100, SlowFast features are extracted with 32-frame windows (stride 16), trained on the designated split and evaluated with mAP@[0.1:0.1:0.5], aligning with standard TAD practice</cite> For egocentric, multi-object scenarios, detection and grounding capabilities are crucial, and methods that jointly model objects and interactions can improve localization precision around ambiguous boundaries.<cite id="84a715cb-1">Spatio-temporal action detection with multi-object interaction emphasizes modeling interactions and occlusion to improve spatial localization; datasets differ in temporal duration and annotation granularity</cite>

Practical takeaway: Use a VLM backbone (e.g., SlowFast/I3D/Swin) pretrained on large-scale video datasets and add a TAD or grounding head for dense localization; audio and language modules can boost performance in multimodal settings like DEL-style systems.<cite id="9568f81b-2">Combining visual (I3D/SlowFast) and audio (VGGish) features with language support improves dense event localization across benchmarks</cite>

# Best-practice “best pretrained” choices by scenario

1) Dense TAD on egocentric, long-duration videos (Epic-Kitchens, HACS-like):

Snippet: In this challenge, we employ the video classification methods and pretrain them on Kinetics600 [4] dataset firstly. Snippet: EPIC-KITCHENS is the largest egocentric dataset, captured in a non-scripted manner, and recorded in participants' kitchens. We specialise the SLS for this task as follows: 

• SLS-PT for AR in EPIC-KITCHENS: 

-SLS-1-X-X: standard pre-training, in this case would be any image-based pre-training. 

-SLS-2-X-X: Relevant pre-training would be video pretraining (e.g. large scale video datasets such as Kinetics [2] or HowTo100M [13]). 

• SLS-TL for AR in EPIC-KITCHENS: 

-SLS-X-1-X: Would be utilising no temporal information about action segments or instances per video, i.e. video-level labels of actions are only known, without their rough or exact locations. 

-SLS-X-2-X: Would utilise weak temporal labels, known as single timestamps in EPIC-KITCHENS [14]. These are rough single time points within or close to the action of interest. 

-SLS-X-3-X: Full temporal labels (i.e. start-end times) without any spatial labels have been used. 

-SLS-X-4-X: Methods have taken advantage of spatio-temporal labels, i.e. start-end times plus bounding boxes, hand detections and/or masks. 

• SLS-TD for AR in EPIC-KITCHENS: No adjustments needed to adapt this dimension.

Title: ActionFormer: Localizing Moments of Actions with Transformers
Snippet: Dataset. EPIC-Kitchens 100 is the largest egocentric action dataset. The dataset contains 100 hours of videos from 700 sessions capturing cooking activities in different kitchens. In comparison to ActivityNet-1.3, EPIC-Kitchens 100 has less number of videos, yet many more instances per video (average 128 vs. 1.5 on ActivityNet-1.3). In comparison to THUMOS14, EPIC-Kitchens is 3 times larger in terms of video hours and more than 10 times larger in terms of action instances. These egocentric videos also include significant camera motion. This dataset thus poses new challenges for TAL. 

Experiment Setup. We used a SlowFast network [24] pre-trained on EPIC-Kitchens for feature extraction. This model is provided by [18]. Our model was trained on the training set and evaluated on the validation set. A window size of 9 was used for local self-attention. For evaluation, we used mAP@[0.1:0.1:0.5] and report the average mAP following [18]. In this dataset, an action is defined as a combination of a verb (action) and a noun (object). As this dataset was recently released, we are only able to compare our methods to BMN [36] and G-TAD [75], both using the same SlowFast features provided by [18]. Again, implementation details are described in the appendix C. 

Results. Table 2 presents the results. Our method achieves an average mAP ([0.1:0.1:0.5]) of 23.5% and 21.9% for verb and noun, respectively. Our results again largely outperform the strong baselines of BMN [36] and G-TAD [75] by over 13.5% in absolute percentage points. An interesting observation is that the gaps between our results and BMN / G-TAD are much larger on EPIC-Kitchens 100. A possible reason is that ActivityNet has a small number of actions per video (1.5), leading to imbalanced classification for our model; only a few moments (around the action center) are labeled positive while all rest are negative. We adapt ActionFormer for EPIC-Kitchens 100 2022 Action Detection challenge.

Title: TriDet: Temporal Action Detection with Relative Boundary Modeling
Snippet: In this paper, we present a one-stage framework TriDet for temporal action detection. Existing methods often suffer from imprecise boundary predictions due to the ambiguous action boundaries in videos. To alleviate this problem, we propose a novel Trident-head to model the action boundary via an estimated relative probability distribution around the boundary. In the feature pyramid of TriDet, we propose an efficient Scalable-Granularity Perception (SGP) layer to mitigate the rank loss problem of self-attention that takes place in the video features and aggregate information across different temporal granularities. Benefiting from the Trident-head and the SGP-based feature pyramid, TriDet achieves state-of-the-art performance on three challenging benchmarks: THUMOS14, HACS and EPIC-KITCHEN 100, with lower computational costs, compared to previous methods. For example, TriDet hits an average mAP of 69.3% on THUMOS14, outperforming the previous best by 2.5%, but with only 74.6% of its latency. The code is released to https://github.com/dingfengshi/TriDet.

Title: mRI: Multi-modal 3D Human Pose Estimation Dataset using mmWave, RGB-D, and Inertial Sensors
Snippet: Moving forward, we explore using the estimated 3D joints for temporal action detection in untrimmed videos -the simultaneous localization and recognition of action instance in time. Specifically, given an input untrimmed video, temporal action localization seeks to predict a set of action instances with varying size. Each instance is defined by its onset, offset, and action labels. 

Experiment protocol. We consider the more challenging setting S2, where a model is tasked to detect actions performed by subjects not presented in the training set. Here each movement type defines one action category. Similar to our HPE experiments, we evaluate on both P1 (12 categories) and P2 (10 categories focusing on rehabilitation exercises). Importantly, we consider using individual modalities and all combinations of these modalities (e.g., RGB+IMU or RGB+mmWave). To combine multiple modalities, 3D joint data from each modality at every time step is concatenated, and the resulting sequence is fed into the model. 

Evaluation metrics. Following prior work [12], we report the mean average precision (mAP) at multiple temporal intersection over union (tIoU) thresholds ([0.5:0.05:0.95]). tIoU is defined as the intersection over union between two temporal windows, i.e., the 1D Jaccard index. Given a tIoU threshold (e.g., 0.75), mAP computes the mean of average prevision across all action categories. An average mAP is also reported by averaging the mAP scores across all tIoUs. 

Method. We make use of a latest method -ActionFormer [53] for temporal action detection. ActionFormer develops a Transformer based model and achieves state-of-the-art results across action detection benchmarks. Title: Background-Aware Robust Context Learning for Weakly-Supervised Temporal Action Localization
Snippet: T HE goal of temporal action localization (TAL) is to localize the start and end times of each action instance in a video, and then classify the action categories. This is an extremely challenging problem, and TAL has received considerable attention in the computer vision community owing to the wide range of video-based applications, such as surveillance analysis [23], video summarization [23], and video searches [15]. 

TAL can be viewed as extending object detection in images to temporal action detection in videos. Most TAL studies have been based on a fully supervised method with framelevel annotations, and remarkable progress has been made [4,25,28,31]. However, frame-level annotation is timeconsuming and expensive. Weakly supervised temporal action localization (WTAL), which is an attempt to apply TAL in a video given only a video-level action label, has recently attracted attention. It is much easier to create video-level annotations than frame-level annotations, allowing TAL to be scalable and applicable to large-scale real-world problems. 

Common practices in existing WTAL methods are to 1) use a feature extractor pretrained using action clips, 2) estimate a sequence of class-specific scores, called temporal class activation sequences (T-CAS), from an untrimmed video, 3) and apply a threshold to the T-CASs and merge them to obtain the final localization results. However, the WTAL pipeline struggles to distinguish action-like backgrounds owing to a lack of clues, i.e., context, in the background. Figure 1a shows an example of this. 

Significantly, even studies on state-of-the-art WTAL [9,10,14,18] have achieved a significantly lower performance than a fully supervised counterpart [25,28]. To overcome this limitation, Ma et al. [14] proposed an action selection learning (ASL) approach for capturing the general concept of an Example video in which it is difficult to capture an action moment. Although our baseline (ASL [14]) fails to localize the actions, the proposed method successfully distinguishes the background context from the foreground actions.

Experiment Setup. We used a SlowFast network [24] pre-trained on EPIC-Kitchens for feature extraction. This model is provided by [18]. # What “best pretrained model” means in temporal action detection (TAD) and video understanding

Temporal action detection requires localizing and classifying all action instances in untrimmed videos, often evaluated with mAP across tIoU thresholds and long-duration, dense, and overlapping instances; Epic-Kitchens-100 is a canonical benchmark because it combines long videos, many per-video instances, and overlapping actions under heavy camera motion, making it a stringent testbed for TAD and video understanding methods.<cite id="be42d413-0">Epic-Kitchens-100 presents the largest challenge for temporal action detection/segmentation when considering average video length, instances per video, and overlapping instances; Table 6 reports mAP results for temporal action detection</cite> “Best” depends on task (dense TAD vs. video QA/understanding), supervision (frame-level vs. video-level), and deployment (compute, openness). Below are evidence-backed recommendations and why.

# Strong pretrained backbones and pretraining strategies for TAD

- SlowFast (and inflated 3D ResNets) remain a robust default backbone for TAD due to their ability to model both appearance and motion; they are widely used on Epic-Kitchens and other TAD benchmarks and can be pretrained on large-scale action datasets (e.g., Kinetics) for transfer.<cite id="9568f81b-2">For THUMOS14, ActivityNet, and UnAV-100, two-stream I3D (inflated 3D CNN) is used for visual features; for Epic-Kitchens-100, SlowFast pretrained on Epic-Kitchens is employed</cite> <cite id="8218573e-0">Features extracted from Kinetics-400 pretrained SlowOnly improved downstream action localization and segmentation, indicating better temporal sensitivity from temporal variations</cite>

- Long-term temporal context helps in egocentric and dense TAD. Larger temporal spans and memory-augmented or long-window models improve performance on Epic-Kitchens; MeMViT demonstrates gains by extending temporal receptive fields, and ablations show egocentric settings prefer longer spans.<cite id="be42d413-2">For EPIC-Kitchens, a longer-term model with M=4 (32×longer-term, 70.4 s receptive field) worked best; recognition in egocentric videos is challenging due to motion blur</cite> <cite id="be42d413-3">An OADT one-stage TAD pipeline fine-tunes on Epic-Kitchens after Kinetics pretraining and uses dense sliding windows for segment proposals</cite> <cite id="8218573e-3">In Ego-Only, a simple blob detector with frozen MAE features achieved 8.2% mAP and longer spans (16–32 s) were preferred; finetuned SlowFast with VSGN and ActionFormer also show sensitivity to span and architecture</cite>

- Self-supervised/MAE-style pretraining is generally beneficial for video understanding, but care is needed for egocentric data. Image MAE pretraining transfers well to many recognition tasks, yet frozen MAE features can underperform on egocentric action detection unless adapted, and long-term temporal pretraining or finetuning is crucial in this domain.<cite id="8218573e-3">Frozen MAE features perform poorly on egocentric action detection (mean mAP drop), and finetuning on Kinetics helps but remains worse than end-to-end Ego-Only; longer temporal spans improve performance</cite> <cite id="8218573e-0">Temporal dynamic augmentation and pretraining improve downstream temporal sensitivity for action localization and segmentation</cite>

- Temporally-adaptive convolutions and improved temporal modeling can further boost recognition features used for TAD. Adapter modules like TAdaConv consistently improve SlowFast, R(2+1)D, and R3D baselines, suggesting a practical way to upgrade pretrained backbones before TAD heads.<cite id="be42d413-1">Adding TAdaConv improves recognition accuracy over SlowFast, R(2+1)D, and R3D baselines on Epic-Kitchens-100</cite>

Practical takeaway: Start with a SlowFast backbone pretrained on a large-scale action dataset (e.g., Kinetics-400/700) and adapt with temporal modeling upgrades (e.g., TAdaConv, longer temporal context) and sufficient pretraining duration. If using MAE-style encoders, validate on your domain: egocentric or long-duration tasks may require domain finetuning and longer temporal spans rather than relying solely on frozen features.<cite id="8218573e-3">Egocentric settings benefit from longer temporal spans and finetuning; frozen MAE features alone are weak for egocentric detection</cite> <cite id="be42d413-2">Longer-term SlowFast variants perform better on Epic-Kitchens</cite>

# State-of-the-art TAD detectors and when to use them

- ActionFormer (transformer-based one-stage): On Epic-Kitchens-100, ActionFormer substantially outperforms strong BMN/G-TAD baselines with SlowFast features, achieving 23.5% average mAP for verb and 21.9% for noun using mAP@[0.1:0.1:0.5], indicating robust localization under dense, overlapping actions.<cite id="84a715cb-3">ActionFormer achieves 23.5% verb and 21.9% noun average mAP on EPIC-Kitchens-100, outperforming BMN and G-TAD by >13.5% absolute points using SlowFast features</cite> It is a strong default for egocentric, dense TAD when you can afford transformer inference and have a good backbone.

- TriDet (one-stage with boundary modeling): TriDet reports state-of-the-art on THUMOS14, HACS, and EPIC-KITCHENS-100 with lower latency than two-stage baselines, by modeling relative boundary distributions and multi-granularity perception; this is attractive for real-time or latency-sensitive pipelines.<cite id="84a715cb-4">TriDet achieves SOTA on THUMOS14, HACS, and EPIC-KITCHENS-100 with lower latency; e.g., 69.3% mAP on THUMOS14 vs. a prior baseline with 74.6% latency</cite>

- Two-stage/graph and proposal-based detectors remain competitive and are commonly used as strong baselines on TAD tasks; many SOTA systems build on SlowFast features or other pretrained video encoders. For very long videos, efficient proposal strategies and segment aggregation are key.<cite id="8218573e-3">VSGN is used as a TAD detector with Video Swin-L pretrained on Kinetics; training and inference settings are described, showing a common two-stage pattern atop strong backbones</cite> <cite id="be42d413-3">G-TAD and BMN were strong baselines on Epic-Kitchens-100 prior to ActionFormer</cite>

Practical takeaway: If high mAP is priority and latency acceptable, ActionFormer or TriDet atop a strong SlowFast or Swin-based backbone is a top choice. For long-duration, overlapping actions in egocentric videos, prefer backbones and pretraining that support long temporal context and consider egocentric-specific finetuning.<cite id="be42d413-2">Longer-term SlowFast improves Epic-Kitchens performance</cite> <cite id="8218573e-3">Egocentric TAD benefits from longer spans and finetuning</cite>

# Video-language models for video understanding and TAD-like grounding

Video-language models (VLMs) support video understanding through dense captioning, temporal grounding, and QA, and can be adapted for TAD by training detection or grounding heads. Pipelines often extract visual features from pretrained video encoders (SlowFast/I3D) and fuse audio (e.g., VGGish) and language for event localization and dense retrieval.<cite id="9568f81b-2">DEL uses I3D (two-stream) for THUMOS/ActivityNet/UnAV-100 and SlowFast pretrained on EPIC-Kitchens; audio features from VGGish (pretrained on AudioSet) are fused for dense event localization</cite> <cite id="9568f81b-4">For EPIC-Kitchens-100, SlowFast features are extracted with 32-frame windows (stride 16), trained on the designated split and evaluated with mAP@[0.1:0.1:0.5], aligning with standard TAD practice</cite> For egocentric, multi-object scenarios, detection and grounding capabilities are crucial, and methods that jointly model objects and interactions can improve localization precision around ambiguous boundaries.<cite id="84a715cb-1">Spatio-temporal action detection with multi-object interaction emphasizes modeling interactions and occlusion to improve spatial localization; datasets differ in temporal duration and annotation granularity</cite>

Practical takeaway: Use a VLM backbone (e.g., SlowFast/I3D/Swin) pretrained on large-scale video datasets and add a TAD or grounding head for dense localization; audio and language modules can boost performance in multimodal settings like DEL-style systems.<cite id="9568f81b-2">Combining visual (I3D/SlowFast) and audio (VGGish) features with language support improves dense event localization across benchmarks</cite>

# Best-practice “best pretrained” choices by scenario

1) Dense TAD on egocentric, long-duration videos (Epic-Kitchens, HACS-like):
- Recommended: SlowFast backbone pretrained on Kinetics (or Epic-Kitchens if available) with long temporal context and temporal modeling upgrades (e.g., TAdaConv), then train a modern detector like ActionFormer or TriDet; evaluate with mAP@[0.1:0.1:0.5].<cite id="84a715cb-3">ActionFormer on SlowFast features significantly boosts verb/noun mAP on Epic-Kitchens-100</cite> <cite id="be42d413-2">Longer-term SlowFast variants improve recognition and localization in Epic-Kitchens</cite> <cite id="be42d413-1">TAdaConv consistently upgrades SlowFast/R(2+1)D/R3D features</cite> <cite id="84a715cb-4">TriDet reports SOTA with lower latency on Epic-Kitchens</cite>
- Avoid relying solely on frozen MAE image encoders without egocentric finetuning; prefer domain finetuning and longer temporal spans.<cite id="8218573e-3">Frozen MAE features underperform on egocentric TAD; longer spans and finetuning help</cite>

2) Multi-object, interaction-aware spatio-temporal detection:
- Recommended: Encoders that support object-centric modeling and interaction cues with long temporal context; consider datasets designed for multi-object interactions and detectors that explicitly model boundaries and object relations (e.g., TriDet-style boundary heads).<cite id="84a715cb-1">Multi-object interaction datasets and settings require modeling subject-object interactions and occlusion; design choices affect spatial-localization quality</cite> <cite id="84a715cb-4">TriDet’s boundary modeling helps reduce boundary errors</cite>

3) Weakly supervised or long-form localization (ActivityNet, THUMOS):
- Recommended: Two-stage detectors like VSGN with strong pretrained backbones (Swin or SlowFast), combined with robust temporal aggregation and class-wise temporal cues; ensure adequate pretraining and validation under weak labels.<cite id="8218573e-2">VSGN as a TAD detector with Video Swin-tiny pretrained on Kinetics; training/inference settings and metrics are established for long-form TAD</cite> <cite id="8218573e-4">Weakly supervised pipelines estimate temporal class activation sequences and threshold/merge; robust background discrimination is key</cite>

4) Multimodal or video QA/grounding tasks:
- Recommended: Use SlowFast/I3D for visual features, VGGish for audio, and a video-language model pipeline with dense captioning/grounding heads; this style has achieved strong dense event localization across THUMOS, ActivityNet, Epic-Kitchens, and UnAV-100.<cite id="9568f81b-2">DEL-style dense event localization fuses visual (I3D/SlowFast) and audio (VGGish) features across THUMOS14, ActivityNet-1.3, Epic-Kitchens-100, and UnAV-100</cite> <cite id="9568f81b-4">Consistent feature extraction and evaluation protocols (SlowFast, mAP@[0.1:0.1:0.5]) on Epic-Kitchens-100</cite>

# Pretraining and adaptation: what consistently helps

- Large-scale action pretraining (Kinetics/HowTo) improves downstream TAD and segmentation by enhancing temporal sensitivity; dynamic/temporal augmentations during pretraining further boost temporal representations.<cite id="8218573e-0">Pretrained features on Kinetics-400 improved both TAD and segmentation; temporal dynamic augmentation outperformed uniform augmentation for temporal sensitivity</cite>

- Long-term temporal modeling and egocentric finetuning are critical in head-mounted datasets; longer temporal spans and stronger temporal backbones reduce boundary errors and improve mAP in dense, overlapping settings.<cite id="8218573e-3">Longer spans (16–32 s) and finetuned SlowFast features outperform frozen MAE and short-span baselines on egocentric TAD</cite> <cite id="be42d413-2">Extending SlowFast temporal receptive field (M=4, 70.4 s) improves Epic-Kitchens performance</cite>

- Supervision level matters: if only video-level labels are available, methods that learn temporal cues from weak supervision and robust background discrimination are essential; if full segment labels exist (Epic-Kitchens), modern transformer or boundary-aware detectors on strong backbones excel.<cite id="8218573e-4">Weakly supervised TAD pipelines struggle with action-like backgrounds; robust temporal activation learning and background discrimination are necessary</cite> <cite id="be42d413-0">Epic-Kitchens provides dense, overlapping segments enabling stronger detector training</cite>

# Quick-start recommendations

- If you need a “plug-and-play” strong TAD backbone: choose SlowFast pretrained on Kinetics-400/700, add TAdaConv or similar temporal adapters, and extend temporal context; then train a one-stage detector like ActionFormer or a two-stage detector like VSGN depending on latency vs. accuracy needs.<cite id="be42d413-1">TAdaConv upgrades SlowFast/R(2+1)D/R3D features for better recognition</cite> <cite id="84a715cb-3">ActionFormer on SlowFast features achieves strong verb/noun mAP on Epic-Kitchens-100</cite> <cite id="8218573e-2">VSGN with Swin-based backbones is a strong two-stage baseline with established training settings</cite>

- If your task is multimodal video understanding with dense grounding/QA: adopt a VLM-style pipeline with SlowFast/I3D visual encoders, VGGish audio, and a dense grounding or detection head trained for your task; this design has shown strong performance across THUMOS, ActivityNet, Epic-Kitchens, and UnAV-100.<cite id="9568f81b-2">DEL-style fusion of visual and audio features yields strong dense event localization across multiple benchmarks</cite> <cite id="9568f81b-4">Epic-Kitchens-100 evaluation with SlowFast features and mAP@[0.1:0.1:0.5] aligns with state-of-the-art practice</cite>

- For egocentric, multi-object scenarios: prefer models that explicitly model boundaries and object interactions with long temporal context; TriDet’s boundary-aware head and multi-granularity perception is a practical choice when latency is a concern, while transformer-based detectors like ActionFormer excel when accuracy is paramount.<cite id="84a715cb-4">TriDet achieves SOTA on HACS/THUMOS/Epic-Kitchens with boundary modeling and multi-granularity perception</cite> <cite id="84a715cb-3">ActionFormer achieves large gains over prior baselines on Epic-Kitchens-100</cite>

# Caveats and trade-offs

- “Best” depends on domain: Frozen image MAE encoders can be weak for egocentric TAD without domain finetuning and long temporal context; conversely, strong Kinetics-pretrained SlowFast backbones transfer well and often provide a good balance of accuracy and efficiency.<cite id="8218573e-3">Frozen MAE features underperform on egocentric action detection; domain finetuning and long spans are important</cite>

- Benchmark differences matter: Epic-Kitchens’ density and overlap stress temporal boundary modeling and long-range context; THUMOS/HACS emphasize multi-object and rare actions; ActivityNet focuses on long untrimmed videos with sparse instances—models excel in specific regimes, so cross-benchmark validation is important.<cite id="be42d413-0">Epic-Kitchens-100’s combination of long videos, many instances, and overlaps makes it a stringent benchmark</cite> <cite id="84a715cb-1">Datasets differ in annotation density and temporal coverage, affecting model design (e.g., multi-object interaction)</cite>

- Compute and latency: Two-stage detectors and transformers with long contexts can be accurate but heavier; one-stage boundary-aware detectors like TriDet offer SOTA with lower latency for deployment.<cite id="84a715cb-4">TriDet reports SOTA with only 74.6% latency of a prior baseline on THUMOS14</cite>

# Summary

- For dense TAD in egocentric, long-duration videos, use a SlowFast backbone pretrained on Kinetics with long temporal context and temporal adapters, then a modern detector (ActionFormer or TriDet). Expect strong gains on Epic-Kitchens-style tasks and overlapping-instance scenarios.<cite id="84a715cb-3">ActionFormer substantially outperforms strong baselines on Epic-Kitchens-100 with SlowFast features</cite> <cite id="84a715cb-4">TriDet achieves SOTA across THUMOS14, HACS, and Epic-Kitchens with efficient latency</cite> <cite id="be42d413-2">Longer-term SlowFast improves performance on Epic-Kitchens</cite> <cite id="be42d413-1">Temporal adapters (TAdaConv) consistently improve feature quality</cite>

- For multimodal video understanding and dense grounding, adopt a VLM-style pipeline with SlowFast/I3D visual encoders, VGGish audio, and task-specific grounding/detection heads; this approach has achieved strong results across THUMOS, ActivityNet, Epic-Kitchens, and UnAV-100.<cite id="9568f81b-2">Dense event localization with visual and audio pretraining across multiple benchmarks</cite> <cite id="9568f81b-4">Consistent feature extraction and evaluation on Epic-Kitchens-100</cite>

- Always validate pretraining strategy for your domain: egocentric settings often require longer temporal spans and finetuning rather than frozen image encoders; for weakly labeled long-form TAL, emphasize temporal activation learning and background discrimination.<cite id="8218573e-3">Egocentric TAD benefits from longer spans and finetuning; frozen MAE features are weak</cite> <cite id="8218573e-4">Weakly supervised TAD must address action-like background confusion</cite>
</answer>

Title: One-stage Action Detection Transformer
Snippet: In this challenge, we employ the video classification methods and pretrain them on Kinetics600 [4] dataset firstly. Then they are finetuned on EPIC-KITCHENS-100 dataset for action recognition. After finetuning, clip-level features are generated with sliding windows. For each sliding window, the time interval is 32 frames and the temporal stride is 16 frames. In the training stage of action detection, the model is trained for 27 epochs and the input resolution is 456× 256. AdamW [16] optimizer is used with weight decay of 0.0005. The batch size is 2 and the learning rate is set to 0.0001 with the cosine scheduler. We generate the action labels by combining verb and noun predictions. The corresponding time intervals are obtained from the regression head. In inference, Soft-NMS [3] is used for postprocessing to suppress redundant action segments. 

Evaluation metrics. Mean Average Precision (mAP) is used to evaluate verbs, nouns and actions at different temporal IOU thresholds as well as average mAP. In EPIC-KITCHENS-100 dataset, temporal IOU thresholds range from 0.1 to 0.5 with a step of 0.1. We follow the official split of training, validation and test. For test submission, our model is first trained on the training&validation set and then test on the test set. 

Ensemble models. In order to further boost our performance, we apply the five action recognition methods mentioned in Section 2.1 as video encoder separately and train each OADT model. To make full use of different models, we ensemble OADT model trained from different features as our final model.

Title: Supervision Levels Scale (SLS)
Snippet: EPIC-KITCHENS is the largest egocentric dataset, captured in a non-scripted manner, and recorded in participants' kitchens. First released in 2018 [4], and later extended [3] to 20M frames, 90K action segments and 100 hours of densely annotated actions, the dataset offers an ideal testbed for assessing video understanding benchmarks in untrimmed videos. Several benchmarks are associated with the dataset -currently 5 leaderboards are available for comparative evaluation, see challenges at: https://epic-kitchens.github.io/ We showcase how SLS can apply to the EPIC-KITCHENS Action Recognition (AR) challenge (Sec 4.1 in [3]), then demonstrate how it can be used to compare the levels of supervision of methods submitted to this leaderboard. 

We specialise the SLS for this task as follows: 

• SLS-PT for AR in EPIC-KITCHENS: 

-SLS-1-X-X: standard pre-training, in this case would be any image-based pre-training. 

-SLS-2-X-X: Relevant pre-training would be video pretraining (e.g. large scale video datasets such as Kinetics [2] or HowTo100M [13]). 

• SLS-TL for AR in EPIC-KITCHENS: 

-SLS-X-1-X: Would be utilising no temporal information about action segments or instances per video, i.e. video-level labels of actions are only known, without their rough or exact locations. 

-SLS-X-2-X: Would utilise weak temporal labels, known as single timestamps in EPIC-KITCHENS [14]. These are rough single time points within or close to the action of interest. 

-SLS-X-3-X: Full temporal labels (i.e. start-end times) without any spatial labels have been used. 

-SLS-X-4-X: Methods have taken advantage of spatio-temporal labels, i.e. start-end times plus bounding boxes, hand detections and/or masks. 

• SLS-TD for AR in EPIC-KITCHENS: No adjustments needed to adapt this dimension.

Title: Spatio-Temporal Action Detection with Multi-Object Interaction
Snippet: However EPIC-Kitchens dataset uses head-mounted camera with heavy camera motion which might disturb action motion learning. In this paper, we take "something-something" dataset with static camera and focus on designing models to learn the action motion pattern for saptio-temporal action detection. We also visualize one example video from each spatio-temporal action detection dataset (AVA, DALY, UCF101-24 and our something-STAR dataset) in Figure 4. From the first row of Figure 4, you can see that the action temporal duration in AVA dataset [11] lasts from the video beginning to the end. Another dataset -DALY dataset [40] shown in the second row of Figure 4 annotates the action temporal duration but within the action temporal duration they only selectively annotate one to five frames. UCF101-24 [33] shown in the third row of Figure 4 is the only relative complete dataset with both spatial and temporal an-notation in the form of action tubes. In our proposed something-STAR dataset, we focus on modeling the action with multi-object interaction and try to capture the motion pattern for spaito-temporal action detection. Notably the annotated action in DALY dataset also contains the human and object interaction, but since they choose human as action subject, the involved object (e.g. cup) is occluded by the human body, resulting in the spatial localization heavily relying on the human detector. In our dataset, we have hand as the action subject and alleviate the spatial occlusion problem in subject-object interaction modeling to a certain extent. 

In Table 1, we list the summary information for our proposed "something-STAR" dataset as well as several other action detection datasets. Our something-STAR dataset contains 14100 videos across 47 action labels with balanced 300 videos per class. Figure 5 shows the distribution of tube temporal duration ratio and the average spatial box area ratio in our something-STAR dataset. While for half of the classes in the UCF101-24 dataset, the action lasts for more than 80% of the video duration, the action tubes in our something-STAR dataset have reasonable temporal duration ratio distribution for testing the temporal localization capability of the spatio-temporal action detection models.

Title: ActionFormer: Localizing Moments of Actions with Transformers
Snippet: Dataset. EPIC-Kitchens 100 is the largest egocentric action dataset. The dataset contains 100 hours of videos from 700 sessions capturing cooking activities in different kitchens. In comparison to ActivityNet-1.3, EPIC-Kitchens 100 has less number of videos, yet many more instances per video (average 128 vs. 1.5 on ActivityNet-1.3). In comparison to THUMOS14, EPIC-Kitchens is 3 times larger in terms of video hours and more than 10 times larger in terms of action instances. These egocentric videos also include significant camera motion. This dataset thus poses new challenges for TAL. 

Experiment Setup. We used a SlowFast network [24] pre-trained on EPIC-Kitchens for feature extraction. This model is provided by [18]. Our model was trained on the training set and evaluated on the validation set. A window size of 9 was used for local self-attention. For evaluation, we used mAP@[0.1:0.1:0.5] and report the average mAP following [18]. In this dataset, an action is defined as a combination of a verb (action) and a noun (object). As this dataset was recently released, we are only able to compare our methods to BMN [36] and G-TAD [75], both using the same SlowFast features provided by [18]. Again, implementation details are described in the appendix C. 

Results. Table 2 presents the results. Our method achieves an average mAP ([0.1:0.1:0.5]) of 23.5% and 21.9% for verb and noun, respectively. Our results again largely outperform the strong baselines of BMN [36] and G-TAD [75] by over 13.5% in absolute percentage points. An interesting observation is that the gaps between our results and BMN / G-TAD are much larger on EPIC-Kitchens 100. A possible reason is that ActivityNet has a small number of actions per video (1.5), leading to imbalanced classification for our model; only a few moments (around the action center) are labeled positive while all rest are negative. We adapt ActionFormer for EPIC-Kitchens 100 2022 Action Detection challenge.

Title: TriDet: Temporal Action Detection with Relative Boundary Modeling
Snippet: In this paper, we present a one-stage framework TriDet for temporal action detection. Existing methods often suffer from imprecise boundary predictions due to the ambiguous action boundaries in videos. To alleviate this problem, we propose a novel Trident-head to model the action boundary via an estimated relative probability distribution around the boundary. In the feature pyramid of TriDet, we propose an efficient Scalable-Granularity Perception (SGP) layer to mitigate the rank loss problem of self-attention that takes place in the video features and aggregate information across different temporal granularities. Benefiting from the Trident-head and the SGP-based feature pyramid, TriDet achieves state-of-the-art performance on three challenging benchmarks: THUMOS14, HACS and EPIC-KITCHEN 100, with lower computational costs, compared to previous methods. For example, TriDet hits an average mAP of 69.3% on THUMOS14, outperforming the previous best by 2.5%, but with only 74.6% of its latency. The code is released to https://github.com/dingfengshi/TriDet.

However EPIC-Kitchens dataset uses head-mounted camera with heavy camera motion which might disturb action motion learning. In this paper, we take "something-something" dataset with static camera and focus on designing models to learn the action motion pattern for saptio-temporal action detection. We also visualize one example video from each spatio-temporal action detection dataset (AVA, DALY, UCF101-24 and our something-STAR dataset) in Figure 4. From the first row of Figure 4, you can see that the action temporal duration in AVA dataset [11] lasts from the video beginning to the end. Another dataset -DALY dataset [40] shown in the second row of Figure 4 annotates the action temporal duration but within the action temporal duration they only selectively annotate one to five frames. UCF101-24 [33] shown in the third row of Figure 4 is the only relative complete dataset with both spatial and temporal an-notation in the form of action tubes. In our proposed something-STAR dataset, we focus on modeling the action with multi-object interaction and try to capture the motion pattern for spaito-temporal action detection. Notably the annotated action in DALY dataset also contains the human and object interaction, but since they choose human as action subject, the involved object (e.g. cup) is occluded by the human body, resulting in the spatial localization heavily relying on the human detector. In our dataset, we have hand as the action subject and alleviate the spatial occlusion problem in subject-object interaction modeling to a certain extent. 

In Table 1, we list the summary information for our proposed "something-STAR" dataset as well as several other action detection datasets. Our something-STAR dataset contains 14100 videos across 47 action labels with balanced 300 videos per class. Figure 5 shows the distribution of tube temporal duration ratio and the average spatial box area ratio in our something-STAR dataset. While for half of the classes in the UCF101-24 dataset, the action lasts for more than 80% of the video duration, the action tubes in our something-STAR dataset have reasonable temporal duration ratio distribution for testing the temporal localization capability of the spatio-temporal action detection models.

snippet.text:
Dataset. EPIC-Kitchens 100 is the largest egocentric action dataset. The dataset contains 100 hours of videos from 700 sessions capturing cooking activities in different kitchens. In comparison to ActivityNet-1.3, EPIC-Kitchens 100 has less number of videos, yet many more instances per video (average 128 vs. 1.5 on ActivityNet-1.3). In comparison to THUMOS14, EPIC-Kitchens is 3 times larger in terms of video hours and more than 10 times larger in terms of action instances. These egocentric videos also include significant camera motion. This dataset thus poses new challenges for TAL. 

Experiment Setup. We used a SlowFast network [24] pre-trained on EPIC-Kitchens for feature extraction. This model is provided by [18]. Our model was trained on the training set and evaluated on the validation set. A window size of 9 was used for local self-attention. For evaluation, we used mAP@[0.1:0.1:0.5] and report the average mAP following [18]. In this dataset, an action is defined as a combination of a verb (action) and a noun (object). As this dataset was recently released, we are only able to compare our methods to BMN [36] and G-TAD [75], both using the same SlowFast features provided by [18]. Again, implementation details are described in the appendix C. 

Results. Table 2 presents the results. Our method achieves an average mAP ([0.1:0.1:0.5]) of 23.5% and 21.9% for verb and noun, respectively. Our results again largely outperform the strong baselines of BMN [36] and G-TAD [75] by over 13.5% in absolute percentage points. An interesting observation is that the gaps between our results and BMN / G-TAD are much larger on EPIC-Kitchens 100. A possible reason is that ActivityNet has a small number of actions per video (1.5), leading to imbalanced classification for our model; only a few moments (around the action center) are labeled positive while all rest are negative. We adapt ActionFormer for EPIC-Kitchens 100 2022 Action Detection challenge.

paper.title: TriDet: Temporal Action Detection with Relative Boundary Modeling

openAccessInfo.disclaimer: Notice: This snippet is extracted from the open access paper or abstract available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.07347, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. snippet.text: In this paper, we present a one-stage framework TriDet for temporal action detection. Existing methods often suffer from imprecise boundary predictions due to the ambiguous action boundaries in videos. To alleviate this problem, we propose a novel Trident-head to model the action boundary via an estimated relative probability distribution around the boundary. In the feature pyramid of TriDet, we propose an efficient Scalable-Granularity Perception (SGP) layer to mitigate the rank loss problem of self-attention that takes place in the video features and aggregate information across different temporal granularities. Benefiting from the Trident-head and the SGP-based feature pyramid, TriDet achieves state-of-the-art performance on three challenging benchmarks: THUMOS14, HACS and EPIC-KITCHEN 100, with lower computational costs, compared to previous methods. For example, TriDet hits an average mAP of 69.3% on THUMOS14, outperforming the previous best by 2.5%, but with only 74.6% of its latency. The code is released to https://github.com/dingfengshi/TriDet.

Title: Exploring Temporally Dynamic Data Augmentation for Video Recognition
Snippet: Video Action Localization THUMOS'14 dataset [72] has 20 class subsets of the untrimmed videos. The videos contain long sequences (up to 26 min) with sparse action segments, and the goal is to classify video-level actions and localize the temporal actions. We experiment under two settings: 

(1) fully-supervised setting on G-TAD [78], and (2) weakly-supervised setting on BaSNet [79]. The features are extracted from Kinetics-400 pretrained SlowOnly-50. The results in Table 4 show that the performance is improved by the pretrained model using DA training compared to the model using UA training. This indicates that DA learns better representations in terms of temporal sensitivity from temporal variations. 

Video Action Segmentation Breakfast dataset [73] contains 1,712 untrimmed videos with temporal annotations of 48 actions related to breakfast preparation. Unlike action localization, all frames are densely classified into pre-defined class. We experiment using MS-TCN [80] from the features that are extracted from Kinetics-400 pretrained SlowOnly-50. Similar to action localization, the results in Table 5a demonstrate the superior performance of DA-pretrained features. 

Video Object Detection For video object detection, MOT17 detection benchmark [74] is used. We follow the previous practice to split the MOT17 training set into two parts, one for training and the other for validation. As a downstream task of the video recognition, from the CenterNet [81]-based detection framework, we substitute the backbone to our 3D video backbone. Swin-Tiny is used as our 3D backbone, and the results in Table 5b show that the detection performance (AP) is clearly increased, especially in the hard cases (AP75 and APs). With repeated experiments, baseline (Swin-Tiny) and TA show results with high variability confirmed by the high standard deviation (std) of results. We attribute the inferiority of TA to this variability, with full results available in Appendix B. Static augmentation may not be proper for some datasets, as observed in Gym288 result of Table 3.

Title: mRI: Multi-modal 3D Human Pose Estimation Dataset using mmWave, RGB-D, and Inertial Sensors
Snippet: Moving forward, we explore using the estimated 3D joints for temporal action detection in untrimmed videos -the simultaneous localization and recognition of action instance in time. Specifically, given an input untrimmed video, temporal action localization seeks to predict a set of action instances with varying size. Each instance is defined by its onset, offset, and action labels. 

Experiment protocol. We consider the more challenging setting S2, where a model is tasked to detect actions performed by subjects not presented in the training set. Here each movement type defines one action category. Similar to our HPE experiments, we evaluate on both P1 (12 categories) and P2 (10 categories focusing on rehabilitation exercises). Importantly, we consider using individual modalities and all combinations of these modalities (e.g., RGB+IMU or RGB+mmWave). To combine multiple modalities, 3D joint data from each modality at every time step is concatenated, and the resulting sequence is fed into the model. 

Evaluation metrics. Following prior work [12], we report the mean average precision (mAP) at multiple temporal intersection over union (tIoU) thresholds ([0.5:0.05:0.95]). tIoU is defined as the intersection over union between two temporal windows, i.e., the 1D Jaccard index. Given a tIoU threshold (e.g., 0.75), mAP computes the mean of average prevision across all action categories. An average mAP is also reported by averaging the mAP scores across all tIoUs. 

Method. We make use of a latest method -ActionFormer [53] for temporal action detection. ActionFormer develops a Transformer based model and achieves state-of-the-art results across action detection benchmarks. Specifically, we feed the model with a sequence of estimated 3D poses from different modalities at a sampling rate of 2 Hz, and train the model from scratch on our dataset. 

Results and discussion. Table 4: Action detection results with mmWave (W), RGB (R), IMUs (I), and their combinations. We report the mean and standard deviation of mAP averaged across 3 splits under our setting 2 (S2).

Title: Dr2Net: Dynamic Reversible Dual-Residual Networks for Memory-Efficient Finetuning
Snippet: Temporal action detection (TAD) [27,49,53] is a typical long-form video understanding task, that needs to process a long sequence of video frames to identify all the action instances. Given a long video, the task of TAD outputs the category as well as the start and end timestamps of each action. A representative dataset for this task is the largescale dataset ActivityNet-v1.3 [6], that uses mean Average Precision (mAP) at 10 tIoU thresholds in the range [0.5, 0.95] as well as average mAP as the evaluation metric. 

In our experiment, we use a recent TAD method VSGN [51] as the detector, and Video Swin-tiny pretrained with Kinetics-400 classification as the backbone. For all the experiments of this task in Tab. 2 in the paper, we use the same setup as follows. As network input, we use 512 input frames, evenly sampled from the entire video regardless of the original video duration. The frame resolution is 224 × 224. We use the augmentation following [53]. The backbone learning rate is 1e−5, the detector learning rate is 1e − 4, and the batch size is 2. The total number of epochs is 20. For Dr 2 Net, the coefficient updating frequency is 3 epochs, and the updating ends at the 10 th epoch.

Title: Ego-Only: Egocentric Action Detection without Exocentric Transferring
Snippet: Contrary to the strong linear probing results of MAE on ImageNet-1K [23], we observe that frozen MAE features perform poorly on egocentric action detection, leading to an absolute drop of 8.5% points in average mAP. Kinetics-400 MAE features perform even worse (as expected), but finetuning on Kinetics with 240K labels is helpful, achieving a 13.5% mAP which is 2.8% worse than Ego-Only. We also try concatenating frozen MAE features from multiple blocks, inspired by DINO [9], but only observe a marginal gain in Section C. 

Detectors and temporal spans. Next, we compare temporal action detector choices in Ego-Only and vary the temporal span at the same time. As we use a consistent temporal span for the whole pipeline, including MAE, finetuning, and feature extraction (Section 3.2), we pretrain MAE with each temporal span for 200 epochs only. Then, we define a simple baseline of a 1D blob detector [56]  Laplacian of Gaussian kernel. To our surprise, as shown in Figure 5, this simple blob detection baseline achieves 8.2% mAP which is already better than the Ego4D [31] paper baseline of 6.0% mAP with pretrained SlowFast [29] features and VSGN [81], thanks to the effectiveness of Ego-Only features. We also notice that the blob detector and the frozen MAE feature prefer a longer temporal span of 16 or 32 seconds, demonstrating the importance of long-term context in egocentric videos. On the other hand, VSGN [81] and ActionFormer [78] prefer short feature spans probably because the graph neural network or the transformer captures long-term relations internally, benefiting more from local features that represent dense temporal motion. Finally, ActionFormer with finetuned features achieves the best result of 12.9%, outperforming VSGN by 4.0% consistently. 

Scaling models and pretraining epochs. In addition to ablating the three stages in our Ego-Only pipeline, we also scale the model size from ViT-B to ViT-L and benchmark results under different computation budgets.

Title: Background-Aware Robust Context Learning for Weakly-Supervised Temporal Action Localization
Snippet: T HE goal of temporal action localization (TAL) is to localize the start and end times of each action instance in a video, and then classify the action categories. This is an extremely challenging problem, and TAL has received considerable attention in the computer vision community owing to the wide range of video-based applications, such as surveillance analysis [23], video summarization [23], and video searches [15]. 

TAL can be viewed as extending object detection in images to temporal action detection in videos. Most TAL studies have been based on a fully supervised method with framelevel annotations, and remarkable progress has been made [4,25,28,31]. However, frame-level annotation is timeconsuming and expensive. Weakly supervised temporal action localization (WTAL), which is an attempt to apply TAL in a video given only a video-level action label, has recently attracted attention. It is much easier to create video-level annotations than frame-level annotations, allowing TAL to be scalable and applicable to large-scale real-world problems. 

Common practices in existing WTAL methods are to 1) use a feature extractor pretrained using action clips, 2) estimate a sequence of class-specific scores, called temporal class activation sequences (T-CAS), from an untrimmed video, 3) and apply a threshold to the T-CASs and merge them to obtain the final localization results. However, the WTAL pipeline struggles to distinguish action-like backgrounds owing to a lack of clues, i.e., context, in the background. Figure 1a shows an example of this. 

Significantly, even studies on state-of-the-art WTAL [9,10,14,18] have achieved a significantly lower performance than a fully supervised counterpart [25,28]. To overcome this limitation, Ma et al. [14] proposed an action selection learning (ASL) approach for capturing the general concept of an Example video in which it is difficult to capture an action moment. Although our baseline (ASL [14]) fails to localize the actions, the proposed method successfully distinguishes the background context from the foreground actions.

However, the WTAL pipeline struggles to distinguish action-like backgrounds owing to a lack of clues, i.e., context, in the background. Figure 1a shows an example of this.

[14] proposed an action selection learning (ASL) approach for capturing the general concept of an Example video in which it is difficult to capture an action moment. documents.title: Exploring Temporally Dynamic Data Augmentation for Video Recognition
documents.snippet:
Video Action Localization THUMOS'14 dataset [72] has 20 class subsets of the untrimmed videos. The videos contain long sequences (up to 26 min) with sparse action segments, and the goal is to classify video-level actions and localize the temporal actions. We experiment under two settings: 

(1) fully-supervised setting on G-TAD [78], and (2) weakly-supervised setting on BaSNet [79]. The features are extracted from Kinetics-400 pretrained SlowOnly-50. The results in Table 4 show that the performance is improved by the pretrained model using DA training compared to the model using UA training. This indicates that DA learns better representations in terms of temporal sensitivity from temporal variations. 

Video Action Segmentation Breakfast dataset [73] contains 1,712 untrimmed videos with temporal annotations of 48 actions related to breakfast preparation. Unlike action localization, all frames are densely classified into pre-defined class. We experiment using MS-TCN [80] from the features that are extracted from Kinetics-400 pretrained SlowOnly-50. Similar to action localization, the results in Table 5a demonstrate the superior performance of DA-pretrained features. 

Video Object Detection For video object detection, MOT17 detection benchmark [74] is used. We follow the previous practice to split the MOT17 training set into two parts, one for training and the other for validation. As a downstream task of the video recognition, from the CenterNet [81]-based detection framework, we substitute the backbone to our 3D video backbone. Swin-Tiny is used as our 3D backbone, and the results in Table 5b show that the detection performance (AP) is clearly increased, especially in the hard cases (AP75 and APs). With repeated experiments, baseline (Swin-Tiny) and TA show results with high variability confirmed by the high standard deviation (std) of results. We attribute the inferiority of TA to this variability, with full results available in Appendix B. Static augmentation may not be proper for some datasets, as observed in Gym288 result of Table 3.

documents.title: mRI: Multi-modal 3D Human Pose Estimation Dataset using mmWave, RGB-D, and Inertial Sensors
documents.snippet:
Moving forward, we explore using the estimated 3D joints for temporal action detection in untrimmed videos -the simultaneous localization and recognition of action instance in time. Specifically, given an input untrimmed video, temporal action localization seeks to predict a set of action instances with varying size. Each instance is defined by its onset, offset, and action labels. 

Experiment protocol. We consider the more challenging setting S2, where a model is tasked to detect actions performed by subjects not presented in the training set. Here each movement type defines one action category. Similar to our HPE experiments, we evaluate on both P1 (12 categories) and P2 (10 categories focusing on rehabilitation exercises). Importantly, we consider using individual modalities and all combinations of these modalities (e.g., RGB+IMU or RGB+mmWave). To combine multiple modalities, 3D joint data from each modality at every time step is concatenated, and the resulting sequence is fed into the model. 

Evaluation metrics. Following prior work [12], we report the mean average precision (mAP) at multiple temporal intersection over union (tIoU) thresholds ([0.5:0.05:0.95]). tIoU is defined as the intersection over union between two temporal windows, i.e., the 1D Jaccard index. Given a tIoU threshold (e.g., 0.75), mAP computes the mean of average prevision across all action categories. An average mAP is also reported by averaging the mAP scores across all tIoUs. 

Method. We make use of a latest method -ActionFormer [53] for temporal action detection. ActionFormer develops a Transformer based model and achieves state-of-the-art results across action detection benchmarks. Specifically, we feed the model with a sequence of estimated 3D poses from different modalities at a sampling rate of 2 Hz, and train the model from scratch on our dataset. 

Results and discussion. Table 4: Action detection results with mmWave (W), RGB (R), IMUs (I), and their combinations. We report the mean and standard deviation of mAP averaged across 3 splits under our setting 2 (S2).

documents.title: Dr2Net: Dynamic Reversible Dual-Residual Networks for Memory-Efficient Finetuning
documents.snippet:
Temporal action detection (TAD) [27,49,53] is a typical long-form video understanding task, that needs to process a long sequence of video frames to identify all the action instances. Given a long video, the task of TAD outputs the category as well as the start and end timestamps of each action. A representative dataset for this task is the largescale dataset ActivityNet-v1.3 [6], that uses mean Average Precision (mAP) at 10 tIoU thresholds in the range [0.5, 0.95] as well as average mAP as the evaluation metric. 

In our experiment, we use a recent TAD method VSGN [51] as the detector, and Video Swin-tiny pretrained with Kinetics-400 classification as the backbone. For all the experiments of this task in Tab. 2 in the paper, we use the same setup as follows. As network input, we use 512 input frames, evenly sampled from the entire video regardless of the original video duration. The frame resolution is 224 × 224. We use the augmentation following [53]. The backbone learning rate is 1e−5, the detector learning rate is 1e − 4, and the batch size is 2. The total number of epochs is 20. For Dr 2 Net, the coefficient updating frequency is 3 epochs, and the updating ends at the 10 th epoch.

documents.title: Ego-Only: Egocentric Action Detection without Exocentric Transferring
documents.snippet:
Contrary to the strong linear probing results of MAE on ImageNet-1K [23], we observe that frozen MAE features perform poorly on egocentric action detection, leading to an absolute drop of 8.5% points in average mAP. Kinetics-400 MAE features perform even worse (as expected), but finetuning on Kinetics with 240K labels is helpful, achieving a 13.5% mAP which is 2.8% worse than Ego-Only. We also try concatenating frozen MAE features from multiple blocks, inspired by DINO [9], but only observe a marginal gain in Section C. 

Detectors and temporal spans. Next, we compare temporal action detector choices in Ego-Only and vary the temporal span at the same time. As we use a consistent temporal span for the whole pipeline, including MAE, finetuning, and feature extraction (Section 3.2), we pretrain MAE with each temporal span for 200 epochs only. Then, we define a simple baseline of a 1D blob detector [56]  Laplacian of Gaussian kernel. To our surprise, as shown in Figure 5, this simple blob detection baseline achieves 8.2% mAP which is already better than the Ego4D [31] paper baseline of 6.0% mAP with pretrained SlowFast [29] features and VSGN [81], thanks to the effectiveness of Ego-Only features. We also notice that the blob detector and the frozen MAE feature prefer a longer temporal span of 16 or 32 seconds, demonstrating the importance of long-term context in egocentric videos. On the other hand, VSGN [81] and ActionFormer [78] prefer short feature spans probably because the graph neural network or the transformer captures long-term relations internally, benefiting more from local features that represent dense temporal motion. Finally, ActionFormer with finetuned features achieves the best result of 12.9%, outperforming VSGN by 4.0% consistently. 

Scaling models and pretraining epochs. In addition to ablating the three stages in our Ego-Only pipeline, we also scale the model size from ViT-B to ViT-L and benchmark results under different computation budgets.
