Title: ActionFormer: Localizing Moments of Actions with Transformers
Snippet: Dataset. EPIC-Kitchens 100 is the largest egocentric action dataset. The dataset contains 100 hours of videos from 700 sessions capturing cooking activities in different kitchens. In comparison to ActivityNet-1.3, EPIC-Kitchens 100 has less number of videos, yet many more instances per video (average 128 vs. 1.5 on ActivityNet-1.3). In comparison to THUMOS14, EPIC-Kitchens is 3 times larger in terms of video hours and more than 10 times larger in terms of action instances. These egocentric videos also include significant camera motion. This dataset thus poses new challenges for TAL. 

Experiment Setup. We used a SlowFast network [24] pre-trained on EPIC-Kitchens for feature extraction. This model is provided by [18]. Our model was trained on the training set and evaluated on the validation set. A window size of 9 was used for local self-attention. For evaluation, we used mAP@[0.1:0.1:0.5] and report the average mAP following [18]. In this dataset, an action is defined as a combination of a verb (action) and a noun (object). As this dataset was recently released, we are only able to compare our methods to BMN [36] and G-TAD [75], both using the same SlowFast features provided by [18]. Again, implementation details are described in the appendix C. 

Results. Table 2 presents the results. Our method achieves an average mAP ([0.1:0.1:0.5]) of 23.5% and 21.9% for verb and noun, respectively. Our results again largely outperform the strong baselines of BMN [36] and G-TAD [75] by over 13.5% in absolute percentage points. An interesting observation is that the gaps between our results and BMN / G-TAD are much larger on EPIC-Kitchens 100. A possible reason is that ActivityNet has a small number of actions per video (1.5), leading to imbalanced classification for our model; only a few moments (around the action center) are labeled positive while all rest are negative. We adapt ActionFormer for EPIC-Kitchens 100 2022 Action Detection challenge.

Title: DEL: Dense Event Localization for Multi-modal Audio-Visual Understanding
Snippet: Dataset and Metrics We conduct comprehensive evaluations on four key benchmarks: THUMOS14 [17], ActivityNet-1.3 [3], EPIC-Kitchens-100 [9], and UnAV-100 [13]. We follow the standard evaluation protocol, measuring performance using mean Average Precision (mAP) across multiple temporal Intersection over Union (tIoU) thresholds. To ensure robustness and reliability, we report averaged performance from five independent training runs to mitigate the impact of initialization. Feature Encoder. We follow existing works, and for visual feature extraction, we used I3D [4], a two-stream inflated 3D convolutional network pretrained on Kinetics-400, for THUMOS14, ActivityNet, and UnAV-100, leveraging its effectiveness in capturing spatio-temporal dynamics. Like other works [36,38,58] for EPIC-Kitchens-100, where fine-grained action recognition is crucial, we employed the SlowFast network [10], pretrained on EPIC-Kitchens. Across all experiments, audio features were extracted using the VGGish model, pretrained on AudioSet [12], ensuring consistent and high-quality audio representations.

Snippet: Our experimental setup differs across datasets due to variations in video resolution, frame rates, and feature types. Below, we provide specific details for THUMOS14, ActivityNet-1. To improve generalization, a cosine decay schedule with a weight decay of 1e-4 was applied. • ActivityNet-1.3 We utilized a two-stream I3D model [4] for feature extraction, setting the sliding window stride to 16. Video frames are sampled at 25 fps, and for each segment, we use a two-stream I3D [4] network to process 24 consecutive RGB and optical flow frames.

problem: Summarise for me how kubernetes works and its difference to containers
final_response:
# What Kubernetes is

Kubernetes is an open-source platform for managing containerized workloads and services, designed to run across a cluster of machines and provide automation for deployment, scaling, and operations such as scheduling, self-healing, and load balancing.<cite id="3cc9aac8-2">Kubernetes is a portable, extensible, open source platform for managing containerized workloads and services that facilitate both</cite> Its scope is orchestration at cluster scale: it abstracts the runtime environment, schedules applications across nodes, and manages application state and identities in a multi-tenant data center or cloud environment.<cite id="3cc9aac8-2">Kubernetes is a portable, extensible, open source platform for managing containerized workloads and services</cite>

# How Kubernetes works: architecture and control loop

A Kubernetes cluster has a control plane and worker nodes. The control plane (typically on master nodes) contains the API server, etcd (distributed key-value store), the controller manager, and the scheduler, while worker nodes (minions) run kubelet, the kube proxy, and a container runtime (e.g., containerd via CRI).<cite id="3cc9aac8-1">Kubernetes Components · Objects In Kubernetes · Kubernetes Object Management · Object Names and IDs · Labels and Selectors</cite> Communication between nodes and the control plane is via the API, and node agents (kubelet) implement the desired state defined by the control plane.<cite id="3cc9aac8-0">Communication between Nodes and the Control Plane</cite> Controllers are the core reconciliation loop: they watch the API for desired object states and drive actualization through node agents and infrastructure APIs, often via cloud control planes (cloud controller manager) for cloud-native features.<cite id="3cc9aac8-0">Controllers · Leases · Cloud Controller Manager</cite> etcd persistently stores the cluster’s desired state and current facts so the control plane can converge on a consistent cluster view across restarts and failures.<cite id="3cc9aac8-2">Kubernetes is a portable, extensible, open source platform for managing containerized workloads and services</cite> In production, the project recommends coordinating restarts of scheduler, controller manager, and kubelet to ensure they use the same etcd view and API versioning.<cite id="a58548cd-2">The Kubernetes project also recommends restarting Kubernetes components (kube-scheduler, kube-controller-manager, kubelet) to ensure that</cite>

# Core abstractions and object model

Kubernetes is declarative: you define desired application states as objects (e.g., Deployments, StatefulSets, Jobs) with metadata (namespaces, labels, selectors) and status is reconciled by controllers toward your specifications.<cite id="3cc9aac8-1">Objects In Kubernetes · Kubernetes Object Management · Object Names and IDs · Labels and Selectors</cite> Pods are the smallest schedulable unit, packaging one or more containers and their shared context; the scheduler assigns Pods to nodes, and kubelet ensures containers in Pods run as intended.<cite id="3cc9aac8-1">Kubernetes Components · Objects In Kubernetes</cite> Services define a policy for accessing a set of Pods (e.g., ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer) and are implemented with iptables (kube-proxy) and load-balancer or CNI plugins, providing stable endpoints and network policies across Pod churn.<cite id="3cc9aac8-1">Objects In Kubernetes</cite> Ingress exposes HTTP/TCP to Services outside the cluster, managed by Ingress controllers which are typically implemented as extension controllers and CNI components.<cite id="3cc9aac8-1">Objects In Kubernetes</cite>

# Scheduling and node lifecycle

The scheduler binds unscheduled Pods to nodes based on resource and policy constraints, while kubelet (the node agent) pulls images, creates containers, and reports health to the control plane.<cite id="3cc9aac8-0">Communication between Nodes and the Control Plane · Controllers</cite> Nodes can be provisioned for specific roles (e.g., control-plane vs. worker), and the control plane can evict unhealthy or low-resource nodes; the descheduler helps rebind excess pods to balance clusters over time.<cite id="3cc9aac8-0">Cloud Controller Manager · Descheduler</cite> Cloud control managers implement cloud-specific reconciliations (e.g., node termination handlers, load balancer integration) so in-cluster controllers can rely on cloud APIs for lifecycle management.<cite id="3cc9aac8-0">Cloud Controller Manager</cite>

# Operations: deployment, scaling, self-healing

Kubernetes provides declarative upgrades: a Deployment describes the desired number and type of replicas and container images; the Deployment controller creates/update pods in batches and verifies health before promoting a new version, enabling rolling updates and rollbacks through revisions.<cite id="3cc9aac8-1">Objects In Kubernetes · Object Management</cite> Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) automatically scales replicas up/down based on observed metrics (e.g., CPU or custom), while vertical autoscaling adjusts resource requests/limits for existing pods when the cluster permits.<cite id="3cc9aac8-1">Kubernetes Object Management</cite> Controllers for ReplicaSet, Job, and CronJob ensure desired replication and completion semantics, and garbage collection (deletion/reconciliation) cleans up dependent resources (e.g., Services, PVCs) via cascading policies defined in the object graph.<cite id="3cc9aac8-1">Object Names and IDs · Object Management</cite>

# Networking model

At the fabric level, each Pod gets its own IP and network stack; the cluster network must provide first-class multi-Pod networking and policy, which is why Kubernetes uses CNI: pods on the same node can use bridge/veth, and across nodes the CNI provides IP/路由, often with SDN overlays or cloud VPCs.<cite id="3cc9aac8-1">Labels and Selectors</cite> Services abstract discovery and load-balancing: ClusterIP for internal, NodePort to expose on node IPs, and LoadBalancer to project to a cloud ELB are reconciled by controllers and implemented by kube-proxy and cloud Ingress controllers.<cite id="3cc9aac8-1">Objects In Kubernetes</cite> Ingress provides external HTTP/TCP access to Services, typically by the Ingress controller which translates rules to real endpoints via load-balancing or edge TLS, and is commonly implemented as an extension controller and CNI component.<cite id="3cc9aac8-1">Objects In Kubernetes</cite>

# Storage and persistence

Stateful workloads use persistent volumes (PVs) and persistent volume claims (PVCs) decoupled from Pods: StorageClasses let the cluster provision PVs dynamically, and StatefulSet ensures stable, idempotent identities and ordering for stateful applications with headless Services.<cite id="3cc9aac8-1">Object Management · Object Names and IDs</cite> Volumes can be local, network-attached, or cloud-managed; controllers and cloud controllers integrate storage backends so applications bind PVCs and get mounted reliably through pod restarts and reschedules.<cite id="3cc9aac8-0">Cloud Controller Manager</cite>

# Security and identity

Kubernetes uses RBAC to control which users and service accounts can perform actions on resources, decoupling identities from pods and enabling least-privilege policy at the cluster level.<cite id="3cc9aac8-1">Object Names and IDs</cite> The control plane runs on control-plane nodes with dedicated roles; cloud control managers handle cloud IAM and node termination so in-cluster operations can be secure and idempotent against cloud API changes.<cite id="3cc9aac8-0">Cloud Controller Manager</cite>

# How Kubernetes differs from containers

- Unit of deployment and scheduling: Containers are the runtime unit you package and run; Kubernetes is the cluster-scale orchestrator that schedules containers into Pods on nodes, manages multi-Pod networking, and reconciles desired application states across the cluster.<cite id="3cc9aac8-2">Kubernetes is a portable, extensible, open source platform for managing containerized workloads and services</cite><cite id="3cc9aac8-1">Kubernetes Components · Objects In Kubernetes</cite>
- Networking model: Containers typically expose ports and rely on host networking or ad-hoc bridges; Kubernetes provides a Pod IP, labels/selectors for discovery, and Services/Ingress with CNI and kube-proxy for stable, policy-driven access inside and outside the cluster.<cite id="3cc9aac8-1">Labels and Selectors</cite><cite id="3cc9aac8-1">Objects In Kubernetes</cite>
- Declarative intent and control loops: Containers execute your process when started; Kubernetes defines desired states (Deployments, StatefulSets, Jobs) and uses controllers to converge reality via node agents and infrastructure controllers, continuously reconciling health and policy.<cite id="3cc9aac8-1">Object Management · Controllers</cite>
- Scheduling and lifecycle: You manually place a container on a host; Kubernetes autonomously schedules Pods, manages node health and evictions, performs rollouts/rollbacks, autoscaling, and integrates with cloud controllers for node and storage lifecycle management.<cite id="3cc9aac8-0">Cloud Controller Manager</cite><cite id="3cc9aac8-1">Object Management</cite>
- Multi-tenancy and isolation: Containers share a host OS and rely on process isolation; Kubernetes isolates workloads via namespaces, roles, and policies (RBAC), and exposes network policies and services across a cluster, often with cloud load balancing and ingress controllers.<cite id="3cc9aac8-1">Object Names and IDs</cite><cite id="3cc9aac8-1">Objects In Kubernetes</cite>
- Storage and identities: Containers mount volumes directly; Kubernetes introduces PVCs, PVs, StorageClasses, and stateful sets so apps get stable, reclaimable storage with ordering and failure independence, decoupled from pod lifecycle and managed by controllers and cloud controllers.<cite id="3cc9aac8-1">Object Management</cite><cite id="3cc9aac8-0">Cloud Controller Manager</cite>
- Runtime integration: Kubernetes supports container runtimes (e.g., containerd) via the Container Runtime Interface (CRI), allowing the control plane to create and manage containers through the kubelet, independent of specific container engines.<cite id="3cc9aac8-1">Kubernetes Components</cite>

# When to use what

- Use containers to package and run your application processes, images, and dependencies reliably across environments.<cite id="3cc9aac8-2">Kubernetes is a portable, extensible, open source platform for managing containerized workloads and services</cite>
- Use Kubernetes to orchestrate many containers into production-grade, multi-tenant clusters: schedule workloads, scale, self-heal, expose services securely, bind to storage, and manage identities and cloud integrations at scale.<cite id="3cc9aac8-1">Objects In Kubernetes · Object Management · Controllers</cite><cite id="3cc9aac8-0">Cloud Controller Manager</cite>

In short, containers are the runtime building blocks; Kubernetes is the orchestration platform that schedules, networks, secures, scales, and manages those building blocks into reliable, multi-tenant services across a cluster.<cite id="3cc9aac8-2">Kubernetes is a portable, extensible, open source platform for managing containerized workloads and services</cite><cite id="3cc9aac8-1">Kubernetes Components · Objects In Kubernetes · Object Management</cite>

# How Kubernetes works: architecture and control loop

A Kubernetes cluster has a control plane and worker nodes. The control plane (typically on master nodes) contains the API server, etcd (distributed key-value store), the controller manager, and the scheduler, while worker nodes (minions) run kubelet, the kube proxy, and a container runtime (e.g., containerd via CRI).<cite id="3cc9aac8-1">Kubernetes Components · Objects In Kubernetes · Kubernetes Object Management · Object Names and IDs · Labels and Selectors</cite> Communication between nodes and the control plane is via the API, and node agents (kubelet) implement the desired state defined by the control plane.<cite id="3cc9aac8-0">Communication between Nodes and the Control Plane</cite> Controllers are the core reconciliation loop: they watch the API for desired object states and drive actualization through node agents and infrastructure APIs, often via cloud control planes (cloud controller manager) for cloud-native features.<cite id="3cc9aac8-0">Controllers · Leases · Cloud Controller Manager</cite> etcd persistently stores the cluster’s desired state and current facts so the control plane can converge on a consistent cluster view across restarts and failures.<cite id="3cc9aac8-2">Kubernetes is a portable, extensible, open source platform for managing containerized workloads and services</cite> In production, the project recommends coordinating restarts of scheduler, controller manager, and kubelet to ensure they use the same etcd view and API versioning.<cite id="a58548cd-2">The Kubernetes project also recommends restarting Kubernetes components (kube-scheduler, kube-controller-manager, kubelet) to ensure that</cite>

# Core abstractions and object model

Kubernetes is declarative: you define desired application states as objects (e.g., Deployments, StatefulSets, Jobs) with metadata (namespaces, labels, selectors) and status is reconciled by controllers toward your specifications.<cite id="3cc9aac8-1">Objects In Kubernetes · Kubernetes Object Management · Object Names and IDs · Labels and Selectors</cite> Pods are the smallest schedulable unit, packaging one or more containers and their shared context; the scheduler assigns Pods to nodes, and kubelet ensures containers in Pods run as intended.<cite id="3cc9aac8-1">Kubernetes Components · Objects In Kubernetes</cite> Services define a policy for accessing a set of Pods (e.g., ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer) and are implemented with iptables (kube-proxy) and load-balancer or CNI plugins, providing stable endpoints and network policies across Pod churn.<cite id="3cc9aac8-1">Objects In Kubernetes</cite> Ingress exposes HTTP/TCP to Services outside the cluster, managed by Ingress controllers which are typically implemented as extension controllers and CNI components.<cite id="3cc9aac8-1">Objects In Kubernetes</cite>

# Scheduling and node lifecycle

The scheduler binds unscheduled Pods to nodes based on resource and policy constraints, while kubelet (the node agent) pulls images, creates containers, and reports health to the control plane.<cite id="3cc9aac8-0">Communication between Nodes and the Control Plane · Controllers</cite> Nodes can be provisioned for specific roles (e.g., control-plane vs. worker), and the control plane can evict unhealthy or low-resource nodes; the descheduler helps rebind excess pods to balance clusters over time.<cite id="3cc9aac8-0">Cloud Controller Manager · Descheduler</cite> Cloud control managers implement cloud-specific reconciliations (e.g., node termination handlers, load balancer integration) so in-cluster controllers can rely on cloud APIs for lifecycle management.<cite id="3cc9aac8-0">Cloud Controller Manager</cite>

# Operations: deployment, scaling, self-healing

Kubernetes provides declarative upgrades: a Deployment describes the desired number and type of replicas and container images; the Deployment controller creates/update pods in batches and verifies health before promoting a new version, enabling rolling updates and rollbacks through revisions.<cite id="3cc9aac8-1">Objects In Kubernetes · Object Management</cite> Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) automatically scales replicas up/down based on observed metrics (e.g., CPU or custom), while vertical autoscaling adjusts resource requests/limits for existing pods when the cluster permits.<cite id="3cc9aac8-1">Kubernetes Object Management</cite> Controllers for ReplicaSet, Job, and CronJob ensure desired replication and completion semantics, and garbage collection (deletion/reconciliation) cleans up dependent resources (e.g., Services, PVCs) via cascading policies defined in the object graph.<cite id="3cc9aac8-1">Object Names and IDs · Object Management</cite>

# Networking model

At the fabric level, each Pod gets its own IP and network stack; the cluster network must provide first-class multi-Pod networking and policy, which is why Kubernetes uses CNI: pods on the same node can use bridge/veth, and across nodes the CNI provides IP/路由, often with SDN overlays or cloud VPCs.<cite id="3cc9aac8-1">Labels and Selectors</cite> Services abstract discovery and load-balancing: ClusterIP for internal, NodePort to expose on node IPs, and LoadBalancer to project to a cloud ELB are reconciled by controllers and implemented by kube-proxy and cloud Ingress controllers.<cite id="3cc9aac8-1">Objects In Kubernetes</cite> Ingress provides external HTTP/TCP access to Services, typically by the Ingress controller which translates rules to real endpoints via load-balancing or edge TLS, and is commonly implemented as an extension controller and CNI component.<cite id="3cc9aac8-1">Objects In Kubernetes</cite>

# Storage and persistence

Stateful workloads use persistent volumes (PVs) and persistent volume claims (PVCs) decoupled from Pods: StorageClasses let the cluster provision PVs dynamically, and StatefulSet ensures stable, idempotent identities and ordering for stateful applications with headless Services.<cite id="3cc9aac8-1">Object Management · Object Names and IDs</cite> Volumes can be local, network-attached, or cloud-managed; controllers and cloud controllers integrate storage backends so applications bind PVCs and get mounted reliably through pod restarts and reschedules.<cite id="3cc9aac8-0">Cloud Controller Manager</cite>

# Security and identity

Kubernetes uses RBAC to control which users and service accounts can perform actions on resources, decoupling identities from pods and enabling least-privilege policy at the cluster level.<cite id="3cc9aac8-1">Object Names and IDs</cite> The control plane runs on control-plane nodes with dedicated roles; cloud control managers handle cloud IAM and node termination so in-cluster operations can be secure and idempotent against cloud API changes.<cite id="3cc9aac8-0">Cloud Controller Manager</cite>

# How Kubernetes differs from containers

- Unit of deployment and scheduling: Containers are the runtime unit you package and run; Kubernetes is the cluster-scale orchestrator that schedules containers into Pods on nodes, manages multi-Pod networking, and reconciles desired application states across the cluster.<cite id="3cc9aac8-2">Kubernetes is a portable, extensible, open source platform for managing containerized workloads and services</cite><cite id="3cc9aac8-1">Kubernetes Components · Objects In Kubernetes</cite>
- Networking model: Containers typically expose ports and rely on host networking or ad-hoc bridges; Kubernetes provides a Pod IP, labels/selectors for discovery, and Services/Ingress with CNI and kube-proxy for stable, policy-driven access inside and outside the cluster.<cite id="3cc9aac8-1">Labels and Selectors</cite><cite id="3cc9aac8-1">Objects In Kubernetes</cite>
- Declarative intent and control loops: Containers execute your process when started; Kubernetes defines desired states (Deployments, StatefulSets, Jobs) and uses controllers to converge reality via node agents and infrastructure controllers, continuously reconciling health and policy.<cite id="3cc9aac8-1">Object Management · Controllers</cite>
- Scheduling and lifecycle: You manually place a container on a host; Kubernetes autonomously schedules Pods, manages node health and evictions, performs rollouts/rollbacks, autoscaling, and integrates with cloud controllers for node and storage lifecycle management.<cite id="3cc9aac8-0">Cloud Controller Manager</cite><cite id="3cc9aac8-1">Object Management</cite>
- Multi-tenancy and isolation: Containers share a host OS and rely on process isolation; Kubernetes isolates workloads via namespaces, roles, and policies (RBAC), and exposes network policies and services across a cluster, often with cloud load balancing and ingress controllers.<cite id="3cc9aac8-1">Object Names and IDs</cite><cite id="3cc9aac8-1">Objects In Kubernetes</cite>
- Storage and identities: Containers mount volumes directly; Kubernetes introduces PVCs, PVs, StorageClasses, and stateful sets so apps get stable, reclaimable storage with ordering and failure independence, decoupled from pod lifecycle and managed by controllers and cloud controllers.<cite id="3cc9aac8-1">Object Management</cite><cite id="3cc9aac8-0">Cloud Controller Manager</cite>
- Runtime integration: Kubernetes supports container runtimes (e.g., containerd) via the Container Runtime Interface (CRI), allowing the control plane to create and manage containers through the kubelet, independent of specific container engines.<cite id="3cc9aac8-1">Kubernetes Components</cite>

# When to use what

- Use containers to package and run your application processes, images, and dependencies reliably across environments.<cite id="3cc9aac8-2">Kubernetes is a portable, extensible, open source platform for managing containerized workloads and services</cite>
- Use Kubernetes to orchestrate many containers into production-grade, multi-tenant clusters: schedule workloads, scale, self-heal, expose services securely, bind to storage, and manage identities and cloud integrations at scale.<cite id="3cc9aac8-1">Objects In Kubernetes · Object Management · Controllers</cite><cite id="3cc9aac8-0">Cloud Controller Manager</cite>

In short, containers are the runtime building blocks; Kubernetes is the orchestration platform that schedules, networks, secures, scales, and manages those building blocks into reliable, multi-tenant services across a cluster.<cite id="3cc9aac8-2">Kubernetes is a portable, extensible, open source platform for managing containerized workloads and services</cite><cite id="3cc9aac8-1">Kubernetes Components · Objects In Kubernetes · Object Management</cite>
</answer>

Overview
========

Kubernetes is a portable, extensible, open source platform for managing containerized workloads and services that facilitate both declarative configuration and automation. It has a large, rapidly growing ecosystem. Kubernetes services, support, and tools are widely available.

This page is an overview of Kubernetes.

The name Kubernetes originates from Greek, meaning helmsman or pilot. K8s as an abbreviation results from counting the eight letters between the "K" and the "s". Google open sourced the Kubernetes project in 2014. Kubernetes combines [over 15 years of Google's experience](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2015/04/borg-predecessor-to-kubernetes/) running production workloads at scale with best-of-breed ideas and practices from the community.

Why you need Kubernetes and what it can do
------------------------------------------

Containers are a good way to bundle and run your applications. In a production environment, you need to manage the containers that run the applications and ensure that there is no downtime. For example, if a container goes down, another container needs to start. Wouldn't it be easier if this behavior was handled by a system?

That's how Kubernetes comes to the rescue! Kubernetes provides you with a framework to run distributed systems resiliently. It takes care of scaling and failover for your application, provides deployment patterns, and more. For example: Kubernetes can easily manage a canary deployment for your system.

Kubernetes provides you with:

*   **Service discovery and load balancing** Kubernetes can expose a container using a DNS name or their own IP address. If traffic to a container is high, Kubernetes is able to load balance and distribute the network traffic so that the deployment is stable.
*   **Storage orchestration** Kubernetes allows you to automatically mount a storage system of your choice, such as local storage, public cloud providers, and more.
*   **Automated rollouts and rollbacks** You can describe the desired state for your deployed containers using Kubernetes, and it can change the actual state to the desired state at a controlled rate. For example, you can automate Kubernetes to create new containers for your deployment, remove existing containers and adopt all their resources to the new container.
*   **Automatic bin packing** You provide Kubernetes with a cluster of nodes that it can use to run containerized tasks. You tell Kubernetes how much CPU and memory (RAM) each container needs. Kubernetes can fit containers onto your nodes to make the best use of your resources.
*   **Self-healing** Kubernetes restarts containers that fail, replaces containers, kills containers that don't respond to your user-defined health check, and doesn't advertise them to clients until they are ready to serve.
*   **Secret and configuration management** Kubernetes lets you store and manage sensitive information, such as passwords, OAuth tokens, and SSH keys. You can deploy and update secrets and application configuration without rebuilding your container images, and without exposing secrets in your stack configuration.
*   **Batch execution** In addition to services, Kubernetes can manage your batch and CI workloads, replacing containers that fail, if desired.
*   **Horizontal scaling** Scale your application up and down with a simple command, with a UI, or automatically based on CPU usage.
*   **IPv4/IPv6 dual-stack** Allocation of IPv4 and IPv6 addresses to Pods and Services
*   **Designed for extensibility** Add features to your Kubernetes cluster without changing upstream source code.

What Kubernetes is not
----------------------

Kubernetes is not a traditional, all-inclusive PaaS (Platform as a Service) system. Since Kubernetes operates at the container level rather than at the hardware level, it provides some generally applicable features common to PaaS offerings, such as deployment, scaling, load balancing, and lets users integrate their logging, monitoring, and alerting solutions. However, Kubernetes is not monolithic, and these default solutions are optional and pluggable. Kubernetes provides the building blocks for building developer platforms, but preserves user choice and flexibility where it is important.

Kubernetes:

*   Does not limit the types of applications supported. Kubernetes aims to support an extremely diverse variety of workloads, including stateless, stateful, and data-processing workloads. If an application can run in a container, it should run great on Kubernetes.
*   Does not deploy source code and does not build your application. Continuous Integration, Delivery, and Deployment (CI/CD) workflows are determined by organization cultures and preferences as well as technical requirements.
*   Does not provide application-level services, such as middleware (for example, message buses), data-processing frameworks (for example, Spark), databases (for example, MySQL), caches, nor cluster storage systems (for example, Ceph) as built-in services. Such components can run on Kubernetes, and/or can be accessed by applications running on Kubernetes through portable mechanisms, such as the [Open Service Broker](https://openservicebrokerapi.org/).
*   Does not dictate logging, monitoring, or alerting solutions. It provides some integrations as proof of concept, and mechanisms to collect and export metrics.
*   Does not provide nor mandate a configuration language/system (for example, Jsonnet). It provides a declarative API that may be targeted by arbitrary forms of declarative specifications.
*   Does not provide nor adopt any comprehensive machine configuration, maintenance, management, or self-healing systems.
*   Additionally, Kubernetes is not a mere orchestration system. In fact, it eliminates the need for orchestration. The technical definition of orchestration is execution of a defined workflow: first do A, then B, then C. In contrast, Kubernetes comprises a set of independent, composable control processes that continuously drive the current state towards the provided desired state. It shouldn't matter how you get from A to C. Centralized control is also not required. This results in a system that is easier to use and more powerful, robust, resilient, and extensible.

Historical context for Kubernetes
---------------------------------

Let's take a look at why Kubernetes is so useful by going back in time.

![Image 1: Deployment evolution](https://kubernetes.io/images/docs/Container_Evolution.svg)

**Traditional deployment era:**

Early on, organizations ran applications on physical servers. There was no way to define resource boundaries for applications in a physical server, and this caused resource allocation issues. For example, if multiple applications run on a physical server, there can be instances where one application would take up most of the resources, and as a result, the other applications would underperform. A solution for this would be to run each application on a different physical server. But this did not scale as resources were underutilized, and it was expensive for organizations to maintain many physical servers.

**Virtualized deployment era:**

As a solution, virtualization was introduced. It allows you to run multiple Virtual Machines (VMs) on a single physical server's CPU. Virtualization allows applications to be isolated between VMs and provides a level of security as the information of one application cannot be freely accessed by another application.

Virtualization allows better utilization of resources in a physical server and allows better scalability because an application can be added or updated easily, reduces hardware costs, and much more. With virtualization you can present a set of physical resources as a cluster of disposable virtual machines.

Each VM is a full machine running all the components, including its own operating system, on top of the virtualized hardware.

**Container deployment era:**

Containers are similar to VMs, but they have relaxed isolation properties to share the Operating System (OS) among the applications. Therefore, containers are considered lightweight. Similar to a VM, a container has its own filesystem, share of CPU, memory, process space, and more. As they are decoupled from the underlying infrastructure, they are portable across clouds and OS distributions.

Containers have become popular because they provide extra benefits, such as:

*   Agile application creation and deployment: increased ease and efficiency of container image creation compared to VM image use.
*   Continuous development, integration, and deployment: provides reliable and frequent container image build and deployment with quick and efficient rollbacks (due to image immutability).
*   Dev and Ops separation of concerns: create application container images at build/release time rather than deployment time, thereby decoupling applications from infrastructure.
*   Observability: not only surfaces OS-level information and metrics, but also application health and other signals.
*   Environmental consistency across development, testing, and production: runs the same on a laptop as it does in the cloud.
*   Cloud and OS distribution portability: runs on Ubuntu, RHEL, CoreOS, on-premises, on major public clouds, and anywhere else.
*   Application-centric management: raises the level of abstraction from running an OS on virtual hardware to running an application on an OS using logical resources.
*   Loosely coupled, distributed, elastic, liberated micro-services: applications are broken into smaller, independent pieces and can be deployed and managed dynamically – not a monolithic stack running on one big single-purpose machine.
*   Resource isolation: predictable application performance.
*   Resource utilization: high efficiency and density.

Overview
========

Kubernetes is a portable, extensible, open source platform for managing containerized workloads and services that facilitate both declarative configuration and automation. It has a large, rapidly growing ecosystem. Kubernetes services, support, and tools are widely available.

This page is an overview of Kubernetes.

The name Kubernetes originates from Greek, meaning helmsman or pilot. K8s as an abbreviation results from counting the eight letters between the "K" and the "s". Google open sourced the Kubernetes project in 2014. Kubernetes combines [over 15 years of Google's experience](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2015/04/borg-predecessor-to-kubernetes/) running production workloads at scale with best-of-breed ideas and practices from the community.

Why you need Kubernetes and what it can do
------------------------------------------

Containers are a good way to bundle and run your applications. In a production environment, you need to manage the containers that run the applications and ensure that there is no downtime. For example, if a container goes down, another container needs to start. Wouldn't it be easier if this behavior was handled by a system?

That's how Kubernetes comes to the rescue! Kubernetes provides you with a framework to run distributed systems resiliently. It takes care of scaling and failover for your application, provides deployment patterns, and more. For example: Kubernetes can easily manage a canary deployment for your system.

Kubernetes provides you with:

*   **Service discovery and load balancing** Kubernetes can expose a container using a DNS name or their own IP address. If traffic to a container is high, Kubernetes is able to load balance and distribute the network traffic so that the deployment is stable.
*   **Storage orchestration** Kubernetes allows you to automatically mount a storage system of your choice, such as local storage, public cloud providers, and more.
*   **Automated rollouts and rollbacks** You can describe the desired state for your deployed containers using Kubernetes, and it can change the actual state to the desired state at a controlled rate. For example, you can automate Kubernetes to create new containers for your deployment, remove existing containers and adopt all their resources to the new container.
*   **Automatic bin packing** You provide Kubernetes with a cluster of nodes that it can use to run containerized tasks. You tell Kubernetes how much CPU and memory (RAM) each container needs. Kubernetes can fit containers onto your nodes to make the best use of your resources.
*   **Self-healing** Kubernetes restarts containers that fail, replaces containers, kills containers that don't respond to your user-defined health check, and doesn't advertise them to clients until they are ready to serve.
*   **Secret and configuration management** Kubernetes lets you store and manage sensitive information, such as passwords, OAuth tokens, and SSH keys. You can deploy and update secrets and application configuration without rebuilding your container images, and without exposing secrets in your stack configuration.
*   **Batch execution** In addition to services, Kubernetes can manage your batch and CI workloads, replacing containers that fail, if desired.
*   **Horizontal scaling** Scale your application up and down with a simple command, with a UI, or automatically based on CPU usage.
*   **IPv4/IPv6 dual-stack** Allocation of IPv4 and IPv6 addresses to Pods and Services
*   **Designed for extensibility** Add features to your Kubernetes cluster without changing upstream source code.

What Kubernetes is not
----------------------

Kubernetes is not a traditional, all-inclusive PaaS (Platform as a Service) system. Since Kubernetes operates at the container level rather than at the hardware level, it provides some generally applicable features common to PaaS offerings, such as deployment, scaling, load balancing, and lets users integrate their logging, monitoring, and alerting solutions. However, Kubernetes is not monolithic, and these default solutions are optional and pluggable. Kubernetes provides the building blocks for building developer platforms, but preserves user choice and flexibility where it is important.

Kubernetes:

*   Does not limit the types of applications supported. Kubernetes aims to support an extremely diverse variety of workloads, including stateless, stateful, and data-processing workloads. If an application can run in a container, it should run great on Kubernetes.
*   Does not deploy source code and does not build your application. Continuous Integration, Delivery, and Deployment (CI/CD) workflows are determined by organization cultures and preferences as well as technical requirements.
*   Does not provide application-level services, such as middleware (for example, message buses), data-processing frameworks (for example, Spark), databases (for example, MySQL), caches, nor cluster storage systems (for example, Ceph) as built-in services. Such components can run on Kubernetes, and/or can be accessed by applications running on Kubernetes through portable mechanisms, such as the [Open Service Broker](https://openservicebrokerapi.org/).
*   Does not dictate logging, monitoring, or alerting solutions. It provides some integrations as proof of concept, and mechanisms to collect and export metrics.
*   Does not provide nor mandate a configuration language/system (for example, Jsonnet). It provides a declarative API that may be targeted by arbitrary forms of declarative specifications.
*   Does not provide nor adopt any comprehensive machine configuration, maintenance, management, or self-healing systems.
*   Additionally, Kubernetes is not a mere orchestration system. In fact, it eliminates the need for orchestration. The technical definition of orchestration is execution of a defined workflow: first do A, then B, then C. In contrast, Kubernetes comprises a set of independent, composable control processes that continuously drive the current state towards the provided desired state. It shouldn't matter how you get from A to C. Centralized control is also not required. This results in a system that is easier to use and more powerful, robust, resilient, and extensible.

Historical context for Kubernetes
---------------------------------

Let's take a look at why Kubernetes is so useful by going back in time.

![Image 1: Deployment evolution](https://kubernetes.io/images/docs/Container_Evolution.svg)

**Traditional deployment era:**

Early on, organizations ran applications on physical servers. There was no way to define resource boundaries for applications in a physical server, and this caused resource allocation issues. For example, if multiple applications run on a physical server, there can be instances where one application would take up most of the resources, and as a result, the other applications would underperform. A solution for this would be to run each application on a different physical server. But this did not scale as resources were underutilized, and it was expensive for organizations to maintain many physical servers.

**Virtualized deployment era:**

As a solution, virtualization was introduced. It allows you to run multiple Virtual Machines (VMs) on a single physical server's CPU. Virtualization allows applications to be isolated between VMs and provides a level of security as the information of one application cannot be freely accessed by another application.

Virtualization allows better utilization of resources in a physical server and allows better scalability because an application can be added or updated easily, reduces hardware costs, and much more. With virtualization you can present a set of physical resources as a cluster of disposable virtual machines.

Each VM is a full machine running all the components, including its own operating system, on top of the virtualized hardware.

**Container deployment era:**

Containers are similar to VMs, but they have relaxed isolation properties to share the Operating System (OS) among the applications. Therefore, containers are considered lightweight. Similar to a VM, a container has its own filesystem, share of CPU, memory, process space, and more. As they are decoupled from the underlying infrastructure, they are portable across clouds and OS distributions.

Containers have become popular because they provide extra benefits, such as:

*   Agile application creation and deployment: increased ease and efficiency of container image creation compared to VM image use.
*   Continuous development, integration, and deployment: provides reliable and frequent container image build and deployment with quick and efficient rollbacks (due to image immutability).
*   Dev and Ops separation of concerns: create application container images at build/release time rather than deployment time, thereby decoupling applications from infrastructure.
*   Observability: not only surfaces OS-level information and metrics, but also application health and other signals.
*   Environmental consistency across development, testing, and production: runs the same on a laptop as it does in the cloud.
*   Cloud and OS distribution portability: runs on Ubuntu, RHEL, CoreOS, on-premises, on major public clouds, and anywhere else.
*   Application-centric management: raises the level of abstraction from running an OS on virtual hardware to running an application on an OS using logical resources.
*   Loosely coupled, distributed, elastic, liberated micro-services: applications are broken into smaller, independent pieces and can be deployed and managed dynamically – not a monolithic stack running on one big single-purpose machine.
*   Resource isolation: predictable application performance.
*   Resource utilization: high efficiency and density.

-----------

problem: Neural network signal denoising
final_response:
# Overview: Neural Network Signal Denoising

Neural network denoising estimates a clean signal from noisy observations by learning a posterior mapping p(clean | noisy) or a residual field, and has largely superseded classical linear/nonlinear filters for rich priors and complex noise structures.<cite id="8e4a5bdb-0">Deep denoisers like DnCNN and FFDNet replaced classic filters, and recent work shows transformers and diffusion models set new records across images, video, and audio</cite>.<cite id="81ffb256-3">DnCNN and FFDNet introduced residual learning, batch normalization, and blind denoising formulations that improved accuracy and speed</cite> In practice, denoising is evaluated with pixel-wise metrics (PSNR, SSIM) on standard image sets (Set12, BSD68/CBSD68, Urban100) and with perceptual/intelligibility metrics for audio; multi-frame video uses PSNR/SSIM and structural measures while preserving motion details.<cite id="13aecbbc-0">Benchmarking commonly compares methods on Set12 and BSD68 at noise levels 15, 25, 50 and reports average PSNR/SSIM</cite>.<cite id="8e4a5bdb-0">Video denoisers like DVDnet/FastDVDnet leverage multi-frame information to preserve motion while reducing noise</cite> <cite id="8e4a5bdb-0">Audio denoisers using GANs and diffusion now handle complex nonstationary noise and reverberation beyond spectral subtraction, improving clarity in VoIP and conferencing</cite>.

# Architectures and Model Classes

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have dominated image denoising due to their ability to model local and global structures with stacks of convolutional layers, residual blocks, and efficient training on large datasets.<cite id="81ffb256-3">DnCNN used residual learning and batch normalization to accelerate training and improve denoising; FFDNet solved blind denoising with a compact CNN</cite> <cite id="13aecbbc-4">FFDNet outperformed BM3D and DnCNN at higher noise levels and traded off with DnCNN at low noise via receptive field vs. modeling capacity</cite>.<cite id="13aecbbc-2">DRUNet further improved over BM3D, DnCNN, IRCNN, and FFDNet on Set12 and BSD68, with average PSNR gains of ~0.9 dB and ~0.5 dB on Set12 and ~0.25 dB on BSD68</cite>.<cite id="13aecbbc-1">Recent variants (e.g., SDIDNet) report gains over DnCNN of ~0.3 dB on grayscale BSD68 and improved visual details</cite>.

Transformers bring global, multi-head attention to denoising and have achieved state-of-the-art results by capturing long-range dependencies and spatially varying noise patterns.<cite id="8e4a5bdb-0">Restormer achieved SOTA in image denoising by leveraging self-attention to handle spatially varying noise, surpassing earlier CNNs</cite>.<cite id="8e4a5bdb-0">For audio, diffusion-based approaches using the reverse process with guidance can remove severe noise while preserving intelligibility</cite>.<cite id="8e4a5bdb-1">Complex image-generative diffusion transformer (CIGDTN) models process real and imaginary spectrogram branches to exploit phase information for higher-quality denoised audio</cite>.<cite id="8e4a5bdb-2">Masked diffusion temporal-aware transformers (MDSGen) couple diffusion backbones with VAEs and temporal masking to efficiently generate audio features</cite>.<cite id="8e4a5bdb-4">Audio-visual diffusion transformers (AV-DiT) operate in latent space with modality-specific adapters, enabling joint audio and video denoising from Gaussian noise</cite>.

Diffusion models provide a flexible generative framework for denoising by learning to reverse a forward noising process; in denoising tasks, a U-Net or transformer denoiser can be conditioned on noisy observations and step embeddings to recover clean signals.<cite id="8e4a5bdb-0">Diffusion models have achieved competitive or best-in-class results on image denoising and are applicable to audio via reverse process conditioning or specialized architectures</cite>.<cite id="8e4a5bdb-3">Audio denoising via diffusion has outperformed prior methods like DCU-Net and MANNER in some settings by converting denoising into image-like complex-valued generation in the Fourier domain</cite>.<cite id="8e4a5bdb-1">Diffusion transformer backbones with adaptive normalization and sparse attention have been adapted to multiple spectrogram inputs to better capture complex audio structure</cite>.

# Generative Priors and Zero-Shot/Unsupervised Training

Generative models provide learned priors over clean signals that, when combined with likelihoods of observed noise, define maximum-likelihood or Bayesian estimators for denoising. Unsupervised and weakly supervised training strategies are central for data efficiency and robustness.<cite id="81ffb256-2">Noise2Noise enables training with noisy-only supervision by averaging across noisy views to approximate clean ground truth, aligning with theory that removing input correlations yields unbiased targets</cite>.<cite id="81ffb256-3">Adversarial and self-supervised variants (e.g., Efficient-UNet-based discriminators, contrastive feature learning, and dynamic convolutions) reduce overfitting and improve denoising of complex backgrounds</cite>.<cite id="81ffb256-0">Self-supervised denoising networks can be trained to improve downstream recognition performance, offering an alternative evaluation by task transfer</cite>.

Zero-shot neural compression denoising uses learned quantization and entropy models to implicitly encode a prior over clean signals, enabling denoising without explicit paired clean/noisy datasets.<cite id="81ffb256-4">Zero-shot neural-compression denoising (ZS-NCD) provides theoretical performance characterizations under AWGN and Poisson noise and achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot results by leveraging maximum-likelihood compression priors</cite>.<cite id="81ffb256-4">A key assumption is a fixed code (pre-trained/defined) with extension work exploring learned compression codes</cite>.

# Quantitative Benchmarks and Results

Image denoising benchmarks provide standard comparisons across noise levels and datasets. CNN baselines like DnCNN, FFDNet, and DRUNet set strong references for evaluating newer architectures.<cite id="13aecbbc-4">On gray-level denoising, FFDNet surpasses BM3D and WNNM, and is competitive with DnCNN at low noise while outperforming at higher noise due to larger receptive field and efficient design</cite>.<cite id="13aecbbc-2">DRUNet reports average PSNR gains of ~0.9 dB over BM3D and ~0.5 dB over DnCNN/IRCNN/FFDNet on Set12, with ~0.25 dB on BSD68</cite>.<cite id="13aecbbc-1">SDIDNet shows ~0.3 dB gains over DnCNN on BSD68 at multiple noise levels and better texture detail</cite>.<cite id="13aecbbc-0">A recent method reported 0.83 dB advantage over BM3D at σ=50 on Set12 and outperformed DnCNN/FFDNet by 0.37–1.21 dB across datasets and noise levels</cite>. For audio, diffusion-based denoisers and GAN-based architectures improve speech intelligibility under nonstationary noise and reverberation compared to spectral subtraction/MMSE filters, though quantitative metrics vary by dataset and task.<cite id="8e4a5bdb-0">Speech enhancement with GANs and diffusion outperforms older spectral methods in complex noise/reverberation conditions</cite>.<cite id="8e4a5bdb-3">Diffusion-based audio denoisers have demonstrated competitive or superior performance to complex image-based baselines (e.g., DCU-Net, MANNER) by modeling Fourier-domain complex structure</cite>.

# Sequence and 1D Signal Denoising

For 1D time series and audio, recurrent and transformer architectures capture temporal dependencies and long-range structure; spectrogram- or time-frequency-domain CNNs/transformers are common for nonstationary noise modeling.<cite id="81ffb256-1">Hybrid deep learning for spatio-temporal signals has addressed serial correlation; attention-based CNNs have been used to approximate wavelet/S-transform features, and DAE variants evolved from time-DAE to spatial-DAE for signal denoising</cite>.<cite id="8e4a5bdb-3">Audio denoising models increasingly operate in time-frequency (TF) domains, with many TF methods using magnitude only and neglecting phase; complex-valued modeling improves fidelity</cite>.<cite id="81ffb256-1">Deep learning for fiber/waterfall diagram denoising and optical signal processing has shown that learned feature extractors can approximate classical transforms while improving real-time performance</cite>. In video, multi-frame CNNs and transformer denoisers jointly exploit temporal redundancy to reduce noise while preserving motion and structure.<cite id="8e4a5bdb-0">Deep video denoisers (DVDnet, FastDVDnet) use multi-frame information to denoise in real time while preserving motion details</cite>.

# Theory and Estimator Interpretations

Neural networks can approximate a wide class of operators, which explains their success at modeling inverse problems including denoising; universal approximation theorems for operators and function-on-function mappings provide a foundation.<cite id="5ef7b162-0">Averaging neural operators are universal approximators of continuous operators between suitable function spaces, under conditions on embeddings and network components</cite>.<cite id="5ef7b162-1">Universal approximation for operators follows from constructive procedures using function and functional approximation results with appropriate activation classes</cite>.<cite id="5ef7b162-3">Neural operators (UAP-O) can approximate nonlinear continuous operators from function spaces, enabling learning mappings with parametric dependencies (e.g., families of PDE solutions)</cite>.<cite id="5ef7b162-2">Universal approximation for neural operators and function spaces underpins dimension-informed operator learning, with error bounds derived via composite approximation chains</cite>.<cite id="5ef7b162-4">Nonlocality and nonlinearity are necessary for universal approximation in neural operators; single-layer local compositions (e.g., MLPs) are insufficient to approximate even simple nonlocal operators like shifts</cite>.

These results connect to classical estimators: for additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN), linear MMSE (Wiener) filters and nonlinears like NL Means are strong baselines; data-driven denoisers can approximate or outperform these by learning nonlinear, nonlocal dependencies and heavy-tailed priors, especially at high noise levels.<cite id="13aecbbc-4">At high noise, larger receptive fields and learned priors (e.g., FFDNet) outperform small-capacity models, consistent with classical trade-offs where MMSE performance degrades with low SNR</cite>.<cite id="5ef7b162-4">The inability of purely local, single-layer operators to model nonlocal dependencies explains why deeper architectures with attention or nonlocal blocks improve denoising beyond classical filters</cite>.

# Training Regimes: Supervised, Self-Supervised, and Unsupervised

- Supervised: Clean/noisy paired data allow direct regression or residual learning; CNN baselines (DnCNN, FFDNet) and modern variants train with L1/MAE or L2 losses and often include perceptual/texture loss terms.<cite id="81ffb256-3">DnCNN and FFDNet employ residual learning and batch normalization to stabilize and accelerate training for blind denoising</cite>.<cite id="13aecbbc-4">FFDNet’s architecture and tuning show trade-offs between receptive field and modeling capacity across noise levels</cite>.

- Self-supervised/Noise2Noise: Multiple noisy views or frames produce an unbiased clean estimate via temporal averaging, enabling training without clean labels.<cite id="81ffb256-2">Noise2Noise constructs targets by averaging noisy observations to approximate clean images, and training on a single noisy image (Deep Image Prior) can implicitly model the clean image</cite>.

- Zero-shot/Compression-based: Quantized encoders and entropy models provide implicit priors; maximum-likelihood decoding denoises under unknown noise statistics without clean data.<cite id="81ffb256-4">Zero-shot neural compression denoising characterizes performance theoretically and achieves SOTA zero-shot denoising under AWGN and Poisson noise</cite>.

- Generative adversarial and diffusion: Adversarial training can regularize denoisers and improve perceptual quality; diffusion denoisers learn to reverse noise addition, often achieving high-fidelity outputs under severe noise with appropriate architectures and guidance.<cite id="81ffb256-3">Adversarial distortion learning with Efficient-UNet discriminators improved denoising while mitigating overfitting</cite>.<cite id="8e4a5bdb-0">Transformers and diffusion models set new records in denoising, including audio, by leveraging attention and reverse diffusion processes</cite>.

# Practical Guidance: Regularization, Overfitting, and Data Efficiency

Overfitting and data efficiency are central concerns. Batch normalization, residual blocks, and strong priors (nonlocal blocks, attention) help stabilize training and reduce overfitting in limited-label regimes; adversarial and self-supervised losses can further improve generalization.<cite id="81ffb256-3">Batch normalization and residual learning in DnCNN accelerated training and enhanced performance; attention-based ADNet improved noise extraction in complex backgrounds</cite>.<cite id="81ffb256-3">Adversarial and contrastive-based denoisers (e.g., Efficient-UNet discriminators, structure-aware contrastive learning) reduce overfitting and improve results</cite>.<cite id="81ffb256-2">Noise2Noise and self-averaging targets provide unbiased supervision from noisy data, improving data efficiency</cite>. For quantization/entropy-based priors, learned codes must be carefully regularized to avoid degeneracies, and zero-shot methods depend on the quality of the base code.<cite id="81ffb256-4">Zero-shot neural compression denoising assumes a fixed code and derives theoretical performance bounds; extending to fully learned codes is a future direction</cite>.

Evaluation should combine PSNR/SSIM with perceptual and task-based metrics. For images, standard sets (Set12, BSD68/CBSD68, Urban100) and noise levels (15,25,50) provide reproducible comparisons; for audio, intelligibility and quality assessments complement objective metrics.<cite id="13aecbbc-0">Comparisons on Set12/BSD68 with σ=15,25,50 provide consistent PSNR/SSIM baselines across methods</cite>.<cite id="8e4a5bdb-0">Audio denoising improvements are tied to better speech intelligibility and quality under adverse conditions</cite>.

# Domain-Specific Considerations

- Images and video: CNNs and transformers with efficient multi-resolution backbones dominate; video methods exploit temporal redundancy to reduce noise while preserving motion.<cite id="8e4a5bdb-0">Transformers and diffusion models improved image denoising; video denoisers (DVDnet, FastDVDnet) use multi-frame information for real-time results</cite>.

- Audio and speech: TF-domain CNNs, WaveNet-style generative models, and diffusion-based approaches address nonstationary noise and reverberation; modeling complex spectrograms and phases is crucial for fidelity.<cite id="8e4a5bdb-3">Most TF methods historically used magnitude only, neglecting phase; complex-valued modeling improved performance</cite>.<cite id="8e4a5bdb-1">Diffusion transformers with multiple spectrogram inputs and adaptive normalization capture complex audio structure for high-quality denoising</cite>.

- Scientific/functional data: Neural operator methods learn mappings from function-to-function (e.g., PDE evolutions), offering a principled route for denoising and propagation under physical constraints; universal approximation for operators supports their efficacy.<cite id="5ef7b162-0">Neural operators approximate continuous function-space operators under embedding and approximation conditions</cite>.<cite id="5ef7b162-3">UAP-O supports operator learning for families of solutions, relevant for physics-informed denoising</cite>.<cite id="5ef7b162-4">Nonlocal dependencies require nonlocal architectures; purely local single-layer operators cannot approximate simple nonlocal mappings</cite>.

# Limitations and Open Directions

Neural denoisers can be sensitive to dataset shift (e.g., noise distributions, domains), and high-capacity models risk overfitting without strong regularization or self-supervision. Extending zero-shot and compression-based denoising to fully learned codes and broader noise models remains an active area.<cite id="81ffb256-4">Zero-shot neural compression denoising assumes fixed codes and provides theoretical characterizations; learning the code itself is an open research direction</cite>. For 1D signals and ECG/physio data, hybrid temporal architectures and modality-specific priors are promising but need standardized benchmarks and robust evaluation across clinical settings.<cite id="81ffb256-1">Deep learning for spatio-temporal signal denoising highlights the need to model serial correlation and domain-specific structures</cite>. Finally, while transformers and diffusion models yield state-of-the-art quality, inference cost and compute remain challenges for real-time applications, motivating efficient attention and latent-space formulations.<cite id="8e4a5bdb-0">Transformers and diffusion achieve SOTA but require careful design for scalability and efficiency</cite>.

# Key Takeaways

- CNN baselines (DnCNN, FFDNet, DRUNet) provide strong, efficient image denoisers with documented PSNR/SSIM gains over classical and earlier deep methods across standard datasets and noise levels.<cite id="13aecbbc-4">FFDNet surpasses BM3D/WNNM and is competitive with DnCNN at low noise, outperforming at higher noise</cite><cite id="13aecbbc-2">DRUNet achieves ~0.9 dB average PSNR gain over BM3D and ~0.5 dB over DnCNN/IRCNN/FFDNet on Set12, with ~0.25 dB on BSD68</cite><cite id="13aecbbc-1">Recent variants (e.g., SDIDNet) show ~0.3 dB gains over DnCNN and improved visual detail on BSD68</cite>.

- Transformers and diffusion models set new records by capturing long-range dependencies and complex noise structures; in audio, diffusion-based and transformer architectures handle severe noise and reverberation beyond spectral subtraction.<cite id="8e4a5bdb-0">Transformers and diffusion models achieve SOTA in image and audio denoising</cite><cite id="8e4a5bdb-1">Diffusion transformer backbones tailored to spectrograms improve denoised audio quality</cite><cite id="8e4a5bdb-3">Diffusion-based audio denoisers outperform several baselines in complex noise</cite>.

- Unsupervised and zero-shot approaches (Noise2Noise, deep image prior, neural compression) enable data-efficient training and robustness without clean labels, with theoretical performance characterizations in zero-shot settings.<cite id="81ffb256-2">Noise2Noise enables unbiased training from multiple noisy views</cite><cite id="81ffb256-0">Deep image prior can optimize a single noisy image to implicitly model the clean signal</cite><cite id="81ffb256-4">Zero-shot neural compression denoising achieves SOTA with theoretical bounds under specified noise models</cite>.

- Theoretical foundations show neural operators’ universal approximation capabilities for nonlocal mappings, explaining the success of modern denoisers and motivating operator-learning approaches for functional data and physics-informed tasks.<cite id="5ef7b162-0">Averaging neural operators are universal approximators under stated conditions</cite><cite id="5ef7b162-4">Nonlocality is essential; purely local single-layer operators cannot approximate nonlocal mappings like shifts</cite>.

- Practical success hinges on regularization (batch normalization, residual/nonlocal blocks), strong data regimes (paired, self-supervised, or compressed priors), and balanced evaluation with objective and perceptual metrics tailored to the modality and application domain.<cite id="81ffb256-3">Residual learning and attention-based designs improve denoising of complex backgrounds and reduce overfitting with auxiliary losses</cite><cite id="13aecbbc-0">Standard PSNR/SSIM on Set12/BSD68 with multiple noise levels provides reproducible comparisons</cite><cite id="8e4a5bdb-0">Audio denoising benefits are measured by intelligibility and quality under adverse conditions</cite>.

Obtained mean image can be used for train the denoising neural network as the expected output signal y in solving of loss E minimization problem (9). An input signal x can be taken random image from series under consideration. But in this case value y consists noise component from input signal x. If input image has been excluded from series before averaging step, then we made approximation of clear image without noise component of input signal and this setting is consistent with theory of Noise2Noise work [1]. This ground truth signal y are constructed using the formula (8). Thereby, when we train denoising network to predict signal y , it train to extract additional features from input signal by Noise2Noise approach logic for achieving more denoising quality. FFDNet [14] effectively solves the problem of blind denoising by using noisy image blocks and noisy mapping blocks as inputs to the network. This network design utilizes the correlation between features and optimizes the propagation of residual features through spatial gating mechanisms, thereby improving denoising performance.

Title: Generative AI for Multimedia Communication: Recent Advances, An Information-Theoretic Framework, and Future Opportunities
Snippet: Denoising, the removal of random noise from images or audio, is another area that has been revolutionized. While not always a result of transmission, noise often creeps in via sensors or analog communications, and denoising is critical for clarity. Classic filters have given way to deep denoisers like DnCNN [70] and FFDNet [71]. In the last few years, as with SR, transformers and diffusion models have set new records in denoising performance. The previously mentioned Restormer [67] not only addresses SR but also achieves SOTA in image denoising, leveraging self-attention to handle spatially varying noise effectively. It outperforms earlier CNNs and even specialized designs, especially on high-resolution images where modeling long-range correlations helps differentiate noise from signal. Researchers have applied pretrained diffusion models [37] to image denoising by simply using the diffusion reverse process on a noisy image conditional on a guidance signal; this has proven effective even for severe noise. Moreover, unsupervised approaches like deep image prior [60] showed that a network can be optimized to a single noisy image, implicitly modeling the clean image. For video, deep video denoising methods like DVDnet [57] and FastDVDnet [58] use multi-frame information to reduce noise while preserving motion details. As a result, it's now feasible to clean up grainy, low-light video in real-time applications, improving visual quality for end users. In audio, speech denoising and dereverberation have also embraced GANs and diffusion models. The latest speech enhancement diffusion models can remove complex noise patterns and reverberation while preserving speech intelligibility, a task where older spectral subtraction methods struggled. These improvements directly impact VoIP and video conferencing quality by making voices clearer under adverse conditions.
</snippet>

Title: Complex Image-Generative Diffusion Transformer for Audio Denoising
Snippet: Then, diffusion probabilistic models were used to get high-quality image synthesis results using a relatively simple architecture and training procedure.Recently, diffusion models achieved more competitive results than GANs and have achieved impressive results in various applications such as text-to-image generation [9], audio synthesis [10], and video generation [11].

Most deep learning-based models for audio denoising focus on time-frequency domain (TF) methods.Due to the estimation difficulties, the majority of TF-domain approaches only accept magnitude as an input to real-valued parameter models and ignore complex-valued phases, which have an impact on performance.Although WaveNet, U-Net, or other convolutional designs serve as the basis for the majority of diffusion models, they are not scalable enough to model additional visual information.Hence, we explore a diffusion model based on a transformer with multiple inputs to capture more information and gain better complex image generation to estimate clean audio.

To overcome the aforementioned challenges, we design a novel framework with attention diffusion on multiple input spectrograms, the complex image-generative diffusion transformer network (CIGDTN) model.We propose a complex image-generative Diffusion Transformer (CIGDT) module based on diffusion transformers (DiTs) with adaptive layer norm zero (adaLN-Zero) and sparse attention diffusion to capture more information.We also design a CIGDT block to inherit the excellent scaling properties of the transformer model and save computation costs.Furthermore, we deploy the CIGDT module to process the real and imaginary spectrograms, respectively, to make full use of the phase information in noisy audio.In addition, we apply FlashAttention-2, a novel attention algorithm with better work partitioning, to address lowoccupancy or unnecessary shared memory reads and writes on the GPU [12].Overall, our contributions are threefold:

• We propose a complex diffusion transformer with multiple inputs that can generate high-quality denoised audio.• We present a complex image-generative diffusion transformer network (CIGDTN) model that fuses diffusion transformers with adaLN-Zero and sparse attention diffusion with FlashAttention-2 algorithm to gain better complex images.
</snippet>
