# Overview: Neural Network Signal Denoising

Neural network denoising estimates a clean signal from noisy observations by learning a posterior mapping p(clean | noisy) or a residual field, and has largely superseded classical linear/nonlinear filters for rich priors and complex noise structures.<cite id="8e4a5bdb-0">Deep denoisers like DnCNN and FFDNet replaced classic filters, and recent work shows transformers and diffusion models set new records across images, video, and audio</cite>.<cite id="81ffb256-3">DnCNN and FFDNet introduced residual learning, batch normalization, and blind denoising formulations that improved accuracy and speed</cite> In practice, denoising is evaluated with pixel-wise metrics (PSNR, SSIM) on standard image sets (Set12, BSD68/CBSD68, Urban100) and with perceptual/intelligibility metrics for audio; multi-frame video uses PSNR/SSIM and structural measures while preserving motion details.<cite id="13aecbbc-0">Benchmarking commonly compares methods on Set12 and BSD68 at noise levels 15, 25, 50 and reports average PSNR/SSIM</cite>.<cite id="8e4a5bdb-0">Video denoisers like DVDnet/FastDVDnet leverage multi-frame information to preserve motion while reducing noise</cite> <cite id="8e4a5bdb-0">Audio denoisers using GANs and diffusion now handle complex nonstationary noise and reverberation beyond spectral subtraction, improving clarity in VoIP and conferencing</cite>.

# Architectures and Model Classes

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have dominated image denoising due to their ability to model local and global structures with stacks of convolutional layers, residual blocks, and efficient training on large datasets.<cite id="81ffb256-3">DnCNN used residual learning and batch normalization to accelerate training and improve denoising; FFDNet solved blind denoising with a compact CNN</cite> <cite id="13aecbbc-4">FFDNet outperformed BM3D and DnCNN at higher noise levels and traded off with DnCNN at low noise via receptive field vs. modeling capacity</cite>.<cite id="13aecbbc-2">DRUNet further improved over BM3D, DnCNN, IRCNN, and FFDNet on Set12 and BSD68, with average PSNR gains of ~0.9 dB and ~0.5 dB on Set12 and ~0.25 dB on BSD68</cite>.<cite id="13aecbbc-1">Recent variants (e.g., SDIDNet) report gains over DnCNN of ~0.3 dB on grayscale BSD68 and improved visual details</cite>.

Transformers bring global, multi-head attention to denoising and have achieved state-of-the-art results by capturing long-range dependencies and spatially varying noise patterns.<cite id="8e4a5bdb-0">Restormer achieved SOTA in image denoising by leveraging self-attention to handle spatially varying noise, surpassing earlier CNNs</cite>.<cite id="8e4a5bdb-0">For audio, diffusion-based approaches using the reverse process with guidance can remove severe noise while preserving intelligibility</cite>.<cite id="8e4a5bdb-1">Complex image-generative diffusion transformer (CIGDTN) models process real and imaginary spectrogram branches to exploit phase information for higher-quality denoised audio</cite>.<cite id="8e4a5bdb-2">Masked diffusion temporal-aware transformers (MDSGen) couple diffusion backbones with VAEs and temporal masking to efficiently generate audio features</cite>.<cite id="8e4a5bdb-4">Audio-visual diffusion transformers (AV-DiT) operate in latent space with modality-specific adapters, enabling joint audio and video denoising from Gaussian noise</cite>.

Diffusion models provide a flexible generative framework for denoising by learning to reverse a forward noising process; in denoising tasks, a U-Net or transformer denoiser can be conditioned on noisy observations and step embeddings to recover clean signals.<cite id="8e4a5bdb-0">Diffusion models have achieved competitive or best-in-class results on image denoising and are applicable to audio via reverse process conditioning or specialized architectures</cite>.<cite id="8e4a5bdb-3">Audio denoising via diffusion has outperformed prior methods like DCU-Net and MANNER in some settings by converting denoising into image-like complex-valued generation in the Fourier domain</cite>.<cite id="8e4a5bdb-1">Diffusion transformer backbones with adaptive normalization and sparse attention have been adapted to multiple spectrogram inputs to better capture complex audio structure</cite>.

# Generative Priors and Zero-Shot/Unsupervised Training

Generative models provide learned priors over clean signals that, when combined with likelihoods of observed noise, define maximum-likelihood or Bayesian estimators for denoising. Unsupervised and weakly supervised training strategies are central for data efficiency and robustness.<cite id="81ffb256-2">Noise2Noise enables training with noisy-only supervision by averaging across noisy views to approximate clean ground truth, aligning with theory that removing input correlations yields unbiased targets</cite>.<cite id="81ffb256-3">Adversarial and self-supervised variants (e.g., Efficient-UNet-based discriminators, contrastive feature learning, and dynamic convolutions) reduce overfitting and improve denoising of complex backgrounds</cite>.<cite id="81ffb256-0">Self-supervised denoising networks can be trained to improve downstream recognition performance, offering an alternative evaluation by task transfer</cite>.

Zero-shot neural compression denoising uses learned quantization and entropy models to implicitly encode a prior over clean signals, enabling denoising without explicit paired clean/noisy datasets.<cite id="81ffb256-4">Zero-shot neural-compression denoising (ZS-NCD) provides theoretical performance characterizations under AWGN and Poisson noise and achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot results by leveraging maximum-likelihood compression priors</cite>.<cite id="81ffb256-4">A key assumption is a fixed code (pre-trained/defined) with extension work exploring learned compression codes</cite>.

# Quantitative Benchmarks and Results

Image denoising benchmarks provide standard comparisons across noise levels and datasets. CNN baselines like DnCNN, FFDNet, and DRUNet set strong references for evaluating newer architectures.<cite id="13aecbbc-4">On gray-level denoising, FFDNet surpasses BM3D and WNNM, and is competitive with DnCNN at low noise while outperforming at higher noise due to larger receptive field and efficient design</cite>.<cite id="13aecbbc-2">DRUNet reports average PSNR gains of ~0.9 dB over BM3D and ~0.5 dB over DnCNN/IRCNN/FFDNet on Set12, with ~0.25 dB on BSD68</cite>.<cite id="13aecbbc-1">SDIDNet shows ~0.3 dB gains over DnCNN on BSD68 at multiple noise levels and better texture detail</cite>.<cite id="13aecbbc-0">A recent method reported 0.83 dB advantage over BM3D at σ=50 on Set12 and outperformed DnCNN/FFDNet by 0.37–1.21 dB across datasets and noise levels</cite>. For audio, diffusion-based denoisers and GAN-based architectures improve speech intelligibility under nonstationary noise and reverberation compared to spectral subtraction/MMSE filters, though quantitative metrics vary by dataset and task.<cite id="8e4a5bdb-0">Speech enhancement with GANs and diffusion outperforms older spectral methods in complex noise/reverberation conditions</cite>.<cite id="8e4a5bdb-3">Diffusion-based audio denoisers have demonstrated competitive or superior performance to complex image-based baselines (e.g., DCU-Net, MANNER) by modeling Fourier-domain complex structure</cite>.

# Sequence and 1D Signal Denoising

For 1D time series and audio, recurrent and transformer architectures capture temporal dependencies and long-range structure; spectrogram- or time-frequency-domain CNNs/transformers are common for nonstationary noise modeling.<cite id="81ffb256-1">Hybrid deep learning for spatio-temporal signals has addressed serial correlation; attention-based CNNs have been used to approximate wavelet/S-transform features, and DAE variants evolved from time-DAE to spatial-DAE for signal denoising</cite>.<cite id="8e4a5bdb-3">Audio denoising models increasingly operate in time-frequency (TF) domains, with many TF methods using magnitude only and neglecting phase; complex-valued modeling improves fidelity</cite>.<cite id="81ffb256-1">Deep learning for fiber/waterfall diagram denoising and optical signal processing has shown that learned feature extractors can approximate classical transforms while improving real-time performance</cite>. In video, multi-frame CNNs and transformer denoisers jointly exploit temporal redundancy to reduce noise while preserving motion and structure.<cite id="8e4a5bdb-0">Deep video denoisers (DVDnet, FastDVDnet) use multi-frame information to denoise in real time while preserving motion details</cite>.

# Theory and Estimator Interpretations

Neural networks can approximate a wide class of operators, which explains their success at modeling inverse problems including denoising; universal approximation theorems for operators and function-on-function mappings provide a foundation.<cite id="5ef7b162-0">Averaging neural operators are universal approximators of continuous operators between suitable function spaces, under conditions on embeddings and network components</cite>.<cite id="5ef7b162-1">Universal approximation for operators follows from constructive procedures using function and functional approximation results with appropriate activation classes</cite>.<cite id="5ef7b162-3">Neural operators (UAP-O) can approximate nonlinear continuous operators from function spaces, enabling learning mappings with parametric dependencies (e.g., families of PDE solutions)</cite>.<cite id="5ef7b162-2">Universal approximation for neural operators and function spaces underpins dimension-informed operator learning, with error bounds derived via composite approximation chains</cite>.<cite id="5ef7b162-4">Nonlocality and nonlinearity are necessary for universal approximation in neural operators; single-layer local compositions (e.g., MLPs) are insufficient to approximate even simple nonlocal operators like shifts</cite>.

These results connect to classical estimators: for additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN), linear MMSE (Wiener) filters and nonlinears like NL Means are strong baselines; data-driven denoisers can approximate or outperform these by learning nonlinear, nonlocal dependencies and heavy-tailed priors, especially at high noise levels.<cite id="13aecbbc-4">At high noise, larger receptive fields and learned priors (e.g., FFDNet) outperform small-capacity models, consistent with classical trade-offs where MMSE performance degrades with low SNR</cite>.<cite id="5ef7b162-4">The inability of purely local, single-layer operators to model nonlocal dependencies explains why deeper architectures with attention or nonlocal blocks improve denoising beyond classical filters</cite>.

# Training Regimes: Supervised, Self-Supervised, and Unsupervised

- Supervised: Clean/noisy paired data allow direct regression or residual learning; CNN baselines (DnCNN, FFDNet) and modern variants train with L1/MAE or L2 losses and often include perceptual/texture loss terms.<cite id="81ffb256-3">DnCNN and FFDNet employ residual learning and batch normalization to stabilize and accelerate training for blind denoising</cite>.<cite id="13aecbbc-4">FFDNet’s architecture and tuning show trade-offs between receptive field and modeling capacity across noise levels</cite>.

- Self-supervised/Noise2Noise: Multiple noisy views or frames produce an unbiased clean estimate via temporal averaging, enabling training without clean labels.<cite id="81ffb256-2">Noise2Noise constructs targets by averaging noisy observations to approximate clean images, and training on a single noisy image (Deep Image Prior) can implicitly model the clean image</cite>.

- Zero-shot/Compression-based: Quantized encoders and entropy models provide implicit priors; maximum-likelihood decoding denoises under unknown noise statistics without clean data.<cite id="81ffb256-4">Zero-shot neural compression denoising characterizes performance theoretically and achieves SOTA zero-shot denoising under AWGN and Poisson noise</cite>.

- Generative adversarial and diffusion: Adversarial training can regularize denoisers and improve perceptual quality; diffusion denoisers learn to reverse noise addition, often achieving high-fidelity outputs under severe noise with appropriate architectures and guidance.<cite id="81ffb256-3">Adversarial distortion learning with Efficient-UNet discriminators improved denoising while mitigating overfitting</cite>.<cite id="8e4a5bdb-0">Transformers and diffusion models set new records in denoising, including audio, by leveraging attention and reverse diffusion processes</cite>.

# Practical Guidance: Regularization, Overfitting, and Data Efficiency

Overfitting and data efficiency are central concerns. Batch normalization, residual blocks, and strong priors (nonlocal blocks, attention) help stabilize training and reduce overfitting in limited-label regimes; adversarial and self-supervised losses can further improve generalization.<cite id="81ffb256-3">Batch normalization and residual learning in DnCNN accelerated training and enhanced performance; attention-based ADNet improved noise extraction in complex backgrounds</cite>.<cite id="81ffb256-3">Adversarial and contrastive-based denoisers (e.g., Efficient-UNet discriminators, structure-aware contrastive learning) reduce overfitting and improve results</cite>.<cite id="81ffb256-2">Noise2Noise and self-averaging targets provide unbiased supervision from noisy data, improving data efficiency</cite>. For quantization/entropy-based priors, learned codes must be carefully regularized to avoid degeneracies, and zero-shot methods depend on the quality of the base code.<cite id="81ffb256-4">Zero-shot neural compression denoising assumes a fixed code and derives theoretical performance bounds; extending to fully learned codes is a future direction</cite>.

Evaluation should combine PSNR/SSIM with perceptual and task-based metrics. For images, standard sets (Set12, BSD68/CBSD68, Urban100) and noise levels (15,25,50) provide reproducible comparisons; for audio, intelligibility and quality assessments complement objective metrics.<cite id="13aecbbc-0">Comparisons on Set12/BSD68 with σ=15,25,50 provide consistent PSNR/SSIM baselines across methods</cite>.<cite id="8e4a5bdb-0">Audio denoising improvements are tied to better speech intelligibility and quality under adverse conditions</cite>.

# Domain-Specific Considerations

- Images and video: CNNs and transformers with efficient multi-resolution backbones dominate; video methods exploit temporal redundancy to reduce noise while preserving motion.<cite id="8e4a5bdb-0">Transformers and diffusion models improved image denoising; video denoisers (DVDnet, FastDVDnet) use multi-frame information for real-time results</cite>.

- Audio and speech: TF-domain CNNs, WaveNet-style generative models, and diffusion-based approaches address nonstationary noise and reverberation; modeling complex spectrograms and phases is crucial for fidelity.<cite id="8e4a5bdb-3">Most TF methods historically used magnitude only, neglecting phase; complex-valued modeling improved performance</cite>.<cite id="8e4a5bdb-1">Diffusion transformers with multiple spectrogram inputs and adaptive normalization capture complex audio structure for high-quality denoising</cite>.

- Scientific/functional data: Neural operator methods learn mappings from function-to-function (e.g., PDE evolutions), offering a principled route for denoising and propagation under physical constraints; universal approximation for operators supports their efficacy.<cite id="5ef7b162-0">Neural operators approximate continuous function-space operators under embedding and approximation conditions</cite>.<cite id="5ef7b162-3">UAP-O supports operator learning for families of solutions, relevant for physics-informed denoising</cite>.<cite id="5ef7b162-4">Nonlocal dependencies require nonlocal architectures; purely local single-layer operators cannot approximate simple nonlocal mappings</cite>.

# Limitations and Open Directions

Neural denoisers can be sensitive to dataset shift (e.g., noise distributions, domains), and high-capacity models risk overfitting without strong regularization or self-supervision. Extending zero-shot and compression-based denoising to fully learned codes and broader noise models remains an active area.<cite id="81ffb256-4">Zero-shot neural compression denoising assumes fixed codes and provides theoretical characterizations; learning the code itself is an open research direction</cite>. For 1D signals and ECG/physio data, hybrid temporal architectures and modality-specific priors are promising but need standardized benchmarks and robust evaluation across clinical settings.<cite id="81ffb256-1">Deep learning for spatio-temporal signal denoising highlights the need to model serial correlation and domain-specific structures</cite>. Finally, while transformers and diffusion models yield state-of-the-art quality, inference cost and compute remain challenges for real-time applications, motivating efficient attention and latent-space formulations.<cite id="8e4a5bdb-0">Transformers and diffusion achieve SOTA but require careful design for scalability and efficiency</cite>.

# Key Takeaways

- CNN baselines (DnCNN, FFDNet, DRUNet) provide strong, efficient image denoisers with documented PSNR/SSIM gains over classical and earlier deep methods across standard datasets and noise levels.<cite id="13aecbbc-4">FFDNet surpasses BM3D/WNNM and is competitive with DnCNN at low noise, outperforming at higher noise</cite><cite id="13aecbbc-2">DRUNet achieves ~0.9 dB average PSNR gain over BM3D and ~0.5 dB over DnCNN/IRCNN/FFDNet on Set12, with ~0.25 dB on BSD68</cite><cite id="13aecbbc-1">Recent variants (e.g., SDIDNet) show ~0.3 dB gains over DnCNN and improved visual detail on BSD68</cite>.

- Transformers and diffusion models set new records by capturing long-range dependencies and complex noise structures; in audio, diffusion-based and transformer architectures handle severe noise and reverberation beyond spectral subtraction.<cite id="8e4a5bdb-0">Transformers and diffusion models achieve SOTA in image and audio denoising</cite><cite id="8e4a5bdb-1">Diffusion transformer backbones tailored to spectrograms improve denoised audio quality</cite><cite id="8e4a5bdb-3">Diffusion-based audio denoisers outperform several baselines in complex noise</cite>.

- Unsupervised and zero-shot approaches (Noise2Noise, deep image prior, neural compression) enable data-efficient training and robustness without clean labels, with theoretical performance characterizations in zero-shot settings.<cite id="81ffb256-2">Noise2Noise enables unbiased training from multiple noisy views</cite><cite id="81ffb256-0">Deep image prior can optimize a single noisy image to implicitly model the clean signal</cite><cite id="81ffb256-4">Zero-shot neural compression denoising achieves SOTA with theoretical bounds under specified noise models</cite>.

- Theoretical foundations show neural operators’ universal approximation capabilities for nonlocal mappings, explaining the success of modern denoisers and motivating operator-learning approaches for functional data and physics-informed tasks.<cite id="5ef7b162-0">Averaging neural operators are universal approximators under stated conditions</cite><cite id="5ef7b162-4">Nonlocality is essential; purely local single-layer operators cannot approximate nonlocal mappings like shifts</cite>.

- Practical success hinges on regularization (batch normalization, residual/nonlocal blocks), strong data regimes (paired, self-supervised, or compressed priors), and balanced evaluation with objective and perceptual metrics tailored to the modality and application domain.<cite id="81ffb256-3">Residual learning and attention-based designs improve denoising of complex backgrounds and reduce overfitting with auxiliary losses</cite><cite id="13aecbbc-0">Standard PSNR/SSIM on Set12/BSD68 with multiple noise levels provides reproducible comparisons</cite><cite id="8e4a5bdb-0">Audio denoising benefits are measured by intelligibility and quality under adverse conditions</cite>.
</answer>

Title: Reduction of Noise in Restoration of Images Using Mean and Median Filtering Techniques
Snippet: Since selection of the right denoising procedure plays a major role, it is important to experiment and compare the methods. As future research, we would like to work further on the comparison of the denoising techniques. If the features of the denoised signal are fed into a neural network pattern recognizer, then the rate of successful classification should determine the ultimate measure by which to compare various denoising procedures in image restoration.

Title: Fiber Signal Denoising Algorithm using Hybrid Deep Learning Networks
Snippet: Two-dimensional signal denoising focuses on image denoising of waterfall diagrams. This problem was viewed as an image defuzzification problem in [15], with the fast iterative shrinkage thresholding algorithm utilized to improve image resolution. Although noise can be removed to a certain extent, this method still lacks real-time processing. Deep learning algorithms have made remarkable achievements in image denoising these years [33]. Neural networks can achieve higher denoising accuracy by using a large amount of data for training. Artificial neural networks were first introduced into the field of optical fiber signal denoising in [5] and achieved clearly visible outcomes. An attentionbased convolutional neural network was proposed in [14] to approximate classical methods (wavelet transform and S-transform) results. DAE was first utilized in [15] and further modified from time-DAE to spatial-DAE in [16]. But currently deep-learning based algorithms do not take into account the serial correlation of spatio-temporal signals, ignoring the intrinsic relationship.

Title: Unsupervised Training of Denoising Networks
Snippet: In this work we produce a novel method for training denoising neural network architectures. This approach combine traditional supervised method for training autoencoder neural network architectures and approach produced by authors of Noise2Noise work [1]. 

When we have image series of one scene obtained in different time (see Sect. 3), we can average this image series and made approximation of expected clear image. Obtained mean image can be used for train the denoising neural network as the expected output signal y in solving of loss E minimization problem (9). An input signal x can be taken random image from series under consideration. But in this case value y consists noise component from input signal x. If input image has been excluded from series before averaging step, then we made approximation of clear image without noise component of input signal and this setting is consistent with theory of Noise2Noise work [1]. This ground truth signal y are constructed using the formula (8). Thereby, when we train denoising network to predict signal y , it train to extract additional features from input signal by Noise2Noise approach logic for achieving more denoising quality. Scheme of this approach also is shown (see Fig. 3).

Title: NAF-MEEF: A Nonlinear Activation-Free Network Based on Multi-Scale Edge Enhancement and Fusion for Railway Freight Car Image Denoising
Snippet: The self-supervised denoising methods represented by N2N [9], N2S [10], S2S [11], and VDN [12] lack flexibility in adjusting network parameters, and the extracted features cannot fully represent noise, making it difficult to obtain complex mapping relationships between noisy images and denoised images. 

Supervised learning can effectively address the issues present in the aforementioned self-supervised denoising techniques. DnCNN [13] accelerates the training process and enhances model denoising performance by employing residual learning and batch normalization techniques. FFDNet [14] effectively solves the problem of blind denoising by using noisy image blocks and noisy mapping blocks as inputs to the network. ADNet [15] introduces a denoising convolutional neural network guided by an attention mechanism, enabling finer extraction of noise information from complex backgrounds, thus achieving superior denoising results. ADL [3] introduces an adversarial distortion learning-based denoising method, where both the denoiser and discriminator are implemented using an autoencoder architecture known as Efficient-UNet. This approach effectively mitigates overfitting during training and improves the model's denoising performance. DRAN [16] removes noise from images by integrating attention mechanisms and dynamic convolution operations while preserving critical image details. This network design utilizes the correlation between features and optimizes the propagation of residual features through spatial gating mechanisms, thereby improving denoising performance. 

On this basis, recent research has further explored denoising mechanisms in specific task scenarios. Yang et al. propose DIPKD [17], which enhances lightweight SAR object detection via Selective Noise Suppression, Knowledge Level Decoupling, and Reverse Information Transfer, effectively filtering speckle noise and boosting student model performance. Saidulu and Muduli [18] designed DP-LDCTNet for low-dose CT denoising, combining Dynamic Convolution, a Structure-aware Network trained with contrastive learning, and CT-specific perceptual loss to preserve structural integrity.

Title: Zero-shot denoising via neural compression: Theoretical and algorithmic framework
Snippet: We have studied maximum likelihood compression-based denoising, and provided theoretical characterization of its performance under both AWGN and Poisson noise. Furthermore, we introduced ZS-NCD, a new zero-shot neural-compression-based denoising and demonstrated that it achieves state-of-the-art performance among zero-shot methods, in both AWGN and Poisson denoising. 

The presented theoretical results are derived by assuming a fixed (e.g., pre-trained/defined) compression code. Extending these results to the case of zero-shot learned compression codes is an interesting direction for future research.

In this work we produce a novel method for training denoising neural network architectures. This approach combine traditional supervised method for training autoencoder neural network architectures and approach produced by authors of Noise2Noise work [1]. 

When we have image series of one scene obtained in different time (see Sect. 3), we can average this image series and made approximation of expected clear image. Obtained mean image can be used for train the denoising neural network as the expected output signal y in solving of loss E minimization problem (9). An input signal x can be taken random image from series under consideration. But in this case value y consists noise component from input signal x. If input image has been excluded from series before averaging step, then we made approximation of clear image without noise component of input signal and this setting is consistent with theory of Noise2Noise work [1]. This ground truth signal y are constructed using the formula (8). Thereby, when we train denoising network to predict signal y , it train to extract additional features from input signal by Noise2Noise approach logic for achieving more denoising quality. Scheme of this approach also is shown (see Fig. 3).

documents.title: NAF-MEEF: A Nonlinear Activation-Free Network Based on Multi-Scale Edge Enhancement and Fusion for Railway Freight Car Image Denoising
documents.snippet:
The self-supervised denoising methods represented by N2N [9], N2S [10], S2S [11], and VDN [12] lack flexibility in adjusting network parameters, and the extracted features cannot fully represent noise, making it difficult to obtain complex mapping relationships between noisy images and denoised images. 

Supervised learning can effectively address the issues present in the aforementioned self-supervised denoising techniques. DnCNN [13] accelerates the training process and enhances model denoising performance by employing residual learning and batch normalization techniques. FFDNet [14] effectively solves the problem of blind denoising by using noisy image blocks and noisy mapping blocks as inputs to the network. ADNet [15] introduces a denoising convolutional neural network guided by an attention mechanism, enabling finer extraction of noise information from complex backgrounds, thus achieving superior denoising results. ADL [3] introduces an adversarial distortion learning-based denoising method, where both the denoiser and discriminator are implemented using an autoencoder architecture known as Efficient-UNet. This approach effectively mitigates overfitting during training and improves the model's denoising performance. DRAN [16] removes noise from images by integrating attention mechanisms and dynamic convolution operations while preserving critical image details. This network design utilizes the correlation between features and optimizes the propagation of residual features through spatial gating mechanisms, thereby improving denoising performance. 

On this basis, recent research has further explored denoising mechanisms in specific task scenarios. Yang et al. propose DIPKD [17], which enhances lightweight SAR object detection via Selective Noise Suppression, Knowledge Level Decoupling, and Reverse Information Transfer, effectively filtering speckle noise and boosting student model performance. Saidulu and Muduli [18] designed DP-LDCTNet for low-dose CT denoising, combining Dynamic Convolution, a Structure-aware Network trained with contrastive learning, and CT-specific perceptual loss to preserve structural integrity.

documents.title: Zero-shot denoising via neural compression: Theoretical and algorithmic framework
documents.snippet:
We have studied maximum likelihood compression-based denoising, and provided theoretical characterization of its performance under both AWGN and Poisson noise. Furthermore, we introduced ZS-NCD, a new zero-shot neural-compression-based denoising and demonstrated that it achieves state-of-the-art performance among zero-shot methods, in both AWGN and Poisson denoising. 

The presented theoretical results are derived by assuming a fixed (e.g., pre-trained/defined) compression code. Extending these results to the case of zero-shot learned compression codes is an interesting direction for future research.

Title: Generative AI for Multimedia Communication: Recent Advances, An Information-Theoretic Framework, and Future Opportunities
Snippet: Denoising, the removal of random noise from images or audio, is another area that has been revolutionized. While not always a result of transmission, noise often creeps in via sensors or analog communications, and denoising is critical for clarity. Classic filters have given way to deep denoisers like DnCNN [70] and FFDNet [71]. In the last few years, as with SR, transformers and diffusion models have set new records in denoising performance. The previously mentioned Restormer [67] not only addresses SR but also achieves SOTA in image denoising, leveraging self-attention to handle spatially varying noise effectively. It outperforms earlier CNNs and even specialized designs, especially on high-resolution images where modeling long-range correlations helps differentiate noise from signal. Researchers have applied pretrained diffusion models [37] to image denoising by simply using the diffusion reverse process on a noisy image conditional on a guidance signal; this has proven effective even for severe noise. Moreover, unsupervised approaches like deep image prior [60] showed that a network can be optimized to a single noisy image, implicitly modeling the clean image. For video, deep video denoising methods like DVDnet [57] and FastDVDnet [58] use multi-frame information to reduce noise while preserving motion details. As a result, it's now feasible to clean up grainy, low-light video in real-time applications, improving visual quality for end users. In audio, speech denoising and dereverberation have also embraced GANs and diffusion models. The latest speech enhancement diffusion models can remove complex noise patterns and reverberation while preserving speech intelligibility, a task where older spectral subtraction methods struggled. These improvements directly impact VoIP and video conferencing quality by making voices clearer under adverse conditions.

Title: Complex Image-Generative Diffusion Transformer for Audio Denoising
Snippet: Then, diffusion probabilistic models were used to get high-quality image synthesis results using a relatively simple architecture and training procedure.Recently, diffusion models achieved more competitive results than GANs and have achieved impressive results in various applications such as text-to-image generation [9], audio synthesis [10], and video generation [11].

Most deep learning-based models for audio denoising focus on time-frequency domain (TF) methods.Due to the estimation difficulties, the majority of TF-domain approaches only accept magnitude as an input to real-valued parameter models and ignore complex-valued phases, which have an impact on performance.Although WaveNet, U-Net, or other convolutional designs serve as the basis for the majority of diffusion models, they are not scalable enough to model additional visual information.Hence, we explore a diffusion model based on a transformer with multiple inputs to capture more information and gain better complex image generation to estimate clean audio.

To overcome the aforementioned challenges, we design a novel framework with attention diffusion on multiple input spectrograms, the complex image-generative diffusion transformer network (CIGDTN) model.We propose a complex image-generative Diffusion Transformer (CIGDT) module based on diffusion transformers (DiTs) with adaptive layer norm zero (adaLN-Zero) and sparse attention diffusion to capture more information.We also design a CIGDT block to inherit the excellent scaling properties of the transformer model and save computation costs.Furthermore, we deploy the CIGDT module to process the real and imaginary spectrograms, respectively, to make full use of the phase information in noisy audio.In addition, we apply FlashAttention-2, a novel attention algorithm with better work partitioning, to address lowoccupancy or unnecessary shared memory reads and writes on the GPU [12].Overall, our contributions are threefold:

• We propose a complex diffusion transformer with multiple inputs that can generate high-quality denoised audio.• We present a complex image-generative diffusion transformer network (CIGDTN) model that fuses diffusion transformers with adaLN-Zero and sparse attention diffusion with FlashAttention-2 algorithm to gain better complex images.

Title: Complex Image-Generative Diffusion Transformer for Audio Denoising
Snippet: Audio denoising is the process of estimating better-quality audio signals from a mixture of audio by removing background noise.However, removing background noise from many different sources to produce high-quality audio still makes audio denoising challenging.Conventional audio denoising methods include Wiener filtering, spectral subtraction, minimum mean square error (MMSE) estimation [1], etc.In extremely low SNR and non-stationary noise environments, the performance of these approaches is known to suffer from a significant loss in performance.Deep learning techniques have resulted in multiple new audio denoising techniques to tackle challenges in the domains of speech and audio.Deep audio denoising models may estimate and remove noise from noisy data to obtain denoised audio, or they may directly create denoised audio using the regression technique [2].

[8] first introduced a class of latent variable models motivated by nonequilibrium thermodynamics.Then, diffusion probabilistic models were used to get high-quality image synthesis results using a relatively simple architecture and training procedure.

Title: AV-DiT: Efficient Audio-Visual Diffusion Transformer for Joint Audio and Video Generation
Snippet: To enable the denoising process in the latent space for joint audio and video generation, we propose an audio-visual diffusion transformer (AV-DiT) by leveraging the off-the-shell DiT backbone pre-trained on image-only data, aiming to make full use of its generalization ability to reduce the training cost and model complexity.As shown in Figure 2, our AV-DiT augments the shared image-based DiT with some modality-specific adapters to learn to recover the video and audio modality from Gaussian noise, where the original DiT weights are frozen while inserted parameters are trainable.

rv ×cv , M means the number of video frames, c v is the video channel and r v > 1 denotes the video downsampling ratio.Meanwhile, the audio waveform is transformed into an image-like mel-spectrogram A ∈ R B×T ×F via the STFT operator which is then passed through a pre-trained VAE encoder to obtain the audio latent code z a = E a (A), where z a ∈ R B× T ra × F ra ×ca , T , F and c a denote the temporal, frequency, and channel dimension, respectively, and r a > 1 means the ratio of downsampling audio resolution.In our work, we employ the off-the-shell pre-trained VAEs from image LDM (i.e.Latent Stable Diffusion [2]) and audio LDM (i.e.Tango [11]) to extract the video and audio latent codes respectively and save them locally to reduce the training memory.Furthermore, similar to the ViTs, the z v and z a are transformed into the sequence of tokens by respective patch embedding layers, which are then followed by the positional encoding to yield the video x v ∈ R (B * M )×Lv×D and audio x a ∈ R B×La×D inputs of our proposed multimodal diffusion transformer.In addition, the time information is incorporated into the diffusion transformer blocks via a time embedder.

Title: Nonlocality and Nonlinearity Implies Universality in Operator Learning
Snippet: To achieve a universal approximation property, a neural operator architecture must necessarily define a nonlinear operator. In the context of ordinary neural networks acting as approximators of functions between finite dimensional Euclidean spaces, it is well-known that (nonpolynomial) nonlinearity essentially also represents a sufficient condition for their universal approximation property [46,2,22,12]. This should be contrasted with neural operators, where nonlinearity alone is not sufficient to ensure universality; to illustrate this latter fact, we note that even a single layer of an ordinary neural network actually gives rise to a nonlinear operator, which maps an input function to an output function by composition, 

(2.1) 

Here, W and b represent the weights and biases, respectively, and σ denotes the activation function. Despite being highly nonlinear, operators of such a compositional form cannot be universal. The main reason for this is that any such Ψ is local, in the sense that the value Ψ(u)(x) of the output function at a given evaluation point x depends only on the value of the input function u(x) at that same evaluation point. As a consequence, such mappings are not able to approximate even simple operators Ψ † with a nonlocal dependence on the input, such as the shift operator Ψ † (u)(x) := u(x + h) for fixed h ̸ = 0. 

More specifically, we will focus on the case of a single hidden layer. This results in the following averaging neural operator (ANO) architecture: 

where the lifting and projection mappings, R and Q, are given by (1.1) and (1.3), respectively, with R and Q single-hidden layer neural networks of width d c , and where L is of the form (2.3). 

We note that this ANO is a specific subclass of the NNO. Due to its minimal structure, the ANO depends on only one hyperparameter; the lifting dimension d c . The tunable parameters of ANO are represented by the weight matrix W ∈ R dc×dc and bias b ∈ R dc in the hidden layer L, and the internal weights and biases of the ordinary neural networks R and Q, which define the lifting and projection layers, respectively.

problem: What is the difference between normalizing flows and vae?
final_response:
# Bottom line

- Variational autoencoders (VAEs) learn a generative model by optimizing a lower bound on log-likelihood (the ELBO) that balances reconstruction and a KL regularization, using an encoder-decoder architecture with an approximate latent posterior; this yields amortized inference but does not, in general, give exact likelihoods or independence of latent variables by design.<cite id="6f2dcf9c-0">VAEs maximize a lower bound on the marginal log-likelihood by introducing a variational posterior qφ(z|x) and a generative model pθ, with an objective comprising reconstruction loss plus KL(qφ||pθ(z)), enabling amortized inference but requiring variational approximation</cite><cite id="fc645085-0">After training, the ELBO lower-bounds the true marginal log-likelihood, with a KL gap that induces bias if used as a density estimator</cite><cite id="fc645085-1">VAEs balance reconstruction and KL terms; a dominant KL can cause posterior collapse, while a weak KL can leave “holes” in latent coverage</cite>.

- Normalizing flows model data via a sequence of invertible, differentiable bijections from a simple base distribution, using the change-of-variables formula to obtain tractable log-likelihoods; architectures like RealNVP, MAF, and IAF impose structured Jacobians for efficiency and can be used for generative sampling, density estimation, and even as flexible approximate posteriors in VI.<cite id="5e4e255f-0">Normalizing flows transform a simple prior via invertible functions fφ with easily computed inverses and Jacobian determinants to obtain tractable likelihoods</cite><cite id="5e4e255f-1">Flows compose invertible smooth mappings and, in VI, parameterized to provide expressive approximate posteriors when det-Jacobian is tractable; known families include NICE, RealNVP, MAF, and IAF</cite><cite id="5e4e255f-2">RealNVP stacks bijectors with simple Jacobian determinants; AR flows have lower-triangular Jacobians so the determinant is a product of diagonal terms, enabling efficient density evaluation and factorized modeling</cite><cite id="5e4e255f-3">Block-structure in flow Jacobians (e.g., RealNVP, MAF/IAF) trades expressivity for tractable determinants; AR flows often target density estimation while IAFs suit variational posteriors; continuous-time flows can ensure bijectivity and efficient Jacobians</cite><cite id="5e4e255f-4">Implementations include RealNVP, GLOW, MAF, and IAF; surveys summarize families and design trade-offs</cite>.

# Training objective and inference

- VAEs maximize the evidence lower bound (ELBO) E_q[log pθ(x|z)] − D_KL(qφ(z|x)||p(z)), training an encoder to produce a variational posterior and a decoder to reconstruct data; inference involves sampling from qφ(z|x) and decoding, yielding amortized latent inference but an approximate (not exact) posterior and lower-bound likelihood.<cite id="6f2dcf9c-0">The VAE objective is reconstruction loss minus KL(qφ(z|x)||p(z)), with the variational posterior serving as the inference model</cite><cite id="6f2dcf9c-4">The KL term regularizes the latent space and enforces alignment with a prior, trading off reconstruction and regularization in the ELBO</cite><cite id="fc645085-0">The marginal likelihood is intractable; VAE uses a lower bound with an approximate posterior, introducing a KL gap that biases density estimates</cite>.

- Flows train by fitting an invertible transform to data, typically minimizing a divergence to a data distribution (e.g., KL to the data or adversarial/other losses), and enable exact likelihood evaluation and efficient sampling in both forward and inverse directions due to invertibility and tractable Jacobians.<cite id="5e4e255f-0">Training flows proceeds by minimizing the KL between the data distribution and the flow model, leveraging invertibility and tractable Jacobians for tractable likelihoods</cite><cite id="5e4e255f-3">Bijectivity and efficient Jacobians are ensured by design (e.g., continuous-time gradient flows), supporting both forward and inverse transformations at similar time complexity</cite>.

# Latent variables, dependencies, and expressivity

- In VAEs, the approximate posterior qφ(z|x) is learned and can be arbitrarily factored or structured (e.g., Gaussian) by the encoder; dependencies between latent dimensions are induced by the architecture and training trade-off, and exact independence is not guaranteed, though a dominant KL can push factors toward independence (factorized Gaussians) or cause posterior collapse if too strong.<cite id="6f2dcf9c-0">VAEs learn a variational posterior via an encoder and use it for amortized inference, with the KL term regularizing the posterior relative to a prior</cite><cite id="fc645085-1">Strong KL can cause posterior collapse where latent vectors lose information about the input; weak KL may leave uncovered latent regions, affecting precision</cite><cite id="fc645085-3">Decomposing the KL term (e.g., in β-TCVAE) can target disentanglement by controlling dependencies between x and z</cite>.

Title: Generated Loss and Augmented Training of MNIST VAE
Snippet: The variational autoencoder (VAE) framework (Kingma & Welling, 2013) has been a popular options for training deep generative models. It is a maximum likelihood model and establishes a lower bound (evidence lower bound, ELBO) on the likelihood of observed data by factoring out a latent representation. The VAE encoder is trained to encode training examples into posterior distributions in the latent space, and the VAE decoder is trained to reconstruct the training examples from the latent vectors sampled from these posterior distributions. To maximize ELBO, the model needs to minimize both mistakes in reconstruction ('reconstruction loss') and the difference between the posterior distributions and an assumed prior ('latent loss', measured by KL-divergence). If the latent loss dominates, posterior distributions of the latent vectors collapse to the assumed prior and the latent vector no longer carries any information about the training example (posterior collapse). Models of continuous data types in posterior collapse often hedge their bets by always outputting a weighted average of the training examples. In addition, models capable of autoregression fall back to it in posterior collapse. 

A less severe but more pervasive issue of VAE is low-precision reconstructions and generated samples (Sajjadi et al., 2018). It has been theorized that this issue still comes down to the strength of the KL-divergence term. With strong KL-divergence term, posterior distributions of sampled latent vectors of two distinct training examples overlap and result in ambiguous and therefore low-precision generated samples. On the other hand, there may be holes in the latent space that is not covered by any posterior distributions when the KL-divergence term is weak, and such holes will result in samples unconstrained by training data (Rezende & Viola, 2018). In order to steer clear of the posterior collapse and optimize posterior distributions for generation, the KL-divergence weight β is often introduced as a hyperparameter (Higgins et al., 2017) and sometimes used in conjunction with manual annealing over training steps (Bowman et al., 2015;Sønderby et al., 2016;Akuzawa et al., 2018).
</snippet>

Title: VIVAT: Virtuous Improving VAE Training through Artifact Mitigation
Snippet: The classical VAE, also referred to as KL-VAE, was introduced by [21] and quickly adopted for conditional image generation [52]. The core principle of this approach involves minimizing the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between the latent distribution and a Gaussian prior. Since its inception, this architecture has been widely utilized and extensively modified. Notable architectural innovations include hierarchical VAE [46] and DiffuseVAE [30], the latter employing diffusion processes to refine the blurry VAE outputs. Previous research has also explored the impact of architectural depth in autoencoders [8] and proposed a VAE variant optimized for high compression ratios (up to 128×) [6]. However, the majority of prior work has focused on developing novel loss functions and regularization techniques, such as spectral regularization [46], frequency-domain optimization [18], the integration of Wasserstein distance [44], and more [17,39,24,42,10,43,41,56]. Despite these advancements, most of these contributions have not been widely adopted in large-scale commercial generative models. An alternative approach, VQ-VAE [47], replaces the continuous latent space with a discrete codebook, leading to significant improvements in generative tasks [36,12,54,1]. This method has inspired numerous subsequent modifications [36,57], including VQ-GAN [12], which enhances VQ-VAE through adversarial and perceptual losses. Nevertheless, quantized VAEs are known to produce geometric artifacts, and scaling their latent space dimensions is non-trivial. As a result, KL-VAE remains prevalent in several recent high-profile generative models [7,11,25]. In this work, we further investigate the KL-VAE architecture, aiming to advance its practical potential in reconstruction and generative applications.

Snippet: In this paper, we study two aspects of the variational autoencoder (VAE): the prior distribution over the latent variables and its corresponding posterior. Second, we analyze the family of inverse autoregressive flows (inverse AF) and show that with further improvement, inverse AF could be used as universal approximation to any complicated posterior. # Bottom line

- Variational autoencoders (VAEs) learn a generative model by optimizing a lower bound on log-likelihood (the ELBO) that balances reconstruction and a KL regularization, using an encoder-decoder architecture with an approximate latent posterior; this yields amortized inference but does not, in general, give exact likelihoods or independence of latent variables by design.<cite id="6f2dcf9c-0">VAEs maximize a lower bound on the marginal log-likelihood by introducing a variational posterior qφ(z|x) and a generative model pθ, with an objective comprising reconstruction loss plus KL(qφ||pθ(z)), enabling amortized inference but requiring variational approximation</cite><cite id="fc645085-0">After training, the ELBO lower-bounds the true marginal log-likelihood, with a KL gap that induces bias if used as a density estimator</cite><cite id="fc645085-1">VAEs balance reconstruction and KL terms; a dominant KL can cause posterior collapse, while a weak KL can leave “holes” in latent coverage</cite>.

- Normalizing flows model data via a sequence of invertible, differentiable bijections from a simple base distribution, using the change-of-variables formula to obtain tractable log-likelihoods; architectures like RealNVP, MAF, and IAF impose structured Jacobians for efficiency and can be used for generative sampling, density estimation, and even as flexible approximate posteriors in VI.<cite id="5e4e255f-0">Normalizing flows transform a simple prior via invertible functions fφ with easily computed inverses and Jacobian determinants to obtain tractable likelihoods</cite><cite id="5e4e255f-1">Flows compose invertible smooth mappings and, in VI, parameterized to provide expressive approximate posteriors when det-Jacobian is tractable; known families include NICE, RealNVP, MAF, and IAF</cite><cite id="5e4e255f-2">RealNVP stacks bijectors with simple Jacobian determinants; AR flows have lower-triangular Jacobians so the determinant is a product of diagonal terms, enabling efficient density evaluation and factorized modeling</cite><cite id="5e4e255f-3">Block-structure in flow Jacobians (e.g., RealNVP, MAF/IAF) trades expressivity for tractable determinants; AR flows often target density estimation while IAFs suit variational posteriors; continuous-time flows can ensure bijectivity and efficient Jacobians</cite><cite id="5e4e255f-4">Implementations include RealNVP, GLOW, MAF, and IAF; surveys summarize families and design trade-offs</cite>.

# Training objective and inference

- VAEs maximize the evidence lower bound (ELBO) E_q[log pθ(x|z)] − D_KL(qφ(z|x)||p(z)), training an encoder to produce a variational posterior and a decoder to reconstruct data; inference involves sampling from qφ(z|x) and decoding, yielding amortized latent inference but an approximate (not exact) posterior and lower-bound likelihood.<cite id="6f2dcf9c-0">The VAE objective is reconstruction loss minus KL(qφ(z|x)||p(z)), with the variational posterior serving as the inference model</cite><cite id="6f2dcf9c-4">The KL term regularizes the latent space and enforces alignment with a prior, trading off reconstruction and regularization in the ELBO</cite><cite id="fc645085-0">The marginal likelihood is intractable; VAE uses a lower bound with an approximate posterior, introducing a KL gap that biases density estimates</cite>.

- Flows train by fitting an invertible transform to data, typically minimizing a divergence to a data distribution (e.g., KL to the data or adversarial/other losses), and enable exact likelihood evaluation and efficient sampling in both forward and inverse directions due to invertibility and tractable Jacobians.<cite id="5e4e255f-0">Training flows proceeds by minimizing the KL between the data distribution and the flow model, leveraging invertibility and tractable Jacobians for tractable likelihoods</cite><cite id="5e4e255f-3">Bijectivity and efficient Jacobians are ensured by design (e.g., continuous-time gradient flows), supporting both forward and inverse transformations at similar time complexity</cite>.

# Latent variables, dependencies, and expressivity

- In VAEs, the approximate posterior qφ(z|x) is learned and can be arbitrarily factored or structured (e.g., Gaussian) by the encoder; dependencies between latent dimensions are induced by the architecture and training trade-off, and exact independence is not guaranteed, though a dominant KL can push factors toward independence (factorized Gaussians) or cause posterior collapse if too strong.<cite id="6f2dcf9c-0">VAEs learn a variational posterior via an encoder and use it for amortized inference, with the KL term regularizing the posterior relative to a prior</cite><cite id="fc645085-1">Strong KL can cause posterior collapse where latent vectors lose information about the input; weak KL may leave uncovered latent regions, affecting precision</cite><cite id="fc645085-3">Decomposing the KL term (e.g., in β-TCVAE) can target disentanglement by controlling dependencies between x and z</cite>.

- Flows explicitly construct bijective transforms that can impose factorization or coupling structures on latent variables (e.g., RealNVP’s triangular Jacobians, IAF/MAF’s autoregressive conditionals), enabling controlled dependencies and, when used as the generative transform, direct invertible mappings from complex to simple latent space; when used as posteriors in VI, flows can be more expressive than factor Gaussians.<cite id="5e4e255f-2">AR flow architectures yield lower-triangular Jacobians with efficient determinants and allow modeling P(X) as product of conditionals, supporting factorized/conditional densities</cite><cite id="5e4e255f-1">Normalizing flows have been proposed to enhance the expressiveness of approximate posteriors in VI when the true posterior is unknown</cite><cite id="427de7b6-0">Inverse autoregressive flows can act as universal approximators for complicated posteriors, enabling more flexible VAE parameterizations beyond factorial Gaussians</cite><cite id="427de7b6-4">IAF transforms leverage autoregressive networks with triangular Jacobians to maintain efficient density computation while flexibly transforming latent variables</cite>.

# Likelihoods and sampling guarantees

- VAEs generally do not provide exact log-likelihoods of the observed data unless strong conditions are met; practitioners can use the ELBO to obtain lower bounds and importance-weighted estimates, but KL gaps remain, and reconstruction-centric training can bias density estimates.<cite id="fc645085-0">VAE density estimation uses −ELBO as a lower bound with a residual KL(q||p), introducing theoretical bias if treated as exact likelihood</cite><cite id="fc645085-1">Posterior collapse and KL-strength trade-offs can degrade reconstruction and density fidelity</cite>.

- Flows provide exact likelihoods because the change-of-variables formula makes the log-density tractable, and invertibility allows exact sampling and inversion; this has driven their use in maximum-likelihood training and as flexible priors/posteriors in VI.<cite id="5e4e255f-0">Invertible mappings with tractable Jacobian determinants enable exact likelihood evaluation under the flow model</cite><cite id="5e4e255f-3">Efficient Jacobians and bijectivity are central, with AR/IAF families used for density estimation and as implicitly reversible transforms for posteriors</cite>.

# Architectures and typical components

- VAEs comprise an encoder network producing a posterior over latents, a latent prior, and a decoder mapping latent samples back to data; training involves backprop through sampling and reparameterization to optimize the ELBO.<cite id="6f2dcf9c-0">VAEs encode inputs into latent variables with a variational posterior and decode latent vectors to reconstruct inputs, optimizing the ELBO comprising reconstruction and KL terms</cite><cite id="6f2dcf9c-4">The KL term enforces structure in the latent space, with the ELBO reflecting a trade-off between reconstruction and regularization</cite>.

- Flows comprise a composition of invertible “bijector” modules (e.g., affine coupling in RealNVP, autoregressive transforms in MAF/IAF, spline couplings) designed so inverses and Jacobian determinants are easy to compute; training can be framed as maximum-likelihood or adversarial density fitting, and flows can be used generatively, for density estimation, or as flexible posteriors/priors in VAEs.<cite id="5e4e255f-1">Flows are sequences of invertible smooth mappings; parameterized for VI to provide expressive posteriors when det-Jacobian is tractable</cite><cite id="5e4e255f-3">Block-structured Jacobians in RealNVP/MAF/IAF trade off expressivity and efficiency; AR/IAF roles differ between density estimation and variational posteriors</cite><cite id="427de7b6-2">Linear rational spline flows can serve as effective priors and approximate posteriors in VAEs, with performance competitive to models like Glow and rational quadratic splines</cite>.

# Use cases and when to prefer each

- Choose a VAE when you need amortized latent-variable inference, flexible encoder/decoder structures for representation learning or conditional generation, and a principled trade-off between reconstruction quality and latent regularization; be mindful that density lower bounds are approximate and disentanglement depends on objective design.<cite id="6f2dcf9c-0">VAEs enable amortized inference via an encoder-decoder with an approximate posterior and KL regularization</cite><cite id="fc645085-3">Decomposing and tuning KL components can improve disentanglement at the cost of reconstruction</cite><cite id="fc645085-0">VAE-based density estimates are lower bounds with KL gaps, informing downstream use</cite>.

- Choose a normalizing flow when you need exact likelihoods, efficient maximum-likelihood training, invertible mappings (for data-to-latent and latent-to-data), or highly flexible posteriors/priors in VI; AR/IAF designs also support disentangled latent factor modeling and can be integrated into VAEs to enhance posterior expressivity.<cite id="5e4e255f-0">Change-of-variables with invertible transforms yields tractable likelihoods for exact training and evaluation</cite><cite id="5e4e255f-3">RealNVP/MAF/IAF trade Jacobian structure for efficiency and disentanglement; IAFs are suitable for variational posteriors</cite><cite id="427de7b6-0">Inverse autoregressive flows can approximate complex posteriors, broadening VAE flexibility</cite><cite id="427de7b6-3">Normalizing flows have been used to enhance VAE expressivity of posteriors and priors, and to achieve disentangled latent spaces in related work</cite>.

# Bridges and hybrids

- Normalizing flows and VAEs can be combined: flows can serve as the VAE’s prior or posterior, or as a base density in the variational inference pipeline; empirical studies show such “flow-VAEs” can rival state-of-the-art density models like Glow while retaining fast synthesis.<cite id="427de7b6-2">Rational spline flows used as VAE priors/posteriors achieve performance close to Glow and rational quadratic spline flows</cite><cite id="427de7b6-1">IAFs proposed as scalable, flexible posteriors in VAEs, potentially rivaling or surpassing purely autoregressive models while enabling faster synthesis</cite><cite id="5e4e255f-4">RealNVP and Glow are prominent flow-based generative models used alongside VAEs in practice</cite>.

# Summary comparison

- Objective and inference: VAEs optimize an ELBO with an approximate posterior and amortized inference; flows optimize likelihood under invertible transforms and enable exact likelihoods and efficient sampling/inversion.<cite id="6f2dcf9c-0">VAEs use variational posteriors and ELBO optimization for amortized inference</cite><cite id="5e4e255f-0">Flows train by fitting invertible transforms to data with tractable likelihoods</cite>.

- Latent dependencies: VAEs induce latent dependencies via encoder/decoder and KL trade-offs; flows can impose known dependency structures (e.g., triangular/autoregressive) and can be made more expressive as posteriors via IAF/MAF.<cite id="fc645085-1">KL strength and posterior collapse trade-offs affect latent information</cite><cite id="5e4e255f-2">AR/RealNVP Jacobian structures control conditional dependencies with efficient determinants</cite><cite id="427de7b6-0">IAFs can act as universal posterior approximators</cite>.

- Density estimation vs generative modeling: VAEs are widely used for both but provide lower-bound likelihoods unless special conditions hold; flows are strong density estimators with exact likelihoods and are often used for generative modeling as well.<cite id="fc645085-0">VAE likelihoods are lower-bounded by ELBO with residual KL</cite><cite id="5e4e255f-0">Flows enable tractable exact likelihoods via change-of-variables</cite>.

- Architectures: VAEs have encoder-decoder with variational posterior; flows are stacks of invertible bijectors with structured Jacobians; both have numerous variants and can be hybridized (e.g., flow-VAE, IAF within VAEs, spline flows as priors/posteriors).<cite id="5e4e255f-1">Normalizing flows as enhanced posteriors in VI with tractable Jacobians</cite><cite id="427de7b6-1">IAF as scalable posteriors within VAEs</cite><cite id="427de7b6-2">Spline flows as priors/posteriors in VAEs with performance near state-of-the-art</cite>.
</answer>

Title: How to Train Your VAE
Snippet: Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) have become a cornerstone in generative modeling and representation learning within machine learning. This paper explores a nuanced aspect of VAEs, focusing on interpreting the Kullback-Leibler (KL) Divergence, a critical component within the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) that governs the trade-off between reconstruction accuracy and regularization. Meanwhile, the KL Divergence enforces alignment between latent variable distributions and a prior imposing a structure on the overall latent space but leaves individual variable distributions unconstrained. The proposed method redefines the ELBO with a mixture of Gaussians for the posterior probability, introduces a regularization term to prevent variance collapse, and employs a PatchGAN discriminator to enhance texture realism. snippet.text: Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) have become a cornerstone in generative modeling and representation learning within machine learning. This paper explores a nuanced aspect of VAEs, focusing on interpreting the Kullback-Leibler (KL) Divergence, a critical component within the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) that governs the trade-off between reconstruction accuracy and regularization. Meanwhile, the KL Divergence enforces alignment between latent variable distributions and a prior imposing a structure on the overall latent space but leaves individual variable distributions unconstrained. The proposed method redefines the ELBO with a mixture of Gaussians for the posterior probability, introduces a regularization term to prevent variance collapse, and employs a PatchGAN discriminator to enhance texture realism. Implementation details involve ResNetV2 architectures for both the Encoder and Decoder. The experiments demonstrate the ability to generate realistic faces, offering a promising solution for enhancing VAE-based generative models.

Title: Generated Loss and Augmented Training of MNIST VAE
Snippet: The variational autoencoder (VAE) framework (Kingma & Welling, 2013) has been a popular options for training deep generative models. It is a maximum likelihood model and establishes a lower bound (evidence lower bound, ELBO) on the likelihood of observed data by factoring out a latent representation. The VAE encoder is trained to encode training examples into posterior distributions in the latent space, and the VAE decoder is trained to reconstruct the training examples from the latent vectors sampled from these posterior distributions. To maximize ELBO, the model needs to minimize both mistakes in reconstruction ('reconstruction loss') and the difference between the posterior distributions and an assumed prior ('latent loss', measured by KL-divergence). If the latent loss dominates, posterior distributions of the latent vectors collapse to the assumed prior and the latent vector no longer carries any information about the training example (posterior collapse). Models of continuous data types in posterior collapse often hedge their bets by always outputting a weighted average of the training examples. In addition, models capable of autoregression fall back to it in posterior collapse. 

A less severe but more pervasive issue of VAE is low-precision reconstructions and generated samples (Sajjadi et al., 2018). Snippet: The classical VAE, also referred to as KL-VAE, was introduced by [21] and quickly adopted for conditional image generation [52]. The core principle of this approach involves minimizing the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between the latent distribution and a Gaussian prior. Since its inception, this architecture has been widely utilized and extensively modified. Notable architectural innovations include hierarchical VAE [46] and DiffuseVAE [30], the latter employing diffusion processes to refine the blurry VAE outputs. Previous research has also explored the impact of architectural depth in autoencoders [8] and proposed a VAE variant optimized for high compression ratios (up to 128×) [6]. However, the majority of prior work has focused on developing novel loss functions and regularization techniques, such as spectral regularization [46], frequency-domain optimization [18], the integration of Wasserstein distance [44], and more [17,39,24,42,10,43,41,56]. Despite these advancements, most of these contributions have not been widely adopted in large-scale commercial generative models. An alternative approach, VQ-VAE [47], replaces the continuous latent space with a discrete codebook, leading to significant improvements in generative tasks [36,12,54,1]. This method has inspired numerous subsequent modifications [36,57], including VQ-GAN [12], which enhances VQ-VAE through adversarial and perceptual losses. Nevertheless, quantized VAEs are known to produce geometric artifacts, and scaling their latent space dimensions is non-trivial. As a result, KL-VAE remains prevalent in several recent high-profile generative models [7,11,25]. In this work, we further investigate the KL-VAE architecture, aiming to advance its practical potential in reconstruction and generative applications.

The variational autoencoder (VAE) framework (Kingma & Welling, 2013) has been a popular options for training deep generative models. It is a maximum likelihood model and establishes a lower bound (evidence lower bound, ELBO) on the likelihood of observed data by factoring out a latent representation. The VAE encoder is trained to encode training examples into posterior distributions in the latent space, and the VAE decoder is trained to reconstruct the training examples from the latent vectors sampled from these posterior distributions. To maximize ELBO, the model needs to minimize both mistakes in reconstruction ('reconstruction loss') and the difference between the posterior distributions and an assumed prior ('latent loss', measured by KL-divergence). If the latent loss dominates, posterior distributions of the latent vectors collapse to the assumed prior and the latent vector no longer carries any information about the training example (posterior collapse). Models of continuous data types in posterior collapse often hedge their bets by always outputting a weighted average of the training examples. In addition, models capable of autoregression fall back to it in posterior collapse. 

A less severe but more pervasive issue of VAE is low-precision reconstructions and generated samples (Sajjadi et al., 2018). It has been theorized that this issue still comes down to the strength of the KL-divergence term. With strong KL-divergence term, posterior distributions of sampled latent vectors of two distinct training examples overlap and result in ambiguous and therefore low-precision generated samples. On the other hand, there may be holes in the latent space that is not covered by any posterior distributions when the KL-divergence term is weak, and such holes will result in samples unconstrained by training data (Rezende & Viola, 2018). In order to steer clear of the posterior collapse and optimize posterior distributions for generation, the KL-divergence weight β is often introduced as a hyperparameter (Higgins et al., 2017) and sometimes used in conjunction with manual annealing over training steps (Bowman et al., 2015;Sønderby et al., 2016;Akuzawa et al., 2018).

Title: Learnable Explicit Density for Continuous Latent Space and Variational Inference
Snippet: In this paper, we study two aspects of the variational autoencoder (VAE): the prior distribution over the latent variables and its corresponding posterior. First, we decompose the learning of VAEs into layerwise density estimation, and argue that having a flexible prior is beneficial to both sample generation and inference. Second, we analyze the family of inverse autoregressive flows (inverse AF) and show that with further improvement, inverse AF could be used as universal approximation to any complicated posterior. Our analysis results in a unified approach to parameterizing a VAE, without the need to restrict ourselves to use factorial Gaussians in the latent real space.

Title: An Introduction to Variational Autoencoders
Snippet: E framework is now a commonly used tool for various applications of probabilistic modeling and artificial creativity, and basic implementations are available in most major deep learning software libraries.

For learning flexible inference models, we proposed inverse autoregressive flows (IAF), a type of normalizing flow that allows scaling to high-dimensional latent spaces. An interesting direction for further exploration is comparison with transformations with computationally cheap inverses, such as NICE (Dinh et al., 2014) and Real NVP (Dinh et al., 2016). Application of such transformations in the VAE framework can potentially lead to relatively simple VAEs with a combination of powerful posteriors, priors and decoders. Such architectures can potentially rival or surpass purely autoregressive architectures ( Van den Oord et al., 2016), while allowing much faster synthesis.

The proposed VAE framework remains the only framework in the literature that allows for both discrete and continuous observed variables, allows for efficient amortized latent-variable inference and fast synthesis, and which can produce close to state-of-the-art performance in terms of the log-likelihood of data.

Title: Invertible Generative Modeling using Linear Rational Splines
Snippet: Finally, we test the performance of our proposed model in a variational auto-encoder (VAE) (Kingma and Welling, 2014) setting. In short, in a VAE data points are modeled as realizations of a random variable whose distribution is assumed to be the result of marginalization over a lower-dimensional latent variable. To make this process tractable, the type of prior and approximate posterior random variables need to be determined carefully. Like other flow-based models, linear rational spline flows can be used as effective models for priors and approximate posteriors in a VAE setting. For a detailed explanation on normalizing flows in the context of VAEs, we refer the interested reader to (Rezende and Mohamed, 2015). 

Table 3 shows the quantitative results of VAE simulation using linear rational splines. As can be seen, our proposed model performs almost as well as other models such as Glow (Kingma and Dhariwal, 2018) and rational quadratic splines (Durkan et al., 2019b). 

For more details on the experimental configuration and model samples see Appendices B.4 and C.2, respectively.

Title: Latent mixed-effect models for high-dimensional longitudinal data
Snippet: The literature on extending VAEs' modelling capacity is vast. It spans from extending the expressivity of variational posterior distributions, e.g., using a multivariate Gaussian with a tridiagonal inverse covariance structure (Fortuin et al., 2020) or normalizing flows (Rezende and Mohamed, 2015), to enabling more informative priors compared to the standard normal used in plain VAEs (Kingma and Welling, 2019). Alternative research efforts focus on endowing the model with desirable characteristics, such as a disentangled latent space (Higgins et al., 2016;Zhao et al., 2019). Our work enhances the latent space representation by incorporating auxiliary covariates into the prior, such as time-varying side-profile information.

Title: Adaptive Density Estimation for Generative Models
Snippet: To increase the flexibility of posteriors used over latent variables in variational inference, Kingma et al. [26] proposed a type of normalizing flow called inverse autoregressive flow (IAF). The main benefits of this normalizing flow are its scalability to high dimensions, and its ability to leverage autoregressive neural network, such as those introduced by van den Oord et al. [53]. First, a latent variable vector is sampled using the reparametrization trick [25]: 

Then, mean and variance parameters µ 1 and σ 1 are computed as functions of z 0 using autoregressive models, and a new latent variable z 1 is obtained: 

Since σ 1 and µ 1 are implemented by autoregressive networks, the Jacobian dz1 dz0 is triangular with the values of σ 1 on the diagonal, and the density under the new latent variable remains efficient to compute. This transformation can be repeated an arbitrary number of times for increased flexibility in theory, but in practice a single step is used.

snippet.text: The literature on extending VAEs' modelling capacity is vast. It spans from extending the expressivity of variational posterior distributions, e.g., using a multivariate Gaussian with a tridiagonal inverse covariance structure (Fortuin et al., 2020) or normalizing flows (Rezende and Mohamed, 2015), to enabling more informative priors compared to the standard normal used in plain VAEs (Kingma and Welling, 2019). Alternative research efforts focus on endowing the model with desirable characteristics, such as a disentangled latent space (Higgins et al., 2016;Zhao et al., 2019). Our work enhances the latent space representation by incorporating auxiliary covariates into the prior, such as time-varying side-profile information.

The main benefits of this normalizing flow are its scalability to high dimensions, and its ability to leverage autoregressive neural network, such as those introduced by van den Oord et al. [53]. First, a latent variable vector is sampled using the reparametrization trick [25]: 

Then, mean and variance parameters µ 1 and σ 1 are computed as functions of z 0 using autoregressive models, and a new latent variable z 1 is obtained: 

Since σ 1 and µ 1 are implemented by autoregressive networks, the Jacobian dz1 dz0 is triangular with the values of σ 1 on the diagonal, and the density under the new latent variable remains efficient to compute. This transformation can be repeated an arbitrary number of times for increased flexibility in theory, but in practice a single step is used.

documents.snippet: In this paper, we study two aspects of the variational autoencoder (VAE): the prior distribution over the latent variables and its corresponding posterior. First, we decompose the learning of VAEs into layerwise density estimation, and argue that having a flexible prior is beneficial to both sample generation and inference. Second, we analyze the family of inverse autoregressive flows (inverse AF) and show that with further improvement, inverse AF could be used as universal approximation to any complicated posterior. Our analysis results in a unified approach to parameterizing a VAE, without the need to restrict ourselves to use factorial Gaussians in the latent real space.
