focused on Western countries and especially the United States. Conclusions made when evaluating models against US-centric bias categories do not generalise well to other global contexts and the full spectrum of biases encountered in different sociocultural settings [54]. 

This paper seeks to measure LLM bias in application contexts beyond Western countries, specifically in India, the world's most populous country. There is a small body of existing work studying language model bias in the Indian context, but it is primarily concentrated on word embeddings [1,37,41] and encoder-based LLMs [5,12,68], thus leaving two research gaps. First, it remains unclear to what extent recently-released generative LLMs encode biases in the Indian context. Second, there is a lack of comparative research on the degree or severity of biases among categories which are more prevalent in the West (race and gender), as opposed to others that are more prevalent in India (caste and religion). 

In this work, we aim to bridge these gaps by computing the stereotypical bias levels of popular LLMs in the Indian context and comparing these levels between the Indian and U.S. settings (see Table 1).

Title: StereoMap: Quantifying the Awareness of Human-like Stereotypes in Large Language Models
Snippet: Large Language Models (LLMs), trained on vast amounts of web-crawled data, have been found to encode and perpetuate harmful associations prevalent in the training data. For instance, previous research has demonstrated that LLMs1 exhibit associations between Muslims and violence, as well as between specific gender pronouns (e.g. she) and stereotypical occupations (e.g. homemaker) (Abid et al., 2021;Bolukbasi et al., 2016). To address these concerns, various measurement techniques and mitigation strategies have been developed (Nadeem et al., 2021;Nangia et al., 2020;Schick et al., 2021). For example, benchmark datasets have been proposed to capture stereotyping in LLMs by presenting two contrastive pairs (e.g. (the poor, the rich), (Whites, Asians)) based on various sociodemographic and cultural dimensions (e.g. race, gender, ethnicity), allowing for a comparison of the likelihood of these associations in LLM outputs (Nadeem et al., 2021;Nangia et al., 2020). 

Despite the utility of benchmark datasets for capturing biased stereotyping in LLMs, there have been valid critiques regarding construct validity (what the test is measuring) and the operationalization of the construct (how well the test is measuring it) (Blodgett et al., 2021). These benchmark datasets often rely on crowd-sourced or crowd-worked data itself without a strong theoretical foundation to support the underlying assumptions. While such data can provide valuable insights, we argue that incorporating established and validated theories from psychology can enhance the measurement of stereotypes in LLMs by providing a theoretical framework to identify the dimensions that constitute stereotypes and based on that develop robust metrics and methods for measuring and interpreting stereotypes (Cao et al., 2022;Fraser et al., 2021). To work towards this goal, we propose a framework that we call STEREOMAP, which serves as a comprehensive testbed for measuring stereotypes in LLMs. This framework is grounded in the widely adopted Stereotype Content Model (SCM) put forth by Fiske et al. (2002).

Recent work shows LLMs exhibit implicit bias even when explicitly denying biased views (Bai et al., 2025), with Kumar et al. (2024) finding such biases persist across over 50 LLMs. Benchmarks often test bias in stereotypes in different social contexts (Parrish et al., 2022;Jin et al., 2024;Dong et al., 2023). Despite these advances, no standardized benchmark exists specifically for measuring implicit bias through objective task performance rather than embedding-level or stereotype association analysis.

documents.title: Explicit vs. Implicit: Investigating Social Bias in Large Language Models through Self-Reflection
documents.snippet:
Stereotypes refer to fixed, simplified, and often biased views or beliefs about a particular individual or group (Dovidio, 2010). These views are typically based on characteristics such as race, gender, age, and occupation while often disregarding individual differences (Gilbert and Hixon, 1991). Our study focuses on evaluating the stereotypes reflected in both explicit and implicit biases in LLMs, and defines corresponding quantitative metrics. 

In measuring implicit bias, a stereotype is considered present when the LLM establishes semantic associations between each element of a pair of attributes and its corresponding traditional stereotypical target; otherwise, it is considered absent. This strict definition criterion helps identify the LLM's implicit bias. For example, when the LLM associates stimuli related to White people (such as White names) with positive attributes and stimuli related to Black people (such as Black names) with negative attributes, it is considered to exhibit stereotyping. 

In measuring explicit bias, as this study employs a 5-point Likert scale (Likert, 1932) for evaluation, stereotype expression statements are constructed based on the implicit bias template sentences, associating each element of a pair of attributes with its traditional stereotypical target, and requiring the LLM to make judgments. When the LLM selects "agree" or "strongly agree" and provides corresponding reasons, it is considered to exhibit stereotyping. When the LLM selects "neutral", "disagree", or "strongly disagree", it is considered to show no stereotyping. 

To quantify the experimental results, we define the Stereotypical Score (SC): 

where n stereotype represents the number of stereotypical expressions occurring in either explicit or implicit tests, and N is the total number of experi-ments. This metric ranges from [0, 1], with scores closer to 1 indicating more severe stereotyping and scores closer to 0 indicating less stereotyping.

documents.title: SB-Bench: Stereotype Bias Benchmark for Large Multimodal Models
documents.snippet: SB-bench is the most comprehensive multiple-choice benchmark using real images to evaluate stereotype biases in LMMs. It includes 7,500 triplets of stereotypical images, contextual information, and multiple-choice questions, with each category further divided into several subcategories. SB-bench spans nine diverse domains: Age, Disability Status, Gender Identity, Nationality, Race/Ethnicity, Religion, Sexual Orientation, Physical Appearance, and Socio-Economic Status, with 60 subcategories in total, offering a detailed representation of stereotype biases. We extend the categorization from (Huang & Xiong, 2023) and modify some subcategories for our specific use case. Tab. 2 provides a summary of each bias type, including its definition and an example illustrating attested bias. SB-bench has been meticulously curated through a semi-automated pipeline to create a high-quality real dataset that captures the nuances of these nine bias categories. We show these domains and their subgroups in Fig. 2.

focused on Western countries and especially the United States. Conclusions made when evaluating models against US-centric bias categories do not generalise well to other global contexts and the full spectrum of biases encountered in different sociocultural settings [54]. 

This paper seeks to measure LLM bias in application contexts beyond Western countries, specifically in India, the world's most populous country. There is a small body of existing work studying language model bias in the Indian context, but it is primarily concentrated on word embeddings [1,37,41] and encoder-based LLMs [5,12,68], thus leaving two research gaps. First, it remains unclear to what extent recently-released generative LLMs encode biases in the Indian context. Second, there is a lack of comparative research on the degree or severity of biases among categories which are more prevalent in the West (race and gender), as opposed to others that are more prevalent in India (caste and religion). 

In this work, we aim to bridge these gaps by computing the stereotypical bias levels of popular LLMs in the Indian context and comparing these levels between the Indian and U.S. settings (see Table 1).

documents.title: StereoMap: Quantifying the Awareness of Human-like Stereotypes in Large Language Models
documents.snippet:
Large Language Models (LLMs), trained on vast amounts of web-crawled data, have been found to encode and perpetuate harmful associations prevalent in the training data. For instance, previous research has demonstrated that LLMs1 exhibit associations between Muslims and violence, as well as between specific gender pronouns (e.g. she) and stereotypical occupations (e.g. homemaker) (Abid et al., 2021;Bolukbasi et al., 2016). To address these concerns, various measurement techniques and mitigation strategies have been developed (Nadeem et al., 2021;Nangia et al., 2020;Schick et al., 2021). For example, benchmark datasets have been proposed to capture stereotyping in LLMs by presenting two contrastive pairs (e.g. (the poor, the rich), (Whites, Asians)) based on various sociodemographic and cultural dimensions (e.g. race, gender, ethnicity), allowing for a comparison of the likelihood of these associations in LLM outputs (Nadeem et al., 2021;Nangia et al., 2020). 

Despite the utility of benchmark datasets for capturing biased stereotyping in LLMs, there have been valid critiques regarding construct validity (what the test is measuring) and the operationalization of the construct (how well the test is measuring it) (Blodgett et al., 2021). These benchmark datasets often rely on crowd-sourced or crowd-worked data itself without a strong theoretical foundation to support the underlying assumptions. While such data can provide valuable insights, we argue that incorporating established and validated theories from psychology can enhance the measurement of stereotypes in LLMs by providing a theoretical framework to identify the dimensions that constitute stereotypes and based on that develop robust metrics and methods for measuring and interpreting stereotypes (Cao et al., 2022;Fraser et al., 2021). To work towards this goal, we propose a framework that we call STEREOMAP, which serves as a comprehensive testbed for measuring stereotypes in LLMs. This framework is grounded in the widely adopted Stereotype Content Model (SCM) put forth by Fiske et al. (2002).

problem: how to optimize a genetic algoirthm
final_response:
# Overview

Optimizing a genetic algorithm (GA) means choosing encodings and operators, setting population size and generations, selecting pressure-driven selection and constraint-handling strategies, and deciding when to stop—while balancing exploration and exploitation for the problem’s landscape and evaluation budget.<cite id="b0a7fd64-0">Traditional GAs may explore infeasible regions; handling constraints is essential to find actionable designs</cite><cite id="b0a7fd64-1">Hybrid methods and specialized operators can address feasibility but add parameters and assumptions</cite>. Good practice is to start from a well-tuned baseline, then iterate on ablations for operators, population sizing, and termination, and to adopt multiobjective or constrained strategies as needed.

# 1) Foundations: Encodings, Operators, and Selection

Begin with a baseline configuration and then tune. In practice, binary vs. real-coded encodings are often compared; real-coded GAs commonly use arithmetic crossover and Gaussian mutation, with tournament or rank-based selection and elitism.<cite id="acfccfd5-1">Tournament selection with size 2 is popular for efficiency; arithmetic crossover is widely used with real encodings; Gaussian mutation is a common choice; elitism preserves the best solution</cite><cite id="4016e549-4">A tuned GA found segment-based crossover, Gaussian “by center” mutation, and linear ranking selection to be best for the task</cite>. Selection pressure influences convergence speed and diversity; rank-based or fitness-scaling methods can mitigate premature convergence when landscapes are multimodal.<cite id="4016e549-4">Linear ranking selection gives individuals with lower fitness a chance to be selected, helping reveal alternative configurations</cite>.

Crossover and mutation rates require a balance: too much recombination can disrupt good building blocks; too little mutates the population too slowly. Empirical studies often place crossover near 0.5–0.9 and mutation in the 0.001–0.10 range, with problem-dependent adjustments to avoid premature convergence or slow progress.<cite id="acfccfd5-0">Crossover probabilities of 0.5–1.0 are common, while mutation probabilities of 0.001–0.05 are typical; too high crossover can disrupt traits, and too low mutation slows convergence</cite><cite id="acfccfd5-3">A DeJong-style baseline with 50 individuals and Pc=0.6 was improved by Pm=0.05 for the task</cite><cite id="4016e549-3">A study reported default settings of N=50, pc≈0.25, pm≈0.01; too low or too high mutation/migration rates were disadvantageous</cite>. For multiobjective settings, NSGA-II and its variants are commonly configured with population sizes around tens and fixed or tuned generations; fronts can be relatively insensitive to common (Pc, Pm) combinations, so run multiple settings and compare outcomes.<cite id="acfccfd5-1">An NSGA-II setup used pop=40, generations=40, Pc=0.8, Pm=0.3; similar Pareto fronts across several common (Pc,Pm) combinations indicated limited sensitivity</cite>.

# 2) Population Size and Generations: Quality vs. Cost

Population size and generations jointly determine runtime and convergence. Empirically, increasing population size can speed up convergence but increase runtime per generation; the net effect depends on landscape complexity and evaluation cost.<cite id="0c70f5b7-0">Larger code size slowed population generation but sped evolution; runtime trends included linear and quadratic effects with problem structure</cite><cite id="0c70f5b7-2">Time complexity increased with both population size and generations because selection, crossover, mutation, and evaluations scale with these parameters</cite>. Theory suggests larger populations can reduce time to hit targets by increasing selection pressure and first-hitting probabilities, but they do not universally dominate smaller variants across all problems.<cite id="0c70f5b7-3">Drift/FHT analyses showed increasing population size can lower time complexity and boost first-hitting probabilities, yet (N+N) did not always outperform (1+1) across problems</cite>. 

Pragmatically, small populations with many generations can work well on low-dimensional, smooth landscapes; large populations with fewer generations can explore multiple basins in rugged or disconnected landscapes. Runtime can vary by orders of magnitude with population size; choose sizes that respect evaluation budgets and convergence goals, and validate with early-plateau checks.<cite id="0c70f5b7-4">Population size choices can cause GA runtime to vary by several orders of magnitude; small populations can be effective for small dimension with many generations, while larger populations accelerate convergence in complex problems</cite>. As a rule of thumb, run a parametric study over population sizes and generations to find a sweet spot for your problem’s cost-quality trade-off.<cite id="0c70f5b7-2">A 3D plot of time complexity over population size and generations can guide choosing generations and size for a target budget</cite>.

# 3) Selection, Crossover, and Mutation: Design Choices and Pitfalls

- Selection pressure and diversity: Tournament selection with small size (k=2) is computationally efficient and often effective; rank-based or fitness-scaling methods preserve lower-fitness individuals to maintain diversity and avoid premature convergence.<cite id="acfccfd5-1">Tournament size 2 is used for efficiency and simplicity</cite><cite id="4016e549-4">Linear ranking selection provides a chance to select less-fit individuals, sustaining diversity</cite>.
- Crossover: Arithmetic crossover (blend) and segment-based crossover blend or exchange variable ranges; segment-based crossover can increase diversity by sampling random segments from parents.<cite id="4016e549-4">Segment-based crossover uses random chosen segments from parents and showed strong performance</cite><cite id="4016e549-4">Arithmetic crossover is popular for real encodings</cite>.
- Mutation: Gaussian mutation with small step sizes is widely used; adaptive or schedule-based mutation can counter premature convergence, and dynamic adjustment of Pc and Pm can improve performance, especially with larger populations.<cite id="acfccfd5-1">Gaussian mutation is commonly adopted</cite><cite id="acfccfd5-2">A dynamic approach that starts with high crossover and low mutation, then gradually increases mutation and decreases crossover, was reported more effective for large populations</cite>.
- Over/under-tuning: Both too high crossover and too low mutation can lead to premature convergence; conversely, too low crossover or too high mutation can slow convergence or degrade solution quality. Iteratively sweep these parameters and monitor convergence and diversity.<cite id="acfccfd5-0">High crossover can disrupt inheritance; low mutation slows convergence, high mutation can degrade effectiveness; balanced settings are crucial</cite>.

# 4) Handling Constraints: Penalties, Repair, and Feasibility

When problems have constraints, choose a handling strategy aligned with your objectives and domain knowledge. Penalty methods add constraint violations to the objective but require careful tuning and can cause premature convergence or stagnation if penalties are not set appropriately.<cite id="b0a7fd64-0">Penalty methods are popular but cannot guarantee both feasibility and convergence; large penalties can cause premature convergence, while small penalties may retain infeasible solutions</cite><cite id="b0a7fd64-3">Penalty terms can be added to the objective to drive feasibility, but tuning is required</cite>. Repair methods transform infeasible individuals into feasible ones and can reduce search effort, but may not work well if feasible regions are disconnected and can bias search toward specific repair heuristics.<cite id="b0a7fd64-1">Repair methods map infeasible solutions to feasible ones and can reduce the search space, but may fail for disconnected feasible regions</cite>. Specialized operators and hybrid schemes integrate domain knowledge but add parameters and complexity; select them when penalties and repairs are insufficient.<cite id="b0a7fd64-1">Hybrid GA approaches with other heuristics or mathematical programming can work but require additional parameters and domain knowledge</cite>. For multiobjective constrained problems, hybrid constraint handling (e.g., population trimming plus adaptive penalties) can improve both convergence and diversity compared to baselines.<cite id="b0a7fd64-2">A hybrid technique combining population trimming and adaptive penalties in NSGA-II improved convergence and diversity over state-of-the-art methods on constrained MOPs</cite>. 

Guidelines:
- If feasibility is essential, prefer repair or feasibility-promoting selection until a feasible solution is found, then emphasize refinement.
- If infeasibility is allowed but undesirable, use adaptive penalties with dynamic scaling and feasibility thresholds.
- Prefer methods that align with the problem’s structure (e.g., boundary-aware operators for box constraints).

# 5) Multiobjective Optimization: When and How

For multiple conflicting objectives or unknown Pareto sets, use multiobjective GAs (e.g., NSGA-II, MOEA/D, indicator-based methods) with problem-appropriate settings. NSGA-II commonly uses a population size around tens, steady-state operators, and a fixed number of generations; fronts can be robust to some operator settings, so ablate to confirm.<cite id="acfccfd5-1">NSGA-II with pop=40, generations=40, Pc=0.8, Pm=0.3 produced consistent fronts across several (Pc,Pm) combinations</cite>. For constrained multiobjective problems, integrate constraint handling into selection and replacement to balance feasibility, convergence, and diversity; hybrid strategies can outperform standard baselines.<cite id="b0a7fd64-2">A constrained multiobjective EA with a hybrid constraint-handling technique (population trimming + adaptive penalty) outperformed state-of-the-art NSGA-II variants in convergence and diversity</cite>. If objectives are scalarized (e.g., with weights), validate sensitivity to weights and consider using a set of weights or a posteriori methods to explore the Pareto front.

# 6) Adaptive and Dynamic Parameter Control

Static parameter settings can be suboptimal across changing landscapes. Dynamic adjustment of Pc and Pm can improve exploration-convergence balance, especially as population size varies; for large populations, increasing mutation and decreasing crossover over time improved results in one study.<cite id="acfccfd5-2">A dynamic schedule starting with Pm=0 and Pc=1, gradually increasing mutation and decreasing crossover, outperformed two static tuning methods for large populations</cite>. In practice, you can implement schedule-based or performance-based adjustments (e.g., reduce recombination when diversity drops, increase mutation after early convergence) and monitor diversity metrics and convergence speed.

# 7) Expensive Black-box Optimization: Surrogates and Design Space

When evaluations are expensive, surrogate-assisted GAs can reduce cost by learning from sampled solutions and guiding search. Use surrogates (e.g., Kriging/RBF, Gaussian process surrogates) to replace or approximate expensive evaluations in the genetic loop, and integrate acquisition functions to select the next query points. Additionally, reduce dimensionality or fix nuisance parameters a priori to shrink the search space; this is especially effective when many inputs have weak impact on the objective or constraints. In constrained settings, combine surrogate models with repair or penalty-based feasibility handling to propose feasible candidates efficiently.<cite id="b0a7fd64-1">Hybrid GA approaches that integrate another heuristic or mathematical programming can reduce search effort but require additional parameters and domain knowledge</cite>. Note that surrogate quality is critical; cross-validate models and use warm-start samples from prior runs to stabilize training.

# 8) Termination, Monitoring, and Validation

Terminate when improvements plateau across metrics (e.g., objective values, diversity, or feasibility), the budget is exhausted, or a time/stopping tolerance is met. Combine generation-based and performance-based criteria (e.g., relative change in the best solution or average diversity) to avoid long runs after convergence.<cite id="4016e549-4">A GA can stop at a maximum generation or when the weighted average change in fitness over stalled generations is below a tolerance; storing previously evaluated fitness avoids recomputation</cite>. For multiobjective runs, report hypervolume (set-based metric) and spacing to quantify convergence and diversity, and compute means/variances across multiple runs to assess stability. When comparing configurations, use paired statistical tests or confidence intervals on key metrics to avoid drawing conclusions from noise.

# 9) A Practical Tuning Workflow

1) Choose encoding and constraints: Select real vs. binary encodings and define constraints; implement feasibility checks and pick a baseline constraint-handling strategy (penalty/repair/operator-based).<cite id="b0a7fd64-0">Handling constraints is critical to ensure feasible, actionable designs</cite><cite id="b0a7fd64-1">Repair and hybrid methods can reduce search space but add parameters</cite>.  
2) Set a baseline: Start with a common setup (e.g., tournament size 2, arithmetic crossover, Gaussian mutation, pop≈20–50, generations≈50–100) and a simple penalty or repair scheme; run on a held-out set or early warm-start samples.<cite id="acfccfd5-1">Tournament-2, arithmetic crossover, Gaussian mutation, pop=40, generations=40, Pc=0.8, Pm=0.3</cite><cite id="4016e549-3">Defaults of N=50, pc≈0.25, pm≈0.01 with ~50 iterations to reach a target state</cite>.  
3) Parametric sweeps: Study population size and generations together via a grid or space-filling design; track time complexity and solution quality to find a budget-optimized point.<cite id="0c70f5b7-2">Time complexity increases with population size and generations; use a 3D analysis to guide trade-offs</cite><cite id="0c70f5b7-4">Runtime can vary by orders of magnitude with population size; small populations can work for low-dimensional problems with many generations</cite>.  
4) Tune operators and rates: Sweep Pc and Pm, trying typical ranges and adaptive schedules; prefer methods that maintain diversity and avoid premature convergence.<cite id="acfccfd5-0">Pc≈0.5–1.0 and Pm≈0.001–0.05 with balanced exploration vs. exploitation</cite><cite id="acfccfd5-2">Dynamic adjustment of Pc and Pm improved performance for large populations</cite>.  
5) Select multiobjective vs. scalarization: If multiple objectives, adopt NSGA-II or similar and integrate constraint handling; if scalarizing, test a set of weights and validate Pareto coverage with an a posteriori method.<cite id="acfccfd5-1">NSGA-II parameterization and robustness to some operator settings</cite><cite id="b0a7fd64-2">Hybrid constraint handling improved convergence and diversity for constrained MOPs</cite>.  
6) Add surrogates and design-space reduction: For expensive evaluations, build a surrogate model and use it to guide selection of offspring; reduce dimensions or fix parameters where possible to cut cost.<cite id="b0a7fd64-1">Hybrid methods can reduce search effort but require extra parameters and domain knowledge</cite>.  
7) Set termination and reuse cache: Use generation limits, change-based plateaus, or quality thresholds; cache evaluated individuals to avoid recomputation and speed up iterations.<cite id="4016e549-4">Stop on max generations or small weighted average change; store fitness to save simulation time</cite>.  
8) Validate and compare: Run multiple trials with statistical tests on metrics (e.g., hypervolume, spacing, or convergence/quality), and ablate configurations to ensure improvements are not due to noise or one-time luck.

# 10) Summary of Key Trade-offs

- Exploration vs. convergence: Larger populations and higher crossover/mutation speed up exploration but increase runtime and risk premature convergence if unbalanced.<cite id="0c70f5b7-2">Time complexity rises with population and generations</cite><cite id="acfccfd5-0">High crossover can disrupt traits; high mutation can harm effectiveness</cite>.  
- Generality vs. optimality: Parameter tuning that boosts one problem may degrade others (NFL), so validate across instances when possible.<cite id="0c70f5b7-3">NFL implies algorithmic variants with different parameter tuning can have equal average performance across problems; tuning for one problem can harm others</cite>.  
- Feasibility vs. objective quality: Penalty methods require careful tuning; repair methods can miss disconnected feasible regions; hybrid/domain-aware methods help but add complexity.<cite id="b0a7fd64-0">Penalty tuning is delicate and may fail to guarantee feasibility or convergence</cite><cite id="b0a7fd64-1">Repair methods may not work for disconnected feasible sets</cite>.  
- Multiobjective coverage: Combine constraint handling with diversity-preserving selection and consider hybrid strategies to improve both convergence and diversity on constrained fronts.<cite id="b0a7fd64-2">Hybrid constraint handling in NSGA-II improved convergence and diversity on constrained MOPs</cite>.  
- Cost: For expensive black-box optimization, surrogate models and design-space reduction can dramatically cut evaluations while maintaining solution quality, provided the surrogate is well validated and integrated into the genetic loop.<cite id="b0a7fd64-1">Hybrid GA approaches can reduce search effort but require additional parameters and domain knowledge</cite>.

Following this workflow and attending to these trade-offs can make a GA robust, efficient, and effective for a wide range of optimization problems.

Snippet: Genetic algorithm uses the natural selection process for any search process. We also do the reverse process of considering the mutation ratio to be maximum and crossover ratio to be minimum and slowly decrease the mutation ratio and increase the crossover ratio (MDCI). GAs are particularly effective for solving complex optimization problems where the search space is large and may contain multiple local optima. In this study, we employ a GA to optimize the hyperparameters of our model. The GA is configured with the following parameters: 

• Population Size: The population size is set to 20 individuals (n=20). 

This parameter determines the number of candidate solutions maintained in each generation. 

• Number of Generations: The algorithm runs for 20 generations (g = 20). Each generation involves selection, crossover, mutation, and evaluation processes. 

• Crossover Probability: The crossover probability is 0.5 (cxpb = 0.5). This means that there is a 50% chance that two selected parents will undergo crossover to produce offspring.

Snippet: A solution that satisfies all constraints in an optimization problem is referred to as a "feasible" solution. Traditional GAs may inadvertently explore infeasible regions of the solution space, generating solutions that violate one or more constraints. Such solutions are of no practical value in design problems, as they do not represent viable designs. Therefore, the ability to effectively handle constraints is a critical feature for GAs to be considered a useful tool in design optimization. By incorporating constraint handling, GAs can be adapted to efficiently search for feasible solutions within the constrained solution space, leading to more meaningful and actionable results. 

Several distinct methods of constraint handling in GAs have been researched, varying in application, complexity, and generality [10,11]. The literary history of constraint handling in GAs is broad and somewhat fragmented, as many techniques have been developed in isolation to address particular use-cases. However, in general, constraint handling approaches fall roughly into three groups: penalty methods, repair methods, and specialized operators. 

The most popular method of constraint handling in genetic algorithms is to apply a penalty to infeasible solutions [10,11,12,13]. The techniques described by [11] suggest methods of levying penalties in an effort to guide search towards feasible regions of the search space. Nonetheless, infeasible solutions still appear in the population, with the goal that sufficiently high penalty precludes the candidate from selection in future generations. 

Empirically, penalty methods in stochastic optimization cannot guarantee both the prevention of infeasible solutions and algorithm convergence. In other words, depending on the convergence criterion and configuration of the genetic algorithm, the solutions returned by the algorithm are not guaranteed to be feasible. As discussed in [14], a large penalty for constraint violations may result in premature convergence or stagnation when a feasible solution is found. Conversely, a low penalty may result in infeasible solutions being returned, as they may have higher fitness than the feasible solutions. Indeed, the results of [11] show that, for some methods, infeasible solutions were present in the optimal set of solutions. Therefore, tuning of the penalty factors may be required to achieve desired performance, and the correct tuning of the parameters is not known a-priori.
</snippet>

# Overview

Optimizing a genetic algorithm (GA) means choosing encodings and operators, setting population size and generations, selecting pressure-driven selection and constraint-handling strategies, and deciding when to stop—while balancing exploration and exploitation for the problem’s landscape and evaluation budget.<cite id="b0a7fd64-0">Traditional GAs may explore infeasible regions; handling constraints is essential to find actionable designs</cite><cite id="b0a7fd64-1">Hybrid methods and specialized operators can address feasibility but add parameters and assumptions</cite>. Good practice is to start from a well-tuned baseline, then iterate on ablations for operators, population sizing, and termination, and to adopt multiobjective or constrained strategies as needed.

# 1) Foundations: Encodings, Operators, and Selection

Begin with a baseline configuration and then tune. In practice, binary vs. real-coded encodings are often compared; real-coded GAs commonly use arithmetic crossover and Gaussian mutation, with tournament or rank-based selection and elitism.<cite id="acfccfd5-1">Tournament selection with size 2 is popular for efficiency; arithmetic crossover is widely used with real encodings; Gaussian mutation is a common choice; elitism preserves the best solution</cite><cite id="4016e549-4">A tuned GA found segment-based crossover, Gaussian “by center” mutation, and linear ranking selection to be best for the task</cite>. Selection pressure influences convergence speed and diversity; rank-based or fitness-scaling methods can mitigate premature convergence when landscapes are multimodal.<cite id="4016e549-4">Linear ranking selection gives individuals with lower fitness a chance to be selected, helping reveal alternative configurations</cite>.

Crossover and mutation rates require a balance: too much recombination can disrupt good building blocks; too little mutates the population too slowly. Empirical studies often place crossover near 0.5–0.9 and mutation in the 0.001–0.10 range, with problem-dependent adjustments to avoid premature convergence or slow progress.<cite id="acfccfd5-0">Crossover probabilities of 0.5–1.0 are common, while mutation probabilities of 0.001–0.05 are typical; too high crossover can disrupt traits, and too low mutation slows convergence</cite><cite id="acfccfd5-3">A DeJong-style baseline with 50 individuals and Pc=0.6 was improved by Pm=0.05 for the task</cite><cite id="4016e549-3">A study reported default settings of N=50, pc≈0.25, pm≈0.01; too low or too high mutation/migration rates were disadvantageous</cite>. For multiobjective settings, NSGA-II and its variants are commonly configured with population sizes around tens and fixed or tuned generations; fronts can be relatively insensitive to common (Pc, Pm) combinations, so run multiple settings and compare outcomes.<cite id="acfccfd5-1">An NSGA-II setup used pop=40, generations=40, Pc=0.8, Pm=0.3; similar Pareto fronts across several common (Pc,Pm) combinations indicated limited sensitivity</cite>.

# 2) Population Size and Generations: Quality vs. Cost

Population size and generations jointly determine runtime and convergence. Empirically, increasing population size can speed up convergence but increase runtime per generation; the net effect depends on landscape complexity and evaluation cost.<cite id="0c70f5b7-0">Larger code size slowed population generation but sped evolution; runtime trends included linear and quadratic effects with problem structure</cite><cite id="0c70f5b7-2">Time complexity increased with both population size and generations because selection, crossover, mutation, and evaluations scale with these parameters</cite>. Theory suggests larger populations can reduce time to hit targets by increasing selection pressure and first-hitting probabilities, but they do not universally dominate smaller variants across all problems.<cite id="0c70f5b7-3">Drift/FHT analyses showed increasing population size can lower time complexity and boost first-hitting probabilities, yet (N+N) did not always outperform (1+1) across problems</cite>. 

Pragmatically, small populations with many generations can work well on low-dimensional, smooth landscapes; large populations with fewer generations can explore multiple basins in rugged or disconnected landscapes. Runtime can vary by orders of magnitude with population size; choose sizes that respect evaluation budgets and convergence goals, and validate with early-plateau checks.<cite id="0c70f5b7-4">Population size choices can cause GA runtime to vary by several orders of magnitude; small populations can be effective for small dimension with many generations, while larger populations accelerate convergence in complex problems</cite>. As a rule of thumb, run a parametric study over population sizes and generations to find a sweet spot for your problem’s cost-quality trade-off.<cite id="0c70f5b7-2">A 3D plot of time complexity over population size and generations can guide choosing generations and size for a target budget</cite>.

# 3) Selection, Crossover, and Mutation: Design Choices and Pitfalls

- Selection pressure and diversity: Tournament selection with small size (k=2) is computationally efficient and often effective; rank-based or fitness-scaling methods preserve lower-fitness individuals to maintain diversity and avoid premature convergence.<cite id="acfccfd5-1">Tournament size 2 is used for efficiency and simplicity</cite><cite id="4016e549-4">Linear ranking selection provides a chance to select less-fit individuals, sustaining diversity</cite>.
- Crossover: Arithmetic crossover (blend) and segment-based crossover blend or exchange variable ranges; segment-based crossover can increase diversity by sampling random segments from parents.<cite id="4016e549-4">Segment-based crossover uses random chosen segments from parents and showed strong performance</cite><cite id="4016e549-4">Arithmetic crossover is popular for real encodings</cite>.
- Mutation: Gaussian mutation with small step sizes is widely used; adaptive or schedule-based mutation can counter premature convergence, and dynamic adjustment of Pc and Pm can improve performance, especially with larger populations.<cite id="acfccfd5-1">Gaussian mutation is commonly adopted</cite><cite id="acfccfd5-2">A dynamic approach that starts with high crossover and low mutation, then gradually increases mutation and decreases crossover, was reported more effective for large populations</cite>.
- Over/under-tuning: Both too high crossover and too low mutation can lead to premature convergence; conversely, too low crossover or too high mutation can slow convergence or degrade solution quality. Iteratively sweep these parameters and monitor convergence and diversity.<cite id="acfccfd5-0">High crossover can disrupt inheritance; low mutation slows convergence, high mutation can degrade effectiveness; balanced settings are crucial</cite>.

# 4) Handling Constraints: Penalties, Repair, and Feasibility

When problems have constraints, choose a handling strategy aligned with your objectives and domain knowledge. Penalty methods add constraint violations to the objective but require careful tuning and can cause premature convergence or stagnation if penalties are not set appropriately.<cite id="b0a7fd64-0">Penalty methods are popular but cannot guarantee both feasibility and convergence; large penalties can cause premature convergence, while small penalties may retain infeasible solutions</cite><cite id="b0a7fd64-3">Penalty terms can be added to the objective to drive feasibility, but tuning is required</cite>. Repair methods transform infeasible individuals into feasible ones and can reduce search effort, but may not work well if feasible regions are disconnected and can bias search toward specific repair heuristics.<cite id="b0a7fd64-1">Repair methods map infeasible solutions to feasible ones and can reduce the search space, but may fail for disconnected feasible regions</cite>. Specialized operators and hybrid schemes integrate domain knowledge but add parameters and complexity; select them when penalties and repairs are insufficient.<cite id="b0a7fd64-1">Hybrid GA approaches with other heuristics or mathematical programming can work but require additional parameters and domain knowledge</cite>. For multiobjective constrained problems, hybrid constraint handling (e.g., population trimming plus adaptive penalties) can improve both convergence and diversity compared to baselines.<cite id="b0a7fd64-2">A hybrid technique combining population trimming and adaptive penalties in NSGA-II improved convergence and diversity over state-of-the-art methods on constrained MOPs</cite>. 

Guidelines:
- If feasibility is essential, prefer repair or feasibility-promoting selection until a feasible solution is found, then emphasize refinement.
- If infeasibility is allowed but undesirable, use adaptive penalties with dynamic scaling and feasibility thresholds.
- Prefer methods that align with the problem’s structure (e.g., boundary-aware operators for box constraints).

# 5) Multiobjective Optimization: When and How

For multiple conflicting objectives or unknown Pareto sets, use multiobjective GAs (e.g., NSGA-II, MOEA/D, indicator-based methods) with problem-appropriate settings. NSGA-II commonly uses a population size around tens, steady-state operators, and a fixed number of generations; fronts can be robust to some operator settings, so ablate to confirm.<cite id="acfccfd5-1">NSGA-II with pop=40, generations=40, Pc=0.8, Pm=0.3 produced consistent fronts across several (Pc,Pm) combinations</cite>. For constrained multiobjective problems, integrate constraint handling into selection and replacement to balance feasibility, convergence, and diversity; hybrid strategies can outperform standard baselines.<cite id="b0a7fd64-2">A constrained multiobjective EA with a hybrid constraint-handling technique (population trimming + adaptive penalty) outperformed state-of-the-art NSGA-II variants in convergence and diversity</cite>. If objectives are scalarized (e.g., with weights), validate sensitivity to weights and consider using a set of weights or a posteriori methods to explore the Pareto front.

# 6) Adaptive and Dynamic Parameter Control

Static parameter settings can be suboptimal across changing landscapes. Dynamic adjustment of Pc and Pm can improve exploration-convergence balance, especially as population size varies; for large populations, increasing mutation and decreasing crossover over time improved results in one study.<cite id="acfccfd5-2">A dynamic schedule starting with Pm=0 and Pc=1, gradually increasing mutation and decreasing crossover, outperformed two static tuning methods for large populations</cite>. In practice, you can implement schedule-based or performance-based adjustments (e.g., reduce recombination when diversity drops, increase mutation after early convergence) and monitor diversity metrics and convergence speed.

# 7) Expensive Black-box Optimization: Surrogates and Design Space

When evaluations are expensive, surrogate-assisted GAs can reduce cost by learning from sampled solutions and guiding search. Use surrogates (e.g., Kriging/RBF, Gaussian process surrogates) to replace or approximate expensive evaluations in the genetic loop, and integrate acquisition functions to select the next query points. Additionally, reduce dimensionality or fix nuisance parameters a priori to shrink the search space; this is especially effective when many inputs have weak impact on the objective or constraints. In constrained settings, combine surrogate models with repair or penalty-based feasibility handling to propose feasible candidates efficiently.<cite id="b0a7fd64-1">Hybrid GA approaches that integrate another heuristic or mathematical programming can reduce search effort but require additional parameters and domain knowledge</cite>. Note that surrogate quality is critical; cross-validate models and use warm-start samples from prior runs to stabilize training.

# 8) Termination, Monitoring, and Validation

Terminate when improvements plateau across metrics (e.g., objective values, diversity, or feasibility), the budget is exhausted, or a time/stopping tolerance is met. Combine generation-based and performance-based criteria (e.g., relative change in the best solution or average diversity) to avoid long runs after convergence.<cite id="4016e549-4">A GA can stop at a maximum generation or when the weighted average change in fitness over stalled generations is below a tolerance; storing previously evaluated fitness avoids recomputation</cite>. For multiobjective runs, report hypervolume (set-based metric) and spacing to quantify convergence and diversity, and compute means/variances across multiple runs to assess stability. When comparing configurations, use paired statistical tests or confidence intervals on key metrics to avoid drawing conclusions from noise.

# 9) A Practical Tuning Workflow

1) Choose encoding and constraints: Select real vs. binary encodings and define constraints; implement feasibility checks and pick a baseline constraint-handling strategy (penalty/repair/operator-based).<cite id="b0a7fd64-0">Handling constraints is critical to ensure feasible, actionable designs</cite><cite id="b0a7fd64-1">Repair and hybrid methods can reduce search space but add parameters</cite>.  
2) Set a baseline: Start with a common setup (e.g., tournament size 2, arithmetic crossover, Gaussian mutation, pop≈20–50, generations≈50–100) and a simple penalty or repair scheme; run on a held-out set or early warm-start samples.<cite id="acfccfd5-1">Tournament-2, arithmetic crossover, Gaussian mutation, pop=40, generations=40, Pc=0.8, Pm=0.3</cite><cite id="4016e549-3">Defaults of N=50, pc≈0.25, pm≈0.01 with ~50 iterations to reach a target state</cite>.  
3) Parametric sweeps: Study population size and generations together via a grid or space-filling design; track time complexity and solution quality to find a budget-optimized point.<cite id="0c70f5b7-2">Time complexity increases with population size and generations; use a 3D analysis to guide trade-offs</cite><cite id="0c70f5b7-4">Runtime can vary by orders of magnitude with population size; small populations can work for low-dimensional problems with many generations</cite>.  
4) Tune operators and rates: Sweep Pc and Pm, trying typical ranges and adaptive schedules; prefer methods that maintain diversity and avoid premature convergence.<cite id="acfccfd5-0">Pc≈0.5–1.0 and Pm≈0.001–0.05 with balanced exploration vs. exploitation</cite><cite id="acfccfd5-2">Dynamic adjustment of Pc and Pm improved performance for large populations</cite>.  
5) Select multiobjective vs. scalarization: If multiple objectives, adopt NSGA-II or similar and integrate constraint handling; if scalarizing, test a set of weights and validate Pareto coverage with an a posteriori method.<cite id="acfccfd5-1">NSGA-II parameterization and robustness to some operator settings</cite><cite id="b0a7fd64-2">Hybrid constraint handling improved convergence and diversity for constrained MOPs</cite>.  
6) Add surrogates and design-space reduction: For expensive evaluations, build a surrogate model and use it to guide selection of offspring; reduce dimensions or fix parameters where possible to cut cost.<cite id="b0a7fd64-1">Hybrid methods can reduce search effort but require extra parameters and domain knowledge</cite>.  
7) Set termination and reuse cache: Use generation limits, change-based plateaus, or quality thresholds; cache evaluated individuals to avoid recomputation and speed up iterations.<cite id="4016e549-4">Stop on max generations or small weighted average change; store fitness to save simulation time</cite>.  
8) Validate and compare: Run multiple trials with statistical tests on metrics (e.g., hypervolume, spacing, or convergence/quality), and ablate configurations to ensure improvements are not due to noise or one-time luck.

# 10) Summary of Key Trade-offs

- Exploration vs. convergence: Larger populations and higher crossover/mutation speed up exploration but increase runtime and risk premature convergence if unbalanced.<cite id="0c70f5b7-2">Time complexity rises with population and generations</cite><cite id="acfccfd5-0">High crossover can disrupt traits; high mutation can harm effectiveness</cite>.  
- Generality vs. optimality: Parameter tuning that boosts one problem may degrade others (NFL), so validate across instances when possible.<cite id="0c70f5b7-3">NFL implies algorithmic variants with different parameter tuning can have equal average performance across problems; tuning for one problem can harm others</cite>.  
- Feasibility vs. objective quality: Penalty methods require careful tuning; repair methods can miss disconnected feasible regions; hybrid/domain-aware methods help but add complexity.<cite id="b0a7fd64-0">Penalty tuning is delicate and may fail to guarantee feasibility or convergence</cite><cite id="b0a7fd64-1">Repair methods may not work for disconnected feasible sets</cite>.  
- Multiobjective coverage: Combine constraint handling with diversity-preserving selection and consider hybrid strategies to improve both convergence and diversity on constrained fronts.<cite id="b0a7fd64-2">Hybrid constraint handling in NSGA-II improved convergence and diversity on constrained MOPs</cite>.  
- Cost: For expensive black-box optimization, surrogate models and design-space reduction can dramatically cut evaluations while maintaining solution quality, provided the surrogate is well validated and integrated into the genetic loop.<cite id="b0a7fd64-1">Hybrid GA approaches can reduce search effort but require additional parameters and domain knowledge</cite>.

Following this workflow and attending to these trade-offs can make a GA robust, efficient, and effective for a wide range of optimization problems.

Title: A dynamic approach for parameter tuning in genetic algorithm using crossover and mutation ratios
Snippet: Genetic algorithm uses the natural selection process for any search process. It is an optimization process where integration among different vital parameters like crossover and mutation plays a major role. The parameters have an impact on the algorithm by their probabilities. In this paper we would review the different strategies used for the selection of crossover and mutation ratios and suggest a dynamic approach for modifying the ratios during runtime. We start with a mutation ratio 0% and crossover ratio 100% where the mutation ratio slowly increases and the crossover ratio decreases (MICD). The final mutation ratio will be 0% and crossover ratio will be 100% at the end of the search process. We also do the reverse process of considering the mutation ratio to be maximum and crossover ratio to be minimum and slowly decrease the mutation ratio and increase the crossover ratio (MDCI). We compare the proposed method with two pre-existing parameter tuning methods and found that this dynamic approach of incrementing the mutation and decrementing the crossover value was more effective when the size of the population was large.

Title: A dynamic approach for parameter tuning in genetic algorithm using crossover and mutation ratios
Snippet: Genetic algorithm uses the natural selection process for any search process. It is an optimization process where integration among different vital parameters like crossover and mutation plays a major role. The parameters have an impact on the algorithm by their probabilities. In this paper we would review the different strategies used for the selection of crossover and mutation ratios and suggest a dynamic approach for modifying the ratios during runtime. We start with a mutation ratio 0% and crossover ratio 100% where the mutation ratio slowly increases and the crossover ratio decreases (MICD). The final mutation ratio will be 0% and crossover ratio will be 100% at the end of the search process. We also do the reverse process of considering the mutation ratio to be maximum and crossover ratio to be minimum and slowly decrease the mutation ratio and increase the crossover ratio (MDCI). In the segment-based crossover, random chosen segments of the parents are used to form an offspring [35]. 

When compared to other crossover types, segment based crossover has noteworthy diversity on the gene. As a result, the search space contains various flag sets. As mutation type gauss by center is used, where a random value which is driven from a normal distribution is added to the chosen gene [36]. 

In the linear ranking selection concept, the selection probability of an individual is determined by sorting fitness values with equal intervals between adjacent rank [37]. With linear ranking, individuals with lower fitness values have chance to be chosen. This approach provides to reveal the flags which has not been turned on but may have effect on the execution time.

Title: Improved genetic algorithm for multi-threshold optimization in digital pathology image segmentation
Snippet: To comprehensively understand the performance of the Improved Genetic Algorithm (Improved GA), a detailed analysis of its time complexity has been conducted. Time complexity is a critical metric for evaluating how the execution time of an algorithm scales with the size of the input. In the context of genetic algorithms, the primary time-consuming operations are selection, crossover, mutation, and fitness evaluation. To visually represent the time complexity, an experimental analysis was conducted, and a 3D plot was generated to illustrate the time complexity under various combinations of population size and number of generations. Each point in the plot corresponds to a specific combination of population size and generation, with the color intensity reflecting the magnitude of the time complexity. Text labels were added to provide direct numerical values for each point. The 3D plot of the Time Complexity Analysis of the Improved Genetic Algorithm is shown in Fig. 8. The experimental results indicate that the time complexity increases with both the population size and the number of generations. This is intuitive, as each individual in the population requires processing through selection, crossover, mutation, and fitness evaluation, and these operations are directly proportional to the population size and the number of generations. 

In practical scenarios, the choice of population size and number of generations involves a trade-off between computational efficiency and solution quality. For applications where high-quality solutions are paramount, the Improved GA's superior performance justifies its higher computational demands. The time complexity analysis provides a profound understanding of the Improved GA's performance, aiding in informed decision-making when designing and applying genetic algorithms in practice.

Snippet: An intriguing extension of the NFL and its equation involves considering two configurations of the same method, denoted a(f ) and b(f ). According to the NFL theorem, these two algorithms will have equal average performance over all possible problems. Hence, it can be deduced that tuning the parameters of an algorithm to enhance its effectiveness on a specific problem may adversely affect its effectiveness on other problem instances. This highlights the inherent trade-off between optimality and generality, emphasizing the critical role of parameter tuning. This trade-off in the context of meta-heuristics has been extensively explored and theoretically investigated in various studies. 

The computational time complexity of Evolutionary Algorithms (EA) was examined by He and Yao [51], in which they utilized drift analysis to estimate the average time complexity order of an EA when applied to a problem based on the upper and lower bounds. To extend this, they [52] performed a time complexity analysis on both (1 + 1) and (N + N ) EAs by deriving their First Hitting Time (FHT) on a variety of problems. They directly estimated the FHT of a Markov chain from the transition matrix. Through further empirical studies, they concluded that increasing the population size, one of the key characteristics of EAs, can lower time complexity, boost first-hitting probabilities, and shorten FHT. Nonetheless, they emphasized their results do not imply that (N + N ) will always outperform (1+1) on all possible problems. Given the distribution µ 0 of initial population X 0 conditional on initial state i with the transition probability P, they formulated E[T ] as the mean first hitting time T as follows: 

The significance and importance of parameter tuning on the performance of meta-heuristics was reiterated by Yu et al. [53]. Identifying the population size as the main parameter of Genetic Algorithms (GA), they introduced a population-sizing model for the entropy-based model building. Title: Phi-array: A novel method for fitness visualization and decision making in evolutionary design optimization
Snippet: A real-number encoded genetic algorithm (GA) was used in this study. Values were scaled to nearest integers within the specified lower and upper bounds during initialization and mutation. The following GA strategies were employed: 

• Fixed initialization of population was used for the crossover probability study and random initialization was used for the final optimization; 

• Selection of individuals in a population for genetic operations is based on tournament selection with rank based fitness scaling; 

• Fitness scaling is done by ranking raw fitness scores and the rank of an individual is its position in the sorted scores; 

• Elitism is employed in the form that the single best solution from the previous generation is preserved in the new generation; 

• The GA stops when the specified maximum number of generations is reached or when the weighted average change in the fitness function value over stalled generations is less than the specified function tolerance; and 

• The fitness of each evaluated individual is stored to save computation time spent on simulation. 

Population size for real-encoded genetic algorithms is usually determined by ad-hoc approaches and depends on a researcher's experience [38] of the type of the problem and the solution landscape. The choice of population size has been reported to cause the runtime of the GA to vary by several orders of magnitude [39]. The compute-intensive nature of the physically-based simulation 1 in this study meant that the GA's population size needed to be carefully chosen to reduce overall runtime but not sacrificing the speed of convergence. Previous studies have found that a small population is quite effective [40] when the dimension of the problem is small [41] and the GA is allowed to run for many generations [39]. 

The population size for the GA in this study was, therefore, chosen to be 20. The crossover probability, P c , was set to 0.4, which was based on a parametric study, described in the following section. The mutation probability, P m , was, therefore, 0.6 (P m = 1 − P c ). The maximum number of generations was set to 100 as one of the stopping criteria.

documents.snippet:
To comprehensively understand the performance of the Improved Genetic Algorithm (Improved GA), a detailed analysis of its time complexity has been conducted. Time complexity is a critical metric for evaluating how the execution time of an algorithm scales with the size of the input. In the context of genetic algorithms, the primary time-consuming operations are selection, crossover, mutation, and fitness evaluation. To visually represent the time complexity, an experimental analysis was conducted, and a 3D plot was generated to illustrate the time complexity under various combinations of population size and number of generations. Each point in the plot corresponds to a specific combination of population size and generation, with the color intensity reflecting the magnitude of the time complexity. Text labels were added to provide direct numerical values for each point. The 3D plot of the Time Complexity Analysis of the Improved Genetic Algorithm is shown in Fig. 8. The experimental results indicate that the time complexity increases with both the population size and the number of generations. This is intuitive, as each individual in the population requires processing through selection, crossover, mutation, and fitness evaluation, and these operations are directly proportional to the population size and the number of generations. 

In practical scenarios, the choice of population size and number of generations involves a trade-off between computational efficiency and solution quality. For applications where high-quality solutions are paramount, the Improved GA's superior performance justifies its higher computational demands. The time complexity analysis provides a profound understanding of the Improved GA's performance, aiding in informed decision-making when designing and applying genetic algorithms in practice.

Title: A Lattice-based Method for Optimization in Continuous Spaces with Genetic Algorithms
Snippet: A solution that satisfies all constraints in an optimization problem is referred to as a "feasible" solution. Traditional GAs may inadvertently explore infeasible regions of the solution space, generating solutions that violate one or more constraints. Such solutions are of no practical value in design problems, as they do not represent viable designs. Therefore, the ability to effectively handle constraints is a critical feature for GAs to be considered a useful tool in design optimization. By incorporating constraint handling, GAs can be adapted to efficiently search for feasible solutions within the constrained solution space, leading to more meaningful and actionable results. 

Several distinct methods of constraint handling in GAs have been researched, varying in application, complexity, and generality [10,11]. The literary history of constraint handling in GAs is broad and somewhat fragmented, as many techniques have been developed in isolation to address particular use-cases. However, in general, constraint handling approaches fall roughly into three groups: penalty methods, repair methods, and specialized operators. 

The most popular method of constraint handling in genetic algorithms is to apply a penalty to infeasible solutions [10,11,12,13]. The techniques described by [11] suggest methods of levying penalties in an effort to guide search towards feasible regions of the search space. Nonetheless, infeasible solutions still appear in the population, with the goal that sufficiently high penalty precludes the candidate from selection in future generations. 

Empirically, penalty methods in stochastic optimization cannot guarantee both the prevention of infeasible solutions and algorithm convergence. In other words, depending on the convergence criterion and configuration of the genetic algorithm, the solutions returned by the algorithm are not guaranteed to be feasible. As discussed in [14], a large penalty for constraint violations may result in premature convergence or stagnation when a feasible solution is found. Conversely, a low penalty may result in infeasible solutions being returned, as they may have higher fitness than the feasible solutions. Indeed, the results of [11] show that, for some methods, infeasible solutions were present in the optimal set of solutions. Therefore, tuning of the penalty factors may be required to achieve desired performance, and the correct tuning of the parameters is not known a-priori.

Title: Optimization Design of Automotive Body Stiffness Using a Boundary Hybrid Genetic Algorithm
Snippet: Zhou et al. [14] developed a ranking procedure in accordance with the Pareto strength concept for the bi-objective problem, but with the constraints increasing, the objective function becomes complicated. As pointed out by Runarsson and Yao [15], the multi-objective techniques are difficult to find feasible solutions since most of the time is spent searching infeasible regions. While GA is coupled with another technique (e.g., another heuristic or a mathematical programming approach) to form hybrid methods, the new methods generally require several parameters to work properly, just like penalty methods. The main idea of the repair methods is to transform an infeasible solution into a feasible one, which can reduce the search space by using a repair technique. Furthermore, no special operators or modifications of the fitness function need to be considered in this case. Salcedo et al. [16] proposed a concept of a hybrid genetic algorithm in which the local search (LS) procedure is used as a constraint-handling technique. Later, Li et al. [17] proposed a boundary simulation genetic algorithm (BSGA) to address inequality constraints for GAs and developed a series of genetic operators that would abandon or repair infeasible individuals produced during the search process. However, it was not specified whether the infeasible solutions were abandoned or repaired, and it may not work properly for problems with disconnected feasible regions. Coello [18] has emphasized that a desired constraint-handling technique should be general and incorporate knowledge about the domain, efficiency, etc. Based on the BSGA and hybrid genetic algorithm, a boundary hybrid genetic algorithm (BHGA) that could be applied effectively to engineering is proposed in this paper. In general, the method proposed in this paper has several features, which will be discussed in detail in the following chapters.

Title: A Constrained Multiobjective Evolutionary Algorithm Based on a Hybrid Constraint Handling Technique Using Population Trimming Strategy
Snippet: For constrained multiobjective optimization problems (CMOPs), one of the fundamental issues faced by researchers is how to make comparisons between individuals within the population that results in a balanced selection of better individuals. The selection of better individuals need to be balanced between elitism, diversity and feasibility. In this paper, we propose a hybrid constraint handling technique of population trimming strategy and adaptive penalty function for multiobjective evolutionary algorithm NSGA-II to solve CMOPs. In our approach, a method of objectivization of constraint violations and proportional reduction is used to compare two individuals and trim the population, and as a result the new parent population consisted of the optimal feasible individuals and good infeasible individuals is obtained. To our knowledge, the distant matrix in proportional reduction procedure is firstly proposed for comparison and maintaining diversity in infeasible individuals. Furthermore, an adaptive penalty function method is utilized to give the fitness of individuals in parent population. Numerical simulations indicate that the proposed algorithm outperforms the current state-of-the-art algorithms, e.g. NSGA-II-CD, NAGA-II-WTY, in both convergence and diversity.

Title: A Constraint Optimization path planning for Dynamic Environment
Snippet: Constraint optimization issues involve a variety of design aspects. Constraints are crucial to engineering design since they are frequently imposed in problem statements and can be challenging to satisfy, making search efforts laborious and ineffective. Any stochastic search algorithm's freshly generated solution might not meet the restrictions of the problem after optimization. The penalty method, which penalizes impractical solutions in order to ensure feasible ones, is now the most widely used method for addressing the limitations of a problem. A bracket operator penalty term can be added to the objective function based on the constraint violation, and a penalized function is created. Due to their straightforward structure and implementation, evolutionary algorithms (EAs) have been developed to handle constraint optimization and are having increasing interest. Due to the fact that the initial EAs are essentially unconstrained optimization techniques when managing constraint optimization, they are required to have an additional mechanism to deal with constraints. Several constraint-handling strategies have been proposed, one of them is the penalty function which is used in this reseaech.

Title: A Constraint-Handling Technique for Genetic Algorithms using a Violation Factor
Snippet: One of the key complications in using GA for practical engineering optimization applications is the design of the fitness function. When dealing with constrained problems, we must find a mean to estimate the closeness of an infeasible solution to the feasible region. By simply examining the previously proposed constraint-handling techniques, several key points can be derived about the existing methods. Initially, they are diverse, yet require the definition and fine-tuning of at least one parameter. 

Apart of being an arduous procedure to define and control the penalty terms, we claim that such methods deviate from the essence of the philosophy of the evolutionary algorithms (i.e., techniques based on the principle of natural selection). Arguably, the most widely used algorithm is the genetic algorithm developed by (Holland, 1975). Despite the success of GA's as optimization techniques in many engineering applications, they are mostly applied on unconstrained problems. 

Therefore, the main proposal of the authors is to suggest a constraint-handling technique that preserves the notions of the GA. The key motif is to keep the fitness function equivalent to the designer's objective and eliminate any additional penalty functions. The core structure of GA is analogous to the theory of biological evolution mimicking the principle of the survival of the fittest. The proposed constraint-handling technique is directly inspired from the nature of genetic algorithms, since the objective function is preserved during the evolution process. In this study, we will implement the proposed VCH method inside a genetic algorithm due to its advantages: a) Adaptability: Does not oblige the objective function to be continuous or in algebraic form. b) Robustness: Escapes more easily from local optimums because of its population-based nature. c) Equilibrium: Provide a good balance between exploitation and exploration. Do not need specific domain information, but can be further exploited it if provided. d) Flexibility: GA's are simple and relatively easy to implement.

problem: Find some existing work on LLM and inductive qualitative analysis.
final_response:
# Overview: LLMs for Inductive Qualitative Analysis

Inductive qualitative analysis derives codes, categories, and themes from data without starting from a fixed codebook, often through iterative coding and theoretical sampling (e.g., grounded theory, thematic analysis). Recent work explores how large language models (LLMs) can support or automate inductive coding, codebook induction, and collaborative annotation workflows, as well as how to evaluate their reliability and convergence compared to human coders. <cite id="8e76f9ec-1">Inductive coding is typically carried out by human coders who iteratively interpret, categorize, and refine codes, but it is time-consuming and subject to inconsistency; LLM advances create opportunities to automate parts of the pipeline</cite>. <cite id="8e76f9ec-4">Thematic analysis includes an initial coding phase followed by saturation assessment; recent work examines how well LLMs achieve analytical saturation and proposes a novel measure of Inductive Thematic Saturation using DSPy</cite>.

# Empirical Comparisons: LLMs vs. Humans; Agreement and Reliability

Several studies directly compare LLMs and humans on inductive coding tasks and examine agreement and reliability. <cite id="8e76f9ec-0">A head-to-head study of six open-source LLMs vs. human experts on inductive coding reports a counterintuitive dichotomy: humans perform better on complex sentences while LLMs perform better on simpler ones; experts rated human annotations more favorably by other humans, while some LLMs aligned closer to true labels yet were downrated by experts</cite>. <cite id="de6449b3-4">In a mixed-methods study coding large-scale student–ChatGPT interaction data, interrater reliability reached substantial to near-perfect agreement (e.g., Kappa 0.75–0.91 across categories), and the authors note that LLMs guided by clear schemas can achieve moderate to substantial agreement with human coders</cite>. <cite id="f7e4e0d4-3">A domain application used GPT‑4 to code 24 interviews using a 28‑code codebook nested within 8 broad aspects, reporting a 74% hit rate at detailed code level and 96% at broad code levels, and aligning more closely with human qualitative results than LDA</cite>.

Beyond simple hit-rate comparisons, process-level evaluations highlight complementary strengths. <cite id="8e76f9ec-0">The same study finds systematic deviations in both human and LLM labels relative to a gold standard, underscoring that neither is uniformly better across all data characteristics</cite>. <cite id="de6449b3-0">A grounded-theory tutorial with blind gamers found that ChatGPT 4‑Turbo and manual coding were reliable in many aspects, but ChatGPT showed shortcomings in depth, contextualization, connections, and coding organization compared to manual coding with qualitative software</cite>.

# Frameworks and Automation: Multi-Agent LLM Annotation and Saturation Measurement

Researchers are building frameworks that emulate and extend human qualitative workflows with LLMs. <cite id="8e76f9ec-1">A multi-agent, multi-round LLM annotation framework simulates collaborative annotation for inductive coding without fine-tuning, tracking how codes evolve and align; it introduces process metrics (code stability, semantic self-consistency, opinion-confidence dynamics) and geometric analyses of embedding-space changes to assess coordination</cite>. This work explicitly targets inductive code development and convergence behaviors, distinguishing surface lexical mimicry from deeper semantic alignment. <cite id="8e76f9ec-4">Complementing convergence, “Inductive Thematic Saturation” (ITS) quantifies when initial LLM-produced codes stabilize, offering a measure of codebook adequacy; the authors implement this using the DSPy framework to formalize evaluation and measurement</cite>.

# Datasets and Benchmarks for Qualitative Coding and Codebook Induction

While general LLM benchmarks are abundant, domain-specific benchmarks for qualitative inductive coding remain sparse. <cite id="f7e4e0d4-3">Some applied studies construct codebooks and datasets for LLM coding (e.g., 28 codes across 8 broad aspects from interviews), enabling hit-rate evaluations against human-coded gold standards</cite>. <cite id="8e76f9ec-2">Other work demonstrates codebook generation from thousands of qualitative texts (e.g., student teaching evaluations), showing alignment with a previously coded human codebook, suggesting feasibility of LLM-generated codebooks for inductive thematic analysis</cite>. <cite id="8e76f9ec-3">Theory-grounded studies train or align LLMs (e.g., BERT) to predict qualitative codes derived from a model of social construction of knowledge (IAM), highlighting the importance of theoretical grounding when translating qualitative frameworks into data-driven models</cite>. <cite id="f7e4e0d4-4">At the broader evaluation ecosystem level, new approaches like decentralized arenas and multi-judge LLM evaluation suites are emerging, though these focus on general LLM judging rather than qualitative coding per se</cite>.

# Methodological Workflows and Guidelines for LLM-Assisted Inductive Coding

Methodological papers and tutorials are surfacing practical workflows and cautions for using LLMs in grounded theory and thematic analysis. <cite id="de6449b3-0">A grounded-theory tutorial with ChatGPT 4‑Turbo provides a step-by-step workflow—open coding, axial coding, selective coding—comparing LLM outputs to manual coding with qualitative software; it reports reliability across many aspects, while noting deficits in contextual depth and relational connections</cite>. <cite id="de6449b3-4">The same study offers recommendations and limitations, emphasizing that LLM coding quality depends on prompt schemas, examples, and iterative human oversight to mitigate bias and maintain analytic rigor</cite>.

# Applications: Codebook Induction and Domain Cases

LLMs are being used to generate and refine codebooks across domains. <cite id="8e76f9ec-2">In education, an NLP-based method generated a codebook from 5,000 student evaluations of teaching and showed alignment with a prior human-coded codebook, indicating potential for scalable inductive qualitative analysis</cite>. <cite id="f7e4e0d4-3">In educational stakeholder interviews, GPT‑4 coding using a structured codebook achieved high-level alignment with human results and outperformed a classical topic model on thematic coherence</cite>. <cite id="8e76f9ec-3">In online learning analytics, transformer-based LLMs were evaluated for predicting qualitative codes grounded in the Interaction Analysis Model (IAM), underscoring the role of theoretical grounding when modeling social construction of knowledge in discourse</cite>.

# Limitations, Biases, and Open Challenges

Despite promising results, several limitations recur. <cite id="8e76f9ec-0">Humans and LLMs exhibit complementary but also conflicting error profiles—humans stronger on complex contexts, LLMs on simpler items—so hybrid workflows and calibration are needed</cite>. <cite id="de6449b3-0">LLMs can lack depth and context sensitivity and may miss relational connections among codes compared to trained qualitative coders</cite>. <cite id="8e76f9ec-1">Multi-agent LLM systems may converge due to lexical or surface-level factors rather than shared semantics; proposed metrics aim to separate true semantic consistency from superficial mimicry</cite>. <cite id="8e76f9ec-4">Measuring saturation with LLMs remains an active area; ensuring code quality and stopping rules for induction require careful, possibly formalized, evaluation</cite>. Title: Text Annotation via Inductive Coding: Comparing Human Experts to LLMs in Qualitative Data Analysis
Snippet: This paper investigates the automation of qualitative data analysis, focusing on inductive coding using large language models (LLMs). Unlike traditional approaches that rely on deductive methods with predefined labels, this research investigates the inductive process where labels emerge from the data. The study evaluates the performance of six open-source LLMs compared to human experts. As part of the evaluation, experts rated the perceived difficulty of the quotes they coded. The results reveal a peculiar dichotomy: human coders consistently perform well when labeling complex sentences but struggle with simpler ones, while LLMs exhibit the opposite trend. Additionally, the study explores systematic deviations in both human and LLM generated labels by comparing them to the golden standard from the test set. While human annotations may sometimes differ from the golden standard, they are often rated more favorably by other humans. In contrast, some LLMs demonstrate closer alignment with the true labels but receive lower evaluations from experts.
