Title: Emergent Convergence in Multi-Agent LLM Annotation
Snippet: Inductive coding is a core method in qualitative research, used to identify patterns and themes by assigning semantic labels, or codes, to unstructured text segments (Saldana, 2016;Braun and Clarke, 2021). This process is typically carried out by human coders who iteratively interpret, categorize, and refine codes. Collaborative coding can enhance interpretive depth through discussion and consensus, but it is also time-consuming and subject to inconsistencies caused by individual bias and group effects (MacQueen and Guest, 2008;Bernard, 2016;Bumbuc, 2016). 

Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have created opportunities to automate parts of the qualitative analysis pipeline. While prior work has examined LLMs for individual coding (Chen et al., 2024;Parfenova et al., 2025), little is known about how they behave in multi-agent settings that mirror human annotation teams. In particular, it remains unclear how coordination arises between models, and whether convergence in their outputs reflects shared semantic understanding, lexical mimicry, or other surface-level alignment processes. 

This paper introduces a large-scale simulation framework for multi-agent, multi-round LLM discussions in an inductive coding task. Each model acts as a black-box agent that proposes and revises codes over several rounds, without finetuning or access to internal states. By analyzing only the outputs, we track how codes evolve and align over time, providing an interpretable view of coordination. 

We combine process-level metrics with geometric analysis of output embeddings to capture both lexical and structural aspects of coordination. Our metrics include code stability, semantic self-consistency, and opinion-confidence dynamics, alongside measures of embedding-space geometry such as intrinsic dimensionality, which we interpret as a proxy for semantic compression during convergence. 

Our contributions are: 

1. We present a simulation framework for largescale, black-box multi-agent LLM discussions applied to collaborative annotation. 

2. We propose coordination metrics that capture surface-level stability, semantic consistency, and opinion-confidence alignment, as well as geometric shifts in embedding space.
</snippet>

Title: StatLLM: A Dataset for Evaluating the Performance of Large Language Models in Statistical Analysis
Snippet: The coding capabilities of large language models (LLMs) have opened up new opportunities for automatic statistical analysis in machine learning and data science. However, before their widespread adoption, it is crucial to assess the accuracy of code generated by LLMs. A major challenge in this evaluation lies in the absence of a benchmark dataset for statistical code (e.g., SAS and R). To fill in this gap, this paper introduces StatLLM, an open-source dataset for evaluating the performance of LLMs in statistical analysis. The StatLLM dataset comprises three key components: statistical analysis tasks, LLM-generated SAS code, and human evaluation scores. The first component includes statistical analysis tasks spanning a variety of analyses and datasets, providing problem descriptions, dataset details, and human-verified SAS code. The second component features SAS code generated by ChatGPT 3.5, ChatGPT 4.0, and Llama 3.1 for those tasks. The third component contains evaluation scores from human experts in assessing the correctness, effectiveness, readability, executability, and output accuracy of the LLM-generated code. We also illustrate the unique potential of the established benchmark dataset for (1) evaluating and enhancing natural language processing metrics, (2) assessing and improving LLM performance in statistical coding, and (3) developing and testing of next-generation statistical software - advancements that are crucial for data science and machine learning research.
</snippet>

Title: Re-defining language teacher cognition through a data-driven model: The case of three EFL teachers
Snippet: Grounded theory has a multilevel data analysis process in which the researcher starts with some basic descriptions (open coding), goes on with a conceptual ordering (axial coding) and finalizes with theorization (selective coding) (Patton, 1990). All these processes are shaped with detailed sets of coding processes that occur recursively in a cyclical way. 

The first step of this coding process was open coding in the current study. In this process, the researcher broke the data into chunks and assigned them initial category labels. At the end of open coding, the researcher identified themes to serve as categories in the next step. Since this phase of coding process was similar to qualitative content analysis, the scheme of Creswell (2012) which includes transcription, reading through the data, coding and reaching themes was used in this stage. 

The second step was axial coding in which "the researcher makes connections between categories, thereby attempting to integrate them and group them into more encompassing concepts that subsume several subcategories" (Dörnyei, 2007, p. 261). During axial coding, the researcher selected a core category among open coding categories based on the criteria stated by Strauss and Corbin (1998) considering its frequency in the data and its relevance to other categories, and related other categories to it under the headings of causal conditions, context, intervening conditions, strategies and consequences. In order to systematize this process, the researcher followed the axial coding paradigm presented by Strauss and Corbin (1998) and conducted the same process for two constructs of the study-language teacher cognition and classroom practices-separately (Figure 1). 

In selective coding, the last phase of the process, the researcher integrated and refined the theory from the interrelationship among the categories derived from the axial coding schemes of language teacher cognition and classroom practices (Strauss & Corbin, 1998). A new theoretical insight was generated on the sources and characteristics of each construct and their interconnectedness. At the end, the researcher proposed a framework that would describe the cognition of the participant teachers with regard to their classroom practices and institutional context.
</snippet>

Title: Coproducing Wellbeing Policy: A Theory of Thriving in Financial Hardship
Snippet: Two analysts (authors 1 and 3) conducted the qualitative analysis of the interviews. Note that these researchers were participants in the interviews and thus coded each other's interviews. This provides some rigor in two regards. First, it means that one analyst can cut through theoretical biases the other brought to their interview practice at the coding stage. Second, it means that in coding interview transcripts the analysts are not simply coding their own words. 

The analysts began by using grounded theory (Charmaz, 2006), which is the simple idea that theories based on qualitative research should be 'grounded' in the associated data. In practice, grounded theory involves using 'descriptive' codes to label what is literally said in interviews, returning to earlier data sources iteratively as new codes emerge. A sec-ond round of 'analytical' codes is then used to organise the descriptive codes into clusters, themes, and ultimately theories.

# Overview: LLMs for Inductive Qualitative Analysis

Inductive qualitative analysis derives codes, categories, and themes from data without starting from a fixed codebook, often through iterative coding and theoretical sampling (e.g., grounded theory, thematic analysis). Recent work explores how large language models (LLMs) can support or automate inductive coding, codebook induction, and collaborative annotation workflows, as well as how to evaluate their reliability and convergence compared to human coders. <cite id="8e76f9ec-1">Inductive coding is typically carried out by human coders who iteratively interpret, categorize, and refine codes, but it is time-consuming and subject to inconsistency; LLM advances create opportunities to automate parts of the pipeline</cite>. <cite id="8e76f9ec-4">Thematic analysis includes an initial coding phase followed by saturation assessment; recent work examines how well LLMs achieve analytical saturation and proposes a novel measure of Inductive Thematic Saturation using DSPy</cite>.

# Empirical Comparisons: LLMs vs. Humans; Agreement and Reliability

Several studies directly compare LLMs and humans on inductive coding tasks and examine agreement and reliability. <cite id="8e76f9ec-0">A head-to-head study of six open-source LLMs vs. human experts on inductive coding reports a counterintuitive dichotomy: humans perform better on complex sentences while LLMs perform better on simpler ones; experts rated human annotations more favorably by other humans, while some LLMs aligned closer to true labels yet were downrated by experts</cite>. <cite id="de6449b3-4">In a mixed-methods study coding large-scale student–ChatGPT interaction data, interrater reliability reached substantial to near-perfect agreement (e.g., Kappa 0.75–0.91 across categories), and the authors note that LLMs guided by clear schemas can achieve moderate to substantial agreement with human coders</cite>. <cite id="f7e4e0d4-3">A domain application used GPT‑4 to code 24 interviews using a 28‑code codebook nested within 8 broad aspects, reporting a 74% hit rate at detailed code level and 96% at broad code levels, and aligning more closely with human qualitative results than LDA</cite>.

Beyond simple hit-rate comparisons, process-level evaluations highlight complementary strengths. <cite id="8e76f9ec-0">The same study finds systematic deviations in both human and LLM labels relative to a gold standard, underscoring that neither is uniformly better across all data characteristics</cite>. <cite id="de6449b3-0">A grounded-theory tutorial with blind gamers found that ChatGPT 4‑Turbo and manual coding were reliable in many aspects, but ChatGPT showed shortcomings in depth, contextualization, connections, and coding organization compared to manual coding with qualitative software</cite>.

# Frameworks and Automation: Multi-Agent LLM Annotation and Saturation Measurement

Researchers are building frameworks that emulate and extend human qualitative workflows with LLMs. <cite id="8e76f9ec-1">A multi-agent, multi-round LLM annotation framework simulates collaborative annotation for inductive coding without fine-tuning, tracking how codes evolve and align; it introduces process metrics (code stability, semantic self-consistency, opinion-confidence dynamics) and geometric analyses of embedding-space changes to assess coordination</cite>. This work explicitly targets inductive code development and convergence behaviors, distinguishing surface lexical mimicry from deeper semantic alignment. <cite id="8e76f9ec-4">Complementing convergence, “Inductive Thematic Saturation” (ITS) quantifies when initial LLM-produced codes stabilize, offering a measure of codebook adequacy; the authors implement this using the DSPy framework to formalize evaluation and measurement</cite>.

# Datasets and Benchmarks for Qualitative Coding and Codebook Induction

While general LLM benchmarks are abundant, domain-specific benchmarks for qualitative inductive coding remain sparse. <cite id="f7e4e0d4-3">Some applied studies construct codebooks and datasets for LLM coding (e.g., 28 codes across 8 broad aspects from interviews), enabling hit-rate evaluations against human-coded gold standards</cite>. <cite id="8e76f9ec-2">Other work demonstrates codebook generation from thousands of qualitative texts (e.g., student teaching evaluations), showing alignment with a previously coded human codebook, suggesting feasibility of LLM-generated codebooks for inductive thematic analysis</cite>. <cite id="8e76f9ec-3">Theory-grounded studies train or align LLMs (e.g., BERT) to predict qualitative codes derived from a model of social construction of knowledge (IAM), highlighting the importance of theoretical grounding when translating qualitative frameworks into data-driven models</cite>. <cite id="f7e4e0d4-4">At the broader evaluation ecosystem level, new approaches like decentralized arenas and multi-judge LLM evaluation suites are emerging, though these focus on general LLM judging rather than qualitative coding per se</cite>.

# Methodological Workflows and Guidelines for LLM-Assisted Inductive Coding

Methodological papers and tutorials are surfacing practical workflows and cautions for using LLMs in grounded theory and thematic analysis. <cite id="de6449b3-0">A grounded-theory tutorial with ChatGPT 4‑Turbo provides a step-by-step workflow—open coding, axial coding, selective coding—comparing LLM outputs to manual coding with qualitative software; it reports reliability across many aspects, while noting deficits in contextual depth and relational connections</cite>. <cite id="de6449b3-4">The same study offers recommendations and limitations, emphasizing that LLM coding quality depends on prompt schemas, examples, and iterative human oversight to mitigate bias and maintain analytic rigor</cite>. 

Studies also illustrate how to integrate LLMs into iterative qualitative cycles. <cite id="8e76f9ec-4">Work on inductive thematic saturation proposes formalizing initial coding rounds and measuring when additional coding yields diminishing returns, providing a decision heuristic for when to stop code induction with LLMs</cite>. <cite id="de6449b3-3">Applied qualitative projects using grounded theory describe strategies to reduce bias (e.g., coding blind to interviewer identities, comparing codebooks, and using divergent coding strategies) and achieving conceptual saturation, showing that LLMs can be one component in a multi-layered analytic process</cite>.

# Applications: Codebook Induction and Domain Cases

LLMs are being used to generate and refine codebooks across domains. <cite id="8e76f9ec-2">In education, an NLP-based method generated a codebook from 5,000 student evaluations of teaching and showed alignment with a prior human-coded codebook, indicating potential for scalable inductive qualitative analysis</cite>. <cite id="f7e4e0d4-3">In educational stakeholder interviews, GPT‑4 coding using a structured codebook achieved high-level alignment with human results and outperformed a classical topic model on thematic coherence</cite>. <cite id="8e76f9ec-3">In online learning analytics, transformer-based LLMs were evaluated for predicting qualitative codes grounded in the Interaction Analysis Model (IAM), underscoring the role of theoretical grounding when modeling social construction of knowledge in discourse</cite>.

# Limitations, Biases, and Open Challenges

Despite promising results, several limitations recur. <cite id="8e76f9ec-0">Humans and LLMs exhibit complementary but also conflicting error profiles—humans stronger on complex contexts, LLMs on simpler items—so hybrid workflows and calibration are needed</cite>. <cite id="de6449b3-0">LLMs can lack depth and context sensitivity and may miss relational connections among codes compared to trained qualitative coders</cite>. <cite id="8e76f9ec-1">Multi-agent LLM systems may converge due to lexical or surface-level factors rather than shared semantics; proposed metrics aim to separate true semantic consistency from superficial mimicry</cite>. <cite id="8e76f9ec-4">Measuring saturation with LLMs remains an active area; ensuring code quality and stopping rules for induction require careful, possibly formalized, evaluation</cite>. Finally, benchmarking remains uneven: many studies rely on bespoke datasets and ad hoc gold standards rather than widely shared, theory-aligned qualitative coding benchmarks, limiting comparability and reproducibility. <cite id="f7e4e0d4-3">Even when codebooks are published, they are often domain-specific and not designed for broad external validity</cite>.

# Takeaways and Pointers for Practice

- Use LLMs as scalable co-coders or codebook generators, but validate with human coders and iterative comparison. <cite id="8e76f9ec-0">LLMs and humans complement each other across data complexity</cite>; <cite id="de6449b3-0">LLMs can improve efficiency and code diversity but may miss contextual depth and connections</cite>.
- Embrace hybrid workflows and structured schemas. <cite id="de6449b3-4">Clear coding schemas and examples can raise interrater agreement with LLMs toward moderate-to-substantial levels</cite>; <cite id="de6449b3-0">grounded theory tutorials demonstrate stepwise integration of LLM outputs with manual coding</cite>.
- Monitor convergence and saturation rigorously. <cite id="8e76f9ec-1">Track code stability and semantic consistency across rounds in multi-agent setups</cite>; <cite id="8e76f9ec-4">measure inductive thematic saturation to decide when to stop code induction</cite>.
- Ground theory and domain context. <cite id="8e76f9ec-3">Theory-informed coding frameworks (e.g., IAM) can improve LLM alignment to qualitative concepts</cite>; <cite id="f7e4e0d4-3">domain codebooks enable higher-level agreement with human-coded results</cite>.
- Plan for evaluation and reporting. <cite id="8e76f9ec-0">Report both label-level agreement and qualitative expert judgments</cite>; <cite id="de6449b3-4">use recognized reliability metrics (e.g., Cohen’s Kappa) and document prompt schemas and datasets</cite>.

# Representative Works (by Theme)

- Comparative performance and reliability:
  - <cite id="8e76f9ec-0">Text Annotation via Inductive Coding: Comparing Human Experts to LLMs</cite>.
  - <cite id="de6449b3-4">Mixed-methods coding with LLMs showing Kappa 0.75–0.91 across categories and discussion of LLM agreement with human coders</cite>.
  - <cite id="f7e4e0d4-3">GPT‑4 coding of interviews with 74% hit rate at detailed code level and 96% at broad code levels vs. human qualitative results</cite>.

- Frameworks and automation:
  - <cite id="8e76f9ec-1">Multi-agent LLM annotation for inductive coding with process metrics and embedding-space geometry analyses</cite>.
  - <cite id="8e76f9ec-4">Inductive Thematic Saturation (ITS) measurement with DSPy for LLM-driven initial coding</cite>.

- Codebook induction and applied qualitative analysis:
  - <cite id="8e76f9ec-2">NLP-based codebook generation from 5,000 student evaluations aligning with a human codebook</cite>.
  - <cite id="f7e4e0d4-3">Theory-grounded LLM evaluation (IAM) for predicting qualitative codes online</cite>.

- Methodological guidance and grounded theory:
  - <cite id="de6449b3-0">Practical guide and assessment using ChatGPT for grounded theory with reliability comparisons to manual coding</cite>.
  - <cite id="de6449b3-3">Case study detailing grounded theory procedures and strategies to mitigate bias and reach saturation</cite>.

# Summary

The literature shows that LLMs can assist inductive qualitative analysis by scaling initial coding, generating or refining codebooks, and participating in multi-round, collaborative-like workflows, but they require careful human oversight, structured schemas, and rigorous evaluation to ensure reliability, depth, and theoretical grounding. <cite id="8e76f9ec-1">LLM teams can converge on codes through multi-round discussions, though distinguishing true semantic alignment from surface mimicry remains a key challenge</cite>. <cite id="8e76f9ec-0">Humans and LLMs exhibit complementary strengths across different data characteristics, motivating hybrid workflows</cite>. <cite id="de6449b3-0">Methodological tutorials and empirical comparisons indicate growing reliability and efficiency gains, alongside recognized limitations in contextual depth and relational coding</cite>. <cite id="8e76f9ec-4">Emerging measures like inductive thematic saturation and formal frameworks (e.g., DSPy) begin to standardize evaluation of LLM-driven qualitative induction</cite>.
</answer>

Title: Text Annotation via Inductive Coding: Comparing Human Experts to LLMs in Qualitative Data Analysis
Snippet: This paper investigates the automation of qualitative data analysis, focusing on inductive coding using large language models (LLMs). Unlike traditional approaches that rely on deductive methods with predefined labels, this research investigates the inductive process where labels emerge from the data. The study evaluates the performance of six open-source LLMs compared to human experts. As part of the evaluation, experts rated the perceived difficulty of the quotes they coded. The results reveal a peculiar dichotomy: human coders consistently perform well when labeling complex sentences but struggle with simpler ones, while LLMs exhibit the opposite trend. Additionally, the study explores systematic deviations in both human and LLM generated labels by comparing them to the golden standard from the test set. While human annotations may sometimes differ from the golden standard, they are often rated more favorably by other humans. In contrast, some LLMs demonstrate closer alignment with the true labels but receive lower evaluations from experts.

Title: Emergent Convergence in Multi-Agent LLM Annotation
Snippet: Inductive coding is a core method in qualitative research, used to identify patterns and themes by assigning semantic labels, or codes, to unstructured text segments (Saldana, 2016;Braun and Clarke, 2021). This process is typically carried out by human coders who iteratively interpret, categorize, and refine codes. Collaborative coding can enhance interpretive depth through discussion and consensus, but it is also time-consuming and subject to inconsistencies caused by individual bias and group effects (MacQueen and Guest, 2008;Bernard, 2016;Bumbuc, 2016). 

Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have created opportunities to automate parts of the qualitative analysis pipeline. While prior work has examined LLMs for individual coding (Chen et al., 2024;Parfenova et al., 2025), little is known about how they behave in multi-agent settings that mirror human annotation teams. In particular, it remains unclear how coordination arises between models, and whether convergence in their outputs reflects shared semantic understanding, lexical mimicry, or other surface-level alignment processes. 

This paper introduces a large-scale simulation framework for multi-agent, multi-round LLM discussions in an inductive coding task. Each model acts as a black-box agent that proposes and revises codes over several rounds, without finetuning or access to internal states. By analyzing only the outputs, we track how codes evolve and align over time, providing an interpretable view of coordination. 

We combine process-level metrics with geometric analysis of output embeddings to capture both lexical and structural aspects of coordination. Our metrics include code stability, semantic self-consistency, and opinion-confidence dynamics, alongside measures of embedding-space geometry such as intrinsic dimensionality, which we interpret as a proxy for semantic compression during convergence. 

Our contributions are: 

1. We present a simulation framework for largescale, black-box multi-agent LLM discussions applied to collaborative annotation. 

2. We propose coordination metrics that capture surface-level stability, semantic consistency, and opinion-confidence alignment, as well as geometric shifts in embedding space.

Title: Deep Learning Models for Analyzing Social Construction of Knowledge Online
Snippet: Of particular interest when trying to match a qualitative coder's analysis of social construction of knowledge are deep learning models based on the large language models (LLMs). "Deep learning is a subset of machine learning in which multilayered neural networks learn from vast amounts of data...Deep learning uses multi-layered structures of algorithms called neural networks to draw similar conclusions as humans would" (Oppermann, 2022, pp. 1-2). We define a LLM as a deep learning model trained on a large corpus of text which then allows it to do classifications, translations, problem solving, create documents and images, etc. Examples of LLMs are BERT, ChatGPT, and LLaMA (see Appendix A). This paper explored how a basic feed-forward, NN classifier (doc2vec) and a deep learning model (BERT, a transformer and LLM) can predict a qualitative analyst's coding of the Phases of social construction of knowledge in online discussions when the predication is based on the theoretical foundation of social construction of knowledge as specified by the Interaction Analysis Model (IAM) (Gunawardena et al., 1997). The aim was to situate the deep learning model on a sound theoretical base that can explain how people learn in collaboration with each other. The need for grounding analytics on a sound learning theory base that accounts for collaborative interaction and social construction of knowledge between participants in an online environment is highlighted in the review of 36 social learning analytic studies conducted by Kaliisa and colleagues (2022). This study used the IAM as it stipulates the process of social construction of knowledge to predict a qualitative analyst's coding of discussion transcripts. The study will also use the same coded transcripts found in Megli et al.'s study (2023a;2023b), and demonstrate how a feed-forward NN classifier and a deep learning model could predict the Phases of knowledge construction coded according to the IAM. This study will therefore extend the research completed by our larger research team (Megli et al., 2023a;2023b) where a detailed description of the methods used in the qualitative coding of online transcripts can be found.

Title: Codebook Reduction and Saturation: Novel observations on Inductive Thematic Saturation for Large Language Models and initial coding in Thematic Analysis
Snippet: This paper reflects on the process of performing Thematic Analysis with Large Language Models (LLMs). Specifically, the paper deals with the problem of analytical saturation of initial codes, as produced by LLMs. Thematic Analysis is a well-established qualitative analysis method composed of interlinked phases. A key phase is the initial coding, where the analysts assign labels to discrete components of a dataset. Saturation is a way to measure the validity of a qualitative analysis and relates to the recurrence and repetition of initial codes. In the paper we reflect on how well LLMs achieve analytical saturation and propose also a novel technique to measure Inductive Thematic Saturation (ITS). This novel technique leverages a programming framework called DSPy. The proposed novel approach allows a precise measurement of ITS.

We combine process-level metrics with geometric analysis of output embeddings to capture both lexical and structural aspects of coordination. Our metrics include code stability, semantic self-consistency, and opinion-confidence dynamics, alongside measures of embedding-space geometry such as intrinsic dimensionality, which we interpret as a proxy for semantic compression during convergence. 

Our contributions are: 

1. We present a simulation framework for largescale, black-box multi-agent LLM discussions applied to collaborative annotation. 

2. We propose coordination metrics that capture surface-level stability, semantic consistency, and opinion-confidence alignment, as well as geometric shifts in embedding space.

documents.title: Deep Learning Models for Analyzing Social Construction of Knowledge Online
documents.snippet: Of particular interest when trying to match a qualitative coder's analysis of social construction of knowledge are deep learning models based on the large language models (LLMs). "Deep learning is a subset of machine learning in which multilayered neural networks learn from vast amounts of data...Deep learning uses multi-layered structures of algorithms called neural networks to draw similar conclusions as humans would" (Oppermann, 2022, pp. 1-2). We define a LLM as a deep learning model trained on a large corpus of text which then allows it to do classifications, translations, problem solving, create documents and images, etc. Examples of LLMs are BERT, ChatGPT, and LLaMA (see Appendix A). This paper explored how a basic feed-forward, NN classifier (doc2vec) and a deep learning model (BERT, a transformer and LLM) can predict a qualitative analyst's coding of the Phases of social construction of knowledge in online discussions when the predication is based on the theoretical foundation of social construction of knowledge as specified by the Interaction Analysis Model (IAM) (Gunawardena et al., 1997). The aim was to situate the deep learning model on a sound theoretical base that can explain how people learn in collaboration with each other. The need for grounding analytics on a sound learning theory base that accounts for collaborative interaction and social construction of knowledge between participants in an online environment is highlighted in the review of 36 social learning analytic studies conducted by Kaliisa and colleagues (2022). This study used the IAM as it stipulates the process of social construction of knowledge to predict a qualitative analyst's coding of discussion transcripts. The study will also use the same coded transcripts found in Megli et al.'s study (2023a;2023b), and demonstrate how a feed-forward NN classifier and a deep learning model could predict the Phases of knowledge construction coded according to the IAM. This study will therefore extend the research completed by our larger research team (Megli et al., 2023a;2023b) where a detailed description of the methods used in the qualitative coding of online transcripts can be found.

documents.title: Codebook Reduction and Saturation: Novel observations on Inductive Thematic Saturation for Large Language Models and initial coding in Thematic Analysis
documents.snippet: This paper reflects on the process of performing Thematic Analysis with Large Language Models (LLMs). Specifically, the paper deals with the problem of analytical saturation of initial codes, as produced by LLMs. Thematic Analysis is a well-established qualitative analysis method composed of interlinked phases. A key phase is the initial coding, where the analysts assign labels to discrete components of a dataset. Saturation is a way to measure the validity of a qualitative analysis and relates to the recurrence and repetition of initial codes. In the paper we reflect on how well LLMs achieve analytical saturation and propose also a novel technique to measure Inductive Thematic Saturation (ITS). This novel technique leverages a programming framework called DSPy. The proposed novel approach allows a precise measurement of ITS.

Title: StatLLM: A Dataset for Evaluating the Performance of Large Language Models in Statistical Analysis
Snippet: The coding capabilities of large language models (LLMs) have opened up new opportunities for automatic statistical analysis in machine learning and data science. However, before their widespread adoption, it is crucial to assess the accuracy of code generated by LLMs. A major challenge in this evaluation lies in the absence of a benchmark dataset for statistical code (e.g., SAS and R). To fill in this gap, this paper introduces StatLLM, an open-source dataset for evaluating the performance of LLMs in statistical analysis. The StatLLM dataset comprises three key components: statistical analysis tasks, LLM-generated SAS code, and human evaluation scores. The first component includes statistical analysis tasks spanning a variety of analyses and datasets, providing problem descriptions, dataset details, and human-verified SAS code. The second component features SAS code generated by ChatGPT 3.5, ChatGPT 4.0, and Llama 3.1 for those tasks. The third component contains evaluation scores from human experts in assessing the correctness, effectiveness, readability, executability, and output accuracy of the LLM-generated code. We also illustrate the unique potential of the established benchmark dataset for (1) evaluating and enhancing natural language processing metrics, (2) assessing and improving LLM performance in statistical coding, and (3) developing and testing of next-generation statistical software - advancements that are crucial for data science and machine learning research.

Title: A Dutch Financial Large Language Model
Snippet: Evaluation benchmarks provide valuable information on the performance of a model, allowing us to identify key areas for improvement. Unfortunately, the availability of benchmarks for Dutch LLMs is disproportionally low [28]. There are none existing within the financial context. Currently, evaluation datasets for Dutch LLM have been created by translating English benchmarks into Dutch [13], which lacks a genuine representation of the Dutch language. 

To evaluate the performance of a Dutch financial LLM, a comprehensive and diverse benchmark is required that encompasses various key financial tasks. To this end, we introduce the first Dutch financial evaluation benchmark. It is designed based on our instruction tuning dataset construction method (see Section 3.1.2). This benchmark covers critical tasks essential for effective assessment, such as Sentiment Analysis (SA), News Headline Classification (HC), Named Entity Recognition (NER), Relationship Extraction (RE), and Question Answering (QA).

Title: Adapting to Educate: Conversational AI's Role in Mathematics Education Across Different Educational Contexts
Snippet: Liu and Sun [28] employed GPT-4 to code transcripts of 24 interviews with educational stakeholders, using a developed codebook of 28 codes nested within 8 broad educational aspects. Their findings demonstrated that compared to Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), LLMs were more capable of understanding themes within the text and more closely aligned with human qualitative researchers' results, achieving a hit rate of 74% at the detailed code level and 96% at broad code levels. These results underscored LLMs' ability for consistent judgment and potential to supplement human interpretations. Their findings are consistent with other studies utilizing LLMs for deductive coding [44,49], where LLM's consistent inference and reasoning, combined with appropriate human supervision, potentially enhance the construct validity and reliability of coding results [48]. 

In addition to qualitative analysis, studies (e.g., [9,42]) have shown that LLMs analyze input based on criteria. A comparison of GPT-3.5's evaluation results with humans using the same criteria for the International English Language Testing System (IELTS) academic writing confirmed that LLMs can deliver reliable and criterionbased grading [9]. However, the quality of rubrics for evaluation is crucial. These studies highlight the importance of developing precise rubrics for LLM applications, key to achieving good inter-rater consistency with benchmarks and demonstrating excellent test-retest reliability, thereby systematically assessing the quality and relevance of content. The creation of clear and specific rubrics tailored for educational contexts is essential for enhancing the accuracy and effectiveness of automated content analysis, ensuring consistent and objective analysis, and providing a robust framework for interpreting complex educational data.

Title: A Practical Guide and Assessment on Using ChatGPT to Conduct Grounded Theory: Tutorial
Snippet: Generative large language models (LLMs), such as ChatGPT, have significant potential for qualitative data analysis. This paper aims to provide an early insight into how LLMs can enhance the efficiency of text coding and qualitative analysis, and evaluate their reliability. Using a dataset of semistructured interviews with blind gamers, this study provides a step-by-step tutorial on applying ChatGPT 4-Turbo to the grounded theory approach. The performance of ChatGPT 4-Turbo is evaluated by comparing its coding results with manual coding results assisted by qualitative analysis software. The results revealed that ChatGPT 4-Turbo and manual coding methods exhibited reliability in many aspects. The application of ChatGPT 4-Turbo in grounded theory enhanced the efficiency and diversity of coding and updated the overall grounded theory process. Compared with manual coding, ChatGPT showed shortcomings in depth, context, connections, and coding organization. Limitations and recommendations for applying artificial intelligence in qualitative research were also discussed.

Title: Re-defining language teacher cognition through a data-driven model: The case of three EFL teachers
Snippet: Grounded theory has a multilevel data analysis process in which the researcher starts with some basic descriptions (open coding), goes on with a conceptual ordering (axial coding) and finalizes with theorization (selective coding) (Patton, 1990). All these processes are shaped with detailed sets of coding processes that occur recursively in a cyclical way. 

The first step of this coding process was open coding in the current study. In this process, the researcher broke the data into chunks and assigned them initial category labels. At the end of open coding, the researcher identified themes to serve as categories in the next step. Since this phase of coding process was similar to qualitative content analysis, the scheme of Creswell (2012) which includes transcription, reading through the data, coding and reaching themes was used in this stage. 

The second step was axial coding in which "the researcher makes connections between categories, thereby attempting to integrate them and group them into more encompassing concepts that subsume several subcategories" (Dörnyei, 2007, p. 261). During axial coding, the researcher selected a core category among open coding categories based on the criteria stated by Strauss and Corbin (1998) considering its frequency in the data and its relevance to other categories, and related other categories to it under the headings of causal conditions, context, intervening conditions, strategies and consequences. In order to systematize this process, the researcher followed the axial coding paradigm presented by Strauss and Corbin (1998) and conducted the same process for two constructs of the study-language teacher cognition and classroom practices-separately (Figure 1). 

In selective coding, the last phase of the process, the researcher integrated and refined the theory from the interrelationship among the categories derived from the axial coding schemes of language teacher cognition and classroom practices (Strauss & Corbin, 1998). A new theoretical insight was generated on the sources and characteristics of each construct and their interconnectedness. At the end, the researcher proposed a framework that would describe the cognition of the participant teachers with regard to their classroom practices and institutional context.

Title: Coproducing Wellbeing Policy: A Theory of Thriving in Financial Hardship
Snippet: Two analysts (authors 1 and 3) conducted the qualitative analysis of the interviews. Note that these researchers were participants in the interviews and thus coded each other's interviews. This provides some rigor in two regards. First, it means that one analyst can cut through theoretical biases the other brought to their interview practice at the coding stage. Second, it means that in coding interview transcripts the analysts are not simply coding their own words. 

The analysts began by using grounded theory (Charmaz, 2006), which is the simple idea that theories based on qualitative research should be 'grounded' in the associated data. In practice, grounded theory involves using 'descriptive' codes to label what is literally said in interviews, returning to earlier data sources iteratively as new codes emerge. A sec-ond round of 'analytical' codes is then used to organise the descriptive codes into clusters, themes, and ultimately theories. 

Descriptive codes varied from line-by-line to paragraph-by-paragraph. The analysts discussed whether they were approaching this exercise similarly in terms of label variety/ specificity and text-length, but otherwise did not discuss the actual codes they were using to avoid influencing each other's analysis. After coding around half the material (i.e. around 20/39 interviews), both analysts started again from the beginning to reanalyse early interviews with codes that had emerged later in the process. At completion, the analysts compared codebooks and were pleased to discover that their codes were broadly similar. To evidence this, Table 1 shows the top 7 codes across each analyst. 

The next step in the qualitative analysis was to make sense of the descriptive codes in a way that would produce a model or theory of thriving. At this stage, the analysts adopted divergent strategies to try to address their own biases, check whether different methods yielded different results, and increase the likelihood that we achieved conceptual saturation and organised themes in a neat way. Analyst 1 has a substantial background in wellbeing theory. This allowed him to utilise a theoretical coding approach, applying existing ideas from the interdisciplinary wellbeing literature to organise the descriptive codes into a coherent system. In contrast, analyst 2 had no background in wellbeing studies but experience with qualitative research methods.

Title: How Students (Really) Use ChatGPT: Uncovering Experiences Among Undergraduate Students
Snippet: Interrater reliability was assessed using Cohen's Kappa [93]. As shown in Table 2, results indicated substantial to near-perfect agreement: 0.81 (Information Seeking), 0.85 (Content Generation), 0.83 (Student-ChatGPT Interaction), 0.75 (ChatGPT Response Behavior), and 0.91 (Language Use). Given our observed kappa scores, this aligns with Chae and Davidson's [27] finding that large language models, when guided by a few illustrative examples and a clear coding schema, can achieve moderate to substantial agreement with human coders. (4) Identifying broader patterns: We conducted a follow-up round of qualitative coding to explore how discourse unfolded within and across the five main categories. Through axial coding [127], we analyzed interaction data to identify new concepts and relationships, revealing overlapping themes and subtle transitions between sub-categories (similar to methodology presented in [5]). This analysis enriched our understanding of each category's internal structure and supported more detailed, conceptually grounded descriptions. 

Accomplishing these analytic steps in sequence enabled us to follow the mixed-methods model proposed by Aranda et al. [9], which integrates computational and qualitative approaches to critically analyze large-scale textual data. Specifically, by using axial coding to refine our sub-categories and examine intersections among the main categories, we aligned with their transformative design that combines depth of interpretation with systematic structure discovery, thus advancing a context-sensitive discourse analysis grounded in both theory and data.

snippet.text:
Two analysts (authors 1 and 3) conducted the qualitative analysis of the interviews. Note that these researchers were participants in the interviews and thus coded each other's interviews. This provides some rigor in two regards. First, it means that one analyst can cut through theoretical biases the other brought to their interview practice at the coding stage. Second, it means that in coding interview transcripts the analysts are not simply coding their own words. 

The analysts began by using grounded theory (Charmaz, 2006), which is the simple idea that theories based on qualitative research should be 'grounded' in the associated data. In practice, grounded theory involves using 'descriptive' codes to label what is literally said in interviews, returning to earlier data sources iteratively as new codes emerge. A sec-ond round of 'analytical' codes is then used to organise the descriptive codes into clusters, themes, and ultimately theories. 

Descriptive codes varied from line-by-line to paragraph-by-paragraph. The analysts discussed whether they were approaching this exercise similarly in terms of label variety/ specificity and text-length, but otherwise did not discuss the actual codes they were using to avoid influencing each other's analysis. After coding around half the material (i.e. around 20/39 interviews), both analysts started again from the beginning to reanalyse early interviews with codes that had emerged later in the process. At completion, the analysts compared codebooks and were pleased to discover that their codes were broadly similar. To evidence this, Table 1 shows the top 7 codes across each analyst. 

The next step in the qualitative analysis was to make sense of the descriptive codes in a way that would produce a model or theory of thriving. At this stage, the analysts adopted divergent strategies to try to address their own biases, check whether different methods yielded different results, and increase the likelihood that we achieved conceptual saturation and organised themes in a neat way. Analyst 1 has a substantial background in wellbeing theory. This allowed him to utilise a theoretical coding approach, applying existing ideas from the interdisciplinary wellbeing literature to organise the descriptive codes into a coherent system. In contrast, analyst 2 had no background in wellbeing studies but experience with qualitative research methods.

Interrater reliability was assessed using Cohen's Kappa [93]. As shown in Table 2, results indicated substantial to near-perfect agreement: 0.81 (Information Seeking), 0.85 (Content Generation), 0.83 (Student-ChatGPT Interaction), 0.75 (ChatGPT Response Behavior), and 0.91 (Language Use). Given our observed kappa scores, this aligns with Chae and Davidson's [27] finding that large language models, when guided by a few illustrative examples and a clear coding schema, can achieve moderate to substantial agreement with human coders. (4) Identifying broader patterns: We conducted a follow-up round of qualitative coding to explore how discourse unfolded within and across the five main categories. Through axial coding [127], we analyzed interaction data to identify new concepts and relationships, revealing overlapping themes and subtle transitions between sub-categories (similar to methodology presented in [5]). This analysis enriched our understanding of each category's internal structure and supported more detailed, conceptually grounded descriptions. 

Accomplishing these analytic steps in sequence enabled us to follow the mixed-methods model proposed by Aranda et al. [9], which integrates computational and qualitative approaches to critically analyze large-scale textual data. Specifically, by using axial coding to refine our sub-categories and examine intersections among the main categories, we aligned with their transformative design that combines depth of interpretation with systematic structure discovery, thus advancing a context-sensitive discourse analysis grounded in both theory and data.

documents.title: A Practical Guide and Assessment on Using ChatGPT to Conduct Grounded Theory: Tutorial
documents.snippet: Generative large language models (LLMs), such as ChatGPT, have significant potential for qualitative data analysis. This paper aims to provide an early insight into how LLMs can enhance the efficiency of text coding and qualitative analysis, and evaluate their reliability. Using a dataset of semistructured interviews with blind gamers, this study provides a step-by-step tutorial on applying ChatGPT 4-Turbo to the grounded theory approach. The performance of ChatGPT 4-Turbo is evaluated by comparing its coding results with manual coding results assisted by qualitative analysis software. The results revealed that ChatGPT 4-Turbo and manual coding methods exhibited reliability in many aspects. The application of ChatGPT 4-Turbo in grounded theory enhanced the efficiency and diversity of coding and updated the overall grounded theory process. Compared with manual coding, ChatGPT showed shortcomings in depth, context, connections, and coding organization. Limitations and recommendations for applying artificial intelligence in qualitative research were also discussed.

documents.title: Re-defining language teacher cognition through a data-driven model: The case of three EFL teachers
documents.snippet:
Grounded theory has a multilevel data analysis process in which the researcher starts with some basic descriptions (open coding), goes on with a conceptual ordering (axial coding) and finalizes with theorization (selective coding) (Patton, 1990). All these processes are shaped with detailed sets of coding processes that occur recursively in a cyclical way. 

The first step of this coding process was open coding in the current study. In this process, the researcher broke the data into chunks and assigned them initial category labels. At the end of open coding, the researcher identified themes to serve as categories in the next step. Since this phase of coding process was similar to qualitative content analysis, the scheme of Creswell (2012) which includes transcription, reading through the data, coding and reaching themes was used in this stage. 

The second step was axial coding in which "the researcher makes connections between categories, thereby attempting to integrate them and group them into more encompassing concepts that subsume several subcategories" (Dörnyei, 2007, p. 261). During axial coding, the researcher selected a core category among open coding categories based on the criteria stated by Strauss and Corbin (1998) considering its frequency in the data and its relevance to other categories, and related other categories to it under the headings of causal conditions, context, intervening conditions, strategies and consequences. In order to systematize this process, the researcher followed the axial coding paradigm presented by Strauss and Corbin (1998) and conducted the same process for two constructs of the study-language teacher cognition and classroom practices-separately (Figure 1). 

In selective coding, the last phase of the process, the researcher integrated and refined the theory from the interrelationship among the categories derived from the axial coding schemes of language teacher cognition and classroom practices (Strauss & Corbin, 1998). A new theoretical insight was generated on the sources and characteristics of each construct and their interconnectedness. At the end, the researcher proposed a framework that would describe the cognition of the participant teachers with regard to their classroom practices and institutional context.

problem: Activation Function in deep learning
final_response:
# Why activation functions are needed

Activation functions introduce nonlinearity so that neural networks can learn and approximate complex functions beyond linear compositions of layers.<cite id="e5caefba-3">Activation functions play a crucial role in deep neural networks, introducing non-linearity and enabling the modeling of complex data representations.</cite> Before ReLU-era designs, sigmoid and tanh activations suffered from vanishing gradients in deep networks, which slowed training and degraded optimization.<cite id="e5caefba-1">Deep networks with ReLUs are more easily optimized than networks with sigmoid or tanh units, because gradient is able to flow when the input to the ReLU function is positive.</cite> The adoption of ReLU and its analysis helped shift practice toward architectures that avoid dead neurons and stabilize training in deep models.<cite id="e5caefba-1">Since Krizhevsky et al. (2012) obtained the first place in the 2012 edition of the ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge, deep convolutional neural networks with ReLUs have become common practice, leading to thriving research into ReLU variants.</cite>

# Classic activation families and properties

- Sigmoids and tanh: These saturate for large positive/negative inputs, which can cause vanishing gradients and hinder training in deep stacks.<cite id="e5caefba-1">The use of ReLUs was a breakthrough that enabled the fully supervised training of state-of-the-art deep networks, because gradient is able to flow when the input is positive, unlike saturating Sigmoid and Tanh.</cite>
- ReLU (Rectified Linear Unit): f(x)=max(0,x). It is simple, mitigates vanishing gradients on positive inputs, and has become the default in many areas of deep learning.<cite id="e5caefba-1">ReLU is defined as max(0,x) and became widely adopted after enabling effective training in ImageNet-scale networks.</cite> However, negative inputs are discarded and may “die” if inputs remain negative, causing dead neurons and reduced representational power.<cite id="e5caefba-1">One issue with ReLUs is that the image of the negative domain is always zero, so gradient does not flow through that neuron during backpropagation.</cite>

# ReLU variants: leaky, parametric, randomized, and ELU

- Leaky ReLU (LReLU): Introduces a small negative slope to avoid zero gradients for negative inputs, addressing the dying ReLU problem but with a fixed slope that can be sensitive to hyperparameters.<cite id="e5caefba-2">Leaky Rectified Linear Unit (LReLU) multiplies negative inputs by a small slope to avoid zero gradients, but the optimal slope is challenging and performance can be sensitive to the value.</cite>
- Parametric ReLU (PReLU): Makes the negative slope a learnable parameter, improving flexibility and performance while mitigating dead neurons; it can also lead to overfitting if not regularized.<cite id="e5caefba-2">PReLU generalizes LReLU by learning the leakiness, improving CNN performance with little overfitting risk in experiments.</cite><cite id="e5caefba-3">PReLU treats the negative slope as a trainable parameter but can lead to overfitting.</cite> PReLU and LReLU are computationally similar at inference, with PReLU showing performance gains in some speed-oriented architectures.<cite id="e5caefba-0">At inference time, PReLU is computationally equivalent to LReLU with minimal parameter increase and provides a noticeable performance increase.</cite>
- Randomized ReLU (RReLU): During training, samples a negative slope from a distribution to regularize and reduce overfitting.<cite id="e5caefba-2">Randomized Leaky ReLU (RReLU) draws the negative slope from a distribution to regularize training.</cite>
- Exponential Linear Units (ELU): An S-shaped function that saturates for negative inputs (improving bias shift robustness and noise resilience) and behaves like ReLU for positive inputs; it can accelerate learning and improve performance but may approximate LReLU under Batch Normalization or with small inputs, with limited generalization impact.<cite id="e5caefba-1">ELUs showed significant improvements over ReLUs, with natural ways to combat bias shift and noise robustness, while retaining ReLU-like behavior for positive inputs.</cite><cite id="e5caefba-4">ELU accelerates learning and improves performance, but under some conditions (small inputs or BatchNorm) it approximates LReLU, with negligible generalization impact.</cite>
- Other variants and bounded designs: Research also explores bounded ReLU variants to control output ranges and improve stability in constrained settings, and designs that use negative inputs more effectively (e.g., concatenating positive and inverted negative inputs).<cite id="e5caefba-3">Bounded ReLU variants address unbounded outputs and training instability; other designs concatenate positive and negative parts or combine ReLU with tanh to overcome vanishing gradients.</cite>

# Modern activations: GELU, Swish, and gated units

- GELU (Gaussian Error Linear Unit): A smooth, non-polynomial activation used widely in Transformers and NLP; it is related to SiLU and has similar smooth non-monotonic shapes used as alternatives to ReLU.<cite id="152882b1-2">GELU(x)=xΦ(x) is a non-polynomial activation; related smooth functions include SiLU(x)=x sigmoid(x) and Swish(x)=x sigmoid(βx).</cite><cite id="152882b1-1">GELU has gained popularity in NLP (BERT, GPT-2, GPT-3) and is often compared favorably to GLU-based alternatives in some studies.</cite>
- Swish: A self-gated activation f(x)=x·sigmoid(βx) discovered via a combination of exhaustive search and reinforcement learning; it is smooth and non-monotonic. Empirically, Swish often matches or exceeds ReLU across diverse tasks, with reported gains on ImageNet and deep models, and can train very deep networks better despite having gradient “squishing.”<cite id="6e83c7d5-1">Swish is a smooth, non-monotonic self-gated activation discovered via automated search and has shown consistent gains over ReLU on image classification and machine translation.</cite><cite id="6e83c7d5-1">On ImageNet, replacing ReLUs with Swish improved top-1 accuracy by 0.9% on Mobile NASNet-A and 0.6% on Inception-ResNet-v2.</cite><cite id="6e83c7d5-2">Swish outperforms ReLU in very deep fully connected networks (40–50 layers), challenging the view that ReLU is superior simply because it avoids gradient squishing.</cite> Swish has also influenced gated designs and is a popular choice in modern architectures.<cite id="152882b1-0">Combinations of Swish and gated linear units (GLU) have been found to outperform GeLU in some transformer-style experiments.</cite><cite id="152882b1-3">SwiGLU and GeGLU are widely used gated activation variants in state-of-the-art models like LLaMA and Gemma.</cite>
- Other smooth alternatives: SiLU (x·sigmoid(x)), Mish (x·tanh(softplus(x))) are part of the broader family of smooth, non-monotonic activations and are often benchmarked alongside GELU and Swish.<cite id="152882b1-2">SiLU and Mish are listed among non-polynomial analytic activations related to GELU and Swish.</cite>

# Initialization and scaling: matching activations to variance control

Proper initialization scales weights to maintain stable activation variances and gradient flows, especially with ReLU and its variants. Kaiming (He) initialization is designed for ReLU-like activations and scales weights by fan-in (or fan-out) with a 2 factor to counteract ReLU’s 0.5 variance reduction on positive inputs, whereas Xavier (Glorot) balances forward and backward variances and assumes more symmetric activations.<cite id="e17b00e8-0">Kaiming (He) initialization addresses non-negative outputs of ReLU by scaling weights based on input size, maintaining output variance and stable gradients.</cite><cite id="e17b00e8-1">Kaiming uses a 2 factor to correct for ReLU’s variance reduction; Xavier balances forward and backward variances via an arithmetic mean and assumes symmetric activations, creating a tension between fan-in and fan-out choices.</cite> In practice, ReLU networks initialized with Kaiming often achieve behavior comparable to tanh networks with Xavier, reinforcing the importance of matching initialization to activation characteristics.<cite id="e17b00e8-3">Combining ReLU with ReLU-aware scaled initialization yields similar results to tanh with Xavier initialization.</cite> However, in ResNils, residual path accumulation can still double variance per block without additional mechanisms, motivating careful initialization and normalization choices in deep residual architectures.<cite id="e17b00e8-4">In ResNets, Kaiming initialization keeps per-path variances constant, but residual combinations can double variance through blocks, leading to exploding gradients unless mitigated.</cite>

# Practical behavior and mitigation strategies

Dead neurons and saturation remain key concerns for ReLU-style activations. Introducing a small negative slope (LReLU), learning it (PReLU/RReLU), or adopting S-shaped saturating forms (ELU) can reduce dead neurons and improve robustness to noise and bias shift, at the cost of additional hyperparameters or training complexity.<cite id="e5caefba-1">Leaky and parametric ReLUs mitigate dead neurons by allowing small negative gradients, while ELUs provide natural saturation and noise robustness.</cite><cite id="e5caefba-2">These variants offer adaptability but can add complexity and tuning burden.</cite> In practice, practitioners often see inconsistent gains across tasks and datasets for many alternatives to ReLU; Swish and GELU have become popular defaults in vision and NLP, respectively, with empirical evidence of improvements in some settings.<cite id="6e83c7d5-1">Despite many alternatives, improvements over ReLU are often inconsistent across models and datasets.</cite><cite id="6e83c7d5-1">Swish consistently matches or outperforms ReLU in many tasks and deep models, with notable ImageNet gains.</cite><cite id="152882b1-1">GELU is widely used in NLP and has competitive performance versus GLU-based options in some studies.</cite> Gated linear units (GLU and variants like SwiGLU/GeGLU) apply element-wise gating to control nonlinearity and have seen broad adoption in transformer-style models.<cite id="152882b1-3">SwiGLU and GeGLU are widely used gated activations in modern transformer models such as LLaMA and Gemma.</cite><cite id="152882b1-4">GLU variants replace the outer activation with gating (sigmoid/ReLUs/GELU) and are explored across transformer feed-forward blocks.</cite>

# When to use what: a practitioner’s guide

- Default broad use: ReLU remains simple and effective for many tasks; pair it with ReLU-aware initialization (He/Kaiming) and consider Batch Normalization to stabilize training and reduce dead neuron risk.<cite id="e17b00e8-0">Kaiming initialization is designed for ReLU and maintains stable variances for deep CNNs and similar architectures.</cite><cite id="e5caefba-1">ReLU improves optimization on positive inputs compared to saturating units and underpins modern CNNs.</cite>
- Mitigate dead neurons: Use LReLU/PReLU/RReLU when many activations stay negative; consider ELU for noise robustness and bias-shift mitigation, especially when Batch Normalization is available.<cite id="e5caefba-1">LReLU and PReLU address zero-gradient regions; ELU provides natural saturation and noise robustness.</cite><cite id="e5caefba-4">Under BatchNorm or small inputs, ELU may approximate LReLU with negligible generalization impact.</cite>
- Deep or very deep networks: Swish and smooth alternatives can help with optimization depth and training stability; empirical studies report gains and better scaling in very deep networks.<cite id="6e83c7d5-2">Swish outperforms ReLU in very deep networks (40–50 layers), training deeper models effectively despite gradient squishing.</cite>
- Transformers/NLP: GELU and Swish-based gated units (SwiGLU/GeGLU) are strong defaults; many state-of-the-art language models adopt these choices.<cite id="152882b1-1">GELU is widely used in large language models (BERT, GPT series).</cite><cite id="152882b1-3">SwiGLU/GeGLU are common in modern transformer architectures like LLaMA and Gemma.</cite>
- Initialization must match nonlinearity: Use He/Kaiming for ReLU and its variants; consider Xavier for sigmoid/tanh; be aware of residual path variance accumulation and combine with normalization strategies.<cite id="e17b00e8-1">Kaiming addresses ReLU’s nonlinearity with fan-in/fan-out variants and a 2 factor; Xavier balances forward/backward variances for symmetric activations.</cite><cite id="e17b00e8-4">Residual designs can double variance per block, requiring careful initialization and regularization.</cite>

# Broader trends and open directions

Research continues to explore how to shape nonlinearity for expressivity and optimization, including trainable or specialized activations, smooth non-monotonic functions, and automated discovery.<cite id="e5caefba-2">A wide range of ReLU variants and alternative activations have been proposed, with benefits like adaptability but also increased complexity and tuning needs.</cite><cite id="6e83c7d5-3">Automated search has produced Swish; subsequent work highlights limitations of discrete search spaces and motivates continuous, trainable activations like PWLU to overcome instability and inefficiency issues.</cite> New families like SELU and self-normalizing units target mean/ variance stability and noise robustness, and are often used with or without BatchNorm to achieve consistent internal statistics.<cite id="e5caefba-3">SELU and related exponential activations aim to drive stability and robustness via bounded, saturating behavior and can be used to achieve self-normalizing dynamics.</cite> Across domains, practitioners increasingly mix-and-match activations by task and architecture, guided by empirical performance, training stability, and compute/latency constraints.<cite id="6e83c7d5-0">Many modern deep networks employ activations such as Leaky ReLU, Mish, and Swish, reflecting rapid adoption of alternatives to ReLU.</cite>

# Key takeaways

- ReLU solved vanishing gradients but can cause dead neurons; LReLU/PReLU/RReLU and ELU mitigate this with extra parameters/training complexity.<cite id="e5caefba-1">ReLU improved optimization on positive inputs but discards negative values, risking dead neurons; LReLU/PReLU/RReLU and ELU address this.</cite>
- Swish and GELU are strong general-purpose alternatives with smooth, non-monotonic shapes, and gated variants like SwiGLU/GeGLU are prevalent in Transformers.<cite id="6e83c7d5-1">Swish consistently matches or outperforms ReLU across tasks and deep models.</cite><cite id="152882b1-1">GELU is widely adopted in NLP models.</cite><cite id="152882b1-3">Gated Swish/GELU units are standard in modern transformer architectures.</cite>
- Match initialization to nonlinearity: use He/Kaiming for ReLU-like units and be mindful of residual path variance; Xavier suits sigmoid/tanh, but modern designs often rely on normalization layers.<cite id="e17b00e8-0">Kaiming initialization stabilizes ReLU networks by controlling variance.</cite><cite id="e17b00e8-1">He vs. Xavier trade off forward and backward variance control and require careful fan-in/fan-out selection.</cite><cite id="e17b00e8-4">Residual blocks can still accumulate variance, necessitating additional care.</cite>
- Activation choice interacts with depth, normalization, and dataset/task; empirical comparisons remain important, and recent evidence favors smooth and gated choices in many scenarios, though gains can be task-dependent.<cite id="6e83c7d5-1">Improvements over ReLU are often inconsistent across models/datasets, but Swish shows consistent gains in many benchmarks.</cite><cite id="e5caefba-2">Benefits of alternative activations often come with increased complexity and tuning, so practical guidance favors matching activation to training dynamics and task constraints.</cite>

Title: Don't Fear Peculiar Activation Functions: EUAF and Beyond
Snippet: In recent years, the Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU (Nair and Hinton, 2010)), defined as ReLU(x) = max(0, x), has gained popularity and recognition for its effectiveness in addressing the gradient vanishing and explosion issues encountered with Sigmoid and Tanh activation functions.Thus, ReLU has been widely used in the deep learning community such as industrial fault diagnosis (Liu et al., 2024a) and medical image segmentation (Liu et al., 2024b) .However, ReLU can suffer from the occurrence of a number of "dead neurons", which results in information loss and can hurt the neural network's feature processing ability.To mitigate this issue, several variants of ReLU have been introduced such as Leaky Rectified Linear Unit (LReLU) (Xu et al., 2015), Parametric Rectified Linear Unit (PReLU) (He et al., 2015), Randomized Leaky Rectified Linear Unit (RReLU) (Xu et al., 2015), Exponential Linear Unit (ELU) (Clevert et al., 2015), Gaussian Error Linear Unit (GELU) (Hendrycks and Gimpel, 2016), and Generalized Linear Unit (GENLU) (Fan et al., 2020).Most recently, Goldenstein et al. (2024) proposed Self-Normalizing ReLU or NeLU to ensure that the prediction model is not affected by the noise level during testing.It has been tested in synthetic data and image de-noising tasks.These variants represents a significant advancement in activation function design, offering adaptability and potentially better performance.Whereas, their benefits come with the cost of increased model complexity or computation burden and the need for careful tuning and regularization which inspired researchers to create more different activation functions.

In addition to these ReLU variants, other kinds of activation functions have also been developed.For example, the Swish (Swish(x) = x • sigmoid(βx)) (Ramachandran et al., 2017) was identified through an automated search using a combination of exhaustive and reinforcement learning as an alternative to ReLU.Its similar shape makes it a reasonable proxy for ReLU in deep learning applications.

Title: ULU: A Unified Activation Function
Snippet: Activation functions play a crucial role in deep neural networks, introducing non-linearity and enabling the modeling of complex data representations. The Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) has been widely adopted due to its simplicity and effectiveness in alleviating the vanishing gradient problem. However, ReLU [30] and its variants are not without limitations, prompting researchers to explore alternative activation functions. 

One line of research focuses on addressing the non-utilization of negative values in ReLU. The Leaky ReLU (LReLU) [28] introduces a small negative slope to mitigate the "dying ReLU" problem, but determining the optimal slope remains a challenge. Parametric ReLU (PReLU) addresses this by treating the negative slope as a trainable parameter, although it can lead to overfitting. Other variants, such as Randomized ReLU (RReLU) [41], Concatenated ReLU (CReLU) [36], and Parametric Tan Hyperbolic Linear Unit (P-TELU) [4], attempt to capture useful information from negative inputs. 

Another research direction aims to enhance the limited non-linearity of ReLU. S-shaped ReLU (SReLU) and Multi-bin Trainable Linear Unit (MTLU) [9] in-crease non-linearity by combining multiple linear functions. Elastic ReLU (EReLU) [18] controls non-linearity by randomly drawing slopes during training. Rectified Linear Tanh (ReLTanh) [40]combines ReLU with Tanh to overcome vanishing gradients. 

The unbounded output of ReLU and its variants has also been a concern, as it may lead to training instability, particularly in embedded systems. Bounded ReLU (BReLU) [26] addresses this issue by introducing an upper bound, improving training stability. 

Exponential activation functions, such as Exponential Linear Unit (ELU) [2], Scaled ELU (SELU) [20], Parametric ELU (PELU) [39], and their variants, tackle the gradient diminishing problem of ReLU. These functions exhibit desirable properties like differentiability, negative saturation, and reduced bias shift, providing robustness to noise and improved optimization.
</snippet>

Title: Improving Deep Neural Network with Multiple Parametric Exponential Linear Units
Snippet: Many state of the art deep neural networks have been proposed in recent years, greatly promoting the development of computer vision tasks such as object recognition and object detection. Several elements contributed to such a revolutionary change, for example, big datasets, high-performance hardwares, and regularization techniques. One of the most important elements is the replacement of sigmoid activation function with rectified linear unit (ReLU) [1,2]. ReLU keeps positive inputs and outputs zero for negative inputs. This non-linear function does not suffer from the vanishing gradients, which makes training deep networks possible. 

Recently, more and more efforts have concentrated on the study of activation function. Leaky ReLU [3] was proposed to multiply the negative inputs by a slope factor, which aims to avoid zero gradients. However, according to [3], LReLU has comparable performance with ReLU and is sensitive to the value of the slope. He et al. [4] found that the cost function is differentiable with respect to the slope factor and therefore proposed to optimize the slope through stochastic gradient descent (SGD). This parametric rectified linear unit is named PReLU. Experiments showed that PReLU can improve the performance of convolutional neural networks with little overfitting risk. They also proved that PReLU has the ability of pushing off-diagonal blocks of FIM closer to zero, which enables faster convergence than ReLU. This property is also analyzed in [5]. Clevert et al. [5] presented a new form of activation function, exponential linear unit (ELU). ELU is similar to sigmoid for negative inputs and has the same form as ReLU for positive inputs. It has been proved that ELU is able to bring the gradient closer to the unit natural gradient, which accelerates learning speed and leads to higher performance. However, we found that ELU is approximate to Leaky ReLU under some condition, for example, small inputs or using Batch Normalization [6]. In this case, ELU has negligible impact on the generalization capability and classification performance. We will analysis this in section 4.4. 

In addition to these deterministic activation functions, there is another random version.

GELU has been used in BERT [13], GPT-2 [14], and GPT-3 [15] architectures. Padé activation unit (PAU) has been proposed recently, and it is constructed from the approximation of the Leaky ReLU function by rational polynomials of a given order. Though PAU improves network performance in the image classification problem over ReLU, its variants, and Swish, it has a major drawback. PAU contains many trainable parameters, which significantly increases the network complexity and computational cost. Motivated from these works, we propose activation functions using the smoothing maximum technique. The maximum function is non-smooth at the origin. We want to explore how the smooth approximation of the maximum function (which can be used as an activation function) affects a network's training dynamics and performance. Our experimental evaluation shows that our proposed activation functions are comparatively more effective than ReLU, Mish, Swish, GELU, PAU etc., across different deep learning tasks. We summarise the paper as follows: 

1. We have proposed activation functions by smoothing the maximum function. We show that it can approximate GELU, ReLU, Leaky ReLU or the general Maxout family. 2. We show that the proposed functions outperform widely used activation functions in a variety of deep learning tasks.

Title: Swish: a Self-Gated Activation Function
Snippet: At the heart of every deep network lies a linear transformation followed by an activation function f (•). The activation function plays a major role in the success of training deep neural networks. Currently, the most successful and widely-used activation function is the Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) (Hahnloser et al., 2000;Jarrett et al., 2009;Nair & Hinton, 2010), defined as f (x) = max(x, 0). The use of ReLUs was a breakthrough that enabled the fully supervised training of state-of-the-art deep networks (Krizhevsky et al., 2012). Deep networks with ReLUs are more easily optimized than networks with sigmoid or tanh units, because gradient is able to flow when the input to the ReLU function is positive. Thanks to its simplicity and effectiveness, ReLU has become the default activation function used across the deep learning community. 

While numerous activation functions have been proposed to replace ReLU (Maas et al., 2013;He et al., 2015;Clevert et al., 2015;Klambauer et al., 2017), none have managed to gain the widespread adoption that ReLU enjoys. Many practitioners have favored the simplicity and reliability of ReLU because the performance improvements of the other activation functions tend to be inconsistent across different models and datasets. 

In this work, we propose a new activation function called Swish. Swish is a smooth, non-monotonic function defined as f (x) = x • sigmoid(x). Our extensive experiments show that Swish consistently matches or outperforms ReLU on deep networks applied to a variety of challenging domains such as image classification and machine translation. On ImageNet, replacing ReLUs with Swish units improves top-1 classification accuracy by 0.9% on Mobile NASNet-A (Zoph et al., 2017) and 0.6% on Inception-ResNet-v2 (Szegedy et al., 2017).
</snippet>

As a crucial design choice, the combination of Rectified Linear Units(ReLU) [7,15,25] with deep neural networks shows six times faster in convergence compared to tanh nonlinearties [18]. With nonsaturating gradients, ReLU mitigates the vanishing gradient problem and shows robust performance across different tasks and neural architectures.

Beyond ReLU, many new activation functions have been proposed like Leaky ReLU [23], PReLU [10], ELU [4], SELU [16], etc. These human-designed activation functions are either fixed or have a few learnable parameters. All these variants are similar in shape, and their gains are not consistent across tasks which limits their applications [26]. Besides human-designed activation functions, automatic searched activations function, Swish [26], show better performance across tasks. Swish adopts a tree-structured search space based on unary and binary functions, which is searched by reinforcement learning. Although showing improvements over ReLU, Swish also has its limitations. First, the tree-structured search space is highly discrete and restricted. A slight change in one composing unit may result in an entirely different activation function, making it difficult to search. Second, the sample-based searching method typically requires evaluating hundreds to thousands of candidate activation functions, which is computationally expensive. It is infeasible to use such an inefficient searching process to find specialized activation functions for each dataset or architecture. Instead, the searched Swish is used for most conditions. There are also methods like APL [1] and PAU [24] that use universal approximators as activation functions. Contrary to Swish, they are mostly contiguous with respect to their parameters and can be directly optimized by gradients. However, these methods suffer from complicated formulations that may lead to unstable learning or inefficient inference. Besides, simply using gradients may not be sufficient to fully optimize these formulations.
