# Why activation functions are needed

Activation functions introduce nonlinearity so that neural networks can learn and approximate complex functions beyond linear compositions of layers.<cite id="e5caefba-3">Activation functions play a crucial role in deep neural networks, introducing non-linearity and enabling the modeling of complex data representations.</cite> Before ReLU-era designs, sigmoid and tanh activations suffered from vanishing gradients in deep networks, which slowed training and degraded optimization.<cite id="e5caefba-1">Deep networks with ReLUs are more easily optimized than networks with sigmoid or tanh units, because gradient is able to flow when the input to the ReLU function is positive.</cite> The adoption of ReLU and its analysis helped shift practice toward architectures that avoid dead neurons and stabilize training in deep models.<cite id="e5caefba-1">Since Krizhevsky et al. (2012) obtained the first place in the 2012 edition of the ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge, deep convolutional neural networks with ReLUs have become common practice, leading to thriving research into ReLU variants.</cite>

# Classic activation families and properties

- Sigmoids and tanh: These saturate for large positive/negative inputs, which can cause vanishing gradients and hinder training in deep stacks.<cite id="e5caefba-1">The use of ReLUs was a breakthrough that enabled the fully supervised training of state-of-the-art deep networks, because gradient is able to flow when the input is positive, unlike saturating Sigmoid and Tanh.</cite>
- ReLU (Rectified Linear Unit): f(x)=max(0,x). It is simple, mitigates vanishing gradients on positive inputs, and has become the default in many areas of deep learning.<cite id="e5caefba-1">ReLU is defined as max(0,x) and became widely adopted after enabling effective training in ImageNet-scale networks.</cite> However, negative inputs are discarded and may “die” if inputs remain negative, causing dead neurons and reduced representational power.<cite id="e5caefba-1">One issue with ReLUs is that the image of the negative domain is always zero, so gradient does not flow through that neuron during backpropagation.</cite>

# ReLU variants: leaky, parametric, randomized, and ELU

- Leaky ReLU (LReLU): Introduces a small negative slope to avoid zero gradients for negative inputs, addressing the dying ReLU problem but with a fixed slope that can be sensitive to hyperparameters.<cite id="e5caefba-2">Leaky Rectified Linear Unit (LReLU) multiplies negative inputs by a small slope to avoid zero gradients, but the optimal slope is challenging and performance can be sensitive to the value.</cite>
- Parametric ReLU (PReLU): Makes the negative slope a learnable parameter, improving flexibility and performance while mitigating dead neurons; it can also lead to overfitting if not regularized.<cite id="e5caefba-2">PReLU generalizes LReLU by learning the leakiness, improving CNN performance with little overfitting risk in experiments.</cite><cite id="e5caefba-3">PReLU treats the negative slope as a trainable parameter but can lead to overfitting.</cite> PReLU and LReLU are computationally similar at inference, with PReLU showing performance gains in some speed-oriented architectures.<cite id="e5caefba-0">At inference time, PReLU is computationally equivalent to LReLU with minimal parameter increase and provides a noticeable performance increase.</cite>
- Randomized ReLU (RReLU): During training, samples a negative slope from a distribution to regularize and reduce overfitting.<cite id="e5caefba-2">Randomized Leaky ReLU (RReLU) draws the negative slope from a distribution to regularize training.</cite>
- Exponential Linear Units (ELU): An S-shaped function that saturates for negative inputs (improving bias shift robustness and noise resilience) and behaves like ReLU for positive inputs; it can accelerate learning and improve performance but may approximate LReLU under Batch Normalization or with small inputs, with limited generalization impact.<cite id="e5caefba-1">ELUs showed significant improvements over ReLUs, with natural ways to combat bias shift and noise robustness, while retaining ReLU-like behavior for positive inputs.</cite><cite id="e5caefba-4">ELU accelerates learning and improves performance, but under some conditions (small inputs or BatchNorm) it approximates LReLU, with negligible generalization impact.</cite>
- Other variants and bounded designs: Research also explores bounded ReLU variants to control output ranges and improve stability in constrained settings, and designs that use negative inputs more effectively (e.g., concatenating positive and inverted negative inputs).<cite id="e5caefba-3">Bounded ReLU variants address unbounded outputs and training instability; other designs concatenate positive and negative parts or combine ReLU with tanh to overcome vanishing gradients.</cite>

# Modern activations: GELU, Swish, and gated units

- GELU (Gaussian Error Linear Unit): A smooth, non-polynomial activation used widely in Transformers and NLP; it is related to SiLU and has similar smooth non-monotonic shapes used as alternatives to ReLU.<cite id="152882b1-2">GELU(x)=xΦ(x) is a non-polynomial activation; related smooth functions include SiLU(x)=x sigmoid(x) and Swish(x)=x sigmoid(βx).</cite><cite id="152882b1-1">GELU has gained popularity in NLP (BERT, GPT-2, GPT-3) and is often compared favorably to GLU-based alternatives in some studies.</cite>
- Swish: A self-gated activation f(x)=x·sigmoid(βx) discovered via a combination of exhaustive search and reinforcement learning; it is smooth and non-monotonic. Empirically, Swish often matches or exceeds ReLU across diverse tasks, with reported gains on ImageNet and deep models, and can train very deep networks better despite having gradient “squishing.”<cite id="6e83c7d5-1">Swish is a smooth, non-monotonic self-gated activation discovered via automated search and has shown consistent gains over ReLU on image classification and machine translation.</cite><cite id="6e83c7d5-1">On ImageNet, replacing ReLUs with Swish improved top-1 accuracy by 0.9% on Mobile NASNet-A and 0.6% on Inception-ResNet-v2.</cite><cite id="6e83c7d5-2">Swish outperforms ReLU in very deep fully connected networks (40–50 layers), challenging the view that ReLU is superior simply because it avoids gradient squishing.</cite> Swish has also influenced gated designs and is a popular choice in modern architectures.<cite id="152882b1-0">Combinations of Swish and gated linear units (GLU) have been found to outperform GeLU in some transformer-style experiments.</cite><cite id="152882b1-3">SwiGLU and GeGLU are widely used gated activation variants in state-of-the-art models like LLaMA and Gemma.</cite>
- Other smooth alternatives: SiLU (x·sigmoid(x)), Mish (x·tanh(softplus(x))) are part of the broader family of smooth, non-monotonic activations and are often benchmarked alongside GELU and Swish.<cite id="152882b1-2">SiLU and Mish are listed among non-polynomial analytic activations related to GELU and Swish.</cite>

# Initialization and scaling: matching activations to variance control

Proper initialization scales weights to maintain stable activation variances and gradient flows, especially with ReLU and its variants. Kaiming (He) initialization is designed for ReLU-like activations and scales weights by fan-in (or fan-out) with a 2 factor to counteract ReLU’s 0.5 variance reduction on positive inputs, whereas Xavier (Glorot) balances forward and backward variances and assumes more symmetric activations.<cite id="e17b00e8-0">Kaiming (He) initialization addresses non-negative outputs of ReLU by scaling weights based on input size, maintaining output variance and stable gradients.</cite><cite id="e17b00e8-1">Kaiming uses a 2 factor to correct for ReLU’s variance reduction; Xavier balances forward and backward variances via an arithmetic mean and assumes symmetric activations, creating a tension between fan-in and fan-out choices.</cite> In practice, ReLU networks initialized with Kaiming often achieve behavior comparable to tanh networks with Xavier, reinforcing the importance of matching initialization to activation characteristics.<cite id="e17b00e8-3">Combining ReLU with ReLU-aware scaled initialization yields similar results to tanh with Xavier initialization.</cite> However, in ResNils, residual path accumulation can still double variance per block without additional mechanisms, motivating careful initialization and normalization choices in deep residual architectures.<cite id="e17b00e8-4">In ResNets, Kaiming initialization keeps per-path variances constant, but residual combinations can double variance through blocks, leading to exploding gradients unless mitigated.</cite>

# Practical behavior and mitigation strategies

Dead neurons and saturation remain key concerns for ReLU-style activations. Introducing a small negative slope (LReLU), learning it (PReLU/RReLU), or adopting S-shaped saturating forms (ELU) can reduce dead neurons and improve robustness to noise and bias shift, at the cost of additional hyperparameters or training complexity.<cite id="e5caefba-1">Leaky and parametric ReLUs mitigate dead neurons by allowing small negative gradients, while ELUs provide natural saturation and noise robustness.</cite><cite id="e5caefba-2">These variants offer adaptability but can add complexity and tuning burden.</cite> In practice, practitioners often see inconsistent gains across tasks and datasets for many alternatives to ReLU; Swish and GELU have become popular defaults in vision and NLP, respectively, with empirical evidence of improvements in some settings.<cite id="6e83c7d5-1">Despite many alternatives, improvements over ReLU are often inconsistent across models and datasets.</cite><cite id="6e83c7d5-1">Swish consistently matches or outperforms ReLU in many tasks and deep models, with notable ImageNet gains.</cite><cite id="152882b1-1">GELU is widely used in NLP and has competitive performance versus GLU-based options in some studies.</cite> Gated linear units (GLU and variants like SwiGLU/GeGLU) apply element-wise gating to control nonlinearity and have seen broad adoption in transformer-style models.<cite id="152882b1-3">SwiGLU and GeGLU are widely used gated activations in modern transformer models such as LLaMA and Gemma.</cite><cite id="152882b1-4">GLU variants replace the outer activation with gating (sigmoid/ReLUs/GELU) and are explored across transformer feed-forward blocks.</cite>

# When to use what: a practitioner’s guide

- Default broad use: ReLU remains simple and effective for many tasks; pair it with ReLU-aware initialization (He/Kaiming) and consider Batch Normalization to stabilize training and reduce dead neuron risk.<cite id="e17b00e8-0">Kaiming initialization is designed for ReLU and maintains stable variances for deep CNNs and similar architectures.</cite><cite id="e5caefba-1">ReLU improves optimization on positive inputs compared to saturating units and underpins modern CNNs.</cite>
- Mitigate dead neurons: Use LReLU/PReLU/RReLU when many activations stay negative; consider ELU for noise robustness and bias-shift mitigation, especially when Batch Normalization is available.<cite id="e5caefba-1">LReLU and PReLU address zero-gradient regions; ELU provides natural saturation and noise robustness.</cite><cite id="e5caefba-4">Under BatchNorm or small inputs, ELU may approximate LReLU with negligible generalization impact.</cite>
- Deep or very deep networks: Swish and smooth alternatives can help with optimization depth and training stability; empirical studies report gains and better scaling in very deep networks.<cite id="6e83c7d5-2">Swish outperforms ReLU in very deep networks (40–50 layers), training deeper models effectively despite gradient squishing.</cite>
- Transformers/NLP: GELU and Swish-based gated units (SwiGLU/GeGLU) are strong defaults; many state-of-the-art language models adopt these choices.<cite id="152882b1-1">GELU is widely used in large language models (BERT, GPT series).</cite><cite id="152882b1-3">SwiGLU/GeGLU are common in modern transformer architectures like LLaMA and Gemma.</cite>
- Initialization must match nonlinearity: Use He/Kaiming for ReLU and its variants; consider Xavier for sigmoid/tanh; be aware of residual path variance accumulation and combine with normalization strategies.<cite id="e17b00e8-1">Kaiming addresses ReLU’s nonlinearity with fan-in/fan-out variants and a 2 factor; Xavier balances forward/backward variances for symmetric activations.</cite><cite id="e17b00e8-4">Residual designs can double variance per block, requiring careful initialization and regularization.</cite>

# Broader trends and open directions

Research continues to explore how to shape nonlinearity for expressivity and optimization, including trainable or specialized activations, smooth non-monotonic functions, and automated discovery.<cite id="e5caefba-2">A wide range of ReLU variants and alternative activations have been proposed, with benefits like adaptability but also increased complexity and tuning needs.</cite><cite id="6e83c7d5-3">Automated search has produced Swish; subsequent work highlights limitations of discrete search spaces and motivates continuous, trainable activations like PWLU to overcome instability and inefficiency issues.</cite> New families like SELU and self-normalizing units target mean/ variance stability and noise robustness, and are often used with or without BatchNorm to achieve consistent internal statistics.<cite id="e5caefba-3">SELU and related exponential activations aim to drive stability and robustness via bounded, saturating behavior and can be used to achieve self-normalizing dynamics.</cite> Across domains, practitioners increasingly mix-and-match activations by task and architecture, guided by empirical performance, training stability, and compute/latency constraints.<cite id="6e83c7d5-0">Many modern deep networks employ activations such as Leaky ReLU, Mish, and Swish, reflecting rapid adoption of alternatives to ReLU.</cite>

# Key takeaways

- ReLU solved vanishing gradients but can cause dead neurons; LReLU/PReLU/RReLU and ELU mitigate this with extra parameters/training complexity.<cite id="e5caefba-1">ReLU improved optimization on positive inputs but discards negative values, risking dead neurons; LReLU/PReLU/RReLU and ELU address this.</cite>
- Swish and GELU are strong general-purpose alternatives with smooth, non-monotonic shapes, and gated variants like SwiGLU/GeGLU are prevalent in Transformers.<cite id="6e83c7d5-1">Swish consistently matches or outperforms ReLU across tasks and deep models.</cite><cite id="152882b1-1">GELU is widely adopted in NLP models.</cite><cite id="152882b1-3">Gated Swish/GELU units are standard in modern transformer architectures.</cite>
- Match initialization to nonlinearity: use He/Kaiming for ReLU-like units and be mindful of residual path variance; Xavier suits sigmoid/tanh, but modern designs often rely on normalization layers.<cite id="e17b00e8-0">Kaiming initialization stabilizes ReLU networks by controlling variance.</cite><cite id="e17b00e8-1">He vs. Xavier trade off forward and backward variance control and require careful fan-in/fan-out selection.</cite><cite id="e17b00e8-4">Residual blocks can still accumulate variance, necessitating additional care.</cite>
- Activation choice interacts with depth, normalization, and dataset/task; empirical comparisons remain important, and recent evidence favors smooth and gated choices in many scenarios, though gains can be task-dependent.<cite id="6e83c7d5-1">Improvements over ReLU are often inconsistent across models/datasets, but Swish shows consistent gains in many benchmarks.</cite><cite id="e5caefba-2">Benefits of alternative activations often come with increased complexity and tuning, so practical guidance favors matching activation to training dynamics and task constraints.</cite>

Title: QuickNet: Maximizing Efficiency and Efficacy in Deep Architectures
Snippet: He et al introduced parametric rectified linear units in order to improve performance on the imagenet dataset in 2015. We make the observation that at inference time, the PReLU is computationally equivalent to the Leaky ReLU with a minimal parameter increase, yet provides a noticeable performance increase. Title: Don't Fear Peculiar Activation Functions: EUAF and Beyond
Snippet: In recent years, the Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU (Nair and Hinton, 2010)), defined as ReLU(x) = max(0, x), has gained popularity and recognition for its effectiveness in addressing the gradient vanishing and explosion issues encountered with Sigmoid and Tanh activation functions.Thus, ReLU has been widely used in the deep learning community such as industrial fault diagnosis (Liu et al., 2024a) and medical image segmentation (Liu et al., 2024b) .However, ReLU can suffer from the occurrence of a number of "dead neurons", which results in information loss and can hurt the neural network's feature processing ability.To mitigate this issue, several variants of ReLU have been introduced such as Leaky Rectified Linear Unit (LReLU) (Xu et al., 2015), Parametric Rectified Linear Unit (PReLU) (He et al., 2015), Randomized Leaky Rectified Linear Unit (RReLU) (Xu et al., 2015), Exponential Linear Unit (ELU) (Clevert et al., 2015), Gaussian Error Linear Unit (GELU) (Hendrycks and Gimpel, 2016), and Generalized Linear Unit (GENLU) (Fan et al., 2020).Most recently, Goldenstein et al. Title: ULU: A Unified Activation Function
Snippet: Activation functions play a crucial role in deep neural networks, introducing non-linearity and enabling the modeling of complex data representations. The Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) has been widely adopted due to its simplicity and effectiveness in alleviating the vanishing gradient problem. However, ReLU [30] and its variants are not without limitations, prompting researchers to explore alternative activation functions. 

One line of research focuses on addressing the non-utilization of negative values in ReLU. The Leaky ReLU (LReLU) [28] introduces a small negative slope to mitigate the "dying ReLU" problem, but determining the optimal slope remains a challenge. Parametric ReLU (PReLU) addresses this by treating the negative slope as a trainable parameter, although it can lead to overfitting. Other variants, such as Randomized ReLU (RReLU) [41], Concatenated ReLU (CReLU) [36], and Parametric Tan Hyperbolic Linear Unit (P-TELU) [4], attempt to capture useful information from negative inputs. 

Another research direction aims to enhance the limited non-linearity of ReLU. S-shaped ReLU (SReLU) and Multi-bin Trainable Linear Unit (MTLU) [9] in-crease non-linearity by combining multiple linear functions. Elastic ReLU (EReLU) [18] controls non-linearity by randomly drawing slopes during training. Rectified Linear Tanh (ReLTanh) [40]combines ReLU with Tanh to overcome vanishing gradients. 

The unbounded output of ReLU and its variants has also been a concern, as it may lead to training instability, particularly in embedded systems. Bounded ReLU (BReLU) [26] addresses this issue by introducing an upper bound, improving training stability. 

Exponential activation functions, such as Exponential Linear Unit (ELU) [2], Scaled ELU (SELU) [20], Parametric ELU (PELU) [39], and their variants, tackle the gradient diminishing problem of ReLU. These functions exhibit desirable properties like differentiability, negative saturation, and reduced bias shift, providing robustness to noise and improved optimization.

Title: Improving Deep Neural Network with Multiple Parametric Exponential Linear Units
Snippet: Many state of the art deep neural networks have been proposed in recent years, greatly promoting the development of computer vision tasks such as object recognition and object detection. Several elements contributed to such a revolutionary change, for example, big datasets, high-performance hardwares, and regularization techniques. One of the most important elements is the replacement of sigmoid activation function with rectified linear unit (ReLU) [1,2]. ReLU keeps positive inputs and outputs zero for negative inputs. This non-linear function does not suffer from the vanishing gradients, which makes training deep networks possible. 

Recently, more and more efforts have concentrated on the study of activation function. Leaky ReLU [3] was proposed to multiply the negative inputs by a slope factor, which aims to avoid zero gradients. However, according to [3], LReLU has comparable performance with ReLU and is sensitive to the value of the slope. He et al. [4] found that the cost function is differentiable with respect to the slope factor and therefore proposed to optimize the slope through stochastic gradient descent (SGD). This parametric rectified linear unit is named PReLU. Experiments showed that PReLU can improve the performance of convolutional neural networks with little overfitting risk. They also proved that PReLU has the ability of pushing off-diagonal blocks of FIM closer to zero, which enables faster convergence than ReLU. This property is also analyzed in [5]. Clevert et al. [5] presented a new form of activation function, exponential linear unit (ELU). ELU is similar to sigmoid for negative inputs and has the same form as ReLU for positive inputs. It has been proved that ELU is able to bring the gradient closer to the unit natural gradient, which accelerates learning speed and leads to higher performance. However, we found that ELU is approximate to Leaky ReLU under some condition, for example, small inputs or using Batch Normalization [6]. In this case, ELU has negligible impact on the generalization capability and classification performance. We will analysis this in section 4.4. 

In addition to these deterministic activation functions, there is another random version.

In recent years, the Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU (Nair and Hinton, 2010)), defined as ReLU(x) = max(0, x), has gained popularity and recognition for its effectiveness in addressing the gradient vanishing and explosion issues encountered with Sigmoid and Tanh activation functions.Thus, ReLU has been widely used in the deep learning community such as industrial fault diagnosis (Liu et al., 2024a) and medical image segmentation (Liu et al., 2024b) .However, ReLU can suffer from the occurrence of a number of "dead neurons", which results in information loss and can hurt the neural network's feature processing ability.To mitigate this issue, several variants of ReLU have been introduced such as Leaky Rectified Linear Unit (LReLU) (Xu et al., 2015), Parametric Rectified Linear Unit (PReLU) (He et al., 2015), Randomized Leaky Rectified Linear Unit (RReLU) (Xu et al., 2015), Exponential Linear Unit (ELU) (Clevert et al., 2015), Gaussian Error Linear Unit (GELU) (Hendrycks and Gimpel, 2016), and Generalized Linear Unit (GENLU) (Fan et al., 2020).Most recently, Goldenstein et al. (2024) proposed Self-Normalizing ReLU or NeLU to ensure that the prediction model is not affected by the noise level during testing.It has been tested in synthetic data and image de-noising tasks.These variants represents a significant advancement in activation function design, offering adaptability and potentially better performance.Whereas, their benefits come with the cost of increased model complexity or computation burden and the need for careful tuning and regularization which inspired researchers to create more different activation functions.

In addition to these ReLU variants, other kinds of activation functions have also been developed.For example, the Swish (Swish(x) = x • sigmoid(βx)) (Ramachandran et al., 2017) was identified through an automated search using a combination of exhaustive and reinforcement learning as an alternative to ReLU.Its similar shape makes it a reasonable proxy for ReLU in deep learning applications.

documents.title: ULU: A Unified Activation Function
documents.snippet:
Activation functions play a crucial role in deep neural networks, introducing non-linearity and enabling the modeling of complex data representations. The Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) has been widely adopted due to its simplicity and effectiveness in alleviating the vanishing gradient problem. However, ReLU [30] and its variants are not without limitations, prompting researchers to explore alternative activation functions. 

One line of research focuses on addressing the non-utilization of negative values in ReLU. The Leaky ReLU (LReLU) [28] introduces a small negative slope to mitigate the "dying ReLU" problem, but determining the optimal slope remains a challenge. Parametric ReLU (PReLU) addresses this by treating the negative slope as a trainable parameter, although it can lead to overfitting. Other variants, such as Randomized ReLU (RReLU) [41], Concatenated ReLU (CReLU) [36], and Parametric Tan Hyperbolic Linear Unit (P-TELU) [4], attempt to capture useful information from negative inputs. 

Another research direction aims to enhance the limited non-linearity of ReLU. S-shaped ReLU (SReLU) and Multi-bin Trainable Linear Unit (MTLU) [9] in-crease non-linearity by combining multiple linear functions. Elastic ReLU (EReLU) [18] controls non-linearity by randomly drawing slopes during training. Rectified Linear Tanh (ReLTanh) [40]combines ReLU with Tanh to overcome vanishing gradients. 

The unbounded output of ReLU and its variants has also been a concern, as it may lead to training instability, particularly in embedded systems. Bounded ReLU (BReLU) [26] addresses this issue by introducing an upper bound, improving training stability. 

Exponential activation functions, such as Exponential Linear Unit (ELU) [2], Scaled ELU (SELU) [20], Parametric ELU (PELU) [39], and their variants, tackle the gradient diminishing problem of ReLU. These functions exhibit desirable properties like differentiability, negative saturation, and reduced bias shift, providing robustness to noise and improved optimization.

documents.title: Improving Deep Neural Network with Multiple Parametric Exponential Linear Units
documents.snippet:
Many state of the art deep neural networks have been proposed in recent years, greatly promoting the development of computer vision tasks such as object recognition and object detection. Several elements contributed to such a revolutionary change, for example, big datasets, high-performance hardwares, and regularization techniques. One of the most important elements is the replacement of sigmoid activation function with rectified linear unit (ReLU) [1,2]. ReLU keeps positive inputs and outputs zero for negative inputs. This non-linear function does not suffer from the vanishing gradients, which makes training deep networks possible. 

Recently, more and more efforts have concentrated on the study of activation function. Leaky ReLU [3] was proposed to multiply the negative inputs by a slope factor, which aims to avoid zero gradients. However, according to [3], LReLU has comparable performance with ReLU and is sensitive to the value of the slope. He et al. [4] found that the cost function is differentiable with respect to the slope factor and therefore proposed to optimize the slope through stochastic gradient descent (SGD). This parametric rectified linear unit is named PReLU. Experiments showed that PReLU can improve the performance of convolutional neural networks with little overfitting risk. They also proved that PReLU has the ability of pushing off-diagonal blocks of FIM closer to zero, which enables faster convergence than ReLU. This property is also analyzed in [5]. Clevert et al. [5] presented a new form of activation function, exponential linear unit (ELU). ELU is similar to sigmoid for negative inputs and has the same form as ReLU for positive inputs. It has been proved that ELU is able to bring the gradient closer to the unit natural gradient, which accelerates learning speed and leads to higher performance. However, we found that ELU is approximate to Leaky ReLU under some condition, for example, small inputs or using Batch Normalization [6]. In this case, ELU has negligible impact on the generalization capability and classification performance. We will analysis this in section 4.4. 

In addition to these deterministic activation functions, there is another random version.

Title: SMU: smooth activation function for deep networks using smoothing maximum technique
Snippet: In a deep neural network, activations are either fixed before training or trainable. Researchers have proposed several activations in recent years by combining known functions. Some of these functions have hyperparameters or trainable parameters. In the case of trainable activation functions, parameters are optimized during training. Swish is a popular activation function that can be used as either a constant or trainable activation function, and it shows some good performance in a variety of deep learning tasks like image classification, object detection, machine translation etc. GELU shares similar properties like the Swish activation function, and it gains popularity in the deep learning community due to its efficacy in natural language processing tasks. GELU has been used in BERT [13], GPT-2 [14], and GPT-3 [15] architectures. Padé activation unit (PAU) has been proposed recently, and it is constructed from the approximation of the Leaky ReLU function by rational polynomials of a given order. Though PAU improves network performance in the image classification problem over ReLU, its variants, and Swish, it has a major drawback. PAU contains many trainable parameters, which significantly increases the network complexity and computational cost. Motivated from these works, we propose activation functions using the smoothing maximum technique. The maximum function is non-smooth at the origin. We want to explore how the smooth approximation of the maximum function (which can be used as an activation function) affects a network's training dynamics and performance. Our experimental evaluation shows that our proposed activation functions are comparatively more effective than ReLU, Mish, Swish, GELU, PAU etc., across different deep learning tasks. We summarise the paper as follows: 

1. We have proposed activation functions by smoothing the maximum function. We show that it can approximate GELU, ReLU, Leaky ReLU or the general Maxout family. 2. We show that the proposed functions outperform widely used activation functions in a variety of deep learning tasks.

Title: Do Transformer Modifications Transfer Across Implementations and Applications?
Snippet: We consider various activation functions to replace the ReLU in the feedforward network block. The activation functions that we explored are: (1) GeLU (Hendrycks and Gimpel, 2016), (2) Swish (Ramachandran et al., 2017), (3) Exponential Linear Units (ELU) (Clevert et al., 2015), (4) Scaled exponential linear units (SeLU) (Klambauer et al., 2017), (5) Sigmoid and (6) Softplus. We also explore "Gated Linear Unit" (GLU) variants (Dauphin et al., 2017;Shazeer, 2020) which compose two linear transformations together in an element-wise fashion, i.e. F 1 (x) σ(F 2 (x)) where σ is an activation function and F 1 and F 2 are separate learned affine transformations. We explore modifying σ to be sigmoid activations (denoted as GLU), ReLU activations (denoted as ReGLU), GeLU activations (denoted as GeGLU) or to be a standard linear transformation (no activation, denoted as LiGLU).

Title: Variance Control via Weight Rescaling in LLM Pre-training
Snippet: Kaiming Initialization [2], also known as He Initialization, is a weight initialization technique specifically designed to address the challenges posed by activation functions with non-negative outputs, such as Rectified Linear Units (ReLU) [25]. Unlike Xavier Initialization, which assumes symmetric activation functions such as sigmoid or tanh, Kaiming Initialization accounts for the asymmetric nature of ReLU and its variants, ensuring stable gradient flow during training. 

The key idea behind Kaiming Initialization is to scale the initial weights based on the number of input units in the layer, taking into account the properties of ReLU activations. For a weight matrix W ∈ R nin×nout , where n in and n out are the number of input and output units, respectively, the weights are sampled from a uniform or a normal distribution. 

For the normal distribution, the weights are initialized as: 

For the uniform distribution, the weights are initialized as: 

This initialization strategy ensures that the variance of the outputs remains consistent across layers, preventing issues such as vanishing or exploding gradients in deep networks with ReLU activations. By explicitly considering the rectifying behavior of ReLU, Kaiming Initialization has become a cornerstone for training modern neural networks, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and other architectures that rely heavily on ReLU-based activations.

Title: A scaling calculus for the design and initialization of ReLU networks
Snippet: The most common approaches are the Kaiming (He et al., 2015) (sometimes called He) and Xavier (Glorot & Bengio, 2010) (sometimes called Glorot) initializations. The Kaiming technique for ReLU networks is one of two approaches: 

For the feed-forward network above, assuming random activations, the forward-activation variance will remain constant in expectation throughout the network if fan-in initialization of weights (LeCun et al., 2012) is used, whereas the fan-out variant maintains a constant variance of the backpropagated signal. The constant factor 2 corrects for the variance-reducing effect of the ReLU activation. Although popularized by He et al. (2015), similar scaling was in use in early neural network models that used tanh activation functions (Bottou, 1988). 

These two principles are clearly in conflict; unless n l = n l+1 , either the forward variance or backward variance will become non-constant. No prima facie reason for preferring one initialization over the other is provided. Unfortunately, there is some confusion in the literature as many works reference using Kaiming initialization without specifying if the fan-in or fan-out variant is used. 

The Xavier initialization (Glorot & Bengio, 2010) is the closest to our proposed approach. They balance these conflicting objectives using the arithmetic mean: 

to "... approximately satisfy our objectives of maintaining activation variances and back-propagated gradients variance as one moves up or down the network". This approach to balancing is essentially heuristic, in contrast to the geometric mean approach that our theory directly guides us to. 

Figure 2 shows heat maps of the average singular values for each block of the Hessian of a LeNet model under the initializations considered. The use of geometric initialization results in an equally weighted diagonal, in contrast to the other initializations considered.

Snippet: Random weight initialization could result in unstable variances (vanishing/exploding gradients) of the activations for very deep neural networks. There are a variety of proposed initialization strategies to deal with this issue [24], [29]. 

Xavier Initialization [24] estimates the standard deviation of initial parameters based on the number of input and output channels in a layer. However, Xavier Initialization has problems when initializing networks with a ReLU activation function [1]. Therefore, for ReLU activation networks, Kaiming Initialization [1] is proposed. Kaiming Initialization stabilizes the variances and keeps them constant through the layers of DNNs. In ResNets, the variance of the input and output of residual blocks would remain identical by using this initialization, i.e., Var(F l (x l−1 )) = Var(x l−1 ), where Var(x) denotes the variances for each component of x. However, since the correlations between x l and F l (x l−1 ) are small, then after each residual path we get: 

Thus, the variance doubles after each residual block, and increases exponentially as we stack up multiple residual blocks, leading to an identical problem in the backward pass during training.

Random weight initialization could result in unstable variances (vanishing/exploding gradients) of the activations for very deep neural networks. There are a variety of proposed initialization strategies to deal with this issue [24], [29]. 

Xavier Initialization [24] estimates the standard deviation of initial parameters based on the number of input and output channels in a layer. However, Xavier Initialization has problems when initializing networks with a ReLU activation function [1]. Therefore, for ReLU activation networks, Kaiming Initialization [1] is proposed. Kaiming Initialization stabilizes the variances and keeps them constant through the layers of DNNs. In ResNets, the variance of the input and output of residual blocks would remain identical by using this initialization, i.e., Var(F l (x l−1 )) = Var(x l−1 ), where Var(x) denotes the variances for each component of x. However, since the correlations between x l and F l (x l−1 ) are small, then after each residual path we get: 

Thus, the variance doubles after each residual block, and increases exponentially as we stack up multiple residual blocks, leading to an identical problem in the backward pass during training.

Kaiming Initialization [2], also known as He Initialization, is a weight initialization technique specifically designed to address the challenges posed by activation functions with non-negative outputs, such as Rectified Linear Units (ReLU) [25]. Unlike Xavier Initialization, which assumes symmetric activation functions such as sigmoid or tanh, Kaiming Initialization accounts for the asymmetric nature of ReLU and its variants, ensuring stable gradient flow during training. 

The key idea behind Kaiming Initialization is to scale the initial weights based on the number of input units in the layer, taking into account the properties of ReLU activations. For a weight matrix W ∈ R nin×nout , where n in and n out are the number of input and output units, respectively, the weights are sampled from a uniform or a normal distribution.

This initialization strategy ensures that the variance of the outputs remains consistent across layers, preventing issues such as vanishing or exploding gradients in deep networks with ReLU activations. By explicitly considering the rectifying behavior of ReLU, Kaiming Initialization has become a cornerstone for training modern neural networks, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and other architectures that rely heavily on ReLU-based activations.

The constant factor 2 corrects for the variance-reducing effect of the ReLU activation. Although popularized by He et al. (2015), similar scaling was in use in early neural network models that used tanh activation functions (Bottou, 1988). 

These two principles are clearly in conflict; unless n l = n l+1 , either the forward variance or backward variance will become non-constant. Snippet: In every deep neural network, the selection of the activation function is of great concern. Many activation functions, such as Leaky ReLU, Mish, and Swish, have recently been developed.

Title: Swish: a Self-Gated Activation Function
Snippet: At the heart of every deep network lies a linear transformation followed by an activation function f (•). The activation function plays a major role in the success of training deep neural networks. Currently, the most successful and widely-used activation function is the Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) (Hahnloser et al., 2000;Jarrett et al., 2009;Nair & Hinton, 2010), defined as f (x) = max(x, 0). The use of ReLUs was a breakthrough that enabled the fully supervised training of state-of-the-art deep networks (Krizhevsky et al., 2012). Deep networks with ReLUs are more easily optimized than networks with sigmoid or tanh units, because gradient is able to flow when the input to the ReLU function is positive. Thanks to its simplicity and effectiveness, ReLU has become the default activation function used across the deep learning community. 

While numerous activation functions have been proposed to replace ReLU (Maas et al., 2013;He et al., 2015;Clevert et al., 2015;Klambauer et al., 2017), none have managed to gain the widespread adoption that ReLU enjoys. Many practitioners have favored the simplicity and reliability of ReLU because the performance improvements of the other activation functions tend to be inconsistent across different models and datasets. 

In this work, we propose a new activation function called Swish. Swish is a smooth, non-monotonic function defined as f (x) = x • sigmoid(x). Our extensive experiments show that Swish consistently matches or outperforms ReLU on deep networks applied to a variety of challenging domains such as image classification and machine translation. On ImageNet, replacing ReLUs with Swish units improves top-1 classification accuracy by 0.9% on Mobile NASNet-A (Zoph et al., 2017) and 0.6% on Inception-ResNet-v2 (Szegedy et al., 2017).

Title: Swish: a Self-Gated Activation Function
Snippet: We first compare Swish to the ReLU activation function on a set of small scale experiments, and find that Swish consistently outperforms ReLU. We then benchmark Swish against ReLU and a number of recently proposed activation functions on challenging datasets, and find that Swish matches or exceeds the baselines on nearly all tasks. 

The following sections will describe our experimental settings and results in greater detail. As a summary, Table 1 shows Swish in comparison to each baseline activation function we considered (which are defined in Section 3.2). The results in Table 1 are aggregated by comparing the performance Swish to the performance of different activation functions applied to a variety of models, such as Inception ResNet-v2 (Szegedy et al., 2017) and Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017), across multiple datasets, such as CIFAR, ImageNet, and English→German translation. 2 The improvement of Swish over other activation functions is statistically significant under a one-sided paired sign test. We are interested in whether replacing ReLUs with Swish units can improve the training of deep networks. We train fully connected networks of varying depths on MNIST, with each layer having 1,024 neurons. We do not use residual connections (He et al., 2016a) because they enable the training of arbitrarily deep networks. We use He initialization (He et al., 2015) with BatchNorm (Ioffe & Szegedy, 2015) to lessen the dependence on initialization. The network is optimized using SGD with momentum on a batch size of 128, and for fair comparison, we try the same number of learning rates for each activation function. Figure 6 plots the median result of 3 runs. In our experiments, both activation functions achieve similar performances up to 40 layers. However, as shown in the figure, Swish outperforms ReLU by a large margin in the range between 40 and 50 layers when optimization becomes difficult. In very deep networks, Swish achieves higher test accuracies than ReLU. This result challenges the conventional wisdom that ReLU performs well because it does not squish gradients; Swish is able to train deeper networks despite having gradient squishing properties.

Title: Learning specialized activation functions with the Piecewise Linear Unit
Snippet: Activation functions are fundamental components for modern deep neural networks, which affect both the expressiveness and the optimization of models. As a crucial design choice, the combination of Rectified Linear Units(ReLU) [7,15,25] with deep neural networks shows six times faster in convergence compared to tanh nonlinearties [18]. With nonsaturating gradients, ReLU mitigates the vanishing gradient problem and shows robust performance across different tasks and neural architectures.

Beyond ReLU, many new activation functions have been proposed like Leaky ReLU [23], PReLU [10], ELU [4], SELU [16], etc. These human-designed activation functions are either fixed or have a few learnable parameters. All these variants are similar in shape, and their gains are not consistent across tasks which limits their applications [26]. Besides human-designed activation functions, automatic searched activations function, Swish [26], show better performance across tasks. Swish adopts a tree-structured search space based on unary and binary functions, which is searched by reinforcement learning. Although showing improvements over ReLU, Swish also has its limitations. First, the tree-structured search space is highly discrete and restricted. A slight change in one composing unit may result in an entirely different activation function, making it difficult to search. Second, the sample-based searching method typically requires evaluating hundreds to thousands of candidate activation functions, which is computationally expensive. It is infeasible to use such an inefficient searching process to find specialized activation functions for each dataset or architecture. Instead, the searched Swish is used for most conditions. There are also methods like APL [1] and PAU [24] that use universal approximators as activation functions. Contrary to Swish, they are mostly contiguous with respect to their parameters and can be directly optimized by gradients. However, these methods suffer from complicated formulations that may lead to unstable learning or inefficient inference. Besides, simply using gradients may not be sufficient to fully optimize these formulations.

problem: Can LLMs learn new information when trained on supervised fine-tuning (SFT)?
final_response:
# Short answer

Yes—but usually not by expanding the model’s internal world knowledge. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) used for instruction tuning primarily adapts behavior, formatting, and stylistic choices (e.g., discourse markers, role-play, transitions) while leveraging the model’s pre‑trained knowledge; robust gains in factual knowledge are limited and dataset‑dependent, and narrow or continual fine‑tuning can even overwrite or forget prior knowledge without special techniques to mitigate forgetting.<cite id="af6ca978-0,75bc02a1-0">Recent analyses argue that simple instruction tuning and alignment make models “mainly learn the style or format for interacting with users” by eliciting capabilities already present from pre‑training, with token‑distribution shifts concentrated in stylistic rather than knowledge‑rich tokens</cite><cite id="75bc02a1-4">Work on the “Superficial Alignment Hypothesis” similarly posits that fine‑tuning primarily adjusts response formatting and style rather than imbuing new capabilities</cite><cite id="b5792093-0">Empirically, fine‑tuning can increase activation and sometimes improve reasoning, but also shows inconsistent effects on knowledge‑intensive benchmarks such as MMLU and HellaSwag</cite>.

# What supervised fine-tuning typically changes

- Behavior and style: Instruction‑tuned models become better at following prompts, adopting role‑play, and generating structured, user‑oriented text, but these are largely surface‑level adaptations of style and interaction format rather than learning new latent concepts.<cite id="af6ca978-0">Comparative token‑distribution analyses report that stylistic tokens (e.g., transitional phrases and discourse markers) shift the most after alignment, while contextual words carrying rich knowledge change little</cite><cite id="75bc02a1-4">The superficial alignment hypothesis and related evidence argue SFT mainly adjusts formatting and style</cite>.
- Instruction bias and context use: SFT can introduce biases that make models overly sensitive to prompt surface forms, and can reduce reliance on provided context under conflict, reflecting a shift in strategy rather than an expansion of knowledge.<cite id="75bc02a1-1">Instruction‑tuned models exhibit strong fragility to semantically invariant changes (e.g., option label formats), with large performance drops when labels switch from numeric to Roman numerals</cite><cite id="75bc02a1-2">Studies report loss of context awareness after instruction tuning, with models becoming less reliant on provided context when knowledge conflicts arise</cite>.

# Can SFT actually add or update knowledge?

- Sometimes, but inconsistently: When instruction data includes task‑specific examples with correct answers, fine‑tuning can improve performance on some reasoning tasks; however, broad gains across knowledge benchmarks (e.g., MMLU, HellaSwag) are variable, suggesting limits to true knowledge acquisition rather than uniform style‑only changes.<cite id="b5792093-0">An empirical study finds fine‑tuning significantly improves some activations and reasoning abilities, yet declines in MMLU and HellaSwag imply knowledge‑intensive capabilities can worsen</cite>.
- Knowledge vs. style trade‑offs: Analyses suggest SFT tends to optimize output style and adherence to instructions rather than expanding parametric knowledge, especially when using few‑shot instruction sets; separating knowledge learning from format alignment is proposed to target actual domain knowledge gains.<cite id="af6ca978-0">Evidence indicates distribution shifts are stylistic and that as few as ~1,000 SFT examples can “achieve satisfactory alignment performance” by leveraging prior knowledge</cite><cite id="af6ca978-0">A unified view proposes “knowledge mixture pre‑training” to focus on learning new domain knowledge while preserving general knowledge</cite>.
- Instruction‑tuning vs. pretraining: Large‑scale evaluations show significant differences between pretrained and instruction‑ or fine‑tuned models on many tasks, but instruction‑tuned and fine‑tuned models are not significantly different from each other across several benchmarks, implying instruction tuning often capitalizes on pre‑trained knowledge and formatting rather than adding distinct new knowledge.<cite id="b5792093-3">A comprehensive reassessment finds significant differences between pretrained and instruction‑tuned models, and between pretrained and fine‑tuned models, but no significant differences between instruction‑tuned and fine‑tuned models across multiple benchmarks</cite>.

# Limits and risks: forgetting and overwriting

- Catastrophic forgetting under continual fine‑tuning: Narrow task‑specific SFT or sequential instruction tuning can degrade performance on earlier tasks and benchmarks, erasing prior knowledge unless mitigated.<cite id="74238de8-0">A continual instruction‑finetuning study evaluates retention by re‑testing earlier tasks after each fine‑tuning step and quantifies forgetting as the gap between peak and final performance</cite><cite id="74238de8-4">Empirically, models show significant forgetting after the first instruction tuning; mixing in general instruction data mitigates the decline on benchmarks like MMLU‑human (e.g., 30% vs. 26.8% with instruction‑only)</cite>.
- Overwriting alignment: Fine‑tuning on data that conflicts with prior alignment can reverse or degrade safety and preference alignment, indicating that SFT can overwrite learned behaviors and values when data is not aligned with prior training.<cite id="af6ca978-2">Prior work warns that fine‑tuning aligned LLMs can compromise safety alignment, and that fine‑tuning unaligned LLMs exacerbates verbatim memorization</cite><cite id="af6ca978-3">Re‑emergent misalignment research shows narrow fine‑tuning can overwrite, suppress, or reverse prior alignment</cite>.
- Instruction bias and fragility: SFT can induce strong sensitivity to prompt surface forms and instructions, with large performance swings under semantically equivalent reformulations, suggesting that observed “learning” may be prompt‑format adaptation rather than durable knowledge change.<cite id="75bc02a1-1">Experiments show drastic performance drops (e.g., ~30% on MMLU) when only option labels change despite semantic invariance, and degradation when instructions are removed</cite>.

# When SFT can contribute new knowledge (and when it’s not the right tool)

- Domain‑specific adaptation with SFT plus retrieval or continued pretraining: To learn new domain knowledge, practitioners often combine SFT with retrieval or continued training on domain data, explicitly targeting knowledge acquisition rather than pure instruction following; frameworks argue for decoupling “knowledge learning” from “format alignment.”<cite id="af6ca978-0">A domain‑adaptation framework proposes separating knowledge learning from format alignment, noting that instruction tuning alone tends to elicit existing knowledge and style while shifting stylistic tokens</cite>.
- General instruction data to mitigate forgetting: Adding broad instruction datasets during continual fine‑tuning can help preserve baseline knowledge and reduce catastrophic forgetting, indicating that high‑level instruction guidance can stabilize knowledge alongside task‑specific updates.<cite id="74238de8-4">Mixing general instruction data (e.g., ALPACA) with task‑specific data mitigates forgetting on knowledge benchmarks (e.g., MMLU‑human 30% vs. 26.8% with instruction‑only)</cite>.
- Not a silver bullet for deep knowledge expansion: If the goal is broad, factual knowledge growth, SFT alone is often insufficient; methods that directly target knowledge (e.g., continued pretraining on domain corpora, distillation from preference‑optimized or truth‑ful models) or incorporate retrieval/self‑critique signals tend to be more effective for factual updates than instruction‑only SFT.<cite id="75bc02a1-2">Work on grounding and preference optimization for factuality suggests training‑time approaches to align models with external evidence can strengthen factual knowledge</cite>.

# Practical implications

- Expect behavior and style changes: With SFT, you should primarily plan for improved instruction following, role‑play, and formatting; these are reliable and sizable, even if there is little new world‑knowledge added.<cite id="af6ca978-0">Instruction tuning elicits prior knowledge and improves task capability while concentrating shifts in stylistic tokens</cite><cite id="75bc02a1-4">Evidence supports a superficial alignment pattern where formatting and style dominate</cite>.
- Guard against forgetting and drift: For continual or narrow SFT, monitor performance on earlier or broader benchmarks and consider techniques like mixing general instruction data, larger context windows, or optimizers designed to mitigate forgetting to preserve prior knowledge.<cite id="74238de8-0">Continual instruction fine‑tuning studies quantify forgetting on earlier tasks</cite><cite id="74238de8-4">Mixing general instruction data mitigates knowledge loss</cite><cite id="b5792093-3">A broader reassessment highlights that instruction‑tuned and fine‑tuned models can be statistically similar on many benchmarks, underscoring the need for careful monitoring</cite>.
- For true knowledge expansion, pair SFT with knowledge‑focused methods: Combine SFT with continued domain pretraining, retrieval‑augmented training, or distillation from preference‑optimized models to drive factual updates beyond prompt‑format alignment.<cite id="af6ca978-0">Frameworks explicitly decoupling knowledge learning and format alignment argue for targeted strategies to add new domain knowledge</cite><cite id="75bc02a1-2">Training approaches that integrate retrieval and self‑critique or preference optimization can align models to external evidence and improve factuality</cite>.

# Bottom line

LLMs can “learn” with supervised fine‑tuning—but what they typically learn is better adherence to instructions, safer or chat‑style formatting, and prompt‑format‑dependent strategy, grounded in their pre‑trained knowledge. Reliable acquisition of new factual knowledge generally requires SFT in combination with domain‑specific training signals (retrieval, continued pretraining, or distillation), and even then must be carefully managed to avoid catastrophic forgetting or instruction‑format fragility.<cite id="af6ca978-0">Instruction tuning aligns behavior and elicits prior knowledge, with token‑level shifts concentrated in style</cite><cite id="af6ca978-3">Narrow fine‑tuning can overwrite prior alignment</cite><cite id="b5792093-0">Empirical effects on knowledge benchmarks are inconsistent</cite><cite id="74238de8-4">Mitigation strategies like mixing general instruction data can reduce forgetting</cite><cite id="75bc02a1-1">Instruction bias and fragility can dominate performance</cite>.

Title: SEFE: Superficial and Essential Forgetting Eliminator for Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning
Snippet: The rapid advancement of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) has led to a series of significant works (Liu et al., 2023;Dai et al., 2023;Achiam et al., 2023;Bai et al., 2023b;Liu et al., 2024a;Chen et al., 2024d). Training these models typically involves multiple phases, with pretraining and instruction tuning being two crucial ones. During pre-training, large-scale unsupervised learning endows the model with foundational cognitive skills. In the subsequent instruction tuning phase, the model is refined using instruction-response pairs to enhance its ability to comprehend and respond to user commands. This comprehensive training enables MLLMs to exhibit zero-shot capabilities, allowing them to handle previously unseen instructions. 

However, these zero-shot abilities are often insufficient for MLLMs to specialize in specific domains. To achieve such specialization, targeted multimodal instruction tuning with relevant datasets is commonly employed. Nevertheless, the breadth of tasks that MLLMs are expected to handle is vast, and the requirements are continuously evolving. As demands grow, simply fine-tuning the model with data from new tasks can result in the loss of previously acquired capabilities-a phenomenon known as catastrophic forgetting (McCloskey & Cohen, 1989). Alternatively, retraining the model with both new and old task data each time requirements change is highly resource-intensive. To address this, Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning (MCIT) has emerged (He et al., 2023;Zhu et al., 2024a;Chen et al., 2024a;Zheng et al., 2024;Zeng et al., 2024). This field seeks to enable MLLMs to progressively learn new tasks without losing proficiency in previously mastered ones during incremental instruction tuning. 

Existing methods in MCIT (He et al., 2023;Zhu et al., 2024a;Zheng et al., 2024), like conventional continual learning research, conceptualize catastrophic forgetting as a generalized problem of knowledge loss and have made some progress addressing it. However, our analysis indicates that the nature of forgetting in MCIT extends beyond mere knowledge loss.
</snippet>

Title: MLLM-CBench:A Comprehensive Benchmark for Continual Instruction Tuning of Multimodal LLMs with Chain-of-Thought Reasoning Analysis
Snippet: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have emerged as foundational architectures for cross-modal understanding and generation, demonstrating impressive capabilities across a variety of tasks. Instruction tuning has further enhanced these models by aligning them with human intent and improving task-specific performance through supervised adaptation (Yu et al. 2024). However, real-world deployment demands continuous adaptation to evolving instructions and domain requirements-a paradigm known as continual instruction tuning (He et al. 2023a;Chen et al. 2024a), where the model incrementally learns from new tasks while retaining prior capabilities. 

While significant progress has been made in continual instruction tuning for Large Language Models (LLMs) (Zheng et al. 2025a), the multimodal counterpart remains underexplored. The absence of a rigorous benchmark further impedes progress: existing benchmarks (e.g., EMT (Jia et al. 2025), CITB (He et al. 2023b), CoIN (Chen et al. 2024a)) on continual instruction tuning of MLLMs exhibit critical limitations in the comprehensiveness of evaluation metrics, method coverage, and task challenge -key factors for establishing a rigorous benchmark for continual instruction tuning of MLLMs. (1) Superficial Evaluation Metrics: Prevailing benchmarks prioritize final answer correctness while neglecting granular reasoning process analysis, hindering indepth understanding of the causes behind catastrophic forgetting in MLLMs (Luo et al. 2023). Although CoIN (Chen et al. 2024a) implicitly estimates reasoning knowledge forgetting, the interpretability of the evaluation metric remains inadequate. (2) Limited Investigation of Continual Learning Algorithms and Training Paradigms: Existing works predominantly focus on quantifying catastrophic forgetting under sequential fine-tuning settings, while overlooking the systematic study of existing continual learning algorithms, thereby severely limiting the practical utility of such benchmarks. Furthermore, Reinforcement Finetuning (RFT) has been widely adopted in the post-training of MLLMs and has demonstrated great potential in enhancing their reasoning ability and generalization. Yet its effectiveness in continual instruction tuning remains underexplored.
</snippet>

Title: The Atomic Instruction Gap: Instruction-Tuned LLMs Struggle with Simple, Self-Contained Directives
Snippet: Instruction tuning has significantly improved the 0shot capabilities of large language models (LLMs), enabling complex task execution via natural language prompts (Wei et al., 2022;Iyer et al., 2023;Sanh et al., 2022;Ouyang et al., 2022). However, while prior work focuses on multi-step (Jiang et al., 2024;Chen et al., 2024), or uncommon instructions (Li et al., 2024), the ability of instruction-tuned LLMs (IT-LLMs) to follow atomic instructionssimple, unambiguous directives -remains critically underexplored. This gap is consequential: atomic adherence underpins reliable performance in deterministic applications and compositional reasoning (Hayati et al., 2025;He et al., 2024;Sun et al., 2024). 

We empirically demonstrate that IT-LLMs exhibit profound fragility to semantically invariant atomic instructions, using MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021) and MMLU-Pro (Wang et al., 2024). Through four controlled experiments, we reveal systematic failures. Our work is motivated by two key factors: (1) Real-world relevance -Practical applications often involve tasks coupled with instructions, yet the impact of instruction-following ability on task performance remains unclear. Hence, we pick two knowledge-intensive benchmarks. 

(2) Evaluation practicality -MCQs provide a straightforward format for automated evaluation and have been adopted for assessing LLM capabilities (Robinson et al., 2023). 

Experiment 1 varies option labels (alphabetic, numeric, Roman) with explicit instructions. Despite semantic equivalence, models show drastic performance gaps (e.g., 30.44% drop for Roman vs. numeric labels on MMLU), exposing instruction bias to surface formats. Experiment 2 removes instructions entirely. Performance degrades significantly (e.g., -10.84% for Roman labels on MMLU), confirming instructions' necessity. Experiment 3 deprives options of content, retaining only labels and instructions.
</snippet>

Title: Instruction Tuning with and without Context: Behavioral Shifts and Downstream Impact
Snippet: Instruction Tuning and Its Impact on Context Awareness and Knowledge Use Several works have shown that instruction tuning influences on how LLMs use their parametric knowledge and given input context. Recent studies show loss of context awareness after instruction tuning6 . Goyal et al. (2024) find that models tend to be less reliant on provided context under knowledge conflict as instruction tuning progresses. Similarly, Wang et al. (2024b) attributes this loss to role biases introduced by chat-style prompting templates. Other analysis explore how instruction tuning reshapes behavioral and representational properties of LLMS in attention distribution or attribution (Wu et al., 2023;Gao et al., 2023). Another line of work aim to enhance the model's external context utilization through instruction tuning: overcoming the lostin-the-middle problem (Liu et al., 2023c) in longcontext inputs (An et al., 2024;Begin et al., 2025;He et al., 2023) or better grounding on given context (Lee et al., 2024a;Asai et al., 2024;Tian et al., 2023;Luo et al., 2023). Together, these studies examine how instruction tuning affects the utilization of parametric knowledge versus user-provided context. Our work extends this understanding by examining new axes of how training on datasets with or without relevant context affects a model's grounding ability and its use of parametric knowledge. 

Improving Grounding in Language and Vision-Language Models Prior work have explored multiple directions to strengthen grounding. Inference-time methods modify decoding or introduce post-hoc revision pipelines to better incorporate external knowledge (Shi et al., 2023;Wang et al., 2024a;Gao et al., 2022;Chern et al., 2023). Training-time approaches aim to align models to external evidence, for example using preference optimization for factuality (Tian et al., 2023) or integrating retrieval and self-critique signals as in Self-RAG (Asai et al., 2024).
</snippet>

Title: In-context Learning vs. Instruction Tuning: The Case of Small and Multilingual Language Models
Snippet: Instruction tuning has been the dominant paradigm to adapt LLMs for downstream tasks. The standard pipeline involves SFT on instruction-response datasets (Wei et al., 2021), often complemented with human preference alignment via methods such as RLHF (Ouyang et al., 2022) or DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023). The effectiveness of these approaches has been demonstrated across a variety of domains, leading to substantial improvements in instruction-following capabilities. However, recent studies have suggested that the benefits of instruction tuning might be more superficial that previously thought. Zhou et al. (2024) proposed the Superficial Alignment Hypothesis, arguing that fine-tuning primarily adjust response formatting and style rather than imbuing the models with new capabilities. Further, Lin et al. (2024) found that instruction tuning predominantly shift token distributions related to style and safety disclaimers, with minimal impact on core knowledge retrieval. In this line of work, Hewitt et al. (2024) showed that a base model can exhibit instruction-following behaviour to some extent by applying straightfor-ward rules and adjusting token distributions in a targeted manner. This raises critical questions about whether costly fine-tuning is always necessary for strong instruction-following performance. 

Alternative alignment strategies have been explored, particularly in the context of ICL. Brown et al. (2020) first demonstrated that pretrained models can exhibit strong instruction-following behaviour when provided with appropriate examples in their prompt. As noted above, Lin et al. ( 2024) expanded the use of ICL for instruction followin with URIAL, a method which aligns base LLMs using just three stylistic in-context examples. While URIAL improves instruction adherence significantly, Zhao et al. (2025) showed that it still lags behind fine-tuned models, particularly in multi-turn interactions. They further highlighted that decoding parameters, such as temperature and repetition penalties, significantly influence ICL performance, suggesting that proper hyperparameter tuning is crucial for optimal ICL alignment. Similarly, Han (2023) found that the benefits of ICL are highly sensitive to the quality of in-context examples, with carefully curated demonstrations yielding much stronger alignment that randomly sampled ones.

# Short answer

Yes—but usually not by expanding the model’s internal world knowledge. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) used for instruction tuning primarily adapts behavior, formatting, and stylistic choices (e.g., discourse markers, role-play, transitions) while leveraging the model’s pre‑trained knowledge; robust gains in factual knowledge are limited and dataset‑dependent, and narrow or continual fine‑tuning can even overwrite or forget prior knowledge without special techniques to mitigate forgetting.<cite id="af6ca978-0,75bc02a1-0">Recent analyses argue that simple instruction tuning and alignment make models “mainly learn the style or format for interacting with users” by eliciting capabilities already present from pre‑training, with token‑distribution shifts concentrated in stylistic rather than knowledge‑rich tokens</cite><cite id="75bc02a1-4">Work on the “Superficial Alignment Hypothesis” similarly posits that fine‑tuning primarily adjusts response formatting and style rather than imbuing new capabilities</cite><cite id="b5792093-0">Empirically, fine‑tuning can increase activation and sometimes improve reasoning, but also shows inconsistent effects on knowledge‑intensive benchmarks such as MMLU and HellaSwag</cite>.

# What supervised fine-tuning typically changes

- Behavior and style: Instruction‑tuned models become better at following prompts, adopting role‑play, and generating structured, user‑oriented text, but these are largely surface‑level adaptations of style and interaction format rather than learning new latent concepts.<cite id="af6ca978-0">Comparative token‑distribution analyses report that stylistic tokens (e.g., transitional phrases and discourse markers) shift the most after alignment, while contextual words carrying rich knowledge change little</cite><cite id="75bc02a1-4">The superficial alignment hypothesis and related evidence argue SFT mainly adjusts formatting and style</cite>.
- Instruction bias and context use: SFT can introduce biases that make models overly sensitive to prompt surface forms, and can reduce reliance on provided context under conflict, reflecting a shift in strategy rather than an expansion of knowledge.<cite id="75bc02a1-1">Instruction‑tuned models exhibit strong fragility to semantically invariant changes (e.g., option label formats), with large performance drops when labels switch from numeric to Roman numerals</cite><cite id="75bc02a1-2">Studies report loss of context awareness after instruction tuning, with models becoming less reliant on provided context when knowledge conflicts arise</cite>.

# Can SFT actually add or update knowledge?

- Sometimes, but inconsistently: When instruction data includes task‑specific examples with correct answers, fine‑tuning can improve performance on some reasoning tasks; however, broad gains across knowledge benchmarks (e.g., MMLU, HellaSwag) are variable, suggesting limits to true knowledge acquisition rather than uniform style‑only changes.<cite id="b5792093-0">An empirical study finds fine‑tuning significantly improves some activations and reasoning abilities, yet declines in MMLU and HellaSwag imply knowledge‑intensive capabilities can worsen</cite>.
- Knowledge vs. style trade‑offs: Analyses suggest SFT tends to optimize output style and adherence to instructions rather than expanding parametric knowledge, especially when using few‑shot instruction sets; separating knowledge learning from format alignment is proposed to target actual domain knowledge gains.<cite id="af6ca978-0">Evidence indicates distribution shifts are stylistic and that as few as ~1,000 SFT examples can “achieve satisfactory alignment performance” by leveraging prior knowledge</cite><cite id="af6ca978-0">A unified view proposes “knowledge mixture pre‑training” to focus on learning new domain knowledge while preserving general knowledge</cite>.
- Instruction‑tuning vs. pretraining: Large‑scale evaluations show significant differences between pretrained and instruction‑ or fine‑tuned models on many tasks, but instruction‑tuned and fine‑tuned models are not significantly different from each other across several benchmarks, implying instruction tuning often capitalizes on pre‑trained knowledge and formatting rather than adding distinct new knowledge.<cite id="b5792093-3">A comprehensive reassessment finds significant differences between pretrained and instruction‑tuned models, and between pretrained and fine‑tuned models, but no significant differences between instruction‑tuned and fine‑tuned models across multiple benchmarks</cite>.

# Limits and risks: forgetting and overwriting

- Catastrophic forgetting under continual fine‑tuning: Narrow task‑specific SFT or sequential instruction tuning can degrade performance on earlier tasks and benchmarks, erasing prior knowledge unless mitigated.<cite id="74238de8-0">A continual instruction‑finetuning study evaluates retention by re‑testing earlier tasks after each fine‑tuning step and quantifies forgetting as the gap between peak and final performance</cite><cite id="74238de8-4">Empirically, models show significant forgetting after the first instruction tuning; mixing in general instruction data mitigates the decline on benchmarks like MMLU‑human (e.g., 30% vs. 26.8% with instruction‑only)</cite>.
- Overwriting alignment: Fine‑tuning on data that conflicts with prior alignment can reverse or degrade safety and preference alignment, indicating that SFT can overwrite learned behaviors and values when data is not aligned with prior training.<cite id="af6ca978-2">Prior work warns that fine‑tuning aligned LLMs can compromise safety alignment, and that fine‑tuning unaligned LLMs exacerbates verbatim memorization</cite><cite id="af6ca978-3">Re‑emergent misalignment research shows narrow fine‑tuning can overwrite, suppress, or reverse prior alignment</cite>.
- Instruction bias and fragility: SFT can induce strong sensitivity to prompt surface forms and instructions, with large performance swings under semantically equivalent reformulations, suggesting that observed “learning” may be prompt‑format adaptation rather than durable knowledge change.<cite id="75bc02a1-1">Experiments show drastic performance drops (e.g., ~30% on MMLU) when only option labels change despite semantic invariance, and degradation when instructions are removed</cite>.

# When SFT can contribute new knowledge (and when it’s not the right tool)

- Domain‑specific adaptation with SFT plus retrieval or continued pretraining: To learn new domain knowledge, practitioners often combine SFT with retrieval or continued training on domain data, explicitly targeting knowledge acquisition rather than pure instruction following; frameworks argue for decoupling “knowledge learning” from “format alignment.”<cite id="af6ca978-0">A domain‑adaptation framework proposes separating knowledge learning from format alignment, noting that instruction tuning alone tends to elicit existing knowledge and style while shifting stylistic tokens</cite>.
- General instruction data to mitigate forgetting: Adding broad instruction datasets during continual fine‑tuning can help preserve baseline knowledge and reduce catastrophic forgetting, indicating that high‑level instruction guidance can stabilize knowledge alongside task‑specific updates.<cite id="74238de8-4">Mixing general instruction data (e.g., ALPACA) with task‑specific data mitigates forgetting on knowledge benchmarks (e.g., MMLU‑human 30% vs. 26.8% with instruction‑only)</cite>.
- Not a silver bullet for deep knowledge expansion: If the goal is broad, factual knowledge growth, SFT alone is often insufficient; methods that directly target knowledge (e.g., continued pretraining on domain corpora, distillation from preference‑optimized or truth‑ful models) or incorporate retrieval/self‑critique signals tend to be more effective for factual updates than instruction‑only SFT.<cite id="75bc02a1-2">Work on grounding and preference optimization for factuality suggests training‑time approaches to align models with external evidence can strengthen factual knowledge</cite>.

# Practical implications

- Expect behavior and style changes: With SFT, you should primarily plan for improved instruction following, role‑play, and formatting; these are reliable and sizable, even if there is little new world‑knowledge added.<cite id="af6ca978-0">Instruction tuning elicits prior knowledge and improves task capability while concentrating shifts in stylistic tokens</cite><cite id="75bc02a1-4">Evidence supports a superficial alignment pattern where formatting and style dominate</cite>.
- Guard against forgetting and drift: For continual or narrow SFT, monitor performance on earlier or broader benchmarks and consider techniques like mixing general instruction data, larger context windows, or optimizers designed to mitigate forgetting to preserve prior knowledge.<cite id="74238de8-0">Continual instruction fine‑tuning studies quantify forgetting on earlier tasks</cite><cite id="74238de8-4">Mixing general instruction data mitigates knowledge loss</cite><cite id="b5792093-3">A broader reassessment highlights that instruction‑tuned and fine‑tuned models can be statistically similar on many benchmarks, underscoring the need for careful monitoring</cite>.
- For true knowledge expansion, pair SFT with knowledge‑focused methods: Combine SFT with continued domain pretraining, retrieval‑augmented training, or distillation from preference‑optimized models to drive factual updates beyond prompt‑format alignment.<cite id="af6ca978-0">Frameworks explicitly decoupling knowledge learning and format alignment argue for targeted strategies to add new domain knowledge</cite><cite id="75bc02a1-2">Training approaches that integrate retrieval and self‑critique or preference optimization can align models to external evidence and improve factuality</cite>.

# Bottom line

LLMs can “learn” with supervised fine‑tuning—but what they typically learn is better adherence to instructions, safer or chat‑style formatting, and prompt‑format‑dependent strategy, grounded in their pre‑trained knowledge. Reliable acquisition of new factual knowledge generally requires SFT in combination with domain‑specific training signals (retrieval, continued pretraining, or distillation), and even then must be carefully managed to avoid catastrophic forgetting or instruction‑format fragility.<cite id="af6ca978-0">Instruction tuning aligns behavior and elicits prior knowledge, with token‑level shifts concentrated in style</cite><cite id="af6ca978-3">Narrow fine‑tuning can overwrite prior alignment</cite><cite id="b5792093-0">Empirical effects on knowledge benchmarks are inconsistent</cite><cite id="74238de8-4">Mitigation strategies like mixing general instruction data can reduce forgetting</cite><cite id="75bc02a1-1">Instruction bias and fragility can dominate performance</cite>.
</answer>
