problem: Downlink scheduling of satellite image data
final_response:
# What “Downlink Scheduling of Satellite Image Data” Means

Downlink scheduling arranges when and through which ground stations Earth observation (EO) satellites transmit imaged data to the ground within time windows when the satellite is visible to a station, respecting satellite hardware constraints (e.g., antenna modes), ground-station reception resources, request deadlines and priorities, and mission-level objectives such as maximizing delivered data utility, meeting latency thresholds, and ensuring robustness under weather and pass-geometry variability.<cite id="bf161aeb-0">Downlink scheduling for EO satellites is commonly formulated with per-request parameters (release time, deadline, duration, priority, assigned ground station), urgency classes, visibility masks (pass times), multi-antenna operation modes, and ground-station channel constraints</cite><cite id="bf161aeb-3">Time-varying links and variable ground-station visibility windows are intrinsic to the scheduling problem and must be modeled explicitly</cite>.

# Problem Structure and Core Constraints

A typical instance considers a set of downlink requests with time windows and priorities, where urgent requests must start soon after release and regular requests are scheduled primarily by priority; some requests may require dual downlink (e.g., redundancy across two stations).<cite id="bf161aeb-0">Requests have release/deadline windows, urgency/priority, and some are “dual” requiring two stations; urgent have absolute priority over regular</cite>. Downlinks can only occur during visibility passes; the satellite may support multi-beam (half-power) or single-beam (full-power) downlinking, affecting resource contention and assignment granularity.<cite id="bf161aeb-0">A downlink can be performed only during a station visibility “mask”; a SAR satellite like RADARSAT-2 can use two antennas in half-power to downlink simultaneously or one in full-power</cite>. Ground stations have limited channels and can differ by transmission power and reception capabilities, which influence which downlink assignments are feasible and desirable.<cite id="bf161aeb-0">Each ground station has one or two channels and can be classified by transmission power</cite>.

At system scale, multiple satellites contend for shared ground stations, and downlink windows are scarce; weather-induced path losses (e.g., rain/cloud attenuation) can disrupt or degrade links, making robustness and backup station selection critical for time-sensitive applications.<cite id="9b257d74-2">Contention among many satellites for a few ground stations can cause high latency and onboard retention; weather can induce up to 10 dB attenuation, reducing reliability without additional ground stations</cite>. These constraints motivate joint optimization of communication and downstream processing to meet latency thresholds while minimizing cost.<cite id="9b257d74-4">Ground station scheduling aligns communications and operations with visibility, energy, and data constraints; objectives include maximizing downloaded data while meeting requirements</cite>.

# Objectives and Performance Metrics

Downlink schedulers optimize trade-offs among delivered volume, timeliness, fairness, and robustness. In practice, maximizing utility is central because only successfully transmitted requests yield customer utility; bottlenecks at the downlink can force removal of previously acquired images from use, underscoring the need to prioritize transmittable requests.<cite id="e81e3497-2">Only transmitted images count toward utility; downlink can become a bottleneck where limited ground resources prevent transmission, causing acquisitions to be shelved</cite>. Priority-based objectives often distinguish urgent (time-critical) vs. regular requests, with absolute priority dominance for urgent to minimize critical delays.<cite id="bf161aeb-0">Urgent requests start as soon as possible and dominate scheduling improvements over regular requests</cite>. For multi-satellite settings, objectives may include minimizing latency costs and meeting topic-level completeness/timeliness for user data products, with rewards decaying if deadlines are missed.<cite id="9b257d74-0">Data-topic objectives reward complete transmission before expected time, with sharp decay if deadlines are missed; hybrid PSO+GA methods have been used</cite>.

Online and cloud-integrated schedulers incorporate long-term latency thresholds and system cost into real-time decisions, balancing data delivery and processing to reduce queueing and operational expense.<cite id="9b257d74-4">Lyapunov optimization enables online decisions that incorporate long-term latency thresholds and dynamic pairing without future information, jointly considering communication and computation</cite>.

# Algorithmic Approaches

- Heuristics and metaheuristics: Classical dispatching and improvement methods are widely used to handle time windows, priorities, and visibility constraints. Comparative studies report procedures that schedule urgent and regular requests in consecutive phases and apply GRASP, ejection chains, simulated annealing, and tabu search to reduce tardiness and improve priority adherence.<cite id="9b257d74-0">For RADARSAT-2, a two-phase urgent-then-regular procedure with GRASP, ejection chain, simulated annealing, and tabu search was compared for minimizing downlink tardiness</cite>. Hybrid genetic algorithms and mixed-integer formulations are used to select feasible subsets of requests maximizing utility under ground and satellite resource limits, with extensions toward multi-satellite contention and integrated acquisition–downlink planning as future directions.<cite id="e81e3497-0">Hybrid genetic algorithms generate downlink schedules given an acquisition plan and note the need to extend to multi-satellite settings and integrated scheduling</cite><cite id="e81e3497-2">The downlink selection aims to maximize a utility function under constraints; when resources are limited, not all requests can be transmitted, making it an oversubscribed problem</cite>.

- Exact optimization (MILP/ILP): MILP models capture visibility masks, pass windows, multi-antenna modes, and ground-station channel constraints, and have been proposed for single- and multi-satellite settings with multiple ground stations. These models can be validated on real mission data and scale with time-space network representations of satellite resources and constraints.<cite id="9b257d74-3">A MILP model based on a time-space network assigns mission and communication time windows for multiple satellites and ground stations, validated on actual satellite data</cite>. Earlier work also modeled data transmission tardiness explicitly and compared metaheuristics against MILP-derived lower bounds, highlighting performance trade-offs.<cite id="9b257d74-0">A MILP formulation for single-satellite, multiple-ground-station download scheduling was developed, with iterative methods for nonlinear dynamics and extensions to data-topic objectives</cite>.

- Lyapunov optimization and online control: For federated ground-station networks and cloud-adjacent EO pipelines, Lyapunov-based methods make online downlink and pairing decisions that respect latency thresholds and system cost without requiring future knowledge of satellite passes or ground-link quality, reducing complexity via graph formulations (e.g., bipartite matching with Hungarian algorithm).<cite id="9b257d74-4">SkyGS uses Lyapunov optimization to incorporate long-term latency thresholds into real-time decisions and reduces complexity by transforming the problem into a bipartite graph solved with the Hungarian algorithm</cite>.

- Multi-objective and topic-aware scheduling: When user products consist of multiple data units from different satellites, schedulers can optimize completeness and timeliness via reward functions that penalize partial or late transmissions, using hybrids like particle swarm optimization plus genetic algorithms to navigate combinatorial complexity.<cite id="9b257d74-0">Topic-aware objectives and hybrid PSO+GA algorithms have been proposed to meet completeness/timeliness requirements and manage multi-satellite contributions</cite>.

# Multi-Satellite and Multi-Ground Station Scheduling

EO constellations and multi-GS operations introduce high-dimensional contention. MILP and heuristic frameworks assign satellites to ground stations and then solve station-level scheduling, often via greedy arrival-time rules after assignment, to minimize waiting time and latency cost.<cite id="9b257d74-0">A simulated annealing approach assigns download requests to ground stations, followed by greedy single-station scheduling based on arrival-time considerations</cite>. Federating multiple GSaaS providers expands the feasible downlink graph, reduces onboard queueing, and improves robustness to single-provider weather outages, but requires integrated scheduling that couples communication and processing to meet end-to-end latency thresholds.<cite id="9b257d74-2">Federation of GSaaS increases available downlink opportunities and reduces onboard waiting time, but current methods often optimize communication only, neglecting downstream processing</cite><cite id="9b257d74-4">Jointly optimizing communication and computation enables cost minimization while enforcing latency thresholds in downlink scheduling</cite>.

At system scale, mixed-integer models for multiple satellites and ground stations allocate mission windows and communications to maximize utilization under visibility, energy, and data constraints using time-space networks grounded in real mission data.<cite id="9b257d74-3">An MILP time-space network model assigns time windows for missions and communications across multiple satellites and ground stations, validated with Korean satellite data</cite>. Operational studies emphasize that assuming fixed data volumes can be conservative or inaccurate due to uncertain outputs from compression and diverse imaging conditions, motivating robust designs with bounded capacities or stochastic models.<cite id="9b257d74-0">Assuming maximum data volumes can lead to under-utilization; compression yields uncertain volumes depending on imaged areas and conditions</cite>.

# Priority Handling, Urgency, and Dual Requests

Urgent requests (e.g., disaster response) are scheduled with absolute priority dominance to start close to their release, while regular requests are scheduled by priority and time-window fit. Dual requests require redundancy across two ground stations and increase combinatorial complexity, necessitating formulations that select both station pairs and pass windows that accommodate two simultaneous receptions or sequential handoffs without violating deadlines.<cite id="bf161aeb-0">Urgent vs regular priority handling and dual requests (two-station delivery) are explicit features in industrial RADARSAT-2 downlink scheduling</cite>.

# Visibility Pass Geometry, Link Variability, and Standards Implications

Visibility windows are determined by satellite-ground geometry and are time-varying; for optical and Ka-band links, atmospheric conditions (rain, clouds) and elevation/altitude affect path loss and availability, requiring scheduling policies that account for weather-aware link quality and station selection.<cite id="bf161aeb-3">Optical transmission loss depends on propagation distance, elevation, and meteorological conditions including cloud cover; comprehensive dynamic simulation is needed</cite><cite id="9b257d74-2">Weather-induced attenuation up to 10 dB can disrupt downlinks, making backup ground stations essential for robust scheduling</cite>. These physical and protocol constraints influence scheduler policies such as pass-based scheduling, adaptive coding and modulation, and prioritization of high-elevation, low-loss opportunities to meet deadlines with required bit error rates.<cite id="bf161aeb-0">Satellite image downlink uses defined code rates and bit error rate targets over the satellite–ground data link, with antenna and channel characteristics shaping feasible downlink operations</cite>.

# Integrated Planning and Acquisition–Downlink Coupling

Most operational systems separate planning into image acquisition and downlink scheduling, but the most efficient solutions consider them jointly: acquisition choices constrain downlink feasibility, and downlink bottlenecks can invalidate previously selected acquisitions, leading to re-planning and utility loss.<cite id="e81e3497-0">Downlink schedules depend on acquisition schedules; extending to multi-satellite and integrated acquisition–downlink planning is a key future direction</cite><cite id="e81e3497-2">The downlink bottleneck can cause previously selected imaging to be removed if transmission cannot be arranged, highlighting the need for integrated planning</cite>. Topic-aware and multi-satellite formulations explicitly model cross-satellite data products and their completeness/timeliness requirements to align acquisition and downlink decisions at the product level.<cite id="9b257d74-0">Data topics aggregate units from different satellites with completeness and timeliness requirements, guiding joint scheduling</cite>.

# Practical Systems and Scale

Real EO systems generate massive, near-continuous data volumes (e.g., daily EB-scale from LEO constellations), making downlink scheduling a cost and latency-critical function that must consider both communication and compute to meet end-to-end deadlines and maintain robustness across providers and weather regimes.<cite id="9b257d74-4">LEO constellations can produce on the order of 120 TB/day, requiring downlink and processing that jointly minimize cost and latency while meeting thresholds</cite>. Federated ground networks and cloud-integrated schedulers use Lyapunov-based online optimization and graph algorithms to scale to many satellites, antennas, and data centers while enforcing latency constraints without future-lookahead.<cite id="9b257d74-4">Lyapunov optimization with bipartite matching achieves O(|E||D| + (|S|+|A|)^3) complexity for online pairing and scheduling across edges, data centers, satellites, and antennas</cite>.

# Design Patterns and Implementation Guidance

- Model the pass-based resource: Represent visibility masks, multi-antenna modes, and station channel limits explicitly; include urgency/priority and dual-request constraints; and track on-board storage implications of delayed downlink.<cite id="bf161aeb-0">Visibility masks, antenna modes, station channels, urgency, and dual requests are core elements of industrial EO downlink scheduling</cite>.

- Choose the solver family: 
  - For small-to-medium instances with strong optimality guarantees, use MILP on time-space networks; validate with real mission data when possible.<cite id="9b257d74-3">MILP time-space network models have been validated on actual satellite data for multi-satellite, multi-GS settings</cite>.
  - For dynamic, large-scale, or stochastic environments, use Lyapunov-based online policies to enforce latency thresholds and reduce complexity via graph matching; augment with heuristics (e.g., greedy arrival-time) for station-level sequencing after assignment.<cite id="9b257d74-4">Lyapunov-based online pairing with Hungarian algorithm reduces complexity while enforcing latency thresholds</cite><cite id="9b257d74-0">Greedy arrival-time rules can follow assignment heuristics (e.g., simulated annealing) for station-level scheduling</cite>.
  - For multi-objective and topic-aware objectives, consider hybrid metaheuristics (GA+PSO) to balance completeness, timeliness, and cost under multi-satellite contributions.<cite id="9b257d74-0">Hybrid PSO+GA methods address topic-level completeness/timeliness requirements in multi-satellite settings</cite>.

- Plan integrated and robust: Co-optimize acquisition and downlink where possible; anticipate compression variability and use bounded data sizes or stochastic estimates; design for multi-GS federation and backup to mitigate weather-induced outages and single-provider risk; and incorporate end-to-end latency constraints that include onboard processing queues and network transport to data centers.<cite id="e81e3497-0">Integrated scheduling is needed to mitigate downlink bottlenecks that force shelving acquisitions</cite><cite id="9b257d74-0">Uncertainty in data volumes due to compression complicates planning and motivates robust designs</cite><cite id="9b257d74-2">Federation of GSaaS reduces latency and increases robustness by expanding available downlink opportunities and providing backups against weather</cite><cite id="9b257d74-4">Joint communication–computation scheduling enforces latency thresholds and minimizes system cost</cite>.

# Evidence Gaps and Future Directions

While robust optimization and Lyapunov methods are well-supported for online scheduling with latency constraints, there is less published evidence specifically applying reinforcement learning to EO downlink under realistic pass-based dynamics and protocol constraints. Bridging this gap would involve RL policies trained on historical visibility, weather, and queue states to balance throughput, latency, and fairness across priority classes and GS networks. Additionally, standards-aware schedulers that explicitly exploit CCSDS Space Data Link Control and DVB-S2/S2X features (e.g., adaptive coding/modulation, frame structure, congestion control) could further improve link utilization and latency, but detailed protocol-level scheduling studies remain a niche in the EO literature.<cite id="bf161aeb-0">Current formulations emphasize link code rate and bit error rate targets and antenna modes, indicating where protocol-aware scheduling could add value</cite><cite id="bf161aeb-3">Optical and radio link modeling should incorporate elevation, distance, and meteorological effects, aligning with standards-aware scheduling</cite>.

# Summary

Effective downlink scheduling for satellite image data must model pass-based visibility, heterogeneous and time-varying links, multi-antenna and ground-station constraints, urgency and priority, and the coupling between acquisition and transmission. Heuristics, MILP models, and Lyapunov-based online methods provide complementary levers to maximize delivered utility, meet deadlines, and maintain robustness at mission and constellation scales, with emerging systems integrating ground-station as a service and cloud processing to enforce end-to-end latency while minimizing cost.<cite id="bf161aeb-0">Industrial formulations capture release/deadline windows, urgency/priority, visibility masks, multi-antenna modes, and station channel constraints</cite><cite id="9b257d74-0">Metaheuristics and MILP approaches address tardiness, multi-satellite contention, and topic-level objectives; compression uncertainty motivates robust planning</cite><cite id="9b257d74-2">Multi-GS contention and weather-induced attenuation drive the need for robust, federated ground networks</cite><cite id="9b257d74-4">Lyapunov-based online scheduling with graph algorithms integrates communication and computation to meet latency thresholds and reduce cost at scale</cite>.

Title: Satellite downlink scheduling problem: A case study
Snippet: We consider the problem arising in satellite industry that deals with scheduling downlinks of images assuming that the schedule for image acquisition is already generated. We study RADARSAT-2 satellite that orbits the Earth to acquire images that can be downlinked to a set G of stationary ground stations for further processing. Since the problem has a lot in common with scheduling problems and, in particular, with the Resource Constrained Project Scheduling Problem, our notations are close to the ones used in the scheduling literature. 

Let V be a set of n downlink requests to be scheduled within the planning horizon of 24 hours. For each request j ∈ V , release time r j , deadline d j , downlink duration p j , priority w j and ground station g j ∈ G are prescribed. The interval [r j , d j ] is called the time window of request j. Downlink requests are classified as regular and urgent. The downlink of urgent requests has to start as close as possible to their release times. However, downlinks of regular requests are more flexible and are primarily governed by their priorities. Urgent requests have absolute priority dominance over the regular (non-urgent) requests, i.e., any (small) improvement in downlinking of urgent requests is preferred over large improvements in downlinking of regular requests. Finally, some requests have to be downlinked to two ground stations and we call them dual requests. Each dual request is represented by two requests i, j ∈ V , and we are given a set of pairs (i, j) of dual requests. 

A downlink activity can be carried out only when the satellite is passing over a ground station. This time interval is called visibility mask of the station. The RADARSAT-2 has two antennas for downlinking, and it can work in half-power and full-power setting. When working in half-power setting, the two antennas can work separately and they can independently downlink two different images to one or two different ground stations simultaneously. In full-power setting, the satellite can process only one downlink at a time. 

Each ground station g ∈ G has one or two channels for receiving the downlinked images. Ground stations can also be classified based on their transmission power.
</snippet>

Title: A Hybrid Genetic Algorithm for Satellite Image Downlink Scheduling Problem
Snippet: Most of the literature on satellite mission planning is divided into two categories: optical satellites [1][2][3][4] and Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) satellites [5][6][7][8][9][10][11][12]. The satellite image acquisition and image downlink are two main scheduling problems in satellite mission planning. The image acquisition scheduling is a process of selecting observation tasks (shot strips) generated from customer demands. All selected observation tasks consist of a set of requests as the input of SIDSP. The image downlink scheduling is a process of selecting a subset of downlink requests among the candidate set. Only if the image is successfully transmitted can the utility of the corresponding demand be counted. Considering all kinds of constraints, the subset of requests that can eventually be transmitted, their corresponding ground stations and downlink time windows are the output of SIDSP with the purpose of maximizing the utility function. SIDSP is a complex constrained optimization problem. 

The growing customer demands and the limited ground resources make SIDSP become an oversubscribed scheduling problem. Not all the requests can be scheduled and there are cases that satellite has sufficient conditions for an imaging but cannot arrange a downlink for it, which causes the imaging to be removed from the image acquisition plan and the corresponding customer demand has to be shelved. Image downlink may become a bottleneck in the efficiency of the whole satellite system. Satellite image downlink system is mainly composed of on-board transmission system and ground receiving system. The on-board transmission system includes transmitter and antennas. The ground receiving system includes receiver and antennas. Satellite image downlink mission is to transmit the original or compressed data to the ground station by satelliteground data link under the certain code rate and bit error rate. Satellites can work in two modes: (1) the antennas can work separately and they can independently downlink different images to one or different ground stations simultaneously; (2) only one antenna can work to downlink at a time. Downlink also can be classified into two ways: (1) the observed images are transmitted to the ground station in real time when the observation target and the ground station are simultaneously visible to the satellite; (2) first store observed images in the onboard memory and then transmit data to the ground station when the satellite is passing.

To address the challenge of exponential complexity of the resulting realtime optimizations, we transform the problem into a bipartite graph and apply the Hungarian algorithm to solve it, thereby reducing the computational complexity to O(|E||D| + (|S| + |A|) 3 ), where |E|, |D|, |S| and |A| denote the number of edges, data centers, satellites, and antennas, respectively. In summary, our main contributions are summarized as follows: 

• We propose a novel concept to federate multiple GSaaS from diverse providers into a unified ground station network. 

• During downlink scheduling, we broaden our focus from solely communication to encompass both communication and computation, thereby incorporating satellite data processing into our considerations. • During optimization, SkyGS judiciously considers both the system cost and data latency and effectively minimizes system cost while adhering to the data latency threshold. II. BACKGROUND Satellite orbits and data collection: Emerging LEO constellations for earth observation, such as the Dove constellation, typically operate in polar orbits with an approximate period of 90 minutes. Due to the Earth's rotation, the satellite's ground track shifts westward with each orbit, enabling the scanning of different global sections each time [20]. Equipped with sensors, these satellites capture earth images across various parts of the frequency spectrum, including RGB, radio waves, and infrared. Unlike traditional Earth observation satellites that prioritize and plan their imagery collections based on specific "targeted" areas, often omitting non-prioritized regions [21], emerging Earth observation LEO constellations aim to build a near real-time map of the earth. These satellites continuously collect data, storing images on-board. As measured in work [10], the Dove constellation captures an average of 120TB of data per day. Handling the downlink and processing of such immense volumes of data incurs substantial costs and requires timely execution, underscoring the necessity of considering both system cost and data latency during scheduling.

Title: Satellite Scheduling Problems: A survey of applications in Earth and outer space observation
Snippet: Karapetyan et al. (2015) considered the optimization of the data transmission tardiness in the downlink scheduling problem for Canada's Earth observing satellite, RADARSAT-2, and proposed a schedule generation procedure that schedules urgent and regular requests in two consecutive steps, respecting task priorities. The authors compare the performance of four standard metaheuristics: GRASP, ejection chain, simulated annealing and tabu search. 

In the same year, Spangelo et al. (2015) study the single-satellite multiple-ground stations download scheduling problem. They take into consideration the dynamics of energy consumption and data storage and propose a MILP model of the problem for linear dynamics. An iterative algorithm based on the MILP representation is then developed to solve the non-linear dynamics case. Later, Chen et al. (2020) included the consideration of data topics in the problem. A data topic is required by a particular user and contains a set of observation data units provided by different satellites. Every observation data topic has completeness and timeliness requirements, which are evaluated in the objective function thanks to specific reward functions. The full amount of reward is assigned only if all of the observation data belonging to one topic have been transmitted to the ground station before the expected time, otherwise the value of the observation data will be decaying sharply. To solve the problem, the authors proposed a hybrid scheduling algorithm, combining particle swarm optimization and a genetic algorithm. Liu et al. (2022) address the multi-satellite downlink scheduling problem considering waiting time through the minimization of latency costs. They propose a simulated annealing algorithm with a tabu list to assign the download requests to ground stations, and then solve the single station scheduling problem via greedy approaches based on arrival time considerations. 

The previous works assume prior knowledge of the exact amount of new data generated by observations and stored. In new satellites systems, the execution of sophisticated compression algorithms makes the volume of data generated uncertain, since it depends on the imaged ground area and on the conditions over them. To cope with this problem, the maximum volumes could be assumed for all the tasks, leading to under-utilisation of resources.
</snippet>

Title: The Space Above the Sky: Uniting Global-Scale Ground Station as a Service for Efficient Orbital Data Processing
Snippet: For instance, Leaf Space operates 17 ground stations [16], while SSC operates 10 ground stations [13]. In contrast, the Dove constellation, managed by Planet, comprises over 150 Earth observation LEO satellites [3]. This disparity leads to significant satellite contention and consequently, high data latency. Often, multiple satellites are within the visibility range of one ground station simultaneously, competing for the limited downlink opportunities. Given the scarcity of these opportunities, unmanaged contention can result in substantial data retention onboard the satellites. 

This latency is particularly critical for time-sensitive applications such as flood monitoring [6] and forest fire detection [7]. Moreover, relying on a single ground station provider decreases the robustness of satellite communications against arXiv:2501.00354v1 [cs.NI] 31 Dec 2024 weather variations. The quality of the links between satellites and ground stations is highly susceptible to atmospheric conditions. Attenuation effects, which can be influenced by rain and clouds, may result in signal losses of up to 10 dB, varying with the weather conditions and the signal's frequency [17]. Without additional ground stations serving as backups, satellites must contend with these weather-induced attenuation during data downlink, potentially compromising the reliability and quality of the communication. 

Following the idea of sky computing [18], it is interesting to extend the benefit of sky computing to outer space and examine the possibility of sky GSaaS. Through federating multiple GSaaS from diverse providers, the scale of ground station networks is significantly enhanced. Satellites can downlink data to any station within this collective network, thereby substantially increasing downlink opportunities and reducing data onboard waiting time. 

Despite the huge potential benefits, realizing the federation of GSaaS is non-trivial and faces the following challenges: 

• Compounding interaction of communication and computing: In satellite data downlink scheduling, current methods primarily focus on optimizing the communication aspect, often neglecting the data processing stage. 

For instance, L2D2 optimizes data downlink scheduling between satellites and ground stations [19], while Umbra considers scheduling data from satellites to ground stations and then to the cloud, without addressing subsequent data processing [10]. To be comprehensive, incorporating satellite data processing into downlink scheduling is essential.
</snippet>

Title: Mixed-Integer Linear Programming Model for Scheduling Missions and Communications of Multiple Satellites
Snippet: Satellites have been developed and operated for various purposes. The global satellite market is growing rapidly as the number of satellites and their mission diversity increase. Satellites revolve around the Earth to perform missions and communicate with ground stations repeatedly and sequentially. However, because satellites are orbiting the Earth, there is a limited time window for missions to a specific area and communication with ground stations. Thus, in an environment where multiple satellites and multiple ground stations (MS-MGs) are operated, scheduling missions and communications to maximize the utilization of satellites is a complex problem. For the MS-MG scheduling problem, this study proposes a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model to assign time windows for missions and communications with ground stations to individual satellites. The MILP model is based on the concept of a time-space network and includes constraints reflecting on the space mission environment of satellites. The objective function and constraints of the MILP model were validated through numerical experiments based on actual data from Korean satellites.
</snippet>

Title: Multi-objective approaches to ground station scheduling for optimization of communication with satellites
Snippet: There are thousands of artificial (i.e., man-made) satellites in the Earth's orbit. They are used either for taking pictures of the planet (e.g., to help meteorologists in weather prediction) or for taking pictures of other planets and faraway galaxies (e.g., to help scientists better understand the universe) (NASA 2017). In general, these satellites can be classified as Earth observation satellites, communications satellites, navigation satellites, weather satellites, and space telescopes.

Earth observation satellites (EOSs) are intended for environmental monitoring, meteorology, map making, and others. EOSs acquire images of the Earth's surface according to given observation requests, like earth resources exploration, natural disaster surveillance, or military reconnaissance.

The satellite scheduling problem consists of aligning tasks (like communications and control maneuvers) with resources (ground stations, space stations, and satellites). In the satellite scheduling problem, some resources are stationary, while others are orbiting the earth. To optimally align the tasks and resources several constraints have to be met, which classifies the problem as constraint-optimization one (Pemberton and Galiber 2000).

More specifically, the satellite scheduling problem consists of scheduling communication windows between ground stations and satellites. These include day-today activities of an operational satellite, like configuration of different sensors on the satellite to collect data, maintenance of the satellite status, and transmission of data/ commands between satellites and ground stations. During the allocated communication window the task to be performed should be completed (Xhafa and Ip 2019). The goal of scheduled data downloads from satellites to ground stations is to maximize the total amount of downloaded data while satisfying all visibility, energy, and data requirements; this is also known as Multiple-Satellite, Multiple Ground Station Scheduling Problem (MMSP) (Castaing 2014).

# What “Downlink Scheduling of Satellite Image Data” Means

Downlink scheduling arranges when and through which ground stations Earth observation (EO) satellites transmit imaged data to the ground within time windows when the satellite is visible to a station, respecting satellite hardware constraints (e.g., antenna modes), ground-station reception resources, request deadlines and priorities, and mission-level objectives such as maximizing delivered data utility, meeting latency thresholds, and ensuring robustness under weather and pass-geometry variability.<cite id="bf161aeb-0">Downlink scheduling for EO satellites is commonly formulated with per-request parameters (release time, deadline, duration, priority, assigned ground station), urgency classes, visibility masks (pass times), multi-antenna operation modes, and ground-station channel constraints</cite><cite id="bf161aeb-3">Time-varying links and variable ground-station visibility windows are intrinsic to the scheduling problem and must be modeled explicitly</cite>.

# Problem Structure and Core Constraints

A typical instance considers a set of downlink requests with time windows and priorities, where urgent requests must start soon after release and regular requests are scheduled primarily by priority; some requests may require dual downlink (e.g., redundancy across two stations).<cite id="bf161aeb-0">Requests have release/deadline windows, urgency/priority, and some are “dual” requiring two stations; urgent have absolute priority over regular</cite>. Downlinks can only occur during visibility passes; the satellite may support multi-beam (half-power) or single-beam (full-power) downlinking, affecting resource contention and assignment granularity.<cite id="bf161aeb-0">A downlink can be performed only during a station visibility “mask”; a SAR satellite like RADARSAT-2 can use two antennas in half-power to downlink simultaneously or one in full-power</cite>. Ground stations have limited channels and can differ by transmission power and reception capabilities, which influence which downlink assignments are feasible and desirable.<cite id="bf161aeb-0">Each ground station has one or two channels and can be classified by transmission power</cite>.

At system scale, multiple satellites contend for shared ground stations, and downlink windows are scarce; weather-induced path losses (e.g., rain/cloud attenuation) can disrupt or degrade links, making robustness and backup station selection critical for time-sensitive applications.<cite id="9b257d74-2">Contention among many satellites for a few ground stations can cause high latency and onboard retention; weather can induce up to 10 dB attenuation, reducing reliability without additional ground stations</cite>. These constraints motivate joint optimization of communication and downstream processing to meet latency thresholds while minimizing cost.<cite id="9b257d74-4">Ground station scheduling aligns communications and operations with visibility, energy, and data constraints; objectives include maximizing downloaded data while meeting requirements</cite>.

# Objectives and Performance Metrics

Downlink schedulers optimize trade-offs among delivered volume, timeliness, fairness, and robustness. In practice, maximizing utility is central because only successfully transmitted requests yield customer utility; bottlenecks at the downlink can force removal of previously acquired images from use, underscoring the need to prioritize transmittable requests.<cite id="e81e3497-2">Only transmitted images count toward utility; downlink can become a bottleneck where limited ground resources prevent transmission, causing acquisitions to be shelved</cite>. Priority-based objectives often distinguish urgent (time-critical) vs. regular requests, with absolute priority dominance for urgent to minimize critical delays.<cite id="bf161aeb-0">Urgent requests start as soon as possible and dominate scheduling improvements over regular requests</cite>. For multi-satellite settings, objectives may include minimizing latency costs and meeting topic-level completeness/timeliness for user data products, with rewards decaying if deadlines are missed.<cite id="9b257d74-0">Data-topic objectives reward complete transmission before expected time, with sharp decay if deadlines are missed; hybrid PSO+GA methods have been used</cite>.

Online and cloud-integrated schedulers incorporate long-term latency thresholds and system cost into real-time decisions, balancing data delivery and processing to reduce queueing and operational expense.<cite id="9b257d74-4">Lyapunov optimization enables online decisions that incorporate long-term latency thresholds and dynamic pairing without future information, jointly considering communication and computation</cite>.

# Algorithmic Approaches

- Heuristics and metaheuristics: Classical dispatching and improvement methods are widely used to handle time windows, priorities, and visibility constraints. Comparative studies report procedures that schedule urgent and regular requests in consecutive phases and apply GRASP, ejection chains, simulated annealing, and tabu search to reduce tardiness and improve priority adherence.<cite id="9b257d74-0">For RADARSAT-2, a two-phase urgent-then-regular procedure with GRASP, ejection chain, simulated annealing, and tabu search was compared for minimizing downlink tardiness</cite>. Hybrid genetic algorithms and mixed-integer formulations are used to select feasible subsets of requests maximizing utility under ground and satellite resource limits, with extensions toward multi-satellite contention and integrated acquisition–downlink planning as future directions.<cite id="e81e3497-0">Hybrid genetic algorithms generate downlink schedules given an acquisition plan and note the need to extend to multi-satellite settings and integrated scheduling</cite><cite id="e81e3497-2">The downlink selection aims to maximize a utility function under constraints; when resources are limited, not all requests can be transmitted, making it an oversubscribed problem</cite>.

- Exact optimization (MILP/ILP): MILP models capture visibility masks, pass windows, multi-antenna modes, and ground-station channel constraints, and have been proposed for single- and multi-satellite settings with multiple ground stations. These models can be validated on real mission data and scale with time-space network representations of satellite resources and constraints.<cite id="9b257d74-3">A MILP model based on a time-space network assigns mission and communication time windows for multiple satellites and ground stations, validated on actual satellite data</cite>. Earlier work also modeled data transmission tardiness explicitly and compared metaheuristics against MILP-derived lower bounds, highlighting performance trade-offs.<cite id="9b257d74-0">A MILP formulation for single-satellite, multiple-ground-station download scheduling was developed, with iterative methods for nonlinear dynamics and extensions to data-topic objectives</cite>.

- Lyapunov optimization and online control: For federated ground-station networks and cloud-adjacent EO pipelines, Lyapunov-based methods make online downlink and pairing decisions that respect latency thresholds and system cost without requiring future knowledge of satellite passes or ground-link quality, reducing complexity via graph formulations (e.g., bipartite matching with Hungarian algorithm).<cite id="9b257d74-4">SkyGS uses Lyapunov optimization to incorporate long-term latency thresholds into real-time decisions and reduces complexity by transforming the problem into a bipartite graph solved with the Hungarian algorithm</cite>.

- Multi-objective and topic-aware scheduling: When user products consist of multiple data units from different satellites, schedulers can optimize completeness and timeliness via reward functions that penalize partial or late transmissions, using hybrids like particle swarm optimization plus genetic algorithms to navigate combinatorial complexity.<cite id="9b257d74-0">Topic-aware objectives and hybrid PSO+GA algorithms have been proposed to meet completeness/timeliness requirements and manage multi-satellite contributions</cite>.

# Multi-Satellite and Multi-Ground Station Scheduling

EO constellations and multi-GS operations introduce high-dimensional contention. MILP and heuristic frameworks assign satellites to ground stations and then solve station-level scheduling, often via greedy arrival-time rules after assignment, to minimize waiting time and latency cost.<cite id="9b257d74-0">A simulated annealing approach assigns download requests to ground stations, followed by greedy single-station scheduling based on arrival-time considerations</cite>. Federating multiple GSaaS providers expands the feasible downlink graph, reduces onboard queueing, and improves robustness to single-provider weather outages, but requires integrated scheduling that couples communication and processing to meet end-to-end latency thresholds.<cite id="9b257d74-2">Federation of GSaaS increases available downlink opportunities and reduces onboard waiting time, but current methods often optimize communication only, neglecting downstream processing</cite><cite id="9b257d74-4">Jointly optimizing communication and computation enables cost minimization while enforcing latency thresholds in downlink scheduling</cite>.

At system scale, mixed-integer models for multiple satellites and ground stations allocate mission windows and communications to maximize utilization under visibility, energy, and data constraints using time-space networks grounded in real mission data.<cite id="9b257d74-3">An MILP time-space network model assigns time windows for missions and communications across multiple satellites and ground stations, validated with Korean satellite data</cite>. Operational studies emphasize that assuming fixed data volumes can be conservative or inaccurate due to uncertain outputs from compression and diverse imaging conditions, motivating robust designs with bounded capacities or stochastic models.<cite id="9b257d74-0">Assuming maximum data volumes can lead to under-utilization; compression yields uncertain volumes depending on imaged areas and conditions</cite>.

# Priority Handling, Urgency, and Dual Requests

Urgent requests (e.g., disaster response) are scheduled with absolute priority dominance to start close to their release, while regular requests are scheduled by priority and time-window fit. Dual requests require redundancy across two ground stations and increase combinatorial complexity, necessitating formulations that select both station pairs and pass windows that accommodate two simultaneous receptions or sequential handoffs without violating deadlines.<cite id="bf161aeb-0">Urgent vs regular priority handling and dual requests (two-station delivery) are explicit features in industrial RADARSAT-2 downlink scheduling</cite>.

# Visibility Pass Geometry, Link Variability, and Standards Implications

Visibility windows are determined by satellite-ground geometry and are time-varying; for optical and Ka-band links, atmospheric conditions (rain, clouds) and elevation/altitude affect path loss and availability, requiring scheduling policies that account for weather-aware link quality and station selection.<cite id="bf161aeb-3">Optical transmission loss depends on propagation distance, elevation, and meteorological conditions including cloud cover; comprehensive dynamic simulation is needed</cite><cite id="9b257d74-2">Weather-induced attenuation up to 10 dB can disrupt downlinks, making backup ground stations essential for robust scheduling</cite>. These physical and protocol constraints influence scheduler policies such as pass-based scheduling, adaptive coding and modulation, and prioritization of high-elevation, low-loss opportunities to meet deadlines with required bit error rates.<cite id="bf161aeb-0">Satellite image downlink uses defined code rates and bit error rate targets over the satellite–ground data link, with antenna and channel characteristics shaping feasible downlink operations</cite>.

# Integrated Planning and Acquisition–Downlink Coupling

Most operational systems separate planning into image acquisition and downlink scheduling, but the most efficient solutions consider them jointly: acquisition choices constrain downlink feasibility, and downlink bottlenecks can invalidate previously selected acquisitions, leading to re-planning and utility loss.<cite id="e81e3497-0">Downlink schedules depend on acquisition schedules; extending to multi-satellite and integrated acquisition–downlink planning is a key future direction</cite><cite id="e81e3497-2">The downlink bottleneck can cause previously selected imaging to be removed if transmission cannot be arranged, highlighting the need for integrated planning</cite>. Topic-aware and multi-satellite formulations explicitly model cross-satellite data products and their completeness/timeliness requirements to align acquisition and downlink decisions at the product level.<cite id="9b257d74-0">Data topics aggregate units from different satellites with completeness and timeliness requirements, guiding joint scheduling</cite>.

# Practical Systems and Scale

Real EO systems generate massive, near-continuous data volumes (e.g., daily EB-scale from LEO constellations), making downlink scheduling a cost and latency-critical function that must consider both communication and compute to meet end-to-end deadlines and maintain robustness across providers and weather regimes.<cite id="9b257d74-4">LEO constellations can produce on the order of 120 TB/day, requiring downlink and processing that jointly minimize cost and latency while meeting thresholds</cite>. Federated ground networks and cloud-integrated schedulers use Lyapunov-based online optimization and graph algorithms to scale to many satellites, antennas, and data centers while enforcing latency constraints without future-lookahead.<cite id="9b257d74-4">Lyapunov optimization with bipartite matching achieves O(|E||D| + (|S|+|A|)^3) complexity for online pairing and scheduling across edges, data centers, satellites, and antennas</cite>.

# Design Patterns and Implementation Guidance

- Model the pass-based resource: Represent visibility masks, multi-antenna modes, and station channel limits explicitly; include urgency/priority and dual-request constraints; and track on-board storage implications of delayed downlink.<cite id="bf161aeb-0">Visibility masks, antenna modes, station channels, urgency, and dual requests are core elements of industrial EO downlink scheduling</cite>.

- Choose the solver family: 
  - For small-to-medium instances with strong optimality guarantees, use MILP on time-space networks; validate with real mission data when possible.<cite id="9b257d74-3">MILP time-space network models have been validated on actual satellite data for multi-satellite, multi-GS settings</cite>.
  - For dynamic, large-scale, or stochastic environments, use Lyapunov-based online policies to enforce latency thresholds and reduce complexity via graph matching; augment with heuristics (e.g., greedy arrival-time) for station-level sequencing after assignment.<cite id="9b257d74-4">Lyapunov-based online pairing with Hungarian algorithm reduces complexity while enforcing latency thresholds</cite><cite id="9b257d74-0">Greedy arrival-time rules can follow assignment heuristics (e.g., simulated annealing) for station-level scheduling</cite>.
  - For multi-objective and topic-aware objectives, consider hybrid metaheuristics (GA+PSO) to balance completeness, timeliness, and cost under multi-satellite contributions.<cite id="9b257d74-0">Hybrid PSO+GA methods address topic-level completeness/timeliness requirements in multi-satellite settings</cite>.

- Plan integrated and robust: Co-optimize acquisition and downlink where possible; anticipate compression variability and use bounded data sizes or stochastic estimates; design for multi-GS federation and backup to mitigate weather-induced outages and single-provider risk; and incorporate end-to-end latency constraints that include onboard processing queues and network transport to data centers.<cite id="e81e3497-0">Integrated scheduling is needed to mitigate downlink bottlenecks that force shelving acquisitions</cite><cite id="9b257d74-0">Uncertainty in data volumes due to compression complicates planning and motivates robust designs</cite><cite id="9b257d74-2">Federation of GSaaS reduces latency and increases robustness by expanding available downlink opportunities and providing backups against weather</cite><cite id="9b257d74-4">Joint communication–computation scheduling enforces latency thresholds and minimizes system cost</cite>.

# Evidence Gaps and Future Directions

While robust optimization and Lyapunov methods are well-supported for online scheduling with latency constraints, there is less published evidence specifically applying reinforcement learning to EO downlink under realistic pass-based dynamics and protocol constraints. Bridging this gap would involve RL policies trained on historical visibility, weather, and queue states to balance throughput, latency, and fairness across priority classes and GS networks. Additionally, standards-aware schedulers that explicitly exploit CCSDS Space Data Link Control and DVB-S2/S2X features (e.g., adaptive coding/modulation, frame structure, congestion control) could further improve link utilization and latency, but detailed protocol-level scheduling studies remain a niche in the EO literature.<cite id="bf161aeb-0">Current formulations emphasize link code rate and bit error rate targets and antenna modes, indicating where protocol-aware scheduling could add value</cite><cite id="bf161aeb-3">Optical and radio link modeling should incorporate elevation, distance, and meteorological effects, aligning with standards-aware scheduling</cite>.

# Summary

Effective downlink scheduling for satellite image data must model pass-based visibility, heterogeneous and time-varying links, multi-antenna and ground-station constraints, urgency and priority, and the coupling between acquisition and transmission. Heuristics, MILP models, and Lyapunov-based online methods provide complementary levers to maximize delivered utility, meet deadlines, and maintain robustness at mission and constellation scales, with emerging systems integrating ground-station as a service and cloud processing to enforce end-to-end latency while minimizing cost.<cite id="bf161aeb-0">Industrial formulations capture release/deadline windows, urgency/priority, visibility masks, multi-antenna modes, and station channel constraints</cite><cite id="9b257d74-0">Metaheuristics and MILP approaches address tardiness, multi-satellite contention, and topic-level objectives; compression uncertainty motivates robust planning</cite><cite id="9b257d74-2">Multi-GS contention and weather-induced attenuation drive the need for robust, federated ground networks</cite><cite id="9b257d74-4">Lyapunov-based online scheduling with graph algorithms integrates communication and computation to meet latency thresholds and reduce cost at scale</cite>.

Title: Satellite downlink scheduling problem: A case study
Snippet: We consider the problem arising in satellite industry that deals with scheduling downlinks of images assuming that the schedule for image acquisition is already generated. We study RADARSAT-2 satellite that orbits the Earth to acquire images that can be downlinked to a set G of stationary ground stations for further processing. Since the problem has a lot in common with scheduling problems and, in particular, with the Resource Constrained Project Scheduling Problem, our notations are close to the ones used in the scheduling literature. 

Let V be a set of n downlink requests to be scheduled within the planning horizon of 24 hours. For each request j ∈ V , release time r j , deadline d j , downlink duration p j , priority w j and ground station g j ∈ G are prescribed. The interval [r j , d j ] is called the time window of request j. Downlink requests are classified as regular and urgent. The downlink of urgent requests has to start as close as possible to their release times. However, downlinks of regular requests are more flexible and are primarily governed by their priorities. Urgent requests have absolute priority dominance over the regular (non-urgent) requests, i.e., any (small) improvement in downlinking of urgent requests is preferred over large improvements in downlinking of regular requests. Finally, some requests have to be downlinked to two ground stations and we call them dual requests. Each dual request is represented by two requests i, j ∈ V , and we are given a set of pairs (i, j) of dual requests. 

A downlink activity can be carried out only when the satellite is passing over a ground station. This time interval is called visibility mask of the station. The RADARSAT-2 has two antennas for downlinking, and it can work in half-power and full-power setting. When working in half-power setting, the two antennas can work separately and they can independently downlink two different images to one or two different ground stations simultaneously. In full-power setting, the satellite can process only one downlink at a time. 

Each ground station g ∈ G has one or two channels for receiving the downlinked images. Ground stations can also be classified based on their transmission power.

Title: Exploiting potentialities for space-based quantum communication network: downlink quantum key distribution modelling and scheduling analysis
Snippet: These limitations hence suggest that, to improve the SatQKD efficiency, an efficient scheduling of downlink to the set of OGSs is required. 

Investigations of observation duration scheduling problems for Earth observation satellite are being used to execute highly efficient Earth observation tasks. Inspired by the similar satellite-to-ground orbit operations [37,38], the authors of ref. [39] elegantly extended the idea of scheduling downlinks to the scenario of satelliteto-ground QKD. To design a sequence of assignment that the satellite executes, ultimately achieving the optimal schedule, it is typically evaluated in terms of secure keys available. This requirement makes it necessary to have a prior comparison of the expected results of all possible satellite operations. For all of results, the unique characteristics of optical transmission from satellite to ground should be considered. In addition, the communication window for OGSs also have variable durations that depend on various factors in the satellite scenario. Taken together, atmospheric conditions, transmission path lengths and orbital propagations should be considered in a comprehensive, dynamic simulation of SatQKD. 

In this work, we develop a comprehensive modelling framework of SatQKD. We consider orbital propagations to determine orbital parameters at each time step, the time-varied satellite-to-ground channel loss including beam diffractions and atmosphere effects can be as a function of propagation distance and elevation angle. Moreover, Incorporated with the local meteorological data to loss model, the cloud cover contribution to transmission disturbance is quantified, thus a recreation of the quasi-experimental scenario. Choosing the Micius satellite experimental setting for paradigms of satellite applications, we simulate a course of Micius satellite flying across the ground stations built on the specific locations of Chinese nodes, and estimated the maximum number of keys that is possible to deliver to the ground nodes during a specific week. Furthermore, we listed the satellite-to-ground downlink optical transmission loss for all ground nodes, and capture its variations by selection of the orbital altitudes for a satellite. Meanwhile, we provide a trade-off consideration between the duration available for communications and its corresponding average link loss during an orbit, which could be used to support decisions involving the locations of ground stations and the selection of the orbital parameters for a satellite. Lastly, we demonstrate that the use of schedule is an effective way in networking a system of OGSs.

Title: A Hybrid Genetic Algorithm for Satellite Image Downlink Scheduling Problem
Snippet: Most of the literature on satellite mission planning is divided into two categories: optical satellites [1][2][3][4] and Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) satellites [5][6][7][8][9][10][11][12]. The satellite image acquisition and image downlink are two main scheduling problems in satellite mission planning. The image acquisition scheduling is a process of selecting observation tasks (shot strips) generated from customer demands. All selected observation tasks consist of a set of requests as the input of SIDSP. The image downlink scheduling is a process of selecting a subset of downlink requests among the candidate set. Only if the image is successfully transmitted can the utility of the corresponding demand be counted. Considering all kinds of constraints, the subset of requests that can eventually be transmitted, their corresponding ground stations and downlink time windows are the output of SIDSP with the purpose of maximizing the utility function. SIDSP is a complex constrained optimization problem. 

The growing customer demands and the limited ground resources make SIDSP become an oversubscribed scheduling problem. Not all the requests can be scheduled and there are cases that satellite has sufficient conditions for an imaging but cannot arrange a downlink for it, which causes the imaging to be removed from the image acquisition plan and the corresponding customer demand has to be shelved. Image downlink may become a bottleneck in the efficiency of the whole satellite system. Satellite image downlink system is mainly composed of on-board transmission system and ground receiving system. The on-board transmission system includes transmitter and antennas. The ground receiving system includes receiver and antennas. Satellite image downlink mission is to transmit the original or compressed data to the ground station by satelliteground data link under the certain code rate and bit error rate. Satellites can work in two modes: (1) the antennas can work separately and they can independently downlink different images to one or different ground stations simultaneously; (2) only one antenna can work to downlink at a time. Downlink also can be classified into two ways: (1) the observed images are transmitted to the ground station in real time when the observation target and the ground station are simultaneously visible to the satellite; (2) first store observed images in the onboard memory and then transmit data to the ground station when the satellite is passing.

snippet.text:
Most of the literature on satellite mission planning is divided into two categories: optical satellites [1][2][3][4] and Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) satellites [5][6][7][8][9][10][11][12]. The satellite image acquisition and image downlink are two main scheduling problems in satellite mission planning. The image acquisition scheduling is a process of selecting observation tasks (shot strips) generated from customer demands. All selected observation tasks consist of a set of requests as the input of SIDSP. The image downlink scheduling is a process of selecting a subset of downlink requests among the candidate set. Only if the image is successfully transmitted can the utility of the corresponding demand be counted. Considering all kinds of constraints, the subset of requests that can eventually be transmitted, their corresponding ground stations and downlink time windows are the output of SIDSP with the purpose of maximizing the utility function. SIDSP is a complex constrained optimization problem. 

The growing customer demands and the limited ground resources make SIDSP become an oversubscribed scheduling problem. Not all the requests can be scheduled and there are cases that satellite has sufficient conditions for an imaging but cannot arrange a downlink for it, which causes the imaging to be removed from the image acquisition plan and the corresponding customer demand has to be shelved. Image downlink may become a bottleneck in the efficiency of the whole satellite system. Satellite image downlink system is mainly composed of on-board transmission system and ground receiving system. The on-board transmission system includes transmitter and antennas. The ground receiving system includes receiver and antennas. Satellite image downlink mission is to transmit the original or compressed data to the ground station by satelliteground data link under the certain code rate and bit error rate. Satellites can work in two modes: (1) the antennas can work separately and they can independently downlink different images to one or different ground stations simultaneously; (2) only one antenna can work to downlink at a time. Downlink also can be classified into two ways: (1) the observed images are transmitted to the ground station in real time when the observation target and the ground station are simultaneously visible to the satellite; (2) first store observed images in the onboard memory and then transmit data to the ground station when the satellite is passing.

We consider the problem arising in satellite industry that deals with scheduling downlinks of images assuming that the schedule for image acquisition is already generated. We study RADARSAT-2 satellite that orbits the Earth to acquire images that can be downlinked to a set G of stationary ground stations for further processing. Since the problem has a lot in common with scheduling problems and, in particular, with the Resource Constrained Project Scheduling Problem, our notations are close to the ones used in the scheduling literature. 

Let V be a set of n downlink requests to be scheduled within the planning horizon of 24 hours. For each request j ∈ V , release time r j , deadline d j , downlink duration p j , priority w j and ground station g j ∈ G are prescribed. The interval [r j , d j ] is called the time window of request j. Downlink requests are classified as regular and urgent. The downlink of urgent requests has to start as close as possible to their release times. However, downlinks of regular requests are more flexible and are primarily governed by their priorities. Urgent requests have absolute priority dominance over the regular (non-urgent) requests, i.e., any (small) improvement in downlinking of urgent requests is preferred over large improvements in downlinking of regular requests. Finally, some requests have to be downlinked to two ground stations and we call them dual requests. Each dual request is represented by two requests i, j ∈ V , and we are given a set of pairs (i, j) of dual requests. 

A downlink activity can be carried out only when the satellite is passing over a ground station. This time interval is called visibility mask of the station. The RADARSAT-2 has two antennas for downlinking, and it can work in half-power and full-power setting. When working in half-power setting, the two antennas can work separately and they can independently downlink two different images to one or two different ground stations simultaneously. In full-power setting, the satellite can process only one downlink at a time. 

Each ground station g ∈ G has one or two channels for receiving the downlinked images. Ground stations can also be classified based on their transmission power.

Title: Satellite Scheduling Problems: A survey of applications in Earth and outer space observation
Snippet: Karapetyan et al. (2015) considered the optimization of the data transmission tardiness in the downlink scheduling problem for Canada's Earth observing satellite, RADARSAT-2, and proposed a schedule generation procedure that schedules urgent and regular requests in two consecutive steps, respecting task priorities. The authors compare the performance of four standard metaheuristics: GRASP, ejection chain, simulated annealing and tabu search. 

In the same year, Spangelo et al. (2015) study the single-satellite multiple-ground stations download scheduling problem. They take into consideration the dynamics of energy consumption and data storage and propose a MILP model of the problem for linear dynamics. An iterative algorithm based on the MILP representation is then developed to solve the non-linear dynamics case. Later, Chen et al. (2020) included the consideration of data topics in the problem. A data topic is required by a particular user and contains a set of observation data units provided by different satellites. Every observation data topic has completeness and timeliness requirements, which are evaluated in the objective function thanks to specific reward functions. The full amount of reward is assigned only if all of the observation data belonging to one topic have been transmitted to the ground station before the expected time, otherwise the value of the observation data will be decaying sharply. To solve the problem, the authors proposed a hybrid scheduling algorithm, combining particle swarm optimization and a genetic algorithm. Liu et al. (2022) address the multi-satellite downlink scheduling problem considering waiting time through the minimization of latency costs. They propose a simulated annealing algorithm with a tabu list to assign the download requests to ground stations, and then solve the single station scheduling problem via greedy approaches based on arrival time considerations. 

The previous works assume prior knowledge of the exact amount of new data generated by observations and stored. In new satellites systems, the execution of sophisticated compression algorithms makes the volume of data generated uncertain, since it depends on the imaged ground area and on the conditions over them. To cope with this problem, the maximum volumes could be assumed for all the tasks, leading to under-utilisation of resources.

Title: The Space Above the Sky: Uniting Global-Scale Ground Station as a Service for Efficient Orbital Data Processing
Snippet: For instance, Leaf Space operates 17 ground stations [16], while SSC operates 10 ground stations [13]. In contrast, the Dove constellation, managed by Planet, comprises over 150 Earth observation LEO satellites [3]. This disparity leads to significant satellite contention and consequently, high data latency. Often, multiple satellites are within the visibility range of one ground station simultaneously, competing for the limited downlink opportunities. Given the scarcity of these opportunities, unmanaged contention can result in substantial data retention onboard the satellites. 

This latency is particularly critical for time-sensitive applications such as flood monitoring [6] and forest fire detection [7]. Moreover, relying on a single ground station provider decreases the robustness of satellite communications against arXiv:2501.00354v1 [cs.NI] 31 Dec 2024 weather variations. The quality of the links between satellites and ground stations is highly susceptible to atmospheric conditions. Attenuation effects, which can be influenced by rain and clouds, may result in signal losses of up to 10 dB, varying with the weather conditions and the signal's frequency [17]. Without additional ground stations serving as backups, satellites must contend with these weather-induced attenuation during data downlink, potentially compromising the reliability and quality of the communication. 

Following the idea of sky computing [18], it is interesting to extend the benefit of sky computing to outer space and examine the possibility of sky GSaaS. Through federating multiple GSaaS from diverse providers, the scale of ground station networks is significantly enhanced. Satellites can downlink data to any station within this collective network, thereby substantially increasing downlink opportunities and reducing data onboard waiting time. 

Despite the huge potential benefits, realizing the federation of GSaaS is non-trivial and faces the following challenges: 

• Compounding interaction of communication and computing: In satellite data downlink scheduling, current methods primarily focus on optimizing the communication aspect, often neglecting the data processing stage. 

For instance, L2D2 optimizes data downlink scheduling between satellites and ground stations [19], while Umbra considers scheduling data from satellites to ground stations and then to the cloud, without addressing subsequent data processing [10]. To be comprehensive, incorporating satellite data processing into downlink scheduling is essential.

Title: Mixed-Integer Linear Programming Model for Scheduling Missions and Communications of Multiple Satellites
Snippet: Satellites have been developed and operated for various purposes. The global satellite market is growing rapidly as the number of satellites and their mission diversity increase. Satellites revolve around the Earth to perform missions and communicate with ground stations repeatedly and sequentially. However, because satellites are orbiting the Earth, there is a limited time window for missions to a specific area and communication with ground stations. Thus, in an environment where multiple satellites and multiple ground stations (MS-MGs) are operated, scheduling missions and communications to maximize the utilization of satellites is a complex problem. For the MS-MG scheduling problem, this study proposes a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model to assign time windows for missions and communications with ground stations to individual satellites. The MILP model is based on the concept of a time-space network and includes constraints reflecting on the space mission environment of satellites. The objective function and constraints of the MILP model were validated through numerical experiments based on actual data from Korean satellites.

Title: Multi-objective approaches to ground station scheduling for optimization of communication with satellites
Snippet: There are thousands of artificial (i.e., man-made) satellites in the Earth's orbit. They are used either for taking pictures of the planet (e.g., to help meteorologists in weather prediction) or for taking pictures of other planets and faraway galaxies (e.g., to help scientists better understand the universe) (NASA 2017). In general, these satellites can be classified as Earth observation satellites, communications satellites, navigation satellites, weather satellites, and space telescopes.

Earth observation satellites (EOSs) are intended for environmental monitoring, meteorology, map making, and others. EOSs acquire images of the Earth's surface according to given observation requests, like earth resources exploration, natural disaster surveillance, or military reconnaissance.

The satellite scheduling problem consists of aligning tasks (like communications and control maneuvers) with resources (ground stations, space stations, and satellites). In the satellite scheduling problem, some resources are stationary, while others are orbiting the earth. To optimally align the tasks and resources several constraints have to be met, which classifies the problem as constraint-optimization one (Pemberton and Galiber 2000).

More specifically, the satellite scheduling problem consists of scheduling communication windows between ground stations and satellites. These include day-today activities of an operational satellite, like configuration of different sensors on the satellite to collect data, maintenance of the satellite status, and transmission of data/ commands between satellites and ground stations. During the allocated communication window the task to be performed should be completed (Xhafa and Ip 2019). The goal of scheduled data downloads from satellites to ground stations is to maximize the total amount of downloaded data while satisfying all visibility, energy, and data requirements; this is also known as Multiple-Satellite, Multiple Ground Station Scheduling Problem (MMSP) (Castaing 2014).

In contrast, the Dove constellation, managed by Planet, comprises over 150 Earth observation LEO satellites [3]. This disparity leads to significant satellite contention and consequently, high data latency. Often, multiple satellites are within the visibility range of one ground station simultaneously, competing for the limited downlink opportunities. Given the scarcity of these opportunities, unmanaged contention can result in substantial data retention onboard the satellites. 

This latency is particularly critical for time-sensitive applications such as flood monitoring [6] and forest fire detection [7]. Moreover, relying on a single ground station provider decreases the robustness of satellite communications against arXiv:2501.00354v1 [cs.NI] 31 Dec 2024 weather variations. The quality of the links between satellites and ground stations is highly susceptible to atmospheric conditions. Attenuation effects, which can be influenced by rain and clouds, may result in signal losses of up to 10 dB, varying with the weather conditions and the signal's frequency [17]. Without additional ground stations serving as backups, satellites must contend with these weather-induced attenuation during data downlink, potentially compromising the reliability and quality of the communication. 

Following the idea of sky computing [18], it is interesting to extend the benefit of sky computing to outer space and examine the possibility of sky GSaaS. Through federating multiple GSaaS from diverse providers, the scale of ground station networks is significantly enhanced. Satellites can downlink data to any station within this collective network, thereby substantially increasing downlink opportunities and reducing data onboard waiting time. 

Despite the huge potential benefits, realizing the federation of GSaaS is non-trivial and faces the following challenges: 

• Compounding interaction of communication and computing: In satellite data downlink scheduling, current methods primarily focus on optimizing the communication aspect, often neglecting the data processing stage. 

For instance, L2D2 optimizes data downlink scheduling between satellites and ground stations [19], while Umbra considers scheduling data from satellites to ground stations and then to the cloud, without addressing subsequent data processing [10]. To be comprehensive, incorporating satellite data processing into downlink scheduling is essential.

Satellites revolve around the Earth to perform missions and communicate with ground stations repeatedly and sequentially. However, because satellites are orbiting the Earth, there is a limited time window for missions to a specific area and communication with ground stations. Thus, in an environment where multiple satellites and multiple ground stations (MS-MGs) are operated, scheduling missions and communications to maximize the utilization of satellites is a complex problem.
