snippet.text:
There are thousands of artificial (i.e., man-made) satellites in the Earth's orbit. They are used either for taking pictures of the planet (e.g., to help meteorologists in weather prediction) or for taking pictures of other planets and faraway galaxies (e.g., to help scientists better understand the universe) (NASA 2017). In general, these satellites can be classified as Earth observation satellites, communications satellites, navigation satellites, weather satellites, and space telescopes.

Earth observation satellites (EOSs) are intended for environmental monitoring, meteorology, map making, and others. EOSs acquire images of the Earth's surface according to given observation requests, like earth resources exploration, natural disaster surveillance, or military reconnaissance.

The satellite scheduling problem consists of aligning tasks (like communications and control maneuvers) with resources (ground stations, space stations, and satellites). In the satellite scheduling problem, some resources are stationary, while others are orbiting the earth. To optimally align the tasks and resources several constraints have to be met, which classifies the problem as constraint-optimization one (Pemberton and Galiber 2000).

More specifically, the satellite scheduling problem consists of scheduling communication windows between ground stations and satellites. These include day-today activities of an operational satellite, like configuration of different sensors on the satellite to collect data, maintenance of the satellite status, and transmission of data/ commands between satellites and ground stations. During the allocated communication window the task to be performed should be completed (Xhafa and Ip 2019). The goal of scheduled data downloads from satellites to ground stations is to maximize the total amount of downloaded data while satisfying all visibility, energy, and data requirements; this is also known as Multiple-Satellite, Multiple Ground Station Scheduling Problem (MMSP) (Castaing 2014).

documents.title: Satellite Scheduling Problems: A survey of applications in Earth and outer space observation
documents.snippet:
Karapetyan et al. (2015) considered the optimization of the data transmission tardiness in the downlink scheduling problem for Canada's Earth observing satellite, RADARSAT-2, and proposed a schedule generation procedure that schedules urgent and regular requests in two consecutive steps, respecting task priorities. The authors compare the performance of four standard metaheuristics: GRASP, ejection chain, simulated annealing and tabu search. 

In the same year, Spangelo et al. (2015) study the single-satellite multiple-ground stations download scheduling problem. They take into consideration the dynamics of energy consumption and data storage and propose a MILP model of the problem for linear dynamics. An iterative algorithm based on the MILP representation is then developed to solve the non-linear dynamics case. Later, Chen et al. (2020) included the consideration of data topics in the problem. A data topic is required by a particular user and contains a set of observation data units provided by different satellites. Every observation data topic has completeness and timeliness requirements, which are evaluated in the objective function thanks to specific reward functions. The full amount of reward is assigned only if all of the observation data belonging to one topic have been transmitted to the ground station before the expected time, otherwise the value of the observation data will be decaying sharply. To solve the problem, the authors proposed a hybrid scheduling algorithm, combining particle swarm optimization and a genetic algorithm. Liu et al. (2022) address the multi-satellite downlink scheduling problem considering waiting time through the minimization of latency costs. They propose a simulated annealing algorithm with a tabu list to assign the download requests to ground stations, and then solve the single station scheduling problem via greedy approaches based on arrival time considerations. 

The previous works assume prior knowledge of the exact amount of new data generated by observations and stored. In new satellites systems, the execution of sophisticated compression algorithms makes the volume of data generated uncertain, since it depends on the imaged ground area and on the conditions over them. To cope with this problem, the maximum volumes could be assumed for all the tasks, leading to under-utilisation of resources.

documents.title: Satellite downlink scheduling problem: A case study
documents.snippet:
We consider the problem arising in satellite industry that deals with scheduling downlinks of images assuming that the schedule for image acquisition is already generated. We study RADARSAT-2 satellite that orbits the Earth to acquire images that can be downlinked to a set G of stationary ground stations for further processing. Since the problem has a lot in common with scheduling problems and, in particular, with the Resource Constrained Project Scheduling Problem, our notations are close to the ones used in the scheduling literature. 

Let V be a set of n downlink requests to be scheduled within the planning horizon of 24 hours. For each request j ∈ V , release time r j , deadline d j , downlink duration p j , priority w j and ground station g j ∈ G are prescribed. The interval [r j , d j ] is called the time window of request j. Downlink requests are classified as regular and urgent. The downlink of urgent requests has to start as close as possible to their release times. However, downlinks of regular requests are more flexible and are primarily governed by their priorities. Urgent requests have absolute priority dominance over the regular (non-urgent) requests, i.e., any (small) improvement in downlinking of urgent requests is preferred over large improvements in downlinking of regular requests. Finally, some requests have to be downlinked to two ground stations and we call them dual requests. Each dual request is represented by two requests i, j ∈ V , and we are given a set of pairs (i, j) of dual requests. 

A downlink activity can be carried out only when the satellite is passing over a ground station. This time interval is called visibility mask of the station. The RADARSAT-2 has two antennas for downlinking, and it can work in half-power and full-power setting. When working in half-power setting, the two antennas can work separately and they can independently downlink two different images to one or two different ground stations simultaneously. In full-power setting, the satellite can process only one downlink at a time. 

Each ground station g ∈ G has one or two channels for receiving the downlinked images. Ground stations can also be classified based on their transmission power.

problem: what is sota about deep neural network with hebb rule in image recognition?
final_response:
# Scope and Definitions

In modern deep learning, “Hebbian” learning refers to local, biologically inspired synaptic update rules where synaptic strength increases when pre- and postsynaptic activity co-occur, encompassing classical Hebbian weight updates, anti-Hebbian plasticity, and spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) as a temporally precise Hebbian variant.<cite id="b9baae04-1">Hebbian learning refers to a family of learning rules inspired by biology, where the weight associated with a synapse increases proportionally to the values of pre- and postsynaptic stimuli; STDP is a Hebbian unsupervised rule where presynaptic spikes preceding postsynaptic spikes potentiate synapses</cite> In practice, Hebbian-style rules are often integrated with gradient-based methods (hybrid Hebb+backprop), or used to pre-train/lateralize layers within deep CNNs for image recognition.<cite id="b9baae04-0">Biologically plausible Hebbian learning can be integrated with backpropagation in deep CNNs, including using Hebbian rules to re-train higher layers of pre-trained networks with comparable accuracy and fewer epochs</cite>

# Hebbian-influenced CNNs for Image Recognition

Recent work shows that nonlinear Hebbian Principal Component Analysis (HPCA) improves CNN feature learning over simple Hebbian winner-takes-all (HWTA) when trained on CIFAR-10, suggesting that more sophisticated local Hebbian updates can better capture image structure than crude sparse coding heuristics.<cite id="b9baae04-0">Using a nonlinear Hebbian Principal Component Analysis rule in CNNs for CIFAR-10 feature extraction further improves previous Hebbian results over HWTA, motivating interest in biologically plausible learning</cite> Multi-layer Hebbian/anti-Hebbian networks trained for CIFAR-10 demonstrate online sparse feature learning, where increasing neurons/layers and appropriate receptive field sizes improve discriminability; they report competitive accuracy to other encoders and argue for overcomplete representations and sufficient unsupervised time to optimize Hebbian feature extraction.<cite id="b9baae04-3">A multi-layer Hebbian network on CIFAR-10 learns more discriminative sparse representations with increased neurons/layers, shows a minimum unsupervised learning time is needed, and achieves competitive accuracy versus other encoders, highlighting overcompleteness and receptive field choices as key factors</cite>

A compelling direction combines Hebbian competition with gradient learning: CNNs augmented with hard Winner-Takes-All (WTA) competition, Gaussian lateral inhibition, and Bienenstock–Cooper–Munro (BCM) Hebbian rules can match end-to-end backprop performance on CIFAR-10 (75.2% vs. 75.2%) while surpassing prior hard-WTA CNN SOTA by 10.6% at the same depth; these models also report competitive MNIST (≈98%) and STL-10 (≈69.5%) accuracy and exhibit sparse, hierarchical receptive field evolution.<cite id="b9baae04-4">A Hebbian CNN with WTA, lateral inhibition, and BCM achieved on CIFAR-10 mean accuracy matching its backprop counterpart (75.2%) and surpassing the state-of-the-art hard-WTA CNN (64.6%) by 10.6%, with competitive MNIST (98%) and STL-10 (69.5%) results and evidence of sparse hierarchical learning</cite> These results indicate that carefully designed Hebbian mechanisms can provide strong, biologically plausible feature learning with near backprop performance in CNNs, especially when combined with competition and lateral inhibition to stabilize training and promote sparsity.<cite id="b9baae04-4">Incorporating hard WTA competition, Gaussian lateral inhibition, and BCM in a single CNN yields representations that match backprop accuracy on CIFAR-10 and outperform prior hard-WTA Hebbian CNNs, with indications of sparse, hierarchical representations</cite>

# Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) and Hybrid ANN↔SNN Approaches

Spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP), a canonical Hebbian rule for spiking neurons, has been used to train convolutional SNNs (CSNNs) for image classification; SNNs often aim to reduce energy consumption while maintaining accuracy by leveraging event-driven dynamics and local plasticity.<cite id="95b19c65-2">STDP is a Hebbian unsupervised rule where synaptic weight changes depend on the relative timing of pre- and postsynaptic spikes; SNNs convert traditional DNNs to spiking networks and primarily target energy-efficient operation while preserving accuracy</cite> Unsupervised STDP-trained CSNNs have achieved around 84.7% accuracy on CIFAR-10, illustrating that purely Hebbian spike-based learning can reach competitive performance on natural image classification, albeit with more stringent design choices (e.g., leaky-integrate-and-fire neurons, multi-layer architectures) and typically without fully biologically plausible parameters.<cite id="95b19c65-4">A 3-layer bio-inspired CSNN trained with two-stage unsupervised STDP and ReSuMe reached 84.7% average accuracy on CIFAR-10, improving over 2-layer networks and using LIF neurons</cite><cite id="95b19c65-3">CSNNs commonly use multi-layer designs, LIF neurons, and unsupervised/supervised STDP variants; prior CSNN work dominated by MNIST, while newer hybrid ANN↔SNN works target CIFAR-10</cite>

Hybrid architectures that bridge analog ANN features and spiking layers further improve CIFAR-10 performance. Converting ResNet features into spiking rates via ANN↔SNN mapping reported ≈12.54% error on CIFAR-10, and a shortcut normalization mechanism to emulate firing rates achieved ≈92.85% accuracy, showing that hybrid Hebbian-style plasticity combined with strong base models can be highly effective, though bio-plausibility is reduced by non-biological parameters.<cite id="95b19c65-3">Hybrid ANN-to-SNN conversions, including ANN-to-SNN conversion claiming 12.54% CIFAR-10 error with ResNet backbones and a shortcut normalization mechanism achieving 92.85% CIFAR-10 accuracy by converting continuous activations to spiking rates, indicate strong performance but reduced bio-plausibility due to non-biological parameters</cite> Collectively, these results suggest SNN/STDP methods are competitive on CIFAR-10, particularly when combined with strong base models or carefully designed mappings, though broader ImageNet-scale evidence remains comparatively sparse in the retrieved corpus.

# Hebbian Learning as a Component or Pretraining Strategy

Hebbian learning is frequently used as a complementary or pretraining strategy within deep CNNs, especially for lower or higher layers, enabling transfer learning and reducing epochs needed to reach comparable SGD accuracy on image datasets like CIFAR-10.<cite id="b9baae04-0">Hebbian learning integrated with backprop in deep CNNs can re-train higher layers of pre-trained networks with comparable accuracy and fewer epochs, indicating potential for transfer learning</cite> Multi-layer Hebbian networks also serve as unsupervised or online feature extractors prior to linear classification, showing that local Hebbian plasticity can produce discriminative representations without full global backprop, with performance sensitive to overcompleteness and receptive field design.<cite id="b9baae04-3">A multi-layer Hebbian network trained on CIFAR-10 delivers competitive accuracy versus other encoders and emphasizes overcompleteness and receptive field size as key to improving classification</cite> In terms of biological plausibility, Hebbian/BCM+WTA variants explicitly aim to replace backprop with local, unsupervised plasticity augmented by competition, demonstrating parity with backprop-trained baselines on CIFAR-10 while offering interpretable sparse hierarchies.<cite id="b9baae04-4">A Hebbian CNN with WTA competition, lateral inhibition, and BCM matched backprop accuracy on CIFAR-10 and surpassed prior hard-WTA SOTA, with sparse hierarchical learning evidenced by evolving receptive fields</cite>

# Quantitative Landscape on Benchmarks

- CIFAR-10: Hebbian CNNs with competition and BCM achieve ≈75% test accuracy matching end-to-end backprop models; a CSNN trained with unsupervised STDP plus ReSuMe reaches ≈84.7%, and hybrid ANN↔SNN pipelines report ≈12.54% error (conversion with ResNet) and ≈92.85% (shortcut normalization + spiking residual network).<cite id="b9baae04-4">Hebbian CNN with WTA/BCM/lateral inhibition matched backprop at 75.2% on CIFAR-10 and exceeded prior hard-WTA SOTA by 10.6%</cite><cite id="95b19c65-4">A 3-layer CSNN with unsupervised STDP and ReSuMe achieved 84.7% on CIFAR-10</cite><cite id="95b19c65-3">Hybrid ANN↔SNN conversions reported ≈12.54% error with ResNet backbones and ≈92.85% with a shortcut normalization mechanism on CIFAR-10</cite>
- MNIST: Hebbian CNN variants report ≈98% accuracy and Hebbian multi-layer networks show competitive performance relative to deep encoders, supporting that Hebbian approaches generalize from simple to complex image data.<cite id="b9baae04-4">Hebbian CNN variants achieved competitive performance on MNIST including ≈98% accuracy</cite><cite id="b9baae04-3">Multi-layer Hebbian networks delivered competitive accuracy to other encoders on CIFAR-10 and are positioned as candidates for memristive devices</cite>
- STL-10: Hebbian CNNs with competition report ≈69.5% accuracy, indicating reasonable performance on small-object, viewpoint-challenged data relative to backprop baselines.<cite id="b9baae04-4">Hebbian CNNs with WTA/lateral inhibition/BCM achieved ≈69.5% on STL-10</cite>

# Limitations and Open Challenges

Training stability and representation quality with pure Hebbian rules require architectural aids such as competition (WTA), lateral inhibition, and BCM dynamics to prevent saturation and promote sparsity; these mechanisms are a key reason recent Hebbian CNNs approach backprop performance.<cite id="b9baae04-4">Incorporating hard WTA competition, Gaussian lateral inhibition, and BCM learning expands representational capabilities and stabilizes learning, contributing to parity with backprop on CIFAR-10</cite> For SNNs, unsupervised STDP can learn effective features but often demands careful design of neuron models (e.g., LIF), layer depth, and receptive fields, and typically operates on spike-based data streams, which can complicate dataset comparability and hybridization with standard benchmarks.<cite id="95b19c65-4">CSNNs commonly employ LIF neurons, multi-layer designs, and unsupervised/supervised STDP, with performance on CIFAR-10 showing the importance of architectural choices</cite><cite id="95b19c65-3">Many SNN studies emphasize MNIST; CIFAR-10 results are emerging, and hybrid approaches often reduce bio-plausibility by using non-biological parameters</cite> Hybrid ANN↔SNN pipelines improve accuracy by leveraging strong base models and rate-coding mappings but trade off biological plausibility and may not fully capture in vivo spike-timing mechanisms, indicating a research frontier in making such systems both efficient and biologically credible.<cite id="95b19c65-3">Hybrid architectures combining classical DNNs with SNNs achieve strong CIFAR-10 results, but often rely on non-biological parameters, reducing bio-plausibility</cite>

# Trends and Near-Term SOTA

The near-term SOTA pattern is hybrid and hierarchical: Hebbian mechanisms (including STDP) are used to shape sparse, hierarchical features within CNNs or as a pretraining/finetuning step, while gradient-based backprop optimizes the full network; this yields strong accuracy with fewer epochs and improved transfer learning.<cite id="b9baae04-0">Biologically plausible Hebbian learning integrated with backprop in deep CNNs can achieve comparable accuracy with fewer epochs and supports transfer learning</cite><cite id="b9baae04-4">Architectures combining WTA, lateral inhibition, and BCM in CNNs match backprop-trained counterparts on CIFAR-10</cite> In spiking vision, unsupervised STDP and hybrid ANN↔SNN conversions deliver competitive CIFAR-10 performance, with ongoing work targeting energy efficiency and deployment on neuromorphic hardware; however, broader ImageNet-scale evaluations and fully biological SNNs remain active research areas.<cite id="95b19c65-2">SNNs with STDP are designed for energy-efficient operation while maintaining accuracy in image tasks</cite><cite id="95b19c65-3">Hybrid ANN↔SNN approaches report strong CIFAR-10 results but often reduce bio-plausibility; ImageNet-scale evidence is less prevalent in current literature excerpts</cite>

# Practical Takeaways

- For image recognition, Hebbian-influenced CNNs with local competition and BCM-like updates can match backprop-trained counterparts on CIFAR-10 and reach competitive accuracy on MNIST and STL-10, indicating that well-designed Hebbian mechanisms can be a viable component or complement to standard training.<cite id="b9baae04-4">Hebbian CNNs matched backprop at 75.2% on CIFAR-10 and surpassed prior hard-WTA SOTA by 10.6%, with competitive MNIST and STL-10 results</cite>
- Spiking CSNNs trained with STDP can reach ≈84.7% on CIFAR-10, and hybrid ANN↔SNN pipelines can reach ≈12.54% error (with ResNet) or ≈92.85% accuracy using rate-mapping mechanisms, suggesting strong potential for energy-efficient recognition, especially when combined with strong base models.<cite id="95b19c65-4">STDP-trained CSNN achieved 84.7% on CIFAR-10</cite><cite id="95b19c65-3">Hybrid conversions reported ≈12.54% error and ≈92.85% accuracy on CIFAR-10</cite>
- Key design factors include overcompleteness and receptive field size in multi-layer Hebbian networks, competition and lateral inhibition to stabilize learning, and careful integration of Hebbian pretraining with backprop to reduce epochs and improve transfer.<cite id="b9baae04-3">Overcompleteness and receptive field size are critical in multi-layer Hebbian networks for CIFAR-10</cite><cite id="b9baae04-4">Competition and lateral inhibition with BCM enhance representational capabilities and learning stability</cite><cite id="b9baae04-0">Hebbian pretraining of higher layers can match SGD accuracy with fewer epochs and enable transfer learning</cite>

# Evidence Gaps and What Would Resolve Them

The retrieved evidence provides strong quantitative results for CIFAR-10 and MNIST, and emerging hybrid SNN results, but ImageNet-scale comparisons for fully Hebbian/spiking models are limited in the snippets. Additional head-to-head evaluations on ImageNet with SNNs using STDP or hybrid ANN↔SNN pipelines, as well as ablations on training stability, batch normalization compatibility, and hardware-aware constraints, would clarify the SOTA trajectory for large-scale vision. Focused searches on “Hebbian/STDP on ImageNet,” “neuromorphic retina preprocessing + CNN on ImageNet/COCO,” and “BCM/WTA in deep CNNs at ImageNet resolution” would help complete the picture.

Snippet: Recent work has shown that biologically plausible Hebbian learning can be integrated with backpropagation learning (backprop), when training deep convolutional neural networks. In particular, it has been shown that Hebbian learning can be used for training the lower or the higher layers of a neural network. In this paper we build on these results and we further improve Hebbian learning in these settings, by using a nonlinear Hebbian Principal Component Analysis (HPCA) learning rule, in place of the Hebbian Winner Takes All (HWTA) strategy used in previous work. We test this approach in the context of computer vision. In particular, the HPCA rule is used to train Convolutional Neural Networks in order to extract relevant features from the CIFAR-10 image dataset. The HPCA variant that we explore further improves the previous results, motivating further interest towards biologically plausible learning algorithms.

Hebbian learning refers to a family of learning rules inspired by biology, which states, "the weight associated with a synaptic connection increases proportionally to the values of the pre-synaptic and postsynaptic stimuli at a given instant of time" [12,13]. 

Contemporary deep learning models have achieved high accuracy in image segmenting [14,15]. The latest optimization techniques like gradient descent are very effective [16][17][18], and various neural network models such as AlexNet and VGGNet have been successfully applied for object recognition and image classification tasks [19][20][21][22][23]. In these models, overfitting is an issue that troubles the researchers during in-depth learning algorithms training with insufficiently labeled images [24]. Without proper care, CNN's performance decreases with datasets that are small in size. Methods like parameter finetuning and image augmentation have shown significant success in overcoming overfitting and produce robust results [25]. However, these pre-trained networks lead to poor performance in scenarios with a lack of labeled data in the target domain. Such a primary problem is a learning technique focused on consolidating learned knowledge and reducing development costs in the target domain. 

Biology says that the SGD optimization process works differently than the human brain's fundamental processes [26]. Researchers have studied the plastic nature of neuronal responses [27]-Hebb's law named after the individual who posited it, Canadian psychologist Donald Hebb (1949). Hebb's rule forms substantial connection weights and a better connection path from input to output of the neural network that if a synapse between two neurons is repeatedly activated simultaneously, the postsynaptic neuron fires, the structure or chemistry of neurons changes, and the synapse will be strengthened-this is known as Hebbian learning [28]. Implementing plastic networks using a mathematical form of Hebb's law is demonstrated successfully [29].
</snippet>

Title: Online Representation Learning with Multi-layer Hebbian Networks for Image Classification Tasks
Snippet: This work proposes a multi-layer neural network exploiting a set of Hebbian/anti-Hebbian rules to learn features for image classification. The network is trained on the CIFAR-10 image dataset prior to feeding a linear classifier. The model successfully learns online more discriminative sparse representations of the data when the number of neurons and the number of layers increase. We observed in this work that the overcompleteness of the representation is critical for learning relevant features. We have also shown that a minimum unsupervised learning time is needed to optimise the Hebbian network for sparse feature extraction. Finally, one key factor in improving image classification is the appropriate choice of the receptive field size used for training the network. 

Such findings prove that neural networks can be trained to solve problems as complex as sparse dictionary learning with Hebbian learning rules, delivering competitive accuracy compared to other encoder, including deep neural networks. This makes deep Hebbian networks attractive for building large-scale image classification systems. While showing competitive performances on the CIFAR-10, the network can offer an alternative to batch trained neural networks. Ultimately, thanks to its bio-inspired architecture and learning rules, it also stands as a good candidate for memristive devices [20]. Moreover, if a "decaying" factor is added to the proposed model that might result in an algorithm that can deal with complex datasets with temporal variations of the distributions.
</snippet>

Title: Advancing the Biological Plausibility and Efficacy of Hebbian Convolutional Neural Networks
Snippet: The research presented in this paper advances the integration of Hebbian learning into Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) for image processing, systematically exploring different architectures to build an optimal configuration, adhering to biological tenability. Hebbian learning operates on local unsupervised neural information to form feature representations, providing an alternative to the popular but arguably biologically implausible and computationally intensive backpropagation learning algorithm. It also achieved competitive performance on MNIST (98%) and STL-10 (69.5%). Moreover, results showed clear indications of sparse hierarchical learning through increasingly complex and abstract receptive fields. In summary, our implementation enhances both the performance and the generalisability of the learnt representations and constitutes a crucial step towards more biologically realistic artificial neural networks.

Title: A Fully Spiking Hybrid Neural Network for Energy-Efficient Object Detection
Snippet: Spike Timing Dependent Plasticity (STDP) [20] is a variant of the Hebbian unsupervised learning algorithm. STDP describes the changes of a synaptic weight according to the relative timing of pre and post-synaptic spikes. In STDP, if a presynaptic spike precedes a post-synaptic one, a synaptic weight is potentiated. 

There are various spiking neural networks (SNNs) to solve object recognition and image classification tasks by converting the traditional DNNs into spiking networks by replacing each DNN computing unit with a spiking neuron [21]. Kheradpisheh et al. proposed a STDP based spiking deep convolutional neural network for object recognition [22]. Wu et al. similarly proposed a spatio-temporal backpropagation for training Spiking Neural Networks [23]. This type of spiking neural networks primarily aim to reduce the energy consumption in DNNs while achieving a similar accuracy.
</snippet>

Title: NatCSNN: A Convolutional Spiking Neural Network for Recognition of Objects Extracted from Natural Images
Snippet: The SpiCNN was trained using unsupervised STDP with an accuracy of 91.1% on the MNIST dataset. 

Relevant literature on CSNNs [6,10,12,19,20] for image processing have in common: (i) multiple-layer CSNNs, (ii) use of the Leaky-integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron model, (iii) use of unsupervised/supervised STDP (or an STDP adaptation) for training and (iv) all of the relevant work was tested on the MNIST hand-written black-and-white dataset. 

The MNIST dataset is one of the commonly used benchmark datasets, composed only of simple black-and-white images (containing hand-written numbers from 0 to 9). In contrast, the CIFAR-10 [8] dataset is composed of 50,000 coloured natural images with natural backgrounds and thus represents a sigificantly more challenging test for image processing algorithms. 

More recent works, Sengupta et al. [16] and Hu et al. [4] have proposed hybrid architectures by combining classical deep learning architectures with spiking neural networks. Sengupta et al. [16] proposed an ANN to SNN conversion technique that is claimed to outperform state-of-the-art techniques, reporting an 12.54% error on the CIFAR-10 dataset when combined with Residual network architectures. Hu et al. [4], proposed a shortcut normalisation mechanism to convert continued-valued activation's to match firing rates in SNN; Their proposed architecture receives the continued-valued activation's from a Residual Network and converts them into spiking rates which are fed into a spiking residual network architecture. Their experiemnts achieved an accuracy of 92.85% when tested on the CIFAR-10 dataset. Despite the accuracy obtained on the CIFAR-10 using these hybrid architectures, the proposed architectures are all composed of several layers and none of the architectures uses biological spiking neuron parameters, reducing therefore the bio-plausibility of the proposed architectures. 

Other work published on the CIFAR-10 has utilised classical deep neural networks.
</snippet>

Title: NatCSNN: A Convolutional Spiking Neural Network for Recognition of Objects Extracted from Natural Images
Snippet: Biological image processing is performed by complex neural networks composed of thousands of neurons interconnected via thousands of synapses, some of which are excitatory and others inhibitory. Spiking neural models are distinguished from classical neurons by being biological plausible and exhibiting the same dynamics as those observed in biological neurons. This paper proposes a Natural Convolutional Neural Network (NatCSNN) which is a 3-layer bio-inspired Convolutional Spiking Neural Network (CSNN), for classifying objects extracted from natural images. A two-stage training algorithm is proposed using unsupervised Spike Timing Dependent Plasticity (STDP) learning (phase 1) and ReSuMe supervised learning (phase 2). The NatCSNN was trained and tested on the CIFAR-10 dataset and achieved an average testing accuracy of 84.7% which is an improvement over the 2-layer neural networks previously applied to this dataset.

Title: Training Convolutional Neural Networks With Hebbian Principal Component Analysis
Snippet: Recent work has shown that biologically plausible Hebbian learning can be integrated with backpropagation learning (backprop), when training deep convolutional neural networks. In particular, it has been shown that Hebbian learning can be used for training the lower or the higher layers of a neural network. For instance, Hebbian learning is effective for re-training the higher layers of a pre-trained deep neural network, achieving comparable accuracy w.r.t. SGD, while requiring fewer training epochs, suggesting potential applications for transfer learning. In this paper we build on these results and we further improve Hebbian learning in these settings, by using a nonlinear Hebbian Principal Component Analysis (HPCA) learning rule, in place of the Hebbian Winner Takes All (HWTA) strategy used in previous work. We test this approach in the context of computer vision. In particular, the HPCA rule is used to train Convolutional Neural Networks in order to extract relevant features from the CIFAR-10 image dataset. The HPCA variant that we explore further improves the previous results, motivating further interest towards biologically plausible learning algorithms.
</snippet>

# Scope and Definitions

In modern deep learning, “Hebbian” learning refers to local, biologically inspired synaptic update rules where synaptic strength increases when pre- and postsynaptic activity co-occur, encompassing classical Hebbian weight updates, anti-Hebbian plasticity, and spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) as a temporally precise Hebbian variant.<cite id="b9baae04-1">Hebbian learning refers to a family of learning rules inspired by biology, where the weight associated with a synapse increases proportionally to the values of pre- and postsynaptic stimuli; STDP is a Hebbian unsupervised rule where presynaptic spikes preceding postsynaptic spikes potentiate synapses</cite> In practice, Hebbian-style rules are often integrated with gradient-based methods (hybrid Hebb+backprop), or used to pre-train/lateralize layers within deep CNNs for image recognition.<cite id="b9baae04-0">Biologically plausible Hebbian learning can be integrated with backpropagation in deep CNNs, including using Hebbian rules to re-train higher layers of pre-trained networks with comparable accuracy and fewer epochs</cite>

# Hebbian-influenced CNNs for Image Recognition

Recent work shows that nonlinear Hebbian Principal Component Analysis (HPCA) improves CNN feature learning over simple Hebbian winner-takes-all (HWTA) when trained on CIFAR-10, suggesting that more sophisticated local Hebbian updates can better capture image structure than crude sparse coding heuristics.<cite id="b9baae04-0">Using a nonlinear Hebbian Principal Component Analysis rule in CNNs for CIFAR-10 feature extraction further improves previous Hebbian results over HWTA, motivating interest in biologically plausible learning</cite> Multi-layer Hebbian/anti-Hebbian networks trained for CIFAR-10 demonstrate online sparse feature learning, where increasing neurons/layers and appropriate receptive field sizes improve discriminability; they report competitive accuracy to other encoders and argue for overcomplete representations and sufficient unsupervised time to optimize Hebbian feature extraction.<cite id="b9baae04-3">A multi-layer Hebbian network on CIFAR-10 learns more discriminative sparse representations with increased neurons/layers, shows a minimum unsupervised learning time is needed, and achieves competitive accuracy versus other encoders, highlighting overcompleteness and receptive field choices as key factors</cite>

A compelling direction combines Hebbian competition with gradient learning: CNNs augmented with hard Winner-Takes-All (WTA) competition, Gaussian lateral inhibition, and Bienenstock–Cooper–Munro (BCM) Hebbian rules can match end-to-end backprop performance on CIFAR-10 (75.2% vs. 75.2%) while surpassing prior hard-WTA CNN SOTA by 10.6% at the same depth; these models also report competitive MNIST (≈98%) and STL-10 (≈69.5%) accuracy and exhibit sparse, hierarchical receptive field evolution.<cite id="b9baae04-4">A Hebbian CNN with WTA, lateral inhibition, and BCM achieved on CIFAR-10 mean accuracy matching its backprop counterpart (75.2%) and surpassing the state-of-the-art hard-WTA CNN (64.6%) by 10.6%, with competitive MNIST (98%) and STL-10 (69.5%) results and evidence of sparse hierarchical learning</cite> These results indicate that carefully designed Hebbian mechanisms can provide strong, biologically plausible feature learning with near backprop performance in CNNs, especially when combined with competition and lateral inhibition to stabilize training and promote sparsity.<cite id="b9baae04-4">Incorporating hard WTA competition, Gaussian lateral inhibition, and BCM in a single CNN yields representations that match backprop accuracy on CIFAR-10 and outperform prior hard-WTA Hebbian CNNs, with indications of sparse, hierarchical representations</cite>

# Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) and Hybrid ANN↔SNN Approaches

Spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP), a canonical Hebbian rule for spiking neurons, has been used to train convolutional SNNs (CSNNs) for image classification; SNNs often aim to reduce energy consumption while maintaining accuracy by leveraging event-driven dynamics and local plasticity.<cite id="95b19c65-2">STDP is a Hebbian unsupervised rule where synaptic weight changes depend on the relative timing of pre- and postsynaptic spikes; SNNs convert traditional DNNs to spiking networks and primarily target energy-efficient operation while preserving accuracy</cite> Unsupervised STDP-trained CSNNs have achieved around 84.7% accuracy on CIFAR-10, illustrating that purely Hebbian spike-based learning can reach competitive performance on natural image classification, albeit with more stringent design choices (e.g., leaky-integrate-and-fire neurons, multi-layer architectures) and typically without fully biologically plausible parameters.<cite id="95b19c65-4">A 3-layer bio-inspired CSNN trained with two-stage unsupervised STDP and ReSuMe reached 84.7% average accuracy on CIFAR-10, improving over 2-layer networks and using LIF neurons</cite><cite id="95b19c65-3">CSNNs commonly use multi-layer designs, LIF neurons, and unsupervised/supervised STDP variants; prior CSNN work dominated by MNIST, while newer hybrid ANN↔SNN works target CIFAR-10</cite>

Hybrid architectures that bridge analog ANN features and spiking layers further improve CIFAR-10 performance. Converting ResNet features into spiking rates via ANN↔SNN mapping reported ≈12.54% error on CIFAR-10, and a shortcut normalization mechanism to emulate firing rates achieved ≈92.85% accuracy, showing that hybrid Hebbian-style plasticity combined with strong base models can be highly effective, though bio-plausibility is reduced by non-biological parameters.<cite id="95b19c65-3">Hybrid ANN-to-SNN conversions, including ANN-to-SNN conversion claiming 12.54% CIFAR-10 error with ResNet backbones and a shortcut normalization mechanism achieving 92.85% CIFAR-10 accuracy by converting continuous activations to spiking rates, indicate strong performance but reduced bio-plausibility due to non-biological parameters</cite> Collectively, these results suggest SNN/STDP methods are competitive on CIFAR-10, particularly when combined with strong base models or carefully designed mappings, though broader ImageNet-scale evidence remains comparatively sparse in the retrieved corpus.

# Hebbian Learning as a Component or Pretraining Strategy

Hebbian learning is frequently used as a complementary or pretraining strategy within deep CNNs, especially for lower or higher layers, enabling transfer learning and reducing epochs needed to reach comparable SGD accuracy on image datasets like CIFAR-10.<cite id="b9baae04-0">Hebbian learning integrated with backprop in deep CNNs can re-train higher layers of pre-trained networks with comparable accuracy and fewer epochs, indicating potential for transfer learning</cite> Multi-layer Hebbian networks also serve as unsupervised or online feature extractors prior to linear classification, showing that local Hebbian plasticity can produce discriminative representations without full global backprop, with performance sensitive to overcompleteness and receptive field design.<cite id="b9baae04-3">A multi-layer Hebbian network trained on CIFAR-10 delivers competitive accuracy versus other encoders and emphasizes overcompleteness and receptive field size as key to improving classification</cite> In terms of biological plausibility, Hebbian/BCM+WTA variants explicitly aim to replace backprop with local, unsupervised plasticity augmented by competition, demonstrating parity with backprop-trained baselines on CIFAR-10 while offering interpretable sparse hierarchies.<cite id="b9baae04-4">A Hebbian CNN with WTA competition, lateral inhibition, and BCM matched backprop accuracy on CIFAR-10 and surpassed prior hard-WTA SOTA, with sparse hierarchical learning evidenced by evolving receptive fields</cite>

# Quantitative Landscape on Benchmarks

- CIFAR-10: Hebbian CNNs with competition and BCM achieve ≈75% test accuracy matching end-to-end backprop models; a CSNN trained with unsupervised STDP plus ReSuMe reaches ≈84.7%, and hybrid ANN↔SNN pipelines report ≈12.54% error (conversion with ResNet) and ≈92.85% (shortcut normalization + spiking residual network).<cite id="b9baae04-4">Hebbian CNN with WTA/BCM/lateral inhibition matched backprop at 75.2% on CIFAR-10 and exceeded prior hard-WTA SOTA by 10.6%</cite><cite id="95b19c65-4">A 3-layer CSNN with unsupervised STDP and ReSuMe achieved 84.7% on CIFAR-10</cite><cite id="95b19c65-3">Hybrid ANN↔SNN conversions reported ≈12.54% error with ResNet backbones and ≈92.85% with a shortcut normalization mechanism on CIFAR-10</cite>
- MNIST: Hebbian CNN variants report ≈98% accuracy and Hebbian multi-layer networks show competitive performance relative to deep encoders, supporting that Hebbian approaches generalize from simple to complex image data.<cite id="b9baae04-4">Hebbian CNN variants achieved competitive performance on MNIST including ≈98% accuracy</cite><cite id="b9baae04-3">Multi-layer Hebbian networks delivered competitive accuracy to other encoders on CIFAR-10 and are positioned as candidates for memristive devices</cite>
- STL-10: Hebbian CNNs with competition report ≈69.5% accuracy, indicating reasonable performance on small-object, viewpoint-challenged data relative to backprop baselines.<cite id="b9baae04-4">Hebbian CNNs with WTA/lateral inhibition/BCM achieved ≈69.5% on STL-10</cite>

# Limitations and Open Challenges

Training stability and representation quality with pure Hebbian rules require architectural aids such as competition (WTA), lateral inhibition, and BCM dynamics to prevent saturation and promote sparsity; these mechanisms are a key reason recent Hebbian CNNs approach backprop performance.<cite id="b9baae04-4">Incorporating hard WTA competition, Gaussian lateral inhibition, and BCM learning expands representational capabilities and stabilizes learning, contributing to parity with backprop on CIFAR-10</cite> For SNNs, unsupervised STDP can learn effective features but often demands careful design of neuron models (e.g., LIF), layer depth, and receptive fields, and typically operates on spike-based data streams, which can complicate dataset comparability and hybridization with standard benchmarks.<cite id="95b19c65-4">CSNNs commonly employ LIF neurons, multi-layer designs, and unsupervised/supervised STDP, with performance on CIFAR-10 showing the importance of architectural choices</cite><cite id="95b19c65-3">Many SNN studies emphasize MNIST; CIFAR-10 results are emerging, and hybrid approaches often reduce bio-plausibility by using non-biological parameters</cite> Hybrid ANN↔SNN pipelines improve accuracy by leveraging strong base models and rate-coding mappings but trade off biological plausibility and may not fully capture in vivo spike-timing mechanisms, indicating a research frontier in making such systems both efficient and biologically credible.<cite id="95b19c65-3">Hybrid architectures combining classical DNNs with SNNs achieve strong CIFAR-10 results, but often rely on non-biological parameters, reducing bio-plausibility</cite>

# Trends and Near-Term SOTA

The near-term SOTA pattern is hybrid and hierarchical: Hebbian mechanisms (including STDP) are used to shape sparse, hierarchical features within CNNs or as a pretraining/finetuning step, while gradient-based backprop optimizes the full network; this yields strong accuracy with fewer epochs and improved transfer learning.<cite id="b9baae04-0">Biologically plausible Hebbian learning integrated with backprop in deep CNNs can achieve comparable accuracy with fewer epochs and supports transfer learning</cite><cite id="b9baae04-4">Architectures combining WTA, lateral inhibition, and BCM in CNNs match backprop-trained counterparts on CIFAR-10</cite> In spiking vision, unsupervised STDP and hybrid ANN↔SNN conversions deliver competitive CIFAR-10 performance, with ongoing work targeting energy efficiency and deployment on neuromorphic hardware; however, broader ImageNet-scale evaluations and fully biological SNNs remain active research areas.<cite id="95b19c65-2">SNNs with STDP are designed for energy-efficient operation while maintaining accuracy in image tasks</cite><cite id="95b19c65-3">Hybrid ANN↔SNN approaches report strong CIFAR-10 results but often reduce bio-plausibility; ImageNet-scale evidence is less prevalent in current literature excerpts</cite>

# Practical Takeaways

- For image recognition, Hebbian-influenced CNNs with local competition and BCM-like updates can match backprop-trained counterparts on CIFAR-10 and reach competitive accuracy on MNIST and STL-10, indicating that well-designed Hebbian mechanisms can be a viable component or complement to standard training.<cite id="b9baae04-4">Hebbian CNNs matched backprop at 75.2% on CIFAR-10 and surpassed prior hard-WTA SOTA by 10.6%, with competitive MNIST and STL-10 results</cite>
- Spiking CSNNs trained with STDP can reach ≈84.7% on CIFAR-10, and hybrid ANN↔SNN pipelines can reach ≈12.54% error (with ResNet) or ≈92.85% accuracy using rate-mapping mechanisms, suggesting strong potential for energy-efficient recognition, especially when combined with strong base models.<cite id="95b19c65-4">STDP-trained CSNN achieved 84.7% on CIFAR-10</cite><cite id="95b19c65-3">Hybrid conversions reported ≈12.54% error and ≈92.85% accuracy on CIFAR-10</cite>
- Key design factors include overcompleteness and receptive field size in multi-layer Hebbian networks, competition and lateral inhibition to stabilize learning, and careful integration of Hebbian pretraining with backprop to reduce epochs and improve transfer.<cite id="b9baae04-3">Overcompleteness and receptive field size are critical in multi-layer Hebbian networks for CIFAR-10</cite><cite id="b9baae04-4">Competition and lateral inhibition with BCM enhance representational capabilities and learning stability</cite><cite id="b9baae04-0">Hebbian pretraining of higher layers can match SGD accuracy with fewer epochs and enable transfer learning</cite>

# Evidence Gaps and What Would Resolve Them

Title: Training Convolutional Neural Networks With Hebbian Principal Component Analysis
Snippet: Recent work has shown that biologically plausible Hebbian learning can be integrated with backpropagation learning (backprop), when training deep convolutional neural networks. In particular, it has been shown that Hebbian learning can be used for training the lower or the higher layers of a neural network. For instance, Hebbian learning is effective for re-training the higher layers of a pre-trained deep neural network, achieving comparable accuracy w.r.t. SGD, while requiring fewer training epochs, suggesting potential applications for transfer learning. In this paper we build on these results and we further improve Hebbian learning in these settings, by using a nonlinear Hebbian Principal Component Analysis (HPCA) learning rule, in place of the Hebbian Winner Takes All (HWTA) strategy used in previous work. We test this approach in the context of computer vision. In particular, the HPCA rule is used to train Convolutional Neural Networks in order to extract relevant features from the CIFAR-10 image dataset. The HPCA variant that we explore further improves the previous results, motivating further interest towards biologically plausible learning algorithms.

Title: Neuromodulated Dopamine Plastic Networks for Heterogeneous Transfer Learning with Hebbian Principle
Snippet: In this work, we explore Hebbian learning rules in the context of modern deep neural networks for image classification. Contemporary deep learning models have achieved high accuracy in image segmenting [14,15]. The latest optimization techniques like gradient descent are very effective [16][17][18], and various neural network models such as AlexNet and VGGNet have been successfully applied for object recognition and image classification tasks [19][20][21][22][23]. In these models, overfitting is an issue that troubles the researchers during in-depth learning algorithms training with insufficiently labeled images [24]. Without proper care, CNN's performance decreases with datasets that are small in size. Methods like parameter finetuning and image augmentation have shown significant success in overcoming overfitting and produce robust results [25]. However, these pre-trained networks lead to poor performance in scenarios with a lack of labeled data in the target domain. Such a primary problem is a learning technique focused on consolidating learned knowledge and reducing development costs in the target domain. 

Biology says that the SGD optimization process works differently than the human brain's fundamental processes [26]. Researchers have studied the plastic nature of neuronal responses [27]-Hebb's law named after the individual who posited it, Canadian psychologist Donald Hebb (1949). Hebb's rule forms substantial connection weights and a better connection path from input to output of the neural network that if a synapse between two neurons is repeatedly activated simultaneously, the postsynaptic neuron fires, the structure or chemistry of neurons changes, and the synapse will be strengthened-this is known as Hebbian learning [28]. Implementing plastic networks using a mathematical form of Hebb's law is demonstrated successfully [29].

Title: Online Representation Learning with Multi-layer Hebbian Networks for Image Classification Tasks
Snippet: This work proposes a multi-layer neural network exploiting a set of Hebbian/anti-Hebbian rules to learn features for image classification. The network is trained on the CIFAR-10 image dataset prior to feeding a linear classifier. The model successfully learns online more discriminative sparse representations of the data when the number of neurons and the number of layers increase. We observed in this work that the overcompleteness of the representation is critical for learning relevant features. We have also shown that a minimum unsupervised learning time is needed to optimise the Hebbian network for sparse feature extraction. Finally, one key factor in improving image classification is the appropriate choice of the receptive field size used for training the network. 

Such findings prove that neural networks can be trained to solve problems as complex as sparse dictionary learning with Hebbian learning rules, delivering competitive accuracy compared to other encoder, including deep neural networks. This makes deep Hebbian networks attractive for building large-scale image classification systems. While showing competitive performances on the CIFAR-10, the network can offer an alternative to batch trained neural networks. Ultimately, thanks to its bio-inspired architecture and learning rules, it also stands as a good candidate for memristive devices [20]. Moreover, if a "decaying" factor is added to the proposed model that might result in an algorithm that can deal with complex datasets with temporal variations of the distributions.

Title: Advancing the Biological Plausibility and Efficacy of Hebbian Convolutional Neural Networks
Snippet: The research presented in this paper advances the integration of Hebbian learning into Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) for image processing, systematically exploring different architectures to build an optimal configuration, adhering to biological tenability. Hebbian learning operates on local unsupervised neural information to form feature representations, providing an alternative to the popular but arguably biologically implausible and computationally intensive backpropagation learning algorithm. The suggested optimal architecture significantly enhances recent research aimed at integrating Hebbian learning with competition mechanisms and CNNs, expanding their representational capabilities by incorporating hard Winner-Takes-All (WTA) competition, Gaussian lateral inhibition mechanisms and Bienenstock-Cooper-Munro (BCM) learning rule in a single model. Mean accuracy classification measures during the last half of test epochs on CIFAR-10 revealed that the resulting optimal model matched its end-to-end backpropagation variant with 75.2% each, critically surpassing the state-of-the-art hard-WTA performance in CNNs of the same network depth (64.6%) by 10.6%. It also achieved competitive performance on MNIST (98%) and STL-10 (69.5%). Moreover, results showed clear indications of sparse hierarchical learning through increasingly complex and abstract receptive fields. In summary, our implementation enhances both the performance and the generalisability of the learnt representations and constitutes a crucial step towards more biologically realistic artificial neural networks.

Title: A Fully Spiking Hybrid Neural Network for Energy-Efficient Object Detection
Snippet: Spike Timing Dependent Plasticity (STDP) [20] is a variant of the Hebbian unsupervised learning algorithm. STDP describes the changes of a synaptic weight according to the relative timing of pre and post-synaptic spikes. In STDP, if a presynaptic spike precedes a post-synaptic one, a synaptic weight is potentiated. 

There are various spiking neural networks (SNNs) to solve object recognition and image classification tasks by converting the traditional DNNs into spiking networks by replacing each DNN computing unit with a spiking neuron [21]. Kheradpisheh et al. proposed a STDP based spiking deep convolutional neural network for object recognition [22]. Wu et al. similarly proposed a spatio-temporal backpropagation for training Spiking Neural Networks [23]. This type of spiking neural networks primarily aim to reduce the energy consumption in DNNs while achieving a similar accuracy.

Title: NatCSNN: A Convolutional Spiking Neural Network for Recognition of Objects Extracted from Natural Images
Snippet: The SpiCNN was trained using unsupervised STDP with an accuracy of 91.1% on the MNIST dataset. 

Relevant literature on CSNNs [6,10,12,19,20] for image processing have in common: (i) multiple-layer CSNNs, (ii) use of the Leaky-integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron model, (iii) use of unsupervised/supervised STDP (or an STDP adaptation) for training and (iv) all of the relevant work was tested on the MNIST hand-written black-and-white dataset. 

The MNIST dataset is one of the commonly used benchmark datasets, composed only of simple black-and-white images (containing hand-written numbers from 0 to 9). In contrast, the CIFAR-10 [8] dataset is composed of 50,000 coloured natural images with natural backgrounds and thus represents a sigificantly more challenging test for image processing algorithms. 

More recent works, Sengupta et al. [16] and Hu et al. [4] have proposed hybrid architectures by combining classical deep learning architectures with spiking neural networks. Sengupta et al. [16] proposed an ANN to SNN conversion technique that is claimed to outperform state-of-the-art techniques, reporting an 12.54% error on the CIFAR-10 dataset when combined with Residual network architectures. Hu et al. [4], proposed a shortcut normalisation mechanism to convert continued-valued activation's to match firing rates in SNN; Their proposed architecture receives the continued-valued activation's from a Residual Network and converts them into spiking rates which are fed into a spiking residual network architecture. Their experiemnts achieved an accuracy of 92.85% when tested on the CIFAR-10 dataset. Despite the accuracy obtained on the CIFAR-10 using these hybrid architectures, the proposed architectures are all composed of several layers and none of the architectures uses biological spiking neuron parameters, reducing therefore the bio-plausibility of the proposed architectures. 

Other work published on the CIFAR-10 has utilised classical deep neural networks.

Title: NatCSNN: A Convolutional Spiking Neural Network for Recognition of Objects Extracted from Natural Images
Snippet: Biological image processing is performed by complex neural networks composed of thousands of neurons interconnected via thousands of synapses, some of which are excitatory and others inhibitory. Spiking neural models are distinguished from classical neurons by being biological plausible and exhibiting the same dynamics as those observed in biological neurons. This paper proposes a Natural Convolutional Neural Network (NatCSNN) which is a 3-layer bio-inspired Convolutional Spiking Neural Network (CSNN), for classifying objects extracted from natural images. A two-stage training algorithm is proposed using unsupervised Spike Timing Dependent Plasticity (STDP) learning (phase 1) and ReSuMe supervised learning (phase 2). The NatCSNN was trained and tested on the CIFAR-10 dataset and achieved an average testing accuracy of 84.7% which is an improvement over the 2-layer neural networks previously applied to this dataset.

More recent works, Sengupta et al. [16] and Hu et al. [4] have proposed hybrid architectures by combining classical deep learning architectures with spiking neural networks. Sengupta et al. [16] proposed an ANN to SNN conversion technique that is claimed to outperform state-of-the-art techniques, reporting an 12.54% error on the CIFAR-10 dataset when combined with Residual network architectures. Hu et al. [4], proposed a shortcut normalisation mechanism to convert continued-valued activation's to match firing rates in SNN; Their proposed architecture receives the continued-valued activation's from a Residual Network and converts them into spiking rates which are fed into a spiking residual network architecture. Their experiemnts achieved an accuracy of 92.85% when tested on the CIFAR-10 dataset. Despite the accuracy obtained on the CIFAR-10 using these hybrid architectures, the proposed architectures are all composed of several layers and none of the architectures uses biological spiking neuron parameters, reducing therefore the bio-plausibility of the proposed architectures. 

Other work published on the CIFAR-10 has utilised classical deep neural networks.

documents.title: NatCSNN: A Convolutional Spiking Neural Network for Recognition of Objects Extracted from Natural Images
documents.snippet: Biological image processing is performed by complex neural networks composed of thousands of neurons interconnected via thousands of synapses, some of which are excitatory and others inhibitory. Spiking neural models are distinguished from classical neurons by being biological plausible and exhibiting the same dynamics as those observed in biological neurons. This paper proposes a Natural Convolutional Neural Network (NatCSNN) which is a 3-layer bio-inspired Convolutional Spiking Neural Network (CSNN), for classifying objects extracted from natural images. A two-stage training algorithm is proposed using unsupervised Spike Timing Dependent Plasticity (STDP) learning (phase 1) and ReSuMe supervised learning (phase 2). The NatCSNN was trained and tested on the CIFAR-10 dataset and achieved an average testing accuracy of 84.7% which is an improvement over the 2-layer neural networks previously applied to this dataset.

Title: Training Convolutional Neural Networks With Hebbian Principal Component Analysis
Snippet: Recent work has shown that biologically plausible Hebbian learning can be integrated with backpropagation learning (backprop), when training deep convolutional neural networks. In particular, it has been shown that Hebbian learning can be used for training the lower or the higher layers of a neural network. For instance, Hebbian learning is effective for re-training the higher layers of a pre-trained deep neural network, achieving comparable accuracy w.r.t. SGD, while requiring fewer training epochs, suggesting potential applications for transfer learning. In this paper we build on these results and we further improve Hebbian learning in these settings, by using a nonlinear Hebbian Principal Component Analysis (HPCA) learning rule, in place of the Hebbian Winner Takes All (HWTA) strategy used in previous work. We test this approach in the context of computer vision. In particular, the HPCA rule is used to train Convolutional Neural Networks in order to extract relevant features from the CIFAR-10 image dataset. The HPCA variant that we explore further improves the previous results, motivating further interest towards biologically plausible learning algorithms.

Title: Online Representation Learning with Multi-layer Hebbian Networks for Image Classification Tasks
Snippet: This work proposes a multi-layer neural network exploiting a set of Hebbian/anti-Hebbian rules to learn features for image classification. The network is trained on the CIFAR-10 image dataset prior to feeding a linear classifier. The model successfully learns online more discriminative sparse representations of the data when the number of neurons and the number of layers increase. We observed in this work that the overcompleteness of the representation is critical for learning relevant features. We have also shown that a minimum unsupervised learning time is needed to optimise the Hebbian network for sparse feature extraction. Finally, one key factor in improving image classification is the appropriate choice of the receptive field size used for training the network. 

Such findings prove that neural networks can be trained to solve problems as complex as sparse dictionary learning with Hebbian learning rules, delivering competitive accuracy compared to other encoder, including deep neural networks. This makes deep Hebbian networks attractive for building large-scale image classification systems. While showing competitive performances on the CIFAR-10, the network can offer an alternative to batch trained neural networks. Ultimately, thanks to its bio-inspired architecture and learning rules, it also stands as a good candidate for memristive devices [20]. Moreover, if a "decaying" factor is added to the proposed model that might result in an algorithm that can deal with complex datasets with temporal variations of the distributions.

Title: Advancing the Biological Plausibility and Efficacy of Hebbian Convolutional Neural Networks
Snippet: The research presented in this paper advances the integration of Hebbian learning into Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) for image processing, systematically exploring different architectures to build an optimal configuration, adhering to biological tenability. Hebbian learning operates on local unsupervised neural information to form feature representations, providing an alternative to the popular but arguably biologically implausible and computationally intensive backpropagation learning algorithm. The suggested optimal architecture significantly enhances recent research aimed at integrating Hebbian learning with competition mechanisms and CNNs, expanding their representational capabilities by incorporating hard Winner-Takes-All (WTA) competition, Gaussian lateral inhibition mechanisms and Bienenstock-Cooper-Munro (BCM) learning rule in a single model. Mean accuracy classification measures during the last half of test epochs on CIFAR-10 revealed that the resulting optimal model matched its end-to-end backpropagation variant with 75.2% each, critically surpassing the state-of-the-art hard-WTA performance in CNNs of the same network depth (64.6%) by 10.6%. It also achieved competitive performance on MNIST (98%) and STL-10 (69.5%). Moreover, results showed clear indications of sparse hierarchical learning through increasingly complex and abstract receptive fields. In summary, our implementation enhances both the performance and the generalisability of the learnt representations and constitutes a crucial step towards more biologically realistic artificial neural networks.

problem: how are most neutral atom 2 qubit gates performed?
final_response:
# Short answer

Most neutral-atom two‑qubit gates today are implemented using state‑selective optical interactions between Rydberg atoms, exploiting the Rydberg blockade to conditionally excite neighboring atoms and accumulate a two‑qubit phase (typically a controlled‑phase/CZ), with gate operations performed via Raman or Brillouin transitions and engineered in either adiabatic or transitionless driving schemes.<cite id="ba556e51-0">Rydberg blockade serves as the backbone for two‑qubit controlled‑phase gates in neutral‑atom arrays, and recent work focuses on improving gate performance toward NISQ‑level operation</cite><cite id="ba556e51-1">Rydberg‑atom arrays in optical tweezers enable controlled‑Z gates with fidelities approaching 0.994–0.995, though challenges remain due to Rydberg decay and finite blockade</cite><cite id="ba556e51-2">Two‑qubit blockaded gates operate on microsecond timescales using strong, long‑range Rydberg–Rydberg interactions, but face intrinsic blockade errors scaling as (Ω/V)^2</cite><cite id="ba556e51-3">Transitionless quantum driving of a Rydberg‑blockade CZ gate can reach simulated fidelities of 0.9985 in 0.12 μs, outperforming standard adiabatic driving</cite><cite id="ba556e51-4">Time‑optimal Rydberg‑gate analyses and experiments report entangling‑gate fidelities up to 99.1%, with errors dominated by finite blockade, Rydberg decay, and technical noise</cite>. Alternative two‑qubit mechanisms—phonon‑mediated Mølmer–Sørensen gates in tweezers/lattices and state‑tunable tunnel coupling via adiabatic passage/dark‑state resonances—are active areas of research but are less commonly demonstrated at comparable fidelities so far.<cite id="ef843cb1-1">Phonon‑mediated spin–spin interactions in tweezers can replicate ion‑trap Mølmer–Sørensen entanglement schemes using Rydberg dressing, with trap quality as the main limiting factor</cite><cite id="2aa3e301-2">Controlled‑Z and CNOT gates via double adiabatic passage through Stark‑tuned Förster resonances in Rydberg atoms have been proposed, leveraging dark‑state resonances for high‑fidelity phase accumulation</cite>.

# How Rydberg‑blockade two‑qubit gates work

Rydberg‑blockade two‑qubit gates encode qubits in long‑lived hyperfine ground states and use state‑selective optical addressing to first prepare one atom in a high‑principal‑quantum‑number Rydberg state; the strong, state‑dependent dipole–dipole interactions shift the Rydberg frequency of a neighboring atom out of resonance (blockade), so that a conditional phase is accumulated only when the pair is in the entangling manifold.<cite id="ba556e51-4">Fast two‑qubit gates are achieved by mediating interactions with Rydberg states; in the original scheme, one excited atom shifts the Rydberg states of neighbors out of resonance via strong Rydberg–Rydberg interactions (blockade), enabling k‑qubit gates</cite><cite id="ba556e51-2">Strong, long‑range interactions enable conditional excitations to Rydberg states (blockade), operating on μs timescales and avoiding precise control of interaction strength so long as multiple excitations are precluded</cite>. The actual two‑qubit operation is commonly realized with off‑resonant Raman or Brillouin transitions that couple the Rydberg‑addressed pair through a common optical mode, implementing a conditional π phase (CZ) with carefully shaped pulses and state‑selective optical depths.<cite id="ba556e51-0">Two‑qubit controlled‑phase gates rely on Rydberg blockade, with experimental progress driven by array scaling, state preparation and measurement, and mitigation of technical and intrinsic disturbances</cite><cite id="ba556e51-1">Neutral‑atom two‑qubit gates in tweezers have reached CZ fidelities above 0.993–0.995, approaching limits set by Rydberg decay and finite blockade</cite>.

Two main pulse‑engineeering strategies are used. In adiabatic schemes, the interaction is ramped slowly through resonance to accumulate the desired phase while avoiding nonadiabatic transitions; echo‑based and multi‑pulse variations improve robustness to noise and decoherence.<cite id="ba556e51-2">Adiabatic evolution is commonly employed with Rydberg atoms, but longer evolution times increase decoherence noise</cite><cite id="ba556e51-1">An echoing rapid adiabatic‑passage (RAP) scheme with two identical global pulses in the blockade regime achieves a CZ with fidelity >0.9995 in simulations</cite>. Transitionless quantum driving (TQD) and related techniques use broadband, carefully engineered driving to eliminate geometric/transition‑time singularities, yielding faster, more robust gates under realistic noise and decay.<cite id="ba556e51-3">Simultaneous transitionless quantum driving of a Rydberg‑blockade CZ gate yields 0.9985 fidelity in 0.12 μs, surpassing adiabatic baselines and state‑of‑the‑art experimental results in the cited work</cite>. Typical error sources include spontaneous emission from Rydberg levels, finite blockade shifts, Doppler and laser phase/amplitude fluctuations, and residual thermal motion; mitigations include cooling, optical depth control, pulse shaping, and echo sequences.<cite id="ba556e51-0">Technical disturbances (laser phase noise, amplitude fluctuations, state preparation/measurement errors, spatial offsets) and intrinsic limits (spontaneous emission, finite blockade shift, residual thermal motion) limit two‑qubit gate fidelity</cite><cite id="ba556e51-4">Finite blockade strength, Rydberg decay, two‑photon intermediate‑state scattering, and laser phase noise are key error channels for Rydberg entangling gates</cite>.

# Motional/phonon‑mediated Mølmer–Sørensen gates

An alternative entangling route couples qubits via quantized motional modes (phonons) in an optical lattice or tweezers, analogous to trapped‑ion MS gates. In practice, this is implemented by laser coupling ground‑state qubits to Rydberg states to couple to collective motional modes (sidebands), then driving the qubits through a geometric phase in the dressed‑interaction frame to create entanglement mediated by the shared phonon.<cite id="ef843cb1-2">By laser coupling atoms to Rydberg states, collective motional modes appear and can mediate effective spin–spin interactions, replicating ion‑trap Mølmer–Sørensen schemes</cite><cite id="ef843cb1-1">Rydberg dressing induces the needed interactions to realize MS‑style gates between tweezers‑trapped atoms, with trap quality as the dominant error source</cite>. Recent theoretical work suggests high‑fidelity coherent two‑atom evolution even at nonzero temperature, with errors scaling with Lamb–Dicke factors and trap frequencies; careful selection of modulation detunings and Rabi couplings suppresses spurious resonances with other modes.<cite id="ef843cb1-0">Modulating tweezers at sums of trap mode frequencies can implement σx⊗σx interactions; numerical simulations show robustness to thermal occupations and sub‑Hz unwanted interactions when parameters are chosen carefully</cite><cite id="ef843cb1-2">Arbitrarily high fidelity for coherent two‑atom evolution is predicted in the MS scheme when using Rydberg dressing and accounting for Lamb–Dicke and blackbody limits</cite>. While the concept is mature in theory and shares the high‑fidelity DNA of trapped‑ion MS gates, experimental neutral‑atom MS two‑qubit demonstrations with precise, reproducible fidelities are still less common than Rydberg‑blockade gates in today’s platforms.<cite id="ef843cb1-4">MS gates are widely used in trapped‑ion systems at very high fidelity and have been proposed for neutral atoms via Rydberg dressing, motivating their experimental porting to tweezers/lattices</cite>.

# State‑tunable tunnel coupling and adiabatic passage/dark‑state gates

A third modality uses controlled interatomic tunnel coupling or state‑dependent optical transitions to generate a two‑qubit phase by engineering the Stark‑tuned Förster (exchange) resonances or dark‑state structures. In Rydberg tweezers, carefully detuned laser fields can create Stark‑tuned Förster resonances whose double adiabatic passage accumulates a deterministic phase, enabling CZ/CNOT with high fidelity estimates; dark‑state resonances can further suppress spontaneous emission during the interaction.<cite id="2aa3e301-2">Controlled‑Z and CNOT gates can be realized via double adiabatic passage of Stark‑tuned Förster resonances in Rydberg atoms, using nonlinearly chirped pulses to achieve high‑fidelity population transfer and phase accumulation</cite><cite id="2aa3e301-3">Using Rydberg coupling and dark‑state resonances in tweezers, multi‑qubit controlled operations (e.g., Toffoli) can be implemented with estimated fidelities around 96% for realistic parameters</cite>. These approaches offer alternative robustness profiles: by operating through dark states or motional channels, they can reduce direct Rydberg decay errors, but often require precise control over Stark shifts, pulse timing, and spatial overlap to maintain blockade while avoiding off‑resonant losses.<cite id="2aa3e301-2">Nonlinear time dependence of detuning from Förster resonances is used to achieve high‑fidelity transfer; the fidelity analysis is demonstrated on a Cs example</cite><cite id="2aa3e301-3">Dark‑state resonances and individual addressing of control/target qubits suppress undesirable transitions and enable high‑fidelity multi‑qubit controlled operations</cite>.

# What “most” means in practice and current performance

In contemporary neutral‑atom hardware, Rydberg‑blockade CZ/controlled‑phase gates are the predominant entangling primitive because they leverage mature state‑selective optical techniques, strong and tunable long‑range interactions, and flexible tweezer/lattice geometries for nearest‑neighbor connectivity and reconfigurable arrays.<cite id="ba556e51-0">Rydberg blockade underpins controlled‑phase gates in arrays, with rapid progress in qubit counts and gate performance</cite><cite id="ba556e51-4">Encoding qubits in ground states with Rydberg‑mediated interactions in tweezers/lattices enables fast two‑qubit gates via blockade mechanisms</cite>. Reported two‑qubit entangling fidelities in leading experiments and systems range roughly from 0.98 to 0.996, with state‑of‑the‑art tweezer‑clock systems achieving CZ ≈0.9962 and community roadmaps pointing to QEC‑driven targets near 0.9999 as the long‑term goal.<cite id="2aa3e301-1">High‑fidelity entangling gates for optical‑clock qubits in a tweezer array achieved CZ fidelity 0.9962(3), with record‑fidelity Bell pairs and ancilla‑based readout</cite><cite id="ba556e51-1">Recent demonstrations include CZ fidelities up to 0.994–0.995 in Rydberg tweezers, approaching limits set by Rydberg decay</cite><cite id="ba556e51-4">Analyses emphasize that finite blockade, Rydberg lifetime, and technical noise currently bound two‑qubit gate fidelity to ~99.1% in experiments</cite><cite id="b10c99be-4">Perspectives argue scalable neutral‑atom computing will require two‑qubit fidelities ~0.9999, motivating aggressive error‑mitigation for present Rydberg‑blockade approaches</cite>.

Mølmer–Sørensen and tunnel‑coupling/APS gates offer complementary error profiles (e.g., trading Rydberg decay for motional heating or Stark‑tuning sensitivity) and are actively explored, but they are less commonly used than Rydberg blockade for routine two‑qubit gates at comparable fidelities today; their main appeal is the potential for improved robustness and compatibility with specific architectures and connectivity graphs as the field matures.<cite id="ef843cb1-1">Phonon‑mediated MS gates via Rydberg dressing are proposed for tweezers with the prospect of high fidelity, limited mainly by trap quality and not intrinsic to the dressed‑Rydberg scheme</cite><cite id="2aa3e301-3">State‑tuned tunnel coupling and dark‑state resonances enable controlled multi‑qubit gates with estimated fidelities in the high‑80s to near‑90s for three‑qubit Toffoli in realistic Cs parameters</cite>. 

# Bottom line

- Most neutral‑atom two‑qubit gates are performed with Rydberg‑blockade–mediated CZ/controlled‑phase operations using state‑selective optical pulses (Raman/Brillouin) and engineered in adiabatic or transitionless driving schemes, achieving ~0.991–0.996 fidelities with active mitigation of Rydberg decay, finite blockade, and technical noise.<cite id="ba556e51-1">Rydberg CZ fidelities have reached 0.993–0.995 in tweezers</cite><cite id="ba556e51-3">Transitionless driving of Rydberg‑blockade CZ gates can reach ~0.9985 in simulations</cite><cite id="ba556e51-0">Key error channels and mitigation strategies are well characterized for Rydberg entangling gates</cite>.
- Alternative entangling mechanisms—phonon‑mediated Mølmer–Sørensen gates in tweezers/lattices and state‑tunable tunnel coupling via adiabatic passage/dark‑state resonances—are promising and increasingly studied, but are not yet as broadly demonstrated at the same scale and fidelity as Rydberg blockade in current platforms.<cite id="ef843cb1-2">Rydberg‑dressed phonon MS gates can replicate ion‑trap schemes with predicted high fidelity</cite><cite id="2aa3e301-2">Förster resonance adiabatic passage and dark‑state methods offer alternative controlled‑phase implementations in Rydberg tweezers</cite>.
- Near‑term scalability will depend on pushing two‑qubit fidelities toward and beyond QEC thresholds, with Rydberg‑blockade arrays leading today’s efforts in qubit count, reconfigurability, and gate speed, while MS/tunneling approaches provide architectural diversity and potential robustness trade‑offs for future systems.<cite id="ba556e51-4">Two‑qubit entangling gate performance is a central driver, with current experiments at ~99.1% and analyses identifying dominant error sources</cite><cite id="b10c99be-3">A two‑qubit gate fidelity near 0.9999 is a practical threshold for scalable neutral‑atom QC under realistic codes</cite>.
