problem: can you write a short literature review on the use of artifical intelligence for planning in mass customization manufacturing companies
final_response:
# Scope and Definitions

Mass customization (MC) blends the variety of made-to-order with the cost and throughput targets of mass production, shifting manufacturers toward low-volume, high-mix (LVHM) production to meet individualized customer demands while maintaining competitive pricing and lead times.<cite id="e79ae94f-0">Mass customization challenges supply chains by adapting mass production approaches to high-variety, low-volume production, combining scale-like efficiency with customization flexibility</cite><cite id="e79ae94f-4">Mass customization necessitates a low-volume, high-variety model that produces a broad array of tailor-made products in smaller quantities, transitioning from high-volume, low-variety manufacturing</cite>. This transition increases scheduling and planning complexity due to shorter product life cycles, variable volumes across product families, and the need to integrate small, bespoke orders with platform-based products without undermining overall efficiency.<cite id="e79ae94f-2">Mass customization demand features great variety, shorter product life cycles, and variable volumes; it adds complexity to assembly representation, sequencing, and mixed-model scheduling, requiring holistic approaches</cite><cite id="e79ae94f-3">Managing new product introductions and small customer orders alongside high-volume production is difficult; conventional optimization can be computationally demanding in LVHM environments</cite>.

# Planning Challenges in Mass Customization

Planning in MC must coordinate production reconfiguration, order acceptance, job allocation, and real-time rescheduling under uncertainty (e.g., machine breakdowns, variable processing times, rush orders), while respecting resource, skill, and customer due date constraints.<cite id="649c53e7-0">Single-piece flow and mass customization increase variability (e.g., machining times) and introduce unplanned perturbations like breakdowns and illnesses that trigger replanning; digital twins are proposed to enable fast optimization loops to meet constraints and lead-time targets</cite>. Assembly-focused MC planning adds challenges in reconfigurable line design, delayed differentiation, mixed-model sequencing, and operator integration to maintain throughput and quality under high variety.<cite id="e79ae94f-2">Key assembly planning topics for MC include reconfigurable assembly planning, mixed-model scheduling, and adapting human operator roles amid increased complexity</cite>. At the enterprise level, integrating master production schedules with detailed workforce and resource schedules remains underexplored, and companies struggle to operationalize AI planning due to data readiness and expertise gaps.<cite id="2b6a6117-3">There is a gap in linking the master schedule to detailed planning; reviews show few AI implementations in industrial scheduling and highlight data, expertise, and complexity as main challenges for deploying AI planners</cite>.

# AI Techniques for Planning in Mass Customization

## Reinforcement Learning and Multi-Agent RL

Dynamic scheduling in MC is naturally modeled as a multi-objective, partially observable Markov decision process; RL and multi-agent RL (MARL) learn policies that handle random arrivals, processing-time variability, breakdowns, and conflicting objectives without retraining on every change.<cite id="7ddaeac1-1">Production scheduling is NP-hard and traditionally offline; disturbances from internal and external factors invalidate initial plans, motivating online, robust scheduling; RL-based approaches use composite reward functions to adapt to changes in smart factories</cite><cite id="7ddaeac1-4">Dynamic scheduling under mass personalization requires near-optimal machine and job allocation; MARL has been used for random job arrivals, stochastic processing times, and setup-time randomness, including dueling architectures to prevent conflicting operations and minimize makespan</cite>. Emerging systems combine requirement interpretation with RL-based dispatching: natural-language requirement analysis via LLMs weights KPIs, guiding DRL schedulers that improve productivity and cost metrics compared to baselines in software-defined factories.<cite id="7ddaeac1-2">A federated digital twin with a large language model and deep RL achieved up to 14.9% cost reduction and 13.4% productivity gains versus flow- and job-shop baselines by aligning requirements to KPIs and optimizing job–machine selection in a software-defined factory</cite>.

## Digital Twins for LVHM and Single-Piece Flow

Digital twins mirror physical production dynamics to enable real-time optimization, disruption management, and integrated planning across orders and factory operations under high variability.<cite id="649c53e7-0">Digital twins synchronize physical and virtual systems to run fast optimization and analysis loops; case studies show potential to increase certainty in planning, minimize costs, and meet lead-time constraints in single-piece and mass-customizing environments while supporting individual orders and factory-level production</cite><cite id="649c53e7-3">Digital twins support intelligent workshop scheduling, resource allocation, and active rescheduling via real-time data, and can integrate with MILP models to realize flexible scheduling under internal and external events</cite>. Practical implementations report substantial reductions in order cycle times for small, customized jobs by optimizing job allocation and scheduling with an intelligent simulation-based optimization model within the digital twin framework.<cite id="649c53e7-4">A digital twin-based production optimization system (DTPOS) with intelligent simulation optimization reduced average processing time for small orders from 19 days to 9.59 days (52.63%), indicating timely delivery and improved LVHM scheduling for mass personalization</cite>.

## Constraint Programming, Metaheuristics, and Hybrid Approaches

Beyond RL, heuristic and metaheuristic methods (e.g., genetic algorithms, ant colonies) provide near-optimal schedules but require retraining when settings change, which can halt processes; hybrid human–AI and simulation-optimization approaches mitigate this by retaining policy knowledge and enabling agile adjustments.<cite id="7ddaeac1-4">Heuristics are fast but not suitable across many settings; metaheuristics can find near-optimal schedules but need policy retention or retraining if settings change, risking process halts; RL/MARL offer learning policies that adapt to dynamic changes</cite>. AI-driven customized manufacturing emphasizes multi-agent cooperation, autonomous reconfiguration, and self-organizing scheduling on flexible lines to cope with product variety and dynamic order intake.<cite id="2b6a6117-2">AI-driven strategies such as collective and autonomous intelligence, cross-media reasoning, and multi-agent cooperation enable dynamic reconfiguration and self-organizing scheduling for flexible manufacturing in customized production</cite>.

## Human-in-the-Loop and Integrated Planning

Effective MC planning requires deciding the scope of AI decision-making and how it complements human planners, especially when integrating master schedules with workforce and resource planning; success factors include data availability, real-time usability, and safety in implementation.<cite id="2b6a6117-3">When using AI for planning, firms must determine decision levels and human–AI roles; challenges include data gathering, expertise, and complexity; success factors are real-time usability, user-friendliness, and safety, and only 11 of 37 reviewed AI mentions included implementations</cite>. Sectoral applications in fashion show AI aiding design personalization and production-side scheduling and resource allocation to reduce idle time and adapt to changing orders in real time.<cite id="2b6a6117-4">AI algorithms generate consumer options and predict preferences in design, and optimize production scheduling and resource allocation to reduce idle time and adapt to changing order demands in personalized customization</cite>.

# Case Studies and Quantitative Evidence

- Digital twin + intelligent simulation optimization (DTPOS) in a PCBA SMT line: 52.63% reduction in processing time for small orders and timely delivery performance under LVHM conditions, demonstrating that digital twins can integrate order-level and factory-level planning to meet MC constraints.<cite id="649c53e7-4">A digital twin-based DTPOS reduced average order processing time from 19 days to 9.59 days (52.63%) and achieved timely completion for small orders in a PCBA SMT setting</cite>.
- Federated digital twin with LLM + DRL in a software-defined factory: requirement-aware scheduling improved cost and productivity by up to 14.9% and 13.4% over flow- and job-shop baselines, indicating AI’s ability to weight KPIs and optimize under diverse user needs in MC contexts.<cite id="7ddaeac1-2">The literacy DRL scheduling outperformed flow-shop and job-shop baselines by up to 14.9% (cost) and 13.4% (productivity), showing requirement-driven scheduling benefits</cite>.
- MARL for dynamic job shop/flow shop settings: MARL policies address random job arrivals, stochastic processing times, and breakdowns, reducing conflicts and makespan relative to rule-based dispatching and static heuristics in dynamic MC-like environments.<cite id="7ddaeac1-4">MARL approaches have been applied to random arrivals, processing-time variability, and setup-time randomness, with cooperation mechanisms to prevent conflicts and minimize makespan</cite>.
- Digital twin-enabled planning under single-piece and mass customization: case studies show digital twins can raise planning certainty, manage unplanned events, and integrate with MES to meet cost and lead-time targets in highly variable settings.<cite id="649c53e7-0">Digital twins provide higher certainty in planning under single-piece and mass customizing by synchronizing physical and virtual systems for fast optimization and rescheduling within daily plans</cite><cite id="649c53e7-3">Digital twins enable real-time active workshop scheduling and MILP-based flexible scheduling under internal and external events</cite>.

# Benefits and Limitations

Benefits include improved responsiveness to dynamic orders, reduced idle time and costs, better multi-objective trade-offs, and integration of natural-language requirements with quantitative scheduling goals via LLMs and DRL; digital twins enable real-time data-driven rescheduling and disruption management across LVHM environments.<cite id="7ddaeac1-1">RL-based online scheduling with composite rewards improves robustness to disturbances and supports multi-objective performance in smart factories</cite><cite id="7ddaeac1-2">LLM-guided DRL aligns requirement KPIs and optimizes job–machine selection, outperforming baselines on cost and productivity</cite><cite id="649c53e7-3">Digital twins support real-time active scheduling and flexible planning under disruptions</cite>. Reported case studies show double-digit percentage improvements in certain metrics, indicating tangible gains for MC planning.<cite id="649c53e7-4">A 52.63% reduction in processing time for small orders and timely delivery demonstrate practical benefits of DTPOS</cite>.

Limitations and open challenges include data readiness and skilled expertise barriers to AI deployment, the need for robust multi-criteria reward engineering in RL, retraining and stability issues for metaheuristics when shop-floor settings change, and the underexplored integration of master production scheduling with detailed, AI-driven planning at scale.<cite id="2b6a6117-3">Reviews highlight data gathering, expertise, and complexity as barriers; only a minority of studies report implementations and few address integrating the master schedule into AI-driven planning</cite><cite id="7ddaeac1-1">Most RL scheduling policies struggle with multiple objectives and learning efficiency under real-world variability, motivating careful reward design</cite><cite id="7ddaeac1-4">Metaheuristics require policy retraining when settings shift, risking process halts; RL offers learning but introduces its own engineering challenges</cite>.

# Practical Implications and Recommendations

- Start with digital twin-enabled simulation-optimization to bridge order-level customization with factory-level planning, capturing real-time events and constraints for robust rescheduling in LVHM environments.<cite id="649c53e7-0">Digital twins can synchronize optimization and operations to manage variability and unplanned events in single-piece and mass customization</cite><cite id="649c53e7-3">Integrating digital twins with MES and MILP scheduling enables real-time active rescheduling and resource allocation</cite>.
- Adopt RL/MARL for dynamic dispatching and rescheduling, using composite, requirement-aware rewards and KPIs; where requirements are text-heavy, pair with LLM-based requirement parsing to weight objectives like cost, lead time, and quality.<cite id="7ddaeac1-1">RL with composite rewards supports online, multi-objective scheduling under disturbances</cite><cite id="7ddaeac1-2">LLM-guided DRL selects KPIs from natural-language requirements and optimizes scheduling accordingly</cite><cite id="7ddaeac1-4">MARL variants address randomness and breakdowns with cooperative policies to reduce conflicts and makespan</cite>.
- Integrate workforce and resource planning with the master schedule, using human-in-the-loop decision gates and safety constraints; prioritize data quality, real-time usability, and change management for sustainable adoption.<cite id="2b6a6117-3">Decompose AI decision scope, address data and expertise gaps, and ensure real-time usability and safety; few implementations to date indicate a need for phased integration</cite>.
- For small-batch or single-piece orders, combine heuristic filters with learned policies to reduce search space and maintain throughput, while leveraging digital twins for scenario testing and ramp-up planning.<cite id="7ddaeac1-4">Heuristics can pre-filter actions for RL/MARL to reduce complexity; metaheuristics remain useful for specific settings with retraining considerations</cite><cite id="649c53e7-0">Digital twins support planning under single-piece flow by enabling rapid scenario analysis and rescheduling</cite>.

# Conclusion

AI is increasingly used to plan in mass customization by addressing the planning and scheduling challenges of LVHM production through reinforcement learning, multi-agent learning, digital twins, and hybrid human–AI frameworks that integrate requirement understanding, real-time data, and optimization.<cite id="2b6a6117-2">AI-driven cooperative operation, reconfiguration, and self-organizing scheduling underpin customized manufacturing</cite><cite id="7ddaeac1-4">RL/MARL and simulation-optimization handle dynamic uncertainties in mass personalization scheduling</cite><cite id="649c53e7-0">Digital twins provide fast optimization loops to manage variability and disruptions in customized production</cite>. Early industrial evidence shows significant improvements in scheduling efficiency and delivery performance, but broader adoption hinges on overcoming data, expertise, and integration barriers, and on careful design of multi-criteria policies that align with business and customer requirements.<cite id="2b6a6117-3">Adoption remains limited due to data, expertise, and complexity; success factors include real-time usability and safety</cite><cite id="7ddaeac1-1">RL-based scheduling requires composite reward engineering to balance multiple objectives under real-world disturbances</cite><cite id="649c53e7-4">Case studies demonstrate large reductions in cycle time for small, customized orders via digital twin–based optimization</cite>.

Title: Reinforcement learning for online optimization of job-shop scheduling in a smart manufacturing factory
Snippet: In the last three decades, the world has experienced three times of industrial revolutions, enabling industry with automated machines and information systems to support rapid and innovative product design. The manufacturing industry plays an important role in the development processes of the economy and technology. Today, manufacturing companies face a large number of challenges in a turbulent environment originating from saturated markets, abrupt and unprecedented changes in market demands, an increasing number of product variants, and smaller lot sizes. 1,2 This trend is intensified by production modes such as mass customization and individualization, which guarantee the creation of unique products to meet the requirements of almost every customer. 3 The transformation of traditional industrial markets inevitably leads to the evolution of manufacturing modes. 

Production scheduling is a complex combinatorial problem, more specifically, a non-polynomial-hard (NP-hard) problem, which coordinates manufacturing resources to get optimal sequences and combinations. It is traditionally elaborated in a centralized manner using offline methods and considering the problems are static and deterministic. 4 However, initial production plans often become invalid due to many unexpected events that come from internal (e.g. machine failures, operator absence), external (e.g. rush orders, unavailability of raw materials), or composite factors (e.g. time fluctuation, resource uncertainty). Therefore, scheduling algorithms are required to modify the original schedules for eliminating the disturbances. Early studies focus on rescheduling resources offline to achieve new schedules, which may suspend the manufacturing processes and increase the lead time. 5 Simulation technologies (e.g. multi-agent system) build scheduling algorithms with empirical rules and historical data, but they are limited in achieving optimal schedules in a changeable manufacturing environment. 6 Recently, artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms such as reinforcement learning (RL) are adopted to industrial manufacturing with regard to online scheduling. However, most RL-based scheduling algorithms are inefficient at learning to optimize the decision-making policies when multiple objectives are considered in a smart manufacturing factory. 7 The overall performances of manufacturing systems are influenced by many factors such as order requirements, machine properties, and supply chain profits, which can be transformed into composite reward functions in RLbased scheduling systems. This paper realizes online scheduling based on RL with composite reward functions, which makes manufacturing systems to be more efficient and robust.
</snippet>
<snippet id=7ddaeac1-2>
Title: Literacy Deep Reinforcement Learning-Based Federated Digital Twin Scheduling for the Software-Defined Factory
Snippet: As user requirements become increasingly complex, the demand for product personalization is growing, but traditional hardware-centric production relies on fixed procedures that lack the flexibility to support diverse requirements. Although bespoke manufacturing has been introduced, it provides users with only a few standardized options, limiting its ability to meet a wide range of needs. To address this issue, a new manufacturing concept called the software-defined factory has emerged. It is an autonomous manufacturing system that provides reconfigurable manufacturing services to produce tailored products. Reinforcement learning has been suggested for flexible scheduling to satisfy user requirements. However, fixed rule-based methods struggle to accommodate conflicting needs. This study proposes a novel federated digital twin scheduling that combines large language models and deep reinforcement learning algorithms to meet diverse user requirements in the software-defined factory. The large language model-based literacy module analyzes requirements in natural language and assigns weights to digital twin attributes to achieve highly relevant KPIs, which are used to guide scheduling decisions. The deep reinforcement learning-based scheduling module optimizes scheduling by selecting the job and machine with the maximum reward. Different types of user requirements, such as reducing manufacturing costs and improving productivity, are input and evaluated by comparing the flow-shop scheduling with job-shop scheduling based on reinforcement learning. Experimental results indicate that in requirement case 1 (the manufacturing cost), the proposed method outperforms flow-shop scheduling by up to 14.9% and job-shop scheduling by 5.6%. For requirement case 2 (productivity), it exceeds the flow-shop method by up to 13.4% and the job-shop baseline by 7.2%. The results confirm that the literacy DRL scheduling proposed in this paper can handle the individual characteristics of requirements.
</snippet>

Title: Knowledge graph-enhanced multi-agent reinforcement learning for adaptive scheduling in smart manufacturing
Snippet: Dynamic scheduling problems are essential under mass personalization as they seek (near-) optimal allocation to feasible machines following dynamic scheduling settings (Johnson et al., 2022). Existing approaches to dynamic scheduling problems can be classified into three categories: heuristic methods, meta-heuristic methods, and reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms (Luo et al., 2021). 

Heuristic rules simply allocate operations to machines following predefined rules, such as first-in-first-out and longest-processing time allocation rules. The disadvantages are obvious since they are not suitable for many scheduling settings to optimize scheduling performance (Xie et al., 2019). In contrast, meta-heuristic methods, such as genetic algorithms (Elmaraghy et al., 2000;Qi et al., 2000;Zhang et al., 2013aZhang et al., , 2013b) ) and ant colony algorithms (Merkle et al., 2002;J. Zhang et al., 2013aJ. Zhang et al., , 2013b)), can explore nearoptimal schedules. However, the scheduling policies need to be retained if manufacturing settings are adjusted, and the time-consuming retraining might halt the whole manufacturing process (Al-Hinai & Elmekkawy, 2011;Gao et al., 2015). 

Reinforcement learning is a promising solution to dynamic scheduling problems (Heger & Voss, 2021;Jing et al., 2022;Kuhnle et al., 2021). Random job arrivals is addressed using multi-agent DQN (Johnson et al., 2022) by training with random job arrivals. A multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) approach has been proposed to manage scheduling processes with random processing time (Park et al., 2020). The randomness in setup time is addressed through MARL, with the goal of minimizing makespan (Oh et al., 2022). Stochastic processing times and unplanned machine breakdowns are tackled separately using dueling multi-agent reinforcement learning, which incorporates cooperation mechanisms to prevent conflicting operations (Qin et al., 2023).
</snippet></tool_output>

Title: Digital Twin Based Optimization of a Manufacturing Execution System to Handle High Degrees of Customer Specifications
Snippet: Moving to single-piece flow and mass customization, this is further compounded through the increased variability of machining times. 

Within the highly variable production environment created by single-piece flows and mass customization, additional perturbations can be created. Some can be planned for, such as regular maintenance on the equipment in the machine park, and employees' holidays. These two events (one machine based, and one human based) create additional constraints on the system and the performance. These can, of course, be foreseen and planned for within the planning frames (annual, monthly, weekly, and daily). Additional complications are created by machine breakdowns and employees' illnesses [7]. These cannot be integrated into the planning frames as they are random events that cause replanning and rescheduling within the daily plan, although they have an impact on the system constraints for considerably longer. 

The concept of a digital twins offers new possibilities in the design, operation and optimization of production systems: using models of the systems dynamics and data structures, digital copies of physical systems can be created [8]. By synchronizing the two systems, one can exploit the benefits of both words [9]: the physical world, where the actual value-creation of the production system takes place, and the digital world, which enables fast optimization and analysis loops, whose results are later deployed to the physical system. It is thus a relevant question whether the aforementioned challenges of production planning can be helped by using a digital twin of the production system. Using two case studies, this paper addresses how to provide higher levels of certainty to the planning process to ensure that costs are minimized and lead times are achieved within the constraints of single piece flows and mass customizing using a digital twin. This has to both support individual orders and consider the existing production within the factory. The aim is to integrate an agile planning tool into the existing manufacturing execution system (MES) within the factory.
</snippet>

Title: Design of a Digital Twin in Low-Volume, High-Mix Job Allocation and Scheduling for Achieving Mass Personalization
Snippet: With the advent of Industry 4.0, manufacturers are shifting from mass production to mass customization, designing products to meet unique customer needs [1,2]. This shift begins with the new product development process. Mass production typically involves high-volume, low-variety manufacturing, while mass customization necessitates a low-volume, high-variety model that produces a broad array of tailor-made products in smaller quantities [3]. In order to meet the growing demand for bespoke products, manufacturers are transitioning from a high-volume, low-variety (HVLM) production model to a low-volume, high-variety (LVHM) model. This strategy allows manufacturers to concentrate on specific customer segments and offer a wide variety of product variations, enabling mass customization. Despite the significant challenges associated with this transition, manufacturers must be competitive and maintain a substantial market share in customized products. scaling up, enabling these companies to focus on core propositions and market development. Ultimately, the synergy between human expertise and the digital twin solution drives both operational excellence and social sustainability in the LVHM production landscape.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 provides a literature review on LVHM production, as well as advanced simulation and optimization techniques. Section 3 elaborates on the proposed digital twin model with the ISOM. A case study involving the use of the proposed digital twin model to optimize job allocation and scheduling in the SMT production line for the PCBA process is presented in Section 4. Section 5 discusses the corresponding results and implementation to highlight the value of the proposed digital twin model. Finally, Section 6 draws the conclusion of this research.

Title: Design of a Digital Twin in Low-Volume, High-Mix Job Allocation and Scheduling for Achieving Mass Personalization
Snippet: The research identifies a significant gap in the transition from high-volume, low-variety (HVLM) production models to low-volume, high-variety (LVHM) models in the manufacturing industry, a shift necessitated by the increasing demand for bespoke, mass-customized products. From the extant literature, although there are a number of research studies about the job allocation and scheduling problem in the context of Industry 5.0 [33,34], the research on solving such problems in the LVHM production environment for promoting mass personalization is relatively limited. The challenge lies in managing new product introductions and small customer orders within high-volume production settings without impacting overall efficiency. Existing systems often overlook small-scale orders in favor of high-volume ones, leading to potential disappointment for new or smaller customers and misalignment with corporate strategies and marketing plans. The dynamic nature of the system and the complexity of the job allocation process under mass personalization initiatives further complicate the optimization process. Conventional optimization approaches, while effective, can be computationally demanding in such environments. 

In response to these challenges, research on the digital twin model in the LVHM production environment is urgently needed. This model, unlike traditional production optimization approaches that rely on specific system state assumptions, accommodates dynamic system states and offers optimal solutions through simulation analysis. The research is contextualized within the practical challenge of developing a low-volume, high-variety production workshop to provide manufacturing services to start-ups, a goal that aligns with government initiatives to commercialize research results. The research, therefore, seeks to fill the gap in understanding and implementing mass personalization strategies in line with Industry 5.0 within a low-volume, high-variety production context.

Title: Digital twin for product versus project lifecycles’ development in manufacturing and construction industries
Snippet: Manufacturing is the main phase in which digital twin is applied, and it refers to the process of assembling, manufacturing or producing a product based on specifications defined in the design phase (Son et al., 2022). During this phase, the digital twin has been investigated for flexible scheduling and production, process optimisation and production improving, equipment maintenance and fault diagnosis, energy management, human factors engineering optimisation, as well as real-time data management and tracing. In terms of digital twin implementation to assist production scheduling, intelligent scheduling of workshops enabled by digital twin could solve the problem of inconsistent resource allocation to physical production sites caused by information imbalance, and real-time active workshop scheduling was achieved through data provided by digital twin (Zhang et al., 2022). Nie et al. (2021) enhanced the allocation of resources and resistance to disruption in the production process through the integration of physical and virtual shopfloor with digital twin service systems, enabling a more efficient allocation of resources. 

In addition, a digital twin-based mixed integer linear programming (MILP) scheduling model has been developed, realising flexible scheduling of production based on internal and external temporary events (Tliba et al., 2022). 

Digital twin can also be used to optimise the process and improve the production of products. As one of the main concerns of product production, quality improvement is an important aspect of digital twin applications. Reisch et al. (2022) were able to achieve real-time defect detection during the machining of large metal parts through digital twin and make quantitative assessments to improve the sensitivity of defect detection thereby ensuring machining quality. Also, quality control methods driven by digital twin can be used to accurately predict product quality, evaluate processes and optimise process parameters related to product quality (Zhu & Ji, 2022). In addition, improvements in the production are also manifested in optimisation in the machining and assembly processes. The machining state during the manufacturing process could be simulated by digital twin in real time and enable timely correction and optimisation of machining solutions to improve the machining process (Zhang & Zhu, 2019). Yi et al. (2021) also introduced an intelligent assembly process enabled by the digital twin, capable of being used for assembly process planning, simulation and prediction.
</snippet>

Title: Design of a Digital Twin in Low-Volume, High-Mix Job Allocation and Scheduling for Achieving Mass Personalization
Snippet: The growing consumer demand for unique products has made customization and personalization essential in manufacturing. This shift to low-volume, high-mix (LVHM) production challenges the traditional paradigms and creates difficulties for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Industry 5.0 emphasizes the importance of human workers and social sustainability in adapting to these changes. This study introduces a digital twin design tailored for LVHM production, focusing on the collaboration between human expertise and advanced technologies. The digital twin-based production optimization system (DTPOS) uses an intelligent simulation-based optimization model (ISOM) to balance productivity and social sustainability by optimizing job allocation and scheduling. The digital twin model fosters a symbiotic relationship between human workers and the production process, promoting operational excellence and social sustainability through local innovation and economic growth. A case study was conducted within the context of a printed circuit board assembly (PCBA) using surface mount technology to validate the digital twin model’s efficacy and performance. The proposed DTPOS significantly improved the performance metrics of small orders, reducing the average order processing time from 19 days to 9.59 days—an improvement of 52.63%. The average order-to-delivery time for small orders was 19.47 days, indicating timely completion. These findings highlight the successful transformation from mass production to mass personalization, enabling efficient production capacity utilization and improved job allocation and scheduling. By embracing the principles of Industry 5.0, the proposed digital twin model addresses the challenges of LVHM production, fostering a sustainable balance between productivity, human expertise, and social responsibility.
</snippet></tool_output>

Title: Lean Manual Assembly 4.0: A Systematic Review
Snippet: Mass customization demand is characterized by a combination of great variety, shorter product life cycles, and variable production volumes (medium or high for platform products, very low for personalized products); compared to Industry 2.0's stable market and Industry 3.0's volatile market-in terms of product volume, product variety and delivery time. In this new context, Toyota Production Systems (TPS) may prove limited, and its advantages and disadvantages with regards to seru were analyzed by Yin et al. [11]. The usage of new key digital technologies will bring forward the 4th Industrial Revolution (Industry 4.0), addressing many of the challenges of production systems for mass customization [11,12]. However, looking at isolated systems may not be enough since increased complexity requires a holistic approach to respond successfully and cost-effectively to shifting market demands [13]. Assembly is the final process to create a product, where component sub-assemblies come together into the final product. Demand-driven increasing product variety adds complexity, production cost and lead time to assembly operations, which goes against its goals. In the mass customization landscape, key assembly topics need to be reviewed, evaluated and adapted [2]: assembly representation and sequencing, especially non-sequential assembly; assembly system design-considering line balancing, delayed product differentiation and performance evaluation; assembly system operations-with a focus on exploring reconfigurable assembly planning, mixed-model assembly scheduling, and dealing with complexity resulting from different sources; and the changing role of human operators. In conclusion, mass customization brings increased complexity that needs to be addressed at multiple levels and taking a holistic point of view to ensure that optimizing a subsystem does not negatively affect another subsystem.

Title: Design of a Digital Twin in Low-Volume, High-Mix Job Allocation and Scheduling for Achieving Mass Personalization
Snippet: The research identifies a significant gap in the transition from high-volume, low-variety (HVLM) production models to low-volume, high-variety (LVHM) models in the manufacturing industry, a shift necessitated by the increasing demand for bespoke, mass-customized products. From the extant literature, although there are a number of research studies about the job allocation and scheduling problem in the context of Industry 5.0 [33,34], the research on solving such problems in the LVHM production environment for promoting mass personalization is relatively limited. The challenge lies in managing new product introductions and small customer orders within high-volume production settings without impacting overall efficiency. Existing systems often overlook small-scale orders in favor of high-volume ones, leading to potential disappointment for new or smaller customers and misalignment with corporate strategies and marketing plans. The dynamic nature of the system and the complexity of the job allocation process under mass personalization initiatives further complicate the optimization process. Conventional optimization approaches, while effective, can be computationally demanding in such environments. 

In response to these challenges, research on the digital twin model in the LVHM production environment is urgently needed. This model, unlike traditional production optimization approaches that rely on specific system state assumptions, accommodates dynamic system states and offers optimal solutions through simulation analysis. The research is contextualized within the practical challenge of developing a low-volume, high-variety production workshop to provide manufacturing services to start-ups, a goal that aligns with government initiatives to commercialize research results. The research, therefore, seeks to fill the gap in understanding and implementing mass personalization strategies in line with Industry 5.0 within a low-volume, high-variety production context.
</snippet>

# Scope and Definitions

Mass customization (MC) blends the variety of made-to-order with the cost and throughput targets of mass production, shifting manufacturers toward low-volume, high-mix (LVHM) production to meet individualized customer demands while maintaining competitive pricing and lead times.<cite id="e79ae94f-0">Mass customization challenges supply chains by adapting mass production approaches to high-variety, low-volume production, combining scale-like efficiency with customization flexibility</cite><cite id="e79ae94f-4">Mass customization necessitates a low-volume, high-variety model that produces a broad array of tailor-made products in smaller quantities, transitioning from high-volume, low-variety manufacturing</cite>. This transition increases scheduling and planning complexity due to shorter product life cycles, variable volumes across product families, and the need to integrate small, bespoke orders with platform-based products without undermining overall efficiency.<cite id="e79ae94f-2">Mass customization demand features great variety, shorter product life cycles, and variable volumes; it adds complexity to assembly representation, sequencing, and mixed-model scheduling, requiring holistic approaches</cite><cite id="e79ae94f-3">Managing new product introductions and small customer orders alongside high-volume production is difficult; conventional optimization can be computationally demanding in LVHM environments</cite>.

# Planning Challenges in Mass Customization

Planning in MC must coordinate production reconfiguration, order acceptance, job allocation, and real-time rescheduling under uncertainty (e.g., machine breakdowns, variable processing times, rush orders), while respecting resource, skill, and customer due date constraints.<cite id="649c53e7-0">Single-piece flow and mass customization increase variability (e.g., machining times) and introduce unplanned perturbations like breakdowns and illnesses that trigger replanning; digital twins are proposed to enable fast optimization loops to meet constraints and lead-time targets</cite>. Assembly-focused MC planning adds challenges in reconfigurable line design, delayed differentiation, mixed-model sequencing, and operator integration to maintain throughput and quality under high variety.<cite id="e79ae94f-2">Key assembly planning topics for MC include reconfigurable assembly planning, mixed-model scheduling, and adapting human operator roles amid increased complexity</cite>. At the enterprise level, integrating master production schedules with detailed workforce and resource schedules remains underexplored, and companies struggle to operationalize AI planning due to data readiness and expertise gaps.<cite id="2b6a6117-3">There is a gap in linking the master schedule to detailed planning; reviews show few AI implementations in industrial scheduling and highlight data, expertise, and complexity as main challenges for deploying AI planners</cite>.

# AI Techniques for Planning in Mass Customization

## Reinforcement Learning and Multi-Agent RL

Dynamic scheduling in MC is naturally modeled as a multi-objective, partially observable Markov decision process; RL and multi-agent RL (MARL) learn policies that handle random arrivals, processing-time variability, breakdowns, and conflicting objectives without retraining on every change.<cite id="7ddaeac1-1">Production scheduling is NP-hard and traditionally offline; disturbances from internal and external factors invalidate initial plans, motivating online, robust scheduling; RL-based approaches use composite reward functions to adapt to changes in smart factories</cite><cite id="7ddaeac1-4">Dynamic scheduling under mass personalization requires near-optimal machine and job allocation; MARL has been used for random job arrivals, stochastic processing times, and setup-time randomness, including dueling architectures to prevent conflicting operations and minimize makespan</cite>. Emerging systems combine requirement interpretation with RL-based dispatching: natural-language requirement analysis via LLMs weights KPIs, guiding DRL schedulers that improve productivity and cost metrics compared to baselines in software-defined factories.<cite id="7ddaeac1-2">A federated digital twin with a large language model and deep RL achieved up to 14.9% cost reduction and 13.4% productivity gains versus flow- and job-shop baselines by aligning requirements to KPIs and optimizing job–machine selection in a software-defined factory</cite>.

## Digital Twins for LVHM and Single-Piece Flow

Digital twins mirror physical production dynamics to enable real-time optimization, disruption management, and integrated planning across orders and factory operations under high variability.<cite id="649c53e7-0">Digital twins synchronize physical and virtual systems to run fast optimization and analysis loops; case studies show potential to increase certainty in planning, minimize costs, and meet lead-time constraints in single-piece and mass-customizing environments while supporting individual orders and factory-level production</cite><cite id="649c53e7-3">Digital twins support intelligent workshop scheduling, resource allocation, and active rescheduling via real-time data, and can integrate with MILP models to realize flexible scheduling under internal and external events</cite>. Practical implementations report substantial reductions in order cycle times for small, customized jobs by optimizing job allocation and scheduling with an intelligent simulation-based optimization model within the digital twin framework.<cite id="649c53e7-4">A digital twin-based production optimization system (DTPOS) with intelligent simulation optimization reduced average processing time for small orders from 19 days to 9.59 days (52.63%), indicating timely delivery and improved LVHM scheduling for mass personalization</cite>.

## Constraint Programming, Metaheuristics, and Hybrid Approaches

Beyond RL, heuristic and metaheuristic methods (e.g., genetic algorithms, ant colonies) provide near-optimal schedules but require retraining when settings change, which can halt processes; hybrid human–AI and simulation-optimization approaches mitigate this by retaining policy knowledge and enabling agile adjustments.<cite id="7ddaeac1-4">Heuristics are fast but not suitable across many settings; metaheuristics can find near-optimal schedules but need policy retention or retraining if settings change, risking process halts; RL/MARL offer learning policies that adapt to dynamic changes</cite>. AI-driven customized manufacturing emphasizes multi-agent cooperation, autonomous reconfiguration, and self-organizing scheduling on flexible lines to cope with product variety and dynamic order intake.<cite id="2b6a6117-2">AI-driven strategies such as collective and autonomous intelligence, cross-media reasoning, and multi-agent cooperation enable dynamic reconfiguration and self-organizing scheduling for flexible manufacturing in customized production</cite>.

## Human-in-the-Loop and Integrated Planning

Effective MC planning requires deciding the scope of AI decision-making and how it complements human planners, especially when integrating master schedules with workforce and resource planning; success factors include data availability, real-time usability, and safety in implementation.<cite id="2b6a6117-3">When using AI for planning, firms must determine decision levels and human–AI roles; challenges include data gathering, expertise, and complexity; success factors are real-time usability, user-friendliness, and safety, and only 11 of 37 reviewed AI mentions included implementations</cite>. Sectoral applications in fashion show AI aiding design personalization and production-side scheduling and resource allocation to reduce idle time and adapt to changing orders in real time.<cite id="2b6a6117-4">AI algorithms generate consumer options and predict preferences in design, and optimize production scheduling and resource allocation to reduce idle time and adapt to changing order demands in personalized customization</cite>.

# Case Studies and Quantitative Evidence

- Digital twin + intelligent simulation optimization (DTPOS) in a PCBA SMT line: 52.63% reduction in processing time for small orders and timely delivery performance under LVHM conditions, demonstrating that digital twins can integrate order-level and factory-level planning to meet MC constraints.<cite id="649c53e7-4">A digital twin-based DTPOS reduced average order processing time from 19 days to 9.59 days (52.63%) and achieved timely completion for small orders in a PCBA SMT setting</cite>.
- Federated digital twin with LLM + DRL in a software-defined factory: requirement-aware scheduling improved cost and productivity by up to 14.9% and 13.4% over flow- and job-shop baselines, indicating AI’s ability to weight KPIs and optimize under diverse user needs in MC contexts.<cite id="7ddaeac1-2">The literacy DRL scheduling outperformed flow-shop and job-shop baselines by up to 14.9% (cost) and 13.4% (productivity), showing requirement-driven scheduling benefits</cite>.
- MARL for dynamic job shop/flow shop settings: MARL policies address random job arrivals, stochastic processing times, and breakdowns, reducing conflicts and makespan relative to rule-based dispatching and static heuristics in dynamic MC-like environments.<cite id="7ddaeac1-4">MARL approaches have been applied to random arrivals, processing-time variability, and setup-time randomness, with cooperation mechanisms to prevent conflicts and minimize makespan</cite>.
- Digital twin-enabled planning under single-piece and mass customization: case studies show digital twins can raise planning certainty, manage unplanned events, and integrate with MES to meet cost and lead-time targets in highly variable settings.<cite id="649c53e7-0">Digital twins provide higher certainty in planning under single-piece and mass customizing by synchronizing physical and virtual systems for fast optimization and rescheduling within daily plans</cite><cite id="649c53e7-3">Digital twins enable real-time active workshop scheduling and MILP-based flexible scheduling under internal and external events</cite>.

# Benefits and Limitations

Benefits include improved responsiveness to dynamic orders, reduced idle time and costs, better multi-objective trade-offs, and integration of natural-language requirements with quantitative scheduling goals via LLMs and DRL; digital twins enable real-time data-driven rescheduling and disruption management across LVHM environments.<cite id="7ddaeac1-1">RL-based online scheduling with composite rewards improves robustness to disturbances and supports multi-objective performance in smart factories</cite><cite id="7ddaeac1-2">LLM-guided DRL aligns requirement KPIs and optimizes job–machine selection, outperforming baselines on cost and productivity</cite><cite id="649c53e7-3">Digital twins support real-time active scheduling and flexible planning under disruptions</cite>. Reported case studies show double-digit percentage improvements in certain metrics, indicating tangible gains for MC planning.<cite id="649c53e7-4">A 52.63% reduction in processing time for small orders and timely delivery demonstrate practical benefits of DTPOS</cite>.

Limitations and open challenges include data readiness and skilled expertise barriers to AI deployment, the need for robust multi-criteria reward engineering in RL, retraining and stability issues for metaheuristics when shop-floor settings change, and the underexplored integration of master production scheduling with detailed, AI-driven planning at scale.<cite id="2b6a6117-3">Reviews highlight data gathering, expertise, and complexity as barriers; only a minority of studies report implementations and few address integrating the master schedule into AI-driven planning</cite><cite id="7ddaeac1-1">Most RL scheduling policies struggle with multiple objectives and learning efficiency under real-world variability, motivating careful reward design</cite><cite id="7ddaeac1-4">Metaheuristics require policy retraining when settings shift, risking process halts; RL offers learning but introduces its own engineering challenges</cite>.

# Practical Implications and Recommendations

- Start with digital twin-enabled simulation-optimization to bridge order-level customization with factory-level planning, capturing real-time events and constraints for robust rescheduling in LVHM environments.<cite id="649c53e7-0">Digital twins can synchronize optimization and operations to manage variability and unplanned events in single-piece and mass customization</cite><cite id="649c53e7-3">Integrating digital twins with MES and MILP scheduling enables real-time active rescheduling and resource allocation</cite>.
- Adopt RL/MARL for dynamic dispatching and rescheduling, using composite, requirement-aware rewards and KPIs; where requirements are text-heavy, pair with LLM-based requirement parsing to weight objectives like cost, lead time, and quality.<cite id="7ddaeac1-1">RL with composite rewards supports online, multi-objective scheduling under disturbances</cite><cite id="7ddaeac1-2">LLM-guided DRL selects KPIs from natural-language requirements and optimizes scheduling accordingly</cite><cite id="7ddaeac1-4">MARL variants address randomness and breakdowns with cooperative policies to reduce conflicts and makespan</cite>.
- Integrate workforce and resource planning with the master schedule, using human-in-the-loop decision gates and safety constraints; prioritize data quality, real-time usability, and change management for sustainable adoption.<cite id="2b6a6117-3">Decompose AI decision scope, address data and expertise gaps, and ensure real-time usability and safety; few implementations to date indicate a need for phased integration</cite>.
- For small-batch or single-piece orders, combine heuristic filters with learned policies to reduce search space and maintain throughput, while leveraging digital twins for scenario testing and ramp-up planning.<cite id="7ddaeac1-4">Heuristics can pre-filter actions for RL/MARL to reduce complexity; metaheuristics remain useful for specific settings with retraining considerations</cite><cite id="649c53e7-0">Digital twins support planning under single-piece flow by enabling rapid scenario analysis and rescheduling</cite>.

# Conclusion

AI is increasingly used to plan in mass customization by addressing the planning and scheduling challenges of LVHM production through reinforcement learning, multi-agent learning, digital twins, and hybrid human–AI frameworks that integrate requirement understanding, real-time data, and optimization.<cite id="2b6a6117-2">AI-driven cooperative operation, reconfiguration, and self-organizing scheduling underpin customized manufacturing</cite><cite id="7ddaeac1-4">RL/MARL and simulation-optimization handle dynamic uncertainties in mass personalization scheduling</cite><cite id="649c53e7-0">Digital twins provide fast optimization loops to manage variability and disruptions in customized production</cite>. Early industrial evidence shows significant improvements in scheduling efficiency and delivery performance, but broader adoption hinges on overcoming data, expertise, and integration barriers, and on careful design of multi-criteria policies that align with business and customer requirements.<cite id="2b6a6117-3">Adoption remains limited due to data, expertise, and complexity; success factors include real-time usability and safety</cite><cite id="7ddaeac1-1">RL-based scheduling requires composite reward engineering to balance multiple objectives under real-world disturbances</cite><cite id="649c53e7-4">Case studies demonstrate large reductions in cycle time for small, customized orders via digital twin–based optimization</cite>.
</answer>

Title: Time autonomy in personnel planning: Requirements and solution approaches in the context of intelligent scheduling from a holistic organizational perspective
Snippet: Even though some companies have shown interest in including employee preferences in scheduling, there is no algorithm that can effectively address this requirement (Özder et al. 2020, p. 19). Özder et al. (2020, p. 19) further point out another research gap in the literature that is specifically relevant for manufacturing applications: The inclusion of a master schedule in personnel scheduling that has not been addressed yet. The Master Production Schedule (MPS) acts as a bridge, translating broad production plans into specific, detailed schedules. These schedules pinpoint the exact production timelines for individual end items or models, allowing for the prioritization of critical items (Kiran 2019). 

From the literature review, that was conducted for the purpose of this paper, the following findings can be stated: 

If Artificial Intelligence (AI) is used for planning purposes, it is essential to determine how and to which level it can make decisions. Shrestha et al. (2019) introduce a framework for how human decision-making-combined with AI-based decision-making-can be utilized as starting point for creating a concept. Gabriel et al. ( 2022) discuss AI's potential to support humans and, in the case of personnel scheduling, planners. However, the main challenges in using AI for scheduling are: gathering the required data, expertise and complexity. Hence, their work presents a concept of how AI can be used. Rischmeyer (2021) presents a general idea of the possibility of using AI for automated workforce planning and explains the challenges and the advantages of having an AI tool for planning. It further recognizes real-time, user-friendliness and safety as the success factors of an AI planner and explains how an implementation project should be managed. 

Out of 37 articles, where AI was mentioned, only 11 included an own AI implementation. However, no ML approach could be identified in the review, that specifically tackled the focus of this paper. Instead, it has been ap-to other problems. For example, Denkena et al. (2017) used deep learning to determine the employee influence on setup and processing time in a manufacturing setup. Mo et al. (2020) used natural language processing techniques in construction to prioritize the tasks and assign them to the correct employee with the right skill.

In addition, AI technology can monitor production progress in real time and adjust production strategies in a timely manner to adapt to changing order demands.

From the literature review, that was conducted for the purpose of this paper, the following findings can be stated: 

If Artificial Intelligence (AI) is used for planning purposes, it is essential to determine how and to which level it can make decisions. Shrestha et al. ( 2022) discuss AI's potential to support humans and, in the case of personnel scheduling, planners. Rischmeyer (2021) presents a general idea of the possibility of using AI for automated workforce planning and explains the challenges and the advantages of having an AI tool for planning. It further recognizes real-time, user-friendliness and safety as the success factors of an AI planner and explains how an implementation project should be managed. 

Out of 37 articles, where AI was mentioned, only 11 included an own AI implementation. However, no ML approach could be identified in the review, that specifically tackled the focus of this paper. Instead, it has been ap-to other problems. For example, Denkena et al. (2017) used deep learning to determine the employee influence on setup and processing time in a manufacturing setup. Mo et al. (2020) used natural language processing techniques in construction to prioritize the tasks and assign them to the correct employee with the right skill.

Title: Reinforcement learning for online optimization of job-shop scheduling in a smart manufacturing factory
Snippet: In the last three decades, the world has experienced three times of industrial revolutions, enabling industry with automated machines and information systems to support rapid and innovative product design. The manufacturing industry plays an important role in the development processes of the economy and technology. Today, manufacturing companies face a large number of challenges in a turbulent environment originating from saturated markets, abrupt and unprecedented changes in market demands, an increasing number of product variants, and smaller lot sizes. 1,2 This trend is intensified by production modes such as mass customization and individualization, which guarantee the creation of unique products to meet the requirements of almost every customer. 3 The transformation of traditional industrial markets inevitably leads to the evolution of manufacturing modes. 

Production scheduling is a complex combinatorial problem, more specifically, a non-polynomial-hard (NP-hard) problem, which coordinates manufacturing resources to get optimal sequences and combinations. It is traditionally elaborated in a centralized manner using offline methods and considering the problems are static and deterministic. 4 However, initial production plans often become invalid due to many unexpected events that come from internal (e.g. machine failures, operator absence), external (e.g. rush orders, unavailability of raw materials), or composite factors (e.g. time fluctuation, resource uncertainty). Therefore, scheduling algorithms are required to modify the original schedules for eliminating the disturbances. Early studies focus on rescheduling resources offline to achieve new schedules, which may suspend the manufacturing processes and increase the lead time. 5 Simulation technologies (e.g. multi-agent system) build scheduling algorithms with empirical rules and historical data, but they are limited in achieving optimal schedules in a changeable manufacturing environment. 6 Recently, artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms such as reinforcement learning (RL) are adopted to industrial manufacturing with regard to online scheduling. However, most RL-based scheduling algorithms are inefficient at learning to optimize the decision-making policies when multiple objectives are considered in a smart manufacturing factory. 7 The overall performances of manufacturing systems are influenced by many factors such as order requirements, machine properties, and supply chain profits, which can be transformed into composite reward functions in RLbased scheduling systems. This paper realizes online scheduling based on RL with composite reward functions, which makes manufacturing systems to be more efficient and robust.

Title: Literacy Deep Reinforcement Learning-Based Federated Digital Twin Scheduling for the Software-Defined Factory
Snippet: As user requirements become increasingly complex, the demand for product personalization is growing, but traditional hardware-centric production relies on fixed procedures that lack the flexibility to support diverse requirements. Although bespoke manufacturing has been introduced, it provides users with only a few standardized options, limiting its ability to meet a wide range of needs. To address this issue, a new manufacturing concept called the software-defined factory has emerged. It is an autonomous manufacturing system that provides reconfigurable manufacturing services to produce tailored products. Reinforcement learning has been suggested for flexible scheduling to satisfy user requirements. However, fixed rule-based methods struggle to accommodate conflicting needs. This study proposes a novel federated digital twin scheduling that combines large language models and deep reinforcement learning algorithms to meet diverse user requirements in the software-defined factory. The large language model-based literacy module analyzes requirements in natural language and assigns weights to digital twin attributes to achieve highly relevant KPIs, which are used to guide scheduling decisions. The deep reinforcement learning-based scheduling module optimizes scheduling by selecting the job and machine with the maximum reward. Different types of user requirements, such as reducing manufacturing costs and improving productivity, are input and evaluated by comparing the flow-shop scheduling with job-shop scheduling based on reinforcement learning. Experimental results indicate that in requirement case 1 (the manufacturing cost), the proposed method outperforms flow-shop scheduling by up to 14.9% and job-shop scheduling by 5.6%. For requirement case 2 (productivity), it exceeds the flow-shop method by up to 13.4% and the job-shop baseline by 7.2%. The results confirm that the literacy DRL scheduling proposed in this paper can handle the individual characteristics of requirements.

Title: Knowledge graph-enhanced multi-agent reinforcement learning for adaptive scheduling in smart manufacturing
Snippet: Dynamic scheduling problems are essential under mass personalization as they seek (near-) optimal allocation to feasible machines following dynamic scheduling settings (Johnson et al., 2022). Existing approaches to dynamic scheduling problems can be classified into three categories: heuristic methods, meta-heuristic methods, and reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms (Luo et al., 2021). 

Heuristic rules simply allocate operations to machines following predefined rules, such as first-in-first-out and longest-processing time allocation rules. The disadvantages are obvious since they are not suitable for many scheduling settings to optimize scheduling performance (Xie et al., 2019). In contrast, meta-heuristic methods, such as genetic algorithms (Elmaraghy et al., 2000;Qi et al., 2000;Zhang et al., 2013aZhang et al., , 2013b) ) and ant colony algorithms (Merkle et al., 2002;J. Zhang et al., 2013aJ. Zhang et al., , 2013b)), can explore nearoptimal schedules. However, the scheduling policies need to be retained if manufacturing settings are adjusted, and the time-consuming retraining might halt the whole manufacturing process (Al-Hinai & Elmekkawy, 2011;Gao et al., 2015). 

Reinforcement learning is a promising solution to dynamic scheduling problems (Heger & Voss, 2021;Jing et al., 2022;Kuhnle et al., 2021). Random job arrivals is addressed using multi-agent DQN (Johnson et al., 2022) by training with random job arrivals. A multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) approach has been proposed to manage scheduling processes with random processing time (Park et al., 2020). The randomness in setup time is addressed through MARL, with the goal of minimizing makespan (Oh et al., 2022). Stochastic processing times and unplanned machine breakdowns are tackled separately using dueling multi-agent reinforcement learning, which incorporates cooperation mechanisms to prevent conflicting operations (Qin et al., 2023).

Title: Digital Twin Based Optimization of a Manufacturing Execution System to Handle High Degrees of Customer Specifications
Snippet: Moving to single-piece flow and mass customization, this is further compounded through the increased variability of machining times. 

Within the highly variable production environment created by single-piece flows and mass customization, additional perturbations can be created. Some can be planned for, such as regular maintenance on the equipment in the machine park, and employees' holidays. These two events (one machine based, and one human based) create additional constraints on the system and the performance. These can, of course, be foreseen and planned for within the planning frames (annual, monthly, weekly, and daily). Additional complications are created by machine breakdowns and employees' illnesses [7]. These cannot be integrated into the planning frames as they are random events that cause replanning and rescheduling within the daily plan, although they have an impact on the system constraints for considerably longer. 

The concept of a digital twins offers new possibilities in the design, operation and optimization of production systems: using models of the systems dynamics and data structures, digital copies of physical systems can be created [8]. By synchronizing the two systems, one can exploit the benefits of both words [9]: the physical world, where the actual value-creation of the production system takes place, and the digital world, which enables fast optimization and analysis loops, whose results are later deployed to the physical system. It is thus a relevant question whether the aforementioned challenges of production planning can be helped by using a digital twin of the production system. Using two case studies, this paper addresses how to provide higher levels of certainty to the planning process to ensure that costs are minimized and lead times are achieved within the constraints of single piece flows and mass customizing using a digital twin. This has to both support individual orders and consider the existing production within the factory. The aim is to integrate an agile planning tool into the existing manufacturing execution system (MES) within the factory.

Title: Design of a Digital Twin in Low-Volume, High-Mix Job Allocation and Scheduling for Achieving Mass Personalization
Snippet: With the advent of Industry 4.0, manufacturers are shifting from mass production to mass customization, designing products to meet unique customer needs [1,2]. This shift begins with the new product development process. Mass production typically involves high-volume, low-variety manufacturing, while mass customization necessitates a low-volume, high-variety model that produces a broad array of tailor-made products in smaller quantities [3]. In order to meet the growing demand for bespoke products, manufacturers are transitioning from a high-volume, low-variety (HVLM) production model to a low-volume, high-variety (LVHM) model. This strategy allows manufacturers to concentrate on specific customer segments and offer a wide variety of product variations, enabling mass customization. Despite the significant challenges associated with this transition, manufacturers must be competitive and maintain a substantial market share in customized products. scaling up, enabling these companies to focus on core propositions and market development. Ultimately, the synergy between human expertise and the digital twin solution drives both operational excellence and social sustainability in the LVHM production landscape.

Ultimately, the synergy between human expertise and the digital twin solution drives both operational excellence and social sustainability in the LVHM production landscape. 

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 provides a literature review on LVHM production, as well as advanced simulation and optimization techniques. Section 3 elaborates on the proposed digital twin model with the ISOM. A case study involving the use of the proposed digital twin model to optimize job allocation and scheduling in the SMT production line for the PCBA process is presented in Section 4. Section 5 discusses the corresponding results and implementation to highlight the value of the proposed digital twin model. Finally, Section 6 draws the conclusion of this research.

Title: Design of a Digital Twin in Low-Volume, High-Mix Job Allocation and Scheduling for Achieving Mass Personalization
Snippet: The research identifies a significant gap in the transition from high-volume, low-variety (HVLM) production models to low-volume, high-variety (LVHM) models in the manufacturing industry, a shift necessitated by the increasing demand for bespoke, mass-customized products. From the extant literature, although there are a number of research studies about the job allocation and scheduling problem in the context of Industry 5.0 [33,34], the research on solving such problems in the LVHM production environment for promoting mass personalization is relatively limited. The challenge lies in managing new product introductions and small customer orders within high-volume production settings without impacting overall efficiency. Existing systems often overlook small-scale orders in favor of high-volume ones, leading to potential disappointment for new or smaller customers and misalignment with corporate strategies and marketing plans. The dynamic nature of the system and the complexity of the job allocation process under mass personalization initiatives further complicate the optimization process. Conventional optimization approaches, while effective, can be computationally demanding in such environments. 

In response to these challenges, research on the digital twin model in the LVHM production environment is urgently needed. This model, unlike traditional production optimization approaches that rely on specific system state assumptions, accommodates dynamic system states and offers optimal solutions through simulation analysis. The research is contextualized within the practical challenge of developing a low-volume, high-variety production workshop to provide manufacturing services to start-ups, a goal that aligns with government initiatives to commercialize research results. The research, therefore, seeks to fill the gap in understanding and implementing mass personalization strategies in line with Industry 5.0 within a low-volume, high-variety production context.

Title: Digital twin for product versus project lifecycles’ development in manufacturing and construction industries

Title: Design of a Digital Twin in Low-Volume, High-Mix Job Allocation and Scheduling for Achieving Mass Personalization

Moving to single-piece flow and mass customization, this is further compounded through the increased variability of machining times. 

Within the highly variable production environment created by single-piece flows and mass customization, additional perturbations can be created. Some can be planned for, such as regular maintenance on the equipment in the machine park, and employees' holidays. These two events (one machine based, and one human based) create additional constraints on the system and the performance. These can, of course, be foreseen and planned for within the planning frames (annual, monthly, weekly, and daily). Additional complications are created by machine breakdowns and employees' illnesses [7]. These cannot be integrated into the planning frames as they are random events that cause replanning and rescheduling within the daily plan, although they have an impact on the system constraints for considerably longer. 

The concept of a digital twins offers new possibilities in the design, operation and optimization of production systems: using models of the systems dynamics and data structures, digital copies of physical systems can be created [8]. By synchronizing the two systems, one can exploit the benefits of both words [9]: the physical world, where the actual value-creation of the production system takes place, and the digital world, which enables fast optimization and analysis loops, whose results are later deployed to the physical system. It is thus a relevant question whether the aforementioned challenges of production planning can be helped by using a digital twin of the production system. Using two case studies, this paper addresses how to provide higher levels of certainty to the planning process to ensure that costs are minimized and lead times are achieved within the constraints of single piece flows and mass customizing using a digital twin. This has to both support individual orders and consider the existing production within the factory. The aim is to integrate an agile planning tool into the existing manufacturing execution system (MES) within the factory.

snippet.text:
The research identifies a significant gap in the transition from high-volume, low-variety (HVLM) production models to low-volume, high-variety (LVHM) models in the manufacturing industry, a shift necessitated by the increasing demand for bespoke, mass-customized products. From the extant literature, although there are a number of research studies about the job allocation and scheduling problem in the context of Industry 5.0 [33,34], the research on solving such problems in the LVHM production environment for promoting mass personalization is relatively limited. The challenge lies in managing new product introductions and small customer orders within high-volume production settings without impacting overall efficiency. Existing systems often overlook small-scale orders in favor of high-volume ones, leading to potential disappointment for new or smaller customers and misalignment with corporate strategies and marketing plans. The dynamic nature of the system and the complexity of the job allocation process under mass personalization initiatives further complicate the optimization process. Conventional optimization approaches, while effective, can be computationally demanding in such environments. 

In response to these challenges, research on the digital twin model in the LVHM production environment is urgently needed. This model, unlike traditional production optimization approaches that rely on specific system state assumptions, accommodates dynamic system states and offers optimal solutions through simulation analysis. The research is contextualized within the practical challenge of developing a low-volume, high-variety production workshop to provide manufacturing services to start-ups, a goal that aligns with government initiatives to commercialize research results. The research, therefore, seeks to fill the gap in understanding and implementing mass personalization strategies in line with Industry 5.0 within a low-volume, high-variety production context.

Title: Lean Manual Assembly 4.0: A Systematic Review
Snippet: Mass customization demand is characterized by a combination of great variety, shorter product life cycles, and variable production volumes (medium or high for platform products, very low for personalized products); compared to Industry 2.0's stable market and Industry 3.0's volatile market-in terms of product volume, product variety and delivery time. In this new context, Toyota Production Systems (TPS) may prove limited, and its advantages and disadvantages with regards to seru were analyzed by Yin et al. [11]. The usage of new key digital technologies will bring forward the 4th Industrial Revolution (Industry 4.0), addressing many of the challenges of production systems for mass customization [11,12]. However, looking at isolated systems may not be enough since increased complexity requires a holistic approach to respond successfully and cost-effectively to shifting market demands [13]. Assembly is the final process to create a product, where component sub-assemblies come together into the final product. Demand-driven increasing product variety adds complexity, production cost and lead time to assembly operations, which goes against its goals. In the mass customization landscape, key assembly topics need to be reviewed, evaluated and adapted [2]: assembly representation and sequencing, especially non-sequential assembly; assembly system design-considering line balancing, delayed product differentiation and performance evaluation; assembly system operations-with a focus on exploring reconfigurable assembly planning, mixed-model assembly scheduling, and dealing with complexity resulting from different sources; and the changing role of human operators. In conclusion, mass customization brings increased complexity that needs to be addressed at multiple levels and taking a holistic point of view to ensure that optimizing a subsystem does not negatively affect another subsystem.

In this new context, Toyota Production Systems (TPS) may prove limited, and its advantages and disadvantages with regards to seru were analyzed by Yin et al. [11]. The usage of new key digital technologies will bring forward the 4th Industrial Revolution (Industry 4.0), addressing many of the challenges of production systems for mass customization [11,12]. However, looking at isolated systems may not be enough since increased complexity requires a holistic approach to respond successfully and cost-effectively to shifting market demands [13]. Assembly is the final process to create a product, where component sub-assemblies come together into the final product. Demand-driven increasing product variety adds complexity, production cost and lead time to assembly operations, which goes against its goals. In the mass customization landscape, key assembly topics need to be reviewed, evaluated and adapted [2]: assembly representation and sequencing, especially non-sequential assembly; assembly system design-considering line balancing, delayed product differentiation and performance evaluation; assembly system operations-with a focus on exploring reconfigurable assembly planning, mixed-model assembly scheduling, and dealing with complexity resulting from different sources; and the changing role of human operators. In conclusion, mass customization brings increased complexity that needs to be addressed at multiple levels and taking a holistic point of view to ensure that optimizing a subsystem does not negatively affect another subsystem.
