# Overview: What “open challenges” in fuzzing mean

Recent surveys and community discussions identify fuzzing challenges across technique design, deployment at scale, and evaluation reproducibility, spanning input generation, state management, and integration with static analysis or symbolic execution in both research and practice.<cite id="1342fe45-0">There have been multiple surveys tracing fuzzing’s evolution from 2017 onward, highlighting obstacles such as coverage-based guidance, input generation, and the integration of static/taint analysis, machine learning, and format-specific methods, along with dedicated surveys for embedded systems and ML-in-fuzzing<cite id="1342fe45-0">These surveys analyze gaps between the full input space and “defect space” and summarize open challenges and opportunities</cite><cite id="1342fe45-2">A Shonan meeting summary and follow-on survey explicitly catalog open challenges for fuzzing and symbolic execution from practitioner perspectives</cite>. In industry continuous integration, platforms like OSS-Fuzz often test drivers and system code in single-threaded modes due to practical difficulties, underscoring open problems in multithreaded fuzzing effectiveness and efficiency.<cite id="1342fe45-4">OSS-Fuzz tests driver programs in single-threaded mode because of fuzzing difficulty and inefficiency</cite><cite id="1342fe45-4">A dedicated grey-box fuzzing technique is needed for input-dependent and interleaving-dependent paths in multithreaded programs</cite>.

# Effectiveness across diverse targets and languages

A core challenge is that many fuzzers are tailored to specific formats (e.g., protocols, web browsers) or programming models, limiting generalizability and creating coverage gaps across real-world binaries and compiled artifacts.<cite id="1342fe45-0">Surveys document design decisions at each fuzzing stage and emphasize gaps between general input spaces and defect spaces across diverse targets</cite><cite id="1342fe45-1">Protocol fuzzing surveys discuss state-of-the-art techniques and open challenges in that domain</cite>. For WebAssembly (Wasm), cross-compiler and platform differences mean vulnerabilities may manifest only in certain compiled forms; moreover, binary-only analysis is common (third-party libraries or legacy code), yet Wasm lacks many of the oracles built into native fuzzing toolchains, requiring new instrumentation and oracles for memory safety.<cite id="6c037045-0">WebAssembly is a widely compiled target with low-level semantics and broad deployment (browsers, serverless, smart contracts), making its security highly relevant</cite><cite id="6c037045-1">A Wasm-focused fuzzer is desirable because targeting a specific source language covers only a fraction of real-world binaries; source may be unavailable and build/compiler constraints complicate adoption</cite><cite id="6c037045-1">Behavior in Wasm can differ from native compilation due to different mitigations and semantics, so fuzzing another platform is insufficient to expose Wasm-specific memory bugs</cite>. Recent work addresses these gaps by building binary-only Wasm fuzzers with instrumentation (e.g., canaries) and Wasm-specific coverage/oracles, demonstrating effective path exploration and crash discovery without source.<cite id="6c037045-3">A first binary-only greybox fuzzer for Wasm integrates AFL’s input generation with binary instrumentation that provides coverage and canaries, and a Wasm VM, showing effective path exploration and crashes in large Wasm binaries without source</cite><cite id="6c037045-3">Binaries hardened with canary instrumentation show low runtime overhead and thwart previously published exploits</cite>.

Mobile and GUI targets remain particularly difficult. Android system services and GUI applications are challenging: extracting interfaces for native services, instrumenting without source, and generating valid inputs for GUI event loops often require substantial engineering and special-purpose approaches.<cite id="95c97c9b-0">Fuzzing Android native system services requires extracting C++ interfaces and performing generative fuzzing; the approach identified dozens of vulnerabilities but is performance- and engineering-intensive</cite><cite id="95c97c9b-2">GUI applications are widely recognized as challenging for fuzzing; fuzzing with AFL++ “is not possible without modifying the source code,” motivating higher-level abstractions that can handle GUI and other difficult subjects</cite>. Specialized systems like Efuzz target program environments (including GUI and network services) to unify fuzzing across diverse user-mode targets, highlighting the need for general-purpose engines beyond traditional file/protocol fuzzers.<cite id="95c97c9b-2">Efuzz is designed to test a broad spectrum of user-mode programs, including GUI and network protocols, addressing the recognized challenge status of these targets and demonstrating feasibility where general fuzzers fail</cite>.

# State management, performance, and scaling

Fuzzing’s state explosion and performance bottlenecks persist, especially when coordinating multiple fuzzers or distributing workloads. Parallel and distributed fuzzing introduce task conflicts (duplicate mutations, redundant path executions), heavy synchronization overheads, and resource allocation trade-offs that reduce throughput and waste compute.<cite id="4702818a-2">In parallel/distributed fuzzing, absent global scheduling and timely synchronization leads to task conflicts and resource waste; even with shared seeds and scheduling, synchronization overhead grows with instances and must be carefully traded off against effectiveness</cite><cite id="4702818a-2">Computing power allocation across instances is another open challenge to optimize resource-saving in distributed fuzzing</cite>. Even in continuous fuzzing infrastructures, practical constraints lead to single-threaded testing for difficult targets, reflecting unresolved performance and correctness trade-offs in multithreaded settings.<cite id="1342fe45-4">OSS-Fuzz tests drivers in single-threaded mode due to fuzzing difficulty and inefficiency</cite>.

Protocol fuzzing engines (e.g., AFLNet and its successors) illustrate another scaling challenge: many network services are hard to fuzz with off-the-shelf engines, and specialized or hypervisors/VM-based approaches are needed to achieve acceptable coverage and throughput, yet compatibility and maintenance burdens remain.<cite id="95c97c9b-2">AFLNet is recommended for network services, but many ProFuzzBench subjects are incompatible with AFL++ and even hypervisor-based accelerations like Nyx-Net only work on a subset, indicating portability and coverage limits</cite><cite id="95c97c9b-2">Nyx-Net improves throughput via hypervisor-based snapshots, but compatibility gaps with common protocol subjects persist</cite>.

# Concurrency and multithreaded program fuzzing

A persistent open challenge is robustly exercising and detecting concurrency defects (races, deadlocks) and concurrency-dependent vulnerabilities in user-space multithreaded programs. General-purpose greybox fuzzers often cannot explore interleaving-induced states and thus miss a significant class of bugs; early community sentiment and industrial practice reflect this difficulty, with single-threaded testing adopted for safety.<cite id="4702818a-4">General greybox fuzzers are usually unaware of multithreading and cannot effectively explore interleaving-dependent states, leaving input- and interleaving-dependent bugs undetected</cite><cite id="4702818a-4">Industry practice in OSS-Fuzz tests drivers in single-threaded mode due to difficulty and inefficiency in fuzzing multithreaded code</cite>. Recent thread-aware techniques introduce instrumentations to distinguish thread interleavings, seed selection guided by concurrency feedback, and interleaving control mechanisms (priority manipulation, sleep injection, synchronization barriers), improving detection of race conditions and related vulnerabilities; yet, coverage remains limited and techniques vary in openness and scope.<cite id="4702818a-0">Thread-aware instrumentations and seed/execution optimization enable effective bug hunting in multithreaded programs, with new vulnerabilities and bugs reported</cite><cite id="4702818a-3">Existing concurrency-aware fuzzers differ in scope and openness; none fully open-source fuzzer meeting multi-vulnerability detection in user programs was found, motivating specialized approaches like interleaving control and thread-aware feedback</cite><cite id="4702818a-1">Datasets and thread-aware fuzzing approaches (e.g., MUZZ) have spurred reproducible research on concurrent applications, but the need for broader, standardized evaluations persists</cite>.

# Orchestration, collaboration, and evaluation

Combining multiple fuzzers and techniques (collaborative fuzzing) is promising but faces open problems in selecting complementary components, integrating heterogeneous feedback, and avoiding interference or redundancy.<cite id="1342fe45-3">Collaborative fuzzing (e.g., Enfuzz, Collabfuzz) coordinates multiple fuzzers to cover missed program spaces, but the main challenge is identifying the most effective combinations and avoiding conflicts when techniques are not orthogonal</cite>. Platform-level efforts like UNIFUZZ highlight the need for holistic, metrics-driven evaluation to address inconsistencies in benchmarks and reproducibility across studies, pointing to gaps in standardized metrics and fair comparison frameworks.<cite id="1342fe45-4">UNIFUZZ discusses issues in the current fuzzing research field and proposes a platform to evaluate fuzzers, indicating the importance of holistic and metrics-driven assessment</cite>.

# Specialized engines, input validity, and system targets

Many effective fuzzers target specific system-level constraints, such as protocol state machines or system call semantics, requiring specialized engines and validation oracles. For instance, protocol fuzzing engines for network services often build on VMs/hypervisors or tailored schedulers to achieve high coverage, while libFuzzer-style engines require validated inputs for system libraries; both approaches reflect open challenges in balancing generality with domain-specific constraints.<cite id="95c97c9b-2">Protocol fuzzers like AFLNet and Nyx-Net demonstrate specialized engines and hypervisor-based acceleration to achieve better coverage/throughput, yet compatibility and maintenance challenges remain</cite><cite id="6c037045-3">Wasm-focused binary instrumentation and VM integration provide coverage and oracles otherwise absent in native toolchains, enabling effective end-to-end fuzzing</cite>. For Android, both on-device and system-level fuzzing require careful interface identification, parameter mutation strategies, and instrumentation, with performance and engineering effort being substantial barriers to broad coverage.<cite id="95c97c9b-0">On Android, extracting interfaces for native system services and performing generative fuzzing is a core challenge; the approach is effective but performance- and engineering-intensive</cite><cite id="95c97c9b-4">An on-device Android fuzzing framework combines conventional Intent fuzzing with system API fuzzing via reflection, highlighting the need to identify exposed surfaces and mutate parameters effectively</cite>.

# Emerging directions: semantic guidance, AI/ML, and determinism

Semantic- and model-guided fuzzing (e.g., using ML for seed selection, corpus minimization, or coverage modeling) is an active area, but open challenges include ensuring safety/validity of generated inputs, integrating models with coverage feedback, and generalizing across diverse targets and languages.<cite id="1342fe45-0">Surveys of ML in fuzzing catalog applications to input generation, seed selection, and corpus minimization, while noting the need to study algorithms, preprocessing, datasets, and evaluation metrics for ML-based fuzzing</cite>. For WebAssembly, deterministic execution and instrumentation-based hardening/oracles show promise for reliable bug discovery and regression prevention, but balancing performance overheads and compatibility across compilers/platforms remains an open engineering problem.<cite id="6c037045-3">Binary instrumentation for canaries and coverage in Wasm enables effective fuzzing and hardening with low runtime overhead, demonstrating a viable path for deterministic-style defenses and testing</cite><cite id="6c037045-1">Differences in mitigation strategies across Wasm compilation targets and platforms complicate portability of fuzzing oracles and results</cite>.

# Practical adoption barriers and platform integration

Even with strong research advances, adoption in production CI/CD is hindered by target-specific constraints, seed engineering, and maintenance costs for specialized harnesses. Continuous fuzzing platforms adopt conservative defaults (e.g., single-threaded tests) when fuzzing multithreaded targets is difficult or slow, reflecting real-world risk management rather than optimal technical solutions.<cite id="1342fe45-4">OSS-Fuzz’s single-threaded testing practice for drivers illustrates risk-driven operational constraints when multithreaded fuzzing is difficult and inefficient</cite>. On mobile, effective fuzzing often requires deep platform knowledge for exposed components and system APIs, with on-device setups adding complexity around instrumentation and log capture; despite this, fuzzing remains an effective but resource-intensive pathway to discover vulnerabilities.<cite id="95c97c9b-0">Fuzzing Android native services is effective but performance- and engineering-intensive, emphasizing both opportunity and cost</cite><cite id="95c97c9b-4">On-device frameworks combine intent and system API fuzzing via reflection, illustrating practical integration patterns and constraints</cite>.

# Summary of open challenges

- Generalization across diverse targets and languages (e.g., Wasm binaries across compilers, GUI and protocol heterogeneity) and the lack of universal oracles.<cite id="6c037045-1">A fuzzer aimed at one source language covers only a fraction of Wasm binaries; source unavailability and build/compiler constraints complicate adoption</cite><cite id="95c97c9b-2">GUI applications are challenging for mainstream fuzzers, often requiring source modification or higher-level abstractions</cite>.
- State explosion, performance bottlenecks, and resource efficiency in parallel/distributed fuzzing, including task conflicts, synchronization overheads, and compute allocation.<cite id="4702818a-2">Task conflicts and synchronization overheads reduce resource efficiency in parallel/distributed fuzzing, with open problems in global scheduling and information sharing</cite>.
- Concurrency-aware fuzzing for multithreaded programs: exercising interleavings, detecting races and deadlocks, and doing so efficiently and at scale; current practice often defaults to single-threaded testing.<cite id="4702818a-4">General greybox fuzzers are unaware of multithreading and cannot explore interleaving-dependent states; OSS-Fuzz tests drivers in single-threaded mode due to difficulty and inefficiency</cite><cite id="4702818a-0">Thread-aware instrumentations and seed strategies improve detection of concurrency issues in real-world programs</cite>.
- Orchestration and collaborative fuzzing: selecting complementary techniques, integrating heterogeneous feedback, and avoiding interference or redundancy; standardized, holistic evaluation frameworks are still maturing.<cite id="1342fe45-3">Collaborative fuzzing aims to complement different fuzzers but faces challenges in choosing effective combinations and handling non-orthogonal techniques</cite><cite id="1342fe45-4">UNIFUZZ motivates metrics-driven, holistic evaluation to address field-wide issues</cite>.
- Specialized engines and input validity for system/protocol targets and embedded environments, with portability and maintenance costs; protocol fuzzing engines often require VM/hypervisor support and still face compatibility limits.<cite id="95c97c9b-2">AFLNet and Nyx-Net show specialized engines and accelerations, yet many subjects remain incompatible with mainstream fuzzers</cite><cite id="6c037045-3">Wasm-specific instrumentation and VM integration enable coverage/oracles otherwise absent in native toolchains</cite>.
- Adoption barriers and operational constraints in CI/CD and mobile platforms, where effective fuzzing requires substantial engineering and is resource-intensive, yet remains a key pathway for discovering real-world vulnerabilities.<cite id="95c97c9b-0">Fuzzing Android native services is effective but performance- and engineering-intensive</cite><cite id="1342fe45-4">OSS-Fuzz’s conservative single-threaded approach reflects unresolved practical challenges in multithreaded fuzzing</cite>.

These challenges are interrelated: advances in instrumentation and oracles (e.g., Wasm canaries) enable better state tracking; thread-aware feedback and interleaving control improve concurrency testing; and collaborative, metrics-driven evaluation frameworks can help compare and integrate heterogeneous techniques at scale.<cite id="6c037045-3">Binary instrumentation for canaries and coverage in Wasm supports effective fuzzing and hardening with low overhead</cite><cite id="4702818a-0">Thread-aware instrumentations and optimized seed/execution strategies improve detection of multithreading-relevant bugs and vulnerabilities</cite><cite id="1342fe45-4">Holistic, metrics-driven platforms like UNIFUZZ aim to address evaluation and reproducibility issues in the fuzzing research field</cite>.
</answer>

Title: The progress, challenges, and perspectives of directed greybox fuzzing
Snippet: Fuzzing surveys. So far there have been several surveys on fuzzing. As far as we can find, Fell 118 conducted the first review on fuzzing in 2017, which introduced the basic scheme of fuzzing and the existing tools on protocols fuzzing and web browser fuzzing. Li et al. presented an overview of fuzzing solutions by the year 2017 and discussed techniques that could make the fuzzing process smarter and more efficient, including static analysis, taint analysis, machine learning, and format method. Liang et al. 6 summarized 18 typical fuzzers ranging from 2004 to 2017. They discussed the key obstacles and some stateof-the-art technologies that aim to overcome or mitigate these obstacles. In 2019, Manès et al. 2 gave a detailed survey on 63 modern fuzzers. They explored the design decisions at every stage of fuzzing by surveying the related literature. Böhme et al. 119 summarized the open challenges and opportunities for fuzzing and symbolic execution as they emerged in discussions among researchers and practitioners in a Shonan Meeting. Finally, Zhu et al. 119 gave the most up-to-date survey on fuzzing to narrow down the gaps between the entire input space and the defect space. The survey reviews and analyzes the gaps as well as their solutions, considering both breadth and depth. In addition to surveys on common fuzzing, there are also surveys focused on subclasses of fuzzing. Eisele et al. reviewed the fuzzing approaches for embedded systems 120 . They gave a formal definition of embedded fuzzing and grouped the approaches according to how the execution environment is served to the system under test. Saavedra et al. 121 reviewed the machine learning applications in fuzzing, including deep learning, neural networks, and reinforcement learning. They discussed successful applications of machine learning to fuzzing, such as input generation, seed selection, and corpus minimization. Wang et al. also gave a review of fuzzing based on machine learning techniques 122 . They identified six different stages in which machine learning has been used and studied the machine learning-based fuzzing models from the selection of machine learning algorithm, pre-processing methods, datasets, evaluation metrics, and hyperparameters setting.

Snippet: One of our challenges is to identify the optimal fuzzer configuration from a vast array of techniques, and collaborative fuzzing -a method of coordinating multiple different fuzzers during testing -is a related area of interest. Enfuzz [15] and Collabfuzz [35] are the initial attempts to coordinate various types of fuzzers to enhance the results. The motivation behind these works is that when different fuzzers are combined and run together, the program space missed by one fuzzer can be covered and complemented by others. The main challenge of collaborative fuzzing is to identify the most effective combination of fuzzers to use. 

However, the ultimate goal of these collaborative fuzzing frameworks and our work differs. What collaborative fuzzing answers is the combination of pre-made fuzzers complementing each other when they are run together. On the other hand, our work aims to give the best choice of techniques to fuzz when you use a single fuzzer to fuzz. This is not what collaborative fuzzing answers for us. 

Additionally, we reiterate that the key differences that distinguishes our study from prior research is that prior studies employed fuzzers that do not share the same baseline. The fact that using fuzzers that cannot be decomposed into orthogonal approaches will mistify the individual contribution of its techniques.

documents.snippet:
One of our challenges is to identify the optimal fuzzer configuration from a vast array of techniques, and collaborative fuzzing -a method of coordinating multiple different fuzzers during testing -is a related area of interest. Enfuzz [15] and Collabfuzz [35] are the initial attempts to coordinate various types of fuzzers to enhance the results. The motivation behind these works is that when different fuzzers are combined and run together, the program space missed by one fuzzer can be covered and complemented by others. The main challenge of collaborative fuzzing is to identify the most effective combination of fuzzers to use. 

However, the ultimate goal of these collaborative fuzzing frameworks and our work differs. What collaborative fuzzing answers is the combination of pre-made fuzzers complementing each other when they are run together. On the other hand, our work aims to give the best choice of techniques to fuzz when you use a single fuzzer to fuzz. This is not what collaborative fuzzing answers for us. 

Additionally, we reiterate that the key differences that distinguishes our study from prior research is that prior studies employed fuzzers that do not share the same baseline. The fact that using fuzzers that cannot be decomposed into orthogonal approaches will mistify the individual contribution of its techniques.

Title: Fuzzm: Finding Memory Bugs through Binary-Only Instrumentation and Fuzzing of WebAssembly
Snippet: WebAssembly is an increasingly important bytecode language [20,55,56] with low-level semantics, fast execution, and a multitude of source languages compiling to it. It is widely supported in browsers 1 and used by diverse web applications [24], for "serverless" cloud computing [21,52], in smart contract platforms [23,36,46], to sandbox libraries in native applications [40,58], and even as a universal bytecode by standlone WebAssembly runtimes [1,2,13]. 

Given its importance, the security of WebAssembly is also becoming more and more relevant. While WebAssembly prevents some security issues by design, source-level vulnerabilities may still propagate to WebAssembly binaries [8,30,37]. 

Recent work [30] has shown that, surprisingly, memory vulnerabilities in WebAssembly binaries can sometimes be even more easily exploited than when the same source code is compiled to native architectures. One reason is the lack of mitigations, such as stack canaries, page protection flags, or hardened memory allocators [30]. 

To find vulnerabilities, greybox fuzzing has proven to be an effective technique [9,22,32,47,59]. For example, Google's OSS-Fuzz project has found thousands of vulnerabilities in widely used software [3,51]. A greybox fuzzer automatically generates inputs that explore the target program and eventually trigger a vulnerability. For that, it requires (i) lightweight feedback from the execution, e.g., coverage information, to guide the input generation, and (ii) runtime oracles that make a vulnerability apparent, e.g., by crashing the program. 

A greybox fuzzer for WebAssembly would be highly desirable, but several characteristics of WebAssembly must be taken into account. First, WebAssembly is a compilation target for multiple source languages, including C, C++, Rust, Go, and many others [24]. A fuzzer aimed at a specific source language hence could analyze only a fraction of all real-world binaries.

Title: Fuzzm: Finding Memory Bugs through Binary-Only Instrumentation and Fuzzing of WebAssembly
Snippet: A fuzzer aimed at a specific source language hence could analyze only a fraction of all real-world binaries. Second, the source code of a WebAssembly binary may not be available, e.g., when analyzing third-party websites, third-party libraries, or in-house legacy applications. Even if the source code is available, adopting a fuzzer into the development workflow is made harder if it requires changes to the build system, or specific (versions of) compilers. Third, even when compiling from the same source code, the securityrelevant behavior of a program compiled to WebAssembly may differ from the same program being compiled to native code [30]. As we illustrate in Section 3, whether a vulnerability can be exploited depends on how the semantics of the source language are compiled and which mitigations the target platform provides. As a result, fuzzing a program compiled for another platform, e.g., x86 [16], is insufficient to expose memory bugs in WebAssembly. Taken together, these characteristics motivate a fuzzer targeted at WebAssembly binaries. However, despite the overall success of greybox fuzzing and the increasing importance of WebAssembly, such a fuzzer currently does not exist. This paper presents Fuzzm 2 , the first binary-only greybox fuzzer for WebAssembly. Its main components, shown in Figure 1, address several interesting technical challenges. First, unlike native programs, WebAssembly lacks several builtin oracles that native fuzzers rely on for finding suspicious program behavior. For example, none of the current compilers targeting WebAssembly adds stack canaries [14,45], and due to WebAssembly's linear memory, overflows from, e.g., stack to heap data remain unnoticed [30]. While tools like AddressSanitizer [50] can instrument source code to detect memory-related misbehavior, they do not apply to binaries. Instead, our stack and heap canary instrumentation rewrites binaries to detect over-and underflows on the stack and heap.

Title: ESFuzzer: An Efficient Way to Fuzz WebAssembly Interpreter
Snippet: WebAssembly code is designed to run in a sandboxed environment, such as a web browser, providing a high level of security and isolation from the underlying operating system and hardware. This enables the execution of untrusted code in a web browser without compromising the security and integrity of the user’s system. This paper discusses the challenges associated with using fuzzing tools to identify vulnerabilities or bugs in WebAssembly interpreters. Our approach, known as ESFuzzer, introduces an efficient method for fuzzing WebAssembly interpreters using an Equivalent-Statement concept and the Stack Repair Algorithm. The samples generated by our approach successfully passed code validation. In addition, we developed effective mutation strategies to enhance the efficacy of our approach. ESFuzzer has demonstrated its ability to generate code that achieves 100% WebAssembly validation testing and achieves code coverage that is more than twice that of libFuzzer. Furthermore, the 24-h experiment results show that ESFuzzer performs ten times more efficiently than libFuzzer.

Title: Fuzzm: Finding Memory Bugs through Binary-Only Instrumentation and Fuzzing of WebAssembly
Snippet: • The first binary-only fuzzer for WebAssembly programs. 

• A binary instrumentation that inserts stack and heap canaries, which can be used to harden existing WebAssembly programs and as an oracle in our fuzzer (Section 4). • Integration of the AFL fuzzer and its tried-and-tested input generation, a binary-only instrumentation that provides compatible coverage information, and a WebAssembly VM, for efficient end-to-end fuzzing (Section 5). • Empirical evidence that Fuzzm effectively explores paths and finds crashes in well-known programs compiled to WebAssembly, and in large, real-world WebAssembly binaries without source code (Section 6), and • Empirical evidence that binaries hardened with our canary instrumentations run with low runtime overhead and effectively thwart previously published exploits (Section 6).

Title: Dynamic Security Analysis on Android: A Systematic Literature Review
Snippet: Liu et al. [81] developed a fuzzer, named Fans, for Android native system services. On Android, system services are mainly implemented in Java or C++ and we differentiate between native (implemented in C++) and normal system services (implemented in Java). One of the challenges Liu et al. address is how to extract the interfaces of native system services and perform generative fuzzing on these interfaces. Fans was able to identify 30 unique vulnerabilities in native system services during a 30 days fuzzing run. In addition, 138 unique Java exceptions were found, which could indicate further vulnerabilities. These results emphasis that fuzzing on Android is an effective but performance and engineering intense way of finding vulnerabilities.

Title: VLM-Fuzz: Vision Language Model Assisted Recursive Depth-first Search Exploration for Effective UI Testing of Android Apps
Snippet: This section introduces relevant background on Android UI fuzzing and its challenges.

Title: Program Environment Fuzzing
Snippet: Subject Programs. Efuzz is a generic fuzzer capable of testing a broad spectrum of user-mode programs in Linux. Given the scope of applications that Efuzz can fuzz, we shall focus on two core categories of program: network protocols and (Graphical) User Interface GUI/UI applications that interact with a human user via the windowing system or terminal. These two categories have been recognized as challenging for fuzzing [7]. For example, fuzzing GUI applications with AFL++ [1] is "not possible without modifying the source code". 3 Since Efuzz works at the abstraction of the kernel/user-mode boundary, it can fuzz GUI applications and other difficult subjects without special handling. By targeting challenging fuzzing targets, we aim to demonstrate the generality of Efuzz. 

In total, we collect 20 subjects as detailed in Table 1. For network protocols, we collect subjects from ProFuzzBench [27], a widelyused benchmarking platform for evaluating the network-enabled fuzzers. However, for GUI applications under Linux, there is no existing fuzzing dataset. We therefore select subjects from frequentlyused and well-known applications and frameworks, including text editors (UI), visual shells (UI), GNOME desktop environment (GUI), Qt (GUI), and the underlying windowing system (GUI). 

Comparisons. To the best of our knowledge, no existing fuzzers target the full program environment. In the realm of fuzzing network protocols, AFLNet is the first network fuzzer, and also recommended by AFL++ for fuzzing network services. Nyx-Net enhances the fuzzing throughput of AFLNet by introducing innovative hypervisor-based snapshots. Unfortunately, we cannot compare with AFL++ since it does not work on many of the network protocols. As shown in the paper of Nyx-Net [34], AFL++ only works on 5 of the ProFuzzBench subjects. Furthermore, for these 5 subjects, Performance Metrics. We evaluate the performance of Efuzz based on three primary metrics: bug-finding capability, code coverage, and fuzzing throughput.

Title: Fully automated functional fuzzing of Android apps for detecting non-crashing logic bugs
Snippet: We implemented Genie as an automated, end-to-end functional fuzzing tool for Android apps. Given an app as input, it outputs any likely distinct bug reports. Genie was built upon DroidBot [Li et al. 2017] and significantly extended Stoat's model mining algorithm [Su et al. 2017]. It was written in Python and JavaScript (5,671 lines of Python for the core algorithms; 1,035 lines of Python for parallel fuzzing, and 386 lines of JavaScript for bug report visualization). Specifically, it uses AccessibilityService [Accessibility 2020] to collect GUI layouts, the APTED algorithm [Pimentel 2020] to compute tree edit distance, ADB [ADB 2020] to send GUI events, including touch, long-touch, edit, and navigation (e.g., back, scroll). We have made Genie publicly available at https:// github.com/ functional-fuzzing-android-apps/ home.

Title: Understanding Android VoIP Security: A System-Level Vulnerability Assessment
Snippet: Fig. 4. The on-device fuzzing framework, with not only the conventional Intent fuzzing but also the creative system API fuzzing based on Java reflection. 

On-Device Fuzzing Framework. As shown in Fig. 4, we develop an on-device fuzzing framework based on Drozer [18]. We use a drozer console on PC to control the fuzzing process on a test phone via its drozer agent. We deliver fuzzing commands through Android's adb forward command and receive fuzzing logs through the adb logcat command. For both Intent and system API fuzzing, we perform these three steps: identifying exposed surfaces, mutating parameters, and recording logs. 

On-Device Intent Fuzzing. In the Intent fuzzing, exposed surfaces are VoIP apps' exported components that can be accessed by any other third-party apps on the same phone. We identify these exported components by analyzing component information in the app's AndroidManifest.xml file. To mutate Intent parameters, we try both empty (i.e., null) parameters and the parameters that satisfy a component's data schemes (e.g., content:// and vk.voip). 

On-Device System API Fuzzing. In the system API fuzzing, exposed surfaces are those unprotected system service interfaces. We identify them by using Java reflection to invoke Android ServiceManager's listServices function, which can list not only all the available system service interfaces but also their accepted parameter types. We then launch targeted fuzzing against these exposed service interfaces according to their parameter types.

On-Device Fuzzing Framework. As shown in Fig. 4, we develop an on-device fuzzing framework based on Drozer [18]. We use a drozer console on PC to control the fuzzing process on a test phone via its drozer agent. We deliver fuzzing commands through Android's adb forward command and receive fuzzing logs through the adb logcat command. For both Intent and system API fuzzing, we perform these three steps: identifying exposed surfaces, mutating parameters, and recording logs. 

On-Device Intent Fuzzing. In the Intent fuzzing, exposed surfaces are VoIP apps' exported components that can be accessed by any other third-party apps on the same phone. We identify these exported components by analyzing component information in the app's AndroidManifest.xml file. To mutate Intent parameters, we try both empty (i.e., null) parameters and the parameters that satisfy a component's data schemes (e.g., content:// and vk.voip). 

On-Device System API Fuzzing. In the system API fuzzing, exposed surfaces are those unprotected system service interfaces. We identify them by using Java reflection to invoke Android ServiceManager's listServices function, which can list not only all the available system service interfaces but also their accepted parameter types. We then launch targeted fuzzing against these exposed service interfaces according to their parameter types.

documents.title: Dynamic Security Analysis on Android: A Systematic Literature Review
documents.snippet: Liu et al. [81] developed a fuzzer, named Fans, for Android native system services. On Android, system services are mainly implemented in Java or C++ and we differentiate between native (implemented in C++) and normal system services (implemented in Java). One of the challenges Liu et al. address is how to extract the interfaces of native system services and perform generative fuzzing on these interfaces. Fans was able to identify 30 unique vulnerabilities in native system services during a 30 days fuzzing run. In addition, 138 unique Java exceptions were found, which could indicate further vulnerabilities. These results emphasis that fuzzing on Android is an effective but performance and engineering intense way of finding vulnerabilities.

Subject Programs. Efuzz is a generic fuzzer capable of testing a broad spectrum of user-mode programs in Linux. Given the scope of applications that Efuzz can fuzz, we shall focus on two core categories of program: network protocols and (Graphical) User Interface GUI/UI applications that interact with a human user via the windowing system or terminal. These two categories have been recognized as challenging for fuzzing [7]. For example, fuzzing GUI applications with AFL++ [1] is "not possible without modifying the source code". 3 Since Efuzz works at the abstraction of the kernel/user-mode boundary, it can fuzz GUI applications and other difficult subjects without special handling. By targeting challenging fuzzing targets, we aim to demonstrate the generality of Efuzz. 

In total, we collect 20 subjects as detailed in Table 1. For network protocols, we collect subjects from ProFuzzBench [27], a widelyused benchmarking platform for evaluating the network-enabled fuzzers. However, for GUI applications under Linux, there is no existing fuzzing dataset. We therefore select subjects from frequentlyused and well-known applications and frameworks, including text editors (UI), visual shells (UI), GNOME desktop environment (GUI), Qt (GUI), and the underlying windowing system (GUI). 

Comparisons. To the best of our knowledge, no existing fuzzers target the full program environment. In the realm of fuzzing network protocols, AFLNet is the first network fuzzer, and also recommended by AFL++ for fuzzing network services. Nyx-Net enhances the fuzzing throughput of AFLNet by introducing innovative hypervisor-based snapshots. Unfortunately, we cannot compare with AFL++ since it does not work on many of the network protocols. As shown in the paper of Nyx-Net [34], AFL++ only works on 5 of the ProFuzzBench subjects. Furthermore, for these 5 subjects, Performance Metrics. We evaluate the performance of Efuzz based on three primary metrics: bug-finding capability, code coverage, and fuzzing throughput.

documents.title: Fully automated functional fuzzing of Android apps for detecting non-crashing logic bugs
documents.snippet: We implemented Genie as an automated, end-to-end functional fuzzing tool for Android apps. Given an app as input, it outputs any likely distinct bug reports. Genie was built upon DroidBot [Li et al. 2017] and significantly extended Stoat's model mining algorithm [Su et al. 2017]. It was written in Python and JavaScript (5,671 lines of Python for the core algorithms; 1,035 lines of Python for parallel fuzzing, and 386 lines of JavaScript for bug report visualization). Specifically, it uses AccessibilityService [Accessibility 2020] to collect GUI layouts, the APTED algorithm [Pimentel 2020] to compute tree edit distance, ADB [ADB 2020] to send GUI events, including touch, long-touch, edit, and navigation (e.g., back, scroll). We have made Genie publicly available at https:// github.com/ functional-fuzzing-android-apps/ home.

Title: MUZZ: Thread-aware Grey-box Fuzzing for Effective Bug Hunting in Multithreaded Programs
Snippet: We detect them by replaying the seeds generated by MUZZ with stateof-the-art concurrency-bug detectors such as TSan. Note that B m may not be revealed during fuzzing since they do not necessarily result in memory corruption crashes. In the remaining sections, when referring to multithreading-relevant bugs, we always mean the combination of concurrency-bugs and concurrency-vulnerabilities, i.e., V m ∪ B m . 

We summarize the contributions of our work as follows: 1) We develop three novel thread-aware instrumentations for grey-box fuzzing that can distinguish the execution states caused by thread-interleavings. 

2) We optimize seed selection and execution strategies based on the runtime feedback provided by the instrumentations, which help generate more effective seeds concerning the multithreading context. 

3) We integrate these analyses into MUZZ for an effective bug hunting in multithreaded programs. Experiments on 12 realworld programs show that MUZZ outperforms other fuzzers like AFL and MOPT in detecting concurrency-vulnerabilities and revealing concurrency-bugs. 4) MUZZ detected 8 new concurrency-vulnerabilities and 19 new concurrency-bugs, with 4 CVE IDs assigned. Considering the small portion of concurrency-vulnerabilities recorded in the CVE database, the results are promising.

Title: UltraFuzz: Towards Resource-Saving in Distributed Fuzzing
Snippet: Parallel fuzzing first evolves from a naive method, i.e., the parallel mode of AFL (i.e., AFL-P), which simply runs multiple fuzzer instances with the same target simultaneously. Each instance of AFL binds a core and periodically re-scans the top-level sync directory for any test cases found in other instances. Multi-core parallel fuzzing represents the evolution of the naive method. However, the parallelism at this stage is limited by intra-machine. Distributed fuzzing [30,31] extends intra-machine parallelism to multiple machines connected by a network, allowing using more computing resources. Then, the researcher takes a step further by sharing seeds between fuzzer instances. In this mode, the program starts to schedule tasks between fuzzing instances to alleviate task conflicts [32,33]. To optimize parallel fuzzing towards resource-saving, we still need to overcome the following technical challenges. 

(1) Task conflicts. In parallel fuzzing, owing to the absence of global scheduling and timely update of fuzzing information among the instances, different fuzzing instances may mutate the same seeds or generate redundant test cases that execute the same path, causing task conflicts, which will lead to a severe waste of testing resources. Though some tools, such as P-fuzz [32] and PAFL [33], try to synchronize fuzzing information among fuzzing instances, a centralized scheduling scheme is still required to optimize parallel fuzzing from a global perspective. 

(2) Synchronization overhead. In parallel fuzzing, various fuzzing information can be shared among fuzzing instances to increase performance, such as seeds, coverage, hangs, and crashes. However, the synchronization overhead inevitably deducts the performance, and such deduction becomes more severe as instances increase. Thus, what information to share and how to share it is critical, especially in a distributed environment. To alleviate performance deduction and improve resource efficiency, some approaches [30][31][32]34] adopt periodical synchronization to achieve a tradeoff between effectiveness and efficiency. However, timely updating of fuzzing status is critical to avoid task conflict. 

(3) Computing power allocation.

Title: Combining BMC and Fuzzing Techniques for Finding Software Vulnerabilities in Concurrent Programs
Snippet: Here, we organize these past efforts according to five categories in the taxonomy of Table I. The first three categories concern the usability of each fuzzer: whether they apply to user programs or operating system code (Scope), which type of bugs they are able to detect (Vulnerabilities), and whether their code is easily accessible (Open Source). In this regard, none of the existing state-of-the-art fuzzers satisfy our research requirements. That is, there is no fully open-source fuzzer that can detect multiple concurrency vulnerabilities in user programs. We address this gap by introducing our own concurrency-aware fuzzer in Section IV. 

The last two categories concern the fuzzing techniques themselves. Specifically, the general fuzzing strategy in Algorithm 1 requires some adaptations to produce good results on concurrent programs. First and foremost, a mechanism to force the execution of a large number of different interleaving is required (Interleaving Control). Existing fuzzers like MUZZ [23] and ConAFL [34] manipulate the thread priorities at assembly level, others like Krace [44] inject sleep instruction to force a context switch, while AutoInter-fuzzing [42] and Conzzer [45] instrument the code with explicit synchronization barriers or thread locks. Alternatively, the interleaving exploration can be left to the natural non-determinism of the operating system like in ConFuzz [43]. Lastly, some authors propose to change the feedback to the input mutation engine in an attempt to guide the fuzzer towards more interesting interleavings (Mutation Feedback). We mark such attempts as Thread-Aware as opposed to the default Branch Coverage metrics used in sequential fuzzing. We provide more information on these state-of-the-art fuzzers in Section VII-B.

Title: MUZZ: Thread-aware Grey-box Fuzzing for Effective Bug Hunting in Multithreaded Programs
Snippet: Despite the great success of GBFs in detecting vulnerabilities, there are few efforts on fuzzing user-space multithreaded programs. General-purpose GBFs usually cannot explore thread-interleaving introduced execution states due to their unawareness of multithreading. Therefore, they cannot effectively detect concurrency-vulnerabilities inherently buried in sophisticated program flows [30]. In a discussion in 2015 [64], the author of AFL, Michal Zalewski, even suggests that "it's generally better to have a single thread". In fact, due to the difficulty and inefficiency, the fuzzing driver programs in Google's continuous fuzzing platform OSS-fuzz are all tested in single-threaded mode [15]. Also, by matching unions of keyword patterns "race*", "concurren*" and "thread*" in the MITRE CVE database [48], we found that only 202 CVE records are relevant to concurrency-vulnerabilities out of the 70438 assigned CVE IDs ranging from CVE-2014-* to CVE-2018-*. In particular, we observed that, theoretically, at most 4 CVE records could be detected by grey-box fuzzers that work on user-space programs. 

As a result, there are no practical fuzzing techniques to test input-dependent user-space multithreaded programs and detect bugs or vulnerabilities inside them. To this end, we present a dedicated grey-box fuzzing technique, MUZZ, to reveal bugs by exercising input-dependent and interleavingdependent paths. We categorize the targeted multithreadingrelevant bugs into two major groups: 

• concurrency-vulnerabilities (V m ): they correspond to memory corruption vulnerabilities that occur in a multithreading context. These vulnerabilities can be detected during the fuzzing phase. • concurrency-bugs (B m ): they correspond to the bugs like data-races, atomicity-violations, deadlocks, etc. We detect them by replaying the seeds generated by MUZZ with stateof-the-art concurrency-bug detectors such as TSan.

problem: Explainable AI on Sentimental Analysis
final_response:
# Explainable AI for Sentiment Analysis: Why It Matters, How It Works, and How to Evaluate It

## 1) Why XAI is critical for sentiment analysis
Sentiment analysis models increasingly drive high-stakes decisions in customer support, finance, politics, and social services, but many state-of-the-art systems are based on deep neural networks that are hard to audit and inspect, limiting trust and accountability, especially under regulations like the GDPR’s “right to explanation.” <cite id="bbed8d5a-0">The reduced explainability of deep models used for sentiment analysis is a recognized barrier to adoption</cite> and integrating XAI can improve both transparency and model performance by surfacing decision factors and enabling targeted debugging. <cite id="bbed8d5a-3">In one study using a fine-tuned GPT-2 for sentiment analysis of ME vulnerabilities, the model achieved 72.88% congruence with human labels overall and 85.7% accuracy in a language domain, illustrating both the potential utility and the need for interpretability to align with human judgments</cite>. <cite id="bbed8d5a-4">As LLMs become dominant for sentiment tasks, their “black-box” nature heightens the need for user-oriented explainability to foster trust and make outputs actionable</cite>.

## 2) XAI methods for sentiment: categories and representative techniques
XAI approaches for sentiment fall into two broad categories: post-hoc, model-agnostic explainers; and model-specific mechanisms built into architectures. Below are widely used families with examples and typical uses.

### 2.1 Post-hoc, model-agnostic explanations (text-focused)
- Local perturbation and surrogate modeling: LIME creates local surrogate models and highlights the features most influential for a prediction; in sentiment, this surfaces key words driving positive/negative/neutral labels. <cite id="bbed8d5a-1">LIME and SHAP have been applied to sentiment models to reveal which features drive predictions, with SHAP providing more stable attributions across instances</cite>. <cite id="00918d34-0">LIME approximates a complex classifier locally and identifies impactful words for sentiment decisions</cite>.
- Gradient-based and unified attribution: Methods like Integrated Gradients (IG), DeepLIFT, and LRP compute feature relevance from model gradients or decompositions; SHAP is often positioned as a unifying framework that connects LIME, LRP, and DeepLIFT through Shapley value concepts. <cite id="00918d34-2">SHAP is considered a gold standard due to its theoretical grounding and broad applicability; it unifies LIME, LRP, and DeepLIFT and extends to phrase/hierarchical interactions</cite>. <cite id="00918d34-3">Recent sentiment studies use combinations of gradients (IG), LRP, and KernelSHAP to explain BERT-based sentiment classifiers</cite>.
- Model-agnostic instance-level and global explanations: LIME and KernelSHAP are commonly used to produce instance-level heatmaps and global feature contribution rankings for sentiment. <cite id="00918d34-1">In a multilingual finance-oriented setup, LIME heatmaps and SHAP word contributions were integrated to explain BERT predictions across Sinhala, English, and code-mixed content</cite>.
- Practical coverage and limitations: While useful, explainers for real-world text are still limited; many studies focus on benchmark datasets rather than production scenarios. <cite id="00918d34-0">Despite widespread use, there is limited research applying LIME/SHAP to sentiment in real-world app-review settings, highlighting an opportunity gap</cite>.

### 2.2 Model-specific mechanisms that add interpretability
- Attention in RNNs and Transformers: Attention weights in BiLSTM/GRU and BERT can highlight words or spans driving sentiment; these mechanisms are widely adopted in sentiment models. <cite id="961823a4-0">Attention-enhanced BiLSTM/GRU and BERT models are used to focus on words with sentiment tendencies, improving classification while providing attention-based salience for explanation</cite>. <cite id="961823a4-1">BERT’s self-attention assigns importance to words to capture context, which is valuable for sentiment analysis and topic modeling</cite>. <cite id="961823a4-2">Attention has been added to RNN-based sentiment methods to model connections between words and targets, and BERT has become a state-of-the-art, interpretable backbone via attention</cite>.
- Prototype-based and rule-like explanations: Prototype methods present representative examples per class (e.g., positive/negative) and the features used to classify them, improving interpretability for non-technical users compared to raw attention weights. <cite id="961823a4-3">Prototype-based DNNs argue for visualizing reasoning via prototypes; attention alone is sometimes controversial and geared toward expert users</cite>.
- Context decomposition and hierarchical explanations: Methods that decompose model predictions into words and phrases can reveal contrasting sentiments or contributing n-grams. <cite id="961823a4-3">Context decomposition methods (e.g., Murdoch et al.) analyze LSTM predictions by identifying words/phrases of contrasting sentiment and how they combine into the final prediction</cite>.
- Critical perspective on attention: Although popular, attention weights do not always correspond to human-intuitive explanations and can be misinterpreted; this motivates combining attention with post-hoc methods or prototype rationales. <cite id="961823a4-3">Research has questioned attention as a faithful explanation for non-technical users, noting controversies and the need for more interpretable, user-centered approaches</cite>.

## 3) Evaluating explanations: faithfulness, plausibility, and user studies
Faithfulness and plausibility are central to assessing explanation quality in sentiment analysis. Faithfulness measures whether explanations reflect the model’s actual decision process, while plausibility measures whether explanations align with human understanding.

- Faithfulness metrics and perturbation-based tests: Activation patching and perturbation-based evaluations probe whether changing explained features changes predictions, testing whether explanations support the model’s behavior. <cite id="cd7049e5-0">Recent work argues that many faithfulness tests focus on consistency under perturbations rather than true reflection of internal reasoning; activation analyses can assess whether explanations support the explained answer</cite>. <cite id="cd7049e5-1">Metrics like Faithfulness Violation Test assess importance–polarity consistency and correlation with probability change, complementing traditional faithfulness evaluations</cite>.
- Faithfulness vs. model architecture and explainers: Empirical comparisons show architecture and explainer choice influence faithfulness. <cite id="cd7049e5-2">A sentiment dataset study found that model architecture (simpler LSTM vs. complex transformers) and explainer type affect faithfulness, with attention-based interpretations often ranking highest, and model-specific designs (e.g., SKEP incorporating sentiment knowledge) improving faithfulness under some methods</cite>. <cite id="cd7049e5-2">Plausibility trends differed: LIME consistently outperformed other methods on plausibility, while attention-based explanations performed worst in that study, and there was a gap between model accuracy and plausibility</cite>.
- Plausibility and user-centric evaluation: When gold rationales are unavailable, user studies and plausibility metrics can complement faithfulness measures. <cite id="cd7049e5-4">A user-centric evaluation introduced plausibility, coherence, and perfidiousness metrics for natural language explanations in sentiment analysis and offensive language detection, using user studies to assess how well explanations convinced and aligned with text</cite>.
- Benchmarks and datasets for explainable sentiment: New datasets explicitly support evaluation of interpretability and fairness. <cite id="cd7049e5-2">A sentiment dataset evaluates multiple models with different interpretation methods under faithfulness and plausibility criteria</cite>. <cite id="cd7049e5-3">TeSent introduces a large Telugu sentiment dataset with human-annotated rationales and models trained with and without rationales to support explainability and fairness evaluation in low-resource languages</cite>. <cite id="cd7049e5-1">Benchmarks like ERASER include document labels and human-recognized explanation snippets, enabling rationale-based evaluation when ground truth rationales exist</cite>.

## 4) Domain-specific and multilingual considerations
XAI for sentiment must address language, domain, and social context to be actionable.

- Finance and risk: Multilingual XAI can align with domain policies and mitigate bias. <cite id="00918d34-1">A financial services study combined SHAP/LIME with BERT to explain sentiment across Sinhala, English, and code-mixed content, used aspect-based sentiment to focus on banking services, and reviewed SHAP/LIME outputs to ensure consistency and proportional class representation to mitigate bias</cite>.
- Politics and social media: Political sentiment analysis requires explainability to interpret trends and support transparency. <cite id="bbed8d5a-2">A Bengali political sentiment dataset highlights future work on applying LIME/SHAP and exploring GPT/ Claude LLMs to analyze political sentiment with explainability, including reasoning about causes and handling explicit/implicit opinions</cite>.
- Socio-technical applications: XAI can bridge model predictions and human judgments in sensitive domains. <cite id="bbed8d5a-3">In analyzing ME vulnerabilities with a fine-tuned GPT-2, XAI-supported sentiment analysis achieved 72.88% congruence with human labels and domain-specific accuracy of 85.7%, offering a template for aligning AI and human assessments</cite>.
- Multilingual and low-resource settings: New benchmarks emphasize explainability and fairness in under-studied languages. <cite id="cd7049e5-3">TeSent provides a 21,119-instance Telugu dataset with human rationales and multiple fine-tuned models to assess explainability and fairness in a language with limited prior evaluation</cite>.

## 5) Common pitfalls and what to look out for
Several issues recur when applying XAI to sentiment, and diagnostics can guide method selection.

- Sarcasm, irony, and code-switching: These phenomena can confound feature attribution and attention, producing misleading “explanations” that highlight cues with opposite polarity. XAI pipelines should include human-in-the-loop review and domain-specific lexicons. <cite id="bbed8d5a-0">Surveys emphasize that explainability challenges are heightened in customer-facing sentiment tasks where context and tone are critical</cite>. <cite id="00918d34-1">In code-mixed and short texts, LIME heatmaps and SHAP contributions require manual review to validate consistency and mitigate bias</cite>.
- Attention as a proxy: Attention weights may not reflect true decision factors; combining attention with post-hoc attribution and prototype examples provides a more robust view. <cite id="961823a4-3">Research has questioned the interpretability of attention for non-experts and noted controversies about attention being a valid explanation</cite>.
- Plausibility–accuracy gap: Models can be accurate yet produce implausible explanations, and vice versa. <cite id="cd7049e5-2">Studies observe a gap between model accuracy and plausibility, with LIME often improving plausibility but attention-based explanations sometimes performing worse on plausibility</cite>.
- Evaluation limits: When gold rationales are absent, faithfulness testing must rely on perturbations and user studies, which can be noisy. <cite id="cd7049e5-1">Existing faithfulness tests may not fully capture whether explanations mirror internal reasoning; activation-based analyses and metrics that combine importance correlation and polarity consistency can help</cite>. <cite id="cd7049e5-4">User studies provide practical feedback on plausibility and coherence but require careful design to avoid bias</cite>.

## 6) A practical XAI workflow for sentiment analysis
Putting these insights together, a pragmatic workflow is:

1) Choose a model class and baseline: Start with an interpretable backbone (e.g., attention-enabled BiLSTM/GRU or BERT) for strong accuracy and a natural source of attention weights. <cite id="961823a4-0">Attention-enhanced RNNs and BERT are widely used for sentiment and provide inherent salience signals</cite>.
2) Add post-hoc attribution: Layer on SHAP (global and local) and IG/DeepLIFT/LRP to cross-validate feature importance and capture interactions at word/phrase level. <cite id="00918d34-2">SHAP’s unifying theory and extensions to phrases/interactions provide robust, model-agnostic attributions</cite>. <cite id="00918d34-3">IG/LRP/KernelSHAP are common in BERT-based sentiment explanations</cite>.
3) Generate instance-level and global views: Use LIME for instance-level heatmaps and SHAP global contributions; consider prototype examples per sentiment to make non-technical users more comfortable. <cite id="961823a4-3">Prototype-based explanations can improve intuitive interpretability compared to raw attention</cite>. <cite id="00918d34-1">In multilingual settings, combine LIME heatmaps and SHAP contributions with aspect-based breakdowns</cite>.
4) Evaluate faithfulness and plausibility: 
- Use perturbation-based tests and activation patching where possible; compute importance–polarity and behavior consistency. <cite id="cd7049e5-0">Activation patching assesses whether explanations support the model’s answers</cite>. <cite id="cd7049e5-1">Metrics that combine importance–probability correlation and polarity consistency help quantify faithfulness</cite>.
- Compare methods on your dataset for faithfulness and plausibility; expect trade-offs (e.g., LIME better plausibility, attention sometimes lower plausibility). <cite id="cd7049e5-2">Empirical comparisons show architecture and explainer choice affect faithfulness and plausibility, with LIME often outperforming others on plausibility</cite>.
- When gold rationales are absent, run user studies to measure plausibility, coherence, and perfidiousness (faithfulness to alternative labels). <cite id="cd7049e5-4">User-centric metrics and studies can evaluate natural language explanations in the absence of gold rationales</cite>.
5) Address domain and language constraints: Curate domain-specific lexicons, review code-mixed inputs, and ensure balanced, representative data to reduce bias. <cite id="00918d34-1">Manual review of SHAP/LIME outputs and balanced class distribution help mitigate bias in multilingual finance sentiment</cite>. <cite id="cd7049e5-3">Use datasets and models designed for explainability and fairness in low-resource languages like Telugu</cite>.
6) Iterate and monitor: Continuously audit explanations for sarcasm/irony and domain shifts; update models and explanations as policies and data change. <cite id="bbed8d5a-0">Surveys emphasize that explainability must be integrated into the development lifecycle to address DL model limitations in sentiment analysis</cite>.

## 7) Key takeaways
- XAI is essential for sentiment analysis to meet regulatory, trust, and governance needs, and can also improve model performance and diagnostic capability. <cite id="bbed8d5a-0">Explainability is a core barrier to adopting deep sentiment models</cite> and <cite id="bbed8d5a-3">auditing against human labels can reveal gaps and areas for improvement</cite>.
- Combine model-specific mechanisms (e.g., attention in BERT/RNNs) with post-hoc attribution (SHAP/LIME/IG/LRP) and prototype explanations to provide multiple, complementary views. <cite id="961823a4-0">Attention enhances both performance and local salience</cite>; <cite id="00918d34-2">SHAP/LIME/DeepLIFT/LRP offer robust, model-agnostic attributions and interaction-aware explanations</cite>; <cite id="961823a4-3">prototype methods can make explanations more accessible to non-experts</cite>.
- Evaluate faithfulness and plausibility with perturbation and activation-based tests, rationale metrics when available, and user studies; expect trade-offs and plan for continuous auditing. <cite id="cd7049e5-0">Activation patching provides insight into whether explanations support the model’s answers</cite>, <cite id="cd7049e5-2">architecture and explainer choice shape faithfulness and plausibility</cite>, and <cite id="cd7049e5-4">user studies offer practical plausibility and coherence assessments</cite>.
- Tailor XAI to domain and language constraints, including finance, politics, and multilingual/low-resource settings, using aspect-based explanations and manual review to handle code-mixing and bias. <cite id="00918d34-1">Finance and multilingual use cases benefit from SHAP/LIME with aspect-based breakdowns and manual validation</cite>, and <cite id="cd7049e5-3">new benchmarks like TeSent support explainability and fairness in Telugu</cite>.

By integrating these methods and evaluations into the sentiment analysis pipeline, practitioners can deliver models that are not only accurate but also transparent, auditable, and aligned with human expectations.

Explainability (Arrieta et al., 2020;Ali et al., 2023;Longo et al., 2024) can be considered an essential component of artificial intelligence. The following definition, proposed in (Arrieta et al., 2020), considers the two fundamental elements when we discuss explanations: understanding and audience. 

Given an audience, an explainable AI (XAI) is one that produces details or reasons to make its functioning clear or easy to understand. 

Today we can find a vast literature with different technical approximations to produce explanations for different AI systems. This research area, widely known as Explainable AI (XAI), has grown exponentially in the last few years, leading to recent discussions on its maturity and challenges (Ali et al., 2023;Longo et al., 2024). Title: Towards Faithful Natural Language Explanations: A Study Using Activation Patching in Large Language Models
Snippet: The advent of Large Language Models (LLMs) has revolutionized the field of Natural Language Processing (NLP), enabling machines to perform considerably well across a wide array of tasks ranging from commonsense reasoning (Achiam et al., 2023) to producing high-quality training data (Yeo et al., 2024). Moreover, LLMs can generate highly plausible Natural Language Explanations (NLE) to support their answer, such as adopting the Chainof-Thought (CoT) prompting method (Wei et al., 2022). Despite their apparent sophistication, the trustworthiness of these explanations is not guaranteed and their underlying faithfulness (Jie et al., 2024) should be carefully scrutinized. 

However, it is unclear amongst the existing approaches (Atanasova et al., 2023;Lanham et al., 2023;Wiegreffe et al., 2020;Parcalabescu and Frank, 2023), which is best suited for measuring faithfulness. A commonly referenced definition of faithfulness follows as such: "The faithfulness of an interpretation is a measure of how well it accurately reflects the underlying reasoning process of the model" (Jacovi and Goldberg, 2020). Following this definition, we can be certain that a truly faithful explanation leads to goals such as instilling trust (Cambria et al., 2023;Yeo et al., 2023) in the receiving audience or enabling actionable insights given the information revealed by the explanation. 

A recent work, Parcalabescu and Frank (2023) argues that existing faithfulness tests are not designed to measure the faithfulness under the referenced definition, but rather the ability of models to return consistent answers under various perturbed settings. Albeit these tests are still considered valid, the findings of these tests may be unreliable and inconsistent across different benchmarks. In this work, we study the internal computations of the model to assess the level of faithfulness of an explanation in supporting the explained answer.
</snippet>

Title: TeSent: A Benchmark Dataset for Fairness-aware Explainable Sentiment Classification in Telugu
Snippet: Although, several benchmarks are available for fairness evaluation in sentiment classification for English and other resource friendly languages (Díaz et al., 2018;Thelwall, 2018;Kiritchenko and Mohammad, 2018;Goldfarb-tarrant et al., 2023), no real initiative for the same has been taken for Telugu and other Indic languages. 

Explainability has become a critical pillar in machine learning research, driven by the increasing need for transparency, accountability, and human trust in AI systems-especially in high-stakes domains and under regulatory frameworks such as the GDPR's "right to explanation" (European Parliament and Council of the European Union). A class of explainability methods, known as post-hoc explainers, has gained popularity for auditing model behavior with respect to predictions (Bhatt et al., 2020). However, the effectiveness of such explainers remains dependent on two key properties (Lyu et al., 2024): faithfulness, which measures how accurately an explanation reflects the model's true reasoning process; and plausibility, which assesses how well the explanation aligns with human intuition and understanding. Sentiment classification models are increasingly being deployed in highstakes decision making systems which have significant social and economic impact (Du et al., 2024). There is a pressing need for sentiment classification benchmarks to assess explainability aspects, and for datasets to be curated in a manner that facilitates such evaluation-an area that existing benchmarks, particularly for Telugu and other low-resource languages, have largely ignored.

Title: A Multi-Task Text Classification Pipeline with Natural Language Explanations: A User-Centric Evaluation in Sentiment Analysis and Offensive Language Identification in Greek Tweets
Snippet: As the proposed pipeline consists of two models, each accomplishing a different task, we evaluate each model separately. Additionally, since the tasks of sentiment analysis and offensive language identification have gold standard annotations in the dataset, our user-centred study is focused only on evaluating the second part of the pipeline, namely the generated explanations, for which no ground truth rationales are available. To that end, we used the F1-Score and Balanced Accuracy metrics to evaluate the performance of the classifier part of the pipeline, while for the explanation generator, we conducted a user-centred evaluation through a user study. 

As there are no ground truth rationales for the datasets we used, we cannot evaluate our explanations using metrics such as Simulatability [15]. Additionally, since we have explanations in natural language, we cannot use unsupervised metrics such as faithfulness-based metrics. Based on these facts, the most appropriate way to evaluate our explanations is through a user study. 

We evaluate the quality of the created explanations through a user study using three different metrics. Specifically, we employ the Plausibility metric, designed for natural language explanations. This metric quantifies how plausible the provided explanation is to the predicted sentiment according to the input text. A plausible explanation should explain to the user the reason why the sentiment was selected for that input text, even if that sentiment is incorrect. Based on that, this metric tries to quantify how convincing the explanation is to the end user. 

The second metric is called Coherence and quantifies how coherent the explanation is. A coherent explanation should be very close to a human written text, being devoid of syntactical or grammatical errors. On the other hand, an explanation with very low coherence would be akin to a text with randomly placed words, without any context or meaning. 

For the final metric, we propose Perfidisouness which aims to quantify how good a generated explanation is for each instance, concerning a label other than the predicted one. Specifically, an explanation with high Perfidiousness should be faithful to any label other the predicted one, while achieving low values when the explanation is faithful to the predicted label.

Title: Decoding Consumer Sentiments: Advanced NLP Techniques for Analyzing Smartphone Reviews
Snippet: This section describes the model chosen for the sentiment classification and topic modeling tasks. 

For sentiment classification, we selected the BERT (bidirectional encoder representations from transformers) model due to its superior ability to understand the context of words in textual data. BERT's effectiveness in sentiment analysis makes it an ideal choice for our study, given its capacity to discern the nuanced shifts in meaning that context imparts to words. 

BERT stands out in natural language processing (NLP) due to its attention mechanism, which enables it to focus on different parts of the text, mirroring human reading comprehension. Unlike traditional linear models, its bidirectional approach allows for a comprehensive understanding of word context from both preceding and following text. Pre-training on a vast corpus equips BERT with an intricate understanding of language subtleties, enhancing its performance even before fine-tuning for specific tasks like sentiment classification. Pretraining a language model like BERT involves training the model on a large dataset to learn language patterns and structures. This process allows the model to quickly adapt to and excel in new tasks with comparatively less task-specific data, making it particularly effective for sentiment classification. 

BERT is based on the transformer architecture, which relies on mechanisms to process input text. The key mathematical components of BERT related to the scope of this research include: 

Self-Attention Mechanism: BERT uses the self-attention mechanism (Vaswani et al., 2017) to weigh the importance of different words in a sentence relative to each other. This means that every word can pay attention to other words, helping it understand the context better. This is mathematically represented as: 

where Q (query), K (key), and V (value) are matrices derived from the input embeddings, and dk is the dimension of the key vectors. The dot product of Q and K is scaled by and passed through a softmax function to obtain the attention weights, which are then multiplied by V (Vaswani et al., 2017). 

Self-attention plays a key role in understanding and capturing contextual relationships and long-range dependencies in text data. This makes it highly valuable for tasks like sentiment analysis and topic modeling, where context and relationships between words significantly impact the results (Vaswani et al., 2017).

Title: Enhancing User Trust and Interpretability in AI-Driven Feature Request Detection for Mobile App Reviews: An Explainable Approach
Snippet: Several explainable AI techniques have been created to improve the interpretability of models. One of these techniques, known as Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME) developed by Ribeiro et al. [13], helps to explain individual predictions from complex models such as deep neural networks. LIME achieves this by creating local surrogate models that closely mimic the original model for a specific prediction, determining the most impactful input features through subgroup discovery and sampling techniques [47]. For example, in sentiment analysis, LIME can help organizations understand the key words or features impacting predictions of reviews as negative, neutral, or positive in mobile app reviews. 

Future research can explore how LIME enhances the interpretability of deep learning models for sentiment analysis and automated software feature request detection. LIME and SHAP are two widely used explainable AI methods. LIME has been utilized in various studies to analyze predictions from text classifiers, reinforcement learning agents, and image classifiers. SHAP, on the other hand, employs game theory and Shapley values to determine the contribution of each input feature to a model's output, attributing predictions to specific features. Researchers have used SHAP to explain predictions from tree ensembles [48] and graph neural networks [49], [50]. Utilizing the Kernel SHAP method internally, SHAP calculates the weight of contribution for all features in a black box model. 

Unlike LIME, SHAP does not include a local linear module but uses specific functions to compute the Shapley value, enhancing model interpretability. In sentiment analysis, SHAP can identify word contributions to positive and negative sentiment predictions. Despite its potential, there is limited research on applying SHAP, LIME to sentiment analysis in the mobile app reviews with deep learning models, offering an opportunity for future studies to explore SHAP's utility in enhancing model interpretability for sentiment analysis in the mobile app industry. 

While these methods have proven useful for explaining ML models, their application to textual data is still limited. Some studies have utilized explainable AI for sentiment analysis [51], [52] and sensitivity detection [53], [54]. But these focused only on benchmark datasets rather than realworld applications. Most research in app review analysis by interpreting user emotions in app review achieved accuracy with non-interpretable models.
</snippet>

Title: GrammarSHAP: An Efficient Model-Agnostic and Structure-Aware NLP Explainer
Snippet: Several local explainability techniques exist to interpret predictions produced by NLP models (Arrieta et al., 2020). Among them, features attribution (or feature relevance) approaches quantify each input component's contribution to the model's output, i.e. how each feature affects the observed prediction. Methods in this category are available in a large variety: gradient-based (Simonyan et al., 2014;Sundararajan et al., 2017), neuralnetwork specific e.g. LRP (Bach et al., 2015) and DeepLIFT (Shrikumar et al., 2017), and modelagnostic e.g. LIME (Ribeiro et al., 2016). SHAP (Lundberg and Lee, 2017)-particularly relevant for our methodology-is by many considered to be a gold standard thanks to its solid theoretical background and broad applicability. This framework builds a unified view of methods like LIME, LRP, and DeepLIFT and the game-theoretic concept of Shapley values (Shapley, 1953). 

More recent works address the limitations of word-level relevance scores by focusing on phraselevel and hierarchical explanations. The proposed approaches analyze and quantify words' interactions through exhaustive search (Tsang et al., 2018), combining their contextual decomposition scores (Singh et al., 2018), or via measuring SHAP interaction values along a predefined tree structure (Lundberg et al., 2018). Chen and Jordan (2020) combines a linguistic parse tree with Banzhaf values (Banzhaf III, 1964) to capture meaningful interactions in text inputs. (Chen et al., 2020), instead, propose to detect directly feature interaction without resorting to external structures. They propose a hierarchical explainability method that, in a topdown fashion, breaks down text components in shorter phrases and words based on the weakest detected interactions.
