# Overview

Hallucination and bias are tightly linked failure modes in modern AI systems: biased training data and internalized priors can drive models to generate plausible but incorrect or unfair content, while hallucinations often manifest as biased errors that are overconfident and hard to detect.<cite id="7af62802-1">Hallucination remains a fundamental obstacle to the reliability and safety of large language models and arises from data curation practices, pretraining biases, decoding dynamics, and insufficient human-aligned evaluation protocols</cite><cite id="7af62802-3">AI hallucination is fluent but inaccurate generation; surveys attribute it to overfitting, model complexity, and bias in training data, with a taxonomy distinguishing data-driven versus model-driven causes</cite>. Below, we synthesize definitions, mechanisms, empirical findings, and mitigation strategies that connect the two phenomena.

# Definitions and Taxonomy

Hallucination is typically defined as plausible but factually incorrect, unfaithful to input, or unsupported content generated by models, appearing “real” yet wrong.<cite id="7af62802-1">Hallucination in language and multimodal models is the generation of nonsensical or inaccurate content that undermines reliability</cite><cite id="844fbd25-0">Hallucinations correspond to plausible yet nonfactual content generated by an LM</cite><cite id="844fbd25-4">Hallucinations include intrinsic hallucination (contradictions with source context) and extrinsic hallucination (content unverifiable by context or external knowledge), as well as faithfulness hallucinations (violations of user instructions or logical consistency)</cite>. Bias, in this context, refers to systematic and repeatable errors that produce unfair outcomes by privileging arbitrary groups or distortions in representation, which can be present in data, annotations, representations, models, or research design.<cite id="844fbd25-0">Bias is a systematic and repeatable error creating unfair outcomes; LMs inherit five sources of bias (data, annotations, vector representations, models, research design)</cite><cite id="844fbd25-0">Biases become problematic when propagated or amplified through model hallucinations, with inherent pretraining data biases leading to inequalities in information representation and knowledge gaps</cite>.

A useful taxonomy distinguishes whether hallucinations stem from data/content bias versus model-driven errors, and whether they are faithful to inputs yet incorrect (faithfulness hallucination) or fabricate content outright (factual hallucination).<cite id="7af62802-3">Hallucinations may arise from data and from modeling; surveys categorize causes into data-driven and model-driven hallucinations</cite><cite id="844fbd25-4">Faithfulness hallucinations include factual distortions and instruction violations, complementing intrinsic and extrinsic hallucination types</cite>.

# Mechanisms Linking Bias and Hallucination

1) Statistical and Conceptual Priors from Training Data. Models internalize distributional statistics and priors from biased corpora, which can cause them to favor spurious associations and “fill in” missing information with incorrect but plausible content.<cite id="7af62802-1">Pretraining biases and data curation practices are systemic sources of hallucinations</cite><cite id="844fbd25-1">LVLM hallucinations are linked to co-occurrence bias and over-reliance on language priors; attention dynamics (e.g., over-textual attention, attention sinks) can distort grounding and amplify hallucinations</cite>. In vision-language models, concept association bias and overreliance on statistical priors lead to cross-modal errors (e.g., attributing a frequent attribute to an object not present in the image).<cite id="844fbd25-2">Concept Association Bias occurs when VLMs infer missing concepts across modalities; statistical bias from unimodal priors leads to hallucinations, evidenced by binary questions probing frequent attribute/relationship combinations</cite>.

2) Spurious Correlations and Social/Nationality Biases. Biases embedded in data can create spurious correlations that models exploit, producing high-confidence but incorrect outputs that evade standard detection or finetuning.<cite id="6e7ae460-4">Spurious correlations in training data (e.g., name–nationality) induce high-confidence hallucinations resistant to uncertainty metrics and refusal finetuning</cite>. Empirically, social bias can be a causal driver of faithfulness hallucinations, with anti-stereotype inputs inducing higher hallucination rates than in-line or pro-stereotype inputs.<cite id="6e7ae460-0">Using a structural causal modeling approach and a Bias Intervention Dataset, experiments show biases are significant causes of faithfulness hallucinations, with varying directions of effect across bias states</cite><cite id="6e7ae460-3">Across seven LLMs, hallucination rates were highest for anti-stereotype data, followed by non-stereotype, and lowest for pro-stereotype, consistent across bias types</cite>.

3) Geographical and Spatial Biases. Distortions in geographic knowledge representation reflect dataset biases and can propagate into hallucinations about locations and spatial relations.<cite id="844fbd25-0">Biased data and annotations contribute to knowledge gaps and data-related hallucinations; gender and nationality biases are particularly associated with hallucinations, and spatial disparities in geographic knowledge appear when biases are amplified through hallucinations</cite>.

4) Attention and Grounding Dynamics. In multimodal models, attention over textual context and under-attention to visual tokens can couple with learned priors to produce hallucinated outputs that contradict visual evidence, especially when priors are strong and modality grounding is weak.<cite id="844fbd25-1">LVLMs may pay more attention to text than visuals, with co-occurrence bias and language priors contributing to hallucinations; attention sinks and anchor tokens can distort grounding and amplify errors</cite><cite id="844fbd25-2">Hidden representation analyses show hallucinations arise from localized subspaces encoding spurious biases; spectral representation filtering targets these modes to suppress object hallucinations</cite>.

# Empirical Evidence

- Social-bias causal experiments: By manipulating bias states and measuring hallucination rates, studies show that social bias significantly increases faithfulness hallucinations, with anti-stereotype conditions eliciting the most errors across multiple models.<cite id="6e7ae460-0">Experiments reveal biases are significant causes of faithfulness hallucinations with model- and bias-state-dependent effects</cite><cite id="6e7ae460-3">Anti-stereotype texts produced the highest hallucination rates (e.g., >12% for several LLMs, with some models exceeding 20%), followed by non-stereotype and pro-stereotype</cite>.

- Geographic distortions: Evaluations show that biases in data/annotations propagate into spatial knowledge gaps and distortions, which appear as hallucinations in geographic content generation or response selection, mirroring the dataset bias distribution.<cite id="844fbd25-0">Geographic biases are identified and compared against training dataset distributions; distortions reduce task performance and manifest as hallucinations in spatial information</cite>.

- VLM priors and concept association: VLMs exhibit concept association bias and overreliance on statistical priors, producing attribute or relationship hallucinations when cross-modal inferences conflict with visual evidence.<cite id="844fbd25-2">Concept Association Bias and statistical priors drive cross-modal hallucinations; binary probes demonstrate reliance on frequent co-occurrences</cite>.

- RAG’s partial mitigation and remaining biases: Even with retrieval grounding, hallucinations persist because models can fabricate, misrepresent, or contradict retrieved content, and evaluation remains challenging—highlighting that both data bias and model tendencies contribute jointly.<cite id="844fbd25-4">RAG seeks to mitigate hallucinations by grounding in trusted contexts but does not fully eliminate them; models still add unsupported details, misrepresent information, or contradict contexts, and detection struggles</cite>.

# Interplay and Detection Challenges

High-confidence hallucinations often arise from spurious correlations and strong priors, making them difficult to catch with confidence-based detectors or simple refusal finetuning, which underscores a key interaction between bias and hallucination: biased spurious features can dominate decoding even when world knowledge is correct.<cite id="6e7ae460-4">Spurious correlations induce high-confidence hallucinations that evade uncertainty signals and refusal finetuning, indicating robust overreliance on biased features</cite>. In multimodal settings, attention dynamics can further amplify these errors by privileging textual or prior knowledge over visual evidence, especially in object or attribute hallucinations.<cite id="844fbd25-1">Over-text attention and attention sinks distort grounding and amplify hallucinations</cite><cite id="844fbd25-2">Principal-component analysis of hidden states reveals low-rank hallucination modes tied to spurious biases that can be targeted for suppression</cite>.

# Mitigations That Bridge Both Issues

- Data- and representation-level debiasing: Curating diverse, representative data and filtering spurious correlations can reduce the priors that trigger hallucinations; representational analyses can identify and suppress low-rank modes encoding biased errors in VLMs.<cite id="844fbd25-2">Spectral Representation Filtering identifies hallucination modes tied to spurious biases and suppresses object hallucinations with inference efficiency</cite>.

- Grounding and attention control: Improving cross-modal grounding (e.g., stronger visual token attention, avoiding attention sinks) reduces reliance on language priors and mitigates cross-modal hallucinations.<cite id="844fbd25-1">Enhancing visual attention and mitigating co-occurrence bias can curb hallucinations by improving grounding</cite>.

- Retrieval augmentation with careful evaluation: RAG can reduce factual hallucinations by anchoring to external sources, though residual hallucinations and detection challenges remain, requiring robust faithfulness evaluation at both summarization and RAG-specific levels.<cite id="844fbd25-4">RAG reduces but does not eliminate hallucinations; dedicated leaderboards and faithfulness evaluation (including LLM-as-a-judge) are used to benchmark and monitor</cite>.

- Lifecycle governance: Holistic pipelines spanning data curation, training objectives, decoding, and evaluation can address both bias and hallucination as intertwined risks, rather than in isolation.<cite id="7af62802-1">Hallucination is systemic across the AI lifecycle, arising from data curation and pretraining biases; scalable supervision, robust benchmarks, and uncertainty modeling are needed</cite>.

# Summary

In practice, AI hallucinations often emerge from biased representations and priors learned from training data, which guide models to produce plausible but incorrect content; conversely, bias is amplified when these priors are propagated and distorted in generation, especially under attention and grounding failures.<cite id="7af62802-1">Pretraining biases and data curation shape systemic hallucinations across the lifecycle</cite><cite id="844fbd25-0">Biases become problematic when propagated or amplified through hallucinations, reflecting inequalities in information representation and knowledge gaps</cite><cite id="844fbd25-1">Overreliance on language priors and weak visual grounding contribute to hallucinations in LVLMs</cite>. Empirical studies show that manipulating bias states increases or decreases hallucination rates, and that spurious correlations can yield overconfident, hard-to-detect errors, reinforcing the intertwined nature of the two problems.<cite id="6e7ae460-0">Social bias causally contributes to faithfulness hallucinations</cite><cite id="6e7ae460-3">Anti-stereotype bias states elicit the highest hallucination rates across multiple LLMs</cite><cite id="6e7ae460-4">Spurious correlations induce high-confidence hallucinations that resist standard mitigation</cite>. Effective solutions therefore target both sources—debiasing data/representations and strengthening grounding and evaluation—together reduce both bias and hallucination risks in deployed systems.<cite id="844fbd25-2">Targeting spurious bias subspaces in representations suppresses object hallucinations</cite><cite id="844fbd25-4">RAG and faithfulness evaluation help, but require continued monitoring due to persistent hallucinations</cite>.
</answer>

Title: I Think, Therefore I Hallucinate: Minds, Machines, and the Art of Being Wrong
Snippet: Databases and Search Strategy. We reviewed peer-reviewed studies, preprints, and conference papers from major academic databases, including PubMed (human research), PsycINFO (cognitive and clinical studies), arXiv (AI-related work), and IEEE Xplore (engineering perspectives). 

• Keywords: human hallucinations, predictive processing, Bayesian perception,schizophrenia and hallucination, AI confabulation, large language model hallucination, auto regressive modeling, and related terms. 

• Initial Hits: Approximately 300 articles were retrieved, from which we retained abstracts explicitly addressing hallucinations (or analogous terms like "confabulation," "fabrication," "illusion") in either humans or AI models. 

Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria. 

• Inclusion: Papers that discussed underlying mechanisms of hallucinations (e.g., top-down priors, neural correlates, model architectures, or training objectives) and provided empirical or theoretical insights on generating or mitigating such phenomena. 

• Exclusion: Publications focusing on phenomena only tangentially related to hallucinations (e.g., purely artistic illusions) or AI error modes unrelated to confabulations (e.g., classification failures without mention of fabricated content). 

All abstracts that passed this initial screening were read in full to confirm relevance and methodological rigor. Discrepancies were resolved by a review team of two cognitive neuroscientists and one machine learning researcher, ensuring included works contributed uniquely to understanding hallucinations in either domain.

Title: Never Compromise to Vulnerabilities: A Comprehensive Survey on AI Governance
Snippet: Hallucination remains a fundamental obstacle to the reliability and safety of large language models (LLMs) and multimodal large language models (MLLMs). Although existing mitigation strategies across data preprocessing, training objectives, and inference mechanisms have shown promise, they often lack robustness, generalizability, and scalability across real-world tasks, domains, and modalities. Current solutions tend to be fragmented, focusing on narrow benchmarks or handcrafted settings, which limits their effectiveness in open-ended or safety-critical deployments. Moreover, hallucination is not merely a localized model design flaw but a systemic challenge that spans the entire AI lifecycle. It arises from data curation practices, pretraining biases, decoding dynamics, and insufficient human-aligned evaluation protocols. As foundation models evolve toward greater autonomy and multimodal capability, the risks of hallucination become more opaque, harder to trace, and more consequential in practice. 

Future research must therefore go beyond surface-level fixes and pursue holistic solutions. This includes developing scalable and adaptive supervision pipelines (e.g., weak supervision, human-AI collaborative filtering), designing robust benchmarks that simulate real-world uncertainty and ambiguity, and integrating epistemic uncertainty modeling into both generation and evaluation. Additionally, advancing introspective and self-corrective mechanisms-such as reasoning rollback, contrastive decoding, and multimodal grounding validation-will be essential to align model behavior with factual integrity and user intent. Bridging efforts across NLP, vision, HCI, and cognitive science will be key to mitigating hallucinations in increasingly complex AI systems.

Title: AlphaIntellect at SemEval-2024 Task 6: Detection of Hallucinations in Generated Text
Snippet: AI hallucination refers to a phenomenon where a Large Language Model (LLM) -usually Generative AI or a computer vision tool produces nonsensical and inaccurate outputs (Maleki et al., 2024).Thus, this leads to fluent but inaccurate generations.The term 'hallucination' is usually associated with human or animal brains but from the standpoint of machines, hallucinations refer to these inaccurately produced outputs.

Hallucinations in generative models may arise due to multiple factors such as overfitting during model training, complexity of the model, and bias in training data.According to multiple surveys (Huang et al., 2023), Hallucinations in natural language models may arise primarily due to two reasons -Hallucinations due to data and hallucinations during modeling.

Hallucinations in AI models may prove to be a threat in multiple scenarios such as healthcare where a model may not be able to predict the existence of the exact condition that needs to be treated.

Hallucinations in fluent over generations may also lead to the spread of misinformation.

The most pressing problem in the modern-day natural language generation landscape is that the existing metrics (Bandi et al., 2023) can mostly detect fluency in generation rather than accuracy.

To deal with this issue, several studies have explored different techniques, such as Knowledge Graph Integration, Bias Detection, and Mitigation (Rawte et al., 2023).Building upon this prior research, our work proposes training tailormade deep learning models and using Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) based architectures to identify cases of hallucinations.

To deal with this scenario, a task (Mickus et al., 2024) was proposed to build a system to detect instances of hallucinations in generated text.

Title: I Think, Therefore I Hallucinate: Minds, Machines, and the Art of Being Wrong
Snippet: Since this research does not involve direct experimentation, our approach is theoretical and comparative, drawing on: 

• Neuroscience research on human perception, hallucinations, and predictive processing. 

• Machine learning studies on AI hallucinations in large language models. 

• A systematic comparison between human and AI hallucinations, focusing on shared mechanisms, functional roles, and potential ways to improve AI cognition. 

We propose a taxonomy of hallucinations-sensory, cognitive, factual, and contextual-to analyze hallucinations in biological and artificial systems. By synthesizing research from cognitive science, neuroscience, and AI, this paper aims to reshape how we understand and approach hallucinations in intelligent systems.

AI hallucination refers to a phenomenon where a Large Language Model (LLM) -usually Generative AI or a computer vision tool produces nonsensical and inaccurate outputs (Maleki et al., 2024).Thus, this leads to fluent but inaccurate generations.The term 'hallucination' is usually associated with human or animal brains but from the standpoint of machines, hallucinations refer to these inaccurately produced outputs.

Hallucinations in generative models may arise due to multiple factors such as overfitting during model training, complexity of the model, and bias in training data.According to multiple surveys (Huang et al., 2023), Hallucinations in natural language models may arise primarily due to two reasons -Hallucinations due to data and hallucinations during modeling.

Hallucinations in AI models may prove to be a threat in multiple scenarios such as healthcare where a model may not be able to predict the existence of the exact condition that needs to be treated.

Hallucinations in fluent over generations may also lead to the spread of misinformation.

The most pressing problem in the modern-day natural language generation landscape is that the existing metrics (Bandi et al., 2023) can mostly detect fluency in generation rather than accuracy.

To deal with this issue, several studies have explored different techniques, such as Knowledge Graph Integration, Bias Detection, and Mitigation (Rawte et al., 2023).Building upon this prior research, our work proposes training tailormade deep learning models and using Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) based architectures to identify cases of hallucinations.

To deal with this scenario, a task (Mickus et al., 2024) was proposed to build a system to detect instances of hallucinations in generated text.

documents.title: I Think, Therefore I Hallucinate: Minds, Machines, and the Art of Being Wrong
documents.snippet:
Since this research does not involve direct experimentation, our approach is theoretical and comparative, drawing on: 

• Neuroscience research on human perception, hallucinations, and predictive processing. 

• Machine learning studies on AI hallucinations in large language models. 

• A systematic comparison between human and AI hallucinations, focusing on shared mechanisms, functional roles, and potential ways to improve AI cognition. 

We propose a taxonomy of hallucinations-sensory, cognitive, factual, and contextual-to analyze hallucinations in biological and artificial systems. By synthesizing research from cognitive science, neuroscience, and AI, this paper aims to reshape how we understand and approach hallucinations in intelligent systems.

Title: Exploring Causal Effect of Social Bias on Faithfulness Hallucinations in Large Language Models
Snippet: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success in various tasks, yet they remain vulnerable to faithfulness hallucinations, where the output does not align with the input. In this study, we investigate whether social bias contributes to these hallucinations, a causal relationship that has not been explored. A key challenge is controlling confounders within the context, which complicates the isolation of causality between bias states and hallucinations. To address this, we utilize the Structural Causal Model (SCM) to establish and validate the causality and design bias interventions to control confounders. In addition, we develop the Bias Intervention Dataset (BID), which includes various social biases, enabling precise measurement of causal effects. Experiments on mainstream LLMs reveal that biases are significant causes of faithfulness hallucinations, and the effect of each bias state differs in direction. We further analyze the scope of these causal effects across various models, specifically focusing on unfairness hallucinations, which are primarily targeted by social bias, revealing the subtle yet significant causal effect of bias on hallucination generation.

Title: Exploring Causal Effect of Social Bias on Faithfulness Hallucinations in Large Language Models
Snippet: Before testing causality, we first compared hallucination rates across different bias states. The hallucination rate is defined as the ratio of the number of hallucination samples to the total number of samples. Figure 4 provides a visual summary of hallucination rates for various LLMs. Analyzing the performance of these models reveals several key findings. 

Most models show high hallucination rates across all three bias states. Five LLMs, including Llama-3 and Qwen2.5, exceed 12% on anti-stereotype texts. The seven selected LLMs exhibit significant performance differences. For example, GPT-4o-mini maintains hallucination rates below 6% in all bias states, while Llama-3.2 exceeds 20%. Considering that Llama-3.2 has a smaller scale compared to the other models, its relatively poorer performance is understandable. 

Takeaway. All seven models show the trend: Anti-stereotype data have the highest hallucination rates, followed by Non-stereotype, and Pro-stereotype the lowest. This trend is also consistent across different types of social bias, indicating a significant correlation between bias state and hallucination.

Title: When Bias Pretends to Be Truth: How Spurious Correlations Undermine Hallucination Detection in LLMs
Snippet: Hallucinations in large language models (LLMs), characterized by confidently generating incorrect or nonexistent information, emerge as a major barrier to their safe and reliable deployment (Ji et al., 2023;Zhang et al., 2025b;Tonmoy et al., 2024). Understanding and mitigating hallucinations requires identifying their diverse origins and devising robust interventions at different stages of the model development lifecycle. 

Previous research identifies two primary sources of hallucinations in large language models: inaccuracies in pretraining data and inherent limitations in models' memorization and processing capabilities. Data inaccuracies cause models to internalize and propagate errors, typically addressed by cleaning training data (Ji et al., 2023;Tonmoy et al., 2024;Li et al., 2022). Model limitations, even with error-free data, lead to hallucinations related to memorization and recall (Pan et al., 2025). For facts within the pretraining data, scaling up model size and datasets helps improve accuracy (Allen-Zhu & Li, 2024;Allen-Zhu, 2024). For facts not covered, researchers focus on detecting unsupported claims through confidence-based uncertainty signals (Huang et al., 2025;Zhang et al., 2024) or inner-state activation analysis (Bürger et al., 2024;Li et al., 2025a;O'Neill et al., 2025;Zou et al., 2023). Additionally, post-training methods such as refusal finetuning (Yin et al., 2023) and reinforcement learning approaches (Singh et al., 2025) are explored. However, a critical question remains: are these known interventions sufficient? Figure 1: Spurious correlations induce high-confidence hallucinations that evade detection and mitigation. Statistical biases in training data (e.g., name-nationality) lead to consistent errors resistant to uncertainty metrics and refusal fine-tuning.

Title: Evaluation of geographical distortions in language models
Snippet: These models are often referred to as large language models (LLMs), not only because of the size of their neural architectures but also because of the enormous scale of their training data. These models still contain the five sources of bias present in any NLP project (Hovy & Prabhumoye, 2021), namely, biases in the data, annotations, vector representations, models and research design. We define bias as a systematic and repeatable error that creates unfair outcomes, such as privileging one arbitrary group of users over others. Biases become problematic when they are propagated or amplified through model hallucinations (Wan et al., 2023). Hallucinations correspond to plausible yet nonfactual content (Huang et al., 2025) generated by an LM. Inherent biases in pretraining data can lead to inequalities in information representation and contribute to knowledge gaps, ultimately resulting in data-related hallucinations (Huang et al., 2025). Certain types of bias are particularly associated with hallucinations, notably those related to gender (Wan et al., 2023) and nationality (Venkit et al., 2023). 

In this study, we focus on the biases inherent to spatial information representation. While social biases such as gender, sexual orientation, and ethnicity are often studied (Navigli et al., 2023), they rarely include biases related to geographical knowledge representation (Mai et al., 2023). These distortions in representation lead to decreased performance on downstream tasks (Decoupes et al., 2023). 

The main goal of this paper is to provide an evaluation framework for both MLMs and CLMs to identify two biases: spatial disparity of geographic knowledge and geographic distortion, and compare them with the spatial distribution of locations in the training datasets. The evaluation is both reproducible 1 and scalable to all LMs. A short version of this work appeared in (Decoupes et al., 2025). Title: MAP: Mitigating Hallucinations in Large Vision-Language Models with Map-Level Attention Processing
Snippet: Hallucinations is a widely studied problem in Large Language Models (LLMs), commonly defined as the generation of text that is factually inaccurate or unsupported by the input context (Rawte, Sheth, and Das 2023;Sriramanan et al. 2024;Huang et al. 2025). In the realm of Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs), hallucinations refer to outputs that conflict with the visual content, such as mentioning nonexistent objects or misrepresenting visual attributes (Li et al. 2023a). This hallucination issue is particularly pronounced in multi-modal tasks such as image captioning (Rohrbach et al. 2018;Li et al. 2023b) and visual question answering (Antol et al. 2015;Goyal et al. 2017). 

Layer 32 

Criss-Cross Attention (Broadcast) Although the exact causes of hallucinations remain unclear, several factors are believed to contribute to their occurrence. Some studies (Liu, Zheng, and Chen 2024;Jiang et al. 2025;Sarkar et al. 2025a) have revealed that LVLMs are prone to pay more attention to the textual context while paying inadequate attention to visual tokens, which may result in hallucinated generations. Moreover, studies (Zhou et al. 2023;Tu et al. 2025;Zhu et al. 2025) also point out that co-occurrence bias (i.e., the tendency to predict objects that frequently appear together) and over-reliance on language priors can both contribute to hallucinations. Furthermore, works like (Huang et al. 2024;Kang et al. 2025) has observed issues such as attention sinks and anchor tokens, which may distort grounding and amplify hallucinations.

Title: Suppressing VLM Hallucinations with Spectral Representation Filtering
Snippet: Vision-language models (VLMs) have achieved remarkable success in bridging visual perception and natural language processing [5,24,35,36,44], powering diverse applications such as image captioning, visual question answering (VQA), and multimodal reasoning. By integrating pre-trained vision encoders with large language models (LLMs), these systems generate fluent, context-aware descriptions of visual scenes. Despite their prowess, VLMs remain plagued by object hallucinations (OH): the fabrication of objects, attributes, or spatial relations absent from the input image, often stemming from linguistic priors or distributional biases in training data [3,15,16,29,41]. 

Existing mitigation strategies fall into two categories: decoding-time adjustments, such as constrained beam search [11] or logit debiasing [8,19], which modulate generation to promote grounded outputs; and post-hoc refinements such as Woodpecker [37], LURE [43]), and the reference-guided editing method HALC [6]. While these yield gains in controlled scenarios, they introduce substantial overhead, often 5-10x inference slowdowns, demand task-specific adaptations, or rely on external resources. We address this gap with a gradient-free, inferenceefficient correction paradigm that operates at the representational level. Through covariance analysis of hidden states from paired truthful and hallucinatory generations, we identify low-rank hallucination modes, principal directions of variance that encode spurious biases. As visualized in Fig. 1, UMAP projections of hidden activations reveal that truthful (blue) and hallucinatory (amber) representations, are highly separable in different layers. This structured divergence indicates that hallucinations emerge from localized subspaces within the model's latent geome-Figure 2. Qualitative comparison of captions generated by LLaVA and mPLUG-Owl2 before and after applying Spectral Representation Filtering (SRF). The baseline model hallucinates non-existent fruits such as apples and bananas, while SRF suppresses these errors.

Title: Data-Driven Calibration of Prediction Sets in Large Vision-Language Models Based on Inductive Conformal Prediction
Snippet: Large Vision-Language Models. Early-stage research primarily focused on generating text responses from image and text inputs. Building upon this foundation, subsequent studies have significantly expanded the capabilities and application domains of LVLMs. Recent advances further enhance fine-grained parsing abilities, enabling precise control over localized regions (e.g., bounding boxes or key points) beyond holistic image understanding. These developments have facilitated the widespread deployment of LVLMs in critical fields such as medical diagnosis, embodied robotics interaction, and autonomous driving. However, the complexity of multimodal interactions introduces new challenges-for instance, inconsistencies in cross-modal information fusion may degrade output reliability. In high-risk scenarios like healthcare and autonomous systems, unreliable model responses could lead to severe safety hazards, underscoring the necessity of accurate hallucination detection. Unlike traditional methods reliant on external validation, this work proposes quantifying the intrinsic uncertainty of LVLMs to identify hallucinations, establishing a novel theoretical foundation for building safe and dependable human-AI collaborative systems. 

Hallucinations in Large Language Models. In natural language processing Yang et al. [2025b], hallucination refers to generated content that appears plausible but deviates from source material or factual accuracy, originating from psychological concepts of perceiving non-existent realities Lin et al. [2023], Kuhn et al. [2023], Farquhar et al. [2024], Wang et al. [2025a], Yang et al. [2024]. This phenomenon manifests primarily as two types: intrinsic hallucination (direct contradictions with source context) and extrinsic hallucination (content unverifiable through original context or external knowledge bases). This hallucination issue is particularly pronounced in multi-modal tasks such as image captioning (Rohrbach et al. 2018;Li et al. 2023b) and visual question answering (Antol et al. 2015;Goyal et al. 2017). 

Layer 32 

Criss-Cross Attention (Broadcast) Although the exact causes of hallucinations remain unclear, several factors are believed to contribute to their occurrence. Some studies (Liu, Zheng, and Chen 2024;Jiang et al. 2025;Sarkar et al. 2025a) have revealed that LVLMs are prone to pay more attention to the textual context while paying inadequate attention to visual tokens, which may result in hallucinated generations. Moreover, studies (Zhou et al. 2023;Tu et al. 2025;Zhu et al. 2025) also point out that co-occurrence bias (i.e., the tendency to predict objects that frequently appear together) and over-reliance on language priors can both contribute to hallucinations. Vision-language models (VLMs) have achieved remarkable success in bridging visual perception and natural language processing [5,24,35,36,44], powering diverse applications such as image captioning, visual question answering (VQA), and multimodal reasoning. Despite their prowess, VLMs remain plagued by object hallucinations (OH): the fabrication of objects, attributes, or spatial relations absent from the input image, often stemming from linguistic priors or distributional biases in training data [3,15,16,29,41]. 

Existing mitigation strategies fall into two categories: decoding-time adjustments, such as constrained beam search [11] or logit debiasing [8,19], which modulate generation to promote grounded outputs; and post-hoc refinements such as Woodpecker [37], LURE [43]), and the reference-guided editing method HALC [6]. While these yield gains in controlled scenarios, they introduce substantial overhead, often 5-10x inference slowdowns, demand task-specific adaptations, or rely on external resources. We address this gap with a gradient-free, inferenceefficient correction paradigm that operates at the representational level. Through covariance analysis of hidden states from paired truthful and hallucinatory generations, we identify low-rank hallucination modes, principal directions of variance that encode spurious biases. As visualized in Fig. 1, UMAP projections of hidden activations reveal that truthful (blue) and hallucinatory (amber) representations, are highly separable in different layers. This structured divergence indicates that hallucinations emerge from localized subspaces within the model's latent geome-Figure 2. Qualitative comparison of captions generated by LLaVA and mPLUG-Owl2 before and after applying Spectral Representation Filtering (SRF). The baseline model hallucinates non-existent fruits such as apples and bananas, while SRF suppresses these errors.

Building upon this foundation, subsequent studies have significantly expanded the capabilities and application domains of LVLMs. Recent advances further enhance fine-grained parsing abilities, enabling precise control over localized regions (e.g., bounding boxes or key points) beyond holistic image understanding. problem: Find papers on how weight evolve through training in a transformer
final_response:
# Overview

This collection highlights recent papers that study how transformer weights change during training, spanning theory on attention and gradient dynamics, empirical layer-wise evolution of weight statistics, continual pretraining and fine-tuning, and head-level specialization. These works collectively map trajectories of weight matrices across epochs, layers, and tasks, and connect them to optimization choices, initialization scaling, and architectural design. <cite id="84db4750-2">Transformers exhibit incremental learning dynamics where the difference between initial and trained weights increases in rank over time</cite> and <cite id="84db4750-3">depth-dependent variance patterns emerge during pretraining, with shallow layers adapting quickly and deep layers adjusting more slowly</cite>. <cite id="9bb56ffa-2">Continual pretraining can improve perplexity and downstream transfer but also induces learning and forgetting that depend on model size and domain sequence</cite>, while <cite id="7d9a1368-0">attention heads can specialize into functional roles like “induction heads” during pretraining, supporting in-context learning</cite>. <cite id="19962e5b-1">NTK-based analyses show when and why transformers’ training dynamics stabilize and converge under different widths and initializations</cite>, and <cite id="19962e5b-4">global convergence can be achieved under multiple scaling regimes, with faster rates under certain initializations and over-parameterization regimes</cite>.

# Theoretical Analyses of Attention and Gradient Dynamics

Several papers analyze how attention weights evolve under optimization and what convergence behavior to expect. <cite id="84db4750-0">A one-layer transformer with softmax attention trained by GD exhibits phase-like behavior in attention dynamics for in-context learning; in imbalanced settings, a four-phase evolution emerges that characterizes interactions between dominant and under-represented features</cite>. <cite id="84db4750-1">In a formal phase 1 analysis, linear and attention layers show coupled dynamics: attention weights increase on tokens consistent with positive samples and suppress attention on non-leading tokens in negative samples, while token scores and attention allocation shift to dominant positions over time</cite>. These results connect training time to how attention distributions concentrate on informative tokens.

Convergence and stability are also studied through kernel and spectral lenses. <cite id="19962e5b-1">Under NTK initialization and appropriate scaling, the limiting NTK matrix of a transformer can be derived and used to show global convergence of GD with high probability, with stability of the NTK during training controlled via the spectral norm of the Hessian</cite>. <cite id="19962e5b-4">Comparative theory shows separations across scaling (τ0 = d−1/2 vs d−1), initialization (LeCun/He vs NTK), and architecture; for example, shallow transformers can converge globally under both scalings, but τ0 = d−1/2 admits faster convergence for large widths, and LeCun/He can yield faster convergence than NTK initialization</cite>. These analyses tie initialization scales and width to the trajectory of weight updates and to convergence speed.

# Empirical Evolution of Layer-wise Weights During Pretraining

Beyond theory, studies track how individual weight matrices change as training progresses. <cite id="84db4750-3">In a 12-layer GPT-2-style transformer trained with AdamW, attention Q/K/V projection weights show depth-dependent variance dynamics: lower layers expand their standard deviation rapidly in early pretraining, while higher layers change more slowly and smoothly, eventually stabilizing near narrower equilibrium distributions; weight matrices become sparser post-training, with a few large-magnitude entries dominating</cite>. <cite id="84db4750-2">Complementing this, theoretical and experimental evidence shows transformers follow incremental learning dynamics where the rank of the difference between initial and trained weights increases gradually, indicating staged growth of representational power</cite>. Together, these findings suggest asymmetric adaptation across depth: early, strong updates in shallow layers, followed by slower equilibrium in deeper layers.

Spectral and NTK-based diagnostics connect these empirical patterns to dynamics and prioritization. <cite id="19962e5b-2">Layerwise NTK (LNTK) decompositions show that layer convergence is governed by eigenvalues of the layer’s integral NTK; using layer-specific learning rates ηl ≈ 2/λl1 aligns updates with principal eigenvectors, leveraging spectral bias to speed learning along dominant directions</cite>. <cite id="19962e5b-3">A NTK-based test loss and Hessian-aware model selection framework (LENSLLM) characterizes fine-tuning transition phases and links intrinsic learning dynamics (via NTK) to dataset size and pre-trained knowledge, offering practical guidance on when and how to stop fine-tuning</cite>.

# Continual Pretraining, Weight Drift, and Specialization Across Domains/Tasks

Continual pretraining studies how weights evolve when a model is pretrained on multiple, changing corpora or domains. <cite id="9bb56ffa-2">A new continual domain-adaptive pretraining benchmark finds that continual pretraining consistently improves perplexity across <1.5B models and boosts downstream GPT-2 performance; larger models benefit more and smaller models show higher sensitivity to both learning and forgetting, while sequences of semantically similar domains enhance specialization and transfer, whereas randomized domains may yield better general transfer and final performance</cite>. <cite id="9bb56ffa-0">Surveys of continual pretraining in language models trace prior work showing multi-stage pretraining on in-domain, then task-specific data to enable temporal reasoning or mixed-language translation, contrasting with efficient in-domain continual pretraining that generalizes across tasks</cite>.

These dynamics have implications for avoiding catastrophic forgetting and stabilizing updates. <cite id="9bb56ffa-1">In speech and other modalities, continual learning strategies (rehearsal, regularization, and architecture expansion) are used to mitigate forgetting when adapting to new distributions; low-rank adapters allow rapid adaptation with minimal weight perturbation, highlighting how selective parameter updates can steer weight evolution while preserving prior knowledge</cite>. <cite id="9bb56ffa-4">Pragmatically, gradual unfreezing and gradient sparsification (e.g., GradDrop variants) can improve masked fine-tuning by controlling which weights are updated per epoch or layer, stabilizing training when tuning large pretrained models</cite>.

# Head-Level Specialization and Functional Roles of Attention

At the head level, multi-head attention modules often exhibit functional specialization as models are trained on diverse tasks or data. <cite id="7d9a1368-0">Developmental analyses identify “induction heads” that track repetitions of target tokens to support next-token prediction, with emergence of these patterns coinciding with improved in-context learning; subsequent work links these heads causally to solving sequence-tracking tasks</cite>. <cite id="7d9a1368-2">Analyses across tasks show consistent head roles, including syntax and coreference heads in BERT, alignment and position-specialized heads in machine translation, and heads that attend to rare words, indicating that attention heads can specialize along interpretable functions</cite>.

Multi-task settings further reveal how heads specialize and can be leveraged or pruned. <cite id="7d9a1368-1">Head importance scores and pruning procedures quantify functional specialization after training, and targeted training can enhance role-specific heads to promote specialization across tasks</cite>. <cite id="7d9a1368-4">Related work demonstrates head redundancy and diversity mechanisms, with pruning and lottery-ticket-style approaches showing that many heads contribute little post-training, while diversity-promoting regularization and mixture-of-experts variants can distribute specialization across heads for different inputs</cite>.

# Optimization, Initialization, and Scaling Effects on Weight Trajectories

Optimization choices and initialization scales shape how weights evolve, from early movement to convergence. <cite id="84db4750-4">Recent analyses show GD on self-attention with feedforward layers can achieve linear convergence under proper initialization (e.g., LeCun, He, NTK), though assumptions (e.g., identity feedforward weights) limit generality, highlighting how initialization and architecture constrain dynamics</cite>. <cite id="19962e5b-4">Comparative theory suggests that quadratic over-parameterization can suffice for global convergence in shallow transformers, and that certain initializations (LeCun/He) can yield faster convergence than NTK initialization, helping explain limited practical use of NTK for transformers</cite>. 

Spectral tools offer guidance for layerwise update scheduling. <cite id="19962e5b-2">By diagnosing LNTK eigenvalues, practitioners can choose layer-specific learning rates and prioritize layers with slower-converging directions, aligning weight updates with the model’s intrinsic learning dynamics and spectral bias toward principal components</cite>. <cite id="19962e5b-3">NTK-based model selection frameworks explicitly capture the competition between pre-trained knowledge, fine-tuning data scale, and dynamics, supporting early stopping and resource allocation strategies</cite>.

# Practical Observations on Weight Statistics and Sparsity

Empirical measurements reveal concrete patterns in how weights evolve and stabilize. <cite id="84db4750-3">During pretraining, lower-depth attention heads show rapid expansion and then stabilization of weight variance, while higher layers exhibit slower, smoother growth and sparser distributions with many near-zero entries and a small fraction of large magnitudes</cite>. <cite id="84db4750-2">The incremental rank increase in trained–initial weight differences suggests a staged growth of the model’s representational capacity, with rank gaps accumulating as tasks become more complex</cite>. These patterns inform monitoring and regularization strategies (e.g., controlling depth-wise variance growth, encouraging or constraining sparsity), and they align with the spectral insights above.

# Putting It Together and Open Questions

- Attention dynamics: <cite id="84db4750-0">Phase-wise evolution and concentration of attention on informative tokens</cite> indicate that training steers attention distributions toward functional selectivity.
- Depth and layers: <cite id="84db4750-3">Shallow layers update strongly early and stabilize quickly, while deeper layers adjust more slowly</cite>, and <cite id="19962e5b-2">spectral bias suggests prioritizing layers and directions that guide faster convergence</cite>.
- Continual adaptation: <cite id="9bb56ffa-2">Continual pretraining improves perplexity and downstream tasks but induces domain-specific specialization and forgetting patterns that depend on model size and domain sequences</cite>, with techniques like adapters and gradual unfreezing controlling the weight-drift surface area.
- Heads and tasks: <cite id="7d9a1368-0">Induction heads and task-specialized attention</cite> show that multi-task and multi-domain training can yield interpretable head roles and specialization.

Open challenges include quantifying cross-optimizer differences in long-horizon training, understanding when and how to regularize rank growth, and extending NTK-based convergence analyses to deeper, more realistic transformer stacks with residual connections and complex objectives. Title: In-Context Convergence of Transformers
Snippet: In this work, we investigated the training dynamics of a one-layer transformer with softmax attention trained by GD for in-context learning. We analyzed two settings respectively with balanced and imbalanced features, and proved the guaranteed convergence to a vanishing in-context prediction error by detailing the evolution of attention dynamics for both settings. Title: Towards Geospatial Foundation Models via Continual Pretraining
Snippet: Continual pretraining has been primarily introduced in the natural language domain [17,18,28], in order to improve large language models (LLM). [17] illustrates the viability of two additional stages of pretraining, using in-domain data (domain-adaptive), and then even further using task-specific data (task-adaptive). [18] proposes a continual training paradigm for enabling temporal reasoning abilities to pretrained language models. [28] focus on using continual pretraining to enable mixed language neural machine translation. In the vision domain, [23] employs a BYOL [16] style continual pretraining paradigm for 2D medical image segmentation. [36] explores a hierarchical pretraining approach for task adaptation. However, they primarily focus on adapting to a specific downstream task at a time, employing three training stages on top of an existing pretrained model for each task individually. In contrast, we employ one efficient in-domain pretraining setting that can generalize to many downstream tasks, as illustrated in Section 4. Furthermore, rather than directly loading the pretrained weights from existing models as initialization, we find instead that leveraging the representations as an auxiliary distillation objective during the pretraining process enables learning stronger representations.

Title: Weight Factorization and Centralization for Continual Learning in Speech Recognition
Snippet: Large-scale multilingual speech models [1] have become the backbone of speech applications, thanks to the high performance achieved in multiple languages, enabled by scaling the models, computation and data. Despite such achievement, the one-size-fit-all solution might still require further finetuning, in order to optimize the performance on certain tasks or datasets, for example dealing with code-switching [2,3] or low-resourced languages [4,5]. Dealing with such data is crucial in many systems such as simultaneous speech translation systems [6,7]. There is a variety of methods that allow for fast and efficient adaptation, such as using low-dimensional adapters [8,9], but this has often been treated as a one-off solution. More appropriately, we can treat the models as continual learning agents, in a scenario that these agents continually learn to adapt to the datasets without losing the previously learned knowledge. In fact, it only takes a few updates on a new dataset with a completely different distribution than the training data (which is not accessible when it comes to foundational models) to cause catastrophic forgetting, when the improvement on the downstream task is compromised with the rapid deterioration of the original model. 

The continual learning research area currently addresses this challenge primarily through three approaches: rehearsalbased techniques rely on a portion of the training data to partially recover performance loss [10,11]; regularization techniques penalize gradients or weights from deviating from their * Equal contribution original state [12]; and architecture-based techniques expand the model capacity [13,14] to accommodate new data-or a combination of these approaches altogether [15]. It is imperative to find solutions for continual learning on top of foundational models, especially when access to data is limited or unavailable, which makes many techniques difficult to apply. 

On the other hand, having a strong foundation also enables other possibilities compared to approaches that rely on training models from scratch. First of all, the foundational models can be adapted on new small datasets very rapidly with lowrank adapters, which are additional weights assigned to specific datasets/tasks. These weights are invoked only when these tasks are identified or given during inference.
</snippet>

Title: Investigating Continual Pretraining in Large Language Models: Insights and Implications
Snippet: Continual learning (CL) in large language models (LLMs) is an evolving domain that focuses on developing efficient and sustainable training strategies to adapt models to emerging knowledge and achieve robustness in dynamic environments. Our primary emphasis is on continual domain-adaptive pretraining, a process designed to equip LLMs with the ability to integrate new information from various domains while retaining previously learned knowledge. Since existing works concentrate mostly on continual fine-tuning for a limited selection of downstream tasks or training domains, we introduce a new benchmark designed to measure the adaptability of LLMs to changing pretraining data landscapes. We further examine the impact of model size on learning efficacy and forgetting, as well as how the progression and similarity of emerging domains affect the knowledge transfer within these models. Our findings uncover several key insights: (i) continual pretraining consistently improves<1.5B models studied in this work and is also superior to domain adaptation, (ii) larger models always achieve better perplexity than smaller ones when continually pretrained on the same corpus, (iii) smaller models are particularly sensitive to continual pretraining, showing the most significant rates of both learning and forgetting, (iv) continual pretraining boosts downstream task performance of GPT-2 family, (v) continual pretraining enables LLMs to specialize better when the sequence of domains shows semantic similarity while randomizing training domains leads to better transfer and final performance otherwise. We posit that our research establishes a new benchmark for CL in LLMs, providing a more realistic evaluation of knowledge retention and transfer across diverse domains.
</snippet>

Title: Gradient Sparsification For Masked Fine-Tuning of Transformers
Snippet: Fine-tuning pretrained transformer models for downstream tasks has been the defacto standard in natural language processing due to the recent successes of large-scale masked language modeling [1]- [4]. This is usually achieved in one of two ways: (1) freeze the gradients of the pretrained portion of the network and perform stochastic gradient descent (SGD) on a newly added task-specific layer/s or (2) perform SGD on both the pretrained and newly added layer/s. However, freezing all gradients of the pretrained layers can be too restrictive, particularly when the downstream task is dissilmilar to the task of language modeling used during pretraining [5]. In contrast, unfreezing all layers may lead to negative transfer whereby irrelevant features are tuned for a downstream task or stability issues may arise when performing stochastic gradient descent for a large number of parameters [6]. Gradual unfreezing [7] is an alternative method that only tunes a subset of k layers and freezes the remaining layers for an epoch. In each successive epoch, the next subset of k layers are tuned and this is iterated in a top-down fashion, i.e., unfreeze top k subset of layers to the bottom k subset of layers. Gradual unfreezing reduces training time by reducing the number of gradient updates after backpropagation. For the sole purpose of improving fine-tuning performance, gradual unfreezing could benefit from sparse gradient dropout alternatives that allow at least a subset of weights of all layers to be tuned at each epoch. Concretely, instead of restricting the freezing of gradients for whole layers, we can mask a percentage of gradients in all layers to allow gradients to flow through the whole network.

# Overview

This collection highlights recent papers that study how transformer weights change during training, spanning theory on attention and gradient dynamics, empirical layer-wise evolution of weight statistics, continual pretraining and fine-tuning, and head-level specialization. These works collectively map trajectories of weight matrices across epochs, layers, and tasks, and connect them to optimization choices, initialization scaling, and architectural design. <cite id="84db4750-2">Transformers exhibit incremental learning dynamics where the difference between initial and trained weights increases in rank over time</cite> and <cite id="84db4750-3">depth-dependent variance patterns emerge during pretraining, with shallow layers adapting quickly and deep layers adjusting more slowly</cite>. <cite id="9bb56ffa-2">Continual pretraining can improve perplexity and downstream transfer but also induces learning and forgetting that depend on model size and domain sequence</cite>, while <cite id="7d9a1368-0">attention heads can specialize into functional roles like “induction heads” during pretraining, supporting in-context learning</cite>. <cite id="19962e5b-1">NTK-based analyses show when and why transformers’ training dynamics stabilize and converge under different widths and initializations</cite>, and <cite id="19962e5b-4">global convergence can be achieved under multiple scaling regimes, with faster rates under certain initializations and over-parameterization regimes</cite>.

# Theoretical Analyses of Attention and Gradient Dynamics

Several papers analyze how attention weights evolve under optimization and what convergence behavior to expect. <cite id="84db4750-0">A one-layer transformer with softmax attention trained by GD exhibits phase-like behavior in attention dynamics for in-context learning; in imbalanced settings, a four-phase evolution emerges that characterizes interactions between dominant and under-represented features</cite>. <cite id="84db4750-1">In a formal phase 1 analysis, linear and attention layers show coupled dynamics: attention weights increase on tokens consistent with positive samples and suppress attention on non-leading tokens in negative samples, while token scores and attention allocation shift to dominant positions over time</cite>. These results connect training time to how attention distributions concentrate on informative tokens.

Convergence and stability are also studied through kernel and spectral lenses. <cite id="19962e5b-1">Under NTK initialization and appropriate scaling, the limiting NTK matrix of a transformer can be derived and used to show global convergence of GD with high probability, with stability of the NTK during training controlled via the spectral norm of the Hessian</cite>. <cite id="19962e5b-4">Comparative theory shows separations across scaling (τ0 = d−1/2 vs d−1), initialization (LeCun/He vs NTK), and architecture; for example, shallow transformers can converge globally under both scalings, but τ0 = d−1/2 admits faster convergence for large widths, and LeCun/He can yield faster convergence than NTK initialization</cite>. These analyses tie initialization scales and width to the trajectory of weight updates and to convergence speed.

# Empirical Evolution of Layer-wise Weights During Pretraining

Beyond theory, studies track how individual weight matrices change as training progresses. <cite id="84db4750-3">In a 12-layer GPT-2-style transformer trained with AdamW, attention Q/K/V projection weights show depth-dependent variance dynamics: lower layers expand their standard deviation rapidly in early pretraining, while higher layers change more slowly and smoothly, eventually stabilizing near narrower equilibrium distributions; weight matrices become sparser post-training, with a few large-magnitude entries dominating</cite>. <cite id="84db4750-2">Complementing this, theoretical and experimental evidence shows transformers follow incremental learning dynamics where the rank of the difference between initial and trained weights increases gradually, indicating staged growth of representational power</cite>. Together, these findings suggest asymmetric adaptation across depth: early, strong updates in shallow layers, followed by slower equilibrium in deeper layers.

Spectral and NTK-based diagnostics connect these empirical patterns to dynamics and prioritization. <cite id="19962e5b-2">Layerwise NTK (LNTK) decompositions show that layer convergence is governed by eigenvalues of the layer’s integral NTK; using layer-specific learning rates ηl ≈ 2/λl1 aligns updates with principal eigenvectors, leveraging spectral bias to speed learning along dominant directions</cite>. <cite id="19962e5b-3">A NTK-based test loss and Hessian-aware model selection framework (LENSLLM) characterizes fine-tuning transition phases and links intrinsic learning dynamics (via NTK) to dataset size and pre-trained knowledge, offering practical guidance on when and how to stop fine-tuning</cite>.

# Continual Pretraining, Weight Drift, and Specialization Across Domains/Tasks

Continual pretraining studies how weights evolve when a model is pretrained on multiple, changing corpora or domains. <cite id="9bb56ffa-2">A new continual domain-adaptive pretraining benchmark finds that continual pretraining consistently improves perplexity across <1.5B models and boosts downstream GPT-2 performance; larger models benefit more and smaller models show higher sensitivity to both learning and forgetting, while sequences of semantically similar domains enhance specialization and transfer, whereas randomized domains may yield better general transfer and final performance</cite>. <cite id="9bb56ffa-0">Surveys of continual pretraining in language models trace prior work showing multi-stage pretraining on in-domain, then task-specific data to enable temporal reasoning or mixed-language translation, contrasting with efficient in-domain continual pretraining that generalizes across tasks</cite>.

These dynamics have implications for avoiding catastrophic forgetting and stabilizing updates. <cite id="9bb56ffa-1">In speech and other modalities, continual learning strategies (rehearsal, regularization, and architecture expansion) are used to mitigate forgetting when adapting to new distributions; low-rank adapters allow rapid adaptation with minimal weight perturbation, highlighting how selective parameter updates can steer weight evolution while preserving prior knowledge</cite>. <cite id="9bb56ffa-4">Pragmatically, gradual unfreezing and gradient sparsification (e.g., GradDrop variants) can improve masked fine-tuning by controlling which weights are updated per epoch or layer, stabilizing training when tuning large pretrained models</cite>.

# Head-Level Specialization and Functional Roles of Attention

At the head level, multi-head attention modules often exhibit functional specialization as models are trained on diverse tasks or data. <cite id="7d9a1368-0">Developmental analyses identify “induction heads” that track repetitions of target tokens to support next-token prediction, with emergence of these patterns coinciding with improved in-context learning; subsequent work links these heads causally to solving sequence-tracking tasks</cite>. <cite id="7d9a1368-2">Analyses across tasks show consistent head roles, including syntax and coreference heads in BERT, alignment and position-specialized heads in machine translation, and heads that attend to rare words, indicating that attention heads can specialize along interpretable functions</cite>.

Multi-task settings further reveal how heads specialize and can be leveraged or pruned. <cite id="7d9a1368-1">Head importance scores and pruning procedures quantify functional specialization after training, and targeted training can enhance role-specific heads to promote specialization across tasks</cite>. <cite id="7d9a1368-4">Related work demonstrates head redundancy and diversity mechanisms, with pruning and lottery-ticket-style approaches showing that many heads contribute little post-training, while diversity-promoting regularization and mixture-of-experts variants can distribute specialization across heads for different inputs</cite>.

# Optimization, Initialization, and Scaling Effects on Weight Trajectories

Optimization choices and initialization scales shape how weights evolve, from early movement to convergence. <cite id="84db4750-4">Recent analyses show GD on self-attention with feedforward layers can achieve linear convergence under proper initialization (e.g., LeCun, He, NTK), though assumptions (e.g., identity feedforward weights) limit generality, highlighting how initialization and architecture constrain dynamics</cite>. <cite id="19962e5b-4">Comparative theory suggests that quadratic over-parameterization can suffice for global convergence in shallow transformers, and that certain initializations (LeCun/He) can yield faster convergence than NTK initialization, helping explain limited practical use of NTK for transformers</cite>. 

Spectral tools offer guidance for layerwise update scheduling. <cite id="19962e5b-2">By diagnosing LNTK eigenvalues, practitioners can choose layer-specific learning rates and prioritize layers with slower-converging directions, aligning weight updates with the model’s intrinsic learning dynamics and spectral bias toward principal components</cite>. <cite id="19962e5b-3">NTK-based model selection frameworks explicitly capture the competition between pre-trained knowledge, fine-tuning data scale, and dynamics, supporting early stopping and resource allocation strategies</cite>.

# Practical Observations on Weight Statistics and Sparsity

Empirical measurements reveal concrete patterns in how weights evolve and stabilize. <cite id="84db4750-3">During pretraining, lower-depth attention heads show rapid expansion and then stabilization of weight variance, while higher layers exhibit slower, smoother growth and sparser distributions with many near-zero entries and a small fraction of large magnitudes</cite>. <cite id="84db4750-2">The incremental rank increase in trained–initial weight differences suggests a staged growth of the model’s representational capacity, with rank gaps accumulating as tasks become more complex</cite>. These patterns inform monitoring and regularization strategies (e.g., controlling depth-wise variance growth, encouraging or constraining sparsity), and they align with the spectral insights above.

# Putting It Together and Open Questions

- Attention dynamics: <cite id="84db4750-0">Phase-wise evolution and concentration of attention on informative tokens</cite> indicate that training steers attention distributions toward functional selectivity.
- Depth and layers: <cite id="84db4750-3">Shallow layers update strongly early and stabilize quickly, while deeper layers adjust more slowly</cite>, and <cite id="19962e5b-2">spectral bias suggests prioritizing layers and directions that guide faster convergence</cite>.
- Continual adaptation: <cite id="9bb56ffa-2">Continual pretraining improves perplexity and downstream tasks but induces domain-specific specialization and forgetting patterns that depend on model size and domain sequences</cite>, with techniques like adapters and gradual unfreezing controlling the weight-drift surface area.
- Heads and tasks: <cite id="7d9a1368-0">Induction heads and task-specialized attention</cite> show that multi-task and multi-domain training can yield interpretable head roles and specialization.

Open challenges include quantifying cross-optimizer differences in long-horizon training, understanding when and how to regularize rank growth, and extending NTK-based convergence analyses to deeper, more realistic transformer stacks with residual connections and complex objectives. Nonetheless, the body of work above provides a practical and theoretical map of how transformer weights evolve: they start with small, structured perturbations and gradually expand rank and variance in depth-dependent ways; attention concentrates on informative signals; and continual adaptation induces domain- and task-specific specialization, all shaped by initialization scales, widths, and spectral properties that guide efficient update strategies. <cite id="84db4750-2">Incremental rank growth across training</cite>, <cite id="84db4750-3">depth-dependent variance and sparsity</cite>, <cite id="9bb56ffa-2">continual pretraining trade-offs</cite>, and <cite id="19962e5b-2">spectral/LNTK-guided scheduling</cite> collectively offer a coherent view of transformer weight evolution over time.
</answer>

Title: In-Context Convergence of Transformers
Snippet: In this work, we investigated the training dynamics of a one-layer transformer with softmax attention trained by GD for in-context learning. We analyzed two settings respectively with balanced and imbalanced features, and proved the guaranteed convergence to a vanishing in-context prediction error by detailing the evolution of attention dynamics for both settings. Interestingly, we characterized a four-phase behavior for the imbalanced settings that sheds light on the intricate attention dynamics between dominant and target under-represented features during training. To our knowledge, this is the first work that rigorously analyzed the softmax attention dynamics for in-context learning. Our approach features novel ideas for phase decomposition based on the changes of the dominant role between two types of bilinear attention weights in the learning process, and has the potential to facilitate further theoretical understanding of how transformers perform in other algorithms and learning paradigms.

Title: Transformers learn through gradual rank increase
Snippet: The transformer architecture achieves state of the art performance in various domains, yet we still lack a solid theoretical understanding of its training dynamics [VSP + 17, DCLT19, LOG + 19, DBK + 20]. Nevertheless, the theoretical toolbox has matured over the last years and there are promising new approaches. One important line of work examines the role that initialization scale plays on the trajectory taken by gradient descent [JGH18, COB18, GSJW19, MGW + 20, JGS + 21, SS21, KC22]. When the weights are initialized small, it has been shown for simple networks that an incremental learning behaviour occurs, where functions of increasing complexity are learned in stages. This regime is known to be richer than the large-initialization regime1 , but the incremental learning dynamics are difficult to analyze, and are so far understood only for extremely simple architectures. Can we apply this analysis to transformers? Namely: 

Are there incremental learning dynamics when training a transformer architecture? 

An obstacle is that past work on incremental learning has mainly studied linear networks [Ber22, ACHL19, MKAA21, LLL20, WGL + 19, JGS + 21, GSSD19, SKZ + 23, PF23], with one paper studying nonlinear 2-layer fully-connected networks [BPVF22]. In contrast, transformers have nonlinear attention heads that do not fall under previous analyses: given X ∈ R n×d , an attention head computes attention(X; 

where W K , W Q , W V , W O ∈ R d×d ′ are trainable matrices, and the softmax is applied row-wise. A transformer is even more complex, since it is formed by stacking alternating layers of attention heads and feedforward networks, along with residual connections. 

Main finding Our main finding is that transformers exhibit incremental learning dynamics, where the difference between the trained and initial weights incrementally increases in rank. Our results have a theoretical component and an experimental component.

Title: Weight Initialization and Variance Dynamics in Deep Neural Networks and Large Language Models
Snippet: Setup. To examine how variance evolves in deep transformers, I pretrain a 12-transformer GPT-2-style model built from scratch. Each transformer block includes multihead self-attention and a feed-forward MLP with GELU activation. The model is initialized with a standard configuration (normal distribution, std 0.02 for most modules and xavier normal for the embedding matrix) and trained with AdamW at learning rate 1 × 10 −4 , batch size 16. The experiment tracks the standard deviation of weights in all layers of attention Q/K/V projections. 

Protocol. At each training checkpoint, I (i) compute the standard deviation of the weights for every layer and mod-  Findings. After pretraining, the model exhibits clear depth-dependent variance dynamics. For attention Q/K/V, the lower layers show rapid and pronounced expansion of weight standard deviation during early training-std values increase sharply within the first few thousand iterations, reflecting strong adaptation to raw input statistics. In contrast, higher layers expand much more slowly, with smaller and smoother std growth, indicating that their weights adjust gradually under weaker, residualgradient signals constrained by normalization. When visualizing individual weight matrices, the post-training distributions become noticeably sparser: many near-zero entries remain, while a small fraction of large-magnitude weights dominate, suggesting selective amplification of salient connections. Overall, the variance trajectories reveal a progressive equilibration pattern-fast and volatile adaptation in shallow layers, slower convergence in deeper layers, and eventual stabilization of each layer's variance around a narrow equilibrium band. This asymmetric evolution highlights how transformer depth shapes the flow of statistical adaptation during pretraining.

Title: On the Convergence of Gradient Descent on Learning Transformers with Residual Connections
Snippet: In addition to these studies, a considerable number of works [ZFB24, HCL23, CSWY24, YHLC24, ZSLS25, LWL + 24, MHM23, ACDS23, RWL24, FCJS24, TWCD23, HLY24] have focused on self-attention mechanism-based in-context learning, particularly examining the training dynamics and landscape. However, despite the growing interest in in-context learning, this line of research does not adequately capture the complexities of the training process underlying self-attention mechanisms. The primary reason for this is that in-context learning dynamics are primarily concerned with how models adapt to new tasks during inference, while the training dynamics of self-attention mechanisms within Transformer models focus on the process through which self-attention weights are learned during training. Moreover, in-context learning inherently relies on a specific input matrix structure, which is not directly applicable to the training dynamics of self-attention mechanisms. In response to this gap, recent work [SHZ + 24] investigates the training dynamics of gradient descent for self-attention mechanisms within Transformer models, providing insights into how gradient-based optimization influences the evolution of weight matrices during the training process. Beyond investigating individual components, only recent work [WLCC23] studies the convergence rate of a softmax attention layer combined with a feedforward network using a single ReLU activation function, without imposing any specific restrictions on the input matrix. This work shows that, with proper initialization, gradient descent can achieve a linear convergence rate. Moreover, it demonstrates that under suitable conditions, commonly used initialization schemes such as LeCun and He, and NTK initialization satisfy the requirements for convergence. However, a key limitation of this analysis is the assumption that the weight matrices in the feedforward network are identity matrices, which restricts its applicability to more general settings. Consequently, the results only partially capture the training dynamics of a singlelayer Transformer.

After pretraining, the model exhibits clear depth-dependent variance dynamics. For attention Q/K/V, the lower layers show rapid and pronounced expansion of weight standard deviation during early training-std values increase sharply within the first few thousand iterations, reflecting strong adaptation to raw input statistics.
