Title: Kolmogorov Arnold Networks in Fraud Detection: Bridging the Gap Between Theory and Practice
Snippet: We used five datasets commonly used for fraud detection research, covering domains like credit card transactions, bank account activities, vehicle insurance claims, healthcare provider claims, and e-commerce transactions. The Kaggle-Credit Card Fraud Dataset [30] includes transactions from European cardholders in September 2013, with 492 frauds out of 284,807 transactions. The Bank Account Fraud (BAF) dataset [31] features large-scale, realistic tabular data for evaluating fraud detection models in banking. The Vehicle Claims dataset [32] focuses on unsupervised anomaly detection in vehicle insurance claims. The Healthcare Provider Fraud Detection Analysis Dataset [33] includes inpatient and outpatient claims, and beneficiary details to detect fraudulent healthcare billing activities. Lastly, the IEEE-CIS Fraud Detection Dataset [34] benchmarks machine learning models on e-commerce transactions provided by Vesta Corporation, supporting research to improve fraud alerts and revenue protection.

Title: Supply chain fraud prediction with machine learning and artificial intelligence
Snippet: Given the focus of this dataset on e-commerce transactions in a business-to-consumer (B2C) context, it is important to define the concept of fraud within online retail settings. Fraud within the B2C realm poses distinctive challenges as it frequently involves consumers directly perpetrating fraudulent activities against the company (Yang et al. 2015;W. Yu et al. 2024). In the B2C environment, fraud can be identified through anomalies in order status, wherein consumers engage in deceptive practices to exploit the e-commerce system (Polman and Spruit 2013;Raghava-Raju 2017). These fraudulent activities encompass order cancellation fraud, whereby consumers place orders and subsequently cancel them after the items have been shipped, with the objective of obtaining the goods without payment (Jangra et al. 2023;Marchal and Szyller 2019). Additional forms of B2C fraud encompass the utilisation of stolen or counterfeit credit cards to undertake unauthorised purchases, resulting in chargebacks when the genuine cardholder disputes the transactions (Turaba et al. 2022). Furthermore, deceptive practices involve returning used or damaged goods and falsely claiming them to be in their original condition or substituting items and retaining the original purchases (Wanganoo et al. 2021). In certain instances, consumers may hijack genuine customer accounts to place fraudulent orders or manipulate account details for financial gain (P. Kumar et al. 2017). To effectively combat consumer fraud in the B2C environment, SCM needs advanced detection systems that can analyze order status and customer behaviour patterns for red flags of fraudulent activities. These systems must leverage ML techniques that monitor unusual order cancellation rates, inconsistent payment histories, atypical return patterns, and irregular account activities in the supply chain. 

While predictive analytics has found applications across myriad domains, several promising applications for fraud detection in SCM remain untapped. For instance, predictive analytics can be harnessed to discern fraudulent activities based on payment mediums (electronic or cash) or the buyer's order status (on-site or online). The former, identifying fraud through payment mediums, has been adopted by a handful of companies to notable success. This strategy hinges on analyzing historical payment data to spotlight dubious transactions warranting deeper scrutiny.

# Digital Twins: Literature Review with Focus on Changing Environments and the Generalization Problem

## Definition, Scope, and Motivation
Digital twins (DTs) are virtual representations of physical assets, processes, or systems that enable real-time data streaming, predictive analytics, and bidirectional interaction to inform operations and optimization in applications such as industry, smart cities, and healthcare.<cite id="330cc81f-0">Digital twins are being rapidly developed due to advances in big data, IoT, cloud computing, and AI, with active research and deployment across industrial, smart city, and smart health sectors</cite> <cite id="c476e08b-1">DTs comprise a physical twin in the real world, a virtual twin in cyberspace, and the interactions between them, with cyber-physical interaction being indispensable for deriving data-driven intelligence and feeding actions back to the physical system</cite> <cite id="c476e08b-1">Integration of XR and DTs supports 3D immersive modeling, safe simulations, and workforce training, while online calibration, dynamic learning, and AI enable continual synchronization and intelligence</cite>. Surveys and expert studies emphasize both technical and nontechnical challenges, including social, legal, and governance aspects, and call for structured taxonomies of obstacles to operationalization.<cite id="330cc81f-0">Surveys discuss theoretical underpinnings and application developments, and highlight challenges for future work</cite> <cite id="330cc81f-1">A systematic review and Delphi survey on urban DTs identify and score technical and nontechnical challenges, providing a taxonomy of obstacles and their perceived severity</cite>.

## Challenges from Changing Environments

DTs operate in dynamic environments where data distributions shift, sensors fail or degrade, and physical systems evolve, creating nonstationary conditions that threaten synchronization and predictive fidelity. In smart manufacturing, the DT–physical system coupling depends on high-quality, continuous sensing (e.g., SCADA), and the integration of sensors with DTs enables real-time interaction and optimization; however, data quality issues, missing data, and model uncertainty are pervasive obstacles.<cite id="c476e08b-1">DTs rely on real-time data streaming from advanced sensing systems such as SCADA, with data quality instrumental to modeling, calibration, and optimization</cite> <cite id="c476e08b-1">The twinning and modeling process faces data and model challenges including sensor placement, missing data, and model uncertainty</cite> <cite id="c476e08b-2">Manufacturing cyber-physical systems integrate heterogeneous devices and networks, requiring pattern mining, real-time sensor networks, and deep learning to cope with contextual big data and process variability</cite>. 

Nonstationarity demands continual learning and adaptation to maintain alignment between physical and virtual twins. Evidence from industrial and wireless DT settings shows that synchronization can degrade as environments evolve, and that continual learning (CL) and active learning (AL) are used to keep DTs updated with minimal labels while preserving accuracy in dynamic conditions.<cite id="c476e08b-3">DT-driven cyber-physical systems enable online upgrades and parallel monitoring, but disconnected upgrades are inefficient for adjusting to latent disruptions and dynamic operational changes</cite> <cite id="c476e08b-4">DTs in dynamic wireless networks and intelligent location-based services adopt continual learning frameworks to model evolving affinity between physical and cyber twins and minimize desynchronization, with MLOps used to manage dynamic updates</cite> <cite id="c476e08b-4">In the lumber industry, active learning helps DTs adapt to dynamic environments by selecting and learning from new samples to remain synchronized with real-world changes</cite>. 

Uncertainty is ubiquitous and must be modeled explicitly to ensure reliable operation under environmental variability. A comprehensive framework for DTs recognizes measurement, modeling, and operational uncertainties and demonstrates how probabilistic methods such as Bayesian networks can propagate evidence and update the virtual state in real time; risk-aware DTs (“Risk Twin”) extend this by visualizing reliability indices to support risk-informed control.<cite id="c476e08b-1">Uncertainties in sensing, modeling, and operations are pervasive in DT applications and can compromise deterministic models</cite> <cite id="c476e08b-4">A Bayesian-network-based framework updates digital states via inference with observed data, illustrating probabilistic DT modeling under uncertainty</cite> <cite id="c476e08b-4">Risk Twin operationalizes real-time risk visualization and control by quantifying uncertainties and producing unified risk metrics across structural components</cite>.

## The Generalization Problem: From Domain Shift to Sim2Real

A central limitation of DTs is generalization across environments, time, and use cases. When virtual training environments differ from real-world deployment, models can degrade unless adapted; this is especially acute in perception and control tasks where simulator fidelity and domain gap affect performance.<cite id="04014de6-3">High-fidelity DTs for LiDAR-based intelligent transportation systems can improve learning by generating labeled synthetic data and aligning feature distributions between simulated and real domains, but simulators’ hand-crafted environments are simplified and not streamlined, and post-hoc domain adaptation often requires extra processing</cite> <cite id="04014de6-3">A DT-assisted approach combining graph matching and multi-level domain discriminators improved cross-domain generalization compared to isolated simulator improvements, yet practical gaps remain in creating HiFi DTs for arbitrary locations</cite>. In wireless communications, training deep models on DT-generated synthetic CSI to perform well in real environments is framed explicitly as a domain adaptation problem, with performance bounds tied to distributional discrepancy between synthetic (DT) and real data and mitigation via adaptation losses.<cite id="04014de6-4">Training DL models on DT synthetic data for real-world performance is a domain adaptation problem; theoretical bounds relate generalization error to distribution discrepancy and a model complexity term, motivating adaptation losses to minimize the gap</cite> <cite id="04014de6-4">When DT data resembles real-world data, models trained on DT data can achieve high real-world performance, highlighting the role of DT fidelity in domain adaptation success</cite>. 

Transfer learning with DTs offers a practical path to reduce real-domain labeling and improve robustness by leveraging virtual data to initialize or constrain target-domain learners. In production lines, a source DT generates large, balanced virtual datasets to pre-train a learner, whose shared parameters are then transferred to a target physical workshop where only a small labeled set is used, speeding training and improving robustness without rebuilding the model structure.<cite id="04014de6-1">A DT-assisted transfer learning pipeline trains a source learner on DT-generated virtual data, transfers parameters to a target domain, and uses small labeled real data to fine-tune shared parameters, improving training speed and robustness</cite>. In robotics and intelligent systems, curated DT datasets and multi-modal sensing-communication frameworks are proposed to support sim2real transfer, but they also highlight the need for better alignment and generalization strategies beyond pure physics emulation.<cite id="04014de6-2">SynthSoM-Twin proposes a multi-modal sensing-communication DT dataset to enable sim2real transfer via synesthesia of machines, illustrating data-centric approaches to improve generalization</cite>.

## Methods to Improve Robustness and Generalization

### Continual and Adaptive Learning
Continual learning (CL) and active learning (AL) are used to keep DTs synchronized with evolving environments, reducing desynchronization and enabling online updates. Edge continual learning frameworks and MLOps pipelines manage dynamic updates in DT architectures spanning manufacturing, wireless systems, and location-based services, emphasizing synchronization and adaptation to data drift.<cite id="c476e08b-4">Continual learning frameworks for dynamic DTs over wireless networks emphasize accurate modeling of evolving affinity between physical and cyber twins and minimizing desynchronization, with edge implementations and MLOps for dynamic updates</cite> <cite id="c476e08b-4">DT-based architectures with continual learning in intelligent location services integrate MLOps to adapt to evolving data and task conditions, maintaining accuracy and relevance over time</cite> <cite id="c476e08b-1">Cyber-physical interaction via data synchronization, online calibration, and dynamic learning is essential to derive intelligence and maintain alignment between twins in changing environments</cite>.

### Uncertainty Quantification and Physics-Informed Modeling
UQ and physics-informed approaches help DTs reason about aleatoric (inherent) and epistemic (knowledge gaps) uncertainty, enabling calibration and trust assessment. Literature reviews and applications detail Bayesian and surrogate modeling methods, co-simulation with UQ, and physics-constrained DNNs to improve predictive fidelity and decision support under uncertainty.<cite id="1f33c846-0">UQ distinguishes aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty, with methods including Bayesian surrogates, co-simulation, and calibration/bias correction; physics-constrained DNNs and optimization with uncertainty calibration have been applied to quantify output uncertainty</cite> <cite id="1f33c846-1">Constructing operating DTs involves sensing, data processing, abstraction, and simulation, each contributing uncertainties that impact predictive fidelity and require itemized quantification and management</cite> <cite id="1f33c846-2">UQ and sensitivity analysis are proposed to establish reliability and trustworthiness of DTs, with machine learning-based UQ (e.g., sparse polynomial chaos) and global sensitivity indices suggested for integration</cite>. In structural DTs, probabilistic frameworks such as Bayesian networks and risk-twin architectures provide real-time risk visualization and control by quantifying uncertainties and aggregating component-level reliability metrics.<cite id="1f33c846-4">Probabilistic modeling with Bayesian networks updates digital states under uncertainty, and risk-twin systems visualize reliability indices in real time to support risk-informed control in civil structures</cite>.

### High-Fidelity Digital Twins and Domain Adaptation
High-fidelity DTs that accurately model assets and environments can narrow the sim2real gap by generating realistic synthetic data and aligning distributions between source and target domains. In LiDAR-based perception, high-fidelity DTs combined with domain adaptation modules (e.g., graph matching and domain discriminators) improved cross-dataset generalization compared to simulator-only improvements, while also exposing practical gaps in asset acquisition and streamlined pipeline construction.<cite id="04014de6-3">High-fidelity DTs for LiDAR perception generate labeled synthetic data and learn transferable representations with domain adaptation modules, improving cross-domain performance but requiring complex, non-streamlined asset pipelines</cite>. In MIMO communications, theoretical analyses tie domain discrepancy to generalization error and motivate training objectives that balance DT-derived losses with adaptation terms to bridge distributional gaps.<cite id="04014de6-4">Domain adaptation bounds relate generalization error to discrepancy between DT and real data and a complexity term, guiding loss functions that minimize the gap while leveraging DT data</cite>.

### Data and Infrastructure: Digital Thread and Cross-Domain Integration
Effective generalization depends on robust data pipelines and interoperable representations across the digital thread. In manufacturing, integrated data management, real-time sensor networks, and AI-driven analytics support DT-driven cognitive loops that rapidly reconfigure production parameters, but require resilient connectivity and automated data management to handle big contextual data and process variability.<cite id="c476e08b-2">Manufacturing cyber-physical systems interconnect heterogeneous devices and networks, using pattern mining, real-time sensor networks, and deep learning to expose process connections and adjust to prosumer and environmental changes</cite> <cite id="c476e08b-3">DT-driven cyber-physical systems act as infrastructure for planning and online upgrades, processing collected data to inform control and reconfiguration in response to disruptions and dynamic changes</cite>. In urban DTs, challenge taxonomies and expert scoring highlight the need to address data integration and governance alongside technical barriers, underscoring that generalization is constrained by interoperability and institutional factors beyond algorithms alone.<cite id="330cc81f-1">A Delphi-based review of urban DTs classifies technical and nontechnical challenges and scores their severity, indicating that governance and integration issues are significant barriers to operational DTs</cite>.

## Domain-Specific Illustrations

- Industrial communications: Learnable DTs for electromagnetic environments can model object properties and interactions, achieving high channel prediction accuracy after training and handling environment changes without pilot overhead, demonstrating adaptive modeling under nonstationarity.<cite id="330cc81f-4">A learnable DT reconstructs EM properties and interactions, achieving high channel prediction accuracy post-training and handling environment changes, which is critical for real-world applications</cite> <cite id="04014de6-4">DT-assisted CSI compression/feedback frames learning as domain adaptation, with bounds linking distribution discrepancy to performance and loss functions that leverage DT data to improve real-world performance</cite>.

- Manufacturing and robotics: DT-assisted transfer learning uses virtual data to bootstrap target-domain models with limited labels, improving speed and robustness in fault diagnosis and production lines; DT-enabled XR and immersive interfaces support modeling, training, and real-time interaction, but rely on high-quality, synchronized data streams and address model uncertainty and missing data.<cite id="04014de6-1">DT-assisted transfer learning uses large virtual datasets to initialize target-domain learners, transferring shared parameters to reduce labeling needs and improve robustness</cite> <cite id="c476e08b-1">DTs integrated with XR provide immersive 3D environments for modeling and training, but require data synchronization, online calibration, and dynamic learning to maintain cyber-physical alignment</cite> <cite id="c476e08b-1">Model uncertainty, sensor placement, and missing data are persistent challenges in DT modeling for manufacturing</cite>.

- Smart cities and infrastructure: High-fidelity DTs for perception (e.g., LiDAR-based ITS) and risk-informed structural DTs demonstrate how probabilistic modeling and real-time uncertainty propagation can support generalization and risk control, while also revealing limitations in simulator fidelity and streamlined DT pipeline construction.<cite id="04014de6-3">High-fidelity DTs for LiDAR perception improve cross-domain generalization through distribution alignment but face challenges in realistic environment construction and post-hoc adaptation requirements</cite> <cite id="1f33c846-4">Risk Twin integrates Bayesian inference into DTs to quantify and visualize structural reliability in real time, enabling risk-informed control under environmental and operational uncertainties</cite>.

## Open Problems and Research Gaps

- Bridging the sim2real gap at scale: While high-fidelity DTs and domain adaptation modules improve generalization, creating streamlined, automated pipelines for asset acquisition and environment modeling remains open, especially for arbitrary deployment sites and long-horizon operations.<cite id="04014de6-3">Despite progress, key gaps remain in sim2real lidar learning, including simplified hand-crafted sim environments, reliance on post-hoc UDA, and non-streamlined HiFi DT creation, motivating simpler systematic methods for arbitrary locations</cite>.

- Robust continual learning under nonstationarity: DTs in dynamic environments require CL strategies that mitigate catastrophic forgetting and maintain synchronization under concept drift, with practical integration into MLOps and edge platforms for real-time adaptation.<cite id="c476e08b-4">Continual learning frameworks for dynamic DTs emphasize synchronization and MLOps for managing continual updates in real time</cite>.

- Physics-informed and uncertainty-aware twins: There is a need for standardized UQ practices across domains and for integrating physics constraints with learned models to ensure reliability and calibration under environmental variability and sensor uncertainty.<cite id="1f33c846-1">Uncertainties at each stage of DT construction impact predictive fidelity, calling for itemized quantification and management strategies</cite> <cite id="1f33c846-0">Physics-constrained DNNs and Bayesian calibration methods have been explored, but broader standardization and integration into DT pipelines remain</cite>.

- Data and governance across the digital thread: Generalization is constrained by data quality, interoperability, and governance in complex, multi-stakeholder settings; urban DTs highlight the importance of addressing nontechnical challenges alongside technical ones to realize scalable, trustworthy DTs.<cite id="330cc81f-1">Urban DT challenge taxonomies, informed by Delphi surveys, indicate significant nontechnical barriers related to governance and integration that affect operationalization</cite>.

## Conclusion

DTs promise powerful closed-loop intelligence across sectors, but their value depends on the ability to operate and generalize under changing environments and across diverse contexts. The literature converges on three pillars: continual, synchronization-aware learning; uncertainty quantification and physics-informed modeling; and high-fidelity, adaptable DTs coupled with domain adaptation and transfer learning to bridge sim2real gaps.<cite id="c476e08b-4">Continual learning and active learning are key to maintaining DT synchronization in dynamic environments</cite> <cite id="1f33c846-0">UQ and physics-constrained models help manage aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties and improve calibration</cite> <cite id="04014de6-3">High-fidelity DTs with domain adaptation improve cross-domain performance but face practical pipeline challenges</cite> <cite id="04014de6-1">DT-assisted transfer learning reduces real-label requirements and accelerates robust deployment</cite>. Progress will also hinge on resilient digital threads, interoperable data, and governance frameworks that extend beyond algorithmic advances to support trustworthy, generalizable DT ecosystems across industry and society.<cite id="330cc81f-1">Comprehensive challenge taxonomies for urban DTs emphasize that nontechnical and governance factors are as critical as technical ones for scalable DT operations</cite>.

Snippet: Uncertainty quantification (UQ) is an important aspect of all model-building exercises and has been emphasised as an evaluation criterion in applications ranging from medicine [11] to autonomous vehicles [12]. Models built from data are subject to aleatoric uncertainty which stems from randomness in the data generating process, sensing mechanism, etc. This type of uncertainty is inherent to the system and cannot be reduced by collecting more measurements. On the other hand, epistemic uncertainty stems from the inadequacy of a model to explain the underlying system, and can be reduced by using more data to train the model. As a result, UQ of both digital twin models and DNN models has already been studied in the literature. The authors in [13] made use of Monte Carlo co-simulations with a digital twin and adopted statistical analysis tools to quantify the uncertainty in controlling an agricultural vehicle. A Bayesian model was used for surrogate modelling and UQ of convolutional neural networks learning to solve stochastic partial differential equations in [14]. The uncertainty of surrogate models in reliabilitybased design optimisation was quantified in [15]. UQ of computational thermodynamics models was performed in [16]. Bayesian method-based model calibration and UQ was performed for a physics-based model for predicting the evolution of precipitates during a heat treatment in [17]. Physics-based digital twins can additionally have parametric or structural uncertainty in the model as well as aleatoric uncertainty. These uncertainties have been addressed in the literature with a host of methods such as calibration and bias correction [18]. A physics-constrained deep neural network was developed in [19] to solve partial differential equations, and uncertainty calibration was included in the optimisation to quantify the output uncertainty. 

Uncertainty quantification of DNN models has also attracted significant attention. The authors in [20] proposed a computationally light approach to quantify the aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty for DNNs. The authors proposed the use of assumed density filtering for propagating the input uncertainty through all layers of the model.

Title: Risk twin: real-time risk visualization and control for structural systems
Snippet: However, a prevailing assumption in many Digital Twin systems is that the sensing, modeling, and simulation modules are deterministic [25][26][27][28]. This assumption, however, is not realistic in real-world Digital Twin applications, where uncertainties are pervasive [29]. These uncertainties arise from various sources, including measurement uncertainties due to inaccuracies and variabilities of sensors; modeling uncertainties stemming from limitations and assumptions in computational models; and operational uncertainties, which involve variations in system performance under different real-world conditions and human interactions [30,31]. For instance, stress-sensing devices in structural Digital Twin systems often exhibit high sensitivity to temperature and humidity, causing significant discrepancies in Analog-to-Digital (AD) conversion values for identical stress levels measured under differing conditions, such as noon versus night [32]. These uncertainties can compromise the accuracy of deterministic Digital Twin models. To properly quantify the influence of uncertainties in Digital Twin systems, Kapteyn et al. proposed a comprehensive framework based on Bayesian network [21]. This framework represents the states of physical systems and their digital counterparts as random variables and updates the latter through Bayesian network inference using the observed data. Moreover, two realistic applications of predictive Digital Twin are proposed to illustrate the framework, which have been further explored in subsequent research [12,22]. 

Although the previously discussed methodologies can predict specific quantities of interest, there is an absence of a specialized framework for assessing the risk of structural safety on a unified scale. Such a framework is essential not only for quantifying uncertainties and risks within the structural system, but also for providing a holistic metric of risk across different structural components. For instance, a Digital Twin can monitor quantities such as stress, strain, and moment that collectively contribute to the safety of structural components, but it does not offer a directly comparable metric for the risk of each component. 

To fill this gap, this study introduces Risk Twin, a system designed to analyze and visualize the reliability indices for structural components in real-time, thereby facilitating risk-informed control. 

Building on existing progress of integrating probabilistic analysis within the Digital Twinning technology, this study aims to further advance their application in risk assessment and control of civil structures.
</snippet></tool_output>

# Digital Twins: Literature Review with Focus on Changing Environments and the Generalization Problem

## Definition, Scope, and Motivation
Digital twins (DTs) are virtual representations of physical assets, processes, or systems that enable real-time data streaming, predictive analytics, and bidirectional interaction to inform operations and optimization in applications such as industry, smart cities, and healthcare.<cite id="330cc81f-0">Digital twins are being rapidly developed due to advances in big data, IoT, cloud computing, and AI, with active research and deployment across industrial, smart city, and smart health sectors</cite> <cite id="c476e08b-1">DTs comprise a physical twin in the real world, a virtual twin in cyberspace, and the interactions between them, with cyber-physical interaction being indispensable for deriving data-driven intelligence and feeding actions back to the physical system</cite> <cite id="c476e08b-1">Integration of XR and DTs supports 3D immersive modeling, safe simulations, and workforce training, while online calibration, dynamic learning, and AI enable continual synchronization and intelligence</cite>. Surveys and expert studies emphasize both technical and nontechnical challenges, including social, legal, and governance aspects, and call for structured taxonomies of obstacles to operationalization.<cite id="330cc81f-0">Surveys discuss theoretical underpinnings and application developments, and highlight challenges for future work</cite> <cite id="330cc81f-1">A systematic review and Delphi survey on urban DTs identify and score technical and nontechnical challenges, providing a taxonomy of obstacles and their perceived severity</cite>.

## Challenges from Changing Environments

DTs operate in dynamic environments where data distributions shift, sensors fail or degrade, and physical systems evolve, creating nonstationary conditions that threaten synchronization and predictive fidelity. In smart manufacturing, the DT–physical system coupling depends on high-quality, continuous sensing (e.g., SCADA), and the integration of sensors with DTs enables real-time interaction and optimization; however, data quality issues, missing data, and model uncertainty are pervasive obstacles.<cite id="c476e08b-1">DTs rely on real-time data streaming from advanced sensing systems such as SCADA, with data quality instrumental to modeling, calibration, and optimization</cite> <cite id="c476e08b-1">The twinning and modeling process faces data and model challenges including sensor placement, missing data, and model uncertainty</cite> <cite id="c476e08b-2">Manufacturing cyber-physical systems integrate heterogeneous devices and networks, requiring pattern mining, real-time sensor networks, and deep learning to cope with contextual big data and process variability</cite>. 

Nonstationarity demands continual learning and adaptation to maintain alignment between physical and virtual twins. Evidence from industrial and wireless DT settings shows that synchronization can degrade as environments evolve, and that continual learning (CL) and active learning (AL) are used to keep DTs updated with minimal labels while preserving accuracy in dynamic conditions.<cite id="c476e08b-3">DT-driven cyber-physical systems enable online upgrades and parallel monitoring, but disconnected upgrades are inefficient for adjusting to latent disruptions and dynamic operational changes</cite> <cite id="c476e08b-4">DTs in dynamic wireless networks and intelligent location-based services adopt continual learning frameworks to model evolving affinity between physical and cyber twins and minimize desynchronization, with MLOps used to manage dynamic updates</cite> <cite id="c476e08b-4">In the lumber industry, active learning helps DTs adapt to dynamic environments by selecting and learning from new samples to remain synchronized with real-world changes</cite>. 

Uncertainty is ubiquitous and must be modeled explicitly to ensure reliable operation under environmental variability. A comprehensive framework for DTs recognizes measurement, modeling, and operational uncertainties and demonstrates how probabilistic methods such as Bayesian networks can propagate evidence and update the virtual state in real time; risk-aware DTs (“Risk Twin”) extend this by visualizing reliability indices to support risk-informed control.<cite id="c476e08b-1">Uncertainties in sensing, modeling, and operations are pervasive in DT applications and can compromise deterministic models</cite> <cite id="c476e08b-4">A Bayesian-network-based framework updates digital states via inference with observed data, illustrating probabilistic DT modeling under uncertainty</cite> <cite id="c476e08b-4">Risk Twin operationalizes real-time risk visualization and control by quantifying uncertainties and producing unified risk metrics across structural components</cite>.

## The Generalization Problem: From Domain Shift to Sim2Real

A central limitation of DTs is generalization across environments, time, and use cases. When virtual training environments differ from real-world deployment, models can degrade unless adapted; this is especially acute in perception and control tasks where simulator fidelity and domain gap affect performance.<cite id="04014de6-3">High-fidelity DTs for LiDAR-based intelligent transportation systems can improve learning by generating labeled synthetic data and aligning feature distributions between simulated and real domains, but simulators’ hand-crafted environments are simplified and not streamlined, and post-hoc domain adaptation often requires extra processing</cite> <cite id="04014de6-3">A DT-assisted approach combining graph matching and multi-level domain discriminators improved cross-domain generalization compared to isolated simulator improvements, yet practical gaps remain in creating HiFi DTs for arbitrary locations</cite>. In wireless communications, training deep models on DT-generated synthetic CSI to perform well in real environments is framed explicitly as a domain adaptation problem, with performance bounds tied to distributional discrepancy between synthetic (DT) and real data and mitigation via adaptation losses.<cite id="04014de6-4">Training DL models on DT synthetic data for real-world performance is a domain adaptation problem; theoretical bounds relate generalization error to distribution discrepancy and a model complexity term, motivating adaptation losses to minimize the gap</cite> <cite id="04014de6-4">When DT data resembles real-world data, models trained on DT data can achieve high real-world performance, highlighting the role of DT fidelity in domain adaptation success</cite>. 

Transfer learning with DTs offers a practical path to reduce real-domain labeling and improve robustness by leveraging virtual data to initialize or constrain target-domain learners. In production lines, a source DT generates large, balanced virtual datasets to pre-train a learner, whose shared parameters are then transferred to a target physical workshop where only a small labeled set is used, speeding training and improving robustness without rebuilding the model structure.<cite id="04014de6-1">A DT-assisted transfer learning pipeline trains a source learner on DT-generated virtual data, transfers parameters to a target domain, and uses small labeled real data to fine-tune shared parameters, improving training speed and robustness</cite>. In robotics and intelligent systems, curated DT datasets and multi-modal sensing-communication frameworks are proposed to support sim2real transfer, but they also highlight the need for better alignment and generalization strategies beyond pure physics emulation.<cite id="04014de6-2">SynthSoM-Twin proposes a multi-modal sensing-communication DT dataset to enable sim2real transfer via synesthesia of machines, illustrating data-centric approaches to improve generalization</cite>.

## Methods to Improve Robustness and Generalization

### Continual and Adaptive Learning
Continual learning (CL) and active learning (AL) are used to keep DTs synchronized with evolving environments, reducing desynchronization and enabling online updates. Edge continual learning frameworks and MLOps pipelines manage dynamic updates in DT architectures spanning manufacturing, wireless systems, and location-based services, emphasizing synchronization and adaptation to data drift.<cite id="c476e08b-4">Continual learning frameworks for dynamic DTs over wireless networks emphasize accurate modeling of evolving affinity between physical and cyber twins and minimizing desynchronization, with edge implementations and MLOps for dynamic updates</cite> <cite id="c476e08b-4">DT-based architectures with continual learning in intelligent location services integrate MLOps to adapt to evolving data and task conditions, maintaining accuracy and relevance over time</cite> <cite id="c476e08b-1">Cyber-physical interaction via data synchronization, online calibration, and dynamic learning is essential to derive intelligence and maintain alignment between twins in changing environments</cite>.

### Uncertainty Quantification and Physics-Informed Modeling
UQ and physics-informed approaches help DTs reason about aleatoric (inherent) and epistemic (knowledge gaps) uncertainty, enabling calibration and trust assessment. Literature reviews and applications detail Bayesian and surrogate modeling methods, co-simulation with UQ, and physics-constrained DNNs to improve predictive fidelity and decision support under uncertainty.<cite id="1f33c846-0">UQ distinguishes aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty, with methods including Bayesian surrogates, co-simulation, and calibration/bias correction; physics-constrained DNNs and optimization with uncertainty calibration have been applied to quantify output uncertainty</cite> <cite id="1f33c846-1">Constructing operating DTs involves sensing, data processing, abstraction, and simulation, each contributing uncertainties that impact predictive fidelity and require itemized quantification and management</cite> <cite id="1f33c846-2">UQ and sensitivity analysis are proposed to establish reliability and trustworthiness of DTs, with machine learning-based UQ (e.g., sparse polynomial chaos) and global sensitivity indices suggested for integration</cite>. In structural DTs, probabilistic frameworks such as Bayesian networks and risk-twin architectures provide real-time risk visualization and control by quantifying uncertainties and aggregating component-level reliability metrics.<cite id="1f33c846-4">Probabilistic modeling with Bayesian networks updates digital states under uncertainty, and risk-twin systems visualize reliability indices in real time to support risk-informed control in civil structures</cite>.

### High-Fidelity Digital Twins and Domain Adaptation
High-fidelity DTs that accurately model assets and environments can narrow the sim2real gap by generating realistic synthetic data and aligning distributions between source and target domains. In LiDAR-based perception, high-fidelity DTs combined with domain adaptation modules (e.g., graph matching and domain discriminators) improved cross-dataset generalization compared to simulator-only improvements, while also exposing practical gaps in asset acquisition and streamlined pipeline construction.<cite id="04014de6-3">High-fidelity DTs for LiDAR perception generate labeled synthetic data and learn transferable representations with domain adaptation modules, improving cross-domain performance but requiring complex, non-streamlined asset pipelines</cite>. In MIMO communications, theoretical analyses tie domain discrepancy to generalization error and motivate training objectives that balance DT-derived losses with adaptation terms to bridge distributional gaps.<cite id="04014de6-4">Domain adaptation bounds relate generalization error to discrepancy between DT and real data and a complexity term, guiding loss functions that minimize the gap while leveraging DT data</cite>.

### Data and Infrastructure: Digital Thread and Cross-Domain Integration
Effective generalization depends on robust data pipelines and interoperable representations across the digital thread. In manufacturing, integrated data management, real-time sensor networks, and AI-driven analytics support DT-driven cognitive loops that rapidly reconfigure production parameters, but require resilient connectivity and automated data management to handle big contextual data and process variability.<cite id="c476e08b-2">Manufacturing cyber-physical systems interconnect heterogeneous devices and networks, using pattern mining, real-time sensor networks, and deep learning to expose process connections and adjust to prosumer and environmental changes</cite> <cite id="c476e08b-3">DT-driven cyber-physical systems act as infrastructure for planning and online upgrades, processing collected data to inform control and reconfiguration in response to disruptions and dynamic changes</cite>. In urban DTs, challenge taxonomies and expert scoring highlight the need to address data integration and governance alongside technical barriers, underscoring that generalization is constrained by interoperability and institutional factors beyond algorithms alone.<cite id="330cc81f-1">A Delphi-based review of urban DTs classifies technical and nontechnical challenges and scores their severity, indicating that governance and integration issues are significant barriers to operational DTs</cite>.

## Domain-Specific Illustrations

- Industrial communications: Learnable DTs for electromagnetic environments can model object properties and interactions, achieving high channel prediction accuracy after training and handling environment changes without pilot overhead, demonstrating adaptive modeling under nonstationarity.<cite id="330cc81f-4">A learnable DT reconstructs EM properties and interactions, achieving high channel prediction accuracy post-training and handling environment changes, which is critical for real-world applications</cite> <cite id="04014de6-4">DT-assisted CSI compression/feedback frames learning as domain adaptation, with bounds linking distribution discrepancy to performance and loss functions that leverage DT data to improve real-world performance</cite>.

- Manufacturing and robotics: DT-assisted transfer learning uses virtual data to bootstrap target-domain models with limited labels, improving speed and robustness in fault diagnosis and production lines; DT-enabled XR and immersive interfaces support modeling, training, and real-time interaction, but rely on high-quality, synchronized data streams and address model uncertainty and missing data.<cite id="04014de6-1">DT-assisted transfer learning uses large virtual datasets to initialize target-domain learners, transferring shared parameters to reduce labeling needs and improve robustness</cite> <cite id="c476e08b-1">DTs integrated with XR provide immersive 3D environments for modeling and training, but require data synchronization, online calibration, and dynamic learning to maintain cyber-physical alignment</cite> <cite id="c476e08b-1">Model uncertainty, sensor placement, and missing data are persistent challenges in DT modeling for manufacturing</cite>.

- Smart cities and infrastructure: High-fidelity DTs for perception (e.g., LiDAR-based ITS) and risk-informed structural DTs demonstrate how probabilistic modeling and real-time uncertainty propagation can support generalization and risk control, while also revealing limitations in simulator fidelity and streamlined DT pipeline construction.<cite id="04014de6-3">High-fidelity DTs for LiDAR perception improve cross-domain generalization through distribution alignment but face challenges in realistic environment construction and post-hoc adaptation requirements</cite> <cite id="1f33c846-4">Risk Twin integrates Bayesian inference into DTs to quantify and visualize structural reliability in real time, enabling risk-informed control under environmental and operational uncertainties</cite>.

## Open Problems and Research Gaps

- Bridging the sim2real gap at scale: While high-fidelity DTs and domain adaptation modules improve generalization, creating streamlined, automated pipelines for asset acquisition and environment modeling remains open, especially for arbitrary deployment sites and long-horizon operations.<cite id="04014de6-3">Despite progress, key gaps remain in sim2real lidar learning, including simplified hand-crafted sim environments, reliance on post-hoc UDA, and non-streamlined HiFi DT creation, motivating simpler systematic methods for arbitrary locations</cite>.

- Robust continual learning under nonstationarity: DTs in dynamic environments require CL strategies that mitigate catastrophic forgetting and maintain synchronization under concept drift, with practical integration into MLOps and edge platforms for real-time adaptation.<cite id="c476e08b-4">Continual learning frameworks for dynamic DTs emphasize synchronization and MLOps for managing continual updates in real time</cite>.

- Physics-informed and uncertainty-aware twins: There is a need for standardized UQ practices across domains and for integrating physics constraints with learned models to ensure reliability and calibration under environmental variability and sensor uncertainty.<cite id="1f33c846-1">Uncertainties at each stage of DT construction impact predictive fidelity, calling for itemized quantification and management strategies</cite> <cite id="1f33c846-0">Physics-constrained DNNs and Bayesian calibration methods have been explored, but broader standardization and integration into DT pipelines remain</cite>.

- Data and governance across the digital thread: Generalization is constrained by data quality, interoperability, and governance in complex, multi-stakeholder settings; urban DTs highlight the importance of addressing nontechnical challenges alongside technical ones to realize scalable, trustworthy DTs.<cite id="330cc81f-1">Urban DT challenge taxonomies, informed by Delphi surveys, indicate significant nontechnical barriers related to governance and integration that affect operationalization</cite>.

## Conclusion

DTs promise powerful closed-loop intelligence across sectors, but their value depends on the ability to operate and generalize under changing environments and across diverse contexts. The literature converges on three pillars: continual, synchronization-aware learning; uncertainty quantification and physics-informed modeling; and high-fidelity, adaptable DTs coupled with domain adaptation and transfer learning to bridge sim2real gaps.<cite id="c476e08b-4">Continual learning and active learning are key to maintaining DT synchronization in dynamic environments</cite> <cite id="1f33c846-0">UQ and physics-constrained models help manage aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties and improve calibration</cite> <cite id="04014de6-3">High-fidelity DTs with domain adaptation improve cross-domain performance but face practical pipeline challenges</cite> <cite id="04014de6-1">DT-assisted transfer learning reduces real-label requirements and accelerates robust deployment</cite>. Progress will also hinge on resilient digital threads, interoperable data, and governance frameworks that extend beyond algorithmic advances to support trustworthy, generalizable DT ecosystems across industry and society.<cite id="330cc81f-1">Comprehensive challenge taxonomies for urban DTs emphasize that nontechnical and governance factors are as critical as technical ones for scalable DT operations</cite>.
</answer>

Title: Developments of digital twin technologies in industrial, smart city and healthcare sectors: a survey
Snippet: Digitization and digitalization have already changed our world significantly. Further disruptions are imminent with the ongoing digital transformation, a major component of which is digital twins. As the big data techniques, Internet of Things, cloud computing, and artificial intelligence algorithms advance, the digital twin technology has entered a phase of rapid development. It has been stated to be one of the top ten most promising technologies. Although it is still in its early stages, digital twins are already being widely used in a variety of fields, especially in industry, smart cities, and smart health, which are points that attract most researchers to study. In the literature, there can be seen numerous articles and reviews on digital twins, published every year in these three fields. It is therefore timely, even necessary, to provide an analysis of the published work. This is the motivation behind this article, the focus of which is the major research and application areas of digital twins. The survey first analyzes the recent developments of digital twins, then summarizes the theoretical underpinnings of the technology, and finally concludes with specific developments in various application areas of digital twins. It also discusses the challenges that may be encountered in the future.

Title: Challenges of urban digital twins: A systematic review and a Delphi expert survey
Snippet: Other viewpoints, such as social and legal aspects, are overlooked in present discussions. Motivated by those knowledge gaps, we conduct this review, aiming to: (1) understand urban digital twins in a comprehensive and critical manner; (2) identify and describe urban digital twins' challenges from technical and nontechnical perspectives; (3) demonstrate the severity of each challenge; (4) offer diverse insights from research and industry. Such reflections motivate us to conduct a systematic review to identify challenges in the literature considering both technical and non-technical perspectives. However, such a topic is novel in the research community, leading to a relatively small corpus of papers. Thus, the literature review gives rather an outline of challenges and falls short in gauging how severe each challenge is. To enhance our review, we include a multiple-round Delphi survey distributed to a panel of experts to collect deep insights from academia, industry and governmental organisations. The Delphi survey asks panellists to list challenges to urban digital twins and score the severity of them. We regard this work can contribute to the research community by providing a well-organised taxonomy of challenges with different severity and introducing diverse understandings from a wide range of stakeholders. With such efforts, we believe this research fills the current gaps of techno-optimism urban digital twins' potential by outlining a detailed side of their challenges. Considering that urban digital twins are constantly developing, the classification of identified challenges will be a necessary piece of the jigsaw and enrich the understanding of such topic. The robust research method enables us to augment the results from our systematic review and provide a multi-dimensional and comprehensive overview of challenges to the operation of digital twins. This paper is the first one on the challenges that hinder the operation of urban digital twins and provides multidisciplinary insights across all domains where digital twins are employed. snippet.text:
Other viewpoints, such as social and legal aspects, are overlooked in present discussions. Motivated by those knowledge gaps, we conduct this review, aiming to: (1) understand urban digital twins in a comprehensive and critical manner; (2) identify and describe urban digital twins' challenges from technical and nontechnical perspectives; (3) demonstrate the severity of each challenge; (4) offer diverse insights from research and industry. Such reflections motivate us to conduct a systematic review to identify challenges in the literature considering both technical and non-technical perspectives. However, such a topic is novel in the research community, leading to a relatively small corpus of papers. Thus, the literature review gives rather an outline of challenges and falls short in gauging how severe each challenge is. To enhance our review, we include a multiple-round Delphi survey distributed to a panel of experts to collect deep insights from academia, industry and governmental organisations. The Delphi survey asks panellists to list challenges to urban digital twins and score the severity of them. We regard this work can contribute to the research community by providing a well-organised taxonomy of challenges with different severity and introducing diverse understandings from a wide range of stakeholders. With such efforts, we believe this research fills the current gaps of techno-optimism urban digital twins' potential by outlining a detailed side of their challenges. Considering that urban digital twins are constantly developing, the classification of identified challenges will be a necessary piece of the jigsaw and enrich the understanding of such topic. Title: Integration of digital twin and deep learning in cyber‐physical systems: towards smart manufacturing

Title: Towards Smart Manufacturing Metaverse via Digital Twinning in Extended Reality
Snippet: DT involves a virtual representation of physical manufacturing assets, resources, processes, or systems that enables real-time data streaming, dashboard visualization, predictive analytics, and intelligence distillation [18,19]. Broadly, there are three core components in the DT -physical twin in the real world, DT in virtual space, and interactions between physical and digital twins. The twinning and modeling process is non-trivial, often encountering data and model challenges such as sensor placement, missing data, model uncertainty [20,21]. XR, including VR, AR, and MR, has gained popularity in recent years as a new tool to support DT modeling in 3D immersive environments. The integration of XR and DT can also provide a safe and controlled environment for manufacturing simulations in workforce training. 

Here, we argue that "digital twin" means a twin in the cyberspace, while "physical twin" means a twin in the physical world. The term of "digital twin" does not explicitly cover three core components -physical twin, digital twin, and interactions between physical and virtual twins. In fact, cyber-physical interaction is indis-pensable to derive data-driven intelligence and simultaneously feed actions or insights back to the physical twin of a real-world factory. Therefore, cyber-physical twin (or Phygital Twin) is a more appropriate term that refers to the process to build the digital twin with data from a physical twin, and further enable cyber-physical interactions through data synchronization, online calibration, dynamic learning, and artificial intelligence. 

As shown in Fig. 2, advanced sensing systems (e.g., supervisory control and data acquisition -SCADA) are critical to streaming the data or signals from the physical twin to the digital twin. The quality of data is instrumental to modeling, calibration, simulation, and optimization in the digital twin. In turn, the integration of sensors with DT offers an unprecedented opportunity of 3D immersive environment to visualize the operational statuses of machines and engage in real-time interactions between digital and physical machines. Further, analytics in the DT help optimize managerial decisions such as job scheduling, process control, predictive maintenance, and feed actions back into the physical twin. After all, smart manufacturing operations depend greatly on the seamless cyber-physical twinning and integration.

Title: Sustainable, Smart, and Sensing Technologies for Cyber-Physical Manufacturing Systems: A Systematic Literature Review
Snippet: The carrying out of manufacturing cyber-physical systems necessitates accessing huge quantities of sensors, actuators, appliances, and groundbreaking production infrastructure devices with connected integrated networking processors [12][13][14]23,36,[43][44][45][46][47], constituting an exemplary coherent machinery. Combination of all cyber-physical data devices into an integrated management system can assist heterogeneous digital twin models in inspecting contextual big data and accomplishing the operational upgrade (e.g., production system robustness). Throughout manufacturing processes, the digital twin assimilates instantaneous production contextual big data from work-in-process, prosumers, and machinery. Vast omnipresent data requires the adequate operational mining tools to be turned into functional input. Pattern mining, real-time sensor networks, and deep learning-assisted smart process planning deploy contextual big data [36,[48][49][50] and expose the intricate connections among work-in-process, machinery, and operational features latent or intrinsic in the manufacturing process. The cyber-physical networked production systems can interconnect by deploying conventional interfaces, inspect contextual big data to forecast failures while processing, set up manufacturing services at the Internet of Things-enabled sustainability level, and adjust to prosumer alterations socially. The manufacturing cyber-physical system possesses progressively automated linkages and networking [23,36,[51][52][53], becoming quite resilient with the cutting-edge computing and monitoring infrastructures. Manufacturing cyber-physical systems integrate groundbreaking connectivity to gather instantaneous data produced by physical manufacturing systems and automated data management, machine learning analytics, and cyber computation. The computerized twin-driven production cognitive loop swiftly redesigns the customized requests into the monitoring parameters of the cyber-physical manufacturing system that significantly enhances operational efficiency from preparation to production. The digital twin integrates a connection to the inspection storage that includes contextual big data concerning distinct components and statistical allotments for assemblages of components.

Title: Sustainable, Smart, and Sensing Technologies for Cyber-Physical Manufacturing Systems: A Systematic Literature Review
Snippet: While cutting-edge sensing and streamlining infrastructure management is prevalent in smart manufacturing, assimilating the digital twin model throughout the groundbreaking production infrastructure constitutes an essential component between the physical and the cyber application layers of a cyber-physical system. Digital twin-driven manufacturing cyber-physical systems are a feasible proposal for parallel monitoring of smart plants. The digital twin is leveraged for supervising and parallel monitoring of the manufacturing system, enabling online upgrade of the cyber-physical production system [23,[36][37][38][39] developed on contextual big data. A cyber-physical system is a combination of physical devices interconnecting across a virtual cyberspace by use of a data transferring network. Each physical device has its cyber component as a digital image of the concrete device, catalyzing digital twin models. The digital twin can inspect and supervise the physical entity that can transfer data to optimize and integrate its virtual model. The digital twin model represents a precise and instantaneous cyber duplicate of a physical production system that adequately mirrors all of its functionalities, assimilating big contextual data as regards work-in-process and machine, and being deployed as an infrastructure for manufacturing planning, networked upgrade, and swift remodeling. The digital twin functions as a paradigm transition, integrating production operations into manufacturing cyber-physical systems. Inconsistent with the standard simulation design, the digital twin component constitutes a confirmation tool for lifecycle integral upgrading solution and not only visual presentation of reproducing unpredictable events or reporting the outcomes. Developed on the leading-edge infrastructures by use of big data technologies [36,[40][41][42], cyber-physical manufacturing systems gather sensory information from operational machines and work-in-processes and transmit them to the higher level networked parallel monitoring component operating throughout the digital twin computation module. Such a connected component processes the collected data, lets the physical system know the outcomes, and conveys control commands to generate indispensable alterations throughout the physical realm, or redesigns system parameters. By integrating semi-physical paralleling technology and swift networking optimization approach, one will advance an adequate iterative process, as a disconnected upgrade is inefficient in adjusting to latent disruptions and dynamic operational alterations.

Title: TWIN-ADAPT: Continuous Learning for Digital Twin-Enabled Online Anomaly Classification in IoT-Driven Smart Labs
Snippet: The importance of continual learning in digital twins (DTs) is highlighted in both the lumber industry [45] and dynamic digital twin frameworks over wireless networks [46]. In the lumber industry, Active Learning (AL) methods are leveraged to address the challenges of dynamic environments, ensuring that DTs actively select and learn from new data samples to remain adaptive and synchronized with real-world changes. Similarly, in dynamic digital twins over wireless networks, a novel edge continual learning framework has been proposed to accurately model the evolving affinity between physical and cyber twins, emphasizing synchronization and minimizing de-synchronization, which is crucial for robust and reliable real-world communication. Lombardo et al.,in [47], developed a digital twin-based architecture for Intelligent Location-Based Services (I-LBSs) with continual learning (CL), integrating MLOps to manage dynamic updates and adapt to evolving data and task conditions. In summary, a variety of continual learning strategies have been explored in the digital twin space that are essential in maintaining the accuracy and relevance of DTs across space and time. This emphasizes the need for efficient continual learning strategies for digital twins, particularly in the context of anomaly detection and identification in real-time streams, which is critical for industrial cyber-physical systems that are susceptible to data distribution changes.

documents.snippet: The importance of continual learning in digital twins (DTs) is highlighted in both the lumber industry [45] and dynamic digital twin frameworks over wireless networks [46]. This emphasizes the need for efficient continual learning strategies for digital twins, particularly in the context of anomaly detection and identification in real-time streams, which is critical for industrial cyber-physical systems that are susceptible to data distribution changes.

Snippet: The idea of digital-twin-assisted simulation modeling for perception tasks is quite recent. Li et al. [52] constructed a high-fidelity digital twin for the first time to generate a labeled synthetic image dataset. They further applied a graph-matching module to align feature distributions between the simulated and real domains. By combining this along a multi-task network (object detection and segmentation) and employing multi-level domain discriminators, transferable representations are learned. In [53], researchers presented a realistic synthetic lidar dataset particularly focused on replicating the geometric and distributional properties of the KITTI and nuScenes datasets. They found, through cross-dataset generalization experiments, that the models trained on their LUCID dataset achieved the best cross-dataset generalization performance, a mean cross-dataset average precision (AP-CDP) delta of -0.18 and average recall (AR-CDP) delta of -0.16, outperforming other real and synthetic datasets. 

This digital twin-assisted simulation approach demonstrated an improved performance compared to isolated improvements of sensor physics and to prior UDA methods, highlighting its significance. However, digital-twin modeling can be a sophisticated process, particularly, because of all the digital asset (such as buildings, roads, road users, etc.) required to construct the map. Research Gaps and Motivation: Despite the above progress, several key gaps remain in Sim2Real lidar learning: (1) Though, simulators incorporate improved lidar-sensor physics and noise models, their built-in environments are completely hand-crafted and are in most cases too much simplified to be used for Sim2Real learning; (2) Domain adaptation methods are primarily post-hoc corrective solutions, requiring further processing and feature-level domain adaptions; and (3) although HiFi DT modeling has emerged for lidar-based simulations, however, the process to create HiFi DTs is not streamlined. Our paper, inspired by exciting research in the domain, introduces a novel much simpler systematic method to create HiFi DTs for arbitrarily any location, using only public information.

Title: Uncertainty-aware deep learning for digital twin-driven monitoring: Application to fault detection in power lines
Snippet: Uncertainty quantification (UQ) is an important aspect of all model-building exercises and has been emphasised as an evaluation criterion in applications ranging from medicine [11] to autonomous vehicles [12]. Models built from data are subject to aleatoric uncertainty which stems from randomness in the data generating process, sensing mechanism, etc. This type of uncertainty is inherent to the system and cannot be reduced by collecting more measurements. On the other hand, epistemic uncertainty stems from the inadequacy of a model to explain the underlying system, and can be reduced by using more data to train the model. As a result, UQ of both digital twin models and DNN models has already been studied in the literature. The authors in [13] made use of Monte Carlo co-simulations with a digital twin and adopted statistical analysis tools to quantify the uncertainty in controlling an agricultural vehicle. A Bayesian model was used for surrogate modelling and UQ of convolutional neural networks learning to solve stochastic partial differential equations in [14]. The uncertainty of surrogate models in reliabilitybased design optimisation was quantified in [15]. UQ of computational thermodynamics models was performed in [16]. Bayesian method-based model calibration and UQ was performed for a physics-based model for predicting the evolution of precipitates during a heat treatment in [17]. Physics-based digital twins can additionally have parametric or structural uncertainty in the model as well as aleatoric uncertainty. These uncertainties have been addressed in the literature with a host of methods such as calibration and bias correction [18]. A physics-constrained deep neural network was developed in [19] to solve partial differential equations, and uncertainty calibration was included in the optimisation to quantify the output uncertainty. 

Uncertainty quantification of DNN models has also attracted significant attention. The authors in [20] proposed a computationally light approach to quantify the aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty for DNNs. The authors proposed the use of assumed density filtering for propagating the input uncertainty through all layers of the model.

Title: Risk twin: real-time risk visualization and control for structural systems
Snippet: However, a prevailing assumption in many Digital Twin systems is that the sensing, modeling, and simulation modules are deterministic [25][26][27][28]. This assumption, however, is not realistic in real-world Digital Twin applications, where uncertainties are pervasive [29]. These uncertainties arise from various sources, including measurement uncertainties due to inaccuracies and variabilities of sensors; modeling uncertainties stemming from limitations and assumptions in computational models; and operational uncertainties, which involve variations in system performance under different real-world conditions and human interactions [30,31]. For instance, stress-sensing devices in structural Digital Twin systems often exhibit high sensitivity to temperature and humidity, causing significant discrepancies in Analog-to-Digital (AD) conversion values for identical stress levels measured under differing conditions, such as noon versus night [32]. These uncertainties can compromise the accuracy of deterministic Digital Twin models. To properly quantify the influence of uncertainties in Digital Twin systems, Kapteyn et al. proposed a comprehensive framework based on Bayesian network [21]. This framework represents the states of physical systems and their digital counterparts as random variables and updates the latter through Bayesian network inference using the observed data. Moreover, two realistic applications of predictive Digital Twin are proposed to illustrate the framework, which have been further explored in subsequent research [12,22]. 

Although the previously discussed methodologies can predict specific quantities of interest, there is an absence of a specialized framework for assessing the risk of structural safety on a unified scale. Such a framework is essential not only for quantifying uncertainties and risks within the structural system, but also for providing a holistic metric of risk across different structural components. For instance, a Digital Twin can monitor quantities such as stress, strain, and moment that collectively contribute to the safety of structural components, but it does not offer a directly comparable metric for the risk of each component. 

To fill this gap, this study introduces Risk Twin, a system designed to analyze and visualize the reliability indices for structural components in real-time, thereby facilitating risk-informed control. 

Building on existing progress of integrating probabilistic analysis within the Digital Twinning technology, this study aims to further advance their application in risk assessment and control of civil structures.

snippet.text:
However, a prevailing assumption in many Digital Twin systems is that the sensing, modeling, and simulation modules are deterministic [25][26][27][28]. This assumption, however, is not realistic in real-world Digital Twin applications, where uncertainties are pervasive [29]. These uncertainties arise from various sources, including measurement uncertainties due to inaccuracies and variabilities of sensors; modeling uncertainties stemming from limitations and assumptions in computational models; and operational uncertainties, which involve variations in system performance under different real-world conditions and human interactions [30,31]. For instance, stress-sensing devices in structural Digital Twin systems often exhibit high sensitivity to temperature and humidity, causing significant discrepancies in Analog-to-Digital (AD) conversion values for identical stress levels measured under differing conditions, such as noon versus night [32]. These uncertainties can compromise the accuracy of deterministic Digital Twin models. To properly quantify the influence of uncertainties in Digital Twin systems, Kapteyn et al. proposed a comprehensive framework based on Bayesian network [21]. This framework represents the states of physical systems and their digital counterparts as random variables and updates the latter through Bayesian network inference using the observed data. Moreover, two realistic applications of predictive Digital Twin are proposed to illustrate the framework, which have been further explored in subsequent research [12,22]. 

Although the previously discussed methodologies can predict specific quantities of interest, there is an absence of a specialized framework for assessing the risk of structural safety on a unified scale. Such a framework is essential not only for quantifying uncertainties and risks within the structural system, but also for providing a holistic metric of risk across different structural components. For instance, a Digital Twin can monitor quantities such as stress, strain, and moment that collectively contribute to the safety of structural components, but it does not offer a directly comparable metric for the risk of each component. 

To fill this gap, this study introduces Risk Twin, a system designed to analyze and visualize the reliability indices for structural components in real-time, thereby facilitating risk-informed control. 

Building on existing progress of integrating probabilistic analysis within the Digital Twinning technology, this study aims to further advance their application in risk assessment and control of civil structures.

Uncertainty quantification (UQ) is an important aspect of all model-building exercises and has been emphasised as an evaluation criterion in applications ranging from medicine [11] to autonomous vehicles [12]. Models built from data are subject to aleatoric uncertainty which stems from randomness in the data generating process, sensing mechanism, etc. This type of uncertainty is inherent to the system and cannot be reduced by collecting more measurements. On the other hand, epistemic uncertainty stems from the inadequacy of a model to explain the underlying system, and can be reduced by using more data to train the model. As a result, UQ of both digital twin models and DNN models has already been studied in the literature. The authors in [13] made use of Monte Carlo co-simulations with a digital twin and adopted statistical analysis tools to quantify the uncertainty in controlling an agricultural vehicle. A Bayesian model was used for surrogate modelling and UQ of convolutional neural networks learning to solve stochastic partial differential equations in [14]. The uncertainty of surrogate models in reliabilitybased design optimisation was quantified in [15]. UQ of computational thermodynamics models was performed in [16]. Bayesian method-based model calibration and UQ was performed for a physics-based model for predicting the evolution of precipitates during a heat treatment in [17]. Physics-based digital twins can additionally have parametric or structural uncertainty in the model as well as aleatoric uncertainty. These uncertainties have been addressed in the literature with a host of methods such as calibration and bias correction [18]. A physics-constrained deep neural network was developed in [19] to solve partial differential equations, and uncertainty calibration was included in the optimisation to quantify the output uncertainty. 

Uncertainty quantification of DNN models has also attracted significant attention. The authors in [20] proposed a computationally light approach to quantify the aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty for DNNs. The authors proposed the use of assumed density filtering for propagating the input uncertainty through all layers of the model.
