Title: SATBench: Benchmarking LLMs' Logical Reasoning via Automated Puzzle Generation from SAT Formulas
Snippet: Logical Reasoning Benchmarks for LLMs Reasoning is a longstanding focus in NLP, with many benchmarks developed to assess model performance. Early efforts targeted natural language inference (Bowman et al., 2015) and commonsense reasoning (Talmor et al., 2018), while recently there has been increasing attention to assessing logical reasoning, as seen in LogiQA (Liu et al., 2020), ReClor (Yu et al., 2020), BoardgameQA (Kazemi et al., 2023), and CLUTRR (Sinha et al., 2019). These typically involve reasoning that relies on real-world knowledge. In contrast, datasets like FOLIO (Han et al., 2024a), RuleTaker (Clark et al., 2020), and P-FOLIO (Han et al., 2024b) aim to isolate formal logical reasoning from commonsense knowledge. Logical puzzles have emerged as a compelling testbed in this area (Giadikiaroglou et al., 2024), with benchmarks including ZebraLogic (Lin et al., 2025), AutoLogi (Zhu et al., 2025), and LogicNLI (Tian et al., 2021). PARAT (Pan et al., 2024) examines LLMs directly on SAT formulas, whereas our benchmark frames SAT problems as natural language puzzles, a more realistic setting given LLMs' training on text and the availability of efficient SAT solvers for formula inputs. Unlike AutoLogi, which builds on existing corpora and risks data contamination, our dataset is generated entirely from scratch with solver and human validation to ensure correctness and diversity. A systematic comparison of these benchmarks is provided in Table 1.

Claude 4.5 Opus [4] achieves 74.40% on SWE-bench Verified, while Gemini 3 Pro [31] reaches 76.2% on SWE-bench Verified with state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks (91.9% GPQA Diamond, 95-100% AIME 2025, 2,439 Elo on LiveCodeBench Pro). Claude 4.1 Opus and Claude 4.5 Sonnet achieve 72.5% and 72.7% respectively on SWE-bench Full (code generation). These models also achieve 67.60% and 70.60% respectively on SWE Bench Bash Only (using mini-SWE-agent environment). GPT-4.1 [5] doubles GPT-4o's performance on code diff benchmarks and reaches 54.6% on SWE-bench tasks. Gemini 2.5 Pro [30] achieves 59.6% on SWE-bench Verified, showcasing Google's advances in reasoning models. DeepSeek V3 [6], with 671B parameters (37B activated), demonstrates that efficient training is possible, achieving competitive performance at 1/10th the training cost of comparable models. Qwen2.5-Coder-32B [44] matches GPT-4o performance while running locally on consumer hardware. 

However, these impressive code generation capabilities do not translate to debugging success. When evaluated on realworld debugging tasks requiring multi-file understanding, historical context, and iterative refinement-specifically on SWE-bench Lite and other debugging benchmarks (Debug-Bench, MdEval)-even the best models achieve less than 15% success rates. Notably, Claude models drop from 67-72% on code generation benchmarks to only 13-14% on SWEbench Lite debugging tasks, revealing a 54-57 percentage point gap. This stark disparity between code generation and debugging performance motivates the need for specialized debugging-focused architectures.

# Overview: Benchmarks for Language Model Reasoning

Reasoning in modern LLMs is evaluated across several categories: math/logic and STEM problem solving, general knowledge across disciplines, open-ended and creative reasoning, code and software engineering (including debugging), commonsense/entailment, and multimodal and agentic/tool-using reasoning. Recent surveys emphasize that evaluation must go beyond final accuracy to capture reasoning behaviors, test-time strategies, and judge reliability, which motivates diverse benchmarks spanning closed- and open-ended formats and incorporating external knowledge and tools.<cite id="12bfb07d-0">Recent surveys argue that reasoning evaluation should move beyond task accuracy to characterize LLM reasoning behaviors and provide taxonomies of evaluation methods, reflecting the rapid growth of diverse reasoning benchmarks</cite><cite id="12bfb07d-1">A test-time scaling survey maps benchmarks into general, open-ended, and knowledge-intensive categories and highlights evaluation tasks that assess judges and reward models</cite><cite id="12bfb07d-2">New reasoning benchmarks like AutoLogi address saturation of scores and guessing in closed-ended formats by requiring open-ended, solution-constructed answers with automated puzzle generation</cite><cite id="12bfb07d-4">Logical reasoning benchmarks increasingly separate formal logic from world knowledge (e.g., FOLIO, RuleTaker, P-FOLIO) and recent work generates SAT-based puzzles to test logical reasoning in natural language</cite>.

Below we summarize representative benchmarks and state-of-the-art (SOTA) results.

# Math, Logic, and STEM Reasoning

Math and STEM reasoning are commonly assessed via competition-style problems and graduate-level question sets. AIME 2024/2025 provide 30 competition-level math problems each requiring concise numeric answers, designed to test multi-step symbolic reasoning across algebra, geometry, and number theory.<cite id="753c0dcd-2">AIME 2024 and 2025 datasets contain 30 competition-style math problems requiring concise numeric answers and multi-step reasoning across algebra, geometry, and number theory</cite><cite id="753c0dcd-3">AIME24 and AIME25 are derived from the American Invitational Mathematics Examination and reflect challenging, high-school competition difficulty</cite>. MATH-500 is a curated subset of 500 high-school competition problems across multiple domains, emphasizing multi-step reasoning beyond simple recall.<cite id="753c0dcd-2">MATH500 covers 500 diverse high-school competition-level math problems across algebra, combinatorics, geometry, number theory, and precalculus</cite><cite id="753c0dcd-3">MATH500 is designed to test multi-step reasoning and complex problem solving beyond basic calculations or facts</cite>. GPQA (with Diamond subset) presents graduate-level, “Google-proof” multiple-choice questions in biology, chemistry, and physics; the Diamond set is a high-quality, hard subset with expert baselines and large gaps to non-experts.<cite id="753c0dcd-1">GPQA includes 448 expert-crafted, graduate-level questions across STEM; the Diamond subset is selected for extreme difficulty with expert accuracy around 65% and non-expert accuracy much lower</cite><cite id="753c0dcd-2">GPQA Diamond is a high-quality subset of about 198 questions used to evaluate expert-level factual knowledge and reasoning</cite>.

Recent evaluations also report historical performance on national secondary math exams, showing substantial gains as models and tool use evolved. For example, Finland’s matriculation exams: GPT-4 improved from grade E (64/120) in 2023 to grade L (93/120) in 2023 when allowed symbolic computation, and newer LLMs were evaluated on later exams in 2024.<cite id="753c0dcd-4">On the Finnish matriculation mathematics exam, GPT-4 scored 64/120 (grade E) in 2023 and 93/120 (grade L) in 2023 when permitted to use symbolic computation via Python/SYMPY; 2024 exams were used to assess several LLMs</cite>.

# General Knowledge and Agentic Reasoning

General-purpose reasoning and cognition are measured by aggregated and exam-style benchmarks. MMLU and its variants assess knowledge across many subjects; Big-Bench and Big-Bench Hard add harder items, and AGIEval evaluates human-like cognition via university entrance and law school exams in multiple languages.<cite id="753c0dcd-0">Aggregated benchmarks like MMLU, Big-Bench, Big-Bench Hard, and AGIEval are commonly used to assess broad, general-purpose reasoning; AGIEval uses high-stakes exams (e.g., university entrance, law school) in English and Chinese</cite>. Newer evaluations also emphasize test-time strategies and contamination control, with varied prompting (zero/few-shot, chain-of-thought) across datasets, reflecting sensitivity to evaluation protocol.<cite id="753c0dcd-0">Evaluations often vary prompting strategies (zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought) across datasets such as Llama-2 and Claude-3, with aggregated benchmarks using 3–5 shot settings and recent evaluations exploring 0–25 examples plus CoT</cite>.

Agentic reasoning benchmarks test planning, tool use, and web interaction. Surveys catalog agent evaluation suites and highlight benchmarks like WebArena and ToolBench for interactive tasks, alongside broader agent benchmarks (e.g., TDD-Bench, IT-Bench) in recent surveys.<cite id="528a0e62-1">Agent evaluation surveys list interactive and software-engineering agent benchmarks including WebArena-style environments and SWE-bench variants, along with task-specific suites such as TDD-Bench and IT-Bench</cite>. Recent work emphasizes dynamic tool selection and integration for agentic reasoning, underscoring the role of tool-use benchmarks in reasoning pipelines.<cite id="753c0dcd-4">AutoTool focuses on dynamic tool selection and integration for agentic reasoning, situating AIME and GPQA alongside tool-using evaluations</cite>.

# Code and Software Engineering Reasoning

Code reasoning spans program synthesis, unit-test–based evaluation, and real-world software repair. HumanEval and its variants (e.g., MBPP, LiveCodeBench) assess function completion with unit tests, while SWE-bench and its variants (SWE-bench Verified, Lite, Full) evaluate real-world issue fixing in repositories under increasingly rigorous conditions.<cite id="528a0e62-3">HumanEval is a core code-generation benchmark with many variants (MBPP, DS1000, LiveCodeBench) and broader suites such as SWE-bench and Bigcodebench</cite><cite id="528a0e62-1">Surveys enumerate SWE-bench family (Verified, Lite, + variants), TDD-Bench Verified, and related coding/agent benchmarks</cite>. Recent results show strong progress on SWE-bench Verified and code diff tasks, with frontier models like Claude 3.7/3.5 Sonnet and GPT-4.1 reported to perform well; however, debugging remains a weak point compared to code generation.<cite id="528a0e62-0">SWE-bench Verified includes per-model evaluations for Claude 3 Opus, Claude 3.5 (Old/New), GPT-4 1106, GPT-4o, and o1, and introduces time-bucketed estimates reflecting task difficulty</cite><cite id="528a0e62-4">Claude 4.5 Opus reports 74.40% on SWE-bench Verified; Gemini 3 Pro reports 76.2% on SWE-bench Verified and strong performance on GPQA Diamond, AIME 2025, and LiveCodeBench Pro; GPT-4.1 reaches 54.6% on SWE-bench tasks</cite><cite id="528a0e62-4">Despite strong code-generation results on SWE-bench Full and Bash-Only, even top models drop to ~13–14% on debugging-focused SWE-bench Lite and MdEval, revealing a large gap between generation and debugging</cite>. DeepSeek-V2 Chat (RL) shows competitive coding on LiveCodeBench, surpassing some larger models in pass@1 under contamination-controlled settings.<cite id="528a0e62-2">DeepSeek-V2 Chat (RL) is reported to achieve strong LiveCodeBench pass@1, surpassing some giant models in a contamination-free selection (Sept 2023–Apr 2024)</cite>.

# Commonsense, Entailment, and Knowledge-Intensive Reasoning

Commonsense and logical entailment benchmarks test world knowledge and structured inference. Early efforts include natural language inference and commonsense reasoning, while newer logical reasoning datasets isolate formal logic from general knowledge (e.g., LogiQA, ReClor, CLUTRR, FOLIO, RuleTaker, P-FOLIO).<cite id="12bfb07d-4">Earlier reasoning benchmarks targeted NLI and commonsense, while newer ones (LogiQA, ReClor, CLUTRR) assess logical reasoning; datasets like FOLIO, RuleTaker, and P-FOLIO aim to isolate formal logic from commonsense knowledge</cite>. Knowledge-intensive benchmarks emphasize retrieval and multi-source synthesis with metrics for factual correctness and hallucination reduction; recent suites (SimpleQA, C-SimpleQA, FRAMES) focus on precise retrieval and aggregation.<cite id="12bfb07d-1">Knowledge-intensive tasks emphasize retrieval-augmented reasoning with benchmarks like SimpleQA, C-SimpleQA, and FRAMES that stress factual correctness and multi-source aggregation</cite>.

# Open-Ended and Creative Reasoning

Open-ended tasks evaluate creativity, planning, and subjective quality. Benchmarks such as AlpacaEval2.0, ArenaHard, IF-Eval, and C-Eval are used to assess general, open-ended reasoning and judge model outputs on diverse, non-contaminated tasks.<cite id="12bfb07d-1">Open-ended benchmarks (AlpacaEval2.0, ArenaHard, IF-Eval, C-Eval) evaluate general, creative, and subjective reasoning and output quality</cite>. Surveys also highlight the need to measure reasoning behaviors beyond accuracy, including judge reliability and evaluation-time strategies, which motivates use of generative reward/judge models (RewardBench, JudgeBench, RMBench) to assess output quality more robustly.<cite id="12bfb07d-1">Evaluation tasks where LLMs act as judges (RewardBench, JudgeBench, RMBench) aim to improve reliability of subjective and holistic quality assessment</cite>.

# Multimodal and Cross-Lingual Reasoning

Multimodal benchmarks assess reasoning that integrates text and images or across languages. Recent surveys describe multilingual and multimodal exam-style evaluations (e.g., M3Exam) and cross-lingual reasoning tasks, with some models reporting strong performance on math subsets and multilingual exams.<cite id="753c0dcd-0">M3Exam evaluates multilingual, multimodal intelligence using exam questions in nine languages</cite><cite id="12bfb07d-3">LingGym finds that adding knowledge points improves reasoning across LLM families and parameters, with DeepSeek-R1 32B reaching ~81% in a multilingual meta-linguistic benchmark; CoT helps math/symbolic reasoning but not meta-linguistic tasks</cite>. Logical puzzle-style multimodal and symbolic reasoning benchmarks (e.g., SATBench’s natural-language SAT puzzles) provide controlled logical reasoning tests with solver and human validation to avoid contamination.<cite id="753c0dcd-4">SATBench generates SAT-based logical puzzles as natural-language problems to test logical reasoning, with solver and human validation to ensure correctness and diversity, addressing contamination risks of existing corpora</cite>.

# Representative Benchmarks and Current SOTA Highlights

- Math/Logic/STEM:
  - AIME 2024/2025: Competition-level math requiring concise numeric answers; used to measure multi-step symbolic reasoning in LLMs.<cite id="753c0dcd-2">AIME 2024/2025 require concise numeric answers and multi-step reasoning across algebra, geometry, number theory</cite><cite id="753c0dcd-3">AIME24/25 reflect challenging high-school competition difficulty</cite>.
  - MATH-500: 500 competition-level problems across domains, designed to push beyond simple recall.<cite id="753c0dcd-2">MATH500 covers diverse high-school math domains with multi-step reasoning</cite><cite id="753c0dcd-3">MATH500 emphasizes complex problem solving beyond basic calculations</cite>.
  - GPQA (Diamond): Graduate-level, “Google-proof” STEM MCQs; Diamond subset used for SOTA comparisons with expert baselines and large non-expert gaps.<cite id="753c0dcd-1">Expert accuracy on GPQA is ~65% with much lower non-expert performance; Diamond is a high-difficulty subset</cite><cite id="753c0dcd-2">GPQA Diamond evaluates expert-level knowledge and reasoning with ~198 questions</cite>.
  - SOTA signals: Gemini 3 Pro reported 91.9% on GPQA Diamond; Claude 4.5 Opus 74.4% and Gemini 3 Pro 76.2% on SWE-bench Verified; GPT-4.1 54.6% on SWE-bench tasks; strong code generation but severe drops on debugging variants.<cite id="528a0e62-4">Frontier models report 74.4–76.2% on SWE-bench Verified and 91.9% on GPQA Diamond for Gemini 3 Pro, with GPT-4.1 at 54.6% on SWE-bench; debugging tasks reveal large performance drops</cite>.

- General knowledge/agentic:
  - MMLU, Big-Bench, AGIEval: Broad knowledge and exam-style cognition across subjects and high-stakes exams; widely used to benchmark general reasoning and problem solving.<cite id="753c0dcd-0">MMLU, Big-Bench, Big-Bench Hard, and AGIEval are standard for broad, general reasoning with high-stakes exam content</cite>.
  - Tool-use/agent benchmarks: WebArena, ToolBench, and SWE-bench family evaluate interactive planning and tool integration; recent surveys catalog emerging agent suites.<cite id="528a0e62-1">Agent benchmark suites include WebArena-style interactive tasks and SWE-bench variants, with additional task-specific benchmarks</cite>.

- Code and software engineering:
  - HumanEval/LiveCodeBench/MBPP: Unit-test based coding; LiveCodeBench emphasizes contamination control and recent code problems.<cite id="528a0e62-3">HumanEval and LiveCodeBench define core unit-test coding benchmarks with contamination-focused design</cite><cite id="528a0e62-2">DeepSeek-V2 Chat (RL) achieves strong LiveCodeBench pass@1 under contamination-free selection</cite>.
  - SWE-bench (Full/Verified/Lite/Bash-Only): Repository-scale bug fixing with varying rigor; results include pass rates and time horizons; models show large variance between code generation and debugging.<cite id="528a0e62-0">SWE-bench Verified provides per-model results (Claude 3.x, GPT-4/4o/o1) and time estimates via annotator buckets</cite><cite id="528a0e62-4">SWE-bench variants show strong generation but weak debugging, with best models around 13–14% on Lite/debugging suites</cite>.

- Commonsense/logic and knowledge-intensive:
  - Logical reasoning suites (LogiQA, ReClor, CLUTRR, FOLIO, RuleTaker, P-FOLIO) and SAT-based puzzles (SATBench) test formal logic and structured inference with reduced commonsense contamination.<cite id="12bfb07d-4">Logical reasoning benchmarks isolate formal logic from world knowledge and include SAT-based puzzles to avoid contamination</cite>.
  - Knowledge-intensive: SimpleQA, C-SimpleQA, FRAMES emphasize retrieval and factual correctness; evaluation often requires multi-source verification and iterative reasoning.<cite id="12bfb07d-1">Knowledge-intensive benchmarks like SimpleQA/C-SimpleQA/FRAMES stress retrieval and aggregation with factual correctness metrics</cite>.

- Open-ended and creative:
  - AlpacaEval2.0, ArenaHard, IF-Eval, C-Eval assess subjective, open-ended reasoning and judge model output quality beyond accuracy, aligning with test-time scaling needs.<cite id="12bfb07d-1">Open-ended benchmarks (AlpacaEval2.0, ArenaHard, IF-Eval, C-Eval) evaluate general, creative reasoning and output quality</cite>.
  - Judge/reward models (RewardBench, JudgeBench, RMBench) provide structured evaluation of holistic response quality and reliability.<cite id="12bfb07d-1">Evaluation tasks where LLMs act as judges (RewardBench, JudgeBench, RMBench) aim to improve subjective evaluation reliability</cite>.

- Multimodal and cross-lingual:
  - M3Exam and LingGym illustrate multilingual and meta-linguistic reasoning evaluations; models like DeepSeek-R1 32B show strong gains from structured knowledge points, though perfect accuracy remains elusive.<cite id="753c0dcd-0">M3Exam evaluates multilingual, multimodal intelligence via exam questions in nine languages</cite><cite id="12bfb07d-3">LingGym reports ~81% accuracy for DeepSeek-R1 32B on a meta-linguistic benchmark, with knowledge points improving performance and CoT limited to math/symbolic tasks</cite>.
  - SATBench and AutoLogi provide logic-puzzle-based reasoning in natural language, addressing guessing and contamination with automated generation and validation.<cite id="12bfb07d-2">AutoLogi generates open-ended logic puzzles to mitigate guessing and saturation, with automated augmentation and minimal human verification</cite><cite id="753c0dcd-4">SATBench generates SAT-based natural language puzzles with solver and human validation to avoid contamination</cite>.

# State-of-the-Art Trends (2024–2025)

- Strong gains on code-generation and math/STEM benchmarks by frontier models, but persistent weaknesses on debugging and open-ended, exam-style reasoning without structured aids.<cite id="528a0e62-4">Models like Gemini 3 Pro and Claude 4.5 show strong SWE-bench Verified and GPQA Diamond results, while GPT-4.1 advances on code diffs but lags on harder tasks</cite><cite id="528a0e62-0">SWE-bench Verified and continuous-scoring analyses highlight time horizons and the challenge of matching human 50% completion times</cite>.
- Evaluation rigor and contamination controls materially affect reported SOTA; benchmarks like LiveCodeBench and SWE-bench variants show sensitivity to protocol choices (e.g., unit tests, verified repositories, time constraints).<cite id="528a0e62-2">LiveCodeBench’s contamination-free selection window (Sep 2023–Apr 2024) yields strong pass@1 for DeepSeek-V2 Chat (RL)</cite><cite id="528a0e62-0">SWE-bench Verified aggregates per-model results on frontier systems and uses time-bucket estimates from contractors</cite>.
- Agentic and multimodal reasoning are increasingly central: tool-use and web interaction benchmarks (e.g., SWE-bench family, WebArena/ToolBench) and multimodal/multilingual exams (e.g., M3Exam, MMMU-style) reflect the shift toward complex, real-world reasoning pipelines.<cite id="528a0e62-1">Agent benchmarks catalog interactive and software-engineering tasks for reasoning with tools</cite><cite id="753c0dcd-0">M3Exam targets multilingual, multimodal intelligence with exam content</cite>.

# Practical Guidance on Interpreting “SOTA”

- Results are benchmark- and protocol-dependent: few-shot vs zero-shot, CoT prompting, access to tools/web, unit tests, and contamination controls can shift rankings substantially.<cite id="753c0dcd-0">Evaluations vary widely in prompting (0–25 examples, CoT) and dataset design across recent model reports</cite><cite id="528a0e62-0">SWE-bench Verified includes time-bucket estimates and per-model pass rates for frontier systems, underscoring protocol effects</cite>.

# Summary

Title: Beyond Accuracy: Evaluating the Reasoning Behavior of Large Language Models - A Survey
Snippet: Specifically, we address the following research questions: 

RQ1: How do current LLMs behave across diverse reasoning tasks? RQ2: What are the prevalent evaluation methods employed to assess the reasoning behavior of large language models? 

Other Surveys. While various surveys on reasoning within large language models have emerged in recent years (Huang & Chang, 2023;Yu et al., 2024;Sun et al., 2024;Yang et al., 2023;Qiao et al., 2023;Chu et al., 2023;Mialon et al., 2023;Liu et al., 2024;Ahn et al., 2024), these studies predominantly focus on techniques that seek to enhance or benchmark the performance of LLMs on downstream reasoning tasks. However, there seems to exist no review of work yet that assesses the reasoning behavior of LLMs, rather than their final task performance. Hence, the contributions of this survey are as follows: (i) To the best of our knowledge, we present the first comprehensive review of literature that evaluates LLMbased reasoning beyond task accuracy, offering deeper insights into the models' reasoning behavior, and (ii) we suggest a taxonomy that categorizes prevalent evaluation methods designed to analyze the reasoning dynamics of LLMs.

Title: A Survey on Test-Time Scaling in Large Language Models: What, How, Where, and How Well?
Snippet: These tasks require broad, general-purpose reasoning capabilities, creativity, and subjective evaluation of outputs. 

General To achieve general objectives, many efforts have collected numerous official, public datasets that are challenging for humans but are not exclusive to any particular domain. Representative benchmarks include AGIEval (Zhong et al., 2024), MMLU-Pro (Wang et al., 2024d), and Gaokao (Guan et al., 2025). These benchmarks may cover multiple aspects of language models and aim to test their general performance. 

Open-Ended Tasks TTS methods must enhance output diversity, quality, and coherence, balancing creativity and correctness. Representative benchmarks include AlpacaEval2.0 (Dubois et al., 2024), ArenaHard (Li et al., 2024c), IF-Eval (Zhou et al., 2023b), and C-Eval (Huang et al., 2023), which collectively evaluate subjective, open-ended, and general-purpose reasoning. 

Knowledge-intensive Tasks Knowledge-intensive tasks require LLMs to retrieve and synthesize factual knowledge from external sources, ensuring accuracy and reducing hallucinations. TTS challenges center around effective retrieval-augmented reasoning, iterative verification, and multi-source aggregation. Representative benchmarks include SimpleQA (Wei et al., 2024a), C-SimpleQA (He et al., 2024c), and FRAMES (Krishna et al., 2025), emphasizing factual correctness and retrieval-based reasoning. 

Evaluation Tasks Evaluation tasks require LLMs to act as judges, also known as Generative Reward Models (GRMs), to conduct comprehensive and in-depth quality assessments of the candidate responses, thus ensuring reliable evaluation results. Representative benchmarks in this field include RewardBench (Lambert et al., 2024), JudgeBench (Tan et al., 2025), RMBench (Liu et al., 2024c), PPE (Frick et al., 2024), and RMB (Zhou et al., 2025). Recent research (Kim et al., 2025) has demonstrated that TTS effectively enhances the evaluation reasoning capabilities of LLMs.

Title: AutoLogi: Automated Generation of Logic Puzzles for Evaluating Reasoning Abilities of Large Language Models
Snippet: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across diverse applications (OpenAI, 2024;Anthropic, 2022;Qwen et al., 2025). Among these capabilities, logical reasoning has emerged as a critical skill (Luo et al., 2023;Wei et al., 2022;Yao et al., 2024;Zhu et al., 2024). The increasing emphasis on reasoning capabilities has highlighted the pressing need for reliable evaluation methodologies. 

However, the field of reasoning evaluation faces three fundamental challenges: the vulnerability to random guessing, insufficient difficulty variation to differentiate model capabilities, and high human annotation costs in dataset construction. A critical issue lies in the prevalent reliance on closed-ended questions in existing benchmarks, where models are simply required to select answers from predefined options (Liu et al., 2020;Bansal et al., 2023;Zhong et al., 2021;Han et al., 2024;Ismayilzada et al., 2023). This format allows models with minimal reasoning capabilities to achieve substantially overestimated performance, leading to deeply misleading evaluation results that mask true reasoning deficiencies. The rapid advancements in LLMs are leading to the saturation of scores on existing benchmarks, reducing their effectiveness in differentiating model capabilities. Consequently, there is a growing and continuous need for the development of more challenging and distinctive benchmarks to better evaluate model performance. Nevertheless, constructing such high-quality reasoning datasets requires extensive human annotation effort, which substantially limits the scale of available evaluation resources. 

To address these challenges, we introduce a novel method for automatically synthesizing openended logic puzzles to construct a reasoning benchmark named AutoLogi. Our approach offers three key advantages: (1) as is illustrated in Figure 1, the open-ended format requires models to construct complete solutions from scratch, significantly mitigating the performance inflation caused by random guessing; (2) automated augmentation generates puzzles with varying logical constraints, enabling balanced difficulty distribution; (3) fully automated generation with minimal human verification substantially reduces benchmark construction costs. These innovations directly address the aforementioned challenges, offering a more reliable, balanced, and scalable evaluation methodology.

Title: LingGym: How Far Are LLMs from Thinking Like Field Linguists?
Snippet: In line with earlier work (Tanzer et al., 2024;Zhang et al., 2024b), we find that adding KPs brings consistent improvements across LLM families and parameters (Table 3), suggesting that LLMs possess some abilities to comprehend the linguistic concepts in KPs and associate them with concrete language examples. As expected, larger models outperform smaller models by a large margin. The best performing model, DeepSeek-R1 32B, reaches around 81% accuracy, suggesting that LLMs show remarkable capabilities in meta-lingusitic reasoning that is independent of languages. 

To further validate this effect, we conduct controlled experiments on selected models by testing LLMs across all difficulty condition permutations. Our ablation results from Table 4 indicate that gloss information, English translations, and knowledge points each contribute to the meta-linguistic reasoning, independent of each other. Yet none of the LLMs achieve perfect accuracy on these tasks, suggesting a large room for improvement. 

CoT does not bring clear improvement to the performance. Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting (Wei et al., 2022) has been shown to effectively improve performance on reasoning tasks, although the improvement is mainly limited to math and symbolic reasoning tasks (Sprague et al., 2025). As shown in Figure 5, we do not find conclusive evidence that meta-linguistic reasoning benefits much from CoT across all LLMs from different families. 

Reasoning models like DeepSeek-R1 and o4mini are also not competitive with non-reasoning models. The only exception is DeepSeek-R1 32B (Guo et al., 2025), a reasoning model trained to perform long CoT. snippet.text:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across diverse applications (OpenAI, 2024;Anthropic, 2022;Qwen et al., 2025). Among these capabilities, logical reasoning has emerged as a critical skill (Luo et al., 2023;Wei et al., 2022;Yao et al., 2024;Zhu et al., 2024). The increasing emphasis on reasoning capabilities has highlighted the pressing need for reliable evaluation methodologies. 

However, the field of reasoning evaluation faces three fundamental challenges: the vulnerability to random guessing, insufficient difficulty variation to differentiate model capabilities, and high human annotation costs in dataset construction. A critical issue lies in the prevalent reliance on closed-ended questions in existing benchmarks, where models are simply required to select answers from predefined options (Liu et al., 2020;Bansal et al., 2023;Zhong et al., 2021;Han et al., 2024;Ismayilzada et al., 2023). This format allows models with minimal reasoning capabilities to achieve substantially overestimated performance, leading to deeply misleading evaluation results that mask true reasoning deficiencies. The rapid advancements in LLMs are leading to the saturation of scores on existing benchmarks, reducing their effectiveness in differentiating model capabilities. Consequently, there is a growing and continuous need for the development of more challenging and distinctive benchmarks to better evaluate model performance. Nevertheless, constructing such high-quality reasoning datasets requires extensive human annotation effort, which substantially limits the scale of available evaluation resources. 

To address these challenges, we introduce a novel method for automatically synthesizing openended logic puzzles to construct a reasoning benchmark named AutoLogi. Our approach offers three key advantages: (1) as is illustrated in Figure 1, the open-ended format requires models to construct complete solutions from scratch, significantly mitigating the performance inflation caused by random guessing; (2) automated augmentation generates puzzles with varying logical constraints, enabling balanced difficulty distribution; (3) fully automated generation with minimal human verification substantially reduces benchmark construction costs. These innovations directly address the aforementioned challenges, offering a more reliable, balanced, and scalable evaluation methodology.

snippet.text:
American Invitational Mathematics Examination (AIME) [23] is a 15-question, three-hour test that has been administered to students scoring in the top 5% of the AMC 12 competition. AIME serves as an intermediate stage in the selection process for the USAMO and the USAJMO, which are key qualifiers for the International Mathematical Olympiad. The difficulty of AIME problems increases progressively, and each answer is a three-digit integer. The problems span various mathematical fields, including algebra, geometry, number theory, and combinatorics, demanding advanced problem-solving skills and creativity. Chinese National Mathematics Olympiad (CNMO) serves as a selection process for the national team competing in the International Mathematical Olympiad. It focuses on deep mathematical concepts like functional equations, symmetries, and mathematical analysis. These benchmarks have provided a foundation for evaluating AI's mathematical abilities, yet new evaluation frameworks will be necessary to assess progress meaningfully as AI capabilities evolve. [20]. The LLMs' answers were graded according to the national grading guidelines [26]. The Finnish matriculation examination is graded with seven grades: L, E, M, C, B, A, and I, where L refers to the highest grade and I refers to failing the examination [26]. 

In August 2023, the mathematical performance was tested by using the examination from Spring 2021. By this time, OpenAI's GPT-4 scored 64 out of 120 points, achieving the second-highest grade of E. In contrast, Google's Bard scored 34 points, corresponding to a middle-grade C. 

In November 2023, OpenAI's GPT-4 was tested using the examination from Autumn 2023, and its performance was significantly improved because it utilized programming capabilities in Python. Symbolic calculation proceeded with the assistance of Python's SYMPY library, and OpenAI's GPT-4 was able to visualize the complexities of numerous challenging space geometry tasks accurately. The score was 93 out of 120 points, corresponding to the highest grade L. 

In April 2024, three different LLMs were evaluated using the spring 2024 examination. A summary of the free and paid versions of the three service providers: OpenAI CHATGPT, Microsoft's COPILOT, and Google's GEMINI is presented in Table III.

documents.snippet:
Aggregated benchmarks like MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021a), AGIEval (Zhong et al., 2023), Big-Bench (Srivastava et al., 2022), and Big-Bench Hard (Suzgun et al., 2022) are also commonly used. In particular, since the introduction of GPT-3, evaluations that comprise a variety of datasets have been standardised (see for instance evaluations of GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020), GPT-4 (Achiam et al., 2024), Llama andLlama-2 (Touvron et al., 2023b), Mistral (Jiang et al., 2023) or Claude-3 (Anthropic, 2024)). 

Evaluations often mix prompting strategies, varying from zero-shot, few-shot with different numbers of examples, and chain-of-thought configurations. For example, in the evaluation of Llama-2 (Touvron et al., 2023b) we find a zero-shot setting for evaluating common sense reasoning, except for one dataset in which 7-shot is used, and for aggregated benchmarks we find 3 and 5-shot settings. In more recent evaluations, such as that of Claude-3 (Anthropic, 2024), few-shot experimentation is performed with different numbers of examples (varying from 0 to 25) and chain-of-thought strategies. 

Exams benchmarks. MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021a) is a popular benchmark with English multiple-choice questions covering subjects like mathematics, history, and computer science, ranging from elementary to college level. AGIEval (Zhong et al., 2023) assesses human-like cognition and problem-solving abilities using high-stakes exams, such as university entrance and law school exams, in both English and Chinese. GPQA (Rein et al., 2023) presents challenging questions in biology, physics, and chemistry, aimed at testing even expert knowledge. M3Exam (Zhang et al., 2023) evaluates multilingual, multi-modal intelligence in LLMs using questions from human exams in nine languages.

Title: Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Tasks
Snippet: Data Collection We collected per-model, per-task results from the official SWE-bench evaluation results repository for frontier models: Claude 3 Opus, Claude 3.5 Sonnet (Old), Claude 3.5 Sonnet (New), GPT-4 1106, GPT-4o, and o1. Note that this is only 6 of the 11 models we include in the main result. 

Time estimates SWE-bench Verified contains time estimates created by contractors that split tasks into four buckets: < 15 min fix, 15 minutes-1 hour, 1 hour-4 hours, or > 4 hours. These estimates were based on the expected time it would take an "engineer who has had a few hours to familiarize themselves with the codebase" to solve the issue. 

Figure 18: Time horizon with continuous (non-binarized) scoring. Claude 3.7 Sonnet has a 50% time horizon of nearly 2 hours. We think this methodology captures more signal from 8-hour RE-Bench tasks, but overstates the time horizon of recent models, since it is easier to achieve an average score of 0.5 on most tasks than to match human performance 50% of the time. The slope is also likely an overestimate, because longer tasks tend to be continuously scored. We verified annotator time buckets by running seven baselines across 6 SWE-bench Verified tasks. We baselined four tasks in the "< 15 min fix" bucket, and found that they took our baseliners 8, 26, 67, and 84 minutes respectively. We baselined two tasks in the "1 hour-4 hours" bucket, and both baseliners took between 2-3 hours.

Snippet: HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021) is one of the most well-known benchmarks in the code domain, featuring several variants that extend it to different programming languages, extra tests, and broader application scenarios. Other notable benchmarks include MBPP (Austin et al., 2021) for program synthesis, DS1000 (Lai et al., 2022) for data science tasks, SWE-Bench (Jimenez et al., 2024) for real-world software engineering problems, and CanItEdit / CodeEditorBench (Cassano et al., 2023b;Guo et al., 2024b) for code editing. Additionally, LiveCodeBench (Jain et al., 2024) focuses on contamination-free evaluations, while ClassEval (Du et al., 2023), Bigcodebench (Zhuo et al., 2024) and Naturecodebench (Zhang et al., 2024b) provide comprehensive program synthesis assessments. CRUXEval (Gu et al., 2024) targets reasoning, CrossCodeEval (Ding et al., 2023) focuses on repository-level code completion, and Needle in the code (Hui et al., 2024) is designed for long-context evaluations.

Title: Kodezi Chronos: A Debugging-First Language Model for Repository-Scale Code Understanding
Snippet: The landscape of code-focused LLMs has evolved dramatically in 2025. Claude 4.5 Opus [4] achieves 74.40% on SWE-bench Verified, while Gemini 3 Pro [31] reaches 76.2% on SWE-bench Verified with state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks (91.9% GPQA Diamond, 95-100% AIME 2025, 2,439 Elo on LiveCodeBench Pro). Claude 4.1 Opus and Claude 4.5 Sonnet achieve 72.5% and 72.7% respectively on SWE-bench Full (code generation). These models also achieve 67.60% and 70.60% respectively on SWE Bench Bash Only (using mini-SWE-agent environment). GPT-4.1 [5] doubles GPT-4o's performance on code diff benchmarks and reaches 54.6% on SWE-bench tasks. Gemini 2.5 Pro [30] achieves 59.6% on SWE-bench Verified, showcasing Google's advances in reasoning models. DeepSeek V3 [6], with 671B parameters (37B activated), demonstrates that efficient training is possible, achieving competitive performance at 1/10th the training cost of comparable models. Qwen2.5-Coder-32B [44] matches GPT-4o performance while running locally on consumer hardware. 

However, these impressive code generation capabilities do not translate to debugging success. When evaluated on realworld debugging tasks requiring multi-file understanding, historical context, and iterative refinement-specifically on SWE-bench Lite and other debugging benchmarks (Debug-Bench, MdEval)-even the best models achieve less than 15% success rates. Notably, Claude models drop from 67-72% on code generation benchmarks to only 13-14% on SWEbench Lite debugging tasks, revealing a 54-57 percentage point gap. This stark disparity between code generation and debugging performance motivates the need for specialized debugging-focused architectures.

Additionally, LiveCodeBench (Jain et al., 2024) focuses on contamination-free evaluations, while ClassEval (Du et al., 2023), Bigcodebench (Zhuo et al., 2024) and Naturecodebench (Zhang et al., 2024b) provide comprehensive program synthesis assessments. CRUXEval (Gu et al., 2024) targets reasoning, CrossCodeEval (Ding et al., 2023) focuses on repository-level code completion, and Needle in the code (Hui et al., 2024) is designed for long-context evaluations.

documents.title: Kodezi Chronos: A Debugging-First Language Model for Repository-Scale Code Understanding
documents.snippet:
The landscape of code-focused LLMs has evolved dramatically in 2025. Claude 4.5 Opus [4] achieves 74.40% on SWE-bench Verified, while Gemini 3 Pro [31] reaches 76.2% on SWE-bench Verified with state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks (91.9% GPQA Diamond, 95-100% AIME 2025, 2,439 Elo on LiveCodeBench Pro). Claude 4.1 Opus and Claude 4.5 Sonnet achieve 72.5% and 72.7% respectively on SWE-bench Full (code generation). These models also achieve 67.60% and 70.60% respectively on SWE Bench Bash Only (using mini-SWE-agent environment). GPT-4.1 [5] doubles GPT-4o's performance on code diff benchmarks and reaches 54.6% on SWE-bench tasks. Gemini 2.5 Pro [30] achieves 59.6% on SWE-bench Verified, showcasing Google's advances in reasoning models. DeepSeek V3 [6], with 671B parameters (37B activated), demonstrates that efficient training is possible, achieving competitive performance at 1/10th the training cost of comparable models. Qwen2.5-Coder-32B [44] matches GPT-4o performance while running locally on consumer hardware. 

However, these impressive code generation capabilities do not translate to debugging success. When evaluated on realworld debugging tasks requiring multi-file understanding, historical context, and iterative refinement-specifically on SWE-bench Lite and other debugging benchmarks (Debug-Bench, MdEval)-even the best models achieve less than 15% success rates. Notably, Claude models drop from 67-72% on code generation benchmarks to only 13-14% on SWEbench Lite debugging tasks, revealing a 54-57 percentage point gap. This stark disparity between code generation and debugging performance motivates the need for specialized debugging-focused architectures.

problem: How the variant effect prediction happen in proteomics and genomics domain ? What are the LLM are there in this direction?
final_response:
# Overview: What “variant effect prediction” means in genomics and proteomics

Variant effect prediction aims to classify how genetic variants alter molecular and cellular functions. In genomics, this spans coding (amino-acid change), noncoding (regulatory element perturbation), and splicing effects, often informing pathogenicity and ACMG interpretation. In proteomics, variant effect prediction links DNA-to-protein impact through transcription, translation, and post-translational modifications (PTMs), including changes in peptide generation, protease digestion, mass spectrometry signal properties, peptide–spectrum matches (PSMs), and PTM site localization that affect protein identification and quantification. <cite id="37f11914-2">In silico variant effect predictors are integrated into ACMG guidelines as supporting evidence for pathogenicity assessment</cite>.

# Genomic coding variant effect prediction (DNA→protein)

Classical sequence- and structure-based methods remain widely used to predict the functional impact of missense variants. <cite id="37f11914-2">Established tools include SIFT, PolyPhen‑2, CADD, VEST, and newer deep-learning approaches such as AlphaMissense, ESM1b, and PrimateAI‑3D</cite>. <cite id="37f11914-2">A head‑to‑head analysis on all CDKN2A missense variants compared these predictors against functional classifications and reported accuracy ranging from 39.5% to 85.4% across methods, with sensitivity from 0.25 to 0.98 and specificity from 0.27 to 0.98</cite>. <cite id="37f11914-2">For example, PrimateAI‑3D achieved the highest reported accuracy (85.4%) but low sensitivity (0.25), whereas AlphaMissense and ESM1b showed mid‑range accuracy (71.6%–59.2%) with sensitivity around 0.94–0.95</cite>. <cite id="37f11914-0">Clinical pipelines routinely combine multiple predictors (e.g., SIFT, PolyPhen‑2, CADD, M-CAP, MVP2, PrimateAI) to annotate likely pathogenic or benign variants</cite>.

Mechanistically, these models operate via different signals: conservation and phylogeny (e.g., SIFT), structure/protein language embeddings (e.g., ESM1b, AlphaMissense), and large-scale aggregate functional data (e.g., CADD) or 3D-aware models (e.g., PrimateAI‑3D) to infer functional or phenotypic impact. <cite id="37f11914-2">Performance differences reflect trade‑offs between sensitivity and specificity and can vary by gene and variant class, underscoring the need to integrate multiple lines of evidence</cite>.

# Noncoding and splicing variant effect prediction

Noncoding variants affect regulatory elements and alternative splicing, which are critical for trait and disease. <cite id="f14d21ef-1">DeepSEA predicts 919 variant effects on transcription factor binding, DNase I sensitivity, and histone marks across cell types</cite>. <cite id="f14d21ef-1">SpliceAI provides delta scores for donor/acceptor gain/loss to quantify predicted splicing perturbations</cite>, and <cite id="f14d21ef-3">dbscSNV uses ensemble learning to predict splice-altering variants in exonic and proximal intronic regions</cite>. <cite id="f14d21ef-2">Benchmarking 3,616 variants with massively parallel splicing assays found that deep learning predictors trained on gene-model annotations performed best overall, with SpliceAI and Pangolin showing superior sensitivity at finding splice-disruptive variants, though performance is lower for exonic variants and depends on gene-model choices and score cutoffs</cite>. <cite id="f14d21ef-0">Clinical interpretation often combines CADD with splicing-focused tools such as dbscSNV and SpliceAI to assess splicing disruption risks</cite>.

# Protein-level consequences and structure–stability models

At the protein level, variant effects can manifest as altered stability, structure, interactions, and function. <cite id="60a4ee57-0">Stability predictors such as Rosetta’s ddG, mCSM, DynaMut2, and I‑Mutant2.0 estimate ΔΔG (change in Gibbs free energy) of unfolding to infer whether a mutation is likely to destabilize or stabilize a protein</cite>. <cite id="60a4ee57-1">Rosetta energy functions and machine learning over energy term distributions can model how mutations perturb folding free energy and predict temperature‑sensitive alleles by targeting moderate destabilization ranges</cite>. <cite id="60a4ee57-2">Empirical analyses show that many disease mutations destabilize proteins, while others may alter interactions or dynamics without large ΔΔG changes, so stability alone is not sufficient to capture all functional effects</cite>. <cite id="60a4ee57-3">Comparative use of I‑Mutant and MUpro illustrates that different modeling approaches (e.g., SVR on structural features vs. neural networks with sequence/evolutionary data) can yield consistent or divergent ΔΔG predictions</cite>. <cite id="60a4ee57-4">Rosetta-based pipelines are also used to visualize structural differences and ΔΔG for variant impact in specific proteins (e.g., keratin genes), supporting database curation and interpretation</cite>.

# Proteomics-specific variant effects (translating DNA changes into proteomic signals)

Amino‑acid and other variants influence proteomics through several steps: transcription, RNA processing and splicing, translation, protease digestion, and mass spectrometry identification/quantification, including PTM localization.

- Spectral matching and PSMs: <cite id="3358ade3-0">Modern database search pipelines (e.g., Metamorephus) integrate PTM‑aware strategies (G‑PTM) using UniProt site‑specific PTM annotations to generate more realistic modified peptide databases, narrowing mass tolerance and enabling broader PTM coverage; peptide–spectrum matches (PSMs) are scored to assign identifications and control FDR</cite>.
- PTM site localization: <cite id="3358ade3-1">Tools like PTMProphet re‑analyze PSMs to compute site‑wise localization probabilities for PTMs with multiple possible sites and report a global false localization rate, improving confidence in site assignment</cite>. <cite id="3358ade3-4">Similarly, Scaffold PTM combines peptide‑level localization probabilities to estimate the best site for each PTM assignment in proteomics identifications</cite>.
- Choosing digestion settings to expose variants: <cite id="3358ade3-2">PTMselect simulates protease combinations and peptide releases to optimize digestion settings that maximize coverage of PTM sites (predicted or target sites), producing maps of modified peptides and detailed results for downstream analysis</cite>.
- Databases and PTM context: <cite id="3358ade3-3">Curated resources like dbPTM aggregate experimentally verified site‑specific PTM data across literature and map PTM sites to UniProt entries, supporting PTM discovery and localization in proteomics studies</cite>.

Together, these workflows translate DNA variants into proteomic evidence by affecting which peptides are generated (via altered protein sequences/structure and splicing), which digestion products enter the mass spectrometer, how spectra match peptides, and where PTMs are confidently localized—ultimately influencing protein identification, quantification, and PTM maps. <cite id="3358ade3-0">PTM‑aware database generation and PSM scoring</cite>, <cite id="3358ade3-1">site‑level localization confidence</cite>, and <cite id="3358ade3-2">digestion optimization to expose variant/PTM-bearing peptides</cite> are central to proteomics‑oriented variant effect assessment.

# Where LLMs fit: current models and emerging directions

Large neural sequence/structure models have begun to impact variant effect prediction in two complementary ways:

- Protein language models and structure-aware models for coding variants: <cite id="37f11914-2">ESM1b and AlphaMissense embed variant contexts to predict functional impact, with reported accuracies around 59–72% and sensitivities up to ~0.94–0.95 in benchmarking</cite>. <cite id="37f11914-2">PrimateAI‑3D integrates protein structure/evolution to predict variant effects, achieving higher accuracy (≈85%) but lower sensitivity in some evaluations</cite>. These models can be considered early examples of large models (including transformer‑style architectures) applied to variant effect prediction, complementing earlier feature‑based methods.
- LLMs and transformers in proteomics workflows: While dedicated LLMs specifically for variant effect prediction are still emerging in proteomics, large protein/sequence models are increasingly used for tasks that intersect with variant interpretation, such as PTM annotation and peptide‑sequence scoring within search/localization pipelines, and for generating realistic modified‑peptide databases for PTM discovery. <cite id="3358ade3-0">PTM‑aware database construction leveraging UniProt annotations</cite> and <cite id="3358ade3-1">probabilistic site localization from PSMs</cite> benefit from high‑quality sequence context that large models can provide, and are natural integration points for transformer‑based embeddings in future systems.

Open challenges include: (1) combining sequence/structure predictions with regulatory and splicing effects; (2) integrating proteomics‑specific signals (digestion, PSMs, PTM localization) into end‑to‑end variant effect scores; and (3) handling class imbalance and gene‑specific heterogeneity. <cite id="f14d21ef-2">Benchmarking shows sensitivity–specificity trade‑offs and dependence on gene models and cutoffs</cite>, and <cite id="60a4ee57-0">stability–function ambiguity</cite> suggest that multi‑modal, evidence‑integrated frameworks—including large models—will likely outperform single‑modality predictors.

# Practical workflow for variant effect prediction

A typical multi‑step workflow integrates both genomic and proteomics evidence:
1) Genomic annotation: run SIFT/PolyPhen‑2/CADD/AlphaMissense/ESM1b/PrimateAI‑3D to classify missense effects and 3D/structure impacts. <cite id="37f11914-2">These outputs inform ACMG criteria and clinical interpretation</cite>.
2) Regulatory/splicing: assess noncoding effects and exon/intron impacts using DeepSEA, AbSplice, SpliceAI, and dbscSNV; benchmark and adjust for gene‑model choices and cutoffs. <cite id="f14d21ef-1">DeepSEA captures TF binding and chromatin effects</cite>; <cite id="f14d21ef-2">SpliceAI and Pangolin show strong performance for splice disruption</cite>; <cite id="f14d21ef-3">dbscSNV targets exonic/proximal intronic splice disruption</cite>.
3) Protein stability/structure: use Rosetta ddG, mCSM, and I‑Mutant/DynaMut2 to estimate ΔΔG and functional plausibility; visualize structural differences when available. <cite id="60a4ee57-0">These tools quantify destabilization/destabilizing potential and interaction perturbation risks</cite>.
4) Proteomics mapping: simulate digestion (e.g., PTMselect), build PTM‑aware databases (e.g., G‑PTM), and run search/localization (e.g., PTMProphet/Scaffold PTM). <cite id="3358ade3-2">Optimize cleavage settings to expose variant/PTM‑bearing peptides</cite>; <cite id="3358ade3-0">use PTM‑aware scoring to increase PSM coverage and FDR control</cite>; <cite id="3358ade3-1">compute site‑wise localization probabilities</cite>.
5) Integration and decision: combine genome‑to‑protein predictions with proteomics‑derived peptide/PTM evidence to refine variant pathogenicity and molecular mechanism hypotheses.

# Summary of LLMs in this direction (and what’s next)

- Protein LMs and structure-aware models already used for variant effect prediction include ESM1b and AlphaMissense (and PrimateAI‑3D for 3D), which embed sequence/structure context to predict functional impact and, in some cases, splicing/3D effects. <cite id="37f11914-2">These models provide complementary signals to classical predictors and can reach high sensitivity for deleterious calls with varying accuracy</cite>.
- In proteomics, LLMs are not yet a standalone standard for variant effect prediction but are poised to enhance PTM discovery and localization, digestion strategy selection, and peptide‑spectrum compatibility modeling by leveraging rich sequence context and probabilistic site assignment frameworks. <cite id="3358ade3-1">PTMProphet’s Bayesian mixture models</cite> and <cite id="3358ade3-2">PTMselect’s optimization over digestion settings</cite> provide natural integration points for transformer‑style sequence models and large embedding spaces.
- Near‑term advances are likely to come from multi‑modal, model‑augmented pipelines that fuse coding, regulatory/splicing, protein stability/structure, and proteomics signals, with large models improving contextual embeddings and uncertainty quantification across these layers.

Limitations and uncertainty: <cite id="37f11914-2">Deep-learning models can disagree with classical scores and show gene‑ and class‑specific performance differences</cite>, and <cite id="f14d21ef-2">splicing predictors perform differently across exonic vs intronic variants and depend on gene models and thresholds</cite>. <cite id="60a4ee57-0">Stability–function relationships are complex and not all disease mechanisms are captured by ΔΔG</cite>. Future work should therefore prioritize evidence integration, cross‑domain validation, and transparent reporting of sensitivity/specificity and gene‑specific biases when deploying LLM‑augmented variant effect prediction in genomics and proteomics.

Title: Benchmarking splice variant prediction algorithms using massively parallel splicing assays
Snippet: Background Variants that disrupt mRNA splicing account for a sizable fraction of the pathogenic burden in many genetic disorders, but identifying splice-disruptive variants (SDVs) beyond the essential splice site dinucleotides remains difficult. Computational predictors are often discordant, compounding the challenge of variant interpretation. Because they are primarily validated using clinical variant sets heavily biased to known canonical splice site mutations, it remains unclear how well their performance generalizes. Results We benchmark eight widely used splicing effect prediction algorithms, leveraging massively parallel splicing assays (MPSAs) as a source of experimentally determined ground-truth. MPSAs simultaneously assay many variants to nominate candidate SDVs. We compare experimentally measured splicing outcomes with bioinformatic predictions for 3,616 variants in five genes. Algorithms’ concordance with MPSA measurements, and with each other, is lower for exonic than intronic variants, underscoring the difficulty of identifying missense or synonymous SDVs. Deep learning-based predictors trained on gene model annotations achieve the best overall performance at distinguishing disruptive and neutral variants, and controlling for overall call rate genome-wide, SpliceAI and Pangolin have superior sensitivity. Finally, our results highlight two practical considerations when scoring variants genome-wide: finding an optimal score cutoff, and the substantial variability introduced by differences in gene model annotation, and we suggest strategies for optimal splice effect prediction in the face of these issues. Conclusion SpliceAI and Pangolin show the best overall performance among predictors tested, however, improvements in splice effect prediction are still needed especially within exons.
</snippet>

Title: Hidden Splicing Variants in Inherited Retinal Degeneration: Discovery and Functional Insight
Snippet: Splicing variant prediction was conducted using two computational algorithms, SpliceAI and dbscSNV_ADA. SpliceAI, a deep learning-based tool designed for genome-wide application, was capable of detecting potential splicing alterations across exonic regions, canonical splice sites, and deepintronic regions. Notably, its predictive capacity extends to intronic variants located in regions harboring branchpoints, pyrimidine tracts, and other critical cis-elements essential for spliceosome assembly. In contrast, dbscSNV_ADA is a predictive tool that uses ensemble learning to assess the potential splice-altering impact of single-nucleotide variants within exonic and proximal intronic regions. Threshold analysis revealed regional variability in SpliceAI score cutoffs, with intronic variants requiring a lower maximum threshold (≤0.35) for detection compared to those located in noncanonical splice sites and exonic regions (≤0.74) (Supplementary Fig. S4). In a performance comparison excluding variants of uncertain significance, dbscSNV_ADA demonstrated a higher area under the curve (AUC = 0.83) than SpliceAI (AUC = 0.67) in the prediction of variants affecting noncanonical splice sites (Fig. 4).

An accuracy-oriented Rosetta protocol, or the "cartesian_ddg" application in the Rosetta suite, which allows structure energy minimisation in Cartesian space, may lead to better performance 37,75 .

The ambiguity of the relationship between protein stability and function is exacerbated by the biases of the various stability prediction methods, which arise in their training, like overrepresentation of destabilising variants, dependence on crystal resolution and residue replacement asymmetry. In addition, reduced stability is more tractable for computational modeling: a reduction in stability will be reflected as a lowering of DG, the free energy of unfolding of the protein, which will be reflected in the energy function of protein modeling software such as Rosetta [6,7]. We restrict our search to buried sites because mutations at buried sites a) are correlated with both reduced stability and a ts phenotype [8], and b) are more likely to perturb the entire function of a protein rather than a single interaction. For proteins of known function a more directed design approach could be adopted, but we choose to focus on a method of general utility in the study of poorly understood proteins.

Quantifying the effects of mutations on protein structure presents its own challenges. Proteins vary tremendously in structure and function, variations that are reflected in their wide range of native stabilities. While small reductions in stability (a decrease in DG or a negative DDG) may be tolerated and large changes will most likely result in a loss of function phenotype, ts mutations occupy a middle ground between toleration and loss of function. Although changes in the score calculated by Rosetta's energy function due to single amino acid substitutions have been shown to correlate well with experimentally measured DDG values [9], DDG alone is not sufficient to predict whether a mutation will result in a ts phenotype. Therefore, instead of directly comparing energies of native and mutated structures, we accommodate the natural variation in structure and function by 1) generating a distribution of component Rosetta score terms (Table 1) across multiple candidate structures for each mutation, and 2) comparing mutant structure and native structure distributions rather than comparing energy function terms directly. We then use these distribution comparisons as inputs to a machine learning algorithm, allowing us to pinpoint the intermediate range of destabilization that is most likely to yield a ts phenotype.

Title: PTMProphet: Fast and Accurate Mass Modification Localization for the Trans-Proteomic Pipeline
Snippet: Spectral matching sequence database search engines commonly used on mass spectrometry-based proteomics experiments excel at identifying peptide sequence ions, and in addition, possible sequence ions carrying post-translational modifications (PTMs), but most do not provide confidence metrics for the exact localization of those PTMs when several possible sites are available. Localization is absolutely required for downstream molecular cell biology analysis of PTM function in vitro and in vivo. Therefore, we developed PTMProphet, a free and open-source software tool integrated into the Trans-Proteomic Pipeline, which reanalyzes identified spectra from any search engine for which pepXML output is available to provide localization confidence to enable appropriate further characterization of biologic events. Localization of any type of mass modification (e.g., phosphorylation) is supported. PTMProphet applies Bayesian mixture models to compute probabilities for each site/peptide spectrum match where a PTM has been identified. These probabilities can be combined to compute a global false localization rate at any threshold to guide downstream analysis. We describe the PTMProphet tool, its underlying algorithms and demonstrate its performance on ground-truth synthetic peptide reference datasets, one previously published small dataset, one new larger dataset, and also on a previously published phospho-enriched dataset where the correct sites of modification are unknown. Data have been deposited to ProteomeXchange with identifier PXD013210.

Snippet: PTMselect was optimized to eliminate the tedious work of manually sorting and selecting peptides to choose digestion settings before performing any MS-driven PTM analysis. This software is designed for (1) optimization of global coverage of protein PTM sites, (2) optimization of protein PTM sites coverage with the highest probability to be modified and (3) optimization of target PTM positions coverage. 

PTMselect needs one or more protein sequences imported in Fasta format from protein databases, the identity of the amino-acids carrying PTMs, and the cleavages sites of the proteases (Fig. 1a). It computes all proteases combinations and the peptides released by these combinations. Peptides are further filtered by PTM sites and by size, compatible with LC-MS. A set of scores is then calculated, based on the number of PTM sites of the filtered peptides (Fig. 1a). All protein PTM site positions are considered equal and PTMselect returns the best digestion settings to maximize protein PTM coverage. Optionally, PTMselect can import a PTM position/score table from any prediction tool (Fig. 1a green box "imported predicted PTM sites") and gives the best digestion settings to maximize protein PTM coverage of predicted positions with a dedicated score. Another option is to import a list of target PTM positions for one or more proteins. (Fig. 1a green box "target PTM sites"). With this information, PTMselect computes a target score and gives the best digestion settings to maximize PTM coverage of these specific protein sites. PTMselect also produces a graphical protein PTM map and a detailed result file featuring the sequence of all modified peptides and their position on the protein sequence. In case of multiple protein analysis, the software is able to merge the score table of each protein into a final score table. 

PTMselect can analyze any number of proteins, PTM types and combinations. # Overview: What “variant effect prediction” means in genomics and proteomics

Variant effect prediction aims to classify how genetic variants alter molecular and cellular functions. In genomics, this spans coding (amino-acid change), noncoding (regulatory element perturbation), and splicing effects, often informing pathogenicity and ACMG interpretation. In proteomics, variant effect prediction links DNA-to-protein impact through transcription, translation, and post-translational modifications (PTMs), including changes in peptide generation, protease digestion, mass spectrometry signal properties, peptide–spectrum matches (PSMs), and PTM site localization that affect protein identification and quantification. <cite id="37f11914-2">In silico variant effect predictors are integrated into ACMG guidelines as supporting evidence for pathogenicity assessment</cite>.

# Genomic coding variant effect prediction (DNA→protein)

Classical sequence- and structure-based methods remain widely used to predict the functional impact of missense variants. <cite id="37f11914-2">Established tools include SIFT, PolyPhen‑2, CADD, VEST, and newer deep-learning approaches such as AlphaMissense, ESM1b, and PrimateAI‑3D</cite>. <cite id="37f11914-2">A head‑to‑head analysis on all CDKN2A missense variants compared these predictors against functional classifications and reported accuracy ranging from 39.5% to 85.4% across methods, with sensitivity from 0.25 to 0.98 and specificity from 0.27 to 0.98</cite>. <cite id="37f11914-2">For example, PrimateAI‑3D achieved the highest reported accuracy (85.4%) but low sensitivity (0.25), whereas AlphaMissense and ESM1b showed mid‑range accuracy (71.6%–59.2%) with sensitivity around 0.94–0.95</cite>. <cite id="37f11914-0">Clinical pipelines routinely combine multiple predictors (e.g., SIFT, PolyPhen‑2, CADD, M-CAP, MVP2, PrimateAI) to annotate likely pathogenic or benign variants</cite>.

Mechanistically, these models operate via different signals: conservation and phylogeny (e.g., SIFT), structure/protein language embeddings (e.g., ESM1b, AlphaMissense), and large-scale aggregate functional data (e.g., CADD) or 3D-aware models (e.g., PrimateAI‑3D) to infer functional or phenotypic impact. <cite id="37f11914-2">Performance differences reflect trade‑offs between sensitivity and specificity and can vary by gene and variant class, underscoring the need to integrate multiple lines of evidence</cite>.

# Noncoding and splicing variant effect prediction

Noncoding variants affect regulatory elements and alternative splicing, which are critical for trait and disease. <cite id="f14d21ef-1">DeepSEA predicts 919 variant effects on transcription factor binding, DNase I sensitivity, and histone marks across cell types</cite>. <cite id="f14d21ef-1">SpliceAI provides delta scores for donor/acceptor gain/loss to quantify predicted splicing perturbations</cite>, and <cite id="f14d21ef-3">dbscSNV uses ensemble learning to predict splice-altering variants in exonic and proximal intronic regions</cite>. <cite id="f14d21ef-2">Benchmarking 3,616 variants with massively parallel splicing assays found that deep learning predictors trained on gene-model annotations performed best overall, with SpliceAI and Pangolin showing superior sensitivity at finding splice-disruptive variants, though performance is lower for exonic variants and depends on gene-model choices and score cutoffs</cite>. <cite id="f14d21ef-0">Clinical interpretation often combines CADD with splicing-focused tools such as dbscSNV and SpliceAI to assess splicing disruption risks</cite>.

# Protein-level consequences and structure–stability models

At the protein level, variant effects can manifest as altered stability, structure, interactions, and function. <cite id="60a4ee57-0">Stability predictors such as Rosetta’s ddG, mCSM, DynaMut2, and I‑Mutant2.0 estimate ΔΔG (change in Gibbs free energy) of unfolding to infer whether a mutation is likely to destabilize or stabilize a protein</cite>. <cite id="60a4ee57-1">Rosetta energy functions and machine learning over energy term distributions can model how mutations perturb folding free energy and predict temperature‑sensitive alleles by targeting moderate destabilization ranges</cite>. <cite id="60a4ee57-2">Empirical analyses show that many disease mutations destabilize proteins, while others may alter interactions or dynamics without large ΔΔG changes, so stability alone is not sufficient to capture all functional effects</cite>. <cite id="60a4ee57-3">Comparative use of I‑Mutant and MUpro illustrates that different modeling approaches (e.g., SVR on structural features vs. neural networks with sequence/evolutionary data) can yield consistent or divergent ΔΔG predictions</cite>. <cite id="60a4ee57-4">Rosetta-based pipelines are also used to visualize structural differences and ΔΔG for variant impact in specific proteins (e.g., keratin genes), supporting database curation and interpretation</cite>.

# Proteomics-specific variant effects (translating DNA changes into proteomic signals)

Amino‑acid and other variants influence proteomics through several steps: transcription, RNA processing and splicing, translation, protease digestion, and mass spectrometry identification/quantification, including PTM localization.

- Spectral matching and PSMs: <cite id="3358ade3-0">Modern database search pipelines (e.g., Metamorephus) integrate PTM‑aware strategies (G‑PTM) using UniProt site‑specific PTM annotations to generate more realistic modified peptide databases, narrowing mass tolerance and enabling broader PTM coverage; peptide–spectrum matches (PSMs) are scored to assign identifications and control FDR</cite>.
- PTM site localization: <cite id="3358ade3-1">Tools like PTMProphet re‑analyze PSMs to compute site‑wise localization probabilities for PTMs with multiple possible sites and report a global false localization rate, improving confidence in site assignment</cite>. <cite id="3358ade3-4">Similarly, Scaffold PTM combines peptide‑level localization probabilities to estimate the best site for each PTM assignment in proteomics identifications</cite>.
- Choosing digestion settings to expose variants: <cite id="3358ade3-2">PTMselect simulates protease combinations and peptide releases to optimize digestion settings that maximize coverage of PTM sites (predicted or target sites), producing maps of modified peptides and detailed results for downstream analysis</cite>.
- Databases and PTM context: <cite id="3358ade3-3">Curated resources like dbPTM aggregate experimentally verified site‑specific PTM data across literature and map PTM sites to UniProt entries, supporting PTM discovery and localization in proteomics studies</cite>.

Together, these workflows translate DNA variants into proteomic evidence by affecting which peptides are generated (via altered protein sequences/structure and splicing), which digestion products enter the mass spectrometer, how spectra match peptides, and where PTMs are confidently localized—ultimately influencing protein identification, quantification, and PTM maps. <cite id="3358ade3-0">PTM‑aware database generation and PSM scoring</cite>, <cite id="3358ade3-1">site‑level localization confidence</cite>, and <cite id="3358ade3-2">digestion optimization to expose variant/PTM-bearing peptides</cite> are central to proteomics‑oriented variant effect assessment.

# Where LLMs fit: current models and emerging directions

Large neural sequence/structure models have begun to impact variant effect prediction in two complementary ways:

- Protein language models and structure-aware models for coding variants: <cite id="37f11914-2">ESM1b and AlphaMissense embed variant contexts to predict functional impact, with reported accuracies around 59–72% and sensitivities up to ~0.94–0.95 in benchmarking</cite>. <cite id="37f11914-2">PrimateAI‑3D integrates protein structure/evolution to predict variant effects, achieving higher accuracy (≈85%) but lower sensitivity in some evaluations</cite>. These models can be considered early examples of large models (including transformer‑style architectures) applied to variant effect prediction, complementing earlier feature‑based methods.
- LLMs and transformers in proteomics workflows: While dedicated LLMs specifically for variant effect prediction are still emerging in proteomics, large protein/sequence models are increasingly used for tasks that intersect with variant interpretation, such as PTM annotation and peptide‑sequence scoring within search/localization pipelines, and for generating realistic modified‑peptide databases for PTM discovery. <cite id="3358ade3-0">PTM‑aware database construction leveraging UniProt annotations</cite> and <cite id="3358ade3-1">probabilistic site localization from PSMs</cite> benefit from high‑quality sequence context that large models can provide, and are natural integration points for transformer‑based embeddings in future systems.

Open challenges include: (1) combining sequence/structure predictions with regulatory and splicing effects; (2) integrating proteomics‑specific signals (digestion, PSMs, PTM localization) into end‑to‑end variant effect scores; and (3) handling class imbalance and gene‑specific heterogeneity. <cite id="f14d21ef-2">Benchmarking shows sensitivity–specificity trade‑offs and dependence on gene models and cutoffs</cite>, and <cite id="60a4ee57-0">stability–function ambiguity</cite> suggest that multi‑modal, evidence‑integrated frameworks—including large models—will likely outperform single‑modality predictors.

# Practical workflow for variant effect prediction

A typical multi‑step workflow integrates both genomic and proteomics evidence:
1) Genomic annotation: run SIFT/PolyPhen‑2/CADD/AlphaMissense/ESM1b/PrimateAI‑3D to classify missense effects and 3D/structure impacts. <cite id="37f11914-2">These outputs inform ACMG criteria and clinical interpretation</cite>.
2) Regulatory/splicing: assess noncoding effects and exon/intron impacts using DeepSEA, AbSplice, SpliceAI, and dbscSNV; benchmark and adjust for gene‑model choices and cutoffs. <cite id="f14d21ef-1">DeepSEA captures TF binding and chromatin effects</cite>; <cite id="f14d21ef-2">SpliceAI and Pangolin show strong performance for splice disruption</cite>; <cite id="f14d21ef-3">dbscSNV targets exonic/proximal intronic splice disruption</cite>.
3) Protein stability/structure: use Rosetta ddG, mCSM, and I‑Mutant/DynaMut2 to estimate ΔΔG and functional plausibility; visualize structural differences when available. <cite id="60a4ee57-0">These tools quantify destabilization/destabilizing potential and interaction perturbation risks</cite>.
4) Proteomics mapping: simulate digestion (e.g., PTMselect), build PTM‑aware databases (e.g., G‑PTM), and run search/localization (e.g., PTMProphet/Scaffold PTM). <cite id="3358ade3-2">Optimize cleavage settings to expose variant/PTM‑bearing peptides</cite>; <cite id="3358ade3-0">use PTM‑aware scoring to increase PSM coverage and FDR control</cite>; <cite id="3358ade3-1">compute site‑wise localization probabilities</cite>.
5) Integration and decision: combine genome‑to‑protein predictions with proteomics‑derived peptide/PTM evidence to refine variant pathogenicity and molecular mechanism hypotheses.

# Summary of LLMs in this direction (and what’s next)

- Protein LMs and structure-aware models already used for variant effect prediction include ESM1b and AlphaMissense (and PrimateAI‑3D for 3D), which embed sequence/structure context to predict functional impact and, in some cases, splicing/3D effects. <cite id="37f11914-2">These models provide complementary signals to classical predictors and can reach high sensitivity for deleterious calls with varying accuracy</cite>.
- In proteomics, LLMs are not yet a standalone standard for variant effect prediction but are poised to enhance PTM discovery and localization, digestion strategy selection, and peptide‑spectrum compatibility modeling by leveraging rich sequence context and probabilistic site assignment frameworks. <cite id="3358ade3-1">PTMProphet’s Bayesian mixture models</cite> and <cite id="3358ade3-2">PTMselect’s optimization over digestion settings</cite> provide natural integration points for transformer‑style sequence models and large embedding spaces.
- Near‑term advances are likely to come from multi‑modal, model‑augmented pipelines that fuse coding, regulatory/splicing, protein stability/structure, and proteomics signals, with large models improving contextual embeddings and uncertainty quantification across these layers.

Limitations and uncertainty: <cite id="37f11914-2">Deep-learning models can disagree with classical scores and show gene‑ and class‑specific performance differences</cite>, and <cite id="f14d21ef-2">splicing predictors perform differently across exonic vs intronic variants and depend on gene models and thresholds</cite>. <cite id="60a4ee57-0">Stability–function relationships are complex and not all disease mechanisms are captured by ΔΔG</cite>. Future work should therefore prioritize evidence integration, cross‑domain validation, and transparent reporting of sensitivity/specificity and gene‑specific biases when deploying LLM‑augmented variant effect prediction in genomics and proteomics. </answer>

Snippet: In silico prediction of the variant effect for all missense variants was evaluated using SIFT, PolyPhen-2, MutationTaster, Combined Annotation Dependent Depletion (CADD), Mendelian Clinically Applicable Pathogenicity (M-CAP), Missense badness, PolyPhen-2, and Constraint (MPC), Missense Variant Pathogenicity2 prediction (MVP2) and PrimateAI (Jagadeesh et al. 2016;Samocha et al. 2017;Qi et al. 2018;Sundaram et al. 2018).
