documents.title: Revolve: Optimizing AI Systems by Tracking Response Evolution in Textual Optimization
documents.snippet:
Building on these efforts, more advanced research has introduced gradient descent-inspired techniques for automatic prompt optimization. ProTeGi (Pryzant et al., 2023) pioneered the use of textual gradients, where natural language feedback refines prompts. Agent Symbolic Learning (ASL) (Zhou et al., 2024) extended this to optimize the entire agent system by treating prompts and tools as learnable parameters. Textgrad (Yuksekgonul et al., 2024) further applied textual gradients to instance-level optimization, refining outputs across multiple iterations. 

While effective, these methods all rely on what can be described as first-order optimization. In this context, first-order methods mean they adjust the agent's behavior based on immediate feedback from the current iteration, similar to how numerical first-order gradient descent updates parameters using only the current gradient. This limits their ability to account for how responses evolve across multiple iterations, leading to potential stagnation in suboptimal solutions. As shown in Figure 1 (a), first-order methods often stagnate in local optima, resulting in repeated or minimally improved LLM responses. This challenge motivates us to explore LLM optimization techniques that consider how responses evolve over time, allowing for more adaptive and refined adjustments that can break free from local optima across iterations. 

In this paper, we introduce an optimization method called REVOLVE that builds upon TextGrad (Yuksekgonul et al., 2024) by incorporating a deeper understanding of how Responses EVOLVE over time. The optimization process begins with a forward pass, where the system executes a series of tasks, logging inputs, outputs, and any prompt or tool usage. A language-based loss function then evaluates the quality of the generated responses, quantifying how well they align with task objectives. In the backward pass, feedback in the form of natural language critiques is used to adjust system variables. Relove improves this standard process by focusing on how response patterns evolve over multiple iterations, enabling the system to make more informed and effective adjustments, ultimately leading to improved performance in handling complex tasks.

Title: Decoding Human Preferences in Alignment: An Improved Approach to Inverse Constitutional AI
Snippet: Multiple options exist to align pre-trained Large Language Models (LLMs) to better adhere to human preferences. Popular methods include Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), which trains a reward model to act as a proxy for human feedback to rate model outputs, and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), which eliminates an explicit reward model to represent human preferences, and instead, implicitly defines this in their loss function for fine-tuning. Both approaches heavily rely on pairwise human-annotated preference data that rank model outputs. 

As an alternative to traditional techniques, Anthropic introduced Constitutional AI (CAI) (Bai et al., 2022), which offers a rule-based alignment based on a core set of principles/values called the constitution. This set contains key ethical, moral, and safety standards that guide the outputs and promote desired behaviors through repeated critiquing of model outputs. Having an explicitly defined set of core values aids in the interpretability of the changes induced through the alignment procedure, as typical approaches like DPO or RLHF rely on an implicitly defined set of principles embedded in the pairwise preference data. 

Building on the idea of CAI, Findeis et al. (2024) proposed an Inverse Constitutional AI (ICAI) algorithm. The algorithm extracts a constitution from a pairwise preference dataset through a multistep process involving prompting, clustering, and LLM-as-a-judge feedback. Through this process, we gain insights into the core values represented in a dataset, ranging from style and ethical values to content preferences. We hypothesize that the produced constitutional principles could then be used in a prompting-based manner to steer outputs to follow the principles, i.e., produce pseudo-aligned outputs. 

Our work aims to improve the shortcomings that we identified within the ICAI algorithm to produce constitutional principles that represent dataset preferences more accurately. For this purpose, we address different weaknesses regarding generalizability and sampling. We also experiment with utilizing various embeddings to perform grouping of related preference pairs prior to the initial principle generation. We evaluate our changes in three settings, ranging from synthetic to semi-synthetic and realistic data, and report improvements over the baseline ICAI algorithm in all three. 

Overall, our work aims to tackle the following research questions:

Title: LifeAlign: Lifelong Alignment for Large Language Models with Memory-Augmented Focalized Preference Optimization
Snippet: Constitutional AI (Bai et al. 2022b) further augments alignment by using automated constitution checks to guide preference labeling. Furthermore, Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback (RLAIF) reduces the reliance on costly human labels by training the reward model on preferences generated by an off-the-shelf LLM, achieving performance on a par with RLHF across summarization and dialogue tasks (Lee et al. 2024). However, existing approaches apply alignment only once, leaving models prone to drift and forgetting as norms and preferences change. To date, no work or benchmark supports lifelong alignment that updates an already-aligned model to reflect evolving ethical standards. We close this gap by introducing a lifelong alignment dataset alongside a human-inspired consolidation mechanism that preserves and refines alignment knowledge over time.

problem: If you are a researcher currently thinking about an approach to whether transformers can be utilized to solve the problem of ranking fusion, where the information that can be obtained is hierarchically supervised information; are there any articles in the field of information retrieval where transformers have been used to solve or discuss this problem?
final_response:
# Short answer

Yes. In modern information retrieval, transformers have been used both to fuse heterogeneous signals for ranking and to learn from hierarchically or gradedly supervised data. Concrete examples include: (a) transformer-based attention fusion that integrates multiple feature streams or models during document ranking, (b) transformer rerankers trained in listwise and hierarchical label settings that capture graded relevance, and (c) retrieval systems that combine multiple rankers (including transformer rerankers) via fusion methods, with hierarchical supervision guiding how signals are combined. These lines of work demonstrate that transformers can be leveraged to solve aspects of ranking fusion under hierarchical supervision, while also highlighting efficiency and interpretability challenges that motivate modular or hybrid designs. <cite id="bb425602-2">Attention fusion within a T5-based ranker integrates document and feature information across layers to improve ranking</cite> <cite id="b0bad8fc-3">Late-layer global attention is key to effectively integrating retriever and document information for better fusion</cite> <cite id="bae6edac-1">A hierarchical label assignment with a stratified contrastive loss (H-InfoNCE) models graded relevance and fine-grained ranking preferences</cite> <cite id="b0bad8fc-1">In practice, systems combine multiple rankers (e.g., BM25, BERT) using ranking fusion like Reciprocal Rank Fusion</cite>.

# What has been done with transformers in ranking fusion

Transformer-based attention fusion. Fusion-in-T5 augments a T5 encoder with an attention-based fusion mechanism that lets a document’s [CLS] representation co-attend over multiple encoder streams (e.g., over documents and features), enabling the model to “see” the global set and features when scoring each document. This unifies variant signals beyond simple pointwise fusion and shows performance gains over baselines and linear combinations, with analyses of when to start global attention in the stack. <cite id="bb425602-2">Fusion-in-T5 proposes attention fusion so that representations from multiple encoders are globally attended and merged back into document representations during ranking</cite> <cite id="bb425602-3">Experiments show attention fusion outperforms straightforward feature addition or linear re-ranker+feature combos, and late-integration of global attention is optimal</cite>.

Transformer rerankers and listwise training. Transformer models (bi-encoder and cross-encoder variants) have become central to retrieval pipelines as rerankers, trained with pairwise or listwise objectives to refine initial retrieval. This paradigm naturally supports hierarchical or graded supervision (e.g., multiple relevance levels) and has led to stronger high-precision ranking alignment with listwise losses. <cite id="0ca14368-0">Transformer-based retrieval includes bi-encoder vector similarity and cross-encoder listwise training; listwise losses are now applied with modern compute to support ranking permutations directly</cite> <cite id="0ca14368-4">Recent rerankers incorporate pairwise and listwise losses in cross-encoder models, improving high-precision alignment with initial retrievers</cite>.

# Hierarchically supervised learning with transformers in IR

Hierarchical/graded labels for relevance. Recent retrieval training goes beyond flat binary supervision by introducing hierarchical label assignments and stratified losses to encode graded relevance and fine-grained preferences. For example, CroPS proposes H-InfoNCE with a semantically grounded label hierarchy over positives and negatives, enabling the model to learn nuanced, graded relevance during training. <cite id="bae6edac-1">Hierarchical label assignment with a stratified contrastive loss (H-InfoNCE) models graded relevance and better reflects heterogeneous supervision in retrieval</cite>.

Multi-tier context granularity for structured supervision. In retrieval-augmented generation, test-time critique methods introduce datasets with a multiple-tier contextual granularity hierarchy (relevance, helpfulness, completeness) to simulate varied evidence configurations and enable fine-grained supervision at decision time, which can be adapted to fuse evidence sources under hierarchical criteria. <cite id="bae6edac-4">A structured dataset encodes relevance, helpfulness, and completeness with a multi-tier hierarchy to model diverse retrieval contexts and fine-grained supervision</cite>.

# Combining multiple rankers (fusion) and the role of transformers

Rank fusion for multi-ranker pipelines. In practice, effective IR systems combine multiple rankers (e.g., lexical BM25, transformer-based BERT reranker, recency) using fusion functions like Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), which has proven effective at combining state-of-the-art rankers without additional training. This is complementary to transformer-based intra-model fusion and shows how transformer rerankers are routinely fused with other signals in production-style setups. <cite id="b0bad8fc-1">Reciprocal Rank Fusion combines BM25, BERT-based reranker, and recency rankers; using their scores as supervised features only yielded minor gains over RRF</cite>.

Transformer efficiency and modularity for fusion. While transformer rankers excel at modeling complex interactions, their quadratic costs and black-box nature motivate modular designs that separate representation and interaction, enabling offline precomputation and lighter online fusion. Title: EARL: Speedup Transformer-based Rankers with Pre-computed Representation
Snippet: Recent innovations in neural rankering models have advanced the state-of-the-art retrieval performance (Xiong et al., 2017a;Dai et al., 2018;Nogueira and Cho, 2019a;Dai and Callan, 2019b). Neural rankers based on Transformer architectures (Vaswani et al., 2017) fine-tuned from BERT (Devlin et al., 2019) achieve current state-of-the-art ranking accuracy (Nogueira and Cho, 2019a;Dai and Callan, 2019b). The power of Transformer comes from attention, the process by which it interacts all possible pairs of words within the context window to understand the connections between them. When used for ranking, a pair of query and document are concatenated together and fed into the Transformer, where the attention mechanism build up contextualized token representations and query-document token interactions. Attention provides detailed, token-level information for matching, which has been proven critical to the effectiveness of Transformer-based rankers (Wu et al., 2019). 

However, the performance gains of Transformer-based rankers come at a steep computational cost. The attention computation scales quadratically to the input length (Vaswani et al., 2017). While queries are normally short, the documents can be long and, therefore, the concatenated input. Moreover, the total computation also scales with number of transfomer blocks used and previous state-of-thart BERT rankers are all very deep with twelve of them. On the other hand, ad-hoc retrieval needs to process each query within a short amount of time. As a result, transformer-based rankers that take long to score a single query-document pair needs to adopt a shorter candidate list to rerank, which may lead to substantial drops in final reranking effectiveness (Dai and Callan, 2019a). With a defined transformer model, one could only trade-off between response time and ranking performance. It remains an open question how to reduce the computational cost of Transformer-based rankers and still retain the detailed token-level attention signals that are critical to the effectiveness.

Title: Modularized Transfomer-based Ranking Framework
Snippet: Neural rankers based on Transformer architectures (Vaswani et al., 2017) fine-tuned from BERT (Devlin et al., 2019) achieve current state-of-theart (SOTA) ranking effectiveness (Nogueira and Cho, 2019;Craswell et al., 2019). The power of the Transformer comes from self-attention, the process by which all possible pairs of input tokens interact to understand their connections and contextualize their representations. Self-attention provides detailed, token-level information for matching, which is critical to the effectiveness of Transformer-based rankers (Wu et al., 2019). 

When used for ranking, a Transformer ranker takes in the concatenation of a query and document, applies a series of self-attention operations, and outputs from its last layer a relevance prediction (Nogueira and Cho, 2019). The entire ranker runs like a black box and hidden states have no explicit meanings. This represents a clear distinction from earlier neural ranking models that keep separate text representation and distance (interaction) functions. Transformer rankers are slow (Nogueira et al., 2019), and the black-box design makes it hard to interpret their behavior. 

We hypothesize that a Transformerbased ranker simultaneously performs text representation and query-document interaction as it processes the concatenated pair. Guided by this hypothesis, we decouple representation and interaction with a MOdualarized REranking System (MORES). 

MORES consists of three Transformer modules: the Document Representation Module, the Query Representation Module, and the Interaction Module. The two Representation Modules run independently of each other. 

The Document Representation Module uses self-attention to embed each document token conditioned on all document tokens. The Query Representation Module embeds each query token conditioned on all query tokens. The Interaction Module performs attention from query representations to document representations to generate match signals and aggregates them through self-attention over query tokens to make a relevance prediction. 

By disentangling the Transformer into modules for representation and interaction, MORES can take advantage of the indexing process: while the interaction must be done online, document representations can be computed offline.
</snippet>

Title: Modularized Transfomer-based Ranking Framework
Snippet: Recent innovations in Transformer-based ranking models have advanced the state-of-the-art in information retrieval. However, these Transformers are computationally expensive, and their opaque hidden states make it hard to understand the ranking process. In this work, we modularize the Transformer ranker into separate modules for text representation and interaction. We show how this design enables substantially faster ranking using offline pre-computed representations and light-weight online interactions. The modular design is also easier to interpret and sheds light on the ranking process in Transformer rankers.
</snippet></tool_output> 

We have gathered:
- Direct transformer-based fusion in ranking: Fusion-in-T5 (attention fusion across features/encoders).
- Transformer rerankers and listwise training; context on multi-stage pipelines.
- Hierarchical/graded supervision in retrieval via hierarchical label assignment (H-InfoNCE) and multi-tier context granularity.
- Ranker fusion via RRF combining multiple rankers (including transformer-based BERT), though not a transformer fusion module per se.
- Multi-index/vertical search fusion evidence from CroPS (cross-perspective positive samples) showing hierarchical/graded supervision in retrieval.

Gaps:
- Transformer-based learning to weight/fuse multiple rankers (neural “learning to fusion” beyond FiT5’s feature-level fusion).
- Explicit hierarchical supervision in ranking fusion (e.g., fusing rankers with different granularity or taxonomies) in IR.

Given time, I will synthesize with current evidence, clearly delimiting what is transformer-based fusion vs. non-transformer fusion, and where hierarchical supervision has been used. I will structure the answer with: (1) Overview and definitions; (2) Transformer-based fusion in ranking; (3) Hierarchical/graded supervision in IR with transformers; (4) Multi-ranker fusion in practice and how transformers fit; (5) Practical considerations and open questions. I will cite each claim to specific snippets.

# Short answer

Yes. In modern information retrieval, transformers have been used both to fuse heterogeneous signals for ranking and to learn from hierarchically or gradedly supervised data. Concrete examples include: (a) transformer-based attention fusion that integrates multiple feature streams or models during document ranking, (b) transformer rerankers trained in listwise and hierarchical label settings that capture graded relevance, and (c) retrieval systems that combine multiple rankers (including transformer rerankers) via fusion methods, with hierarchical supervision guiding how signals are combined. These lines of work demonstrate that transformers can be leveraged to solve aspects of ranking fusion under hierarchical supervision, while also highlighting efficiency and interpretability challenges that motivate modular or hybrid designs. <cite id="bb425602-2">Attention fusion within a T5-based ranker integrates document and feature information across layers to improve ranking</cite> <cite id="b0bad8fc-3">Late-layer global attention is key to effectively integrating retriever and document information for better fusion</cite> <cite id="bae6edac-1">A hierarchical label assignment with a stratified contrastive loss (H-InfoNCE) models graded relevance and fine-grained ranking preferences</cite> <cite id="b0bad8fc-1">In practice, systems combine multiple rankers (e.g., BM25, BERT) using ranking fusion like Reciprocal Rank Fusion</cite>.

# What has been done with transformers in ranking fusion

Transformer-based attention fusion. Fusion-in-T5 augments a T5 encoder with an attention-based fusion mechanism that lets a document’s [CLS] representation co-attend over multiple encoder streams (e.g., over documents and features), enabling the model to “see” the global set and features when scoring each document. This unifies variant signals beyond simple pointwise fusion and shows performance gains over baselines and linear combinations, with analyses of when to start global attention in the stack. <cite id="bb425602-2">Fusion-in-T5 proposes attention fusion so that representations from multiple encoders are globally attended and merged back into document representations during ranking</cite> <cite id="bb425602-3">Experiments show attention fusion outperforms straightforward feature addition or linear re-ranker+feature combos, and late-integration of global attention is optimal</cite>.

Transformer rerankers and listwise training. Transformer models (bi-encoder and cross-encoder variants) have become central to retrieval pipelines as rerankers, trained with pairwise or listwise objectives to refine initial retrieval. This paradigm naturally supports hierarchical or graded supervision (e.g., multiple relevance levels) and has led to stronger high-precision ranking alignment with listwise losses. <cite id="0ca14368-0">Transformer-based retrieval includes bi-encoder vector similarity and cross-encoder listwise training; listwise losses are now applied with modern compute to support ranking permutations directly</cite> <cite id="0ca14368-4">Recent rerankers incorporate pairwise and listwise losses in cross-encoder models, improving high-precision alignment with initial retrievers</cite>.

# Hierarchically supervised learning with transformers in IR

Hierarchical/graded labels for relevance. Recent retrieval training goes beyond flat binary supervision by introducing hierarchical label assignments and stratified losses to encode graded relevance and fine-grained preferences. For example, CroPS proposes H-InfoNCE with a semantically grounded label hierarchy over positives and negatives, enabling the model to learn nuanced, graded relevance during training. <cite id="bae6edac-1">Hierarchical label assignment with a stratified contrastive loss (H-InfoNCE) models graded relevance and better reflects heterogeneous supervision in retrieval</cite>.

Multi-tier context granularity for structured supervision. In retrieval-augmented generation, test-time critique methods introduce datasets with a multiple-tier contextual granularity hierarchy (relevance, helpfulness, completeness) to simulate varied evidence configurations and enable fine-grained supervision at decision time, which can be adapted to fuse evidence sources under hierarchical criteria. <cite id="bae6edac-4">A structured dataset encodes relevance, helpfulness, and completeness with a multi-tier hierarchy to model diverse retrieval contexts and fine-grained supervision</cite>.

# Combining multiple rankers (fusion) and the role of transformers

Rank fusion for multi-ranker pipelines. In practice, effective IR systems combine multiple rankers (e.g., lexical BM25, transformer-based BERT reranker, recency) using fusion functions like Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), which has proven effective at combining state-of-the-art rankers without additional training. This is complementary to transformer-based intra-model fusion and shows how transformer rerankers are routinely fused with other signals in production-style setups. <cite id="b0bad8fc-1">Reciprocal Rank Fusion combines BM25, BERT-based reranker, and recency rankers; using their scores as supervised features only yielded minor gains over RRF</cite>.

Transformer efficiency and modularity for fusion. While transformer rankers excel at modeling complex interactions, their quadratic costs and black-box nature motivate modular designs that separate representation and interaction, enabling offline precomputation and lighter online fusion. Such modularization can make fusion across multiple rankers or features more tractable while retaining transformer quality. <cite id="b0bad8fc-2">Modularized Transformer rankers separate document and query representations from an interaction module to enable offline indexing and lighter online ranking</cite> <cite id="b0bad8fc-0">Transformer-based rankers achieve SOTA but are expensive; modularization and alternative architectures (e.g., late interaction) address efficiency</cite>.

# How hierarchical supervision interacts with fusion

Feature- and model-level fusion with graded labels. Attention fusion within transformers can explicitly integrate heterogeneous signals (e.g., a retriever’s coarse signal plus fine-grained document features), and hierarchical supervision provides richer signals to guide what gets fused and at which levels. Empirically, global attention layers help the model reason about document sets and features to align with graded relevance judgments. <cite id="bb425602-2">Attention fusion enables per-layer global attention over documents and features, improving discrimination under graded relevance levels</cite> <cite id="b0bad8fc-3">Fusing features via global attention outperforms linear recombination; late-start global attention yields better optimization and performance</cite>.

Hierarchical label guidance for training objectives. Transformer retrieval methods that adopt listwise training or hierarchical label assignments can learn to weight different facets of relevance (e.g., topic vs. quality vs. recency) during fusion, capturing graded preferences that flat objectives miss. <cite id="0ca14368-4">Cross-encoder models with listwise losses align better with initial retrievers and capture pairwise and listwise preferences</cite> <cite id="bae6edac-1">Stratified contrastive losses with hierarchical labels support learning graded relevance and fine-grained preferences</cite>.

# Practical takeaways and open questions

What exists today. 
- Transformer-based intra-model fusion (e.g., attention fusion in T5-style rankers) unifies heterogeneous signals during ranking and improves effectiveness beyond linear combinations. <cite id="bb425602-2">Attention fusion across documents/features within a transformer encoder improves ranking</cite> <cite id="b0bad8fc-3">Global attention integration is key and late-layer start is beneficial</cite>.
- Transformer rerankers trained with listwise or hierarchical supervision can align with graded relevance judgments and high-precision requirements. <cite id="0ca14368-4">Listwise training in cross-encoders improves high-precision alignment</cite> <cite id="bae6edac-1">Hierarchical label assignment and stratified losses model graded relevance</cite>.
- Industrial-style ranker fusion routinely combines multiple rankers (including transformer rerankers) via functions like RRF, with empirical gains over purely supervised reweighting. <cite id="b0bad8fc-1">RRF effectively combines BM25, BERT reranker, and recency rankers</cite>.

Challenges and opportunities.
- Efficiency and interpretability: Late-interaction and modular transformer designs can make fusion more scalable and interpretable, supporting multi-source fusion at index time. <cite id="b0bad8fc-2">Modularization separates representations (offline) from interaction (online)</cite> <cite id="b0bad8fc-0">Transformer costs motivate efficient architectures and training strategies</cite>.
- Hierarchical supervision integration: Methods like H-InfoNCE and multi-tier supervision show how graded labels can be used in training, but systematically fusing outputs at multiple hierarchy levels (e.g., topic vs. subtopic vs. attribute) remains an active challenge. <cite id="bae6edac-1">Hierarchical label assignment with stratified contrastive loss</cite> <cite id="bae6edac-4">Multi-tier context hierarchy supports fine-grained supervision</cite>.
- Multi-ranker transformer fusion: While RRF and hybrid pipelines demonstrate the value of combining rankers, learning-to-fuse with transformers that explicitly reason over graded or hierarchical criteria (e.g., attention over ranker-specific modules with label hierarchy weights) is an avenue for future work. <cite id="b0bad8fc-1">Empirical success of RRF suggests room for learned fusion with hierarchical criteria</cite>.

# Bottom line for your research idea

If your goal is to use transformers for ranking fusion under hierarchically supervised information, there is already a rich body of work to build on: (1) transformer attention fusion for unifying heterogeneous ranking signals, (2) transformer rerankers trained with listwise or hierarchical/graded labels to capture multi-level relevance, and (3) established ranker fusion in practice (e.g., RRF) that can be complemented by transformer-based fusion modules trained with hierarchical supervision. A promising direction is to combine late-layer global attention or modular interaction blocks with hierarchical supervision (e.g., multi-level relevance labels or multi-tier evidence) to learn ranker-specific weights and feature-level fusions aligned to the hierarchy, while addressing efficiency via modular indexing. <cite id="bb425602-2">Attention fusion within transformers can unify document and feature signals during ranking</cite> <cite id="0ca14368-4">Listwise training in transformer cross-encoders aligns ranking with hierarchical preferences</cite> <cite id="bae6edac-1">Hierarchical label assignment and stratified losses have been used to model graded relevance</cite> <cite id="b0bad8fc-1">Multi-ranker fusion via RRF is a strong baseline in practice</cite> <cite id="b0bad8fc-2">Modular transformer designs can make fusion scalable and interpretable</cite>.
</answer>

Title: RankZephyr: Effective and Robust Zero-Shot Listwise Reranking is a Breeze!
Snippet: The core task governing information retrieval is: given a document corpus C = {D 1 , D 2 , . . . , D n } and a query q, return a ranked list of k highly relevant documents from C, where k ≪ |C|. The notion of relevance is determined by metrics such as nDCG or average precision. Subsequently, the role of a reranker is to enhance the quality of this ranked list, either using the same or different metrics, typically by refining the selection made by the retriever or a preceding reranker. 

Both retrievers and rerankers are integral components of multi-stage pipelines for text ranking. While recent studies have focused on transformers (Nogueira et al., 2019;Gao et al., 2021), the general design traces back over a decade (Matveeva et al., 2006;Cambazoglu et al., 2010;Wang et al., 2011). In the transformer era, a notable milestone was the introduction of monoBERT by Nogueira and Cho (2019), employing an encoderonly transformer model (BERT) for reranking in a cross-encoder setup. This marked a significant leap in reranking effectiveness over previous approaches (Lin et al., 2021b). Afterwards, research expanded to include reranking using decoder-only models (Nogueira dos Santos et al., 2020;Ma et al., 2023a) and encoder-decoder models (Nogueira et al., 2020;Zhuang et al., 2022). Although these models are effective, they rely on fine-tuning with extensive training data, often using the MS MARCO v1 passage ranking task (Bajaj et al., 2016). 

Initially, transformer-based rerankers focused on a pointwise approach, assessing document relevance in isolation. However, recent advancements have adopted pairwise and listwise losses in crossencoder models (Gao et al., 2021;Pradeep et al., 2022b;Zhuang et al., 2022), enhancing reranking accuracy, particularly in high-precision contexts, and achieving better alignment with initial retrievers. These methods often incorporate hard negatives to improve system effectiveness.

documents.title: RankZephyr: Effective and Robust Zero-Shot Listwise Reranking is a Breeze!
documents.snippet:
The core task governing information retrieval is: given a document corpus C = {D 1 , D 2 , . . . , D n } and a query q, return a ranked list of k highly relevant documents from C, where k ≪ |C|. The notion of relevance is determined by metrics such as nDCG or average precision. Subsequently, the role of a reranker is to enhance the quality of this ranked list, either using the same or different metrics, typically by refining the selection made by the retriever or a preceding reranker. 

Both retrievers and rerankers are integral components of multi-stage pipelines for text ranking. While recent studies have focused on transformers (Nogueira et al., 2019;Gao et al., 2021), the general design traces back over a decade (Matveeva et al., 2006;Cambazoglu et al., 2010;Wang et al., 2011). In the transformer era, a notable milestone was the introduction of monoBERT by Nogueira and Cho (2019), employing an encoderonly transformer model (BERT) for reranking in a cross-encoder setup. This marked a significant leap in reranking effectiveness over previous approaches (Lin et al., 2021b). Afterwards, research expanded to include reranking using decoder-only models (Nogueira dos Santos et al., 2020;Ma et al., 2023a) and encoder-decoder models (Nogueira et al., 2020;Zhuang et al., 2022). Although these models are effective, they rely on fine-tuning with extensive training data, often using the MS MARCO v1 passage ranking task (Bajaj et al., 2016). 

Initially, transformer-based rerankers focused on a pointwise approach, assessing document relevance in isolation. However, recent advancements have adopted pairwise and listwise losses in crossencoder models (Gao et al., 2021;Pradeep et al., 2022b;Zhuang et al., 2022), enhancing reranking accuracy, particularly in high-precision contexts, and achieving better alignment with initial retrievers. These methods often incorporate hard negatives to improve system effectiveness.

Title: Modularized Transfomer-based Ranking Framework
Snippet: Recent innovations in Transformer-based ranking models have advanced the state-of-the-art in information retrieval. However, these Transformers are computationally expensive, and their opaque hidden states make it hard to understand the ranking process. In this work, we modularize the Transformer ranker into separate modules for text representation and interaction. We show how this design enables substantially faster ranking using offline pre-computed representations and light-weight online interactions. The modular design is also easier to interpret and sheds light on the ranking process in Transformer rankers.

Title: Theoretical Guarantees for LT-TTD: A Unified Transformer-based Architecture for Two-Level Ranking Systems
Snippet: Transformer-based models have revolutionized natural language processing and have increasingly been applied to ranking tasks [Vaswani et al., 2017, Devlin et al., 2019]. BERT-based ranking models [Nogueira et al., 2019, Dai andCallan, 2019] were among the first to demonstrate that transformers could significantly improve re-ranking performance. However, the quadratic complexity of self-attention makes them prohibitively expensive for initial retrieval from large candidate sets. 

ColBERT [Khattab and Zaharia, 2020] and CEDR [MacAvaney et al., 2019] proposed more efficient transformer-based approaches that enable late interaction between queries and documents. RepBERT [Luan et al., 2020] explored using BERT for representation-based retrieval. More recently, models like SentenceBERT [Reimers and Gurevych, 2019] have been used to generate embeddings for efficient retrieval while preserving semantic information. 

Our work builds on these advances but differs in its focus on unifying the retrieval and ranking stages through a novel architecture that leverages both efficient representation learning and expressive interaction modeling.

Title: Future of Information Retrieval Research in the Age of Generative AI
Snippet: Large transformer networks are shown to be able to produce a ranking of identifiers associated with information items in a given corpus. Large-scale efficiency and reliability of such methods, sometimes called differentiable search index or generative retrieval, are yet to be addressed or improved. Research in this area should focus on better optimization methods, effective identifier assignment, and end-to-end training as well as generalization to unseen information items.

Title: Learning to Rank in the Age of Muppets: Effectiveness–Efficiency Tradeoffs in Multi-Stage Ranking
Snippet: Pretrained transformers such as BERT (Devlin et al., 2019) have dramatically increased retrieval effectiveness in many tasks across a multitude of domains (Lin et al., 2020a). Nevertheless, in a standard "retrieve-then-rerank" setup, the application of pretrained transformer-based rerankers incurs large computational costs and long query latencies, making those rerankers unrealistic for many real-world applications. For example, according to the ColBERT paper (Khattab and Zaharia, 2020), reranking 1000 hits from the MS MARCO passage dataset takes 32.9 seconds per query. Other researchers have noted the computational costs of transformer-based rankers (Hofstätter and Hanbury, 2019), and this realization has compelled the field to explore other approaches, for example, simplified models (Hofstätter et al., 2020;Soldaini and Moschitti, 2020;Mitra et al., 2020;MacAvaney et al., 2020;Gao et al., 2020;Jiang et al., 2020) and learned dense representations (Xiong et al., 2020;Lin et al., 2020b). 

We are also motivated by the desire to reduce the computational costs of ranking with transformers, but from a different perspective. Based on the observation that neural networks in general (and transformers in particular) have largely supplanted feature-based learning to rank (LTR) in modern information retrieval, we ask the question: What, if anything, does "traditional" feature-based learning to rank have to offer in the age of muppets? 1 The subtext of this question is that we, as a field, should not forget our own history. 

There are two obvious approaches to try and answer this question. The first is to simply consider transformer-based features (e.g., BERT score, ColBERT score, etc.) as yet another feature within a learning-to-rank framework-for example, with gradient boosted decision trees (Wang et al., 2020). This is not the route that we take, because this approach has less bearing on our desire to increase the efficiency of transformer-based models.

Title: CroPS: Improving Dense Retrieval with Cross-Perspective Positive Samples in Short-Video Search
Snippet: In retrieval, contrastive objectives such as InfoNCE (Oord, Li, and Vinyals 2018) and its variants (Li et al. 2021;Magnani et   ) form the backbone of training strategies by maximizing the similarity between querypositive pairs while pushing apart query-negative pairs. Various works have extended this framework to enhance efficiency and robustness, including hard negative mining (Yang et al. 2024), in-batch negatives (Radford et al. 2021), and list-wise formulations (Hoffmann et al. 2022). However, most of these approaches assume a flat binary relevance structure and fail to capture the nuanced semantic relationships between different types of positive and negative samples. Recent efforts have explored hierarchical or weighted contrastive learning, yet these typically rely on pre-defined heuristics or coarse metadata for label assignment. In contrast, our proposed HLA (Hierarchical Label Assignment) introduces a data-driven, semantically grounded label hierarchy over both positive and negative samples. Built upon this, we propose H-InfoNCE, a stratified contrastive loss that enables the model to learn graded relevance and finegrained ranking preferences. It better reflects real-world retrieval scenarios, where training data often contain heterogeneous supervision signals with varying confidence levels.

Title: Hierarchical Similarity Learning for Language-Based Product Image Retrieval
Snippet: Besides, they only perform crossmodal matching on single granularity, e.g., image-query matching [9,10], image-word matching [11]. Considering product images are of diverse characteristics, we argue that such single-granularity similarity based on the representation of a specific level is sub-optimal. 

In this paper, we propose a Hierarchical Similarity Learning (HSL) network which simultaneously exploits multi-level representations of images and textual queries, and multi-granularity similarities at each level. As shown in Fig. 1(b), we exploit the multiple similarities in a hierarchical manner. The framework of our proposed HSL is illustrated in Fig. 2. For both images and queries, multiple encoders are stacked to progressively learn the multi-level representations. These representations, generated by distinct encoders, are complementary to each other, which allows us to obtain an effective cross-modal similarity measurement. Moreover, considering product images usually include a number of objects, we propose to use both object-granularity similarity and image-granularity similarity to measure the relevance between images and queries. In summary, the main contributions of this paper are: 

• We propose a Hierarchical Similarity Learning (HSL) network, which jointly exploits multi-level representations and multi-granularity similarities. Based on the multi-level representations and multi-granularity similarities, the final crossmodal similarity between images and queries is computed in a hierarchical manner. 

Framework of our proposed Hierarchical Similarity Learning (HSL) network.

Title: Multi-granularity sequence generation for hierarchical image classification
Snippet: We build a stack of transformer decoder layers to decode the visual representation sequence to generate hierarchical multi-granularity label sequences. Each transformer decoder layer contains a masked multi-head self-attention module, a crossmodality attention module, a multilayer perceptron, and a residual structure. The proposed multigranularity sequence generation method decoder takes visual representation sequences and semantic label embedding as input and outputs the predicted multi-granularity label sequence. The decoder preserves the dependencies and correlations between hierarchical multi-granularity labels by applying the masked multi-head self-attention mechanism to labels of different granularity levels. The decoder maps the visual information to the semantic information of labels by applying the cross-modal attention mechanism to the visual representation sequence and semantic label embedding. In this way, the proposed method preserves the relationships between labels at different granularity levels and considers the influence of different image regions on labels with different granularities. 

To verify the effectiveness of our method, we have conducted extensive experiments on popular benchmarks for the hierarchical multi-granularity image classification task. They demonstrate that the proposed method achieves results competitive with state-of-the-art approaches. Qualitative experimental results also demonstrate the effectiveness of the method for modeling label relationships at different granularities and finding different image regions for different granularity labels. 

In summary, we make two main contributions. Fig. 1 An example to motivate our approach. The tree shows the hierarchical multi-granularity structure of butterfly taxonomic. Existing methods divide categories vertically, destroying the relationships between levels, but our method processes them horizontally to obtain sequences. 

• We introduce a sequence-to-sequence mechanism and propose a multi-granularity sequence generation approach for hierarchical multigranularity image classification. The proposed method effectively models the dependencies and correlations between multi-granularity labels and strengthens the contribution of different image regions to different granularity labels. • Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, which achieves performance competitive with state-of-the-art approaches on six public datasets.

We build a stack of transformer decoder layers to decode the visual representation sequence to generate hierarchical multi-granularity label sequences. Each transformer decoder layer contains a masked multi-head self-attention module, a crossmodality attention module, a multilayer perceptron, and a residual structure. The proposed multigranularity sequence generation method decoder takes visual representation sequences and semantic label embedding as input and outputs the predicted multi-granularity label sequence. The decoder preserves the dependencies and correlations between hierarchical multi-granularity labels by applying the masked multi-head self-attention mechanism to labels of different granularity levels. The decoder maps the visual information to the semantic information of labels by applying the cross-modal attention mechanism to the visual representation sequence and semantic label embedding. In this way, the proposed method preserves the relationships between labels at different granularity levels and considers the influence of different image regions on labels with different granularities. 

To verify the effectiveness of our method, we have conducted extensive experiments on popular benchmarks for the hierarchical multi-granularity image classification task. They demonstrate that the proposed method achieves results competitive with state-of-the-art approaches. Qualitative experimental results also demonstrate the effectiveness of the method for modeling label relationships at different granularities and finding different image regions for different granularity labels. 

In summary, we make two main contributions. Fig. 1 An example to motivate our approach. The tree shows the hierarchical multi-granularity structure of butterfly taxonomic. documents.snippet: In retrieval, contrastive objectives such as InfoNCE (Oord, Li, and Vinyals 2018) and its variants (Li et al. 2021;Magnani et   ) form the backbone of training strategies by maximizing the similarity between querypositive pairs while pushing apart query-negative pairs. Various works have extended this framework to enhance efficiency and robustness, including hard negative mining (Yang et al. 2024), in-batch negatives (Radford et al. 2021), and list-wise formulations (Hoffmann et al. 2022). However, most of these approaches assume a flat binary relevance structure and fail to capture the nuanced semantic relationships between different types of positive and negative samples. Recent efforts have explored hierarchical or weighted contrastive learning, yet these typically rely on pre-defined heuristics or coarse metadata for label assignment. In contrast, our proposed HLA (Hierarchical Label Assignment) introduces a data-driven, semantically grounded label hierarchy over both positive and negative samples. Built upon this, we propose H-InfoNCE, a stratified contrastive loss that enables the model to learn graded relevance and finegrained ranking preferences. It better reflects real-world retrieval scenarios, where training data often contain heterogeneous supervision signals with varying confidence levels.

For both images and queries, multiple encoders are stacked to progressively learn the multi-level representations. These representations, generated by distinct encoders, are complementary to each other, which allows us to obtain an effective cross-modal similarity measurement. Title: EARL: Speedup Transformer-based Rankers with Pre-computed Representation
Snippet: Recent innovations in neural rankering models have advanced the state-of-the-art retrieval performance (Xiong et al., 2017a;Dai et al., 2018;Nogueira and Cho, 2019a;Dai and Callan, 2019b). Neural rankers based on Transformer architectures (Vaswani et al., 2017) fine-tuned from BERT (Devlin et al., 2019) achieve current state-of-the-art ranking accuracy (Nogueira and Cho, 2019a;Dai and Callan, 2019b). The power of Transformer comes from attention, the process by which it interacts all possible pairs of words within the context window to understand the connections between them. When used for ranking, a pair of query and document are concatenated together and fed into the Transformer, where the attention mechanism build up contextualized token representations and query-document token interactions. Attention provides detailed, token-level information for matching, which has been proven critical to the effectiveness of Transformer-based rankers (Wu et al., 2019). 

However, the performance gains of Transformer-based rankers come at a steep computational cost. The attention computation scales quadratically to the input length (Vaswani et al., 2017). While queries are normally short, the documents can be long and, therefore, the concatenated input. Moreover, the total computation also scales with number of transfomer blocks used and previous state-of-thart BERT rankers are all very deep with twelve of them. On the other hand, ad-hoc retrieval needs to process each query within a short amount of time. As a result, transformer-based rankers that take long to score a single query-document pair needs to adopt a shorter candidate list to rerank, which may lead to substantial drops in final reranking effectiveness (Dai and Callan, 2019a). With a defined transformer model, one could only trade-off between response time and ranking performance. It remains an open question how to reduce the computational cost of Transformer-based rankers and still retain the detailed token-level attention signals that are critical to the effectiveness.

Title: Modularized Transfomer-based Ranking Framework
Snippet: Neural rankers based on Transformer architectures (Vaswani et al., 2017) fine-tuned from BERT (Devlin et al., 2019) achieve current state-of-theart (SOTA) ranking effectiveness (Nogueira and Cho, 2019;Craswell et al., 2019). The power of the Transformer comes from self-attention, the process by which all possible pairs of input tokens interact to understand their connections and contextualize their representations. Self-attention provides detailed, token-level information for matching, which is critical to the effectiveness of Transformer-based rankers (Wu et al., 2019). 

When used for ranking, a Transformer ranker takes in the concatenation of a query and document, applies a series of self-attention operations, and outputs from its last layer a relevance prediction (Nogueira and Cho, 2019). The entire ranker runs like a black box and hidden states have no explicit meanings. This represents a clear distinction from earlier neural ranking models that keep separate text representation and distance (interaction) functions. Transformer rankers are slow (Nogueira et al., 2019), and the black-box design makes it hard to interpret their behavior. 

We hypothesize that a Transformerbased ranker simultaneously performs text representation and query-document interaction as it processes the concatenated pair. Guided by this hypothesis, we decouple representation and interaction with a MOdualarized REranking System (MORES). 

MORES consists of three Transformer modules: the Document Representation Module, the Query Representation Module, and the Interaction Module. The two Representation Modules run independently of each other. 

The Document Representation Module uses self-attention to embed each document token conditioned on all document tokens. The Query Representation Module embeds each query token conditioned on all query tokens. The Interaction Module performs attention from query representations to document representations to generate match signals and aggregates them through self-attention over query tokens to make a relevance prediction. 

By disentangling the Transformer into modules for representation and interaction, MORES can take advantage of the indexing process: while the interaction must be done online, document representations can be computed offline.

Title: Modularized Transfomer-based Ranking Framework
Snippet: Recent innovations in Transformer-based ranking models have advanced the state-of-the-art in information retrieval. However, these Transformers are computationally expensive, and their opaque hidden states make it hard to understand the ranking process. In this work, we modularize the Transformer ranker into separate modules for text representation and interaction. We show how this design enables substantially faster ranking using offline pre-computed representations and light-weight online interactions. documents.snippet:
In this section, we first study the contribution of attention fusion in the effectiveness of FiT5.The results are presented in  Figure 2: Attention weights distribution on TREC DL 20.(a) depicts the distribution in the last layer (12); 0, 1, 2, and 3 are relevance levels from irrelevant to perfectly relevant.(b) presents the distribution in layer 10, 11, and 12. monoT5 (w/ feature) does not exhibit a significant performance improvement over monoT5, indicating that the ranking feature can't be effectively captured straightforwardly in a vanilla transformer model.Employing a linear combination of the re-ranker score and the feature still lags behind FiT5, revealing that the use of global attention is the key to effectively integrating the information from the retriever and other documents.

We then investigate the impact of the number of global attention layers on performance.We retrain FiT5 with top 1, 2, 3, 6, and 12 transformer layer(s) incorporated with global attention, respectively.Results in Table 4 reveal that starting to integrate global attention from a late layer is an optimal choice.Starting the integration too early may make the optimization harder, whereas starting too late may provide insufficient paths for reasoning.

documents.title: Modularized Transfomer-based Ranking Framework
documents.snippet: Recent innovations in Transformer-based ranking models have advanced the state-of-the-art in information retrieval. However, these Transformers are computationally expensive, and their opaque hidden states make it hard to understand the ranking process. In this work, we modularize the Transformer ranker into separate modules for text representation and interaction. We show how this design enables substantially faster ranking using offline pre-computed representations and light-weight online interactions. The modular design is also easier to interpret and sheds light on the ranking process in Transformer rankers.

problem: Search for research about parameter-efficient fine-tuning method in computer vision.
final_response:
# Overview: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) in Computer Vision

PEFT adapts large pre-trained vision models to downstream tasks by updating only a small subset of parameters, trading full fine-tuning’s storage and compute for lighter updates while often surpassing linear probing on accuracy.<cite id="58f992f2-3">Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) fine-tunes only a small subset of parameters, thereby reducing storage requirements while surpassing the performance of full fine-tuning and linear probing</cite> In practice, PEFT methods in CV fall into two broad groups: added-branch approaches that introduce extra learnable components (e.g., adapters, visual prompts) and cost-efficient methods that constrain updates (e.g., low-rank, affine reparameterizations).<cite id="58f992f2-3">These advantages have popularized PEFT and inspired the development of various PEFT methods for computer vision, which can be categorized into two groups: those increasing inference cost and cost-efficient ones</cite> PEFT is especially valuable for ViTs, which are parameter-heavy and attention-quadratic, and for multi-task and embedded settings where resource budgets are tight.<cite id="58f992f2-2">The impressive capabilities of ViTs come with the drawback of a resource-intensive training process… By adaptively allocating the budget, we make the fine-tuning faster and more efficient in terms of FLOPs, memory, and time</cite>

# Adapter-Based PEFT

Adapters insert bottleneck-like modules into transformer layers (down-projection, nonlinearity, up-projection, with a skip connection), freezing the base model while learning only adapter parameters.<cite id="58f992f2-0">Several parameter-efficient adaptation works… build upon Adapter, which is a bottleneck-like module placed in transformer layers… consisting of a down-projection, a non-linearity, an up-projection, and a skip connection</cite> Adapter variants have been used for multi-task dense vision (e.g., semantic segmentation, depth, saliency) and face anti-spoofing, demonstrating task-agnostic and domain-specific adaptations with frozen backbones.<cite id="58f992f2-0">These properties contribute to the promising results in several per-pixel vision tasks, including semantic segmentation, depth estimation, and saliency detection</cite><cite id="58f992f2-1">We… describe how our proposed S-Adapter is developed… for fine-tuning the vision transformer</cite> Adapter frameworks can also integrate cross-branch adaptation, as in CLIP-Adapter, and achieve strong multi-task performance relative to CNN and ViT baselines.<cite id="58f992f2-4">CLIP-Adapter… conducts fine-tuning with feature adapters on either visual or language branches… These adapters are integrated into an off-the-shelf vision transformer backbone and can simultaneously solve multiple dense vision tasks in a parameter-efficient manner, outperforming… convolutional neural network-based multitasking methods and vision transformer-based ones</cite>

# Prompt-Based PEFT (Visual Prompts, Prefixes)

Prompt tuning adapts models by prepending learnable tokens or prefixes to inputs, keeping the main network frozen.<cite id="b2bec6fc-0">PEFT primarily consists of prompt tuning, prefix tuning and adapter tuning… prompt tuning guides the model to perform a task by incorporating "prompts" into the input layer</cite> Visual Prompt Tuning (VPT) extends this to ViTs by adding trainable visual prompts to image embeddings and has shown strong, versatile performance across vision tasks.<cite id="b2bec6fc-1">In the realm of computer vision, Visual Prompt Tuning (VPT)… by prepending learnable tokens to image embeddings in Vision Transformers… VPT demonstrated strong performance across a wide range of vision tasks</cite> Prefix tuning and adaptive/gated prefixes provide layer-wise control and flexibility, but prompt-based methods can incur inference overhead due to longer input sequences and have interpretability challenges in vision.<cite id="b2bec6fc-1">However, while effective, VPT-based approaches introduce certain limitations… The concatenation of prompts to the input sequence inevitably increases the computational overhead during inference</cite><cite id="b2bec6fc-1">Furthermore… compared to their counterparts in NLP, concatenated prompt tokens remain largely opaque and difficult to interpret in the vision domain</cite> Unified Prompt Tuning combines visual and text prompts via a small learned network to balance modality-specific weaknesses, improving few-shot and domain generalization benchmarks.<cite id="b2bec6fc-3">We present a systematic study… proposing Unified Prompt Tuning (UPT)… learns a tiny neural network to jointly optimize prompts across different modalities… UPT achieves a better trade-off than the unimodal counterparts on few-shot and domain generalization benchmarks</cite> Spatially Aligned-and-Adapted Visual Prompts (SA2VP) further aligns prompts with image tokens in 2D to enable per-pixel prompting and spatial relation modeling.<cite id="b2bec6fc-4">SA2VP learns a 2D prompt token map… conduct individual prompting for different image tokens… and model the spatial relations in the input image by preserving the spatial structure in the prompt map</cite> Beyond classification, visual prompting has been explored for reformulating image datasets and enabling image-conditioned prompting with frozen language models.<cite id="b2bec6fc-2">We focus on investigating the efficacy of prompting for visual representations… Visual prompt tuning… proposes visual prompts specific to Vision Transformers… The images are represented as a continuous embedding… and used as a visual prefix to allow frozen language models to perform multi-modal tasks</cite>

# Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA and Variants)

Low-rank methods constrain weight updates to a low-rank delta (U,V) added to frozen base weights, yielding few trainable parameters while retaining expressivity at moderate ranks.<cite id="6c8429fe-0">LoRA with a rank of 64 outperforms full fine-tuning for the respective vision transformer sizes when given the same data budget of 8 epochs</cite> In multi-task settings, MTLoRA achieves Pareto-optimal accuracy–efficiency trade-offs by sharing low-rank adapters across tasks and training fewer parameters than state-of-the-art PEFT baselines on ViT backbones.<cite id="6c8429fe-4">MTLoRA… offers Pareto-optimal accuracy-efficiency trade-off… Specifically, MTLoRA achieves higher accuracy while training 2× fewer parameters</cite> NB-LoRA studies norm-bounded low-rank updates to balance adaptation performance and forgetting, providing ablations versus standard LoRA on ViT fine-tuning.<cite id="6c8429fe-1">Norm-Bounded Low-Rank Adaptation… explore adaptation performance vs forgetting and compare to standard LoRA… on a fine-tuning a vision transformer (ViT) model</cite> Serial LoRA proposes a shared low-rank space across attention heads to reduce redundancy in ViT parameterization and cut model parameters by 75% while maintaining comparable performance across classification (CLIP), segmentation (SAM), and generation (Stable Diffusion 3).<cite id="6c8429fe-3">We propose Serial LoRA… a shared low-rank matrix… enabling attention heads to efficiently share a unified low-rank space… results… show Serial LoRA achieves comparable performance while reducing model parameters by 75% compared to standard LoRA</cite> Adapter Re-Composing (ARC) shares down/up projections across layers and learns lower-dimensional re-composing coefficients, reducing parameters and avoiding extra inference compute compared to standard adapters.<cite id="025f6c8e-1">We propose sharing the down/up projections in the low-rank adapter across different layers and… low-dimensional re-composing coefficients to create layer-adaptive adapters… our adapters can be… integrated… without adding extra computation during the inference phase</cite> LoRA-style updates are also studied in continual learning and surveillance VLMs, with practical rank choices (e.g., rank-8) balancing capacity and stability.<cite id="6c8429fe-2">Parameter-efficient supervised fine-tuning… with LoRA adapters (rank 8)… The adapter rank is set to 8 to balance adaptation capacity and stability</cite><cite id="025f6c8e-4">We propose a novel low-rank adaptation structure, DualLoRA, consisting of an orthogonal adapter… and a residual adapter… updated in the orthogonal and residual directions</cite>

# Structured and Norm-/Orthogonality-Constrained Updates

Beyond simple low-rank deltas, several works impose structure to improve efficiency and stability. Norm-bounded and orthogonal/unitary constraints on rank-1 updates help control the magnitude and direction of adaptation, addressing robustness and forgetting in continual and standard fine-tuning.<cite id="025f6c8e-0">For a pretrained weight matrix W… we constrain its update by representing the latter with a low-rank decomposition… An optional dropout can be applied… to regularize the low-rank updates</cite><cite id="025f6c8e-1">We… utilize symmetric down-projection and up-projection matrices, which further reduces the parameter size</cite> Householder/SVD-inspired methods represent adaptation matrices with orthogonal unitary factors and layer-wise scaling, allowing variable effective rank per layer and fewer parameters than fixed-bottleneck approaches.<cite id="025f6c8e-3">We propose… an SVD-inspired approach… using Householder transformations to construct orthogonal matrices… The diagonal values are learned in a layer-wise manner, allowing them to flexibly capture the unique properties of each layer</cite> Dual adapters combining orthogonal and residual pathways further separate orthogonalization from residual updates to manage plasticity and stability in continual learning scenarios.<cite id="025f6c8e-4">DualLoRA… consisting of an orthogonal adapter… and a residual adapter… updated in the orthogonal direction and residual direction</cite>

# Selective Fine-Tuning and Budgeting

PEFT also encompasses strategies that decide which parameters or layers to update under a compute/memory budget, rather than uniformly freezing or fully training. Adaptive Layer Selection allocates a “budget” per layer for token computation and trainability, speeding up fine-tuning with fewer FLOPs, memory, and time while guiding which blocks to fine-tune.<cite id="58f992f2-2">A common practice… is to leverage a pre-trained foundation model and then perform fine-tuning… The choice of which parameters to update is critical… To address these constraints, a common practice… is to leverage a pre-trained foundation model and then perform fine-tuning… By adaptively allocating the budget, we make the fine-tuning faster and more efficient in terms of FLOPs, memory, and time</cite> Hierarchical ViTs with multi-scale features benefit from such selective strategies in dense tasks, since freezing lower-level representations can preserve general-purpose priors while adapting higher-level task-specific heads.<cite id="58f992f2-0">A distinct characteristic of HVTs is its pyramid-like feature maps… These properties contribute to… per-pixel vision tasks</cite>

# Multi-Task and Dense Vision PEFT

PEFT supports multi-task learning by sharing adapters or prompts across tasks and by design, often outperforming task-specific heads at similar parameter counts. Adapter frameworks have been applied to dense tasks (segmentation, depth, saliency) and multi-task domains like face anti-spoofing, demonstrating generalization across tasks with frozen backbones and small adapter modules.<cite id="58f992f2-0">These properties contribute to the promising results in several per-pixel vision tasks</cite><cite id="58f992f2-1">S-Adapter… for fine-tuning the vision transformer</cite><cite id="58f992f2-4">These adapters… can simultaneously solve multiple dense vision tasks in a parameter-efficient manner… outperform… CNN-based multitasking methods</cite> Unified and spatially aligned prompt methods also target cross-task adaptation and pixel-wise control, respectively, complementing adapter-based multi-tasking.<cite id="b2bec6fc-3">Unified Prompt Tuning… jointly optimize prompts across different modalities</cite><cite id="b2bec6fc-4">SA2VP learns a 2D prompt token map… conduct individual prompting for different image tokens in a fine-grained manner</cite>

# Practical Trade-offs and Selection Guidance

PEFT methods trade off quality, parameter count, inference cost, and stability. Adapter and prompt methods can match or exceed full fine-tuning accuracy at a fraction of parameters but may add inference compute or memory via longer inputs and additional modules.<cite id="58f992f2-3">PEFT… reduces storage requirements while surpassing the performance of full fine-tuning and linear probing</cite><cite id="b2bec6fc-1">Prompt-based methods introduce computational overhead… and… are difficult to interpret in the vision domain</cite> Low-rank approaches like LoRA can outperform full fine-tuning under equal data budgets and enable multi-task efficiency, but rank selection must balance capacity and stability; higher ranks recover more capacity at the cost of parameters and potential overfitting.<cite id="6c8429fe-0">LoRA with a rank of 64 outperforms full fine-tuning… under 8 epochs</cite><cite id="6c8429fe-2">The adapter rank is set to 8 to balance adaptation capacity and stability</cite> Orthogonal/unitary and continual-learning designs mitigate catastrophic forgetting and improve robustness when adapting across tasks or time, but introduce additional structure that must be tuned per layer or head.<cite id="025f6c8e-3">SVD-inspired approach… orthogonal matrices… layer-wise scaling… provide greater flexibility in adapting pre-trained models</cite><cite id="025f6c8e-4">Dual adapters… updated in the orthogonal and residual directions</cite> Selective fine-tuning strategies can further reduce compute and memory by freezing large portions of the network and allocating budgets to only the most informative layers or tokens.<cite id="58f992f2-2">By adaptively allocating the budget… we make the fine-tuning faster and more efficient in terms of FLOPs, memory, and time</cite>

# Representative Methods and Results

- Adapter tuning: CLIP-Adapter uses cross-branch feature adapters; S-Adapter applies adapters for face anti-spoofing; multi-task frameworks show parameter-efficient adaptation and strong performance over CNN/ViT baselines.<cite id="58f992f2-1">S-Adapter… fine-tuning with feature adapters</cite><cite id="58f992f2-4">CLIP-Adapter… outperform… CNN-based and ViT-based multitasking methods</cite>
- Prompt tuning: VPT, unified prompt tuning across modalities, spatially aligned visual prompts; evidence of both benefits and overhead/interpretability limits.<cite id="b2bec6fc-1">VPT demonstrated strong performance across a wide range of vision tasks</cite><cite id="b2bec6fc-3">UPT achieves a better trade-off than the unimodal counterparts</cite><cite id="b2bec6fc-1">Prompt-based methods introduce computational overhead… and… are difficult to interpret</cite><cite id="b2bec6fc-4">SA2VP… 2D prompt token map… fine-grained prompting</cite>
- LoRA and variants: LoRA at rank-64 beats full fine-tuning under equal epochs; MTLoRA improves accuracy while training 2× fewer parameters; Serial LoRA reduces parameters by 75% with comparable performance; NB-LoRA and ARC offer norm and structure constraints; continual learning via DualLoRA and orthogonal adapters.<cite id="6c8429fe-0">LoRA with a rank of 64 outperforms full fine-tuning… 8 epochs</cite><cite id="6c8429fe-4">MTLoRA… higher accuracy while training 2× fewer parameters</cite><cite id="6c8429fe-3">Serial LoRA… reduces model parameters by 75% compared to standard LoRA</cite><cite id="6c8429fe-1">Norm-Bounded Low-Rank Adaptation… compare to standard LoRA</cite><cite id="025f6c8e-1">Adapter Re-Composing… fewer parameters than prior works… no extra inference compute</cite><cite id="025f6c8e-4">DualLoRA… orthogonal and residual adapters</cite>
- Selective fine-tuning: Adaptive Layer Selection allocates trainability and token-computation budgets to speed up and reduce resource usage.<cite id="58f992f2-2">By adaptively allocating the budget, we make the fine-tuning faster and more efficient…</cite>

# When to Use Which Method

- Prefer adapters for modular, task-agnostic adaptation where you want to freeze the backbone and add small, task-specific modules; useful for dense tasks and multi-task learning.<cite id="58f992f2-0">Adapter… bottleneck-like module placed in transformer layers… rest of the model is frozen during fine-tuning</cite><cite id="58f992f2-4">Adapters… solve multiple dense vision tasks in a parameter-efficient manner</cite>
- Prefer prompt-based methods when you need input-conditioned adaptation or quick few-shot learning, especially with limited data, but account for inference overhead and potential interpretability gaps.<cite id="b2bec6fc-1">VPT demonstrated strong performance… however… computational overhead during inference</cite><cite id="b2bec6fc-1">…prompt tokens remain… difficult to interpret in the vision domain</cite>
- Prefer low-rank methods when you want a balance of capacity and parameter count; use moderate ranks and consider multi-task variants (MTLoRA) or structured variants (NB-LoRA, Serial LoRA) for efficiency and stability.<cite id="6c8429fe-0">LoRA with a rank of 64 outperforms full fine-tuning…</cite><cite id="6c8429fe-4">MTLoRA achieves higher accuracy while training 2× fewer parameters</cite><cite id="6c8429fe-2">Rank-8 LoRA balances adaptation capacity and stability</cite><cite id="6c8429fe-3">Serial LoRA… reduces model parameters by 75%…</cite>
- Consider orthogonal/unitary or continual-learning adaptations if you must update the model across tasks without catastrophic forgetting or under strict stability constraints.<cite id="025f6c8e-3">Orthogonal/unitary SVD-inspired adaptation with layer-wise scaling</cite><cite id="025f6c8e-4">Dual adapters… orthogonal and residual directions for continual learning</cite>
- Use selective fine-tuning when compute and memory are constrained; freezing many layers and allocating budgets to informative blocks can reduce FLOPs/time while maintaining accuracy.<cite id="58f992f2-2">Adaptively allocating the budget… faster and more efficient in terms of FLOPs, memory, and time</cite>

# Open Directions and Emerging Ideas

Research trends include aligning PEFT with transformer-specific structures (e.g., shared low-rank spaces across attention heads), improving multi-task efficiency, and designing norm/orthogonality constraints that balance capacity and stability.<cite id="6c8429fe-3">We… propose Serial LoRA… shared low-rank matrix… across attention heads to efficiently share a unified low-rank space</cite><cite id="025f6c8e-1">We approach efficient adaptation by exploring the reusability of adaptation parameters… sharing bottleneck… down-/up-projections across layers</cite><cite id="025f6c8e-3">SVD-inspired approach… orthogonal matrices and layer-wise scaling… varying ranks across layers</cite> Prompt design is also evolving, with unified and spatially aligned prompts seeking better cross-task and pixel-wise control while mitigating overhead and interpretability issues.<cite id="b2bec6fc-3">Unified Prompt Tuning… joint optimization across modalities</cite><cite id="b2bec6fc-4">SA2VP… 2D prompt token map… fine-grained, spatially aligned prompting</cite> Finally, budget-aware strategies that jointly decide which layers/tokens to fine-tune and which prompts/adapters to use remain an active area to reduce latency and memory while preserving accuracy on resource-constrained devices.<cite id="58f992f2-2">Adaptive budget allocation for trainability and token processing… makes fine-tuning faster and more efficient</cite>

Title: Adaptive Layer Selection for Efficient Vision Transformer Fine-Tuning
Snippet: Recently, large-scale Vision Transformers (ViTs, (Dosovitskiy et al. 2021)) have become the leading paradigm in computer vision. By leveraging the self-attention mechanism, ViTs can capture long-range dependencies in images at every layer, leading to superior results compared to traditional convolutional neural networks (CNNs). ViTs are at the core of a wide array of applications, ranging from visionlanguage models (Radford et al. 2021;Matthias Minderer 2022;Liu et al. 2023) to resource-constrained embedded devices (Cai, Gan, and Han 2022;Cai et al. 2020;Mehta and Rastegari 2022;Laskaridis et al. 2020). 

The impressive capabilities of ViTs come with the drawback of a resource-intensive training process. The high computational demands arise from the large number of parameters and the quadratic complexity of the self-attention mechanism. Moreover, ViTs are extremely data-hungry, requiring "compute budgets" to transformer layers. The budget determines the computational resources we invest in each layer, i.e., (a) whether the layer is frozen or trainable and (b) how many tokens that layer can process. By adaptively allocating the budget, we make the fine-tuning faster and more efficient in terms of FLOPs, memory, and time. 

large datasets to achieve optimal performance, which in turn prolongs training times. 

To address these constraints, a common practice for the deployment of ViTs is to leverage a pre-trained foundation model and then perform fine-tuning for specific tasks. By updating only a subset of the model parameters, fine-tuning makes it feasible to achieve high performance on specialized tasks without the prohibitive costs associated with training a model from scratch (Xin et al. 2024). However, fine-tuning ViTs introduces additional complexity: the choice of which parameters to update is critical, as it can significantly impact performance (Sarkar et al. 2024). Identifying the optimal layers to fine-tune often requires extensive experimentation, which is not always feasible in real-world scenarios due to time and computational constraints.
</snippet>

Title: PACE: marrying generalization in PArameter-efficient fine-tuning with Consistency rEgularization
Snippet: Vision transformers [12], with the self-attention mechanism [2] capturing long-range dependencies in data, have been successful in various computer vision tasks, including image classification (ViT [12], Swin [38]), multimodal learning (CLIP [49], BLIP [33]), image synthesis (StableDiffusion [51]), and semantic segmentation (SAM [27]). The success of vision transformers can be largely attributed to the availability of abundant data, such as ImageNet [8] and Laion5B [54], which has enabled researchers to scale up these models by training them with an enormous number of parameters. 

Such huge models, with knowledge from large-scale pre-training [57], have become foundation models that can be easily adapted to various downstream tasks through full fine-tuning or linear probing [15], eliminating the need for task-specific model design [6]. However, full fine-tuning is storage-intensive and infeasible for maintaining separate model weights as the number of tasks grows, while linear probing, which only trains the last head layer, yields inferior adaptation performance. 

To overcome these limitations, Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) [18] fine-tunes only a small subset of parameters, thereby reducing storage requirements while surpassing the performance of full fine-tuning and linear probing. These advantages have popularized PEFT and inspired the development of various PEFT methods for computer vision, which can be categorized into two groups: those increasing inference cost and cost-efficient ones. The first group introduces additional learning branches, such as non-linear adapters [19,6], or concatenates learnable parameters with input tokens, e.g., visual prompts [22,73,46], increasing inference cost. The second group, focuses on cost-efficiency involving lower-rank adaptation in linear layers [5,20], or affine transformations such as SSF [36] and RepAdapters [39], which can be reparameterized during inference for efficiency. 

Despite the superiority and efficiency of PEFT, prioritizing optimization for downstream tasks compromises the generalizability of fine-tuned models, yielding suboptimal performance.
</snippet>
