Snippet: Despite effectiveness, current LoRA has not well considered the structural characteristic of vision transformer. This makes us rethink how to better align PEFT methods with the architectural nuances of vision transformers, ensuring scalability and efficiency in fine-tuning large-scale vision models. 

Generally, in vision transformers, the multi-head attention (MHA) mechanism and the QKV design tend to use larger feature dimensions and more attention heads to enhance the model's ability to capture relationships across multiple feature spaces. However, the fine-tuning process must adjust parameters across the individual feature spaces of Q, K, V, and O for each attention head. this parallel structure leads to an arXiv:2503.17750v1 [cs.CV] 22 Mar 2025 increase in fine-tuning parameters, making adaptation more computationally expensive. This paper explores a fundamental question: Is there a shared low-rank LoRA space that can efficiently adapt the transformer structure? We hypothesize that such a unified LoRA space could capture underlying parameter commonalities across feature subspaces, reducing redundancy and the number of parameters required for finetuning. This concept serves as the foundation that motivates us to propose a more efficient LoRA method to finetuning vision foundation models with the transformer structure. 

To validate this hypothesis, we propose Serial LoRA, a novel variant specifically designed to address the parameterintensive parallel structure in Transformers. Serial LoRA employs a shared low-rank matrix that can be serially composite with the attention mechanism, as shown in Fig. 1, enabling the attention heads to efficiently share a unified low-rank space. This design extracts underlying parameter commonalities across heads, significantly reducing redundancy and finetuning costs. Our comprehensive evaluations across various transformer-based vision foundation models demonstrate the effectiveness of Serial LoRA. Specifically, we conduct extensive experiments on 24 datasets spanning three major vision tasks: image classification using CLIP, semantic segmentation with SAM, and image generation based on Stable Diffusion 3. The results consistently show that Serial LoRA achieves comparable performance while reducing model parameters by 75% compared to standard LoRA.

Among them, prompt tuning guides the model to perform a task by incorporating "prompts" into the input layer. For example, Jia et al. [11] developed Multi-modal Prompt Learning (MaPLe), which designs coupled vision-language cues and progressively models feature relationships to enable richer contextual learning. In comparison, prefix tuning achieves more flexible and efficient optimization by adding learnable prefixes to the input and performing layer-wise weighting to help the model extract task-specific features. For instance, Wu et al. [38] proposed Adaptive Prefix Tuning (APT) by using a gating mechanism to dynamically optimize prefixes for learning layer-specific representations. However, both prompt tuning and prefix tuning mainly adapt to the task by designing specific input structures, which limits their capacity for multi-task learning. As a result, adapter tuning has become one of the most commonly used methods within PEFT. It achieves efficient fine-tuning without modifying the original model parameters by inserting Adapter modules with a small number of parameters between specific layers of the pre-trained model. Title: Achieving More with Less: Additive Prompt Tuning for Rehearsal-Free Class-Incremental Learning
Snippet: In recent years, parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods [11,13,14,17,24,43] have gained significant attention as alternatives to full model fine-tuning. These approaches aim to adapt large pre-trained models to downstream tasks by updating only a small subset of parameters, offering a more efficient and scalable solution. 

Prompt tuning [23], one of the most prominent PEFT approaches, was initially introduced in natural language processing. It began with discrete text templates designed to guide model behavior, which later evolved into continuous prompt tuning [24], where learnable vectors are optimized to better align with task-specific objectives. In the realm of computer vision, Visual Prompt Tuning (VPT) [17] extended this concept to visual tasks by prepending learnable tokens to image embeddings in Vision Transformers. VPT demonstrated strong performance across a wide range of vision tasks, showcasing the versatility of prompt-based methods. 

However, while effective, VPT-based approaches intro-duce certain limitations. The concatenation of prompts to the input sequence inevitably increases the computational overhead during inference, making them less efficient in practice. Furthermore, compared to their counterparts in NLP, concatenated prompt tokens remain largely opaque and difficult to interpret in the vision domain. As such, in this work, we propose a refined framework that rethinks how visual prompts should be designed and utilized.
</snippet>

Title: Unified Vision and Language Prompt Learning
Snippet: Prompt tuning, a parameter- and data-efficient transfer learning paradigm that tunes only a small number of parameters in a model's input space, has become a trend in the vision community since the emergence of large vision-language models like CLIP. We present a systematic study on two representative prompt tuning methods, namely text prompt tuning and visual prompt tuning. A major finding is that none of the unimodal prompt tuning methods performs consistently well: text prompt tuning fails on data with high intra-class visual variances while visual prompt tuning cannot handle low inter-class variances. To combine the best from both worlds, we propose a simple approach called Unified Prompt Tuning (UPT), which essentially learns a tiny neural network to jointly optimize prompts across different modalities. Extensive experiments on over 11 vision datasets show that UPT achieves a better trade-off than the unimodal counterparts on few-shot learning benchmarks, as well as on domain generalization benchmarks. Code and models will be released to facilitate future research.
</snippet>

Title: Efficient Adaptation of Large Vision Transformer via Adapter Re-Composing
Snippet: We adopt a low-rank design for the adapter using a bottleneck operation but propose a novel approach. Unlike other methods that place the adapter in different layers and directly learn different parameters for each adapter to cater to layer-wise variation, we propose sharing the down/up projections in the low-rank adapter across different layers and simply learning low-dimensional re-scaling coefficients to recompose the linear projections into layer-adaptive adapters. The idea of Adapter Re-Composing (ARC) is motivated by the observation that naturally derived adaptation matrices can exhibit extremely low-rank characteristics, even when not explicitly designed as such. This implies the possibility of using a shared "basis" to re-compose the adapters. Furthermore, we design the low-rank adapters using symmetric down-projection and up-projection matrices, which further reduces the parameter size. Due to their linear nature and careful positioning design, our adapters can be seamlessly integrated into the pre-trained network, as in [7; 9; 10], without adding extra computation during the inference phase. 

We evaluate our method on various large Vision Transformer models, including ViT-B [1] and its variants such as ViT-L [1], ViT-H [1], and Swin-B [11], using 24 downstream image classification benchmark datasets. The experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves compelling transfer learning performance while maintaining a smaller parameter size. 

The key contributions of this paper are summarized as follows: 

• We approach efficient pre-trained model adaptation from a novel perspective by exploring the reusability of adaptation parameters, which goes beyond existing works that primarily focus on the lightweight design of adapter structures. 

• We introduce the Adapter Re-Composing (ARC) strategy, which shares bottleneck operation's down-/up-projections across layers and utilizes lower-dimensional re-composing coefficients to create layer-adaptive adapters. This approach enables fewer parameters than prior works. 

• Our parameter sharing scheme in the ARC method prevents a linear increase in parameter size with the number of layers, ensuring better scalability, particularly for larger-scale models. 

• Through extensive experiments on various Vision Transformer variations and numerous downstream tasks, we show that our method achieves highly competitive transfer learning performance while maintaining a relatively low level of additional parameter.
</snippet>

Title: Efficient Adaptation of Pre-trained Vision Transformer via Householder Transformation
Snippet: A common strategy for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) of pre-trained Vision Transformers (ViTs) involves adapting the model to downstream tasks by learning a low-rank adaptation matrix. This matrix is decomposed into a product of down-projection and up-projection matrices, with the bottleneck dimensionality being crucial for reducing the number of learnable parameters, as exemplified by prevalent methods like LoRA and Adapter. However, these low-rank strategies typically employ a fixed bottleneck dimensionality, which limits their flexibility in handling layer-wise variations. To address this limitation, we propose a novel PEFT approach inspired by Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) for representing the adaptation matrix. SVD decomposes a matrix into the product of a left unitary matrix, a diagonal matrix of scaling values, and a right unitary matrix. We utilize Householder transformations to construct orthogonal matrices that efficiently mimic the unitary matrices, requiring only a vector. The diagonal values are learned in a layer-wise manner, allowing them to flexibly capture the unique properties of each layer. This approach enables the generation of adaptation matrices with varying ranks across different layers, providing greater flexibility in adapting pre-trained models. Experiments on standard downstream vision tasks demonstrate that our method achieves promising fine-tuning performance.
</snippet>

PEFT also encompasses strategies that decide which parameters or layers to update under a compute/memory budget, rather than uniformly freezing or fully training. Adaptive Layer Selection allocates a “budget” per layer for token computation and trainability, speeding up fine-tuning with fewer FLOPs, memory, and time while guiding which blocks to fine-tune.<cite id="58f992f2-2">A common practice… is to leverage a pre-trained foundation model and then perform fine-tuning… The choice of which parameters to update is critical… To address these constraints, a common practice… is to leverage a pre-trained foundation model and then perform fine-tuning… By adaptively allocating the budget, we make the fine-tuning faster and more efficient in terms of FLOPs, memory, and time</cite> Hierarchical ViTs with multi-scale features benefit from such selective strategies in dense tasks, since freezing lower-level representations can preserve general-purpose priors while adapting higher-level task-specific heads.<cite id="58f992f2-0">A distinct characteristic of HVTs is its pyramid-like feature maps… These properties contribute to… per-pixel vision tasks</cite>

# Multi-Task and Dense Vision PEFT

PEFT supports multi-task learning by sharing adapters or prompts across tasks and by design, often outperforming task-specific heads at similar parameter counts. Adapter frameworks have been applied to dense tasks (segmentation, depth, saliency) and multi-task domains like face anti-spoofing, demonstrating generalization across tasks with frozen backbones and small adapter modules.<cite id="58f992f2-0">These properties contribute to the promising results in several per-pixel vision tasks</cite><cite id="58f992f2-1">S-Adapter… for fine-tuning the vision transformer</cite><cite id="58f992f2-4">These adapters… can simultaneously solve multiple dense vision tasks in a parameter-efficient manner… outperform… CNN-based multitasking methods</cite> Unified and spatially aligned prompt methods also target cross-task adaptation and pixel-wise control, respectively, complementing adapter-based multi-tasking.<cite id="b2bec6fc-3">Unified Prompt Tuning… jointly optimize prompts across different modalities</cite><cite id="b2bec6fc-4">SA2VP learns a 2D prompt token map… conduct individual prompting for different image tokens in a fine-grained manner</cite>

# Practical Trade-offs and Selection Guidance

PEFT methods trade off quality, parameter count, inference cost, and stability. - LoRA and variants: LoRA at rank-64 beats full fine-tuning under equal epochs; MTLoRA improves accuracy while training 2× fewer parameters; Serial LoRA reduces parameters by 75% with comparable performance; NB-LoRA and ARC offer norm and structure constraints; continual learning via DualLoRA and orthogonal adapters.<cite id="6c8429fe-0">LoRA with a rank of 64 outperforms full fine-tuning… 8 epochs</cite><cite id="6c8429fe-4">MTLoRA… higher accuracy while training 2× fewer parameters</cite><cite id="6c8429fe-3">Serial LoRA… reduces model parameters by 75% compared to standard LoRA</cite><cite id="6c8429fe-1">Norm-Bounded Low-Rank Adaptation… compare to standard LoRA</cite><cite id="025f6c8e-1">Adapter Re-Composing… fewer parameters than prior works… no extra inference compute</cite><cite id="025f6c8e-4">DualLoRA… orthogonal and residual adapters</cite>
- Selective fine-tuning: Adaptive Layer Selection allocates trainability and token-computation budgets to speed up and reduce resource usage.<cite id="58f992f2-2">By adaptively allocating the budget, we make the fine-tuning faster and more efficient…</cite>

# When to Use Which Method

- Prefer adapters for modular, task-agnostic adaptation where you want to freeze the backbone and add small, task-specific modules; useful for dense tasks and multi-task learning.<cite id="58f992f2-0">Adapter… bottleneck-like module placed in transformer layers… rest of the model is frozen during fine-tuning</cite><cite id="58f992f2-4">Adapters… solve multiple dense vision tasks in a parameter-efficient manner</cite>

These properties contribute to the promising results in several per-pixel vision tasks, including semantic segmentation [13,14,26], depth estimation [27], and saliency detection [28]. Title: Adaptive Layer Selection for Efficient Vision Transformer Fine-Tuning
Snippet: Recently, large-scale Vision Transformers (ViTs, (Dosovitskiy et al. 2021)) have become the leading paradigm in computer vision. By leveraging the self-attention mechanism, ViTs can capture long-range dependencies in images at every layer, leading to superior results compared to traditional convolutional neural networks (CNNs). ViTs are at the core of a wide array of applications, ranging from visionlanguage models (Radford et al. 2021;Matthias Minderer 2022;Liu et al. 2023) to resource-constrained embedded devices (Cai, Gan, and Han 2022;Cai et al. 2020;Mehta and Rastegari 2022;Laskaridis et al. 2020). 

The impressive capabilities of ViTs come with the drawback of a resource-intensive training process. The high computational demands arise from the large number of parameters and the quadratic complexity of the self-attention mechanism. Moreover, ViTs are extremely data-hungry, requiring "compute budgets" to transformer layers. The budget determines the computational resources we invest in each layer, i.e., (a) whether the layer is frozen or trainable and (b) how many tokens that layer can process. By adaptively allocating the budget, we make the fine-tuning faster and more efficient in terms of FLOPs, memory, and time. 

large datasets to achieve optimal performance, which in turn prolongs training times. 

To address these constraints, a common practice for the deployment of ViTs is to leverage a pre-trained foundation model and then perform fine-tuning for specific tasks. By updating only a subset of the model parameters, fine-tuning makes it feasible to achieve high performance on specialized tasks without the prohibitive costs associated with training a model from scratch (Xin et al. 2024). However, fine-tuning ViTs introduces additional complexity: the choice of which parameters to update is critical, as it can significantly impact performance (Sarkar et al. 2024). Identifying the optimal layers to fine-tune often requires extensive experimentation, which is not always feasible in real-world scenarios due to time and computational constraints.

Title: PACE: marrying generalization in PArameter-efficient fine-tuning with Consistency rEgularization
Snippet: Vision transformers [12], with the self-attention mechanism [2] capturing long-range dependencies in data, have been successful in various computer vision tasks, including image classification (ViT [12], Swin [38]), multimodal learning (CLIP [49], BLIP [33]), image synthesis (StableDiffusion [51]), and semantic segmentation (SAM [27]). The success of vision transformers can be largely attributed to the availability of abundant data, such as ImageNet [8] and Laion5B [54], which has enabled researchers to scale up these models by training them with an enormous number of parameters. 

Such huge models, with knowledge from large-scale pre-training [57], have become foundation models that can be easily adapted to various downstream tasks through full fine-tuning or linear probing [15], eliminating the need for task-specific model design [6]. However, full fine-tuning is storage-intensive and infeasible for maintaining separate model weights as the number of tasks grows, while linear probing, which only trains the last head layer, yields inferior adaptation performance. 

To overcome these limitations, Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) [18] fine-tunes only a small subset of parameters, thereby reducing storage requirements while surpassing the performance of full fine-tuning and linear probing. These advantages have popularized PEFT and inspired the development of various PEFT methods for computer vision, which can be categorized into two groups: those increasing inference cost and cost-efficient ones. The first group introduces additional learning branches, such as non-linear adapters [19,6], or concatenates learnable parameters with input tokens, e.g., visual prompts [22,73,46], increasing inference cost. The second group, focuses on cost-efficiency involving lower-rank adaptation in linear layers [5,20], or affine transformations such as SSF [36] and RepAdapters [39], which can be reparameterized during inference for efficiency. 

Despite the superiority and efficiency of PEFT, prioritizing optimization for downstream tasks compromises the generalizability of fine-tuned models, yielding suboptimal performance.

Title: Solution for SMART-101 Challenge of ICCV Multi-modal Algorithmic Reasoning Task 2023
Snippet: Vision Adapters [1,2] are a recent development in the field of AI that aims to enhance the capabilities of existing models. For instance, the Vision Transformer Adapter is the first multi-task vision transformer adapter that learns generalizable task affinities which can be applied to novel tasks and domains. Another research is the CLIP-Adapter [2] proposed by Peng Gao et al., which conducts fine-tuning with feature adapters on either visual or language branches. This approach has shown significant progress in visual rep-resentation learning. These adapters are integrated into an off-the-shelf vision transformer backbone and can simultaneously solve multiple dense vision tasks in a parameterefficient manner. They outperform not only the existing convolutional neural network-based multitasking methods but also the vision transformer-based ones.

Snippet: Despite effectiveness, current LoRA has not well considered the structural characteristic of vision transformer. Generally, in vision transformers, the multi-head attention (MHA) mechanism and the QKV design tend to use larger feature dimensions and more attention heads to enhance the model's ability to capture relationships across multiple feature spaces. This design extracts underlying parameter commonalities across heads, significantly reducing redundancy and finetuning costs. Title: Representation Discrepancy Bridging Method for Remote Sensing Image-Text Retrieval
Snippet: However, it is computationally intensive and requires significant training time. In contrast, PEFT achieves efficient domain adaptation with minimal resources by reducing the number of fine-tuning parameters and computational overhead. PEFT primarily consists of prompt tuning [35], prefix tuning [36] and adapter tuning [17]. Among them, prompt tuning guides the model to perform a task by incorporating "prompts" into the input layer. For example, Jia et al. [37] proposed Visual Prompt Tuning (VPT), which introduces trainable visual prompts while keeping the main model parameters frozen, providing an efficient alternative to fine-tuning. Khattak et al. [11] developed Multi-modal Prompt Learning (MaPLe), which designs coupled vision-language cues and progressively models feature relationships to enable richer contextual learning. In comparison, prefix tuning achieves more flexible and efficient optimization by adding learnable prefixes to the input and performing layer-wise weighting to help the model extract task-specific features. For instance, Wu et al. [38] proposed Adaptive Prefix Tuning (APT) by using a gating mechanism to dynamically optimize prefixes for learning layer-specific representations. However, both prompt tuning and prefix tuning mainly adapt to the task by designing specific input structures, which limits their capacity for multi-task learning. As a result, adapter tuning has become one of the most commonly used methods within PEFT. It achieves efficient fine-tuning without modifying the original model parameters by inserting Adapter modules with a small number of parameters between specific layers of the pre-trained model. Gao et al. [39] proposed CLIP-Adapter, which enhances VLP model fine-tuning by introducing feature adapters instead of using traditional Prompt Tuning methods. Recently, Yuan et al. [12] introduced a Parameter-Efficient Transfer Learning (PETL) framework that facilitates the transfer of visionlanguage knowledge from the natural image domain to remote sensing, and presented MRS-Adapter to improve multi-modal fusion for RSITR tasks. Generally, Adapter tuning has gained popularity in PEFT by optimizing a small number of plug-and-play modules. 

Although current PEFT methods have significantly improved the performance of RSITR models, they typically employ symmetric adapter architectures.

Title: Achieving More with Less: Additive Prompt Tuning for Rehearsal-Free Class-Incremental Learning
Snippet: In recent years, parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods [11,13,14,17,24,43] have gained significant attention as alternatives to full model fine-tuning. These approaches aim to adapt large pre-trained models to downstream tasks by updating only a small subset of parameters, offering a more efficient and scalable solution. 

Prompt tuning [23], one of the most prominent PEFT approaches, was initially introduced in natural language processing. It began with discrete text templates designed to guide model behavior, which later evolved into continuous prompt tuning [24], where learnable vectors are optimized to better align with task-specific objectives. In the realm of computer vision, Visual Prompt Tuning (VPT) [17] extended this concept to visual tasks by prepending learnable tokens to image embeddings in Vision Transformers. VPT demonstrated strong performance across a wide range of vision tasks, showcasing the versatility of prompt-based methods. 

However, while effective, VPT-based approaches intro-duce certain limitations. The concatenation of prompts to the input sequence inevitably increases the computational overhead during inference, making them less efficient in practice. Furthermore, compared to their counterparts in NLP, concatenated prompt tokens remain largely opaque and difficult to interpret in the vision domain. As such, in this work, we propose a refined framework that rethinks how visual prompts should be designed and utilized.

Title: Exploring Visual Prompts for Adapting Large-Scale Models
Snippet: There have been initial approaches that attempt to prompt with images. Similar to prefix tuning, Frozen [44] creates a image-conditional prompt by training a vision encoder using gradients from a frozen language model. The images are represented as a continuous embedding from the vision encoder and used as a visual prefix to allow frozen language models to perform multi-modal tasks. CPT [46] converts visual grounding into a fill-in-the-blank problem by creating visual prompts with colored blocks and color-based textual prompts. However, both of these approaches focus on extending the capabilities of a language-based model. On the other hand, we focus on investigating the efficacy of prompting for visual representations and image classification datasets. In other words, we assume that the pre-trained model consists of a visual encoder and focus on reformulating image datasets. Visual prompt tuning [20] is concurrent work that proposes visual prompts specific to Vision Transformers [11]. It uses deep prompt tuning [27,36,29] by prepending a set of tunable parameters to each Transformer encoder layer.

Title: Unified Vision and Language Prompt Learning
Snippet: Prompt tuning, a parameter- and data-efficient transfer learning paradigm that tunes only a small number of parameters in a model's input space, has become a trend in the vision community since the emergence of large vision-language models like CLIP. We present a systematic study on two representative prompt tuning methods, namely text prompt tuning and visual prompt tuning. A major finding is that none of the unimodal prompt tuning methods performs consistently well: text prompt tuning fails on data with high intra-class visual variances while visual prompt tuning cannot handle low inter-class variances. To combine the best from both worlds, we propose a simple approach called Unified Prompt Tuning (UPT), which essentially learns a tiny neural network to jointly optimize prompts across different modalities. Extensive experiments on over 11 vision datasets show that UPT achieves a better trade-off than the unimodal counterparts on few-shot learning benchmarks, as well as on domain generalization benchmarks. Code and models will be released to facilitate future research.

Title: SA2VP: Spatially Aligned-and-Adapted Visual Prompt
Snippet: Adapting large pre-trained vision models to a specific downstream vision task via parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) has proven to be an effective and efficient strategy, particularly in the scenarios where the training data is limited. It not only distills the prior knowledge relevant to the downstream task from the pre-trained model to achieve better performance, but also substantially improves the training Figure 1: Typical methods for visual prompting tuning follow the sequential modeling paradigm which learns an unordered sequence of prompts prefixed to the image representation. All prompt tokens play the same role of prompting for all image tokens. In contrast, our SA 2 VP learns a 2D prompt token map, which aligns with the image token map spatially. As a result, our SA 2 VP is able to 1) conduct individual prompting for different image tokens in a fine-grained manner and 2) model the spatial relations in the input image by preserving the spatial structure in the prompt map. 

efficiency by incurring only a small amount of parametertuning overhead. As a prominent PEFT method, prompt tuning has achieved remarkable success in NLP field and is being explored its potential in computer vision (Bahng et al. 2022;Huang et al. 2023;Jia et al. 2022;Das et al. 2023;Han et al. 2023;Bar et al. 2022). 

Most of existing methods for visual prompt tuning (Jia et al. 2022;Das et al. 2023;Han et al. 2023) follow the sequential modeling paradigm, which stems from the learning way of prompt in NLP, as shown in Figure 1. A prominent example is VPT (Jia et al. 2022), which encodes an input image as a sequential representation using pre-trained vision Transformer models and then learns a set of prompt tokens as auxiliary input prefixed to the image representation. The learned vision prompts are expected to distill the relevant knowledge from the pre-trained model, thereby adapting the pre-trained model to the downstream target task. While such sequential modeling paradigm of visual prompts has shown great promise, it suffers from two potential limitations.

documents.title: Achieving More with Less: Additive Prompt Tuning for Rehearsal-Free Class-Incremental Learning
documents.snippet:
In recent years, parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods [11,13,14,17,24,43] have gained significant attention as alternatives to full model fine-tuning. These approaches aim to adapt large pre-trained models to downstream tasks by updating only a small subset of parameters, offering a more efficient and scalable solution. 

Prompt tuning [23], one of the most prominent PEFT approaches, was initially introduced in natural language processing. It began with discrete text templates designed to guide model behavior, which later evolved into continuous prompt tuning [24], where learnable vectors are optimized to better align with task-specific objectives. In the realm of computer vision, Visual Prompt Tuning (VPT) [17] extended this concept to visual tasks by prepending learnable tokens to image embeddings in Vision Transformers. VPT demonstrated strong performance across a wide range of vision tasks, showcasing the versatility of prompt-based methods. 

However, while effective, VPT-based approaches intro-duce certain limitations. The concatenation of prompts to the input sequence inevitably increases the computational overhead during inference, making them less efficient in practice. Furthermore, compared to their counterparts in NLP, concatenated prompt tokens remain largely opaque and difficult to interpret in the vision domain. As such, in this work, we propose a refined framework that rethinks how visual prompts should be designed and utilized.

documents.title: Exploring Visual Prompts for Adapting Large-Scale Models
documents.snippet: There have been initial approaches that attempt to prompt with images. Similar to prefix tuning, Frozen [44] creates a image-conditional prompt by training a vision encoder using gradients from a frozen language model. The images are represented as a continuous embedding from the vision encoder and used as a visual prefix to allow frozen language models to perform multi-modal tasks. CPT [46] converts visual grounding into a fill-in-the-blank problem by creating visual prompts with colored blocks and color-based textual prompts. However, both of these approaches focus on extending the capabilities of a language-based model. On the other hand, we focus on investigating the efficacy of prompting for visual representations and image classification datasets. In other words, we assume that the pre-trained model consists of a visual encoder and focus on reformulating image datasets. Visual prompt tuning [20] is concurrent work that proposes visual prompts specific to Vision Transformers [11]. It uses deep prompt tuning [27,36,29] by prepending a set of tunable parameters to each Transformer encoder layer.

documents.title: Unified Vision and Language Prompt Learning
documents.snippet: Prompt tuning, a parameter- and data-efficient transfer learning paradigm that tunes only a small number of parameters in a model's input space, has become a trend in the vision community since the emergence of large vision-language models like CLIP. We present a systematic study on two representative prompt tuning methods, namely text prompt tuning and visual prompt tuning. A major finding is that none of the unimodal prompt tuning methods performs consistently well: text prompt tuning fails on data with high intra-class visual variances while visual prompt tuning cannot handle low inter-class variances. To combine the best from both worlds, we propose a simple approach called Unified Prompt Tuning (UPT), which essentially learns a tiny neural network to jointly optimize prompts across different modalities. Extensive experiments on over 11 vision datasets show that UPT achieves a better trade-off than the unimodal counterparts on few-shot learning benchmarks, as well as on domain generalization benchmarks. Code and models will be released to facilitate future research.

documents.title: SA2VP: Spatially Aligned-and-Adapted Visual Prompt
documents.snippet:
Adapting large pre-trained vision models to a specific downstream vision task via parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) has proven to be an effective and efficient strategy, particularly in the scenarios where the training data is limited. It not only distills the prior knowledge relevant to the downstream task from the pre-trained model to achieve better performance, but also substantially improves the training Figure 1: Typical methods for visual prompting tuning follow the sequential modeling paradigm which learns an unordered sequence of prompts prefixed to the image representation. All prompt tokens play the same role of prompting for all image tokens. In contrast, our SA 2 VP learns a 2D prompt token map, which aligns with the image token map spatially. As a result, our SA 2 VP is able to 1) conduct individual prompting for different image tokens in a fine-grained manner and 2) model the spatial relations in the input image by preserving the spatial structure in the prompt map. 

efficiency by incurring only a small amount of parametertuning overhead. As a prominent PEFT method, prompt tuning has achieved remarkable success in NLP field and is being explored its potential in computer vision (Bahng et al. 2022;Huang et al. 2023;Jia et al. 2022;Das et al. 2023;Han et al. 2023;Bar et al. 2022). 

Most of existing methods for visual prompt tuning (Jia et al. 2022;Das et al. 2023;Han et al. 2023) follow the sequential modeling paradigm, which stems from the learning way of prompt in NLP, as shown in Figure 1. A prominent example is VPT (Jia et al. 2022), which encodes an input image as a sequential representation using pre-trained vision Transformer models and then learns a set of prompt tokens as auxiliary input prefixed to the image representation. The learned vision prompts are expected to distill the relevant knowledge from the pre-trained model, thereby adapting the pre-trained model to the downstream target task. While such sequential modeling paradigm of visual prompts has shown great promise, it suffers from two potential limitations.

Title: Efficient Adaptation of Large Vision Transformer via Adapter Re-Composing
Snippet: We adopt a low-rank design for the adapter using a bottleneck operation but propose a novel approach. Unlike other methods that place the adapter in different layers and directly learn different parameters for each adapter to cater to layer-wise variation, we propose sharing the down/up projections in the low-rank adapter across different layers and simply learning low-dimensional re-scaling coefficients to recompose the linear projections into layer-adaptive adapters. The idea of Adapter Re-Composing (ARC) is motivated by the observation that naturally derived adaptation matrices can exhibit extremely low-rank characteristics, even when not explicitly designed as such. This implies the possibility of using a shared "basis" to re-compose the adapters. Furthermore, we design the low-rank adapters using symmetric down-projection and up-projection matrices, which further reduces the parameter size. Due to their linear nature and careful positioning design, our adapters can be seamlessly integrated into the pre-trained network, as in [7; 9; 10], without adding extra computation during the inference phase. 

We evaluate our method on various large Vision Transformer models, including ViT-B [1] and its variants such as ViT-L [1], ViT-H [1], and Swin-B [11], using 24 downstream image classification benchmark datasets. The experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves compelling transfer learning performance while maintaining a smaller parameter size. 

The key contributions of this paper are summarized as follows: 

• We approach efficient pre-trained model adaptation from a novel perspective by exploring the reusability of adaptation parameters, which goes beyond existing works that primarily focus on the lightweight design of adapter structures. 

• We introduce the Adapter Re-Composing (ARC) strategy, which shares bottleneck operation's down-/up-projections across layers and utilizes lower-dimensional re-composing coefficients to create layer-adaptive adapters. This approach enables fewer parameters than prior works. 

• Our parameter sharing scheme in the ARC method prevents a linear increase in parameter size with the number of layers, ensuring better scalability, particularly for larger-scale models. 

• Through extensive experiments on various Vision Transformer variations and numerous downstream tasks, we show that our method achieves highly competitive transfer learning performance while maintaining a relatively low level of additional parameter.

Title: Efficient Adaptation of Pre-trained Vision Transformer via Householder Transformation
Snippet: A common strategy for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) of pre-trained Vision Transformers (ViTs) involves adapting the model to downstream tasks by learning a low-rank adaptation matrix. This matrix is decomposed into a product of down-projection and up-projection matrices, with the bottleneck dimensionality being crucial for reducing the number of learnable parameters, as exemplified by prevalent methods like LoRA and Adapter. However, these low-rank strategies typically employ a fixed bottleneck dimensionality, which limits their flexibility in handling layer-wise variations. To address this limitation, we propose a novel PEFT approach inspired by Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) for representing the adaptation matrix. SVD decomposes a matrix into the product of a left unitary matrix, a diagonal matrix of scaling values, and a right unitary matrix. We utilize Householder transformations to construct orthogonal matrices that efficiently mimic the unitary matrices, requiring only a vector. The diagonal values are learned in a layer-wise manner, allowing them to flexibly capture the unique properties of each layer. This approach enables the generation of adaptation matrices with varying ranks across different layers, providing greater flexibility in adapting pre-trained models. Experiments on standard downstream vision tasks demonstrate that our method achieves promising fine-tuning performance.

Title: Replay-Free Continual Low-Rank Adaptation with Dynamic Memory
Snippet: The subspace for updating the model becomes more constrained as the gradients are projected into a subspace orthogonal to all feature subspaces from the previous tasks. Subsequent studies [2,13,23,27] ease the stringent constraints of orthogonality to expand the optimization subspace in a new task, considering the stability-plasticity trade-off. Inspired by the prior studies, we propose a novel low-rank adaptation structure, DualLoRA, consisting of an orthogonal adapter O := A o B o ∈ R d×d and a residual adapter R := A r B r ∈ R d×d that are updated in the orthogonal direction and residual direction, as shown in Fig 2 . We follow the strategy in the existing PEFT continual learning schemes [12,17,20,25,26], using pre-trained vision transformers (ViTs) as backbone models throughout this paper.

problem: Research on realizing highly compressible vae by creating vae that further compresses and restores the latent vector of vae
final_response:
# Goal and Intuition

The goal is to make variational autoencoders (VAEs) “highly compressible” by adding mechanisms that further compress and faithfully restore their latent representations. Strong compression can be achieved by (i) making the initial latent as structured and disentangled as possible, and (ii) stacking additional layers or models that operate on that latent to remove remaining redundancy while preserving perceptual content. In practice, this yields two-stage pipelines (e.g., autoencoder then VAE), hierarchical/stacked VAEs with multiple latent scales, and quantized or discrete latent codes that enable extreme compression ratios, all trained to balance rate and distortion through VAE objectives or explicit rate–distortion trade-offs.<cite id="5c835148-1">The Vector Quantized Variational Autoencoder (VQ-VAE) learns to compress high-dimensional inputs into a discretized latent space and reconstruct them, with an encoder that outputs continuous latents followed by codebook quantization and a decoder that reconstructs from the quantized codes</cite><cite id="fe630f28-1">β-VAEs generalize VAEs for representation learning and lossy compression by trading off latent information (“bit rate”) against reconstruction distortion, and hierarchical VAEs extend this by adding multiple latent layers whose rates can be split and tuned</cite><cite id="fe630f28-2">Deep hierarchical VAEs employ multiscale latents z = {z1, ..., zL} with priors factorized across scales to capture coarse-to-fine structure, improving flexibility and expressiveness for compression</cite>.

# Architectural Patterns to Compress and Restore Latents

## Two-stage modeling: autoencoder + VAE in latent space

A practical route is to first compress with a deterministic autoencoder and then model the autoencoder’s latent with a VAE. This offloads fine-grained detail coding to the autoencoder, allowing the VAE to focus on structural, semantically meaningful components and achieve high-fidelity synthesis at competitive scores.<cite id="5c835148-1">In a two-stage setup, an autoencoder compresses images into semantic features, which are then modeled with a deep VAE; the VAE focuses on structural components while the autoencoder retains fine-grained details, yielding realistic generation on high-resolution datasets with FID 9.34 on ImageNet‑256 comparable to BigGAN</cite>. This pattern directly realizes “a VAE that further compresses and restores the latent vector of a VAE” by having a second VAE refine and reconstruct a prior model’s latent representation.

## Hierarchical/stacked VAEs (VAE layers or VAE within a hierarchical architecture)

Hierarchical VAEs introduce multiple latent layers that encode different levels of detail, often with priors conditioned on previous latents. This coarse-to-fine structure both improves reconstruction and naturally supports allocating bits across scales for compression–distortion trade-offs.<cite id="fe630f28-0">A hierarchical VAE enriches a standard VAE with multiple latent spaces, where each layer is trained to encode different levels of detail; the loss can factor priors/posteriors across layers and condition higher layers on lower ones</cite><cite id="fe630f28-2">ResNet-style hierarchical VAEs use multiscale latents with z1 lowest-dimensional and zL largest, and extend the VAE objective to supervise multiscale latents; temporal priors can be added for practical compression in video</cite>. VQ‑VAE‑2 extends this idea with hierarchical quantized codebooks at multiple resolutions, enabling multi-scale discrete latents for high-resolution synthesis and compression-like efficiency.<cite id="a4108b19-2">VQ‑VAE‑2 upgrades VQ‑VAE by adding multiple hierarchical layers with different quantized codebooks at different hierarchies; for example, a two-layer network on ImageNet and a three-layer on FFHQ use smaller bottom/top maps with 512 codebooks of 64-dim latents</cite>.

## Quantized/discrete latents and quantized hierarchies

Discrete latent codes replace continuous Gaussians with finite codebooks, yielding a natural lossy compression fit and often improving perceptual quality at low rates when combined with hierarchical structure. VQ‑VAE and its successors demonstrate this principle across images and videos, and hierarchical quantized autoencoders (HQA) show extreme compression with maintained semantics.<cite id="5c835148-0">VQ‑VAE replaces continuous latents with discrete codebook indices; subsequent hierarchical VQ‑VAE variants add multiple latent codes to improve quality</cite><cite id="a4108b19-0">HQA trains hierarchical VQ‑VAEs with stochastic posterior over codes and shows that, under extreme compression (e.g., 9 bpp in an 8×8 2D latent corresponding to 171× compression, and 9 bpp in a 4×4 latent corresponding to 683× compression), reconstructions retain semantic features on CelebA and MNIST</cite><cite id="a4108b19-4">Quantized hierarchies can be built by training a higher-layer VQ‑VAE on top of a pre-trained lower-layer model; the combined encoder–decoder–codebook system compresses twice (bottom→top→bottom) and mitigates mode-covering by exchanging input-space mode collapse for latent-space mode covering, acting as a metaprior over hierarchical structure</cite>. In video, unified VAE architectures (e.g., MAGVITV2, W.A.LT) adopt this paradigm with strong downsampling and small fixed latent dimensions per frame, enabling efficient joint image–video compression.<cite id="5c835148-3">Unified VAE architectures like MAGVITV2 and W.A.LT support joint image–video compression; encoders typically downsample spatially by 8× and temporally by 4× with a 16-d latent, reconstructing frames from compact latents</cite><cite id="970ef064-2">Latent diffusion pipelines use VAEs to compress inputs into compact latents for efficient generation, motivating specialized VAEs for dynamic human motion with unified architectures</cite>.

## Autoregressive or flow-based coding of quantized VAE latents

Once a VQ‑VAE produces fixed-size discrete codes, an autoregressive (AR) model or better yet a VAE with structured prior can further compress these codes for a fixed distortion. This “compression-augmented VAE” idea leverages the discrete latent as a side information token sequence to be modeled more efficiently by an AR prior or a hierarchical VAE layer.<cite id="a4108b19-3">After training a VQ‑VAE, it is common to use an autoregressive model (e.g., PixelCNN or transformers) to learn the joint distribution over sequences of codebook indices; this AR model can then be used to lower the compression rate at a fixed distortion via arithmetic coding</cite>. In hierarchical VAEs, the prior across scales can also be designed to be factorial or structured, improving rate efficiency by capturing dependencies between scales and frames.<cite id="fe630f28-0">Hierarchical VAEs often represent priors and posteriors as factorial normals conditioned on previous latents, enabling independent allocation of information across scales</cite><cite id="fe630f28-2">Practical compression variants introduce temporal priors in addition to multiscale latents, improving expressivity for temporal data</cite>.

# Techniques That Make Latents More Compressible

## Disentanglement and structured priors

β‑VAEs and related variants explicitly trade off latent information against distortion, enabling control over how much each latent encodes distinct factors, which is crucial for compression because disentangled factors are easier to quantize or sparsify without visible artifacts.<cite id="fe630f28-1">β‑VAEs introduce a rate term representing latent information and allow tuning the trade-off between bit rate and distortion; hierarchical VAEs generalize this to multiple latent layers, with rates per layer that can be independently tuned</cite>. Factorial priors across latent scales in hierarchical VAEs further encourage independence between scales, simplifying compression and aiding rate allocation.<cite id="fe630f28-0">In hierarchical VAEs, the prior can be factorized as p(zl | z<l) with factorial normal distributions, conditioning higher layers on lower ones to capture hierarchical structure</cite>.

## Sparsity and quantization-aware training

Quantized hierarchies and stochastic posteriors in VQ‑VAEs support sparse, structured latent codes that better match natural data manifolds. This reduces mode-covering and allows extreme compression by encoding only high-density regions, with the second VAE/hierarchy restoring perceptual content through multi-scale decoding.<cite id="a4108b19-4">Quantized hierarchies mitigate mode-covering by moving it from input space to latent space and act as metapriors exploiting hierarchical structure; top-level 1‑bit codes reference a bottom-level structure, ensuring reconstructions fall in high-density regions</cite><cite id="a4108b19-0">Stochastic posteriors over codes in hierarchical VQ‑VAEs naturally motivate MSE losses for higher layers and improve performance under extreme compression on CelebA/MNIST</cite>.

## Coarse-to-fine and temporal structure for videos

Snippet: Hierarchical VAEs are latent variable models that train a generator p(x|z) to reconstruct data x from a sequence of latent variables z := {z 1 , . . . , z N } sampled from a learned posterior. The posterior encodes information about the data necessary for reconstruction, but is also incentivized to be close to a prior distribution. The posterior and prior are generally factorized normal distributions of the form q(z|x) := N i=1 q(z i |z <i , x) and p(z) := N i=1 p(z i |z <i ) respectively. The generator, posterior, and prior are trained jointly to maximize a lower bound on the data log-likelihood: 

The objective in Equation 1 is analogous to minimizing a lossless codelength of the data, with the reconstruction loss describing the distortion measured in nats, and KL terms representing the rate (Chen et al., 2016). However, if most bits in a natural image encode barely perceptible details, then this lossless compression task is dominated by the perceptual compression component. In other words, a VAE trying to minimize its loss would do so by mastering highlevel features while ignoring the image's semantics, since the former make up the majority of the image's codelength. This problem disappears when training in the latent space since high-frequency details have already been removed by the autoencoder. Thus to minimize its loss, a latent-space VAE must learn the complex dependencies between image concepts. Fortunately, it can dedicate all its capacity to this single task without spending any on learning details. This is especially important for deep VAEs, since it redistributes not only parameters but also latent groups.

Title: Hierarchical Quantized Autoencoders
Snippet: Despite progress in training neural networks for lossy image compression, current approaches fail to maintain both perceptual quality and abstract features at very low bitrates. Encouraged by recent success in learning discrete representations with Vector Quantized Variational Autoencoders (VQ-VAEs), we motivate the use of a hierarchy of VQ-VAEs to attain high factors of compression. We show that the combination of stochastic quantization and hierarchical latent structure aids likelihood-based image compression. This leads us to introduce a novel objective for training hierarchical VQ-VAEs. Our resulting scheme produces a Markovian series of latent variables that reconstruct images of high-perceptual quality which retain semantically meaningful features. We provide qualitative and quantitative evaluations on the CelebA and MNIST datasets.

Snippet: The VQ-VAE model is introduced in [33], and it builds on the variational autoencoder (VAE) model [29,34] by generalizing ideas from classical image compression methods such as jpeg. Given a dataset of observations x (1) , x (2) , . . . , x (N) , the goal of a VAE is to learn, without supervision, a lower-dimensional representation in terms of latent variables z. It is composed of an encoder E, which maps the input image into latent variables, and a decoder, which reconstructs the image from the compressed representation. In other words, the decoder network models the joint distribution p(x|z)p(z) , while the encoder models the posterior distribution q(z|x) . 

In the VQ-VAE framework, the prior distribution is based on K prototype latent vectors e (1) , e (2) , . . . , e (K) of dimension D, which quantizes the latent maps E(x), generated by the encoder. There are exactly K different latent vectors to choose from, so each pixel on the latent maps is represented with the nearest quantizing vector. In Razavi et al. [13], the VQ-VAE-2 is presented, which is the upgrade of the VQ-VAE to include multiple hierarchical layers that provide different quantized codebooks at different hierarchies. The decoder then reconstructs the image using the latent maps conditioning the higher layers, which have smaller resolutions than the lower ones. In the original setup, the 24-bit image used as input had a 256 × 256 resolution, which was reduced to a 64 × 64 bottom map and a 32 × 32 top map with K = 512 = 2 9 different quantizing vectors of D = 64 dimensions. In [13], the authors presented a two-layer network trained on ImageNet [35] and a threelayer network trained on FFHQ [36] for generating high-resolution photorealistic facial images.

Title: Neural Distributed Source Coding
Snippet: Vector-Quantized VAE (VQ-VAE) [18] is a specific type of VAE [20], [27] with a discrete latent variable, even when the input is continuous. Because the latent code is discrete and has fixed size, VQ-VAEs are a natural fit for lossy compression. Indeed, many existing works have explored its use in various compression tasks, ranging from music generation to highresolution image synthesis [28]- [32]. 

A VQ-VAE consists of three components: an encoder, a decoder, and a codebook. The main difference between VQ-VAE and a regular VAE is that the output of the encoder is quantized to the nearest vector in the codebook. During training, all three components are jointly optimized. During inference, the encoder compresses the input into a lower-dimensional representation of vectors which are quantized to the latent vectors in the codebook. These quantized representations are passed through the decoder, which reconstructs the image. Once a VQ-VAE is trained, it is common to use an autoregressive model, such as PixelCNN [33] or transformers [34], to achieve a lower rate for a fixed distortion value. The autoregressive model learns the joint distribution for the ordered set of latent codebook vectors used to represent each input to the VQ-VAE; this model can be used to lower the compression rate of the VQ-VAE via arithmetic coding [35].
</snippet>

Title: Hierarchical Quantized Autoencoders

The two layer system works as follows: a given datapoint is encoded by the bottom 2-bit layer. The result is then encoded by the top layer. After quantization, the result is decoded by the top layer, quantized again by the bottom layer before decoding through the bottom layer to the input space. This scheme is a simplification of the Hierarchical Quantized Autoencoder (HQA) described in depth in Section 4.2. 

The reconstruction density produced by the full HQA scheme is shown in Figure 1c. The quantized hierarchy has successfully modelled the original density function and shows no mode-covering behaviour. Note the top level representation of this quantized hierarchy has the same information bottleneck as the original 1 bit VQ-VAE that failed to model the density function. 

Each of the bottom layer's 4 codes corresponds to a region of high density in the input space. Therefore, the single bit top layer will imperfectly model the latent space of the bottom layer for the same reasons that explain modecovering. However, by quantizing the prediction of the top layer to a code of the bottom layer, the reconstructions will always fall in regions of high density in the input space. 

This result shows that, under a given information bottleneck, quantized hierarchies allow for fundamentally different density modelling behaviour than equivalent single layer systems. 

Therefore, we propose quantized hierarchies to mitigate the mode-covering behaviour shown by likelihood-based systems for the following reasons: 

• Hierarchy: By choosing to model a distribution using a hierarchical latent space of increasingly compressed representations, mode-covering behaviour in the input space can be exchanged for mode-covering behaviour in the latent space. This also acts as a good metaprior to match the hierarchical structure of natural data (Lázaro-Gredilla et al., 2016). 

• Quantization: Quantization allows for the resolution of mode-covering behaviour in latent space, ensuring realistic reconstructions that fall in regions of high density in the input space.

# Goal and Intuition

The goal is to make variational autoencoders (VAEs) “highly compressible” by adding mechanisms that further compress and faithfully restore their latent representations. Strong compression can be achieved by (i) making the initial latent as structured and disentangled as possible, and (ii) stacking additional layers or models that operate on that latent to remove remaining redundancy while preserving perceptual content. In practice, this yields two-stage pipelines (e.g., autoencoder then VAE), hierarchical/stacked VAEs with multiple latent scales, and quantized or discrete latent codes that enable extreme compression ratios, all trained to balance rate and distortion through VAE objectives or explicit rate–distortion trade-offs.<cite id="5c835148-1">The Vector Quantized Variational Autoencoder (VQ-VAE) learns to compress high-dimensional inputs into a discretized latent space and reconstruct them, with an encoder that outputs continuous latents followed by codebook quantization and a decoder that reconstructs from the quantized codes</cite><cite id="fe630f28-1">β-VAEs generalize VAEs for representation learning and lossy compression by trading off latent information (“bit rate”) against reconstruction distortion, and hierarchical VAEs extend this by adding multiple latent layers whose rates can be split and tuned</cite><cite id="fe630f28-2">Deep hierarchical VAEs employ multiscale latents z = {z1, ..., zL} with priors factorized across scales to capture coarse-to-fine structure, improving flexibility and expressiveness for compression</cite>.

# Architectural Patterns to Compress and Restore Latents

## Two-stage modeling: autoencoder + VAE in latent space

A practical route is to first compress with a deterministic autoencoder and then model the autoencoder’s latent with a VAE. This offloads fine-grained detail coding to the autoencoder, allowing the VAE to focus on structural, semantically meaningful components and achieve high-fidelity synthesis at competitive scores.<cite id="5c835148-1">In a two-stage setup, an autoencoder compresses images into semantic features, which are then modeled with a deep VAE; the VAE focuses on structural components while the autoencoder retains fine-grained details, yielding realistic generation on high-resolution datasets with FID 9.34 on ImageNet‑256 comparable to BigGAN</cite>. This pattern directly realizes “a VAE that further compresses and restores the latent vector of a VAE” by having a second VAE refine and reconstruct a prior model’s latent representation.

## Hierarchical/stacked VAEs (VAE layers or VAE within a hierarchical architecture)

Hierarchical VAEs introduce multiple latent layers that encode different levels of detail, often with priors conditioned on previous latents. This coarse-to-fine structure both improves reconstruction and naturally supports allocating bits across scales for compression–distortion trade-offs.<cite id="fe630f28-0">A hierarchical VAE enriches a standard VAE with multiple latent spaces, where each layer is trained to encode different levels of detail; the loss can factor priors/posteriors across layers and condition higher layers on lower ones</cite><cite id="fe630f28-2">ResNet-style hierarchical VAEs use multiscale latents with z1 lowest-dimensional and zL largest, and extend the VAE objective to supervise multiscale latents; temporal priors can be added for practical compression in video</cite>. VQ‑VAE‑2 extends this idea with hierarchical quantized codebooks at multiple resolutions, enabling multi-scale discrete latents for high-resolution synthesis and compression-like efficiency.<cite id="a4108b19-2">VQ‑VAE‑2 upgrades VQ‑VAE by adding multiple hierarchical layers with different quantized codebooks at different hierarchies; for example, a two-layer network on ImageNet and a three-layer on FFHQ use smaller bottom/top maps with 512 codebooks of 64-dim latents</cite>.

## Quantized/discrete latents and quantized hierarchies

Discrete latent codes replace continuous Gaussians with finite codebooks, yielding a natural lossy compression fit and often improving perceptual quality at low rates when combined with hierarchical structure. VQ‑VAE and its successors demonstrate this principle across images and videos, and hierarchical quantized autoencoders (HQA) show extreme compression with maintained semantics.<cite id="5c835148-0">VQ‑VAE replaces continuous latents with discrete codebook indices; subsequent hierarchical VQ‑VAE variants add multiple latent codes to improve quality</cite><cite id="a4108b19-0">HQA trains hierarchical VQ‑VAEs with stochastic posterior over codes and shows that, under extreme compression (e.g., 9 bpp in an 8×8 2D latent corresponding to 171× compression, and 9 bpp in a 4×4 latent corresponding to 683× compression), reconstructions retain semantic features on CelebA and MNIST</cite><cite id="a4108b19-4">Quantized hierarchies can be built by training a higher-layer VQ‑VAE on top of a pre-trained lower-layer model; the combined encoder–decoder–codebook system compresses twice (bottom→top→bottom) and mitigates mode-covering by exchanging input-space mode collapse for latent-space mode covering, acting as a metaprior over hierarchical structure</cite>. In video, unified VAE architectures (e.g., MAGVITV2, W.A.LT) adopt this paradigm with strong downsampling and small fixed latent dimensions per frame, enabling efficient joint image–video compression.<cite id="5c835148-3">Unified VAE architectures like MAGVITV2 and W.A.LT support joint image–video compression; encoders typically downsample spatially by 8× and temporally by 4× with a 16-d latent, reconstructing frames from compact latents</cite><cite id="970ef064-2">Latent diffusion pipelines use VAEs to compress inputs into compact latents for efficient generation, motivating specialized VAEs for dynamic human motion with unified architectures</cite>.

## Autoregressive or flow-based coding of quantized VAE latents

Once a VQ‑VAE produces fixed-size discrete codes, an autoregressive (AR) model or better yet a VAE with structured prior can further compress these codes for a fixed distortion. This “compression-augmented VAE” idea leverages the discrete latent as a side information token sequence to be modeled more efficiently by an AR prior or a hierarchical VAE layer.<cite id="a4108b19-3">After training a VQ‑VAE, it is common to use an autoregressive model (e.g., PixelCNN or transformers) to learn the joint distribution over sequences of codebook indices; this AR model can then be used to lower the compression rate at a fixed distortion via arithmetic coding</cite>. In hierarchical VAEs, the prior across scales can also be designed to be factorial or structured, improving rate efficiency by capturing dependencies between scales and frames.<cite id="fe630f28-0">Hierarchical VAEs often represent priors and posteriors as factorial normals conditioned on previous latents, enabling independent allocation of information across scales</cite><cite id="fe630f28-2">Practical compression variants introduce temporal priors in addition to multiscale latents, improving expressivity for temporal data</cite>.

# Techniques That Make Latents More Compressible

## Disentanglement and structured priors

β‑VAEs and related variants explicitly trade off latent information against distortion, enabling control over how much each latent encodes distinct factors, which is crucial for compression because disentangled factors are easier to quantize or sparsify without visible artifacts.<cite id="fe630f28-1">β‑VAEs introduce a rate term representing latent information and allow tuning the trade-off between bit rate and distortion; hierarchical VAEs generalize this to multiple latent layers, with rates per layer that can be independently tuned</cite>. Factorial priors across latent scales in hierarchical VAEs further encourage independence between scales, simplifying compression and aiding rate allocation.<cite id="fe630f28-0">In hierarchical VAEs, the prior can be factorized as p(zl | z<l) with factorial normal distributions, conditioning higher layers on lower ones to capture hierarchical structure</cite>.

## Sparsity and quantization-aware training

Quantized hierarchies and stochastic posteriors in VQ‑VAEs support sparse, structured latent codes that better match natural data manifolds. This reduces mode-covering and allows extreme compression by encoding only high-density regions, with the second VAE/hierarchy restoring perceptual content through multi-scale decoding.<cite id="a4108b19-4">Quantized hierarchies mitigate mode-covering by moving it from input space to latent space and act as metapriors exploiting hierarchical structure; top-level 1‑bit codes reference a bottom-level structure, ensuring reconstructions fall in high-density regions</cite><cite id="a4108b19-0">Stochastic posteriors over codes in hierarchical VQ‑VAEs naturally motivate MSE losses for higher layers and improve performance under extreme compression on CelebA/MNIST</cite>.

## Coarse-to-fine and temporal structure for videos

For videos, hierarchical VAEs with multiscale latents and temporal priors capture global motion and detailed dynamics separately, enabling efficient compression and restoration of latent motion/content components.<cite id="fe630f28-2">Hierarchical VAEs with temporal priors add time dependence to multiscale latents, improving flexibility for practical compression in video</cite>. Specialized VAEs for human motion adopt unified architectures and strong downsampling with small fixed latent sizes, reflecting the same principle of separating global and detailed motion in compact latent space.<cite id="970ef064-2">A unified VAE architecture for video downsample spatially by 8× and temporally by 4×, using 16‑dimensional latents, to achieve efficient compression and reconstruction for complex motion</cite><cite id="970ef064-4">Hi‑VAE extracts hierarchical motion representations by applying two compression modules (global and detailed motion) and reconstructs via a diffusion-based decoder, illustrating multi-stage latent compression for video</cite>.

# Rate–Distortion Practice and Evidence

Quantitative evidence shows that hierarchical/discrete approaches can reach extreme compression with perceptual quality. For images, hierarchical quantized autoencoders report very low bits per sample (e.g., 9 bpp in 4×4 latents) corresponding to hundreds of-fold compression while retaining semantic features, and VQ‑VAE‑2 demonstrates multi-resolution codebooks for high-resolution synthesis with compact latents.<cite id="a4108b19-0">HQA reports 9 bpp in an 8×8 latent (171× compression) and 9 bpp in a 4×4 latent (683× compression) on CelebA and MNIST with high-quality reconstructions and diverse stochastic decodes</cite><cite id="a4108b19-2">VQ‑VAE‑2 uses two- or three-layer hierarchical codebooks (e.g., 512 codebooks of 64-dim latents at 32×32 and 64×64 maps) for high-resolution facial image synthesis</cite>. In generative quality, a two-stage autoencoder→VAE pipeline achieves strong FID on ImageNet‑256, indicating that further modeling of a latent representation can preserve identity/detail while benefiting from compression objectives.<cite id="5c835148-1">A deep VAE trained in the autoencoder’s latent space achieves FID 9.34 on ImageNet‑256, comparable to BigGAN, supporting that latent-space VAEs can focus on high-level structure while the autoencoder retains fine details</cite>.

For hierarchical VAEs, principled rate–distortion control is possible by splitting the total latent rate across scales and tuning each layer independently, with theoretical bounds and large-scale experiments guiding where to allocate bits for downstream tasks and reconstruction quality.<cite id="fe630f28-1">In hierarchical VAEs, the rate can be split into contributions per latent layer, enabling independent tuning; theoretical bounds on downstream performance as functions of per-layer rates are derived and verified experimentally</cite>. In video, hierarchical and temporal priors improve expressivity and practical compression, aligning with the need to compress motion and content separately at low bitrates.<cite id="fe630f28-2">Introducing temporal priors in hierarchical VAEs enhances expressiveness for compression, beyond multiscale latents alone</cite><cite id="5c835148-3">Unified VAE architectures for joint image–video compression use strong downsampling and small latents to achieve efficient latent representations for dynamic content</cite>.

# Putting It Together: Design Recipes

- Two-stage VAE compressor: Train an autoencoder to remove high-frequency detail, then train a VAE on the autoencoder’s latent to learn semantic structure. This decouples fine detail (lossy) from structure (probabilistic), enabling large compression while maintaining quality; reconstruction passes first decode the VAE latent, then the autoencoder restores pixels.<cite id="5c835148-1">Two-stage autoencoder→VAE focuses the VAE on structure and leaves fine details to the autoencoder, achieving high-fidelity synthesis with strong compression characteristics</cite>.

- Hierarchical VAE with quantized latents: Use VQ‑VAEs at multiple scales (VQ‑VAE‑2 or HQA) to encode coarse-to-fine information with factorial priors across layers. Stochastic posteriors and multi-codebook hierarchies reduce mode-covering and enable extreme bitrates, while multi-scale decoding restores content and detail progressively.<cite id="a4108b19-0">HQA’s hierarchical VQ‑VAEs with stochastic codes achieve extreme compression (171×–683×) with semantic preservation on CelebA and MNIST</cite><cite id="a4108b19-4">Quantized hierarchies encode at multiple resolutions and mitigate mode-covering by leveraging a metaprior over latent layers</cite><cite id="a4108b19-2">VQ‑VAE‑2 demonstrates multi-resolution codebooks for high-resolution synthesis with compact latents</cite>.

- Compression-augmented VAEs: After obtaining VQ codes, train an autoregressive or hierarchical VAE layer to model the sequence/code distribution and produce shorter side information at fixed distortion; arithmetic coding or tokenization of the AR/prior outputs yields further rate reduction.<cite id="a4108b19-3">AR models (e.g., PixelCNN/transformers) can learn the joint distribution over VQ code sequences and be used to lower the rate via arithmetic coding at a target distortion</cite><cite id="fe630f28-0">Factorial priors conditioned on previous latents support structured compression in hierarchical VAEs</cite>.

- Video-specific latent compression: Adopt temporal priors and motion/content separation in hierarchical VAEs; use strong downsampling and small fixed latent dimensions per frame, as in unified VAE architectures for joint image–video tasks; consider two-stage global/detailed motion encoders to separate coarse kinematics from fine dynamics before reconstruction.<cite id="fe630f28-2">Temporal priors with multiscale latents improve hierarchical VAEs for video compression and reconstruction</cite><cite id="5c835148-3">Unified VAEs for video compress with large downsampling and 16‑D latents to enable efficient reconstruction</cite><cite id="970ef064-4">Hi‑VAE uses two compression modules (global and detailed motion) on a video VAE to achieve efficient reconstruction via a diffusion-based decoder</cite>.

# Trade-offs and Practical Guidance

- Rate–distortion allocation across layers: In hierarchical VAEs, allocate higher bits to latents that carry the most task-relevant or perceptual information and fewer bits to high-frequency residuals; theoretical analyses provide guidance on downstream performance vs. per-layer rates and help locate the optimal operating point.<cite id="fe630f28-1">Per-layer rates can be split and tuned; theoretical and empirical bounds guide where to target in rate space for given applications</cite>.

- Mode-covering and artifact control: Extreme compression with quantized latents can induce mode-covering; hierarchical quantization and stochastic posteriors shift mode collapse into latent space and maintain realistic reconstructions by conditioning higher-level codes on lower-level structures.<cite id="a4108b19-4">Quantized hierarchies mitigate input-space mode-covering by trading it for latent-space mode-covering, aided by a metaprior structure that keeps reconstructions within high-density regions</cite>.

- Reconstruction quality vs. compression: Two-stage pipelines can preserve identity/detail while enabling aggressive compression of the latent; however, the autoencoder must be carefully trained to retain perceptual content, and the VAE must balance KL regularization to avoid over-regularization of semantics.<cite id="5c835148-1">The two-stage autoencoder→VAE achieves strong FID while separating fine details from structural learning, supporting efficient compression with high-fidelity outputs</cite><cite id="fe630f28-1">β‑VAE rate–distortion trade-offs and hierarchical extensions require careful tuning to balance compression and reconstruction quality</cite>.

- Modality-specific considerations: Video demands temporal priors and motion/content separation; unified VAE architectures with strong downsampling and small latents are effective. For images, hierarchical quantized autoencoders provide extreme compression, while high-resolution generative tasks benefit from VQ‑VAE‑2’s multi-scale codebooks.<cite id="5c835148-3">Unified VAE architectures for video emphasize downsampling and small latents for efficient compression of dynamic content</cite><cite id="a4108b19-2">VQ‑VAE‑2 supports high-resolution synthesis with compact, multi-scale latents</cite>.

# Open Problems and Research Directions

- Optimal hierarchical priors/posteriors: Beyond factorial normals, designing structured, possibly autoregressive or flow-based priors across latent scales could further reduce rates while maintaining reconstruction quality, especially for complex natural scenes and videos.<cite id="fe630f28-0">Hierarchical VAEs currently use factorial normal priors conditioned on lower latents, suggesting room for richer priors that capture latent dependencies</cite><cite id="fe630f28-2">Temporal priors are an active area for practical compression in hierarchical VAEs</cite>.

- Universal compression with learned priors: Combining quantized VAE latents with learned side-information compressors (AR or flow-based) remains promising; better tokenization and arithmetic coding tailored to discrete latent codes can close remaining rate gaps at fixed distortion.<cite id="a4108b19-3">AR models can compress VQ code sequences; integrating more powerful structured priors and coding schemes is a path to lower rates</cite>.

- Evaluation at extreme rates: More standardized benchmarks at ultra-low bitrates for both perceptual quality and semantic preservation (e.g., HQA regimes) would help compare methods and guide hyperparameter choices for different applications.<cite id="a4108b19-0">HQA demonstrates extreme compression with semantic retention, motivating broader evaluation protocols at ultra-low bitrates</cite>.

# Summary

Realizing highly compressible VAEs can be approached by (1) making the initial latent as structured and disentangled as possible, (2) stacking additional VAE layers or a second VAE to further compress and reconstruct that latent, and (3) leveraging discrete/quantized latents and hierarchical quantization to push compression to extreme regimes while preserving perceptual content. Empirical results show that two-stage autoencoder→VAE pipelines, hierarchical/quantized VAEs, and AR-compressed quantized latents can achieve strong generative quality alongside large compression ratios, with principled rate–distortion control across latent layers guiding practical trade-offs in application design.<cite id="5c835148-1">A two-stage autoencoder→VAE achieves high-fidelity generation while enabling compression of the latent space</cite><cite id="a4108b19-0">Hierarchical quantized autoencoders reach extreme compression (e.g., 171×–683×) with semantic feature preservation</cite><cite id="a4108b19-2">VQ‑VAE‑2 demonstrates multi-scale quantized latents for high-resolution synthesis</cite><cite id="fe630f28-1">Hierarchical VAEs allow per-layer rate allocation with theoretical guidance for targeting optimal rate–distortion points</cite><cite id="a4108b19-3">Autoregressive models can compress VQ‑VAE latent code sequences to reduce rate at fixed distortion</cite><cite id="fe630f28-2">Hierarchical and temporal priors in VAEs improve expressiveness and practical compression for video</cite><cite id="5c835148-3">Unified VAE architectures for video use strong downsampling and small latents to enable efficient compression and reconstruction</cite>.
</answer>

Title: High Fidelity Image Synthesis With Deep VAEs In Latent Space
Snippet: We present fast, realistic image generation on high-resolution, multimodal datasets using hierarchical variational autoencoders (VAEs) trained on a deterministic autoencoder's latent space. In this two-stage setup, the autoencoder compresses the image into its semantic features, which are then modeled with a deep VAE. Title: Trading Information between Latents in Hierarchical Variational Autoencoders
Snippet: Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) were originally motivated (Kingma&Welling, 2014) as probabilistic generative models in which one performs approximate Bayesian inference. The proposal of $\beta$-VAEs (Higgins et al., 2017) breaks this interpretation and generalizes VAEs to application domains beyond generative modeling (e.g., representation learning, clustering, or lossy data compression) by introducing an objective function that allows practitioners to trade off between the information content ("bit rate") of the latent representation and the distortion of reconstructed data (Alemi et al., 2018). In this paper, we reconsider this rate/distortion trade-off in the context of hierarchical VAEs, i.e., VAEs with more than one layer of latent variables. We identify a general class of inference models for which one can split the rate into contributions from each layer, which can then be tuned independently. We derive theoretical bounds on the performance of downstream tasks as functions of the individual layers' rates and verify our theoretical findings in large-scale experiments. Our results provide guidance for practitioners on which region in rate-space to target for a given application.
