Title: Impact of Temporary Fork on the Evolution of Mining Pools in Blockchain Networks: An Evolutionary Game Analysis
Snippet: There has been a rich body of previous work on blockchain network and mining pool. In the following, we introduce related work regarding temporary fork, game theory, the impact of uncle block rewards and the decentralization in blockchain networks, respectively. 

Temporary Fork in Blockchain Networks. Due to the network propagation delay, blockchain networks may face inconsistencies in form of temporary forks. There are several papers studying the delay and temporary fork in blockchain networks from a networking perspective. In [12], authors analyze Bitcoin from a networking perspective and show that the propagation delay in the network is the primary cause for blockchain forks. Literature [9] provides an empirical analysis of the announcement and propagation of Bitcoin blocks that caused blockchain forks. 

Authors in [36] analyze the blockchain protocol in asynchronous networks. In [37], authors model the Bitcoin consensus and network protocols to develop the theoretical analysis for fork in Bitcoin network. In [38], authors try to reduce forks in the blockchain via probabilistic verification. Nevertheless, existing research efforts mainly focus on the impacting factors from the blockchain system point of view such as block size and network propagation delay. Along a different line from the previous work, we focus on the computing power perspective and propose a detailed model of temporary fork with heterogeneous computing power. 

Game Theory in Blockchain Networks. Blockchain is a distributed, decentralized, public ledger. Due to the decentralization of the blockchain network, game theory [26] is an ideal modeling tool to analyze the interactions within the blockchain network [39], where evolutionary games [31] can be used to analyzing the dynamic interactions and the evolution of the blockchain networks. The evolutionary game for consensus provision in blockchain networks with shards is investigated in [40]. Literature [41] proposes an evolutionary game theoretical analysis on block withholding attack in PoW blockchain. 

A closely related work [25] develops an evolutionary game to study the dynamic process of mining pool selection.
</snippet></tool_output><think>

Title: To EVM or Not to EVM: Blockchain Compatibility and Network Effects
Snippet: Let there be three blockchain platforms: two EVM-compatible blockchains, P 1 and P 2 , and one EVM-incompatible blockchain, P 3 . There are two firms, an incumbent A on P 1 , and a new entrant B. 

Blockchain Platforms. Blockchains P 1 ,P 2 , and P 3 have existing user bases N 1 ,N 2 , and N 3 respectively. A larger user base leads to a larger positive network effect for users, and firms account for this effect when choosing platforms. We assume that N 1 > N 2 = N 3 . That is, the EVM-compatible blockchain P 1 has the largest existing user base. Readers can think of P 1 as the Ethereum blockchain which has seen the widest adoption amongst users and developers. P 2 and P 3 are two newer, alternative layer-1 blockchains that compete with Ethereum. P 2 is EVM-compatible (e.g. Binance Smart Chain), and P 3 is not (e.g. Algorand). 

Firms. Firms A and B build similar applications on blockchain, such as a decentralized exchange (DEX) or a lending service. We assume that the product offered by the firms are inter-operable, meaning that if they are built on the same blockchain, they both benefit from the network effect of each other's users. An example of this would be DEXes on the same chain: with the rise of DEX aggregators, the liquidity found on multiple DEXes on the same blockchain can often be atomically accessed by users at the same time. This would not be true if they were built on two different blockchains. We assume that firm A is already built on the largest blockchain P 1 at the start of the game. Firm B is a new entrant who will choose a blockchain to launch its application in period t = 0. The game will then proceed as a two-stage Bertrand competition, where in each of the two periods t = 1, 2, the two firms set prices for their services, denoted as p At , p Bt respectively, to maximize their aggregate payoff.
</snippet>

Title: Blockchain technology for supply chain traceability: A game-theoretic analysis between e-platforms
Snippet: By combing the above literature, we summarise the gaps between this paper and the relevant literature as follows: First, the above studies are all theoretical and applied studies on today's popular technology, blockchain. Most articles reveal that the adoption of blockchain technology plays a major role in enhancing the competitiveness of enterprises in various industries. Similar to the above studies, we also discuss the impact of blockchain technology on supply chain operations. However, many articles use qualitative methods to analyse the benefits of blockchain characteristics for a single-channel supply chain. While some articles have quantitatively studied the impact of blockchain technology on the profitability of supply chain members through a gaming approach, very few articles have studied the impact of blockchain technology on competition between two e-tailing platforms based on an e-commerce context. Therefore, based on the above studies, this paper focuses on competition between e-retailers in a dual-channel supply chain to further understand the value of blockchain adoption by discussing the relevance factors such as consumer sensitivity to blockchain, agency agreements, and brand value effects. Second, the above articles have deeply studied the horizontal competition issues of dualchannel supply chain members. Similar to the above reviewed literature, this paper also focuses on horizontal competition between two retailers. Moreover, they do not combine the blockchain with the brand value effect to study the dual-channel supply chain competition of two e-tailers. Therefore, this paper focuses on blockchain technology adoption decisions for competing platforms. Specifically, weighing the relationship between the brand spillover effects of blockchain technology and the cost of blockchain usage in an online dualchannel competitive environment is key to the analysis. Third, the above studies are all based on the heterogeneity of consumers from different perspectives. Similar to the above reviewed literature, this paper also focuses on the heterogeneity of consumers.

Title: To EVM or Not to EVM: Blockchain Compatibility and Network Effects
Snippet: We study the competition between blockchains in a multi-chain environment, where a dominant EVM-compatible blockchain (e.g., Ethereum) co-exists with an alternative EVM-compatible (e.g., Avalanche) and an EVM-incompatible (e.g., Algorand) blockchain. While EVM compatibility allows existing Ethereum users and developers to migrate more easily over to the alternative layer-1, EVM incompatibility might allow the firms to build more loyal and "sticky'' user base, and in turn a more robust ecosystem. As such, the choice to be EVM-compatible is not merely a technological decision, but also an important strategic decision. In this paper, we develop a game theoretic model to study this competitive dynamic, and find that at equilibrium, new entrants/developers tend to adopt the dominant blockchain. To avoid adoption failure, the alternative blockchains have to either (1) directly subsidize the new entrant firms or (2) offer better features, which in practice can take form in lower transaction costs, faster finality, or larger network effects. We find that it is easier for EVM-compatible blockchains to attract users through direct subsidy, while it is more efficient for EVM-incompatible blockchains to attract users through offering better features/products.

# Overview: Why Game Theory for Blockchain Adoption

Game theory is widely used to analyze blockchain because strategic interactions among users, miners/validators, and developers determine whether a protocol change or new chain will be adopted and how equilibria form across the network.<cite id="f42b5b5e-0">Game theory is widely used to study security, mining management, and economic issues in blockchain networks, enabling analysis of optimal strategies via equilibrium solutions</cite><cite id="f42b5b5e-2">Game-theoretic models capture roles, behaviors, and system performance to understand and optimize strategies under rationality and incentive constraints in blockchain</cite><cite id="f42b5b5e-4">Game theory has been used to analyze consensus node strategies, predict interactions, and design incentive mechanisms that prevent misconduct</cite>. Adoption decisions—by users, validators, enterprises, and developers—are inherently strategic and often characterized by externalities, complementarities, and coordination frictions, which game-theoretic frameworks can formalize.

# Protocol Upgrades and Fork Adoption: Coordination and Threshold Effects

Protocol upgrades are implemented via soft or hard forks, creating adoption thresholds: most nodes must update for a soft fork (backwards-compatible) while a non-backward-compatible change splits the network at a hard fork.<cite id="a3546f28-0">Soft forks are backward-compatible upgrades requiring most node operators to update, whereas hard forks are backward-incompatible and lead to permanent chain divergence</cite><cite id="a3546f28-3">A hard fork arises when an upgrade is non-backward compatible, requiring all nodes to upgrade; miners vote on adoption, and acceptance can trigger a hard fork</cite><cite id="8e95fe2f-2">Hard forks require all participants to update; soft forks can be adopted without universal upgrades, with risk of suboptimal outcomes in change processes</cite>. Adoption is a coordination problem across heterogeneous actors under delay and uncertainty, where a critical mass of adopters determines success; evolutionary games are often used to model dynamic convergence to equilibria where adoption is either widespread or fails due to low participation.<cite id="8e95fe2f-4">Evolutionary games model dynamic interactions and adoption processes in blockchain networks, including pool selection and attack-withholding dynamics, capturing gradual change toward equilibria</cite><cite id="f42b5b5e-3">An evolutionary game among core enterprises, SMEs, and financial institutions models bounded rationality, dynamic strategy adjustment, and adoption probabilities (guarantee, compliance, blockchain model) over time</cite>.

# Signaling, Cheap Talk, and Governance Under Uncertainty

Governance choices (e.g., UASF/SegWit-like proposals) often rely on signals, communication, and strategic voting rather than complete common knowledge, creating opportunities for cheap talk and misinformation equilibria. Surveys and governance analyses emphasize that upgrade processes can suffer from suboptimal or fraudulent outcomes when coordination is imperfect, highlighting the need for signaling and reputation mechanisms to align stakeholders’ expectations and reduce coordination failure risk.<cite id="8e95fe2f-2">Protocol change processes can lead to fraud or sub-optimal outcomes, underscoring governance risks when aligning diverse communities</cite><cite id="a3546f28-1">Ethereum-like networks use governance procedures to propose and vote on upgrades, which can be implemented via hard or soft forks depending on the change and social structure</cite>. In such settings, signaling models (sender–receiver games) and equilibrium refinements help assess when credible commitments or verifiable signals can sustain adoption, versus when multiple equilibria with delayed or failed adoption occur.

# Enterprise and Platform Adoption: Network Effects and Compatibility

At the enterprise and platform level, adoption is driven by network externalities among users and complements (developers, dApps, liquidity), and compatibility choices (e.g., EVM support). Two-sided market and platform-competition models capture how incumbent and entrant firms choose platforms, set prices, and invest in features, with equilibria determined by user and developer network effects and migration frictions.<cite id="6a6d2324-1">A two-stage Bertrand competition model with firm entry studies platform choice under network effects, where larger user bases confer positive externalities and firms compete on prices across EVM-compatible and incompatible chains</cite><cite id="6a6d2324-4">A game-theoretic model of multi-chain competition (dominant EVM-compatible vs alternatives) shows new entrants tend to adopt the dominant chain; to avoid adoption failure, alternatives must subsidize or offer better features (lower fees, faster finality, stronger network effects)</cite><cite id="6a6d2324-0">A non-cooperative two-stage competitive game models promotion of service providers and rivalry between blockchain platforms to draw consumers, linking service quality and incentives to competition outcomes</cite>. These models generalize to two-sided markets where users and developers exhibit cross-side network effects, and to compatibility decisions where EVM support reduces migration costs and accelerates ecosystem adoption.<cite id="6a6d2324-1">Interoperability across firms on the same chain strengthens network effects, as applications benefit from each other’s user base</cite><cite id="6a6d2324-4">EVM compatibility is a strategic decision affecting migration ease and competitive dynamics, with equilibrium adoption patterns shaped by subsidies and feature quality</cite>.

# Staking and Validator Adoption: Coordination, Investment, and Slashing

In proof-of-stake systems, validator adoption depends on the cost of staking, slashing penalties, expected block rewards, and the security externalality that all validators benefit from a well-protected network. Coordination and moral-hazard games explain why some nodes may underinvest in validator participation unless penalties and incentives align, and why slashing rules and deposit sizes are designed to internalize the security externalality and deter equivocation.<cite id="f42b5b5e-0">Game-theoretic analyses of blockchain economic and energy trading, and incentive mechanisms, inform how slashing and staking rules shape validator behavior</cite><cite id="f42b5b5e-2">Mechanism design within game-theoretic models is used to align incentives so rational, self-interested nodes act desirably under equilibrium</cite>. Evolutionary games have also been applied to mining and pool selection dynamics, which extend to staking pools as similar strategic coordination problems under heterogeneous stake sizes and penalties.<cite id="8e95fe2f-4">Evolutionary game analyses include consensus provision with shards, block withholding attacks, and mining pool selection, illustrating dynamic coordination under heterogeneity</cite>.

# Supply-Chain and Industry-Wide Adoption: Bounded Rationality and Multi-Actor Interactions

Adoption at the enterprise ecosystem level (e.g., supply chains) is naturally modeled with evolutionary/replicator games that incorporate bounded rationality, learning, and multiple stakeholders. These models track how core enterprises, SMEs, and financial institutions adjust strategies over time (e.g., adoption of a blockchain-enabled guarantee model, compliance, or a blockchain versus traditional process), and identify conditions under which adoption equilibria are efficient or fail due to low participation or miscoordination.<cite id="f42b5b5e-3">An evolutionary game among core enterprises, SMEs, and financial institutions formalizes bounded rationality, dynamic strategy adjustment, and adoption probabilities (guarantee provision, compliance, blockchain model choice), with risk-neutral players and explicit strategy payoffs</cite>. Such models can be extended to include information provision and verification costs, as well as reputational and regulatory considerations that shift payoffs and tipping points for adoption.

# Mechanism Design and Incentive Compatibility for Adoption

Beyond static coordination, mechanism design and incentive-compatibility analyses are central to adoption because upgrade rules, slashing, and subsidy schedules must align private incentives with social optima. Game-theoretic surveys emphasize designing mechanisms that prevent attacks and misconduct while encouraging adoption, and highlight challenges when actors are not purely rational or when extreme malicious behavior is possible.<cite id="f42b5b5e-0">Game-theoretic approaches inform incentive mechanism design for blockchain, including rules to address security and economic issues</cite><cite id="f42b5b5e-2">Rationality and selfishness assumptions underpin game-theoretic analyses, but attackers may act maliciously regardless of cost; mechanisms must address such extremes</cite><cite id="f42b5b5e-4">Incentive mechanisms can prevent nodes from misconduct or attacks and coordinate voluntary decisions among consensus nodes</cite>. In platform and governance settings, mechanism design connects signaling/cheap talk and voting protocols to adoption outcomes, ensuring that credible, verifiable messages and voting rights induce efficient upgrades and ecosystem migration.

# Practical Modeling Guidance and Trade-offs

- Choose model class by adoption bottleneck: coordination/evolutionary games for threshold phenomena and dynamic learning; signaling/cheap talk for governance with incomplete information; platform competition/network-effects for enterprise/developer migration; mechanism design for incentive alignment of upgrades and staking.<cite id="8e95fe2f-4">Evolutionary games capture dynamic adoption and strategy evolution in decentralized settings</cite><cite id="a3546f28-0">Soft vs hard fork mechanics create distinct adoption thresholds and divergence risks</cite><cite id="6a6d2324-4">Platform competition and network effects determine whether new entrants adopt dominant chains and what remedies (subsidies, features) avoid adoption failure</cite>.
- Incorporate heterogeneity and delays: heterogeneous computing power or stake sizes and propagation delays materially affect equilibria and tipping points for adoption; these factors should be included when modeling miner/pool or validator dynamics and upgrade voting windows.<cite id="8e95fe2f-4">Heterogeneous computing power and propagation delays shape fork and pool dynamics, which evolutionary models can capture</cite>.
- Anticipate governance risk: upgrade processes can fail or deviate from socially optimal outcomes due to information frictions and strategic behavior; models should include channels for credible signaling, transparency, and penalties to reduce coordination failures.<cite id="8e95fe2f-2">Protocol change processes face risks of fraud or suboptimal outcomes, motivating careful governance design</cite><cite id="a3546f28-1">Governance procedures vary across networks and may use forks or votes; adoption outcomes depend on social structure and change type</cite>.

# Takeaways

- Adoption on blockchains is best understood through coordination and evolutionary games that capture threshold effects and learning dynamics among miners/validators and enterprises, signaling/cheap talk when governance is at stake, and platform-competition models with network externalities for ecosystem migration.<cite id="a3546f28-0">Soft and hard forks encode distinct adoption thresholds and divergence risks for protocol upgrades</cite><cite id="8e95fe2f-4">Evolutionary games model dynamic interactions and adoption equilibria in decentralized settings</cite><cite id="6a6d2324-4">Network effects and compatibility shape platform adoption, with new entrants tending to adopt dominant chains unless compensated by subsidies or superior features</cite>. These models, grounded in game-theoretic incentives and mechanism design, provide actionable levers—credible signals, well-calibrated slashing and subsidies, and feature-led or subsidization strategies—to increase the likelihood of successful, efficient adoption outcomes.<cite id="f42b5b5e-0">Game-theoretic incentive mechanisms can address security and economic issues central to adoption</cite><cite id="f42b5b5e-4">Incentive mechanisms align node behavior and support voluntary, coordinated upgrades</cite>.
</answer>

Title: A Survey on Blockchain: A Game Theoretical Perspective
Snippet: Over the past decade, blockchain technology has attracted tremendous attention from both academia and industry. The popularity of blockchains was originated from the concept of crypto-currencies to serve as a decentralized and tamper-proof transaction data ledger. Nowadays, blockchains as the key framework in the decentralized public data-ledger have been applied to a wide range of scenarios far beyond crypto-currencies, such as the Internet of Things, healthcare, and insurance. This survey aims to fill the gap between a large number of studies on blockchain networks, where game theory emerges as an analytical tool, and the lack of a comprehensive survey on the game theoretical approaches applied in blockchain-related issues. In this survey, we review the game models proposed to address common issues in the blockchain network. The focus is placed on security issues, e.g., selfish mining, majority attack and denial of service attack, issues regarding mining management, e.g., computational power allocation, reward allocation, and pool selection, as well as issues regarding blockchain economic and energy trading. Additionally, we discuss the advantages and disadvantages of these selected game theoretical models and solutions. Finally, we highlight important challenges and future research directions of applying game theoretical approaches to incentive mechanism design and the combination of blockchain with other technologies.

Title: Blockchain Systems, Technologies, and Applications: A Methodology Perspective
Snippet: As an analysis tool, game theory is widely used to study security, mining, and resource allocation problems in blockchain networks. A game model can be built by capturing the characteristic of the addressed problem in terms of the role of blockchain users, behavior of blockchain decision-maker and the performance of blockchain system. Thus, the game modling can help researchers understand the impact of different strategy and analyze the optimal strategy based on equilibrium solution. 

Meanwhile, some problems are still remaining to be addressed as follows. 

1) Some necessary information should be collected and exchanged in game theory, for example, the selling price of edge server for mining task offloading and the computing resources used by miners for mining. Schedule the communication resource into the game theory need to be well investigated. 2) Furthermore, to achieve the equilibrium solution, multiround iterations in game theory are needed usually, but the corresponding overhead should be considered. The overhead which cause commnuication delay, would generate significant impact on the performance and the security of blockchain system. Next, efficient and lightweight game theoretic mechanism for blockchain system should be investigated. 3) Rationality and selfishness are the basic assumptions in game theory. However, these assumptions might be invalid especially for the malicious attacker, whose purpose is to launch an attacking to ruin the blockchain system regardless of the cost. Therefore, how to understand and study this extreme malicious action in order to improve security and privacy should be studied in the future.

Title: Blockchain and Supply-Chain Financing: An Evolutionary Game Approach with Guarantee Considerations
Snippet: Based on the dynamic game relationship analysis among the three parties involved, the following six assumptions were proposed and organized sequentially for the model's development:

(1) As the main entities in the game, the core enterprise, SMEs, and financial institutions all pursue the maximization of their own interests under conditions of incomplete information acquisition; (2) Financial institutions, core enterprises, and SMEs all possess bounded rationality and have the capability to dynamically adjust their strategies over time and in response to the environment within the evolutionary game theory.Other entities may potentially influence any of the three parties are not considered in this game process; (3) In the scenario where the blockchain model is utilized, it is assumed all information uploaded to the blockchain by the three parties is authentic and free from any malpractice; (4) The revenue generated from the core enterprise's guarantee provision is less than the revenue derived from its own operations; (5) All three parties involved in the game are considered to be risk-neutral;

(6) The probability that the core enterprise chooses to provide a guarantee is denoted as x, with a corresponding probability of 1 − x for not providing a guarantee.The probability that SMEs opt for compliance is denoted as y, and the probability of choosing to default is 1 − y.The probability that financial institutions select the blockchain model is represented by z, with a probability of 1 − z for selecting the traditional model.The parameters and their corresponding symbols are shown in Table 1.

Title: Game Theory Application Resources Management and Distribution in Blockchain Network
Snippet: In recent times, game theory has been gradually exploited for research and application in Blockchain. It is basically the mathematical model that studies the strategic interactions between players to make reasonable decisions, if imposed on the Blockchain platform, game theory has analyzed the strategy of the consensus nodes. Through the interactions between them such as understanding and predicting mutually exploiting behaviors, then having optimal response strategy based on balance. Furthermore, game theory can be used to develop incentive mechanisms that prevent nodes from misconduct or initiate attacks. As such, referring to game theory is voluntary decision-making with all consensus of the nodes in the Blockchain network. 

In a game, each player makes his or her own strategy to maximize its utility, based on the other player's strategy [1]. Referring to game theory, it is necessary to mention the following terms: Game: Any situation where the outcome depends on the actions of two or more decision makers (players). 

• Player: The player is the decision-maker in the game. Inside Blockchain, the player can be a miner, a mining pool or a blockchain user 

• Convenience: Gadget, meaning payout, interest, or revenue that reflects a player's expected outcome * Strategy: A complete plan of action that the player will use depending on the circumstances that arise in the game. In general, a player's utility is determined not only on the player's strategy, but also on the strategy of the other players. Due to the different strategies nodes implement to maximize their own strategy of utilities, nodes can attach new verification blocks to different blocks in the Blockchain * Reasonableness: A reasonable player, means always watching, if the Player always maximizes his payout Game theory pursues two basic assumptions. One is that an individual or group of individuals is a participant in the game and the goal is to gain benefits (be it to win or minimize his losses). Second, participating players always calculate in advance of their decisions according to the principle of reason to try to get more utility for themselves. 

This article will present the problem of using game theory to simulate a resource optimization method for blockchain network to achieve the best efficiency.

documents.snippet:
In recent times, game theory has been gradually exploited for research and application in Blockchain. It is basically the mathematical model that studies the strategic interactions between players to make reasonable decisions, if imposed on the Blockchain platform, game theory has analyzed the strategy of the consensus nodes. Through the interactions between them such as understanding and predicting mutually exploiting behaviors, then having optimal response strategy based on balance. Furthermore, game theory can be used to develop incentive mechanisms that prevent nodes from misconduct or initiate attacks. As such, referring to game theory is voluntary decision-making with all consensus of the nodes in the Blockchain network. 

In a game, each player makes his or her own strategy to maximize its utility, based on the other player's strategy [1]. Referring to game theory, it is necessary to mention the following terms: Game: Any situation where the outcome depends on the actions of two or more decision makers (players). 

• Player: The player is the decision-maker in the game. Inside Blockchain, the player can be a miner, a mining pool or a blockchain user 

• Convenience: Gadget, meaning payout, interest, or revenue that reflects a player's expected outcome * Strategy: A complete plan of action that the player will use depending on the circumstances that arise in the game. In general, a player's utility is determined not only on the player's strategy, but also on the strategy of the other players. Due to the different strategies nodes implement to maximize their own strategy of utilities, nodes can attach new verification blocks to different blocks in the Blockchain * Reasonableness: A reasonable player, means always watching, if the Player always maximizes his payout Game theory pursues two basic assumptions. One is that an individual or group of individuals is a participant in the game and the goal is to gain benefits (be it to win or minimize his losses). Second, participating players always calculate in advance of their decisions according to the principle of reason to try to get more utility for themselves. 

This article will present the problem of using game theory to simulate a resource optimization method for blockchain network to achieve the best efficiency.

Snippet: Summary: The software upgrades of a blockchain platform are implemented as forks of the blockchain. 

Context: After a blockchain platform is deployed, developers upgrade the blockchain to meet new requirements. 

Problem: The code of a blockchain platform is stand-alone. Any changes may affect the historical ledger contents. How can developers implement upgrades to a blockchain platform without affecting the historical ledger contents? 

Forces: 

• Upgradability guarantee. Blockchain needs to be upgraded to fix software bugs, and implement new functionalities. • Adaptability improvement. Blockchain needs to adapt to the varying requirements of diverse application scenarios. • Blockchain property preservation. The fundamental properties of a blockchain, e.g., immutability, must not be affected by software upgrades. Solution: Fig. 9 is a graphical representation of protocol forking, which can be applied to upgrade a deployed blockchain. The upgrades and evolution require a series of formalised development procedures. Upgrades accepted by the community are implemented and released as new versions via protocol forking. Specifically, there exist two types of upgrades in blockchain: soft fork and hard fork. Soft forks mean backward-compatible upgrades, which require the majority of node operators to install the latest version of a blockchain platform. After soft fork, appending blocks need to adhere to both new and old on-chain protocols. Blocks that violate the new protocol will be abandoned by the platform (as the dotted block N+2 in Fig. 9 (a)). On the contrary, hard forks refer to the backward-incompatible upgrades, which lead to permanent divergences of a blockchain. After hard fork, a blockchain is split into two separate instances. One instance employs the old protocol while the other one follows new rules. The two instances will operate as two distinct blockchain platforms, as illustrated in Fig. 9 (b). Please note that protocol forking in the context of blockchain governance refers to intentional software upgrades. Accidental forkings where multiple block validators intend to append new blocks at the same time are out of the scope of this paper.

Title: Deciphering DeFi: A Comprehensive Analysis and Visualization of Risks in Decentralized Finance
Snippet: Changes to the protocol: Changes to the blockchain protocol can happen via hard forks, soft forks, protocol upgrades, or modifications from a governance process. A hard fork is a modification to the blockchain protocol that is not backward-compatible, requiring all network participants to update to the latest version of the program. A soft fork is a backward-compatible update to the blockchain protocol that may be executed without needing all users to upgrade their software. Some blockchain protocols, including Ethereum, have a method for executing protocol upgrades. Depending on the nature of the modifications being made, these enhancements may be introduced via a hard fork or a soft fork. Some blockchain networks provide a governance procedure that enables users to propose and vote on protocol modifications. The execution method for these modifications depends on the specific network, the type of proposed change, and the community's social structure. They can be implemented through a hard fork, a soft fork, or another method. There is the risk of fraud or sub-optimal outcomes of these change processes, as described in Barrera and Hurder (2018). • Centralization: Consensus protocols, such as proof-of-work (PoW) or proof-of-stake (PoS), might be susceptible to centralization, which occurs when a small number of users control a considerable majority of the network's computational capacity (Gencer et al. (2018)). This is called a 51% attack. PoS protocols depend on a limited set of validators to validate transactions and establish consensus on the blockchain's state. If these validators are hacked or do not function in the best interests of the network, it might pose a risk to DeFi users. Further risks specific to the used consensus protocols are: selfish mining, pool hopping attack, Sybil attack, or nothing at stake attack.

Title: An Overview of Forks and Coordination in Blockchain Development
Snippet: If an upgrade in the blockchain process is non-backward compatible with the existing blockchain implementation, it is termed as a hard fork. It can result from a rule change such that the client software and virtual machines validating transactions and blocks according to the old rule will consider it invalid and redundant, hence requiring upgrades of all the nodes involved. One of the prime examples of this is the hard fork of Bitcoin and Bitcoin Cash. Imagine in a blockchain process, after the nth block, some rules in the node were changed, or an upgrade in the blockchain protocol was proposed. The miner nodes (peers on the peerto-peer network) are required to vote on the adoption and incorporation of these changes. In case the incumbent process is elected, no changes would occur, but if the upgrade is elected and made, it could trigger a "hard fork" in the chain. For instance, any block mined using old protocols would become invalid and could not be chained to the block mined with the new protocol as depicted in [22].

Title: Impact of Temporary Fork on the Evolution of Mining Pools in Blockchain Networks: An Evolutionary Game Analysis
Snippet: There has been a rich body of previous work on blockchain network and mining pool. In the following, we introduce related work regarding temporary fork, game theory, the impact of uncle block rewards and the decentralization in blockchain networks, respectively. 

Temporary Fork in Blockchain Networks. Due to the network propagation delay, blockchain networks may face inconsistencies in form of temporary forks. There are several papers studying the delay and temporary fork in blockchain networks from a networking perspective. In [12], authors analyze Bitcoin from a networking perspective and show that the propagation delay in the network is the primary cause for blockchain forks. Literature [9] provides an empirical analysis of the announcement and propagation of Bitcoin blocks that caused blockchain forks. 

Authors in [36] analyze the blockchain protocol in asynchronous networks. In [37], authors model the Bitcoin consensus and network protocols to develop the theoretical analysis for fork in Bitcoin network. In [38], authors try to reduce forks in the blockchain via probabilistic verification. Nevertheless, existing research efforts mainly focus on the impacting factors from the blockchain system point of view such as block size and network propagation delay. Along a different line from the previous work, we focus on the computing power perspective and propose a detailed model of temporary fork with heterogeneous computing power. 

Game Theory in Blockchain Networks. Blockchain is a distributed, decentralized, public ledger. Due to the decentralization of the blockchain network, game theory [26] is an ideal modeling tool to analyze the interactions within the blockchain network [39], where evolutionary games [31] can be used to analyzing the dynamic interactions and the evolution of the blockchain networks. The evolutionary game for consensus provision in blockchain networks with shards is investigated in [40]. Literature [41] proposes an evolutionary game theoretical analysis on block withholding attack in PoW blockchain. 

A closely related work [25] develops an evolutionary game to study the dynamic process of mining pool selection.

Problem: The code of a blockchain platform is stand-alone. Any changes may affect the historical ledger contents. How can developers implement upgrades to a blockchain platform without affecting the historical ledger contents? 

Forces: 

• Upgradability guarantee. Blockchain needs to be upgraded to fix software bugs, and implement new functionalities. • Adaptability improvement. Blockchain needs to adapt to the varying requirements of diverse application scenarios. • Blockchain property preservation. The fundamental properties of a blockchain, e.g., immutability, must not be affected by software upgrades. Solution: Fig. 9 is a graphical representation of protocol forking, which can be applied to upgrade a deployed blockchain. The upgrades and evolution require a series of formalised development procedures. Upgrades accepted by the community are implemented and released as new versions via protocol forking. Specifically, there exist two types of upgrades in blockchain: soft fork and hard fork. Soft forks mean backward-compatible upgrades, which require the majority of node operators to install the latest version of a blockchain platform. After soft fork, appending blocks need to adhere to both new and old on-chain protocols. Blocks that violate the new protocol will be abandoned by the platform (as the dotted block N+2 in Fig. 9 (a)). On the contrary, hard forks refer to the backward-incompatible upgrades, which lead to permanent divergences of a blockchain. After hard fork, a blockchain is split into two separate instances. One instance employs the old protocol while the other one follows new rules. The two instances will operate as two distinct blockchain platforms, as illustrated in Fig. 9 (b). Please note that protocol forking in the context of blockchain governance refers to intentional software upgrades. Accidental forkings where multiple block validators intend to append new blocks at the same time are out of the scope of this paper.

snippet.text: Changes to the protocol: Changes to the blockchain protocol can happen via hard forks, soft forks, protocol upgrades, or modifications from a governance process. A hard fork is a modification to the blockchain protocol that is not backward-compatible, requiring all network participants to update to the latest version of the program. A soft fork is a backward-compatible update to the blockchain protocol that may be executed without needing all users to upgrade their software. Some blockchain protocols, including Ethereum, have a method for executing protocol upgrades. Depending on the nature of the modifications being made, these enhancements may be introduced via a hard fork or a soft fork. Some blockchain networks provide a governance procedure that enables users to propose and vote on protocol modifications. The execution method for these modifications depends on the specific network, the type of proposed change, and the community's social structure. They can be implemented through a hard fork, a soft fork, or another method. There is the risk of fraud or sub-optimal outcomes of these change processes, as described in Barrera and Hurder (2018). • Centralization: Consensus protocols, such as proof-of-work (PoW) or proof-of-stake (PoS), might be susceptible to centralization, which occurs when a small number of users control a considerable majority of the network's computational capacity (Gencer et al. (2018)). This is called a 51% attack. PoS protocols depend on a limited set of validators to validate transactions and establish consensus on the blockchain's state. If these validators are hacked or do not function in the best interests of the network, it might pose a risk to DeFi users. Further risks specific to the used consensus protocols are: selfish mining, pool hopping attack, Sybil attack, or nothing at stake attack.

snippet.text:
There has been a rich body of previous work on blockchain network and mining pool. In the following, we introduce related work regarding temporary fork, game theory, the impact of uncle block rewards and the decentralization in blockchain networks, respectively. 

Temporary Fork in Blockchain Networks. Due to the network propagation delay, blockchain networks may face inconsistencies in form of temporary forks. There are several papers studying the delay and temporary fork in blockchain networks from a networking perspective. In [12], authors analyze Bitcoin from a networking perspective and show that the propagation delay in the network is the primary cause for blockchain forks. Literature [9] provides an empirical analysis of the announcement and propagation of Bitcoin blocks that caused blockchain forks. 

Authors in [36] analyze the blockchain protocol in asynchronous networks. In [37], authors model the Bitcoin consensus and network protocols to develop the theoretical analysis for fork in Bitcoin network. In [38], authors try to reduce forks in the blockchain via probabilistic verification. Nevertheless, existing research efforts mainly focus on the impacting factors from the blockchain system point of view such as block size and network propagation delay. Along a different line from the previous work, we focus on the computing power perspective and propose a detailed model of temporary fork with heterogeneous computing power. 

Game Theory in Blockchain Networks. Blockchain is a distributed, decentralized, public ledger. Due to the decentralization of the blockchain network, game theory [26] is an ideal modeling tool to analyze the interactions within the blockchain network [39], where evolutionary games [31] can be used to analyzing the dynamic interactions and the evolution of the blockchain networks. The evolutionary game for consensus provision in blockchain networks with shards is investigated in [40]. Literature [41] proposes an evolutionary game theoretical analysis on block withholding attack in PoW blockchain. 

A closely related work [25] develops an evolutionary game to study the dynamic process of mining pool selection.

snippet.text: Any software or operating system needs periodic upgrades to fix errors or add new functionalities. For the blockchain system, those updates are called a "fork". There are two kinds of forks, i.e., hard fork and soft fork. Figure 1 shows an example of a hard fork. The blockchain system is a decentralized network. All the nodes on the network need to follow the same rules. The set of rules is known as the protocol. In Fig. 1, the blue block is called a divergence block, where the blockchain system updates its protocol. When a protocol is updated, and the new protocol is not backwards-compatible. Some nodes on the blockchain do not accept the new protocol, and they choose to use the old version. Thus, the blockchain forks into 2 incompatible blockchains, which run the new and old protocol, respectively.

documents.title: An Overview of Forks and Coordination in Blockchain Development
documents.snippet: If an upgrade in the blockchain process is non-backward compatible with the existing blockchain implementation, it is termed as a hard fork. It can result from a rule change such that the client software and virtual machines validating transactions and blocks according to the old rule will consider it invalid and redundant, hence requiring upgrades of all the nodes involved. One of the prime examples of this is the hard fork of Bitcoin and Bitcoin Cash. Imagine in a blockchain process, after the nth block, some rules in the node were changed, or an upgrade in the blockchain protocol was proposed. The miner nodes (peers on the peerto-peer network) are required to vote on the adoption and incorporation of these changes. In case the incumbent process is elected, no changes would occur, but if the upgrade is elected and made, it could trigger a "hard fork" in the chain. For instance, any block mined using old protocols would become invalid and could not be chained to the block mined with the new protocol as depicted in [22].

Title: Blockchain Technology Empirical Studies on the Demand of Distributed Network
Snippet: Blockchain technology has become a new model for encryption, unsustainability and confidence in both consumers and suppliers (SPs) in order to increase the quality of services. A game theory framework is used to simulate a competitive market with the existing platform controlled by a centralizer as a confidant third party to provide an economic overview of such a Blockchain-based platform sector. The portals serve as a mediator in this industry and provide consumers with services delivered by SPs. The key reasons for blockchain based network market performance are I how engagement by SPs represents its service efficiency (QoS) and (ii) how SPs are empowered to contribute their services, such as the virtual environment. A non-cooperative two-stage competitive game is used in our game formulation, whereby the first stage model how to promote SPs on a blockchain basis and the second stage modeleves rivalry between platforms to draw consumers. We therefore have an equilibrium analysis that offers a valuable description of the effect on competition among platforms and SPs’ equilibrium reward policy of the service quality of the blockchain network. Our numerical analysis reveals that the incentive to balance is increasing proportionately to the Fault tolerance of a blockchain-based network when the incentive is unfavourable if the number of participating SPs has a non-increasing QoS.

Title: To EVM or Not to EVM: Blockchain Compatibility and Network Effects
Snippet: Let there be three blockchain platforms: two EVM-compatible blockchains, P 1 and P 2 , and one EVM-incompatible blockchain, P 3 . There are two firms, an incumbent A on P 1 , and a new entrant B. 

Blockchain Platforms. Blockchains P 1 ,P 2 , and P 3 have existing user bases N 1 ,N 2 , and N 3 respectively. A larger user base leads to a larger positive network effect for users, and firms account for this effect when choosing platforms. We assume that N 1 > N 2 = N 3 . That is, the EVM-compatible blockchain P 1 has the largest existing user base. Readers can think of P 1 as the Ethereum blockchain which has seen the widest adoption amongst users and developers. P 2 and P 3 are two newer, alternative layer-1 blockchains that compete with Ethereum. P 2 is EVM-compatible (e.g. Binance Smart Chain), and P 3 is not (e.g. Algorand). 

Firms. Firms A and B build similar applications on blockchain, such as a decentralized exchange (DEX) or a lending service. We assume that the product offered by the firms are inter-operable, meaning that if they are built on the same blockchain, they both benefit from the network effect of each other's users. An example of this would be DEXes on the same chain: with the rise of DEX aggregators, the liquidity found on multiple DEXes on the same blockchain can often be atomically accessed by users at the same time. This would not be true if they were built on two different blockchains. We assume that firm A is already built on the largest blockchain P 1 at the start of the game. Firm B is a new entrant who will choose a blockchain to launch its application in period t = 0. The game will then proceed as a two-stage Bertrand competition, where in each of the two periods t = 1, 2, the two firms set prices for their services, denoted as p At , p Bt respectively, to maximize their aggregate payoff.

Title: Blockchain technology for supply chain traceability: A game-theoretic analysis between e-platforms
Snippet: By combing the above literature, we summarise the gaps between this paper and the relevant literature as follows: First, the above studies are all theoretical and applied studies on today's popular technology, blockchain. Most articles reveal that the adoption of blockchain technology plays a major role in enhancing the competitiveness of enterprises in various industries. Similar to the above studies, we also discuss the impact of blockchain technology on supply chain operations. However, many articles use qualitative methods to analyse the benefits of blockchain characteristics for a single-channel supply chain. While some articles have quantitatively studied the impact of blockchain technology on the profitability of supply chain members through a gaming approach, very few articles have studied the impact of blockchain technology on competition between two e-tailing platforms based on an e-commerce context. Therefore, based on the above studies, this paper focuses on competition between e-retailers in a dual-channel supply chain to further understand the value of blockchain adoption by discussing the relevance factors such as consumer sensitivity to blockchain, agency agreements, and brand value effects. Second, the above articles have deeply studied the horizontal competition issues of dualchannel supply chain members. Similar to the above reviewed literature, this paper also focuses on horizontal competition between two retailers. However, the above literature studies fierce competition between online retailers and offline retailers. This paper mainly focuses on competition between two e-tailers. Although there are a few articles that explore the effect of brand value, these articles do not take blockchain technology into consideration. Moreover, they do not combine the blockchain with the brand value effect to study the dual-channel supply chain competition of two e-tailers. Therefore, this paper focuses on blockchain technology adoption decisions for competing platforms. Specifically, weighing the relationship between the brand spillover effects of blockchain technology and the cost of blockchain usage in an online dualchannel competitive environment is key to the analysis. Third, the above studies are all based on the heterogeneity of consumers from different perspectives. Similar to the above reviewed literature, this paper also focuses on the heterogeneity of consumers.

Title: To EVM or Not to EVM: Blockchain Compatibility and Network Effects
Snippet: We study the competition between blockchains in a multi-chain environment, where a dominant EVM-compatible blockchain (e.g., Ethereum) co-exists with an alternative EVM-compatible (e.g., Avalanche) and an EVM-incompatible (e.g., Algorand) blockchain. While EVM compatibility allows existing Ethereum users and developers to migrate more easily over to the alternative layer-1, EVM incompatibility might allow the firms to build more loyal and "sticky'' user base, and in turn a more robust ecosystem. As such, the choice to be EVM-compatible is not merely a technological decision, but also an important strategic decision. In this paper, we develop a game theoretic model to study this competitive dynamic, and find that at equilibrium, new entrants/developers tend to adopt the dominant blockchain. To avoid adoption failure, the alternative blockchains have to either (1) directly subsidize the new entrant firms or (2) offer better features, which in practice can take form in lower transaction costs, faster finality, or larger network effects. We find that it is easier for EVM-compatible blockchains to attract users through direct subsidy, while it is more efficient for EVM-incompatible blockchains to attract users through offering better features/products.

documents.title: Blockchain technology for supply chain traceability: A game-theoretic analysis between e-platforms
documents.snippet: By combing the above literature, we summarise the gaps between this paper and the relevant literature as follows: First, the above studies are all theoretical and applied studies on today's popular technology, blockchain. Most articles reveal that the adoption of blockchain technology plays a major role in enhancing the competitiveness of enterprises in various industries. Similar to the above studies, we also discuss the impact of blockchain technology on supply chain operations. However, many articles use qualitative methods to analyse the benefits of blockchain characteristics for a single-channel supply chain. While some articles have quantitatively studied the impact of blockchain technology on the profitability of supply chain members through a gaming approach, very few articles have studied the impact of blockchain technology on competition between two e-tailing platforms based on an e-commerce context. Therefore, based on the above studies, this paper focuses on competition between e-retailers in a dual-channel supply chain to further understand the value of blockchain adoption by discussing the relevance factors such as consumer sensitivity to blockchain, agency agreements, and brand value effects. Second, the above articles have deeply studied the horizontal competition issues of dualchannel supply chain members. Similar to the above reviewed literature, this paper also focuses on horizontal competition between two retailers. However, the above literature studies fierce competition between online retailers and offline retailers. This paper mainly focuses on competition between two e-tailers. Although there are a few articles that explore the effect of brand value, these articles do not take blockchain technology into consideration. Moreover, they do not combine the blockchain with the brand value effect to study the dual-channel supply chain competition of two e-tailers. Therefore, this paper focuses on blockchain technology adoption decisions for competing platforms. Specifically, weighing the relationship between the brand spillover effects of blockchain technology and the cost of blockchain usage in an online dualchannel competitive environment is key to the analysis. Third, the above studies are all based on the heterogeneity of consumers from different perspectives. Similar to the above reviewed literature, this paper also focuses on the heterogeneity of consumers.

documents.title: To EVM or Not to EVM: Blockchain Compatibility and Network Effects
documents.snippet: We study the competition between blockchains in a multi-chain environment, where a dominant EVM-compatible blockchain (e.g., Ethereum) co-exists with an alternative EVM-compatible (e.g., Avalanche) and an EVM-incompatible (e.g., Algorand) blockchain. While EVM compatibility allows existing Ethereum users and developers to migrate more easily over to the alternative layer-1, EVM incompatibility might allow the firms to build more loyal and "sticky'' user base, and in turn a more robust ecosystem. As such, the choice to be EVM-compatible is not merely a technological decision, but also an important strategic decision. In this paper, we develop a game theoretic model to study this competitive dynamic, and find that at equilibrium, new entrants/developers tend to adopt the dominant blockchain. To avoid adoption failure, the alternative blockchains have to either (1) directly subsidize the new entrant firms or (2) offer better features, which in practice can take form in lower transaction costs, faster finality, or larger network effects. We find that it is easier for EVM-compatible blockchains to attract users through direct subsidy, while it is more efficient for EVM-incompatible blockchains to attract users through offering better features/products.

problem: optimal search algorithm applied to people moving around a facility
final_response:
# Overview

Optimal search in facilities with moving people typically requires modeling human motion and environment structure, specifying a cost (e.g., time, energy, overlap), and optimizing over policies or plans under uncertainty. The literature covers dynamic network and moving-target search formulations, POMDP-based Bayesian search on occupancy grids, structured coverage patterns, and multi-robot patrolling against mobile adversaries. These methods provide varying guarantees: exact dynamic-programming solutions for finite-horizon problems, provably near-optimal policies via submodularity, and heuristic or adversarially optimal strategies when preferences or unknowns are present. <cite id="1b7f8a97-2">Dynamic programming and greedy approximations are combined with a FAB (frontier-aware best) scheme for moving target search</cite><cite id="1b7f8a97-4">Sweep-line/frontier allocation optimizes robot usage and coverage quality for known environments</cite><cite id="5097dbb5-0">Bayesian grid-based search and coverage are NP-hard, but greedy policies achieve within (1−1/e) of optimal due to submodularity</cite><cite id="c3961c13-0">Adversarial patrolling and pursuit–evasion provide time-optimal capture/patrolling strategies under specific assumptions</cite>.

# Models of People and Facilities

Facility search can be modeled at multiple abstraction levels, each with different assumptions and optimality properties. Graph/polygonal models discretize space or motion and turn search into path/planning over states with sensing/overlap costs; these problems are NP-hard in general. <cite id="5097dbb5-0">Graph-based models treat sensing and motion as discrete, polygonal models assume full 360-degree view and infinite range, and Bayesian models partition space into cells with detection probabilities, with all three often NP-hard</cite>. When human motion must be realistic, social force models (SFM) capture repulsive/attractive interactions and pedestrian-specific behaviors like edge effects and vision-limited neighborhoods. <cite id="c1411ee1-0">The social-force model, originating in the 1990s, simulates pedestrian movement via forces decaying with distance and has been extended with friction, respect mechanisms, and anisotropic interactions</cite><cite id="c1411ee1-1">Efficient neighbor search in SFM can be achieved by mesh-based spatial hashing to reduce complexity from O(N^2) to O(N)</cite><cite id="c1411ee1-4">Enhanced SFM variants incorporate walking-edge and vision sight to balance shortest-path routing with corridor use and collision avoidance</cite>.

# Algorithms and Optimality Guarantees

Dynamic search for moving targets. For moving target search, dynamic programming can find optimal observation allocations, with greedy heuristics and upper bounds; a FAB algorithm iterates stationary solutions to handle motion. <cite id="1b7f8a97-2">A dynamic programming algorithm computes optimal stationary allocations; greedy heuristics provide efficient approximations, and a FAB algorithm iterates these to solve the moving-target case with numerical comparisons across target motion models</cite>. Frontier sweep and allocation. In known environments, sweep-line/frontier methods allocate robots along a marching frontier; optimization focuses on minimizing robot count for a minimum sensing probability or maximizing coverage quality with a fixed robot budget. <cite id="1b7f8a97-4">For a 2D bounded workspace with a pre-determined sweep schedule (frontier at each time), the problem reduces to placing robots along the frontier to meet a minimum sensing quality per point, minimizing the number of robots or maximizing minimum quality; dual problems trade off robots and coverage</cite>. Structured coverage patterns. Triangular-grid patterns provide blanket coverage with asymptotic optimality in the number of robots needed, enabling systematic sweep strategies. <cite id="1b7f8a97-3">Triangular grid coverage guarantees a complete blanket of a region and is asymptotically optimal in the minimum number of robots required for complete coverage of arbitrary bounded areas; robots can execute sweep by moving between grid vertices</cite>. Near-optimal coverage with submodularity. When coverage is cast as selecting informative positions under sensing models, submodularity yields guarantees from greedy selection. <cite id="5097dbb5-0">Coverage with real sensor specs is NP-hard but submodular; greedy algorithms achieve a (1−1/e) approximation to the optimum, providing near-optimal guarantees in cluttered environments</cite><cite id="5097dbb5-1">Path-entropy frontier selection improves area coverage by prioritizing goals whose paths reveal the most unknown cells</cite>.

Bayesian search and POMDPs in facilities. Occupancy-grid Bayesian frameworks and POMDP planners handle partial observability and long horizons, often via grid discretization of states and hierarchical decompositions. <cite id="5097dbb5-2">POMDP planners produce belief-space waypoints for search and tracking; discretization of targets into grids enables use of discrete POMDP solvers; hierarchical and hybrid POMDP/MDP methods address long horizons and mixed observability, with recent methods solving continuous-state search problems up to 10 dimensions via variational techniques</cite><cite id="5097dbb5-4">Occupancy grid mapping represents continuous space as cells with Bayesian probabilities; POMDPs extend MDPs by mapping state to observations, fitting naturally with robotic search under uncertainty</cite>. In partially mapped, multi-robot settings, LOMDP/POMDP formulations coordinate teams to find goals in unseen space with centralized planning over shared partial maps. <cite id="5097dbb5-3">A LOMDP/POMDP formulation for multi-robot teams with occupancy-grid beliefs coordinates collective actions to minimize expected distance to a point-goal in unseen space, using belief-space Bellman updates</cite>.

# Human Motion Realism: Integrating Social Force with Optimization

Combining pedestrian dynamics with search/evacuation planning can improve realism and performance. <cite id="c1411ee1-0">The social force model captures repulsive and goal forces and has been calibrated and extended to handle crowded environments and anisotropic interactions</cite>. Integrating SFM density maps with optimally guided path planning can reduce evacuation times by routing away from congested areas. <cite id="c1411ee1-2">An MDP-based optimally guided path planner that uses SFM density maps assigns negative rewards to congested states, yielding at least 4.31 s (5.1%) average evacuation-time reduction in a 50-person case and 8.8 s savings in dense scenarios; a time-dependent MDP is proposed to further adapt rewards in real time</cite>. For indoor scenarios, enhanced SFM variants address edge effects and vision limits to better reflect how pedestrians distribute near walls and choose sighted paths. <cite id="c1411ee1-4">Walking-edge preference forces and vision-sight constraints in modified SFM capture trade-offs between shortest paths and corridor use for safe, efficient movement</cite>.

# Multi-Robot Patrolling and Indoor Pursuit–Evasion

Optimal or adversarially robust patrolling in buildings relates to pursuit–evasion, with time-optimal clearance or capture under graph/visibility assumptions. <cite id="c3961c13-0">Patrolling with adversaries can be framed as a non-cooperative game; related pursuit–evasion assumes evaders seek to avoid capture, and hide-and-seek on graphs guarantees finite-time capture under specific assumptions</cite>. In perimeter-like facilities, coordinated robot teams can patrol by maintaining evenly spaced formations and randomized headings to maximize minimum capture utility; the optimal strategy can be to choose movement probabilities that maximize worst-case capture utility. <cite id="c3961c13-0">For a perimeter modeled as a ring divided into cells, synchronized robots in evenly spaced formation and probabilistic direction changes yield a patrolling strategy optimized to maximize the minimum expected utility; the optimal solution reduces to selecting the heading probability p that maximizes this minimum</cite>. Against adaptive criminals, dynamic programming gives optimal but computationally heavy patrol allocation, while greedy slice-by-step planning approximates it with lower complexity. <cite id="c3961c13-1">Dynamic programming yields optimal but O(C^2 N T_u) patrol allocation; a greedy algorithm with O(C N T_u) complexity iterates one-step lookaheads to minimize expected crime at each step, updating the suspect distribution and proceeding until the horizon</cite>.

# Practical Algorithm Selection and Deployment

- Known static facility, probabilistic target locations: Use Bayesian grid search with POMDP planning; if sensing models yield submodular gains, deploy a greedy frontier-selection policy for near-optimal coverage with guarantees. <cite id="5097dbb5-0">Bayesian grid-based search is NP-hard but admits (1−1/e) greedy guarantees via submodularity, enabling near-optimal coverage with real sensor constraints</cite><cite id="5097dbb5-2">Discrete/variational POMDP solvers and hierarchical POMDPs support long-horizon search/tracking in buildings</cite>. 
- Known dynamic environment (moving people/obstacles) with a sweepable layout: Use sweep-line/frontier allocation optimized for coverage quality or robot count; structured grid-based sweeps (triangular) provide systematic motion and asymptotically optimal robot counts. <cite id="1b7f8a97-4">Frontier sweep schedules with optimized robot placement guarantee minimum sensing quality or minimize robots</cite><cite id="1b7f8a97-3">Triangular grid patterns are asymptotically optimal for robot coverage and support sweep strategies between vertices</cite>. 
- Moving targets with uncertain motion: Employ dynamic programming or FAB for moving target search to allocate observation effort and adjust to target dynamics; combine SFM with optimization to anticipate congestion and improve routing. <cite id="1b7f8a97-2">Dynamic programming and FAB handle moving targets with comparisons across motion models</cite><cite id="c1411ee1-2">Integrating SFM density into MDP routing reduced evacuation times by 5–10% in simulations</cite>. 
- Adversarial or criminal activity: Use game-theoretic patrolling and pursuit–evasion variants to define time-optimal or utility-maximizing strategies against adaptive opponents; consider formation-based randomized headings and periodic reversals to maximize worst-case outcomes. <cite id="c3961c13-0">Adversarial patrolling selects probabilities over headings to maximize minimum capture utility; related pursuit–evasion guarantees finite-time capture under graph assumptions</cite><cite id="c3961c13-1">Greedy one-step lookahead allocation approximates optimal patrol deployment against adaptive criminals with lower complexity</cite>. 
- Unknown/partially mapped facilities with teams: Use multi-robot LOMDP/POMDP with shared occupancy grids and centralized planning to expand coverage and reduce expected search cost as maps reveal over time. <cite id="5097dbb5-3">LOMDP/POMDP formulations coordinate multi-robot teams over shared partial occupancy grids to minimize expected distance to unseen goals</cite>.

# Caveats and Open Considerations

Most formal optimality results assume a known, complete facility model and well-specified sensing/transition dynamics; integrating full social-force realism and large human populations increases model dimensionality and complexity. <cite id="5097dbb5-2">POMDP methods rely on discretization or approximate inference for continuous states and high-dimensional observations</cite><cite id="c1411ee1-0">SFM calibration and superposition assumptions can be problematic when extrapolating from pairwise measurements to dense crowds</cite>. Some guarantees (e.g., (1−1/e)) rely on submodularity of the coverage objective; violations due to human interactions or dynamic blockages can degrade performance. <cite id="5097dbb5-0">Submodularity-based near-optimality applies under specific sensing models and remains a useful approximation in cluttered environments</cite>. Finally, adversarial patrolling and pursuit–evasion optimality often hinge on assumptions about objectives and information; translating these to real security settings requires careful validation of assumptions and possibly hybrid strategies. <cite id="c3961c13-0">Patrolling and pursuit–evasion assumptions (e.g., evader avoids capture, no entry to areas of interest) differ from general security scenarios and motivate hybrid designs</cite>.

# Summary

For people moving around a facility, optimal search strategies fall into four evidenced families: (1) dynamic moving-target search with dynamic programming and FAB for allocating observation effort and handling motion; (2) sweep-line/frontier and structured-grid coverage with optimized robot placement and asymptotic optimality in robot counts; (3) Bayesian/POMDP search over occupancy grids with near-optimal guarantees via submodularity and practical multi-robot coordination; and (4) adversarial patrolling/pursuit–evasion with time-optimal or utility-maximizing policies under explicit assumptions. Integrating pedestrian social-force dynamics with optimization improves realism and can reduce evacuation times, while deployment must weigh model assumptions, computational cost, and guarantees against the specific facility and threat model. <cite id="1b7f8a97-2">Dynamic programming and FAB provide exact and approximate solutions for moving targets</cite><cite id="1b7f8a97-4">Frontier sweep and robot allocation optimize coverage quality and robot counts in known environments</cite><cite id="1b7f8a97-3">Triangular-grid coverage offers asymptotically optimal robot counts and systematic sweeps</cite><cite id="5097dbb5-0">Bayesian grid search with submodular coverage yields (1−1/e) guarantees</cite><cite id="c1411ee1-2">SFM-guided routing reduces evacuation times in simulations</cite><cite id="c3961c13-0">Adversarial patrolling and pursuit–evasion provide game-theoretic time/coverage optimality under stated assumptions</cite>.

Title: Optimal Allocation of Many Robot Guards for Sweep-Line Coverage
Snippet: Searching for a static or moving target in a planar environment is a classic problem in robotics [1]- [5]. The setting applies to many real-world applications, including searching for lost person/object, checking for potential hazards, and generally, search and rescue tasks conducted in a known environment. Research tackling this problem mostly focuses on devising a search plan with different types of objectives, such as minimizing the total length of the frontier of the search schedule from the start to the end [6], minimizing the number of robots used for the search plan in a visibilitybased robot sensing model [7], and so on. 

In certain cases, the high-level plan for searching a given region may be already pre-determined and fixed. For example, in search and rescue efforts, a frequently carried out plan is to perform a single sweep of an environment with a marching frontier, which is easy to execute when many participating robots/agents are involved. The high-level search plan may also be determined by existing algorithms that compute only the search frontier. However, even in the case where the search plan consists of pre-determined sweep (frontier) lines, it remains non-trivial to find an optimal organization of the mobile robots to execute the search plan, for either minimizing the number of robots needed for a given sensing probability requirement or utilizing a fixed number of robots to maximize the minimum sensing probability of locating something in the environment. 

In this work, we address the challenge of how to best allocate many robots to execute a pre-determined search schedule for a known environment. More specifically, for a two-dimensional closed and bounded workspace, and a known search schedule which gives a search frontier for any given time, the robot guards are required to stay on the search frontier to carry out the sensing task. Because each robot's coverage quality deteriorates with distance, their relative placement on the frontier must be carefully decided to maximize the coverage quality. For the setup, we focus on the problem of finding the minimum number of robots required to execute a pre-determined sweep schedule such that a minimum sensing quality is guaranteed for each point in the workspace. Solutions to this minimization problem readily translate to solutions for maximizing the coverage quality for a fixed number of robots, which is a dual problem.

Title: Single-file pedestrian dynamics: a review of agent-following models
Snippet: The social-force model (SFM) [37] is considered the first model that describes the movement of pedestrians by means of repulsive forces that decay exponentially with distance. It is conceptually predated by the model of Hirai and Tarui (see Sec. 3.2) which uses algebraic forces. The SFM was first developed in the 1990s, and since then it has been widely used to study pedestrian dynamics in various settings. The SFM allows for the simulation of pedestrian behavior and the prediction of crowd movement in different scenarios, such as evacuation from a building. Over the years, it has undergone various modifications and enhancements to improve its accuracy in simulating pedestrian dynamics and to address its difficulties in describing certain scenarios (see Section 3.3). Researchers have added physical forces (e.g. friction), improved numerical efficiency, and introduced mechanisms such as the "respect mechanism" [81] to improve the performance especially in crowded environments. 

In [69], an approach for calibration of the SFM by using experimental measurements to adjust the repulsive force was proposed. The updated repulsive force takes into account both the distance and the angle between the direction of movement and the vector that connects the positions of the two pedestrians. This approach of considering both distance and angle dependencies is commonly used in other models, starting from [40], in order to account for the anisotropic behavior of pedestrians. Recent results show that rescaling of the social force model yields in a first-order Optimal Velocity model if inertia is neglected [68]. This over-damped limit of SFM (see also Appendix D) can formally performed by letting the social forces becoming corrections to the optimal velocity. The exponential Weidmann pedestrian OV model [113] is then recovered if we restrict interactions to the next neighbor. 

However, it is important to note that these measurements were primarily done with only two pedestrians and then extrapolated to a crowd with multiple individuals, which assumes that the superposition of forces can be applied in this context. This assumption, however, will turn out to be problematic and experimentally not sustainable (see Section 3.3).
</snippet>

Title: Deep adaptive learning for safe and efficient navigation of pedestrian dynamics
Snippet: Based on the work conducted in this study, this research successfully incorporates a social force model into an optimally guided path planning model, for the evacuation of a group of pedestrians. Pedestrian navigation safety is critical to saving lives and preventing injury in a multitude of emergencies such as active shooter incidents and fires. By integrating the two models, we can further optimize mobility in emergency evacuation situations. Our optimally guided path planning model incorporates the social force model's density map and assigns highly congested areas to negative reward states. The negative reward states are used to avoid congested areas and pathways and advise pedestrians to follow the optimally guided path. For simulation I, the baseline example evacuation time was an average 84.95 s. Utilizing the two integrated models, we were able to show a reduction in the average evacuation time of at least 4.31 s or a 5.1% evacuation time decrease. The total evacuation time was able to be reduced to a total average of 75.9 s and a 10.6% decrease in average evacuation time compared to the baseline example. For simulation II, in a more dense environment, the baseline example's evacuation time was an average of 165.3 s. Integrating the two modelling techniques, we were able to provide a total evacuation time savings of 8.8 s. In simulation I, where 50 pedestrians are present, the optimal effect of path optimization is splitting the pedestrians evenly. Fifty percent of the pedestrians followed the social force model, and the remaining 50% follow the optimally guided path. This provides a 10.1% evacuation time savings. In simulation II, where 200 pedestrians are present, the optimal effect of path optimization is to allow 10% of pedestrians to follow the optimally guided path. Following this approach provided an average time savings of 8.8 s.
