Title: Analysis and Augmentation of Human Performance on Telerobotic Search Problems
Snippet: There are three major models for spatial search: graph-based models, polygonal models, and Bayesian models. The graphbased model is based on the assumption that sensing and robots' motion can be treated as discrete quantities, making it possible to model the problem using a graph [8]. The polygonal model is based on the assumptions that the environment can be described through polygons, the range of sensors is infinite, and the field of view is 360 degrees [9]. The challenge is either to cover the whole environment by using the fewest sensors, or maximize the coverage by using a fixed number of sensors. Bayesian search is based on the assumption that the search space can be divided into finite cells/graphs and that each cell represents individual probability of detection [10]. The goal is to determine the optimal path to find the target(s), according to the probability distribution function (PDF) [11], [12]. Although each model relies on different assumptions and uses different objectives, viewed from a computational standpoint, they are all NP-hard problems [8]- [10]. 

Another way to maximize the coverage in the search space is by using cognitive-based adaptive optimization (CAO), which was proposed for optimization problems that had unknown objective functions but available sensing measurements [13]. It was applied to maximize the coverage using a fixed number of robots equipped with sensors in 3D environments [14]. The CAO framework gives coverage results without prior information about either the objective function or the environment [15] and works even if the environment is non-convex. However, in contrast to the aforementioned approaches, CAO cannot provide theoretical lower bounds on coverage. 

To take advantage of Bayesian models and the submodularity found in coverage problems, the grid map approach was proposed [7]: Coverage is computed combining the measurements from sensor positions, real sensing scans, and a known grid map. This problem was shown to be NP-hard [6]. Since maximal coverage is a submodular maximization problem, greedy algorithms are able to achieve solutions over (1-1/e) of the optimum. The advantage of this approach is that it provides a near-optimal guarantee using real sensor specifications (e.g., range and angle) and works even in cluttered environments.
</snippet>

In MDP, all states are known to the agent to make an optimal solution, but in POMDP, the agent only has an observation O to relate the states. # Overview

Optimal search in facilities with moving people typically requires modeling human motion and environment structure, specifying a cost (e.g., time, energy, overlap), and optimizing over policies or plans under uncertainty. The literature covers dynamic network and moving-target search formulations, POMDP-based Bayesian search on occupancy grids, structured coverage patterns, and multi-robot patrolling against mobile adversaries. These methods provide varying guarantees: exact dynamic-programming solutions for finite-horizon problems, provably near-optimal policies via submodularity, and heuristic or adversarially optimal strategies when preferences or unknowns are present. <cite id="1b7f8a97-2">Dynamic programming and greedy approximations are combined with a FAB (frontier-aware best) scheme for moving target search</cite><cite id="1b7f8a97-4">Sweep-line/frontier allocation optimizes robot usage and coverage quality for known environments</cite><cite id="5097dbb5-0">Bayesian grid-based search and coverage are NP-hard, but greedy policies achieve within (1−1/e) of optimal due to submodularity</cite><cite id="c3961c13-0">Adversarial patrolling and pursuit–evasion provide time-optimal capture/patrolling strategies under specific assumptions</cite>.

# Models of People and Facilities

Facility search can be modeled at multiple abstraction levels, each with different assumptions and optimality properties. Graph/polygonal models discretize space or motion and turn search into path/planning over states with sensing/overlap costs; these problems are NP-hard in general. <cite id="5097dbb5-0">Graph-based models treat sensing and motion as discrete, polygonal models assume full 360-degree view and infinite range, and Bayesian models partition space into cells with detection probabilities, with all three often NP-hard</cite>. When human motion must be realistic, social force models (SFM) capture repulsive/attractive interactions and pedestrian-specific behaviors like edge effects and vision-limited neighborhoods. <cite id="c1411ee1-0">The social-force model, originating in the 1990s, simulates pedestrian movement via forces decaying with distance and has been extended with friction, respect mechanisms, and anisotropic interactions</cite><cite id="c1411ee1-1">Efficient neighbor search in SFM can be achieved by mesh-based spatial hashing to reduce complexity from O(N^2) to O(N)</cite><cite id="c1411ee1-4">Enhanced SFM variants incorporate walking-edge and vision sight to balance shortest-path routing with corridor use and collision avoidance</cite>.

# Algorithms and Optimality Guarantees

Dynamic search for moving targets. For moving target search, dynamic programming can find optimal observation allocations, with greedy heuristics and upper bounds; a FAB algorithm iterates stationary solutions to handle motion. <cite id="1b7f8a97-2">A dynamic programming algorithm computes optimal stationary allocations; greedy heuristics provide efficient approximations, and a FAB algorithm iterates these to solve the moving-target case with numerical comparisons across target motion models</cite>. Frontier sweep and allocation. In known environments, sweep-line/frontier methods allocate robots along a marching frontier; optimization focuses on minimizing robot count for a minimum sensing probability or maximizing coverage quality with a fixed robot budget. <cite id="1b7f8a97-4">For a 2D bounded workspace with a pre-determined sweep schedule (frontier at each time), the problem reduces to placing robots along the frontier to meet a minimum sensing quality per point, minimizing the number of robots or maximizing minimum quality; dual problems trade off robots and coverage</cite>. Structured coverage patterns. Triangular-grid patterns provide blanket coverage with asymptotic optimality in the number of robots needed, enabling systematic sweep strategies. <cite id="1b7f8a97-3">Triangular grid coverage guarantees a complete blanket of a region and is asymptotically optimal in the minimum number of robots required for complete coverage of arbitrary bounded areas; robots can execute sweep by moving between grid vertices</cite>. Near-optimal coverage with submodularity. When coverage is cast as selecting informative positions under sensing models, submodularity yields guarantees from greedy selection. <cite id="5097dbb5-0">Coverage with real sensor specs is NP-hard but submodular; greedy algorithms achieve a (1−1/e) approximation to the optimum, providing near-optimal guarantees in cluttered environments</cite><cite id="5097dbb5-1">Path-entropy frontier selection improves area coverage by prioritizing goals whose paths reveal the most unknown cells</cite>.

Bayesian search and POMDPs in facilities. Occupancy-grid Bayesian frameworks and POMDP planners handle partial observability and long horizons, often via grid discretization of states and hierarchical decompositions. <cite id="5097dbb5-2">POMDP planners produce belief-space waypoints for search and tracking; discretization of targets into grids enables use of discrete POMDP solvers; hierarchical and hybrid POMDP/MDP methods address long horizons and mixed observability, with recent methods solving continuous-state search problems up to 10 dimensions via variational techniques</cite><cite id="5097dbb5-4">Occupancy grid mapping represents continuous space as cells with Bayesian probabilities; POMDPs extend MDPs by mapping state to observations, fitting naturally with robotic search under uncertainty</cite>. In partially mapped, multi-robot settings, LOMDP/POMDP formulations coordinate teams to find goals in unseen space with centralized planning over shared partial maps. <cite id="5097dbb5-3">A LOMDP/POMDP formulation for multi-robot teams with occupancy-grid beliefs coordinates collective actions to minimize expected distance to a point-goal in unseen space, using belief-space Bellman updates</cite>.

# Human Motion Realism: Integrating Social Force with Optimization

Combining pedestrian dynamics with search/evacuation planning can improve realism and performance. <cite id="c1411ee1-0">The social force model captures repulsive and goal forces and has been calibrated and extended to handle crowded environments and anisotropic interactions</cite>. Integrating SFM density maps with optimally guided path planning can reduce evacuation times by routing away from congested areas. <cite id="c1411ee1-2">An MDP-based optimally guided path planner that uses SFM density maps assigns negative rewards to congested states, yielding at least 4.31 s (5.1%) average evacuation-time reduction in a 50-person case and 8.8 s savings in dense scenarios; a time-dependent MDP is proposed to further adapt rewards in real time</cite>. For indoor scenarios, enhanced SFM variants address edge effects and vision limits to better reflect how pedestrians distribute near walls and choose sighted paths. <cite id="c1411ee1-4">Walking-edge preference forces and vision-sight constraints in modified SFM capture trade-offs between shortest paths and corridor use for safe, efficient movement</cite>.

# Multi-Robot Patrolling and Indoor Pursuit–Evasion

Optimal or adversarially robust patrolling in buildings relates to pursuit–evasion, with time-optimal clearance or capture under graph/visibility assumptions. <cite id="c3961c13-0">Patrolling with adversaries can be framed as a non-cooperative game; related pursuit–evasion assumes evaders seek to avoid capture, and hide-and-seek on graphs guarantees finite-time capture under specific assumptions</cite>. In perimeter-like facilities, coordinated robot teams can patrol by maintaining evenly spaced formations and randomized headings to maximize minimum capture utility; the optimal strategy can be to choose movement probabilities that maximize worst-case capture utility. <cite id="c3961c13-0">For a perimeter modeled as a ring divided into cells, synchronized robots in evenly spaced formation and probabilistic direction changes yield a patrolling strategy optimized to maximize the minimum expected utility; the optimal solution reduces to selecting the heading probability p that maximizes this minimum</cite>. Against adaptive criminals, dynamic programming gives optimal but computationally heavy patrol allocation, while greedy slice-by-step planning approximates it with lower complexity. <cite id="c3961c13-1">Dynamic programming yields optimal but O(C^2 N T_u) patrol allocation; a greedy algorithm with O(C N T_u) complexity iterates one-step lookaheads to minimize expected crime at each step, updating the suspect distribution and proceeding until the horizon</cite>.

# Practical Algorithm Selection and Deployment

- Known static facility, probabilistic target locations: Use Bayesian grid search with POMDP planning; if sensing models yield submodular gains, deploy a greedy frontier-selection policy for near-optimal coverage with guarantees. <cite id="5097dbb5-0">Bayesian grid-based search is NP-hard but admits (1−1/e) greedy guarantees via submodularity, enabling near-optimal coverage with real sensor constraints</cite><cite id="5097dbb5-2">Discrete/variational POMDP solvers and hierarchical POMDPs support long-horizon search/tracking in buildings</cite>. 
- Known dynamic environment (moving people/obstacles) with a sweepable layout: Use sweep-line/frontier allocation optimized for coverage quality or robot count; structured grid-based sweeps (triangular) provide systematic motion and asymptotically optimal robot counts. <cite id="1b7f8a97-4">Frontier sweep schedules with optimized robot placement guarantee minimum sensing quality or minimize robots</cite><cite id="1b7f8a97-3">Triangular grid patterns are asymptotically optimal for robot coverage and support sweep strategies between vertices</cite>. 
- Moving targets with uncertain motion: Employ dynamic programming or FAB for moving target search to allocate observation effort and adjust to target dynamics; combine SFM with optimization to anticipate congestion and improve routing. <cite id="1b7f8a97-2">Dynamic programming and FAB handle moving targets with comparisons across motion models</cite><cite id="c1411ee1-2">Integrating SFM density into MDP routing reduced evacuation times by 5–10% in simulations</cite>. 
- Adversarial or criminal activity: Use game-theoretic patrolling and pursuit–evasion variants to define time-optimal or utility-maximizing strategies against adaptive opponents; consider formation-based randomized headings and periodic reversals to maximize worst-case outcomes. <cite id="c3961c13-0">Adversarial patrolling selects probabilities over headings to maximize minimum capture utility; related pursuit–evasion guarantees finite-time capture under graph assumptions</cite><cite id="c3961c13-1">Greedy one-step lookahead allocation approximates optimal patrol deployment against adaptive criminals with lower complexity</cite>. 
- Unknown/partially mapped facilities with teams: Use multi-robot LOMDP/POMDP with shared occupancy grids and centralized planning to expand coverage and reduce expected search cost as maps reveal over time. <cite id="5097dbb5-3">LOMDP/POMDP formulations coordinate multi-robot teams over shared partial occupancy grids to minimize expected distance to unseen goals</cite>.

# Caveats and Open Considerations

Most formal optimality results assume a known, complete facility model and well-specified sensing/transition dynamics; integrating full social-force realism and large human populations increases model dimensionality and complexity. <cite id="5097dbb5-2">POMDP methods rely on discretization or approximate inference for continuous states and high-dimensional observations</cite><cite id="c1411ee1-0">SFM calibration and superposition assumptions can be problematic when extrapolating from pairwise measurements to dense crowds</cite>. Some guarantees (e.g., (1−1/e)) rely on submodularity of the coverage objective; violations due to human interactions or dynamic blockages can degrade performance. <cite id="5097dbb5-0">Submodularity-based near-optimality applies under specific sensing models and remains a useful approximation in cluttered environments</cite>. Finally, adversarial patrolling and pursuit–evasion optimality often hinge on assumptions about objectives and information; translating these to real security settings requires careful validation of assumptions and possibly hybrid strategies. <cite id="c3961c13-0">Patrolling and pursuit–evasion assumptions (e.g., evader avoids capture, no entry to areas of interest) differ from general security scenarios and motivate hybrid designs</cite>.

# Summary

For people moving around a facility, optimal search strategies fall into four evidenced families: (1) dynamic moving-target search with dynamic programming and FAB for allocating observation effort and handling motion; (2) sweep-line/frontier and structured-grid coverage with optimized robot placement and asymptotic optimality in robot counts; (3) Bayesian/POMDP search over occupancy grids with near-optimal guarantees via submodularity and practical multi-robot coordination; and (4) adversarial patrolling/pursuit–evasion with time-optimal or utility-maximizing policies under explicit assumptions. Integrating pedestrian social-force dynamics with optimization improves realism and can reduce evacuation times, while deployment must weigh model assumptions, computational cost, and guarantees against the specific facility and threat model. <cite id="1b7f8a97-2">Dynamic programming and FAB provide exact and approximate solutions for moving targets</cite><cite id="1b7f8a97-4">Frontier sweep and robot allocation optimize coverage quality and robot counts in known environments</cite><cite id="1b7f8a97-3">Triangular-grid coverage offers asymptotically optimal robot counts and systematic sweeps</cite><cite id="5097dbb5-0">Bayesian grid search with submodular coverage yields (1−1/e) guarantees</cite><cite id="c1411ee1-2">SFM-guided routing reduces evacuation times in simulations</cite><cite id="c3961c13-0">Adversarial patrolling and pursuit–evasion provide game-theoretic time/coverage optimality under stated assumptions</cite>.

Title: Single-file pedestrian dynamics: a review of agent-following models
Snippet: The social-force model (SFM) [37] is considered the first model that describes the movement of pedestrians by means of repulsive forces that decay exponentially with distance. It is conceptually predated by the model of Hirai and Tarui (see Sec. 3.2) which uses algebraic forces. The SFM was first developed in the 1990s, and since then it has been widely used to study pedestrian dynamics in various settings. The SFM allows for the simulation of pedestrian behavior and the prediction of crowd movement in different scenarios, such as evacuation from a building. Over the years, it has undergone various modifications and enhancements to improve its accuracy in simulating pedestrian dynamics and to address its difficulties in describing certain scenarios (see Section 3.3). Researchers have added physical forces (e.g. friction), improved numerical efficiency, and introduced mechanisms such as the "respect mechanism" [81] to improve the performance especially in crowded environments. 

In [69], an approach for calibration of the SFM by using experimental measurements to adjust the repulsive force was proposed. The updated repulsive force takes into account both the distance and the angle between the direction of movement and the vector that connects the positions of the two pedestrians. This approach of considering both distance and angle dependencies is commonly used in other models, starting from [40], in order to account for the anisotropic behavior of pedestrians. Recent results show that rescaling of the social force model yields in a first-order Optimal Velocity model if inertia is neglected [68]. This over-damped limit of SFM (see also Appendix D) can formally performed by letting the social forces becoming corrections to the optimal velocity. The exponential Weidmann pedestrian OV model [113] is then recovered if we restrict interactions to the next neighbor. 

However, it is important to note that these measurements were primarily done with only two pedestrians and then extrapolated to a crowd with multiple individuals, which assumes that the superposition of forces can be applied in this context. This assumption, however, will turn out to be problematic and experimentally not sustainable (see Section 3.3).

Title: Deep adaptive learning for safe and efficient navigation of pedestrian dynamics
Snippet: Based on the work conducted in this study, this research successfully incorporates a social force model into an optimally guided path planning model, for the evacuation of a group of pedestrians. Pedestrian navigation safety is critical to saving lives and preventing injury in a multitude of emergencies such as active shooter incidents and fires. By integrating the two models, we can further optimize mobility in emergency evacuation situations. Our optimally guided path planning model incorporates the social force model's density map and assigns highly congested areas to negative reward states. The negative reward states are used to avoid congested areas and pathways and advise pedestrians to follow the optimally guided path. For simulation I, the baseline example evacuation time was an average 84.95 s. Utilizing the two integrated models, we were able to show a reduction in the average evacuation time of at least 4.31 s or a 5.1% evacuation time decrease. The total evacuation time was able to be reduced to a total average of 75.9 s and a 10.6% decrease in average evacuation time compared to the baseline example. For simulation II, in a more dense environment, the baseline example's evacuation time was an average of 165.3 s. Integrating the two modelling techniques, we were able to provide a total evacuation time savings of 8.8 s. In simulation I, where 50 pedestrians are present, the optimal effect of path optimization is splitting the pedestrians evenly. Fifty percent of the pedestrians followed the social force model, and the remaining 50% follow the optimally guided path. This provides a 10.1% evacuation time savings. In simulation II, where 200 pedestrians are present, the optimal effect of path optimization is to allow 10% of pedestrians to follow the optimally guided path. Following this approach provided an average time savings of 8.8 s. 

In the future, we will expand the current MDP framework to a Time-Dependent MDP (TDMP). The time-dependent MDP will incorporate dynamic reward changing based on the social force models' movement in current time. Using a TDMP may reduce the overall evacuation time by providing optimal routing choices in real-time with rewards being updated at each time step. Expanding our current modelling framework will allow for incorporation of a more robust and dynamic reward function.

Pedestrian navigation safety is critical to saving lives and preventing injury in a multitude of emergencies such as active shooter incidents and fires. By integrating the two models, we can further optimize mobility in emergency evacuation situations. Our optimally guided path planning model incorporates the social force model's density map and assigns highly congested areas to negative reward states. The negative reward states are used to avoid congested areas and pathways and advise pedestrians to follow the optimally guided path. For simulation I, the baseline example evacuation time was an average 84.95 s. Utilizing the two integrated models, we were able to show a reduction in the average evacuation time of at least 4.31 s or a 5.1% evacuation time decrease. The total evacuation time was able to be reduced to a total average of 75.9 s and a 10.6% decrease in average evacuation time compared to the baseline example. For simulation II, in a more dense environment, the baseline example's evacuation time was an average of 165.3 s. Integrating the two modelling techniques, we were able to provide a total evacuation time savings of 8.8 s. In simulation I, where 50 pedestrians are present, the optimal effect of path optimization is splitting the pedestrians evenly. Fifty percent of the pedestrians followed the social force model, and the remaining 50% follow the optimally guided path. This provides a 10.1% evacuation time savings. In simulation II, where 200 pedestrians are present, the optimal effect of path optimization is to allow 10% of pedestrians to follow the optimally guided path. Following this approach provided an average time savings of 8.8 s. 

In the future, we will expand the current MDP framework to a Time-Dependent MDP (TDMP). The time-dependent MDP will incorporate dynamic reward changing based on the social force models' movement in current time. Using a TDMP may reduce the overall evacuation time by providing optimal routing choices in real-time with rewards being updated at each time step. Expanding our current modelling framework will allow for incorporation of a more robust and dynamic reward function.

documents.snippet:
The social-force model (SFM) [37] is considered the first model that describes the movement of pedestrians by means of repulsive forces that decay exponentially with distance. It is conceptually predated by the model of Hirai and Tarui (see Sec. 3.2) which uses algebraic forces. The SFM was first developed in the 1990s, and since then it has been widely used to study pedestrian dynamics in various settings. The SFM allows for the simulation of pedestrian behavior and the prediction of crowd movement in different scenarios, such as evacuation from a building. Over the years, it has undergone various modifications and enhancements to improve its accuracy in simulating pedestrian dynamics and to address its difficulties in describing certain scenarios (see Section 3.3). Researchers have added physical forces (e.g. friction), improved numerical efficiency, and introduced mechanisms such as the "respect mechanism" [81] to improve the performance especially in crowded environments. 

In [69], an approach for calibration of the SFM by using experimental measurements to adjust the repulsive force was proposed. The updated repulsive force takes into account both the distance and the angle between the direction of movement and the vector that connects the positions of the two pedestrians. This approach of considering both distance and angle dependencies is commonly used in other models, starting from [40], in order to account for the anisotropic behavior of pedestrians. Recent results show that rescaling of the social force model yields in a first-order Optimal Velocity model if inertia is neglected [68]. This over-damped limit of SFM (see also Appendix D) can formally performed by letting the social forces becoming corrections to the optimal velocity. The exponential Weidmann pedestrian OV model [113] is then recovered if we restrict interactions to the next neighbor. 

However, it is important to note that these measurements were primarily done with only two pedestrians and then extrapolated to a crowd with multiple individuals, which assumes that the superposition of forces can be applied in this context. This assumption, however, will turn out to be problematic and experimentally not sustainable (see Section 3.3).

Title: A Formal Framework for Mobile Robot Patrolling in Arbitrary Environments with Adversaries
Snippet: Game theoretical approaches model a patrolling situation as a non-cooperative game [10] between the patrollers and the intruder. Two are the main approaches proposed in the literature for robotic patrolling with adversaries: one does not explicitly model the preferences of the adversaries [7], whereas the other one does [8,9]. Before reviewing these approaches, we note that similar strategic problems have been addressed in the pursuit-evasion field (e.g., [11,12]) and by hide-and-seek approaches [13], where a hider can hide itself in a vertex of an arbitrary graph and a seeker can move along the graph to seek the hider within a finite time. However, some assumptions, including the fact that the evader's goal is only to avoid capture and not to enter an area of interest, make the pursuit-evasion problem not directly comparable with the patrolling problem we are considering.

We now describe the main approach that does not model the intruder preferences. In [7], the authors consider the problem of patrolling a perimeter divided in cells, each one giving access to an area of interest, by employing a team of synchronized mobile robots acting in turns. The perimeter is considered as a ring whose cells require the same time, say d turns, to the intruder for entering. The robots keep an evenly separated formation by moving in a coordinated fashion. (The authors show that this patrolling configuration is optimal for their settings.) The patrolling strategy does not depend on the specific cells in which the robots are. The authors present different movement models for the robots. In the simplest one, all the robots move clockwise with probability p or move counterclockwise with probability 1 − p. In the most realistic movement model, all the patrollers move to the cells they are headed to with probability p and reverse their heading, staying in their current cells for a turn, with probability 1 − p. The intruder is assumed to be in the position to repeatedly observe the actions of the patroller (staying hidden), derive a correct belief over the patroller's strategy, and attack the cell for which the probability to be captured is the smallest one (this is because no preferences over the cells are considered). The optimal patrolling strategy amounts to choose the value of p that maximizes the minimum expected utility for the patrollers or

Title: Analysis and Augmentation of Human Performance on Telerobotic Search Problems
Snippet: There are three major models for spatial search: graph-based models, polygonal models, and Bayesian models. The graphbased model is based on the assumption that sensing and robots' motion can be treated as discrete quantities, making it possible to model the problem using a graph [8]. The polygonal model is based on the assumptions that the environment can be described through polygons, the range of sensors is infinite, and the field of view is 360 degrees [9]. The challenge is either to cover the whole environment by using the fewest sensors, or maximize the coverage by using a fixed number of sensors. Bayesian search is based on the assumption that the search space can be divided into finite cells/graphs and that each cell represents individual probability of detection [10]. The goal is to determine the optimal path to find the target(s), according to the probability distribution function (PDF) [11], [12]. Although each model relies on different assumptions and uses different objectives, viewed from a computational standpoint, they are all NP-hard problems [8]- [10]. 

Another way to maximize the coverage in the search space is by using cognitive-based adaptive optimization (CAO), which was proposed for optimization problems that had unknown objective functions but available sensing measurements [13]. It was applied to maximize the coverage using a fixed number of robots equipped with sensors in 3D environments [14]. The CAO framework gives coverage results without prior information about either the objective function or the environment [15] and works even if the environment is non-convex. However, in contrast to the aforementioned approaches, CAO cannot provide theoretical lower bounds on coverage. 

To take advantage of Bayesian models and the submodularity found in coverage problems, the grid map approach was proposed [7]: Coverage is computed combining the measurements from sensor positions, real sensing scans, and a known grid map. This problem was shown to be NP-hard [6]. Since maximal coverage is a submodular maximization problem, greedy algorithms are able to achieve solutions over (1-1/e) of the optimum. The advantage of this approach is that it provides a near-optimal guarantee using real sensor specifications (e.g., range and angle) and works even in cluttered environments.

Title: Active SLAM Utility Function Exploiting Path Entropy
Snippet: In this article, we have presented a utility function that selects the most favorable frontier goal location within an occupancy grid map for a reliable A-SLAM with an area coverage task. The proposed utility function incorporates path entropy to select the frontier goal location which has the highest amount of unknown cells within its path thus maximizing the area coverage. Using simulation and experimental results on publicly available environment maps we have proved the efficiency of our approach as compared to similar methods. As a future prospective, we plan to incorporate our method in a multi-robot scenario utilizing efficient frontier-sharing for maximum environment exploration.

Title: Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes in Robotics: A Survey
Snippet: A POMDP planner produces waypoints for a robot in [32], [52], deferring the traversal task to a lower level controller. Hierarchical POMDPs for visual problem solving are suggested in [144], [174], and a tree with multiple levels of progressively finerscale POMDPs is considered in [48]. A hybrid approach that uses an MDP model when a target is visible and a POMDP model when not is proposed in [172]. Hiearchical methods can address long planning horizons by planning on a higher level of abstraction. 

Discretization of the target state allows the application of discrete POMDP solvers to tracking and search problems. Grid-based discretization is used in, e.g., [48], [99], [32], [129]. State space factorization is used for object oriented POMDPs in [160], [175], and mixed observability -the fact that some factors of the state may be fully observable -is exploited in [108], [56]. 

Others directly solve continuous-state tracking and search problems [27], [97], [11], [29]. Multi-modality in dynamics that differ depending on the state is considered in [27]. In [97] Bayesian optimization is applied to directly search for policies while simulation rollouts are used to evaluate policies. For unmanned aerial vehicle collision avoidance with a continuousstate formulation, [11] proposes to use Monte Carlo value iteration. Up to ten continuous state space dimensions in a search problem are handled by the recent variational method that parametrizes the POMDP using Gaussian mixtures [29]. 

Using image data with POMDP methods has been proposed for object search [174], [160], [170], [162], [175], tracking [142], exploration [97], [156], query answering [144], and object pose estimation [46], [7]. Instead of using images directly as observations in the POMDP which would be computationally prohibitively expensive, the images are abstracted into a low-dimensional representation.

Title: Learning Augmented, Multi-Robot Long-Horizon Navigation in Partially Mapped Environments
Snippet: Our multi-robot team is placed in a partially-mapped environment and tasked to find a point-goal located in unseen space in minimum expected cost (distance). Each robot is equipped with a planar laser scanner, which it uses to localize and build an accurate map of its local surroundings, a problem setting recently coined by Merlin et al. [17] as a Locally Observable Markov Decision Process (LOMDP). We assume lossless communication between robots so that all robots have an up-to-date partial map represented as an occupancy grid, as revealed by all members of the team and the poses of each robot-collectively, the team's belief b t . Planning is centrally coordinated, and so at each time step, the team's collective action a t specifies how each robot should move so as to make progress towards the unseen goal in an effort to minimize the expected cost.

Formally, we represent this problem as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process [18], [19] (POMDP). The expected cost Q under this model can be written via a belief space variant of the Bellman equation [20]:

is the cost accumulated by reaching belief state b t+1 from b t by taking action a t .

Title: A Design Framework of Exploration, Segmentation, Navigation, and Instruction (ESNI) for the Lifecycle of Intelligent Mobile Agents as a Method for Mapping an Unknown Built Environment
Snippet: The occupancy grid mapping refers to a representation that the continuous space in the environment was partitioned into different cells. Each cell has a Bayesian probability to indicate whether it is 1 (occupied) or 0 (empty). The representation is simply the situation of mobile robots and has become the dominant paradigm for embodied agent environments [39]. Occupancy grid mapping (OGM) method is used in module: segmentation to convert the simulation into grid map. Partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) [36] is a stochastic process that describes the discrete states for embodied agents in an environment. Formally, Markov decision process (MDP) is represented by a tuple, (S, A, T, R, γ), where S is all possible states, action domain is the set of all possible actions, transition function T = T(s, a, s ) = Probability(s'|s, a) is a set of conditional probabilities between states, R is a reward function, and γ is the discount factor. In MDP, all states are known to the agent to make an optimal solution, but in POMDP, the agent only has an observation O to relate the states. The tuple representing POMDP has additional two elements, O and Z: the observations space O is the set of all possible observations and Z is the set of conditional observation probabilities [37].

The advantage of this approach is that it provides a near-optimal guarantee using real sensor specifications (e.g., range and angle) and works even in cluttered environments.

A POMDP planner produces waypoints for a robot in [32], [52], deferring the traversal task to a lower level controller. Hierarchical POMDPs for visual problem solving are suggested in [144], [174], and a tree with multiple levels of progressively finerscale POMDPs is considered in [48]. A hybrid approach that uses an MDP model when a target is visible and a POMDP model when not is proposed in [172]. Hiearchical methods can address long planning horizons by planning on a higher level of abstraction. 

Discretization of the target state allows the application of discrete POMDP solvers to tracking and search problems. Grid-based discretization is used in, e.g., [48], [99], [32], [129]. State space factorization is used for object oriented POMDPs in [160], [175], and mixed observability -the fact that some factors of the state may be fully observable -is exploited in [108], [56]. 

Others directly solve continuous-state tracking and search problems [27], [97], [11], [29]. Multi-modality in dynamics that differ depending on the state is considered in [27]. In [97] Bayesian optimization is applied to directly search for policies while simulation rollouts are used to evaluate policies. For unmanned aerial vehicle collision avoidance with a continuousstate formulation, [11] proposes to use Monte Carlo value iteration. Up to ten continuous state space dimensions in a search problem are handled by the recent variational method that parametrizes the POMDP using Gaussian mixtures [29]. 

Using image data with POMDP methods has been proposed for object search [174], [160], [170], [162], [175], tracking [142], exploration [97], [156], query answering [144], and object pose estimation [46], [7]. Instead of using images directly as observations in the POMDP which would be computationally prohibitively expensive, the images are abstracted into a low-dimensional representation.

Each robot is equipped with a planar laser scanner, which it uses to localize and build an accurate map of its local surroundings, a problem setting recently coined by Merlin et al. [17] as a Locally Observable Markov Decision Process (LOMDP). We assume lossless communication between robots so that all robots have an up-to-date partial map represented as an occupancy grid, as revealed by all members of the team and the poses of each robot-collectively, the team's belief b t . Planning is centrally coordinated, and so at each time step, the team's collective action a t specifies how each robot should move so as to make progress towards the unseen goal in an effort to minimize the expected cost.

snippet.text: The occupancy grid mapping refers to a representation that the continuous space in the environment was partitioned into different cells. Each cell has a Bayesian probability to indicate whether it is 1 (occupied) or 0 (empty). The representation is simply the situation of mobile robots and has become the dominant paradigm for embodied agent environments [39]. Occupancy grid mapping (OGM) method is used in module: segmentation to convert the simulation into grid map. Partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) [36] is a stochastic process that describes the discrete states for embodied agents in an environment. Formally, Markov decision process (MDP) is represented by a tuple, (S, A, T, R, γ), where S is all possible states, action domain is the set of all possible actions, transition function T = T(s, a, s ) = Probability(s'|s, a) is a set of conditional probabilities between states, R is a reward function, and γ is the discount factor. In MDP, all states are known to the agent to make an optimal solution, but in POMDP, the agent only has an observation O to relate the states. The tuple representing POMDP has additional two elements, O and Z: the observations space O is the set of all possible observations and Z is the set of conditional observation probabilities [37].

documents.snippet:
There are three major models for spatial search: graph-based models, polygonal models, and Bayesian models. The graphbased model is based on the assumption that sensing and robots' motion can be treated as discrete quantities, making it possible to model the problem using a graph [8]. The polygonal model is based on the assumptions that the environment can be described through polygons, the range of sensors is infinite, and the field of view is 360 degrees [9]. The challenge is either to cover the whole environment by using the fewest sensors, or maximize the coverage by using a fixed number of sensors. Bayesian search is based on the assumption that the search space can be divided into finite cells/graphs and that each cell represents individual probability of detection [10]. The goal is to determine the optimal path to find the target(s), according to the probability distribution function (PDF) [11], [12]. Although each model relies on different assumptions and uses different objectives, viewed from a computational standpoint, they are all NP-hard problems [8]- [10]. 

Another way to maximize the coverage in the search space is by using cognitive-based adaptive optimization (CAO), which was proposed for optimization problems that had unknown objective functions but available sensing measurements [13]. It was applied to maximize the coverage using a fixed number of robots equipped with sensors in 3D environments [14]. The CAO framework gives coverage results without prior information about either the objective function or the environment [15] and works even if the environment is non-convex. However, in contrast to the aforementioned approaches, CAO cannot provide theoretical lower bounds on coverage. 

To take advantage of Bayesian models and the submodularity found in coverage problems, the grid map approach was proposed [7]: Coverage is computed combining the measurements from sensor positions, real sensing scans, and a known grid map. This problem was shown to be NP-hard [6]. Since maximal coverage is a submodular maximization problem, greedy algorithms are able to achieve solutions over (1-1/e) of the optimum. The advantage of this approach is that it provides a near-optimal guarantee using real sensor specifications (e.g., range and angle) and works even in cluttered environments.

problem: how to improve chunk retrieval with contrastive learning?
final_response:
# Overview: Why contrastive learning for chunk retrieval

Dense retrieval replaces lexical matching with continuous embeddings of queries and chunks, enabling semantic matching without exact keyword overlap and often surpassing BM25 in open-domain QA and passage search when paired with strong encoders and suitable negatives<cite id="ae11352f-0">In contrast to sparse lexical methods, dense retrieval uses continuous vector embeddings to represent queries and documents; DPR showed that BERT-based dual encoders trained on question–answer pairs can surpass BM25 in open-domain QA</cite><cite id="ae11352f-1">Dense retrieval embeds queries and documents into a shared space and computes similarity via an inner product; DPR trained on question–answer pairs outperformed sparse methods on benchmarks like Natural Questions and TriviaQA</cite>. However, performance hinges on contrastive objectives and negative sampling: early dense retrievers required large-scale labeled training data and careful negative strategies to avoid coarse-grained scoring and overfitting<cite id="ae11352f-0">Early models struggled with generalization, requiring large-scale labeled datasets and appropriate negative sampling strategies in contrastive learning</cite><cite id="ae11352f-1">Dense retrieval training often relies on contrastive learning distinguishing relevant and irrelevant pairs; dual encoders can be limited by coarse-grained similarity, and training stability and negative sampling are challenges</cite>.

# 1) Contrastive objectives and negative mining for retrieval

A core lever is how you form positives/negatives during training. Static negatives from lexical retrievers (e.g., BM25) can be challenging but risk overfitting; dynamic negatives refresh hard examples during training and typically improve contrastive optimization<cite id="721977ac-1">Static negatives like BM25 provide lexical contrast but can overfit; dynamic negatives introduced in ANCE and STAR adapt during training but require re-indexing and more compute</cite>. Practical strategies include:
- In-batch negatives: sample other documents from the same batch as negatives for a given query; focusing on the hardest in-batch positives can improve top-rank performance<cite id="721977ac-3">Hard in-batch negatives: sample most similar positives from other queries in the batch; hard negatives help top ranking while uniform negatives help bottom ranking</cite>.
- Uniform negatives across the corpus: complement hard negatives by sampling from the entire collection to diversify distribution and mitigate overfitting to in-batch sets<cite id="721977ac-3">Uniform negatives from the entire corpus provide complementary value to hard negatives and help bottom ranking while reducing overfitting</cite>.
- Large-batch dynamic negatives (ANCE-like): retrieve a large candidate set, compute nearest neighbors under current parameters as negatives, and update weights over time; warmup from uniform negatives to hard negatives and linearly decay uniform weights improves convergence<cite id="721977ac-3">Dynamic negatives: sample a large batch, select top-K most similar via current parameters without updating yet, combine with other sources, and warmup with uniform negatives while increasing hard-negative weight over time</cite><cite id="721977ac-4">ANCE selects hard negatives from the entire dataset per batch using retrieval and KNN; a self-learning pipeline iteratively fine-tunes with generated ANCE data, and pairwise training with circle loss is beneficial for hard negatives</cite>.
- Hard negative mining in stage-2 fine-tuning: after an initial retriever, sample top-k negatives with that retriever and train a second-stage encoder with contrastive loss to better align task-specific semantics<cite id="721977ac-2">Hard negative mining selects hard negatives from a dataset using a fine-tuned dense retriever and trains a second backbone encoder with contrastive cross-entropy loss, crucial for enhancing dense retrievers</cite>.
- Pairwise losses and specialized schedules: when positives and negatives are similar, pairwise losses (e.g., circle loss) and localized contrastive estimation can sharpen decision boundaries and align with retriever outputs<cite id="721977ac-4">Pairwise training with circle loss and localized contrastive estimation improve reranking when positives and negatives are nuanced; self- and teacher-based ANCE pipelines are used for bi-encoders and cross-encoders</cite><cite id="721977ac-0">Localized Contrastive Estimation demonstrated hard negatives improve cross-encoder reranking; even advanced pretraining like Condenser benefits from hard negatives</cite>.

Scalability tips: cross-batch memory and gradient caching allow large effective batch sizes for contrastive learning without prohibitive memory, enabling multi-positive training and better embeddings<cite id="ae11352f-0">RocketQA improved contrastive training with cross-batch memory for more diverse negative samples</cite><cite id="721977ac-4">Gao and Callan (2021) devised a gradient cache technique that upper-bounds peak memory usage for contrastive learning and can be adapted for co-Condenser pretraining</cite>.

# 2) Encoder designs tailored to chunks: dual encoders, late interaction, and efficiency

Dual-encoder bi-archs remain efficient for large corpora, with DPR as a canonical example for question–passage retrieval<cite id="ae11352f-1">DPR uses dual BERT encoders for questions and passages and trains on QA corpora</cite>. Late-interaction and multi-vector approaches mitigate the “representation bottleneck” by operating at token granularity:
- ColBERT retains token-level embeddings and aggregates token-wise similarities (e.g., MaxSim), enabling fine-grained matching and compatibility with vector similarity indexes for high-throughput retrieval<cite id="4a4e29a0-4">ColBERT postpones interaction until after encoding and uses MaxSim over token-level embeddings, enabling vector-similarity indexes and re-ranking with 170× speedups and reduced FLOPs while outperforming non-BERT baselines</cite><cite id="4a4e29a0-1">ColBERT computes per-query-token similarity to document tokens and sums max-similarities, preserving contextual richness while supporting offline document indexing and efficient retrieval</cite><cite id="4a4e29a0-3">ColBERT addresses the representation bottleneck by postponing interaction and generating token sequences, capturing fine-grained matching signals and outperforming bi-encoder baselines across benchmarks</cite>.
- Contriever extends this paradigm with contrastive pre-training on diverse, potentially unsupervised corpora, improving zero-shot retrieval and generalization; off-the-shelf Contriever often outperforms standard BERT baselines and reduces the benefit of data augmentation when strong contrastive pretraining is already present<cite id="b37dd068-0">Contriever uses contrastive learning to cluster query–document pairs, enabling zero-shot semantic search and question answering across domains</cite><cite id="b37dd068-1">Contriever is a stronger base model than BERT-BASE, consistently outperforming in zero-shot retrieval and post-MS MARCO fine-tuning; augmentation yields smaller gains for models with stronger contrastive pretraining like E5-Base</cite>.
- Practical multi-vector indexing: modern systems combine multiple retrieval modes (dense, sparse, multi-vector) to improve coverage and precision, especially for long contexts and multimodal retrieval<cite id="b37dd068-0">BGE-M3 integrates dense, lexical, and multi-vector retrieval for multilingual, multimodal retrieval</cite><cite id="4a4e29a0-2">Multi-vector dense models like ColBERT approximate cross-encoder joint attention with bi-encoder efficiency; Jina-ColBERT-v2 shows strong multilingual retrieval and supports long contexts, with Matryoshka Representation Loss enabling 50% lower dimension with insignificant performance loss</cite>.

# 3) Contrastive pretraining and data curation at scale

State-of-the-art pipelines emphasize two-stage training with large-scale pretraining and targeted fine-tuning:
- E5: large-batch contrastive pretraining with unlabeled data and in-batch negatives, followed by supervised fine-tuning with hard negative mining; this two-stage scheme improves adaptability across tasks and domains<cite id="b37dd068-2">E5 uses a two-stage contrastive approach: unlabeled pretraining with in-batch negatives at large scale, then supervised fine-tuning with hard negative mining</cite>.
- BGE: leverages RetroMAE-style pretraining to recover clean text from noisy inputs, then contrastive learning with large batch and in-batch negatives, plus instruction-based fine-tuning for broad task coverage<cite id="b37dd068-2">BGE uses RetroMAE to recover clean text from polluted embeddings, followed by contrastive pretraining with large batch in-batch negatives and task-specific fine-tuning</cite>.
- Nomic embedding models: combine unsupervised contrastive pretraining with supervised fine-tuning, longer contexts, and architectural tweaks (e.g., rotary positions, SwiGLU), supporting efficient scaling to very long inputs for embedding tasks<cite id="b37dd068-2">Nomic embedding models emphasize longer sequence lengths and efficient architectures, and employ both unsupervised contrastive pretraining and supervised contrastive fine-tuning to boost embedding performance</cite>.
- Quality filtering and consistency: consistency-based filtering and noise reduction during pretraining improve data quality and downstream retrieval effectiveness<cite id="b37dd068-2">To maintain data quality, CCPairs uses consistency-based filtering; BGE and related pipelines rely on large-batch in-batch negatives and hard negative mining to improve retrieval quality</cite>.

Enabling techniques:
- Gradient cache: allows near-constant peak memory for large-batch contrastive training and can be adapted to co-Condenser-like pretraining, making strong contrastive objectives feasible on limited accelerators<cite id="721977ac-4">A gradient cache technique upper-bounds peak memory in contrastive learning and adapts to co-Condenser pretraining</cite>.

# 4) Hybrid sparse–dense and multi-vector indexing

Combining lexical and dense signals often improves recall and robustness:
- Sparse priors + dense reranking: BM25/TF–IDF as coarse filters and DPR/ColBERT as rerankers have been effective; late interaction models can serve as re-rankers atop term-based indexes to capture nuanced semantic relations<cite id="4a4e29a0-4">ColBERT can serve as a re-ranker atop term-based retrieval, leveraging vector similarity indexes to retrieve top-k results efficiently and substantially improving recall over non-BERT baselines</cite><cite id="ae11352f-1">DPR’s coarse-grained similarity can be complemented by late-interaction or multi-view methods and advanced distillation to improve dense retrieval</cite>.
- Multi-vector indexes and ANN search: vector databases use approximate nearest neighbor search over high-dimensional embeddings, and multi-vector schemes (e.g., ColBERT) support richer similarity aggregation while retaining efficiency via precomputation and indexing<cite id="b37dd068-3">VectorDBs store and retrieve high-dimensional embeddings for semantic similarity via ANN search, and recent contrastive and multimodal pretraining improve embedding quality for RAG</cite><cite id="4a4e29a0-1">ColBERT’s token-level representations enable offline precomputation and vector-similarity indexes, supporting efficient large-scale retrieval</cite>.
- Key-aware/conditional retrieval: keyed caching and conditional retrieval pipelines can exploit query context to select appropriate retrieval backbones or stages, improving long-context and multistep retrieval scenarios<cite id="4a4e29a0-3">A conditional retrieval mechanism uses a first retriever to inform a second retriever that understands relationships among the original query, retrieved document, and candidates, addressing context-dependent relations</cite>.

# 5) Chunking and long-context strategies

How you form “chunks” matters as much as how you embed them:
- Chunking methods: fixed-length windows and sentence-based chunks are common; optimizing chunk boundaries for retrieval (e.g., content-aware indexing) can improve recall at query time<cite id="ae11352f-3">Fixed-length and sentence chunking are common; content-aware chunking can utilize retriever strengths and further improve retrieval performance</cite>.
- Long-context retrieval and multi-hop: late-interaction and multi-vector retrievers support longer contexts and fine-grained matching across evidence spans; mixed-objective learning at the sentence level can avoid contrastive conflicts in document-level training and yield stronger empirical results<cite id="ae11352f-2">A multi-task mixed-objective framework bypasses contrastive conflicts in document/passage-level contrastive learning by performing dense sentence-level retrieval, showing stronger empirical performance</cite><cite id="4a4e29a0-2">Jina-ColBERT-v2 targets long-context and multilingual retrieval, demonstrating strong performance across tasks</cite>.
- Domain adaptation: hard negatives mined from enterprise data and localized contrastive estimation can align retrieval with domain-specific patterns and user behavior, improving reranking when negatives match retriever outputs<cite id="721977ac-1">Static negatives can overfit domain-specific corpora; dynamic negatives and localized contrastive estimation improve performance and reranking alignment</cite><cite id="721977ac-0">Hard negatives integrated into cross-encoder training improved reranking accuracy when negatives aligned with retriever outputs</cite>.

# 6) Evaluation and ablations

Assess improvements with retrieval metrics and training analyses:
- Recall@k on passage/document retrieval benchmarks (e.g., MS MARCO, TREC CAR) and zero-shot transfer; late-interaction models like ColBERT show strong recall gains while maintaining low latency<cite id="4a4e29a0-4">ColBERT re-ranking delivers over 170× speedup and outperforms non-BERT baselines on MS MARCO and TREC CAR</cite>.
- Ablations on negative strategies: dynamic vs static negatives, uniform vs hard negatives, and pairwise vs pointwise losses; observe effects on top vs bottom ranks and convergence stability, with warmup schedules helping stability<cite id="721977ac-3">Hard negatives improve top ranks while uniform negatives help bottom ranks; dynamic negatives improve performance over static; warmup and weight linear updates aid convergence</cite><cite id="721977ac-4">Pairwise training with circle loss and ANCE-style pipelines improve hard-negative scenarios and cross-encoder alignment</cite>.
- Model scaling: stronger contrastively pre-trained encoders (E5, Contriever) may show smaller gains from additional augmentation, indicating diminishing marginal benefit of certain data strategies once pretraining is strong<cite id="b37dd068-1">Augmentation yields smaller improvements for strongly contrastive-pretrained models like E5-Base and Contriever compared to BERT-BASE</cite>.
- Long-context and multilingual coverage: multi-vector and multilingual models (e.g., Jina-ColBERT-v2, BGE-M3) improve across languages and modalities, and reduce storage with minimal accuracy loss via representation loss ablations<cite id="4a4e29a0-2">Jina-ColBERT-v2 supports long context and multilingual retrieval with Matryoshka Representation Loss enabling 50% smaller dimension with insignificant performance impact</cite><cite id="b37dd068-0">BGE and BGE-M3 are designed for multilingual and multimodal retrieval with contrastive training and hybrid retrieval methods</cite>.

# Practical recipe to improve chunk retrieval with contrastive learning

- Choose a backbone and objective:
  - Start with a strong dual-encoder and contrastive objective; if fine-grained matching is crucial, adopt late-interaction (ColBERT/Contriever/Jina-ColBERT) or multi-vector indexing<cite id="4a4e29a0-4">Late interaction and MaxSim in ColBERT improve fine-grained matching and efficiency</cite><cite id="b37dd068-0">Contriever uses contrastive learning to cluster query–document pairs for effective zero-shot retrieval</cite><cite id="4a4e29a0-2">Jina-ColBERT-v2 demonstrates strong multilingual/long-context retrieval with reduced dimensions via representation loss</cite>.
- Curate negatives and schedule training:
  - Use a mix of in-batch, uniform corpus, and large-batch dynamic negatives (ANCE-like) with warmup; consider pairwise losses (circle loss) and localized contrastive estimation for hard cases; adopt cross-batch memory and gradient cache to scale batch sizes<cite id="721977ac-3">Combine hard in-batch negatives, uniform negatives, and large-batch dynamic negatives with warmup schedules to improve top and bottom ranks and convergence</cite><cite id="721977ac-4">ANCE-style pipelines and pairwise training with circle loss improve hard-negative training and cross-encoder alignment</cite><cite id="ae11352f-0">Cross-batch memory (RocketQA) and gradient cache enable larger effective batch sizes for contrastive learning</cite>.
- Stage-wise pretraining and fine-tuning:
  - Follow two-stage pipelines: large-scale unsupervised contrastive pretraining with in-batch negatives, then supervised fine-tuning with hard negative mining and domain corpora; apply consistency filtering to reduce noisy pairs and improve data quality<cite id="b37dd068-2">Two-stage pipelines (unsupervised large-batch contrastive pretraining followed by supervised hard-negative fine-tuning) and consistency-based filtering improve retrieval quality</cite>.
- Combine sparse and dense signals:
  - Use BM25 or lexical indexes as coarse filters and dense retrievers (or late-interaction models) as re-rankers; build multi-vector indexes and employ ANN search for scalability and relevance cut support<cite id="4a4e29a0-4">Serve late-interaction retrievers as re-rankers atop term-based indexes using vector similarity search for high throughput and improved recall</cite><cite id="b37dd068-3">ANN search over vector embeddings underpins scalable semantic retrieval in RAG systems</cite>.
- Optimize chunking and long-context:
  - Design chunk boundaries to maximize retrieval signal (content-aware chunking); for multi-hop and long-context, leverage late-interaction and conditional retrieval to contextualize follow-up retrieval stages<cite id="ae11352f-3">Content-aware indexing and optimized chunking can improve retrieval performance beyond fixed-length or sentence-based chunking</cite><cite id="4a4e29a0-3">Conditional retrieval uses prior retrieved documents to inform a second-stage retriever that understands query–document–candidate relations</cite>.
- Evaluate and iterate:
  - Measure recall@k (10/100/1000) and zero-shot/generalization; ablate negative strategies and losses; for very strong pretrainings, test marginal gains from extra augmentation and instead focus on domain-specific negative mining and reranking<cite id="4a4e29a0-4">ColBERT’s recall gains and efficiency on MS MARCO and TREC CAR</cite><cite id="b37dd068-1">Augmentation benefits diminish for strongly contrastive-pretrained models; focus on domain-specific negatives and alignment</cite>.

# Trade-offs and implementation notes

- Compute and memory: dynamic negatives and large-batch training increase compute; gradient cache and cross-batch memory mitigate memory, enabling scalable contrastive learning<cite id="721977ac-1">Dynamic negatives improve training but require periodic re-indexing and more compute</cite><cite id="721977ac-4">Gradient cache upper-bounds peak memory for contrastive learning and adapts to co-Condenser pretraining</cite><cite id="ae11352f-0">Cross-batch memory in RocketQA increases diversity of negatives</cite>.

Title: Hard Negative Mining for Domain-Specific Retrieval in Enterprise Systems
Snippet: The role of hard negatives in training dense retrieval models has been widely studied. Static negatives, such as BM25 (Robertson and Walker, 1994), provide lexical similarity but fail to capture semantic relevance, often leading to overfitting (Qu et al., 2020). Dynamic negatives, introduced in ANCE (Xiong et al., 2020) and STAR (Zhan et al., 2021), adapt during training to provide more challenging contrasts but require significant computational resources due to periodic re-indexing. Our framework addresses these limitations by dynamically identifying semantically challenging negatives using clustering and dimensionality reduction, ensuring scalability and adaptability. 

Further studies have explored advanced methods for negative sampling in cross-encoder models (Meghwani, 2024). Localized Contrastive Estimation (LCE) (Guo et al., 2023) integrates hard negatives into cross-encoder training, improving the reranking performance when negatives align with the output of the retriever. Similarly, (Pradeep et al., 2022) demonstrated the importance of hard negatives even when models undergo advanced pretraining techniques, such as condenser (Gao and Callan, 2021). Our work builds on these efforts by offering a scalable approach, which can be applied to any domain-heavy enterprise data.

Title: ColPali: Efficient Document Retrieval with Vision Language Models
Snippet: ColBERT (Contextualized Late Interaction over BERT) is a retrieval model designed to balance speed and effectiveness in information retrieval tasks (Khattab & Zaharia, 2020). Traditional retrieval models are typically categorized based on their type of interaction: either processing queries and documents independently for efficiency (bi-encoders) or jointly to capture rich contextual relationships (crossencoders). ColBERT combines the advantages of both approaches through a novel late interaction mechanism. 

Queries and documents are encoded separately using BERT, enabling offline pre-computation of document representations for scalability. Instead of pooling embeddings into a single vector, ColBERT retains token-level embeddings and employs a MaxSim operator to compute fine-grained similarity scores. For each query token, the model determines the maximum similarity with document tokens, summing these scores to compute relevance. 

This architecture preserves the contextual richness of deep language models while significantly improving computational efficiency. By delaying the interaction step, ColBERT supports vector similarity indexing, facilitating end-to-end retrieval from large collections without prohibitive costs. Empirical evaluations on passage search datasets demonstrate that ColBERT achieves competitive effectiveness compared to existing BERT-based models (Devlin et al., 2018), while executing queries orders of magnitude faster and with drastically reduced computational requirements.
</snippet>

Title: Extracting Document Relations from Search Corpus by Marginalizing over User Queries
Snippet: Dense Passage Retrieval (DPR) [6] revolutionized information retrieval by replacing traditional sparse retrieval methods (such as BM25) with dense vector representations learned through deep learning. DPR encodes queries and passages into dense vectors using dual-encoder architectures, typically based on BERT [5], and performs retrieval by computing similarity in the embedding space. 

While DPR and similar bi-encoder approaches achieve strong retrieval performance, they suffer from the representation bottleneck problem: all information about a passage must be compressed into a single dense vector. This limitation led to the development of late interaction models such as ColBERT [7]. 

ColBERT (Contextualized Late Interaction over BERT) addresses the representation bottleneck by postponing the interaction between query and document representations until after encoding. Instead of producing single vectors, ColBERT generates a sequence of contextualized embeddings for each token in both queries and documents. The similarity between a query q and document d is computed as: Score(q, d) 

where 

q and E (j) d are the contextualized embeddings of the i-th query token and j-th document token, respectively. 

This late interaction mechanism allows ColBERT to capture fine-grained matching signals between query and document tokens. ColBERT has demonstrated superior performance across various retrieval benchmarks and has been adopted in numerous applications requiring high-quality document retrieval. 

The choice of ColBERT as our retrieval backbone is motivated by its ability to capture nuanced relationships between queries and documents, which is crucial for our conditional retrieval mechanism where the second retriever must understand the relationship between the original query, the first retrieved document, and candidate documents for the second retrieval step. Our approach addresses these limitations by leveraging the query marginalization process in MC-RAG to discover document relationships in an unsupervised manner, without requiring predefined relationship types or labeled training data. The conditional retrieval mechanism allows us to capture context-dependent relationships that vary based on user queries and information needs.

Title: UncertaintyRAG: Span-Level Uncertainty Enhanced Long-Context Modeling for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
Snippet: There has been extensive research on Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), with one critical aspect being the development of a robust representation model that effectively clusters sentence information with query information in high-dimensional space. In our work, we compare our approach with several influential and open-source methods from prior studies. This section provides a detailed overview of these methods. 

Contriever (Izacard et al., 2021) is a dense retrieval model designed to improve performance and generalization through unsupervised training on diverse datasets. It uses contrastive learning to generate embeddings, bringing semantically related query-document pairs closer together while pushing irrelevant pairs apart. This method allows Contriever to effectively handle tasks like semantic search and question answering, even in zero-shot scenarios. By relying on unsupervised learning, it adapts well to various domains without needing annotated data, making it versatile for information retrieval tasks. BGE (Xiao et al., 2023b) is a large-scale multilingual text embedding model developed by the Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence (BAAI), designed for tasks such as semantic retrieval and ranking across multiple languages. Pre-trained on extensive multilingual datasets, BGE encodes text into dense vector representations optimized for semantic similarity tasks, where the relationship between query and document pairs is captured by comparing their vector embeddings. 

The model is primarily trained using contrastive learning, which teaches it to minimize the distance between embeddings of relevant query-document pairs while maximizing the distance for irrelevant pairs. The RAG system converts raw data from multiple modalities, including text, images, and audio, into high-dimensional vector embeddings using pretrained models such as OpenAI's Ada [16], Cohere [3], Sentence-BERT [19], CLIP [18], and BLIP [11]. Unlike traditional keyword-based retrieval, which relies on exact term matching, vectorization allows for semantic similarity search by mapping data points into a shared continuous space where proximity reflects conceptual similarity [14]. Recent advancements in contrastive learning [5] and multimodal pretraining [1] have further improved the quality and generalizability of vector representations. These models leverage large-scale self-supervised objectives to produce embeddings that capture deeper semantic relationships across diverse data types. As a result, vectorization is now a fundamental component of modern retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems. 

When a user submits a query, it is vectorized using the same embedding model. The query vector is then used to retrieve the most relevant vectors from the database using approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search [8,13,10]. Unlike exact k-nearest neighbor (k-NN) search [4], which requires a linear scan or an exact tree-based search over all data points, ANN algorithms trade off a small amount of retrieval accuracy for significant gains in efficiency.
