snippet.text:
After NeRFs [22], 3D Gaussian Splatting [15] has recently become very popular for capturing a 3D scene and rendering it from novel points of view. 3D Gaussian Splatting optimizes the positions, orientations, appearances (represented as spherical harmonics), and alpha blending of many tiny 3D Gaussians on the basis of a set of training images of the scene to capture the scene geometry and appearance. Because rendering the Gaussians is much faster than rendering a neural field, 3D Gaussian Splatting is much faster than NeRFs and can capture a scene in a few minutes. 

While the Gaussians allow very realistic renderings of the scene, it is still however challenging to extract the sur-Figure 2. Our algorithm can extract a highly detailed mesh from any 3D Gaussian Splatting scene [15] within minutes on a single GPU (top: Renderings of our meshes without texture, bottom: Renderings of the meshes with bound Gaussians). 

face of the scene from them: As shown in Figure 3, after optimization by 3D Gaussian Splatting, the Gaussians do not take an ordered structure in general and do not correspond well to the actual surface of the scene. In addition to the surface itself, it is also often desirable to represent the scene as a mesh, which remains the representation of choice in many pipelines: A mesh-based representation allows for powerful tools for editing, sculpting, animating, and relighting the scene. Because the Gaussians after Gaussian Splatting are unstructured, it is very challenging to extract a mesh from them. Note that this is also challenging with NeRFs albeit for different reasons. 

In this paper, we first propose a regularization term that encourages the Gaussians to be well distributed over the scene surface so that the Gaussians capture much better the scene geometry, as shown in Figure 3. Our approach is to derive a volume density from the Gaussians under the assumption that the Gaussians are flat and well distributed over the scene surface. By minimizing the difference between this density and the actual one computed from the Gaussians during optimization, we encourage the 3D Gaussians to represent well the surface geometry.

problem: What are the state-of-the-art work for 3D Mesh Generation from Multi-view 2d images?
final_response:
# Scope and Definitions

We consider “3D mesh generation from multi-view 2D images” as recovering a watertight triangle mesh (with textures, when available) of an object or scene from two or more calibrated RGB images. Methods span classical photogrammetry/MVS with post-processing meshing, neural radiance/geometry fields that require surface extraction, and end-to-end or two-stage learning pipelines that synthesize auxiliary views and reconstruct meshes. Recent work emphasizes large 3D reconstruction models (LRMs), differentiable rendering, and Gaussian/implicit representations, with meshing achieved via Marching Cubes from SDFs, Poisson/TSDF fusion, or specialized post-processing and mesh-regularized optimization.

# Taxonomy and Trends (2022–2025)

Recent surveys and holistic models emphasize a shift from multi-stage photogrammetry/MVS toward unified learning-based pipelines and generalizable neural reconstruction. Classical pipelines integrate SfM, MVS, and mesh surface extraction; deep methods seek higher efficiency and accuracy while avoiding the cost and sensitivity of per-scene optimization, often leveraging neural volumetric representations and differentiable rendering to output meshes directly or near-directly.<cite id="85dc42c9-3">Classically, multi-view mesh reconstruction is addressed via SfM, MVS, and mesh extraction; recent deep methods target higher efficiency/accuracy, using neural volumetric representations and differentiable rendering to output meshes; per-scene optimization with radiance fields can be converted to meshes (Marching Cubes) but quality is not guaranteed, motivating SDF or direct mesh extraction</cite> Learning-based two-stage strategies generate consistent multi-view images (often with diffusion) and then feed them to a reconstruction model, improving multi-view consistency and mesh fidelity on large-scale datasets such as Google Scanned Objects and Objaverse.<cite id="85dc42c9-0">A two-stage design generates main views and synthesizes additional views with a diffusion-based dense view interpolation module, then reconstructs a high-quality mesh via a tri-plane-based LRM; experiments on GSO and Objaverse show quantitative and qualitative improvements in reconstruction accuracy, multi-view consistency, and fidelity</cite> Holistic frameworks also couple NeRF refinement with differentiable mesh representations and per-instance texture refinement to enhance mesh quality end-to-end.<cite id="85dc42c9-1">A holistic design modifies an LRM and fine-tunes a NeRF with a differentiable mesh representation, plus an efficient per-instance texture refinement process, to enhance mesh quality from multi-view images</cite> Multi-view diffusion plus 3D latent/decoder approaches first build a consistent latent 3D code and then synthesize novel views and a mesh, emphasizing continuity, isotropy, and occlusion consistency.<cite id="85dc42c9-4">A 4-view input is used to establish a consistent 3D latent code conditioned on multi-view images; a 3D decoder performs novel view synthesis informed by aligned representations and occluded detail features; the goal is continuity/isotropy of edges, occlusion delineation, and physical realism</cite>

# Neural Radiance/Geometry Fields and Mesh Extraction

NeRF-style radiance fields and their variants are a core SOTA scene representation for multi-view 3D reconstruction; meshes are typically extracted from SDFs or by isosurfacing and post-processing. Many works train an SDF-optimized neural field and use Marching Cubes to get an initial mesh, followed by refinement to reduce artifacts and improve detail.<cite id="314da0ea-2">NeRF and variants learn volumetric scene functions from multi-view images; recent studies adopt SDF to represent surfaces and extract meshes via Marching Cubes or Dual Contouring, but post-extraction can lose detail and introduce artifacts; refinement methods like NVdiffrec and NeRF2Mesh improve quality but face instabilities and limited connectivity adjustments</cite> Practical pipelines still commonly convert NeRF-derived fields to meshes with marching cubes and visualize the results, underscoring the centrality of this extraction step.<cite id="314da0ea-0">Meshes are extracted from NeRF results with the marching cubes algorithm, illustrating standard practice for converting NeRF reconstructions to meshes</cite> Optimization tricks such as bisection steps in Marching Cubes and Eikonal-style constraints are explored to mitigate staircase artifacts from imperfect SDFs and improve mesh quality at convergence.<cite id="314da0ea-1">Augmenting Marching Cubes with multi-step bisection root finding improves surface extraction quality for imperfect SDFs; authors note the need to re-examine objectives like Eikonal constraints for better mesh quality</cite>

Beyond NeRF, learning-based MVS and implicit surface reconstruction integrate depth estimation and surface fusion, often culminating in Poisson or TSDF-based meshes, but face challenges with occlusion, sensor noise, and global consistency across redundant stages.<cite id="a57243b0-1">Learning-based MVS methods have advanced reconstruction but still grapple with complex computations and global inconsistencies from depth estimation, filtering, fusion, and surface reconstruction stages</cite><cite id="a57243b0-4">Traditional MVS yields dense point clouds that are triangulated or fused via TSDF and Poisson reconstruction to meshes; these classical techniques struggle with incomplete data, occlusions, and noise, producing partial or hole-ridden reconstructions</cite> Modern pipelines also note that per-scene optimization for radiance/implicit fields can be slow, motivating feed-forward generalizable models that avoid dense per-object optimization while maintaining high fidelity.<cite id="85dc42c9-3">Recent methods based on NeRF reconstruct volumetric radiance fields with per-scene optimization; while convertible to meshes, they require significant time; feed-forward reconstruction models trained on large-scale 3D datasets offer speed and generalization</cite>

# Gaussian Splatting and Surface Extraction Innovations

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) and its variants have rapidly advanced multi-view 3D reconstruction with fast training and real-time rendering; extracting high-quality meshes from millions of Gaussians remains challenging, prompting specialized meshing techniques. SuGaR introduces a surface-aligned Gaussian regularization and Poisson reconstruction from rendered depth maps to obtain editable meshes within minutes, outperforming SDF-based mesh extraction in speed and rendering quality.<cite id="46f3a972-1">SuGaR regularizes 3D Gaussians to align with surfaces and uses Poisson reconstruction on rendered depth maps to extract meshes; retrieval is done within minutes compared to hours for SDF-based methods while improving rendering quality, enabling editing and refinement</cite> GOF proposes deriving Gaussian Opacity Fields directly from 3D Gaussians to enable level-set surface extraction and a tetrahedron-grid meshing scheme, avoiding Poisson/TSDF fusion and addressing fine geometry and background reconstruction issues reported in prior Gaussian-based methods.<cite id="46f3a972-0">GOF derives Gaussian Opacity Fields consistent with volume rendering to enable direct level-set surface extraction and tetrahedron-grid meshing without Poisson/TSDF; prior Gaussian-based methods faced fine geometry and background reconstruction challenges</cite><cite id="46f3a972-3">3DGS demonstrates photorealistic NVS with efficient training; SuGaR and 2DGS extend to meshing via Poisson and TSDF fusion, respectively, but struggle with fine-grained geometry and background regions due to inconsistencies between mesh extraction and volume rendering; GOF targets these issues</cite> MILo introduces a mesh-in-the-loop training objective that differentiably extracts and backpropagates mesh geometry/connectivity during Gaussian splatting optimization, yielding higher-quality meshes with far fewer vertices while preserving detail, which improves practicality for downstream applications.<cite id="46f3a972-4">MILo differentiably extracts and optimizes a mesh (vertices and connectivity) from Gaussian parameters during optimization, enforcing bidirectional consistency and producing meshes with almost 10× fewer vertices while preserving fine details, benefiting applications like simulation and animation</cite>

# Multi-View Stereo and Photogrammetry Pipelines (and Deep MVS)

Classical multi-view pipelines estimate per-view depth maps and fuse them via TSDF or Poisson reconstruction to obtain meshes; modern deep MVS methods seek efficiency and quality by operating on points or features and integrating visibility reasoning. Point-based architectures like VA-Point-MVSNet process scenes as point clouds with visibility-aware feature aggregation and iterative refinement, improving time/memory efficiency and reconstruction quality on benchmarks.<cite id="a57243b0-0">VA-Point-MVSNet processes scenes as point clouds with a visibility-aware multi-view feature aggregation module and iterative refinement (PointFlow), improving reconstruction quality and time/memory efficiency on synthetic and real data</cite> Surveys and overviews emphasize that while learning-based MVS advances accuracy, the classical pipeline (dense correspondences → triangulation → surface reconstruction) still dominates and motivates integrated, end-to-end approaches to reduce redundancy and inconsistencies.<cite id="a57243b0-1">Traditional MVS estimates per-view depth and fuses via Poisson or Delaunay triangulation; learning-based MVS has advanced but faces complexity and global inconsistencies from depth, filtering, fusion, and surface steps</cite> Practical multi-sensor fusion and real-time systems often rely on TSDF fusion and Poisson reconstruction for robust meshing, though they can yield partial or holey surfaces under occlusion and noise, motivating combined or learned fusion strategies.<cite id="a57243b0-4">Volumetric TSDF/kinect fusion yields real-time reconstruction; Poisson surface reconstruction from oriented point clouds produces smooth watertight surfaces; however, incomplete data and occlusions lead to partial or hole-ridden meshes</cite>

# Learning-Based Multi-View Image-to-Mesh Pipelines

State-of-the-art pipelines increasingly combine generative models with 3D reconstruction. Two-stage strategies generate dense, consistent multi-view images (including auxiliary views) and then reconstruct meshes using large 3D reconstruction models. Examples include diffusion-based dense view interpolation feeding a tri-plane-based LRM for high-quality mesh and texture, and latent 3D generative models that synthesize novel views from a 3D code and then a mesh.<cite id="85dc42c9-0">A diffusion-based dense view interpolation module synthesizes coherent intermediate views that, together with main views, are processed by a tri-plane-based LRM to reconstruct high-quality geometry and textures</cite><cite id="85dc42c9-4">A consistent 3D latent code is established from multi-view inputs; a 3D decoder performs novel view synthesis and supports mesh reconstruction with attention to edge continuity, occlusion, and realism</cite> Holistic systems also refine meshes and textures via differentiable rendering and per-instance optimization tied to NeRFs, enhancing realism and editability.<cite id="85dc42c9-1">An LRM plus NeRF fine-tuned with a differentiable mesh representation and per-instance texture refinement improves multi-view-to-3D mesh quality</cite> In broader generative modeling from videos/images, NeRF-to-mesh conversion remains standard (marching cubes), while research explores improved SDF optimization and mesh extraction to reduce artifacts for downstream use.<cite id="314da0ea-0">NeRF reconstructions are converted to meshes via marching cubes in video-to-3D generative pipelines</cite><cite id="314da0ea-2">SDF-based NeRF refinements and mesh extraction (Marching Cubes/Dual Contouring) can suffer detail loss and artifacts, motivating specialized refinement and extraction strategies</cite>

# Domain-Specific: Faces and Objects

For faces and hands, multi-view 2D-to-3D methods often leverage strong shape priors and templates, combined with multi-view consistency and neural rendering. Large reconstruction models and differentiable mesh representations are used to refine geometry and textures from multi-view images, improving realism and enabling per-instance texture optimization.<cite id="85dc42c9-1">A holistic multi-view-to-3D design with differentiable mesh representation and per-instance texture refinement enhances mesh quality</cite> In broader 3D object settings, sparse-view and multi-view diffusion strategies synthesize auxiliary views and feed them to mesh LRM backbones to increase coverage and reduce multi-view inconsistency, which is a common failure mode for single-image-only reconstructions.<cite id="85dc42c9-0">Dense view interpolation addresses multi-view inconsistency and provides better constraints for mesh reconstruction from sparse inputs</cite>

# Practical Trade-offs and Meshing Choices

Choice of meshing strategy strongly affects mesh quality and speed. SDF optimization with Marching Cubes/Dual Contouring is widely used but can suffer from staircase artifacts and detail loss; improvements include bisection-based extraction and Eikonal constraints, and post-/joint optimization of meshes with the neural field or Gaussians for better surface quality and editability.<cite id="314da0ea-1">Bisection-based Marching Cubes improves mesh extraction from imperfect SDFs; authors argue for re-examining objectives such as Eikonal constraints</cite><cite id="314da0ea-2">Post-extraction artifacts and limited connectivity adjustments motivate mesh refinement (e.g., NVdiffrec, NeRF2Mesh), though instabilities can arise from random SDF initialization</cite> Poisson and TSDF fusion are robust and yield watertight meshes from dense depth or point clouds but can produce noisy or low-detail surfaces in background regions and thin structures, especially under sparse or occluded views; Gaussian-based methods with Poisson/TSDF or new opacity-field and mesh-in-the-loop approaches (SuGaR, GOF, MILo) aim to overcome these limitations by aligning primitives to surfaces or integrating mesh gradients during optimization.<cite id="46f3a972-3">Poison/TSDF-based meshing from Gaussian splatting or depth maps can struggle with fine geometry and background regions due to inconsistent objectives; GOF proposes opacity fields and tailored meshing to address these issues</cite><cite id="46f3a972-4">MILo’s mesh-in-the-loop optimization reduces vertex count while preserving detail, improving practicality</cite><cite id="46f3a972-1">SuGaR achieves fast, editable meshes via surface-aligned Gaussians and Poisson reconstruction, outperforming SDF-based extraction in speed and rendering quality</cite> Finally, per-scene optimization provides high fidelity but is slow, while feed-forward generalizable models deliver speed and scalability at the cost of potential detail loss and sensitivity to training data coverage.<cite id="85dc42c9-3">Per-scene NeRF optimization yields high-quality radiance fields but is time-consuming; feed-forward generalizable models trained on large 3D datasets provide speed and generalization</cite>

# Representative SOTA Methods and What They Offer

- NeRF/SDF pipelines with improved mesh extraction and refinement: marching-cubes-based extraction with bisection steps; SDF optimization with Eikonal-like constraints; refinement via differentiable surface rendering or vertex/density optimization; widely used baseline for multi-view reconstructions and their meshed outputs.<cite id="314da0ea-0">NeRF-to-mesh conversion via marching cubes is standard in multi-view 3D pipelines</cite><cite id="314da0ea-1">Bisection Marching Cubes mitigates staircase artifacts in SDF extraction</cite><cite id="314da0ea-2">SDF-based NeRF surface extraction and refinement methods (NVdiffrec, NeRF2Mesh) target artifact reduction and better connectivity</cite>
- Gaussian Splatting with meshing innovations: 3DGS and 2DGS for fast NVS; SuGaR for surface-aligned Gaussians and Poisson-based mesh extraction with minutes-scale turnaround and better rendering/editability; GOF for opacity fields enabling direct level-set meshing; MILo for mesh-in-the-loop optimization with fewer vertices and high detail.<cite id="46f3a972-3">3DGS and 2DGS demonstrate efficient NVS with TSDF/Poisson-based meshing but face fine geometry/background challenges</cite><cite id="46f3a972-1">SuGaR enables fast, editable meshes from Gaussians using Poisson reconstruction and surface alignment</cite><cite id="46f3a972-0">GOF provides direct surface extraction from Gaussians without Poisson/TSDF, addressing prior limitations</cite><cite id="46f3a972-4">MILo integrates differentiable mesh extraction into Gaussian splatting optimization to improve mesh quality and efficiency</cite>
- Learning-based multi-view-to-mesh LRM pipelines: tri-plane-based mesh LRM fed by diffusion-synthesized views (CDI3D), holistic NeRF+mesh+texture refinement (GTR), and latent/decoder-based multi-view generative approaches (VI3DRM); all emphasize multi-view consistency, occlusion handling, and high-fidelity geometry/textures.<cite id="85dc42c9-0">CDI3D’s two-stage diffusion plus tri-plane LRM improves multi-view consistency and mesh quality on GSO/Objaverse</cite><cite id="85dc42c9-1">GTR refines geometry and texture via NeRF with differentiable mesh and per-instance texture optimization</cite><cite id="85dc42c9-4">VI3DRM builds consistent 3D latent codes and uses a 3D decoder for novel view synthesis and meshing with emphasis on occlusion and surface continuity</cite>
- Deep MVS and photogrammetry-derived meshing: visibility-aware point-based MVS (VA-Point-MVSNet) for efficient, high-quality point clouds; classical TSDF/Poisson meshing remains robust for many settings but can be partial under occlusion/noise; integrated learning-based MVS reduces redundancy and improves quality while retaining classical fusion strengths.<cite id="a57243b0-0">VA-Point-MVSNet improves reconstruction quality and efficiency via visibility-aware aggregation and iterative refinement</cite><cite id="a57243b0-4">TSDF and Poisson reconstruction produce robust meshes but can be incomplete under occlusions and noise, motivating fusion/learning advances</cite><cite id="a57243b0-1">Learning-based MVS advances accuracy but inherits complexity and inconsistency from classical stages</cite>

# Benchmarks and Evaluation

Recent SOTA papers evaluate on large-scale multi-view datasets such as Google Scanned Objects and Objaverse, as well as diverse real-world images, focusing on reconstruction accuracy, multi-view consistency, and visual fidelity for geometry and textures. Title: Gaussian Opacity Fields: Efficient Adaptive Surface Reconstruction in Unbounded Scenes
Snippet: Inspired by the impressive NVS performance of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [Kerbl et al. 2023], researchers have proposed to utilize 3D Gaussians for surface reconstruction. Recent efforts [Chen et al. 2023b;Yu et al. 2024b] have integrated 3D Gaussians with neural implicit surfaces, optimizing a Signed Distance Function (SDF) network and 3D Gaussians jointly. While these approaches mark some advancements, they also inherit the shortcomings associated with implicit surfaces as previously discussed. Other studies have focused on surface extraction from optimized Gaussian primitives through post-processing techniques [Dai et al. 2024;Guédon and Lepetit 2023;Huang et al. 2024;Turkulainen et al. 2024]. Notably, SuGaR [Guédon and Lepetit 2023] and GaussianSurfels [Dai et al. 2024] adopt Poisson surface reconstruction [Kazhdan and Hoppe 2013] to extract meshes from rendered depth maps. Meanwhile, 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) [Huang et al. 2024] employs TSDF fusion for this purpose. Though these methods achieve improved reconstructions, they face challenges in capturing fine-grained geometry and adequately reconstructing background areas. In this work, we derive Gaussian Opacity Fields directly from 3D Gaussians. Our GOF is consistent with the volume rendering process for rendering RGB images. It enables direct surface extraction by identifying a level set, without resorting to Poisson reconstruction and TSDF fusion. Additionally, we propose a tetrahedron grid-based technique for mesh extraction, resulting in adaptive and detailed meshes.

Title: SuGaR: Surface-Aligned Gaussian Splatting for Efficient 3D Mesh Reconstruction and High-Quality Mesh Rendering
Snippet: We propose a method to allow precise and extremely fast mesh extraction from 3D Gaussian Splatting [15]. Gaussian Splatting has recently become very popular as it yields realistic rendering while being significantly faster to train than NeRFs. It is however challenging to extract a mesh from the millions of tiny 3D Gaussians as these Gaussians tend to be unorganized after optimization and no method has been proposed so far. Our first key contribution is a regularization term that encourages the Gaussians to align well with the surface of the scene. We then introduce a method that exploits this alignment to extract a mesh from the Gaussians using Poisson reconstruction, which is fast, scalable, and preserves details, in contrast to the Marching Cubes algorithm usually applied to extract meshes from Neural SDFs. Finally, we introduce an optional refinement strategy that binds Gaussians to the surface of the mesh, and jointly optimizes these Gaussians and the mesh through Gaussian splatting rendering. This enables easy editing, sculpting, animating, and relighting of the Gaussians by manipulating the mesh instead of the Gaussians themselves. Retrieving such an editable mesh for realistic rendering is done within minutes with our method, compared to hours with the state-of-the-art method on SDFs, while providing a better rendering quality.

Title: R2-Mesh: Reinforcement Learning Powered Mesh Reconstruction via Geometry and Appearance Refinement
Snippet: NeRF (Mildenhall et al. 2020) and its variants (Müller et al. 2022;Chen et al. 2022;Fridovich-Keil et al. 2022;Sun, Sun, and Chen 2022) significantly advance 3D scene reconstruction through a volumetric scene function learned from multi-view images. Some works explore the possibility of generating meshes simultaneously during the training of NeRF models. A notable example is MobileNeRF (Chen et al. 2023). However, the generated polygonal mesh lacks surface smoothness since the mesh topology is fixed at the initial stage. Most recent studies (Wang et al. 2021(Wang et al. , 2023;;Long et al. 2022;Yariv et al. 2021;Oechsle, Peng, and Geiger 2021;Munkberg et al. 2022;Hasselgren, Hofmann, and Munkberg 2022) adopt SDF to represent geometric surfaces. Some of these works (Wang et al. 2021(Wang et al. , 2023;;Long et al. 2022;Yariv et al. 2021;Oechsle, Peng, and Geiger 2021) leverage the ray-marching volumetric rendering formula of NeRF, optimize the SDF to achieve accurate scene representations. They then apply classical isosurfacing algorithms, such as Marching Cubes (Lorensen and Cline 1998) and Dual Contouring (Ju et al. 2002), to extract the mesh. However, this post-extraction leads to loss of detail and surface artifacts that degrade the quality of the extracted mesh. Some studies conduct mesh refinement processes to further enhance the geometric quality. NVdiffrec (Munkberg et al. 2022) utilizes mesh differentiable surface rendering to optimize the SDF, but due to the random initialization of the SDF, it can lead to training instabilities and the presence of floating artifacts. NeRF2Mesh (Tang et al. 2023) performs mesh refinement by optimizing the vertices' positions and face density based on rendering errors, but the connectivity between vertices cannot be fully adjusted.
</snippet>

# Scope and Definitions

We consider “3D mesh generation from multi-view 2D images” as recovering a watertight triangle mesh (with textures, when available) of an object or scene from two or more calibrated RGB images. Methods span classical photogrammetry/MVS with post-processing meshing, neural radiance/geometry fields that require surface extraction, and end-to-end or two-stage learning pipelines that synthesize auxiliary views and reconstruct meshes. Recent work emphasizes large 3D reconstruction models (LRMs), differentiable rendering, and Gaussian/implicit representations, with meshing achieved via Marching Cubes from SDFs, Poisson/TSDF fusion, or specialized post-processing and mesh-regularized optimization.

# Taxonomy and Trends (2022–2025)

Recent surveys and holistic models emphasize a shift from multi-stage photogrammetry/MVS toward unified learning-based pipelines and generalizable neural reconstruction. Classical pipelines integrate SfM, MVS, and mesh surface extraction; deep methods seek higher efficiency and accuracy while avoiding the cost and sensitivity of per-scene optimization, often leveraging neural volumetric representations and differentiable rendering to output meshes directly or near-directly.<cite id="85dc42c9-3">Classically, multi-view mesh reconstruction is addressed via SfM, MVS, and mesh extraction; recent deep methods target higher efficiency/accuracy, using neural volumetric representations and differentiable rendering to output meshes; per-scene optimization with radiance fields can be converted to meshes (Marching Cubes) but quality is not guaranteed, motivating SDF or direct mesh extraction</cite> Learning-based two-stage strategies generate consistent multi-view images (often with diffusion) and then feed them to a reconstruction model, improving multi-view consistency and mesh fidelity on large-scale datasets such as Google Scanned Objects and Objaverse.<cite id="85dc42c9-0">A two-stage design generates main views and synthesizes additional views with a diffusion-based dense view interpolation module, then reconstructs a high-quality mesh via a tri-plane-based LRM; experiments on GSO and Objaverse show quantitative and qualitative improvements in reconstruction accuracy, multi-view consistency, and fidelity</cite> Holistic frameworks also couple NeRF refinement with differentiable mesh representations and per-instance texture refinement to enhance mesh quality end-to-end.<cite id="85dc42c9-1">A holistic design modifies an LRM and fine-tunes a NeRF with a differentiable mesh representation, plus an efficient per-instance texture refinement process, to enhance mesh quality from multi-view images</cite> Multi-view diffusion plus 3D latent/decoder approaches first build a consistent latent 3D code and then synthesize novel views and a mesh, emphasizing continuity, isotropy, and occlusion consistency.<cite id="85dc42c9-4">A 4-view input is used to establish a consistent 3D latent code conditioned on multi-view images; a 3D decoder performs novel view synthesis informed by aligned representations and occluded detail features; the goal is continuity/isotropy of edges, occlusion delineation, and physical realism</cite>

# Neural Radiance/Geometry Fields and Mesh Extraction

NeRF-style radiance fields and their variants are a core SOTA scene representation for multi-view 3D reconstruction; meshes are typically extracted from SDFs or by isosurfacing and post-processing. Many works train an SDF-optimized neural field and use Marching Cubes to get an initial mesh, followed by refinement to reduce artifacts and improve detail.<cite id="314da0ea-2">NeRF and variants learn volumetric scene functions from multi-view images; recent studies adopt SDF to represent surfaces and extract meshes via Marching Cubes or Dual Contouring, but post-extraction can lose detail and introduce artifacts; refinement methods like NVdiffrec and NeRF2Mesh improve quality but face instabilities and limited connectivity adjustments</cite> Practical pipelines still commonly convert NeRF-derived fields to meshes with marching cubes and visualize the results, underscoring the centrality of this extraction step.<cite id="314da0ea-0">Meshes are extracted from NeRF results with the marching cubes algorithm, illustrating standard practice for converting NeRF reconstructions to meshes</cite> Optimization tricks such as bisection steps in Marching Cubes and Eikonal-style constraints are explored to mitigate staircase artifacts from imperfect SDFs and improve mesh quality at convergence.<cite id="314da0ea-1">Augmenting Marching Cubes with multi-step bisection root finding improves surface extraction quality for imperfect SDFs; authors note the need to re-examine objectives like Eikonal constraints for better mesh quality</cite>

Beyond NeRF, learning-based MVS and implicit surface reconstruction integrate depth estimation and surface fusion, often culminating in Poisson or TSDF-based meshes, but face challenges with occlusion, sensor noise, and global consistency across redundant stages.<cite id="a57243b0-1">Learning-based MVS methods have advanced reconstruction but still grapple with complex computations and global inconsistencies from depth estimation, filtering, fusion, and surface reconstruction stages</cite><cite id="a57243b0-4">Traditional MVS yields dense point clouds that are triangulated or fused via TSDF and Poisson reconstruction to meshes; these classical techniques struggle with incomplete data, occlusions, and noise, producing partial or hole-ridden reconstructions</cite> Modern pipelines also note that per-scene optimization for radiance/implicit fields can be slow, motivating feed-forward generalizable models that avoid dense per-object optimization while maintaining high fidelity.<cite id="85dc42c9-3">Recent methods based on NeRF reconstruct volumetric radiance fields with per-scene optimization; while convertible to meshes, they require significant time; feed-forward reconstruction models trained on large-scale 3D datasets offer speed and generalization</cite>

# Gaussian Splatting and Surface Extraction Innovations

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) and its variants have rapidly advanced multi-view 3D reconstruction with fast training and real-time rendering; extracting high-quality meshes from millions of Gaussians remains challenging, prompting specialized meshing techniques. SuGaR introduces a surface-aligned Gaussian regularization and Poisson reconstruction from rendered depth maps to obtain editable meshes within minutes, outperforming SDF-based mesh extraction in speed and rendering quality.<cite id="46f3a972-1">SuGaR regularizes 3D Gaussians to align with surfaces and uses Poisson reconstruction on rendered depth maps to extract meshes; retrieval is done within minutes compared to hours for SDF-based methods while improving rendering quality, enabling editing and refinement</cite> GOF proposes deriving Gaussian Opacity Fields directly from 3D Gaussians to enable level-set surface extraction and a tetrahedron-grid meshing scheme, avoiding Poisson/TSDF fusion and addressing fine geometry and background reconstruction issues reported in prior Gaussian-based methods.<cite id="46f3a972-0">GOF derives Gaussian Opacity Fields consistent with volume rendering to enable direct level-set surface extraction and tetrahedron-grid meshing without Poisson/TSDF; prior Gaussian-based methods faced fine geometry and background reconstruction challenges</cite><cite id="46f3a972-3">3DGS demonstrates photorealistic NVS with efficient training; SuGaR and 2DGS extend to meshing via Poisson and TSDF fusion, respectively, but struggle with fine-grained geometry and background regions due to inconsistencies between mesh extraction and volume rendering; GOF targets these issues</cite> MILo introduces a mesh-in-the-loop training objective that differentiably extracts and backpropagates mesh geometry/connectivity during Gaussian splatting optimization, yielding higher-quality meshes with far fewer vertices while preserving detail, which improves practicality for downstream applications.<cite id="46f3a972-4">MILo differentiably extracts and optimizes a mesh (vertices and connectivity) from Gaussian parameters during optimization, enforcing bidirectional consistency and producing meshes with almost 10× fewer vertices while preserving fine details, benefiting applications like simulation and animation</cite>

# Multi-View Stereo and Photogrammetry Pipelines (and Deep MVS)

Classical multi-view pipelines estimate per-view depth maps and fuse them via TSDF or Poisson reconstruction to obtain meshes; modern deep MVS methods seek efficiency and quality by operating on points or features and integrating visibility reasoning. Point-based architectures like VA-Point-MVSNet process scenes as point clouds with visibility-aware feature aggregation and iterative refinement, improving time/memory efficiency and reconstruction quality on benchmarks.<cite id="a57243b0-0">VA-Point-MVSNet processes scenes as point clouds with a visibility-aware multi-view feature aggregation module and iterative refinement (PointFlow), improving reconstruction quality and time/memory efficiency on synthetic and real data</cite> Surveys and overviews emphasize that while learning-based MVS advances accuracy, the classical pipeline (dense correspondences → triangulation → surface reconstruction) still dominates and motivates integrated, end-to-end approaches to reduce redundancy and inconsistencies.<cite id="a57243b0-1">Traditional MVS estimates per-view depth and fuses via Poisson or Delaunay triangulation; learning-based MVS has advanced but faces complexity and global inconsistencies from depth, filtering, fusion, and surface steps</cite> Practical multi-sensor fusion and real-time systems often rely on TSDF fusion and Poisson reconstruction for robust meshing, though they can yield partial or holey surfaces under occlusion and noise, motivating combined or learned fusion strategies.<cite id="a57243b0-4">Volumetric TSDF/kinect fusion yields real-time reconstruction; Poisson surface reconstruction from oriented point clouds produces smooth watertight surfaces; however, incomplete data and occlusions lead to partial or hole-ridden meshes</cite>

# Learning-Based Multi-View Image-to-Mesh Pipelines

State-of-the-art pipelines increasingly combine generative models with 3D reconstruction. Two-stage strategies generate dense, consistent multi-view images (including auxiliary views) and then reconstruct meshes using large 3D reconstruction models. Examples include diffusion-based dense view interpolation feeding a tri-plane-based LRM for high-quality mesh and texture, and latent 3D generative models that synthesize novel views from a 3D code and then a mesh.<cite id="85dc42c9-0">A diffusion-based dense view interpolation module synthesizes coherent intermediate views that, together with main views, are processed by a tri-plane-based LRM to reconstruct high-quality geometry and textures</cite><cite id="85dc42c9-4">A consistent 3D latent code is established from multi-view inputs; a 3D decoder performs novel view synthesis and supports mesh reconstruction with attention to edge continuity, occlusion, and realism</cite> Holistic systems also refine meshes and textures via differentiable rendering and per-instance optimization tied to NeRFs, enhancing realism and editability.<cite id="85dc42c9-1">An LRM plus NeRF fine-tuned with a differentiable mesh representation and per-instance texture refinement improves multi-view-to-3D mesh quality</cite> In broader generative modeling from videos/images, NeRF-to-mesh conversion remains standard (marching cubes), while research explores improved SDF optimization and mesh extraction to reduce artifacts for downstream use.<cite id="314da0ea-0">NeRF reconstructions are converted to meshes via marching cubes in video-to-3D generative pipelines</cite><cite id="314da0ea-2">SDF-based NeRF refinements and mesh extraction (Marching Cubes/Dual Contouring) can suffer detail loss and artifacts, motivating specialized refinement and extraction strategies</cite>

# Domain-Specific: Faces and Objects

For faces and hands, multi-view 2D-to-3D methods often leverage strong shape priors and templates, combined with multi-view consistency and neural rendering. Large reconstruction models and differentiable mesh representations are used to refine geometry and textures from multi-view images, improving realism and enabling per-instance texture optimization.<cite id="85dc42c9-1">A holistic multi-view-to-3D design with differentiable mesh representation and per-instance texture refinement enhances mesh quality</cite> In broader 3D object settings, sparse-view and multi-view diffusion strategies synthesize auxiliary views and feed them to mesh LRM backbones to increase coverage and reduce multi-view inconsistency, which is a common failure mode for single-image-only reconstructions.<cite id="85dc42c9-0">Dense view interpolation addresses multi-view inconsistency and provides better constraints for mesh reconstruction from sparse inputs</cite>

# Practical Trade-offs and Meshing Choices

Choice of meshing strategy strongly affects mesh quality and speed. SDF optimization with Marching Cubes/Dual Contouring is widely used but can suffer from staircase artifacts and detail loss; improvements include bisection-based extraction and Eikonal constraints, and post-/joint optimization of meshes with the neural field or Gaussians for better surface quality and editability.<cite id="314da0ea-1">Bisection-based Marching Cubes improves mesh extraction from imperfect SDFs; authors argue for re-examining objectives such as Eikonal constraints</cite><cite id="314da0ea-2">Post-extraction artifacts and limited connectivity adjustments motivate mesh refinement (e.g., NVdiffrec, NeRF2Mesh), though instabilities can arise from random SDF initialization</cite> Poisson and TSDF fusion are robust and yield watertight meshes from dense depth or point clouds but can produce noisy or low-detail surfaces in background regions and thin structures, especially under sparse or occluded views; Gaussian-based methods with Poisson/TSDF or new opacity-field and mesh-in-the-loop approaches (SuGaR, GOF, MILo) aim to overcome these limitations by aligning primitives to surfaces or integrating mesh gradients during optimization.<cite id="46f3a972-3">Poison/TSDF-based meshing from Gaussian splatting or depth maps can struggle with fine geometry and background regions due to inconsistent objectives; GOF proposes opacity fields and tailored meshing to address these issues</cite><cite id="46f3a972-4">MILo’s mesh-in-the-loop optimization reduces vertex count while preserving detail, improving practicality</cite><cite id="46f3a972-1">SuGaR achieves fast, editable meshes via surface-aligned Gaussians and Poisson reconstruction, outperforming SDF-based extraction in speed and rendering quality</cite> Finally, per-scene optimization provides high fidelity but is slow, while feed-forward generalizable models deliver speed and scalability at the cost of potential detail loss and sensitivity to training data coverage.<cite id="85dc42c9-3">Per-scene NeRF optimization yields high-quality radiance fields but is time-consuming; feed-forward generalizable models trained on large 3D datasets provide speed and generalization</cite>

# Representative SOTA Methods and What They Offer

- NeRF/SDF pipelines with improved mesh extraction and refinement: marching-cubes-based extraction with bisection steps; SDF optimization with Eikonal-like constraints; refinement via differentiable surface rendering or vertex/density optimization; widely used baseline for multi-view reconstructions and their meshed outputs.<cite id="314da0ea-0">NeRF-to-mesh conversion via marching cubes is standard in multi-view 3D pipelines</cite><cite id="314da0ea-1">Bisection Marching Cubes mitigates staircase artifacts in SDF extraction</cite><cite id="314da0ea-2">SDF-based NeRF surface extraction and refinement methods (NVdiffrec, NeRF2Mesh) target artifact reduction and better connectivity</cite>
- Gaussian Splatting with meshing innovations: 3DGS and 2DGS for fast NVS; SuGaR for surface-aligned Gaussians and Poisson-based mesh extraction with minutes-scale turnaround and better rendering/editability; GOF for opacity fields enabling direct level-set meshing; MILo for mesh-in-the-loop optimization with fewer vertices and high detail.<cite id="46f3a972-3">3DGS and 2DGS demonstrate efficient NVS with TSDF/Poisson-based meshing but face fine geometry/background challenges</cite><cite id="46f3a972-1">SuGaR enables fast, editable meshes from Gaussians using Poisson reconstruction and surface alignment</cite><cite id="46f3a972-0">GOF provides direct surface extraction from Gaussians without Poisson/TSDF, addressing prior limitations</cite><cite id="46f3a972-4">MILo integrates differentiable mesh extraction into Gaussian splatting optimization to improve mesh quality and efficiency</cite>
- Learning-based multi-view-to-mesh LRM pipelines: tri-plane-based mesh LRM fed by diffusion-synthesized views (CDI3D), holistic NeRF+mesh+texture refinement (GTR), and latent/decoder-based multi-view generative approaches (VI3DRM); all emphasize multi-view consistency, occlusion handling, and high-fidelity geometry/textures.<cite id="85dc42c9-0">CDI3D’s two-stage diffusion plus tri-plane LRM improves multi-view consistency and mesh quality on GSO/Objaverse</cite><cite id="85dc42c9-1">GTR refines geometry and texture via NeRF with differentiable mesh and per-instance texture optimization</cite><cite id="85dc42c9-4">VI3DRM builds consistent 3D latent codes and uses a 3D decoder for novel view synthesis and meshing with emphasis on occlusion and surface continuity</cite>
- Deep MVS and photogrammetry-derived meshing: visibility-aware point-based MVS (VA-Point-MVSNet) for efficient, high-quality point clouds; classical TSDF/Poisson meshing remains robust for many settings but can be partial under occlusion/noise; integrated learning-based MVS reduces redundancy and improves quality while retaining classical fusion strengths.<cite id="a57243b0-0">VA-Point-MVSNet improves reconstruction quality and efficiency via visibility-aware aggregation and iterative refinement</cite><cite id="a57243b0-4">TSDF and Poisson reconstruction produce robust meshes but can be incomplete under occlusions and noise, motivating fusion/learning advances</cite><cite id="a57243b0-1">Learning-based MVS advances accuracy but inherits complexity and inconsistency from classical stages</cite>

# Benchmarks and Evaluation

Recent SOTA papers evaluate on large-scale multi-view datasets such as Google Scanned Objects and Objaverse, as well as diverse real-world images, focusing on reconstruction accuracy, multi-view consistency, and visual fidelity for geometry and textures. Two-stage diffusion+LRM and latent 3D generative approaches report improvements over prior state of the art in these metrics, while NeRF/Gaussian-based methods are commonly assessed via mesh quality after extraction and refinement (e.g., artifact reduction, detail preservation, and rendering realism).<cite id="85dc42c9-0">Experiments on GSO and Objaverse show improvements in reconstruction accuracy, multi-view consistency, and visual fidelity for the proposed two-stage diffusion+LRM pipeline</cite><cite id="46f3a972-1">SuGaR reports faster and higher-quality mesh extraction and rendering compared to SDF-based methods</cite><cite id="314da0ea-2">Studies discuss artifacts and refinement outcomes for NeRF-derived meshes, reflecting standard evaluation criteria for mesh realism and detail</cite>

# Practical Guidance

- If you have many multi-view photos and need robust, watertight meshes quickly, TSDF fusion plus Poisson surface reconstruction remains a strong baseline, especially when paired with modern MVS or sensor fusion; consider COLMAP-based SfM/MVS and oriented point cloud processing.<cite id="a57243b0-4">TSDF and Poisson reconstruction are standard and robust, though occlusions/noise can create holes; multi-sensor fusion improves coverage</cite>
- For high fidelity and interactive rendering, NeRF/SDF pipelines with improved mesh extraction (bisection Marching Cubes) and mesh refinement (e.g., NVdiffrec, NeRF2Mesh) are effective; they are slower per scene but deliver high-quality surfaces suitable for downstream graphics tasks.<cite id="314da0ea-1">Bisection Marching Cubes improves SDF-extracted mesh quality</cite><cite id="314da0ea-2">Refinement methods address artifacts and connectivity limitations of NeRF-derived meshes</cite>
- For speed and editability, Gaussian Splatting with SuGaR/GOF/MILo is compelling: surface-aligned Gaussians, opacity fields, and mesh-in-the-loop optimization yield editable meshes with fewer vertices and faster turnaround than SDF-based extraction, especially for complex scenes.<cite id="46f3a972-1">SuGaR achieves fast, editable meshes via Poisson extraction from surface-aligned Gaussians</cite><cite id="46f3a972-0">GOF enables direct, adaptive mesh extraction from Gaussians without TSDF/Poisson</cite><cite id="46f3a972-4">MILo reduces vertex count by 10× while preserving detail through mesh-in-the-loop training</cite>
- If you can synthesize additional views (diffusion-based interpolation or latent 3D generation), feed them to a mesh LRM or decoder to improve coverage and consistency; this two-stage strategy is a leading SOTA pattern for sparse-view reconstructions on large-scale datasets.<cite id="85dc42c9-0">Dense view interpolation plus tri-plane LRM improves multi-view consistency and mesh quality on GSO/Objaverse</cite><cite id="85dc42c9-4">Latent 3D generative approaches build consistent 3D codes and synthesize meshes with strong geometric/occlusion properties</cite>

# Limitations and Open Problems

Despite progress, several challenges remain. Per-scene optimization is still a bottleneck for scalability, and mesh extraction from implicit/Gaussian representations can produce artifacts or lose fine geometry; background and thin structure recovery remain difficult without strong regularization and consistent objectives across rendering and meshing.<cite id="85dc42c9-3">Per-scene optimization is time-consuming; feed-forward models trade detail for speed</cite><cite id="46f3a972-3">Prior Gaussian-based meshing struggles with fine geometry and background regions due to inconsistent objectives between rendering and extraction</cite><cite id="314da0ea-2">SDF-based extraction and refinement can still exhibit artifacts and limited connectivity adjustments</cite> Occlusions, motion, and sensor noise in real-world multi-view settings continue to degrade mesh quality, motivating robust MVS, multi-sensor fusion, and better priors for surface completion and topology handling.<cite id="a57243b0-4">Occlusions and sensor noise cause partial or holey reconstructions, motivating fusion and robust reconstruction</cite>

# Summary

- NeRF/SDF pipelines remain foundational for multi-view 3D reconstruction, with mesh extraction via Marching Cubes and refinements addressing artifacts and detail retention.<cite id="314da0ea-0">NeRF meshes via marching cubes are standard</cite><cite id="314da0ea-1">Bisection Marching Cubes improves extraction quality</cite><cite id="314da0ea-2">Refinement methods reduce artifacts and improve connectivity</cite>
- Gaussian Splatting has transformed speed and quality, and recent meshing advances (SuGaR, GOF, MILo) deliver editable, detailed meshes with fewer vertices and faster turnaround.<cite id="46f3a972-1">SuGaR: surface-aligned Gaussians and Poisson extraction for fast, editable meshes</cite><cite id="46f3a972-0">GOF: opacity fields for direct meshing from Gaussians</cite><cite id="46f3a972-4">MILo: mesh-in-the-loop optimization for high-quality, sparse meshes</cite>
- Learning-based multi-view pipelines that synthesize auxiliary views and use large 3D reconstruction models or latent decoders are state of the art for sparse-view reconstructions on large datasets, improving multi-view consistency and visual fidelity.<cite id="85dc42c9-0">Two-stage diffusion+LRM improves accuracy and consistency on GSO/Objaverse</cite><cite id="85dc42c9-1">NeRF+mesh refinement with per-instance texture optimization</cite><cite id="85dc42c9-4">Latent 3D generative approaches with consistent 3D codes and decoders</cite>
- Classical MVS/photogrammetry with TSDF/Poisson meshing remains robust and widely used, while deep MVS reduces redundancy and improves efficiency and quality in challenging settings.<cite id="a57243b0-0">VA-Point-MVSNet improves efficiency and quality via visibility-aware point-based MVS</cite><cite id="a57243b0-1">Learning-based MVS advances but inherits classical pipeline issues</cite><cite id="a57243b0-4">TSDF/Poisson meshing is robust but can be incomplete under occlusions/noise</cite>

Title: CDI3D: Cross-guided Dense-view Interpolation for 3D Reconstruction
Snippet: Meanwhile, we design a tilt camera pose trajectory to capture views with different elevations and perspectives to maximize the coverage of the object's surface. Finally, the interpolated views, along with the main views, are processed by a tri-plane-based mesh reconstruction model, which extracts robust tokens and reconstructs a high-quality 3D mesh with detailed geometry and texture. As shown in Fig. 1 (Ours), this design guarantees both multi-view consistency and high-quality image generation. 

Our main contributions are summarized as follows. First, we propose CDI3D, an LRM-based framework for highquality 3D mesh reconstruction from a single image. By disentangling the process into two distinct stages: main-view generation and view interpolation, CDI3D leverages a 2D diffusion model to generate main views and introduces an Dense View Interpolation (DVI) module to synthesize additional views with superior multi-view consistency. This twostage design ensures better constraints and smooth transitions between views, effectively addressing the multi-view inconsistency issues that hinder existing methods. Second, we develop the DVI module, which employs 2D diffusion-based multiview interpolation to generate coherent intermediate views between neighboring main views. These interpolated views, combined with the main views, are processed by a tri-planebased LRM to enhance the geometric and textural details of the reconstructed 3D mesh, which significantly improves the quality of both geometry and texture reconstruction, ensuring high-fidelity 3D generation. Third, we design a tilt camera pose trajectory that captures views from various angles and elevations, ensuring that the object is observed from a wider range of viewpoints and providing more complete input for the 3D mesh reconstruction process. Besides, we conduct extensive experiments on the Google Scanned Objects (GSO) dataset [35], Objaverse dataset [3], [4] and diverse type of images collected from the web, demonstrating that CDI3D outperforms state-of-the-art methods both quantitatively and qualitatively in terms of 3D reconstruction accuracy, multiview consistency, and visual fidelity.

Title: MeshLRM: Large Reconstruction Model for High-Quality Mesh
Snippet: Mesh Reconstruction.Despite the existence of various 3D representations, meshes remain the most widely used format in industrial 3D engines.Reconstructing high-quality meshes from multi-view images is a long-standing challenge in computer vision and graphics.Classically, this is addressed via a complex multi-stage photogrammetry pipeline, integrating techniques such as structure from motion (SfM) [1,49,55], multi-view stereo (MVS) [19,50], and mesh surface extraction [27,39].Recently, deep learning-based methods have also been proposed to address these problems for higher efficiency and accuracy [11,24,25,58,62,75].However, the photogrammety pipeline is not only costly, requiring dense input images and long processing time, but also often suffers from low-quality mesh rendering.Our approach enables sparse-view mesh reconstruction through direct feed-forward network inference in an end-to-end manner.We leverage neural volumetric representations and differentiable rendering, training our model to output high-quality meshes that can render realistic images.

Neural Reconstruction.Neural rendering techniques have recently gained significant attention for their ability to produce high-quality 3D reconstructions for realistic rendering [28,37,41,80].Most recent methods are based on NeRF [41] and reconstruct scenes as various volumetric radiance fields [6,18,41,42,72] with per-scene rendering optimization.Though radiance fields can be converted into meshes with Marching Cubes [39], the quality of the resulting mesh is not guaranteed.Previous methods have aimed to transform radiance fields into implicit surface representations (SDFs) [43,63,76], enhancing mesh quality from Marching Cubes.In addition, some methods [47,59,70,77] attempt to directly extract meshes from radiance fields using differentiable surface rendering.However, these methods all require dense input images and long per-scene optimization time, which our approach avoids.

On the other hand, generalizable neural reconstruction has been explored, often leveraging MVS-based cost volumes [7,26,38] or directly aggregating multiview features along pixels' projective epipolar lines [57,65,79].

Title: VI3DRM:Towards meticulous 3D Reconstruction from Sparse Views via Photo-Realistic Novel View Synthesis
Snippet: As depicted in Figure 3, our approach processes RGB images from four distinct camera viewpoints of the same object. The goal is to produce a precise 3D representation that faithfully reconstructs every occluded region of the real object with both realism and consistency. A high-quality multiview 3D mesh reconstruction should demonstrate fidelity in several critical aspects: continuity and isotropy of edges, clear delineation of occluded regions, and physical realism when viewed from arbitrary perspectives. 

Instead of directly producing full 3D reconstructions from images captured from multiple camera viewpoints, our approach first establishes a consistent 3D representation within the latent space, conditioned on the initial set of multi-view images. Leveraging these 3D latent codes, our method then generates novel view synthesis via a 3D decoder. Finally, the interpolated views, along with the main views, are processed by a tri-plane-based mesh reconstruction model, which extracts robust tokens and reconstructs a high-quality 3D mesh with detailed geometry and texture. As shown in Fig. 1 (Ours), this design guarantees both multi-view consistency and high-quality image generation. 

Our main contributions are summarized as follows. First, we propose CDI3D, an LRM-based framework for highquality 3D mesh reconstruction from a single image. By disentangling the process into two distinct stages: main-view generation and view interpolation, CDI3D leverages a 2D diffusion model to generate main views and introduces an Dense View Interpolation (DVI) module to synthesize additional views with superior multi-view consistency. This twostage design ensures better constraints and smooth transitions between views, effectively addressing the multi-view inconsistency issues that hinder existing methods. Second, we develop the DVI module, which employs 2D diffusion-based multiview interpolation to generate coherent intermediate views between neighboring main views. These interpolated views, combined with the main views, are processed by a tri-planebased LRM to enhance the geometric and textural details of the reconstructed 3D mesh, which significantly improves the quality of both geometry and texture reconstruction, ensuring high-fidelity 3D generation. Third, we design a tilt camera pose trajectory that captures views from various angles and elevations, ensuring that the object is observed from a wider range of viewpoints and providing more complete input for the 3D mesh reconstruction process. Besides, we conduct extensive experiments on the Google Scanned Objects (GSO) dataset [35], Objaverse dataset [3], [4] and diverse type of images collected from the web, demonstrating that CDI3D outperforms state-of-the-art methods both quantitatively and qualitatively in terms of 3D reconstruction accuracy, multiview consistency, and visual fidelity.

Title: Gaussian Opacity Fields: Efficient Adaptive Surface Reconstruction in Unbounded Scenes
Snippet: Inspired by the impressive NVS performance of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [Kerbl et al. 2023], researchers have proposed to utilize 3D Gaussians for surface reconstruction. Recent efforts [Chen et al. 2023b;Yu et al. 2024b] have integrated 3D Gaussians with neural implicit surfaces, optimizing a Signed Distance Function (SDF) network and 3D Gaussians jointly. While these approaches mark some advancements, they also inherit the shortcomings associated with implicit surfaces as previously discussed. Other studies have focused on surface extraction from optimized Gaussian primitives through post-processing techniques [Dai et al. 2024;Guédon and Lepetit 2023;Huang et al. 2024;Turkulainen et al. 2024]. Notably, SuGaR [Guédon and Lepetit 2023] and GaussianSurfels [Dai et al. 2024] adopt Poisson surface reconstruction [Kazhdan and Hoppe 2013] to extract meshes from rendered depth maps. Meanwhile, 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) [Huang et al. 2024] employs TSDF fusion for this purpose. Though these methods achieve improved reconstructions, they face challenges in capturing fine-grained geometry and adequately reconstructing background areas. In this work, we derive Gaussian Opacity Fields directly from 3D Gaussians. Our GOF is consistent with the volume rendering process for rendering RGB images. It enables direct surface extraction by identifying a level set, without resorting to Poisson reconstruction and TSDF fusion. Additionally, we propose a tetrahedron grid-based technique for mesh extraction, resulting in adaptive and detailed meshes.

Title: SuGaR: Surface-Aligned Gaussian Splatting for Efficient 3D Mesh Reconstruction and High-Quality Mesh Rendering
Snippet: We propose a method to allow precise and extremely fast mesh extraction from 3D Gaussian Splatting [15]. Gaussian Splatting has recently become very popular as it yields realistic rendering while being significantly faster to train than NeRFs. It is however challenging to extract a mesh from the millions of tiny 3D Gaussians as these Gaussians tend to be unorganized after optimization and no method has been proposed so far. Our first key contribution is a regularization term that encourages the Gaussians to align well with the surface of the scene. We then introduce a method that exploits this alignment to extract a mesh from the Gaussians using Poisson reconstruction, which is fast, scalable, and preserves details, in contrast to the Marching Cubes algorithm usually applied to extract meshes from Neural SDFs. Finally, we introduce an optional refinement strategy that binds Gaussians to the surface of the mesh, and jointly optimizes these Gaussians and the mesh through Gaussian splatting rendering. This enables easy editing, sculpting, animating, and relighting of the Gaussians by manipulating the mesh instead of the Gaussians themselves. Retrieving such an editable mesh for realistic rendering is done within minutes with our method, compared to hours with the state-of-the-art method on SDFs, while providing a better rendering quality.

Title: Gaussian Opacity Fields: Efficient Adaptive Surface Reconstruction in Unbounded Scenes
Snippet: To extract detailed surfaces, it renders depth maps to generate a sparse high-resolution voxel grid and applies a heuristic fusion technique to label the voxels as inside or outside. Marching cube algorithm [Lorensen and Cline 1998] is applied to extract a high-resolution mesh with hundreds of millions of points and thousands of millions of triangles, which is then simplified using slow post-processing techniques [Garland and Heckbert 1997]. Notably, as it focuses on NVS rather than surface reconstruction, the extracted meshes are noisy and contain fewer details in the background region, probably due to lack of regularization and contracted space [Barron et al. 2022a] fusion. 

More recently, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [Kerbl et al. 2023] represents complex scenes as a set of 3D Gaussians, demonstrating photorealistic NVS results while trained efficiently and rendered in real-time. It has been quickly extended to surface reconstruction [Chen et al. 2023b;Guédon and Lepetit 2023;Huang et al. 2024;Yu et al. 2024b]. Notably, SuGaR [Guédon and Lepetit 2023] regularizes the 3D Gaussians to align with surfaces and employs Poisson surface reconstruction [Kazhdan and Hoppe 2013] to extract a mesh from rendered depth maps. 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) [Huang et al. 2024] uses 2D Gaussians instead of 3D Gaussians as a scene representation for better surface representation and utilizes TSDF fusion to reconstruct a mesh. While these methods have shown improved reconstruction, they struggle with extracting fine-grained geometry [Guédon and Lepetit 2023] and reconstructing background regions [Huang et al. 2024]. A primary challenge is the inconsistency between mesh extraction and volume rendering during training. Specifically, Poisson reconstruction ignores the opacity and scale of Gaussian primitives and rendered depth maps are not sufficiently reliable. Moreover, TSDF fusion struggles to accurately model thin structures and to reconstruct unbounded scenes.

Title: MILo: Mesh-In-the-Loop Gaussian Splatting for Detailed and Efficient Surface Reconstruction
Snippet: Fig. 1. Mesh-in-the-Loop Gaussian Splatting. Our method introduces a novel differentiable mesh extraction framework that operates during the optimization of 3D Gaussian Splatting representations. At every training iteration, we differentiably extract a mesh-including both vertex locations and connectivitydirectly from Gaussian parameters. This enables gradient flow from the mesh to Gaussians, allowing us to promote bidirectional consistency between volumetric (Gaussians) and surface (extracted mesh) representations. This approach guides Gaussians toward configurations better suited for surface reconstruction, resulting in higher quality meshes with significantly fewer vertices. In this example, our method reconstructs the entire bicycle scene-including background-with almost 10 times fewer vertices than previous methods while preserving fine geometric details. Our framework can be plugged into any Gaussian splatting representation, increasing performance while generating an order of magnitude fewer mesh vertices. MILo makes the reconstructions more practical for downstream applications like physics simulations and animation.

documents.title: Gaussian Opacity Fields: Efficient Adaptive Surface Reconstruction in Unbounded Scenes
documents.snippet: Inspired by the impressive NVS performance of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [Kerbl et al. 2023], researchers have proposed to utilize 3D Gaussians for surface reconstruction. Recent efforts [Chen et al. 2023b;Yu et al. 2024b] have integrated 3D Gaussians with neural implicit surfaces, optimizing a Signed Distance Function (SDF) network and 3D Gaussians jointly. While these approaches mark some advancements, they also inherit the shortcomings associated with implicit surfaces as previously discussed. Other studies have focused on surface extraction from optimized Gaussian primitives through post-processing techniques [Dai et al. 2024;Guédon and Lepetit 2023;Huang et al. 2024;Turkulainen et al. 2024]. Notably, SuGaR [Guédon and Lepetit 2023] and GaussianSurfels [Dai et al. 2024] adopt Poisson surface reconstruction [Kazhdan and Hoppe 2013] to extract meshes from rendered depth maps. Meanwhile, 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) [Huang et al. 2024] employs TSDF fusion for this purpose. Though these methods achieve improved reconstructions, they face challenges in capturing fine-grained geometry and adequately reconstructing background areas. In this work, we derive Gaussian Opacity Fields directly from 3D Gaussians. Our GOF is consistent with the volume rendering process for rendering RGB images. It enables direct surface extraction by identifying a level set, without resorting to Poisson reconstruction and TSDF fusion. Additionally, we propose a tetrahedron grid-based technique for mesh extraction, resulting in adaptive and detailed meshes.

documents.title: SuGaR: Surface-Aligned Gaussian Splatting for Efficient 3D Mesh Reconstruction and High-Quality Mesh Rendering
documents.snippet: We propose a method to allow precise and extremely fast mesh extraction from 3D Gaussian Splatting [15]. Gaussian Splatting has recently become very popular as it yields realistic rendering while being significantly faster to train than NeRFs. It is however challenging to extract a mesh from the millions of tiny 3D Gaussians as these Gaussians tend to be unorganized after optimization and no method has been proposed so far. Our first key contribution is a regularization term that encourages the Gaussians to align well with the surface of the scene. We then introduce a method that exploits this alignment to extract a mesh from the Gaussians using Poisson reconstruction, which is fast, scalable, and preserves details, in contrast to the Marching Cubes algorithm usually applied to extract meshes from Neural SDFs. Finally, we introduce an optional refinement strategy that binds Gaussians to the surface of the mesh, and jointly optimizes these Gaussians and the mesh through Gaussian splatting rendering. This enables easy editing, sculpting, animating, and relighting of the Gaussians by manipulating the mesh instead of the Gaussians themselves. Retrieving such an editable mesh for realistic rendering is done within minutes with our method, compared to hours with the state-of-the-art method on SDFs, while providing a better rendering quality.

To extract detailed surfaces, it renders depth maps to generate a sparse high-resolution voxel grid and applies a heuristic fusion technique to label the voxels as inside or outside. Marching cube algorithm [Lorensen and Cline 1998] is applied to extract a high-resolution mesh with hundreds of millions of points and thousands of millions of triangles, which is then simplified using slow post-processing techniques [Garland and Heckbert 1997]. Notably, as it focuses on NVS rather than surface reconstruction, the extracted meshes are noisy and contain fewer details in the background region, probably due to lack of regularization and contracted space [Barron et al. 2022a] fusion. 

More recently, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [Kerbl et al. 2023] represents complex scenes as a set of 3D Gaussians, demonstrating photorealistic NVS results while trained efficiently and rendered in real-time. It has been quickly extended to surface reconstruction [Chen et al. 2023b;Guédon and Lepetit 2023;Huang et al. 2024;Yu et al. 2024b]. Notably, SuGaR [Guédon and Lepetit 2023] regularizes the 3D Gaussians to align with surfaces and employs Poisson surface reconstruction [Kazhdan and Hoppe 2013] to extract a mesh from rendered depth maps. 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) [Huang et al. 2024] uses 2D Gaussians instead of 3D Gaussians as a scene representation for better surface representation and utilizes TSDF fusion to reconstruct a mesh. While these methods have shown improved reconstruction, they struggle with extracting fine-grained geometry [Guédon and Lepetit 2023] and reconstructing background regions [Huang et al. 2024]. A primary challenge is the inconsistency between mesh extraction and volume rendering during training. Specifically, Poisson reconstruction ignores the opacity and scale of Gaussian primitives and rendered depth maps are not sufficiently reliable. Moreover, TSDF fusion struggles to accurately model thin structures and to reconstruct unbounded scenes.

Title: Visibility-Aware Point-Based Multi-View Stereo Network
Snippet: We present a novel visibility-aware point-based architecture for high-resolution multi-view stereo reconstruction. Instead of building a high-resolution cost volume, our proposed VA-Point-MVSNet processes the scene as a point cloud directly. The PointFlow module concentrates on the neighborhood of the target surface and refines the predicted depth map iteratively, which therefore achieves improved time and memory efficiency. Experiments on synthetic data and real data demonstrate that the visibilityaware multi-view feature aggregation module can improve the reconstruction quality significantly by considering visibility, and VA-Point-MVSNet is able to produce high-quality reconstruction point clouds on benchmarks. Additionally, VA-Point-MVSNet is applicable to foveated depth inference to greatly reducing unnecessary computation, which cannot be easily implemented for cost-volume-based methods.

Title: High-Precision 3D Reconstruction in Complex Scenes via Implicit Surface Reconstruction Enhanced by Multi-Sensor Data Fusion
Snippet: Traditional pipelines for 3D reconstruction typically use geometry-based or photometric methods. Multi-view stereo (MVS) systems rely on finding dense correspondences among images of a static scene, then performing 3D triangulation to recover shape. Volumetric approaches, such as TSDF fusion [6] and kinect fusion, fuse range scans into a global truncated signed distance function (TSDF), yielding real-time reconstruction. Poisson surface reconstruction from oriented point clouds can produce smooth, watertight surfaces. However, these classical techniques often struggle with incomplete data, strong occlusions, or sensor noise, leading to partial or hole-ridden reconstructions, as shown in Figure 2. We also note that established tools such as COLMAP are widely used for structure-from-motion and multi-view stereo from RGB images, but they do not natively fuse LiDAR or depth modalities at a learned feature level. In real-world environments with clutter or occlusions, each sensor might capture only a subset of the scene's surface. Combining multiple sensors boosts coverage and reduces blind spots. Title: R2-Mesh: Reinforcement Learning Powered Mesh Reconstruction via Geometry and Appearance Refinement
Snippet: NeRF (Mildenhall et al. 2020) and its variants (Müller et al. 2022;Chen et al. 2022;Fridovich-Keil et al. 2022;Sun, Sun, and Chen 2022) significantly advance 3D scene reconstruction through a volumetric scene function learned from multi-view images. Some works explore the possibility of generating meshes simultaneously during the training of NeRF models. A notable example is MobileNeRF (Chen et al. 2023). However, the generated polygonal mesh lacks surface smoothness since the mesh topology is fixed at the initial stage. Most recent studies (Wang et al. 2021(Wang et al. , 2023;;Long et al. 2022;Yariv et al. 2021;Oechsle, Peng, and Geiger 2021;Munkberg et al. 2022;Hasselgren, Hofmann, and Munkberg 2022) adopt SDF to represent geometric surfaces. Some of these works (Wang et al. 2021(Wang et al. , 2023;;Long et al. 2022;Yariv et al. 2021;Oechsle, Peng, and Geiger 2021) leverage the ray-marching volumetric rendering formula of NeRF, optimize the SDF to achieve accurate scene representations. They then apply classical isosurfacing algorithms, such as Marching Cubes (Lorensen and Cline 1998) and Dual Contouring (Ju et al. 2002), to extract the mesh. However, this post-extraction leads to loss of detail and surface artifacts that degrade the quality of the extracted mesh. Some studies conduct mesh refinement processes to further enhance the geometric quality. NVdiffrec (Munkberg et al. 2022) utilizes mesh differentiable surface rendering to optimize the SDF, but due to the random initialization of the SDF, it can lead to training instabilities and the presence of floating artifacts. NeRF2Mesh (Tang et al. 2023) performs mesh refinement by optimizing the vertices' positions and face density based on rendering errors, but the connectivity between vertices cannot be fully adjusted.
