Zhang documented these workload challenges through interviews with engineering faculty advisors, revealing that advisors struggle to balance personalized guidance with limited time resources, often resulting in rushed meetings that fail to address students' complex needs. In addition, hiring full-time academic advisors may not be feasible given resource limitations [3]. Beyond workload pressures and resource constraints, advisors must also keep track of a plethora of resources and information to provide accurate planning, which may require additional training and awareness whenever new requirements are introduced [7,52]. 

Méndez et al. observed that advisors must synthesize information about students' academic histories, personal circumstances, and career aspirations while considering program requirements, prerequisite chains, and course availability-all within brief advising sessions. This complexity is further illustrated in queries requiring multi-source reasoning, such as determining whether "Build LLM Agent" counts toward graduation requirements-a question that cannot be answered from a single document but requires synthesizing course listings, requirement definitions, and potential naming variations across different systems [33]. 

These challenges highlight the need for tools that can support advisors by integrating distributed resources and handling complex queries. To that end, we developed an advising chatbot (Advising-Wise) to answer students' questions and provide advisors with timely access to up-to-date information.

documents.title: Bilingual AI-Driven Chatbot for Academic Advising
Robo academic advisor: Can chatbots and artificial intelligence replace human interaction?
documents.snippet:
Purpose: Chatbots and artificial intelligence (AI) have the potential to alleviate some of the challenges faced by humans. Faculties frequently swamped with teaching and research may find it difficult to act in a parental role for students by offering them individualized advice. Hence, the primary purpose of this study is to review the literature on chatbots and AI in light of their role in auto-advising systems. The authors aimed to gain insights into the most pertinent topics and concerns related to robo academic advisor and identify any gaps in the literature that could serve as potential avenues for further research.
Design/methodology/approach: The research employs a systematic literature review and bibliometric techniques to find 67 primary papers that have been published between 1984 and 2023. Using the Scopus database, the researchers built a summary of the literature on chatbots and AI in academic advice.
Findings: Chatbot applications can be a promising approach to address the challenges of balancing personalized student advising with automation. More empirical research is required, especially on chatbots and other AI-based advising systems, to understand their effectiveness and how they can be integrated into educational settings.
Research limitations/implications: This research’s sample size may restrict its findings’ generalizability. Furthermore, the study’s focus on chatbots may overlook the potential benefits of other AI technologies in enhancing robo academic advising systems. Future research could explore the impact of robo academic advisors in diverse societal backgrounds to gain a more comprehensive understanding of their implications.
Practical implications: Higher educational institutions (HEIs) should establish a robo academic advising system that serves various stakeholders. The system’s chatbots and AI features must be user-friendly, considering the customers’ familiarity with robots.
Originality/value: This study contributes to a better understanding of HEIs’ perceptions of the adoption of chatbots and AI in academic advising by providing insightful information about the main forces behind robo academic advising, illuminating the most frequently studied uses of chatbots and AI in academic advising.

documents.title: Bias-Aware AI Chatbot for Engineering Advising at the University of Maryland A. James Clark School of Engineering
documents.snippet:
The transition from secondary to higher education requires students to make crucial decisions regarding their areas of studies. Specifically, students matriculating into the A. James Clark School of Engineering must choose from 22 programs. UMD's traditional college advising system provides necessary guidance to students during these decisions. Yet the current system exhibits notable limitations: appointment wait times, intimidating formal environments, and reduced information retention, all of which create barriers to academic guidance [Fox, 2022]. 

Artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots have proven complementary tools to address the accessibility limitations in traditional advising, academic or otherwise. These adaptive systems offer distinct advantages including continuous availability, minimizing social barriers, and standardized information delivery [Hasal et al., 2021]. Implementing a chatbot alternative suggests a potential for enhanced accessibility to academic advising services, particularly for students who may be reluctant to engage with traditional advising.

documents.title: An exploratory study of students’ perceptions of advice and support services in a science university
documents.snippet:
Providing optional bilingual advising services or allowing code-switching in advising conversations may significantly reduce student anxiety, improve clarity in communication, and ultimately enhance the effectiveness of advising relationships. Doing so would move beyond linguistic inclusivity and toward cognitive empathy-acknowledging the real psychological cost of learning and help-seeking in a second language. 

Toward a strategic blended advising model: human empathy meets AI scalability As higher education institutions embrace digital transformation, the promise of AI-driven tools-such as academic advising chatbots and virtual scheduling assistants-has become increasingly attractive. These tools offer round-the-clock availability, standardization, and cost efficiency, particularly in large or decentralized universities. However, this study's findings reinforce a crucial boundary: while technology can extend access, it cannot replace the relational depth, contextual judgment, and emotional attunement that human advisors provide. 

Rather than viewing AI as a full substitute, a more strategic approach lies in adopting a blended advising model grounded in task delegation. Under such a model, routine, transactional tasks-such as course registration, deadline reminders, or policy FAQs-are handled by conversational AI platforms. These tasks are rule-based, require minimal emotional nuance, and benefit from speed and scale. Delegating them to AI frees up valuable human advisor capacity to focus on higher-order responsibilities that students repeatedly identified as most meaningful: personalized academic guidance, empathetic listening, and culturally sensitive problem-solving. This model is not simply about efficiency-it reflects a shift in priorities. Students in this study emphasized the importance of being heard, understood, and guided through complex decision-making processes. These are tasks that demand emotional intelligence, narrative understanding, and trust-qualities that current AI systems, despite advances, cannot fully replicate. Therefore, preserving the human dimension in advising is not optional; it is essential for addressing the emotional and identity-related challenges students face, especially in high-pressure health sciences programs. 

Furthermore, AI-generated insights-such as predictive alerts based on course performance or disengagement patterns-can be used to proactively inform human advisors. In this way, technology supports-not replaces-human empathy by equipping advisors with timely, data-driven signals to intervene meaningfully.

problem: Are there any articles focusing on the use of attention mechanisms in ranking? Where the weights generated by the attention mechanism are fused as weights for the base ranking?
final_response:
Yes. Several strands of the literature apply attention mechanisms to ranking and explicitly use the attention-derived weights to fuse multiple base representations, features, or components into a ranking or scoring function. These include learning‑to‑rank (LTR) models in information retrieval, transformer-based listwise rankers, and recommender/ad systems where attention learns to weight user features or historical behavior before fusion into a final relevance score. <cite id="27b16e93-0">The attention mechanism is demonstrated to focus on distinct aspects of the input and extract more relevant information, motivating its use to combine different embeddings of queries and results in a ranking model.

# Classic LTR with attention: weighting and fusing base signals for listwise ranking
- An Attention-Based Deep Net for Learning to Rank (ANN, 2017) applies attention to listwise LTR and uses it to incorporate multiple embeddings for queries and results, with “double attention” over query and results and a decoder for listwise ranking. <cite id="27b16e93-0">It applies attention to listwise LTR, takes different embeddings of queries and results into account by incorporating them with attention, and applies double attention mechanisms to both queries and search results</cite> <cite id="27b16e93-2">The model uses attention to better incorporate different embeddings of queries and results and applies a decoder to learn listwise ranks</cite>. 
- Attention-based listwise models such as Attention Rank and the Deep Listwise Context Model (DLCM) use attention to compute a listwise score by explicitly modeling inter-item dependencies and allocating more optimization effort to high-relevance items. <cite id="a27e57ce-2">Attention Rank is a listwise function that uses a rectified exponential allocation to focus optimization on high-relevance results and can be integrated with unbiased LTR</cite> <cite id="a27e57ce-1">The Deep Listwise Context Model uses a recurrent neural network to take other inputs into account when reranking; transformer-based self-attention has been used to learn from listwise contexts, treating a list of items as a sequence</cite> <cite id="a27e57ce-2">The DLCM with Attention Rank trains 2–20× faster than listwise baselines while computing ranking loss based on ranked lists</cite>. 
- Query-aware and user-aware attention further emphasize that attention learns to weight relevant parts of the query and context before fusion into a ranking signal. <cite id="9c1e0b45-0">In neural ranking, attention learns to weight words and sub-phrases within documents and co-attention learns joint pairwise attentions over document and query; the paper reframes attention as feature augmentation for subsequent layers in ranking models</cite> <cite id="9c1e0b45-1">A context-aware neural ranking model introduces attention at both levels of a hierarchical RNN to identify dependency structure between search context and activities, enhancing document ranking and query suggestion</cite>.

# Transformer-based listwise rankers and cross-attention for personalization
- Transformer-based listwise ranking models use self-attention to capture inter-item relationships directly, producing listwise scores that depend on the entire list, which is orthogonal to how transformers are used to compute item feature vectors. <cite id="a27e57ce-1">Listwise Transformer approaches apply self-attention over sequences of items to learn from listwise contexts, providing listwise scores that depend on all items in the list</cite> <cite id="a27e57ce-1">This form of listwise attention is orthogonal to using transformers to compute individual item feature vectors</cite>. 
- Recent listwise LTR work formalizes training objectives with listwide labels, again centered on listwise attention mechanisms. <cite id="a27e57ce-4">RankFormer targets ranking formalized as listwise problems and discusses listwise Transformer models as a core component</cite>. 
- For personalized ranking, cross-attention aligns user embeddings with item features to weight and fuse information relevant to the user, extending attention-based ranking to user–item alignment. <cite id="a27e57ce-3">Cross-Attention-Rank incorporates user features via cross-attention, aligning user embeddings with item features for personalized ranking</cite>.

# Recommender/ad systems as ranking with attention-based weighting
- Deep Interest Network (DIN) and successors use attention to adaptively weight users’ historical behaviors, producing an adaptive representation that is fused into final click/relevance prediction—essentially a ranking task in ads/personalization. <cite id="3e167731-0">The attention network in DIN is a natural way to incorporate user history into personalized recommendation; Search Ranking DIN (DIN‑S) adapts DIN to ranking by including query-side features and modifying attention scores with a zero unit for non-correlated queries</cite> <cite id="3e167731-4">AFM uses attention networks to learn attention weights over feature interactions, and DIN weights users’ historical behaviors adaptively, capturing diversity in user interests</cite>. 
- Variants extend this pattern with hierarchical/multi-head attention and field-aware mechanisms to learn more precise weights over features and their interactions. <cite id="3e167731-1">DIN uses attention to capture how user interest varies towards ads to obtain adaptive representations; DIEN introduces an attentional updated GRU to model interest drifting; multi-head self-attention and hierarchical attention capture higher-order feature interactions</cite> <cite id="3e167731-2">DHAN combines deep interest with hierarchical attention to learn over user behaviors, with simplified structures referring to DIN and DIEN</cite> <cite id="3e167731-3">Attention-over-Attention (AFAFM) applies feature-level and interaction-level attention to discriminate the importance of feature interactions, contrasting with DIN’s local activation units for adaptive sequential weighting</cite> <cite id="3e167731-0">DIN‑S appends a zero score to regular attention scores before softmax to handle queries uncorrelated with past actions</cite>. 
- These ad/recommendation models are directly applicable to ranking pipelines where multiple candidate items are scored and ordered; the attention weights over user context or features serve as coefficients fused into the final relevance score. <cite id="3e167731-0">DIN‑S introduces query-side features to participate in attention with the historical sequence and adapts DIN’s attention to the search ranking setting</cite> <cite id="3e167731-4">Attention networks are introduced to learn attention weights for feature interactions in recommendation, improving prediction and capturing user interests</cite>.

# Broader context and fusion at the ranking pipeline
- Beyond attention within a single model, pipelines often fuse multiple rankers or modules using learned weights, which complements attention-based weighting inside a base ranker. <cite id="9c1e0b45-2">Weighted Reciprocal Rank Fusion (WRRF) dynamically adjusts module-specific weights to combine neural, legal, and case modules’ predicted ranks, prioritizing neural retrieval at top ranks and increasing symbolic module weight where confidence wanes</cite>. 
- Survey-style discussions of self-attention in retrieval emphasize that attention computes similarity-based weights and performs a weighted combination (often termed a weighted sum or attentional alignment), which is conceptually the same as fusing base representations with attention coefficients. <cite id="9c1e0b45-3">Self-attention determines correlation by computing similarities between word vectors, normalizing to weights, and combining via a weighted sum to obtain attention scores/representations</cite>. 
- In neural LTR broadly, attention has been used both as a feature extractor and as a way to provide hints for subsequent layers—both roles amount to learning weights over inputs that are then fused in downstream scoring. <cite id="9c1e0b45-0">Attention is traditionally used as a feature extractor (dynamic pooling), but the paper reimagines it as feature augmentation to provide hints for subsequent layers in neural ranking</cite>.

# Takeaways and where to start
- If your goal is “attention weights as fusion weights for a base ranking model,” two practical patterns recur: (1) listwise LTR with attention over items/queries (e.g., ANN, Attention Rank, DLCM/RankFormer) to weight and fuse item context into a listwise score; and (2) attention over user features or history in ad/recommendation ranking (e.g., DIN/DIEN/DHAN/AFM/AFAFM) to learn coefficients that adaptively combine base signals for each candidate. <cite id="27b16e93-0">Attention-based LTR can combine different embeddings of queries and results via learned weights for listwise ranking</cite> <cite id="3e167731-0">DIN and DIN‑S use attention to weight historical behaviors and adapt to ranking with query-side features and adjusted attention scores</cite> <cite id="a27e57ce-1">Transformer-based self-attention over item sequences provides listwise attention coefficients independent of item-vector transformers</cite> <cite id="3e167731-3">AFAFM applies attention-over-attention to learn weights over features and interactions for fusion</cite>. 
- Implementation-wise, expect attention modules that compute query/item or feature-level similarities, apply softmax or learned scoring to produce weights, and then take a weighted sum or pointwise product with base representations before the final ranking score. <cite id="9c1e0b45-3">Attention computes similarities, normalizes to weights, and combines via a weighted sum, producing attention scores/representations</cite> <cite id="27b16e93-0">Double attention mechanisms over queries and results help summarize relevant information before decoding listwise scores</cite>. 
- Finally, if you have multiple heterogeneous rankers or modules, consider learned fusion (e.g., WRRF) to combine their outputs, complementing attention-based internal weighting. <cite id="9c1e0b45-2">WRRF dynamically assigns weights to different module rankings to produce a final fused ranking</cite>.

In sum, there is a substantial body of work explicitly using attention to learn weights that fuse base representations or features into ranking models, spanning classic LTR (ANN, Attention Rank, DLCM), modern listwise Transformer rankers (RankFormer), and recommender/ad systems (DIN/DIEN/DHAN/AFM/AFAFM) that adaptively weight user context and features for final relevance prediction. <cite id="27b16e93-0">An attention-based deep net for ranking applies double attention to fuse embeddings for listwise ranking</cite> <cite id="a27e57ce-2">Attention-based listwise models compute ranking losses over full lists and can be trained efficiently while focusing on high-relevance items</cite> <cite id="3e167731-0">DIN and DIN‑S adapt attention to ranking by incorporating query-side features and modifying attention scores for zero-relevance cases</cite> <cite id="3e167731-4">AFM and DIN learn attention weights over feature interactions and user history to improve prediction, directly applicable to ranking</cite> <cite id="a27e57ce-1">Listwise self-attention over item sequences provides an alternative pathway to attention-based fusion of base signals in ranking</cite>.

A distinction is made with (neural) Information Retrieval [17], which often applies (neural) ranking to obtain information related to a query from a single collection of information resources. Though that field aims to find the most relevant resources, it has less of a focus on the LTR objectives themselves and more so on the relevance of individual information resources. Instead, we assume that a limited selection of relevant items has already been made, and our model should now put the most relevant of these on top. 

Traditional LTR [25] employs a pointwise scoring function, i.e. one that computes an individual score for each item independently, and only then compares those scores in pairwise [7] or listwise [10] loss functions. Yet the actual utility of items may depend on the rest of the list, e.g. an item may be much more desireable if it is the cheapest in the selection. Methods have therefore been proposed to compute listwise scores directly, i.e. scores that depend on the features of all items in the list. To this end, Ai et al. [1] proposed the Deep Listwise Context Model, which uses a recurrent neural network to take other inputs into account when reranking the top documents in information retrieval. This approach was further formalized to general multivariate scoring functions [3]. 

A list of items can be seen as a sequence, hence many approaches from Natural Language Processing (NLP) can readily be applied to ranking. Most notably, the Transformer [38] architecture has been used to learn from listwise ranking contexts using self-attention, which we refer to as listwise Transformers [24, 30-32, 34, 37, 42]. As a sequence-to-sequence architecture, the Transformer here considers sequences of items instead of words. This form of listwise attention is thus orthogonal to any usage Transformers that may be used to compute the feature vectors of individual items.
</snippet>

Title: Multi-Cast Attention Networks for Retrieval-based Question Answering and Response Prediction
Snippet: Modeling textual relevance between document query pairs lives at the heart of information retrieval (IR) research. Intuitively, this enables a wide assortment of real life applications, ranging from standard web search to automated chatbots. The key idea is that these systems learn a scoring function between document-query pairs, providing a ranked list of candidates as an output. A considerable fraction of such IR systems are focused on short textual documents, e.g., answering facts based questions or selecting the best response in the context of a chat-based system. The application of retrieval-based response and question answering (QA) systems is overall versatile, potentially serving as a powerful standalone domain-specific system or a crucial component in larger, general purpose chat systems such as Alexa. This paper presents a universal neural ranking model for such tasks. 

Neural networks (or deep learning) have garnered considerable attention for retrieval-based systems [8,27,29,39,52]. Notably, the dominant state-of-the-art systems for many benchmarks are now neural models, almost completely dispensing with traditional feature engineering techniques altogether. In these systems, convolutional or recurrent networks are empowered with recent techniques such as neural attention [1,25,39], achieving very competitive results on standard benchmarks. The key idea of attention is to extract only the most relevant information that is useful for prediction. In the context of textual data, attention learns to weight words and sub-phrases within documents based on how important they are. In the same vein, co-attention mechanisms [5,28,50,54] are a form of attention mechanisms that learn joint pairwise attentions, with respect to both document and query. 

Attention is traditionally used and commonly imagined as a feature extractor. It's behavior can be thought of as a dynamic form of pooling as it learns to select and compose different words to form the final document representation. This paper re-imagines attention as a form of feature augmentation method. Attention is casted with the purpose of not compositional learning or pooling but to provide hints for subsequent layers. To the best of our knowledge, this is a new way to exploit attention in neural ranking models. We begin by describing not only its advantages but also how it handles the weaknesses of existing models designed today.
</snippet>

Extensive experiment comparisons against a rich set of baseline methods and an in-depth ablation analysis confirm the value of our proposed approach for modeling search context buried in search tasks.

The attention mechanism focuses on a subset of the details relevant to our objective instead of assessing the entire picture simultaneously. The core of the attention mechanism lies in selecting the portion of detail to concentrate on based on our goals and continually analyzing it. By calculating the similarity of word vectors, self-attention determines the degree of correlation between the current word and other words for the image captioning task. Typically, two-word vectors have smaller distance angles and greater products the closer their meanings are to each other. By normalizing the similarity, weights are generated. The attention score also referred to as the level of attention of the current word to other words, is obtained by multiplying the weights by the word vectors and summing them. Title: EcoDetect-YOLOv2: A High-Performance Model for Multi-Scale Waste Detection in Complex Surveillance Environments
Snippet: The attention mechanism, inspired by human visual perception and neural information processing, has been extensively applied in deep learning [20]. This mechanism dynamically allocates computational resources, allowing models to focus on critical feature information while suppressing irrelevant signals, thereby improving feature representation and task awareness. Furthermore, attention mechanisms effectively reduce model redundancy, enhance robustness against noise, and improve network generalization. 

In conventional neural networks, all input features are typically treated equally, leading to computational inefficiency and reduced generalization capability [21]. However, in many practical tasks, only a subset of input features significantly influences the final prediction. Treating all features uniformly can introduce unnecessary computational overhead. Additionally, deep neural networks are often regarded as "black-box" models with limited interpretability. The incorporation of attention mechanisms enables weight visualization, enhancing model interpretability and facilitating network optimization. 

Attention mechanisms have demonstrated outstanding performance across various deep learning tasks. For instance, in image classification, attention mechanisms enable models to focus on discriminative regions, improving classification accuracy. In text summarization, these mechanisms help identify key information in source text, generating more precise and concise summaries [22]. By optimizing feature selection and information filtering, attention mechanisms have achieved significant advancements in computer vision, natural language processing, and speech recognition, establishing themselves as a pivotal research direction in deep learning.

The attention mechanism, inspired by human visual perception and neural information processing, has been extensively applied in deep learning [20]. This mechanism dynamically allocates computational resources, allowing models to focus on critical feature information while suppressing irrelevant signals, thereby improving feature representation and task awareness. Furthermore, attention mechanisms effectively reduce model redundancy, enhance robustness against noise, and improve network generalization. 

In conventional neural networks, all input features are typically treated equally, leading to computational inefficiency and reduced generalization capability [21]. However, in many practical tasks, only a subset of input features significantly influences the final prediction. Treating all features uniformly can introduce unnecessary computational overhead. Additionally, deep neural networks are often regarded as "black-box" models with limited interpretability. The incorporation of attention mechanisms enables weight visualization, enhancing model interpretability and facilitating network optimization. 

Attention mechanisms have demonstrated outstanding performance across various deep learning tasks. For instance, in image classification, attention mechanisms enable models to focus on discriminative regions, improving classification accuracy. In text summarization, these mechanisms help identify key information in source text, generating more precise and concise summaries [22]. By optimizing feature selection and information filtering, attention mechanisms have achieved significant advancements in computer vision, natural language processing, and speech recognition, establishing themselves as a pivotal research direction in deep learning.

documents.snippet: In information retrieval, learning to rank constructs a machine-based ranking model which given a query, sorts the search results by their degree of relevance or importance to the query. Neural networks have been successfully applied to this problem, and in this paper, we propose an attention-based deep neural network which better incorporates different embeddings of the queries and search results with an attention-based mechanism. This model also applies a decoder mechanism to learn the ranks of the search results in a listwise fashion. The embeddings are trained with convolutional neural networks or the word2vec model. We demonstrate the performance of this model with image retrieval and text querying data sets.

The attention mechanism focuses on a subset of the details relevant to our objective instead of assessing the entire picture simultaneously. The core of the attention mechanism lies in selecting the portion of detail to concentrate on based on our goals and continually analyzing it. By calculating the similarity of word vectors, self-attention determines the degree of correlation between the current word and other words for the image captioning task. Typically, two-word vectors have smaller distance angles and greater products the closer their meanings are to each other. By normalizing the similarity, weights are generated. The attention score also referred to as the level of attention of the current word to other words, is obtained by multiplying the weights by the word vectors and summing them. Title: RankFormer: Listwise Learning-to-Rank Using Listwide Labels
Snippet: Learning-to-Rank (LTR) provides tools, e.g. objective functions, to learn from feedback labels such that a ranking model is improved. 

To this end, neural ranking uses neural networks as the model. 

A distinction is made with (neural) Information Retrieval [17], which often applies (neural) ranking to obtain information related to a query from a single collection of information resources. Though that field aims to find the most relevant resources, it has less of a focus on the LTR objectives themselves and more so on the relevance of individual information resources. Instead, we assume that a limited selection of relevant items has already been made, and our model should now put the most relevant of these on top. 

Traditional LTR [25] employs a pointwise scoring function, i.e. one that computes an individual score for each item independently, and only then compares those scores in pairwise [7] or listwise [10] loss functions. Yet the actual utility of items may depend on the rest of the list, e.g. an item may be much more desireable if it is the cheapest in the selection. Methods have therefore been proposed to compute listwise scores directly, i.e. scores that depend on the features of all items in the list. To this end, Ai et al. [1] proposed the Deep Listwise Context Model, which uses a recurrent neural network to take other inputs into account when reranking the top documents in information retrieval. This approach was further formalized to general multivariate scoring functions [3]. 

A list of items can be seen as a sequence, hence many approaches from Natural Language Processing (NLP) can readily be applied to ranking. Most notably, the Transformer [38] architecture has been used to learn from listwise ranking contexts using self-attention, which we refer to as listwise Transformers [24, 30-32, 34, 37, 42]. As a sequence-to-sequence architecture, the Transformer here considers sequences of items instead of words. This form of listwise attention is thus orthogonal to any usage Transformers that may be used to compute the feature vectors of individual items.

For instance, for a text query, it may be embedded with tf-idf, LSA (Landauer et al., 1998), or word2vec (Mikolov et al., 2013), and it is unclear how to combine such information with learning to rank. Meanwhile, the attention mechanism is demonstrated to be successful in focusing on distinct aspects of the input, and extracting more relevant information for the output, thereby incorporating different features (Bahdanau et al., 2015;Cho et al., 2015). Therefore, we develop a learning to rank model with an attention mechanism which can help us better summarize information from the query and search results, and applies a decoder mechanism to rank all the search results, therefore providing a flexible list-wise ranking approach which can be applied to both image retrieval and text querying. Our model has the following contributions: (1) it applies the attention mechanism to listwise learning to rank problems, which we think is novel in the learning to rank literature; (2) it takes different embeddings of queries and search results into account, incorporating them with the attention mechanism; (3) double attention mechanisms are applied to both queries and search results. 

Section 2 reviews the RankNet, similarity matching, and the attention mechanism in details. Section 3 constructs arXiv:1702.06106v1 [cs.LG] 20 Feb 2017 the attention-based deep net for ranking, and discusses how to calibrate the model. Section 4 demonstrates the performance of our model on image retrieval and text querying data sets. Section 5 discusses about potential future research and concludes the paper.

documents.snippet:
Learning-to-Rank (LTR) provides tools, e.g. objective functions, to learn from feedback labels such that a ranking model is improved. 

To this end, neural ranking uses neural networks as the model. 

A distinction is made with (neural) Information Retrieval [17], which often applies (neural) ranking to obtain information related to a query from a single collection of information resources. Though that field aims to find the most relevant resources, it has less of a focus on the LTR objectives themselves and more so on the relevance of individual information resources. Instead, we assume that a limited selection of relevant items has already been made, and our model should now put the most relevant of these on top. 

Traditional LTR [25] employs a pointwise scoring function, i.e. one that computes an individual score for each item independently, and only then compares those scores in pairwise [7] or listwise [10] loss functions. Yet the actual utility of items may depend on the rest of the list, e.g. an item may be much more desireable if it is the cheapest in the selection. Methods have therefore been proposed to compute listwise scores directly, i.e. scores that depend on the features of all items in the list. To this end, Ai et al. [1] proposed the Deep Listwise Context Model, which uses a recurrent neural network to take other inputs into account when reranking the top documents in information retrieval. This approach was further formalized to general multivariate scoring functions [3]. 

A list of items can be seen as a sequence, hence many approaches from Natural Language Processing (NLP) can readily be applied to ranking. Most notably, the Transformer [38] architecture has been used to learn from listwise ranking contexts using self-attention, which we refer to as listwise Transformers [24, 30-32, 34, 37, 42]. As a sequence-to-sequence architecture, the Transformer here considers sequences of items instead of words. This form of listwise attention is thus orthogonal to any usage Transformers that may be used to compute the feature vectors of individual items.

Title: Multi-Cast Attention Networks for Retrieval-based Question Answering and Response Prediction
Snippet: Modeling textual relevance between document query pairs lives at the heart of information retrieval (IR) research. Intuitively, this enables a wide assortment of real life applications, ranging from standard web search to automated chatbots. The key idea is that these systems learn a scoring function between document-query pairs, providing a ranked list of candidates as an output. A considerable fraction of such IR systems are focused on short textual documents, e.g., answering facts based questions or selecting the best response in the context of a chat-based system. The application of retrieval-based response and question answering (QA) systems is overall versatile, potentially serving as a powerful standalone domain-specific system or a crucial component in larger, general purpose chat systems such as Alexa. This paper presents a universal neural ranking model for such tasks. 

Neural networks (or deep learning) have garnered considerable attention for retrieval-based systems [8,27,29,39,52]. Notably, the dominant state-of-the-art systems for many benchmarks are now neural models, almost completely dispensing with traditional feature engineering techniques altogether. In these systems, convolutional or recurrent networks are empowered with recent techniques such as neural attention [1,25,39], achieving very competitive results on standard benchmarks. The key idea of attention is to extract only the most relevant information that is useful for prediction. In the context of textual data, attention learns to weight words and sub-phrases within documents based on how important they are. In the same vein, co-attention mechanisms [5,28,50,54] are a form of attention mechanisms that learn joint pairwise attentions, with respect to both document and query. 

Attention is traditionally used and commonly imagined as a feature extractor. It's behavior can be thought of as a dynamic form of pooling as it learns to select and compose different words to form the final document representation. This paper re-imagines attention as a form of feature augmentation method. Attention is casted with the purpose of not compositional learning or pooling but to provide hints for subsequent layers. To the best of our knowledge, this is a new way to exploit attention in neural ranking models. We begin by describing not only its advantages but also how it handles the weaknesses of existing models designed today.

Title: Context Attentive Document Ranking and Query Suggestion
Snippet: We present a context-aware neural ranking model to exploit users' on-task search activities and enhance retrieval performance. In particular, a two-level hierarchical recurrent neural network is introduced to learn search context representation of individual queries, search tasks, and corresponding dependency structure by jointly optimizing two companion retrieval tasks: document ranking and query suggestion. To identify variable dependency structure between search context and users' ongoing search activities, attention at both levels of recurrent states are introduced. Extensive experiment comparisons against a rich set of baseline methods and an in-depth ablation analysis confirm the value of our proposed approach for modeling search context buried in search tasks.

Snippet: Within our general approach, we first train a neural ranking model with the Fast Geometric Ensembling (FGE) technique, which outputs N different model checkpoints, saved at different phases of the training process. The different checkpoints are used to re-rank initial lists with the top 1000 passages for each test query, resulting in the generation of N ranked lists. For the initial rankings, we used the DeepCT first-stage retrieval algorithm, which extends BM25 with context-aware term weights derived from a BERT model [8]. Finally, the N different ranked lists are used as input to a fusion method, which combines the scores to produce a final re-ranked list. # Generative AI Competencies Framework: Core Areas, Technical Skills, and Governance

## Why a Competency Framework for Generative AI
Generative AI (GenAI) tools are reshaping work and learning across domains, creating a need for a coherent set of knowledge, skills, and ethical/legal capabilities that go beyond traditional digital or AI literacy. A competency-based model helps individuals and organizations use GenAI responsibly, avoid overreliance, and integrate human-AI collaboration effectively as technologies evolve rapidly and new use cases emerge continuously. <cite id="2f0b6859-0">The ability to comprehend, assess, and employ generative AI technologies is fundamental to empower individuals to engage with and contribute to an AI-driven world, combining technical proficiency with adaptive usage, ethical considerations, and legal awareness</cite> <cite id="2f0b6859-3">Generative AI literacy is a long-term, continuous process, with competencies spanning knowledge, skills, abilities, and behaviors, and requiring progression from basic tool use to content assessment, prompt engineering, and programming, with ethical, contextual, and legal competencies placed toward the end</cite> <cite id="2f0b6859-2">Because GenAI spans domains, domain-specific sub-skills and ethical considerations will be needed across industries</cite>.

## Broad Competency Models and Education Initiatives
Recent work proposes a "Generative AI Literacy" competency-based model with twelve defining competencies that scaffold learning from foundational knowledge to advanced skills and ethical/legal reasoning. The model emphasizes progression and inclusivity, positioning competencies for learners from consumers to developers and across sectors. <cite id="2f0b6859-0">The framework enumerates twelve key competencies to build knowledge and skills essential for understanding and using GenAI systems, aiming to guide individuals to engage effectively and responsibly across domains</cite> <cite id="2f0b6859-3">The competencies follow a logical progression: general basis of knowledge and skills to know and use GenAI tools; ability to detect AI-generated content; technical skills in content assessment and prompt engineering; programming; and finally knowledge of contexts, ethical implications, and legal aspects</cite> <cite id="2f0b6859-4">The model can underpin curricula from elementary to higher education, professional development, and community programs, and it is intended to evolve as technology advances</cite>.

Internationally, UNESCO has advanced education-oriented competency guidance. <cite id="4f774975-0">UNESCO's AI Competency Framework for Students focuses on four areas: human-centered thinking, AI ethics, technical applications, and system design, complementing earlier guidance for GenAI in education and research that emphasizes a human-centered approach, data privacy, ethical standards, and enhanced teacher training</cite>. In Europe, legislative and governance context is shaping competency needs. <cite id="3eee75f8-2">The European Parliament and Commission's work on the AI Act has increased attention to risks, regulation, and governance of AI systems, underscoring the need for AI literacy in public and professional contexts</cite>.

## Core Knowledge and Skills
A foundational layer of competencies includes:
- **Understanding GenAI capabilities and limits**: Knowing what GenAI can and cannot do across text, images, audio, video, and code; recognizing common failure modes and overreliance risks. <cite id="2f0b6859-3">The model begins with a general basis of knowledge and skills to know and use GenAI tools, followed by the ability to detect AI-generated content</cite> <cite id="2f0b6859-2">GenAI spans multiple modalities and domains, requiring distinct understanding relative to other AI tools</cite>.
- **Prompting and interaction design**: Foundational skills in crafting prompts, iterative refinement, and interacting with models to elicit reliable outputs. <cite id="2f0b6859-3">Technical skills include content assessment and prompt engineering as a core competency in progression</cite>.
- **Critical evaluation and verification**: Detecting AI-generated content, assessing provenance, and validating outputs. <cite id="2f0b6859-3">The competency set explicitly includes the ability to detect AI-generated content as a foundational skill prior to more advanced technical competencies</cite>.
- **Programming and tool fluency**: Integration with coding and development workflows; using APIs and iterative prototyping. <cite id="2f0b6859-3">Programming is positioned as part of the technical progression after core prompting and content assessment skills</cite>.
- **Context, ethics, and legal awareness**: Understanding ethical implications, legal obligations, and domain norms. <cite id="2f0b6859-3">Knowledge of contexts, ethical implications, and legal aspects are placed later in the progression to emphasize their importance for responsible use</cite>.

## Technical Capabilities for Effective Human–AI Collaboration
Beyond core literacy, practitioners need technical capabilities that support safe, reliable, and collaborative use of GenAI:
- **System integration and workflows**: Embedding GenAI into processes (e.g., writing, design, research) with checks and balances against hallucinations and bias. <cite id="2f0b6859-2">Because applications span domains, finer, specific sub-skills and ethical considerations are required, indicating the need for workflow-level competencies</cite> <cite id="2f0b6859-0">Moving from consumers to interpreters of AI models enables users to optimize tool utilization for problem-solving and collaborate with AI</cite>.
- **Evaluation and testing**: Methods to assess model outputs for accuracy, reliability, and robustness in task-specific contexts. <cite id="3eee75f8-4">Standardized Testing and Assessment Guidelines (STAGER) propose checklists for evaluating GenAI proficiency in medical competency testing, illustrating sector-specific evaluation frameworks</cite>.
- **Data and privacy practices**: Competence in data selection, consent, anonymization, and privacy-preserving techniques when training or fine-tuning. <cite id="4f774975-0">UNESCO's guidance emphasizes data privacy in GenAI use in education and research, signaling the need for privacy-aware competencies</cite>.
- **Rag and evidence grounding**: Skills to retrieve, integrate, and cite authoritative sources to mitigate hallucinations. <cite id="3eee75f8-0">A retrieval-augmented generation approach was used to project shifts in workforce competencies and identify vulnerable roles, underscoring the importance of grounding and retrieval skills in evolving job requirements</cite>.
- **Security and safety**: Identifying and mitigating prompt injection, misuse, and exposure of sensitive information. <cite id="3eee75f8-3">Work bringing worker voice into GenAI highlights both potential positive and negative uses and raises compensation and governance questions, pointing to the need for safety and responsible use competencies</cite>.

## Domain-Specific Competencies
Domain-specific competencies tailor core skills to sectoral needs and risk profiles:

This paper adopts the aforementioned definition of competency given by the National Institute of Health, which groups competencies into knowledge, skills, abilities, or behaviors [70]. Alongside, this paper defines generative AI literacy as a long-term, continuous process by which several core competencies, allowing to effectively and responsibly understand, assess, and work with generative AI technologies, have been identified, acquired, practiced, and mastered. 

Based on existing literature on AI literacy, digital literacy, prompt engineering, generative AI, and related topics, including surveys and reviews, peer-reviewed publications, gray literature, and books, this work identifies twelve specific competencies to define the concept of generative AI literacy acknowledging the varied nature of engaging with generative AI.

Title: Complementarity, Augmentation, or Substitutivity? The Impact of Generative Artificial Intelligence on the U.S. Federal Workforce
Snippet: This study investigates the near-future impacts of generative artificial intelligence (AI) technologies on occupational competencies across the U.S. federal workforce. We develop a multi-stage Retrieval-Augmented Generation system to leverage large language models for predictive AI modeling that projects shifts in required competencies and to identify vulnerable occupations on a knowledge-by-skill-by-ability basis across the federal government workforce. This study highlights policy recommendations essential for workforce planning in the era of AI. We integrate several sources of detailed data on occupational requirements across the federal government from both centralized and decentralized human resource sources, including from the U.S. Office of Personnel Management (OPM) and various federal agencies. While our preliminary findings suggest some significant shifts in required competencies and potential vulnerability of certain roles to AI-driven changes, we provide nuanced insights that support arguments against abrupt or generic approaches to strategic human capital planning around the development of generative AI. The study aims to inform strategic workforce planning and policy development within federal agencies and demonstrates how this approach can be replicated across other large employment institutions and labor markets.

Snippet: With the rapid spread of Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems across all domains, the concept of AI literacy ("a set of competencies that enables individuals to critically evaluate AI technologies" [61]) has become increasingly important and necessary in the past few years. The legislative work on the European AI Act [32] done by the European Parliament and European Commission has also contributed to increasing attention towards the risks and challenges posed by systems and tools based on AI models, as well as viable ways to regulate them [41,42]. 

Generative models have found applications across many sectors, reflecting their adaptability and potential impact [58,78,81]. As governments worldwide increasingly digitalize their operations and services, there is a growing intersection between AI and governance. Generative AI technologies can transform communication, public engagement, and decision-making processes with and within governmental bodies [13]. Understanding the implications, challenges, and opportunities presented by generative AI is vital for researchers and practitioners in the field of digital government to make informed decisions about its usage and adoption. At the same time, a literate workforce is better equipped to identify and mitigate potential risks, ensuring that the deployment of generative AI in government processes is accompanied by risk assessment and mitigation strategies. With the transformation of the digital government arena, generative AI literacy is essential for future-proofing government operations. Professionals who understand generative AI can proactively adapt to emerging technologies, ensuring sustained relevance and effectiveness of digital government initiatives. 

The concept of AI literacy has also emerged as a fundamental set of competencies to have during the AI era. However, the recent explosion of generative AI, spearheaded by ChatGPT, the Large Language Model (LLM) developed by OpenAI, has created the need for a more definite set of skills, abilities, and knowledge, specific to the scope and applications of generative AI. The need for specific generative AI literacy arises from the following factors. First, the functionality to generate new text, images, music, videos, and code requires a distinct understanding of what generative AI can and cannot do compared to other existing AI tools. Second, generative AI's transdisciplinarity has implications for various fields, such as writing, design, and scientific research [78].

# Generative AI Competencies Framework: Core Areas, Technical Skills, and Governance

## Why a Competency Framework for Generative AI
Generative AI (GenAI) tools are reshaping work and learning across domains, creating a need for a coherent set of knowledge, skills, and ethical/legal capabilities that go beyond traditional digital or AI literacy. A competency-based model helps individuals and organizations use GenAI responsibly, avoid overreliance, and integrate human-AI collaboration effectively as technologies evolve rapidly and new use cases emerge continuously. <cite id="2f0b6859-0">The ability to comprehend, assess, and employ generative AI technologies is fundamental to empower individuals to engage with and contribute to an AI-driven world, combining technical proficiency with adaptive usage, ethical considerations, and legal awareness</cite> <cite id="2f0b6859-3">Generative AI literacy is a long-term, continuous process, with competencies spanning knowledge, skills, abilities, and behaviors, and requiring progression from basic tool use to content assessment, prompt engineering, and programming, with ethical, contextual, and legal competencies placed toward the end</cite> <cite id="2f0b6859-2">Because GenAI spans domains, domain-specific sub-skills and ethical considerations will be needed across industries</cite>.

## Broad Competency Models and Education Initiatives
Recent work proposes a "Generative AI Literacy" competency-based model with twelve defining competencies that scaffold learning from foundational knowledge to advanced skills and ethical/legal reasoning. The model emphasizes progression and inclusivity, positioning competencies for learners from consumers to developers and across sectors. <cite id="2f0b6859-0">The framework enumerates twelve key competencies to build knowledge and skills essential for understanding and using GenAI systems, aiming to guide individuals to engage effectively and responsibly across domains</cite> <cite id="2f0b6859-3">The competencies follow a logical progression: general basis of knowledge and skills to know and use GenAI tools; ability to detect AI-generated content; technical skills in content assessment and prompt engineering; programming; and finally knowledge of contexts, ethical implications, and legal aspects</cite> <cite id="2f0b6859-4">The model can underpin curricula from elementary to higher education, professional development, and community programs, and it is intended to evolve as technology advances</cite>.

Internationally, UNESCO has advanced education-oriented competency guidance. <cite id="4f774975-0">UNESCO's AI Competency Framework for Students focuses on four areas: human-centered thinking, AI ethics, technical applications, and system design, complementing earlier guidance for GenAI in education and research that emphasizes a human-centered approach, data privacy, ethical standards, and enhanced teacher training</cite>. In Europe, legislative and governance context is shaping competency needs. <cite id="3eee75f8-2">The European Parliament and Commission's work on the AI Act has increased attention to risks, regulation, and governance of AI systems, underscoring the need for AI literacy in public and professional contexts</cite>.

## Core Knowledge and Skills
A foundational layer of competencies includes:
- **Understanding GenAI capabilities and limits**: Knowing what GenAI can and cannot do across text, images, audio, video, and code; recognizing common failure modes and overreliance risks. <cite id="2f0b6859-3">The model begins with a general basis of knowledge and skills to know and use GenAI tools, followed by the ability to detect AI-generated content</cite> <cite id="2f0b6859-2">GenAI spans multiple modalities and domains, requiring distinct understanding relative to other AI tools</cite>.
- **Prompting and interaction design**: Foundational skills in crafting prompts, iterative refinement, and interacting with models to elicit reliable outputs. <cite id="2f0b6859-3">Technical skills include content assessment and prompt engineering as a core competency in progression</cite>.
- **Critical evaluation and verification**: Detecting AI-generated content, assessing provenance, and validating outputs. <cite id="2f0b6859-3">The competency set explicitly includes the ability to detect AI-generated content as a foundational skill prior to more advanced technical competencies</cite>.
- **Programming and tool fluency**: Integration with coding and development workflows; using APIs and iterative prototyping. <cite id="2f0b6859-3">Programming is positioned as part of the technical progression after core prompting and content assessment skills</cite>.
- **Context, ethics, and legal awareness**: Understanding ethical implications, legal obligations, and domain norms. <cite id="2f0b6859-3">Knowledge of contexts, ethical implications, and legal aspects are placed later in the progression to emphasize their importance for responsible use</cite>.

## Technical Capabilities for Effective Human–AI Collaboration
Beyond core literacy, practitioners need technical capabilities that support safe, reliable, and collaborative use of GenAI:
- **System integration and workflows**: Embedding GenAI into processes (e.g., writing, design, research) with checks and balances against hallucinations and bias. <cite id="2f0b6859-2">Because applications span domains, finer, specific sub-skills and ethical considerations are required, indicating the need for workflow-level competencies</cite> <cite id="2f0b6859-0">Moving from consumers to interpreters of AI models enables users to optimize tool utilization for problem-solving and collaborate with AI</cite>.
- **Evaluation and testing**: Methods to assess model outputs for accuracy, reliability, and robustness in task-specific contexts. <cite id="3eee75f8-4">Standardized Testing and Assessment Guidelines (STAGER) propose checklists for evaluating GenAI proficiency in medical competency testing, illustrating sector-specific evaluation frameworks</cite>.
- **Data and privacy practices**: Competence in data selection, consent, anonymization, and privacy-preserving techniques when training or fine-tuning. <cite id="4f774975-0">UNESCO's guidance emphasizes data privacy in GenAI use in education and research, signaling the need for privacy-aware competencies</cite>.
- **Rag and evidence grounding**: Skills to retrieve, integrate, and cite authoritative sources to mitigate hallucinations. <cite id="3eee75f8-0">A retrieval-augmented generation approach was used to project shifts in workforce competencies and identify vulnerable roles, underscoring the importance of grounding and retrieval skills in evolving job requirements</cite>.
- **Security and safety**: Identifying and mitigating prompt injection, misuse, and exposure of sensitive information. <cite id="3eee75f8-3">Work bringing worker voice into GenAI highlights both potential positive and negative uses and raises compensation and governance questions, pointing to the need for safety and responsible use competencies</cite>.

## Domain-Specific Competencies
Domain-specific competencies tailor core skills to sectoral needs and risk profiles:
- **Education and research**: Human-centered design of AI literacy modules; teacher training; ethical, legal, and privacy considerations in educational use. <cite id="4f774975-0">UNESCO's guidance for GenAI in education and research emphasizes a human-centered approach, data privacy, ethical standards, and enhanced teacher training</cite> <cite id="4f774975-3">A human-centered AI literacy module for tertiary institutions outlines constructs providing core competence for students, staff, and professionals</cite>.
- **Healthcare and public-sector applications**: Reliability, validity, and safety in clinical and governmental decision support; evaluation checklists; governance alignment with regulations. <cite id="3eee75f8-4">The STAGER checklist provides a validated set of dimensions for evaluating GenAI reliability for medical competency testing, reflecting the need for rigorous, domain-specific assessment competencies</cite> <cite id="3eee75f8-2">GenAI's impact on government operations and the AI Act's regulatory context elevate the need for risk assessment and governance competencies in public-sector use</cite>.
- **Workforce and labor markets**: Mapping occupational competency shifts and designing policies and training programs. <cite id="3eee75f8-0">A multi-stage RAG-based approach projected knowledge–skill–ability shifts in federal workforce competencies and potential vulnerability of roles to AI-driven changes, informing targeted workforce planning and training</cite> <cite id="3eee75f8-3">A framework for bringing worker voice into GenAI emphasizes inclusive governance and aligning use with workforce and societal interests</cite>.
- **Software engineering and development**: Prompt engineering, code generation, unit testing, CI/CD integration, and documentation; safe integration with retrieval and review processes. <cite id="2f0b6859-3">The competency progression includes programming and prompt engineering as technical skills, with ethical and legal competencies for context in code-generation workflows</cite> <cite id="2f0b6859-2">Domain-specific sub-skills are needed as industry applications vary, indicating the need for specialized software-engineering competencies around GenAI</cite>.

## Governance, Ethics, and Legal Competencies
Responsible deployment requires competencies in governance, ethics, and law:
- **Risk assessment and management**: Identifying and mitigating risks such as bias, hallucinations, security vulnerabilities, and operational disruption. <cite id="3eee75f8-2">The AI Act's focus on risks and regulation underscores the need for risk assessment and mitigation strategies when deploying GenAI in government and other high-stakes contexts</cite>.
- **Ethics and values**: Human-centered design, fairness, transparency, accountability, and sustainability in GenAI systems. <cite id="4f774975-0">UNESCO's AI Competency Framework emphasizes human-centered thinking and AI ethics as core areas for students</cite> <cite id="2f0b6859-3">Ethical implications are a late-stage competency in the progression, reflecting their centrality to responsible use</cite>.
- **Privacy, security, and data governance**: Compliance with data protection laws, privacy-by-design, secure coding practices, and safe data handling. <cite id="4f774975-0">UNESCO guidance highlights data privacy as a key concern for GenAI in education and research</cite>.
- **Intellectual property and licensing**: Understanding copyright, licensing, ownership, and fair use when generating, reusing, or training on content. <cite id="2f0b6859-0">Legal awareness is explicitly integrated into the competency model to support responsible and creative use</cite>.
- **Responsible disclosure and safety**: Reporting vulnerabilities, handling sensitive information, and establishing safety protocols for GenAI systems. <cite id="3eee75f8-3">Worker-voice frameworks highlight governance tensions and the need for policies that balance benefits and risks for business, workforce, and society</cite>.

## Implementation and Learning Pathways
Organizations and institutions can operationalize the framework through layered programs:
- **Curricula and lifelong learning**: Embed the competency progression into education from K–12 through higher education and professional development, with continuous reskilling. <cite id="2f0b6859-4">The twelve-competency model serves as a foundation for curricula across levels, including professional development and community outreach</cite>.
- **Professional development and upskilling**: Targeted programs for workers and teams to address shifting competencies and role-specific needs. <cite id="3eee75f8-0">Projected shifts in required competencies across federal roles inform targeted training and workforce planning</cite>.
- **Human–AI collaboration design**: Foster communication, trust, and symbiotic relationships through practice-based training and design exercises. <cite id="2f0b6859-4">The model calls for frameworks that facilitate effective human–AI collaboration, emphasizing communication, trust, and productive symbiosis</cite>.
- **Evaluation and quality assurance**: Adopt sector-specific checklists and benchmarks to validate AI-enhanced workflows. <cite id="3eee75f8-4">The STAGER checklist exemplifies how to structure and validate GenAI assessments in medical competency contexts</cite>.

## Governance and Evolution of the Framework
Competency needs evolve with rapid model advances and new applications, requiring governance and iterative updates:
- **Monitoring and revision**: Establish processes to review and update competency sets as models, tools, and regulations change. <cite id="2f0b6859-0">The authors emphasize that GenAI literacy is an evolving set of skills and that the framework should be revised and updated as technology evolves</cite>.
- **Stakeholder collaboration**: Engage educators, employers, workers, and policymakers to align competencies with societal and labor-market needs. <cite id="2f0b6859-4">Stakeholders are urged to collaboratively design and implement initiatives fostering AI literacy across levels</cite> <cite id="3eee75f8-3">Bringing worker voice into GenAI development and use can align competencies and governance with workforce and societal interests</cite>.
- **Policy alignment**: Align competency frameworks with international guidance and sectoral regulation (e.g., UNESCO guidance; EU AI Act context). <cite id="4f774975-0">UNESCO's frameworks and guidance provide policy-aligned directions for education and student competencies</cite> <cite id="3eee75f8-2">The EU AI Act's regulatory focus elevates governance competencies in high-stakes domains like government and healthcare</cite>.

## Summary: The Competency Framework in Practice
- **Foundational literacy**: Understanding GenAI capabilities and limits; detecting AI-generated content; basic prompting and programming fluency. <cite id="2f0b6859-3">Progression from foundational knowledge and tool use to content assessment and prompt engineering, followed by programming</cite>.
- **Technical proficiency**: Evaluation and testing; retrieval augmentation and grounding; security and privacy practices; system integration and workflow design; safety and responsible disclosure. <cite id="3eee75f8-4">Sector-specific evaluation checklists for reliability</cite> <cite id="3eee75f8-0">Competency mapping and shifts using RAG for workforce planning</cite> <cite id="4f774975-0">Privacy and ethics emphasis in education and research</cite>.
- **Domain-specific expertise**: Education and research modules; healthcare reliability and regulation; software engineering and development workflows; public-sector risk and governance. <cite id="4f774975-3">Human-centered AI literacy module design</cite> <cite id="3eee75f8-2">AI Act-informed governance in public and high-stakes contexts</cite> <cite id="2f0b6859-2">Need for industry-specific sub-skills</cite>.
- **Governance, ethics, and law**: Risk assessment; ethical design; privacy and security; IP and licensing; responsible disclosure; alignment with regulatory frameworks. <cite id="3eee75f8-2">Regulatory context and risk mitigation in government and healthcare</cite> <cite id="4f774975-0">UNESCO's human-centered, ethical, and privacy-focused guidance</cite> <cite id="2f0b6859-0">Legal awareness and ethical considerations integrated into literacy</cite>.
- **Implementation and governance**: Curricula, professional development, human–AI collaboration frameworks, and evaluation checklists, with iterative updates and stakeholder engagement. <cite id="2f0b6859-4">Programmatic uses across education and workforce</cite> <cite id="3eee75f8-3">Worker-voice frameworks for inclusive governance</cite>.

This framework is not static: organizations should pilot competencies in use cases (e.g., RAG pipelines, evaluation workflows), gather feedback, and update training and policies as models and regulations evolve, ensuring that GenAI competencies remain aligned with both technological progress and societal expectations. <cite id="2f0b6859-0">As technology advances, revisions to competencies may be necessary, and institutions should integrate them into curricula and training initiatives</cite> <cite id="3eee75f8-2">The evolving regulatory landscape further necessitates ongoing competency development and governance alignment</cite>.
</answer>

Title: Generative AI Literacy: Twelve Defining Competencies
Snippet: As previously mentioned, the rapid rise of generative AI tools and their widespread adoption in various disciplines have created a unique set of skills specific to these novel tools, which go beyond the traditional competencies associated with data literacy, digital literacy, or AI literacy. This paper aims to identify a set of competencies that are necessary for users to develop to effectively comprehend and utilize generative tools. This paper adopts the aforementioned definition of competency given by the National Institute of Health, which groups competencies into knowledge, skills, abilities, or behaviors [70]. Alongside, this paper defines generative AI literacy as a long-term, continuous process by which several core competencies, allowing to effectively and responsibly understand, assess, and work with generative AI technologies, have been identified, acquired, practiced, and mastered. 

Based on existing literature on AI literacy, digital literacy, prompt engineering, generative AI, and related topics, including surveys and reviews, peer-reviewed publications, gray literature, and books, this work identifies twelve specific competencies to define the concept of generative AI literacy acknowledging the varied nature of engaging with generative AI. 

As illustrated by Figure 1, the ordering of these competencies is purposeful and follows a logical progression to represent a structured learning path reflecting a continuum of learning, as continuous self-learning is transversal to all the other capabilities. The initial focus is on creating the general basis of knowledge and skill to know and use generative AI tools, followed by knowing how to detect AI-generated content. These develop into more technical skills related to the use of generative AI, with content assessment, prompt engineering, and programming. Then, the three interrelated competencies regarding the knowledge of the contexts, ethical implication, and legal aspects, are intentionally placed towards the end to underline their significance. This approach allows individuals to progressively acquire skills and knowledge, encouraging a user-centric learning experience. 

All the competencies of this Competency-Based Model for generative AI literacy are outlined in Table 3, with a more detailed explanation in Section 5. Table 3 includes examples of the positive implications of being proficient with each capability, as well as the negative implications of not acquiring the specific competency. The work lists twelve key competencies to build the knowledge and skills that are essential for understanding and using generative AI systems. The ability to comprehend, assess, and employ generative AI technologies will be fundamental to empower individuals to engage with and contribute to an AI-driven world effectively. Generative AI literacy goes beyond technical proficiency and requires combining it with other proficiencies such as adaptive usage, ethical considerations, and legal awareness. Thus, the competencies outlined here are not confined to specialists; rather, they cater to a broader audience, reflecting the growing integration of AI into various aspects of daily life. 

Developing generative AI literacy facilitates informed decision-making and participation in AI-driven initiatives and skills to understand, create, and use generative AI systems will ensure realistic expectations, enabling users to leverage AI technologies effectively while avoiding overreliance on their capabilities. By developing these capacities, individuals can use AI as a collaborator within their domain and AI as a tutor/guide for other subjects. 

Generative AI literacy is not a static set of skills, but an evolving one. The framework presented here serves as a starting point and, as AI technologies evolve, researchers should revise these competencies and update them. With growing AI applications, the integration of these competencies into educational curricula, training programs, and professional development initiatives is imperative. Stakeholders are urged to collaboratively design and implement initiatives fostering generative AI literacy at various levels. The competencies lay the groundwork for a potential global standardization of generative AI literacy and nurture a new generation of AI-literate individuals who are not passive consumers but active contributors to the ongoing developments of generative AI.

As previously mentioned, the rapid rise of generative AI tools and their widespread adoption in various disciplines have created a unique set of skills specific to these novel tools, which go beyond the traditional competencies associated with data literacy, digital literacy, or AI literacy. This paper aims to identify a set of competencies that are necessary for users to develop to effectively comprehend and utilize generative tools. This paper adopts the aforementioned definition of competency given by the National Institute of Health, which groups competencies into knowledge, skills, abilities, or behaviors [70]. Alongside, this paper defines generative AI literacy as a long-term, continuous process by which several core competencies, allowing to effectively and responsibly understand, assess, and work with generative AI technologies, have been identified, acquired, practiced, and mastered. 

Based on existing literature on AI literacy, digital literacy, prompt engineering, generative AI, and related topics, including surveys and reviews, peer-reviewed publications, gray literature, and books, this work identifies twelve specific competencies to define the concept of generative AI literacy acknowledging the varied nature of engaging with generative AI. 

As illustrated by Figure 1, the ordering of these competencies is purposeful and follows a logical progression to represent a structured learning path reflecting a continuum of learning, as continuous self-learning is transversal to all the other capabilities. The initial focus is on creating the general basis of knowledge and skill to know and use generative AI tools, followed by knowing how to detect AI-generated content. These develop into more technical skills related to the use of generative AI, with content assessment, prompt engineering, and programming. Then, the three interrelated competencies regarding the knowledge of the contexts, ethical implication, and legal aspects, are intentionally placed towards the end to underline their significance. This approach allows individuals to progressively acquire skills and knowledge, encouraging a user-centric learning experience.

Non-profit organizations and community initiatives focused on AI education can utilize these competencies as a guiding framework for designing literacy outreach programs. By aligning with these competencies, these programs can effectively reach individuals from diverse backgrounds and empower them with essential AI literacy skills, fostering a more inclusive and knowledgeable society equipped to navigate the AI era. 6.3.6 Impact Analysis. Title: The Human-Centred Design of a Universal Module for Artificial Intelligence Literacy in Tertiary Education Institutions
Snippet: Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) is heralding a new era in AI for performing a spectrum of complex tasks that are indistinguishable from humans. Alongside language and text, Generative AI models have been built for all other modalities of digital data, image, video, audio, and code. The full extent of Generative AI and its opportunities, challenges, contributions, and risks are still being explored by academic researchers, industry practitioners, and government policymakers. While this deep understanding of Generative AI continues to evolve, the lack of fluency, literacy, and effective interaction with Generative and conventional AI technologies are common challenges across all domains. Tertiary education institutions are uniquely positioned to address this void. In this article, we present the human-centred design of a universal AI literacy module, followed by its four primary constructs that provide core competence in AI to coursework and research students and academic and professional staff in a tertiary education setting. In comparison to related work in AI literacy, our design is inclusive due to the collaborative approach between multiple stakeholder groups and is comprehensive given the descriptive formulation of the primary constructs of this module with exemplars of how they activate core operational competence across the four groups.
