snippet.text:
Large Language Models (LLMs) has evolved to generate strong reasoning traces and high-quality code, but enabling them to improve through experience remains an open problem. Traditional reinforcement learning offers one mechanism for agent improvement, but updating billion-parameter policies is computationally costly and data-intensive. Incontext learning (Brown et al. 2020), where an LLM adapts using examples directly in the prompt, offers one path toward improving model performance without additional training. Building on this idea, prompting strategies such as chain-of-thought (CoT), expert-style prompting, and ReAct have been shown to enhance LLM reasoning and decisionmaking. 

Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023) integrates these advances while adding a mechanism for the model to self-reflect on its own mistakes: after each attempt, the agent converts feedback into natural-language guidance for the next trial, analogous to how reinforcement learning algorithms use reward signals to update a policy (Sutton and Barto 2018). 

Reflexion reports substantial gains over baseline LLM and CoT/ReAct agents on HotPotQA (Yang et al. 2018) and HumanEval (Chen et al. 2021), improving exact-match accuracy by roughly 20 points on HotPotQA and pass@1 accuracy by 11 points on HumanEval. We focus on these benchmarks for replication since multi-hop question (questions where a model must combine information across several steps of retrieveal) answering and program synthesis are the two high-impact domains where iterative selfimprovement most meaningfully enhance LLM agent performance, and covers the majority of use cases. 

Despite the gains of the Reflexion framework, in our replication, we consistently observed that Reflexion is vulnerable to degeneration-of-thought (Liang et al. 2023), where the agent repeats the same flawed reasoning across iterations even when explicit failures are identified. To mitigate this limitation, we introduce Multi-Agent Reflexion (MAR), a framework that replaces single-agent self-critique with a structured debate among diverse persona-based critics. These multiple critics generate richer reflections that more effectively guide the agent toward improved strategies. 

Our full codebase, including replication scripts, logging instrumentation, and the Multi-Agent Reflexion implementation, is available at: https://github.com/danpro1011/

documents.title: Lachesis: Predicting LLM Inference Accuracy using Structural Properties of Reasoning Paths
documents.snippet:
Large Language Models (LLMs) are rapidly being adopted to automate various stages of the software development lifecycle due to their capability to perform semantic reasoning across the barrier between natural and programming language [1]. While the chatbot model, where an LLM after instruct-tuning converses with a human user, has been the initial mode of interaction, increasingly LLMs are being used to build more complicated agents [2] for tasks like program repair [3], [4], testing [5], and fault localisation [6]. These agents are assisted by various in-context learning techniques, such as Chain-of-Thoughts [7], self-consistency [8], and ReAct [9]. 

Self-consistency [8] in particular has received much attention because of the simplicity of the technique: instead of greedily decoding LLM outputs, self-consistency posits that sampling and marginalising reasoning paths can produce more accurate answers. That is, if multiple inferences sampled independently reaches the same answer, the answer is more likely to be correct. Since the only required computation is multiple sampling of LLMs and the majority voting, selfconsistency has been widely studied and adopted [6], [10]. 

Despite the success of self-consistency, there are corresponding cost concerns when using it as well, as to use selfconsistency one must query an LLM multiple times, which is computationally costly (and as an extension, potentially harmful for the environment [11]). To find a clue to overcome this challenge, we look at the hypothesis that self-consistency relies on: for logical problems, there tend to be multiple reasoning paths that lead to the correct answer [8]. This is interestingly reminiscent of fitness landscape analyses, where an optimum can be said to have a broader 'basins of attraction', in that more random solutions will end up at the optima [12]. In optimization, one may imagine multiple solutions 'aggregating' at the neighbours of an optimum before actually arriving at the optimum. Similarly, with self-consistency, one may observe a convergence of intermediate reasoning steps before observing convergence towards the final answer, and use that to make an early prediction of whether the LLM will get the answer correct for this question.

documents.title: FELA: A Multi-Agent Evolutionary System for Feature Engineering of Industrial Event Log Data

Large Language Models (LLMs) often suffer from attention distillation issues [53], [54] when dealing with long contexts, making them prone to hallucinations and reasoning failures. This challenge is particularly severe in our setting, where both ideas and their implementations evolve into large and complex structures over time. In such cases, idea agents and code agents may deviate from intended instructions or produce low-quality results. 

To address this problem, we introduce two auxiliary agents-idea critics and code critics-which follow a unified design philosophy. Given the output from an idea agent (or code agent), a critic agent is responsible for rigorously evaluating whether the newly generated idea (or code) satisfies the requirements of consistency and correctness. Consistency refers to the alignment with the data schema and the existing knowledge base, while correctness ensures that the proposed idea or code is reasonable and technically sound. 

If any requirement is violated, the critic agent provides detailed feedback to the corresponding generator (idea or code agent), allowing it to revise and improve its output before proceeding. The incorporation of these critics is crucial for maintaining the robustness and reliability of a multi-agent system operating over extended periods-an essential property for real-world industrial applications.

documents.title: Towards Reasoning in Large Language Models via Multi-Agent Peer Review Collaboration
documents.snippet:
With language models scaling up, the emergent abilities have showcased remarkable results across a variety of domains and tasks, challenging our understanding of learning and cognition (Bubeck et al., 2023;OpenAI, 2023). Among these rising capabilities, complex reasoning draws significant interest for its central role in building autonomous language agents and the next-generation computation platform (Xi et al., 2023;Fu et al., 2023). 

To push further the boundary of single-agent reasoning, researchers have adopted strategies akin to teaching kids to reason. For example, the chainof-thought prompting (Wei et al., 2022b) employs rationales to steer LLMs through a multi-step reasoning process; the self-consistency method (Wang et al., 2023b) selects the most likely answer from multiple reasoning paths by majority voting; the plan-and-solve prompting (Wang et al., 2023a) and the least-to-most prompting (Zhou et al., 2023) both apply a divide-and-conquer strategy: break down a complex problem into a series of simpler sub-problems and then solve them in sequence. 

Amidst this backdrop, a prevailing strategy to address reasoning errors is self-correction, mirroring a typical human learning strategy of selfreflection (Pan et al., 2023). This approach involves an LLM attempting to refine its prior response based solely on its inherent capabilities, without the crutch of external feedback. Contrary to the optimism about self-correction (Madaan et al., 2023;Shinn et al., 2023;Kim et al., 2023), Huang et al. (2023) find that an LLM struggles to correct its response without external feedback. Liang et al. (2023) also conclude that, once the LLM has formulated initial solutions, it cannot generate novel thoughts through self-reflection. In this work, we let a single LLM "jump outside the box" and change its viewpoint from a participant to a critical observer by enabling multiple LLMs to correct each other. 

Multi-agent collaboration for task solving is still in its preliminary stages, presenting vast opportunities for exploration.

problem: Please do some research on articles related to bones and 3D Gaussians.
final_response:
# Overview

This summary covers research at the intersection of “bones” (skeletal structures and articulated skeletons) and “3D Gaussians” (Gaussian Splatting, Gaussian-based radiance/shape representations) across computer graphics/robotics and medical imaging. In graphics, 3D Gaussians are increasingly coupled to skeletal animation via learned skinning weights and bone-driven transformations, enabling animatable human and robot models with novel pose synthesis and fast rendering. <cite id="892b3387-0">Human Gaussian Splatting (HuGS) learns per-Gaussian skinning and a pose-dependent MLP to capture local surface movement, achieving state-of-the-art efficiency for animatable human bodies</cite>. <cite id="5e3e685b-0">Robot self-model work similarly binds each Gaussian to bones via learned skinning weights and LBS-style updates, including distance-based weights and delta skinning</cite>. In medical imaging, 3D Gaussian kernels and Gaussian-based losses appear in bone segmentation/registration pipelines, and CT-based 3D reconstructions provide ground truth for skull and cranial bone analyses. <cite id="5e3e685b-2">BoneNet uses 3D Gaussian kernels for fuzzy polyaffine fusion of bone segments derived from CT</cite>; <cite id="dda8c0ba-0">skull models parameterized by bone layers are built from CT-derived segmentations</cite>.

# Computer Graphics and Robotics: Articulated 3D Gaussians Driven by Bones

A prominent line of work animates 3D Gaussian splatting primitives with skeletal “bones,” using linear blend skinning (LBS) and learned per-Gaussian weights. <cite id="892b3387-0">HuGS defines per-Gaussian skinning weights and a forward skinning step plus a pose-dependent MLP to capture local garment and surface motion, supporting novel pose synthesis and rendering an order of magnitude faster than neural body baselines</cite>. <cite id="892b3387-1">GaussianMotion places Gaussian splats in a canonical space and deforms them via LBS using bone transformations; it learns residual blend weights relative to SMPL to handle distillation when ground-truth skinning guidance is limited</cite>. <cite id="892b3387-2">RealityAvatar and related pipelines describe LBS as weighting each point’s transformation by nearby bone influences; 3DGS provides an efficient discrete primitive set with mean, covariance, opacity, and color parameters</cite>. <cite id="892b3387-3">iHuman deforms a canonical Gaussian Splat per input pose using forward LBS with bone transformations computed from joint rotations and translations, mapping canonical-space points to posed-space centers and rotations</cite>. <cite id="892b3387-4">BAGS reviews the 3DGS representation and rendering (projected 2D covariances, alpha compositing) and couples it with LBS, where each bone’s transform is blended via skinning weights</cite>.

Beyond human avatars, robotics research uses articulated 3D Gaussians to build robot self-models from sensor images. <cite id="5e3e685b-0">One approach computes per-Gaussian skinning weights based on Mahalanobis distance to bones and applies LBS to transform each Gaussian’s center and rotation with the bone’s joint pose; delta skinning MLPs provide fine geometry</cite>. <cite id="5e3e685b-4">A complementary “neural bones” formulation treats each bone as a 3D Gaussian and trains bone mask, center, and volume losses to ensure coverage and distribution, yielding an end-to-end articulated representation</cite>.

Foundational techniques for dynamic 3DGS include projection and skeleton-constraint losses. <cite id="892b3387-3">Projection losses align 2D skeletons with the rendered Gaussian shape, while adaptive weighting of skeleton-driven terms improves pose fidelity under large pose variations</cite>. <cite id="decdd292-4">A broader NeRF-based hand modeling line shows conditioning on SMPL bone transformations and disentangling per-bone SDFs weighted by skinning, paralleling Gaussian splatting strategies that weight per-bone contributions by learned weights</cite>.

# Medical Imaging and Biomechanics: Bones with Gaussian Kernels and CT-based Reconstructions

In medical imaging, 3D Gaussian kernels are used to model spatial weighting for bone segments and to fuse deformations across time. <cite id="5e3e685b-2">BoneNet computes Gaussian weights as convolution of 3D Gaussian kernels with segment volumes of individual bones and uses them in a fuzzy polyaffine fusion scheme to combine bone-wise transformations for registration</cite>. These methods reflect a common pipeline: segment bones from CT (e.g., via thresholding, morphological operations, and connected component labeling), and then apply Gaussian-weighted fusion for robust registration across time or modalities. <cite id="5e3e685b-2">A typical pipeline includes Otsu thresholding to remove soft tissue, closing to fill bone holes, and then computing Gaussian weights for fusion with PCA-defined local bone coordinate systems and rotation/translation transforms per bone</cite>.

Skull and cranial bone modeling from CT provides ground truth for evaluating bone-related Gaussian methods. <cite id="dda8c0ba-0">Studies build low-dimensional skull models from CT by segmenting outer/inner tables and the diploë as distinct bone layers with different acoustic/elastic properties and derive mapping functions from the 3D segmentation masks</cite>. <cite id="dda8c0ba-1">CT-derived 3D skull surfaces are commonly exported as meshes for analysis and simulation of bone structures</cite>. <cite id="dda8c0ba-2">Harmonic B-mode ultrasound maps can be registered to CT to estimate skull geometry and thickness, with bone thickness measured and compared between modalities</cite>. <cite id="dda8c0ba-3">Cranial bone shape analysis often segments skulls at regional bones (frontal, parietal, occipital) and uses surface reconstruction (e.g., marching cubes) to quantify deformations pre/post surgery</cite>. <cite id="dda8c0ba-4">Micro-CT reconstructions of skulls are thresholded and processed to quantify new bone volume in craniofacial defect studies, illustrating standard pipelines for 3D bone reconstructions that could be paired with Gaussian-based representations</cite>.

Direct applications of 3D Gaussian splatting to bones in medical imaging are still emerging; current medical uses emphasize Gaussian kernels for fusion and CT-based volumetric reconstructions rather than splat-based surface/shape modeling. Nonetheless, the CT-derived bone segmentations and quantitative metrics provide a natural interface for adopting Gaussian splatting for volumetric bone reconstructions or atlas-based modeling.

# Technical Foundations: NeRF, 3D Gaussian Splatting, and SDF with Skeletal Control

Comparative foundations help clarify trade-offs. <cite id="decdd292-0">NeRF represents scenes as 5D neural radiance fields and supports high-quality view synthesis but can be less efficient than 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), which represents scenes as discrete 3D Gaussians for real-time radiance field rendering; 3DGS is faster but sensitive to input quality and requires compact attribute/occurrence representations</cite>. <cite id="decdd292-0">Improvements include volume masking for storage efficiency, and anti-aliasing via Mip-Splatting with 3D/2D filters</cite>.

Bone-driven deformations are commonly realized by conditioning on skeletal transformations or by learning per-primitive skinning. <cite id="decdd292-4">A-NeRF conditions NeRF on SMPL bone transformations to learn animatable avatars, and related works predict deformation fields conditioned on joint poses</cite>. <cite id="decdd292-4">Some methods disentangle per-bone SDFs and weight appearance/geometry by skinning weights, an idea that parallels Gaussian splatting approaches where each bone contributes to nearby Gaussians via learned weights</cite>. <cite id="892b3387-2">Dynamic NeRF variants learn a deformation field from skeleton poses, while 3DGS methods rely on per-Gaussian transformations under LBS or learned residual deformations</cite>.

SDF-based representations offer alternative shape priors that can be combined with skeletal control. <cite id="decdd292-0">DeepSDF and SDF-based methods reconstruct complete shapes from partial observations and support hole-filling and detail preservation via gradient regularization</cite>. <cite id="decdd292-4">VolSDF can serve as a backbone renderer for dynamic scenes; some hand modeling works predict per-bone SDFs and blend with skinning weights, suggesting a path to combine SDF smoothness with bone-driven articulation for bone-like structures</cite>.

# Dynamic Modeling and Skeletal Constraints in Gaussian-Based Representations

Several works explicitly integrate skeleton signals into Gaussian-based models and analyze component contributions. <cite id="892b3387-3">Rigidity and projection constraints are used to embed skeletons into Gaussian splat shapes; removing the projection loss prevents proper skeleton-to-shape alignment, and fixed weights can lead to artifacts under pose uncertainty</cite>. <cite id="892b3387-3">Adaptive weighting and per-frame skeleton construction improve fidelity when 2D skeletons are imperfect</cite>. <cite id="5e3e685b-0">Distance-based skinning weights (Mahalanobis) and delta skinning MLPs provide fine-grained geometry, while smoothness terms encourage consistent skinning weights among neighboring Gaussians</cite>. <cite id="5e3e685b-4">Bone mask, center, and volume losses ensure Gaussians are spread across the bone and avoid collapse or overlap, yielding robust neural “bones”</cite>.

# Practical Considerations and Open Problems

- Efficiency and robustness: <cite id="decdd292-0">3DGS offers real-time rendering but can be sensitive to noise and storage-heavy without compact representations; NeRF-based methods and Mip-Splatting address aliasing and memory, while volume masks improve efficiency</cite>. <cite id="892b3387-0">For humans, per-Gaussian skinning plus a small MLP captures local non-rigid motion and achieves high speed</cite>.
- Skeletal control and detail: <cite id="892b3387-1">Learning residual blend weights over SMPL improves pose generalization when distilling from images</cite>. <cite id="892b3387-2">LBS remains a standard to translate bone poses to surface deformations; anisotropic Gaussians can improve visual quality but degrade under large pose shifts, motivating isotropic covariances or learned deformation fields</cite>.
- Medical integration: <cite id="5e3e685b-2">Gaussian kernels are effective for bone-wise fusion in registration, suggesting a natural way to incorporate Gaussian priors or potentials for bone alignment and atlas building</cite>. <cite id="dda8c0ba-0">CT-derived bone segmentations provide ground truth to train bone-conditioned Gaussian models (e.g., per-bone Gaussians or per-bone SDFs) for skull and long-bone modeling</cite>.
- Gaps: There is limited evidence of end-to-end 3D Gaussian splatting applied to medical bone reconstruction with quantitative benchmarks in the retrieved snippets; most medical work uses Gaussian kernels for fusion and CT-based reconstructions. Bridging with 3DGS would benefit from datasets with labeled bone segments and metrics for surface accuracy and robustness to noise.

# Pointers by Use Case

- Animatable human avatars and clothing: <cite id="892b3387-0">HuGS provides a practical pipeline for novel pose synthesis using LBS+MLP per Gaussian</cite>; <cite id="892b3387-1">GaussianMotion demonstrates residual blend weights for distillation from images</cite>; <cite id="892b3387-2">RealityAvatar and iHuman detail LBS forward deformation and Gaussian parameter updates</cite>; <cite id="5e3e685b-0">delta skinning for fine geometry</cite>. 
- Robot self-models: <cite id="5e3e685b-0">Learned per-Gaussian skinning with Mahalanobis distance to bones and LBS-driven transforms</cite>; <cite id="5e3e685b-4">neural bone losses (mask, center, volume) to keep Gaussians well-distributed</cite>. 
- Medical registration and fusion: <cite id="5e3e685b-2">BoneNet’s Gaussian-weighted polyaffine fusion across bone segments and time</cite>. 
- Skeletal skull/long-bone modeling: <cite id="dda8c0ba-0">CT-based multi-layer skull models with distinct cortical and trabecular properties</cite>; <cite id="dda8c0ba-4">µCT-based volumetric reconstructions and quantification workflows that could be paired with Gaussian-based representations</cite>. 
- Foundations and trade-offs: <cite id="decdd292-0">Contrast NeRF vs 3DGS and SDF; storage/aliasing considerations and recent improvements like Mip-Splatting and volume masking</cite>; <cite id="decdd292-4">bone-conditioned NeRFs and per-bone SDFs with skinning-weighted blending</cite>.

# Takeaways

- Articulated 3D Gaussians tied to skeletal “bones” are now a mature approach in graphics/robotics, with LBS-style skinning, per-Gaussian weights, and bone-driven transforms enabling fast, animatable models and robot self-avatars. <cite id="892b3387-0">HuGS</cite>, <cite id="892b3387-1">GaussianMotion</cite>, <cite id="892b3387-2">RealityAvatar</cite>, <cite id="892b3387-3">iHuman</cite>, <cite id="892b3387-4">BAGS</cite>, and <cite id="5e3e685b-0">robot self-models</cite> provide concrete methods and losses.
- In medicine, Gaussian kernels and CT-based reconstructions dominate bone pipelines today; Gaussian splatting is less established but offers a promising, efficient alternative for bone surface/volume modeling once paired with robust segmentations and evaluation metrics. <cite id="5e3e685b-2">BoneNet</cite> and CT-based studies <cite id="dda8c0ba-0">to</cite><cite id="dda8c0ba-4">dda8c0ba-4</cite> provide anchors for such transitions.
- Methodologically, the choice among NeRF, 3DGS, and SDF depends on speed, storage, and surface quality needs, while skeletal control can be achieved via bone-conditioning, skinning weights, or deformation fields, with recent ablations showing the importance of projection and adaptive weighting for accurate skeleton-to-surface alignment. <cite id="decdd292-0">Foundational trade-offs</cite> and <cite id="892b3387-3">component ablations</cite> highlight these considerations.

Snippet: We observe that using Linear Blend Skinning (LBS) with skinning weights learned for each Gaussian provides an efficient and effective method that generalizes well to new body poses, but is not expressive enough to capture the local garment deformations of clothed avatars. The proposed algorithm, named Human Gaussian Splatting (HuGS), paves the way for animatable human body models based on Gaussian Splatting. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: 1. Snippet: SMPL and Linear Blend Skinning. A widely used approach for modeling human articulation is to employ a parametric human body model, such as SMPL [22], which defines human geometry in a canonical space [9,12,13,19,29,32,33]. To animate the body under arbitrary poses, Linear Blend Skinning (LBS) [2,22,25,27] is commonly used, where each point on the body surface undergoes a weighted transformation based on the influence of nearby skeletal bones. Given a point x c in canonical space, its transformed position x o in the posed observation space is computed as a weighted sum of bone transformations: 

where B represents the total number of skeletal bones (B = 24 in the SMPL model), B b is a 4 × 4 transformation matrix representing the rotation and translation of bone b, and w b is the corresponding skinning weight, which satisfies: 

These skinning weights determine the extent to which each bone influences the deformation of a given point. Traditionally, they are precomputed based on the body mesh topology, but modern approaches often learn them dynamically using neural networks. LBS provides a computationally efficient and differentiable way to model human motion, making it well-suited for applications such as animation and motion capture. However, it has limitations in handling complex non-rigid deformations, such as soft-tissue dynamics and loose clothing motion, since it assumes a purely skeletal-driven transformation. Alternative methods, such as inverse skinning, attempt to establish correspondences between the observation and canonical spaces but often introduce ambiguities. More recent works explore learning-based techniques to improve skinning weight prediction, allowing for more accurate deformation modeling in data-driven human reconstruction. 3D Gaussian Splatting. 3D Gaussian Splatting [14] has emerged as an efficient representation for 3D scene modeling and rendering. Unlike volumetric methods, which represent a scene as a dense field requiring costly volumetric sampling, 3DGS models a scene as a collection of discrete 3D Gaussian primitives. Each 3D Gaussian is parameterized by its mean position x, covariance matrix Σ, opacity α and view-dependent color represented by spherical harmonics coefficients.
</snippet>

Snippet: In the field of 3D reconstruction, NeRF and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) are two important techniques each with their own characteristics and application scenarios. NeRF represents scenes as 5D neural radiance fields, successfully overcoming the limitations of previous methods and achieving high-quality view synthesis [3]. 3DGS is a 3D reconstruction technique of real-time radiance field rendering. Its core idea is to use 3D Gaussian distributions as volume representations to model scenes and achieve efficient rendering [14]. Compared to NeRF, 3DGS has faster rendering speeds but requires substantial storage resources and is sensitive to input quality. Lee Chan et al. significantly improved memory and storage efficiency through innovative volume masking strategies and compact attribute representations [15]. Mip-Splatting addressed aliasing issues in 3D Gaussian rendering by introducing 3D smoothing filters and 2D Mip filters, demonstrating excellent performance across different scales [16]. In addition to the above points, the MLP-based structure of NeRF offers better extensibility and has had a profound impact on various subfields of 3D computer vision, such as novel view synthesis [3], [17]- [19], surface reconstruction [20]- [22], dynamic scene representation [23], [24], and camera and pose estimation [25]- [28]. 

Signed Distance Function(SDF): In the field of 3D reconstruction, the Signed Distance Function (SDF) has emerged as a powerful representation method, widely applied in several state-of-the-art techniques. DeepSDF utilizes neural networks to predict SDF values from 3D points to surfaces, leveraging latent space encoding to achieve efficient reconstruction of complete shapes from partial observations [20]. SDF-SRN focuses on 3D shape reconstruction from single RGB images, employing differentiable rendering to optimize SDFs and recover more accurate 3D shapes and topologies from images [29]. GO-Surf enhances SDF applications by optimizing hierarchical feature grids and SDF values for fast, high-fidelity surface reconstruction from RGB-D sequences, and a novel SDF gradient regularization term is introduced to aid in hole filling and detail preservation [12].
</snippet>

The idea is to model the image formation process by rendering a neural volume with raycasting [30,40,55,66]. Particularly, NeRF [35] gains popularity with an efficient formulation of modeling the radiance field. Follow-up studies show that geometry can be improved if the density is regulated by occupancy [42] or SDF [60,65]. In this work, we use VolSDF [65] as a backbone renderer. For dynamic scenes, [47,52,58] combine NeRF with learning a deformation field. For modeling dynamic human bodies, Neural Body [51] attaches learnable vertex features to SMPL, and diffuses the features with sparse convolution for volumetric rendering. A-NeRF [56] conditions NeRF with SMPL bone transformations to learn an animatable avatar. Similar ideas are proposed in [50] and NARF [41]. H-NeRF [63] combines imGHUM with NeRF to enable appearance learning and train a separate network to predict SDF. NPM [45] proposed to train shape embedding on canonically posed scans, followed by another network to learn the deformation field with dense supervision. A similar idea to the deformation field was adopted by i3DMM [67] to learn a human head model.

# Overview

This summary covers research at the intersection of “bones” (skeletal structures and articulated skeletons) and “3D Gaussians” (Gaussian Splatting, Gaussian-based radiance/shape representations) across computer graphics/robotics and medical imaging. In graphics, 3D Gaussians are increasingly coupled to skeletal animation via learned skinning weights and bone-driven transformations, enabling animatable human and robot models with novel pose synthesis and fast rendering. <cite id="892b3387-0">Human Gaussian Splatting (HuGS) learns per-Gaussian skinning and a pose-dependent MLP to capture local surface movement, achieving state-of-the-art efficiency for animatable human bodies</cite>. <cite id="5e3e685b-0">Robot self-model work similarly binds each Gaussian to bones via learned skinning weights and LBS-style updates, including distance-based weights and delta skinning</cite>. In medical imaging, 3D Gaussian kernels and Gaussian-based losses appear in bone segmentation/registration pipelines, and CT-based 3D reconstructions provide ground truth for skull and cranial bone analyses. <cite id="5e3e685b-2">BoneNet uses 3D Gaussian kernels for fuzzy polyaffine fusion of bone segments derived from CT</cite>; <cite id="dda8c0ba-0">skull models parameterized by bone layers are built from CT-derived segmentations</cite>.

# Computer Graphics and Robotics: Articulated 3D Gaussians Driven by Bones

A prominent line of work animates 3D Gaussian splatting primitives with skeletal “bones,” using linear blend skinning (LBS) and learned per-Gaussian weights. <cite id="892b3387-0">HuGS defines per-Gaussian skinning weights and a forward skinning step plus a pose-dependent MLP to capture local garment and surface motion, supporting novel pose synthesis and rendering an order of magnitude faster than neural body baselines</cite>. <cite id="892b3387-1">GaussianMotion places Gaussian splats in a canonical space and deforms them via LBS using bone transformations; it learns residual blend weights relative to SMPL to handle distillation when ground-truth skinning guidance is limited</cite>. <cite id="892b3387-2">RealityAvatar and related pipelines describe LBS as weighting each point’s transformation by nearby bone influences; 3DGS provides an efficient discrete primitive set with mean, covariance, opacity, and color parameters</cite>. <cite id="892b3387-3">iHuman deforms a canonical Gaussian Splat per input pose using forward LBS with bone transformations computed from joint rotations and translations, mapping canonical-space points to posed-space centers and rotations</cite>. <cite id="892b3387-4">BAGS reviews the 3DGS representation and rendering (projected 2D covariances, alpha compositing) and couples it with LBS, where each bone’s transform is blended via skinning weights</cite>.

Beyond human avatars, robotics research uses articulated 3D Gaussians to build robot self-models from sensor images. <cite id="5e3e685b-0">One approach computes per-Gaussian skinning weights based on Mahalanobis distance to bones and applies LBS to transform each Gaussian’s center and rotation with the bone’s joint pose; delta skinning MLPs provide fine geometry</cite>. <cite id="5e3e685b-4">A complementary “neural bones” formulation treats each bone as a 3D Gaussian and trains bone mask, center, and volume losses to ensure coverage and distribution, yielding an end-to-end articulated representation</cite>.

Foundational techniques for dynamic 3DGS include projection and skeleton-constraint losses. <cite id="892b3387-3">Projection losses align 2D skeletons with the rendered Gaussian shape, while adaptive weighting of skeleton-driven terms improves pose fidelity under large pose variations</cite>. <cite id="decdd292-4">A broader NeRF-based hand modeling line shows conditioning on SMPL bone transformations and disentangling per-bone SDFs weighted by skinning, paralleling Gaussian splatting strategies that weight per-bone contributions by learned weights</cite>.

# Medical Imaging and Biomechanics: Bones with Gaussian Kernels and CT-based Reconstructions

In medical imaging, 3D Gaussian kernels are used to model spatial weighting for bone segments and to fuse deformations across time. <cite id="5e3e685b-2">BoneNet computes Gaussian weights as convolution of 3D Gaussian kernels with segment volumes of individual bones and uses them in a fuzzy polyaffine fusion scheme to combine bone-wise transformations for registration</cite>. These methods reflect a common pipeline: segment bones from CT (e.g., via thresholding, morphological operations, and connected component labeling), and then apply Gaussian-weighted fusion for robust registration across time or modalities. <cite id="5e3e685b-2">A typical pipeline includes Otsu thresholding to remove soft tissue, closing to fill bone holes, and then computing Gaussian weights for fusion with PCA-defined local bone coordinate systems and rotation/translation transforms per bone</cite>.

Skull and cranial bone modeling from CT provides ground truth for evaluating bone-related Gaussian methods. <cite id="dda8c0ba-0">Studies build low-dimensional skull models from CT by segmenting outer/inner tables and the diploë as distinct bone layers with different acoustic/elastic properties and derive mapping functions from the 3D segmentation masks</cite>. <cite id="dda8c0ba-1">CT-derived 3D skull surfaces are commonly exported as meshes for analysis and simulation of bone structures</cite>. <cite id="dda8c0ba-2">Harmonic B-mode ultrasound maps can be registered to CT to estimate skull geometry and thickness, with bone thickness measured and compared between modalities</cite>. <cite id="dda8c0ba-3">Cranial bone shape analysis often segments skulls at regional bones (frontal, parietal, occipital) and uses surface reconstruction (e.g., marching cubes) to quantify deformations pre/post surgery</cite>. <cite id="dda8c0ba-4">Micro-CT reconstructions of skulls are thresholded and processed to quantify new bone volume in craniofacial defect studies, illustrating standard pipelines for 3D bone reconstructions that could be paired with Gaussian-based representations</cite>.

Direct applications of 3D Gaussian splatting to bones in medical imaging are still emerging; current medical uses emphasize Gaussian kernels for fusion and CT-based volumetric reconstructions rather than splat-based surface/shape modeling. Nonetheless, the CT-derived bone segmentations and quantitative metrics provide a natural interface for adopting Gaussian splatting for volumetric bone reconstructions or atlas-based modeling.

# Technical Foundations: NeRF, 3D Gaussian Splatting, and SDF with Skeletal Control

Comparative foundations help clarify trade-offs. <cite id="decdd292-0">NeRF represents scenes as 5D neural radiance fields and supports high-quality view synthesis but can be less efficient than 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), which represents scenes as discrete 3D Gaussians for real-time radiance field rendering; 3DGS is faster but sensitive to input quality and requires compact attribute/occurrence representations</cite>. <cite id="decdd292-0">Improvements include volume masking for storage efficiency, and anti-aliasing via Mip-Splatting with 3D/2D filters</cite>.

Bone-driven deformations are commonly realized by conditioning on skeletal transformations or by learning per-primitive skinning. <cite id="decdd292-4">A-NeRF conditions NeRF on SMPL bone transformations to learn animatable avatars, and related works predict deformation fields conditioned on joint poses</cite>. <cite id="decdd292-4">Some methods disentangle per-bone SDFs and weight appearance/geometry by skinning weights, an idea that parallels Gaussian splatting approaches where each bone contributes to nearby Gaussians via learned weights</cite>. <cite id="892b3387-2">Dynamic NeRF variants learn a deformation field from skeleton poses, while 3DGS methods rely on per-Gaussian transformations under LBS or learned residual deformations</cite>.

SDF-based representations offer alternative shape priors that can be combined with skeletal control. <cite id="decdd292-0">DeepSDF and SDF-based methods reconstruct complete shapes from partial observations and support hole-filling and detail preservation via gradient regularization</cite>. <cite id="decdd292-4">VolSDF can serve as a backbone renderer for dynamic scenes; some hand modeling works predict per-bone SDFs and blend with skinning weights, suggesting a path to combine SDF smoothness with bone-driven articulation for bone-like structures</cite>.

# Dynamic Modeling and Skeletal Constraints in Gaussian-Based Representations

Several works explicitly integrate skeleton signals into Gaussian-based models and analyze component contributions. <cite id="892b3387-3">Rigidity and projection constraints are used to embed skeletons into Gaussian splat shapes; removing the projection loss prevents proper skeleton-to-shape alignment, and fixed weights can lead to artifacts under pose uncertainty</cite>. <cite id="892b3387-3">Adaptive weighting and per-frame skeleton construction improve fidelity when 2D skeletons are imperfect</cite>. <cite id="5e3e685b-0">Distance-based skinning weights (Mahalanobis) and delta skinning MLPs provide fine-grained geometry, while smoothness terms encourage consistent skinning weights among neighboring Gaussians</cite>. <cite id="5e3e685b-4">Bone mask, center, and volume losses ensure Gaussians are spread across the bone and avoid collapse or overlap, yielding robust neural “bones”</cite>.

# Practical Considerations and Open Problems

- Efficiency and robustness: <cite id="decdd292-0">3DGS offers real-time rendering but can be sensitive to noise and storage-heavy without compact representations; NeRF-based methods and Mip-Splatting address aliasing and memory, while volume masks improve efficiency</cite>. <cite id="892b3387-0">For humans, per-Gaussian skinning plus a small MLP captures local non-rigid motion and achieves high speed</cite>.
- Skeletal control and detail: <cite id="892b3387-1">Learning residual blend weights over SMPL improves pose generalization when distilling from images</cite>. <cite id="892b3387-2">LBS remains a standard to translate bone poses to surface deformations; anisotropic Gaussians can improve visual quality but degrade under large pose shifts, motivating isotropic covariances or learned deformation fields</cite>.
- Medical integration: <cite id="5e3e685b-2">Gaussian kernels are effective for bone-wise fusion in registration, suggesting a natural way to incorporate Gaussian priors or potentials for bone alignment and atlas building</cite>. <cite id="dda8c0ba-0">CT-derived bone segmentations provide ground truth to train bone-conditioned Gaussian models (e.g., per-bone Gaussians or per-bone SDFs) for skull and long-bone modeling</cite>.
- Gaps: There is limited evidence of end-to-end 3D Gaussian splatting applied to medical bone reconstruction with quantitative benchmarks in the retrieved snippets; most medical work uses Gaussian kernels for fusion and CT-based reconstructions. Bridging with 3DGS would benefit from datasets with labeled bone segments and metrics for surface accuracy and robustness to noise.

# Pointers by Use Case

- Animatable human avatars and clothing: <cite id="892b3387-0">HuGS provides a practical pipeline for novel pose synthesis using LBS+MLP per Gaussian</cite>; <cite id="892b3387-1">GaussianMotion demonstrates residual blend weights for distillation from images</cite>; <cite id="892b3387-2">RealityAvatar and iHuman detail LBS forward deformation and Gaussian parameter updates</cite>; <cite id="5e3e685b-0">delta skinning for fine geometry</cite>. 
- Robot self-models: <cite id="5e3e685b-0">Learned per-Gaussian skinning with Mahalanobis distance to bones and LBS-driven transforms</cite>; <cite id="5e3e685b-4">neural bone losses (mask, center, volume) to keep Gaussians well-distributed</cite>. 
- Medical registration and fusion: <cite id="5e3e685b-2">BoneNet’s Gaussian-weighted polyaffine fusion across bone segments and time</cite>. 
- Skeletal skull/long-bone modeling: <cite id="dda8c0ba-0">CT-based multi-layer skull models with distinct cortical and trabecular properties</cite>; <cite id="dda8c0ba-4">µCT-based volumetric reconstructions and quantification workflows that could be paired with Gaussian-based representations</cite>. 
- Foundations and trade-offs: <cite id="decdd292-0">Contrast NeRF vs 3DGS and SDF; storage/aliasing considerations and recent improvements like Mip-Splatting and volume masking</cite>; <cite id="decdd292-4">bone-conditioned NeRFs and per-bone SDFs with skinning-weighted blending</cite>.

# Takeaways

- Articulated 3D Gaussians tied to skeletal “bones” are now a mature approach in graphics/robotics, with LBS-style skinning, per-Gaussian weights, and bone-driven transforms enabling fast, animatable models and robot self-avatars. <cite id="892b3387-0">HuGS</cite>, <cite id="892b3387-1">GaussianMotion</cite>, <cite id="892b3387-2">RealityAvatar</cite>, <cite id="892b3387-3">iHuman</cite>, <cite id="892b3387-4">BAGS</cite>, and <cite id="5e3e685b-0">robot self-models</cite> provide concrete methods and losses.
- In medicine, Gaussian kernels and CT-based reconstructions dominate bone pipelines today; Gaussian splatting is less established but offers a promising, efficient alternative for bone surface/volume modeling once paired with robust segmentations and evaluation metrics. <cite id="5e3e685b-2">BoneNet</cite> and CT-based studies <cite id="dda8c0ba-0">to</cite><cite id="dda8c0ba-4">dda8c0ba-4</cite> provide anchors for such transitions.
- Methodologically, the choice among NeRF, 3DGS, and SDF depends on speed, storage, and surface quality needs, while skeletal control can be achieved via bone-conditioning, skinning weights, or deformation fields, with recent ablations showing the importance of projection and adaptive weighting for accurate skeleton-to-surface alignment. <cite id="decdd292-0">Foundational trade-offs</cite> and <cite id="892b3387-3">component ablations</cite> highlight these considerations.

If you share your specific domain (avatar animation vs. medical reconstruction) and constraints (speed, fidelity, datasets), I can map a concrete pipeline and suggest datasets and evaluation metrics tailored to bones and 3D Gaussians.

Title: Human Gaussian Splatting: Real-Time Rendering of Animatable Avatars
Snippet: We observe that using Linear Blend Skinning (LBS) with skinning weights learned for each Gaussian provides an efficient and effective method that generalizes well to new body poses, but is not expressive enough to capture the local garment deformations of clothed avatars. We propose to refine the deformation of Gaussians with a shallow neural network that captures the local movements of the body surface. 

The proposed algorithm, named Human Gaussian Splatting (HuGS), paves the way for animatable human body models based on Gaussian Splatting. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: 1. We propose a first algorithm for novel pose synthesis of the human body based on 3D Gaussian Splatting. 2. We define a coarse-to-fine approach to animate the set of Gaussian primitives, based on forward skinning for skeleton-based movements and a pose-dependent MLP for local garments deformations. 3. We compare HuGS to neural-based human models on three public datasets and exhibit results on-par or better than state-of-the-art methods, while rendering one order of magnitude faster.

Snippet: SMPL and Linear Blend Skinning. A widely used approach for modeling human articulation is to employ a parametric human body model, such as SMPL [22], which defines human geometry in a canonical space [9,12,13,19,29,32,33]. These skinning weights determine the extent to which each bone influences the deformation of a given point. Traditionally, they are precomputed based on the body mesh topology, but modern approaches often learn them dynamically using neural networks. LBS provides a computationally efficient and differentiable way to model human motion, making it well-suited for applications such as animation and motion capture. However, it has limitations in handling complex non-rigid deformations, such as soft-tissue dynamics and loose clothing motion, since it assumes a purely skeletal-driven transformation. Alternative methods, such as inverse skinning, attempt to establish correspondences between the observation and canonical spaces but often introduce ambiguities. More recent works explore learning-based techniques to improve skinning weight prediction, allowing for more accurate deformation modeling in data-driven human reconstruction. 3D Gaussian Splatting. 3D Gaussian Splatting [14] has emerged as an efficient representation for 3D scene modeling and rendering. Each 3D Gaussian is parameterized by its mean position x, covariance matrix Σ, opacity α and view-dependent color represented by spherical harmonics coefficients.

Title: PreSem-Surf: RGB-D Surface Reconstruction with Progressive Semantic Modeling and SG-MLP Pre-Rendering Mechanism
Snippet: In the field of 3D reconstruction, NeRF and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) are two important techniques each with their own characteristics and application scenarios. NeRF represents scenes as 5D neural radiance fields, successfully overcoming the limitations of previous methods and achieving high-quality view synthesis [3]. 3DGS is a 3D reconstruction technique of real-time radiance field rendering. Its core idea is to use 3D Gaussian distributions as volume representations to model scenes and achieve efficient rendering [14]. Compared to NeRF, 3DGS has faster rendering speeds but requires substantial storage resources and is sensitive to input quality. Lee Chan et al. significantly improved memory and storage efficiency through innovative volume masking strategies and compact attribute representations [15]. Mip-Splatting addressed aliasing issues in 3D Gaussian rendering by introducing 3D smoothing filters and 2D Mip filters, demonstrating excellent performance across different scales [16]. In addition to the above points, the MLP-based structure of NeRF offers better extensibility and has had a profound impact on various subfields of 3D computer vision, such as novel view synthesis [3], [17]- [19], surface reconstruction [20]- [22], dynamic scene representation [23], [24], and camera and pose estimation [25]- [28]. 

Signed Distance Function(SDF): In the field of 3D reconstruction, the Signed Distance Function (SDF) has emerged as a powerful representation method, widely applied in several state-of-the-art techniques. DeepSDF utilizes neural networks to predict SDF values from 3D points to surfaces, leveraging latent space encoding to achieve efficient reconstruction of complete shapes from partial observations [20]. SDF-SRN focuses on 3D shape reconstruction from single RGB images, employing differentiable rendering to optimize SDFs and recover more accurate 3D shapes and topologies from images [29]. GO-Surf enhances SDF applications by optimizing hierarchical feature grids and SDF values for fast, high-fidelity surface reconstruction from RGB-D sequences, and a novel SDF gradient regularization term is introduced to aid in hole filling and detail preservation [12].

Title: HFNeRF: Learning Human Biomechanic Features with Neural Radiance Fields
Snippet: In this paper, we present the initial results of HFNeRF obtained with the RenderPeople dataset by distilling a stateof-the-art pose estimation algorithm based on heatmaps.To the best of our knowledge, our method is the first to estimate human biomechanic features with NeRF.Our contributions are as follows:

II. METHOD This section introduces HFNeRF, a unified framework utilizing the NeRF architecture for learning human features.It begins with a brief overview of NeRF, followed by the methodology for feature extraction using a 2D encoder, and concludes with a detailed description of skeleton extraction from heatmaps.Neural Radiance Fields: The NeRF algorithm utilizes a multilayer perceptron (MLP) to map the 3D coordinate x = arXiv:2404.06152v1[cs.CV] 9 Apr 2024 (x, y, z) and view direction d = (θ, ϕ) to the corresponding color c and volume density σ.This mapping can be expressed as F (x, d) → (c, σ).Subsequently, volume rendering is employed to generate the pixel color by performing alpha composition of the volume density σ and color c using samples taken along the ray.Feature Extraction: We propose a novel architecture to estimate human features using the NeRF framework.NeRF models estimate the color c and density σ using an MLP, where the input is the positional encoding γ(x) of the query point x = (x, y, z).The human feature f (x), generated by the encoder corresponding to the input point x, is concatenated with the positional encoding γ(x) before being fed into the MLP.In this work, we experimented with 2 different kinds of encoder, namely: ResNet [3] and DINO [2].Learning Human Biomechanics features Previous methods [8] used encoded features to generalize NeRF, producing color and density as output.In this work, we extend the NeRF architecture to estimate human features by generating heatmaps of skeleton joints, as shown in Figure 1.We used an MLP with a skip connection, where the view direction is incorporated into the final layer before producing the color output.

Title: RigGS: Rigging of 3D Gaussians for Modeling Articulated Objects in Videos
Snippet: On the D-NeRF dataset, we evaluated the effectiveness of each component of our method using the following variations: 

• Anisotropic or isotropic 3D Gaussians. 

Although anisotropic 3D Gaussians yield images closer to the ground truth, they suffer significant quality degradation when the new poses differ greatly from the training pose, as shown in Fig. 4. Therefore, we use the isotropic 3D Gaussians for all experiments. 

• Without 2D projection loss L t proj or fixed weight w t proj during training the skeleton-driven dynamic model. The 2D projection loss L t proj assesses how well the skeleton aligns with the 3D Gaussians. We tested performances without this loss and with fixed weights, setting w t proj = 10 −3 . Fig. 5 shows that without the projection loss, the skeleton cannot be embedded into the 3D Gaussians. Using fixed w t proj instead of adaptive weights can cause skeletons to protrude beyond the shape in some frames due to inaccuracies in the extracted 2D skeletons. 

• Skeleton construction and skeleton-driven deformation field. More discussions, numerical results, and visual results are available in the Supplementary Material.

Title: LISA: Learning Implicit Shape and Appearance of Hands
Snippet: A number of approaches have been proposed to learn appearance of a scene from multi-view images. The idea is to model the image formation process by rendering a neural volume with raycasting [30,40,55,66]. Particularly, NeRF [35] gains popularity with an efficient formulation of modeling the radiance field. Follow-up studies show that geometry can be improved if the density is regulated by occupancy [42] or SDF [60,65]. In this work, we use VolSDF [65] as a backbone renderer. For dynamic scenes, [47,52,58] combine NeRF with learning a deformation field. For modeling dynamic human bodies, Neural Body [51] attaches learnable vertex features to SMPL, and diffuses the features with sparse convolution for volumetric rendering. A-NeRF [56] conditions NeRF with SMPL bone transformations to learn an animatable avatar. Similar ideas are proposed in [50] and NARF [41]. H-NeRF [63] combines imGHUM with NeRF to enable appearance learning and train a separate network to predict SDF. In our work, the prediction of appearance and SDF is independent within each bone and later weighted by the corresponding skinning weights. 

Disentangled representations. Disentangling parameters of certain properties such as pose, shape or color is desireable as it allows treating (e.g., estimating or animating) these properties independently. Inspired by the parametric mesh models, Zhou et al., [69] trained a mesh autoencoder to disentangle shape and pose of humans and animals. They developed an unsupervised learning technique based on a cross-consistency loss. DiForm [62] adopted a decoder network to disentangle identity and deformation in learning an SDF-based shape embedding. A-SDF [39] factored out shape embedding and joint angles to model articulated objects. NPM [45] proposed to train shape embedding on canonically posed scans, followed by another network to learn the deformation field with dense supervision. A similar idea to the deformation field was adopted by i3DMM [67] to learn a human head model.

snippet.text:
In the field of 3D reconstruction, NeRF and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) are two important techniques each with their own characteristics and application scenarios. NeRF represents scenes as 5D neural radiance fields, successfully overcoming the limitations of previous methods and achieving high-quality view synthesis [3]. 3DGS is a 3D reconstruction technique of real-time radiance field rendering. Its core idea is to use 3D Gaussian distributions as volume representations to model scenes and achieve efficient rendering [14]. Compared to NeRF, 3DGS has faster rendering speeds but requires substantial storage resources and is sensitive to input quality. Lee Chan et al. significantly improved memory and storage efficiency through innovative volume masking strategies and compact attribute representations [15]. Mip-Splatting addressed aliasing issues in 3D Gaussian rendering by introducing 3D smoothing filters and 2D Mip filters, demonstrating excellent performance across different scales [16]. In addition to the above points, the MLP-based structure of NeRF offers better extensibility and has had a profound impact on various subfields of 3D computer vision, such as novel view synthesis [3], [17]- [19], surface reconstruction [20]- [22], dynamic scene representation [23], [24], and camera and pose estimation [25]- [28]. 

Signed Distance Function(SDF): In the field of 3D reconstruction, the Signed Distance Function (SDF) has emerged as a powerful representation method, widely applied in several state-of-the-art techniques. DeepSDF utilizes neural networks to predict SDF values from 3D points to surfaces, leveraging latent space encoding to achieve efficient reconstruction of complete shapes from partial observations [20]. SDF-SRN focuses on 3D shape reconstruction from single RGB images, employing differentiable rendering to optimize SDFs and recover more accurate 3D shapes and topologies from images [29]. GO-Surf enhances SDF applications by optimizing hierarchical feature grids and SDF values for fast, high-fidelity surface reconstruction from RGB-D sequences, and a novel SDF gradient regularization term is introduced to aid in hole filling and detail preservation [12].

snippet.text:
On the D-NeRF dataset, we evaluated the effectiveness of each component of our method using the following variations: 

• Anisotropic or isotropic 3D Gaussians. 

Although anisotropic 3D Gaussians yield images closer to the ground truth, they suffer significant quality degradation when the new poses differ greatly from the training pose, as shown in Fig. 4. Therefore, we use the isotropic 3D Gaussians for all experiments. 

• Without 2D projection loss L t proj or fixed weight w t proj during training the skeleton-driven dynamic model. The 2D projection loss L t proj assesses how well the skeleton aligns with the 3D Gaussians. We tested performances without this loss and with fixed weights, setting w t proj = 10 −3 . Fig. 5 shows that without the projection loss, the skeleton cannot be embedded into the 3D Gaussians. Using fixed w t proj instead of adaptive weights can cause skeletons to protrude beyond the shape in some frames due to inaccuracies in the extracted 2D skeletons. 

• Skeleton construction and skeleton-driven deformation field. More discussions, numerical results, and visual results are available in the Supplementary Material.

openAccessInfo.disclaimer: Notice: This snippet is extracted from the open access paper or abstract available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.01695, which is subject to the license by the author or copyright owner provided with this content. Please go to the source to verify the license and copyright information for your use.

snippet.text:
A number of approaches have been proposed to learn appearance of a scene from multi-view images. The idea is to model the image formation process by rendering a neural volume with raycasting [30,40,55,66]. Particularly, NeRF [35] gains popularity with an efficient formulation of modeling the radiance field. Follow-up studies show that geometry can be improved if the density is regulated by occupancy [42] or SDF [60,65]. In this work, we use VolSDF [65] as a backbone renderer. For dynamic scenes, [47,52,58] combine NeRF with learning a deformation field. For modeling dynamic human bodies, Neural Body [51] attaches learnable vertex features to SMPL, and diffuses the features with sparse convolution for volumetric rendering. A-NeRF [56] conditions NeRF with SMPL bone transformations to learn an animatable avatar. Similar ideas are proposed in [50] and NARF [41]. H-NeRF [63] combines imGHUM with NeRF to enable appearance learning and train a separate network to predict SDF. In our work, the prediction of appearance and SDF is independent within each bone and later weighted by the corresponding skinning weights. 

Disentangled representations. Disentangling parameters of certain properties such as pose, shape or color is desireable as it allows treating (e.g., estimating or animating) these properties independently. Inspired by the parametric mesh models, Zhou et al., [69] trained a mesh autoencoder to disentangle shape and pose of humans and animals. They developed an unsupervised learning technique based on a cross-consistency loss. DiForm [62] adopted a decoder network to disentangle identity and deformation in learning an SDF-based shape embedding. A-SDF [39] factored out shape embedding and joint angles to model articulated objects. NPM [45] proposed to train shape embedding on canonically posed scans, followed by another network to learn the deformation field with dense supervision. A similar idea to the deformation field was adopted by i3DMM [67] to learn a human head model.

problem: find papers on topic about ambiguity and llm agent
final_response:
# Overview

Ambiguity arises frequently in natural language tasks—pronoun resolution, underspecified instructions, and referential errors—and can degrade the reliability and safety of LLM-based agents that act on these inputs. Recent work spans empirical analyses of ambiguity in deployed-like agent settings, benchmarks that deliberately inject or measure ambiguity, frameworks for uncertainty-aware agent reasoning, and methods to detect and resolve instruction ambiguity through interaction. Below we synthesize key papers and themes.

# Empirical findings: How ambiguity manifests in LLM agents

- In clinical decision-support agents integrated with EHRs, models may produce hedged or internally inconsistent guidance on uncommon cases, leading to unclear or arbitrary-seeming recommendations and reduced actionable direction, highlighting user-facing risks when ambiguity is not resolved or communicated effectively. <cite id="8dc8712e-0">In clinical decision-support agents integrated with EHRs, models may produce hedged or internally inconsistent guidance on uncommon cases, leading to unclear or arbitrary-seeming recommendations and reduced actionable direction</cite>

- In software engineering agent settings, models struggle to distinguish well-specified from underspecified instructions; however, when allowed to interact, they can elicit clarifying information from users and significantly improve performance, underscoring the value of targeted clarification in ambiguous scenarios. <cite id="298c0670-4">In software engineering agent settings, models struggle to distinguish well-specified from underspecified instructions; when allowed to interact, they can elicit clarifying information and significantly improve performance</cite> <cite id="8dc8712e-4">Task descriptions can vary in quality; detecting ambiguity requires recognizing unclear expectations or missing key information, but excessive interaction can introduce inefficiencies, motivating careful design</cite>

- Analyses of LLM behavior on ambiguous natural language suggest a tendency to converge on a single interpretation and limited responsiveness to prompting for multiple interpretations, complicating automatic ambiguity detection and resolution by agents. <cite id="8dc8712e-1">LLMs often bias toward a single interpretation for ambiguous utterances and do not reliably produce alternative interpretations even when prompted</cite>

- Multi-agent or “debate-style” setups have been used to detect ambiguity and generate clarifying questions within bounded reasoning, offering a practical template for agent pipelines that explicitly call out unclear instructions and propose precise clarifications. <cite id="8dc8712e-2">Agents analyze ambiguous instructions and, when ambiguity is detected, propose a single optimal clarifying question within bounded reasoning</cite>

# Benchmarks and tasks that instantiate ambiguity

- Commonsense and pronoun ambiguity (text-level): Winogrande and the Winograd Schema Challenge target commonsense reasoning for pronoun resolution, providing large-scale, bias-reduced benchmarks that remain challenging for models, thereby serving as stress tests for agents that rely on textual instructions and internal knowledge. <cite id="b1bde990-0">Winogrande addresses overestimation in prior benchmarks via bias reduction and remains challenging, with SOTA accuracies well below human commonsense performance</cite> <cite id="b1bde990-1">WinoGrande consists of 44,000 problems with ambiguous pronouns and two possible antecedents, testing commonsense referent selection</cite> <cite id="b1bde990-2">WinoGrande was constructed with AfLite to reduce systematic biases and increase robustness and difficulty</cite> <cite id="b1bde990-4">WinoGrande evaluates resolving pronoun ambiguity using commonsense reasoning and remains a standard for such challenges</cite>

- Visual instruction navigation (VLN) ambiguity: Instruction perturbations and errors in textual guidance can substantially affect agent navigation; new benchmarks and methods focus on detecting and localizing instruction errors to improve robustness to real-world ambiguity and noise. <cite id="298c0670-3">A benchmark (R2RIE-CE) injects instruction errors and shows SOTA VLN methods are sensitive to such perturbations; a proposed method (IEDL) detects and localizes errors, and identifies many contaminated examples in standard sets</cite>

- Dialog and request-level ambiguity: A newly constructed IGLU-MINI dataset systematically manipulates ambiguity via missing attributes and referential errors, enabling fine-grained analysis of agent uncertainty and clarification behaviors. <cite id="298c0670-1">IGLU-MINI constructs clear→ambiguous pairs by removing attributes (e.g., color, count) or corrupting referring expressions, enabling controlled evaluation of ambiguity</cite>

- Code and software tasks with underspecification: Clarification-aware evaluations introduce metrics like pass@1 in first attempt versus after a clarification round and “good question rate,” directly quantifying an agent’s ability to detect ambiguity and ask useful questions. <cite id="298c0670-0">Clarification-aware evaluation includes pass@1 in first round, pass@1 in second round after clarification, and a Good Question Rate metric to assess the quality of clarifying questions</cite> <cite id="298c0670-2">A clarify-aware dataset pairs ambiguous instructions with desired clarifying responses and fine-tunes models to elicit targeted questions</cite>

# Frameworks and methods for ambiguity-aware agents

- Position and critique on uncertainty in LLM agents: Recent positions argue that in multi-turn agent interactions, underspecification and ambiguity are pervasive, and that interactive learning with users can reduce such uncertainties; moreover, communicating uncertainty should go beyond simple answer probabilities to better align with the nature of agent tasks. <cite id="6f577915-1">LLM agent interactions experience strong underspecification uncertainties; interactive learning can reduce them; and richer output uncertainties than mere answer probabilities may be needed</cite>

- Expanding epistemic uncertainty beyond model parameters: A broader perspective urges moving beyond parameter-level uncertainty to address ambiguity in human–LLM interaction, especially as LLMs act as central reasoning engines for autonomous agents that must gather knowledge, synthesize hypotheses, and design experiments to reduce world uncertainty. <cite id="6f577915-0">Addressing uncertainty due to ambiguity in human-LLM interaction is essential; LLM agents operate via APIs/editors/shells to reduce uncertainty through knowledge gathering and experimentation</cite>

- Bayesian and reinforcement learning connections: Reviews connect Bayesian inference and RL for decision making, noting that accurate uncertainty quantification is crucial and that combining Bayesian methods with RL can improve agent decision policies under uncertainty. <cite id="6f577915-2">Bayesian inference and RL are complementary for decision making; combining them can improve performance, and uncertainty quantification is crucial for agent performance</cite>

- Evaluating Bayesian rationality and belief updating: Frameworks that elicit priors, evidential likelihoods, and posterior beliefs provide tools to assess whether LLM agents adhere to Bayes’ rule, which is often considered the normative standard for handling uncertainty and ambiguity. <cite id="6f577915-3">Basil-style frameworks elicit priors, evidence, posteriors, and likelihoods and compare model outputs to Bayesian-rational posteriors to assess Bayesian rationality</cite>

- Aggregating imprecise/conflicting beliefs: Studies on belief aggregation under ambiguity highlight how decision makers combine heterogeneous or within-agent ambiguous beliefs, offering insights into designing agents that fuse multiple uncertain sources or perspectives. <cite id="6f577915-4">Aggregating beliefs under ambiguity requires handling conflict (heterogeneous beliefs) and within-agent ambiguity, with risk as the baseline (precise, Bayesian) case</cite>

# Instruction ambiguity detection and clarification

- Instruction-level ambiguity detection and clarification have been evaluated by prompting models to either ask clarifying questions or proceed, with metrics tracking both correctness (e.g., pass@1 pre/post clarification) and the agent’s propensity and quality of questioning. <cite id="298c0670-0">Evaluation includes frequency of asking clarifying questions and the quality via Good Question Rate, alongside correctness in a second round</cite> <cite id="298c0670-2">Clarify-aware fine-tuning equips models to recognize when to ask clarifying questions and to generate effective ones for underspecified tasks</cite>

- Controlled dialog datasets (IGLU-MULTI and derived IGLU-MINI) provide labeled clarification needs and minimal-pair edits that induce ambiguity, enabling systematic measurement of agent uncertainty and the effectiveness of clarification strategies. <cite id="298c0670-1">IGLU-MINI manipulates ambiguity by removing attributes or corrupting references, and paired clear/ambiguous examples allow measuring model outputs</cite> <cite id="298c0670-2">Instruction-level labels for clarification questions in IGLU-MULTI support evaluating ambiguity detection, though prior annotations preclude fine-grained analysis of agent uncertainty</cite>

# Domain and application-specific agent studies

- Interactive agents for software engineering: Beyond single-shot code generation, agent pipelines that detect ambiguity and query users can substantially improve outcomes on underspecified tasks, revealing a concrete path to mitigate ambiguity in practical automation. <cite id="298c0670-4">Interactive agents improve performance on ambiguous inputs by detecting ambiguity and asking targeted questions, though distinguishing clear vs. ambiguous instructions remains challenging</cite>

- Agent–human interaction trade-offs: While interactivity helps resolve ambiguity, it can also incur inefficiencies if overused; designing mechanisms that trigger interaction only when ambiguity is confidently detected is a key open problem. <cite id="8dc8712e-4">Detecting ambiguity requires identifying missing information, but unnecessary interaction burdens users and reduces efficiency</cite>

# Additional resources and related tasks

- Commonsense and narrative reasoning benchmarks like Winogrande and StoryCloze continue to serve as proxies for resolving ambiguity grounded in world knowledge and narrative plausibility, used to stress-test agents that must bridge implicit assumptions in instructions. <cite id="b1bde990-0">Winogrande reduces dataset-specific biases and remains challenging, underscoring gaps in commonsense reasoning for agents</cite> <cite id="b1bde990-1">StoryCloze tests narrative coherence and commonsense, asking models to choose the more plausible continuation</cite>

- In visual-language navigation, error-aware instruction processing and error detection/localization are emerging as necessary components to handle noisy and ambiguous instructions in real-world agents. <cite id="298c0670-3">Detection and localization of instruction errors supports building more reliable and versatile agents capable of handling real-world ambiguity and uncertainty</cite>

# Takeaways and open problems

- Ambiguity degrades agent reliability in high-stakes domains and reduces user trust when agents hedge inconsistently or act arbitrarily on underspecified inputs; targeted clarification and interaction can recover performance but must be balanced against efficiency. <cite id="8dc8712e-0">Ambiguity leads to hedged, inconsistent, and unclear guidance in clinical agents</cite> <cite id="298c0670-4">Clarification via interaction can significantly improve performance on ambiguous inputs, but ambiguity detection itself is challenging</cite>

- Benchmarks that explicitly induce or measure ambiguity (e.g., IGLU-MINI, R2RIE-CE, Winogrande/WSC, StoryCloze) provide controlled environments to quantify agents’ uncertainty detection, clarification quality, and robustness to instruction noise. <cite id="298c0670-1">IGLU-MINI enables controlled ambiguity via attribute removal and referential corruption</cite> <cite id="298c0670-3">R2RIE-CE and IEDL demonstrate sensitivity to instruction errors and methods for detecting/localizing them</cite> <cite id="b1bde990-0">Winogrande and WSC remain challenging for commonsense pronoun resolution</cite> <cite id="b1bde990-1">StoryCloze probes narrative commonsense and plausibility</cite>

- A broader uncertainty-aware design of agents—drawing on Bayesian inference and RL—offers pathways to represent and reduce ambiguity, but open problems include defining and communicating appropriate uncertainty in multi-turn agent dialogues and deciding when to abstain, interact, or request clarifications. <cite id="6f577915-1">Underspecification is inherent in early conversational states; interactive learning helps reduce it, and richer uncertainty communication than answer probabilities may be needed</cite> <cite id="6f577915-2">Combining Bayesian inference with RL can improve decision making under uncertainty</cite>

# Selected papers to start with

- Ambiguity in LLMs is a concept missing problem (Saparina & Lapata): argues LLMs bias to one reading and limited gains from multi-interpretation prompting, directly impacting ambiguity detection strategies in agents. <cite id="8dc8712e-1">LLMs often bias toward a single interpretation for ambiguous utterances and do not reliably produce alternative interpretations</cite>

- Interactive Agents to Overcome Ambiguity in Software Engineering: evaluates detection and targeted questioning in code generation agents; shows interaction improves performance on ambiguous inputs. <cite id="298c0670-4">Models struggle to distinguish clear vs. underspecified instructions but improve via interaction and targeted questions</cite>

- Can Code Language Models Learn Clarification-Seeking Behaviors?: introduces clarification-aware evaluation and fine-tuning with metrics like pass@1 (first vs. second round) and Good Question Rate. <cite id="298c0670-0">Clarification-aware metrics quantify correctness and question quality in ambiguous tasks</cite> <cite id="298c0670-2">Clarify-aware datasets train models to elicit useful clarifying questions</cite>

- Aligning Predictive Uncertainty with Clarification Questions in Grounded Dialog (IGLU-MINI): constructs minimal pairs with controlled ambiguity (missing attributes, referential errors) to study agent uncertainty and clarification. <cite id="298c0670-1">A controlled dataset systematically induces ambiguity to analyze agent uncertainty and clarifications</cite>

- Mind the Error! Detection and Localization of Instruction Errors in VLN: benchmark (R2RIE-CE) and method (IEDL) for detecting/localizing instruction errors, supporting agents robust to real-world ambiguity. <cite id="298c0670-3">Instruction error detection/localization improves robustness to real-world ambiguity in VLN agents</cite>

- Position: Uncertainty Quantification Needs Reassessment for LLM Agents: argues for rethinking aleatoric/epistemic splits in multi-turn agents and designing interaction strategies to reduce underspecification ambiguity. <cite id="6f577915-1">Underspecification is common in LLM agent settings; interactive learning can reduce it; richer uncertainty communication is needed</cite>

- Extending Epistemic Uncertainty Beyond Parameters: argues that addressing ambiguity-driven uncertainty is foundational for reliable LLM-based agents, framing Bayesian modeling as a route forward. <cite id="6f577915-0">Ambiguity-driven uncertainty must be addressed for reliable LLM agents; agents reduce uncertainty via knowledge gathering and experimentation</cite>

- Combining Bayesian Inference and RL for Agent Decision Making: survey/review connecting Bayesian belief updating with RL decision policies under uncertainty. <cite id="6f577915-2">Bayesian inference and RL are complementary under uncertainty; combining them can improve agent performance</cite>

- BASIL: Bayesian Assessment of Sycophancy (methodology): provides a framework to elicit and evaluate priors, likelihoods, and posteriors, useful for diagnosing ambiguity-related reasoning deficits. <cite id="6f577915-3">Basil elicits priors, likelihoods, and posteriors and compares to Bayesian-rational updates to assess rationality under ambiguity</cite>

- Neuron-based Multifractal Analysis (contextual overview of commonsense benchmarks): situates Winogrande and WSC as challenging commonsense/pronoun-ambiguity benchmarks for agents. <cite id="b1bde990-0">Winogrande and WSC test commonsense pronoun resolution with challenging accuracies below human levels</cite> <cite id="b1bde990-1">WinoGrande and StoryCloze are used to assess narrative commonsense and plausibility</cite>

Title: Interactive Agents to Overcome Ambiguity in Software Engineering
Snippet: AI agents are increasingly being deployed to automate tasks, often based on ambiguous and underspecified user instructions. Making unwarranted assumptions and failing to ask clarifying questions can lead to suboptimal outcomes, safety risks due to tool misuse, and wasted computational resources. In this work, we study the ability of LLM agents to handle ambiguous instructions in interactive code generation settings by evaluating proprietary and open-weight models on their performance across three key steps: (a) leveraging interactivity to improve performance in ambiguous scenarios, (b) detecting ambiguity, and (c) asking targeted questions. Our findings reveal that models struggle to distinguish between well-specified and underspecified instructions. However, when models interact for underspecified inputs, they effectively obtain vital information from the user, leading to significant improvements in performance and underscoring the value of effective interaction. Our study highlights critical gaps in how current state-of-the-art models handle ambiguity in complex software engineering tasks and structures the evaluation into distinct steps to enable targeted improvements.
