# What "multimedia document adaptation" entails

Multimedia document adaptation refers to transforming and tailoring digital documents that combine multiple modalities—text, images, video, structured graphics, and interactive elements—so they perform well across varying user contexts, devices, and downstream tasks such as retrieval, summarization, and presentation quality. In service-oriented systems, adaptation cycles are triggered by user context requests and orchestrated by components that manage content, quality, and adaptation logic to select appropriate transformations (e.g., subtitle generation, format conversion, or summarization) for a given scenario. <cite id="4bad69f2-1">A multimedia document typically integrates static media (text, graphics) and continuous media (audio/video), plus structured media (HTML/SMIL/SVG) and embedded programs; a good scenario balances complementary multimedia elements for effective information presentation</cite> <cite id="4bad69f2-2">An adaptation architecture centered on a Multimedia Document Manager, QoS Manager, and Adaptation Manager collaborates to find the best adaptation for a document in context</cite> <cite id="4bad69f2-4">Concrete adaptation actions include speech-to-text, video-to-images, translation, format conversion, and text summarization, executed as services to transform the document objects for the user's context</cite>.

# Core adaptation strategies

## 1) Pipeline/service-level adaptation (A4M-style architectures)
Adaptation can begin at the system level, where a service layer applies transformations to document objects based on user context (device, bandwidth, language, accessibility needs). This includes: 
- Structural and perceptual conversions (e.g., muting audio with subtitles, converting videos to image sequences, changing media formats) and 
- Semantics-level enrichments (e.g., language translation, text summarization). <cite id="4bad69f2-4">A prototype adapted web contents via actions such as speech-to-text, video-to-images, translation, format change, and text summarizing, orchestrated by an adaptation service per user profile</cite>. 
These services can be combined with QoS-aware orchestration to ensure the selected adaptations meet performance and experience targets while preserving information fidelity. <cite id="4bad69f2-2">The Adaptation Manager works with QoS and document managers to reach consensus on the best adaptation under constraints</cite>.

## 2) Cross-modal dense retrieval for documents
For retrieval-focused adaptation, the goal is to align textual queries with multimedia document content (e.g., screenshots of PDFs, web pages, slides) or to align document images with text. Modern approaches:
- Leverage contrastive learning, multilingual adapters, and distillation to train dense retrievers that embed both text and visuals for efficient matching. <cite id="29f0b723-3">Universal Multimodal Embedding work (e.g., VLM2Vec, MMEB) and its MMEB-V2 extension incorporate visual document tasks, emphasizing query- and task-driven embeddings for cross-modal retrieval</cite> <cite id="29f0b723-4">Multilingual dense retrievers use strategies like task-specific LoRA adapters, separate text/image encoders (Jina), VLM-based embedding conversion (VLM2Vec), self-knowledge distillation (xVLM2Vec), and large-scale multilingual encoders (BGE-M3)</cite>.
- Build document-specific benchmarks and frameworks that respect complex layouts and long-form context. <cite id="792e6865-3">DocMMIR proposes a unified framework and benchmark for document-level multi-modal retrieval across Wikipedia articles, arXiv papers, and slides, addressing whole-document structure beyond snippet-level settings</cite> <cite id="792e6865-1">GlobalDoc introduces cross-modal pretext tasks (learning-to-mine, learning-to-unify, learning-to-reorganize) at page level to better capture document layout and content for industrial document retrieval</cite> <cite id="792e6865-2">DIR research highlights the need for cross-modal retrieval over document images that jointly models OCR-derived text and visual layout to overcome limitations of single-modal image retrieval</cite>.

Training strategies commonly include:
- Contrastive losses with hard negative mining and positive-aware mining to improve ranking quality. <cite id="29f0b723-3">MMEB emphasizes multi-stage contrastive learning and NV-Retriever introduces positive-aware mining to remove false negatives</cite>.
- Adapter modules and distillation to adapt foundation encoders to document tasks and multilingual settings efficiently. <cite id="29f0b723-4">Task-specific LoRA adapters (Jina-embeddings-v3/v4), VLM2Vec conversion via contrastive training, and self-knowledge distillation (xVLM2Vec) are used to adapt vision-language models for document retrieval</cite> <cite id="29f0b723-0">Surveys discuss adapting and distilling large multimodal foundation models (e.g., CLIP) into smaller students for domain generalization and aligning prompts via learnable vectors</cite>.
- Matryoshka representation learning to balance quality and efficiency by enabling flexible embedding dimensions. <cite id="29f0b723-4">Matryoshka representation learning is adopted to support flexible embeddings for deployment efficiency in multimodal retrieval</cite>.

## 3) Web-scale multimodal pretraining (foundation models)
Adapting models to handle web-native multimedia documents often starts with large-scale pretraining on diverse web corpora that include text, images, and mixed modalities, followed by task-specific fine-tuning. <cite id="d4897f73-0">M6 collected a massive Chinese M6-Corpus from webpages across domains (encyclopedias, Q&A, forums, product descriptions) and proposed a multimodal transformer (M6) pretrained on multitask objectives, scaling to 10B/100B parameter models that support both single- and cross-modal understanding and generation</cite> <cite id="d4897f73-3">M6 demonstrates cross-modal generation (e.g., text-guided image generation) and general-purpose multimodal understanding, showing versatility across downstream applications</cite>. Such pretraining endows models with prior knowledge over real-world document structures (navigation menus, headers, tables, images) and multimodal correspondences, reducing the need for task-specific data.

For multilingual and cross-script document retrieval, specialized training and evaluation are crucial: <cite id="29f0b723-4">xVLM2Vec extends to multilingual scenarios via self-knowledge distillation but was limited to European languages, motivating broader coverage</cite> <cite id="792e6865-4">M3DR targets universal multilingual multimodal document retrieval across diverse scripts, ablation studies on loss functions and negative sampling strategies guide effective multilingual training</cite>.

## 4) Long-document and LLM-based adaptation
When the unit of adaptation is a long document (papers, reports, legal texts), LLM-centric approaches focus on context utilization, faithfulness, and efficiency. <cite id="e6ac2000-0">Analyses show that decoder-only and encoder-decoder LLMs maintain robustness when relevant info is within their training-time context, but performance degrades when relevant content is placed in the middle of longer inputs, with encoder-decoder models sometimes better leveraging context via bidirectional processing</cite>. To handle long contexts and enable retrieval-augmented workflows:
- Summarization and highlight-aware finetuning can improve focus and controllability. <cite id="e6ac2000-3">Flan-T5-based systems can be finetuned with highlight-aware inputs (e.g., Multi-Review Fusion-in-Context) and reinforced learning with dual rewards to improve faithfulness and coverage around marked spans</cite> <cite id="e6ac2000-1">Legal text modeling benefits from domain-aware preprocessing and using larger Flan-T5 variants (Base/Large/XL/XXL) to capture nuanced terminology and structure</cite>.
- Knowledge distillation transfers ChatGPT-like capabilities into efficient FLAN-T5 variants for document understanding and tabular/RAG tasks. <cite id="e6ac2000-4">Distilling ChatGPT 3.5 into FLAN-T5 with curriculum learning improves performance on document tasks (e.g., TabFact), with larger T5 models benefiting more from structured curricula</cite>.
- Multilingual document similarity and retrieval can be improved by enriching non-English content with high-quality English summaries. <cite id="e6ac2000-2">In OpenMSD, Flan-PaLM2-generated summaries outperform top-N translation summaries and, together with enriched documents, boost MAP scores by 7–16% across test types for multilingual scientific document similarity</cite>.

# Practical adaptation pipelines

A comprehensive multimedia document adaptation pipeline typically combines:
- Structural analysis and OCR to expose text and layout from document images/screenshots and PDFs. <cite id="792e6865-2">Document image retrieval pipelines integrate OCR to turn document images into text for cross-modal matching, while avoiding loss from purely visual features</cite>.
- Cross-modal alignment: pretrain or fine-tune encoders on document-specific corpora using contrastive and retrieval losses, optionally adding multilingual adapters or distilling from VLMs to capture fine-grained visual-text correspondences in layouts, tables, and figures. <cite id="792e6865-3">DocMMIR provides a unified benchmark and framework for whole-document retrieval across modalities and domains</cite> <cite id="29f0b723-4">Adapter-based and distillation-based strategies (LoRA, self-knowledge distillation) adapt encoders for document retrieval</cite> <cite id="29f0b723-3">Positive-aware negative mining and multi-stage contrastive training improve ranking quality in multimodal embeddings</cite>.
- Long-document generation and summarization: for RAG and interactive querying, use LLMs (Flan-T5/UL2) with highlight-aware finetuning, RL for faithfulness, or distillation to produce concise, faithful summaries and fusions of document content. <cite id="e6ac2000-3">Highlight-aware finetuning and RL with dual rewards improve fusion around user-specified spans</cite> <cite id="e6ac2000-4">Curriculum-based distillation transfers complex reasoning into FLAN-T5 variants for document tasks</cite>.
- QoS orchestration: select transformations at runtime (e.g., subtitle generation for hearing-impaired users, image resampling for small screens, bandwidth-aware streaming) using an adaptation manager that respects latency, quality, and accessibility constraints. <cite id="4bad69f2-2">An Adaptation Manager coordinates with document and QoS managers to pick optimal adaptations</cite> <cite id="4bad69f2-4">Adaptation services include speech-to-text, video-to-images, translation, format conversion, and summarization</cite>.

# Evaluation and benchmarks

Document adaptation should be evaluated on tasks that reflect end-user needs and deployment scenarios:
- Cross-modal retrieval: text-to-document image retrieval (DIR), document screenshot retrieval, and visual document benchmarks (VisDoc via MMEB-V2) with metrics like recall@k, MRR, and MAP. <cite id="29f0b723-3">MMEB and MMEB-V2 define broad cross-modal benchmarks including visual document tasks, emphasizing query-driven embeddings and evaluation across multimodal retrieval scenarios</cite> <cite id="792e6865-2">DIR benchmarks stress OCR-based text retrieval over document images and the need to capture layout and visual style for fine-grained matching</cite>.
- Whole-document understanding: document-level multi-modal IR across Wikipedia, arXiv, slides with unified inputs and diverse queries; assess both uni-modal and cross-modal settings. <cite id="792e6865-3">DocMMIR introduces a unified benchmark spanning multiple document types and modalities for document-level retrieval</cite> <cite id="792e6865-1">GlobalDoc proposes page-level pretext tasks and new downstream tasks to evaluate generalization in industrial settings</cite>.
- Multilingual and zero/few-shot settings: measure performance across languages/scripts and unseen domains; use multilingual retrievers and distillation. <cite id="792e6865-4">M3DR systematically evaluates multilingual visual document retrieval across diverse scripts with ablations on loss and negative sampling</cite> <cite id="29f0b723-4">Self-knowledge distillation and adapter approaches are used to extend multilingual capabilities beyond European languages</cite>.
- Long-document generation: evaluate context sensitivity, middle-span robustness, faithfulness, and coverage; test highlight-aware summarization and fusion. <cite id="e6ac2000-0">Decoder-only and encoder-decoder LLMs show sensitivity to placing relevant information in the middle of long contexts, guiding prompt and retrieval strategies</cite> <cite id="e6ac2000-3">Highlight-aware finetuning and RL improve faithfulness and coverage around specified spans</cite> <cite id="e6ac2000-2">Summaries from Flan-PaLM2 improve multilingual document similarity metrics over simple translation snippets</cite>.
- Web-scale generalization: pretrain on large mixed-modality web corpora (e.g., M6) and test zero/few-shot cross-modal tasks and domain transfer. <cite id="d4897f73-0">M6-Corpus spans massive webpages across domains and the M6 model is pretrained for multimodal understanding and generation, enabling transfer to diverse downstream tasks</cite> <cite id="29f0b723-0">Surveys emphasize adapting foundation models to downstream tasks and modeling prompt context for better generalization</cite>.

# Trade-offs and when to choose which approach

- Pipeline vs. model adaptation: Service-level adaptations (A4M) are immediate and QoS-aware but can lose information or require heavy orchestration; model-based adaptations (cross-modal retrievers, foundation models) learn richer multimodal correspondences but need large labeled or pseudo-labeled corpora and careful evaluation. <cite id="4bad69f2-2">Adaptation orchestration must balance user context with system constraints</cite> <cite id="792e6865-2">Purely visual or purely text pipelines miss layout and semantics, motivating cross-modal retrieval</cite>.
- General vs. specialized: Web-scale pretraining (M6) offers broad coverage and transfer, but domain-specific fine-tuning and multilingual distillation are often necessary for high accuracy. <cite id="d4897f73-3">M6 shows general multimodal capabilities and cross-modal generation, yet downstream tasks often benefit from task-specific fine-tuning</cite> <cite id="29f0b723-4">Adapter and distillation methods efficiently adapt pre-trained encoders to document retrieval and multilingual settings</cite>.
- Ranking quality vs. efficiency: Contrastive training with hard negatives and positive-aware mining improves retrieval quality, while Matryoshka and adapter modules help manage latency and resource constraints. <cite id="29f0b723-3">Positive-aware mining reduces false negatives and multi-stage contrastive learning strengthens embeddings</cite> <cite id="29f0b723-4">Matryoshka enables flexible embedding dimensions for deployment efficiency; LoRA adapters reduce parameter count while maintaining performance</cite>.
- Long-document controllability vs. faithfulness: LLM-based adaptation with highlight-aware finetuning and RL improves focus but must guard against hallucinations; distillation can make these capabilities more efficient for production RAG systems. <cite id="e6ac2000-3">Highlight-aware finetuning and RL with dual rewards improve faithfulness and coverage around user-specified spans</cite> <cite id="e6ac2000-4">Curriculum distillation transfers complex reasoning into FLAN-T5 variants for document tasks</cite>.

# A step-by-step adaptation recipe

1) Profile the document space: collect representative web/multimedia documents across domains, extract text and structure (OCR/layout), and tag modalities and metadata. <cite id="792e6865-2">OCR-based pipelines convert document images into text to enable cross-modal retrieval while preserving layout cues</cite> <cite id="d4897f73-0">Webpage-derived corpora spanning encyclopedias, Q&A, forums, and products provide broad coverage for pretraining</cite>.

2) Choose the adaptation target:
- If improving retrieval: build cross-modal retrieval training data and select a backbone (e.g., CLIP-like encoders) plus document-specific pretext tasks (layout alignment, page-level contrastive). <cite id="792e6865-1">Page-level cross-modal pretext tasks (L2M, L2U, L2R) improve document representation learning</cite> <cite id="29f0b723-3">MMEB and Think-then-embed emphasize instruction-driven, query-aware embeddings for multimodal retrieval</cite>.
- If general multimodal understanding: pretrain a foundation model on mixed modalities (e.g., M6-style) and fine-tune for specific tasks (classification, generation, retrieval). <cite id="d4897f73-0">M6 pretrains on massive web multimodal data and supports both single- and cross-modal tasks at scale</cite>.
- If multilingual: add adapter/distillation and multilingual negatives; consider self-supervised cross-lingual alignment. <cite id="29f0b723-4">LoRA adapters, separate encoders, and self-knowledge distillation support multilingual retrieval; M3DR targets diverse scripts</cite>.

3) Engineer long-document support:
- For LLM-based interfaces, use highlight-aware prompts, RL for faithfulness, or distill to smaller FLAN-T5 variants; generate summaries to aid retrieval and RAG. <cite id="e6ac2000-3">Highlight-aware finetuning and RL improve fusion around specified spans in long documents</cite> <cite id="e6ac2000-4">Curriculum distillation transfers capabilities into efficient FLAN-T5 models for document tasks</cite> <cite id="e6ac2000-2">High-quality summaries (Flan-PaLM2) improve multilingual document similarity and retrieval</cite>.

4) Orchestrate QoS-aware deployment:
- Select runtime adaptations (e.g., subtitle generation, image downsampling, format conversion, summarization) based on user context and constraints via an adaptation manager. <cite id="4bad69f2-2">The Adaptation Manager collaborates with QoS and document managers to choose optimal adaptations</cite> <cite id="4bad69f2-4">Adaptation services include speech-to-text, translation, format change, and summarization to fit user contexts</cite>.

5) Evaluate comprehensively:
- Use cross-modal retrieval metrics (recall@k, MRR, MAP) on DIR and document-level benchmarks; test zero/few-shot and multilingual transfers; assess long-context robustness and faithfulness for LLM tasks. <cite id="792e6865-3">DocMMIR evaluates document-level cross-modal retrieval across domains and modalities</cite> <cite id="792e6865-4">M3DR conducts systematic ablations for multilingual visual document retrieval</cite> <cite id="29f0b723-0">Surveys outline test-time adaptation and domain generalization for multimodal models</cite> <cite id="e6ac2000-0">Long-context sensitivity analyses guide placement of key content and retrieval strategies</cite>.

# Summary

Effective multimedia document adaptation combines service-level transformations with model-based learning to align text and multimodal content, scale via web-pretraining, and handle long, multilingual documents through LLM-centric techniques and retrieval. The choice of strategy depends on deployment constraints, data availability, and evaluation goals, with architectures like A4M for runtime adaptations, cross-modal retrieval frameworks (DocMMIR, GlobalDoc) and benchmarks (MMEB-V2, DIR) for measurement, and foundation models (e.g., M6) and multilingual distillation (e.g., M3DR) for broad generalization and efficiency. <cite id="4bad69f2-1">A multimedia document integrates text, graphics, and structured/continuous media</cite> <cite id="4bad69f2-2">Adaptation orchestration coordinates document, QoS, and adaptation managers</cite> <cite id="4bad69f2-4">Adaptation services include speech-to-text, translation, format conversion, and summarization</cite> <cite id="792e6865-3">DocMMIR provides a unified document-level multi-modal IR benchmark and framework</cite> <cite id="29f0b723-3">MMEB and universal multimodal embeddings emphasize query- and instruction-driven embeddings for cross-modal retrieval</cite> <cite id="d4897f73-0">M6 pretrains on massive web multimodal corpora and scales to 10B/100B models for multimodal understanding and generation</cite> <cite id="29f0b723-4">Adapters and distillation enable efficient multilingual multimodal retrieval (e.g., M3DR)</cite> <cite id="e6ac2000-0">LLMs show sensitivity to long-context placement, guiding prompt and retrieval design</cite>.

Title: On the use of historical data in context-aware multimedia documents adaptation processes
Snippet: Our prototype supports web contents adaptation according to user contexts without depending on a specific domain of application. The aim is to ensure the genericity of the prototype so that it can be adapted to a wide range of applications using multimedia documents with simple objects (e.g. texts, images, and videos) or those composed of a combination of different types of contents. Generally, there exist several types of document sharing, depending on applications scopes; we cite as examples file transfer protocol (FTP), peer-to-peer sharing and cloud service sharing (e.g. [36], [37]). Regarding our prototype, the HTTP protocol was adopted to share a set of multimedia documents hosted on a server, due to simplicity of implementation. 

The adaptation of multimedia documents takes place by involving a set of adaptation actions. Each adaptation action is performed by executing one or several adaptation services, depending on the nature of the media objects in the documents. The description of the adaptation actions given in Table 5 is as follows: a. Speech to text: it mutes the sounds of auditory objects by replacing them with textual content (sounds on videos are muted and subtitled while audio contents are converted to text). c. Video to images: it converts videos to images sequences. d. Language translation: this action translates media objects written in a source language to the target language specified in the users profile. e. Format change: it changes the format of a media object to another format (e.g. mp3 to mp4). f. Video in smart TV: this action plays video objects in a smart TV since the screen size is larger. g. Text summarizing: this action summarizes the content of text objects.

Title: Advances in Multimodal Adaptation and Generalization: From Traditional Approaches to Foundation Models
Snippet: These challenges highlight that multimodal DA/DG is not merely a variant of traditional unimodal DA/DG, but a field with its own distinct set of challenges, warranting a dedicated and in-depth survey. 

In recent years, MMDA and MMDG have achieved significant progress in areas such as action recognition [18], semantic segmentation [19], cross-modal retrieval [20], and generative modeling [21]. Besides, the emergence of largescale multimodal foundation models (MFMs), such as contrastive language-image pretraining (CLIP) [16] and stable diffusion [22], has opened new research directions for DA and DG. These efforts aim to enhance generalization capabilities using MFMs or adapt MFMs to downstream tasks. For example, Dunlap et al. [23] extend image embeddings to unseen domains using language, while Huang et al. [24] distill CLIP's knowledge into a smaller student model for domain generalization. Additionally, Zhou et al. [25] adapt CLIP-like vision-language models (VLMs) for downstream image recognition by modeling a prompt's context words with learnable vectors. 

Despite significant progress made in the field recently, there is no comprehensive survey that summarizes the main ideas of multimodal adaptation and generalization. This survey paper aims to provide a detailed literature review of algorithms developed over the last decade and to offer insights into existing research gaps and future directions. This paper covers five adaptation scenarios (Fig. 2 and Fig. 3) and is organized as follows. Sec. 2 discusses related research areas, with a generic framework proposed in Sec. 3. Sec. 4 introduces the multimodal domain adaptation problem and highlights major solutions for action recognition and semantic segmentation. Sec. 5 and Sec. 6 present representative methods for multimodal test-time adaptation (MMTTA, a special form of MMDA that focuses on adapting a pre-trained source multimodal model to a target domain online, without accessing source domain data) and domain generalization, respectively. Sec. 7 explores how multimodal foundation models can help improve DA and DG. Sec. 8 reviews methods for adapting MFMs to downstream tasks.

Title: Progressive Modality Cooperation for Multi-Modality Domain Adaptation
Snippet: Under the MMDA setting, the samples from the source and target domains contain both RGB and depth modalities. Since most existing works are not specifically designed for multi-modality domain adaptation, we compare our work with five supervised multi-modality approaches including (1) HHA [4], (2) CNN Features [81], (3) Cross-Modal [5] (4) FusionNet [74] and (5) RCFFusion [82], five single-modality domain adaptation approaches including (6) DAN [30], (7) JAN [32], and (8) CDAN [33], (9) DANN [10], and (10) iCAN [20], and two multi-modality domain adaptation approaches including (11) UFMDA [52] and ( 12) MM-SADA [83]. For all methods, the input samples from the two domains have both modalities. For all single-modality domain adaptation methods, different networks for all modalities are learned separately and the scores from all networks are fused in a late fusion fashion. Similar to our PMC, the baseline method iCAN [20] uses pseudo-labeled target samples for re-training the network. For the multimodality domain adaptation methods [52], [83] designed for the cross-media retrieval tasks, we modified the classifier of their methods in order to fairly compare them with our PMC method. 

From Table I, we observe that single modality domain adaptation approaches using the late fusion strategy generally outperform the multi-modality approaches without using domain adaptation, which shows it is beneficial to explicitly reduce the data distribution mismatch between the two domains. In addition, one of the baseline multi-modality with domain adaptation approach UFMDA concatenates the mid-level features with the attention module. However, the view-specific statistical property may be ignored by simply concatenating the features. The MM-SADA method [83] also extends DANN for the multi-modality tasks by additionally using a modality correspondence classifier for the alignment of different modalities (i.e., RGB and depth).

Title: Advances in Multimodal Adaptation and Generalization: From Traditional Approaches to Foundation Models
Snippet: Multimodal domain adaptation (MMDA) aims at adapting a model trained on a labeled source domain to perform effectively on an unlabeled target domain while leveraging multiple modalities of data (e.g., video, audio, and optical flow). The modality gaps and different levels of distribution shift across modalities make MMDA particularly challenging than unimodal DA. Existing research on MMDA has primarily focused on two tasks: the action recognition task with video, audio, and optical flow modalities, and the semantic segmentation task with LiDAR point cloud and RGB images. While most proposed methods are partly similar and generally applicable to both tasks, we discuss them separately for clarity.

Title: Think Then Embed: Generative Context Improves Multimodal Embedding
Snippet: Recently there has been growing interest in developing Universal Multimodal Embedding (UME) (Gu et al., 2025;Jiang et al., 2024;Meng et al., 2025), where the embedding depends both on the query and task instruction. Representative examples include VLM2Vec (Jiang et al., 2024), which proposes the Massive Multimodal Embedding Benchmark (MMEB), comprising a wide range of cross / multimodal retrieval tasks, as well as non-conventional retrieval tasks such as VQA, grounding, and classification. Subsequently, MMEB-V2 (Meng et al., 2025) is proposed, extending MMEB-V1 to include video and visual document (visdoc) tasks.

Title: M3DR: Towards Universal Multilingual Multimodal Document Retrieval
Snippet: The GTE series [33] employed multi-stage contrastive learning on large-scale multilingual data. Jina-embeddings-v3 [50] introduced task-specific LoRA adapters, while Jina-v4 [15] extended to multimodal multilingual retrieval with separate text and image encoders, achieving strong performance on JVDR benchmark. However, separate encoders may miss fine-grained visual-textual interactions that vision-based approaches capture. VLM2Vec [22] proposed converting VLMs into embedding models through contrastive training on MMEB. xVLM2Vec [45] extended to multilingual scenarios through self-knowledge distillation, though limited to European languages. BGE-M3 [4] supports 100+ languages over text. Unlike these works which focus on textonly multilingual retrieval or limited-language multimodal scenarios, M3DR systematically addresses multilingual visual document retrieval across diverse scripts. Training Strategies. Modern dense retrievers rely on contrastive learning with InfoNCE loss [46] and hard negative mining. NV-Retriever [44] introduced positive-aware mining for effective false negative removal. LLaRA [30] adapted LLMs for retrieval through embedding-based autoencoding. Llama2Vec [31] demonstrated unsupervised adaptation of Llama-2 for dense retrieval. DRAMA [39] leveraged LLMs for diverse data augmentation. Matryoshka representation learning [29] enables flexible embedding dimensions, critical for deployment efficiency. M3DR builds upon these strategies, conducting systematic ablations on loss functions, negative sampling, and Matryoshka training, identifying optimal configurations for multilingual multimodal document retrieval.

snippet.text: Multimodal domain adaptation (MMDA) aims at adapting a model trained on a labeled source domain to perform effectively on an unlabeled target domain while leveraging multiple modalities of data (e.g., video, audio, and optical flow). The modality gaps and different levels of distribution shift across modalities make MMDA particularly challenging than unimodal DA. Existing research on MMDA has primarily focused on two tasks: the action recognition task with video, audio, and optical flow modalities, and the semantic segmentation task with LiDAR point cloud and RGB images. While most proposed methods are partly similar and generally applicable to both tasks, we discuss them separately for clarity.

snippet.text: The GTE series [33] employed multi-stage contrastive learning on large-scale multilingual data. Jina-embeddings-v3 [50] introduced task-specific LoRA adapters, while Jina-v4 [15] extended to multimodal multilingual retrieval with separate text and image encoders, achieving strong performance on JVDR benchmark. However, separate encoders may miss fine-grained visual-textual interactions that vision-based approaches capture. VLM2Vec [22] proposed converting VLMs into embedding models through contrastive training on MMEB. xVLM2Vec [45] extended to multilingual scenarios through self-knowledge distillation, though limited to European languages. BGE-M3 [4] supports 100+ languages over text. Unlike these works which focus on textonly multilingual retrieval or limited-language multimodal scenarios, M3DR systematically addresses multilingual visual document retrieval across diverse scripts. Training Strategies. Modern dense retrievers rely on contrastive learning with InfoNCE loss [46] and hard negative mining. NV-Retriever [44] introduced positive-aware mining for effective false negative removal. LLaRA [30] adapted LLMs for retrieval through embedding-based autoencoding. Llama2Vec [31] demonstrated unsupervised adaptation of Llama-2 for dense retrieval. DRAMA [39] leveraged LLMs for diverse data augmentation. Matryoshka representation learning [29] enables flexible embedding dimensions, critical for deployment efficiency. M3DR builds upon these strategies, conducting systematic ablations on loss functions, negative sampling, and Matryoshka training, identifying optimal configurations for multilingual multimodal document retrieval.

documents.snippet:
These challenges highlight that multimodal DA/DG is not merely a variant of traditional unimodal DA/DG, but a field with its own distinct set of challenges, warranting a dedicated and in-depth survey. 

In recent years, MMDA and MMDG have achieved significant progress in areas such as action recognition [18], semantic segmentation [19], cross-modal retrieval [20], and generative modeling [21]. Besides, the emergence of largescale multimodal foundation models (MFMs), such as contrastive language-image pretraining (CLIP) [16] and stable diffusion [22], has opened new research directions for DA and DG. These efforts aim to enhance generalization capabilities using MFMs or adapt MFMs to downstream tasks. For example, Dunlap et al. [23] extend image embeddings to unseen domains using language, while Huang et al. [24] distill CLIP's knowledge into a smaller student model for domain generalization. Additionally, Zhou et al. [25] adapt CLIP-like vision-language models (VLMs) for downstream image recognition by modeling a prompt's context words with learnable vectors. 

Despite significant progress made in the field recently, there is no comprehensive survey that summarizes the main ideas of multimodal adaptation and generalization. This survey paper aims to provide a detailed literature review of algorithms developed over the last decade and to offer insights into existing research gaps and future directions. This paper covers five adaptation scenarios (Fig. 2 and Fig. 3) and is organized as follows. Sec. 2 discusses related research areas, with a generic framework proposed in Sec. 3. Sec. 4 introduces the multimodal domain adaptation problem and highlights major solutions for action recognition and semantic segmentation. Sec. 5 and Sec. 6 present representative methods for multimodal test-time adaptation (MMTTA, a special form of MMDA that focuses on adapting a pre-trained source multimodal model to a target domain online, without accessing source domain data) and domain generalization, respectively. Sec. 7 explores how multimodal foundation models can help improve DA and DG. Sec. 8 reviews methods for adapting MFMs to downstream tasks.

Title: Generalized Contrastive Learning for Multi-Modal Retrieval and Ranking
Snippet: Information Retrieval (IR) datasets are designed to assess the retrieval and ranking capabilities of various models. However, comprehensive ranking information is notably lacking in most available datasets. Popular text datasets such as MSMARCO [43], NQ [32] and FEVER [60] contain large-scale corpus with sufficient number of unique queries, but they only capture a binary relationship between the queries and the documents. Some text datasets such as TREC-Covid [63], TREC-News [10] and NFCorpus [5] offer nonbinary relevance but they are limited to three to five relevance level while having small number of unique queries as shown in Table 1. 

The matter got worse for cross-modal text to image retrieval, where popular methods use image captioning datasets such as COCO [36], Flickr30k [48] and Visual Genome [31] to benchmark their retrieval performances. These image caption datasets along with other largescale cross-modal datasets such as LAION-400M [56], RedCaps [12] and CC12M [6] typically assumes a one-to-one mapping between text and image without rankings. They are designed for cross-modal pretraining and captioning but not representative of retrieval tasks in general. Another limitation of these datasets is their division into train, dev and test [59]. This conventional split does not reflect real-world challenge. It lacks detailed evaluations on novel queries with existing documents, novel documents with existing queries, or completely zero-shot query-document pairs.

Title: GlobalDoc: A Cross-Modal Vision-Language Framework for Real-World Document Image Retrieval and Classification
Snippet: The second task, Content-based DIR, evaluates our model's representation learning capability in both uni-modal and cross-modal document image retrieval settings. This task integrates language and vision cues to create a more versatile and flexible system for industrial document data usage, as illustrated in Fig. 1. The key contributions of our work can be summarized in two-folds: 

• We propose three novel pretext tasks for our page-level document pretraining strategy: two cross-modal objectives, learning-to-mine (L2M) and learning-to-unify (L2U); and a learning-to-reorganize (L2R) task to restructure the representation space for each modality. 

• We developed two new downstream tasks to better evaluate GlobalDoc's performance in challenging industrial online settings, and showcase it's generalizing capabilities and assessment in both uni-modal and cross-modal scenarios. 

• We conduct a comprehensive analysis and evaluation of our model's performance on standard VDU benchmark tasks (DIC and VIE), to show the effectiveness of vision-and-language based approaches when compared with SOTA methods utilizing the relative positional encodings (as layout modality).

Title: Towards Natural Language-Based Document Image Retrieval: New Dataset and Benchmark
Snippet: With the rapid development of mobile cameras and smartphones, document images become one of the most con- venient ways to record and disseminate information. As an important part of information retrieval (IR), document image retrieval (DIR) aims to accurately and efficiently retrieve relevant document images from large repositories based on user queries. 

As illustrated in Fig. 1, considering the type of queries, existing DIR methods can be categorized into two paradigms: query-by-image and query-by-text. Specifically, query-by-image methods [2,3,11,16,37,38,40] directly extract features from query and document images for matching. The extraction of image features primarily considers visual information, which limits DIR within the same coarse semantic class, e.g., newspaper or receipt. Comparatively, query-by-text [25,63,73] resorts to Optical Character Recognition (OCR) engines [48][49][50][51]71] to extract words from document images. The retrieval models mainly focus on enhancing the textual representations of queries and documents, while commonly struggling to capture the extensive and comprehensive visual features presented in documents, such as visual elements, display styles, content layout, etc. 

To summarize, the current retrieval methods are restricted to single-modality matching, which inevitably results in information loss and noise for the original text or image domain. Consequently, it is necessary to design a cross-modal retrieval model for DIR that can handle text queries and visual documents simultaneously (see Fig. 1 (c)). This new DIR task is non-trivial as it involves multiple research areas, including text understanding, document image understanding, and cross-modal learning, and is also a crucial component of various downstream tasks. 

An intuitive solution is to directly apply existing crossmodal retrieval methods [8,31,33,52,68] on this task. However, most of these methods are dedicated to modeling the correspondence between textual descriptions and natural images, rather than document images. The lack of a dedicated, fine-grained DIR dataset prevents existing models from obtaining sufficient supervised signals, thereby limiting their performance on DIR tasks.

Title: DocMMIR: A Framework for Document Multi-modal Information Retrieval
Snippet: With the emergence of the Large Pre-training Model, the Pre-trained Multi-modal Retrieval Models (i.e., CLIP (Radford et al., 2021)) and Large Visual Language Models (i.e., BLIP2 (Li et al., 2023), ALIGN (Jia et al., 2021)), trained on vast image-text corpora, have achieved state-of-the-art * Equal Contribution. 

† Corresponding Author. 

results on tasks such as cross-modal retrieval, image captioning, and visual question answering by capturing fine-grained cross-modal alignment. Despite these advances in image-text retrieval, applying MLLMs to conduct document-level retrieval remains challenging. Real-world documents (Wikipedia articles, scientific papers, slide decks, etc.) often contain complex page layouts with text, figures, tables, and other formats. Off-the-shelf MLLMs typically encode images or text snippets in isolation and lack awareness of longer document context or multi-page structure. Existing studies fail to fully address the complexity of realworld document structures, leading to several critical limitations, as illustrated in Table 1. First, most multi-modal document retrieval benchmarks are constrained to fine-grained snippet-level settings, lacking support for whole-document retrieval. Second, the diversity of domains represented in current datasets is limited-many focus on narrow scientific or web-centric sources, overlooking broader cross-domain applicability. Third, some approaches treat whole-document screenshots as unified inputs and show promising results on specific domains, but this strategy assumes visual capture and still ignores semantic layout. These limitations hinder the comprehensive evaluation and development of MLLMs for document-level multi-modal information retrieval. 

To address these gaps, we introduce DocM-MIR: a unified framework for Document-level Multi-Modal Information Retrieval across various domains (demonstrated in Figure 1). We curate a large-scale benchmark with a unified structure that includes documents and queries from diverse sources (Wikipedia articles, arXiv papers, and slide presentations), each containing a mixture of modalities.

Title: Towards Natural Language-Based Document Image Retrieval: New Dataset and Benchmark
Snippet: Traditional content-based DIR methods [2,3,11,16,37,38,40] achieve retrieval by extracting features and computing similarities between the query image and the document images. This matching process can be performed either at the global level or at the single-word level. Besides, common cross-modal retrieval methods [8,13,30,31,52,68] perform retrieval in natural scenes through techniques like image-text matching. Motivated by this, Wang et al. [58] achieve accurate scene text retrieval through matching proposals and query words. However, the queries within these methods are represented for simple classes or single words with coarse semantics. DIR based on semantic-rich queries remains unexplored. 

Among recent DIR methods, PHD [11] explores an image-to-image retrieval method for historical documents. TransferDoc [7] adopts document category retrieval on existing datasets with classification labels [20]. However, these methods do not effectively utilize the information from image and text modalities. VILE [70] generates web page images from existing retrieval datasets [14] and utilizes these images as auxiliary information for text retrieval. Concurrent studies [18,42] employ document screenshots, such as those from PDFs or Wikipedia pages, and utilize large visual-language encoders for alignment modeling. Nevertheless, these approaches are difficult to generalize to DIR in large-scale real-world scenarios.

As an important part of information retrieval (IR), document image retrieval (DIR) aims to accurately and efficiently retrieve relevant document images from large repositories based on user queries. 

As illustrated in Fig. 1, considering the type of queries, existing DIR methods can be categorized into two paradigms: query-by-image and query-by-text. Specifically, query-by-image methods [2,3,11,16,37,38,40] directly extract features from query and document images for matching. The extraction of image features primarily considers visual information, which limits DIR within the same coarse semantic class, e.g., newspaper or receipt. Comparatively, query-by-text [25,63,73] resorts to Optical Character Recognition (OCR) engines [48][49][50][51]71] to extract words from document images. The retrieval models mainly focus on enhancing the textual representations of queries and documents, while commonly struggling to capture the extensive and comprehensive visual features presented in documents, such as visual elements, display styles, content layout, etc. 

To summarize, the current retrieval methods are restricted to single-modality matching, which inevitably results in information loss and noise for the original text or image domain. Consequently, it is necessary to design a cross-modal retrieval model for DIR that can handle text queries and visual documents simultaneously (see Fig. 1 (c)). This new DIR task is non-trivial as it involves multiple research areas, including text understanding, document image understanding, and cross-modal learning, and is also a crucial component of various downstream tasks. 

An intuitive solution is to directly apply existing crossmodal retrieval methods [8,31,33,52,68] on this task. However, most of these methods are dedicated to modeling the correspondence between textual descriptions and natural images, rather than document images. The lack of a dedicated, fine-grained DIR dataset prevents existing models from obtaining sufficient supervised signals, thereby limiting their performance on DIR tasks.

documents.title: DocMMIR: A Framework for Document Multi-modal Information Retrieval
documents.snippet:
With the emergence of the Large Pre-training Model, the Pre-trained Multi-modal Retrieval Models (i.e., CLIP (Radford et al., 2021)) and Large Visual Language Models (i.e., BLIP2 (Li et al., 2023), ALIGN (Jia et al., 2021)), trained on vast image-text corpora, have achieved state-of-the-art * Equal Contribution. 

† Corresponding Author. 

results on tasks such as cross-modal retrieval, image captioning, and visual question answering by capturing fine-grained cross-modal alignment. Despite these advances in image-text retrieval, applying MLLMs to conduct document-level retrieval remains challenging. Real-world documents (Wikipedia articles, scientific papers, slide decks, etc.) often contain complex page layouts with text, figures, tables, and other formats. Off-the-shelf MLLMs typically encode images or text snippets in isolation and lack awareness of longer document context or multi-page structure. Existing studies fail to fully address the complexity of realworld document structures, leading to several critical limitations, as illustrated in Table 1. First, most multi-modal document retrieval benchmarks are constrained to fine-grained snippet-level settings, lacking support for whole-document retrieval. Second, the diversity of domains represented in current datasets is limited-many focus on narrow scientific or web-centric sources, overlooking broader cross-domain applicability. Third, some approaches treat whole-document screenshots as unified inputs and show promising results on specific domains, but this strategy assumes visual capture and still ignores semantic layout. These limitations hinder the comprehensive evaluation and development of MLLMs for document-level multi-modal information retrieval. 

To address these gaps, we introduce DocM-MIR: a unified framework for Document-level Multi-Modal Information Retrieval across various domains (demonstrated in Figure 1). We curate a large-scale benchmark with a unified structure that includes documents and queries from diverse sources (Wikipedia articles, arXiv papers, and slide presentations), each containing a mixture of modalities.

documents.title: Towards Natural Language-Based Document Image Retrieval: New Dataset and Benchmark
documents.snippet:
Traditional content-based DIR methods [2,3,11,16,37,38,40] achieve retrieval by extracting features and computing similarities between the query image and the document images. This matching process can be performed either at the global level or at the single-word level. Besides, common cross-modal retrieval methods [8,13,30,31,52,68] perform retrieval in natural scenes through techniques like image-text matching. Motivated by this, Wang et al. [58] achieve accurate scene text retrieval through matching proposals and query words. However, the queries within these methods are represented for simple classes or single words with coarse semantics. DIR based on semantic-rich queries remains unexplored. 

Among recent DIR methods, PHD [11] explores an image-to-image retrieval method for historical documents. TransferDoc [7] adopts document category retrieval on existing datasets with classification labels [20]. However, these methods do not effectively utilize the information from image and text modalities. VILE [70] generates web page images from existing retrieval datasets [14] and utilizes these images as auxiliary information for text retrieval. Concurrent studies [18,42] employ document screenshots, such as those from PDFs or Wikipedia pages, and utilize large visual-language encoders for alignment modeling. Nevertheless, these approaches are difficult to generalize to DIR in large-scale real-world scenarios.

Title: M6: A Chinese Multimodal Pretrainer
Snippet: Pretraining has become a focus in the research in natural language processing (NLP) [1,2,7,16,18,19,27,31,37,44,49]. The recent GPT-3 with over 175 billion parameters demonstrates that large models trained on big data have extremely large capacity and it can outperform the state-of-the-arts in downstream tasks especially in the zero-shot setting. Also, the rapid development of pretraining in NLP sparkles cross-modal pretraining. A number of studies [4,11,17,22,24,25,28,29,38,51] have created new state-of-the-art performances for various cross-modal downstream tasks. 

A pity is that most recent studies focus on the pretraining on English data. There are lack of both large-scale datasets in Chinese and large-scale models pretrained on the data of Chinese. Therefore, in this work, we develop a large-scale dataset M6-Corpus, which consists of over 1.9TB images and 292GB texts. To the best of our knowledge, this is the largest dataset in Chinese for pretraining in both multimodality and natural language. The dataset collected from the webpages consists of different types of data and covers a large scale of domains, including encyclopedia, question answering, forum discussion, product description, etc. Also, we design sophisticated cleaning procedures to ensure that the data are of high quality. 

Furthermore, in order to sufficiently leverage such a large amount of high-quality data, we propose to build an extremely large model that can process data of multiple modalities and adapt to different types of downstream tasks. Thus we propose a novel model called M6, referring to MultiModality-to-MultiModality Multitask Mega-transformer. The model is based on the transformer, and it is pretrained with multiple tasks. Pretraining endows the model with the capability of single-modality and multimodality understanding and generation. Based on the architecture of M6, we build M6-10B and M6-100B, which are scaled up to 10 billion and 100 billion parameters respectively.

Title: NSUT-NLP at CASE 2022 Task 1: Multilingual Protest Event Detection using Transformer-based Models
Snippet: Pre-training in NLP refers to moulding a large collection of unannotated text input into generalpurpose language representations. It is useful as it  prevents having to start from scratch when training a new model for downstream tasks. Because it offers a stronger model initialization, pre-training improves generalization performance and aids in convergence on downstream tasks. Pretraining can be considered a form of regularization that avoids overfitting on smaller datasets with relatively few human-annotated examples. On many NLP tasks, pre-training models followed by fine-tuning them for downstream tasks, have demonstrated good performance (Erhan et al., 2010). 

The model used in our system is based on the BERT architecture. Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) (Devlin et al., 2019) is a transformer-based (Vaswani et al., 2017) pre-trained language model that was created with the objective of fine-tuning a pre-trained model yields better performance. The pretraining phase of BERT includes two tasks. Firstly, Masked Language Modeling (MLM) is where certain words are randomly masked in a sequence. About 15% of the words in a sequence are masked. The model then attempts to predict the masked words. Secondly, Next Sentence Prediction (NSP), where the model has an additional loss function, NSP loss, indicates if the second sequence follows the first one. Around 50% of the inputs are a pair, and they randomly chose the other 50. 

Our system uses a multimodal BERT (mBERT) specifically, bert-base-multilingual-cased which has been trained on 104 languages with the largest Wikipedia content. Since the size of Wikipedias for different languages varies, exponentially smoothed weighting of the data is performed to under-sample resource-rich languages and over-sample low-resource languages. The model has 12 layers of transformer blocks with 768 hidden dimensions conditioned on 12 self-attention heads. In total, the model has 110M trained parameters.

Title: M6: A Chinese Multimodal Pretrainer
Snippet: In this work, we propose the largest dataset M6-Corpus for pretraining in Chinese, which consists of over 1.9TB images and 292GB texts. The dataset has large coverage over domains, including encyclopedia, question answering, forum discussion, common crawl, etc. We propose a method called M6 that is able to process information of multiple modalities and perform both single-modal and cross-modal understanding and generation. The model is scaled to large model with 10B and 100B parameters with sophisticated deployment, and both models are the largest multimodal pretrained models. We apply the model to a series of downstream applications, showing its versatility. More specifically, we design a downstream task of text-guided image generation, and the finetuned M6 can reach superior performance by producing images of high quality. 

In the future, we will continue the pretraining of extremely large models by increasing the scale of data and models to explore the limit of performance, and we also endeavor to search for more downstream applications for further generalization.

Title: Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
Snippet: Figure 8 compares the performance of decoder-only and encoder-decoder models. When Flan-UL2 is evaluated on sequences within its 2048-token training-time context window (Figure 8; left subplot), its performance is relatively robust to changes in the position of relevant information within the input context (1.9% absolute difference between best-and worst-case performance). When evaluated on settings with sequences longer than 2048 tokens (Figure 8; center and right), Flan-UL2 performance begins to degrade when relevant information is placed in the middle. Flan-T5-XXL shows a similar trend, where longer input contexts result in a greater performance degradation when placing relevant information in the middle of the input context. We hypothesize that encoder-decoder models may make better use of their context windows because their bidirectional encoder allows processing each document in the context of future documents, potentially improving relative importance estimation between documents.

Title: Leveraging open-source models for legal language modeling and analysis: a case study on the Indian constitution
Snippet: Tokenization involves breaking down the text into individual tokens or words, forming the basic units of input for the language model.In legal documents, specialized vocabulary and terminology may pose challenges for traditional tokenization techniques.To address this, we utilized domain-specific tokenization libraries tailored to legal text, which can handle complex linguistic structures and preserve the integrity of legal terms and phrases during preprocessing.

7 An overview of the different types of Flan-T5 models Google/Flan-T5-Small: This model has the smallest capacity among the Flan-T5 variants.It typically contains fewer parameters compared to larger models, making it more lightweight and suitable for tasks where computational resources are limited or where inference speed is a primary concern.Google/Flan-T5-Base: The Base variant of the Flan-T5 model offers a moderate capacity, striking a balance between model size and performance.It contains more parameters than the small variant, allowing it to capture more complex patterns and relationships in the data, while still being relatively efficient in terms of memory and computational resources.

Google/Flan-T5-Large: The Large variant of the Flan-T5 model is characterized by its significantly larger capacity compared to the Base model.With more parameters, the large model can capture finer-grained details and nuances in the input data, leading to improved performance on various natural language processing tasks.However, training and inference with the large model may require more computational resources and time.Google/Flan-T5-XL: The XL variant of the Flan-T5 model represents a further increase in capacity and complexity.With even more parameters than the large model, the XL model offers enhanced representational power, enabling it to handle larger datasets and more challenging tasks.However, this comes at the cost of increased computational requirements and longer training times.

Google/Flan-T5-XXL: The XXL variant of the Flan-T5 model [7] is the largest and most powerful among the Flan-T5 models.With an even greater number of parameters, the XXL model can capture highly intricate patterns and relationships in the input data, leading to state-of-the-art performance on a wide range of natural language processing tasks.

Title: OpenMSD: Towards Multilingual Scientific Documents Similarity Measurement
Snippet: The enriched documents are used to train and test mSpt DC∪CC , the strongest variant of mSpt. The results of the proposed method on IDT and ODT are presented in Table 5 and 6, respectively. Firstly, we find that using the Flan-PaLM2-generated summaries consistently yields better performance than the top-N translation summaries; we believe this is because Flan-PaLM2 considers the whole abstract when generating the summaries, and hence its summaries are more informative and comprehensive than the top-N translation summaries. Secondly, compared to the SOTA baselines, using the enriched documents significantly boosting the MAP scores by 7% and 16% in IDT and ODT, respectively. Compared to the vanilla mSpt DC∪CC , using Flan-PaLM2generated summaries yields marginally (not significantly) better performance in IDT, and significantly better performance in ODT. These results suggest that enriching the non-English papers with high-quality English summaries can significantly improve the multilingual models' performance for papers in non-English and unseen languages.

Title: Multi-Review Fusion-in-Context
Snippet: We examine several baseline models for solving the FiC task.The input to a model is a document set with spans marked within the documents (highlights), and the model is trained to generate a fused passage around the highlights.

Models with full input.Using the training set of our dataset, we finetune a large language model, marking the highlights in the input via designated mark-ups, following Slobodkin et al. (2022).Specifically, we finetune a flan-t5-large model (Chung et al., 2022), that exhibited enhanced performance in tasks requiring constrained generation (Sanh et al., 2022;Wei et al., 2022).We will refer to this model as Flan-T5 H ('H' for 'Highlights').We develop an additional variant of Flan-T5 H , which we further finetune using Reinforcement Learning (RL), following the method in 2022) combined with a dual-reward policy (Pasunuru and Bansal, 2018), alternating between our NLI-based faithfulness and trained coverage metrics ( §5) as rewards.We also examine the performance of a one-shot GPT-4 model (OpenAI, 2023), guided with an example of the task. 10

Models with highlights only.To reveal the importance of the surrounding context, we also train a flan-t5-large model only with a concatenation of the highlights as the input (excluding surrounding context).We denote this variant Flan-T5 only-H .

Models without highlights.Finally, we examine flan-t5-large in a standard summarization setting, where it is finetuned with the input review-set without the highlighted spans, denoting this variant Flan-T5 no-H .It offers insights into the model's ability to pick up on signals that point to highlights.

Title: Leveraging Distillation Techniques for Document Understanding: A Case Study with FLAN-T5
Snippet: We distilled document understanding knowledge from ChatGPT 3.5 into FLAN-T5 of three different sizes small, base and large while employing curriculum learning. The results are promising: While FLAN-T5 SMALL struggles with most datasets, its performance on TabFact is surprisingly close to that of the teacher. FLAN-T5 LARGE even managed to surpass the teacher's performance on TabFact. Further, the results suggest that the larger T5 models utilize more pronounced learning curricula better than their smaller counterparts. A starting point for future work is the evaluation of larger student models, such as FLAN-T5 XL and FLAN-T5 XXL and different learning curricula. Another point of interest is investigation into other document representations and their utility for knowledge distillation.

snippet.text: The enriched documents are used to train and test mSpt DC∪CC , the strongest variant of mSpt. The results of the proposed method on IDT and ODT are presented in Table 5 and 6, respectively. Firstly, we find that using the Flan-PaLM2-generated summaries consistently yields better performance than the top-N translation summaries; we believe this is because Flan-PaLM2 considers the whole abstract when generating the summaries, and hence its summaries are more informative and comprehensive than the top-N translation summaries. Secondly, compared to the SOTA baselines, using the enriched documents significantly boosting the MAP scores by 7% and 16% in IDT and ODT, respectively. Compared to the vanilla mSpt DC∪CC , using Flan-PaLM2generated summaries yields marginally (not significantly) better performance in IDT, and significantly better performance in ODT. We examine several baseline models for solving the FiC task.The input to a model is a document set with spans marked within the documents (highlights), and the model is trained to generate a fused passage around the highlights.

Models with full input.Using the training set of our dataset, we finetune a large language model, marking the highlights in the input via designated mark-ups, following Slobodkin et al. (2022).Specifically, we finetune a flan-t5-large model (Chung et al., 2022), that exhibited enhanced performance in tasks requiring constrained generation (Sanh et al., 2022;Wei et al., 2022).We will refer to this model as Flan-T5 H ('H' for 'Highlights').We develop an additional variant of Flan-T5 H , which we further finetune using Reinforcement Learning (RL), following the method in 2022) combined with a dual-reward policy (Pasunuru and Bansal, 2018), alternating between our NLI-based faithfulness and trained coverage metrics ( §5) as rewards.We also examine the performance of a one-shot GPT-4 model (OpenAI, 2023), guided with an example of the task. 10

Models with highlights only.To reveal the importance of the surrounding context, we also train a flan-t5-large model only with a concatenation of the highlights as the input (excluding surrounding context).We denote this variant Flan-T5 only-H .

Models without highlights.Finally, we examine flan-t5-large in a standard summarization setting, where it is finetuned with the input review-set without the highlighted spans, denoting this variant Flan-T5 no-H .It offers insights into the model's ability to pick up on signals that point to highlights.

snippet.text: We distilled document understanding knowledge from ChatGPT 3.5 into FLAN-T5 of three different sizes small, base and large while employing curriculum learning. The results are promising: While FLAN-T5 SMALL struggles with most datasets, its performance on TabFact is surprisingly close to that of the teacher. FLAN-T5 LARGE even managed to surpass the teacher's performance on TabFact. Further, the results suggest that the larger T5 models utilize more pronounced learning curricula better than their smaller counterparts. A starting point for future work is the evaluation of larger student models, such as FLAN-T5 XL and FLAN-T5 XXL and different learning curricula. Another point of interest is investigation into other document representations and their utility for knowledge distillation.

documents.title: Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
documents.snippet: Figure 8 compares the performance of decoder-only and encoder-decoder models. When Flan-UL2 is evaluated on sequences within its 2048-token training-time context window (Figure 8; left subplot), its performance is relatively robust to changes in the position of relevant information within the input context (1.9% absolute difference between best-and worst-case performance). When evaluated on settings with sequences longer than 2048 tokens (Figure 8; center and right), Flan-UL2 performance begins to degrade when relevant information is placed in the middle. Flan-T5-XXL shows a similar trend, where longer input contexts result in a greater performance degradation when placing relevant information in the middle of the input context. We hypothesize that encoder-decoder models may make better use of their context windows because their bidirectional encoder allows processing each document in the context of future documents, potentially improving relative importance estimation between documents.

problem: Summarize approaches to Cost Optimized Workflow Scheduling for AI workloads (inference, training)
final_response:
# Scope and Goals

Cost-optimized workflow scheduling for AI spans both inference and training and typically balances monetary cost (e.g., on-demand vs. spot/preemptible compute), latency/SLOs, throughput, and energy, under heterogeneous accelerators and dynamic resource availability.<cite id="853ed2bf-1">The Cost-aware Dynamic Workflow Scheduling problem aims to minimize VM rental cost and SLA violation penalties while scheduling DAG workflows with diverse structures under dynamic arrivals and resource fluctuations</cite>. <cite id="853ed2bf-4">AI workflows mix heterogeneous tasks—training may span many nodes, while inference often needs fractions of individual GPUs—creating scheduling challenges across diverse compute resources</cite>.

# Inference: Model- and Orchestration-Side Cost Optimization

Model-side techniques reduce per-request compute and memory, enabling use of smaller instances and lowering cost. <cite id="2f93aca9-0">Common model serving optimizations include model compression via quantization, sparsification, and knowledge distillation, as well as architectural streamlining like multi-query or grouped-query attention to reduce key-value heads</cite>. <cite id="2f93aca9-1">Knowledge distillation trains small models to mimic larger ones; pruning removes redundant computation; and quantization approximates arithmetic to cut latency and memory</cite>. <cite id="2f93aca9-2">Empirically, knowledge distillation can improve both inference time and model size across software engineering tasks but may degrade task-dependent effectiveness, with larger losses in code search/summarization</cite>. <cite id="2f93aca9-2">Quantization often reduces model size but can increase inference time on GPUs (up to 2–3× in some code tasks), though CPU settings may see speedups; pruning yields limited overall gains but can deliver notable CPU speed-ups for specific tasks and configurations</cite>. <cite id="2f93aca9-3">For Mixture-of-Experts models, expert pruning, low-rank decomposition, and expert quantization reduce parameters and compute; however, low-bit quantization can cause significant performance degradation in generative tasks unless error is bounded, and error-bounded lossy compression of expert parameters can preserve fidelity while reducing storage/transfer</cite>. <cite id="2f93aca9-4">Case studies (e.g., DistilBERT) show that combining distillation, quantization, and pruning can preserve much of the teacher model’s performance while accelerating CPU inference</cite>.

Beyond model compression, parallelization strategies map inference workloads efficiently onto available accelerators to reduce unit cost per request. <cite id="2f93aca9-0">Data parallelism replicates weights across devices to serve concurrent requests; model parallelism—pipeline, tensor, sequence, and context parallelism—splits layers, tensors, sequences, or context across devices to fit memory and improve utilization</cite>.

Orchestration and placement further reduce inference cost by matching request patterns to appropriate resources and locations. <cite id="414827f3-0">Preemptible and spot-priced cloud instances offer large discounts but no uptime guarantees; schedulers that embrace preemption and auto-scaling can keep utilization high and meet SLAs by rescheduling evicted pods</cite>. <cite id="853ed2bf-4">Dynamic workflows that span multiple compute types enable placing inference tasks on heterogeneous resources to match their GPU/latency needs</cite>. <cite id="414827f3-2">Priority and co-scheduling mechanisms can preempt lower-priority training to accommodate surging inference loads, scaling inference pods to meet SLAs while temporarily reducing training concurrency</cite>.

# Training: Distributed Scheduling, Preemption, and Cluster Integration

Training jobs benefit from cluster-aware schedulers that manage data- and model-parallel replicas, inter-GPU/topo-aware placement, and efficient use of spot/preemptible resources. <cite id="414827f3-3">Kubernetes-based schedulers for distributed deep learning combine autoscaling and gang scheduling to improve training speed, with one system improving training speed by over 26% versus the default Kubernetes scheduler</cite>. <cite id="414827f3-4">A learning-based scheduler (DL2) dynamically resizes resources per job and outperforms fairness and heuristic schedulers on average job completion time in Kubernetes; a container scheduler (SpeCon) for short-lived DL workloads reduces individual job completion times by up to 41.5%, system performance by 14.8%, and makespan by 24.7% via speculative migrations and progress-aware placement</cite>. <cite id="414827f3-1">A Kubernetes edge–cloud framework (KaiS) using graph neural networks and multi-agent RL increased throughput by 14.3% and reduced scheduling cost by 34.7% compared to baselines</cite>. <cite id="414827f3-0">In practice, preemptible pools can deliver hundreds of thousands of GPU hours without impacting other services when paired with priority and transparent failover, and spot instances can run without eviction issues in some GKE deployments</cite>.

Production frameworks provide controllers that mediate between inference demand and ongoing training. <cite id="414827f3-2">An operator for ML platforms can prioritize inference, preempt training workers (e.g., TFJobs) when necessary, and coordinate with Horizontal Pod Autoscalers and the native Kubernetes scheduler to reallocate GPUs, maintaining inference SLAs while allowing training to continue with minimal checkpoints impacted</cite>.

# Learning-Based and Dynamic Scheduling

Reinforcement learning and graph-based methods adapt policies to heterogeneous, dynamic AI workflows. <cite id="853ed2bf-1">A DRL-based workflow scheduler (GATES) learns to minimize cost and SLA penalties under dynamic arrivals and rapidly fluctuating resources, tailored to the graph-structure diversity of real AI pipelines</cite>. <cite id="853ed2bf-2">Online retraining of inference scheduling policies using multi-agent RL improved makespans to meet deadlines across task sizes, outperforming pre-trained policies and highlighting trade-offs between learning frequency and computational overhead</cite>. <cite id="414827f3-1">Learning-based schedulers in Kubernetes environments have shown double-digit gains in throughput and cost reduction versus heuristics, with frameworks that model GNN embeddings and multi-agent control improving system-level decision-making</cite>.

Hybrid offline–online methods combine learned priors with optimization to handle large feasible spaces. <cite id="2f93aca9-0">Hybrid offline–online scheduling for LLM inference integrates with model serving techniques (quantization, distillation, parallelization) and uses scheduling strategies that are orthogonal to model changes, enabling joint optimization of request routing, batching, and resource allocation under latency and cost constraints</cite>.

# Energy-Aware and Multi-Objective Scheduling

Energy-aware schedulers reduce operational costs by optimizing power and utilization, while respecting SLOs. <cite id="853ed2bf-3">Murakkab’s adaptive runtime integrates workflow orchestration and cluster management for resource-aware scheduling and proactive resource management, yielding about 3.4× speedup and 4.5× higher energy efficiency in preliminary evaluations while maintaining end-to-end result quality</cite>. <cite id="853ed2bf-1">Cost-aware policies explicitly penalize SLA violations alongside rental costs, aligning economic and quality objectives</cite>. <cite id="414827f3-4">Systems that adapt resource allocation between best-effort and latency-sensitive workloads can raise average CPU utilization from 15% to 60% without violating SLOs, demonstrating feasible multi-objective improvements</cite>.

# Cross-Cutting Strategies: Placement, Heterogeneity, and Orchestration

Effective cost-optimized scheduling must handle heterogeneous accelerators and non-IID AI tasks, and it often requires integrating workflow orchestration with cluster schedulers. <cite id="853ed2bf-3">Tight coupling of application logic with execution configurations and the disconnect between orchestration and cluster management lead to over- or under-provisioning, degrading resource efficiency and performance</cite>. <cite id="853ed2bf-4">Dynamic, AI-specific workflows with heterogeneous tasks complicate scheduling, but also enable cross-resource placement (edge–cloud, GPU clusters) to balance cost, latency, and throughput</cite>. <cite id="414827f3-3">Gang scheduling, autoscaling, and task migration tailored to ML (e.g., labels for job classes, weights for priorities) improve fairness and efficiency for distributed training</cite>.

# Practical Trade-offs and Open Challenges

- Accuracy–efficiency trade-offs: <cite id="2f93aca9-2">Distillation and pruning can reduce cost and latency but may degrade task-dependent effectiveness, especially for complex code-generation tasks</cite>. <cite id="2f93aca9-3">Low-bit quantization risks performance regressions in MoE generative inference unless compression error is bounded</cite>.
- Stability with preemption: <cite id="414827f3-0">Spot/preemptible resources lower cost but introduce evictions; robust priority classes, failover, and autoscaling are needed to preserve SLAs</cite>.
- Heterogeneity and observability: <cite id="853ed2bf-4">Training and inference have different resource footprints and latencies, requiring fine-grained monitoring and topology-aware placement</cite>.
- Learning complexity: <cite id="853ed2bf-2">Online RL can improve scheduling quality but increases computational cost for learning, and policies must generalize beyond pretraining scenarios</cite>.

# Takeaways

- Combine model-side optimizations (distillation, quantization, pruning, MoE expert reduction) with serving parallelism to reduce unit cost and memory footprint for inference, then match requests to appropriate resources and locations using priority, preemption, and autoscaling for spot instances.<cite id="2f93aca9-0">Model compression and architectural streamlining reduce compute and memory for inference</cite><cite id="2f93aca9-2">Distillation/pruning/quantization trade offs vary by task and environment</cite><cite id="414827f3-0">Preemption and spot instances lower cost with proper failover</cite>.
- For training, use cluster-aware schedulers with gang scheduling and autoscaling, dynamic resource resizing, and migration to improve throughput and utilization on heterogeneous GPU clusters, while protecting SLOs with priorities and reservations.<cite id="414827f3-3">Distributed training schedulers on Kubernetes improve training speed via autoscaling and gang scheduling</cite><cite id="414827f3-4">DL2 and SpeCon reduce completion time and makespan via learning and migration</cite>.
- Employ learning-based schedulers (DRL, GNN/multi-agent) and hybrid offline–online methods to handle dynamic, heterogeneous AI DAGs, balancing cost, latency, and SLA violations.<cite id="853ed2bf-1">DRL policies learn to minimize cost and SLA penalties under dynamic arrivals</cite><cite id="853ed2bf-2">Online RL retraining improves makespan and deadline satisfaction</cite><cite id="414827f3-1">Edge–cloud learning-based schedulers improve throughput and reduce cost</cite>.
- Integrate workflow orchestration with cluster management to achieve energy- and cost-aware operation without sacrificing accuracy, and use multi-objective formulations that jointly optimize cost, utilization, and SLO compliance.<cite id="853ed2bf-3">Integrated runtimes deliver 3.4× speedup and 4.5× energy efficiency</cite><cite id="414827f3-4">Adaptive partitioning raises utilization while preserving SLOs</cite>.

These approaches collectively enable cost-optimized scheduling for AI workflows across inference and training by aligning model and system-level optimizations, embracing heterogeneity and dynamicity, and using learning-based control to navigate complex, multi-objective trade spaces.
