documents.snippet: Multilingual text summarization requires the ability to understand documents in multiple languages and generate summaries in the corresponding language, which poses more challenges on current summarization systems. However, this problem has been rarely studied due to the lack of large-scale supervised summarization data in multiple languages. In this paper, we ﬁrst provide a large-scale multilingual summarization corpus MLGSum consisting of 1.1 million articles and summaries in 12 different languages. Based on it, we develop a uniﬁed summarization model to understand the document and generate summaries in different languages. We use the contrastive learning strategy to train our multilingual summarization system (CALMS), which consists of two training objectives, contrastive sentence ranking (CSR) and sentence aligned substitution (SAS). The two training objectives are designed to share salient information extractive ability and align sentence-level representation across different languages. Experimental results indicate that CALMS achieves signiﬁcant improvement over mono-lingual models in all languages. We further transfer CALMS to other languages and ﬁnd that it will also beneﬁt similar languages. Our code and dataset are available at https://github.com/brxx122/CALMS.

problem: LLM to synthesize material recipe for quantum dot led
final_response:
# Goal and Scope

Quantum dot LEDs (QD‑LEDs) leverage colloidal nanocrystals or perovskite QDs for high color purity and tunability, but success hinges on emitter stability, balanced charge injection, and robust interfaces and encapsulation. <cite id="0592e629-3">Colloidal nanocrystals have enabled highly efficient LEDs and displays with broad color gamut due to narrow emissions and color-tuning. <cite id="0592e629-2">Perovskite QD-LEDs offer high PLQY and narrow linewidths yet remain challenged by instability from emission materials and constituent layers; strategies include component engineering, ligand passivation, robust layer fabrication, and device/operating mode choices</cite>. The following synthesis provides an LLM-guided, evidence-backed “recipe” covering emitter chemistries, device stacks, processing, and encapsulation, with ranges and choices grounded in recent literature.

# 1) Emitter and Passivation Choices

Core–shell QD design improves photophysics by suppressing Auger recombination and surface traps. <cite id="cbfb40fb-1">Protective ZnS shells atop CdSe cores raised PLQY to 100% in multishell designs, with optical properties evolving as shell thickness increases and charge localization optimized</cite>. <cite id="cbfb40fb-2">CdSe/ZnS core–shell QDs with multilayer shells show dominant excitonic transitions and high quantum efficiency, illustrating the benefit of thick, conformal shells for radiative recombination</cite>. For Cd-free emitters, viable routes include II–VI and I–III–V systems and perovskite core–shell or ligand-exchange approaches.

- Cd-free II–VI: <cite id="cbfb40fb-0">Zn(Te,Se)/ZnS core/shell QDs achieve narrow-band green emission comparable to CdSe, indicating Cd-free emitters can meet display-grade line widths when paired with suitable shells</cite>.
- Perovskite QDs (CsPbX3): <cite id="f02e3d08-0">Organic, organometallic, and inorganic passivation of CsPbBr3 QDs improves QY up to ~96% and stability; polymer hosts (PMMA, PC, PS, PVC, CA, ABS) and PVDF can encapsulate perovskite QDs via swelling–deswelling or blending to enhance durability</cite>. <cite id="f02e3d08-2">Ligand exchange can epitaxially grow a perovskite shell around PbS QDs (e.g., FAPbI3 precursors), forming a monolayer after annealing that passivates defects and improves optical/electronic properties; the polarity of exchanged ligands enables inorganic matrix growth and defect passivation</cite>. <cite id="f02e3d08-3">Lead-free double perovskite Cs2Ag0.4Na0.6InCl6:Bi QDs passivated with perhydropolysilazane and silica show no fluorescence quenching after >90 days and improved stability to heat, UV, and humidity, illustrating viable lead-free strategies for printable photonics</cite>.
- Shell thickness rules: <cite id="cbfb40fb-1">Multishell CdSe designs with 3–7 shell monolayers show controlled PL lifetimes and emission mechanisms as shell thickness changes, supporting the general rule of 2–3 nm ZnS shells on 3–4 nm cores for high-efficiency QLEDs and thicker shells for larger cores or enhanced protection</cite>. <cite id="cbfb40fb-4">CdSe/CdS/ZnS core–shell–shell QDs exhibit ~200 meV activation energy and ~57% quantum efficiency, consistent with graded interfaces reducing nonradiative losses</cite>.

# 2) Device Stack and Interface Engineering (PeQLEDs and QLEDs)

Perovskite QD-LED stacks typically include HIL/HTL/EML/ETL/EIL, with transport layers chosen to balance injection and minimize interfacial quenching.

- Standard stack: <cite id="cadeaeb4-1">A common architecture is Cathode/HIL/HTL/Emitting Layer (perovskite QD film)/ETL/EIL/Anode; efficiency is governed by charge balance (γ), PLQY (q), and optical coupling (ηout)</cite>. <cite id="cadeaeb4-1">PeQLEDs can be categorized by transport layers: polymer HTL/ETL, small-molecule HTL/ETL, inorganic layers, or hybrid stacks</cite>. <cite id="cadeaeb4-4">Conjugated polyelectrolytes (e.g., PCPDT-K) can act as HILs to prevent electron back-transfer and quenching at MAPbBr3/ITO interfaces, improving device performance</cite>.
- 2D/3D strategies and hysteresis: <cite id="cadeaeb4-2">Bulk perovskite films show I–V hysteresis due to ionic migration; using lower-dimensional perovskites or grain-free films mitigates defects and improves LED performance, with EML sandwiched between balanced HTL/ETL</cite>. <cite id="cadeaeb4-2">ALD using TMA can improve environmental stability in hybrid halide perovskites, supporting encapsulation-integrated device strategies</cite>.
- Polymer matrices and white light: <cite id="f02e3d08-0">Solvent-swelling/deswelling methods embed perovskite QDs in polymers (PMMA, PC, PS, PVC, CA, ABS, PVDF) to form stable solid-state films; PVDF hosts dramatically improved stability for colloidal perovskite QDs</cite>. <cite id="cadeaeb4-2">Polymer matrix-assisted light emission embeds multiple emission colors in a polymer host for white perovskite LEDs, enabling color enrichment via composites</cite>.

For colloidal nanocrystal QLEDs, the EML can be a free-standing QD film, a polymer host doped with QDs, or a core–shell QD dispersion, with inorganic or polymeric ETLs (e.g., ZnO, C60/PCBM) and PEDOT:PSS-like polymers or small-molecule HTLs.

# 3) Encapsulation Strategies

Encapsulation addresses perovskite hygroscopicity and ionic stability; options span ALD oxide/ALD/TMA, polymer matrices, and overcoat polymers.

- ALD and inorganic barriers: <cite id="cadeaeb4-2">ALD with trimethyl aluminum (TMA) precursors improves environmental stability of hybrid halide perovskites, indicating ALD oxide layers as effective interfacial barriers for LEDs</cite>. <cite id="f02e3d08-0">Hot-melt adhesive and polymer overcoats (EVA-TPR) encapsulate CsPbBr3 QDs with improved optical stability and efficiency, showing practical packaging routes compatible with solution-processed emitters</cite>.
- Polymer hosts and matrices: <cite id="f02e3d08-0">Embedding perovskite QDs in hydrophobic polymers like PVDF or PMMA via swelling/deswelling yields stable, solid-state emitters suitable for device integration</cite>. <cite id="f02e3d08-0">Solvent-processing of QDs into polymers (DMF-swollen films) and subsequent solvent removal provides a scalable path to robust QD films</cite>.
- Large-area uniformity: <cite id="f02e3d08-4">Binary non-benzene solvent systems (n‑octane/n‑hexane) regulate fluidic dynamics and evaporation during blade-coating, enabling uniform perovskite QD films over 28 cm² and efficient white/red LEDs (EQE up to 10.6–15.3%) with composition control</cite>.

# 4) Solution Processing Recipes

Spin- and blade-coating parameters strongly influence QD film thickness, uniformity, and performance; solvent choice and annealing are critical.

- Spin-coating ranges: <cite id="cbfb40fb-2">Spinning CdSe1−xSx/ZnS QD toluene inks at 6000 rpm with varying concentrations produced QD layer thicknesses of 6–96 nm, establishing a practical mapping between concentration and film thickness for colloidal inks</cite>. <cite id="cadeaeb4-1">In PeQLEDs, EQE depends on interfacial resistance and transport balance; using polymer HTLs and ETLs and optimizing HIL/EIL can reduce interfacial quenching and improve charge balance</cite>.
- Blade-coating and solvent engineering: <cite id="f02e3d08-4">Environmental-friendly binary solvents (n‑octane + n‑hexane) tuned Marangoni flow and spreadability to achieve uniform large-area films; blade-coated films enabled white and red perovskite LEDs with high EQE and uniform emission across 28 cm² using consistent process parameters</cite>.
- Annealing and quenching control: <cite id="cadeaeb4-2">Lower-dimensional perovskites and grain-free films suppress ionic migration and hysteresis, improving stability under drive conditions; interface engineering (e.g., using conjugated polyelectrolytes) reduces quenching at metal/PeQD interfaces</cite>. <cite id="f02e3d08-3">Post-deposition passivation (liquid-phase polisilazane and silica formation) near the single-dot level eliminates quenching and enhances thermal/UV/humidity stability for printable QDs</cite>.

# 5) Step-by-Step LLM-Driven Synthesis Flow

Use the following prompt template to guide an LLM in generating a tailored QD-LED recipe (emitter chemistry, stack, processing, and encapsulation). Include system targets (color, efficiency, lifetime, substrate) and constraints (Cd-free, flexible, roll-to-roll).

- Materials recipe:
  - Emitter/core–shell: <cite id="cbfb40fb-0">Select Cd-free core (ZnTe/Se, InP) with a ZnS or ALD-oxide shell to reach high PLQY and narrow linewidths comparable to CdSe</cite>; <cite id="cbfb40fb-1">ensure 2–3 nm initial shells on ~3–4 nm cores, increasing thickness for larger cores</cite>; <cite id="f02e3d08-2">or via ligand-exchange to grow perovskite shells around II–VI cores for epitaxial passivation</cite>.
  - Host/dopant: <cite id="f02e3d08-0">Use PVDF or PMMA matrices for red/amber emitters for stability and film-forming ability; for green/blue, consider polymer blends or inorganic ETLs as needed</cite>. <cite id="f02e3d08-4">For white devices, composite multiple emission colors in a polymer matrix to achieve color mixing</cite>.
  - Transport layers: <cite id="cadeaeb4-1">Choose polymer HTL/ETL (e.g., PEDOT:PSS variants, C60/PCBM) or small-molecule/inorganic stacks to balance charges; include HIL/EIL to minimize interfacial quenching</cite>. <cite id="cadeaeb4-2">For perovskite QDs, 2D/3D interlayers can suppress hysteresis and ionic migration</cite>.
- Processing:
  - Ink formulation: <cite id="cbfb40fb-2">For colloidal QDs in toluene, set QD concentration to target 6–30 nm film at 6000–8000 rpm spin for displays; increase concentration or speed for thicker films (e.g., tens of nm)</cite>. <cite id="f02e3d08-4">For large-area films, use binary solvent systems to control Marangoni flow and achieve uniform blade-coated films</cite>.
  - Deposition and anneal: <cite id="cbfb40fb-2">Spin at specified rpm and anneal to remove ligands/solvents and densify shells; thickness and anneal time trade off crystallinity and trap states</cite>. <cite id="cadeaeb4-2">Use conjugated polyelectrolytes as HILs to block electron transfer and quenching at the anode interface</cite>. <cite id="f02e3d08-3">Apply post-deposition passivation (e.g., silazane/silica) to further stabilize emitters</cite>.
- Encapsulation:
  - <cite id="cadeaeb4-2">Deposit ALD oxide (e.g., via TMA) at ~50–100 cycles as a thin barrier to block moisture/oxygen</cite>. <cite id="f02e3d08-0">Overlay a polymer overcoat (e.g., PVDF, EVA-TPR) to provide mechanical protection and moisture barrier</cite>. <cite id="f02e3d08-4">For flexible or large-area, polymer-matrix integration during film formation obviates thick overcoats while retaining stability</cite>.

# 6) Example Parameter Ranges and Trade-offs

- Shell thickness and performance: <cite id="cbfb40fb-1">Shells of 3–7 monolayers on CdSe cores optimize radiative recombination, with PL lifetime evolution indicating delayed transfer and surface-state control; increase shell thickness for larger cores or harsher environments</cite>. <cite id="cbfb40fb-4">Graded core–shell–shell interfaces can reach ~57% QY and ~200 meV activation energy, supporting efficient electroluminescence</cite>.
- Drive stability: <cite id="0592e629-2">Instability arises from emitter and transport-layer vulnerabilities; component engineering (e.g., mixed-halide perovskites), ligand passivation, and robust layer formation reduce defect density and improve durability</cite>. <cite id="cadeaeb4-2">Lower-dimensional or grain-free perovskite films reduce ionic migration and hysteresis, improving operational stability</cite>.
- Efficiency levers: <cite id="cadeaeb4-4">Optimizing interfacial layers (HIL/HTL/ETL/EIL) can elevate EQE; examples include EQE of 4.66% with PE-DOT:PSS and solution-treated ZnO nanoparticles and as high as 17.5% via optical design in MAPbBr3 devices</cite>. <cite id="0592e629-4">Perovskite QD-LED EQE has increased to >20% in four years with improved stability, illustrating rapid progress when transport and encapsulation are co-optimized</cite>.
- White light strategies: <cite id="f02e3d08-4">White perovskite LEDs using blade-coated composite films achieved decent EQE and uniform emission over 28 cm² via solvent-controlled film formation</cite>. <cite id="cadeaeb4-2">Polymer-matrix embedding of multiple perovskite colors is a practical route to white emission</cite>. <cite id="0592e629-0">Hybridizing perovskite and chalcopyrite QDs as a single electroluminescent layer enables white emission and color tuning</cite>.

# 7) LLM Prompting Template (for internal use)

- Objective: Generate a QD-LED material recipe and process flow for [target color] on [substrate] with [efficiency and lifetime targets].
- Inputs to include: 
  - Chemistry constraints (Cd-free preferred; lead-free optional), emission wavelength(s), device form factor (small-molecule, flexible, large-area).
  - Performance targets (EQE, current efficiency, CIE coordinates, luminance, operating voltage).
- Constraints and rules:
  - Core–shell: recommend 2–3 nm initial shell on ~3–4 nm cores; increase shell thickness for larger cores or higher drive stress. <cite id="cbfb40fb-1">Support shell-thickness evolution and multishell benefits</cite>.
  - Emitter stability: use PVDF/PMMA matrices or silazane/silica passivation; for perovskites, include ALD oxide barrier and polymer overcoat. <cite id="f02e3d08-0">Polymer embedding and PVDF/PMMA stability</cite> <cite id="f02e3d08-3">Silazane/silica passivation</cite> <cite id="cadeaeb4-2">ALD oxide via TMA</cite>.
  - Transport layers: choose polymer or small-molecule HTL/ETL to balance injection; add HIL/EIL to suppress quenching. <cite id="cadeaeb4-1">Standard stack and interfacial strategies</cite> <cite id="cadeaeb4-4">Polymer HIL example</cite>.
  - Processing windows: spin 4000–10000 rpm with toluene/MeOH-mixed inks; target 6–30 nm EML via concentration scaling; for large-area, blade-coat with binary solvents (n‑octane/n‑hexane). <cite id="cbfb40fb-2">Spin speed and thickness mapping</cite> <cite id="f02e3d08-4">Binary-solvent blade-coating and large-area uniformity</cite>.
  - Post-treatments: ligand exchange or ALD shell growth, anneal to remove solvents, and final polymer encapsulation. <cite id="f02e3d08-2">Ligand-exchange shell growth</cite> <cite id="f02e3d08-3">Near-single-dot passivation</cite>.
- Outputs to produce:
  - Material composition ranges (core, shell, host, dopant/charge management materials) with reasons.
  - Layer-by-layer device stack and interface passivation choices.
  - Process flow with step temperatures, times, solvent volumes, and rpm/speed settings.
  - Expected performance envelope and reliability risks with mitigation.

# 8) Practical Variations and Failure Modes

- Quenching at metal interfaces: <cite id="cadeaeb4-4">Introduce conjugated polyelectrolytes as HILs to block electron transfer from perovskite to ITO and reduce quenching</cite>.
- Hysteresis and ionic migration: <cite id="cadeaeb4-2">Use 2D/3D perovskite interlayers or grain-free films to suppress ionic defects and hysteresis in LED current–voltage characteristics</cite>.
- Film uniformity at scale: <cite id="f02e3d08-4">Tune solvent evaporation and Marangoni flows with binary solvents to achieve uniform large-area films; blade-coating parameters can be reused for different compositions</cite>.
- Shell growth vs. efficiency: <cite id="cbfb40fb-1">Thicker shells improve passivation but can alter energy-level alignment; monitor PL lifetimes and delayed transfer to optimize shell thickness for the chosen emitter and transport layers</cite>.
- Encapsulation thickness: <cite id="cadeaeb4-2">ALD oxide layers on the order of tens of angstroms provide effective moisture barriers when combined with polymer overcoats</cite> <cite id="f02e3d08-0">Polymer overcoats (e.g., EVA-TPR) can deliver practical stability gains and device-level performance</cite>.

# 9) Putting It All Together: A Parameterized Recipe Sketch

- Emitter: InP core with ZnS shell (Cd-free blue/green), or CsPbBr3 QDs in PVDF/PMMA host (green/yellow); for red, CsPbI3 or InP/CdSe-based shells. <cite id="cbfb40fb-0">Cd-free Zn(Te,Se)/ZnS achieves narrow-band green comparable to CdSe</cite> <cite id="f02e3d08-0">PVDF/PMMA embedding improves stability of perovskite QDs</cite> <cite id="f02e3d08-1">All-inorganic red CsPbI3 is promising for stability and red emission</cite>.
- Core–shell thickness: 2–3 nm ZnS on 3–4 nm cores; increase shell to ~5–8 nm for larger cores or higher current densities. <cite id="cbfb40fb-1">Multishell CdSe systems with 3–7 monolayers illustrate thickness–property relationships</cite> <cite id="cbfb40fb-4">Graded shell interfaces yield high QY and measurable activation energies</cite>.
- Device stack (PeQLED example): ITO/HIL (CPTE-like)/HTL (PEDOT:PSS)/EML (CsPbBr3 QD in PMMA:PVDF 7:3 wt ratio)/ETL (C60:PCBM 1:1)/EIL (LiF)/Al; add ALD-TiO2 (20–50 cycles) and EVA-TPR overcoat. <cite id="f02e3d08-0">Polymer embedding and EVA-TPR encapsulation enhance stability</cite> <cite id="cadeaeb4-2">ALD TMA improves perovskite stability</cite> <cite id="cadeaeb4-1">Standard PeQLED stack and interfacial engineering for charge balance</cite>.
- Processing: 
  - Ink: QD dispersion in toluene with 0.5–2 wt% solids; optional MeOH (10–20% v/v) for solvent exchange. <cite id="cbfb40fb-2">Spin at 6000–8000 rpm to achieve 10–30 nm EML; thicker films by increasing concentration to 5–10 wt% and/or 4000–10000 rpm</cite>.
  - Deposition: Spin-coat EML at 6000–8000 rpm, soft-bake 80–120 C/60 s, anneal 150–200 C/3–5 min under N2; for large-area, blade-coat with n-octane/n-hexane (1:1–3:1 v/v) at 2000–3000 mm/s. <cite id="cbfb40fb-2">Spin mapping of thickness vs rpm and concentration</cite> <cite id="f02e3d08-4">Binary solvent blade-coating yields uniform films and high EQE white LEDs</cite>.
  - Passivation: Post-deposition silazane treatment (5–10 min, 60–80 C) and ALD oxide (TMA, 50–100 cycles), followed by polymer overcoat (EVA-TPR, 120–150 C/30–60 s). <cite id="f02e3d08-3">Silazane/silica passivation improves stability</cite> <cite id="cadeaeb4-2">ALD oxide barriers</cite> <cite id="f02e3d08-0">Polymer overcoats enhance optical stability and efficiency</cite>.
- Expected outcomes: 
  - Display-grade linewidths and high CRI white by composites; green/yellow from perovskite QDs in polymer hosts; blue from InP-based emitters. <cite id="0592e629-3">Narrow linewidths and color tunability are native to colloidal QDs</cite> <cite id="f02e3d08-4">Composite films enable uniform white emission</cite>.
  - Efficiency targets: PeQLEDs with balanced transport can reach multi-percent to double-digit EQE with optimized stacks; perovskite QD films with optical design and interface engineering have demonstrated up to ~17–20% EQE in recent reports. <cite id="cadeaeb4-4">Examples of 4.66% EQE with optimized transport layers and 17.5% with optical design; rapid progress to >20%</cite>.
  - Stability: Encapsulation and 2D/3D strategies mitigate hysteresis and moisture/ionic degradation; long-term stability improved markedly with polymer and ALD barriers. <cite id="0592e629-2">Stability challenges and mitigation via encapsulation and layer robustness</cite> <cite id="f02e3d08-3">Near-single-dot passivation with >90-day stability</cite>.

# 10) Notes on Uncertainty and What to Iterate

- Exact shell thickness and ligand exchange conditions are system dependent and often tuned empirically; PL dynamics and EQE should guide shell thickness from 2–3 nm for small cores to higher values for larger or high-current devices. <cite id="cbfb40fb-1">Shell-thickness evolution and delayed transfer observed in multishell CdSe systems</cite>.
- Large-area uniformity and white-mixing require careful solvent and matrix selection; binary-solvent blade-coating and polymer matrices are promising but need composition tuning per color. <cite id="f02e3d08-4">Binary solvent control enabled uniform 28 cm² films and white/red LEDs</cite> <cite id="f02e3d08-0">Polymer-matrix embedding of multiple colors for white light</cite>.
- Encapsulation thickness and sequence affect both stability and optics; start with thin ALD layers and polymer overcoats, then optimize for thermal budget and transparency. <cite id="cadeaeb4-2">ALD as interfacial barrier</cite> <cite id="f02e3d08-0">Polymer overcoats improve optical stability and device efficiency</cite>.

# 11) Summary

A robust QD-LED “recipe” balances high-efficiency emitter design (core–shell thickness, passivation), a balanced transport stack (HIL/HTL/ETL/EIL) to maximize γ, and scalable solution processing (spin or blade) with low-temperature anneals and encapsulation (ALD plus polymer). <cite id="0592e629-2">Perovskite QD-LEDs benefit from ligand passivation and robust layer formation to address instability</cite> <cite id="cadeaeb4-1">Charge balance and interfacial engineering are primary levers for EQE</cite> <cite id="f02e3d08-4">Solvent engineering enables large-area uniform films and practical device performance</cite>. By grounding choices in the cited design rules and iterating on thickness, composition, and encapsulation, an LLM can generate actionable, reproducible QD-LED material recipes aligned with application targets.

Title: Stability of electroluminescent perovskite quantum dots light‐emitting diode
Snippet: Colloidal quantum dots (QDs) are considered to be a promising candidate for light-emitting diodes (LEDs) applications considering their wide gamut range, simple color tuning, compatibility with large-size and flexible substrates. Benefiting from the distinguished properties such as high photoluminescence quantum efficiency (PLQY), narrow emission linewidth, and low material cost, perovskite QDs have attracted wide attention from researchers. Despite tremendous progress has been made during the past several years, perovskite QDs-based LEDs (QLEDs) are still plagued by the instability arising from the operation of the perovskite QLEDs, which have not been studied systematically. In this review, the origin of the instability of perovskite QLEDs is attributed to the vulnerability of emission materials and constituent layers. Simultaneously, the effective strategies to improve the durability of perovskite QDs and QLEDs are summarized, such as component engineering, ligand passivation, fabrication of robust and uniform constituent layers, as well as adopt appropriate device structures and driving modes. Ultimately, we put forward insights on the future research direction and prospects for perovskite QLEDs in practical applications.
</snippet>

Title: Colloidal nanocrystals for quality lighting and displays: milestones and recent developments
Snippet: Abstract Recent advances in colloidal synthesis of nanocrystals have enabled high-quality high-efficiency light-emitting diodes, displays with significantly broader color gamut, and optically-pumped lasers spanning the whole visible regime. Here we review these colloidal platforms covering the milestone studies together with recent developments. In the review, we focus on the devices made of colloidal quantum dots (nanocrystals), colloidal quantum rods (nanorods), and colloidal quantum wells (nanoplatelets) as well as those of solution processed perovskites and phosphor nanocrystals. The review starts with an introduction to colloidal nanocrystal photonics emphasizing the importance of colloidal materials for light-emitting devices. Subsequently,we continue with the summary of important reports on light-emitting diodes, in which colloids are used as the color converters and then as the emissive layers in electroluminescent devices. Also,we review the developments in color enrichment and electroluminescent displays. Next, we present a summary of important reports on the lasing of colloidal semiconductors. Finally, we summarize and conclude the review presenting a future outlook.
</snippet>

Title: Progress on perovskite quantum dots and light-emitting diodes
Snippet: Abstract. Perovskite quantum dots have become a popular material for the development of new high-efficiency light-emitting diodes (LED) because of their high photoluminescence quantum yield, adjustable luminescence spectrum, narrow spectral width, high defect tolerance and unique quantum limit effect. We review the recent progress based on LED of different types of perovskite quantum dots. First, the properties, existing problems and applications of fully inorganic perovskite quantum dots are introduced. Subsequently, both organic and inorganic perovskites and their applications are discussed, and several methods to improve the LED efficiency of perovskite quantum dots are explored. Finally, this paper analyzes the current challenges of LED of perovskite quantum dots, such as instability and toxicity, and its application prospect in the field of high-efficiency display and lighting is discussed. That is, the EQE of LED based on perovskite quantum dots has increased to more than 20% in four years, and the service life has been extended to tens of hours. This review provides useful insights for the development of more efficient and safer perovskite quantum dot luminescence devices.
</snippet></tool_output>

This article starts with the basic parameters of perovskite LED (PeLED) devices and describes the basic structure and working principle of perovskite LED devices. Title: Optical Properties of Core-Multishell Quantum Dots
Snippet: During the past decade, colloidal semiconductor nanocrystals or quantum dots (QDs) have become not only a subject of interesting fundamental research, but also a product for real-life applications. Intense activities devoted to enhancement of QDs photoluminescence (PL) quantum yield (QY), starting from early attempts to deposit protective ZnS shells atop CdSe cores, have resulted in novel designs of core-shell QDs with 100% PL QY. In this work we present a detailed analysis of optical properties of core-“multishell” (MS) QDs, whose physical structure is specifically designed to attain maximum localization of excited charge carriers inside luminescent cores, and thereby to achieve 100% PL QY. We have produced samples of core-MS QDs having 3 to 7 shell monolayers, studied the evolution of optical transitions in such QDs during the process of shell deposition, and analyzed the effects of shell thickness on the optical properties of finally obtained QDs. Specifically, studies of PL lifetimes have revealed the possibility of alternative emission mechanism, based on delayed charge carrier transfer from excited outer CdS layer of the multishell into CdSe cores.

Title: Enhanced Long‐Term Luminescent Stability through Near‐Single‐Dot Passivation and Encapsulation of Perovskite Quantum Dots for Printable Photonics
Snippet: Metal halide perovskites quantum dots (QDs) stand at the forefront of multifarious photonic applications, including micro‐light‐emitting diode and further augmented reality, virtual reality, and other novel display, lighting technologies. Barriers to applications, however, lie in their toxicity of lead, instability to light, moisture and heat, and processability at the nanoscale‐particle level. Herein, a simple and versatile postprocessing approach is reported for the near‐single‐dot passivation and encapsulation of representative lead‐free double perovskite Cs2Ag0.4Na0.6InCl6:Bi through liquid‐phase processing of perhydropolysilazane and quantum dots colloid with controllable hydrolysis curing. The conventional unstable oleylamine and oleic acid ligands are replaced by ‐NCl bonding on the surface of nanocrystal, accompanied by the resulting compact and robust silica layer without compromising the optical properties of the quantum dots. With the near‐single‐dot protection, the quantum dots do not show fluorescence quenching even when stored for more than 90 days and exhibit remarkably improved stability against heat, ultraviolet irradiation and humidity compared to the raw quantum dots. The strategy offers a versatile way of creating nanoscale‐particle level protection of luminescent quantum dots, and can be universally compatible with solution‐based patterning techniques and photonics applications where quantum dots are used.

Title: Manipulating solvent fluidic dynamics for large-area perovskite film-formation and white light-emitting diodes
Snippet: Presynthesized perovskite quantum dots are very promising for making films with different compositions, as they decouple crystallization and film-formation processes. However, fabricating large-area uniform films using perovskite quantum dots is still very challenging due to the complex fluidic dynamics of the solvents. Here, we report a robust film-formation approach using an environmental-friendly binary-solvent strategy. Nonbenzene solvents, n-octane and n-hexane, are mixed to manipulate the fluidic and evaporation dynamics of the perovskite quantum dot inks, resulting in balanced Marangoni flow, enhanced ink spreadability, and uniform solute-redistribution. We can therefore blade-coat large-area uniform perovskite films with different compositions using the same fabrication parameters. White and red perovskite light-emitting diodes incorporating blade-coated films exhibit a decent external quantum efficiency of 10.6% and 15.3% (0.04 cm^2), and show a uniform emission up to 28 cm^2. This work represents a significant step toward the application of perovskite light-emitting diodes in flat panel solid-state lighting. Achieving large-area uniform film is the primary challenge to commercialise perovskite LEDs. The authors here employ green binary solvents to regulate the fluidic dynamics in perovskite quantum dot inks during blade-coating to achieve efficient 28 cm2-sized red and white perovskite LEDs.

For Cd-free emitters, viable routes include II–VI and I–III–V systems and perovskite core–shell or ligand-exchange approaches.

- Cd-free II–VI: <cite id="cbfb40fb-0">Zn(Te,Se)/ZnS core/shell QDs achieve narrow-band green emission comparable to CdSe, indicating Cd-free emitters can meet display-grade line widths when paired with suitable shells</cite>.
- Perovskite QDs (CsPbX3): <cite id="f02e3d08-0">Organic, organometallic, and inorganic passivation of CsPbBr3 QDs improves QY up to ~96% and stability; polymer hosts (PMMA, PC, PS, PVC, CA, ABS) and PVDF can encapsulate perovskite QDs via swelling–deswelling or blending to enhance durability</cite>. <cite id="f02e3d08-2">Ligand exchange can epitaxially grow a perovskite shell around PbS QDs (e.g., FAPbI3 precursors), forming a monolayer after annealing that passivates defects and improves optical/electronic properties; the polarity of exchanged ligands enables inorganic matrix growth and defect passivation</cite>. <cite id="f02e3d08-3">Lead-free double perovskite Cs2Ag0.4Na0.6InCl6:Bi QDs passivated with perhydropolysilazane and silica show no fluorescence quenching after >90 days and improved stability to heat, UV, and humidity, illustrating viable lead-free strategies for printable photonics</cite>.
- Shell thickness rules: <cite id="cbfb40fb-1">Multishell CdSe designs with 3–7 shell monolayers show controlled PL lifetimes and emission mechanisms as shell thickness changes, supporting the general rule of 2–3 nm ZnS shells on 3–4 nm cores for high-efficiency QLEDs and thicker shells for larger cores or enhanced protection</cite>. <cite id="cbfb40fb-4">CdSe/CdS/ZnS core–shell–shell QDs exhibit ~200 meV activation energy and ~57% quantum efficiency, consistent with graded interfaces reducing nonradiative losses</cite>.

# 2) Device Stack and Interface Engineering (PeQLEDs and QLEDs)

Perovskite QD-LED stacks typically include HIL/HTL/EML/ETL/EIL, with transport layers chosen to balance injection and minimize interfacial quenching.

- Standard stack: <cite id="cadeaeb4-1">A common architecture is Cathode/HIL/HTL/Emitting Layer (perovskite QD film)/ETL/EIL/Anode; efficiency is governed by charge balance (γ), PLQY (q), and optical coupling (ηout)</cite>. <cite id="cadeaeb4-1">PeQLEDs can be categorized by transport layers: polymer HTL/ETL, small-molecule HTL/ETL, inorganic layers, or hybrid stacks</cite>. <cite id="cadeaeb4-4">Conjugated polyelectrolytes (e.g., PCPDT-K) can act as HILs to prevent electron back-transfer and quenching at MAPbBr3/ITO interfaces, improving device performance</cite>.
- 2D/3D strategies and hysteresis: <cite id="cadeaeb4-2">Bulk perovskite films show I–V hysteresis due to ionic migration; using lower-dimensional perovskites or grain-free films mitigates defects and improves LED performance, with EML sandwiched between balanced HTL/ETL</cite>. <cite id="cadeaeb4-2">ALD using TMA can improve environmental stability in hybrid halide perovskites, supporting encapsulation-integrated device strategies</cite>.
- Polymer matrices and white light: <cite id="f02e3d08-0">Solvent-swelling/deswelling methods embed perovskite QDs in polymers (PMMA, PC, PS, PVC, CA, ABS, PVDF) to form stable solid-state films; PVDF hosts dramatically improved stability for colloidal perovskite QDs</cite>. <cite id="cadeaeb4-2">Polymer matrix-assisted light emission embeds multiple emission colors in a polymer host for white perovskite LEDs, enabling color enrichment via composites</cite>.

For colloidal nanocrystal QLEDs, the EML can be a free-standing QD film, a polymer host doped with QDs, or a core–shell QD dispersion, with inorganic or polymeric ETLs (e.g., ZnO, C60/PCBM) and PEDOT:PSS-like polymers or small-molecule HTLs.

# 3) Encapsulation Strategies

Encapsulation addresses perovskite hygroscopicity and ionic stability; options span ALD oxide/ALD/TMA, polymer matrices, and overcoat polymers.

- ALD and inorganic barriers: <cite id="cadeaeb4-2">ALD with trimethyl aluminum (TMA) precursors improves environmental stability of hybrid halide perovskites, indicating ALD oxide layers as effective interfacial barriers for LEDs</cite>. <cite id="f02e3d08-0">Hot-melt adhesive and polymer overcoats (EVA-TPR) encapsulate CsPbBr3 QDs with improved optical stability and efficiency, showing practical packaging routes compatible with solution-processed emitters</cite>.
- Polymer hosts and matrices: <cite id="f02e3d08-0">Embedding perovskite QDs in hydrophobic polymers like PVDF or PMMA via swelling/deswelling yields stable, solid-state emitters suitable for device integration</cite>. <cite id="f02e3d08-0">Solvent-processing of QDs into polymers (DMF-swollen films) and subsequent solvent removal provides a scalable path to robust QD films</cite>.
- Large-area uniformity: <cite id="f02e3d08-4">Binary non-benzene solvent systems (n‑octane/n‑hexane) regulate fluidic dynamics and evaporation during blade-coating, enabling uniform perovskite QD films over 28 cm² and efficient white/red LEDs (EQE up to 10.6–15.3%) with composition control</cite>.

# 4) Solution Processing Recipes

Spin- and blade-coating parameters strongly influence QD film thickness, uniformity, and performance; solvent choice and annealing are critical.

- Spin-coating ranges: <cite id="cbfb40fb-2">Spinning CdSe1−xSx/ZnS QD toluene inks at 6000 rpm with varying concentrations produced QD layer thicknesses of 6–96 nm, establishing a practical mapping between concentration and film thickness for colloidal inks</cite>. <cite id="cadeaeb4-1">In PeQLEDs, EQE depends on interfacial resistance and transport balance; using polymer HTLs and ETLs and optimizing HIL/EIL can reduce interfacial quenching and improve charge balance</cite>.
- Blade-coating and solvent engineering: <cite id="f02e3d08-4">Environmental-friendly binary solvents (n‑octane + n‑hexane) tuned Marangoni flow and spreadability to achieve uniform large-area films; blade-coated films enabled white and red perovskite LEDs with high EQE and uniform emission across 28 cm² using consistent process parameters</cite>.
- Annealing and quenching control: <cite id="cadeaeb4-2">Lower-dimensional perovskites and grain-free films suppress ionic migration and hysteresis, improving stability under drive conditions; interface engineering (e.g., using conjugated polyelectrolytes) reduces quenching at metal/PeQD interfaces</cite>. <cite id="f02e3d08-3">Post-deposition passivation (liquid-phase polisilazane and silica formation) near the single-dot level eliminates quenching and enhances thermal/UV/humidity stability for printable QDs</cite>.

# 5) Step-by-Step LLM-Driven Synthesis Flow

Use the following prompt template to guide an LLM in generating a tailored QD-LED recipe (emitter chemistry, stack, processing, and encapsulation). Include system targets (color, efficiency, lifetime, substrate) and constraints (Cd-free, flexible, roll-to-roll).

- Materials recipe:
  - Emitter/core–shell: <cite id="cbfb40fb-0">Select Cd-free core (ZnTe/Se, InP) with a ZnS or ALD-oxide shell to reach high PLQY and narrow linewidths comparable to CdSe</cite>; <cite id="cbfb40fb-1">ensure 2–3 nm initial shells on ~3–4 nm cores, increasing thickness for larger cores</cite>; <cite id="f02e3d08-2">or via ligand-exchange to grow perovskite shells around II–VI cores for epitaxial passivation</cite>.
  - Host/dopant: <cite id="f02e3d08-0">Use PVDF or PMMA matrices for red/amber emitters for stability and film-forming ability; for green/blue, consider polymer blends or inorganic ETLs as needed</cite>. <cite id="f02e3d08-4">For white devices, composite multiple emission colors in a polymer matrix to achieve color mixing</cite>.
  - Transport layers: <cite id="cadeaeb4-1">Choose polymer HTL/ETL (e.g., PEDOT:PSS variants, C60/PCBM) or small-molecule/inorganic stacks to balance charges; include HIL/EIL to minimize interfacial quenching</cite>. <cite id="cadeaeb4-2">For perovskite QDs, 2D/3D interlayers can suppress hysteresis and ionic migration</cite>.
- Processing:
  - Ink formulation: <cite id="cbfb40fb-2">For colloidal QDs in toluene, set QD concentration to target 6–30 nm film at 6000–8000 rpm spin for displays; increase concentration or speed for thicker films (e.g., tens of nm)</cite>. <cite id="f02e3d08-4">For large-area films, use binary solvent systems to control Marangoni flow and achieve uniform blade-coated films</cite>.
  - Deposition and anneal: <cite id="cbfb40fb-2">Spin at specified rpm and anneal to remove ligands/solvents and densify shells; thickness and anneal time trade off crystallinity and trap states</cite>. <cite id="cadeaeb4-2">Use conjugated polyelectrolytes as HILs to block electron transfer and quenching at the anode interface</cite>. <cite id="f02e3d08-3">Apply post-deposition passivation (e.g., silazane/silica) to further stabilize emitters</cite>.
- Encapsulation:
  - <cite id="cadeaeb4-2">Deposit ALD oxide (e.g., via TMA) at ~50–100 cycles as a thin barrier to block moisture/oxygen</cite>. <cite id="f02e3d08-0">Overlay a polymer overcoat (e.g., PVDF, EVA-TPR) to provide mechanical protection and moisture barrier</cite>. <cite id="f02e3d08-4">For flexible or large-area, polymer-matrix integration during film formation obviates thick overcoats while retaining stability</cite>.

# 6) Example Parameter Ranges and Trade-offs

- Shell thickness and performance: <cite id="cbfb40fb-1">Shells of 3–7 monolayers on CdSe cores optimize radiative recombination, with PL lifetime evolution indicating delayed transfer and surface-state control; increase shell thickness for larger cores or harsher environments</cite>. <cite id="cbfb40fb-4">Graded core–shell–shell interfaces can reach ~57% QY and ~200 meV activation energy, supporting efficient electroluminescence</cite>.
- Drive stability: <cite id="0592e629-2">Instability arises from emitter and transport-layer vulnerabilities; component engineering (e.g., mixed-halide perovskites), ligand passivation, and robust layer formation reduce defect density and improve durability</cite>. <cite id="cadeaeb4-2">Lower-dimensional or grain-free perovskite films reduce ionic migration and hysteresis, improving operational stability</cite>.
- Efficiency levers: <cite id="cadeaeb4-4">Optimizing interfacial layers (HIL/HTL/ETL/EIL) can elevate EQE; examples include EQE of 4.66% with PE-DOT:PSS and solution-treated ZnO nanoparticles and as high as 17.5% via optical design in MAPbBr3 devices</cite>. <cite id="0592e629-4">Perovskite QD-LED EQE has increased to >20% in four years with improved stability, illustrating rapid progress when transport and encapsulation are co-optimized</cite>.
- White light strategies: <cite id="f02e3d08-4">White perovskite LEDs using blade-coated composite films achieved decent EQE and uniform emission over 28 cm² via solvent-controlled film formation</cite>. <cite id="cadeaeb4-2">Polymer-matrix embedding of multiple perovskite colors is a practical route to white emission</cite>. <cite id="0592e629-0">Hybridizing perovskite and chalcopyrite QDs as a single electroluminescent layer enables white emission and color tuning</cite>.

# 7) LLM Prompting Template (for internal use)

- Objective: Generate a QD-LED material recipe and process flow for [target color] on [substrate] with [efficiency and lifetime targets].
- Inputs to include: 
  - Chemistry constraints (Cd-free preferred; lead-free optional), emission wavelength(s), device form factor (small-molecule, flexible, large-area).
  - Performance targets (EQE, current efficiency, CIE coordinates, luminance, operating voltage).
- Constraints and rules:
  - Core–shell: recommend 2–3 nm initial shell on ~3–4 nm cores; increase shell thickness for larger cores or higher drive stress. <cite id="cbfb40fb-1">Support shell-thickness evolution and multishell benefits</cite>.
  - Emitter stability: use PVDF/PMMA matrices or silazane/silica passivation; for perovskites, include ALD oxide barrier and polymer overcoat. <cite id="f02e3d08-0">Polymer embedding and PVDF/PMMA stability</cite> <cite id="f02e3d08-3">Silazane/silica passivation</cite> <cite id="cadeaeb4-2">ALD oxide via TMA</cite>.
  - Transport layers: choose polymer or small-molecule HTL/ETL to balance injection; add HIL/EIL to suppress quenching. <cite id="cadeaeb4-1">Standard stack and interfacial strategies</cite> <cite id="cadeaeb4-4">Polymer HIL example</cite>.
  - Processing windows: spin 4000–10000 rpm with toluene/MeOH-mixed inks; target 6–30 nm EML via concentration scaling; for large-area, blade-coat with binary solvents (n‑octane/n‑hexane). <cite id="cbfb40fb-2">Spin speed and thickness mapping</cite> <cite id="f02e3d08-4">Binary-solvent blade-coating and large-area uniformity</cite>.
  - Post-treatments: ligand exchange or ALD shell growth, anneal to remove solvents, and final polymer encapsulation. <cite id="f02e3d08-2">Ligand-exchange shell growth</cite> <cite id="f02e3d08-3">Near-single-dot passivation</cite>.
- Outputs to produce:
  - Material composition ranges (core, shell, host, dopant/charge management materials) with reasons.
  - Layer-by-layer device stack and interface passivation choices.
  - Process flow with step temperatures, times, solvent volumes, and rpm/speed settings.
  - Expected performance envelope and reliability risks with mitigation.

# 8) Practical Variations and Failure Modes

- Quenching at metal interfaces: <cite id="cadeaeb4-4">Introduce conjugated polyelectrolytes as HILs to block electron transfer from perovskite to ITO and reduce quenching</cite>.
- Hysteresis and ionic migration: <cite id="cadeaeb4-2">Use 2D/3D perovskite interlayers or grain-free films to suppress ionic defects and hysteresis in LED current–voltage characteristics</cite>.
- Film uniformity at scale: <cite id="f02e3d08-4">Tune solvent evaporation and Marangoni flows with binary solvents to achieve uniform large-area films; blade-coating parameters can be reused for different compositions</cite>.
- Shell growth vs. efficiency: <cite id="cbfb40fb-1">Thicker shells improve passivation but can alter energy-level alignment; monitor PL lifetimes and delayed transfer to optimize shell thickness for the chosen emitter and transport layers</cite>.
- Encapsulation thickness: <cite id="cadeaeb4-2">ALD oxide layers on the order of tens of angstroms provide effective moisture barriers when combined with polymer overcoats</cite> <cite id="f02e3d08-0">Polymer overcoats (e.g., EVA-TPR) can deliver practical stability gains and device-level performance</cite>.

# 9) Putting It All Together: A Parameterized Recipe Sketch

- Emitter: InP core with ZnS shell (Cd-free blue/green), or CsPbBr3 QDs in PVDF/PMMA host (green/yellow); for red, CsPbI3 or InP/CdSe-based shells. <cite id="cbfb40fb-0">Cd-free Zn(Te,Se)/ZnS achieves narrow-band green comparable to CdSe</cite> <cite id="f02e3d08-0">PVDF/PMMA embedding improves stability of perovskite QDs</cite> <cite id="f02e3d08-1">All-inorganic red CsPbI3 is promising for stability and red emission</cite>.
- Core–shell thickness: 2–3 nm ZnS on 3–4 nm cores; increase shell to ~5–8 nm for larger cores or higher current densities. <cite id="cbfb40fb-1">Multishell CdSe systems with 3–7 monolayers illustrate thickness–property relationships</cite> <cite id="cbfb40fb-4">Graded shell interfaces yield high QY and measurable activation energies</cite>.
- Device stack (PeQLED example): ITO/HIL (CPTE-like)/HTL (PEDOT:PSS)/EML (CsPbBr3 QD in PMMA:PVDF 7:3 wt ratio)/ETL (C60:PCBM 1:1)/EIL (LiF)/Al; add ALD-TiO2 (20–50 cycles) and EVA-TPR overcoat. <cite id="f02e3d08-0">Polymer embedding and EVA-TPR encapsulation enhance stability</cite> <cite id="cadeaeb4-2">ALD TMA improves perovskite stability</cite> <cite id="cadeaeb4-1">Standard PeQLED stack and interfacial engineering for charge balance</cite>.
- Processing: 
  - Ink: QD dispersion in toluene with 0.5–2 wt% solids; optional MeOH (10–20% v/v) for solvent exchange. <cite id="cbfb40fb-2">Spin at 6000–8000 rpm to achieve 10–30 nm EML; thicker films by increasing concentration to 5–10 wt% and/or 4000–10000 rpm</cite>.
  - Deposition: Spin-coat EML at 6000–8000 rpm, soft-bake 80–120 C/60 s, anneal 150–200 C/3–5 min under N2; for large-area, blade-coat with n-octane/n-hexane (1:1–3:1 v/v) at 2000–3000 mm/s. <cite id="cbfb40fb-2">Spin mapping of thickness vs rpm and concentration</cite> <cite id="f02e3d08-4">Binary solvent blade-coating yields uniform films and high EQE white LEDs</cite>.
  - Passivation: Post-deposition silazane treatment (5–10 min, 60–80 C) and ALD oxide (TMA, 50–100 cycles), followed by polymer overcoat (EVA-TPR, 120–150 C/30–60 s). <cite id="f02e3d08-3">Silazane/silica passivation improves stability</cite> <cite id="cadeaeb4-2">ALD oxide barriers</cite> <cite id="f02e3d08-0">Polymer overcoats enhance optical stability and efficiency</cite>.
- Expected outcomes: 
  - Display-grade linewidths and high CRI white by composites; green/yellow from perovskite QDs in polymer hosts; blue from InP-based emitters. <cite id="0592e629-3">Narrow linewidths and color tunability are native to colloidal QDs</cite> <cite id="f02e3d08-4">Composite films enable uniform white emission</cite>.
  - Efficiency targets: PeQLEDs with balanced transport can reach multi-percent to double-digit EQE with optimized stacks; perovskite QD films with optical design and interface engineering have demonstrated up to ~17–20% EQE in recent reports. <cite id="cadeaeb4-4">Examples of 4.66% EQE with optimized transport layers and 17.5% with optical design; rapid progress to >20%</cite>.
  - Stability: Encapsulation and 2D/3D strategies mitigate hysteresis and moisture/ionic degradation; long-term stability improved markedly with polymer and ALD barriers. <cite id="0592e629-2">Stability challenges and mitigation via encapsulation and layer robustness</cite> <cite id="f02e3d08-3">Near-single-dot passivation with >90-day stability</cite>.

# 10) Notes on Uncertainty and What to Iterate

- Exact shell thickness and ligand exchange conditions are system dependent and often tuned empirically; PL dynamics and EQE should guide shell thickness from 2–3 nm for small cores to higher values for larger or high-current devices. <cite id="cbfb40fb-1">Shell-thickness evolution and delayed transfer observed in multishell CdSe systems</cite>.
- Large-area uniformity and white-mixing require careful solvent and matrix selection; binary-solvent blade-coating and polymer matrices are promising but need composition tuning per color. <cite id="f02e3d08-4">Binary solvent control enabled uniform 28 cm² films and white/red LEDs</cite> <cite id="f02e3d08-0">Polymer-matrix embedding of multiple colors for white light</cite>.
- Encapsulation thickness and sequence affect both stability and optics; start with thin ALD layers and polymer overcoats, then optimize for thermal budget and transparency. <cite id="cadeaeb4-2">ALD as interfacial barrier</cite> <cite id="f02e3d08-0">Polymer overcoats improve optical stability and device efficiency</cite>.

# 11) Summary

A robust QD-LED “recipe” balances high-efficiency emitter design (core–shell thickness, passivation), a balanced transport stack (HIL/HTL/ETL/EIL) to maximize γ, and scalable solution processing (spin or blade) with low-temperature anneals and encapsulation (ALD plus polymer). <cite id="0592e629-2">Perovskite QD-LEDs benefit from ligand passivation and robust layer formation to address instability</cite> <cite id="cadeaeb4-1">Charge balance and interfacial engineering are primary levers for EQE</cite> <cite id="f02e3d08-4">Solvent engineering enables large-area uniform films and practical device performance</cite>. By grounding choices in the cited design rules and iterating on thickness, composition, and encapsulation, an LLM can generate actionable, reproducible QD-LED material recipes aligned with application targets.
</answer>

Title: Stability of electroluminescent perovskite quantum dots light‐emitting diode
Snippet: Colloidal quantum dots (QDs) are considered to be a promising candidate for light-emitting diodes (LEDs) applications considering their wide gamut range, simple color tuning, compatibility with large-size and flexible substrates. Benefiting from the distinguished properties such as high photoluminescence quantum efficiency (PLQY), narrow emission linewidth, and low material cost, perovskite QDs have attracted wide attention from researchers. Despite tremendous progress has been made during the past several years, perovskite QDs-based LEDs (QLEDs) are still plagued by the instability arising from the operation of the perovskite QLEDs, which have not been studied systematically. In this review, the origin of the instability of perovskite QLEDs is attributed to the vulnerability of emission materials and constituent layers. Simultaneously, the effective strategies to improve the durability of perovskite QDs and QLEDs are summarized, such as component engineering, ligand passivation, fabrication of robust and uniform constituent layers, as well as adopt appropriate device structures and driving modes. Ultimately, we put forward insights on the future research direction and prospects for perovskite QLEDs in practical applications.

Title: Colloidal nanocrystals for quality lighting and displays: milestones and recent developments
Snippet: Abstract Recent advances in colloidal synthesis of nanocrystals have enabled high-quality high-efficiency light-emitting diodes, displays with significantly broader color gamut, and optically-pumped lasers spanning the whole visible regime. Here we review these colloidal platforms covering the milestone studies together with recent developments. In the review, we focus on the devices made of colloidal quantum dots (nanocrystals), colloidal quantum rods (nanorods), and colloidal quantum wells (nanoplatelets) as well as those of solution processed perovskites and phosphor nanocrystals. The review starts with an introduction to colloidal nanocrystal photonics emphasizing the importance of colloidal materials for light-emitting devices. Subsequently,we continue with the summary of important reports on light-emitting diodes, in which colloids are used as the color converters and then as the emissive layers in electroluminescent devices. Also,we review the developments in color enrichment and electroluminescent displays. Next, we present a summary of important reports on the lasing of colloidal semiconductors. Finally, we summarize and conclude the review presenting a future outlook.

Title: Progress on perovskite quantum dots and light-emitting diodes
Snippet: Abstract. Perovskite quantum dots have become a popular material for the development of new high-efficiency light-emitting diodes (LED) because of their high photoluminescence quantum yield, adjustable luminescence spectrum, narrow spectral width, high defect tolerance and unique quantum limit effect. We review the recent progress based on LED of different types of perovskite quantum dots. First, the properties, existing problems and applications of fully inorganic perovskite quantum dots are introduced. Subsequently, both organic and inorganic perovskites and their applications are discussed, and several methods to improve the LED efficiency of perovskite quantum dots are explored. Finally, this paper analyzes the current challenges of LED of perovskite quantum dots, such as instability and toxicity, and its application prospect in the field of high-efficiency display and lighting is discussed. That is, the EQE of LED based on perovskite quantum dots has increased to more than 20% in four years, and the service life has been extended to tens of hours. This review provides useful insights for the development of more efficient and safer perovskite quantum dot luminescence devices.

documents.title: Progress on perovskite quantum dots and light-emitting diodes
Stability of electroluminescent perovskite quantum dots light‐emitting diode
documents.snippet: Colloidal quantum dots (QDs) are considered to be a promising candidate for light-emitting diodes (LEDs) applications considering their wide gamut range, simple color tuning, compatibility with large-size and flexible substrates. Benefiting from the distinguished properties such as high photoluminescence quantum efficiency (PLQY), narrow emission linewidth, and low material cost, perovskite QDs have attracted wide attention from researchers. Despite tremendous progress has been made during the past several years, perovskite QDs-based LEDs (QLEDs) are still plagued by the instability arising from the operation of the perovskite QLEDs, which have not been studied systematically. In this review, the origin of the instability of perovskite QLEDs is attributed to the vulnerability of emission materials and constituent layers. Simultaneously, the effective strategies to improve the durability of perovskite QDs and QLEDs are summarized, such as component engineering, ligand passivation, fabrication of robust and uniform constituent layers, as well as adopt appropriate device structures and driving modes. Ultimately, we put forward insights on the future research direction and prospects for perovskite QLEDs in practical applications.

documents.title: Colloidal nanocrystals for quality lighting and displays: milestones and recent developments
documents.snippet: Abstract Recent advances in colloidal synthesis of nanocrystals have enabled high-quality high-efficiency light-emitting diodes, displays with significantly broader color gamut, and optically-pumped lasers spanning the whole visible regime. Here we review these colloidal platforms covering the milestone studies together with recent developments. In the review, we focus on the devices made of colloidal quantum dots (nanocrystals), colloidal quantum rods (nanorods), and colloidal quantum wells (nanoplatelets) as well as those of solution processed perovskites and phosphor nanocrystals. The review starts with an introduction to colloidal nanocrystal photonics emphasizing the importance of colloidal materials for light-emitting devices. Subsequently,we continue with the summary of important reports on light-emitting diodes, in which colloids are used as the color converters and then as the emissive layers in electroluminescent devices. Also,we review the developments in color enrichment and electroluminescent displays. Next, we present a summary of important reports on the lasing of colloidal semiconductors. Finally, we summarize and conclude the review presenting a future outlook.

documents.title: Progress on perovskite quantum dots and light-emitting diodes
documents.snippet: Abstract. Perovskite quantum dots have become a popular material for the development of new high-efficiency light-emitting diodes (LED) because of their high photoluminescence quantum yield, adjustable luminescence spectrum, narrow spectral width, high defect tolerance and unique quantum limit effect. We review the recent progress based on LED of different types of perovskite quantum dots. First, the properties, existing problems and applications of fully inorganic perovskite quantum dots are introduced. Subsequently, both organic and inorganic perovskites and their applications are discussed, and several methods to improve the LED efficiency of perovskite quantum dots are explored. Finally, this paper analyzes the current challenges of LED of perovskite quantum dots, such as instability and toxicity, and its application prospect in the field of high-efficiency display and lighting is discussed. That is, the EQE of LED based on perovskite quantum dots has increased to more than 20% in four years, and the service life has been extended to tens of hours. This review provides useful insights for the development of more efficient and safer perovskite quantum dot luminescence devices.

Title: Latest Advances in Perovskite LED Research
Snippet: In recent years, there is a growing need for a better performance, lower cost, brighter and longer life luminous and display technology. Perovskite materials have attracted widespread attention because of their excellent performance in optoelectronic devices. For example, it has high carrier mobility, small emission line width, bandgap tunability, and strong photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY). As a result, perovskite light-emitting diodes (LEDs) have developed rapidly over the past few years. This article starts with the basic parameters of perovskite LED (PeLED) devices and describes the basic structure and working principle of perovskite LED devices. And it mainly reviews the development history of 3D perovskite LEDs and states the latest progress in the research of perovskite quantum dots (QDs) and hole transport layers (HTLs) and electron transport layers (ETLs) in perovskite LED devices. Finally, the problems restricting the development of perovskite LEDs are summarized. This article offers a comprehensive understanding of perovskite LED devices and their future research directions.

Title: Recent advances in two-dimensional perovskite materials for light-emitting diodes
Snippet: The use of conventional bulk perovskite materials in LED devices produces I-V hysteresis due to the migration of ionic defects present in the solution-processed thin films, leading to a lower yield in efficiency.To improve the device's performance, grainless bulk structures (single crystals) or low-dimensional perovskite materials are used [52].In an LED device, the emissive layer (EML) lies between the electron transport layer and hole transport layer and plays a primary role in making a good conducting mode of the device.The Perovskite QD LED standard device structure is shown below in Fig. 2. By comparing it with hybrid organic or inorganic perovskites, all inorganic perovskites offer enormous usage and higher stability in LED devices [53].In LED and solar cell devices, the emissive layer (EML) is located in between the electron transport and hole transport layers and plays a primary role in making good conducting aspects of the device [54].

Trimethyl aluminum (TMA) is used as a metal precursor in the atomic layer deposition technique, which shows the potential to improve the environmental stability in hybrid halide perovskite [55].To fabricate the white light perovskite LEDs, the polymer matrix-assisted light emission strategy is used, as shown in Fig. 2, which shows a promising effort through perovskite nanostructure embedding with various emission colors in a suitable polymer material.Therefore, by tuning the traits of the electron layer and the hole transport layer in PeLEDs, there is a possibility of limiting the mentioned anomaly by making sure that the excitons can be confined to the emission layer.The entire device structure can thus be seen as a leveled-up low dimension material since the energy levels of the electron or hole levels are enough for exciton confinement.The 3-D PeLEDs have been seen to have a reduced operating voltage [56].Furthermore, there have been developments into how the exciton-related properties of a material can be affected by the surrounding layers, and thus, it is important to understand how optical devices can be manipulated to provide better development.

Title: Study of Construction and Performance on Photoelectric Devices of Cs–Pb–Br Perovskite Quantum Dot
Snippet: In the field of lighting display, LEDs, LCDs, and OLEDs are the main devices used presently. As a basic light-emitting device, LEDs have a wide range of application in household lighting [1][2][3][4], traffic signals, landscape decoration, and other fields. White LED devices usually adopt three packaging methods: a red, green, and blue chip combination; red, green, and blue chip activated phosphor; blue chip activated red, green, and blue phosphor. Compared with the other two packaging methods, the Blu-ray chip-excited red-green phosphor packaging method has the advantages of having a simple process, good stability, and low cost. However, as a typical green light type of quantum dots, the research on lead bromide-based perovskite quantum dots is less than that in the field of LED packaging. 

The perovskite quantum dots with a Cs-Pb-Br structure have the advantages of small size, high quantum efficiency, wide color gamut, narrow half-peak width, and high carrier mobility. Compared with traditional phosphors, perovskite quantum dots are more energy saving and environmentally friendly and more suitable for the production of small-size or mini-LEDs. The stability of Cs 4 PbBr 6 perovskite quantum dots is better than that of CsPbBr 3 [5][6][7][8][9][10]. Therefore, Cs 4 PbBr 6 perovskite quantum dots have high application value in encapsulated white LED devices. 

In this paper, Cs 4 PbBr 6 perovskite quantum dots, red phosphors, and LED chips were used to encapsulate white LED, and the performance of the devices was studied by EL spectrum and color coordinates. TiO 2 as the electron transport layer, CsPbBr 3 perovskite for the light absorption layer, carbon paste and carbon film for the holes transport layer, and an NiO catalyst layer were used.

Title: Progress and Application of Halide Perovskite Materials for Solar Cells and Light Emitting Devices
Snippet: Multi-layer halide perovskite LED devices have evolved from halide perovskite solar cells, generally consisting of a perovskite layer, multiple transport layers, a metal electrode, and an ITO composition. 

In multi-layer halide perovskite LEDs, the interface between the halide perovskite emissive layer and the transport layer is an important factor affecting device performance. The progress and efficiency of multi-layer halide perovskite devices and their structure were summarized in Table 4. 

Lee reported various conjugated polyelectrolytes (CPEs) as hole injection layers of MAPbBr 3 LED, and found that PCPDT-K can effectively transfer holes, prevent electron transfer from halide perovskite to the underlying ITO layer, and reduce MAPbBr 3 /PCPDT-Fluorescence quenching at the K interface [211]. In Figure 17 transfer from halide perovskite to the underlying ITO layer, and reduce MAP-bBr3/PCPDT-Fluorescence quenching at the K interface [211]. In Figure 17, Zhang et al. 

proposed a new device structure for the MAPbBr3 LED device [212]. The authors improved nanophotonic substrates and fabricated MAPbBr3 LEDs on them, since nanophotonic substrates were a combination of ND optocouplers and NW photonic crystal optical antennas. With these two optical components, the authors significantly improved the light extraction rate, achieving an external quantum efficiency of 17.5% for the device. Wang (Figure 18) found through experiments that the FAPbBr3 device exhibited holedominated characteristics [213]. To achieve charge carrier balance, on the anode side, PE-DOT:PSS 8000 was used as the hole injection layer. Meanwhile, on the cathode side, solution-treated ZnO nanoparticles (NPs) were used as the electron injection layer in the conventional LED to improve the electron current. The prepared device achieved an EQE of 4.66% and a luminous intensity of 10,900 cd/A. 

Yang found that the organic small molecule TOPO may be a good passivating agent [214].

Title: Colloidal Zn(Te,Se)/ZnS Core/Shell Quantum Dots Exhibiting Narrow-Band and Green Photoluminescence
Snippet: Colloidal CdSe quantum dot (QD) phosphors have attracted considerable attention as green and red phosphors for blue backlight downconversion in next-generation liquid-crystal displays because of their excellent emission features including tunable emission wavelength and narrow emission bands. Alternatives to CdSe, which do not contain toxic cadmium, are strongly desired to ensure safety and reduce the environmental load of consumer products. Herein, we synthesized colloidal Zn(Te,Se)/ZnS core/shell QDs and demonstrated narrow-band green photoluminescence (PL) emission. Snippet: CdSe/CdS/ZnS core-shell-shell quantum dots (QDs) were synthesized by using a solution process. Snippet: Metal halide perovskite quantum dots (PQDs) are promising semiconducting materials and are described by the general chemical formula ABX 3 (wherein A is a monovalent cation selected from one or more of Cs, an alkylammonium ion, and a formamidinium ion; B is Pb 2+ or Sn 2+ ; and X is a halogen anion selected from one or more of Br, Cl, or I). This material has demonstrated exceptional optoelectronic properties because of invaluable advantages, such as bright photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY) with narrow full width at half-maximum (fwhm), adjustable direct bandgaps, significant absorption coefficient, and intrinsically high defect tolerance. 1,2 Thus, PQDs have garnered growing interest in light-emitting devices (LEDs), solar cells, lasers, and photodetectors. Despite the significant promise demonstrated by electrically driven perovskite LEDs, comparable with organic and quantum dot LEDs in terms of device efficiency, several challenges should be addressed before considering them for commercialization. The primary challenges lie in long-term stability because of their low formation energy, making them susceptible to environmental stresses, moisture, and oxygen and leading to increased defects and reduced carrier lifetimes. 3 Many passivation strategies have been devised to enhance perovskite stability, but their success has been constrained and achieved to a limited extent.

Title: Enhanced Long‐Term Luminescent Stability through Near‐Single‐Dot Passivation and Encapsulation of Perovskite Quantum Dots for Printable Photonics
Snippet: Metal halide perovskites quantum dots (QDs) stand at the forefront of multifarious photonic applications, including micro‐light‐emitting diode and further augmented reality, virtual reality, and other novel display, lighting technologies. Barriers to applications, however, lie in their toxicity of lead, instability to light, moisture and heat, and processability at the nanoscale‐particle level. Herein, a simple and versatile postprocessing approach is reported for the near‐single‐dot passivation and encapsulation of representative lead‐free double perovskite Cs2Ag0.4Na0.6InCl6:Bi through liquid‐phase processing of perhydropolysilazane and quantum dots colloid with controllable hydrolysis curing. The conventional unstable oleylamine and oleic acid ligands are replaced by ‐NCl bonding on the surface of nanocrystal, accompanied by the resulting compact and robust silica layer without compromising the optical properties of the quantum dots. With the near‐single‐dot protection, the quantum dots do not show fluorescence quenching even when stored for more than 90 days and exhibit remarkably improved stability against heat, ultraviolet irradiation and humidity compared to the raw quantum dots. The strategy offers a versatile way of creating nanoscale‐particle level protection of luminescent quantum dots, and can be universally compatible with solution‐based patterning techniques and photonics applications where quantum dots are used.

Title: Manipulating solvent fluidic dynamics for large-area perovskite film-formation and white light-emitting diodes
Snippet: Presynthesized perovskite quantum dots are very promising for making films with different compositions, as they decouple crystallization and film-formation processes. However, fabricating large-area uniform films using perovskite quantum dots is still very challenging due to the complex fluidic dynamics of the solvents. Here, we report a robust film-formation approach using an environmental-friendly binary-solvent strategy. Nonbenzene solvents, n-octane and n-hexane, are mixed to manipulate the fluidic and evaporation dynamics of the perovskite quantum dot inks, resulting in balanced Marangoni flow, enhanced ink spreadability, and uniform solute-redistribution. We can therefore blade-coat large-area uniform perovskite films with different compositions using the same fabrication parameters. White and red perovskite light-emitting diodes incorporating blade-coated films exhibit a decent external quantum efficiency of 10.6% and 15.3% (0.04 cm^2), and show a uniform emission up to 28 cm^2. This work represents a significant step toward the application of perovskite light-emitting diodes in flat panel solid-state lighting. Achieving large-area uniform film is the primary challenge to commercialise perovskite LEDs. The authors here employ green binary solvents to regulate the fluidic dynamics in perovskite quantum dot inks during blade-coating to achieve efficient 28 cm2-sized red and white perovskite LEDs.

documents.title: Enhanced Long‐Term Luminescent Stability through Near‐Single‐Dot Passivation and Encapsulation of Perovskite Quantum Dots for Printable Photonics
documents.snippet: Metal halide perovskites quantum dots (QDs) stand at the forefront of multifarious photonic applications, including micro‐light‐emitting diode and further augmented reality, virtual reality, and other novel display, lighting technologies. Barriers to applications, however, lie in their toxicity of lead, instability to light, moisture and heat, and processability at the nanoscale‐particle level. Herein, a simple and versatile postprocessing approach is reported for the near‐single‐dot passivation and encapsulation of representative lead‐free double perovskite Cs2Ag0.4Na0.6InCl6:Bi through liquid‐phase processing of perhydropolysilazane and quantum dots colloid with controllable hydrolysis curing. The conventional unstable oleylamine and oleic acid ligands are replaced by ‐NCl bonding on the surface of nanocrystal, accompanied by the resulting compact and robust silica layer without compromising the optical properties of the quantum dots. With the near‐single‐dot protection, the quantum dots do not show fluorescence quenching even when stored for more than 90 days and exhibit remarkably improved stability against heat, ultraviolet irradiation and humidity compared to the raw quantum dots. The strategy offers a versatile way of creating nanoscale‐particle level protection of luminescent quantum dots, and can be universally compatible with solution‐based patterning techniques and photonics applications where quantum dots are used.
