problem: what best approach to compare research project descriptions for text similarity
final_response:
# Overview: What “Best” Means for Project-Description Similarity
<cite id="6a119da2-2">There is no single “best” algorithm for comparing project descriptions; the appropriate approach depends on the task (e.g., near-duplicate detection, proposal grouping by theme, recommendation, or retrieval) and the domain characteristics (e.g., jargon, structure, and length), and it should be validated for each new project with representative data</cite>. <cite id="6a119da2-3">Different similarity metrics capture different axes of similarity (lexical overlap vs. semantic proximity), so combining multiple measures and aggregating results often yields more robust comparisons than a single metric</cite>.

# Step 1 — Clarify Goals, Unit of Comparison, and Ground Truth
- Decide whether you compare whole proposals, sections (title/abstract, methods, outcomes), or extracted entities (keywords, PI names). <cite id="5067b01e-1">In retrieval-style setups, a common unit is document chunks generated by a chunking strategy, which are then embedded and scored with cosine similarity before being used by a generator</cite>. 
- Plan evaluation: if ranking proposals by relevance, use graded or binary human judgments; if clustering, prepare gold clusters or expert labels. <cite id="6a119da2-3">Multiple algorithms measure similarity differently; normalize or rank outputs and aggregate to get a holistic “overall similarity” view</cite>.

# Step 2 — Baseline: TF–IDF + Cosine, N‑grams, and Keyword Overlap
A robust baseline for project descriptions is a bag‑of‑words pipeline with TF–IDF weighting and cosine similarity across terms, optionally extended with n‑grams and keyword overlap metrics.
- Implementation: segment into sentences or paragraphs; remove stopwords; compute TF–IDF per document; represent each proposal as a TF–IDF vector and score pairs with cosine; consider variants such as unweighted or weighted averages and project-level aggregation. <cite id="6a119da2-0">A study computed TF–IDF per term, formed document vectors, and used cosine similarity for mission statements vs. project descriptions, including sum/average/weighted variants and aggregation across projects with expense weights</cite>.
- N‑grams and overlap: <cite id="6a119da2-4">Term extraction and keyword overlap (e.g., Jaccard, Dice) are established methods for document similarity and have been used in scientific and policy document comparisons</cite>. 
- When to use: this approach is fast, interpretable, and effective for lexical overlap and frequency-based relevance in structured project texts; it also serves as a strong anchor for ablation and comparison with semantic methods. <cite id="6a119da2-2">Because methods are task- and domain-specific, start with this baseline and iterate</cite>.

# Step 3 — Modern Embeddings: Sentence and Paragraph Encoders (SBERT/USE)
For semantic similarity beyond keywords, train or use sentence/paragraph embeddings and compare with cosine distance.
- Why embeddings: <cite id="804f7181-0">SBERT produces sentence-level vectors where semantically similar sentences are closer in embedding space; USE similarly encodes sentences or short paragraphs for similarity and clustering</cite>. <cite id="804f7181-2">SBERT embeddings have been shown to be superior in quality to averaging word vectors (GloVe/Word2Vec) or taking BERT’s [CLS] token and benefit from fine-tuning on IR-relevant data</cite>. <cite id="804f7181-3">Contextually aware SBERT embeddings capture word order and dependencies, yielding more accurate semantic similarity than shallow baselines</cite>.
- What to compare: <cite id="9c62b9c1-0">SBERT typically uses cosine similarity between sentence embeddings for comparison</cite>. <cite id="9c62b9c1-1">Fine-tuned SBERT significantly outperforms prior sentence encoders (InferSent, USE) on seven STS tasks by large margins and achieves higher SentEval scores</cite>. <cite id="9c62b9c1-2">On the STS benchmark, tuned SBERT (86.1 dev, 83.7 test) outperforms USE (82.5/76.6) and InferSent (80.1/75.6), while a language-agnostic BERT variant (LaBSE) shows lower STS performance, indicating that task tuning matters</cite>. <cite id="9c62b9c1-3">SBERT’s siamese/triplet training and cosine scoring maintain accuracy while enabling efficient retrieval and clustering</cite>.
- Practical guidance: 
  - Start with SBERT (distilroberta-stsb or roberta-stsb-large) and compute cosine similarities; for multilingual project descriptions, consider LaBSE but verify on your domain. <cite id="9c62b9c1-2">LaBSE can underperform English-tuned SBERT on fine-grained STS tasks</cite>. 
  - If you need paragraph-level semantics (long projects), encode paragraphs directly; for speed, use content-aware chunking to limit context fragmentation. <cite id="5067b01e-0">Content-aware chunking preserves semantic coherence and reduces chunking errors compared to naive delimiters</cite>. 
  - When to prefer embeddings: when near-duplicates differ lexically (synonyms, paraphrases), when ranking by thematic similarity is crucial, or when you can afford latency for more accurate retrieval. <cite id="9c62b9c1-1">SBERT reduces expensive pairwise model use by enabling efficient nearest-neighbor search via precomputed embeddings and cosine scoring</cite>.

# Step 4 — Long Documents: Chunking, Summarization, and Hierarchical Indexing
Project descriptions are often long and hierarchical; handle them with chunking, multi-view representations, and hierarchical retrieval.
- Chunking strategies: <cite id="5067b01e-0">Naive sentence/paragraph splits can fragment semantics; content-aware chunking segments by the document’s content structure to preserve coherence</cite>. <cite id="5067b01e-2">Hierarchical or recursive chunking (sections→paragraphs→sentences) allows multiple-granularity retrieval but often lacks integrated reranking that leverages mid-sized chunks effectively</cite>.
- Summarization-based navigation: <cite id="5067b01e-0">Converting a long document into a tree of summary nodes and navigating from question to relevant summaries can improve long-document QA and retrieval</cite>. <cite id="5067b01e-0">Recursive embedding, clustering, and multi-level summarization can build a hierarchical index for faster, more focused retrieval</cite>.
- Multi-view indexing: <cite id="5067b01e-3">Represent chunks in raw text, keyword lists, and summary views; content-aware chunking and multi-view indexing significantly improve long-document QA</cite>.
- Retrieval pipeline: <cite id="5067b01e-1">In RAG-style setups, chunk a document, embed query and chunks, score with cosine similarity, select top‑k chunks, and pass them to a generator or comparator</cite>.
- When to use: if projects exceed memory/attention limits or require section-specific matching (e.g., methods vs. outcomes), chunk and index semantically; if you need global similarity summaries, use multi-view or summarization trees. <cite id="5067b01e-4">Graph-based comparative summarization can model commonality and distinction at the phrase level across document pairs, benefiting clustering, recommendation, and IR tasks</cite>.

# Step 5 — Combine Multiple Views: Title, Abstract, Keywords, Sections, and Tags
Highly reliable project comparison often benefits from multi-view fusion: lexical and semantic across title, abstract, methods, outcomes, and metadata.
- Title/abstract similarity: <cite id="804f7181-0">Lexical similarity can be computed via TF–IDF and cosine for title/abstract pairs; semantic similarity via SBERT/USE</cite>. <cite id="804f7181-4">In news recommendation, title similarity used edit-distance metrics and TF–IDF, while article similarity combined Sentence Transformer, BERTopic, and Lemmatized TF–IDF; section similarity used Jaccard; tag similarity used Jaccard on tag lists</cite>.
- Keywords and tags: <cite id="6a119da2-4">Scientific document similarity has long used term extraction and keyword overlap (e.g., Jaccard) to capture topical proximity</cite>. <cite id="804f7181-4">Jaccard and Dice overlap on keywords and tags are effective and interpretable measures for topical similarity</cite>.
- Practical fusion: compute per-view scores (TF–IDF cosine for lexical, SBERT cosine for semantic, Jaccard for keywords/tags) and aggregate them into a composite similarity (e.g., weighted sum by content importance). <cite id="6a119da2-3">Aggregating multiple algorithms that measure different similarity notions yields a more robust overall degree of similarity than any single method</cite>.

# Step 6 — Evaluation: Metrics, Protocols, and Human Feedback
- Ranking tasks: use graded relevance labels and rank-based metrics (nDCG@k, Kendall’s tau) or binary click/accept data with AUC/precision@k. <cite id="6a119da2-3">Because different algorithms emphasize different aspects of “similarity,” normalize or rank outputs and aggregate, but do not directly compare raw scores across metrics</cite>.
- Retrieval and clustering: <cite id="9c62b9c1-1">For IR-style evaluation (recall@k, MAP), SBERT-based embeddings often outperform classical baselines on STS; cosine similarity is standard for comparing embeddings</cite>. <cite id="804f7181-2">For clustering or grouping, SBERT embeddings with cosine linkage and silhouette analysis provide quality assessments</cite>. 
- Human judgments: <cite id="6a119da2-0">Domain-specific alignment (e.g., mission vs. project descriptions) benefits from expert labeling to calibrate thresholds and weighting schemes</cite>. <cite id="6a119da2-2">Given domain particularities, include human experts or labeled pairs in evaluation for each new project</cite>.
- Baseline ablations: compare TF–IDF cosine, SBERT cosine, and Jaccard/Dice keyword overlap to understand which contributes most for your corpus; include long-document variants with chunking and multi-view scoring. <cite id="6a119da2-4">Keyword overlap and term extraction have strong baselines in scientific and policy domains</cite>.

# Step 7 — Practical Trade-offs and Deployment
- Latency and scale: <cite id="9c62b9c1-1">Precompute SBERT embeddings and index with approximate nearest-neighbor structures to make cosine retrieval online scalable</cite>. <cite id="9c62b9c1-1">Efficient hardware and indexing can reduce nearest-neighbor search from hours to milliseconds for large collections</cite>.
- Domain adaptation: <cite id="804f7181-2">Fine-tune SBERT or domain-specific encoders on in-domain IR or similarity data to improve performance</cite>. <cite id="9c62b9c1-2">English-only STS-tuned models can outperform language-agnostic variants on English project texts, so prefer domain-tuned encoders when possible</cite>.
- Explainability and governance: TF–IDF + Jaccard provide interpretable features (terms, n‑grams, keywords) useful for audit trails; embeddings can be post-hoc explained via attention or nearest neighbors. <cite id="6a119da2-0">Weighted TF–IDF with expense-weighted aggregation can reflect program priorities and produce interpretable similarity scores</cite>. <cite id="804f7181-3">SBERT’s cosine similarity yields precise semantic matching while remaining more lightweight than full generative reranking in many settings</cite>.
- Deduplication and near-duplicate detection: <cite id="6a119da2-2">Task-specific optimization often leads to better performance than generic models; for deduplication, combine lexical shingling with SBERT to catch paraphrases and synonymic rewrites</cite>.

# Example End-to-End Workflow for Research Project Comparisons
1) Data preparation: segment each project into title, abstract, methods, outcomes, and tags/keywords; extract n‑grams (2–4‑grams) for sections. <cite id="5067b01e-0">Use content-aware chunking for long sections to preserve semantic units</cite>. 
2) Baseline: compute TF–IDF (unigrams) for each section; score pairwise cosine and aggregate across sections (e.g., weighted by section importance). <cite id="6a119da2-0">Implement sum/average/weighted variants and aggregate across projects as needed</cite>. 
3) Embeddings: generate SBERT sentence embeddings for sections and full projects; compute cosine similarity; optionally fine-tune SBERT on in-domain pairs. <cite id="9c62b9c1-1">SBERT with cosine scoring and fine-tuning outperforms prior sentence encoders on STS tasks and enables efficient retrieval</cite>. 
4) Multi-view fusion: compute Jaccard/Dice for keywords and tags; combine TF–IDF cosine, SBERT cosine, and keyword overlap into a composite score. <cite id="804f7181-4">Use Jaccard for sets (keywords/tags) and section-level overlap; combine with semantic and lexical measures</cite>. 
5) Long documents: if projects are very long, chunk content-awarely, index with multi-view (raw, keywords, summaries), and retrieve top‑k chunks for comparison or generation. <cite id="5067b01e-3">Content-aware chunking and multi-view indexing improve retrieval for long documents</cite>. 
6) Evaluation: establish human-labeled relevance or grouping gold standards; report ranking metrics (nDCG@k, precision@k) and clustering quality (silhouette), and compare against TF–IDF and keyword-only baselines. <cite id="6a119da2-3">Aggregate across multiple algorithms to reflect different similarity notions</cite>. 
7) Deployment: precompute embeddings, deploy approximate nearest-neighbor search, and include an explainer that highlights contributing terms/n‑grams and top semantic chunks. <cite id="9c62b9c1-1">Indexing and precomputation enable efficient semantic search at scale</cite>.

# Summary: Recommended “Best Practice” Stack
- Start with a TF–IDF + cosine baseline and n‑gram/keyword overlap to capture lexical overlap and domain terms; this is fast, interpretable, and a strong baseline. <cite id="6a119da2-0">A concrete implementation with TF–IDF and cosine for mission vs. project descriptions demonstrates practical effectiveness</cite>. 
- Add SBERT/USE sentence embeddings with cosine similarity to capture semantic similarity and paraphrase tolerance; fine-tune on in-domain data when possible. <cite id="9c62b9c1-1">SBERT achieves substantial gains over prior sentence encoders on STS tasks and supports efficient retrieval</cite>. 
- For long documents, use content-aware chunking, hierarchical or summarization trees, and multi-view indexing (raw, keywords, summaries); integrate into a retrieval pipeline that scores chunks with cosine and aggregates to document-level similarity. <cite id="5067b01e-0">Content-aware chunking reduces semantic fragmentation; summarization trees and multi-view indexes aid long-document retrieval</cite>. 
- Combine multiple views (title/abstract/sections/tags) and metrics (cosine, Jaccard, Dice) into a composite score; validate with human judgments and ranking metrics (nDCG@k, precision@k, silhouette). <cite id="6a119da2-3">Different algorithms capture different similarity axes; aggregation is valid and informative</cite>. 
- Choose and tune methods to your domain and constraints; expect to iterate and benchmark per project due to domain specificity. <cite id="6a119da2-2">Method selection should be reviewed and validated for each new project</cite>.

Title: Explainable identification of similarities between entities for discovery in large text
Snippet: In the modern digital landscape, the need for effective methods to analyze, compare and interpret large textual data is paramount. The ability to detect patterns of similarities between text documents can provide immediate insights that would otherwise be difficult to make. For instance, users who study certain political figures can use large amounts of text to identify certain similarities between them. Researchers in the medical domain can identify similarities or common causes between two clinical conditions by comparing a large corpus of medical records that describe these conditions. Similarly, health records associated with certain drugs or vaccines can be compared to identify symptoms or side effects, which can be analyzed even by scanning user-generated documents through social media. In the humanities domain, comparisons can be used to identify specific similarities between novels, literary styles, or characters. But despite the potential usefulness of the ability to quickly perform an explainable identification of similarities between documents, such algorithms have yet attracted relatively little attention. 

Automatic analysis of text has been studied intensively for tasks such as automatic document classification [1][2][3][4], automatic translation of documents [5,6], document summarization [7][8][9], and automatic generation of documents, which is often done through large language models [10]. 

Text document comparison is a common feature in modern word processors, but its goal is merely to compare and match words and sentences in the body of the text. It cannot be used effectively for comparing specific topics of similarities discussed in the documents. Therefore, while automatic document comparison is commonly used feature, it is irrelevant to the task of identifying specific similarities between two or more entities as they are studied through the text documents. 

One of the most common forms of identifying similarities between documents is automatic plagiarism detection [11][12][13][14][15]. Other research efforts focused on similarities between scientific documents, including similarities in keywords and references [16]. The complexity for finding the most similar sentence pair in a collection of 10,000 sentences is reduced from 65 hours with BERT to the computation of 10,000 sentence embeddings (~5 seconds with SBERT) and computing cosinesimilarity (~0.01 seconds). # Overview: What “Best” Means for Project-Description Similarity
<cite id="6a119da2-2">There is no single “best” algorithm for comparing project descriptions; the appropriate approach depends on the task (e.g., near-duplicate detection, proposal grouping by theme, recommendation, or retrieval) and the domain characteristics (e.g., jargon, structure, and length), and it should be validated for each new project with representative data</cite>. <cite id="6a119da2-3">Different similarity metrics capture different axes of similarity (lexical overlap vs. semantic proximity), so combining multiple measures and aggregating results often yields more robust comparisons than a single metric</cite>.

# Step 1 — Clarify Goals, Unit of Comparison, and Ground Truth
- Decide whether you compare whole proposals, sections (title/abstract, methods, outcomes), or extracted entities (keywords, PI names). <cite id="5067b01e-1">In retrieval-style setups, a common unit is document chunks generated by a chunking strategy, which are then embedded and scored with cosine similarity before being used by a generator</cite>. 
- Plan evaluation: if ranking proposals by relevance, use graded or binary human judgments; if clustering, prepare gold clusters or expert labels. <cite id="6a119da2-3">Multiple algorithms measure similarity differently; normalize or rank outputs and aggregate to get a holistic “overall similarity” view</cite>.

# Step 2 — Baseline: TF–IDF + Cosine, N‑grams, and Keyword Overlap
A robust baseline for project descriptions is a bag‑of‑words pipeline with TF–IDF weighting and cosine similarity across terms, optionally extended with n‑grams and keyword overlap metrics.
- Implementation: segment into sentences or paragraphs; remove stopwords; compute TF–IDF per document; represent each proposal as a TF–IDF vector and score pairs with cosine; consider variants such as unweighted or weighted averages and project-level aggregation. <cite id="6a119da2-0">A study computed TF–IDF per term, formed document vectors, and used cosine similarity for mission statements vs. project descriptions, including sum/average/weighted variants and aggregation across projects with expense weights</cite>.
- N‑grams and overlap: <cite id="6a119da2-4">Term extraction and keyword overlap (e.g., Jaccard, Dice) are established methods for document similarity and have been used in scientific and policy document comparisons</cite>. 
- When to use: this approach is fast, interpretable, and effective for lexical overlap and frequency-based relevance in structured project texts; it also serves as a strong anchor for ablation and comparison with semantic methods. <cite id="6a119da2-2">Because methods are task- and domain-specific, start with this baseline and iterate</cite>.

# Step 3 — Modern Embeddings: Sentence and Paragraph Encoders (SBERT/USE)
For semantic similarity beyond keywords, train or use sentence/paragraph embeddings and compare with cosine distance.
- Why embeddings: <cite id="804f7181-0">SBERT produces sentence-level vectors where semantically similar sentences are closer in embedding space; USE similarly encodes sentences or short paragraphs for similarity and clustering</cite>. <cite id="804f7181-2">SBERT embeddings have been shown to be superior in quality to averaging word vectors (GloVe/Word2Vec) or taking BERT’s [CLS] token and benefit from fine-tuning on IR-relevant data</cite>. <cite id="804f7181-3">Contextually aware SBERT embeddings capture word order and dependencies, yielding more accurate semantic similarity than shallow baselines</cite>.
- What to compare: <cite id="9c62b9c1-0">SBERT typically uses cosine similarity between sentence embeddings for comparison</cite>. <cite id="9c62b9c1-1">Fine-tuned SBERT significantly outperforms prior sentence encoders (InferSent, USE) on seven STS tasks by large margins and achieves higher SentEval scores</cite>. <cite id="9c62b9c1-2">On the STS benchmark, tuned SBERT (86.1 dev, 83.7 test) outperforms USE (82.5/76.6) and InferSent (80.1/75.6), while a language-agnostic BERT variant (LaBSE) shows lower STS performance, indicating that task tuning matters</cite>. <cite id="9c62b9c1-3">SBERT’s siamese/triplet training and cosine scoring maintain accuracy while enabling efficient retrieval and clustering</cite>.
- Practical guidance: 
  - Start with SBERT (distilroberta-stsb or roberta-stsb-large) and compute cosine similarities; for multilingual project descriptions, consider LaBSE but verify on your domain. <cite id="9c62b9c1-2">LaBSE can underperform English-tuned SBERT on fine-grained STS tasks</cite>. 
  - If you need paragraph-level semantics (long projects), encode paragraphs directly; for speed, use content-aware chunking to limit context fragmentation. <cite id="5067b01e-0">Content-aware chunking preserves semantic coherence and reduces chunking errors compared to naive delimiters</cite>. 
  - When to prefer embeddings: when near-duplicates differ lexically (synonyms, paraphrases), when ranking by thematic similarity is crucial, or when you can afford latency for more accurate retrieval. <cite id="9c62b9c1-1">SBERT reduces expensive pairwise model use by enabling efficient nearest-neighbor search via precomputed embeddings and cosine scoring</cite>.

# Step 4 — Long Documents: Chunking, Summarization, and Hierarchical Indexing
Project descriptions are often long and hierarchical; handle them with chunking, multi-view representations, and hierarchical retrieval.
- Chunking strategies: <cite id="5067b01e-0">Naive sentence/paragraph splits can fragment semantics; content-aware chunking segments by the document’s content structure to preserve coherence</cite>. <cite id="5067b01e-2">Hierarchical or recursive chunking (sections→paragraphs→sentences) allows multiple-granularity retrieval but often lacks integrated reranking that leverages mid-sized chunks effectively</cite>.
- Summarization-based navigation: <cite id="5067b01e-0">Converting a long document into a tree of summary nodes and navigating from question to relevant summaries can improve long-document QA and retrieval</cite>. <cite id="5067b01e-0">Recursive embedding, clustering, and multi-level summarization can build a hierarchical index for faster, more focused retrieval</cite>.
- Multi-view indexing: <cite id="5067b01e-3">Represent chunks in raw text, keyword lists, and summary views; content-aware chunking and multi-view indexing significantly improve long-document QA</cite>.
- Retrieval pipeline: <cite id="5067b01e-1">In RAG-style setups, chunk a document, embed query and chunks, score with cosine similarity, select top‑k chunks, and pass them to a generator or comparator</cite>.
- When to use: if projects exceed memory/attention limits or require section-specific matching (e.g., methods vs. outcomes), chunk and index semantically; if you need global similarity summaries, use multi-view or summarization trees. <cite id="5067b01e-4">Graph-based comparative summarization can model commonality and distinction at the phrase level across document pairs, benefiting clustering, recommendation, and IR tasks</cite>.

# Step 5 — Combine Multiple Views: Title, Abstract, Keywords, Sections, and Tags
Highly reliable project comparison often benefits from multi-view fusion: lexical and semantic across title, abstract, methods, outcomes, and metadata.
- Title/abstract similarity: <cite id="804f7181-0">Lexical similarity can be computed via TF–IDF and cosine for title/abstract pairs; semantic similarity via SBERT/USE</cite>. <cite id="804f7181-4">In news recommendation, title similarity used edit-distance metrics and TF–IDF, while article similarity combined Sentence Transformer, BERTopic, and Lemmatized TF–IDF; section similarity used Jaccard; tag similarity used Jaccard on tag lists</cite>.
- Keywords and tags: <cite id="6a119da2-4">Scientific document similarity has long used term extraction and keyword overlap (e.g., Jaccard) to capture topical proximity</cite>. <cite id="804f7181-4">Jaccard and Dice overlap on keywords and tags are effective and interpretable measures for topical similarity</cite>.
- Practical fusion: compute per-view scores (TF–IDF cosine for lexical, SBERT cosine for semantic, Jaccard for keywords/tags) and aggregate them into a composite similarity (e.g., weighted sum by content importance). <cite id="6a119da2-3">Aggregating multiple algorithms that measure different similarity notions yields a more robust overall degree of similarity than any single method</cite>.

# Step 6 — Evaluation: Metrics, Protocols, and Human Feedback
- Ranking tasks: use graded relevance labels and rank-based metrics (nDCG@k, Kendall’s tau) or binary click/accept data with AUC/precision@k. <cite id="6a119da2-3">Because different algorithms emphasize different aspects of “similarity,” normalize or rank outputs and aggregate, but do not directly compare raw scores across metrics</cite>.
- Retrieval and clustering: <cite id="9c62b9c1-1">For IR-style evaluation (recall@k, MAP), SBERT-based embeddings often outperform classical baselines on STS; cosine similarity is standard for comparing embeddings</cite>. <cite id="804f7181-2">For clustering or grouping, SBERT embeddings with cosine linkage and silhouette analysis provide quality assessments</cite>. 
- Human judgments: <cite id="6a119da2-0">Domain-specific alignment (e.g., mission vs. project descriptions) benefits from expert labeling to calibrate thresholds and weighting schemes</cite>. <cite id="6a119da2-2">Given domain particularities, include human experts or labeled pairs in evaluation for each new project</cite>.
- Baseline ablations: compare TF–IDF cosine, SBERT cosine, and Jaccard/Dice keyword overlap to understand which contributes most for your corpus; include long-document variants with chunking and multi-view scoring. <cite id="6a119da2-4">Keyword overlap and term extraction have strong baselines in scientific and policy domains</cite>.

# Step 7 — Practical Trade-offs and Deployment
- Latency and scale: <cite id="9c62b9c1-1">Precompute SBERT embeddings and index with approximate nearest-neighbor structures to make cosine retrieval online scalable</cite>. <cite id="9c62b9c1-1">Efficient hardware and indexing can reduce nearest-neighbor search from hours to milliseconds for large collections</cite>.
- Domain adaptation: <cite id="804f7181-2">Fine-tune SBERT or domain-specific encoders on in-domain IR or similarity data to improve performance</cite>. <cite id="9c62b9c1-2">English-only STS-tuned models can outperform language-agnostic variants on English project texts, so prefer domain-tuned encoders when possible</cite>.
- Explainability and governance: TF–IDF + Jaccard provide interpretable features (terms, n‑grams, keywords) useful for audit trails; embeddings can be post-hoc explained via attention or nearest neighbors. <cite id="6a119da2-0">Weighted TF–IDF with expense-weighted aggregation can reflect program priorities and produce interpretable similarity scores</cite>. <cite id="804f7181-3">SBERT’s cosine similarity yields precise semantic matching while remaining more lightweight than full generative reranking in many settings</cite>.
- Deduplication and near-duplicate detection: <cite id="6a119da2-2">Task-specific optimization often leads to better performance than generic models; for deduplication, combine lexical shingling with SBERT to catch paraphrases and synonymic rewrites</cite>.

# Example End-to-End Workflow for Research Project Comparisons
1) Data preparation: segment each project into title, abstract, methods, outcomes, and tags/keywords; extract n‑grams (2–4‑grams) for sections. <cite id="5067b01e-0">Use content-aware chunking for long sections to preserve semantic units</cite>. 
2) Baseline: compute TF–IDF (unigrams) for each section; score pairwise cosine and aggregate across sections (e.g., weighted by section importance). <cite id="6a119da2-0">Implement sum/average/weighted variants and aggregate across projects as needed</cite>. 
3) Embeddings: generate SBERT sentence embeddings for sections and full projects; compute cosine similarity; optionally fine-tune SBERT on in-domain pairs. <cite id="9c62b9c1-1">SBERT with cosine scoring and fine-tuning outperforms prior sentence encoders on STS tasks and enables efficient retrieval</cite>. 
4) Multi-view fusion: compute Jaccard/Dice for keywords and tags; combine TF–IDF cosine, SBERT cosine, and keyword overlap into a composite score. <cite id="804f7181-4">Use Jaccard for sets (keywords/tags) and section-level overlap; combine with semantic and lexical measures</cite>. 
5) Long documents: if projects are very long, chunk content-awarely, index with multi-view (raw, keywords, summaries), and retrieve top‑k chunks for comparison or generation. <cite id="5067b01e-3">Content-aware chunking and multi-view indexing improve retrieval for long documents</cite>. 
6) Evaluation: establish human-labeled relevance or grouping gold standards; report ranking metrics (nDCG@k, precision@k) and clustering quality (silhouette), and compare against TF–IDF and keyword-only baselines. <cite id="6a119da2-3">Aggregate across multiple algorithms to reflect different similarity notions</cite>. 
7) Deployment: precompute embeddings, deploy approximate nearest-neighbor search, and include an explainer that highlights contributing terms/n‑grams and top semantic chunks. <cite id="9c62b9c1-1">Indexing and precomputation enable efficient semantic search at scale</cite>.

# Summary: Recommended “Best Practice” Stack
- Start with a TF–IDF + cosine baseline and n‑gram/keyword overlap to capture lexical overlap and domain terms; this is fast, interpretable, and a strong baseline. <cite id="6a119da2-0">A concrete implementation with TF–IDF and cosine for mission vs. project descriptions demonstrates practical effectiveness</cite>. 
- Add SBERT/USE sentence embeddings with cosine similarity to capture semantic similarity and paraphrase tolerance; fine-tune on in-domain data when possible. <cite id="9c62b9c1-1">SBERT achieves substantial gains over prior sentence encoders on STS tasks and supports efficient retrieval</cite>. 
- For long documents, use content-aware chunking, hierarchical or summarization trees, and multi-view indexing (raw, keywords, summaries); integrate into a retrieval pipeline that scores chunks with cosine and aggregates to document-level similarity. <cite id="5067b01e-0">Content-aware chunking reduces semantic fragmentation; summarization trees and multi-view indexes aid long-document retrieval</cite>. 
- Combine multiple views (title/abstract/sections/tags) and metrics (cosine, Jaccard, Dice) into a composite score; validate with human judgments and ranking metrics (nDCG@k, precision@k, silhouette). <cite id="6a119da2-3">Different algorithms capture different similarity axes; aggregation is valid and informative</cite>. 
- Choose and tune methods to your domain and constraints; expect to iterate and benchmark per project due to domain specificity. <cite id="6a119da2-2">Method selection should be reviewed and validated for each new project</cite>. 
</answer>

Title: Predicting Mission Alignment and Preventing Mission Drift: Do Revenue Sources Matter?
Snippet: Mission alignment. This variable measures the textual similarity between the mission statement and project description. To calculate text similarity, we employ a bag-of-words model. First, we performed sentence segmentation on the text using the Python Jieba library (Junyi, 2016) and extracted words from all sentences in the statements. Then we removed the stop words (for example, and he, is shi, of de, etc.) or commas and for each pair of the mission statement and program description for a foundation, we calculated the tf-idf score for each remaining word in the text to evaluate its importance (Leskovec, Rajaraman, & Ullman, 2014, p. 8). The tf-idf score is calculated as tf-idf (t,d,D)=f t,d •log(N/|{d D:t d}| where f t,d is the frequency of word t in document d, N is the total number of documents, and |{d D:t d}| is the number of documents in which term t appears. This method picks up the most important words in each document while being able to rule out words that are merely frequent but without contextual significance (for example, "the"). Finally, we calculated the similarity between two documents by representing each document as a vector containing the tf-idf score of each word in the document and calculated the cosine similarity between the two vectors. 

We calculated four different cosine similarity values: the sum value, the average value, the weighted sum, and the weighted average. The dataset contains multiple program descriptions but only one mission statement for each institution. For each foundation, we first compute the textual similarity between each pair of program description and mission statement then take the sum of all similarity values as the sum cosine similarity. Dividing the sum cosine similarity by the number of a foundation's projects is the average cosine similarity. Weighting the similarity values by the percentage of program expense in proportion to the total expense, we get the weighted sum and weighted average cosine similarity.

Title: Comparing published scientific journal articles to their pre-print versions
Snippet: We applied several text comparison algorithms to the corresponding sections of the pre-print and final published versions of papers in our test data set. These algorithms, described in detail below, were selected to quantify different notions of "similarity" between texts. We normalized the output values of each algorithm to lie between 1 and 0, with 1 indicating that the texts were effectively identical, and 0 indicating complete dissimilarity. Different algorithms necessarily measured any apparent degree of dissimilarity in different ways, so the outputs of the algorithms cannot be compared directly, but it is nonetheless valid to interpret the aggregation of these results as a general indication of the overall degree of similarity between two texts along several different axes of comparison.

Title: Explainable identification of similarities between entities for discovery in large text
Snippet: In the modern digital landscape, the need for effective methods to analyze, compare and interpret large textual data is paramount. The ability to detect patterns of similarities between text documents can provide immediate insights that would otherwise be difficult to make. For instance, users who study certain political figures can use large amounts of text to identify certain similarities between them. Researchers in the medical domain can identify similarities or common causes between two clinical conditions by comparing a large corpus of medical records that describe these conditions. Similarly, health records associated with certain drugs or vaccines can be compared to identify symptoms or side effects, which can be analyzed even by scanning user-generated documents through social media. In the humanities domain, comparisons can be used to identify specific similarities between novels, literary styles, or characters. But despite the potential usefulness of the ability to quickly perform an explainable identification of similarities between documents, such algorithms have yet attracted relatively little attention. 

Automatic analysis of text has been studied intensively for tasks such as automatic document classification [1][2][3][4], automatic translation of documents [5,6], document summarization [7][8][9], and automatic generation of documents, which is often done through large language models [10]. 

Text document comparison is a common feature in modern word processors, but its goal is merely to compare and match words and sentences in the body of the text. It cannot be used effectively for comparing specific topics of similarities discussed in the documents. Therefore, while automatic document comparison is commonly used feature, it is irrelevant to the task of identifying specific similarities between two or more entities as they are studied through the text documents. 

One of the most common forms of identifying similarities between documents is automatic plagiarism detection [11][12][13][14][15]. Other research efforts focused on similarities between scientific documents, including similarities in keywords and references [16]. Term extraction was also used to determine document similarities [17]. Domains in which automatic document similarities are commonly used for include law [18,19] and accounting [20]. Using machine learning, the task of clustering was applied to text documents to identify the most similar documents inside a text corpus [21]. Similarities between text documents can also be done using stylistic elements of the writing [22,23].

Title: Identifying Similar Test Cases That Are Specified in Natural Language
Snippet: Differently from word embedding, sentence embedding is the representation of a whole sentence with a real-valued (and usually high-dimensional) numeric vector. In this work, we use three different techniques to extract sentence embeddings (SBERT, USE, and TF-IDF). Fig. 1b presents two examples of pre-processed test steps along with part of their sentence embeddings obtained by the SBERT, USE, and TF-IDF techniques. Next, we explain how each sentence embedding technique works.

Sentence-BERT (SBERT) is a BERT-based framework that allows us to directly extract numeric representations of full sentences [43]. The embeddings of sentences that are semantically similar are close in the embedding space. We can use this information for different purposes, such as identifying paraphrases and clustering similar sentences. For instance, the SBERT embeddings of the two test steps presented in Fig. 1b are close in the embedding space (i.e., have a small distance between them). Among several generic and task-specific SBERT pre-trained models that are available, 2 three models are suitable for our task (identifying similar test steps): paraphrase-distilroberta-base-v1, stsb-roberta-base, and stsb-roberta-large. While the first model is optimized to identify paraphrases and was trained on large scale paraphrase data, the second and third ones are the base and large versions of a model that was optimized for semantic textual similarity.

Universal Sentence Encoder (USE) is an embedding technique that can be used to directly extract embeddings from sentences, phrases, or short paragraphs to be used in another task, such as textual similarity and clustering tasks [5]. With a similar behavior to SBERT, the two examples presented in Fig. 1b have close embedding vectors.

Finally, we also used the TF-IDF (Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency) method to represent sentences. TF-IDF computes the importance of a word to a document by combining the word frequency in the document and the word frequency across all the other documents [21], [22], [46

Title: Quantifying the Relevance of Youth Research Cited in the US Policy Documents
Snippet: We used TF-IDF vectorizer to generate the documentterm matrix and 11 different transformer-based pretrained Large Language Models (LLMs) within the Sentence-BERT (SBERT) [39] framework to generate sentence embeddings of the preprocessed texts. Sentence embeddings play a pivotal role in enhancing the capabilities of information retrieval systems, particularly by improving semantic search. This technique is a core component of natural language processing (NLP) that involves transforming entire sentences into fixedsize numerical vectors that encapsulate their semantic meaning. These embeddings facilitate the comparison of sentences based on their semantic similarity, enabling the identification of relationships between sentences beyond mere keyword matching. By converting both queries and documents into vector representations, it can assess semantic similarity using metrics such as cosine similarity, which allows for the retrieval of semantically relevant documents rather than those that only match specific terms. In this work, we used SBERT among various sentence embedding models since it is widely recognized for its superior performance in semantic textual similarity tasks. 

Table II briefly overviews the pretrained LLMs used for generating embedding of the texts in our experiment. The selection of the models was according to the following criteria: 

1) We included the bert-large-uncased model (model 2 in Table II) as the base model. 2) Next, we searched for other transformer models in the HugginFace using the following criteria: 'sentence similarity' as the task, 'English' as the language, and sorting based on 'most likes' and 'most downloads'. We had models 3-6 in Table II according to these criteria. 3) In addition to these, we have considered some pretrained language models that are trained on a vast amount of documents relevant to the field of interest. Models 7-12 in Table II follow that criterion. To get the policy relevance score for each research article, we calculated the cosine similarities of embeddings (TF-IDF vectorized output for TF-IDF vectorizer) for each research article and corresponding citing policy documents. Finally, we averaged that similarity values of each research article with the corresponding citing policy document(s) and returned that score as our final relevance score for that particular research article.

Title: Unsupervised document summarization using pre-trained sentence embeddings and graph centrality
Snippet: After extracting the sentences, the next step is to produce the sentence embedding of each sentence using SBERT (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019), which is a Transformer-based (Vaswani et al., 2017) model built on top of BERT (Devlin et al., 2018) that takes as input sentences and produces sentence embeddings that can be compared with cosine similarity, which is given by the following formula: 

As shown in (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019), these sentence embeddings are superior in quality than taking the CLS token of BERT or averaging the sentence embeddings of the words in the sentence produced by BERT, GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014), or Word2Vec (Mikolov et al., 2013). snippet.text:
We used TF-IDF vectorizer to generate the documentterm matrix and 11 different transformer-based pretrained Large Language Models (LLMs) within the Sentence-BERT (SBERT) [39] framework to generate sentence embeddings of the preprocessed texts. Sentence embeddings play a pivotal role in enhancing the capabilities of information retrieval systems, particularly by improving semantic search. This technique is a core component of natural language processing (NLP) that involves transforming entire sentences into fixedsize numerical vectors that encapsulate their semantic meaning. These embeddings facilitate the comparison of sentences based on their semantic similarity, enabling the identification of relationships between sentences beyond mere keyword matching. By converting both queries and documents into vector representations, it can assess semantic similarity using metrics such as cosine similarity, which allows for the retrieval of semantically relevant documents rather than those that only match specific terms. In this work, we used SBERT among various sentence embedding models since it is widely recognized for its superior performance in semantic textual similarity tasks. 

Table II briefly overviews the pretrained LLMs used for generating embedding of the texts in our experiment. The selection of the models was according to the following criteria: 

1) We included the bert-large-uncased model (model 2 in Table II) as the base model. 2) Next, we searched for other transformer models in the HugginFace using the following criteria: 'sentence similarity' as the task, 'English' as the language, and sorting based on 'most likes' and 'most downloads'. We had models 3-6 in Table II according to these criteria. 3) In addition to these, we have considered some pretrained language models that are trained on a vast amount of documents relevant to the field of interest. Models 7-12 in Table II follow that criterion. To get the policy relevance score for each research article, we calculated the cosine similarities of embeddings (TF-IDF vectorized output for TF-IDF vectorizer) for each research article and corresponding citing policy documents. Finally, we averaged that similarity values of each research article with the corresponding citing policy document(s) and returned that score as our final relevance score for that particular research article.

Title: Sentence-BERT: Sentence Embeddings using Siamese BERT-Networks
Snippet: We evaluate the performance of SBERT for common Semantic Textual Similarity (STS) tasks. State-of-the-art methods often learn a (complex) regression function that maps sentence embeddings to a similarity score. However, these regression functions work pair-wise and due to the combinatorial explosion those are often not scalable if the collection of sentences reaches a certain size. Instead, we always use cosine-similarity to compare the similarity between two sentence embeddings. We ran our experiments also with negative Manhatten and negative Euclidean distances as similarity measures, but the results for all approaches remained roughly the same.

Title: Sentence-BERT: Sentence Embeddings using Siamese BERT-Networks
Snippet: / Euclidean distance, semantically similar sentences can be found. These similarity measures can be performed extremely efficient on modern hardware, allowing SBERT to be used for semantic similarity search as well as for clustering. The complexity for finding the most similar sentence pair in a collection of 10,000 sentences is reduced from 65 hours with BERT to the computation of 10,000 sentence embeddings (~5 seconds with SBERT) and computing cosinesimilarity (~0.01 seconds). By using optimized index structures, finding the most similar Quora question can be reduced from 50 hours to a few milliseconds (Johnson et al., 2017).

We fine-tune SBERT on NLI data, which creates sentence embeddings that significantly outperform other state-of-the-art sentence embedding methods like InferSent (Conneau et al., 2017) and Universal Sentence Encoder . On seven Semantic Textual Similarity (STS) tasks, SBERT achieves an improvement of 11.7 points compared to InferSent and 5.5 points compared to Universal Sentence Encoder. On SentEval (Conneau and Kiela, 2018), an evaluation toolkit for sentence embeddings, we achieve an improvement of 2.1 and 2.6 points, respectively.

SBERT can be adapted to a specific task. It sets new state-of-the-art performance on a challenging argument similarity dataset (Misra et al., 2016) and on a triplet dataset to distinguish sentences from different sections of a Wikipedia article (Dor et al., 2018).

The paper is structured in the following way: Section 3 presents SBERT, section 4 evaluates SBERT on common STS tasks and on the challenging Argument Facet Similarity (AFS) corpus (Misra et al., 2016). Section 5 evaluates SBERT on SentEval. In section 6, we perform an ablation study to test some design aspect of SBERT. In section 7, we compare the computational efficiency of SBERT sentence embeddings in contrast to other state-of-the-art sentence embedding methods.

SBERT and SRoBERTa is evaluated on common STS tasks and transfer learning tasks, where it outperforms other state-of-the-art sentence embeddings methods. SBERT is fine-tuned on NLI data, which creates sentence embeddings that significantly outperform other state-of-the-art sentence embedding methods like InferSent [5] and Universal Sentence Encoder on seven Semantic Textual Similarity (STS) tasks.

snippet.text: In this section, we analyze the efficacy of our three main techniques to improve the performance of the sentence vector. We evaluate the performance of TA-SBERT for semantic textual similarity (STS) and classification tasks. For evaluation of STS tasks, we use the cosine similarity to compare the similarity between two sentence vectors. The Pearson's and Spearman's rank correlation coefficients are calculated between the cosine similarity of the sentence vectors and gold labels. For classification tasks, we use the SentEval [25] toolkit for measuring the quality of the sentence vector. We use pre-trained BERT and RoBERTa from Hugging Face 1 [26]

documents.title: Sentence-BERT: Sentence Embeddings using Siamese BERT-Networks
documents.snippet: We evaluate the performance of SBERT for common Semantic Textual Similarity (STS) tasks. State-of-the-art methods often learn a (complex) regression function that maps sentence embeddings to a similarity score. However, these regression functions work pair-wise and due to the combinatorial explosion those are often not scalable if the collection of sentences reaches a certain size. Instead, we always use cosine-similarity to compare the similarity between two sentence embeddings. We ran our experiments also with negative Manhatten and negative Euclidean distances as similarity measures, but the results for all approaches remained roughly the same.

These similarity measures can be performed extremely efficient on modern hardware, allowing SBERT to be used for semantic similarity search as well as for clustering. The complexity for finding the most similar sentence pair in a collection of 10,000 sentences is reduced from 65 hours with BERT to the computation of 10,000 sentence embeddings (~5 seconds with SBERT) and computing cosinesimilarity (~0.01 seconds). By using optimized index structures, finding the most similar Quora question can be reduced from 50 hours to a few milliseconds (Johnson et al., 2017).

We fine-tune SBERT on NLI data, which creates sentence embeddings that significantly outperform other state-of-the-art sentence embedding methods like InferSent (Conneau et al., 2017) and Universal Sentence Encoder . On seven Semantic Textual Similarity (STS) tasks, SBERT achieves an improvement of 11.7 points compared to InferSent and 5.5 points compared to Universal Sentence Encoder. On SentEval (Conneau and Kiela, 2018), an evaluation toolkit for sentence embeddings, we achieve an improvement of 2.1 and 2.6 points, respectively.

SBERT can be adapted to a specific task. It sets new state-of-the-art performance on a challenging argument similarity dataset (Misra et al., 2016) and on a triplet dataset to distinguish sentences from different sections of a Wikipedia article (Dor et al., 2018).

The paper is structured in the following way: Section 3 presents SBERT, section 4 evaluates SBERT on common STS tasks and on the challenging Argument Facet Similarity (AFS) corpus (Misra et al., 2016). Section 5 evaluates SBERT on SentEval. In section 6, we perform an ablation study to test some design aspect of SBERT. In section 7, we compare the computational efficiency of SBERT sentence embeddings in contrast to other state-of-the-art sentence embedding methods.

Title: Multi-view Content-aware Indexing for Long Document Retrieval
Snippet: Sentence chunking involves dividing textual content based on sentences.Recursive chunking employs various delimiters, such as paragraph separators, newline characters, or spaces, to recursively segment the text.However, these methods often fail to preserve semantic integrity of critical content.In contrast, contentaware chunking (Section 3.1) chunk the text by the smallest subdivision according to the document's content structure.This ensures each chunk to be semantically coherent, thus reducing chunking error.

Long Document Retrieval.Traditional retrieval methods such as BM25 and DPR only retrieve short consecutive chunks from the retrieval corpus, limiting the overall understanding of the context of long documents.To overcome this drawback, several methods focusing on long document retrieval have been proposed.Nie et al. (2022) propose a compressive graph selector network to select questionrelated chunks from the long document and then use the selected short chunks for answer generation.AttenWalker (Nie et al., 2023) addresses the task of incorporating long-range information by employing a meticulously crafted answer generator.Chen et al. (2023) convert the long document into a tree of summary nodes.Upon receiving a question, LLM navigates this tree to find relevant summaries until sufficient information is gathered.Sarthi et al. (2024) utilize recursive embedding, clustering, and summarizing chunks of text to build a tree with different levels of summarization.However, existing methods only consider the retrieval of long documents from one view, limiting the semantic completeness and coherence.

Title: Hierarchical Re-ranker Retriever (HRR)
Snippet: Layered or Recursive Chunking Various hierarchical retrieval methods have been proposed to exploit multiple levels of granularity within a document. A document might be divided into sections (parent level), paragraphs (child level), and sentences (leaf level). Approaches such as C2P Retriever + Reranker attempt to retrieve large chunks first and then drill down into sub-chunks. Although these methods capture different resolutions of context, they often lack an integrated reranking mechanism that effectively leverages mid-sized chunks (e.g., 512 tokens) for relevance scoring.

Title: Multi-view Content-aware Indexing for Long Document Retrieval
Snippet: In this paper, we propose a new approach: Multiview Content-aware indexing (MC-indexing) for more effective retrieval of long document.Specially, we propose a long document QA dataset which annotates not only the question-answer pair, but also the document structure and the document scope to answer this question.We propose a content-aware chunking method to segment the document into content chunks according to its organizational content structure.We design a multiview indexing method to represent each content chunk in raw-text, keywords, and summary views.Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that content-aware chunking can eliminate chunking errors, and multi-view indexing can significantly benefit long DocQA.For future work, we would like to explore how to use the hierarchical document structure for more effective retrieval.Moreover, we would like to train or finetune a retriever that can generate more fine-grained or nuanced embeddings across multiple views.

Title: Comparative Document Analysis for Large Text Corpora
Snippet: In this paper, we study the problem of phrase-based comparative summarization for a document pair, called comparative document analysis (CDA), and propose a general graph-based approach to model semantic commonality and pairwise distinction for phrases. We cast the phrase selection problems into joint optimization problems based on the proposed novel measures. Experiment results demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed method on text corpora of different domains. Interesting future work includes extending CDA to consider different comparison aspects [30,13] and to exploit the hierarchical semantic relations between phrases. CDA is general and can be applied as a primitive step for sentence-based comparative summarization [10,29]. It can potentially benefit many other text applications such as content recommendation, document clustering and relevance feedback in information retrieval [21].

# 3D Gaussian Splatting and Diffusion: What They Are, How They Relate, and How They're Combined

## Overview: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) and Diffusion for 3D
3D Gaussian Splatting represents a scene as a collection of trainable 3D Gaussian primitives with per-Gaussian color and opacity, and renders them by projecting and compositing Gaussians on the image plane; this yields fast, explicit geometry and efficient differentiable rendering suitable for real-time novel view synthesis and 3D reconstruction.<cite id="d22d0fb6-1">3D Gaussian Splatting uses a collection of learnable 3D Gaussian ellipsoids, with mean, covariance (rotation+scale), opacity, and SH-encoded color; it projects Gaussians to 2D and composites them for rendering.</cite> <cite id="d22d0fb6-4">Compared to NeRF, 3DGS enables less training time and high-quality, real-time novel view synthesis; it uses an explicit, differentiable representation and alpha compositing to update Gaussian parameters by gradient descent.</cite> <cite id="10c2ba46-0">3DGS is a differentiable rendering pipeline that represents scenes with 3D Gaussians and splats them onto the image plane using an efficient, tile-based, depth-sorted alpha compositing approach; it can be >100× faster than volumetric NeRF-style rendering.</cite> 

Diffusion models have become a strong prior for 3D by training or distilling from 2D generative models, enabling text-to-3D and view-consistent synthesis; key techniques include NeuS's SDF-constrained density fields, latent diffusion, and score-distillation sampling (SDS) that optimizes 3D representations to match a diffusion model's data distribution.<cite id="064ae4cf-0">NeuS adapts NeRF by parameterizing density as a function of signed distance and adding Eikonal regularization for surface-consistent densities, and many works follow with encodings and hybrid surface constraints.</cite> <cite id="064ae4cf-1">Latent diffusion and Stable Diffusion set a strong 2D prior; DreamFusion introduced SDS to train NeRFs with a 2D diffusion critic, and many follow-ups use SDS, 3D-aware latent diffusion (e.g., Zero-1-to-3), or 2D diffusion priors with 3D optimization.</cite> <cite id="064ae4cf-3">ED-NeRF and related work transfer diffusion priors (e.g., CLIP-guided and Stable Diffusion) to NeRFs via SDS, enabling text-guided editing and generation.</cite> <cite id="064ae4cf-4">Diffusion models are now standard for high-quality image generation; DreamFusion's SDS transfers 3D-awareness from latent diffusion, and methods like SparseFusion and Zero-1-to-3 condition diffusion on 3D cues; DreamGaussian applies SDS directly to Gaussian splatting scenes.</cite> 

## 3D Gaussian Splatting: Representation, Rendering, and Training
3DGS parameterizes each Gaussian with position, anisotropic covariance (often via rotation quaternion and scale), opacity (alpha), and view-dependent color; color is commonly represented with spherical harmonics (SH) to compactly encode lighting/view-direction dependence.<cite id="d22d0fb6-1">Each Gaussian is parameterized by mean, covariance (q, s), opacity, and SH-based color; during rendering, Gaussians are projected to 2D and composited.</cite> <cite id="10c2ba46-0">A Gaussian is defined by mean, rotation, scale (forming a 3×3 covariance), color, and opacity; in camera space, the projected 2D covariance is used in efficient tile-based rasterization and alpha compositing.</cite> <cite id="10c2ba46-4">An alternative compact parameterization uses center, radius, and opacity, with color and opacity updated by gradient descent to minimize pixel differences between rendered and ground-truth images.</cite> 

Rendering proceeds by rasterizing tiles on the image plane and accumulating Gaussian contributions in depth order with alpha compositing; because Gaussians are explicit primitives, there is no NeRF-style MLP evaluation at render time, enabling fast inference and training throughput.<cite id="10c2ba46-0">Tile-based rasterization (e.g., 16×16) finds depth-sorted influencing Gaussians and composites them efficiently; this avoids volumetric ray-marching and is extremely fast compared to NeRF-style rendering.</cite> <cite id="10c2ba46-4">3DGS allows differentiable projection and alpha blending, enabling closed-form or learned per-Gaussian functions to be optimized by backpropagation to minimize rendered–image error.</cite> 

Training optimizes Gaussian parameters (means, covariance, color, opacity) to minimize L1/L2 or perceptual losses between multi-view renderings and observations; unlike NeRF, there is no implicit MLP at query time, but the number of Gaussians and their parameters drive memory and compute, especially for high-quality scenes and large views.<cite id="10c2ba46-4">The eight parameterized values (position, radius, RGB, opacity) are updated via gradient descent to reduce rendered–image differences.</cite> <cite id="10c2ba46-2">Per-Gaussian parameters include rotation (quaternion), scale, opacity, and SH coefficients; 3DGS avoids MLP evaluation at render time, improving speed and quality, but explicit representations increase parameter count and memory pressure as Gaussians increase for higher quality.</cite> 

Key advantages and limitations of 3DGS include real-time rendering and explicit geometry, but challenges such as aliasing, view-dependent color fidelity with SH bases, and efficiency for specular/sharp-angled surfaces motivate extensions and alternative kernels.<cite id="d22d0fb6-3">3DGS achieves real-time rendering with less training time than NeRF and high-quality novel view synthesis, but SH encoding struggles with complex view-dependent effects.</cite> <cite id="d22d0fb6-0">Gaussian kernels cannot produce sharp angular cutoffs without many small primitives, limiting efficiency for specular materials; extensions include higher-dimensional Gaussians and conditional splatting (e.g., N-DG, 6DGS), and alternative kernels such as Beta, exponential, convex, and Student-t splats for edges and high-frequency detail.</cite> 

## 3DGS Extensions and Variants
Recent work extends 3DGS in several directions: improved sampling and filtering (Mip-Splatting), 2D radiance field formulations (2DGS), conditional/extended view bases (6DGS/N-DG), and alternative primitive distributions (Beta/convex/heavy-tailed) to better capture edges, flat surfaces, and high-frequency details or sharp specular highlights.<cite id="d22d0fb6-0">N-Dimensional Gaussians and 6D Gaussian Splatting extend encoding/view dependence; Beta and generalized exponential kernels, as well as Gabor splats, address sharp edges and high-frequency details; 3D convex and Student-t splats target flat surfaces and heavy tails.</cite> <cite id="d22d0fb6-3">Mip-Splatting limits Gaussian frequency with two sampling filters to approximate a box filter and reduce aliasing; 2DGS incorporates depth distortion and normal consistency for geometrically precise radiance fields.</cite> <cite id="10c2ba46-1">Dynamic Gaussian splatting and related methods extend 3DGS to videos by densifying and pruning Gaussians across frames, enabling dynamic scenes.</cite> 

## Diffusion Models for 3D: NeuS and Latent Diffusion/SDS
NeuS adapts NeRFs for surface reconstruction by encoding signed distance fields and adding surface regularization (Eikonal) to resolve ambiguous NeRF densities, yielding more regular and multi-view consistent surfaces; subsequent work adds SFM-based constraints, warping/normal regularization, and encodings to improve featureless regions and convergence.<cite id="064ae4cf-0">NeuS parameterizes NeRF density as a rapidly decreasing function of signed distance and enforces Eikonal consistency; later works incorporate SFM points, warping-based losses, normal regularization, and hybrid encodings to stabilize and improve surface reconstruction.</cite> 

Latent diffusion models (e.g., Stable Diffusion) and score-distillation sampling (SDS) enable training 3D representations with diffusion priors: DreamFusion optimizes a 3D scene by matching rendered views to a frozen text-to-image diffusion model's data distribution across timesteps, yielding 3D-awareness from 2D priors; multiview consistency is improved by conditioning diffusion on poses and by 3D-aware latent diffusion trained on large-scale 3D datasets.<cite id="064ae4cf-1">Latent diffusion and Stable Diffusion provide strong 2D generative priors; DreamFusion introduced SDS to train NeRFs by matching a pre-trained diffusion model's score, and many works follow with pose-conditioned diffusion, SDS variants, 3D-aware latent diffusion (Zero-1-to-3), or NeRF denoising in 3D space.</cite> <cite id="064ae4cf-4">Zero-1-to-3 and related methods re-train latent diffusion with camera embeddings to improve 3D consistency; other approaches denoise directly in 3D and supervise in 2D, or use diffusion as a 2D prior with joint NeRF optimization.</cite> <cite id="064ae4cf-3">SDS has been used to transfer diffusion models' 3D priors to NeRFs for text-guided editing and generation, building on CLIP and Stable Diffusion as denoising surrogates in latent space.</cite> 

## Combining 3DGS with Diffusion: SDS for Gaussians and DreamGaussian-style Pipelines
Several recent methods couple 3DGS with diffusion priors or use diffusion objectives directly to optimize Gaussian splatting, leveraging fast rendering to drive diffusion-based supervision and vice versa.<cite id="10c2ba46-4">Dynamic 3DGS uses deformation MLPs to move Gaussians in canonical space conditioned by time, enabling diffusion or other priors to guide optimization of explicit 3D splatting representations.</cite> <cite id="3bf3e346-0">SDS in DreamFusion optimizes a 3D scene by matching rendered images to a diffusion model's data distribution; 3DGS provides an efficient scene representation with anisotropic Gaussians, color, and opacity, rendered via tile-based compositing and Gaussian evaluation along rays.</cite> <cite id="3bf3e346-1">A quantitative evaluation of SDS-based text-to-3D reports trade-offs among viewpoint conditioning, timestep schedules, variational distillation, accelerated NeRFs, and improved efficiency using Gaussian Splatting; Title: NeuSD: Surface Completion With Multi-View Text-to-Image Diffusion
Snippet: Implicit surface reconstruction. Since its introduction, Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) [29] achieved impressive photorealistic results in novel view synthesis. However, NeRF is a poor representation for multi-view surface reconstruction, since its density field is highly ambiguous and ill-regularized. To adapt NeRF to surface reconstruction, several works [43,52,53] proposed Neural Implicit Surfaces. NeuS [43] specifically, implicitly parameterizes the NeRF density as a rapidly decreasing function of the signed distance to the surface (SDF), and maintains the consistency of the SDF using an Eikonal penalty [19]. Subsequent works proposed constraining the implicit surface using the points obtained with Structure-from-Motion [17], improving multi-view consistency via a warping-based loss term [14], improving performance in featureless areas via a normal-based regularization [42,44], or improving accuracy and convergence speed by using multi-resolution hash encoding [45] or hybrid representations of the surface [15]. While some works extended NeuS or NeRF to sparse image sampling [27,54], still the vast majority of the work is concerned with the reconstruction of the visible part of the surface only, and is not applicable as is in our setting with a partially observed surface. 2D diffusion for 3D generation. Diffusion generative networks started as a fascinating concept and gradually made their way to the state of art through the recent years. Their idea for inference is to start from the Gaussian noise and gradually remove noise with the help of the denoising network step-by-step in the so-called reverse diffusion process. 

The training samples for the denoising network are drawn from the forward diffusion process, where real photos are taken and the noise is added to them. The denoising network can be conditioned on additional input such as 2D segmentation mask [58], depth map, or text prompt. Latent diffusion [35] was the first work that achieved generating very high-quality 2D images from a general-case text prompt-conditioned generative image model. Later, Stable Diffusion extended this work and went viral by producing near-photorealistic samples from user requests.

With the emergence of text-to-image embedding models like CLIP (Radford et al., 2021), various methods have been proposed to train implicit networks that can generate new objects solely from text prompts (Jain et al., 2022). This trend has been accelerated with the advent of text-to-image diffusion generation models such as Stable Diffusion (Rombach et al., 2022), particularly through the score distillation sampling (SDS) (Poole et al., 2022) which conveys the representation of the text-to-image model to NeRF model. However, the challenge of editing pre-trained 3D implicit networks according to specific conditions still remains as an open problem due to the constraints of tasks: maintaining the integrity of the original 3D images while making desired modifications. As an initial work, several approaches (Wang et al., 2022;2023a) tried to edit the pre-trained NeRF models based on text conditions, utilizing the pre-trained CLIP model to fine-tune the parameters of NeRF models.

Snippet: NeRF [25] revolutionized novel view synthesis by implicitly training a multi-layer perception (MLP) to map 3D coordinates and view directions to color and density for volume rendering. While NeRF achieved state-of-the-art (SOTA) quality in NVS, it requires a dense set of input images to render photo-realistic views. Additionally, NeRF is scene-specific and cannot generalize to unseen targets. Many works incrementally improved NeRF in image quality [2,3,14,41], training time [14,37], and extended its capabilities [14,29,37,42]. We particularly focus on fewshot NVS, the problem of generating novel views of a scene when given one or a small number of source images. Pixel-NeRF [44] addressed this problem by training an image encoder with a NeRF module for scene-agnostic performance. GeNVS [6] utilizes a PixelNeRF-like pipeline to produce geometry-aware priors for a powerful diffusion model [20] for few-shot NVS. 

Diffusion models are now the standard in high-quality image generation [17,20,26,35,36] by iteratively denoising the raw image space. Latent diffusion models (LDMs) [21,31] instead iteratively denoise a latent space representation of data, efficiently generating high-quality images. Dream-Fusion [28] presented score-distillation-sampling (SDS), which showed that a web-scale text-to-image latent diffusion model [31] implicitly learned 3D information. SDS uses a fixed diffusion model as a critic to train a NeRF. SparseFusion [46] adopts SDS for few-shot NVS by conditioning the LDM with a view-aligned feature grid. Zero-1to-3 [24,32] extends the concept in SparseFusion to re-train the LDM with camera pose embeddings to produce better SDS scenes. DreamGaussian [38] uses the concept of SDS for Gaussian splatting [23] scenes instead of a NeRF.
