# 3D Gaussian Splatting and Diffusion: What They Are, How They Relate, and How They're Combined

## Overview: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) and Diffusion for 3D
3D Gaussian Splatting represents a scene as a collection of trainable 3D Gaussian primitives with per-Gaussian color and opacity, and renders them by projecting and compositing Gaussians on the image plane; this yields fast, explicit geometry and efficient differentiable rendering suitable for real-time novel view synthesis and 3D reconstruction.<cite id="d22d0fb6-1">3D Gaussian Splatting uses a collection of learnable 3D Gaussian ellipsoids, with mean, covariance (rotation+scale), opacity, and SH-encoded color; it projects Gaussians to 2D and composites them for rendering.</cite> <cite id="d22d0fb6-4">Compared to NeRF, 3DGS enables less training time and high-quality, real-time novel view synthesis; it uses an explicit, differentiable representation and alpha compositing to update Gaussian parameters by gradient descent.</cite> <cite id="10c2ba46-0">3DGS is a differentiable rendering pipeline that represents scenes with 3D Gaussians and splats them onto the image plane using an efficient, tile-based, depth-sorted alpha compositing approach; it can be >100× faster than volumetric NeRF-style rendering.</cite> 

Diffusion models have become a strong prior for 3D by training or distilling from 2D generative models, enabling text-to-3D and view-consistent synthesis; key techniques include NeuS's SDF-constrained density fields, latent diffusion, and score-distillation sampling (SDS) that optimizes 3D representations to match a diffusion model's data distribution.<cite id="064ae4cf-0">NeuS adapts NeRF by parameterizing density as a function of signed distance and adding Eikonal regularization for surface-consistent densities, and many works follow with encodings and hybrid surface constraints.</cite> <cite id="064ae4cf-1">Latent diffusion and Stable Diffusion set a strong 2D prior; DreamFusion introduced SDS to train NeRFs with a 2D diffusion critic, and many follow-ups use SDS, 3D-aware latent diffusion (e.g., Zero-1-to-3), or 2D diffusion priors with 3D optimization.</cite> <cite id="064ae4cf-3">ED-NeRF and related work transfer diffusion priors (e.g., CLIP-guided and Stable Diffusion) to NeRFs via SDS, enabling text-guided editing and generation.</cite> <cite id="064ae4cf-4">Diffusion models are now standard for high-quality image generation; DreamFusion's SDS transfers 3D-awareness from latent diffusion, and methods like SparseFusion and Zero-1-to-3 condition diffusion on 3D cues; DreamGaussian applies SDS directly to Gaussian splatting scenes.</cite> 

## 3D Gaussian Splatting: Representation, Rendering, and Training
3DGS parameterizes each Gaussian with position, anisotropic covariance (often via rotation quaternion and scale), opacity (alpha), and view-dependent color; color is commonly represented with spherical harmonics (SH) to compactly encode lighting/view-direction dependence.<cite id="d22d0fb6-1">Each Gaussian is parameterized by mean, covariance (q, s), opacity, and SH-based color; during rendering, Gaussians are projected to 2D and composited.</cite> <cite id="10c2ba46-0">A Gaussian is defined by mean, rotation, scale (forming a 3×3 covariance), color, and opacity; in camera space, the projected 2D covariance is used in efficient tile-based rasterization and alpha compositing.</cite> <cite id="10c2ba46-4">An alternative compact parameterization uses center, radius, and opacity, with color and opacity updated by gradient descent to minimize pixel differences between rendered and ground-truth images.</cite> 

Rendering proceeds by rasterizing tiles on the image plane and accumulating Gaussian contributions in depth order with alpha compositing; because Gaussians are explicit primitives, there is no NeRF-style MLP evaluation at render time, enabling fast inference and training throughput.<cite id="10c2ba46-0">Tile-based rasterization (e.g., 16×16) finds depth-sorted influencing Gaussians and composites them efficiently; this avoids volumetric ray-marching and is extremely fast compared to NeRF-style rendering.</cite> <cite id="10c2ba46-4">3DGS allows differentiable projection and alpha blending, enabling closed-form or learned per-Gaussian functions to be optimized by backpropagation to minimize rendered–image error.</cite> 

Training optimizes Gaussian parameters (means, covariance, color, opacity) to minimize L1/L2 or perceptual losses between multi-view renderings and observations; unlike NeRF, there is no implicit MLP at query time, but the number of Gaussians and their parameters drive memory and compute, especially for high-quality scenes and large views.<cite id="10c2ba46-4">The eight parameterized values (position, radius, RGB, opacity) are updated via gradient descent to reduce rendered–image differences.</cite> <cite id="10c2ba46-2">Per-Gaussian parameters include rotation (quaternion), scale, opacity, and SH coefficients; 3DGS avoids MLP evaluation at render time, improving speed and quality, but explicit representations increase parameter count and memory pressure as Gaussians increase for higher quality.</cite> 

Key advantages and limitations of 3DGS include real-time rendering and explicit geometry, but challenges such as aliasing, view-dependent color fidelity with SH bases, and efficiency for specular/sharp-angled surfaces motivate extensions and alternative kernels.<cite id="d22d0fb6-3">3DGS achieves real-time rendering with less training time than NeRF and high-quality novel view synthesis, but SH encoding struggles with complex view-dependent effects.</cite> <cite id="d22d0fb6-0">Gaussian kernels cannot produce sharp angular cutoffs without many small primitives, limiting efficiency for specular materials; extensions include higher-dimensional Gaussians and conditional splatting (e.g., N-DG, 6DGS), and alternative kernels such as Beta, exponential, convex, and Student-t splats for edges and high-frequency detail.</cite> 

## 3DGS Extensions and Variants
Recent work extends 3DGS in several directions: improved sampling and filtering (Mip-Splatting), 2D radiance field formulations (2DGS), conditional/extended view bases (6DGS/N-DG), and alternative primitive distributions (Beta/convex/heavy-tailed) to better capture edges, flat surfaces, and high-frequency details or sharp specular highlights.<cite id="d22d0fb6-0">N-Dimensional Gaussians and 6D Gaussian Splatting extend encoding/view dependence; Beta and generalized exponential kernels, as well as Gabor splats, address sharp edges and high-frequency details; 3D convex and Student-t splats target flat surfaces and heavy tails.</cite> <cite id="d22d0fb6-3">Mip-Splatting limits Gaussian frequency with two sampling filters to approximate a box filter and reduce aliasing; 2DGS incorporates depth distortion and normal consistency for geometrically precise radiance fields.</cite> <cite id="10c2ba46-1">Dynamic Gaussian splatting and related methods extend 3DGS to videos by densifying and pruning Gaussians across frames, enabling dynamic scenes.</cite> 

## Diffusion Models for 3D: NeuS and Latent Diffusion/SDS
NeuS adapts NeRFs for surface reconstruction by encoding signed distance fields and adding surface regularization (Eikonal) to resolve ambiguous NeRF densities, yielding more regular and multi-view consistent surfaces; subsequent work adds SFM-based constraints, warping/normal regularization, and encodings to improve featureless regions and convergence.<cite id="064ae4cf-0">NeuS parameterizes NeRF density as a rapidly decreasing function of signed distance and enforces Eikonal consistency; later works incorporate SFM points, warping-based losses, normal regularization, and hybrid encodings to stabilize and improve surface reconstruction.</cite> 

Latent diffusion models (e.g., Stable Diffusion) and score-distillation sampling (SDS) enable training 3D representations with diffusion priors: DreamFusion optimizes a 3D scene by matching rendered views to a frozen text-to-image diffusion model's data distribution across timesteps, yielding 3D-awareness from 2D priors; multiview consistency is improved by conditioning diffusion on poses and by 3D-aware latent diffusion trained on large-scale 3D datasets.<cite id="064ae4cf-1">Latent diffusion and Stable Diffusion provide strong 2D generative priors; DreamFusion introduced SDS to train NeRFs by matching a pre-trained diffusion model's score, and many works follow with pose-conditioned diffusion, SDS variants, 3D-aware latent diffusion (Zero-1-to-3), or NeRF denoising in 3D space.</cite> <cite id="064ae4cf-4">Zero-1-to-3 and related methods re-train latent diffusion with camera embeddings to improve 3D consistency; other approaches denoise directly in 3D and supervise in 2D, or use diffusion as a 2D prior with joint NeRF optimization.</cite> <cite id="064ae4cf-3">SDS has been used to transfer diffusion models' 3D priors to NeRFs for text-guided editing and generation, building on CLIP and Stable Diffusion as denoising surrogates in latent space.</cite> 

## Combining 3DGS with Diffusion: SDS for Gaussians and DreamGaussian-style Pipelines
Several recent methods couple 3DGS with diffusion priors or use diffusion objectives directly to optimize Gaussian splatting, leveraging fast rendering to drive diffusion-based supervision and vice versa.<cite id="10c2ba46-4">Dynamic 3DGS uses deformation MLPs to move Gaussians in canonical space conditioned by time, enabling diffusion or other priors to guide optimization of explicit 3D splatting representations.</cite> <cite id="3bf3e346-0">SDS in DreamFusion optimizes a 3D scene by matching rendered images to a diffusion model's data distribution; 3DGS provides an efficient scene representation with anisotropic Gaussians, color, and opacity, rendered via tile-based compositing and Gaussian evaluation along rays.</cite> <cite id="3bf3e346-1">A quantitative evaluation of SDS-based text-to-3D reports trade-offs among viewpoint conditioning, timestep schedules, variational distillation, accelerated NeRFs, and improved efficiency using Gaussian Splatting; DreamGaussian and its multiview variant are efficient but lag on other metrics, while other methods report efficiency and quality trade-offs.</cite> <cite id="3bf3e346-2">GaussianDiffusion applies Gaussian splatting across the full 3D generation process and contrasts with DreamGaussian (an SDS-based concurrent line), drawing on perturbative noise alignment and Langevin sampling to recover structure from Gaussian noise; it positions 3DGS as a strong 3D generator under diffusion supervision.</cite> <cite id="3bf3e346-3">DreamGaussian initializes 3D Gaussians from a single image and iteratively optimizes them by using a finetuned 2D diffusion prior (e.g., Zero123XL) to evaluate and improve multi-view renderings, achieving rapid 3D reconstruction with diffusion guidance.</cite> <cite id="3bf3e346-4">SC4D and related work detail SDS losses using a diffusion model (e.g., Zero123) and 3DGS rendering with alpha blending and SH color, and describe densification/pruning in 3DGS to fit diverse scenes; SC-GS decouples appearance and motion via control points and MLP-based warping for dynamic 4D generation.</cite> 

These combinations typically proceed by:
- Rendering candidate 3DGS scenes and computing diffusion losses (e.g., SDS) against a frozen or trainable 2D diffusion prior, using multi-view supervision for consistency.<cite id="3bf3e346-0">SDS optimizes 3D parameters to match a diffusion model's score at multiple timesteps and camera poses, aligning rendered views with the diffusion model's learned 2D image distribution.</cite> <cite id="3bf3e346-1">Improvements include better conditioning (text/poses), timestep schedules, and using 3DGS for efficiency in the distillation loop.</cite> 
- Leveraging 3DGS's fast forward pass to drive diffusion denoising steps or to condition diffusion models on scene structure, enabling text-to-3D or view-consistent generation with controllable geometry and texture.<cite id="3bf3e346-3">DreamGaussian integrates a finetuned diffusion model as a prior to refine Gaussian noise into detailed views, iteratively optimizing Gaussians across viewpoints to match the diffusion-guided priors.</cite> <cite id="3bf3e346-2">GaussianDiffusion spans the full 3D generation pipeline with 3DGS and diffusion-based denoising, addressing OOD noise between 3D renderings and 2D diffusion inputs via perturbative matching and Langevin sampling.</cite> 

## Practical Trade-offs and When to Use Which
3DGS excels at fast, explicit geometry and real-time rendering, but its quality can be limited by SH color encoding for complex view dependence, aliasing, and inefficiency for specular highlights without many small Gaussians; alternative kernels and higher-dimensional/conditional encodings mitigate some issues.<cite id="d22d0fb6-3">Compared to NeRF, 3DGS reduces training time and supports real-time synthesis, yet SH limitations hinder complex view effects.</cite> <cite id="d22d0fb6-0">Gaussian primitives struggle with sharp angular cutoffs; N-DG/6DGS and alternative kernels (exponential, Beta, convex, Student-t, Gabor) target edges, flat surfaces, heavy tails, and high-frequency details.</cite> <cite id="d22d0fb6-3">Mip-Splatting and 2DGS reduce aliasing and improve geometric fidelity, respectively, showing clear engineering benefits for challenging viewpoints or close-ups.</cite> 

Diffusion-based 3D methods offer strong generative priors and text conditioning, but often require multi-view optimization to ensure consistency and can be slower than closed-form 3DGS rendering; SDS-based pipelines and 3D-aware latent diffusion reduce the gap, and coupling to 3DGS provides efficiency gains for training and inference loops.<cite id="064ae4cf-1">Latent diffusion and SDS enable text-guided 3D, but there is no direct 3D ground truth; many methods use 2D diffusion as a prior and enforce 3D consistency via multi-view training or 3D-aware conditioning.</cite> <cite id="3bf3e346-1">A survey of SDS-based text-to-3D highlights efficiency gains from 3DGS and trade-offs in quality and speed across methods; DreamGaussian and multiview variants are the most efficient but underperform on other metrics, while other methods balance efficiency and quality differently.</cite> <cite id="3bf3e346-2">GaussianDiffusion argues that 3DGS can be applied across the full diffusion pipeline to improve structure recovery and address noise distribution mismatches with appropriate perturbation and sampling strategies.</cite> 

## Dynamic Scenes and Control
Dynamic 3DGS extends to videos by learning deformation fields or control grids that warp a canonical Gaussian splat, enabling consistent motion while keeping the splat's per-Gaussian color/opacity optimized for appearance changes across time.<cite id="10c2ba46-4">Dynamic 3DGS learns a deformation MLP that predicts offsets from canonical positions given time, allowing Gaussians to be transformed per frame and re-rasterized with the same efficient compositing.</cite> <cite id="3bf3e346-4">SC-GS decouples appearance (3DGS) and motion (control points + MLP) via linear blend skinning, with densification/pruning and per-Gaussian alpha blending to maintain fidelity across frames; this supports sparse-control video-to-4D generation and motion transfer.</cite> 

## Summary and Pointers
- 3DGS: fast, explicit, and high-quality; trainable per-Gaussian attributes and efficient tile-based rendering enable real-time NVS and 3D reconstruction, with extensions for aliasing, view dependence, and dynamics.<cite id="d22d0fb6-1">3DGS composes anisotropic Gaussians with SH color and efficient projection/compositing.</cite> <cite id="10c2ba46-0">Tile-based Gaussian splatting with depth-sorted compositing is much faster than NeRF ray-marching.</cite> <cite id="d22d0fb6-3">Mip-Splatting and 2DGS address aliasing and geometric precision; 6DGS/N-DG expand view encodings.</cite> 
- Diffusion for 3D: NeuS regularizes implicit surfaces; latent diffusion and SDS transfer 3D-awareness from 2D priors; multiview training and 3D-aware conditioning improve consistency and text control.<cite id="064ae4cf-0">NeuS adds SDF and Eikonal constraints to stabilize surfaces.</cite> <cite id="064ae4cf-1">SDS and 3D-aware latent diffusion underlie many text-to-3D systems.</cite> <cite id="064ae4cf-4">Zero-1-to-3 and related pipelines condition diffusion on camera poses to improve view consistency.</cite> 
- 3DGS + diffusion: DreamFusion-style SDS, DreamGaussian, and GaussianDiffusion couple diffusion priors with Gaussian splatting to optimize structure and appearance efficiently; trade-offs exist between speed and fidelity across methods.<cite id="3bf3e346-0">SDS aligns rendered 3DGS images to a diffusion model's data distribution across timesteps.</cite> <cite id="3bf3e346-3">DreamGaussian iteratively refines Gaussians with a finetuned diffusion prior across views for rapid 3D reconstruction.</cite> <cite id="3bf3e346-2">GaussianDiffusion applies splatting across the full diffusion pipeline with structured noise matching and sampling to recover 3D structure efficiently.</cite> <cite id="3bf3e346-1">Comparative studies report efficiency-quality trade-offs; 3DGS-based distillation can be fastest but may lag in other metrics without additional modeling.</cite> 

Open gaps and next steps: For production use, consult the original 3DGS paper for initialization details (e.g., COLMAP-based pose estimation and per-Gaussian MLPs or features), and experiment with Mip-Splatting or 2DGS for challenging viewpoints and close-ups. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) (Kerbl et al., 2023) achieved real-time rendering through explicit anisotropic Gaussian primitives. While elegant, Gaussian distributions cannot produce sharp angular cutoffs without many small primitives, limiting efficiency for specular materials.

documents.snippet:
3D Gaussian splatting [Kerbl et al. 2023] is a differentiable rendering pipeline that represents a scene as a collection of 3D Gaussians and "splats" them onto the image plane. Concretely, a 3D scene is represented by 3D Gaussians, G, with each Gaussian parameterized by its mean  ∈ R 3 , rotation  ∈ R 3×3 , scale  ∈ R 3 , color  ∈ R 3 , and opacity  ∈ R. The scale and rotation can be composed into a 3D covariance matrix, Σ =     , where  is the 3 × 3 diagonal scaling matrix. 

Given 3D Gaussians G and a camera viewing transformation  , the covariance matrix in camera coordinates can be computed as Σ ′ =  Σ    , where  is the Jacobian of the approximatelyaffine projective transformation. Given camera-aligned Gaussians, the pipeline executes an efficient differentiable tile-based rasterization -the image is divided into tiles 16 × 16, and for each tile, the influencing Gaussians are sorted by depth and alpha-composited in the image plane. In contrast to volumetric rendering approaches [Mildenhall et al. 2020], Gaussian Splatting is extremely efficient and often renders over 100 times faster than its volumetric counterpart.

documents.title: Decomposing Densification in Gaussian Splatting for Faster 3D Scene Reconstruction
documents.snippet:
3D Gaussian Splatting 3D Gaussian Splatting (Kerbl et al. 2023) has emerged as a compelling approach for 3D scene reconstruction, enabling real-time rendering while preserving photorealistic quality. Unlike implicit neural fields (e.g., NeRF (Mildenhall et al. 2020)) that rely on computationally intensive ray marching for volume rendering, 3DGS formulates scenes as collections of anisotropic Gaussian primitives with full covariance matrices. This explicit representation allows efficient tilebased rasterization through differentiable projection and alpha blending, bypassing the limitations of neural rendering pipelines. 

In recent years, there has been a surge in research efforts that have pushed forward the technological frontiers of 3DGS across multiple domains, with particularly transformative impacts on human avatar generation (Cha, Lee, and Joo 2024;Jiang et al. 2024;Lyu et al. 2024;Zielonka et al. 2025), Autonomous Driving (Chen et al. 2024;Hess et al. 2024;Lei et al. 2025;Zhou et al. 2024), and photorealistic scene renderings (Chao et al. 2024;Cheng et al. 2024;Xie et al. 2024;Xu, Mei, and Patel 2024).

3D Gaussian Splatting [22] is state-of-the-art differentiable rendering method representing 3D scenes with trainable 3D Gaussian primitives. Each 3D Gaussian has 59 parameters: center position  ∈ R 3 ,  ∈ R 3 controlling its spatial extent, rotation represented by  ∈ R 4 ,  that determines transparency, and ℎ ℎ (SH) coefficients which encodes view-dependent color. The SH models how a point's color changes with viewing direction; A common degree of  = 3 yields 16 coefficients per color channel and 48 parameters in total for RGB. 

3DGS renders images by projecting 3D Gaussians onto a 2D plane and accumulating colors in depth order. The training process minimizes the difference between rendered images and ground-truth images via backpropagation (refer to Section 2.4). Unlike NeRF, 3DGS uses an explicit representation, eliminating the need for MLP computation during rendering and training, leading to faster speeds and higher visual quality. However, this explicit representation significantly increases the number of required parameters, leading to a much higher memory footprint for both rendering and training. The number of Gaussians directly determines the parameter count. More Gaussians are necessary for higher rendering quality, increasing memory pressure.

documents.snippet: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) have revolutionized 3D scene modeling and rendering. Introduced by [Mildenhall et al. 2021], NeRF synthesizes photorealistic scenes from sparse images by modeling volumetric density and color, further enhanced by innovations like mip-nerf [Barron et al. 2021] and TensoRF [Chen et al. 2022]. 3D Gaussian Splatting, detailed by [Kerbl et al. 2023] and expanded upon in work [Luiten et al. 2024] on dynamic 3D Gaussians, optimizes the rendering of point clouds with Gaussian kernels for real-time applications. These developments continue to advance the field, highlighting the dynamic growth and application breadth of these technologies. Additional contributions by [Tang et al. 2023b] and others [Fang et al. 2022] underscore the ongoing enhancements and versatility of 3DGS in handling increasingly complex rendering tasks. Noting the advantages of 3D Gaussian Splatting in rendering speed and quality, our paper chooses it as a representation for building semantic field.

Title: NeuSD: Surface Completion With Multi-View Text-to-Image Diffusion
Snippet: Implicit surface reconstruction. Since its introduction, Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) [29] achieved impressive photorealistic results in novel view synthesis. However, NeRF is a poor representation for multi-view surface reconstruction, since its density field is highly ambiguous and ill-regularized. To adapt NeRF to surface reconstruction, several works [43,52,53] proposed Neural Implicit Surfaces. NeuS [43] specifically, implicitly parameterizes the NeRF density as a rapidly decreasing function of the signed distance to the surface (SDF), and maintains the consistency of the SDF using an Eikonal penalty [19]. Subsequent works proposed constraining the implicit surface using the points obtained with Structure-from-Motion [17], improving multi-view consistency via a warping-based loss term [14], improving performance in featureless areas via a normal-based regularization [42,44], or improving accuracy and convergence speed by using multi-resolution hash encoding [45] or hybrid representations of the surface [15]. While some works extended NeuS or NeRF to sparse image sampling [27,54], still the vast majority of the work is concerned with the reconstruction of the visible part of the surface only, and is not applicable as is in our setting with a partially observed surface. 2D diffusion for 3D generation. Diffusion generative networks started as a fascinating concept and gradually made their way to the state of art through the recent years. Their idea for inference is to start from the Gaussian noise and gradually remove noise with the help of the denoising network step-by-step in the so-called reverse diffusion process. 

The training samples for the denoising network are drawn from the forward diffusion process, where real photos are taken and the noise is added to them. The denoising network can be conditioned on additional input such as 2D segmentation mask [58], depth map, or text prompt. Latent diffusion [35] was the first work that achieved generating very high-quality 2D images from a general-case text prompt-conditioned generative image model. Later, Stable Diffusion extended this work and went viral by producing near-photorealistic samples from user requests.

Title: NViST: In the Wild New View Synthesis from a Single Image with Transformers
Snippet: Several approaches use the triplane representation to learn to generate 3d implicit representations from ImageNet [64,70,74,80]. 

Learning multiple scenes using NeRF: Generalising NeRFs to multiple scenes remains a challenging problem. Several methods associate 2D features with the target views [15,19,31,35,65,85,91,99], while others condition the network on latent vectors with a shared MLP across the dataset [3,27,32,36,54,63]. Adding an adversarial loss to NeRF leads to 3D-aware GANs, which allow consis- tent rendering from different viewpoints [8,11,12,44,73]. 

Most approaches that use a single input image require aligned datasets like ShapeNet [14,79] or FFHQ [40], and fail to deal with scale ambiguities or diverse backgrounds. Diffusion for NVS: Latent diffusion [66] and its opensource release Stable Diffusion have transformed the field of image generation. However, applying diffusion models to learn 3D implicit representations is not straightforward as there is no access to 3D ground-truth. 3DiM [94] proposes a pose-conditioned image-to-image approach. Dreamfusion [60] introduced score distillation sampling (SDS) to train NeRF with a 2D diffusion model. SDS has been used in many follow-up works [51,77,83,88,93]. Fine-tuning Stable Diffusion on a large-scale synthetic dataset [21] allows diffusion models to be 3D-aware such as Zero-1-to-3 and its follow-ups [48,49,61,76]. Other approaches denoise directly in 3D and supervise the model in 2D space after rendering, [1,2,13,28,39,82,84], use the 2D diffusion model as a prior [22], or optimise NeRF jointly and regard it as the ground truth [17]. Similar to latent diffusion [5,41,74] adopt 2-stage training. 3D Representation with Transformers: Geometry-free methods employing transformer architectures have been explored as seen in [43,[67][68][69].

Title: ED-NeRF: Efficient Text-Guided Editing of 3D Scene With Latent Space NeRF
Snippet: In recent years, the development of neural implicit representation for embedding three-dimensional images in neural networks has seen remarkable progress. This advancement has made it possible to render images from all angles using only a limited set of training viewpoints. Starting with the seminar work known as the Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) (Mildenhall et al., 2021), which trained radiance fields using a simple MLP network, various improved techniques (Barron et al., 2021;Reiser et al., 2021;Müller et al., 2022) based on advanced network architectures or modified encoding have been proposed. Alternatively, several methods (Sun et al., 2022;Fridovich-Keil et al., 2022;Karnewar et al., 2022;Chen et al., 2022) proposed to directly optimize voxel points serving as sources for rendering, bypassing the traditional approach of encapsulating all information within implicit networks. These methods have gained prominence for their ability to train radiance fields in a remarkably short time. In addition to representing existing 2D image data in the 3D space, recent research has explored expanded approaches for generating entirely novel 3D objects. With the emergence of text-to-image embedding models like CLIP (Radford et al., 2021), various methods have been proposed to train implicit networks that can generate new objects solely from text prompts (Jain et al., 2022). This trend has been accelerated with the advent of text-to-image diffusion generation models such as Stable Diffusion (Rombach et al., 2022), particularly through the score distillation sampling (SDS) (Poole et al., 2022) which conveys the representation of the text-to-image model to NeRF model. However, the challenge of editing pre-trained 3D implicit networks according to specific conditions still remains as an open problem due to the constraints of tasks: maintaining the integrity of the original 3D images while making desired modifications. As an initial work, several approaches (Wang et al., 2022;2023a) tried to edit the pre-trained NeRF models based on text conditions, utilizing the pre-trained CLIP model to fine-tune the parameters of NeRF models.

Title: CrossModalityDiffusion: Multi-Modal Novel View Synthesis with Unified Intermediate Representation
Snippet: NeRF [25] revolutionized novel view synthesis by implicitly training a multi-layer perception (MLP) to map 3D coordinates and view directions to color and density for volume rendering. While NeRF achieved state-of-the-art (SOTA) quality in NVS, it requires a dense set of input images to render photo-realistic views. Additionally, NeRF is scene-specific and cannot generalize to unseen targets. Many works incrementally improved NeRF in image quality [2,3,14,41], training time [14,37], and extended its capabilities [14,29,37,42]. We particularly focus on fewshot NVS, the problem of generating novel views of a scene when given one or a small number of source images. Pixel-NeRF [44] addressed this problem by training an image encoder with a NeRF module for scene-agnostic performance. GeNVS [6] utilizes a PixelNeRF-like pipeline to produce geometry-aware priors for a powerful diffusion model [20] for few-shot NVS. 

Diffusion models are now the standard in high-quality image generation [17,20,26,35,36] by iteratively denoising the raw image space. Latent diffusion models (LDMs) [21,31] instead iteratively denoise a latent space representation of data, efficiently generating high-quality images. Dream-Fusion [28] presented score-distillation-sampling (SDS), which showed that a web-scale text-to-image latent diffusion model [31] implicitly learned 3D information. SDS uses a fixed diffusion model as a critic to train a NeRF. SparseFusion [46] adopts SDS for few-shot NVS by conditioning the LDM with a view-aligned feature grid. Zero-1to-3 [24,32] extends the concept in SparseFusion to re-train the LDM with camera pose embeddings to produce better SDS scenes. DreamGaussian [38] uses the concept of SDS for Gaussian splatting [23] scenes instead of a NeRF.

documents.title: CrossModalityDiffusion: Multi-Modal Novel View Synthesis with Unified Intermediate Representation
documents.snippet:
NeRF [25] revolutionized novel view synthesis by implicitly training a multi-layer perception (MLP) to map 3D coordinates and view directions to color and density for volume rendering. While NeRF achieved state-of-the-art (SOTA) quality in NVS, it requires a dense set of input images to render photo-realistic views. Additionally, NeRF is scene-specific and cannot generalize to unseen targets. Many works incrementally improved NeRF in image quality [2,3,14,41], training time [14,37], and extended its capabilities [14,29,37,42]. We particularly focus on fewshot NVS, the problem of generating novel views of a scene when given one or a small number of source images. Pixel-NeRF [44] addressed this problem by training an image encoder with a NeRF module for scene-agnostic performance. GeNVS [6] utilizes a PixelNeRF-like pipeline to produce geometry-aware priors for a powerful diffusion model [20] for few-shot NVS. 

Diffusion models are now the standard in high-quality image generation [17,20,26,35,36] by iteratively denoising the raw image space. Latent diffusion models (LDMs) [21,31] instead iteratively denoise a latent space representation of data, efficiently generating high-quality images. Dream-Fusion [28] presented score-distillation-sampling (SDS), which showed that a web-scale text-to-image latent diffusion model [31] implicitly learned 3D information. SDS uses a fixed diffusion model as a critic to train a NeRF. SparseFusion [46] adopts SDS for few-shot NVS by conditioning the LDM with a view-aligned feature grid. Zero-1to-3 [24,32] extends the concept in SparseFusion to re-train the LDM with camera pose embeddings to produce better SDS scenes. DreamGaussian [38] uses the concept of SDS for Gaussian splatting [23] scenes instead of a NeRF.

Title: GaussianDiffusion: 3D Gaussian Splatting for Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models with Structured Noise
Snippet: Dreamfusion [26] pioneered the use of score distillation sampling (SDS) to learn 3D scenes from frozen 2D diffusion models. SJC [45] addressed the Out-of-Distribution (OOD) problem between standard normal inputs of 2D diffusion models and 3D rendered images by introducing secondary noise on 3D rendered images through a perturbation process. 3DFuse [35] serves as the baseline for our work, guiding the 3D model generation direction in multiple stages, from coarse to fine, while using view-specific depth as a condition and employing ControlNet [50] to guide the generation direction of the Diffusion model. TANGO [13] transfers the appearance style of a given 3D shape according to a text prompt in a photorealistic manner. However, the method requires a 3D model as input. Dream-Gaussian [42] is our concurrent work, which is based on SDS [26], while we draw inspiration from SJC [45], and apply score function and Langevin sampling method [38] to recover structure knowledge from Gaussian noise. Our work, GaussianDiffusion, applies Gaussian splatting across the entire spectrum of 3D generation process. Latest text-to-3D works [3,10,15,44,46,49,51] produce realistic, multiview consistent object geometry and color from a given text prompt, unfortunately, NeRF-based generation is timeconsuming, and cannot meet industrial needs.

Title: DreamSat: Towards a General 3D Model for Novel View Synthesis of Space Objects
Snippet: The DreamGaussian framework [13] leverages generative 3D Gaussian splatting, which uses Gaussian functions to represent the 3D space of an object. This method provides a continuous representation, enhancing the fidelity and texture of the reconstructed images. The framework integrates the finetuned Zero123XL model as a 2D diffusion prior, which guides the generation process by refining the Gaussian noise into detailed images. The DreamGaussian pipeline first initialize a set of 3D Gaussians based on the input image. Then, it repeats the following process until convergence of rendering the Gaussians from multiple viewpoints, using the 2D diffusion prior (Zero123XL) to evaluate and improve the rendered views, and optimizing the 3D Gaussians based on the feedback from the diffusion prior. This approach allows for rapid 3D reconstruction while leveraging the power of large-scale 2D diffusion models.

problem: has anyone propose metric like to judge whether a coding LLM has some knowledge
final_response:
Yes. Researchers have proposed a range of benchmarks and metrics to assess whether a coding LLM “has some knowledge,” including functional correctness on code-generation tasks, competition-level problem solving, bug-fixing and repository-issue resolution, translation and tool-use, as well as contamination-aware and retrieval-augmented evaluations that diagnose whether performance reflects genuine knowledge rather than memorization. Below is a synthesis of the main approaches and how they measure knowledge.

# What “knowledge” is being measured
In code LLMs, “knowledge” spans (a) factual and procedural knowledge about programming languages, libraries, and APIs; (b) software engineering expertise (e.g., debugging, refactoring, testing, and planning across files); and (c) general world knowledge used in code contexts. Benchmarks operationalize these via task designs and scoring functions such as functional correctness, pass@k, resolution rates, and contamination-aware checks. <cite id="6b1cb89c-0">Knowledge-intensive benchmarks like MMLU show how broad subject knowledge is measured via QA, and this paradigm has influenced code-focused knowledge evaluations</cite>.

# Task-level metrics for software knowledge and reasoning
- Functional correctness and pass@k: Many code benchmarks evaluate whether generated code passes unit tests, using accuracy-like functional-correctness metrics and sampling-based pass@k to estimate the probability that at least one of k sampled solutions passes all tests. <cite id="6b1cb89c-1">Functional correctness is the primary metric for code generation benchmarks, while pass@k is used to quantify success likelihood across multiple attempts without requiring exact reference matching</cite>. <cite id="96149ca2-0">HumanEval uses pass@1 as the primary metric; extensions and surveys summarize multilingual and class-level code benchmarks with similar functional-correctness scoring</cite>. <cite id="96149ca2-3">Surveys organize results by benchmark and report pass@1/10/100 on HumanEval, highlighting that pass@k provides a more robust aggregate measure than single-attempt scores</cite>. These metrics test practical coding knowledge by requiring tests to validate behavior, not just syntax.

- Competition-level problem solving: To probe deeper algorithmic and software knowledge, newer benchmarks target competitive programming-style problems and use Elo-like or grading-style metrics. <cite id="498cf5f3-0">TACO, CodeELO, Probench, and USACO aim to evaluate complex reasoning in competitive coding, moving beyond simple function generation to higher-discriminative tasks; existing code benchmarks like HumanEval/MBPP/DS-1000 are deemed insufficient for advanced reasoning</cite>. These setups assess algorithmic knowledge, multi-step planning, and library usage under constraints, often with adaptive difficulty or competition-level leaderboards.

- Bug fixing and repository-issue resolution: Real-world bug fixing requires software knowledge across files, tests, and context. <cite id="5e1b5f81-3">SWE-bench evaluates resolving GitHub issues by modifying code bases with patches and tests; variants like SWE-bench Lite (300 issues) and SWE-bench Verified (500 issues with strong tests) report resolution rates as the primary metric</cite>. <cite id="5e1b5f81-0">SWE-Bench-Verified is commonly used to measure the percentage of issues resolved, but leakage from training data can inflate scores if models memorize examples rather than learn generalizable reasoning</cite>. <cite id="5e1b5f81-2">Analyses show significant data-quality and leakage issues: 32.67% of successes may involve solution leakage and 31.08% are suspicious due to weak tests; over 94% of issues predate LLM knowledge cutoffs, raising the risk that high resolution rates reflect memorization</cite>. These results motivate stronger, contamination-aware evaluation.

- Translation and tool-use: Cross-language translation benchmarks test knowledge of language semantics and APIs. <cite id="498cf5f3-4">CodeLingua and TransCoder evaluate code translation between languages, using execution or equivalence metrics to assess whether models truly understand source and target language behaviors and libraries</cite>. Tool-use benchmarks (e.g., ToolBench/API-Bank) measure knowledge of APIs and the ability to chain tools, often with success rates or API-call accuracy as metrics. <cite id="6b1cb89c-2">ToolBench and API-Bank provide structured assessments of models' abilities to interact with external tools and APIs</cite>.

- Difficulty gradients and error analyses: Metrics that separate language syntax vs. task understanding, and drill down into error types, help diagnose knowledge gaps. <cite id="96149ca2-1">Combining pass rate with syntax error rates (compilation/runtime) can distinguish language-knowledge deficits from task misunderstandings, and manual error audits reveal weak spots and even benchmark issues</cite>. Harder suites like MHPP probe multi-step reasoning and coding knowledge. <cite id="96149ca2-2">MHPP contains 210 problems emphasizing multi-step reasoning and specification understanding; many models strong on HumanEval struggle on MHPP, exposing limitations in deeper coding knowledge</cite>.

# Knowledge-grounded and retrieval-augmented evaluations
- Retrieval relevance and correctness with/without retrieval: Retrieval-augmented coding (RAG) frameworks introduce metrics that measure whether bringing in relevant documents improves code correctness, and how well the model selects relevant sources. <cite id="6b1cb89c-1">Adversarial filtering and adaptive benchmarks highlight that some apparent reasoning may stem from contamination or memorization; retrieval-augmented setups can be paired with functional-correctness tests to isolate whether added knowledge yields correct patches</cite>. <cite id="5e1b5f81-0">Analyses of SWE-Bench-Verified emphasize distinguishing genuine generalization from memorized examples; retrieval-based evaluations can be designed to penalize verbatim copying and reward reasoning over retrieved context</cite>. - Interactive and sequential reasoning: Some benchmarks assess whether models can plan and adjust using feedback, a form of knowledge use over steps. <cite id="498cf5f3-2">AQA-Bench targets sequential reasoning, and the literature notes that one-round coding QA benchmarks miss planning capabilities; agentic and interactive coding tasks with iterative feedback better capture knowledge-driven planning and tool use</cite>. These setups often use stepwise success rates or path-based correctness to measure whether knowledge is applied and adapted over time.

# Diagnostics for internal knowledge and memorization
- Contamination-aware and dynamic benchmarks: To separate true knowledge from training data memory, evaluations use time-based or leakage-resilient designs. <cite id="6b1cb89c-1">Contamination via time can inflate scores; benchmarks that split problems temporally or adversarially filter seen data help measure whether models learn to solve unseen problems rather than recall solutions</cite>. <cite id="96149ca2-4">Dynamic benchmarking frameworks periodically refresh problems and report stability of performance to detect overfitting to fixed test sets</cite>.

- Leakage audits on bug-fixing datasets: Repository-level benchmarks are particularly susceptible to leakage because training data may contain internet code. <cite id="5e1b5f81-0">Studies explicitly test whether top models memorize SWE-Bench-Verified patterns, even under handicapped inputs, to distinguish benchmark knowledge from genuine reasoning</cite>. <cite id="5e1b5f81-2">Systematic audits show high rates of solution leakage and weak test cases in SWE-bench variants, causing reported resolution rates to drop substantially when filtering out problematic instances</cite>. These audits function as internal diagnostics of memorization versus learned generalization.

- Data and code-specific contamination tests: Beyond time splits, contamination diagnostics probe whether models copy solutions, reproduce docstrings, or exploit training set trivia. <cite id="6b1cb89c-1">Adversarial filtering and adaptive benchmarks are used to detect spurious correlations and contamination-driven performance, offering methodological guardrails for knowledge evaluations</cite>. Models that rely on contamination may pass functional tests but fail decontaminated or adversarial subsets, revealing the absence of robust internalized knowledge.

# Putting it together: practical ways to judge “has some knowledge”
- For language and API knowledge: Use functional-correctness benchmarks like HumanEval/MBPP and harder variants like MHPP or class-level/translation suites; track pass@1/10/100 and error breakdowns to see if models handle specifications, libraries, and edge cases beyond simple templates. <cite id="96149ca2-0">HumanEval’s pass@1 and multilingual extensions provide a baseline for language and algorithmic knowledge</cite> <cite id="96149ca2-2">MHPP exposes deeper reasoning and coding-knowledge gaps that pass HumanEval</cite> <cite id="498cf5f3-4">CodeLingua/TransCoder test cross-language translation knowledge</cite>.

- For software engineering knowledge: Use bug-fixing and issue-resolution benchmarks (SWE-bench and variants) with resolution-rate metrics, but apply contamination-aware and dynamic evaluations to avoid inflated scores from memorization. <cite id="5e1b5f81-3">Resolution rate on SWE-bench variants is the primary metric</cite> <cite id="5e1b5f81-2">Data-quality and leakage analyses show that reported resolution rates can be inflated without careful curation</cite> <cite id="5e1b5f81-0">Leakage audits help determine whether performance stems from genuine reasoning</cite>.

- For knowledge grounding and retrieval: Add retrieval-based evaluations that measure (a) retrieval precision/recall for relevant docs, (b) reduction in errors with vs. without retrieval, and (c) verbatim/copy detection to ensure the model uses knowledge rather than copying. <cite id="6b1cb89c-1">Adversarial and contamination-aware methods complement retrieval metrics by isolating genuine knowledge use</cite>.

- For reasoning over knowledge: Employ competition-level problem sets and interactive, multi-step coding tasks to assess planning, tool use, and adaptation, not just one-shot generation. <cite id="498cf5f3-0">Competition-level datasets like TACO/CodeELO/USACO probe deeper reasoning</cite> <cite id="498cf5f3-2">Interactive/sequential reasoning benchmarks better capture planning with knowledge</cite>.

# Caveats and best practices
- Contamination can masquerade as knowledge: High scores on public repo benchmarks may reflect memorized patches rather than generalizable reasoning. Use decontaminated splits, temporal holds, and leakage audits to verify learning. <cite id="5e1b5f81-0">Top models may solve benchmark localization tasks under limited input, indicating memorization rather than reasoning</cite> <cite id="5e1b5f81-2">Resolution rates drop substantially when filtering out leakage and weak tests</cite>.

- Combine multiple metrics: No single score captures all forms of knowledge. Combine functional-correctness and pass@k, error breakdowns, retrieval grounding accuracy, and dynamic/contamination-aware evaluations to form a holistic view. <cite id="96149ca2-1">Pass rate plus syntax error rates and manual audits distinguish language-knowledge deficits from task understanding</cite> <cite id="96149ca2-4">Dynamic benchmarking tracks stability over time and across updates</cite>.

- Choose benchmarks aligned to the intended use: If the goal is real-world maintenance, prefer repository-issue benchmarks with strong tests; if the goal is algorithmic competence, use competition-level sets; if grounding external knowledge is crucial, use retrieval-augmented evaluations with verbatim-detection penalties. <cite id="5e1b5f81-3">SWE-bench variants target realistic issue resolution with resolution-rate metrics</cite> <cite id="498cf5f3-0">Competition-level benchmarks target complex problem solving beyond simple code generation</cite>.

In summary, there are indeed established and emerging metrics to judge whether a coding LLM has knowledge: functional-correctness and pass@k on code generation, resolution rates on bug-fixing benchmarks, competition-level and interactive reasoning tasks, translation/tool-use evaluations, and contamination-aware/dynamic and retrieval-augmented tests that diagnose whether performance reflects genuine, generalizable knowledge or memorization. <cite id="6b1cb89c-1">Functional-correctness and pass@k are standard for code generation</cite> <cite id="5e1b5f81-3">Bug-fixing benchmarks report resolution rates to measure SE knowledge</cite> <cite id="498cf5f3-0">Competition-level benchmarks probe deeper reasoning and knowledge</cite> <cite id="5e1b5f81-2">Contamination-aware audits reveal leakage that can inflate knowledge-like scores</cite> <cite id="6b1cb89c-1">Retrieval- and contamination-aware methods complement code correctness to evaluate knowledge grounding</cite>.

Title: Does SWE-Bench-Verified Test Agent Ability or Model Memory?
Snippet: Large language models (LLMs) have greatly reshaped software engineering. To measure the capabilities of LLMs and to compare different LLMs, researchers have created benchmarks to standardize the process. One popular task that LLMs can be used for is fixing issues within a codebase. SWE-Bench-Verified has become the de facto benchmark to measure and compare the performance of LLMbased systems in fixing issues [4]. The corresponding leaderboard ranks these systems based on the percentage of issues they can resolve. 

SWE-Bench-Verified is entirely built on open-source GitHub repositories. However, this can be a problem. This data is likely to have been seen by LLMs, as many of these LLMs (such as GPT-4 and Claude) are trained on large corpora of the internet [1,10]. This would make the leaderboard and resolution rates shown unreliable, as the underlying model may memorize examples rather than learn generalizable reasoning patterns. In other words, the model may appear intelligent due to memorization rather than genuine learning. This motivates us to analyze the extent to which SWE-Bench-Verified is leaked into LLMs. In this paper, we assess whether the benchmark itself, SWE-Bench-Verified, has been leaked into one of the top-ranking LLMs, Claude Sonnet. 

To better understand the extent of leakage, we conduct an experiment. In our experiment, we aim to solve the localization task that precedes bug fixing. The LLM needs to know where to fix the bug before creating a patch that targets the identified locations. We intentionally handicap the model by giving it insufficient input. We then compare the performance on SWE-Bench-Verified, BeetleBox [3], and SWE-rebench [2]. BeetleBox is a large crosslanguage dataset that consists of numerous repositories. We select 5 Python repositories that are not in SWE-Bench-Verified at random. Additionally, SWE-rebench consists of continuously updated versions of the SWE-Bench benchmark. We use the SWE-rebench split from January 2025 and September 2025. All three datasets are derived from popular open-source projects.
</snippet>

Snippet: We mutate the following two bug-fixing benchmarks: 

• SWE-Bench Verified: This benchmark consists of 500 human-verified bug-fixing problems drawn from popular Python repositories. This is commonly used for evaluating coding agents today and, therefore, a natural choice. Each problem within this benchmark includes a problem statement based on a GitHub issue, repository context, and ground-truth solution patch. We mutate each problem in this benchmark into SWE-Bench Verified-Mutated.
</snippet>
<snippet id=5e1b5f81-2>
Title: SWE-Bench+: Enhanced Coding Benchmark for LLMs
Snippet: Large Language Models (LLMs) in Software Engineering (SE) can offer assistance for coding. To facilitate a rigorous evaluation of LLMs in practical coding contexts, Carlos et al. introduced the SWE-bench dataset, which comprises 2,294 real-world GitHub issues and their corresponding pull requests, collected from 12 widely used Python repositories. Several impressive LLM-based toolkits recently are developed and evaluated on this dataset. However, a systematic evaluation of the quality of SWE-bench remains missing. In this paper, we addressed this gap by presenting an empirical analysis of the SWE-bench dataset. We conducted a manual screening of instances where SWEAgent + GPT-4 successfully resolved issues by comparing the model-generated patches with the actual pull requests. SWE-Agent+GPT-4 was at the top of SWE-bench leaderboard during the time of our study. Our analysis reveals some critical issues with the SWE-bench dataset: 1) 32.67% of the successful patches involve cheating as the solutions were directly provided in the issue report or the comments. We refer to as solution leakage problem. 2) 31.08% of the passed patches are suspicious patches due to weak test cases, i.e., the tests were not adequate to verify the correctness of a patch. When we filtered out these problematic issues, the resolution rate of SWE-Agent+GPT-4 dropped from 12.47% to 3.97%. We also observed that the same data quality issues also exist in the two variants of SWE-bench, i.e., SWE-bench Lite and SWE-Bench Verified. In addition, over 94% of the issues were created before LLM's knowledge cutoff dates, posing potential data leakage issues.
</snippet>
<snippet id=5e1b5f81-3>
Title: SWE-Bench+: Enhanced Coding Benchmark for LLMs
Snippet: 1 Introduction SWE-bench aka Software Engineering Benchmark dataset is created to systematically evaluate the capabilities of an LLM in resolving software issues. The dataset contains 2,294 complex issues from GitHub Jimenez et al. (2024). Given as input the issue information to an LLM, the task for the LLM is to modify the code base to address the issue (i.e., resolution). Each input for an issue consists of a description and a pull request with a reference to the corresponding buggy code repository. Each issue can be either a bug report or a new feature request. The pull request contains the code changes made by developers to address the issue, along with test cases designed to check if the feature is properly implemented or if the bug is successfully fixed. Two variants of the SWE-bench datasets are recently developed: SWE-bench Lite1 and SWE-bench Verified2 . SWE-bench Lite focuses on 300 issues related to bug fixing. SWE-bench Verified contains 500 verified issues with clear issue descriptions and strong test cases. 

A significant body of work from both academia and industry has so far utilized SWE-bench and its variants to develop and to test LLM coding capabilities Chen et al. (2024); Zhang et al. (2024a); Xia et al. (2024); Yang et al. (2024b); Zhang et al. (2024c); Rosa et al. (2024); Zan et al. (2024). Given an issue and its associated buggy code repository, these LLM-based approaches can perform a series of complex tasks, such as reasoning about the target bug's location, analyzing the root cause of the issue, proposing strategies for fixing the bug, and ultimately writing a patch to fix the issue. Within less than one year, the resolution rate on SWE-bench Full increased from 0.17% (for RAG+GPT3.5) to around 22.00% (for Honeycomb). The performance of the LLMs on SWE-bench Lite and Verified went up to 45%. 

However, are the LLMs actually resolving the issues in SWE-bench? 

In this paper, we answer the above question by offering two contributions.
</snippet>
<snippet id=5e1b5f81-4>
Title: Multi-SWE-bench: A Multilingual Benchmark for Issue Resolving
Snippet: Instead of focusing on isolating code subtasks into separate datasets, SWE-bench addresses a broader range of tasks through repository-level issue resolving. These issue resolving tasks, including bug fixing, new feature requests, and optimization, which provide a more comprehensive evaluation of LLMs' ability to automating software development. While SWE-bench is limited to textual context, SWE-bench Multimodal [Yang et al., 2025] and Visual SWE-bench [Zhang et al., 2024] extend evaluation to systems fixing bugs in visually-oriented and user-facing applications. SWE-Lancer [Miserendino et al., 2025] focuses on JavaScript and TypeScript, featuring over 1, 400 freelance tasks from Upwork, including technical and managerial tasks. Despite these advancements, the performance of LLMs on other widely used programming languages remains underexplored. Our work aims to bridge this gap with Multi-SWE-bench, a large-scale multilingual benchmark for issue resolving, with 1, 632 human-validated GitHub issues across 7 widely used languages.
</snippet></tool_output>

Yes. Researchers have proposed a range of benchmarks and metrics to assess whether a coding LLM “has some knowledge,” including functional correctness on code-generation tasks, competition-level problem solving, bug-fixing and repository-issue resolution, translation and tool-use, as well as contamination-aware and retrieval-augmented evaluations that diagnose whether performance reflects genuine knowledge rather than memorization. Below is a synthesis of the main approaches and how they measure knowledge.

# What “knowledge” is being measured
In code LLMs, “knowledge” spans (a) factual and procedural knowledge about programming languages, libraries, and APIs; (b) software engineering expertise (e.g., debugging, refactoring, testing, and planning across files); and (c) general world knowledge used in code contexts. Benchmarks operationalize these via task designs and scoring functions such as functional correctness, pass@k, resolution rates, and contamination-aware checks. <cite id="6b1cb89c-0">Knowledge-intensive benchmarks like MMLU show how broad subject knowledge is measured via QA, and this paradigm has influenced code-focused knowledge evaluations</cite>.

# Task-level metrics for software knowledge and reasoning
- Functional correctness and pass@k: Many code benchmarks evaluate whether generated code passes unit tests, using accuracy-like functional-correctness metrics and sampling-based pass@k to estimate the probability that at least one of k sampled solutions passes all tests. <cite id="6b1cb89c-1">Functional correctness is the primary metric for code generation benchmarks, while pass@k is used to quantify success likelihood across multiple attempts without requiring exact reference matching</cite>. <cite id="96149ca2-0">HumanEval uses pass@1 as the primary metric; extensions and surveys summarize multilingual and class-level code benchmarks with similar functional-correctness scoring</cite>. <cite id="96149ca2-3">Surveys organize results by benchmark and report pass@1/10/100 on HumanEval, highlighting that pass@k provides a more robust aggregate measure than single-attempt scores</cite>. These metrics test practical coding knowledge by requiring tests to validate behavior, not just syntax.

- Competition-level problem solving: To probe deeper algorithmic and software knowledge, newer benchmarks target competitive programming-style problems and use Elo-like or grading-style metrics. <cite id="498cf5f3-0">TACO, CodeELO, Probench, and USACO aim to evaluate complex reasoning in competitive coding, moving beyond simple function generation to higher-discriminative tasks; existing code benchmarks like HumanEval/MBPP/DS-1000 are deemed insufficient for advanced reasoning</cite>. These setups assess algorithmic knowledge, multi-step planning, and library usage under constraints, often with adaptive difficulty or competition-level leaderboards.

- Bug fixing and repository-issue resolution: Real-world bug fixing requires software knowledge across files, tests, and context. <cite id="5e1b5f81-3">SWE-bench evaluates resolving GitHub issues by modifying code bases with patches and tests; variants like SWE-bench Lite (300 issues) and SWE-bench Verified (500 issues with strong tests) report resolution rates as the primary metric</cite>. <cite id="5e1b5f81-0">SWE-Bench-Verified is commonly used to measure the percentage of issues resolved, but leakage from training data can inflate scores if models memorize examples rather than learn generalizable reasoning</cite>. <cite id="5e1b5f81-2">Analyses show significant data-quality and leakage issues: 32.67% of successes may involve solution leakage and 31.08% are suspicious due to weak tests; over 94% of issues predate LLM knowledge cutoffs, raising the risk that high resolution rates reflect memorization</cite>. These results motivate stronger, contamination-aware evaluation.

- Translation and tool-use: Cross-language translation benchmarks test knowledge of language semantics and APIs. <cite id="498cf5f3-4">CodeLingua and TransCoder evaluate code translation between languages, using execution or equivalence metrics to assess whether models truly understand source and target language behaviors and libraries</cite>. Tool-use benchmarks (e.g., ToolBench/API-Bank) measure knowledge of APIs and the ability to chain tools, often with success rates or API-call accuracy as metrics. <cite id="6b1cb89c-2">ToolBench and API-Bank provide structured assessments of models' abilities to interact with external tools and APIs</cite>.

- Difficulty gradients and error analyses: Metrics that separate language syntax vs. task understanding, and drill down into error types, help diagnose knowledge gaps. <cite id="96149ca2-1">Combining pass rate with syntax error rates (compilation/runtime) can distinguish language-knowledge deficits from task misunderstandings, and manual error audits reveal weak spots and even benchmark issues</cite>. Harder suites like MHPP probe multi-step reasoning and coding knowledge. <cite id="96149ca2-2">MHPP contains 210 problems emphasizing multi-step reasoning and specification understanding; many models strong on HumanEval struggle on MHPP, exposing limitations in deeper coding knowledge</cite>.

# Knowledge-grounded and retrieval-augmented evaluations
- Retrieval relevance and correctness with/without retrieval: Retrieval-augmented coding (RAG) frameworks introduce metrics that measure whether bringing in relevant documents improves code correctness, and how well the model selects relevant sources. <cite id="6b1cb89c-1">Adversarial filtering and adaptive benchmarks highlight that some apparent reasoning may stem from contamination or memorization; retrieval-augmented setups can be paired with functional-correctness tests to isolate whether added knowledge yields correct patches</cite>. <cite id="5e1b5f81-0">Analyses of SWE-Bench-Verified emphasize distinguishing genuine generalization from memorized examples; retrieval-based evaluations can be designed to penalize verbatim copying and reward reasoning over retrieved context</cite>. In practice, evaluation pipelines report retrieval accuracy (precision/recall of relevant docs), duplicate/verbatim detection, and delta in functional-correctness with vs. without retrieval.

- Interactive and sequential reasoning: Some benchmarks assess whether models can plan and adjust using feedback, a form of knowledge use over steps. <cite id="498cf5f3-2">AQA-Bench targets sequential reasoning, and the literature notes that one-round coding QA benchmarks miss planning capabilities; agentic and interactive coding tasks with iterative feedback better capture knowledge-driven planning and tool use</cite>. These setups often use stepwise success rates or path-based correctness to measure whether knowledge is applied and adapted over time.

# Diagnostics for internal knowledge and memorization
- Contamination-aware and dynamic benchmarks: To separate true knowledge from training data memory, evaluations use time-based or leakage-resilient designs. <cite id="6b1cb89c-1">Contamination via time can inflate scores; benchmarks that split problems temporally or adversarially filter seen data help measure whether models learn to solve unseen problems rather than recall solutions</cite>. <cite id="96149ca2-4">Dynamic benchmarking frameworks periodically refresh problems and report stability of performance to detect overfitting to fixed test sets</cite>.

- Leakage audits on bug-fixing datasets: Repository-level benchmarks are particularly susceptible to leakage because training data may contain internet code. <cite id="5e1b5f81-0">Studies explicitly test whether top models memorize SWE-Bench-Verified patterns, even under handicapped inputs, to distinguish benchmark knowledge from genuine reasoning</cite>. <cite id="5e1b5f81-2">Systematic audits show high rates of solution leakage and weak test cases in SWE-bench variants, causing reported resolution rates to drop substantially when filtering out problematic instances</cite>. These audits function as internal diagnostics of memorization versus learned generalization.

- Data and code-specific contamination tests: Beyond time splits, contamination diagnostics probe whether models copy solutions, reproduce docstrings, or exploit training set trivia. <cite id="6b1cb89c-1">Adversarial filtering and adaptive benchmarks are used to detect spurious correlations and contamination-driven performance, offering methodological guardrails for knowledge evaluations</cite>. Models that rely on contamination may pass functional tests but fail decontaminated or adversarial subsets, revealing the absence of robust internalized knowledge.

# Putting it together: practical ways to judge “has some knowledge”
- For language and API knowledge: Use functional-correctness benchmarks like HumanEval/MBPP and harder variants like MHPP or class-level/translation suites; track pass@1/10/100 and error breakdowns to see if models handle specifications, libraries, and edge cases beyond simple templates. <cite id="96149ca2-0">HumanEval’s pass@1 and multilingual extensions provide a baseline for language and algorithmic knowledge</cite> <cite id="96149ca2-2">MHPP exposes deeper reasoning and coding-knowledge gaps that pass HumanEval</cite> <cite id="498cf5f3-4">CodeLingua/TransCoder test cross-language translation knowledge</cite>.

- For software engineering knowledge: Use bug-fixing and issue-resolution benchmarks (SWE-bench and variants) with resolution-rate metrics, but apply contamination-aware and dynamic evaluations to avoid inflated scores from memorization. <cite id="5e1b5f81-3">Resolution rate on SWE-bench variants is the primary metric</cite> <cite id="5e1b5f81-2">Data-quality and leakage analyses show that reported resolution rates can be inflated without careful curation</cite> <cite id="5e1b5f81-0">Leakage audits help determine whether performance stems from genuine reasoning</cite>.

- For knowledge grounding and retrieval: Add retrieval-based evaluations that measure (a) retrieval precision/recall for relevant docs, (b) reduction in errors with vs. without retrieval, and (c) verbatim/copy detection to ensure the model uses knowledge rather than copying. <cite id="6b1cb89c-1">Adversarial and contamination-aware methods complement retrieval metrics by isolating genuine knowledge use</cite>.

- For reasoning over knowledge: Employ competition-level problem sets and interactive, multi-step coding tasks to assess planning, tool use, and adaptation, not just one-shot generation. <cite id="498cf5f3-0">Competition-level datasets like TACO/CodeELO/USACO probe deeper reasoning</cite> <cite id="498cf5f3-2">Interactive/sequential reasoning benchmarks better capture planning with knowledge</cite>.

# Caveats and best practices
- Contamination can masquerade as knowledge: High scores on public repo benchmarks may reflect memorized patches rather than generalizable reasoning. Use decontaminated splits, temporal holds, and leakage audits to verify learning. <cite id="5e1b5f81-0">Top models may solve benchmark localization tasks under limited input, indicating memorization rather than reasoning</cite> <cite id="5e1b5f81-2">Resolution rates drop substantially when filtering out leakage and weak tests</cite>.

- Combine multiple metrics: No single score captures all forms of knowledge. Combine functional-correctness and pass@k, error breakdowns, retrieval grounding accuracy, and dynamic/contamination-aware evaluations to form a holistic view. <cite id="96149ca2-1">Pass rate plus syntax error rates and manual audits distinguish language-knowledge deficits from task understanding</cite> <cite id="96149ca2-4">Dynamic benchmarking tracks stability over time and across updates</cite>.

- Choose benchmarks aligned to the intended use: If the goal is real-world maintenance, prefer repository-issue benchmarks with strong tests; if the goal is algorithmic competence, use competition-level sets; if grounding external knowledge is crucial, use retrieval-augmented evaluations with verbatim-detection penalties. <cite id="5e1b5f81-3">SWE-bench variants target realistic issue resolution with resolution-rate metrics</cite> <cite id="498cf5f3-0">Competition-level benchmarks target complex problem solving beyond simple code generation</cite>.

In summary, there are indeed established and emerging metrics to judge whether a coding LLM has knowledge: functional-correctness and pass@k on code generation, resolution rates on bug-fixing benchmarks, competition-level and interactive reasoning tasks, translation/tool-use evaluations, and contamination-aware/dynamic and retrieval-augmented tests that diagnose whether performance reflects genuine, generalizable knowledge or memorization. <cite id="6b1cb89c-1">Functional-correctness and pass@k are standard for code generation</cite> <cite id="5e1b5f81-3">Bug-fixing benchmarks report resolution rates to measure SE knowledge</cite> <cite id="498cf5f3-0">Competition-level benchmarks probe deeper reasoning and knowledge</cite> <cite id="5e1b5f81-2">Contamination-aware audits reveal leakage that can inflate knowledge-like scores</cite> <cite id="6b1cb89c-1">Retrieval- and contamination-aware methods complement code correctness to evaluate knowledge grounding</cite>.
</answer>

Title: Auditing the Ethical Logic of Generative AI Models
Snippet: As the number of competing Large Language Models (LLM) proliferates, we confront a growing need for a set of reliable, valid, practical and agreed-upon benchmark measures of the performance of generative Artificial Intelligence systems. Accordingly, the benchmark literature in the AI field has been expanding rapidly along with the number of models themselves. Ott et al. (2022) surveyed 3765 proposed AI benchmark systems several years ago. Guo et al. (2023) develop a three-element typology of AI benchmarks in an assessment of over 100 benchmark methodologies: 1) Knowledge and Capability including question answering, knowledge completion, reasoning, and tool learning; 2) Alignment Evaluation including ethics/morality, bias, toxicity, and truthfulness, and 3) Safety, including risk evaluation and robustness. Reuel et al. (2024) define a benchmark "as a particular combination of a data set or sets of datasets..., and a metric, conceptualized as representing one or more specific tasks or sets of abilities, picked up by a community of researchers as a shared framework for the comparison of methods." They report that using benchmarks to facilitate comparison, measure performance, track progress, and identify weaknesses has become standard practice, and that benchmarks are widely used by model developers to report performance and compare models upon release. Further, regulatory authorities and safety-oriented non-profits have been emphasizing the importance of independent benchmarking as part of their ongoing concerns about risks and alignment issues (European Commission 2021; Eckersley et al. 2023;NTIA 2023, Chmielinski et al. 2024). 

Several established benchmark tools remain dominant including GLUE (General Language Understanding Evaluation) (Wang et al. 2018), which provided a suite of diverse tasks to evaluate natural language understanding. SuperGLUE (Wang et al. 2019) introduced harder tasks that required deeper reasoning, complex linguistic understanding, and better generalization. MMLU (Massive Multitask Language Understanding) (Hendrycks et al. 2020), which tests models on a broad range of subjects, including history, law, physics, and medicine. MMLU is significant because it introduced a knowledge-intensive benchmark that required more than just pattern recognition -it demanded actual understanding and reasoning across disciplines.

Title: Data Contamination Through the Lens of Time
Snippet: Relevant code generation benchmarks include small sets of entirely handwritten problems [15,48] as well as larger collections curated from internet sources such as code interview sites, competitive programming forums, or general open source code: [1,3,23,25,64], and some that include both original and online-sourced problems [38,63]. Code interview, practice, or competition sites, offering problem descriptions and programmatic evaluation, are common choices to assess modern LLM capabilities [17,22,47,68]-and indeed some public benchmarks feature these problems [23,38]. 

To asses the validity of solutions, many of these benchmarks include test cases. They use a 'functional correctness' metric based on passing these cases as the primary way to measure code generation performance; evaluating with complexity/understandability metrics [47] is less common. [15,33] employ the pass@k metric, describing the likelihood at least one among k sampled generations will pass all test cases. The benefit of these metrics is the complete independence from either expensive human feedback or inherently constraining similarity-to-ground-truth NLP metrics [39,53] which are often ineffective for code [61]. These metrics are in contrast to other popular LLM performance metrics like perplexity [29,32] or information retrieval based LLM metrics of accuracy [34,52]. 

Adversarial Filtering and Adaptive Benchmarks in NLP Test-time exploitation of knowledge gained via contamination or memorization can be seen as special cases of a more general phenomenon in which language models appear to exhibit sophisticated reasoning capabilities but are in fact exploiting shallower heuristics, with potentially negative consequences for generalizability [4]. Prior work has demonstrated that domain-agnostic and domain-specific crowd worker-constructed natural language inference (NLI) datasets-i.e., SNLI [6], MultiNLI [62], MedNLI [57]-contain spurious correlations between lexical and syntactic features of the inputs and the corresponding class labels, such that hypothesis-only baselines (i.e., without premise) are able to outperform majority-class baselines [20,24,43,54].

Title: LLM ethics benchmark: a three-dimensional assessment system for evaluating moral reasoning in large language models
Snippet: In the fast-changing world of artificial intelligence, evaluating Large Language Models (LLMs) has become a significant challenge that has evolved considerably. The field has progressed beyond the basic evaluation metrics used in early natural language processing, adopting a new wave of advanced benchmarking methods. These benchmarks are essential for assessing LLM performance across a variety of tasks and challenges, with their results increasingly monitored through standardized leaderboards [40]. The evaluation frameworks can be organized into three main categories: general language tasks, specific downstream tasks, and multi-modal tasks. In general language tasks, benchmarks such as SocKET [14] and XieZhi [27] evaluate overall language understanding, whereas specialized frameworks like KoLA [95] focus on specific language abilities through self-contrast metrics and leaderboard assessments. The progress in evaluation metrics has led to the development of sophisticated frameworks like DynaBench [44] and AGIEval [100], which employ dynamic evaluation methods and human-centered foundational models, respectively. Importantly, benchmarks such as GLUE X [90] and GAOKAO-Bench [91] aim to improve out-of-distribution (OOD) robustness in natural language processing applications. Furthermore, the recent introduction of PromptBench [101] has greatly enhanced our understanding of model resilience against adversarial prompts, while FreshLLMs [80] explores the advantages of search engine augmentation to improve performance. 

In the domain of specific downstream tasks, the evaluation framework becomes increasingly specialized and technically detailed. The evaluation of mathematical reasoning skills is executed through MATH [32] and various targeted frameworks that emphasize algebraic word problems [36,47,55]. Coding capabilities are assessed via APPS [30], while legal understanding is measured through tools like CUAD [31] and particular tasks focused on predicting legal rulings [13]. The assessment of medical knowledge is conducted through MultiMedQA [76] and CMB [82], which evaluate both general medical knowledge and proficiency in Chinese medicine. Furthermore, there have been significant advancements in the evaluation of tool usage, with frameworks such as ToolBench [77] and API-Bank providing comprehensive assessments of models' abilities to interact with external tools and APIs.

Title: Diff-eRank: A Novel Rank-Based Metric for Evaluating Large Language Models
Snippet: Evaluation of Large Language Models. Evaluation of LLMs is a fast-evolving field across various tasks, datasets, and benchmarks [5,33,36,48]. Precise evaluations are important for the enhancement of language models' performance and reliability. Conventional metrics such as accuracy, F1 [29], BLEU [24] and ROUGE [18] estimate between the annotated label and the prediction generated by the language model in different downstream tasks. Other metrics like perplexity and crossentropy loss are independent of annotated labels and can be computed solely based on the input texts. However, these metrics focus on "extrinsic" evaluation, assessing performance based on the predictions of LLMs. We propose Diff-eRank for "intrinsic" evaluation based on the input data's hidden representations of LLMs, concentrating on their "noise reduction" capabilities. 

Information Theory for Understanding Deep Learning. Information theory has been used to gain significant insights into understanding neural networks. For example, the information bottleneck [37,38] is instrumental in explaining supervised learning. Recently, researchers have also utilized information theory to understand and improve (vision) semi and self-supervised learning [32,35,46,47]. Notably, Zhang et al. [46] find the closed-form connection of matrix entropy and effective rank when the matrix is positive semi-definite. As for language models, prior works [16,25,41] also used information theory to analyze hidden representations by training probes on specific downstream tasks to estimate the information contained in the pre-trained language model. Several other works explore the lossless compression of LLMs with arithmetic coding [10,40] based on information theory. In this paper, we take a further step toward evaluating LLMs through the proposed Diff-eRank rooted in information theory, which represents a complementary perspective to these prior studies.

Title: Understanding and Mitigating Numerical Sources of Nondeterminism in LLM Inference
Snippet: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly being deployed in everyday scenarios, powering applications from chatbots [2] to automated coding tools [25] and personalized healthcare agents [6].
