# Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) for Smart Traffic Management: What Works, Why, and When

## Overview and Problem Formulations
DRL has become a prominent paradigm for smart traffic management because traffic control is a high-dimensional, sequential decision problem with partial observability and strong spatiotemporal dependencies across a transportation network.<cite id="69d266c1-0">A signal control algorithm using deep reinforcement learning was evaluated with waiting time, average speed, and number of stops, showing up to 42% waiting time reduction and 29% speed increase versus fixed-time control under congestion, and highlighting the sensitivity of performance to reward design and the relative strengths of value-based vs. policy-based methods</cite>. DRL methods are commonly prototyped in microsimulation platforms such as SUMO, which expose traffic states via TraCI and allow real-time actuation of signal phases for learning and evaluation loops.<cite id="69d266c1-0">SUMO provides microscopic simulation of vehicles and signals with TraCI for real-time control and measurement of performance metrics like CO2, waiting times, and signal effectiveness</cite><cite id="69d266c1-4">DRL agents can use TraCI to obtain real-time traffic information and manipulate signals within SUMO</cite>.

Two core problem formulations recur: (1) single-intersection signal control, where an agent selects phasing or green-time extensions based on lane occupancy/queue length; and (2) multi-intersection/network control, where coordination across intersections is required and often modeled as multi-agent RL to handle interdependencies and credit assignment.<cite id="69d266c1-1">A DRL agent with a discrete traffic state encoding and Q-learning reduced average delay by 82%, queue length by 66%, and travel time by 20% in SUMO versus a neural network baseline</cite><cite id="69d266c1-2">Multi-agent Q-learning with SUMO+CARLA integrates computer-vision inputs to support distributed, real-time adaptive traffic light control across a network</cite>.

## Algorithms and Benchmarks
DRL methods span value-based (DQN, prioritized DQN), policy-based (A2C, PPO, SAC), and actor-critic variants adapted to continuous action spaces (DDPG, MATD3). Benchmarks typically use SUMO for rapid prototyping and evaluation against fixed-time and actuated baselines, with metrics including delay, queue length, throughput, stops, and emissions.<cite id="69d266c1-0">A DRL signal controller was compared against fixed-time and actuated strategies using waiting time, speed, and stops, and showed large improvements under congestion</cite><cite id="69d266c1-1">A DQN-based agent with experience replay achieved large reductions in delay and queue compared to a neural network controller</cite>. Physics-informed or hybrid designs combine domain models with RL to improve data efficiency and stability, for example mixing historical and synthetic data for ramp metering policies.<cite id="f0fc6680-3">A physics-informed RL ramp metering strategy trained with a mix of historical and synthetic data improved traffic performance and outperformed classical feedback-based control</cite>.

Multi-agent actor-critic methods are favored for network control because they support decentralized execution with centralized training and can encode observations that include neighbors’ states to improve coordination.<cite id="611f30a8-1">A multi-agent DDPG (MADDPG) uses centralized critics with additional information and decentralized actors, enabling cooperation across multiple signalized intersections in SUMO</cite><cite id="611f30a8-2">MATD3 has been proposed for continuous-action multi-agent traffic signal control to address coordination challenges and improve stability</cite>. Recent meta-learning approaches aim to improve generalization across heterogeneous neighbors and training scenarios by learning latent representations of neighbor information and intrinsic rewards for stable policy learning.<cite id="611f30a8-4">A meta-variational intrinsic motivated RL method learns decentralized policies that consider neighbor information in latent form to improve generalizability across varying intersection neighbors</cite>.

## Tasks and Performance: Signal Control, Ramp Metering, and VSL
At the intersection, DRL has repeatedly outperformed fixed-time and actuated controls on delay, queue, and throughput in simulation, with reported improvements often exceeding 60–80% in delay/queue under congestion, though reward design is critical and can dominate outcomes.<cite id="69d266c1-0">Design of reward functions significantly impacts performance; value-based DRL outperformed policy-based methods in one study, with large waiting-time and speed gains versus fixed-time control</cite><cite id="69d266c1-1">A DQN agent achieved 82% delay and 66% queue reductions compared to a neural network baseline</cite>. Event-based data pipelines using inductive-loop actuations can make DRL controllers deployable because observations align with existing detectors, and have shown superior performance to fixed-time and actuated strategies in simulation benchmarks.<cite id="17944e4c-2">A DRL signal control method using event-based detector data defined states and rewards from existing detectors, enabling deployment, and outperformed fixed-time and actuated strategies in simulation</cite>.

Beyond intersections, coordinated ramp metering and variable speed limits (VSL) are natural DRL targets. Learning-based ramp metering spans Q-learning to deep multi-task RL and coordinated settings, and recent work combines ramp metering with VSL via decentralized RL; physics-informed RL further improves data efficiency by bootstrapping from models and historical data.<cite id="f0fc6680-0">Learning-based ramp metering has evolved from ANN to RL; coordinated ramp metering using Q-learning and multi-task DRL has been proposed, and decentralized RL has combined ramp metering with VSL</cite><cite id="f0fc6680-3">Physics-informed RL for ramp metering trained on mixed historical and synthetic data improved performance over classical feedback strategies</cite>. VSL control using Q-learning and neural policies has also been explored, with proactive control signals informed by predictions to improve performance under connected and automated vehicle (CAV) penetration.<cite id="f0fc6680-3">Q-learning and deep RL methods have been used to learn speed limit policies that consider traffic predictions and output control signals proactively</cite>.

## Multi-Agent Coordination: Credit Assignment, Nonstationarity, and Stability
Coordinating multiple intersections is challenging due to nonstationary environments, exploration-exploitation trade-offs, continuous action spaces, and credit assignment across agents. Actor-critic methods with centralized critics and decentralized actors (e.g., MADDPG) and robust continuous-action variants (e.g., MATD3) address these issues by sharing global information during training while keeping per-intersection policies executable in the field.<cite id="611f30a8-1">MADDPG uses centralized learning with critics that use additional information and decentralized execution, improving efficiency in multi-intersection networks</cite><cite id="611f30a8-2">MATD3 is proposed for continuous-action multi-agent traffic signal control to enable coordination and improve learning stability</cite>. Communication and shared rewards can further improve coordination, but require careful design to avoid unshared reward gaming and to handle nonstationarity during training.<cite id="611f30a8-0">Multi-agent systems with V2X-informed observations explored independent and shared rewards for traffic light control, showing significant waiting-time reductions versus periodic control</cite>. Novel training schemes like intrinsic motivation and latent neighbor encoding aim to stabilize learning and improve generalization when neighbor sets vary across days or districts.<cite id="611f30a8-4">MetaVIM introduces latent variables for neighbor information and intrinsic rewards to stabilize decentralized policy learning and improve generalizability across heterogeneous neighbors</cite>.

## Real-World Deployability and Scale
Network- and city-scale deployments are emerging. Studies report decentralized DRL controllers trained at scale and evaluated over thousands of real-world intersections, with promising results and the caveat that more sophisticated neighbor-aware coordination could further improve performance.<cite id="17944e4c-4">A deep RL method for city-level signal control evaluated in a real-world scenario with thousands of intersections achieved satisfactory control with a shared agent, and the authors note that more elaborate coordination among neighboring intersections might further improve performance</cite>. Movement-centric and lane-level control approaches with modern algorithms (e.g., FRAP) have shown significant improvements on real datasets from cities like Cologne and Hangzhou, indicating external validity beyond microsimulations.<cite id="17944e4c-0">A movement-centric DRL signal control (MoveLight) using lane-level control and FRAP achieved significant improvements in queue length, delay, and throughput on real-world datasets from Cologne and Hangzhou compared to existing methods</cite>. Event-based data pipelines align with inductive-loop infrastructure and make controllers closer to deployment, while computer vision with SUMO+CARLA co-simulation supports real-time, distributed control evaluation before rollout.<cite id="17944e4c-2">Event-based DRL uses existing detector data for states and rewards, enabling deployable controllers validated against fixed-time and actuated strategies</cite><cite id="69d266c1-2">A SUMO+CARLA co-simulation with multi-agent Q-learning feeds camera-based vehicle detection into per-intersection agents for real-time control</cite>.

## Challenges and Robustness
Key challenges include nonstationarity from moving peers, exploration-exploitation in dynamic flows, credit assignment across agents, and continuous action spaces; these motivate actor-critic designs and centralized training with decentralized execution.<cite id="611f30a8-1">Deep RL for multi-intersection control faces non-stationarity, exploration-exploitation, multi-agent training, and continuous actions; MADDPG addresses these with centralized critics and decentralized actors</cite>. Safety and stability require careful reward shaping and constraints; studies show reward design can dominate outcomes and that value-based vs. policy-based choices affect performance, underscoring the need for robust objectives and possibly constraint-aware RL.<cite id="69d266c1-0">Reward function design had a great impact on performance, with value-based DRL outperforming policy-based in one study, highlighting sensitivity to objective design</cite>. Data and generalization are also concerns: policies trained in simulation must handle heterogeneous neighbors and unseen districts, motivating meta-learning and latent representations of neighbor context.<cite id="611f30a8-4">MetaVIM learns decentralized policies that represent neighbor information latently to improve generalizability across different neighbor configurations</cite>. Environmental impacts are a growing evaluation dimension; DRL controllers are often assessed for emissions alongside delay and queue, with studies reporting substantial waiting-time reductions that can translate to fuel savings.<cite id="69d266c1-0">DRL signal control reduced waiting time by 42% and increased speed by 29% versus fixed-time control and was evaluated on CO2, waiting times, and signal performance via SUMO</cite>.

## Trends and Best Practices
- Physics-informed and hybrid RL: Combining domain models with RL improves data efficiency and stability, especially for ramp metering and VSL, by bootstrapping from simulations and historical data.<cite id="f0fc6680-3">A physics-informed RL ramp metering strategy trained on mixed historical and synthetic data outperformed classical feedback-based control</cite>.
- Event-based learning and deployable pipelines: Leveraging inductive-loop actuations and detector data reduces integration costs and aligns with existing infrastructure for real-time control loops.<cite id="17944e4c-2">Event-based DRL uses detector-derived states and rewards to create deployable controllers that outperform fixed-time and actuated baselines</cite>.
- Multi-agent coordination: Actor-critic methods (MADDPG, MATD3) with neighbor-aware observations and centralized training but decentralized execution are prevalent; intrinsic motivation and meta-learning improve stability and generalization.<cite id="611f30a8-1">MADDPG centralizes learning with additional information and decentralizes execution for multi-intersection control</cite><cite id="611f30a8-2">MATD3 supports continuous actions in multi-agent settings for traffic control</cite><cite id="611f30a8-4">MetaVIM uses latent variables and intrinsic rewards to stabilize decentralized learning and improve generalizability</cite>.
- Scale and real-world data: Movement-centric and lane-level control with modern RL algorithms have shown gains on real datasets from multiple cities, and city-scale deployments are being reported with promising results and suggested refinements for neighbor-aware coordination.<cite id="17944e4c-0">Movement-centric DRL achieved significant improvements on real datasets from Cologne and Hangzhou</cite><cite id="17944e4c-4">A city-level DRL signal control evaluated with thousands of intersections achieved satisfactory control, with room for improved neighbor coordination</cite>.

## Practical Recommendations
- Start with clear objectives and reward design: Combine queuelength, delay, and safety constraints; validate sensitivity to reward shaping and consider value-based or policy-based methods empirically for the task and dataset.<cite id="69d266c1-0">Reward design significantly impacted outcomes, with value-based DRL outperforming policy-based in one study</cite>.
- Use physics-informed priors and hybrid data: For ramp metering/VSL, mix historical and model-simulated data to improve sample efficiency and avoid poor local optima.<cite id="f0fc6680-3">Physics-informed RL with mixed data improved performance over classical feedback strategies</cite>.
- Prefer multi-agent actor-critic for networks: Use MADDPG/MATD3 with neighbor-aware observations and centralized training, and test decentralized execution in simulation before deployment.<cite id="611f30a8-1">MADDPG’s centralized critics and decentralized actors improved multi-intersection control</cite><cite id="611f30a8-2">MATD3 targets continuous-action multi-agent traffic signal control</cite>.
- Build deployable pipelines with event data: Align states with inductive loops and other detectors; validate against actuated/fixed-time baselines and measure emissions and safety along with throughput.<cite id="17944e4c-2">Event-based DRL leverages existing detectors for deployable controllers and outperforms fixed-time/actuated baselines</cite><cite id="69d266c1-0">SUMO-based evaluation measured waiting time, speed, stops, and emissions</cite>.
- Scale thoughtfully: For citywide control, consider movement-centric or lane-level control and decentralized agents; evaluate coordination mechanisms and shared/global information in training to improve stability and generalization.<cite id="17944e4c-0">Movement-centric lane-level control achieved substantial gains on real datasets</cite><cite id="611f30a8-4">Latent neighbor encoding and intrinsic rewards improve generalizability and stability in decentralized multi-agent settings</cite>.

## Limitations and Open Problems
Evidence from large-scale real-world deployments with comprehensive safety audits remains limited in the literature retrieved here; most high-quality results are from microsimulations and small-to-mid scale networks, though movement-centric and city-level studies are emerging.<cite id="17944e4c-4">City-level DRL signal control was evaluated with thousands of intersections and suggested further improvements from neighbor-aware coordination</cite> Robust safety guarantees, cold-start policies, and continuous monitoring/rollback mechanisms are active needs; reward design sensitivity and nonstationarity persist as primary challenges for reliable field deployment.<cite id="69d266c1-0">Performance was highly sensitive to reward function design, underscoring the need for robust objectives</cite><cite id="611f30a8-1">Multi-agent settings face non-stationarity, exploration, and credit assignment challenges that complicate deployment</cite>.

In summary, DRL has demonstrated substantial improvements in traffic management tasks across intersections, ramps, and networks in simulation and is moving toward real-world deployment, with multi-agent actor-critic methods, physics-informed/hybrid learning, and event-based pipelines as key enablers. Continued progress depends on addressing nonstationarity and credit assignment, ensuring robust reward/objective design, and validating safety and emissions alongside core mobility metrics in large-scale, real-world settings.<cite id="69d266c1-0">DRL controllers reduced waiting time and improved speed versus fixed-time control, with performance strongly dependent on reward design</cite><cite id="611f30a8-1">Actor-critic multi-agent RL with centralized learning and decentralized execution improves control across multiple intersections</cite><cite id="f0fc6680-0">Learning-based ramp metering and coordinated control with RL have advanced rapidly in recent years</cite><cite id="17944e4c-4">City-level DRL signal control evaluated at scale shows promise and highlights the value of neighbor-aware coordination</cite>.
</answer>

Title: Implementation of a Real-Time Analysis Simulation System for Traffic Signal Control Algorithms to Reduce Vehicle Exhaust Emissions and Improve Traffic Flow
Snippet: To overcome the limitations of legacy traffic signal control methods, a signal control algorithm using deep reinforcement learning was studied [19]. This algorithm was evaluated by the waiting time of vehicles approaching the intersection, the average speed, and the number of stops as main performance indicators. Using various reward functions and state definitions, it showed excellent performance, such as a 42% reduction in waiting time and a 29% increase in vehicle speed compared to legacy fixed-time signal control in traffic congestion situations. In particular, it was confirmed that the design of the reward function had a great impact on performance and that a value-based reinforcement learning algorithm provided better results than a policy-based one. This study confirmed the possibility of a traffic signal control system that can dynamically adjust signals in real-time according to traffic volume and suggested a method that can contribute to solving urban traffic congestion problems. 

SUMO [3] is an open-source software for traffic simulation and is a tool that can precisely model individual vehicles, signal systems, and pedestrian movements on the road through microscopic simulation. When information on traffic volume is entered through an XML-formatted file, traffic flow simulation is possible with only SUMO's basic simulation engine. SUMO is an open platform that can be expanded through customization by 3rd party programmers. 

In particular, it can communicate with external programs through TraCI (Traffic Control Interface), so real-time traffic control is possible by applying signal control algorithms in languages such as Python. Through this, various traffic data can be collected from simulations, and CO2 emissions, vehicle waiting times, and signal control performance can be analyzed. However, SUMO has a somewhat high entry barrier because it requires complex settings and various file processing to provide various data formats and functions. In addition, since the visualization function is simple, additional linkage and integration work with various external tools is required to add additional advanced visualization functions. 

A system that effectively controls traffic signals in complex urban traffic situations by combining Model Predictive Control (MPC), Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs), Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs), and Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) has been studied [20]. This system can effectively reflect spatiotemporal characteristics to predict traffic flow more accurately and can optimize signal control by adapting to real-time traffic situations through deep reinforcement learning.

Title: Using a Deep Reinforcement Learning Agent for Traffic Signal Control
Snippet: Ensuring transportation systems are efficient is a priority for modern society. Technological advances have made it possible for transportation systems to collect large volumes of varied data on an unprecedented scale. We propose a traffic signal control system which takes advantage of this new, high quality data, with minimal abstraction compared to other proposed systems. We apply modern deep reinforcement learning methods to build a truly adaptive traffic signal control agent in the traffic microsimulator SUMO. We propose a new state space, the discrete traffic state encoding, which is information dense. The discrete traffic state encoding is used as input to a deep convolutional neural network, trained using Q-learning with experience replay. Our agent was compared against a one hidden layer neural network traffic signal control agent and reduces average cumulative delay by 82%, average queue length by 66% and average travel time by 20%.

Title: Traffic Co-Simulation Framework Empowered by Infrastructure Camera Sensing and Reinforcement Learning
Snippet: The aim of the study was to create a co-simulation framework that supports the optimization of any number of traffic lights in a road network for real-time adaptive traffic management based on computer vision input. It was implemented using CARLA and SUMO, with the traffic signal optimization being performed by multiagent Qlearning. SUMO serves as a reliable and highly customizable traffic microsimulator capable of generating training environment and data for reinforcement learning, while CARLA presents a realistic 3D rendering of the urban landscape complete with a diverse array of vehicles that are being controlled by SUMO. 

The process starts with using a SUMO road network with traffic lights as Q-learning  agents utilizing the sumo_rl Python library (Alegre, 2019) which converts SUMO networks to RL environments based on the stable baselines format, allowing the use of standard RL algorithms that the library offers. Each traffic light is an independent agent taking the current phase, occupancy of incoming lanes, and queue length as the state. Each agent calculates its reward from its incoming lanes based on one of four reward functions tested. The trained list of agents is saved to a Python pickle file to be used in the co-simulation. 

The CARLA simulation was configured to run the same map as the one used for training, and cameras were spawned directly above each traffic light pole. The coordinates of the stopping point of the lane being served by each light were used to point the yaw angle of the camera, along with a 10 degrees downward pitch. Every camera captures its image once per second and stores it to memory. YOLOv5 is used to detect vehicles in the oncoming lane by selecting a region around the center of the camera view so that other irrelevant vehicles are not counted. The object detection is performed for each intersection periodically, and the observation is fed into the corresponding agent from the list in the loaded pickle file. The resulting action of the agent is to choose the next phase for the intersection which is then passed to the SUMO simulation. The SUMO-CARLA bridge synchronizes both simulations to ensure accurate visual representation of the scenario. 

The outlined approach represents a virtual test bed for the real world deployment of a computer vision based, distributed and automated, real-time traffic signal control system.

Title: Optimization Control of Adaptive Traffic Signal with Deep Reinforcement Learning
Snippet: The optimization and control of traffic signals is very important for logistics transportation. It not only improves the operational efficiency and safety of road traffic, but also conforms to the direction of the intelligent, green, and sustainable development of modern cities. In order to improve the optimization effect of traffic signal control, this paper proposes a traffic signal optimization method based on deep reinforcement learning and Simulation of Urban Mobility (SUMO) software for urban traffic scenarios. The intersection training scenario was established using SUMO micro traffic simulation software, and the maximum vehicle queue length and vehicle queue time were selected as performance evaluation indicators. In order to be more relevant to the real environment, the experiment uses Weibull distribution to simulate vehicle generation. Since deep reinforcement learning takes into account both perceptual and decision-making capabilities, this study proposes a traffic signal optimization control model based on the deep reinforcement learning Deep Q Network (DQN) algorithm by considering the realism and complexity of traffic intersections, and first uses the DQN algorithm to train the model in a training scenario. After that, the G-DQN (Grouping-DQN) algorithm is proposed to address the problems that the definition of states in existing studies cannot accurately represent the traffic states and the slow convergence of neural networks. Finally, the performance of the G-DQN algorithm model was compared with the original DQN algorithm model and Advantage Actor-Critic (A2C) algorithm model. The experimental results show that the improved algorithm increased the main indicators in all aspects.

Title: Deep Reinforcement Learning-Based Traffic Signal Control Using High-Resolution Event-Based Data
Snippet: We carry out the experiments based on an open source microscopic traffic simulator SUMO [34]. We obtain the 'real-time' traffic information (e.g., the event data) and manipulate simulated objects (e.g., traffic signals) in SUMO via Traffic Control Interface (traci). Keras and TensorFlow Python libraries are used to implement the deep reinforcement learning-based traffic signal controller.

snippet.text:
The aim of the study was to create a co-simulation framework that supports the optimization of any number of traffic lights in a road network for real-time adaptive traffic management based on computer vision input. It was implemented using CARLA and SUMO, with the traffic signal optimization being performed by multiagent Qlearning. SUMO serves as a reliable and highly customizable traffic microsimulator capable of generating training environment and data for reinforcement learning, while CARLA presents a realistic 3D rendering of the urban landscape complete with a diverse array of vehicles that are being controlled by SUMO. 

The process starts with using a SUMO road network with traffic lights as Q-learning  agents utilizing the sumo_rl Python library (Alegre, 2019) which converts SUMO networks to RL environments based on the stable baselines format, allowing the use of standard RL algorithms that the library offers. Each traffic light is an independent agent taking the current phase, occupancy of incoming lanes, and queue length as the state. Each agent calculates its reward from its incoming lanes based on one of four reward functions tested. The trained list of agents is saved to a Python pickle file to be used in the co-simulation. 

The CARLA simulation was configured to run the same map as the one used for training, and cameras were spawned directly above each traffic light pole. The coordinates of the stopping point of the lane being served by each light were used to point the yaw angle of the camera, along with a 10 degrees downward pitch. Every camera captures its image once per second and stores it to memory. YOLOv5 is used to detect vehicles in the oncoming lane by selecting a region around the center of the camera view so that other irrelevant vehicles are not counted. The object detection is performed for each intersection periodically, and the observation is fed into the corresponding agent from the list in the loaded pickle file. The resulting action of the agent is to choose the next phase for the intersection which is then passed to the SUMO simulation. The SUMO-CARLA bridge synchronizes both simulations to ensure accurate visual representation of the scenario. 

The outlined approach represents a virtual test bed for the real world deployment of a computer vision based, distributed and automated, real-time traffic signal control system.

snippet.text: The optimization and control of traffic signals is very important for logistics transportation. It not only improves the operational efficiency and safety of road traffic, but also conforms to the direction of the intelligent, green, and sustainable development of modern cities. In order to improve the optimization effect of traffic signal control, this paper proposes a traffic signal optimization method based on deep reinforcement learning and Simulation of Urban Mobility (SUMO) software for urban traffic scenarios. The intersection training scenario was established using SUMO micro traffic simulation software, and the maximum vehicle queue length and vehicle queue time were selected as performance evaluation indicators. In order to be more relevant to the real environment, the experiment uses Weibull distribution to simulate vehicle generation. Since deep reinforcement learning takes into account both perceptual and decision-making capabilities, this study proposes a traffic signal optimization control model based on the deep reinforcement learning Deep Q Network (DQN) algorithm by considering the realism and complexity of traffic intersections, and first uses the DQN algorithm to train the model in a training scenario. After that, the G-DQN (Grouping-DQN) algorithm is proposed to address the problems that the definition of states in existing studies cannot accurately represent the traffic states and the slow convergence of neural networks. Finally, the performance of the G-DQN algorithm model was compared with the original DQN algorithm model and Advantage Actor-Critic (A2C) algorithm model. The experimental results show that the improved algorithm increased the main indicators in all aspects.

Title: Optimizing Traffic Lights with Multi-agent Deep Reinforcement Learning and V2X communication
Snippet: We consider a system to optimize duration of traffic signals using multi-agent deep reinforcement learning and Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) communication. This system aims at analyzing independent and shared rewards for multi-agents to control duration of traffic lights. A learning agent traffic light gets information along its lanes within a circular V2X coverage. The duration cycles of traffic light are modeled as Markov decision Processes. We investigate four variations of reward functions. The first two are unshared-rewards: based on waiting number, and waiting time of vehicles between two cycles of traffic light. The third and fourth functions are: shared-rewards based on waiting cars, and waiting time for all agents. Each agent has a memory for optimization through target network and prioritized experience replay. We evaluate multi-agents through the Simulation of Urban MObility (SUMO) simulator. The results prove effectiveness of the proposed system to optimize traffic signals and reduce average waiting cars to 41.5 % as compared to the traditional periodic traffic control system.

Title: A Deep Reinforcement Learning Approach for Traffic Signal Control Optimization
Snippet: Inefficient traffic signal control methods may cause numerous problems, such as traffic congestion and waste of energy. Reinforcement learning (RL) is a trending data-driven approach for adaptive traffic signal control in complex urban traffic networks. Although the development of deep neural networks (DNN) further enhances its learning capability, there are still some challenges in applying deep RLs to transportation networks with multiple signalized intersections, including non-stationarity environment, exploration-exploitation dilemma, multi-agent training schemes, continuous action spaces, etc. In order to address these issues, this paper first proposes a multi-agent deep deterministic policy gradient (MADDPG) method by extending the actor-critic policy gradient algorithms. MADDPG has a centralized learning and decentralized execution paradigm in which critics use additional information to streamline the training process, while actors act on their own local observations. The model is evaluated via simulation on the Simulation of Urban MObility (SUMO) platform. Model comparison results show the efficiency of the proposed algorithm in controlling traffic lights.

With the advent of Deep Learning, reinforcement learning tasks that required processing unstructured data, dealing with high dimensional vector spaces and increased computational needs became easier and tractable. However, a significant challenge in deep reinforcement learning methods is that the agents cannot learn to coordinate and share information with each other to optimize a collective objective. Multiagent Deep Reinforcement Learning uses Deep Reinforcement Learning techniques to control multiple agents present in the environment and enable them to cooperate or compete so as to achieve a collective objective. Since traffic networks have many intersections that are dependent on each other, it is crucial to exploit multiagent deep reinforcement learning techniques to enable the different intersections in the network to work collectively towards reducing traffic congestion. There have been significant contributions in applying multiagent reinforcement learning to traffic signal control in the past, see for instance (Prabhuchandran, Hemanth Kumar, & Bhatnagar, 2014) where the authors have used Multiagent  − Learning to efficiently learn traffic control. In (T Chu, 2019), multiagent advantage actor-critic has been used to enable phase selection for traffic control. In (Ge , 2019), the authors model cooperative traffic signal control using Deep  learning and transfer learning. Title: Effects of Smart Traffic Signal Control on Air Quality
Snippet: Traffic flow is increasing constantly with economic and social growth, and road congestion is a crucial issue in growing urban areas [9,10]. Machine learning methods like reinforcement learning [11][12][13][14] and other artificial intelligence techniques such as fuzzy logic algorithms [4] and swarm intelligence [5] have been applied to improve the management of street intersections regulated with traffic lights (signalized intersections). [15] proposed a new approach of a multi-agent system and reinforcement learning (RL) utilizing a q-learning algorithm with a neural network, and demonstrated its advantages in obtaining an efficient traffic signal control policy. Recently, a specific interest has been shown in the applications of agent-based technologies to traffic and transportation engineering. As an example, [16] studied traffic signal duration with a deep reinforcement learning model. Furthermore [17] developed a RL-based traffic signal control method that employs a graph convolutional neural network analysing a six-intersection area. In addition, [18] proposed a new architecture based on multi-agent systems and RL algorithms to make the signal control system more autonomous, able to learn from its environment and make decisions to optimize road traffic. [19] gave a complete overview on RL-based traffic signal control approaches, including the recent advances in deep RL-based traffic signal control methods. [20] summarised in their review some technical characteristics and the current research status of self-adaptive control methods used so far. [21] and [13], instead, provide comprehensive surveys mainly on studies before the more recent spread of deep reinforcement learning. The present work is mainly based on [8]. For our simulations, we replicated the Andrea Costa and Pasubio areas in pseudo-random and entirely random traffic conditions. Both areas are located in the western outskirts of Bologna (Italy) [22].

Title: MetaVIM: Meta Variationally Intrinsic Motivated Reinforcement Learning for Decentralized Traffic Signal Control
Snippet: Traffic signal control aims to coordinate traffic signals across intersections to improve the traffic efficiency of a district or a city. Deep reinforcement learning (RL) has been applied to traffic signal control recently and demonstrated promising performance where each traffic signal is regarded as an agent. However, there are still several challenges that may limit its large-scale application in the real world. On the one hand, the policy of the current traffic signal is often heavily influenced by its neighbor agents, and the coordination between the agent and its neighbors needs to be considered. Hence, the control of a road network composed of multiple traffic signals is naturally modeled as a multi-agent system, and all agents’ policies need to be optimized simultaneously. On the other hand, once the policy function is conditioned on not only the current agent's observation but also the neighbors’, the policy function would be closely related to the training scenario and cause poor generalizability because the agents in various scenarios often have heterogeneous neighbors. To make the policy learned from a training scenario generalizable to new unseen scenarios, a novel Meta Variationally Intrinsic Motivated (MetaVIM) RL method is proposed to learn the decentralized policy for each intersection that considers neighbor information in a latent way. Specifically, we formulate the policy learning as a meta-learning problem over a set of related tasks, where each task corresponds to traffic signal control at an intersection whose neighbors are regarded as the unobserved part of the state. Then, a learned latent variable is introduced to represent the task's specific information and is further brought into the policy for learning. In addition, to make the policy learning stable, a novel intrinsic reward is designed to encourage each agent's received rewards and observation transition to be predictable only conditioned on its own history. Extensive experiments conducted on CityFlow demonstrate that the proposed method substantially outperforms existing approaches and shows superior generalizability.

MADDPG has a centralized learning and decentralized execution paradigm in which critics use additional information to streamline the training process, while actors act on their own local observations. The model is evaluated via simulation on the Simulation of Urban MObility (SUMO) platform. Model comparison results show the efficiency of the proposed algorithm in controlling traffic lights.

documents.title: Effects of Smart Traffic Signal Control on Air Quality
documents.snippet: Traffic flow is increasing constantly with economic and social growth, and road congestion is a crucial issue in growing urban areas [9,10]. Machine learning methods like reinforcement learning [11][12][13][14] and other artificial intelligence techniques such as fuzzy logic algorithms [4] and swarm intelligence [5] have been applied to improve the management of street intersections regulated with traffic lights (signalized intersections). [15] proposed a new approach of a multi-agent system and reinforcement learning (RL) utilizing a q-learning algorithm with a neural network, and demonstrated its advantages in obtaining an efficient traffic signal control policy. Recently, a specific interest has been shown in the applications of agent-based technologies to traffic and transportation engineering. As an example, [16] studied traffic signal duration with a deep reinforcement learning model. Furthermore [17] developed a RL-based traffic signal control method that employs a graph convolutional neural network analysing a six-intersection area. In addition, [18] proposed a new architecture based on multi-agent systems and RL algorithms to make the signal control system more autonomous, able to learn from its environment and make decisions to optimize road traffic. [19] gave a complete overview on RL-based traffic signal control approaches, including the recent advances in deep RL-based traffic signal control methods. [20] summarised in their review some technical characteristics and the current research status of self-adaptive control methods used so far. [21] and [13], instead, provide comprehensive surveys mainly on studies before the more recent spread of deep reinforcement learning. The present work is mainly based on [8]. For our simulations, we replicated the Andrea Costa and Pasubio areas in pseudo-random and entirely random traffic conditions. Both areas are located in the western outskirts of Bologna (Italy) [22].

documents.title: MetaVIM: Meta Variationally Intrinsic Motivated Reinforcement Learning for Decentralized Traffic Signal Control
documents.snippet: Traffic signal control aims to coordinate traffic signals across intersections to improve the traffic efficiency of a district or a city. Deep reinforcement learning (RL) has been applied to traffic signal control recently and demonstrated promising performance where each traffic signal is regarded as an agent. However, there are still several challenges that may limit its large-scale application in the real world. On the one hand, the policy of the current traffic signal is often heavily influenced by its neighbor agents, and the coordination between the agent and its neighbors needs to be considered. Hence, the control of a road network composed of multiple traffic signals is naturally modeled as a multi-agent system, and all agents’ policies need to be optimized simultaneously. On the other hand, once the policy function is conditioned on not only the current agent's observation but also the neighbors’, the policy function would be closely related to the training scenario and cause poor generalizability because the agents in various scenarios often have heterogeneous neighbors. To make the policy learned from a training scenario generalizable to new unseen scenarios, a novel Meta Variationally Intrinsic Motivated (MetaVIM) RL method is proposed to learn the decentralized policy for each intersection that considers neighbor information in a latent way. Specifically, we formulate the policy learning as a meta-learning problem over a set of related tasks, where each task corresponds to traffic signal control at an intersection whose neighbors are regarded as the unobserved part of the state. Then, a learned latent variable is introduced to represent the task's specific information and is further brought into the policy for learning. In addition, to make the policy learning stable, a novel intrinsic reward is designed to encourage each agent's received rewards and observation transition to be predictable only conditioned on its own history. Extensive experiments conducted on CityFlow demonstrate that the proposed method substantially outperforms existing approaches and shows superior generalizability.

Title: The State-of-the-Art of Coordinated Ramp Control with Mixed Traffic Conditions
Snippet: With the rapid advance in machine learning techniques such as artificial neural network (ANN) and reinforcement learning, more and more learning-based approaches for ramp metering emerge recently. Because of the nonlinear feature of traffic dynamics, learning-based approaches seem to be a shortcut to achieve better performance. 

Zhang et al. proposed a local freeway ramp metering using ANN [41]. The controllers calculate the proportionalintegral (PI) feedback gain using multi-layer feed-forward (MLF) neural network which can be tuned by both historical data and on-line streaming data. Coordinated Ramp metering algorithm using ANN was firstly proposed by Wei and Wu [42]. The coordinated metering rate was trained by a traffic simulation model and expert system. 

The recent breakthroughs of Reinforcement Learning (RL) provide another promising direction for ramp metering. Numerous RL-based algorithms have sprung up in the past five years. A local ramp metering algorithm was developed by Lu and Huang [43]. Fares et al., and Lu et al. proposed a coordinated ramp metering algorithm using Q-Learning technique [44], [45]. Belletti et al. proposed an expert level ramp metering control based on multi-task deep reinforcement learning [46], and Schmidt-Dumont et al. combined ramp metering with variable speed limits based on decentralised reinforcement learning [47].

Title: Traffic Shaping and Hysteresis Mitigation Using Deep Reinforcement Learning in a Connected Driving Environment
Snippet: Recently, the combination of reinforcement learning with CAVs has gained a lot of attention. Han et al. put forward a physics-informed reinforcement learning(RL)-based ramp metering strategy. They train the RL model using a combination of historic data and synthetic data generated from a traffic flow model to avoid falling into an inaccurate training environment. The strategy is applied to both local and coordinated ramp metering, and results show significant improvements to traffic performance and that it outperforms classical feedback-based ramp metering strategies [23]. Earlier implementations utilized reinforcement learning in its classical form by creating a Q-learning model and training it through actions and rewards [24,25]. More recently, the emergence of deep reinforcement learning has also opened the door for further explorations with several studies adopting the Deep Q Network (DQN) and variations of it to tackle multiple problems in traffic management [26,27,28]. Walraven et al. [29] modeled the traffic flow optimization problem as a reinforcement learning problem. They obtain speed limit policies using Q-learning and use neural networks to improve the performance of their policy learning algorithm. Their method considers traffic predictions and outputs control signals proactively. Wen et al. [30] utilized a deep Q network (DQN) to address re-balancing needs that are critical for effective fleet management in shared mobility on-demand systems. They show that DQN performs effectively by reducing wait times for travelers and limiting the distance traveled by vehicles. In another study, Zhou et al. [31] used the Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient algorithm to create a reinforcement-learning-based car-following model for CAVs to obtain appropriate driving behavior to improve travel efficiency, fuel consumption, and safety at signalized intersections in real-time. Other works have utilized multi-agent reinforcement learning for the task of large-scale traffic signal control. Variations of cooperative deep reinforcement learning are used and they demonstrate the ability of their frameworks to alleviate congestion significantly [32,33,34]. 

Taking a closer look at recent works that adopt reinforcement learning as a technique to alleviate traffic congestion, none focus on improving traffic flow within the hysteresis region.

Title: MoveLight: Enhancing Traffic Signal Control through Movement-Centric Deep Reinforcement Learning
Snippet: This paper introduces MoveLight, a novel traffic signal control system that enhances urban traffic management through movement-centric deep reinforcement learning. By leveraging detailed real-time data and advanced machine learning techniques, MoveLight overcomes the limitations of traditional traffic signal control methods. It employs a lane-level control approach using the FRAP algorithm to achieve dynamic and adaptive traffic signal control, optimizing traffic flow, reducing congestion, and improving overall efficiency. Our research demonstrates the scalability and effectiveness of MoveLight across single intersections, arterial roads, and network levels. Experimental results using real-world datasets from Cologne and Hangzhou show significant improvements in metrics such as queue length, delay, and throughput compared to existing methods. This study highlights the transformative potential of deep reinforcement learning in intelligent traffic signal control, setting a new standard for sustainable and efficient urban transportation systems.

Title: Deep Reinforcement Learning-Based Traffic Signal Control Using High-Resolution Event-Based Data
Snippet: In this paper, we propose a deep reinforcement learning-based traffic signal control method which uses high-resolution event-based data, aiming to achieve a cost-effective and efficient adaptive traffic signal control system. High-resolution event-based data (referred to as event data in this paper), which keeps track of vehicle passage and presence by recording vehicle-detector actuation/de-actuation events, contains much more useful information compared with traditional aggregated data [18], and more importantly, it can be easily collected from vehicle-actuated detectors (e.g., inductive loops) with current technologies [19,20]. In the proposed RLTSC system, all observations that are used to define the traffic state and reward signal can be directly measured using the prevailing detectors, which makes the system completely deployable. Giving the event-based data, an encoding method is put forward to define the traffic state and deep learning techniques are employed to automatically extract useful features for traffic signal control, which gives the controller outstanding performance. The proposed method is validated on a microscopic traffic simulator, and benchmarked with two commonly used traffic signal control strategies, i.e., the fixed-time control strategy and the actuated control strategy. The experimental results show that the proposed method outperforms the commonly used control strategies.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 depicts the problem of traffic signal control using the framework of Markov decision processes (MDPs). Section 3 defines key RL elements for traffic signal control based on event data. Section 4 introduces the deep reinforcement learning approach for traffic signal control. Simulation experiments for training and evaluating the proposed method are presented in Section 5. Finally, the paper is concluded in Section 6.

problem: What is the state of the art in cross subject EEG emotion recognition?
final_response:
# Overview and Challenge

Cross-subject EEG emotion recognition aims to train a model on EEG data from some subjects (source) and accurately generalize to unseen subjects (target) while maintaining emotion class separation, despite large inter-subject variability in neural patterns and recording conditions.<cite id="ac484c45-0">The substantial inter-subject variabilities of emotion-related EEG activities pose great challenge for cross-subject emotion recognition, with cross-subject accuracy on SEED as low as 58% for a generic MLP versus 96% intra-subject on the same dataset</cite>.<cite id="ac484c45-0">This gap is attributed to individualized experience and dispositional differences, although subject-invariance of emotion representations has been observed in psychology and neuroscience, motivating domain adaptation and domain generalization approaches</cite>.

# Benchmarks and Protocols

Common benchmarks include SEED, SEED-IV, DEAP (DREAMER), and others; evaluation typically uses subject-wise splits such as leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) for strict cross-subject validation, and one-vs-rest for multi-class settings.<cite id="ac484c45-0">On SEED, simple baselines drop from 96% intra-subject to 58% cross-subject, highlighting the evaluation gap that motivates advanced methods</cite>.<cite id="ac484c45-3">Recent work validates cross-subject performance on SEED and SEED-IV with LOSO and reports average accuracies like 90.27% (SEED) and 73.21% (SEED-IV), illustrating standard reporting norms</cite>.<cite id="ac484c45-1">For DEAP/DREAMER, some transformer and graph-based studies report strong subject-dependent results but note average performance in cross-subject settings, indicating the difficulty of generalization across these datasets</cite>.

# State-of-the-Art Methods and Quantitative Performance

Recent SOTA approaches combine domain adaptation/generalization with fine-tuning to bridge distribution shifts and improve target-domain accuracy under limited labels. A hybrid transfer learning method (DFF-Net) integrates an Emo-DA module with few-shot fine-tuning and reports strong cross-subject results on SEED and SEED-IV.<cite id="18e347be-0">Ablations show DA-only at 71.32% (SEED) and 61.78% (SEED-IV), FT-only at 88.09% (SEED) and 78.31% (SEED-IV), and the combined DFF-Net at 93.37% (SEED) and 83.32% (SEED-IV)</cite>.<cite id="18e347be-1">On full cross-participant tables, DFF-Net achieves mean ACC 93.37% (SEED) with low dispersion (1.88%) and 82.3% (SEED-IV) with 5.38% dispersion, outperforming traditional DA baselines such as DAN, DDC, and DCORAL, and surpassing multi-source DA-only methods like MS-MDA/MS-ADA/SDDA by 2.29% (SEED) and 0.74% (SEED-IV)</cite>.

Multi-source domain adaptation with conditional distribution alignment and targeted sample hybridization improves cross-subject generalization by reducing label-conflicting shifts between source and target.<cite id="ac484c45-3">The method reports 90.27% on SEED (8 of 15 subjects >90%) and 73.21% on SEED-IV, and also achieves 94.16% and 75.05% in cross-session experiments on SEED and SEED-IV</cite>.<cite id="ac484c45-3">It promotes conditional distribution alignment over marginal alignment to mitigate label confusion during adaptation</cite>.

Transformer and graph-based models are increasingly effective when paired with cross-subject strategies. A graph-attention plus transformer encoder (STGATE) demonstrates strong cross-subject performance across SEED, SEED-IV, and DREAMER using LOSO.<cite id="61955c02-2">STGATE reports 90.37% (SEED), 76.43% (SEED-IV), and 76.35% (DREAMER) accuracies, using a dynamic adjacency matrix to learn non-Euclidean spatial relations and capturing time-frequency features with a transformer encoder</cite>. Transformer-focused works also explore cross-dataset fine-tuning and style transfer for broader transferability, though these are more aligned with cross-corpus than strict cross-subject evaluation.<cite id="18e347be-2">A transformer approach evaluates on SEED-IV, SEED, SEED-V, and MPED with cross-dataset fine-tuning</cite>.<cite id="18e347be-4">An emotional EEG style transfer framework sets up source and target domain subject groupings across SEED, SEED-IV, and MPED to study cross-dataset emotion recognition tasks</cite>.

# Modeling Trends

- Domain adaptation and domain generalization remain core to cross-subject ER. They align marginal or conditional distributions to reduce the source–target gap, with adversarial, MMD, CORAL, and multi-source variants.<cite id="ac484c45-0">DA/DG methods aim to minimize distribution discrepancies between source (training subject) and target (test subject)</cite>.<cite id="ac484c45-1">Classical DA (e.g., DAN, MMD) and more recent multi-source DA have been adapted to EEG ER, often combined with fine-tuning when target labels are limited</cite>.<cite id="ac484c45-3">Conditional distribution alignment and sample hybridization address label-conflict issues and improve cross-subject and cross-session results</cite>.<cite id="ac484c45-4">Multi-branch DA architectures that preserve subject-specific features and GCN-based models (e.g., MSFR-GCN) have been proposed for cross-subject/cross-session recognition</cite>.

- Hybrid transfer learning (DA + fine-tuning) is emerging as SOTA. Combining domain-invariant representation learning with target-specific fine-tuning mitigates domain shift while leveraging limited target labels.<cite id="18e347be-0">DFF-Net shows DA-only vs FT-only trade-offs and the combined model’s superior accuracy on SEED/SEED-IV</cite>.<cite id="18e347be-1">The hybrid approach outperforms traditional DA and DA-only baselines on SEED and SEED-IV, and surpasses multi-source DA-only methods by a notable margin</cite>.

- Self-supervised and contrastive learning target subject-invariant representations. Contrastive EEG methods form positive pairs via data augmentations and negative pairs across subjects/sessions to encourage invariance, complementing DA/DG.<cite id="ac484c45-0">Subject-invariance in emotion representations suggests the feasibility of cross-subject ER and motivates learning subject-invariant features</cite>.<cite id="25779d80-1">Contrastive learning frameworks create positive pairs from augmented signals and negative pairs across different subjects/sessions to improve cross-subject generalization</cite>.<cite id="ac484c45-2">Soft contrastive masked modeling (EEG-SCMM) addresses cross-corpus generalization and notes that prior DA methods often require access to labeled source and unlabeled target data</cite>.<cite id="25779d80-2">Pre-training with soft contrastive masked modeling achieves state-of-the-art one-to-one dataset transfer on SEED, SEED-IV, and DEAP and can transfer to datasets with different emotion categories, though fine-tuning per target subject is still needed</cite>.

- Transformers and graph-based models enhance feature extraction and relational modeling. Vision transformers or transformer encoders capture time-frequency context, while graph attention models the non-Euclidean channel topology; both benefit from cross-subject training strategies.<cite id="ac484c45-4">Transformer backbones have been integrated into DA modules (e.g., Emo-DA) for EEG ER</cite>.<cite id="61955c02-2">STGATE combines a transformer encoder for time-frequency features with a spatial-temporal graph attention module, achieving SOTA cross-subject accuracy on SEED, SEED-IV, and DREAMER</cite>.<cite id="61955c02-0">Transformer-based models (e.g., transformer capsule networks) achieve high subject-dependent accuracy on DEAP/DREAMER but are average in cross-subject settings, indicating room for stronger adaptation</cite>.

- Cross-sensory and adversarial domain adaptation variants address additional shifts (e.g., modality, session) and report improved cross-subject performance when pairing temporal convolutional networks with adversarial discriminative domain adaptation.<cite id="61955c02-1">Adversarial DA variants and multi-source DA have been shown to reduce cross-subject and cross-session discrepancies, with transformer+adversarial combinations improving valence/arousal classification</cite>.

# Cross-Corpus and Pre-training Directions

Beyond subject shifts, cross-corpus generalization (transfer across datasets with different distributions and labels) is an active direction. Soft contrastive masked modeling and pre-training seek to learn cross-corpus-invariant features and reduce reliance on target-specific retraining.<cite id="ac484c45-2">Cross-corpus generalization requires models to overcome larger distribution shifts than within-dataset or within-subject settings; existing DA methods often need labeled source and unlabeled target, which limits scalability</cite>.<cite id="25779d80-2">Soft contrastive masked modeling (EEG-SCMM) reports SOTA one-to-one transfer across SEED, SEED-IV, and DEAP and some cross-dataset capability, though subject-specific fine-tuning is still necessary for robust cross-subject use</cite>.<cite id="25779d80-3">Large-scale self-supervised pre-training (e.g., BENDR) demonstrates the potential of contrastive learning on EEG recordings from thousands of people for downstream tasks</cite>.

# Practical Strategies and Components

- Feature engineering and backbone choices: Differential entropy features and spatial mapping are common inputs, with ViT or CNN backbones for feature extraction before DA modules and fine-tuning.<cite id="18e347be-0">DFF-Net uses DE features with spatial mapping and a ViT feature extractor, paired with an Emo-DA module and few-shot fine-tuning</cite>.

- Target-domain strategies under limited labels: When target labels are scarce, semi-supervised or pseudo-labeling with fine-tuning can help, often combined with DA to avoid overfitting to noisy pseudo-labels.<cite id="ac484c45-1">Hybrid transfer learning balances DA (reducing domain gap) with fine-tuning (leveraging limited target labels) to improve cross-subject performance</cite>.

- Class imbalance and multi-label handling: For datasets like DEAP with arousal/valence dimensions and many classes, dimension-wise binary classification and one-vs-rest schemes are prevalent; performance varies across dimensions and subjects.<cite id="61955c02-0">Reported accuracies differ across Valence, Arousal, and Dominance in DEAP/DREAMER, with some models showing average cross-subject performance despite strong subject-dependent results</cite>.

# Representative Results Across Datasets

- SEED/SEED-IV: Hybrid DA+FT (DFF-Net) achieves around 93% and 82% mean accuracy, respectively, with low dispersion, outperforming classical DA and DA-only methods.<cite id="18e347be-0">DFF-Net: 93.37% (SEED) and 83.32% (SEED-IV) with ablation gains from hybrid learning over DA-only or FT-only</cite>.<cite id="18e347be-1">DFF-Net’s mean ACC is 93.37% (SEED, STD 1.88%) and 82.3% (SEED-IV, STD 5.38%), surpassing DAN and multi-source DA baselines</cite>. Multi-source conditional alignment with sample hybridization reports 90.27% (SEED) and 73.21% (SEED-IV).<cite id="ac484c45-3">Conditional distribution alignment and hybridization improve cross-subject and cross-session ER on SEED and SEED-IV</cite>. Graph-attention transformer (STGATE) shows 90.37% (SEED), 76.43% (SEED-IV).<cite id="61955c02-2">STGATE reports 90.37% (SEED) and 76.43% (SEED-IV), with 76.35% on DREAMER</cite>.

- DREAMER/DEAP: Transformer and graph models often excel in subject-dependent settings but show more modest gains in cross-subject. STGATE achieves 76.35% on DREAMER under LOSO.<cite id="61955c02-2">STGATE achieves 76.35% on DREAMER with LOSO</cite>. Transformer-based works report high subject-dependent accuracies on DEAP/DREAMER but note average cross-subject performance, underscoring the adaptability gap.<cite id="61955c02-0">Transformer capsule networks and architecture search frameworks achieve high subject-dependent accuracies on DEAP/DREAMER but average cross-subject results</cite>.

# Evaluation Protocols and Pitfalls

Accurate comparison requires clear protocols: subject-wise splits (LOSO or source-only train, target-only test), fixed train/val/test subject sets, and consistent dimension-wise or multi-class evaluation schemes. Reported numbers should distinguish mean accuracy and dispersion across subjects and note whether results include pseudo-labels or target labels.<cite id="ac484c45-3">Cross-subject experiments on SEED and SEED-IV report mean accuracy and dispersion across subjects, illustrating the importance of subject-wise variability</cite>.<cite id="18e347be-1">Cross-participant tables report mean ACC and STD and compare against traditional DA and hybrid DA+FT methods</cite>. Methods that rely on target labels during fine-tuning or pseudo-labeling should disclose label budgets and selection strategies to avoid overestimating true zero-shot cross-subject capability.<cite id="ac484c45-1">Hybrid transfer learning uses limited target-domain labels for fine-tuning, and the balance between DA and FT affects performance and generalization</cite>.

# Open Challenges and Emerging Directions

- Generalization under label scarcity and heterogeneous shifts: Target-domain label scarcity, cross-session shifts, and cross-corpus domain gaps remain challenging; semi-supervised fine-tuning, target data selection, and distillation are promising but need robust validation.<cite id="ac484c45-3">Target-domain sample selection and test-time strategies (e.g., augmentation) are explored to improve limited-label settings</cite>.<cite id="25779d80-2">Knowledge distillation from target-domain models to source-domain pre-trained models has been applied for cross-subject evaluation across subjects in target datasets</cite>.

- Learning subject-invariant yet class-discriminative representations: Contrastive and masked modeling approaches seek invariance across subjects while preserving emotion separability; integrating augmentation strategies and alignment objectives that respect label structure is key.<cite id="25779d80-1">Contrastive learning with subject/session negatives encourages discriminative and invariant features for cross-subject ER</cite>.<cite id="ac484c45-2">Soft contrastive masked modeling targets cross-corpus generalization and discusses limitations of DA methods requiring labeled/unlabeled access</cite>.

- Scalable and adaptive architectures: Multi-branch DA to preserve subject-specific characteristics, graph-based spatial modeling, and transformer encoders for time-frequency context are advancing adaptability; combining these with principled adaptation objectives and evaluation across multiple datasets is essential.<cite id="ac484c45-4">Multi-branch DA and GCN-based models (e.g., MSFR-GCN) address subject-specificity and spatial relations in EEG ER</cite>.<cite id="61955c02-2">STGATE’s dynamic adjacency and transformer encoder demonstrate improved cross-subject performance across multiple datasets</cite>.

# Takeaways

- Strong SOTA cross-subject EEG emotion recognition is achieved by hybridizing domain adaptation/generalization with targeted fine-tuning, reporting around 90–93% mean accuracy on SEED and mid-70s to high-70s on SEED-IV under LOSO, with recent graph+transformer models also competitive on DREAMER.<cite id="18e347be-0">Hybrid DA+FT (DFF-Net) achieves 93.37% (SEED) and 83.32% (SEED-IV)</cite>.<cite id="18e347be-1">Hybrid methods outperform classical DA and DA-only baselines on SEED/SEED-IV</cite>.<cite id="ac484c45-3">Conditional alignment with sample hybridization yields 90.27% (SEED) and 73.21% (SEED-IV)</cite>.<cite id="61955c02-2">STGATE achieves 90.37% (SEED), 76.43% (SEED-IV), and 76.35% (DREAMER)</cite>.

- Transformers and graphs enhance representational power when coupled with adaptation strategies, but cross-subject performance depends critically on domain-shift handling and label strategies; many transformer works excel in subject-dependent settings but show average cross-subject gains without adaptation.<cite id="61955c02-0">Transformer-based models achieve high subject-dependent accuracy on DEAP/DREAMER but average cross-subject performance</cite>.

- Cross-corpus pre-training and masked modeling are promising to reduce dataset-specific biases and improve transfer, though subject-specific fine-tuning or data selection remains necessary for robust cross-subject deployment.<cite id="25779d80-2">Soft contrastive masked modeling transfers across SEED, SEED-IV, and DEAP and can handle cross-dataset shifts, but fine-tuning per subject is still needed</cite>.

- Rigorous evaluation with subject-wise splits, reported mean accuracy and dispersion across subjects, and transparent disclosure of label usage and adaptation strategies are essential for fair SOTA comparisons.<cite id="ac484c45-3">LOSO evaluations on SEED/SEED-IV report mean and dispersion across subjects</cite>.<cite id="18e347be-1">Cross-participant tables include mean ACC and STD and compare against established baselines</cite>.

Snippet: However, most studies have mainly focused on intrasubject emotion recognition [5]. To reach satisfactory recognition performance, researchers needed to collect sufficient data (generally half an hour to more than one hour) within one subject to learn subject-dependent EEG representations for emotion recognition [14], [23], [24]. This laborious and time-consuming training procedure has become a major bottleneck for the practical use of EEG-based emotion recognition. Therefore, developing emotion recognition methods with good cross-subject generalizability is desirable for realistic applications, especially in the cases of new users [25], [26]. 

The substantial inter-subject variabilities of emotion-related EEG activities posed great challenge for cross-subject emotion recognition [27], [28]. For example, the cross-subject emotion recognition accuracy on the widely used SEED dataset [9], [14] could be as low as 58% with a generic multiple layer perceptron classifier. In comparison, the intra-subject emotion recognition could achieve high accuracy of 96% with the same classifier [29]. The substantial drop in the emotion recognition performance from the intra-subject to the cross-subject scenario could be explained by the well-acknowledged individual difference in EEGbased emotion representations due to factors such as individualized experience and dispositional characteristics [30], [31], [32], [33]. Nonetheless, subject-invariance of emotion representation has also been well documented in the field of psychology and neuroscience [15], [34], [35], [36], [37]. Previous fMRI and EEG studies have identified distinct and stable neural representations for different emotions across subjects [15], [34], [35], [36], [37], suggesting the possibility of developing cross-subject emotion recognition algorithms. 

To address the issue of inter-subject variability, researchers have applied domain adaptation (DA) and domain generalization (DG) methods to cross-subject emotion recognition [26], [38]. The DA methods aim to minimize the discrepancy between data distributions of the source domain (i.e., the training subject) and the target domain (i.e., the testing subject).
</snippet>

Title: Hybrid transfer learning strategy for cross-subject EEG emotion recognition
Snippet: If the labeled data in the target domain is limited, utilizing fine-tuning may become challenging. Therefore, some researchers have begun exploring the application of domain adaptation for cross-subject eeg emotion recognition. For example, Jin et al. (2017) introduced the implementation of the Domain Adaptation Network (DAN) for knowledge migration in EEG-based sentiment identification to tackle the core issue of reducing disparities between the origin participant and destination participant in an attempt to eradicate subject variability. Li et al. (2019) introduced a domain adaptation technique for EEG emotion recognition, enhanced by reducing the classification error on the source domain while simultaneously harmonizing the latent representations of the source and target domains to enhance their similarity. Wang et al. (2021a) introduced a proficient domain adaptation approach using the multi-subject learning paradigm to address crosssubject emotion classification tasks with restricted EEG data. This technique empowers the model to grasp overarching attributes from diverse participants and swiftly adjust to the specific target individual (Wang et al., 2021a). However, only relying on domain adaptation methods may not effectively leverage the available label information in the target domain, which can result in performance degradation. Domain adaptation typically focuses on reducing the performance gap between different domains, especially between the source and target domains. Fine-tuning involves further training on target domain data to adapt to its specific characteristics, thus enhancing the performance of the model in the target domain. Therefore, combining these two techniques can lead to more significant performance improvements, allowing the model to better adapt to cross-subject EEG emotion recognition tasks. However, effectively coordinating both domain adaptation and fine-tuning techniques and harnessing their strengths to reduce inter-domain differences, enhance model adaptability, and ultimately improve emotion recognition accuracy is a challenging task. The challenge of this task lies in the need for careful balance between the two techniques, ensuring that the model can adapt well to the data characteristics of the target domain while preserving its generalization capability. Additionally, the selection of appropriate domain adaptation methods and fine-tuning strategies must also be considered.
</snippet>
<snippet id=ac484c45-2>
Title: EEG-SCMM: Soft Contrastive Masked Modeling for Cross-Corpus EEG-Based Emotion Recognition
Snippet: Emotions are human attitudinal experiences and behavioral responses to objective things, closely related to an individual's health conditions and behavioral patterns [45]. Compared to speech [40], gestures [31], and facial expressions [2], electroencephalography (EEG) offers a more direct and objective measurement of human emotions by capturing brain activity across various scalp locations [16]. Therefore, researchers have increasingly emphasized EEGbased emotion recognition in recent years [50,51,53,56], aiming to advance the development of affective brain-computer interfaces (aBCIs). However, three critical challenges remain to be addressed in current approaches. 

(1) Insufficient Generalization Capability. Most existing EEGbased emotion recognition methods are typically designed for a single dataset, necessitating model retraining when the dataset changes. This requirement significantly limits the scalability and generalizability of the model, hindering its application on different datasets. To address this issue, the concept of cross-corpus has been proposed, which is designed to be generalized across multiple datasets. A cross-corpus model is trained on one dataset and can be directly applied to another without retraining from scratch. This concept, which originated in natural language processing [38,52], has been extended to various domains in recent years [5,35,37]. Although existing EEG-based emotion recognition methods, such as BiDANN [28], TANN [26], and PR-PL [57], have demonstrated superior performance in within-subject or cross-subject tasks within a single dataset, their effectiveness significantly degrades in crosscorpus scenarios, where the differences in data distribution across datasets far exceed the intra-dataset variability [35]. 

(2) Modeling Strategy Limitation. Recently, researchers have explored domain adaptation techniques to address cross-corpus EEG-based emotion recognition [14,58]. This is motivated by their  efficacy to solve the problem of domain shift [10]. Despite initial success, such approaches often require prior access to all labeled source data and unlabeled target data for model training.
</snippet>
<snippet id=ac484c45-3>
Title: Multi-source domain adaptation for EEG emotion recognition based on inter-domain sample hybridization
Snippet: Background Electroencephalogram (EEG) is widely used in emotion recognition due to its precision and reliability. However, the nonstationarity of EEG signals causes significant differences between individuals or sessions, making it challenging to construct a robust model. Recently, domain adaptation (DA) methods have shown excellent results in cross-subject EEG emotion recognition by aligning marginal distributions. Nevertheless, these methods do not consider emotion category labels, which can lead to label confusion during alignment. Our study aims to alleviate this problem by promoting conditional distribution alignment during domain adaptation to improve cross-subject and cross-session emotion recognition performance. Method This study introduces a multi-source domain adaptation common-branch network for EEG emotion recognition and proposes a novel sample hybridization method. This method enables the introduction of target domain data information by directionally hybridizing source and target domain samples without increasing the overall sample size, thereby enhancing the effectiveness of conditional distribution alignment in domain adaptation. Cross-subject and cross-session experiments were conducted on two publicly available datasets, SEED and SEED-IV, to validate the proposed model. Result In cross-subject emotion recognition, our method achieved an average accuracy of 90.27% on the SEED dataset, with eight out of 15 subjects attaining a recognition accuracy higher than 90%. For the SEED-IV dataset, the recognition accuracy also reached 73.21%. Additionally, in the cross-session experiment, we sequentially used two out of the three session data as source domains and the remaining session as the target domain for emotion recognition. The proposed model yielded average accuracies of 94.16 and 75.05% on the two datasets, respectively. Conclusion Our proposed method aims to alleviate the difficulties of emotion recognition from the limited generalization ability of EEG features across subjects and sessions. Though adapting the multi-source domain adaptation and the sample hybridization method, the proposed method can effectively transfer the emotion-related knowledge of known subjects and achieve accurate emotion recognition on unlabeled subjects.
</snippet>
<snippet id=ac484c45-4>
Title: MASTF-net: An EEG Emotion Recognition Network Based on Multi-Source Domain Adaptive Method Based on Spatio-Temporal Image and Frequency Domain Information
Snippet: These studies highlight the potential of EEGbased approaches in diagnosing mental health disorders and facilitating timely intervention. 

The emotion recognition method based on EEG signals can more accurately reflect the changes in the subject's emotions compared to methods based on facial and language information. However, considering the individual differences in EEG signals, it remains challenging to share a network model trained on specific subjects with other subjects for testing. Although this detection method utilizing EEG signals from a single subject improves the efficiency of model training, its application in cross-subject and cross-session scenarios is difficult. 

To address the issue of emotion analysis among multiple subjects, domain adaptation(DA) has been widely employed in this research work. DA improves the learning in the unlabeled target domain through the transfer of knowledge from the source domains, which can significantly reduce the number of labeled samples [13]. 

In practical applications, we often encounter scenarios with multiple source domains, such as in cross-subject emotion analysis research, where EEG data from different subjects are considered as multi-source domain data. In recent years, many researchers have tended to merge multiple source domain data into one domain. For example, Yiming et al. [14] and He and Yiming [15] employed deep adaptive networks (DANs) [16] for emotion recognition based on EEG signals, using maximum mean difference (MMD) [17] as a distance metric between source and target domains. 

The approach of combining multiple source domain data into one domain disrupts the unique characteristics of EEG signals from different subjects, neglecting the differences in EEG among different subjects, resulting in significant biases in cross-subject applications. To address this issue, we introduced a multi-branch structure approach [13], establishing one-to-one DA branches for all target domains and source domains to preserve the specific features of each source domain data. Many similar methods appeared in [13], [18], [19]. Pan and Zheng [18] proposed a MSFR-GCN model for EEG-based emotion and cognition recognition using graph convolutional networks (GCN) to obtain graph representations of EEG signals.
