problem: Teach me about all latest progress on diagnosis, such as counterfactual explanation, of VLM models like CLIP
final_response:
# Overview: What “Diagnosis” Means for VLMs like CLIP

Diagnosis of vision–language models (VLMs) such as CLIP spans two complementary goals: explaining and localizing what evidence drives predictions, and auditing failure modes such as spurious correlations, out-of-distribution (OOD) brittleness, and hallucinations that arise in model use or fine-tuning pipelines.<cite id="9fd0fb73-0">Understanding CLIP representations has moved from high-level alignment to component-level analyses that decompose latent embeddings into human-interpretable concepts, examine attention heads and MLP neurons, and use sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to expose diverse, representation-aligned components</cite>.<cite id="3c8ac24f-0">Recent robustness studies show that while CLIP appears robust to ImageNet-style shifts, specialized benchmarks reveal reliance on spurious features that can break under real-world distribution shifts</cite>.<cite id="3c8ac24f-4">Complementary lines of work investigate object hallucinations in CLIP and downstream LVLMs, and propose targeted fine-tuning strategies to mitigate encoder-level errors</cite>.

A prominent and rapidly evolving thread is counterfactual explanation: constructing plausible, semantically consistent image or image–text edits that invert model decisions or attributes, using these edits to test faithfulness, diagnose priors vs. perception, and steer model behavior.<cite id="4659c81d-4">Counterfactual training and evaluation (e.g., DeFacto) explicitly enforce region-faithful reasoning and abstention when evidence is missing, and improves both answer accuracy and grounding over strong baselines</cite>.<cite id="4659c81d-2">Visual counterfactuals can expose how VLMs compete between memorized world knowledge and in-context pixels, with mechanisms to steer models between reliance on priors versus perceptual input</cite>.<cite id="4659c81d-3">Automated pipelines using diffusion models can scale to multimodal counterfactual datasets (e.g., COCO-Counterfactuals) that stress existing models and improve OOD generalization</cite>.

# Counterfactual Diagnosis and Explanation Methods for VLMs

Counterfactuals provide a principled, model-agnostic route to faithfulness: instead of perturbing pixels arbitrarily, they present alternative but plausible scenarios and measure changes in predictions and rationales.<cite id="4659c81d-1">Compared to classic image saliency, counterfactual methods operate on the original model to generate explanations and aim for faithfulness by design, while classic image counterfactuals often highlight discriminative regions without changing the outcome</cite>.<cite id="4659c81d-4">DeFacto introduces a large-scale counterfactual dataset and region-level reward design, improving both answer accuracy and visual grounding, and demonstrating the necessity of counterfactual supervision for interpretability and robustness</cite>.

Constructing high-quality multimodal counterfactuals remains challenging. Recent work frames it as a text-to-image diffusion task to scale up paired image–text counterfactuals with minimal edits.<cite id="4659c81d-3">COCO-Counterfactuals automatically generates counterfactual images and captions from MS-COCO, passes human evaluation, challenges state-of-the-art multimodal models, and improves OOD generalization when used for data augmentation</cite>. At the image-only level, new methods emphasize semantic consistency and sparse, discriminative edits.<cite id="4659c81d-1">State-of-the-art visual counterfactuals can produce semantically consistent replacements of object parts (e.g., wing vs. head) and limit sparsity to make explanations human-friendly, addressing degeneracy from prior approaches</cite>.

Steering and auditing via counterfactuals can also expose knowledge sources inside VLMs. For instance, plausibly contradictory visual evidence can reveal whether models rely on memorized priors or in-context pixels, and where this switch occurs in the forward pass.<cite id="4659c81d-2">Experiments show MLLMs often favor perceptual input over general knowledge when counterfactual pixels contradict priors, with a transition from knowledge-based to perception-based answers emerging in mid-to-late layers; steering vectors can reliably shift predictions for color and size attributes</cite>. These findings translate to CLIP-based LVLMs, since many (e.g., LLaVA, BLIP, Kosmos-2) use CLIP vision encoders as frozen backbones, making encoder-level failures and biases prominent in downstream behavior.<cite id="3c8ac24f-1">CLIP is widely used as a frozen vision encoder in end-to-end VLMs; evaluating CLIP on OOD tasks reveals shortcomings that propagate to downstream models, motivating encoder-specific tuning</cite>.

Beyond training and auditing, counterfactuals can be used for evaluation. Human-like VLM evaluators and region-level metrics assess whether edits are discriminative and lead to the expected prediction changes.<cite id="4659c81d-4">DeFacto evaluates counterfactual edits with both traditional metrics and VLM-as-a-judge, including region-level analyses and ablations on counterfactual training necessity</cite>.<cite id="4659c81d-3">COCO-Counterfactuals supports evaluation by providing challenging, minimally altered pairs that probe robustness and generalization</cite>. For video understanding, dedicated benchmarks expose the difficulty of multi-hop counterfactual reasoning, and targeted post-training can improve counterfactual reasoning capacity.<cite id="700933b9-2">CounterVQA benchmarks progressive counterfactual reasoning across difficulty levels and finds that models degrade on multi-hop causal chains; a post-training method (CFGPT) distills counterfactual reasoning from language to vision to improve across all levels</cite>.<cite id="700933b9-3">Causally-guided adversarial steering produces counterfactual explanations and is evaluated with both standard metrics and VLM-based human-like evaluation, including case studies and parameter ablations</cite>.

# CLIP-Specific Interpretability and Diagnosis

Component-level analyses of CLIP have advanced along two fronts: concept discovery and attribution, and head/layer diagnostics.

- Concept discovery and sparse autoencoders: Researchers decompose CLIP’s latent space into interpretable components that align with human concepts, revealing both expected and spurious features.<cite id="9fd0fb73-0">Task-agnostic concept discovery shows CLIP embeddings align with human-interpretable concepts, but high-level decompositions miss unexpected or spurious features; SAEs offer finer-grained components and can reveal how they influence predictions</cite>.<cite id="9fd0fb73-1">Follow-up work uses SAEs both to understand CLIP’s representations and to steer behavior via identified interpretable features</cite>. This connects to bias and safety auditing, as discovered components may encode sensitive or spurious associations that affect downstream fairness and robustness.<cite id="3c8ac24f-0">Benchmarks like CounterAnimal assess reliance on spurious features under distribution shift, complementing concept analyses</cite>.

- Head-level roles and conceptual consistency: Attention head analyses assign semantic roles to CLIP’s heads and quantify how consistently a head encodes a concept across layers, linking performance and bias at the architectural level.<cite id="9fd0fb73-2">Interpretability advances decompose CLIP image representations into contributions of individual attention heads and identify text sequences that characterize heads’ semantic roles</cite>.<cite id="9fd0fb73-2">A “conceptual consistency” framework labels heads by the concepts they represent and introduces a Concept Consistency Score (CCS) to measure alignment of heads with specific concepts across layers</cite>.<cite id="9fd0fb73-3">Experiments show high CCS heads are critical for performance: pruning them causes larger drops than random heads, and these heads also drive out-of-domain detection, concept-specific reasoning, and video–language understanding; critically, they can learn spurious correlations that amplify social biases</cite>. This provides a diagnosis tool: models with high CCS on sensitive concepts may achieve strong accuracy while amplifying harms, offering targets for bias mitigation and architectural guidance.

- Region-level attribution and tooling: A range of CLIP- and VLM-specific methods localize important visual regions and concepts, addressing limitations of pixel-level or perturbation-only approaches.<cite id="9fd0fb73-4">VLM-specific attributions include Grad-ECLIP, CLIP-Surgery, MaskCLIP, ECLIP, and M2iB, while pixel-space methods can be unstable or misaligned with CLIP’s representation; a new cluster-importance clustering (CCI) approach aligns with CLIP’s pretrained patch embeddings to produce semantically coherent, faithful attributions</cite>. These methods complement counterfactual diagnosis by identifying where and which concepts drive predictions, which can be cross-validated with counterfactual edits.

# Robustness, Failure Modes, and Mitigation for CLIP-Like Models

Diagnosis is incomplete without rigorous robustness audits. Recent work probes spurious correlations, OOD shifts, and hallucinations in CLIP and LVLMs, and proposes tuning strategies to fix encoder-level weaknesses.

- Spurious features and distribution shift: CLIP’s robustness to ImageNet-style shifts can mask overreliance on spurious features that fail under real-world shifts; new benchmarks are designed to expose and quantify this reliance.<cite id="3c8ac24f-0">CLIP appears robust to ImageNet-oriented shifts, but specialized benchmarks like CounterAnimal reveal reliance on spurious features that break under distribution shift</cite>.<cite id="3c8ac24f-1">Evaluations on OOD benchmarks uncover scenarios where CLIP fails, and these limitations propagate to downstream VLMs using CLIP’s embeddings</cite>.

- 3D awareness and architectural effects: Robustness varies with visual encoder architecture and training choices, and CLIP models can exhibit biases (e.g., shape) that change with fine-tuning.<cite id="3c8ac24f-3">A holistic evaluation finds architecture and training choices (e.g., contrastive loss, fine-tuning) significantly affect robustness and biases such as shape reliance; fine-tuning on ImageNet can diminish some biases</cite>.

- Hallucination audits and encoder fine-tuning: Object hallucinations in CLIP encoders can propagate to LVLMs like LLaVA; targeted fine-tuning mitigates both encoder and downstream hallucinations by emphasizing object-level contrastive signals.<cite id="3c8ac24f-4">A curated OHD-Caps benchmark shows CLIP ViT-L/14 scores positive captions only 19% of the time, indicating substantial object hallucination; fine-tuning with object-level contrastive loss reduces hallucinations in CLIP and, when used as the visual encoder, in LLaVA-1.5</cite>.<cite id="3c8ac24f-2">Expanded POPE, CHAIR, and AMBER evaluations quantify discriminative and generative hallucinations, and show improvements when replacing the CLIP encoder with a fine-tuned version in LLaVA-1.5</cite>.

These findings inform diagnosis workflows: if counterfactuals or concept analyses reveal reliance on spurious attributes, OOD weakness, or object hallucinations, follow with encoder-specific fine-tuning on targeted domains and re-evaluate with the appropriate benchmarks.

# Evaluation Benchmarks and Metrics for Explanations and Counterfactuals

Faithfulness and coverage are central dimensions for evaluating VLM explanations and counterfactuals. Recent benchmarks broaden coverage beyond object-level detection to attributes, relations, and the hallucination–informativeness trade-off.

- LVLM faithfulness and coverage: VALOR-EVAL introduces a multi-dimensional benchmark spanning objects, attributes, and relations, with challenging images selected to probe associative biases; it generalizes CHAIR to evaluate both faithfulness and coverage and reports better correlation with human judgments than prior metrics.<cite id="700933b9-4">VALOR-EVAL’s two-stage LLM-based evaluation generalizes CHAIR to jointly measure faithfulness and coverage, highlighting the critical balance between correctness and informativeness and showing improved human correlation on a challenging, human-annotated benchmark</cite>.

- Counterfactual reasoning in video: CounterVQA assesses progressive counterfactual reasoning, revealing performance gaps on multi-hop causal chains; a post-training method (CFGPT) improves across difficulty levels, indicating a path to train counterfactual reasoning explicitly.<cite id="700933b9-2">CounterVQA exposes degradation on complex multi-hop counterfactuals, and CFGPT distills counterfactual reasoning from language to vision to yield consistent gains</cite>.

- Human-like evaluators for counterfactual edits: Beyond traditional metrics, VLMs can judge whether counterfactual edits are semantically consistent, discriminative, and causally effective, adding an external, human-like evaluation layer.<cite id="700933b9-3">Causally-guided adversarial steering evaluates counterfactuals with both standard metrics and VLM-based human-like evaluation, including ablations and case studies</cite>.<cite id="4659c81d-4">DeFacto similarly uses VLMs as evaluators to assess the quality of counterfactual edits and region-faithful reasoning</cite>.

- Multimodal counterfactual datasets: COCO-Counterfactuals provides a scalable, human-validated dataset of minimally altered image–text pairs to probe robustness and support data augmentation for OOD generalization.<cite id="4659c81d-3">COCO-Counterfactuals scales counterfactual generation via diffusion models, challenges state-of-the-art multimodal models, and improves OOD generalization when used for training</cite>.

# Practical Workflow: Diagnosing a CLIP-Based VLM with Counterfactuals and Concepts

1) Attribute and concept mapping: Use CLIP-specific attribution (e.g., ECLIP, Grad-ECLIP, MaskCLIP, CCI) to identify discriminative regions and concept-level components driving key decisions; validate with SAE or head-level analyses to tie concepts to model internals.<cite id="9fd0fb73-4">CLIP- and VLM-specific attribution tools (Grad-ECLIP, CLIP-Surgery, MaskCLIP, ECLIP, M2iB) and representation-aligned CCI can yield more faithful, localized attributions than pixel-level perturbations</cite>.<cite id="9fd0fb73-1">SAEs can expose diverse, human-interpretable components and, when trained appropriately, be used to steer CLIP-like models via identified features</cite>.<cite id="9fd0fb73-2">Head-level role assignments and Concept Consistency Scores reveal which concepts are consistently encoded and where spurious correlations may lie</cite>.

2) Build targeted counterfactuals: Generate semantically consistent edits that flip key attributed concepts (e.g., color, size, occlusion) or causal factors; measure prediction and rationale changes to test faithfulness and over-reliance on priors versus pixels.<cite id="4659c81d-1">Semantically consistent counterfactual frameworks constrain edits to the same object parts and seek discriminative, sparse changes to produce informative explanations</cite>.<cite id="4659c81d-2">Visual counterfactuals can diagnose competition between world knowledge and in-context perception and provide steering vectors to shift reliance between priors and pixels</cite>.

3) Robustness and bias auditing: Probe spurious feature reliance and OOD brittleness using shift-specific benchmarks (e.g., CounterAnimal) and 3D/attribute corruption evaluations; quantify bias via high-CCS head analyses and sensitive-concept scoring.<cite id="3c8ac24f-0">CounterAnimal exposes spurious-feature reliance under distribution shift</cite>.<cite id="3c8ac24f-3">A holistic CLIP evaluation reveals architecture- and training-induced biases (e.g., shape reliance) and their changes with fine-tuning</cite>.<cite id="9fd0fb73-3">High CCS heads both drive performance and amplify social biases, providing targets for bias audits</cite>.

4) Mitigation and re-evaluation: If failures are encoder-driven (e.g., object hallucinations or spurious attribute reliance), fine-tune the vision encoder with domain-specific, object-level contrastive signals and re-test with discriminative and generative hallucination benchmarks (POPE/CHAIR/AMBER) and counterfactual datasets; track faithfulness and coverage with VALOR-EVAL-like metrics and VLM-as-judge evaluations.<cite id="3c8ac24f-2">Object-level fine-tuning reduces hallucinations in CLIP and downstream LVLMs (e.g., LLaVA-1.5) on multiple benchmarks</cite>.<cite id="700933b9-4">VALOR-EVAL’s faithfulness–coverage framework helps quantify trade-offs and human correlation</cite>.<cite id="4659c81d-3">Counterfactual datasets like COCO-Counterfactuals support robustness and OOD evaluation and can improve generalization when used for augmentation</cite>.<cite id="4659c81d-4">Counterfactual training and VLM-judged evaluation (DeFacto) improve grounding and reasoning faithfulness</cite>.

# Open Challenges and Research Directions

- Spurious-to-faithful trade-offs: Counterfactuals and concept analyses can reveal reliance on spurious features, but training with counterfactual supervision must balance faithfulness with generalization to avoid overfitting to artificial edits.<cite id="3c8ac24f-0">Shift-specific benchmarks show that reliance on spurious features can dominate ImageNet-style evaluations, necessitating targeted audits</cite>.<cite id="700933b9-2">Even strong models struggle with multi-hop counterfactual chains, suggesting limits in causal reasoning that future training must address</cite>.

- Faithfulness–utility tensions: Explanations that are too local or sparse may omit necessary context, while comprehensive explanations can be computationally expensive and introduce hallucinations; evaluation frameworks must jointly measure faithfulness and coverage.<cite id="700933b9-4">VALOR-EVAL highlights the faithfulness–coverage trade-off and its importance for reliable LVLM evaluation</cite>.

- Human-like evaluators and interpretability alignment: VLMs-as-judges can assess counterfactual quality and grounding, but their own biases and hallucinations can propagate; combining human-in-the-loop with automated metrics remains an active area.<cite id="700933b9-3">Using VLM evaluators alongside traditional metrics provides qualitative and quantitative signals for counterfactual quality</cite>.<cite id="700933b9-4">LLM-based evaluation frameworks can improve correlation with human judgments on complex LVLM tasks</cite>.

- CLIP backbone governance: As CLIP is reused across many systems, robust auditing and tuning of its encoders are critical; methods that expose high-impact, high-bias heads and spurious concept components can guide safe deployment and selective fine-tuning at scale.<cite id="3c8ac24f-1">Because many LVLMs freeze CLIP encoders, encoder-level weaknesses affect downstream performance and require efficient tuning strategies</cite>.<cite id="9fd0fb73-3">High CCS heads are both essential for performance and prone to spurious correlations, suggesting prioritized mitigation targets</cite>.

# Key Takeaways

- Counterfactual diagnosis has matured from conceptual tools to scalable datasets and training regimes that improve faithfulness and reasoning in VLMs, with direct relevance to CLIP-based systems through their common use as encoders and the propagation of encoder-level failures.<cite id="4659c81d-4">Counterfactual supervision and evaluation improve answer accuracy and visual grounding in multimodal models</cite>.<cite id="4659c81d-2">Visual counterfactuals reveal and steer between world knowledge and perceptual input, exposing internal competition dynamics</cite>.<cite id="4659c81d-3">Automated multimodal counterfactual datasets stress current models and enhance OOD generalization</cite>.

- CLIP-specific interpretability has advanced with head-level role assignments, concept consistency metrics, and SAE-based component analyses, enabling diagnosis of both capabilities and biases at architectural and concept levels.<cite id="9fd0fb73-2">Head-level analyses and CCS provide performance-critical, concept-aligned diagnostics</cite>.<cite id="9fd0fb73-1">SAEs help understand and steer CLIP’s latent concepts</cite>.

- Robustness audits show that CLIP-like models can be surprisingly vulnerable to spurious features and OOD/3D shifts not captured by standard benchmarks; encoder-specific fine-tuning on object-level signals can mitigate hallucinations in both CLIP and downstream LVLMs.<cite id="3c8ac24f-0">Spurious-feature reliance under distribution shift is a latent risk</cite>.<cite id="3c8ac24f-4">Object-level fine-tuning reduces hallucinations in CLIP and in LLaVA-1.5 across multiple evaluations</cite>.

- Evaluation is evolving toward multi-dimensional faithfulness–coverage metrics and domain-specific counterfactual benchmarks, complemented by human-like VLM evaluators to judge counterfactual plausibility and grounding.<cite id="700933b9-4">VALOR-EVAL generalizes CHAIR to jointly measure faithfulness and coverage with better human correlation</cite>.<cite id="700933b9-2">CounterVQA exposes limits in multi-hop counterfactual reasoning and shows targeted post-training can help</cite>.<cite id="4659c81d-3">COCO-Counterfactuals provides scalable, challenging multimodal pairs for evaluation and augmentation</cite>.<cite id="4659c81d-4">VLM-as-judge evaluations quantify counterfactual quality and faithfulness</cite>.

In practice, a modern diagnosis toolkit for CLIP-like models couples concept- and head-level analyses with counterfactual generation and evaluation, robustness audits under targeted shifts, and encoder-level fine-tuning validated on discriminative and generative benchmarks—closing the loop between explanation, diagnosis, and mitigation.<cite id="9fd0fb73-0">Component-level understanding reveals both intended and spurious features in CLIP</cite>.<cite id="3c8ac24f-3">Architecture and training choices shape robustness and biases, guiding mitigation</cite>.<cite id="4659c81d-2">Counterfactuals expose knowledge–perception dynamics and enable steering</cite>.<cite id="3c8ac24f-4">Encoder-focused fine-tuning reduces hallucinations and improves downstream models</cite>.

Title: Pixels Versus Priors: Controlling Knowledge Priors in Vision-Language Models through Visual Counterfacts
Snippet: In our framework, world knowledge priors refer to linguistic associations between visual attributes and objects that the model has memorized during pretraining. In contrast, visual perception is defined by the in-context visual input, which we manipulate to create counterfactual images. These counterfactuals are designed to challenge the model's world knowledge of visual attributes by presenting plausible but contradictory visual evidence. For example, we contrast the size-related knowledge prior "strawberries are bigger than flies" with the counterfactual "flies are bigger than strawberries," violating expected size relations (see Figure 2). 

Using Visual CounterFact, we find that MLLMs often ignore world knowledge when shown counterfactual images, favoring perceptual input even when prompted for general facts. We then trace where in the forward pass predictions shift from in-weight knowledge (e.g., strawberries are red) to in-context perception (this strawberry is blue), finding that this transition consistently emerges in mid-to-late layers. During this transition, models frequently flip between the two answers, revealing a competition between in-context pixel and inweights prior information, with pixels often overriding priors in the model's output. To control this behavior, we use our Pixels Versus Priors steering to control whether a vision-language model relies on knowledge priors or pixel information. PvP is a novel framework to construct steering vectors for vision-language models that control whether the model responds based on memorized knowledge or in-context visual input. Through this steering, we successfully shift an average of 99.3% of color predictions and 80.8% of size predictions from memorized priors to counterfactual answers. 

Together, these contributions provide a new visual counterfactual benchmark and a mechanism for interpreting and controlling the behavior of vision-language models. We present the necessary foundation for a mechanistic understanding of how MLLMs integrate image input with prior knowledge of visual attributes, bridging the gap between interpretability research in language models and the emerging needs of multimodal models.
</snippet>

Title: COCO-Counterfactuals: Automatically Constructed Counterfactual Examples for Image-Text Pairs
Snippet: Counterfactual examples have proven to be valuable in the field of natural language processing (NLP) for both evaluating and improving the robustness of language models to spurious correlations in datasets. Despite their demonstrated utility for NLP, multimodal counterfactual examples have been relatively unexplored due to the difficulty of creating paired image-text data with minimal counterfactual changes. To address this challenge, we introduce a scalable framework for automatic generation of counterfactual examples using text-to-image diffusion models. We use our framework to create COCO-Counterfactuals, a multimodal counterfactual dataset of paired image and text captions based on the MS-COCO dataset. We validate the quality of COCO-Counterfactuals through human evaluations and show that existing multimodal models are challenged by our counterfactual image-text pairs. Additionally, we demonstrate the usefulness of COCO-Counterfactuals for improving out-of-domain generalization of multimodal vision-language models via training data augmentation.
</snippet>

Title: DeFacto: Counterfactual Thinking with Images for Enforcing Evidence-Grounded and Faithful Reasoning
Snippet: In this work, we introduced DeFacto, the first vision-language reasoning framework explicitly grounded in counterfactual supervision, designed to enforce region-faithful reasoning and abstention behavior when critical evidence is missing. To enable this counterfactual reasoning paradigm, we proposed an automatic pipeline for constructing counterfactual datasets, which leverages language model parsing, open-vocabulary detection, and OCR to mask question-relevant regions without requiring manual annotations. Using this pipeline, we built a counterfactual dataset about 100k images to support training and evaluation. Extensive experiments across multiple diverse benchmarks demonstrate that DeFacto consistently improves both answer accuracy and visual grounding faithfulness over strong baselines. Our ablation studies further confirm the necessity of counterfactual training and region-level reward design in enhancing interpretability and robustness. We believe these findings open new directions for integrating counterfactual supervision into multimodal reasoning systems, with potential extensions to video understanding and embodied AI.

Title: From What to How: Attributing CLIP's Latent Components Reveals Unexpected Semantic Reliance
Snippet: Understanding CLIP representations: A line of work on interpreting CLIP and other visionlanguage models focuses on decomposing latent embeddings into a set of predefined, humaninterpretable concepts [5,54]. These methods generally evaluate alignment to known textual labels but struggle to capture the full diversity of learned features, particularly unexpected or spurious ones.

Alternatively, visual embeddings in CLIP's last layer can be decomposed into a diverse set of interpretable components using SAEs [37,40,25], which have been originally proposed for language models [22,7]. Rao et al. [40] train linear classifiers directly on SAEs activations for downstream-tasks, but, as such, can no longer explain the original CLIP model. Other works based on SAEs [30,48] successfully explain what components encode and represent, yet overlook how they influence specific predictions.

Title: Pruning the Paradox: How CLIP’s Most Informative Heads Enhance Performance While Amplifying Bias
Snippet: Large-scale vision-language (VL) models such as CLIP (Radford et al., 2021) have significantly advanced state-of-the-art performance in vision tasks in recent years. Consequently, CLIP has been extensively used as a foundational model for downstream tasks such as video retrieval, image generation, and segmentation (Luo et al., 2022; Liu   * Work partially completed while at Intel Labs. et al., 2024;Brooks et al., 2023;Esser et al., 2024;Kirillov et al., 2023). This has enabled the construction of compositional models combining CLIP with other foundation models, thereby increasing the functionality of CLIP while also adding complexity to the overall model structure. However, as these models gain prominence in real-world applications, their embedded social biases (Howard et al., 2024;Hall et al., 2023;Seth et al., 2023) have emerged as a critical concern with potentially harmful consequences. Despite the growing body of work documenting these biases, a fundamental question remains: what mechanisms within these models' architectures drive both their impressive capabilities and problematic shortcomings? 

Recent interpretability advances (Gandelsman et al.) have made initial progress by decomposing CLIP's image representations into contributions from individual attention heads, identifying text sequences that characterize different heads' semantic roles. However, this approach provides only a partial view into CLIP's inner workings, leaving a critical missing piece: systematic understanding of the visual concepts encoded at the attention head level-and how these concepts underpin both the model's strengths and its social failures. 

Our work addresses this critical gap through a novel interpretability framework we call "conceptual consistency". This framework systematically analyzes which visual concepts are learned by individual attention heads and how consistently these concepts are processed throughout the model's architecture. First, we identify interpretable structures within the individual heads of the last four layers of the model using a set of text descriptions. To accomplish this, we employ the TEXTSPAN algorithm (Gandelsman et al.), which helps us find the most appropriate text descriptions for each head. After identifying these text descriptions, we assign labels to each head representing the common property shared by the descriptions.
</snippet>
<snippet id=9fd0fb73-3>
Title: Pruning the Paradox: How CLIP’s Most Informative Heads Enhance Performance While Amplifying Bias
Snippet: CLIP is one of the most popular foundation models and is heavily used for many vision-language tasks, yet little is known about its inner workings. As CLIP is increasingly deployed in real-world applications, it is becoming even more critical to understand its limitations and embedded social biases to mitigate potentially harmful downstream consequences. However, the question of what internal mechanisms drive both the impressive capabilities as well as problematic shortcomings of CLIP has largely remained unanswered. To bridge this gap, we study the conceptual consistency of text descriptions for attention heads in CLIP-like models. Specifically, we propose Concept Consistency Score (CCS), a novel interpretability metric that measures how consistently individual attention heads in CLIP models align with specific concepts. Our soft-pruning experiments reveal that high CCS heads are critical for preserving model performance, as pruning them leads to a significantly larger performance drop than pruning random or low CCS heads. Notably, we find that high CCS heads capture essential concepts and play a key role in out-of-domain detection, concept-specific reasoning, and video-language understanding. Moreover, we prove that high CCS heads learn spurious correlations which amplify social biases. These results position CCS as a powerful interpretability metric exposing the paradox of performance and social biases in CLIP models.
</snippet>
<snippet id=9fd0fb73-4>
Title: Concept Regions Matter: Benchmarking CLIP with a New Cluster-Importance Approach
Snippet: Interpretability in Vision-Language Models: Early interpretability efforts applied methods such as attention rollout [1], which aggregates attention weights across layers, and gradient-based techniques like GradCAM [50] and GAME [5], which compute feature importance through gradients. With the advent of CLIP [41] and successors like BLIP [32] and ALBEF [31], researchers developed VLM-specific techniques: Grad-ECLIP [64] extends gradient-based attribution to multimodal settings, CLIP-Surgery [33] identifies important regions through similarity masking, MaskCLIP [66] performs token-level masking to localize influential regions, ECLIP [6] leverages gradientweighted attention, and M2iB [58] employs perturbationbased explanations. Perturbation-driven methods such as RISE [40] further provide model-agnostic saliency through random masking. More recent concept-based approaches like SpLiCE [4] learn sparse concept embeddings, while others [26] use foundation models for concept discovery, building on earlier methods like Concept Bottleneck Models [29]. Yet both VLM-specific and traditional interpretability methods produce noisy, low-level attributions. Pixel-space methods such as SLIC [2], LIME [44], and SHAP [38] rely on superpixels that are not aligned with a model's representation. Perturbation-based approaches including RISE [40], Meaningful/Extremal Perturbations [12,13], and the missingness analysis of [23] mask regions using a missingness token (e.g., black patches, noise, blur), making explanations sensitive to the replacement and often unstable. In contrast, CCI clusters CLIP's pretrained patch embeddings to obtain semantically coherent, representation-aligned regions and attenuate the model's attention to the corresponding patch tokens directly, avoiding pixel-level artifacts, preserving the input distribution, and yielding more faithful and localized attributions.
</snippet></tool_output><think>

Title: A Sober Look at the Robustness of CLIPs to Spurious Features
Snippet: Large vision language models (LVLMs) have demonstrated huge success across a wide range of vision and multi-modal tasks, surpassing conventional ImageNet (-trained) models by a remarkably large margin [1]. LVLMs are typically trained with or based on Contrastive Language Image Pre-training (CLIP) [2] on an unprecedented scale of real-world vision and language data such as LAION [3], which are significantly larger than ImageNet. The huge success of CLIP has presented a paradigm shift for modern vision and vision-language models to conduct the pre-training from ImageNet benchmarks to web-scale multi-modal datasets [4]. 

A key signature of CLIP models is the impressive robustness against various ImageNet-oriented distribution shifts [2], which is shown to be prohibitive to ImageNet models [5]. The performance boosts over ImageNet models seem to suggest that CLIP resolves distribution shifts, thereby sparking a rich discussion about its rationale [6,7,8,9,10]. However, the elephant in the room is that adopted testsets (i.e., ImageNet variants) to evaluate the robustness of CLIPs are primarily designed for ImageNet-based models [5,11]. These datasets may not correctly reflect the exact robustness of CLIP, given that CLIP models are trained on a large amount of data that may include, and possibly extend beyond those ImageNet variants during pre-training [10]. In this paper, we investigate the robustness of CLIP to distribution shifts caused by the presence of spurious features. These features are highly correlated with labels, but this correlation may break down under distributional shifts [12,13,14,15,16,17,18,19,20]. We raise a challenging research question in the following:

Title: Toward a Holistic Evaluation of Robustness in CLIP Models
Snippet: Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) models have shown significant potential, particularly in zero-shot classification across diverse distribution shifts. Building on existing evaluations of overall classification robustness, this work aims to provide a more comprehensive assessment of CLIP by introducing several new perspectives. First, we investigate their robustness to variations in specific visual factors. Second, we assess two critical safety objectives—confidence uncertainty and out-of-distribution detection—beyond mere classification accuracy. Third, we evaluate the finesse with which CLIP models bridge the image and text modalities. Fourth, we extend our examination to 3D awareness in CLIP models, moving beyond traditional 2D image understanding. Finally, we explore the interaction between vision and language encoders within modern large multimodal models (LMMs) that utilize CLIP as the visual backbone, focusing on how this interaction impacts classification robustness. In each aspect, we consider the impact of six factors on CLIP models: model architecture, training distribution, training set size, fine-tuning, contrastive loss, and test-time prompts. Our study uncovers several previously unknown insights into CLIP. For instance, the architecture of the visual encoder in CLIP plays a significant role in their robustness against 3D corruption. CLIP models tend to exhibit a bias towards shape when making predictions. Moreover, this bias tends to diminish after fine-tuning on ImageNet. Vision-language models like LLaVA, leveraging the CLIP vision encoder, could exhibit benefits in classification performance for challenging categories over CLIP alone. Our findings are poised to offer valuable guidance for enhancing the robustness and reliability of CLIP models.
</snippet>

Title: CounterVQA: Evaluating and Improving Counterfactual Reasoning in Vision-Language Models for Video Understanding
Snippet: Vision Language Models (VLMs) have recently shown significant advancements in video understanding, especially in feature alignment, event reasoning, and instruction-following tasks. However, their capability for counterfactual reasoning, inferring alternative outcomes under hypothetical conditions, remains underexplored. This capability is essential for robust video understanding, as it requires identifying underlying causal structures and reasoning about unobserved possibilities, rather than merely recognizing observed patterns. To systematically evaluate this capability, we introduce CounterVQA, a video-based benchmark featuring three progressive difficulty levels that assess different aspects of counterfactual reasoning. Through comprehensive evaluation of both state-of-the-art open-source and closed-source models, we uncover a substantial performance gap: while these models achieve reasonable accuracy on simple counterfactual questions, performance degrades significantly on complex multi-hop causal chains. To address these limitations, we develop a post-training method, CFGPT, that enhances a model's visual counterfactual reasoning ability by distilling its counterfactual reasoning capability from the language modality, yielding consistent improvements across all CounterVQA difficulty levels. Dataset and code will be further released.
</snippet>

Title: VALOR-EVAL: Holistic Coverage and Faithfulness Evaluation of Large Vision-Language Models
Snippet: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) suffer from hallucination issues, wherein the models generate plausible-sounding but factually incorrect outputs, undermining their reliability. A comprehensive quantitative evaluation is necessary to identify and understand the extent of hallucinations in these models. However, existing benchmarks are often limited in scope, focusing mainly on object hallucinations. Furthermore, current evaluation methods struggle to effectively address the subtle semantic distinctions between model outputs and reference data, as well as the balance between hallucination and informativeness. To address these issues, we introduce a multi-dimensional benchmark covering objects, attributes, and relations, with challenging images selected based on associative biases. Moreover, we propose a large language model (LLM)-based two-stage evaluation framework that generalizes the popular CHAIR metric and incorporates both faithfulness and coverage into the evaluation. Experiments on 10 established LVLMs demonstrate that our evaluation metric is more comprehensive and better correlated with humans than existing work when evaluating on our challenging human-annotated benchmark dataset. Our work also highlights the critical balance between faithfulness and coverage of model outputs, and encourages future works to address hallucinations in LVLMs while keeping their outputs informative.

# Overview: What “Diagnosis” Means for VLMs like CLIP

Diagnosis of vision–language models (VLMs) such as CLIP spans two complementary goals: explaining and localizing what evidence drives predictions, and auditing failure modes such as spurious correlations, out-of-distribution (OOD) brittleness, and hallucinations that arise in model use or fine-tuning pipelines.<cite id="9fd0fb73-0">Understanding CLIP representations has moved from high-level alignment to component-level analyses that decompose latent embeddings into human-interpretable concepts, examine attention heads and MLP neurons, and use sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to expose diverse, representation-aligned components</cite>.<cite id="3c8ac24f-0">Recent robustness studies show that while CLIP appears robust to ImageNet-style shifts, specialized benchmarks reveal reliance on spurious features that can break under real-world distribution shifts</cite>.<cite id="3c8ac24f-4">Complementary lines of work investigate object hallucinations in CLIP and downstream LVLMs, and propose targeted fine-tuning strategies to mitigate encoder-level errors</cite>.

A prominent and rapidly evolving thread is counterfactual explanation: constructing plausible, semantically consistent image or image–text edits that invert model decisions or attributes, using these edits to test faithfulness, diagnose priors vs. perception, and steer model behavior.<cite id="4659c81d-4">Counterfactual training and evaluation (e.g., DeFacto) explicitly enforce region-faithful reasoning and abstention when evidence is missing, and improves both answer accuracy and grounding over strong baselines</cite>.<cite id="4659c81d-2">Visual counterfactuals can expose how VLMs compete between memorized world knowledge and in-context pixels, with mechanisms to steer models between reliance on priors versus perceptual input</cite>.<cite id="4659c81d-3">Automated pipelines using diffusion models can scale to multimodal counterfactual datasets (e.g., COCO-Counterfactuals) that stress existing models and improve OOD generalization</cite>.

# Counterfactual Diagnosis and Explanation Methods for VLMs

Counterfactuals provide a principled, model-agnostic route to faithfulness: instead of perturbing pixels arbitrarily, they present alternative but plausible scenarios and measure changes in predictions and rationales.<cite id="4659c81d-1">Compared to classic image saliency, counterfactual methods operate on the original model to generate explanations and aim for faithfulness by design, while classic image counterfactuals often highlight discriminative regions without changing the outcome</cite>.<cite id="4659c81d-4">DeFacto introduces a large-scale counterfactual dataset and region-level reward design, improving both answer accuracy and visual grounding, and demonstrating the necessity of counterfactual supervision for interpretability and robustness</cite>.

Constructing high-quality multimodal counterfactuals remains challenging. Recent work frames it as a text-to-image diffusion task to scale up paired image–text counterfactuals with minimal edits.<cite id="4659c81d-3">COCO-Counterfactuals automatically generates counterfactual images and captions from MS-COCO, passes human evaluation, challenges state-of-the-art multimodal models, and improves OOD generalization when used for data augmentation</cite>. At the image-only level, new methods emphasize semantic consistency and sparse, discriminative edits.<cite id="4659c81d-1">State-of-the-art visual counterfactuals can produce semantically consistent replacements of object parts (e.g., wing vs. head) and limit sparsity to make explanations human-friendly, addressing degeneracy from prior approaches</cite>.

Steering and auditing via counterfactuals can also expose knowledge sources inside VLMs. For instance, plausibly contradictory visual evidence can reveal whether models rely on memorized priors or in-context pixels, and where this switch occurs in the forward pass.<cite id="4659c81d-2">Experiments show MLLMs often favor perceptual input over general knowledge when counterfactual pixels contradict priors, with a transition from knowledge-based to perception-based answers emerging in mid-to-late layers; steering vectors can reliably shift predictions for color and size attributes</cite>. These findings translate to CLIP-based LVLMs, since many (e.g., LLaVA, BLIP, Kosmos-2) use CLIP vision encoders as frozen backbones, making encoder-level failures and biases prominent in downstream behavior.<cite id="3c8ac24f-1">CLIP is widely used as a frozen vision encoder in end-to-end VLMs; evaluating CLIP on OOD tasks reveals shortcomings that propagate to downstream models, motivating encoder-specific tuning</cite>.

Beyond training and auditing, counterfactuals can be used for evaluation. Human-like VLM evaluators and region-level metrics assess whether edits are discriminative and lead to the expected prediction changes.<cite id="4659c81d-4">DeFacto evaluates counterfactual edits with both traditional metrics and VLM-as-a-judge, including region-level analyses and ablations on counterfactual training necessity</cite>.<cite id="4659c81d-3">COCO-Counterfactuals supports evaluation by providing challenging, minimally altered pairs that probe robustness and generalization</cite>. For video understanding, dedicated benchmarks expose the difficulty of multi-hop counterfactual reasoning, and targeted post-training can improve counterfactual reasoning capacity.<cite id="700933b9-2">CounterVQA benchmarks progressive counterfactual reasoning across difficulty levels and finds that models degrade on multi-hop causal chains; a post-training method (CFGPT) distills counterfactual reasoning from language to vision to improve across all levels</cite>.<cite id="700933b9-3">Causally-guided adversarial steering produces counterfactual explanations and is evaluated with both standard metrics and VLM-based human-like evaluation, including case studies and parameter ablations</cite>.

# CLIP-Specific Interpretability and Diagnosis

Component-level analyses of CLIP have advanced along two fronts: concept discovery and attribution, and head/layer diagnostics.

- Concept discovery and sparse autoencoders: Researchers decompose CLIP’s latent space into interpretable components that align with human concepts, revealing both expected and spurious features.<cite id="9fd0fb73-0">Task-agnostic concept discovery shows CLIP embeddings align with human-interpretable concepts, but high-level decompositions miss unexpected or spurious features; SAEs offer finer-grained components and can reveal how they influence predictions</cite>.<cite id="9fd0fb73-1">Follow-up work uses SAEs both to understand CLIP’s representations and to steer behavior via identified interpretable features</cite>. This connects to bias and safety auditing, as discovered components may encode sensitive or spurious associations that affect downstream fairness and robustness.<cite id="3c8ac24f-0">Benchmarks like CounterAnimal assess reliance on spurious features under distribution shift, complementing concept analyses</cite>.

- Head-level roles and conceptual consistency: Attention head analyses assign semantic roles to CLIP’s heads and quantify how consistently a head encodes a concept across layers, linking performance and bias at the architectural level.<cite id="9fd0fb73-2">Interpretability advances decompose CLIP image representations into contributions of individual attention heads and identify text sequences that characterize heads’ semantic roles</cite>.<cite id="9fd0fb73-2">A “conceptual consistency” framework labels heads by the concepts they represent and introduces a Concept Consistency Score (CCS) to measure alignment of heads with specific concepts across layers</cite>.<cite id="9fd0fb73-3">Experiments show high CCS heads are critical for performance: pruning them causes larger drops than random heads, and these heads also drive out-of-domain detection, concept-specific reasoning, and video–language understanding; critically, they can learn spurious correlations that amplify social biases</cite>. This provides a diagnosis tool: models with high CCS on sensitive concepts may achieve strong accuracy while amplifying harms, offering targets for bias mitigation and architectural guidance.

- Region-level attribution and tooling: A range of CLIP- and VLM-specific methods localize important visual regions and concepts, addressing limitations of pixel-level or perturbation-only approaches.<cite id="9fd0fb73-4">VLM-specific attributions include Grad-ECLIP, CLIP-Surgery, MaskCLIP, ECLIP, and M2iB, while pixel-space methods can be unstable or misaligned with CLIP’s representation; a new cluster-importance clustering (CCI) approach aligns with CLIP’s pretrained patch embeddings to produce semantically coherent, faithful attributions</cite>. These methods complement counterfactual diagnosis by identifying where and which concepts drive predictions, which can be cross-validated with counterfactual edits.

# Robustness, Failure Modes, and Mitigation for CLIP-Like Models

Diagnosis is incomplete without rigorous robustness audits. Recent work probes spurious correlations, OOD shifts, and hallucinations in CLIP and LVLMs, and proposes tuning strategies to fix encoder-level weaknesses.

- Spurious features and distribution shift: CLIP’s robustness to ImageNet-style shifts can mask overreliance on spurious features that fail under real-world shifts; new benchmarks are designed to expose and quantify this reliance.<cite id="3c8ac24f-0">CLIP appears robust to ImageNet-oriented shifts, but specialized benchmarks like CounterAnimal reveal reliance on spurious features that break under distribution shift</cite>.<cite id="3c8ac24f-1">Evaluations on OOD benchmarks uncover scenarios where CLIP fails, and these limitations propagate to downstream VLMs using CLIP’s embeddings</cite>.

- 3D awareness and architectural effects: Robustness varies with visual encoder architecture and training choices, and CLIP models can exhibit biases (e.g., shape) that change with fine-tuning.<cite id="3c8ac24f-3">A holistic evaluation finds architecture and training choices (e.g., contrastive loss, fine-tuning) significantly affect robustness and biases such as shape reliance; fine-tuning on ImageNet can diminish some biases</cite>.

- Hallucination audits and encoder fine-tuning: Object hallucinations in CLIP encoders can propagate to LVLMs like LLaVA; targeted fine-tuning mitigates both encoder and downstream hallucinations by emphasizing object-level contrastive signals.<cite id="3c8ac24f-4">A curated OHD-Caps benchmark shows CLIP ViT-L/14 scores positive captions only 19% of the time, indicating substantial object hallucination; fine-tuning with object-level contrastive loss reduces hallucinations in CLIP and, when used as the visual encoder, in LLaVA-1.5</cite>.<cite id="3c8ac24f-2">Expanded POPE, CHAIR, and AMBER evaluations quantify discriminative and generative hallucinations, and show improvements when replacing the CLIP encoder with a fine-tuned version in LLaVA-1.5</cite>.

These findings inform diagnosis workflows: if counterfactuals or concept analyses reveal reliance on spurious attributes, OOD weakness, or object hallucinations, follow with encoder-specific fine-tuning on targeted domains and re-evaluate with the appropriate benchmarks.

# Evaluation Benchmarks and Metrics for Explanations and Counterfactuals

Faithfulness and coverage are central dimensions for evaluating VLM explanations and counterfactuals. Recent benchmarks broaden coverage beyond object-level detection to attributes, relations, and the hallucination–informativeness trade-off.

- LVLM faithfulness and coverage: VALOR-EVAL introduces a multi-dimensional benchmark spanning objects, attributes, and relations, with challenging images selected to probe associative biases; it generalizes CHAIR to evaluate both faithfulness and coverage and reports better correlation with human judgments than prior metrics.<cite id="700933b9-4">VALOR-EVAL’s two-stage LLM-based evaluation generalizes CHAIR to jointly measure faithfulness and coverage, highlighting the critical balance between correctness and informativeness and showing improved human correlation on a challenging, human-annotated benchmark</cite>.

- Counterfactual reasoning in video: CounterVQA assesses progressive counterfactual reasoning, revealing performance gaps on multi-hop causal chains; a post-training method (CFGPT) improves across difficulty levels, indicating a path to train counterfactual reasoning explicitly.<cite id="700933b9-2">CounterVQA exposes degradation on complex multi-hop counterfactuals, and CFGPT distills counterfactual reasoning from language to vision to yield consistent gains</cite>.

- Human-like evaluators for counterfactual edits: Beyond traditional metrics, VLMs can judge whether counterfactual edits are semantically consistent, discriminative, and causally effective, adding an external, human-like evaluation layer.<cite id="700933b9-3">Causally-guided adversarial steering evaluates counterfactuals with both standard metrics and VLM-based human-like evaluation, including ablations and case studies</cite>.<cite id="4659c81d-4">DeFacto similarly uses VLMs as evaluators to assess the quality of counterfactual edits and region-faithful reasoning</cite>.

- Multimodal counterfactual datasets: COCO-Counterfactuals provides a scalable, human-validated dataset of minimally altered image–text pairs to probe robustness and support data augmentation for OOD generalization.<cite id="4659c81d-3">COCO-Counterfactuals scales counterfactual generation via diffusion models, challenges state-of-the-art multimodal models, and improves OOD generalization when used for training</cite>.

# Practical Workflow: Diagnosing a CLIP-Based VLM with Counterfactuals and Concepts

1) Attribute and concept mapping: Use CLIP-specific attribution (e.g., ECLIP, Grad-ECLIP, MaskCLIP, CCI) to identify discriminative regions and concept-level components driving key decisions; validate with SAE or head-level analyses to tie concepts to model internals.<cite id="9fd0fb73-4">CLIP- and VLM-specific attribution tools (Grad-ECLIP, CLIP-Surgery, MaskCLIP, ECLIP, M2iB) and representation-aligned CCI can yield more faithful, localized attributions than pixel-level perturbations</cite>.<cite id="9fd0fb73-1">SAEs can expose diverse, human-interpretable components and, when trained appropriately, be used to steer CLIP-like models via identified features</cite>.<cite id="9fd0fb73-2">Head-level role assignments and Concept Consistency Scores reveal which concepts are consistently encoded and where spurious correlations may lie</cite>.

2) Build targeted counterfactuals: Generate semantically consistent edits that flip key attributed concepts (e.g., color, size, occlusion) or causal factors; measure prediction and rationale changes to test faithfulness and over-reliance on priors versus pixels.<cite id="4659c81d-1">Semantically consistent counterfactual frameworks constrain edits to the same object parts and seek discriminative, sparse changes to produce informative explanations</cite>.<cite id="4659c81d-2">Visual counterfactuals can diagnose competition between world knowledge and in-context perception and provide steering vectors to shift reliance between priors and pixels</cite>.

3) Robustness and bias auditing: Probe spurious feature reliance and OOD brittleness using shift-specific benchmarks (e.g., CounterAnimal) and 3D/attribute corruption evaluations; quantify bias via high-CCS head analyses and sensitive-concept scoring.<cite id="3c8ac24f-0">CounterAnimal exposes spurious-feature reliance under distribution shift</cite>.<cite id="3c8ac24f-3">A holistic CLIP evaluation reveals architecture- and training-induced biases (e.g., shape reliance) and their changes with fine-tuning</cite>.<cite id="9fd0fb73-3">High CCS heads both drive performance and amplify social biases, providing targets for bias audits</cite>.

4) Mitigation and re-evaluation: If failures are encoder-driven (e.g., object hallucinations or spurious attribute reliance), fine-tune the vision encoder with domain-specific, object-level contrastive signals and re-test with discriminative and generative hallucination benchmarks (POPE/CHAIR/AMBER) and counterfactual datasets; track faithfulness and coverage with VALOR-EVAL-like metrics and VLM-as-judge evaluations.<cite id="3c8ac24f-2">Object-level fine-tuning reduces hallucinations in CLIP and downstream LVLMs (e.g., LLaVA-1.5) on multiple benchmarks</cite>.<cite id="700933b9-4">VALOR-EVAL’s faithfulness–coverage framework helps quantify trade-offs and human correlation</cite>.<cite id="4659c81d-3">Counterfactual datasets like COCO-Counterfactuals support robustness and OOD evaluation and can improve generalization when used for augmentation</cite>.<cite id="4659c81d-4">Counterfactual training and VLM-judged evaluation (DeFacto) improve grounding and reasoning faithfulness</cite>.

# Open Challenges and Research Directions

- Spurious-to-faithful trade-offs: Counterfactuals and concept analyses can reveal reliance on spurious features, but training with counterfactual supervision must balance faithfulness with generalization to avoid overfitting to artificial edits.<cite id="3c8ac24f-0">Shift-specific benchmarks show that reliance on spurious features can dominate ImageNet-style evaluations, necessitating targeted audits</cite>.<cite id="700933b9-2">Even strong models struggle with multi-hop counterfactual chains, suggesting limits in causal reasoning that future training must address</cite>.

- Faithfulness–utility tensions: Explanations that are too local or sparse may omit necessary context, while comprehensive explanations can be computationally expensive and introduce hallucinations; evaluation frameworks must jointly measure faithfulness and coverage.<cite id="700933b9-4">VALOR-EVAL highlights the faithfulness–coverage trade-off and its importance for reliable LVLM evaluation</cite>.

- Human-like evaluators and interpretability alignment: VLMs-as-judges can assess counterfactual quality and grounding, but their own biases and hallucinations can propagate; combining human-in-the-loop with automated metrics remains an active area.<cite id="700933b9-3">Using VLM evaluators alongside traditional metrics provides qualitative and quantitative signals for counterfactual quality</cite>.<cite id="700933b9-4">LLM-based evaluation frameworks can improve correlation with human judgments on complex LVLM tasks</cite>.

- CLIP backbone governance: As CLIP is reused across many systems, robust auditing and tuning of its encoders are critical; methods that expose high-impact, high-bias heads and spurious concept components can guide safe deployment and selective fine-tuning at scale.<cite id="3c8ac24f-1">Because many LVLMs freeze CLIP encoders, encoder-level weaknesses affect downstream performance and require efficient tuning strategies</cite>.<cite id="9fd0fb73-3">High CCS heads are both essential for performance and prone to spurious correlations, suggesting prioritized mitigation targets</cite>.

# Key Takeaways

- Counterfactual diagnosis has matured from conceptual tools to scalable datasets and training regimes that improve faithfulness and reasoning in VLMs, with direct relevance to CLIP-based systems through their common use as encoders and the propagation of encoder-level failures.<cite id="4659c81d-4">Counterfactual supervision and evaluation improve answer accuracy and visual grounding in multimodal models</cite>.<cite id="4659c81d-2">Visual counterfactuals reveal and steer between world knowledge and perceptual input, exposing internal competition dynamics</cite>.<cite id="4659c81d-3">Automated multimodal counterfactual datasets stress current models and enhance OOD generalization</cite>.

- CLIP-specific interpretability has advanced with head-level role assignments, concept consistency metrics, and SAE-based component analyses, enabling diagnosis of both capabilities and biases at architectural and concept levels.<cite id="9fd0fb73-2">Head-level analyses and CCS provide performance-critical, concept-aligned diagnostics</cite>.<cite id="9fd0fb73-1">SAEs help understand and steer CLIP’s latent concepts</cite>.

- Robustness audits show that CLIP-like models can be surprisingly vulnerable to spurious features and OOD/3D shifts not captured by standard benchmarks; encoder-specific fine-tuning on object-level signals can mitigate hallucinations in both CLIP and downstream LVLMs.<cite id="3c8ac24f-0">Spurious-feature reliance under distribution shift is a latent risk</cite>.<cite id="3c8ac24f-4">Object-level fine-tuning reduces hallucinations in CLIP and in LLaVA-1.5 across multiple evaluations</cite>.

- Evaluation is evolving toward multi-dimensional faithfulness–coverage metrics and domain-specific counterfactual benchmarks, complemented by human-like VLM evaluators to judge counterfactual plausibility and grounding.<cite id="700933b9-4">VALOR-EVAL generalizes CHAIR to jointly measure faithfulness and coverage with better human correlation</cite>.<cite id="700933b9-2">CounterVQA exposes limits in multi-hop counterfactual reasoning and shows targeted post-training can help</cite>.<cite id="4659c81d-3">COCO-Counterfactuals provides scalable, challenging multimodal pairs for evaluation and augmentation</cite>.<cite id="4659c81d-4">VLM-as-judge evaluations quantify counterfactual quality and faithfulness</cite>.

Title: Pixels Versus Priors: Controlling Knowledge Priors in Vision-Language Models through Visual Counterfacts
Snippet: In our framework, world knowledge priors refer to linguistic associations between visual attributes and objects that the model has memorized during pretraining. In contrast, visual perception is defined by the in-context visual input, which we manipulate to create counterfactual images. These counterfactuals are designed to challenge the model's world knowledge of visual attributes by presenting plausible but contradictory visual evidence. For example, we contrast the size-related knowledge prior "strawberries are bigger than flies" with the counterfactual "flies are bigger than strawberries," violating expected size relations (see Figure 2). 

Using Visual CounterFact, we find that MLLMs often ignore world knowledge when shown counterfactual images, favoring perceptual input even when prompted for general facts. We then trace where in the forward pass predictions shift from in-weight knowledge (e.g., strawberries are red) to in-context perception (this strawberry is blue), finding that this transition consistently emerges in mid-to-late layers. During this transition, models frequently flip between the two answers, revealing a competition between in-context pixel and inweights prior information, with pixels often overriding priors in the model's output. To control this behavior, we use our Pixels Versus Priors steering to control whether a vision-language model relies on knowledge priors or pixel information. PvP is a novel framework to construct steering vectors for vision-language models that control whether the model responds based on memorized knowledge or in-context visual input. Through this steering, we successfully shift an average of 99.3% of color predictions and 80.8% of size predictions from memorized priors to counterfactual answers. 

Together, these contributions provide a new visual counterfactual benchmark and a mechanism for interpreting and controlling the behavior of vision-language models. We present the necessary foundation for a mechanistic understanding of how MLLMs integrate image input with prior knowledge of visual attributes, bridging the gap between interpretability research in language models and the emerging needs of multimodal models.

Title: COCO-Counterfactuals: Automatically Constructed Counterfactual Examples for Image-Text Pairs
Snippet: Counterfactual examples have proven to be valuable in the field of natural language processing (NLP) for both evaluating and improving the robustness of language models to spurious correlations in datasets. Despite their demonstrated utility for NLP, multimodal counterfactual examples have been relatively unexplored due to the difficulty of creating paired image-text data with minimal counterfactual changes. To address this challenge, we introduce a scalable framework for automatic generation of counterfactual examples using text-to-image diffusion models. We use our framework to create COCO-Counterfactuals, a multimodal counterfactual dataset of paired image and text captions based on the MS-COCO dataset. We validate the quality of COCO-Counterfactuals through human evaluations and show that existing multimodal models are challenged by our counterfactual image-text pairs. Additionally, we demonstrate the usefulness of COCO-Counterfactuals for improving out-of-domain generalization of multimodal vision-language models via training data augmentation.

Title: DeFacto: Counterfactual Thinking with Images for Enforcing Evidence-Grounded and Faithful Reasoning
Snippet: In this work, we introduced DeFacto, the first vision-language reasoning framework explicitly grounded in counterfactual supervision, designed to enforce region-faithful reasoning and abstention behavior when critical evidence is missing. To enable this counterfactual reasoning paradigm, we proposed an automatic pipeline for constructing counterfactual datasets, which leverages language model parsing, open-vocabulary detection, and OCR to mask question-relevant regions without requiring manual annotations. Using this pipeline, we built a counterfactual dataset about 100k images to support training and evaluation. Extensive experiments across multiple diverse benchmarks demonstrate that DeFacto consistently improves both answer accuracy and visual grounding faithfulness over strong baselines. Our ablation studies further confirm the necessity of counterfactual training and region-level reward design in enhancing interpretability and robustness. We believe these findings open new directions for integrating counterfactual supervision into multimodal reasoning systems, with potential extensions to video understanding and embodied AI.

Title: From What to How: Attributing CLIP's Latent Components Reveals Unexpected Semantic Reliance
Snippet: Understanding CLIP representations: A line of work on interpreting CLIP and other visionlanguage models focuses on decomposing latent embeddings into a set of predefined, humaninterpretable concepts [5,54]. These methods generally evaluate alignment to known textual labels but struggle to capture the full diversity of learned features, particularly unexpected or spurious ones. 

For a more comprehensive understanding, component-level understanding is essential. To this end, studies have begun to examine attention heads and MLP neurons [18,19,10]. Alternatively, visual embeddings in CLIP's last layer can be decomposed into a diverse set of interpretable components using SAEs [37,40,25], which have been originally proposed for language models [22,7]. Rao et al. [40] train linear classifiers directly on SAEs activations for downstream-tasks, but, as such, can no longer explain the original CLIP model. Other works based on SAEs [30,48] successfully explain what components encode and represent, yet overlook how they influence specific predictions.

Title: Steering CLIP's vision transformer with sparse autoencoders
Snippet: Several works have explored interpreting CLIP's behavior and representations. Studies have investigated CLIP's biases [45], attention layers [18,25], and neurons [19,21]. 

Recent works [4,47] introduce task-agnostic concept discovery, demonstrating that CLIP's internal representations naturally align with human-interpretable concepts. Our work builds upon these findings by using SAEs not only to understand CLIP's representations at a finer degree of resolution, but also to actively steer CLIP's behavior through identified interpretable features.

Title: Pruning the Paradox: How CLIP’s Most Informative Heads Enhance Performance While Amplifying Bias
Snippet: Large-scale vision-language (VL) models such as CLIP (Radford et al., 2021) have significantly advanced state-of-the-art performance in vision tasks in recent years. Consequently, CLIP has been extensively used as a foundational model for downstream tasks such as video retrieval, image generation, and segmentation (Luo et al., 2022; Liu   * Work partially completed while at Intel Labs. et al., 2024;Brooks et al., 2023;Esser et al., 2024;Kirillov et al., 2023). This has enabled the construction of compositional models combining CLIP with other foundation models, thereby increasing the functionality of CLIP while also adding complexity to the overall model structure. However, as these models gain prominence in real-world applications, their embedded social biases (Howard et al., 2024;Hall et al., 2023;Seth et al., 2023) have emerged as a critical concern with potentially harmful consequences. Despite the growing body of work documenting these biases, a fundamental question remains: what mechanisms within these models' architectures drive both their impressive capabilities and problematic shortcomings? 

Recent interpretability advances (Gandelsman et al.) have made initial progress by decomposing CLIP's image representations into contributions from individual attention heads, identifying text sequences that characterize different heads' semantic roles. However, this approach provides only a partial view into CLIP's inner workings, leaving a critical missing piece: systematic understanding of the visual concepts encoded at the attention head level-and how these concepts underpin both the model's strengths and its social failures. 

Our work addresses this critical gap through a novel interpretability framework we call "conceptual consistency". This framework systematically analyzes which visual concepts are learned by individual attention heads and how consistently these concepts are processed throughout the model's architecture. First, we identify interpretable structures within the individual heads of the last four layers of the model using a set of text descriptions. To accomplish this, we employ the TEXTSPAN algorithm (Gandelsman et al.), which helps us find the most appropriate text descriptions for each head. After identifying these text descriptions, we assign labels to each head representing the common property shared by the descriptions.

Title: Pruning the Paradox: How CLIP’s Most Informative Heads Enhance Performance While Amplifying Bias
Snippet: CLIP is one of the most popular foundation models and is heavily used for many vision-language tasks, yet little is known about its inner workings. As CLIP is increasingly deployed in real-world applications, it is becoming even more critical to understand its limitations and embedded social biases to mitigate potentially harmful downstream consequences. However, the question of what internal mechanisms drive both the impressive capabilities as well as problematic shortcomings of CLIP has largely remained unanswered. To bridge this gap, we study the conceptual consistency of text descriptions for attention heads in CLIP-like models. Specifically, we propose Concept Consistency Score (CCS), a novel interpretability metric that measures how consistently individual attention heads in CLIP models align with specific concepts. Our soft-pruning experiments reveal that high CCS heads are critical for preserving model performance, as pruning them leads to a significantly larger performance drop than pruning random or low CCS heads. Notably, we find that high CCS heads capture essential concepts and play a key role in out-of-domain detection, concept-specific reasoning, and video-language understanding. Moreover, we prove that high CCS heads learn spurious correlations which amplify social biases. These results position CCS as a powerful interpretability metric exposing the paradox of performance and social biases in CLIP models.

Title: Concept Regions Matter: Benchmarking CLIP with a New Cluster-Importance Approach
Snippet: Interpretability in Vision-Language Models: Early interpretability efforts applied methods such as attention rollout [1], which aggregates attention weights across layers, and gradient-based techniques like GradCAM [50] and GAME [5], which compute feature importance through gradients. With the advent of CLIP [41] and successors like BLIP [32] and ALBEF [31], researchers developed VLM-specific techniques: Grad-ECLIP [64] extends gradient-based attribution to multimodal settings, CLIP-Surgery [33] identifies important regions through similarity masking, MaskCLIP [66] performs token-level masking to localize influential regions, ECLIP [6] leverages gradientweighted attention, and M2iB [58] employs perturbationbased explanations. Perturbation-driven methods such as RISE [40] further provide model-agnostic saliency through random masking. More recent concept-based approaches like SpLiCE [4] learn sparse concept embeddings, while others [26] use foundation models for concept discovery, building on earlier methods like Concept Bottleneck Models [29]. Yet both VLM-specific and traditional interpretability methods produce noisy, low-level attributions. Pixel-space methods such as SLIC [2], LIME [44], and SHAP [38] rely on superpixels that are not aligned with a model's representation. Perturbation-based approaches including RISE [40], Meaningful/Extremal Perturbations [12,13], and the missingness analysis of [23] mask regions using a missingness token (e.g., black patches, noise, blur), making explanations sensitive to the replacement and often unstable. In contrast, CCI clusters CLIP's pretrained patch embeddings to obtain semantically coherent, representation-aligned regions and attenuate the model's attention to the corresponding patch tokens directly, avoiding pixel-level artifacts, preserving the input distribution, and yielding more faithful and localized attributions.

snippet.text: Interpretability in Vision-Language Models: Early interpretability efforts applied methods such as attention rollout [1], which aggregates attention weights across layers, and gradient-based techniques like GradCAM [50] and GAME [5], which compute feature importance through gradients. With the advent of CLIP [41] and successors like BLIP [32] and ALBEF [31], researchers developed VLM-specific techniques: Grad-ECLIP [64] extends gradient-based attribution to multimodal settings, CLIP-Surgery [33] identifies important regions through similarity masking, MaskCLIP [66] performs token-level masking to localize influential regions, ECLIP [6] leverages gradientweighted attention, and M2iB [58] employs perturbationbased explanations. Perturbation-driven methods such as RISE [40] further provide model-agnostic saliency through random masking. More recent concept-based approaches like SpLiCE [4] learn sparse concept embeddings, while others [26] use foundation models for concept discovery, building on earlier methods like Concept Bottleneck Models [29]. Yet both VLM-specific and traditional interpretability methods produce noisy, low-level attributions. Pixel-space methods such as SLIC [2], LIME [44], and SHAP [38] rely on superpixels that are not aligned with a model's representation. Perturbation-based approaches including RISE [40], Meaningful/Extremal Perturbations [12,13], and the missingness analysis of [23] mask regions using a missingness token (e.g., black patches, noise, blur), making explanations sensitive to the replacement and often unstable. In contrast, CCI clusters CLIP's pretrained patch embeddings to obtain semantically coherent, representation-aligned regions and attenuate the model's attention to the corresponding patch tokens directly, avoiding pixel-level artifacts, preserving the input distribution, and yielding more faithful and localized attributions.

documents.title: From What to How: Attributing CLIP's Latent Components Reveals Unexpected Semantic Reliance
documents.snippet:
Understanding CLIP representations: A line of work on interpreting CLIP and other visionlanguage models focuses on decomposing latent embeddings into a set of predefined, humaninterpretable concepts [5,54]. These methods generally evaluate alignment to known textual labels but struggle to capture the full diversity of learned features, particularly unexpected or spurious ones. 

For a more comprehensive understanding, component-level understanding is essential. To this end, studies have begun to examine attention heads and MLP neurons [18,19,10]. Alternatively, visual embeddings in CLIP's last layer can be decomposed into a diverse set of interpretable components using SAEs [37,40,25], which have been originally proposed for language models [22,7]. Rao et al. [40] train linear classifiers directly on SAEs activations for downstream-tasks, but, as such, can no longer explain the original CLIP model. Other works based on SAEs [30,48] successfully explain what components encode and represent, yet overlook how they influence specific predictions.

documents.title: Steering CLIP's vision transformer with sparse autoencoders
documents.snippet:
Several works have explored interpreting CLIP's behavior and representations. Studies have investigated CLIP's biases [45], attention layers [18,25], and neurons [19,21]. 

Recent works [4,47] introduce task-agnostic concept discovery, demonstrating that CLIP's internal representations naturally align with human-interpretable concepts. Our work builds upon these findings by using SAEs not only to understand CLIP's representations at a finer degree of resolution, but also to actively steer CLIP's behavior through identified interpretable features.
