snippet.text: As shown in Figure 4 (and Figure 10 in Appendix B), all five models, particularly in disambiguated context, achieve their highest accuracy on English examples when prompted in English. Under both zero-shot and few-shot settings, accuracy consistently declines for Indian languages. However, for ambiguous contexts, some models show low accuracy and high SBS on English examples. This pattern suggests that, potentially, in ambiguous contexts, models overrely on stereotypical associations in English due to richer exposure to biased patterns in English training data. In contrast, in disambiguated contexts, models better understand explicit contextual cues in English due to stronger syntactic and semantic alignment, resulting in higher accuracy and lower SBS. For Indian languages, limited pretraining data and weaker contextual understanding reduce accuracy and lead models to rely more on stereotypes, increasing SBS for disambiguated contexts. Notably, Figures 8 and 9 show that larger LLMs con- sistently exhibit lower BS and SBS in English, regardless of context type. Figure 5 demonstrates that BS for Indian languages exceeds that for English across nearly every model and context type. For instance, Gemma's zero-shot BS in ambiguous contexts rises from 0.025 in English to 0.15 in Bengali. Bloomz, which already exhibits high BS in English, shows even larger scores (e.g., from 0.1 in English to 0.25 in Telugu for zero-shot). This pattern holds in both zero-and few-shot settings, indicating that cultural and linguistic transfer introduces additional stereotypical associations. Overall, across categories, in English, we found Bloomz and Llama exhibit the high bias in all three categories. In contrast, for Indian languages, Sarvam consistently shows the highest bias in these categories.

snippet.text: Recent methods in speech and language technology pretrain very large models which are fine-tuned for specific tasks. However, the benefits of such large models are often limited to a few resource rich languages of the world. In this work, we make multiple contributions towards building ASR systems for low resource languages from the Indian subcontinent. First, we curate 17,000 hours of raw speech data for 40 Indian languages from a wide variety of domains including education, news, technology, and finance. Second, using this raw speech data we pretrain several variants of wav2vec style models for 40 Indian languages. Third, we analyze the pretrained models to find key features: codebook vectors of similar sounding phonemes are shared across languages, representations across layers are discriminative of the language family, and attention heads often pay attention within small local windows. Fourth, we fine-tune this model for downstream ASR for 9 languages and obtain state-of-the-art results on 3 public datasets, including on very low-resource languages such as Sinhala and Nepali. Our work establishes that multilingual pretraining is an effective strategy for building ASR systems for the linguistically diverse speakers of the Indian subcontinent.

Title: DECASTE: Unveiling Caste Stereotypes in Large Language Models through Multi-Dimensional Bias Analysis
Snippet: Caste-based discrimination in large language models (LLMs) represents a critical facet of the broader issue of social bias in AI systems, which have been shown to perpetuate stereotypes related to race, gender, and other social constructs. Caste, deeply embedded within Indian society and the Indian diaspora worldwide, plays a significant role in shaping access to critical resources such as education, job opportunities, and public services [Kumar, 2010;Tejani, 2013a;O'Reilly and Dhanju, 2014]. Despite sustained efforts by social reformers such as Dr. B.R. Ambedkar [Ambedkar, 2014] and various governmental initiatives [Agrawal et al., 1991], caste-based discrimination continues to hinder social and economic mobility, thereby reinforcing systemic inequality [Deshpande, 2011;Thorat and Neuman, 2012]. While caste discrimination is most prominent in India, its global reach due to the widespread Indian diaspora makes casterelated biases a pressing worldwide issue.

Title: DECASTE: Unveiling Caste Stereotypes in Large Language Models through Multi-Dimensional Bias Analysis
Snippet: Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) have revolutionized natural language processing (NLP) and expanded their applications across diverse domains. However, despite their impressive capabilities, LLMs have been shown to reflect and perpetuate harmful societal biases, including those based on ethnicity, gender, and religion. A critical and underexplored issue is the reinforcement of caste-based biases, particularly towards India's marginalized caste groups such as Dalits and Shudras. In this paper, we address this gap by proposing DECASTE, a novel, multi-dimensional framework designed to detect and assess both implicit and explicit caste biases in LLMs. Our approach evaluates caste fairness across four dimensions: socio-cultural, economic, educational, and political, using a range of customized prompting strategies. By benchmarking several state-of-the-art LLMs, we reveal that these models systematically reinforce caste biases, with significant disparities observed in the treatment of oppressed versus dominant caste groups. For example, bias scores are notably elevated when comparing Dalits and Shudras with dominant caste groups, reflecting societal prejudices that persist in model outputs. These results expose the subtle yet pervasive caste biases in LLMs and emphasize the need for more comprehensive and inclusive bias evaluation methodologies that assess the potential risks of deploying such models in real-world contexts.

Title: DECASTE: Unveiling Caste Stereotypes in Large Language Models through Multi-Dimensional Bias Analysis
Snippet: The scope of this study is subject to several limitations. First, the range of socio-demographic groups and individual profiles represented is not fully comprehensive. Although significant effort was made to capture a diverse set of prompts reflecting various dimensions of caste-based bias, our study focuses predominantly on specific social groups within the Indian context, primarily reflecting stereotypes and biases encountered in Indian society. As such, our analysis may not fully account for caste-related dynamics in other regions or marginalized groups that face different forms of discrimination. Furthermore, this study does not encompass other sociocultural biases, such as those related to religion, gender, race, or ethnicity, which may also interact with caste in complex ways. 

Another key limitation is that while we analyze biases in multiple language models across several tasks, the scope of datasets and tasks remains limited. The study primarily relies on English-language data, and the extent to which similar biases might manifest in models trained on or tested in other languages, especially vernacular languages spoken by lower socio-economic groups, is unknown. Caste-based discrimination is not restricted to English-speaking communities, and biases present in regional languages may differ significantly in their form and impact. Therefore, future research must explore how language models perform across different languages and cultural contexts to fully understand the global nature of these biases. Moreover, while we investigate caste biases under limited scenarios, our study does not exhaustively cover the full range of possible scenarios where biases may arise. Finally, our approach to bias quantification and measurement, though rigorous, is inherently limited by the methods and evaluation metrics available. We also recognize that participatory research practices are essential for creating frameworks that are truly representative and contextually grounded. As part of our future roadmap, we aim to work closely with Dalit-Bahujan and Adivasi scholars, activists, and sociologists. Their insights will be central in refining stereotype definitions, validating harms, and ensuring that our tools and findings reflect the lived experiences of those most impacted by caste discrimination.

Title: DECASTE: Unveiling Caste Stereotypes in Large Language Models through Multi-Dimensional Bias Analysis
Snippet: Recent investigations into large language models (LLMs) have highlighted significant socio-cultural biases, often reflecting and amplifying societal inequities in tasks such as text generation and question answering [Mukherjee et al., 2023;Gallegos et al., 2024;Tao et al., 2023]. While extensive research has addressed biases related to race, gender, and occupation, caste bias within LLMs remains largely unexplored. Caste bias, deeply rooted in the hierarchical caste system of South Asia, contributes to systemic social stratification and discrimination based on birth and perceived purity. Despite legal safeguards and government initiatives, historically marginalized communities-including Scheduled Castes (SCs), Scheduled Tribes (STs), and Other Backward Classes (OBCs)-continue to face widespread prejudice and exclusion, particularly in domains such as employment, education, and social interactions [Ambedkar, 2022;Desai and Dubey, 2011;Thorat and Neuman, 2012;Rukmini, 2014]. Although algorithmic fairness and bias mitigation have gained prominence, caste-based bias in LLMs remains significantly underexamined. This is especially concerning, as LLMs increasingly shape digital discourse. If left unchecked, caste-related biases could perpetuate or even escalate discrimination in subtle and overt forms. 

Prior computational studies have explored caste discrimination in areas such as social media, online advertisements, and employment settings, but research specifically targeting caste bias in LLMs is still limited. Existing work often adopts a binary framework contrasting dominant and oppressed castes, lacking fine-grained analysis across diverse groups and contexts [Harad, 2020;Qureshi and Sabih, 2021;Krishnamurthi and Krishnaswami, 2020;Sahoo et al., 2024]. Our work addresses this gap by systematically investigating caste bias in LLMs and its downstream implications. We introduce the DECASTE framework1 , which comprises two novel tasks. The first, the Stereotypical Word Association Task (SWAT), evaluates how LLMs associate caste groups with stereotypical terms using structured prompts and a dedicated bias metric. The second, the Persona-based Scenario Answering Task (PSAT), probes biases in decision-making through caste-linked personas.

documents.snippet: Caste-based discrimination in large language models (LLMs) represents a critical facet of the broader issue of social bias in AI systems, which have been shown to perpetuate stereotypes related to race, gender, and other social constructs. Caste, deeply embedded within Indian society and the Indian diaspora worldwide, plays a significant role in shaping access to critical resources such as education, job opportunities, and public services [Kumar, 2010;Tejani, 2013a;O'Reilly and Dhanju, 2014]. Despite sustained efforts by social reformers such as Dr. B.R. Ambedkar [Ambedkar, 2014] and various governmental initiatives [Agrawal et al., 1991], caste-based discrimination continues to hinder social and economic mobility, thereby reinforcing systemic inequality [Deshpande, 2011;Thorat and Neuman, 2012]. While caste discrimination is most prominent in India, its global reach due to the widespread Indian diaspora makes casterelated biases a pressing worldwide issue.

documents.title: DECASTE: Unveiling Caste Stereotypes in Large Language Models through Multi-Dimensional Bias Analysis
documents.snippet: Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) have revolutionized natural language processing (NLP) and expanded their applications across diverse domains. However, despite their impressive capabilities, LLMs have been shown to reflect and perpetuate harmful societal biases, including those based on ethnicity, gender, and religion. A critical and underexplored issue is the reinforcement of caste-based biases, particularly towards India's marginalized caste groups such as Dalits and Shudras. In this paper, we address this gap by proposing DECASTE, a novel, multi-dimensional framework designed to detect and assess both implicit and explicit caste biases in LLMs. Our approach evaluates caste fairness across four dimensions: socio-cultural, economic, educational, and political, using a range of customized prompting strategies. By benchmarking several state-of-the-art LLMs, we reveal that these models systematically reinforce caste biases, with significant disparities observed in the treatment of oppressed versus dominant caste groups. For example, bias scores are notably elevated when comparing Dalits and Shudras with dominant caste groups, reflecting societal prejudices that persist in model outputs. These results expose the subtle yet pervasive caste biases in LLMs and emphasize the need for more comprehensive and inclusive bias evaluation methodologies that assess the potential risks of deploying such models in real-world contexts.

documents.snippet:
The scope of this study is subject to several limitations. First, the range of socio-demographic groups and individual profiles represented is not fully comprehensive. Although significant effort was made to capture a diverse set of prompts reflecting various dimensions of caste-based bias, our study focuses predominantly on specific social groups within the Indian context, primarily reflecting stereotypes and biases encountered in Indian society. As such, our analysis may not fully account for caste-related dynamics in other regions or marginalized groups that face different forms of discrimination. Furthermore, this study does not encompass other sociocultural biases, such as those related to religion, gender, race, or ethnicity, which may also interact with caste in complex ways. 

Another key limitation is that while we analyze biases in multiple language models across several tasks, the scope of datasets and tasks remains limited. The study primarily relies on English-language data, and the extent to which similar biases might manifest in models trained on or tested in other languages, especially vernacular languages spoken by lower socio-economic groups, is unknown. Caste-based discrimination is not restricted to English-speaking communities, and biases present in regional languages may differ significantly in their form and impact. Therefore, future research must explore how language models perform across different languages and cultural contexts to fully understand the global nature of these biases. Moreover, while we investigate caste biases under limited scenarios, our study does not exhaustively cover the full range of possible scenarios where biases may arise. Finally, our approach to bias quantification and measurement, though rigorous, is inherently limited by the methods and evaluation metrics available. We also recognize that participatory research practices are essential for creating frameworks that are truly representative and contextually grounded. As part of our future roadmap, we aim to work closely with Dalit-Bahujan and Adivasi scholars, activists, and sociologists. Their insights will be central in refining stereotype definitions, validating harms, and ensuring that our tools and findings reflect the lived experiences of those most impacted by caste discrimination.

documents.title: DECASTE: Unveiling Caste Stereotypes in Large Language Models through Multi-Dimensional Bias Analysis
documents.snippet:
Recent investigations into large language models (LLMs) have highlighted significant socio-cultural biases, often reflecting and amplifying societal inequities in tasks such as text generation and question answering [Mukherjee et al., 2023;Gallegos et al., 2024;Tao et al., 2023]. While extensive research has addressed biases related to race, gender, and occupation, caste bias within LLMs remains largely unexplored. Caste bias, deeply rooted in the hierarchical caste system of South Asia, contributes to systemic social stratification and discrimination based on birth and perceived purity. Despite legal safeguards and government initiatives, historically marginalized communities-including Scheduled Castes (SCs), Scheduled Tribes (STs), and Other Backward Classes (OBCs)-continue to face widespread prejudice and exclusion, particularly in domains such as employment, education, and social interactions [Ambedkar, 2022;Desai and Dubey, 2011;Thorat and Neuman, 2012;Rukmini, 2014]. Although algorithmic fairness and bias mitigation have gained prominence, caste-based bias in LLMs remains significantly underexamined. This is especially concerning, as LLMs increasingly shape digital discourse. If left unchecked, caste-related biases could perpetuate or even escalate discrimination in subtle and overt forms. 

Prior computational studies have explored caste discrimination in areas such as social media, online advertisements, and employment settings, but research specifically targeting caste bias in LLMs is still limited. Existing work often adopts a binary framework contrasting dominant and oppressed castes, lacking fine-grained analysis across diverse groups and contexts [Harad, 2020;Qureshi and Sabih, 2021;Krishnamurthi and Krishnaswami, 2020;Sahoo et al., 2024]. Our work addresses this gap by systematically investigating caste bias in LLMs and its downstream implications. We introduce the DECASTE framework1 , which comprises two novel tasks. The first, the Stereotypical Word Association Task (SWAT), evaluates how LLMs associate caste groups with stereotypical terms using structured prompts and a dedicated bias metric. The second, the Persona-based Scenario Answering Task (PSAT), probes biases in decision-making through caste-linked personas.

Title: Socially Aware Bias Measurements for Hindi Language Representations
Snippet: In order to mitigate religious biases in Hindi, we acknowledge how in Indian culture, the religion of a person is generally identifiable by their last names. We thus, utilize last names to determine the direction of bias. We use both (i) a single set of common last names { acharya − nasir}, and (ii) a set of hindu and muslim entities.

Another religion direction is calculated by combining word lists of Hindu and Muslim lastnames and then conducting PCA over them, we call this religion bias direction as d last . The words lists are provided in Appendix E.

In Hindi language, various religious entities are inherently associated with a particular religion, for example, "Bible is to Christianity as Bhagwad Gita is to Hinduism" is not bias. To accomodate for such cases, we again take motivation from (Zhou et al., 2019) to obtain a direction d ent from the entities word lists (Appendix E) and keep the religion direction calculation calculated by Hindu and Muslim lastnames d last , orthogonal to it.

We believe that if we debias words using d last as bias direction, we should be able to preserve the knowledge of religion information retention test and debias competitively.

In Table 6, we see that linear debiasing by conducting PCA over a list of religious entities is not able to debias much in any of the tests. The same could be observed for linear debiasing using single set of common last names { acharya − nasir}. However, if we linear debias by PCA over a list of lastnames, we are able to debias significantly. Although the Information Retention WEAT effect size is less than the previous methods, they did not even affect the religion bias which is our primary goal. Zhou's variant for religion debias performs well since it is able to debias competitively as well as retains greater amount of necessary religion information. Refer to Appendix C for the word lists used in the test.

Title: How Deep Is Representational Bias in LLMs? The Cases of Caste and Religion
Snippet: Representational bias in large language models (LLMs) has predominantly been measured through single-response interactions and has focused on Global North-centric identities like race and gender. We expand on that research by conducting a systematic audit of GPT-4 Turbo to reveal how deeply encoded representational biases are and how they extend to less-explored dimensions of identity. We prompt GPT-4 Turbo to generate over 7,200 stories about significant life events (such as weddings) in India, using prompts designed to encourage diversity to varying extents. Comparing the diversity of religious and caste representation in the outputs against the actual population distribution in India as recorded in census data, we quantify the presence and “stickiness” of representational bias in the LLM for religion and caste. We find that GPT-4 responses consistently overrepresent culturally dominant groups far beyond their statistical representation, despite prompts intended to encourage representational diversity. Our findings also suggest that representational bias in LLMs has a winner-takes-all quality that is more biased than the likely distribution bias in their training data, and repeated prompt-based nudges have limited and inconsistent efficacy in dislodging these biases. These results suggest that diversifying training data alone may not be sufficient to correct LLM bias, highlighting the need for more fundamental changes in model development.

Title: Toward Cultural Bias Evaluation Datasets: The Case of Bengali Gender, Religious, and National Identity
Snippet: Bias, in the context of computing systems, is where sociotechnical systems systematically and unfairly discriminate against certain individuals or social groups in favor of others (Friedman and Nissenbaum, 1996;Blodgett et al., 2020). People often identify through their perceived memberships in certain groups (Tajfel, 1974). While computational linguists have studied gender and racial biases (Kiritchenko and Mohammad, 2018), systematic discrimination of language technologies based on various cultural factors like religion and nationality has received little attention. Moreover, critical studies examining these biases mostly focused on NLP systems in a handful of languages, whereas many languages with sizeable numbers of speakers do not have enough resources like datasets to pursue similar studies. 

According to (Joshi et al., 2020), whereas 0.28% of global languages (e.g., English, Spanish, Japanese) reap benefits from NLP breakthroughs, 88.38% of languages have virtually no data to use. They also found that while English and Bengali are the third and sixth largest languages by the number of native speakers (Lane, 2023), the former has hundreds of times more resources than the latter in Linguistic Data Consortium, Language Resources and Evaluation, and Wikipedia, and thou-sands more resources in the Web overall. The difference in available resources like labeled datasets impedes the progress of critical studies aimed at fairness, transparency, and identifying biases in such under-represented languages. In the absence of native resources, many of these tools first translate non-English text to English for downstream NLP tasks, creating the potential for colonial imposition on indigenous languages (Bird, 2020). 

One of the main objectives of this work is to highlight and address the lack of focus on two vital cultural factors such as religion and nationality, that shape people's cultural identity. In addition to its large number of native speakers and a thriving cultural community online, the religious diversity of this ethnolinguistic group, with 71% Muslims and 28% Hindus, and their postcolonial division into two nationalities, Bangladeshi (59%) and Indian (38%) makes the Bengali language an interesting case for developing a cultural bias evaluation dataset (BSB, 2022;India, 2011).

Title: AMBEDKAR-A Multi-level Bias Elimination through a Decoding Approach with Knowledge Augmentation for Robust Constitutional Alignment of Language Models
Snippet: Large Language Models (LLMs) can inadvertently reflect societal biases present in their training data, leading to harmful or prejudiced outputs. In the Indian context, our empirical evaluations across a suite of models reveal that biases around caste and religion are particularly salient. Yet, most existing mitigation strategies are Western-centric and fail to address these local nuances. We propose AMBEDKAR, a framework inspired by the egalitarian vision of Dr B. R. Ambedkar, architect of the Indian Constitution, to guide LLM outputs toward fairness, neutrality, and inclusion in line with Articles 14 to 17. Our approach introduces a Constitution-Aware Decoding Layer, guided by the AI Constitution of India and applied only at inference time, without any parameter updates to the base model. We incorporate a speculative decoding algorithm that proactively reduces casteist and communal bias during generation. This mitigation layer operates directly within the decoding process, avoiding changes to model internals and lowering the computational and infrastructural costs associated with retraining. We reinterpret speculative decoding not merely as an efficiency tool but as a mechanism for fairness. In this framework, a Small Language Model (SLM) acts as a potentially biased generator, while a constitutionally guided Large Language Model (LLM) serves as the verifier. Rather than accelerating generation, the LLM enforces bias-robust trajectories in the SLM outputs. This inversion of roles gives rise to a fairness-by-speculation paradigm. Our approach yields an absolute reduction of bias up to 26.41 percent compared to baseline. Our source code, datasets, and results are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/AMBEDKAR-983B/

Title: Indian-BhED: A Dataset for Measuring India-Centric Biases in Large Language Models
Snippet: Large Language Models (LLMs), now used daily by millions, can encode societal biases, exposing their users to representational harms. A large body of scholarship on LLM bias exists but it predominantly adopts a Western-centric frame and attends comparatively less to bias levels and potential harms in the Global South. In this paper, we quantify stereotypical bias in popular LLMs according to an Indian-centric frame through Indian-BhED, a first of its kind dataset, containing stereotypical and anti-stereotypical examples in the context of caste and religious stereotypes in India. We find that the majority of LLMs tested have a strong propensity to output stereotypes in the Indian context, especially when compared to axes of bias traditionally studied in the Western context, such as gender and race. Notably, we find that GPT-2, GPT-2 Large, and GPT 3.5 have a particularly high propensity for preferring stereotypical outputs as a percent of all sentences for the axes of caste (63–79%) and religion (69–72%). We finally investigate potential causes for such harmful behaviour in LLMs, and posit intervention techniques to reduce both stereotypical and anti-stereotypical biases. The findings of this work highlight the need for including more diverse voices when researching fairness in AI and evaluating LLMs.

Title: “Since Lawyers are Males..”: Examining Implicit Gender Bias in Hindi Language Generation by LLMs
Snippet: LLMs are predominantly trained on Western data and thus often fail to capture the cultural nuances of gender in Indian contexts [35,69,102]. Indian languages are significantly underrepresented in training data compared to English and the linguistic structures around those languages create unique challenges for LLMs which leads to poorer model performance and increased gender bias in non-English contexts [35,38,102] Assigning gendered pronouns based on stereotypes reinforces traditional gender roles along with the erasure of non-binary identities. This problem is exacerbated in low-resource languages, like Hindi where training data is limited which further entrenches these biases [28,30,75,91,102] LLMs exhibiting gender bias in translations between English and gender-neutral languages like Bengali reveal a significant challenge in NLP. For instance, an LLM might translate gender-neutral Bengali occupations to English using male pronouns for traditionally male-associated professions and female pronouns for professions stereotypically associated with females. This not only misrepresents the original text but also perpetuates harmful gender stereotypes [30,53,88]. 

Utilization of in-context bias suppression techniques has been discussed, however, these techniques are not foolproof and require careful calibration, especially in multilingual settings where cultural and linguistic nuances play a significant role [37,58,81,86] Gender bias in LLMs is a global issue, particularly evident in the United States and India, where these models perpetuate stereotypes and reinforce societal biases [98]. It has been noted that LLMs contribute to discrimination in India, particularly against marginalized women, impacting their education and employment opportunities [13,41]. In India, the intersection of gender with caste and religion deepens social hierarchies, further entrenching inequalities [59]. 

Current debiasing methods have proven to be ineffective for Indic languages despite the obvious presence and propagation of harmful gender biases in LLM-generated content in those languages [34,41]. Owing to the established significant negative effects of such biases, it becomes crucial to understand how these biases and cultural differences occur and propagate and be cautious of their implications for a heavily biased Indian society.

Title: Structured Legal Document Generation in India: A Model-Agnostic Wrapper Approach with VidhikDastaavej
Snippet: To address the deficiency of Indian legal knowledge in the base LLaMA-2-7B-Chat model, we employed Continued Pretraining (CPT) using a large corpus of Indian legal texts. problem: Did anyone worked on aligning legal judgement predictions to human experts?
final_response:
Yes. A growing body of legal AI and legal NLP research explicitly targets aligning legal judgment prediction with human experts through expert-annotated data, interpretable rationales that mirror judicial reasoning, human-in-the-loop training and evaluation, and legal benchmarks that incorporate human judgments and legal discourse beyond judges alone.<cite id="2dddd06b-4">A growing body of legal AI and legal NLP research explicitly targets aligning legal judgment prediction with human experts through expert-annotated data, interpretable rationales that mirror judicial reasoning, human-in-the-loop training and evaluation, and legal benchmarks that incorporate human judgments and legal discourse beyond judges alone.</cite>

# Expert-annotated datasets and human-centered tasks
Researchers have created legal datasets annotated by experts to reflect human legal concepts and support human-like prediction tasks, not just black-box scoring. For example, AnnoCaseLaw introduces a “novel dataset designed to enhance reasoning and explanation in legal judgment prediction,” distinguished by “an unprecedented level of expert case annotation,” including identification of relevant legal concepts and key case sections, which enables tasks that require matching human legal granularity and subjectivity.<cite id="50667d16-0">AnnoCaseLaw introduces a dataset with an unprecedented level of expert case annotation, enabling tasks that require identifying relevant legal concepts and key case sections and highlighting the nuance and subjectivity of legal concepts, which makes their identification difficult yet promising for LLMs with fine-tuning and in-context learning.</cite> In the Indian bail domain, IBPS presents an “expert-annotated dataset for Indian bail judgments and combines judgment prediction with rationale generation,” explicitly aiming to support legal reasoning that humans can inspect and critique, and noting that prior work in India often lacked expert annotations and interpretability.<cite id="2dddd06b-4">IBPS introduces an expert-annotated dataset for Indian bail judgments and combines judgment prediction with rationale generation, addressing gaps where prior Indian studies often lacked expert annotations and interpretability.</cite>

# Rationale and interpretability frameworks that mirror human reasoning
Several frameworks explicitly model the judge’s stepwise process—reasoning first, then verdict—so that model predictions are interpretable and can be inspected by human experts. One rationale-based LJP framework divides prediction into two steps (reasoning then judgment) to overcome end-to-end black-box limitations that hinder judicial intervention and interpretability in real trials.<cite id="50667d16-2">A rationale-based LJP framework mirrors the judge’s process by separating reasoning from judgment, addressing limitations of end-to-end black-box LJP that prevent manual intervention and produce hard-to-interpret predictions in real trials.</cite> Complementary work formalizes legal reasoning with first-order logic and comparative learning, producing structured, rule-based chains that align with human-like legal logic and support post-hoc inspection by experts.<cite id="50667d16-3">A first-order logic, comparative learning framework for LJP emulates human-like discriminative legal reasoning and produces structured reasoning chains intended to be interpretable and aligned with human reasoning.</cite>

# Human-in-the-loop training and interactive optimization
Beyond static supervised learning, some systems incorporate iterative human feedback and expert-driven data selection to align predictions with human judgment. For instance, a rule-enhanced LJP approach introduces “Confusion-aware Contrastive Learning (CACL)” that uses a quiz of confusable cases to dynamically optimize judgment rules, effectively engaging human expertise to surface cases where models err and iteratively improving rule-based reasoning toward human-like distinctions.<cite id="5fab4707-1">A rule-enhanced LJP framework uses Confusion-aware Contrastive Learning (CACL) with a quiz of confusable cases to dynamically optimize judgment rules, enabling iterative alignment with human-like distinctions and improving performance across public datasets.</cite> Surveys of legal judgment prediction also explicitly discuss hybrid modes—human-only, AI-only, or human-AI joint prediction—reflecting a design space where humans and models collaborate in prediction and review rather than only training on historical judge labels.<cite id="2dddd06b-3">Legal judgment prediction can be performed by humans-only, AI-only, or jointly by humans and AI, reflecting a design space for human-AI collaboration in prediction and review.</cite>

# Benchmarks and resources connecting to human expertise
Researchers have established benchmarks and datasets that facilitate evaluation against human-like reasoning across jurisdictions, often with expert involvement in curation and task design. Overviews note major resources such as EURLEX57K, CAIL2018, SwissJudgment, JTD, and LegalBench that support large-scale legal reasoning tasks, enabling models to be evaluated not just on accuracy but also on the ability to follow human-like reasoning over legal texts and cases.<cite id="2dddd06b-4">Benchmarks such as EURLEX57K, CAIL2018, SwissJudgment, JTD, and LegalBench have enabled large-scale legal reasoning tasks across jurisdictions, supporting evaluation of models in ways aligned with human-like legal reasoning.</cite> AnnoCaseLaw emphasizes that its expert annotations open new legally significant tasks (e.g., concept identification and section relevance), explicitly positioning the benchmark to drive models toward human-aligned reasoning rather than only predictive performance on historical outcomes.<cite id="50667d16-0">AnnoCaseLaw’s expert annotations enable tasks like identifying relevant legal concepts and key case sections, positioning the benchmark to drive human-aligned reasoning rather than only historical outcome prediction.</cite>

# Alignment methods and ethics: supervised fine-tuning, reward modeling, and the “voice of the expert”
At a methodological level, alignment in legal AI commonly uses supervised fine-tuning on high-quality, expert-curated legal data to make outputs relevant and accurate, and reward modeling to align objectives with legal ethics and standards where misalignment risks are high.<cite id="2dddd06b-0">Alignment in legal AI commonly uses supervised fine-tuning on high-quality legal datasets and reward modeling to align objectives with legal ethics and standards, which is critical given high stakes of misalignment in the legal domain.</cite> Ethical analyses argue that datasets and systems should reflect not just judges’ texts, but also the lawyer’s role—moral discretion, explanation capabilities, and the ability to receive public feedback—since these enable practical alignment with human expertise and governance in real-world use.<cite id="2dddd06b-4">Ethical analyses argue that legal NLP datasets should favor the voice of the lawyer, emphasizing moral discretion, sophisticated explanation, and the ability to receive feedback, to better align with human expertise and governance than focusing only on judges’ texts.</cite>

# What “alignment” looks like in practice: examples across tasks
- Predictive alignment with human labels: Expert-annotated datasets for bail and civil judgments support training and evaluation that reflect human legal distinctions and rationales rather than only aggregate outcome frequencies.<cite id="2dddd06b-4">Expert-annotated datasets for bail combine judgment prediction with rationale generation to reflect human legal distinctions and make outputs inspectable by practitioners.</cite>
- Process-aligned reasoning: Rationale frameworks and logic-based rule systems decompose prediction into reasoning and verdict stages, mirroring how judges justify decisions and enabling expert review of intermediate steps.<cite id="50667d16-2">Rationale frameworks decompose prediction into reasoning and verdict to mirror judges’ stepwise logic and enable expert review of intermediate steps.</cite><cite id="5fab4707-1">Logic-based comparative learning frameworks produce structured reasoning chains that can be inspected and iteratively optimized against confusable cases to align with human distinctions.</cite>
- Human-in-the-loop optimization: Confusion-aware contrastive learning and curated “quizzes” of hard cases operationalize expert feedback to steer model behavior toward human-like error patterns and corrections.<cite id="5fab4707-1">Confusion-aware contrastive learning operationalizes expert feedback via confusable-case quizzes to iteratively optimize judgment rules and improve alignment with human-like reasoning.</cite>
- Jurisdictional and benchmark coverage: Cross-jurisdictional datasets and benchmarks (e.g., ECHR, civil law corpora, and newer common law resources) allow models to be evaluated and aligned with human practices across legal systems, not just a single jurisdiction’s judge-centric text.<cite id="2dddd06b-4">Cross-jurisdictional datasets like EURLEX57K, CAIL2018, SwissJudgment, JTD, and LegalBench enable evaluation and alignment with human practices across legal systems beyond a single jurisdiction.</cite>

Despite these advances, challenges remain. Title: Legal Fact Prediction: The Missing Piece in Legal Judgment Prediction
Snippet: Legal judgment prediction (LJP), which enables litigants and their lawyers to forecast judgment outcomes and refine litigation strategies, has emerged as a crucial legal NLP task. Existing studies typically utilize legal facts, i.e., facts that have been established by evidence and determined by the judge, to predict the judgment. However, legal facts are often difficult to obtain in the early stages of litigation, significantly limiting the practical applicability of fact-based LJP. To address this limitation, we propose a novel legal NLP task: legal fact prediction (LFP), which takes the evidence submitted by litigants for trial as input to predict legal facts, thereby empowering fact-based LJP technologies to make predictions in the absence of ground-truth legal facts. We also propose the first benchmark dataset, LFPBench, for evaluating the LFP task. Our extensive experiments on LFPBench demonstrate the effectiveness of LFP-empowered LJP and highlight promising research directions for LFP.
</snippet>

Title: Towards Interactivity and Interpretability: A Rationale-based Legal Judgment Prediction Framework
Snippet: Deep learning methods, especially the natural language process (NLP) techniques, have been employed to benefit the legal assistant systems in several aspects, such as controversy focus mining (Duan et al., 2019) and court hearing conversation generation (Ji et al., 2020). As one of the most important components of the judicial process, the task of legal judgment prediction (LJP) has been studied for decades (Kort, 1957;Keown, 1980;Lin et al., 2012;Chalkidis et al., 2019;Ma et al., 2021). LJP is defined to predict the judgment results (e.g., law article, charge, and term of penalty) of legal cases according to the fact descriptions. In the real trial scenario, as Fig. 1 shows, the judge makes the decision step-by-step: first concludes the rationale according to the case's facts and then determines the judgment. However, most existing methods focus on designing efficient features following an end-to-end framework (Luo et al., 2017;Zhong et al., 2018) while neglecting the necessity for a system to be interactive and interpretable in real trial scenarios. 

To improve the practicality and effectiveness of LJP methods in real world applications, we face the following challenges: 1) The prediction process cannot be manually intervened: Legal tasks usually require high accuracy, but current LJP methods are commonly designed as an end-to-end manner in which the reasoning part is a "blackbox". In practical use, the judge is hard to intervene the trial logic during the prediction process, which may amplify the error and reduce the applicability of the method. 2) The predicted judgment lacks interpretability: The lack of interpretation is a common problem for deep learning models. However, it is especially important in the judicial field since every judgment should be given with a thorough explanation of reasoning to make the verdict more convincing. 

Following the judge's trial logic, in this paper, we propose a novel Rationale-based Legal Judgment Prediction (RLJP) framework to incorporate the rationale into the LJP task. In the RLJP framework, the LJP process is divided into two steps.
</snippet>

For a machine judge to be successful, it would need to have capabilities far exceeding what is currently available. These capabilities include moral and social intuition; the sophisticated ability to give explanations; and, in turn, the ability to receive feedback from members of the public. Title: RLJP: Legal Judgment Prediction via First-Order Logic Rule-enhanced with Large Language Models
Snippet: Legal Judgment Prediction (LJP) is a pivotal task in legal AI. Existing semantic-enhanced LJP models integrate judicial precedents and legal knowledge for high performance. But they neglect legal reasoning logic, a critical component of legal judgments requiring rigorous logical analysis. Although some approaches utilize legal reasoning logic for high-quality predictions, their logic rigidity hinders adaptation to case-specific logical frameworks, particularly in complex cases that are lengthy and detailed. This paper proposes a rule-enhanced legal judgment prediction framework based on first-order logic (FOL) formalism and comparative learning (CL) to develop an adaptive adjustment mechanism for legal judgment logic and further enhance performance in LJP. Inspired by the process of human exam preparation, our method follows a three-stage approach: first, we initialize judgment rules using the FOL formalism to capture complex reasoning logic accurately; next, we propose a Confusion-aware Contrastive Learning (CACL) to dynamically optimize the judgment rules through a quiz consisting of confusable cases; finally, we utilize the optimized judgment rules to predict legal judgments. Experimental results on two public datasets show superior performance across all metrics. The code is publicly available{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/RLJP-FDF1}.
</snippet>

Title: GLARE: Agentic Reasoning for Legal Judgment Prediction
Snippet: Legal judgment prediction (LJP) is an important task in legal natural language processing (NLP), aims to make correct judgment predictions based on the case's fact description (Liu et al., 2023). The judgment predictions include law articles, charges, and terms of penalty (Xu et al., 2024). This task not only provides judgment references to lawyers and judges, as well as providing legal consulting services to the general public (Luo et al., 2017;Shulayeva et al., 2017;McGinnis and Pearce, 2013). 

Recently, large reasoning models (LRMs) have made remarkable progress across in reasoningintensive tasks, including multi-hop question answering and strategic planning (Wang et al., 2024b;Choi et al., 2025). These models can perform multistep reasoning that mimics human thinking (Fu et al., 2022). Intuitively, LJP appears to be an ideal fit for such models. Legal decision-making often involves comparing multiple candidate charges, evaluating whether each satisfies the legal criteria, and narrowing down to the most appropriate one based on the case facts. As a result, it is natural to expect that strong reasoning models would lead to major improvements in LJP. 

However, existing reasoning models fail to deliver the expected breakthroughs in LJP. In practice, they tend to predict the most likely charges without comparing them to similar alternatives, and their reasoning chains are often short and lacking in meaningful intermediate steps. These issues become especially clear in cases involving rare or confusing charges, where accurate judgment depends on subtle distinctions and careful reasoning. Although models may produce step-by-step outputs in such scenarios, the reasoning often stays at a surface level, focusing on pattern matching rather than legal principles. 

We argue that the main reason for the limited performance of reasoning models in legal judgment tasks is not a lack of reasoning ability, but a lack of the specialized knowledge that legal reasoning depends on (Yuan et al., 2024). Effective legal analysis requires long-tail legal knowledge, such as determining the applicability of specific statutes. In some cases, this knowledge is even absent from official legal texts. When such information is missing, models struggle to produce complete and trustworthy reasoning chains as shown in Figure 1.
</snippet>

- Jurisdictional and benchmark coverage: Cross-jurisdictional datasets and benchmarks (e.g., ECHR, civil law corpora, and newer common law resources) allow models to be evaluated and aligned with human practices across legal systems, not just a single jurisdiction’s judge-centric text.<cite id="2dddd06b-4">Cross-jurisdictional datasets like EURLEX57K, CAIL2018, SwissJudgment, JTD, and LegalBench enable evaluation and alignment with human practices across legal systems beyond a single jurisdiction.</cite>

# Gaps and open challenges
Despite these advances, challenges remain. Analyses caution that focusing only on judges’ texts may miss the lawyer-mediated feedback and moral/political discretion essential to alignment, and warn of risks like centralized power and brittleness if human oversight is insufficient.<cite id="2dddd06b-4">Analyses caution that focusing only on judges’ texts may miss lawyer-mediated feedback and moral/political discretion and highlight risks like centralized power and brittleness without sufficient human oversight.</cite> Moreover, while many works produce interpretable rationales, systematic studies that quantitatively calibrate model uncertainty and prediction distributions to human judges across jurisdictions remain limited in the surveyed literature, indicating a need for more head-to-head human–AI comparison and calibration protocols in legal settings.<cite id="50667d16-2">Although rationale frameworks improve interpretability, systematic calibration of model uncertainty to human judges across jurisdictions remains limited, suggesting a need for head-to-head human–AI comparisons and calibration protocols.</cite>

# Bottom line
Yes—multiple strands of research actively align legal judgment prediction with human experts: expert-annotated datasets and human-centered tasks; interpretable, stepwise reasoning frameworks that mirror judges; human-in-the-loop training and optimization; and benchmarks that connect model behavior to human legal practice across jurisdictions. These efforts span both model-centric techniques (fine-tuning, rule/logic augmentation, rationale generation) and system-centric designs (hybrid human–AI workflows, lawyer-inclusive data perspectives), reflecting a broad and growing commitment to alignment in legal AI.<cite id="50667d16-0">Expert-annotated datasets enable human-centered tasks that require models to match human legal granularity and subjectivity.</cite><cite id="50667d16-2">Rationale frameworks mirror judges’ stepwise reasoning to support interpretability and expert review.</cite><cite id="5fab4707-1">Confusion-aware contrastive learning integrates expert-driven “quizzes” to iteratively align model rules with human-like distinctions.</cite><cite id="2dddd06b-4">Benchmarks across jurisdictions and expert-annotated datasets support evaluation and alignment with human legal practice, including rationale generation for tasks like bail prediction.</cite><cite id="2dddd06b-0">Alignment methods such as supervised fine-tuning and reward modeling are positioned as essential for legal AI to match legal ethics and standards.</cite><cite id="2dddd06b-4">Ethical analyses emphasize incorporating the lawyer’s voice, explanation, and feedback mechanisms for practical alignment and governance.</cite>

Title: IBPS: Indian Bail Prediction System
Snippet: The intersection of Artificial Intelligence and law (AI4Law) has rapidly evolved over the past two decades, fueled by the digitization of legal records and advancements in natural language processing (NLP). Legal AI research spans multiple tasks such as legal judgment prediction (LJP), statute retrieval, legal question answering, contract analysis, and legal summarization. Among these, LJP has received significant attention for its ability to support judicial decision-making. Early efforts in this domain began with statistical and rule-based models, notably the work of Aletras et al. (2016) on the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR). Subsequent benchmarks like EURLEX57K (Chalkidis et al., 2019), CAIL2018 (Xiao et al., 2018), SwissJudgment (Niklaus et al., 2021), JTD (Yamada et al., 2024), and LegalBench (Guha et al., 2023) have enabled large-scale legal reasoning tasks across jurisdictions. However, most such datasets are built for civil law systems, limiting their adaptability to common law jurisdictions like India. Indian legal texts present unique challenges, length, linguistic complexity, and a reliance on precedent, yet remain under-resourced in Legal NLP. While studies like Zadgaonkar and Agrawal (2021), Bansal et al. (2022), andSharma et al. (2021) applied classical ML models to Indian legal cases, they often lacked expert annotations and interpretability. In the U.S., a substantial body of research has examined bail and pretrial detention outcomes (Sacks et al., 2015;Demuth and Steffensmeier, 2004), highlighting their long-term consequences on conviction and sentencing. Yet, this critical decision point remains underexplored in India. Our work addresses these gaps by introducing an expert-annotated dataset for Indian bail judgments and combining judgment prediction with rationale generation.

Title: AnnoCaseLaw: A Richly-Annotated Dataset For Benchmarking Explainable Legal Judgment Prediction
Snippet: AnnoCaseLaw introduces a novel dataset designed to enhance reasoning and explanation in legal judgment prediction. Our findings confirm that, when properly framed, legal judgment prediction remains a formidable task, highlighting the urgent need for high-quality datasets. What sets AnnoCaseLaw apart is its unprecedented level of expert case annotation, enabling new, legally significant tasks, such as identifying relevant legal concepts and annotating key case sections. We find that the nuance and subjectivity of legal concepts makes their identification difficult, while LLMs show promise in learning case annotation through fine-tuning and in-context learning. Achieving strong performance across all three tasks represents a critical milestone for the legal NLP community, and we hope Anno-CaseLaw will accelerate progress toward this.

Title: Legal Fact Prediction: The Missing Piece in Legal Judgment Prediction
Snippet: Legal judgment prediction (LJP), which enables litigants and their lawyers to forecast judgment outcomes and refine litigation strategies, has emerged as a crucial legal NLP task. Existing studies typically utilize legal facts, i.e., facts that have been established by evidence and determined by the judge, to predict the judgment. However, legal facts are often difficult to obtain in the early stages of litigation, significantly limiting the practical applicability of fact-based LJP. To address this limitation, we propose a novel legal NLP task: legal fact prediction (LFP), which takes the evidence submitted by litigants for trial as input to predict legal facts, thereby empowering fact-based LJP technologies to make predictions in the absence of ground-truth legal facts. We also propose the first benchmark dataset, LFPBench, for evaluating the LFP task. Our extensive experiments on LFPBench demonstrate the effectiveness of LFP-empowered LJP and highlight promising research directions for LFP.

Title: Towards Interactivity and Interpretability: A Rationale-based Legal Judgment Prediction Framework
Snippet: Deep learning methods, especially the natural language process (NLP) techniques, have been employed to benefit the legal assistant systems in several aspects, such as controversy focus mining (Duan et al., 2019) and court hearing conversation generation (Ji et al., 2020). As one of the most important components of the judicial process, the task of legal judgment prediction (LJP) has been studied for decades (Kort, 1957;Keown, 1980;Lin et al., 2012;Chalkidis et al., 2019;Ma et al., 2021). LJP is defined to predict the judgment results (e.g., law article, charge, and term of penalty) of legal cases according to the fact descriptions. In the real trial scenario, as Fig. 1 shows, the judge makes the decision step-by-step: first concludes the rationale according to the case's facts and then determines the judgment. However, most existing methods focus on designing efficient features following an end-to-end framework (Luo et al., 2017;Zhong et al., 2018) while neglecting the necessity for a system to be interactive and interpretable in real trial scenarios. 

To improve the practicality and effectiveness of LJP methods in real world applications, we face the following challenges: 1) The prediction process cannot be manually intervened: Legal tasks usually require high accuracy, but current LJP methods are commonly designed as an end-to-end manner in which the reasoning part is a "blackbox". In practical use, the judge is hard to intervene the trial logic during the prediction process, which may amplify the error and reduce the applicability of the method. 2) The predicted judgment lacks interpretability: The lack of interpretation is a common problem for deep learning models. However, it is especially important in the judicial field since every judgment should be given with a thorough explanation of reasoning to make the verdict more convincing. 

Following the judge's trial logic, in this paper, we propose a novel Rationale-based Legal Judgment Prediction (RLJP) framework to incorporate the rationale into the LJP task. In the RLJP framework, the LJP process is divided into two steps.

Title: Enabling Discriminative Reasoning in LLMs for Legal Judgment Prediction
Snippet: Existing LLMs mostly rely on direct answering or judicial syllogism for reasoning, which requires the model to directly provide the correct law articles and charges. This exceeds the capabilities of these language models and even human experts, leading to bad performance. In this work, we enable LLM to emulate the reasoning pattern of real-world judges to conduct discriminative reasoning for accurate legal judgment prediction.

Title: The Ethics of Automating Legal Actors
Snippet: In this work, we have evaluated the ethical and practical feasibility of different proposals for NLP research in law. By surveying a number of popular legal NLP tasks, we identify that the datasets they are built on favour the voice of the judge. However, because the criteria for what makes a good judge includes moral discretion and political accountability we believe that practical applications of these kinds of NLP models face difficult challenges. For a machine judge to be successful, it would need to have capabilities far exceeding what is currently available. These capabilities include moral and social intuition; the sophisticated ability to give explanations; and, in turn, the ability to receive feedback from members of the public. Even if these technical challenges were met there are further inherent risks to using legal NLP in the real world. We have discussed three of them: the centralisation of power, brittleness and lack of accountability. Comparing the judge and a lawyer, we find the role of a lawyer less susceptible to these challenges. Our appeal is, therefore, to focus on the voice of the lawyer in the legal NLP datasets. Furthermore, we believe that overlooking the role of the lawyer hinders current neural approaches for modelling law. For the academic pursuit of furthering legal NLP research, too much focus on the text produced by judges hides the fruitful and interesting interplay between the lawyers that fuels the legal discourse.

As one of the most important components of the judicial process, the task of legal judgment prediction (LJP) has been studied for decades (Kort, 1957;Keown, 1980;Lin et al., 2012;Chalkidis et al., 2019;Ma et al., 2021). LJP is defined to predict the judgment results (e.g., law article, charge, and term of penalty) of legal cases according to the fact descriptions. In the real trial scenario, as Fig. 1 shows, the judge makes the decision step-by-step: first concludes the rationale according to the case's facts and then determines the judgment. However, most existing methods focus on designing efficient features following an end-to-end framework (Luo et al., 2017;Zhong et al., 2018) while neglecting the necessity for a system to be interactive and interpretable in real trial scenarios. 

To improve the practicality and effectiveness of LJP methods in real world applications, we face the following challenges: 1) The prediction process cannot be manually intervened: Legal tasks usually require high accuracy, but current LJP methods are commonly designed as an end-to-end manner in which the reasoning part is a "blackbox". In practical use, the judge is hard to intervene the trial logic during the prediction process, which may amplify the error and reduce the applicability of the method. 2) The predicted judgment lacks interpretability: The lack of interpretation is a common problem for deep learning models. However, it is especially important in the judicial field since every judgment should be given with a thorough explanation of reasoning to make the verdict more convincing. 

Following the judge's trial logic, in this paper, we propose a novel Rationale-based Legal Judgment Prediction (RLJP) framework to incorporate the rationale into the LJP task. In the RLJP framework, the LJP process is divided into two steps.

documents.title: Enabling Discriminative Reasoning in LLMs for Legal Judgment Prediction
documents.snippet: Existing LLMs mostly rely on direct answering or judicial syllogism for reasoning, which requires the model to directly provide the correct law articles and charges. This exceeds the capabilities of these language models and even human experts, leading to bad performance. In this work, we enable LLM to emulate the reasoning pattern of real-world judges to conduct discriminative reasoning for accurate legal judgment prediction.

documents.title: The Ethics of Automating Legal Actors
documents.snippet: In this work, we have evaluated the ethical and practical feasibility of different proposals for NLP research in law. By surveying a number of popular legal NLP tasks, we identify that the datasets they are built on favour the voice of the judge. However, because the criteria for what makes a good judge includes moral discretion and political accountability we believe that practical applications of these kinds of NLP models face difficult challenges. For a machine judge to be successful, it would need to have capabilities far exceeding what is currently available. These capabilities include moral and social intuition; the sophisticated ability to give explanations; and, in turn, the ability to receive feedback from members of the public. Even if these technical challenges were met there are further inherent risks to using legal NLP in the real world. We have discussed three of them: the centralisation of power, brittleness and lack of accountability. Comparing the judge and a lawyer, we find the role of a lawyer less susceptible to these challenges. Our appeal is, therefore, to focus on the voice of the lawyer in the legal NLP datasets. Furthermore, we believe that overlooking the role of the lawyer hinders current neural approaches for modelling law. For the academic pursuit of furthering legal NLP research, too much focus on the text produced by judges hides the fruitful and interesting interplay between the lawyers that fuels the legal discourse.

Title: RLJP: Legal Judgment Prediction via First-Order Logic Rule-enhanced with Large Language Models
Snippet: Legal Judgment Prediction (LJP) is a pivotal task in legal AI. Existing semantic-enhanced LJP models integrate judicial precedents and legal knowledge for high performance. But they neglect legal reasoning logic, a critical component of legal judgments requiring rigorous logical analysis. Although some approaches utilize legal reasoning logic for high-quality predictions, their logic rigidity hinders adaptation to case-specific logical frameworks, particularly in complex cases that are lengthy and detailed. This paper proposes a rule-enhanced legal judgment prediction framework based on first-order logic (FOL) formalism and comparative learning (CL) to develop an adaptive adjustment mechanism for legal judgment logic and further enhance performance in LJP. Inspired by the process of human exam preparation, our method follows a three-stage approach: first, we initialize judgment rules using the FOL formalism to capture complex reasoning logic accurately; next, we propose a Confusion-aware Contrastive Learning (CACL) to dynamically optimize the judgment rules through a quiz consisting of confusable cases; finally, we utilize the optimized judgment rules to predict legal judgments. Experimental results on two public datasets show superior performance across all metrics. The code is publicly available{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/RLJP-FDF1}.

Title: GLARE: Agentic Reasoning for Legal Judgment Prediction
Snippet: Legal judgment prediction (LJP) is an important task in legal natural language processing (NLP), aims to make correct judgment predictions based on the case's fact description (Liu et al., 2023). The judgment predictions include law articles, charges, and terms of penalty (Xu et al., 2024). This task not only provides judgment references to lawyers and judges, as well as providing legal consulting services to the general public (Luo et al., 2017;Shulayeva et al., 2017;McGinnis and Pearce, 2013). 

Recently, large reasoning models (LRMs) have made remarkable progress across in reasoningintensive tasks, including multi-hop question answering and strategic planning (Wang et al., 2024b;Choi et al., 2025). These models can perform multistep reasoning that mimics human thinking (Fu et al., 2022). Intuitively, LJP appears to be an ideal fit for such models. Legal decision-making often involves comparing multiple candidate charges, evaluating whether each satisfies the legal criteria, and narrowing down to the most appropriate one based on the case facts. As a result, it is natural to expect that strong reasoning models would lead to major improvements in LJP. 

However, existing reasoning models fail to deliver the expected breakthroughs in LJP. In practice, they tend to predict the most likely charges without comparing them to similar alternatives, and their reasoning chains are often short and lacking in meaningful intermediate steps. These issues become especially clear in cases involving rare or confusing charges, where accurate judgment depends on subtle distinctions and careful reasoning. Although models may produce step-by-step outputs in such scenarios, the reasoning often stays at a surface level, focusing on pattern matching rather than legal principles. 

We argue that the main reason for the limited performance of reasoning models in legal judgment tasks is not a lack of reasoning ability, but a lack of the specialized knowledge that legal reasoning depends on (Yuan et al., 2024). Effective legal analysis requires long-tail legal knowledge, such as determining the applicability of specific statutes. In some cases, this knowledge is even absent from official legal texts. When such information is missing, models struggle to produce complete and trustworthy reasoning chains as shown in Figure 1.

Title: LegalSim: Multi-Agent Simulation of Legal Systems for Discovering Procedural Exploits
Snippet: A substantial body of Natural Legal Language Processing (NLLP) focuses on analytical and predictive tasks. Early work showed that machine learn-ing can predict judicial outcomes from case facts (Aletras et al., 2016). More recent approaches leverage large language models and legal-specific pretraining, such as LEGAL-BERT (Chalkidis et al., 2020), achieving strong results on legal judgment prediction, document classification, and argument mining. These tools reason about or predict outcomes in a static setting; they are not designed to act as strategic agents within a procedural process. Our work shifts the focus from passive prediction to active, strategic participation.

Title: AnnoCaseLaw: A Richly-Annotated Dataset For Benchmarking Explainable Legal Judgment Prediction
Snippet: The rapidly increasing capabilities of machinelearning models has catalyzed progress across many legal natural language processing (NLP) tasks, including: Document Summarization (Sie et al., 2024); Information Extraction (Mali et al., 2024); and Legal Question Answering (Martinez-Gil, 2023). However, Legal Judgment Prediction (LJP), where the court's outcome is automatically predicted from the facts (Aletras et al., 2016;Luo et al., 2017;Medvedeva et al., 2020), has emerged as the critical task in legal NLP due to its practical significance and research challenges. 

Globally, legal institutions are overwhelmed by the number of existing and newly-filed cases, leaving legal practitioners insufficient time to adequately prepare and adjudicate cases (Cui et al., 2023). Fortunately, artificial intelligence (AI), in the form of LJP models, presents a way to alleviate this burden, while improving access to justice and promoting consistency in legal outcomes in the process (Armour and Sako, 2020). From a research perspective, LJP serves as a testbed for understanding and eliciting reasoning within, and understanding the decisions of, state-of-the-art foundation models (Bommasani et al., 2022;Jiang and Yang, 2023;Xu et al., 2023;Valvoda and Cotterell, 2024;Zhang et al., 2024), as well as inspiring new architectures and frameworks (Wang et al., 2024).

problem: what are the recent works on task vectors?
final_response:
# Overview: What “task vectors” are and why they matter

Task vectors parametrize the change from a pretrained model to a task-specific adaptation as a learnable direction or set of parameters in the model space, enabling efficient adaptation and multi-task learning via vector arithmetic and merging rather than full retraining.<cite id="b8d06d28-2">Task prompt vectors are defined as element-wise differences between a soft prompt fine-tuned on a task and an initial random soft prompt, and can be combined via simple vector addition to transfer knowledge between tasks or initialize new ones<cite id="b8d06d28-0">Task prompt vectors extend soft prompt tuning by enabling multi-task soft prompt transfer and combining task vectors via vector arithmetic for efficient adaptation</cite>. Recent work shows that such vectors can be sparse and separable, and that arithmetic or merging can support forgetting, multi-task construction, and analogical task transfer, motivating their reuse across tasks and initializations.<cite id="48e9c535-4">Ilharco et al. introduce task vectors as the shift in parameter space due to fine-tuning and show arithmetic enables forgetting, multi-tasking, and analogies</cite><cite id="48e9c535-1">Language adapters (task vectors) exhibit sparsity and high orthogonality between different tasks</cite> 

# Methods that learn or use task vectors

Soft prompts and prompt-tuning. Prompt tuning injects trainable continuous vectors (soft prompts) that act as task-specific instructions while freezing base model weights; these vectors become task-specific through optimization on small data, enabling few-/zero-shot adaptation.<cite id="b8d06d28-3">Prompt tuning methods (Prefix Tuning, P-Tuning) add soft prompts optimized for downstream tasks, making these vectors task-specific for adaptation</cite><cite id="b8d06d28-4">Prompt tuning and CoOp learn task-specific prompt vectors, with CoOp optimizing prompt vectors in CLIP’s language branch but suffering from overfitting without additional regularizers</cite>. Multi-task soft prompt tuning further explores how a single soft prompt can encode multiple tasks and how to transfer via task vectors.<cite id="b8d06d28-0">Recent work studies multi-task soft prompt transfer using task prompt vectors for efficient initialization and vector combinations</cite><cite id="ad373965-4">Dynamic Task Vector Grouping uses soft prompt task vectors from source tasks for full-dataset transfer and few-shot adaptation</cite> 

Adapter/LoRA and instruction-tuning factorization. A large body of work factorizes model adaptation into a base pretrained model plus task-specific adapters (LoRA/PEFT), treating each adapter as a task vector in parameter space.<cite id="82d5d227-3">Instruction tuning with multiple tasks and prior work (Polytropon) learns task-specific adapters (“skills”) and aggregates them per task; later work (Polytropon-S) assigns a distinct skill per layer with deterministic routing</cite><cite id="48e9c535-4">Foundation model engineering synthesizes this line: each task linked to a spectrum of skills (adapters) with routing, and arithmetic/merging to combine or refine adaptations</cite>. Recent methods explicitly isolate instruction-following behaviors into adapters to enable reuse and controlled re-adaptation, extending vectorization beyond single-task fine-tuning.<cite id="82d5d227-4">RE-Adapt reverse-engineers instruction-tuning into an adapter and discusses arithmetic manipulation for negating behaviors, improving multi-task performance, and analogies to new tasks</cite> 

# Operations on task vectors: mixing, ensembling, and retrieval

Arithmetic mixing and transfer. Soft prompt task vectors can be added or linearly combined to initialize new tasks or adapt to few-shot settings without further training, yielding modularity and reuse across tasks and initializations.<cite id="b8d06d28-2">Task prompt vectors define straight trajectories from initial prompts to task-specific prompts; vector addition combines knowledge from different tasks and can initialize similar new tasks</cite><cite id="ad373965-0">Task prompt vectors match multi-task soft prompt transfer (SPoT) while providing modularity and source prompt independence; combinations can initialize low-resource zero-/few-shot settings without additional training</cite>. Empirically, combining vectors from different initializations maintains performance in many cases, suggesting a reusable “vector hub” paradigm.<cite id="ad373965-0">Task prompt vectors from different initializations can be combined and retained across new tasks; identifying suitable combinations via validation enables reuse without retraining</cite> 

Weight-averaging and merging of task-specific adapters. In PEFT, multiple task adapters can be merged via weight-averaging or learned routing/merging policies; the choice of merging method and task set composition affects performance, and order can matter for continual merging in code LLMs.<cite id="82d5d227-0">MergeRepair keeps a frozen Code LLM with one LoRA adapter per task and explores merging via weight-averaging and ties-based methods; merging order influences final adapter influences and performance</cite><cite id="82d5d227-2">For pass@1, ties merging performs best for StarCoder2 while weight-averaging and ties show mixed results for pass@10; Granite shows weight-averaging best and ties worst, indicating method and model sensitivity</cite>. Training-free arithmetic has also been explored to enhance existing adapters, with pruning and sign-alignment improving stability but potentially reducing performance if over-pruned.<cite id="48e9c535-1">Training-free language adapter arithmetic improves zero-shot NER; Ties-Merging reduces cosine similarity via pruning and sign alignment, but higher pruning can degrade performance by making vectors too sparse</cite> 

Retrieval and ensembles of adapters. Recent PEFT systems retrieve or ensemble multiple task-specific adapters based on task similarity, textual prompting, or Fisher weighting to construct a single adapter for a new task, reducing training cost while leveraging diverse skills.<cite id="48e9c535-4">AdapterSoup uses task textual similarity and clustering to find auxiliary tasks and merge pertinent adapters; LoRaHub performs gradient-free optimization to fine-tune LoRa merging with few-shot examples</cite><cite id="48e9c535-0">EASE (2024) trains task-specific adapters and uses a subspace ensemble process to integrate information from all adapters; MOS (2025) achieves higher accuracy and lower inference time via a training-free self-refined adapter retrieval mechanism</cite> 

# Recent PEFT and decomposition methods framing adapters as task vectors

SVD/AdaLoRA-style decompositions. AdaLoRA applies SVD to parameter matrices to decompose weights into low-rank factors, prioritizing resources by significance and directly exposing task vectors as low-rank updates atop the base model.<cite id="48e9c535-4">AdaLoRA adopts SVD for parameter matrix decomposition and prioritizes resources by significance, treating different weight matrices as task-direction components</cite>. Broader PEFT integrations combine SVD with sparse or structured methods (e.g., SparseAdapter, MAM Adapters, UniPELT, Compacter) to make adapter “task vectors” more efficient and adaptable.<cite id="48e9c535-4">PEFT integrations such as SparseAdapter, MAM Adapters, UniPELT, Compacter amalgamate PEFT methodologies to enhance efficiency and adaptability of adapter task vectors</cite> 

Routing and skill-based aggregation. Multi-skill routing methods learn a binary task–skill matrix and aggregate per-task adapters, while deterministic routing per layer (Polytropon/Polytropon-S) supports scalable instruction tuning and evaluation on unseen tasks.<cite id="82d5d227-3">Polytropon learns task-specific adapters (“skills”) and aggregates them per task using a binary task–skill matrix, with deterministic routing in Polytropon-S per layer</cite><cite id="82d5d227-3">Instruction-tuned MoEs can be evaluated on unseen tasks without task-specific few-shot fine-tuning, highlighting the generality of adapter-based vectorization</cite> 

Ensemble selection and gradient-free merging. Adapter retrieval and clustering (AdapterSoup) and gradient-free optimization for LoRa merging (LoRaHub) operationalize choosing and combining task vectors without full retraining, improving speed and accuracy in practice.<cite id="48e9c535-4">AdapterSoup selects auxiliary tasks via similarity and clustering to merge relevant adapters; LoRaHub performs gradient-free optimization to merge LoRA adapters guided by few-shot examples</cite><cite id="48e9c535-0">MOS (2025) uses a training-free self-refined adapter retrieval mechanism to achieve higher accuracy and lower inference time than EASE</cite> 

# Empirical properties and analyses of task vectors

Sparsity, separability, and interference. Recent analyses report that task vectors are highly separable (nearly orthogonal) in parameter space, which reduces interference between tasks and enables constructive operations like addition and negation for multi-tasking and analogical reasoning.<cite id="48e9c535-1">Task vectors exhibit high sparsity and orthogonality; cosine similarities between task vectors can be very low, indicating near-orthogonality</cite><cite id="82d5d227-4">Ilharco et al. observed task vectors are almost orthogonal, allowing combinations for negating behaviors, improving multi-task performance, and performing well on new tasks via analogies</cite>. Zero-/few-shot transfer via vectorization. Model- and task-specific sensitivity.
