Title: Current and future state of evaluation of large language models for medical summarization tasks
Snippet: One method for designing LLMs to perform evaluations is through the use of manually curated prompts (Fig. 4). A prompt consists of the task description and instructions provided to an LLM to guide its responses. Two primary prompting strategies are employed in this context: Zero-Shot and Few-Shot 3 . In Zero-Shot prompting, the LLM is given only the task description without any examples before being asked to perform evaluations. Few-Shot prompting provides the task description alongside a few examples to help guide the LLM in generating output. The number of examples varies based on the LLM's architecture, input window limitations, and the point at which the model performs optimally. Typically, between one and five few-shot examples are used. Prompt engineering, through both Zero-Shot and Few-Shot ("in-context learning") approaches (collectively referred to as "hard prompting"), enables an LLM to perform tasks that it was not explicitly trained to do. However, performance can vary significantly depending on the model's pre-training and its relevance to the new task. 

Beyond these manual approaches, a more adaptive strategy involves "soft prompting," also known as machine-learned prompts, which includes techniques like prompt tuning and p-tuning 42 . Soft prompts are learnable parameters added as virtual tokens to a model's input to signal task-specific instructions. Unlike hard prompts, soft prompts are trained and incorporated into the model's input layer, enabling the model to handle a broader range of specialized tasks. Soft prompting has been shown to outperform Few-Shot prompting, especially in large-scale models, as it fine-tunes the model's behavior without altering the core weights. 

Through these methods, LLMs can be instructed to serve as evaluators with instructions on the dimensions and scale needed for a thorough evaluation. Promising results for such methods have already been seen in general domain applications like LLM-EVAL 43 and TALEC 44 . LLM-EVAL is a single prompt approach to employing LLM-based evaluators that can consist of multiple dimensions. This approach reported correlation coefficients between human evaluators and LLM evaluators to have an average increase of nearly 30 points over ROUGE-L.
</snippet>

The Evaluator Prompt needs to instruct the LLM on the task (Prompt), provide the LLM will all the necessary information to make an evaluation (Information), and all the information that defines the guidelines and formatting of the evaluation (Evaluation). 

Beyond these manual approaches, a more adaptive strategy involves "soft prompting," also known as machine-learned prompts, which includes techniques like prompt tuning and p-tuning [84]. Soft prompts are learnable parameters added as virtual tokens to a model's input to signal task-specific instructions. Unlike hard prompts, soft prompts are trained and incorporated into the model's input layer, enabling the model to handle a broader range of specialized tasks. Soft prompting has been shown to outperform Few-Shot prompting, especially in large-scale models, as it fine-tunes the model's behavior without altering the core weights.

# Overview: What “task vectors” are and why they matter

Task vectors parametrize the change from a pretrained model to a task-specific adaptation as a learnable direction or set of parameters in the model space, enabling efficient adaptation and multi-task learning via vector arithmetic and merging rather than full retraining.<cite id="b8d06d28-2">Task prompt vectors are defined as element-wise differences between a soft prompt fine-tuned on a task and an initial random soft prompt, and can be combined via simple vector addition to transfer knowledge between tasks or initialize new ones<cite id="b8d06d28-0">Task prompt vectors extend soft prompt tuning by enabling multi-task soft prompt transfer and combining task vectors via vector arithmetic for efficient adaptation</cite>. Recent work shows that such vectors can be sparse and separable, and that arithmetic or merging can support forgetting, multi-task construction, and analogical task transfer, motivating their reuse across tasks and initializations.<cite id="48e9c535-4">Ilharco et al. introduce task vectors as the shift in parameter space due to fine-tuning and show arithmetic enables forgetting, multi-tasking, and analogies</cite><cite id="48e9c535-1">Language adapters (task vectors) exhibit sparsity and high orthogonality between different tasks</cite> 

# Methods that learn or use task vectors

Soft prompts and prompt-tuning. Prompt tuning injects trainable continuous vectors (soft prompts) that act as task-specific instructions while freezing base model weights; these vectors become task-specific through optimization on small data, enabling few-/zero-shot adaptation.<cite id="b8d06d28-3">Prompt tuning methods (Prefix Tuning, P-Tuning) add soft prompts optimized for downstream tasks, making these vectors task-specific for adaptation</cite><cite id="b8d06d28-4">Prompt tuning and CoOp learn task-specific prompt vectors, with CoOp optimizing prompt vectors in CLIP’s language branch but suffering from overfitting without additional regularizers</cite>. Multi-task soft prompt tuning further explores how a single soft prompt can encode multiple tasks and how to transfer via task vectors.<cite id="b8d06d28-0">Recent work studies multi-task soft prompt transfer using task prompt vectors for efficient initialization and vector combinations</cite><cite id="ad373965-4">Dynamic Task Vector Grouping uses soft prompt task vectors from source tasks for full-dataset transfer and few-shot adaptation</cite> 

Adapter/LoRA and instruction-tuning factorization. A large body of work factorizes model adaptation into a base pretrained model plus task-specific adapters (LoRA/PEFT), treating each adapter as a task vector in parameter space.<cite id="82d5d227-3">Instruction tuning with multiple tasks and prior work (Polytropon) learns task-specific adapters (“skills”) and aggregates them per task; later work (Polytropon-S) assigns a distinct skill per layer with deterministic routing</cite><cite id="48e9c535-4">Foundation model engineering synthesizes this line: each task linked to a spectrum of skills (adapters) with routing, and arithmetic/merging to combine or refine adaptations</cite>. Recent methods explicitly isolate instruction-following behaviors into adapters to enable reuse and controlled re-adaptation, extending vectorization beyond single-task fine-tuning.<cite id="82d5d227-4">RE-Adapt reverse-engineers instruction-tuning into an adapter and discusses arithmetic manipulation for negating behaviors, improving multi-task performance, and analogies to new tasks</cite> 

# Operations on task vectors: mixing, ensembling, and retrieval

Arithmetic mixing and transfer. Soft prompt task vectors can be added or linearly combined to initialize new tasks or adapt to few-shot settings without further training, yielding modularity and reuse across tasks and initializations.<cite id="b8d06d28-2">Task prompt vectors define straight trajectories from initial prompts to task-specific prompts; vector addition combines knowledge from different tasks and can initialize similar new tasks</cite><cite id="ad373965-0">Task prompt vectors match multi-task soft prompt transfer (SPoT) while providing modularity and source prompt independence; combinations can initialize low-resource zero-/few-shot settings without additional training</cite>. Empirically, combining vectors from different initializations maintains performance in many cases, suggesting a reusable “vector hub” paradigm.<cite id="ad373965-0">Task prompt vectors from different initializations can be combined and retained across new tasks; identifying suitable combinations via validation enables reuse without retraining</cite> 

Weight-averaging and merging of task-specific adapters. In PEFT, multiple task adapters can be merged via weight-averaging or learned routing/merging policies; the choice of merging method and task set composition affects performance, and order can matter for continual merging in code LLMs.<cite id="82d5d227-0">MergeRepair keeps a frozen Code LLM with one LoRA adapter per task and explores merging via weight-averaging and ties-based methods; merging order influences final adapter influences and performance</cite><cite id="82d5d227-2">For pass@1, ties merging performs best for StarCoder2 while weight-averaging and ties show mixed results for pass@10; Granite shows weight-averaging best and ties worst, indicating method and model sensitivity</cite>. Training-free arithmetic has also been explored to enhance existing adapters, with pruning and sign-alignment improving stability but potentially reducing performance if over-pruned.<cite id="48e9c535-1">Training-free language adapter arithmetic improves zero-shot NER; Ties-Merging reduces cosine similarity via pruning and sign alignment, but higher pruning can degrade performance by making vectors too sparse</cite> 

Retrieval and ensembles of adapters. Recent PEFT systems retrieve or ensemble multiple task-specific adapters based on task similarity, textual prompting, or Fisher weighting to construct a single adapter for a new task, reducing training cost while leveraging diverse skills.<cite id="48e9c535-4">AdapterSoup uses task textual similarity and clustering to find auxiliary tasks and merge pertinent adapters; LoRaHub performs gradient-free optimization to fine-tune LoRa merging with few-shot examples</cite><cite id="48e9c535-0">EASE (2024) trains task-specific adapters and uses a subspace ensemble process to integrate information from all adapters; MOS (2025) achieves higher accuracy and lower inference time via a training-free self-refined adapter retrieval mechanism</cite> 

# Recent PEFT and decomposition methods framing adapters as task vectors

SVD/AdaLoRA-style decompositions. AdaLoRA applies SVD to parameter matrices to decompose weights into low-rank factors, prioritizing resources by significance and directly exposing task vectors as low-rank updates atop the base model.<cite id="48e9c535-4">AdaLoRA adopts SVD for parameter matrix decomposition and prioritizes resources by significance, treating different weight matrices as task-direction components</cite>. Broader PEFT integrations combine SVD with sparse or structured methods (e.g., SparseAdapter, MAM Adapters, UniPELT, Compacter) to make adapter “task vectors” more efficient and adaptable.<cite id="48e9c535-4">PEFT integrations such as SparseAdapter, MAM Adapters, UniPELT, Compacter amalgamate PEFT methodologies to enhance efficiency and adaptability of adapter task vectors</cite> 

Routing and skill-based aggregation. Multi-skill routing methods learn a binary task–skill matrix and aggregate per-task adapters, while deterministic routing per layer (Polytropon/Polytropon-S) supports scalable instruction tuning and evaluation on unseen tasks.<cite id="82d5d227-3">Polytropon learns task-specific adapters (“skills”) and aggregates them per task using a binary task–skill matrix, with deterministic routing in Polytropon-S per layer</cite><cite id="82d5d227-3">Instruction-tuned MoEs can be evaluated on unseen tasks without task-specific few-shot fine-tuning, highlighting the generality of adapter-based vectorization</cite> 

Ensemble selection and gradient-free merging. Adapter retrieval and clustering (AdapterSoup) and gradient-free optimization for LoRa merging (LoRaHub) operationalize choosing and combining task vectors without full retraining, improving speed and accuracy in practice.<cite id="48e9c535-4">AdapterSoup selects auxiliary tasks via similarity and clustering to merge relevant adapters; LoRaHub performs gradient-free optimization to merge LoRA adapters guided by few-shot examples</cite><cite id="48e9c535-0">MOS (2025) uses a training-free self-refined adapter retrieval mechanism to achieve higher accuracy and lower inference time than EASE</cite> 

# Empirical properties and analyses of task vectors

Sparsity, separability, and interference. Recent analyses report that task vectors are highly separable (nearly orthogonal) in parameter space, which reduces interference between tasks and enables constructive operations like addition and negation for multi-tasking and analogical reasoning.<cite id="48e9c535-1">Task vectors exhibit high sparsity and orthogonality; cosine similarities between task vectors can be very low, indicating near-orthogonality</cite><cite id="82d5d227-4">Ilharco et al. observed task vectors are almost orthogonal, allowing combinations for negating behaviors, improving multi-task performance, and performing well on new tasks via analogies</cite>. In contrast, language adapters (sometimes termed “language vectors”) can be less orthogonal, and naive arithmetic can cause parameter interference unless pruned and aligned.<cite id="48e9c535-1">Language adapters show less orthogonal properties than task vectors; pruning and sign alignment in Ties-Merging mitigate interference for arithmetic merging</cite> 

Zero-/few-shot transfer via vectorization. Multi-task soft prompt tuning and vector transfer methods enable zero-/few-shot adaptation by reusing precomputed task vectors from similar tasks or by combining vectors from diverse initializations without additional training, reducing compute and data needs.<cite id="ad373965-0">Task prompt vector combinations can initialize zero-/few-shot settings without training and maintain performance across tasks, even when combining vectors from different initializations</cite><cite id="b8d06d28-2">Vector addition of task prompt vectors yields efficient adaptation and can initialize new, similar tasks</cite> 

# Representative recent works (2023–2025)

- Task Prompt Vectors for soft prompts: formalize task vectors as soft prompt differences; enable vector addition for transfer, forgetting, and multi-task construction; demonstrate reusability across initializations and zero-/few-shot initialization.<cite id="b8d06d28-2">Task prompt vectors are defined by soft prompt differences; vector arithmetic supports transfer and multi-tasking</cite><cite id="ad373965-0">Task prompt vectors match multi-task transfer while enabling zero-/few-shot initialization and cross-initialization reuse</cite> 

- Adapter/LoRA-based task vectors and instruction-tuning: Polytropon/Polytropon-S learn task-specific adapters and routing; RE-Adapt isolates instruction-following into an adapter; MergeRepair studies weight-averaging, ties, and Fisher-weighted merging in code LLMs.<cite id="82d5d227-3">Polytropon learns task-specific adapters and aggregates them per task; Polytropon-S uses per-layer skills with deterministic routing</cite><cite id="82d5d227-4">RE-Adapt isolates instruction-tuning into an adapter and discusses arithmetic manipulation and non-orthogonality to new domains</cite><cite id="82d5d227-0">MergeRepair evaluates merging strategies (weight-averaging, ties, Fisher-weighted) and shows sensitivity to merging order and task composition</cite> 

- PEFT decompositions and ensembles: AdaLoRA (SVD-based) and integrations (SparseAdapter, MAM, UniPELT, Compacter); AdapterSoup and LoRaHub for retrieval/merging; EASE and MOS for training-efficient ensemble retrieval and training-free adapter selection.<cite id="48e9c535-4">AdaLoRA uses SVD to decompose weights and prioritize resources; integrations combine PEFT for efficiency</cite><cite id="48e9c535-4">Polytropon-style routing and adapter aggregation; LoRaHub gradient-free merging with few-shot guidance</cite><cite id="48e9c535-0">EASE (2024) ensembles task adapters via subspace process; MOS (2025) retrieves adapters training-free with improved accuracy and latency</cite> 

- Cross-architecture and vision-language settings: Prompt-tuning and CoOp in VLMs optimize prompt vectors and face overfitting; multi-model PT (MaPLe, PromptSRC) extend to visual prompts, highlighting generality of vectorization beyond text-only LMs.<cite id="b8d06d28-4">In VLMs, prompt tuning, CoOp, and LoRA define task-specific prompt vectors; CoOp overfits without regularization; multi-model PT adds visual prompts to both branches</cite> 

# Practical considerations and open directions

Model- and task-specific sensitivity. Merging and retrieval quality depend on the model architecture, task similarity, and merging strategy; different methods (weight-averaging vs. ties vs. Fisher weighting) and orders can yield divergent performance in code LLMs, and results can vary across base models.<cite id="82d5d227-0">Merging order and method (ties, weight-averaging, Fisher-weighted) influence final adapter quality and performance in code LLMs</cite><cite id="82d5d227-2">Across StarCoder2 and Granite, different merging strategies show varying strengths (e.g., ties best for pass@1 on StarCoder2, weight-averaging best for pass@10 and Granite)</cite> 

Generalization and identifiability. While task vectors are often near-orthogonal and separable, interference can arise in related domains or with dense adapters; pruning, sign alignment, and selective arithmetic can mitigate issues but may reduce performance if over-applied.<cite id="48e9c535-1">High orthogonality reduces interference but naive arithmetic can still cause issues; pruning and sign alignment improve stability but excessive sparsification harms performance</cite><cite id="82d5d227-4">Unlike orthogonal task vectors, instruction adapters may not be orthogonal to new domains; controlled adaptation strength mitigates interference</cite> 

Engineering and deployment. Recent engineering surveys emphasize modular, reusable task vectors with routing and ensembles to scale instruction tuning and reduce fine-tuning costs, while new PEFT integrations (SVD, sparse/structured updates) target efficiency and memory constraints.<cite id="48e9c535-4">Foundation model engineering highlights task vectors, arithmetic/merging, and PEFT integrations (SVD, sparse/structured) for efficient multi-task instruction tuning and reuse</cite> 

Open questions include robust, model-agnostic vector arithmetic across architectures, principled retrieval and routing under concept drift, and stronger theoretical guarantees for identifiability and interference under composition and domain shift.<cite id="48e9c535-1">Empirical analyses show differing orthogonality patterns across adapters vs. task vectors and sensitivity of arithmetic to pruning, suggesting open needs for principled composition under domain shifts</cite> 

# Takeaways

- Task vectors offer a parameter-space lens on adaptation, enabling arithmetic mixing, merging, and retrieval to reduce training and improve multi-task performance across LMs and VLMs.<cite id="b8d06d28-2">Task prompt vectors support vector addition for transfer and initialization</cite><cite id="82d5d227-3">Adapters (“skills”) and routing enable instruction-tuning factorization and aggregation</cite> 
- Recent systems operationalize these ideas via SVD/LoRA decompositions, retrieval/ensembles (EASE, AdapterSoup, LoRaHub, MOS), and training-free arithmetic, with evidence of high separability and modularity but sensitivity to merging strategy and domain overlap.<cite id="48e9c535-4">SVD-based AdaLoRA and PEFT integrations expose task vectors for efficient reuse</cite><cite id="48e9c535-0">EASE and MOS demonstrate ensembling and training-free retrieval with speed-accuracy trade-offs</cite><cite id="48e9c535-1">Orthogonality and interference patterns guide arithmetic and pruning strategies</cite> 
- Active research frontiers include robust cross-model vectorization, principled retrieval and routing, and theory for identifiability and interference in multi-task and continual settings.<cite id="48e9c535-1">Practical methods like pruning and sign alignment mitigate interference but highlight open challenges</cite> 
</answer>

Title: Pushing Mixture of Experts to the Limit: Extremely Parameter Efficient MoE for Instruction Tuning
Snippet: In divergence from this, our work centers on instruction-tuning with multiple tasks present during fine-tuning. We underscore the efficacy of this approach by rigorously testing up to 11B parameter text-to-text model Raffel et al. (2020), implementing token routing, and strictly emphasizing evaluation on a set of unseen (held-out) tasks to underscore the potential of instruction tuning. In another work, Ponti et al. (2022) introduced Polytropon, which involves learning adapters (termed as 'skills') specific to each task and employing a task-skills binary matrix to determine the skill set associated with each task. In their method, input examples dictate the selection of adapters. These adapters are then aggregated, and the resultant single adapter is integrated into the overall architecture. Extending upon the Polytropon framework, Caccia et al. (2023) implemented a distinct skill set for every layer in their variant named Polytropon-S. They introduce a deterministic routing function, delve into supplementary inductive biases, show effectiveness up to 3B models, and they don't employ MoE style architecture. Our research presents a departure from these two studies. Specifically, our primary experimental setup employs MoEs that do not require any specific task identifier during fine-tuning by the use of their token routing strategy. In this way, we can evaluate our instruction-tuned MoEs on unseen tasks without any further task-specific few-shot fine-tuning. We showed the scaling property of our MoEs in this setting by fine-tuning models up to 11B parameters.

Title: RE-Adapt: Reverse Engineered Adaptation of Large Language Models
Snippet: Previous works have looked at the ability to arithmetically manipulate models to isolate certain behaviors (Ilharco et al., 2023;Mitchell et al., 2024).Ilharco et al. (2023) constructed task vectors by differencing weights between a pretrained model and several corresponding models each fine-tuned for a particular task.They observed for their models that task vectors are almost orthogonal to each other, preventing interference and allowing combinations of the vectors for negating certain behaviors, improving multi-task performance, or performing well on new tasks via more complicated task analogies (Ilharco et al., 2023).We similarly solve for our reverse engineered adapter with a simple differencing, but using a single LLM fine-tuned for multi-task instruction-following.By effectively isolating instruction-tuning into an adapter, we allow further fine-tuning of pretrained models, maximizing knowledge acquisition before readapting their ability to follow instructions.We introduce an optional step for reducing the rank of our RE-Adapter, lowering memory requirements while maintaining or improving performance in some scenarios.Unlike individual task vectors, our multi-purpose RE-Adapters are not assumed to be orthogonal to new training domains.We introduce a technique for mitigating potential interference in Section 3 by controlling the adaptation strength.

Mitchell et al. ( 2024) developed an alternative approach for isolating pretraining knowledge from fine-tuned behaviors which they call emulated fine-tuning.Instead of differencing model weights, emulated fine-tuning considers the difference in outputs between pretrained and fine-tuned versions of a model.By combining this difference with the output of a larger pretrained model, Mitchell et al. (2024) found that they could benefit from the additional pretraining knowledge while still solving the task of the smaller model.Their technique could be extended to meet our goal but requires the storage and forward pass of multiple models for inference.Our approach isolates knowledge and instruction-following into adapters, merged into a single model at no extra cost.

(2023) constructed task vectors by differencing weights between a pretrained model and several corresponding models each fine-tuned for a particular task.They observed for their models that task vectors are almost orthogonal to each other, preventing interference and allowing combinations of the vectors for negating certain behaviors, improving multi-task performance, or performing well on new tasks via more complicated task analogies (Ilharco et al., 2023).We similarly solve for our reverse engineered adapter with a simple differencing, but using a single LLM fine-tuned for multi-task instruction-following.By effectively isolating instruction-tuning into an adapter, we allow further fine-tuning of pretrained models, maximizing knowledge acquisition before readapting their ability to follow instructions.We introduce an optional step for reducing the rank of our RE-Adapter, lowering memory requirements while maintaining or improving performance in some scenarios.Unlike individual task vectors, our multi-purpose RE-Adapters are not assumed to be orthogonal to new training domains.We introduce a technique for mitigating potential interference in Section 3 by controlling the adaptation strength.

Mitchell et al. ( 2024) developed an alternative approach for isolating pretraining knowledge from fine-tuned behaviors which they call emulated fine-tuning.Instead of differencing model weights, emulated fine-tuning considers the difference in outputs between pretrained and fine-tuned versions of a model.By combining this difference with the output of a larger pretrained model, Mitchell et al. (2024) found that they could benefit from the additional pretraining knowledge while still solving the task of the smaller model.Their technique could be extended to meet our goal but requires the storage and forward pass of multiple models for inference.Our approach isolates knowledge and instruction-following into adapters, merged into a single model at no extra cost.

documents.title: Pushing Mixture of Experts to the Limit: Extremely Parameter Efficient MoE for Instruction Tuning
documents.snippet: In divergence from this, our work centers on instruction-tuning with multiple tasks present during fine-tuning. We underscore the efficacy of this approach by rigorously testing up to 11B parameter text-to-text model Raffel et al. (2020), implementing token routing, and strictly emphasizing evaluation on a set of unseen (held-out) tasks to underscore the potential of instruction tuning. In another work, Ponti et al. (2022) introduced Polytropon, which involves learning adapters (termed as 'skills') specific to each task and employing a task-skills binary matrix to determine the skill set associated with each task. In their method, input examples dictate the selection of adapters. These adapters are then aggregated, and the resultant single adapter is integrated into the overall architecture. Extending upon the Polytropon framework, Caccia et al. (2023) implemented a distinct skill set for every layer in their variant named Polytropon-S. They introduce a deterministic routing function, delve into supplementary inductive biases, show effectiveness up to 3B models, and they don't employ MoE style architecture. Our research presents a departure from these two studies. Specifically, our primary experimental setup employs MoEs that do not require any specific task identifier during fine-tuning by the use of their token routing strategy. In this way, we can evaluate our instruction-tuned MoEs on unseen tasks without any further task-specific few-shot fine-tuning. We showed the scaling property of our MoEs in this setting by fine-tuning models up to 11B parameters.

Title: Task Prompt Vectors: Effective Initialization through Multi-Task Soft-Prompt Transfer
Snippet: the source soft prompt every time the set of source tasks changes. ATTEMPT, while having sufficient task modularity, depends heavily on the quality and number of source soft prompts. While task prompt vectors, in general, are able to match the results of full multi-task soft prompt transfer (SPoT), initialization of prompt tuning using task prompt vector combinations also retains high task modularity, which means that new tasks can be added without the necessity of training, ultimately decreasing computational costs considerably. Task prompt vectors thus have both -modularity and source prompt independence -and also retain sufficient multi-task performance. 

High reusability of the task prompt vectors. In our experiments, we demonstrated multiple important properties of task prompt vectors. At first, we showed (Section 4.2) that task prompts and their corresponding task prompt vectors from different initializations do not necessarily point to the same space and that some vector combinations are more similar than others. Despite that, task prompt vectors created from one initialization and applied to a different initialization maintain their performance for the majority of observed tasks. The implication of this finding means that it is possible to combine different task prompt vectors from different initializations. Furthermore, we showed (Section 4.3) that combinations of task prompt vectors for similar tasks maintain their source single-task performance (Figure 3) and that the combinations of task prompt vectors can be used for initialization of prompt tuning in low resource settings (zero-/few-shot settings) on the set of target tasks (Table 2). 

Based on both of these observations, we can very effectively re-use pre-trained task prompt vectors for different tasks and use them in downstream scenarios (even without a need for any further training). Since task prompt vectors are independent of their initialization, we can also re-use pre-trained task prompt vectors shared by other researchers and practitioners (e.g., on a designated vector hub). 

Identification of source task prompt vectors. High reusability of task prompt vectors, however, requires identifying an appropriate source task prompt vector or a combination of them. To identify such a single vector/a combination of vectors, we propose to perform an evaluation on held-out validation sets. Another possible factor that can be included in the identification of an appropriate combination is the similarity of combined tasks.

Title: Current and future state of evaluation of large language models for medical summarization tasks
Snippet: One method for designing LLMs to perform evaluations is through the use of manually curated prompts (Fig. 4). A prompt consists of the task description and instructions provided to an LLM to guide its responses. Two primary prompting strategies are employed in this context: Zero-Shot and Few-Shot 3 . In Zero-Shot prompting, the LLM is given only the task description without any examples before being asked to perform evaluations. Few-Shot prompting provides the task description alongside a few examples to help guide the LLM in generating output. The number of examples varies based on the LLM's architecture, input window limitations, and the point at which the model performs optimally. Typically, between one and five few-shot examples are used. Prompt engineering, through both Zero-Shot and Few-Shot ("in-context learning") approaches (collectively referred to as "hard prompting"), enables an LLM to perform tasks that it was not explicitly trained to do. However, performance can vary significantly depending on the model's pre-training and its relevance to the new task. 

Beyond these manual approaches, a more adaptive strategy involves "soft prompting," also known as machine-learned prompts, which includes techniques like prompt tuning and p-tuning 42 . Soft prompts are learnable parameters added as virtual tokens to a model's input to signal task-specific instructions. Unlike hard prompts, soft prompts are trained and incorporated into the model's input layer, enabling the model to handle a broader range of specialized tasks. Soft prompting has been shown to outperform Few-Shot prompting, especially in large-scale models, as it fine-tunes the model's behavior without altering the core weights. 

Through these methods, LLMs can be instructed to serve as evaluators with instructions on the dimensions and scale needed for a thorough evaluation. Promising results for such methods have already been seen in general domain applications like LLM-EVAL 43 and TALEC 44 . LLM-EVAL is a single prompt approach to employing LLM-based evaluators that can consist of multiple dimensions. This approach reported correlation coefficients between human evaluators and LLM evaluators to have an average increase of nearly 30 points over ROUGE-L.

Title: LM-BFF-MS: Improving Few-Shot Fine-tuning of Language Models based on Multiple Soft Demonstration Memory
Snippet: Prompt-based few-shot fine-tuning, which finetunes based on few-shot examples under a prompting setting, has been widely studied for moderately sized PLMs such as BERT (Devlin et al., 2019) and RoBERTa (Liu et al., 2019). For example, PET reformulates downstream tasks as a masked language modeling problem and performs gradient-based fine-tuning (Schick and Schütze, 2021a,b). Auto-Prompt creates appropriate prompts for a set of discrete tokens using a gradient-guided search (Shin et al., 2020). Null Prompts-simple concatenations of the inputs and [MASK] token-achieve a free of prompt engineering (Logan et al., 2021). Instead of using hard prompts, there have also been works of using continuous vectors of prompt tokens, called soft prompting4 , including the work of Lester et al. (2021), which proposes soft prompts composed of learnable continuous embeddings while freezing the weight of PLMs; and Gu et al. (2021) proposes pre-training prompts by adding soft prompts into the pre-training stage to obtain a better initialization. The demonstration-aware prompt has also been explored by (Gao et al., 2021) with their proposed LM-BFF, where a demonstration is constructed by unmasking the masked prompt on a similar input example. Unlike LM-BFF, which uses a single demonstration per label, our work uses 'multiple' demonstrations that are provided for automatically generated label phrases. In addition, inspired by the method of soft prompting, we use 'soft' demonstration memory based on globally shared soft vectors for prompt tokens, without using hard tokens of the similar context. 3 Fine-tuning with Multiple Soft Demonstration Memory

Figure 3: Anatomy of an Evaluator Prompt An evaluator prompt consists of three sections: Prompt, Information, and Evaluation. All three components are essential for an LLM serving as an evaluator. The Evaluator Prompt needs to instruct the LLM on the task (Prompt), provide the LLM will all the necessary information to make an evaluation (Information), and all the information that defines the guidelines and formatting of the evaluation (Evaluation). 

Beyond these manual approaches, a more adaptive strategy involves "soft prompting," also known as machine-learned prompts, which includes techniques like prompt tuning and p-tuning [84]. Soft prompts are learnable parameters added as virtual tokens to a model's input to signal task-specific instructions. Unlike hard prompts, soft prompts are trained and incorporated into the model's input layer, enabling the model to handle a broader range of specialized tasks. Soft prompting has been shown to outperform Few-Shot prompting, especially in large-scale models, as it fine-tunes the model's behavior without altering the core weights.

documents.title: LM-BFF-MS: Improving Few-Shot Fine-tuning of Language Models based on Multiple Soft Demonstration Memory
documents.snippet: Prompt-based few-shot fine-tuning, which finetunes based on few-shot examples under a prompting setting, has been widely studied for moderately sized PLMs such as BERT (Devlin et al., 2019) and RoBERTa (Liu et al., 2019). For example, PET reformulates downstream tasks as a masked language modeling problem and performs gradient-based fine-tuning (Schick and Schütze, 2021a,b). Auto-Prompt creates appropriate prompts for a set of discrete tokens using a gradient-guided search (Shin et al., 2020). Null Prompts-simple concatenations of the inputs and [MASK] token-achieve a free of prompt engineering (Logan et al., 2021). Instead of using hard prompts, there have also been works of using continuous vectors of prompt tokens, called soft prompting4 , including the work of Lester et al. (2021), which proposes soft prompts composed of learnable continuous embeddings while freezing the weight of PLMs; and Gu et al. (2021) proposes pre-training prompts by adding soft prompts into the pre-training stage to obtain a better initialization. The demonstration-aware prompt has also been explored by (Gao et al., 2021) with their proposed LM-BFF, where a demonstration is constructed by unmasking the masked prompt on a similar input example. Unlike LM-BFF, which uses a single demonstration per label, our work uses 'multiple' demonstrations that are provided for automatically generated label phrases. In addition, inspired by the method of soft prompting, we use 'soft' demonstration memory based on globally shared soft vectors for prompt tokens, without using hard tokens of the similar context. 3 Fine-tuning with Multiple Soft Demonstration Memory

Snippet: Task vectors exhibit high sparsity and orthogonality, as Ilharco et al. (2023) observed. While the former characteristic can be denoted in language vectors (Figure 9), the latter displays different properties, in contrast to task vectors. In Figure 10, we visualise the cosine similarity between evaluated language vectors of language adapters. Notably, the minimal cosine similarity (0.19) surpasses the maximum (0.18) reported by previous research in the task space (Ilharco et al., 2023). (2023), λ ∈ [0.8, 1.8]), and we set Top-K% to the default value of 20 and additionally to 80.

Title: MergeRepair: An Exploratory Study on Merging Task-Specific Adapters in Code LLMs for Automated Program Repair
Snippet: However, we do not observe any specific pattern on the score of the merged adapters with different number of tasks involved in their merging process. In other words, increasing or decreasing the number of task-specific adapters used to build the merged adapters does not necessarily lead to performance degradation or improvement over the APR benchmark. For example, for the StarCoder2 model, the scores of the T1-T2-T3-T4-T5 adapter is higher than the scores of the T1-T5 adapter for all merging techniques, while having more constituent tasks. Conversely, the scores of the T1-T2 adapter is higher than the scores of T1-T2-T3-T4-T5 adapter in the same model for all the merging techniques. As discussed above, we find that the type of the tasks involved in the merged adapters has a higher affect on the performance of the merged adapter rather than the number of the tasks in the merged adapter. 

When comparing the results of the merging methods in terms of the pass@1 scores (i.e., rowwise), ties method performs better than the other two methods applied on the StarCoder2 model whereas dare-ties and weight-averaging perform better if Granite is used as the base model. Surprisingly, ties performs the worst for the latter model and dare-ties and weight-averaging perform close to each other with weight-averaging being slightly better. For pass@10 , a mixed results is observed for the StarCoder2 model, where weight-averaging and ties have better scores. For the Granite model, almost the same pattern exists for the results of the pass@10 scores. More specifically, weight-averaging performs the best for both models with ties being close to weight-averaging for StarCoder2 and the worst for Granite . 

By analyzing the merged adapters that are trained on StarCoder2 model and merged using two adapters, T1-T3 performs better than others, and after that T1-T2 is the second bestperforming adapter with T1-T4 and T1-T5 coming afterwards. This suggests that T3 helps improve the performance of the APR task while the others either degrade the performance or increase it slightly (T1-T2).

# Overview: Why debiasing click signals matters in Learning to Rank

Click-based signals are central to industrial ranking because they are plentiful and low-cost, but they are systematically biased. Higher rank positions enjoy greater visibility (“position bias”), popular items garner more clicks due to prior exposure (“popularity bias”), and top-k display means most items are never shown (“selection/exposure bias”). These biases distort click feedback, making models overfit to rank position and visibility rather than true relevance, and reinforcing “rich-get-richer” dynamics that degrade user experience and ranking quality if left uncorrected.<cite id="fae9da23-1">Click-based LTR is vulnerable to position bias and popularity bias, and these biases amplify within feedback loops, creating a “rich-get-richer” dilemma.</cite><cite id="b8bfa50c-3">Position bias in IR leads to a “few-get-richer” effect, where top-ranked items attract more traffic than others combined, and popularity-based rankings introduce systematic bias.</cite>

Modern approaches fall into two broad families: (1) generative click models that infer latent relevance from observed clicks via probabilistic inference; and (2) counterfactual/unbiased LTR that directly optimizes a debiased ranking objective using inverse propensity weighting (IPW) or doubly-robust estimators, often with learned propensities. Each class has strengths and assumptions; misspecification or unrealistic assumptions can harm performance, so hybrid designs and robustness checks are important in practice.<cite id="a321e48d-1">Unbiased LTR can be divided into click modeling and counterfactual LTR; the latter uses IPW-style reweighting and listwise/pairwise losses, with methods that jointly estimate propensities and relevance.</cite><cite id="fae9da23-3">Click models estimate true relevance under behavioral assumptions; propensity-based methods use IPW with position randomization; econometrics-based approaches attempt to control confounding, but coupling propensities and rankers raises unbiasedness concerns if either is misspecified.</cite>

# Core biases in click feedback and their impact on LTR

Position bias: Users see only a subset of results and are more likely to click items higher in the list, so observed clicks depend on rank even conditional on relevance. If modeled directly, rankers may learn position patterns rather than relevance, and the feedback loop makes high-ranked items ever more clickable.<cite id="fae9da23-1">Higher positions are more prone to being observed and clicked; training on such data can make rankers estimate position order rather than personalized relevance, motivating unbiased LTR that infers P(Y=1|X,D,x_d=1) instead of P(Y=1|X,D).</cite><cite id="b8bfa50c-0">Position bias assumes examination probability depends on rank; in top-k settings, item-selection bias sets θ_r=0 for r>k, making counterfactual evaluation methods only correct position bias when no item-selection bias is present.</cite>

Popularity bias: More popular items receive more impressions and clicks, independent of their current relevance; repeated queries and exposure histories create “rich-get-richer” effects that bias implicit feedback. This inflates scores for already popular items and depresses tail items, degrading diversity and novelty if unaddressed.<cite id="fae9da23-1">Items with higher popularity are more likely to be posted, observed, and clicked, and these biases amplify in feedback loops, contributing to rich-get-richer dynamics.</cite><cite id="b8bfa50c-3">Popularity-based rankings and position bias create “noise” and systematic ranking bias, with a few items attracting most traffic.</cite>

Selection/exposure bias (top-k display): Only the top k items are shown, so all others receive zero exposure and cannot contribute to training signals. This top-k truncation must be explicitly modeled in evaluation and training; naive counterfactual methods that ignore item-selection bias cannot fully correct position bias in such settings.<cite id="b8bfa50c-0">In top-k ranking, items beyond rank k have zero examination probabilities; distinguishing item-selection from position bias is crucial because standard counterfactual evaluation can only correct position bias absent item-selection bias.</cite><cite id="b8bfa50c-1">Expected CTR must account for both position and item-selection bias, with unknown parameters that need estimation; methods must handle top-k display constraints.</cite>

# Causal/counterfactual framing of unbiased LTR

A counterfactual view treats a click as a counterfactual event conditioned on being shown and examined, with the goal of optimizing the expected utility P(Y=1 | X, D, x_d=1) rather than the biased P(Y=1 | X, D). This reframing motivates inverse propensity scoring (IPS), where each observed click is reweighted by the inverse of the probability it was shown/examined at its position, to approximate an interventional distribution. Key assumptions and pitfalls: The examination hypothesis (users click only if examined) and position/item-selection bias models are central; misspecification can bias estimates. Propensity estimation via randomization can harm user experience and is often impractical at scale, while learned propensities may be misspecified; doubly-robust or hybrid estimators and joint learning can improve stability but still inherit model risks.<cite id="fae9da23-3">Click models rely on assumptions about user behavior; two-tower PBM models can fail when confounding exists; propensity-based methods often rely on result randomization that harms UX; joint learning of propensities and rankers raises unbiasedness concerns if either is misspecified.</cite>

# Methods to debias click data and train unbiased rankers

Inverse Propensity Weighting (IPW) and variants: IPW reweights observed clicks by the inverse of the probability of being shown/examined at a given position. Practical implementations estimate position-dependent propensities and apply IPS at the item level; listwise and pairwise extensions exist. Joint methods estimate propensities and relevance simultaneously, improving robustness to sparse clicks and reducing variance. Online A/B tests at commercial systems show these methods improve retrieval performance and relevance relative to biased training.<cite id="a321e48d-1">Unbiased LTR methods include pointwise and listwise IPS baselines with position-bias estimation and joint position-bias and relevance estimation (DLA, PairD), with released implementations for intervention harvesting.</cite><cite id="fae9da23-2">A novel algorithm jointly estimates biases at click and unclick positions and trains via pairwise loss, significantly outperforming prior algorithms and improving relevance in online A/B testing.</cite><cite id="fae9da23-4">Most ULTR algorithms estimate position bias and use IPW; a pairwise method jointly estimates click and unclick position biases and learns an unbiased ranker with empirical gains and production validation.</cite>

Click models (generative approaches): Probabilistic models like the Position-Based Model (PBM) and cascade models infer latent relevance and bias from clicks under behavioral assumptions via maximum likelihood or EM. These can correct position bias by separating relevance from position in the likelihood, but require repeated queries or large exposure for accurate inference and may fail under confounding or tail sparsity.<cite id="a321e48d-1">PBM assumes users click only if examined and relevant; implementations include RegressionEM and neural two-tower models that incorporate bias features beyond position.</cite><cite id="fae9da23-0">Accurate position-bias estimation is crucial; practical alternatives include CTR-per-position online updates, Bayesian Probit regression, and EM-based estimation, with automatic estimation easing maintenance at scale.</cite><cite id="a321e48d-0">Most click models require large amounts of repeat impressions per query–item pair, limiting applicability to tail queries; generative models can be used for relevance inference but inherit assumption risks.</cite>

Selection bias correction (econometrics-style): Two-stage methods like Heckman’s adapt tools from observational economics to model selection into exposure (which items are shown/examined) and then correct outcome models. Practical position-bias estimation and bandit feedback: In production, position-bias parameters can be fixed or learned online; options include CTR-per-position updates, Bayesian Probit regression, and EM. Bandit feedback and PBM-style pipelines emphasize accurate bias estimation because model updates rely on unbiasedness corrections; automatic estimation reduces maintenance and scales across use cases.<cite id="fae9da23-0">Position-bias parameters can be fixed or estimated; three automatic methods are evaluated: per-position CTR updates, Bayesian Probit regression, and EM; fixed hyperparameters can struggle at scale across many use cases.</cite><cite id="a321e48d-2">Accurate position-bias estimation is crucial for unbiased LTR with bandit feedback; practical estimators include per-position CTR learning, supervised Bayesian Probit, and EM, with automatic estimation preferred for scalability.</cite>

# Popularity bias, exposure bias, and “rich-get-richer” dynamics

Popularity bias inflates clicks for already popular items and depresses novel/tail items, creating imbalance and harming diversity. It interacts with position bias and can dominate when popular items also occupy top ranks. Corrective strategies include exposure-aware ranking and reweighting by historical exposure, as well as repeated-query designs to avoid overfitting to prior popularity. Ranking systems must explicitly model and, where possible, mitigate these dynamics to preserve novelty and fairness in exposure.<cite id="fae9da23-1">Popularity bias causes more likely posting, observation, and clicking for popular items, amplifying feedback loops and contributing to rich-get-richer effects.</cite><cite id="b8bfa50c-3">Position bias and popularity lead to “few-get-richer,” with top items attracting disproportionate traffic; popularity-based rankings introduce systematic bias and noise in the ranking signal.</cite><cite id="b8bfa50c-2">Inter-item dependencies and presentation can bias clicks; exposure and item placement influence examination probabilities, reinforcing popularity and position effects.</cite>

Exposure and top-k constraints: In top-k display, exposure is zero beyond the k-th position; evaluation and training must account for item-selection bias. # Fairness and exposure-aware ranking

Fairness in ranking can be defined probabilistically or by exposure. Bias in implicit feedback and inter-item dependencies can create unequal exposure across groups or items, necessitating exposure-aware objectives that control the distribution of clicks or attention across protected groups while maintaining utility. Title: A Novel Algorithm for Unbiased Learning to Rank
Snippet: Although click data is widely used in search systems in practice, so far the inherent bias, most notably position bias, has prevented it from being used in training of a ranker for search, i.e., learning-to-rank. Recently, a number of authors have proposed new techniques referred to as 'unbiased learning-to-rank', which can reduce position bias and train a relatively high-performance ranker using click data. Most of the algorithms, based on the inverse propensity weighting (IPW) principle, first estimate the click bias at each position, and then train an unbiased ranker with the estimated biases using a learning-to-rank algorithm. However, there has not been a method for pairwise learning-to-rank that can jointly conduct debiasing of click data and training of a ranker using a pairwise loss function. In this paper, we propose a novel algorithm, which can jointly estimate the biases at click positions and the biases at unclick positions, and learn an unbiased ranker. Experiments on benchmark data show that our algorithm can significantly outperform existing algorithms. In addition, an online A/B Testing at a commercial search engine shows that our algorithm can effectively conduct debiasing of click data and enhance relevance ranking.

Title: Correcting for Position Bias in Learning to Rank: A Control Function Approach
Snippet: Learning-to-rank (LTR) systems have become a core component in many online applications, from search engines to recommender systems. These systems typically use implicit feedback data, such as user clicks, as a proxy for user preferences due to its ease of collection compared to costly manual human annotations. While valuable, implicit feedback data is prone to biases [2,61], with position bias being particularly pervasive. Position bias is the tendency of users to interact more with higher-ranked documents, regardless of their true relevance [13,27]. This skews click data, causing LTR models to overestimate higher-ranked documents and underestimate lower ones. Training on such biased data degrades ranking performance and reinforces a feedback loop that negatively affects user experience. This is a preprint version. 

State-of-the-art methods that address position bias can be broadly categorized as click models, propensity-based approaches, and econometrics-based models. Click models [9,13,16,54] estimate true relevance of documents by hypothesizing how users browse and maximizing the likelihood of observed clicks. Click models rely on assumptions about complex user click behavior, which sometimes may not hold in practice. Two-tower models [20,59], following the position-based click model (PBM) [47], attempt to disentangle relevance and bias from clicks by modeling them separately, but may fail when confounding exists between the two. Propensity-based methods treat clicks as counterfactual events and re-weight them using inverse propensity weighting (IPW) to achieve relevance-equivalent training loss [28,55]. Propensity estimation often relies on result randomization [28,41,55], which can harm user experience [2,56]. Some methods [2,24,35,52,63] jointly learn propensities and rankers, but coupling the two raises concerns about the unbiasedness if either model is misspecified [1,18,51].
</snippet>

Title: Correcting for Selection Bias in Learning-to-rank Systems
Snippet: Here, we frame the problem of learning to rank as a counterfactual problem of predicting whether a document would have been clicked had it been observed. In order to recover from selection bias for clicked documents, we focus on identifying the relevant documents that were never shown to users. Our formulation is different from previous counterfactual formulations which correct for position bias and study the likelihood of a document being clicked had it been placed in a higher position given that it was placed in a lower position [29]. 

Here, we propose a general framework for recovering from selection bias that stems from both limited choices given to users and position bias. First, we propose Heckman r ank , an algorithm for addressing selection bias in the context of learning-to-rank systems. By adapting Heckman's two-stage method, an econometric tool for addressing selection bias, we account for the limited choice given to users and the fact that some items are more likely to be shown to a user than others. Because this correction method is very general, it is applicable to any type of selection bias in which the system's decision to show documents can be learned from features. Because Heckman r ank treats selection as a binary variable, we propose two bias-correcting ensembles that account for the nuanced probability of being selected due to position bias and combine Heckman r ank with existing position-bias correction methods. 

Our experimental evaluations demonstrate the utility of our proposed method when compared to state-of-the-art algorithms for unbiased learning-to-rank. Our ensemble methods have better accuracy compared to existing unbiased LTR algorithms under realistic selection bias assumptions, especially when the position bias is not severe. Moreover, Heckman r ank is more robust to noise than both ensemble methods and position-bias correcting methods across difference position bias assumptions. The experiments also show that selection bias affects the performance of LTR systems even in the absence of position bias, and Heckman r ank is able to correct for it.

Title: Unbiased Learning to Rank Meets Reality: Lessons from Baidu's Large-Scale Search Dataset
Snippet: The field of unbiased learning-to-rank can be broadly divided into click modeling and counterfactual learning-to-rank.Click modeling encodes assumptions on user behavior into probabilistic models [12,19,26].Assumed effects, such as position bias or item relevance, are represented as (latent) variables that are jointly inferred via maximum likelihood estimation [18].Notable examples include the position-based model (PBM) [19,46], which assumes that users click only on positions they examine and items they find relevant, and the cascade model [19], which assumes that users scroll from top to bottom, click on the first relevant item, then leave the page.In recent years, more complex and flexible click models have been proposed using neural architectures, semantic embeddings, and bias features beyond position [7,14,58,64].We implement two neural versions of the original PBM: RegressionEM [57] and an additive two-tower model popular in industry applications [28,61,63].

The counterfactual learning-to-rank community has historically employed simpler user models such as the PBM [34,56] or the affine model for trust bias [55] and focused on training more effective ranking models, mitigating biases with inverse propensity scoring [34,41,56].Our work includes an extended binary crossentropy loss [6,49] as a pointwise IPS baseline and an extended softmax loss as a listwise IPS baseline [3,9].Both methods require position bias estimations, for which we release the implementation of three intervention harvesting methods (more in Section 3.2).We also include two counterfactual methods jointly estimating position bias and item relevance, the dual learning algorithm (DLA) [3] and pairwise debiasing (PairD) [31].We introduce all unbiased learning to rank methods used in this work in Section 4.
</snippet>

Title: Learning to Rank in the Position Based Model with Bandit Feedback
Snippet: Accurate estimation of the position bias is crucial for unbiased learning-to-rank from implicit click data. We can provide these parameters either as fixed or use an automatic parameter estimation method. Using fixed hyperparameters in a production environment with many different use-cases and continuously expanding use cases can be quite challenging in terms of maintenance and scaling. To avoid that, we evaluate three automatic estimation methods: i) estimate using the click-through rate (CTR) per position by updating them online after observing each record ii) a supervised learning approach leveraging the Bayesian Probit regression (PR) model and iii) bias estimation using an expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm.

Title: Unbiased Learning-to-Rank with Biased Feedback
Snippet: Implicit feedback (e.g., clicks, dwell times, etc.) is an abundant source of data in human-interactive systems. While implicit feedback has many advantages (e.g., it is inexpensive to collect, user centric, and timely), its inherent biases are a key obstacle to its effective use. For example, position bias in search rankings strongly influences how many clicks a result receives, so that directly using click data as a training signal in Learning-to-Rank (LTR) methods yields sub-optimal results. To overcome this bias problem, we present a counterfactual inference framework that provides the theoretical basis for unbiased LTR via Empirical Risk Minimization despite biased data. Using this framework, we derive a Propensity-Weighted Ranking SVM for discriminative learning from implicit feedback, where click models take the role of the propensity estimator. In contrast to most conventional approaches to de-biasing the data using click models, this allows training of ranking functions even in settings where queries do not repeat. Beyond the theoretical support, we show empirically that the proposed learning method is highly effective in dealing with biases, that it is robust to noise and propensity model misspecification, and that it scales efficiently. We also demonstrate the real-world applicability of our approach on an operational search engine, where it substantially improves retrieval performance.
</snippet>

Title: A Novel Algorithm for Unbiased Learning to Rank
Snippet: Although click data is widely used in search systems in practice, so far the inherent bias, most notably position bias, has prevented it from being used in training of a ranker for search, i.e., learning-to-rank. Recently, a number of authors have proposed new techniques referred to as 'unbiased learning-to-rank', which can reduce position bias and train a relatively high-performance ranker using click data. Most of the algorithms, based on the inverse propensity weighting (IPW) principle, first estimate the click bias at each position, and then train an unbiased ranker with the estimated biases using a learning-to-rank algorithm. However, there has not been a method for pairwise learning-to-rank that can jointly conduct debiasing of click data and training of a ranker using a pairwise loss function. In this paper, we propose a novel algorithm, which can jointly estimate the biases at click positions and the biases at unclick positions, and learn an unbiased ranker. Experiments on benchmark data show that our algorithm can significantly outperform existing algorithms. In addition, an online A/B Testing at a commercial search engine shows that our algorithm can effectively conduct debiasing of click data and enhance relevance ranking.

Title: Understanding and Mitigating the Effect of Outliers in Fair Ranking
Snippet: Bias in implicit feedback. Users' implicit feedback, such as clicks, can be a great source of relevance judgment that has been shown to help improve search quality [2]. clicks may be misleading due to different types of bias, which causes the probability of a click to differ from the probability of relevance. Recent work on discovering and correcting for different types of bias in logged click data concerns position bias [19,20], presentation bias [40], selection bias [29], trust bias [2,35], popularity bias [1], and recency bias [12]. Inter-item dependencies affect the perceived relevance of items [13]. We introduce a phenomenon that is anchored in inter-item dependencies and may result in biased clicks. Our work differs from previously discussed types of bias by considering interitem relationships. Showing items as outliers can make them more attractive to users, influencing their perceived relevance. Presentation bias [40] concerns a related effect; bold keywords in titles make some items appear more attractive. However, this definition of attractiveness is independent of other items in the list. Metrikov et al. [25] show that click-through rates can be manipulated by adding more images to top positions next to the ad slots on the search result page; they did not study the effect on item exposure or biased clicks. We focus on the effect of outliers, as an inter-item dependency on the examination probability and item exposure, and introduce it as a potential source of bias in click data. 

Fair ranking. Following [42], we distinguish two ways of measuring fairness of rankings. Work on probability-based fairness determines the probability that a ranking is the result of a fair process [4,10,11,16,34,39,41]. Exposure-based methods determine the expected exposure for each item in the ranking and aim to ensure that this exposure is fairly distributed [6,14,24,26,[31][32][33]38]. Our work belongs to the second category. To estimate the expected exposure of each item or group, we need to take into account different types of bias that the user might have when observing system outputs. Previous work has mostly focused on position bias [6,32,38].

Title: Scalar is Not Enough: Vectorization-based Unbiased Learning to Rank
Snippet: Debiasing Click Data. Most of the current approaches to debiasing click data for ranking are based on the examination hypothesis. 

They can be divided into two groups. The first is to model user's behavior to infer relevance from biased click signals, known as click models [7,8,15,17,18]. However, most click models focus on predicting clicks, and the relevance inference is an afterthought [4]. 

The second group tries to directly learn unbiased ranking models from biased clicks, known as unbiased learning to rank (ULTR). Based on it, Joachims et al. [26] proposed the inverse propensity scoring (IPS) method to reweigh the click signals based on the reciprocal of observation probabilities (called propensity scores) and provide an unbiased estimate of the ranking objective. The propensity scores are estimated by randomized experiments [26,40], which hurts users' experience, unfortunately. To address it, Agarwal et al. [3] and Fang et al. [16] proposed to do intervention harvest by exploiting click logs with multiple ranking models. Nevertheless, they have a relatively narrow scope of application due to the strict assumption to construct interventional sets [14]. Recently, some researchers proposed to jointly estimate relevance and bias [4,20,22,41]. Similar to them, our proposed method could jointly train the ranking model and observation model without intervention. 

On the other side, researchers developed models to extend the scope of bias factors. The bias factors contain position [4,10,20,41], contextual information [16,37], clicks in the same query list [14,38], presentation style [32,44], search intent [36] and result domain [21]. In our work, we don't limit the exact meaning of bias factors, which makes our model more flexible and generic.
