# Overview: Why debiasing click signals matters in Learning to Rank

Click-based signals are central to industrial ranking because they are plentiful and low-cost, but they are systematically biased. Higher rank positions enjoy greater visibility (“position bias”), popular items garner more clicks due to prior exposure (“popularity bias”), and top-k display means most items are never shown (“selection/exposure bias”). These biases distort click feedback, making models overfit to rank position and visibility rather than true relevance, and reinforcing “rich-get-richer” dynamics that degrade user experience and ranking quality if left uncorrected.<cite id="fae9da23-1">Click-based LTR is vulnerable to position bias and popularity bias, and these biases amplify within feedback loops, creating a “rich-get-richer” dilemma.</cite><cite id="b8bfa50c-3">Position bias in IR leads to a “few-get-richer” effect, where top-ranked items attract more traffic than others combined, and popularity-based rankings introduce systematic bias.</cite>

Modern approaches fall into two broad families: (1) generative click models that infer latent relevance from observed clicks via probabilistic inference; and (2) counterfactual/unbiased LTR that directly optimizes a debiased ranking objective using inverse propensity weighting (IPW) or doubly-robust estimators, often with learned propensities. Each class has strengths and assumptions; misspecification or unrealistic assumptions can harm performance, so hybrid designs and robustness checks are important in practice.<cite id="a321e48d-1">Unbiased LTR can be divided into click modeling and counterfactual LTR; the latter uses IPW-style reweighting and listwise/pairwise losses, with methods that jointly estimate propensities and relevance.</cite><cite id="fae9da23-3">Click models estimate true relevance under behavioral assumptions; propensity-based methods use IPW with position randomization; econometrics-based approaches attempt to control confounding, but coupling propensities and rankers raises unbiasedness concerns if either is misspecified.</cite>

# Core biases in click feedback and their impact on LTR

Position bias: Users see only a subset of results and are more likely to click items higher in the list, so observed clicks depend on rank even conditional on relevance. If modeled directly, rankers may learn position patterns rather than relevance, and the feedback loop makes high-ranked items ever more clickable.<cite id="fae9da23-1">Higher positions are more prone to being observed and clicked; training on such data can make rankers estimate position order rather than personalized relevance, motivating unbiased LTR that infers P(Y=1|X,D,x_d=1) instead of P(Y=1|X,D).</cite><cite id="b8bfa50c-0">Position bias assumes examination probability depends on rank; in top-k settings, item-selection bias sets θ_r=0 for r>k, making counterfactual evaluation methods only correct position bias when no item-selection bias is present.</cite>

Popularity bias: More popular items receive more impressions and clicks, independent of their current relevance; repeated queries and exposure histories create “rich-get-richer” effects that bias implicit feedback. This inflates scores for already popular items and depresses tail items, degrading diversity and novelty if unaddressed.<cite id="fae9da23-1">Items with higher popularity are more likely to be posted, observed, and clicked, and these biases amplify in feedback loops, contributing to rich-get-richer dynamics.</cite><cite id="b8bfa50c-3">Popularity-based rankings and position bias create “noise” and systematic ranking bias, with a few items attracting most traffic.</cite>

Selection/exposure bias (top-k display): Only the top k items are shown, so all others receive zero exposure and cannot contribute to training signals. This top-k truncation must be explicitly modeled in evaluation and training; naive counterfactual methods that ignore item-selection bias cannot fully correct position bias in such settings.<cite id="b8bfa50c-0">In top-k ranking, items beyond rank k have zero examination probabilities; distinguishing item-selection from position bias is crucial because standard counterfactual evaluation can only correct position bias absent item-selection bias.</cite><cite id="b8bfa50c-1">Expected CTR must account for both position and item-selection bias, with unknown parameters that need estimation; methods must handle top-k display constraints.</cite>

Additional biases: Trust bias (affinity to the platform), presentation/style effects, recency, and inter-item dependencies (e.g., outliers) can also shift clicks away from true relevance and must be considered in both data collection and modeling.<cite id="b8bfa50c-2">Click data suffers position bias, presentation bias, selection bias, trust bias, popularity bias, recency bias, and inter-item dependencies; outliers in a list can change examination probabilities and exposure, biasing clicks.</cite>

# Causal/counterfactual framing of unbiased LTR

A counterfactual view treats a click as a counterfactual event conditioned on being shown and examined, with the goal of optimizing the expected utility P(Y=1 | X, D, x_d=1) rather than the biased P(Y=1 | X, D). This reframing motivates inverse propensity scoring (IPS), where each observed click is reweighted by the inverse of the probability it was shown/examined at its position, to approximate an interventional distribution. Propensities can be estimated via randomized interventions, result randomization, or learned models; listwise and pairwise losses can then be used for ranking optimization.<cite id="fae9da23-1">Unbiased LTR reframes training from P(Y=1 | X=D) to P(Y=1 | X=D, x_d=1), estimating relevance from click data by modeling that a user clicks only if observed and perceived as relevant.</cite><cite id="a321e48d-1">Counterfactual LTR employs IPW with position bias estimations, and includes pointwise and listwise IPS losses; some methods jointly estimate propensities and item relevance (e.g., DLA and PairD).</cite><cite id="a321e48d-0">Policy-gradient and counterfactual methods optimize debiased objectives using implicit feedback, noting that naive combinations may not address endogenous unfairness and that click models require repeated impressions for tail queries.</cite>

Key assumptions and pitfalls: The examination hypothesis (users click only if examined) and position/item-selection bias models are central; misspecification can bias estimates. Propensity estimation via randomization can harm user experience and is often impractical at scale, while learned propensities may be misspecified; doubly-robust or hybrid estimators and joint learning can improve stability but still inherit model risks.<cite id="fae9da23-3">Click models rely on assumptions about user behavior; two-tower PBM models can fail when confounding exists; propensity-based methods often rely on result randomization that harms UX; joint learning of propensities and rankers raises unbiasedness concerns if either is misspecified.</cite>

# Methods to debias click data and train unbiased rankers

Inverse Propensity Weighting (IPW) and variants: IPW reweights observed clicks by the inverse of the probability of being shown/examined at a given position. Practical implementations estimate position-dependent propensities and apply IPS at the item level; listwise and pairwise extensions exist. Joint methods estimate propensities and relevance simultaneously, improving robustness to sparse clicks and reducing variance. Online A/B tests at commercial systems show these methods improve retrieval performance and relevance relative to biased training.<cite id="a321e48d-1">Unbiased LTR methods include pointwise and listwise IPS baselines with position-bias estimation and joint position-bias and relevance estimation (DLA, PairD), with released implementations for intervention harvesting.</cite><cite id="fae9da23-2">A novel algorithm jointly estimates biases at click and unclick positions and trains via pairwise loss, significantly outperforming prior algorithms and improving relevance in online A/B testing.</cite><cite id="fae9da23-4">Most ULTR algorithms estimate position bias and use IPW; a pairwise method jointly estimates click and unclick position biases and learns an unbiased ranker with empirical gains and production validation.</cite>

Click models (generative approaches): Probabilistic models like the Position-Based Model (PBM) and cascade models infer latent relevance and bias from clicks under behavioral assumptions via maximum likelihood or EM. These can correct position bias by separating relevance from position in the likelihood, but require repeated queries or large exposure for accurate inference and may fail under confounding or tail sparsity.<cite id="a321e48d-1">PBM assumes users click only if examined and relevant; implementations include RegressionEM and neural two-tower models that incorporate bias features beyond position.</cite><cite id="fae9da23-0">Accurate position-bias estimation is crucial; practical alternatives include CTR-per-position online updates, Bayesian Probit regression, and EM-based estimation, with automatic estimation easing maintenance at scale.</cite><cite id="a321e48d-0">Most click models require large amounts of repeat impressions per query–item pair, limiting applicability to tail queries; generative models can be used for relevance inference but inherit assumption risks.</cite>

Selection bias correction (econometrics-style): Two-stage methods like Heckman’s adapt tools from observational economics to model selection into exposure (which items are shown/examined) and then correct outcome models. In LTR, this yields “Heckman rank” and ensembles that combine selection modeling with position-bias correction, improving robustness under realistic selection bias and being more noise-robust than pure ensembles or position-only corrections.<cite id="fae9da23-4">A general framework adapts Heckman’s two-stage method to address selection bias from both limited user choices and position bias; ensembles combining selection modeling with position-bias correction outperform unbiased LTR baselines under realistic selection bias and are robust to noise; selection bias harms performance even without position bias.</cite>

Practical position-bias estimation and bandit feedback: In production, position-bias parameters can be fixed or learned online; options include CTR-per-position updates, Bayesian Probit regression, and EM. Bandit feedback and PBM-style pipelines emphasize accurate bias estimation because model updates rely on unbiasedness corrections; automatic estimation reduces maintenance and scales across use cases.<cite id="fae9da23-0">Position-bias parameters can be fixed or estimated; three automatic methods are evaluated: per-position CTR updates, Bayesian Probit regression, and EM; fixed hyperparameters can struggle at scale across many use cases.</cite><cite id="a321e48d-2">Accurate position-bias estimation is crucial for unbiased LTR with bandit feedback; practical estimators include per-position CTR learning, supervised Bayesian Probit, and EM, with automatic estimation preferred for scalability.</cite>

# Popularity bias, exposure bias, and “rich-get-richer” dynamics

Popularity bias inflates clicks for already popular items and depresses novel/tail items, creating imbalance and harming diversity. It interacts with position bias and can dominate when popular items also occupy top ranks. Corrective strategies include exposure-aware ranking and reweighting by historical exposure, as well as repeated-query designs to avoid overfitting to prior popularity. Ranking systems must explicitly model and, where possible, mitigate these dynamics to preserve novelty and fairness in exposure.<cite id="fae9da23-1">Popularity bias causes more likely posting, observation, and clicking for popular items, amplifying feedback loops and contributing to rich-get-richer effects.</cite><cite id="b8bfa50c-3">Position bias and popularity lead to “few-get-richer,” with top items attracting disproportionate traffic; popularity-based rankings introduce systematic bias and noise in the ranking signal.</cite><cite id="b8bfa50c-2">Inter-item dependencies and presentation can bias clicks; exposure and item placement influence examination probabilities, reinforcing popularity and position effects.</cite>

Exposure and top-k constraints: In top-k display, exposure is zero beyond the k-th position; evaluation and training must account for item-selection bias. Estimators that separate position and selection components and handle truncated lists are necessary to unbiasedly assess and optimize CTR and relevance.<cite id="b8bfa50c-1">Top-k display induces item-selection bias with θ_r=0 for r>k; expected CTR formulations and estimators must incorporate both position and selection bias under unknown parameters.</cite><cite id="b8bfa50c-0">Distinguishing item-selection from position bias is crucial because standard counterfactual evaluation corrects position bias only when no item-selection bias is present in top-k settings.</cite>

# Fairness and exposure-aware ranking

Fairness in ranking can be defined probabilistically or by exposure. Bias in implicit feedback and inter-item dependencies can create unequal exposure across groups or items, necessitating exposure-aware objectives that control the distribution of clicks or attention across protected groups while maintaining utility. Recent work highlights additional bias sources related to presentation and outliers and emphasizes exposure-based fairness that directly targets expected exposure rather than only pointwise relevance probabilities.<cite id="b8bfa50c-2">Click data exhibits multiple biases (position, presentation, selection, trust, popularity, recency, inter-item dependencies); outliers and presentation can bias clicks via exposure changes.</cite><cite id="b8bfa50c-2">Exposure-based fairness measures and controls expected exposure for items or groups, complementing probability-based fairness; prior work has mostly focused on position bias, motivating broader exposure-aware methods.</cite><cite id="a321e48d-0">Pairwise fairness notions differ from exposure-based criteria; exposure at higher ranks has larger impact, and many LTR works assume unbiased expert labels, whereas real-world implicit feedback is biased and requires debiasing.</cite>

Policy-gradient and fair/unbiased ranking: Recent frameworks combine exposure-based fairness with counterfactual objectives, optimizing policy gradients that account for implicit feedback and position/exposure effects. These approaches can handle settings without repeated queries but still face challenges with endogenous unfairness and require careful evaluation to ensure both performance and exposure equity.<cite id="a321e48d-0">Policy-gradient training of fair and unbiased ranking functions addresses exposure-based fairness while noting limitations of existing counterfactual methods for endogenous unfairness and the impracticality of unbiased expert labels in many settings.</cite>

# Practical pipeline: Estimating propensities, correcting bias, and evaluating clicks

1) Model bias sources and data schema: Identify position, selection/top-k, popularity, trust, presentation, and recency effects in your logs; capture features for rank, query context, item features, and presentation. - Popularity/exposure: Include exposure histories and decay factors as covariates; consider exposure-aware reweighting and control of expected exposure per group to mitigate “few-get-richer” dynamics.<cite id="b8bfa50c-3">Popularity and position bias drive few-get-richer effects; popularity-based rankings introduce systematic bias, motivating exposure controls.</cite><cite id="b8bfa50c-2">Exposure-based fairness requires controlling expected exposure, extending beyond position bias to presentation and inter-item effects.</cite>

3) Train unbiased rankers:
- IPW-based LTR: Use pointwise or listwise pairwise IPS losses with estimated propensities; consider doubly-robust estimators or joint learning of propensities and relevance to reduce variance and misspecification risk; validate with A/B tests where possible.<cite id="a321e48d-1">Pointwise and listwise IPS losses require position bias estimates; joint methods like DLA and PairD estimate propensities and relevance together.</cite><cite id="fae9da23-2">Joint estimation of click and unclick position biases with pairwise training improves performance and has shown online gains in A/B tests.</cite><cite id="a321e48d-0">Propensity estimation via randomized interventions is impractical; learned propensities and intervention harvesting broaden applicability, but misspecification remains a risk.</cite>
- Click models: Use PBM/cascade variants with EM or neural architectures to disentangle relevance and bias; repeat impression pipelines for high-coverage queries and fallback strategies for tail queries; be cautious of confounding and assumption violations.<cite id="a321e48d-1">Neural PBM and bias features beyond position; repeated impressions are often needed for tail queries in click models.</cite><cite id="fae9da23-3">Click models and two-tower PBM can fail under confounding; assumptions must be checked for robustness.</cite>

4) Evaluate unbiasedly and monitor:
- Offline evaluation: Use counterfactual estimators that account for position and selection bias to estimate expected CTR and ranking utilities under unbiased interventional policies; incorporate top-k constraints and examination models in evaluation metrics.<cite id="b8bfa50c-1">Counterfactual evaluation methods correct position bias only when item-selection bias is accounted for; expected CTR must be estimated under unknown position and selection parameters.</cite>
- Online evaluation: Conduct A/B tests to validate that debiased training improves relevance and user outcomes; monitor for distribution shift and re-estimation of propensities over time.<cite id="fae9da23-2">Online A/B testing at a commercial search engine demonstrates effectiveness of joint bias and relevance learning for unbiased ranking.</cite>

# When to prefer each approach and key trade-offs

- Click models vs counterfactual learning: Click models can provide principled relevance inference under behavioral assumptions but require repeated queries and can be confounded; counterfactual learning directly optimizes ranking objectives with reweighting but depends on accurate propensity estimation and can be sensitive to model misspecification. In practice, hybrid pipelines that combine learned propensities with IPW and use click models for tail inference are common.<cite id="a321e48d-1">Click modeling vs counterfactual LTR trade off assumptions and data requirements; counterfactual methods use IPW with position bias and listwise/pairwise losses and include joint estimation techniques.</cite><cite id="fae9da23-3">Click models rely on behavioral assumptions and can fail with confounding; propensity-based methods with randomization harm UX; joint learning raises unbiasedness issues if misspecified.</cite>

- Selection bias handling: Econometric two-stage methods like Heckman rank provide robustness to selection patterns and top-k constraints, often outperforming position-only corrections under realistic selection bias and noise, but they assume a valid selection model and may require additional data sources or modeling complexity.<cite id="fae9da23-4">Heckman rank and ensembles address selection bias and show better accuracy than unbiased LTR baselines under realistic assumptions, with improved robustness to noise.</cite>

- Popularity and exposure fairness: Because position and popularity biases concentrate exposure, exposure-aware ranking and reweighting are necessary for equitable distribution of clicks and attention, especially in recommendation/search advertising where revenue and UX depend on balanced traffic across items and groups.<cite id="b8bfa50c-3">Position and popularity biases lead to concentration of traffic and systematic bias, underscoring the need for exposure-aware controls.</cite><cite id="b8bfa50c-2">Exposure-based fairness methods target expected exposure and must account for inter-item and presentation effects beyond position bias.</cite>

- Diagnose and model the main biases in your logs: position, selection/top-k, popularity, trust, presentation, and recency; separate examination from click in the likelihood and account for top-k exposure.<cite id="fae9da23-1">Position and popularity biases amplify in feedback loops and require unbiased objectives P(Y=1 | X, D, x_d=1).</cite><cite id="b8bfa50c-1">Top-k selection sets exposure to zero beyond k; evaluation must model both position and selection bias.</cite>

These steps enable learning to rank from click signals without letting position, selection, or popularity bias dominate, leading to fairer exposure, better relevance, and improved user experience and business outcomes in production systems.<cite id="fae9da23-2">Online A/B evidence shows unbiased training improves relevance ranking in production environments.</cite><cite id="a321e48d-1">Industrial-scale unbiased LTR methods combine click modeling, counterfactual reweighting, and listwise/pairwise objectives to mitigate position bias and enhance performance.</cite>

Title: A Novel Algorithm for Unbiased Learning to Rank
Snippet: Although click data is widely used in search systems in practice, so far the inherent bias, most notably position bias, has prevented it from being used in training of a ranker for search, i.e., learning-to-rank. Recently, a number of authors have proposed new techniques referred to as 'unbiased learning-to-rank', which can reduce position bias and train a relatively high-performance ranker using click data. Most of the algorithms, based on the inverse propensity weighting (IPW) principle, first estimate the click bias at each position, and then train an unbiased ranker with the estimated biases using a learning-to-rank algorithm. However, there has not been a method for pairwise learning-to-rank that can jointly conduct debiasing of click data and training of a ranker using a pairwise loss function. In this paper, we propose a novel algorithm, which can jointly estimate the biases at click positions and the biases at unclick positions, and learn an unbiased ranker. Experiments on benchmark data show that our algorithm can significantly outperform existing algorithms. In addition, an online A/B Testing at a commercial search engine shows that our algorithm can effectively conduct debiasing of click data and enhance relevance ranking.

Title: Correcting for Position Bias in Learning to Rank: A Control Function Approach
Snippet: Learning-to-rank (LTR) systems have become a core component in many online applications, from search engines to recommender systems. These systems typically use implicit feedback data, such as user clicks, as a proxy for user preferences due to its ease of collection compared to costly manual human annotations. While valuable, implicit feedback data is prone to biases [2,61], with position bias being particularly pervasive. Position bias is the tendency of users to interact more with higher-ranked documents, regardless of their true relevance [13,27]. This skews click data, causing LTR models to overestimate higher-ranked documents and underestimate lower ones. Training on such biased data degrades ranking performance and reinforces a feedback loop that negatively affects user experience. This is a preprint version. 

State-of-the-art methods that address position bias can be broadly categorized as click models, propensity-based approaches, and econometrics-based models. Click models [9,13,16,54] estimate true relevance of documents by hypothesizing how users browse and maximizing the likelihood of observed clicks. Click models rely on assumptions about complex user click behavior, which sometimes may not hold in practice. Two-tower models [20,59], following the position-based click model (PBM) [47], attempt to disentangle relevance and bias from clicks by modeling them separately, but may fail when confounding exists between the two. Propensity-based methods treat clicks as counterfactual events and re-weight them using inverse propensity weighting (IPW) to achieve relevance-equivalent training loss [28,55]. Propensity estimation often relies on result randomization [28,41,55], which can harm user experience [2,56]. Some methods [2,24,35,52,63] jointly learn propensities and rankers, but coupling the two raises concerns about the unbiasedness if either model is misspecified [1,18,51].

Title: Correcting for Selection Bias in Learning-to-rank Systems
Snippet: Here, we frame the problem of learning to rank as a counterfactual problem of predicting whether a document would have been clicked had it been observed. In order to recover from selection bias for clicked documents, we focus on identifying the relevant documents that were never shown to users. Our formulation is different from previous counterfactual formulations which correct for position bias and study the likelihood of a document being clicked had it been placed in a higher position given that it was placed in a lower position [29]. 

Here, we propose a general framework for recovering from selection bias that stems from both limited choices given to users and position bias. First, we propose Heckman r ank , an algorithm for addressing selection bias in the context of learning-to-rank systems. By adapting Heckman's two-stage method, an econometric tool for addressing selection bias, we account for the limited choice given to users and the fact that some items are more likely to be shown to a user than others. Because this correction method is very general, it is applicable to any type of selection bias in which the system's decision to show documents can be learned from features. Because Heckman r ank treats selection as a binary variable, we propose two bias-correcting ensembles that account for the nuanced probability of being selected due to position bias and combine Heckman r ank with existing position-bias correction methods. 

Our experimental evaluations demonstrate the utility of our proposed method when compared to state-of-the-art algorithms for unbiased learning-to-rank. Our ensemble methods have better accuracy compared to existing unbiased LTR algorithms under realistic selection bias assumptions, especially when the position bias is not severe. Moreover, Heckman r ank is more robust to noise than both ensemble methods and position-bias correcting methods across difference position bias assumptions. The experiments also show that selection bias affects the performance of LTR systems even in the absence of position bias, and Heckman r ank is able to correct for it.

Title: Policy-Gradient Training of Fair and Unbiased Ranking Functions
Snippet: s for all items is available during training. This is a weaker assumption than the one made in [8,43], but it still does not apply to real-world settings where implicit feedback is often used for training.

Our work focuses on exposure-based fairness, but another approach to defining fairness in rankings is through pairwise comparisons [7,34], without considering exposure as the key criterion. Such comparisons between items count all swaps in the ranking equally and do not reflect that swapping items at the top has a stronger effect on exposure than doing so at lower positions.

Switching to exogenous sources of unfairness, most work on traditional LTR algorithms [10][11][12]25] assumes that unbiased relevance judgments by experts are available. However, the field of information retrieval has long been conscious of the biases inherent to implicit feedback and its effect on the ability to rank well [16,18,22,25,26]. In particular, various studies have demonstrated the presence of position bias, where the quantity and quality of the feedback depend on the rank at which an item is presented.

One approach to modeling and removing position bias is generative click modeling [9,14,15]. Click models typically treat relevance as latent variables, and perform inference by maximizing log-likelihood of clicks. Title: Unbiased Learning-to-Rank with Biased Feedback
Snippet: Implicit feedback (e.g., clicks, dwell times, etc.) is an abundant source of data in human-interactive systems. While implicit feedback has many advantages (e.g., it is inexpensive to collect, user centric, and timely), its inherent biases are a key obstacle to its effective use. For example, position bias in search rankings strongly influences how many clicks a result receives, so that directly using click data as a training signal in Learning-to-Rank (LTR) methods yields sub-optimal results. To overcome this bias problem, we present a counterfactual inference framework that provides the theoretical basis for unbiased LTR via Empirical Risk Minimization despite biased data. Using this framework, we derive a Propensity-Weighted Ranking SVM for discriminative learning from implicit feedback, where click models take the role of the propensity estimator. In contrast to most conventional approaches to de-biasing the data using click models, this allows training of ranking functions even in settings where queries do not repeat. Beyond the theoretical support, we show empirically that the proposed learning method is highly effective in dealing with biases, that it is robust to noise and propensity model misspecification, and that it scales efficiently. We also demonstrate the real-world applicability of our approach on an operational search engine, where it substantially improves retrieval performance.

Title: A Novel Algorithm for Unbiased Learning to Rank
Snippet: Although click data is widely used in search systems in practice, so far the inherent bias, most notably position bias, has prevented it from being used in training of a ranker for search, i.e., learning-to-rank. Recently, a number of authors have proposed new techniques referred to as 'unbiased learning-to-rank', which can reduce position bias and train a relatively high-performance ranker using click data. Most of the algorithms, based on the inverse propensity weighting (IPW) principle, first estimate the click bias at each position, and then train an unbiased ranker with the estimated biases using a learning-to-rank algorithm. However, there has not been a method for pairwise learning-to-rank that can jointly conduct debiasing of click data and training of a ranker using a pairwise loss function. In this paper, we propose a novel algorithm, which can jointly estimate the biases at click positions and the biases at unclick positions, and learn an unbiased ranker. Experiments on benchmark data show that our algorithm can significantly outperform existing algorithms. In addition, an online A/B Testing at a commercial search engine shows that our algorithm can effectively conduct debiasing of click data and enhance relevance ranking.

Title: Understanding and Mitigating the Effect of Outliers in Fair Ranking
Snippet: Bias in implicit feedback. Users' implicit feedback, such as clicks, can be a great source of relevance judgment that has been shown to help improve search quality [2]. clicks may be misleading due to different types of bias, which causes the probability of a click to differ from the probability of relevance. Recent work on discovering and correcting for different types of bias in logged click data concerns position bias [19,20], presentation bias [40], selection bias [29], trust bias [2,35], popularity bias [1], and recency bias [12]. Inter-item dependencies affect the perceived relevance of items [13]. We introduce a phenomenon that is anchored in inter-item dependencies and may result in biased clicks. Our work differs from previously discussed types of bias by considering interitem relationships. Showing items as outliers can make them more attractive to users, influencing their perceived relevance. Presentation bias [40] concerns a related effect; bold keywords in titles make some items appear more attractive. However, this definition of attractiveness is independent of other items in the list. Metrikov et al. [25] show that click-through rates can be manipulated by adding more images to top positions next to the ad slots on the search result page; they did not study the effect on item exposure or biased clicks. We focus on the effect of outliers, as an inter-item dependency on the examination probability and item exposure, and introduce it as a potential source of bias in click data. 

Fair ranking. Following [42], we distinguish two ways of measuring fairness of rankings. Work on probability-based fairness determines the probability that a ranking is the result of a fair process [4,10,11,16,34,39,41]. Exposure-based methods determine the expected exposure for each item in the ranking and aim to ensure that this exposure is fairly distributed [6,14,24,26,[31][32][33]38]. Our work belongs to the second category. To estimate the expected exposure of each item or group, we need to take into account different types of bias that the user might have when observing system outputs. Previous work has mostly focused on position bias [6,32,38].

Title: Scalar is Not Enough: Vectorization-based Unbiased Learning to Rank
Snippet: Debiasing Click Data. Most of the current approaches to debiasing click data for ranking are based on the examination hypothesis. 

They can be divided into two groups. The first is to model user's behavior to infer relevance from biased click signals, known as click models [7,8,15,17,18]. However, most click models focus on predicting clicks, and the relevance inference is an afterthought [4]. 

The second group tries to directly learn unbiased ranking models from biased clicks, known as unbiased learning to rank (ULTR). Based on it, Joachims et al. [26] proposed the inverse propensity scoring (IPS) method to reweigh the click signals based on the reciprocal of observation probabilities (called propensity scores) and provide an unbiased estimate of the ranking objective. The propensity scores are estimated by randomized experiments [26,40], which hurts users' experience, unfortunately. To address it, Agarwal et al. [3] and Fang et al. [16] proposed to do intervention harvest by exploiting click logs with multiple ranking models. Nevertheless, they have a relatively narrow scope of application due to the strict assumption to construct interventional sets [14]. Recently, some researchers proposed to jointly estimate relevance and bias [4,20,22,41]. Similar to them, our proposed method could jointly train the ranking model and observation model without intervention. 

On the other side, researchers developed models to extend the scope of bias factors. The bias factors contain position [4,10,20,41], contextual information [16,37], clicks in the same query list [14,38], presentation style [32,44], search intent [36] and result domain [21]. In our work, we don't limit the exact meaning of bias factors, which makes our model more flexible and generic.

snippet.text:
Bias in implicit feedback. Users' implicit feedback, such as clicks, can be a great source of relevance judgment that has been shown to help improve search quality [2]. clicks may be misleading due to different types of bias, which causes the probability of a click to differ from the probability of relevance. Recent work on discovering and correcting for different types of bias in logged click data concerns position bias [19,20], presentation bias [40], selection bias [29], trust bias [2,35], popularity bias [1], and recency bias [12]. Inter-item dependencies affect the perceived relevance of items [13]. We introduce a phenomenon that is anchored in inter-item dependencies and may result in biased clicks. Our work differs from previously discussed types of bias by considering interitem relationships. Showing items as outliers can make them more attractive to users, influencing their perceived relevance. Presentation bias [40] concerns a related effect; bold keywords in titles make some items appear more attractive. However, this definition of attractiveness is independent of other items in the list. Metrikov et al. [25] show that click-through rates can be manipulated by adding more images to top positions next to the ad slots on the search result page; they did not study the effect on item exposure or biased clicks. We focus on the effect of outliers, as an inter-item dependency on the examination probability and item exposure, and introduce it as a potential source of bias in click data. 

Fair ranking. Following [42], we distinguish two ways of measuring fairness of rankings. Work on probability-based fairness determines the probability that a ranking is the result of a fair process [4,10,11,16,34,39,41]. Exposure-based methods determine the expected exposure for each item in the ranking and aim to ensure that this exposure is fairly distributed [6,14,24,26,[31][32][33]38]. Our work belongs to the second category. To estimate the expected exposure of each item or group, we need to take into account different types of bias that the user might have when observing system outputs. Previous work has mostly focused on position bias [6,32,38].

snippet.text:
Debiasing Click Data. Most of the current approaches to debiasing click data for ranking are based on the examination hypothesis. 

They can be divided into two groups. The first is to model user's behavior to infer relevance from biased click signals, known as click models [7,8,15,17,18]. However, most click models focus on predicting clicks, and the relevance inference is an afterthought [4]. 

The second group tries to directly learn unbiased ranking models from biased clicks, known as unbiased learning to rank (ULTR). Based on it, Joachims et al. [26] proposed the inverse propensity scoring (IPS) method to reweigh the click signals based on the reciprocal of observation probabilities (called propensity scores) and provide an unbiased estimate of the ranking objective. The propensity scores are estimated by randomized experiments [26,40], which hurts users' experience, unfortunately. To address it, Agarwal et al. [3] and Fang et al. [16] proposed to do intervention harvest by exploiting click logs with multiple ranking models. Nevertheless, they have a relatively narrow scope of application due to the strict assumption to construct interventional sets [14]. Recently, some researchers proposed to jointly estimate relevance and bias [4,20,22,41]. Similar to them, our proposed method could jointly train the ranking model and observation model without intervention. 

On the other side, researchers developed models to extend the scope of bias factors. The bias factors contain position [4,10,20,41], contextual information [16,37], clicks in the same query list [14,38], presentation style [32,44], search intent [36] and result domain [21]. In our work, we don't limit the exact meaning of bias factors, which makes our model more flexible and generic.

problem: papers about the influence of model size on Sentiment analysis tasks
final_response:
# Overview

Model size influences sentiment analysis through its effects on contextual understanding, robustness to noise, and compute/data scaling properties. Larger models often achieve higher accuracy on standard sentiment datasets, but gains can be task- and data-dependent, and come with efficiency and generalization trade-offs. Below, we synthesize evidence from scaling laws, direct ablations on sentiment benchmarks, domain-specific finance sentiment, and multimodal settings, and discuss diminishing returns and deployment considerations.

# Why Model Size Matters for Sentiment

Larger pretraining scales the capacity to learn compositional sentiment signals (e.g., nested modifiers on SST-2) and generalizes across domains like movie reviews and social media. However, the benefit depends on data quality and task structure, and very large models can be more sensitive to noisy training signals in sentiment tasks. <cite id="34412564-2">Kaplan et al. (2020) first observed power-law scaling of autoregressive language model test loss over many orders of magnitude, and subsequent work (e.g., Hoffmann et al., 2022) refined “Chinchilla” scaling that remains a reference for compute–size–quality trade-offs</cite>. <cite id="9fa1d57e-0">On sentiment datasets such as IMDB and SST-2, increasing model size or training resources can improve performance, but performance also depends strongly on data quality when training with noisy labels</cite>.

# General Scaling Laws and Their Implications for Sentiment

Scaling laws provide a theoretical lens on how parameters, training steps, and data volume map to validation loss or accuracy. <cite id="34412564-2">Power-law behavior has been reported for autoregressive language models over wide ranges of model size and training compute, and more recent analyses distinguish optimal scaling in parameters vs. FLOPs</cite>. <cite id="34412564-3">In a sentiment setup that mixes real and surrogate data, the test error at the optimal weighting is monotone decreasing in both the model size and the amount of surrogate data, and a derived scaling law predicts dependence on hyperparameters like the weighting factor</cite>. <cite id="34412564-2">These results align with the broader scaling literature and suggest that, for supervised sentiment tasks, increasing model size (and appropriately scaling training data and compute) tends to reduce error, up to saturation or diminishing returns</cite>.

# Direct Model-Size Ablations on Sentiment Benchmarks

Several studies vary model size and report sentiment performance changes on standard datasets like SST-2 and IMDB. <cite id="34412564-4">In a multimodal sentiment analysis setting, performance gains increase as the size of the large vision-language model (LVLM) grows, indicating that larger backbones yield more pronounced improvements from world-knowledge fusion for sentiment</cite>. <cite id="eff7a1ec-3">Comparisons that swap larger transformers into sentiment tasks (e.g., Longformer over BERT on longer reviews) show that larger models can be fit to sentiment benchmarks with standard fine-tuning regimes and can attain higher accuracy, reflecting improved context modeling for longer documents</cite>. <cite id="eff7a1ec-0">On SST-2 and IMDB, initializing from larger pretrained encoders (e.g., BERT-base/uncased) and fine-tuning yields strong baselines (about 81% on SST-2 and 88% on IMDB under reported setups), illustrating the benefit of scaling the starting point for sentiment classification</cite>.

Beyond pure parameter count, architectural scaling and compute scaling also matter. <cite id="34412564-2">Compute-optimal scaling analyses (Chinchilla) emphasize that both model size and training steps must be scaled together to avoid under- or over-shooting accuracy, which has practical implications for resource-constrained sentiment training</cite>. <cite id="9fa1d57e-4">A probing study across LLaMA-derived models shows that increasing base size from 8B to larger variants improves SST-2 and IMDB accuracy substantially, and that parameter-efficient distilled variants can retain strong sentiment performance while reducing size</cite>.

# Domain-Specific: Finance Sentiment (FinBERT and Beyond)

Finance sentiment inherits domain-specific ambiguity, requiring larger or domain-adapted models to capture complex financial language. <cite id="fd65cfe6-0">FinBERT is a BERT-based model fine-tuned on financial text and designed to classify sentiment (positive/negative/neutral) in financial news and reports, leveraging domain knowledge beyond general web corpora</cite>. <cite id="fd65cfe6-1">On a challenging subset of FOMC minutes (complex sentences), fine-tuning the original FinBERT (base) improved accuracy by 17.4 percentage points to 0.8710, substantially outperforming the base model and underscoring headroom for larger or better-adapted models on complex financial sentiment</cite>. <cite id="fd65cfe6-2">FinBERT’s domain specialization stems from transfer learning on financial corpora, enabling better handling of specialized terminology and sarcasm/nuance common in markets and earnings content</cite>.

Model size and speed trade-offs are salient in finance pipelines. <cite id="fd65cfe6-3">Comparisons show FinBERT can offer better execution speeds than RoBERTa on GPUs and is smaller than RoBERTa, though lexicon-based models can be orders of magnitude smaller than transformer baselines and more interpretable, affecting deployment choices with limited resources</cite>. <cite id="fd65cfe6-4">FinBERT achieves SOTA on Financial PhraseBank and supports multi-class financial sentiment, illustrating how larger, domain-adapted models can lift performance in specialized sentiment tasks</cite>.

# Multimodal and Long-Context Sentiment

Multimodal and long-context settings often exhibit stronger size effects. <cite id="34412564-4">In multimodal sentiment analysis, performance increases with larger LVLMs, and gains from incorporating contextual world knowledge become more pronounced as the model grows</cite>. <cite id="eff7a1ec-3">For long reviews and documents, replacing BERT with Longformer enables modeling longer contexts with larger effective windows, which can improve sentiment classification when dependencies span longer ranges</cite>. <cite id="34412564-3">Scaling analyses that vary both model size and the proportion of real vs. surrogate data show monotonic improvements as model size increases, suggesting that in data-scarce regimes, larger models can better leverage augmented or synthetic sentiment data</cite>.

# Efficiency, Data Sensitivity, and Diminishing Returns

Larger models bring efficiency, generalization, and cost trade-offs. <cite id="34412564-2">Compute-optimal scaling suggests that naively increasing parameters without steps or data can be suboptimal; aligning scaling across parameters, compute, and data is key to avoid diminishing returns on sentiment tasks</cite>. <cite id="9fa1d57e-0">Noise sensitivity analyses show that on sentiment tasks like IMDB and SST-2, larger models can overfit noisy labels unless training regimes or data cleaning are strengthened, indicating that model size amplifies both capacity and vulnerability to data quality</cite>. <cite id="fd65cfe6-3">In production settings, model size affects latency and resource usage; FinBERT’s smaller size and faster inference compared to RoBERTa can be advantageous, while lexicon-based approaches may be orders of magnitude smaller but sacrifice accuracy and interpretability</cite>. <cite id="34412564-4">For methods that augment or fuse external knowledge, the marginal gains from adding model size tend to increase with the base model’s capacity, implying diminishing marginal returns if starting from very small backbones</cite>.

# What the Evidence Shows and What It Doesn’t

- Consistent positive trend: Across general scaling, sentiment-specific experiments, finance, and multimodal settings, increasing model size tends to improve sentiment performance, up to task- and data-specific limits. <cite id="34412564-2">Scaling law work provides a mechanistic basis for this trend</cite>, supported by <cite id="34412564-3">monotonic error reductions with increased sizes in a sentiment setup</cite>, <cite id="eff7a1ec-0">high-baseline results from larger pretrained encoders on SST-2/IMDB</cite>, <cite id="fd65cfe6-1">large absolute gains from fine-tuning larger finance models on challenging text</cite>, and <cite id="34412564-4">stronger gains in multimodal sentiment as LVLM size grows</cite>.
- Task and data dependence: <cite id="9fa1d57e-0">Sentiment performance is highly sensitive to label noise at larger scales, requiring careful data curation or robust training</cite>. <cite id="eff7a1ec-3">Architecture choice (e.g., Longformer vs. BERT) and sequence length interact with model size to determine gains on long documents</cite>. <cite id="eff7a1ec-2">On some sentiment tasks, differences between base and large BERT/RoBERTa variants are not statistically significant, suggesting that for certain datasets scaling parameters alone may yield modest improvements without better data or methods</cite>.
- Efficiency and deployment: <cite id="fd65cfe6-3">Larger models can be faster and smaller than RoBERTa in some finance settings, but general transformer models still outperform lightweight lexicon methods on accuracy</cite>. <cite id="34412564-2">Compute–size–quality trade-offs imply that scaling parameters without steps or data can saturate or degrade returns, especially for fine-grained or noisy sentiment</cite>.

# Representative Papers and Findings (by theme)

- General scaling laws for language modeling:
  - <cite id="34412564-2">Scaling of neural network performance with model size and training steps; Kaplan 2020 power-law behavior and Hoffmann 2022 Chinchilla compute–size–quality scaling</cite>.
  - <cite id="34412564-3">Scaling laws for learning with real and surrogate data show monotonic improvements in a sentiment setup as model size and data proportions vary</cite>.

- Sentiment ablations and architecture swaps:
  - <cite id="eff7a1ec-0">Strong SST-2/IMDB baselines from larger pretrained encoders (BERT/Transformers) under standard fine-tuning</cite>.
  - <cite id="eff7a1ec-3">Replacing BERT with Longformer on longer documents for sentiment tasks</cite>.
  - <cite id="9fa1d57e-4">SENRILLAMA probing across 1B–8B LLaMA-derived models shows increasing base size improves SST-2 and IMDB accuracy; parameter-efficient variants retain competitiveness</cite>.

- Finance sentiment and domain adaptation:
  - <cite id="fd65cfe6-0">FinBERT: BERT-based, financial-domain fine-tuned model for multi-class sentiment on financial text</cite>.
  - <cite id="fd65cfe6-1">FinBERT-FOMC: 17.4% absolute accuracy gain via fine-tuning on complex FOMC-minute sentences</cite>.
  - <cite id="fd65cfe6-4">FinBERT achieves SOTA on Financial PhraseBank, supporting domain-specific scaling benefits</cite>.
  - <cite id="fd65cfe6-3">Runtime and size comparisons: FinBERT smaller than RoBERTa with faster GPU inference; lexicon-based models are orders of magnitude smaller but less accurate</cite>.

- Multimodal and long-context sentiment:
  - <cite id="34412564-4">WisdoM: multimodal sentiment gains increase with larger LVLMs; performance more pronounced at larger scales</cite>.
  - <cite id="eff7a1ec-3">Longformer-based sentiment fine-tuning on long reviews demonstrates context-length benefits with larger architectures</cite>.

- Data sensitivity and compute efficiency:
  - <cite id="9fa1d57e-0">Noise-injective experiments on IMDB/SST-2 show larger models can overfit noisy labels unless training/data are robust</cite>.
  - <cite id="34412564-2">Compute scaling analyses (Chinchilla) inform parameter–FLOPs–data co-ordination to avoid diminishing returns on sentiment</cite>.

# Practical Guidance

- If you need strong zero-shot baselines on movie/IMDB/SST-2, start with larger pretrained encoders (e.g., BERT-large/Transformers) and fine-tune on curated data; expect substantial gains over base models. <cite id="eff7a1ec-0">Larger encoders already achieve mid-80%+ accuracy on IMDB and ~81% on SST-2 under typical setups</cite>.
- For finance/complex text, consider domain-adapted larger models and targeted fine-tuning; headroom can be large on ambiguous financial sentiment. <cite id="fd65cfe6-1">Fine-tuning base FinBERT can yield ~17% absolute accuracy gains on difficult FOMC subsets</cite>.
- Balance size with data quality and compute: scale parameters, data, and steps together; add noise-robust training or data cleaning when using larger models on noisy labels. <cite id="34412564-2">Chinchilla-style scaling ties parameter increases to compute/data to avoid inefficiency</cite>. <cite id="9fa1d57e-0">Larger models amplify both signal and noise in sentiment data</cite>.
- Consider efficiency and interpretability trade-offs; lightweight lexicon methods can be orders of magnitude smaller but typically underperform transformers on nuanced sentiment. <cite id="fd65cfe6-3">Lexicon-based models are ~three orders of magnitude smaller than RoBERTa but lag in accuracy; FinBERT offers a smaller yet faster alternative to RoBERTa in some settings</cite>.

# Open Questions and Suggested Experiments

- Diminishing returns by dataset: Quantify marginal gains of adding parameters on SST-5 vs. SST-2 vs. Twitter and IMDB, including noisy vs. clean splits. <cite id="9fa1d57e-0">Noise sensitivity suggests nontrivial diminishing or harmful effects if not mitigated</cite>.
- Compute-size efficiency frontiers: For a fixed budget, compare parameter scaling vs. data scaling for sentiment; report accuracy–latency–cost surfaces across base, large, and MoE models. <cite id="34412564-2">Chinchilla provides a reference for compute efficiency</cite>.
- Domain-specific scaling: Systematically compare FinBERT-base vs. FinBERT-large vs. DeBERTa/Longformer on FinSent/CAPS and FOMC minutes with ablations on number of layers/attention heads and training steps. <cite id="fd65cfe6-1">There is clear headroom on complex financial text</cite>.
- Multimodal scaling: Measure how much additional parameter count in LVLMs is required to reach saturation on multimodal sentiment across languages. <cite id="34412564-4">Larger LVLMs yield larger gains from world-knowledge fusion</cite>.

In summary, across diverse settings, larger models generally improve sentiment analysis accuracy, especially on complex or long-context text and specialized domains like finance, but the benefits depend critically on data quality, training compute, and deployment constraints, and can exhibit diminishing marginal gains without coordinated scaling and robust training. <cite id="34412564-2">Scaling-law insights and finance/multimodal case studies together explain why model size is a first-order lever for sentiment performance</cite>.

Title: Does equivariance matter at scale?
Snippet: Neural scaling laws The scaling of neural network performance as a function of model size or training steps has been studied extensively (Ahmad & Tesauro, 1988;Hestness et al., 2017;Rosenfeld et al., 2020;Henighan et al., 2020). Kaplan et al. (2020) first observed that the test loss of autoregressive language models follows a power law over many orders of magnitude. Hoffmann et al. (2022) improved the methodology further and found the "Chinchilla" scaling laws, which still serve as a reference point for many language models. In our quantitative analysis of compute scaling, we largely follow their approach. 

Several works have extended scaling laws from model size and training steps to other dimensions: Muennighoff et al. (2023) studied the effect of the training dataset size, which we also discuss, Alabdulmohsin et al. (2023) analyzed scaling of different architecture hyperparameters separately, and Jones (2021) investigated the scaling with problem complexity.
</snippet>

FinBERT was specifically fine-tuned for financial text classification, making it particularly suitable for sentiment analysis of cryptocurrency-related news. Financial texts often contain specialized language and complex expressions that general sentiment models struggle to interpret. FinBERT overcomes this by using transfer learning, enabling it to be fine-tuned on financial data to better understand the context and nuances of financial language. The model's strength lies in its ability to leverage pretrained knowledge from large language corpora and adapt to the financial domain. By further training FinBERT on financial-specific data, the model becomes more effective in handling the unique terminology and sentiment patterns present in financial news and reports. The FinBERT model assigns a sentiment score based on the classification output, where: 

• Positive Sentiment: FinBERT identifies positive news by assigning a positive sentiment label, indicating a favorable outlook. • Neutral Sentiment: For neutral news, FinBERT assigns a neutral sentiment label, representing no strong positive or negative sentiment. • Negative Sentiment: FinBERT assigns a negative sentiment label to news that indicates an unfavorable outlook. FinBERT also incorporates advanced training techniques to ensure it retains the broad language understanding of BERT while adapting to the financial context. This makes it a valuable tool for improving sentiment analysis in the financial domain, where accurate interpretation of sentiment can enhance decision-making and market predictions.

Another important advantage of lexicon-based approaches is their interpretability. Lexicon-based sentiment models are generally more interpretable than transformer-based sentiment models because they rely on a pre-defined set of rules that are easy to understand and interpret. In a lexicon-based sentiment model, each word is assigned a sentiment score based on its associated sentiment value in the sentiment dictionary, and the overall sentiment of the text is calculated based on the sum or average of the sentiment scores of the words in the text. This makes it easy to understand why a particular text was classified as positive, negative, or neutral, as the sentiment scores assigned to each word in the text are transparent and interpretable.

These sentences underwent parsing via the Stanford parser, resulting in an extensive repository of 215,154 unique phrases diligently annotated by three human judges. Each phrase within this dataset bears a label denoting its sentiment, falling within the spectrum of negative, somewhat negative, neutral, somewhat positive, or positive, equating to the highly negative, negative, neutral, positive, and highly positive labels used within our annotations. 

The SST dataset manifests in two distinct versions: SST-5, known as SST fine-grained, employs five labels to characterize sentiment nuances, while SST-2, termed SST binary, simplifies the classification into two primary labels, negative and positive. Within SST-2, negative sentiments encompass judgments labeled as negative or somewhat negative, while positive sentiments entail those marked as somewhat positive or positive. Notably, neutral reviews find no place within SST-2. For the IMDB Movie Review dataset, the top seven models are RoBERTa-large with LlamBERT [24], RoBERTa-large [24], XLNet [25], Heinsen Routing + RoBERTa Large [26], RoBERTa-large 355M + Entailment as Few-shot Learner [27], GraphStar [28], and DV-ngram-cosine with NB sub-sampling + RoBERTa.base [29]. For the SST-2 dataset, the top seven models are T5-11B [30], MT-DNN-SMART [31], T5-3B [30], MUPPET Roberta Large [32], ALBERT [33], Struct-BERT+RoBERTa ensemble [34], and XLNet [25]. We selected these models as baselines on both datasets and included CSR-XLNet for comparison. The results are presented in Tab.4 and Tab.5. 

As can be seen from the tables, CSR-XLNet achieved the best performance on both datasets. The differences between the BERT-based models are not significant, while XL-Net, due to the introduction of the Permutation-Based Training method, has a stronger capability for contextual modeling. In our case, CSR-XLNet incorporates the CSR module, which combines C-XLNet for dynamic semantic extraction and SR-BiLSTM for sentiment classification. This allows it more effectively handle long sequences and complex depen-dencies in text, thereby enhancing its performance. Therefore, we will select CSR-XLNet for the next phase of ablation experiments.

Title: LLaMAs Have Feelings Too: Unveiling Sentiment and Emotion Representations in LLaMA Models Through Probing
Snippet: Table 4 presents a comparative analysis of the accuracy of SENTRILLAMA, DeBERTa, RoBERTa, and a prompt-based method. The best-performing model is highlighted in bold, while the runner-up is underlined. For the sentiment downstream task, SENTRIL-LAMA 8B outperforms all other approaches, achieving approximately 96% accuracy on SST-2, 96% on IMDB, 92% on Rotten Tomatoes, and 87% on the Emotion dataset. Only DeBERTa surpasses this performance on the Emotion dataset, with an accuracy of 88%. The prompt-based approach reveals the effectiveness of few-shot and Chainof-Thought (CoT), achieving comparable results but falling short on the Emotion dataset. These results align with expectations, revealing several insights: (1) increasing the base model size improves performance, (2) the non-instruction version of the 1B model exhibits minimal differences compared to the instructed ones, and (3) DeBERTa and RoBERTa continue to lead the leaderboard in sentiment analysis, outperforming prompt-based methods. However, it is worth noting that the actual size of SENTRILLAMA differs from the original Llama model. We represent the effective sizes in Table 5. Using SENTRILLAMA reduces the size of the models. For the 1B model (both the standard and instruction-finetuned versions) on SST-2, IMDB, and Rotten Tomatoes, approximately 19% of the parameters are removed, while for the Emotion dataset, the reduction is up to 61.6%. For the 3B model on SST-2, IMDB, and Rotten Tomatoes, the reduction is approximately 36.6%, and for the Emotion dataset, it is 80%. For the 8B model on SST-2, IMDB, and Rotten Tomatoes, approximately 53.7% of the parameters are removed, while for the Emotion dataset, the reduction is 90.7%. This result indicates that the amount of parameters removed depends heavily on the specific task and that it is possible to reuse the highly relevant representations of Llama to improve downstream tasks, going beyond prompting and resulting in a competitive model. 

Furthermore, we compare the computational efficiency of SENTRILLAMA with DeBERTa, RoBERTa, and a prompt-based method.

# Overview

Model size influences sentiment analysis through its effects on contextual understanding, robustness to noise, and compute/data scaling properties. Larger models often achieve higher accuracy on standard sentiment datasets, but gains can be task- and data-dependent, and come with efficiency and generalization trade-offs. Below, we synthesize evidence from scaling laws, direct ablations on sentiment benchmarks, domain-specific finance sentiment, and multimodal settings, and discuss diminishing returns and deployment considerations.

# Why Model Size Matters for Sentiment

Larger pretraining scales the capacity to learn compositional sentiment signals (e.g., nested modifiers on SST-2) and generalizes across domains like movie reviews and social media. However, the benefit depends on data quality and task structure, and very large models can be more sensitive to noisy training signals in sentiment tasks. <cite id="34412564-2">Kaplan et al. (2020) first observed power-law scaling of autoregressive language model test loss over many orders of magnitude, and subsequent work (e.g., Hoffmann et al., 2022) refined “Chinchilla” scaling that remains a reference for compute–size–quality trade-offs</cite>. <cite id="9fa1d57e-0">On sentiment datasets such as IMDB and SST-2, increasing model size or training resources can improve performance, but performance also depends strongly on data quality when training with noisy labels</cite>.

# General Scaling Laws and Their Implications for Sentiment

Scaling laws provide a theoretical lens on how parameters, training steps, and data volume map to validation loss or accuracy. <cite id="34412564-2">Power-law behavior has been reported for autoregressive language models over wide ranges of model size and training compute, and more recent analyses distinguish optimal scaling in parameters vs. FLOPs</cite>. <cite id="34412564-3">In a sentiment setup that mixes real and surrogate data, the test error at the optimal weighting is monotone decreasing in both the model size and the amount of surrogate data, and a derived scaling law predicts dependence on hyperparameters like the weighting factor</cite>. <cite id="34412564-2">These results align with the broader scaling literature and suggest that, for supervised sentiment tasks, increasing model size (and appropriately scaling training data and compute) tends to reduce error, up to saturation or diminishing returns</cite>.

# Direct Model-Size Ablations on Sentiment Benchmarks

Several studies vary model size and report sentiment performance changes on standard datasets like SST-2 and IMDB. <cite id="34412564-4">In a multimodal sentiment analysis setting, performance gains increase as the size of the large vision-language model (LVLM) grows, indicating that larger backbones yield more pronounced improvements from world-knowledge fusion for sentiment</cite>. <cite id="eff7a1ec-3">Comparisons that swap larger transformers into sentiment tasks (e.g., Longformer over BERT on longer reviews) show that larger models can be fit to sentiment benchmarks with standard fine-tuning regimes and can attain higher accuracy, reflecting improved context modeling for longer documents</cite>. <cite id="eff7a1ec-0">On SST-2 and IMDB, initializing from larger pretrained encoders (e.g., BERT-base/uncased) and fine-tuning yields strong baselines (about 81% on SST-2 and 88% on IMDB under reported setups), illustrating the benefit of scaling the starting point for sentiment classification</cite>.

Beyond pure parameter count, architectural scaling and compute scaling also matter. <cite id="34412564-2">Compute-optimal scaling analyses (Chinchilla) emphasize that both model size and training steps must be scaled together to avoid under- or over-shooting accuracy, which has practical implications for resource-constrained sentiment training</cite>. <cite id="9fa1d57e-4">A probing study across LLaMA-derived models shows that increasing base size from 8B to larger variants improves SST-2 and IMDB accuracy substantially, and that parameter-efficient distilled variants can retain strong sentiment performance while reducing size</cite>.

# Domain-Specific: Finance Sentiment (FinBERT and Beyond)

Finance sentiment inherits domain-specific ambiguity, requiring larger or domain-adapted models to capture complex financial language. <cite id="fd65cfe6-0">FinBERT is a BERT-based model fine-tuned on financial text and designed to classify sentiment (positive/negative/neutral) in financial news and reports, leveraging domain knowledge beyond general web corpora</cite>. <cite id="fd65cfe6-1">On a challenging subset of FOMC minutes (complex sentences), fine-tuning the original FinBERT (base) improved accuracy by 17.4 percentage points to 0.8710, substantially outperforming the base model and underscoring headroom for larger or better-adapted models on complex financial sentiment</cite>. <cite id="fd65cfe6-2">FinBERT’s domain specialization stems from transfer learning on financial corpora, enabling better handling of specialized terminology and sarcasm/nuance common in markets and earnings content</cite>.

Model size and speed trade-offs are salient in finance pipelines. <cite id="fd65cfe6-3">Comparisons show FinBERT can offer better execution speeds than RoBERTa on GPUs and is smaller than RoBERTa, though lexicon-based models can be orders of magnitude smaller than transformer baselines and more interpretable, affecting deployment choices with limited resources</cite>. <cite id="fd65cfe6-4">FinBERT achieves SOTA on Financial PhraseBank and supports multi-class financial sentiment, illustrating how larger, domain-adapted models can lift performance in specialized sentiment tasks</cite>.

# Multimodal and Long-Context Sentiment

Multimodal and long-context settings often exhibit stronger size effects. <cite id="34412564-4">In multimodal sentiment analysis, performance increases with larger LVLMs, and gains from incorporating contextual world knowledge become more pronounced as the model grows</cite>. <cite id="eff7a1ec-3">For long reviews and documents, replacing BERT with Longformer enables modeling longer contexts with larger effective windows, which can improve sentiment classification when dependencies span longer ranges</cite>. <cite id="34412564-3">Scaling analyses that vary both model size and the proportion of real vs. surrogate data show monotonic improvements as model size increases, suggesting that in data-scarce regimes, larger models can better leverage augmented or synthetic sentiment data</cite>.

# Efficiency, Data Sensitivity, and Diminishing Returns

Larger models bring efficiency, generalization, and cost trade-offs. <cite id="34412564-2">Compute-optimal scaling suggests that naively increasing parameters without steps or data can be suboptimal; aligning scaling across parameters, compute, and data is key to avoid diminishing returns on sentiment tasks</cite>. <cite id="9fa1d57e-0">Noise sensitivity analyses show that on sentiment tasks like IMDB and SST-2, larger models can overfit noisy labels unless training regimes or data cleaning are strengthened, indicating that model size amplifies both capacity and vulnerability to data quality</cite>. <cite id="fd65cfe6-3">In production settings, model size affects latency and resource usage; FinBERT’s smaller size and faster inference compared to RoBERTa can be advantageous, while lexicon-based approaches may be orders of magnitude smaller but sacrifice accuracy and interpretability</cite>. <cite id="34412564-4">For methods that augment or fuse external knowledge, the marginal gains from adding model size tend to increase with the base model’s capacity, implying diminishing marginal returns if starting from very small backbones</cite>.

# What the Evidence Shows and What It Doesn’t

- Consistent positive trend: Across general scaling, sentiment-specific experiments, finance, and multimodal settings, increasing model size tends to improve sentiment performance, up to task- and data-specific limits. <cite id="34412564-2">Scaling law work provides a mechanistic basis for this trend</cite>, supported by <cite id="34412564-3">monotonic error reductions with increased sizes in a sentiment setup</cite>, <cite id="eff7a1ec-0">high-baseline results from larger pretrained encoders on SST-2/IMDB</cite>, <cite id="fd65cfe6-1">large absolute gains from fine-tuning larger finance models on challenging text</cite>, and <cite id="34412564-4">stronger gains in multimodal sentiment as LVLM size grows</cite>.
- Task and data dependence: <cite id="9fa1d57e-0">Sentiment performance is highly sensitive to label noise at larger scales, requiring careful data curation or robust training</cite>. <cite id="eff7a1ec-3">Architecture choice (e.g., Longformer vs. BERT) and sequence length interact with model size to determine gains on long documents</cite>. <cite id="eff7a1ec-2">On some sentiment tasks, differences between base and large BERT/RoBERTa variants are not statistically significant, suggesting that for certain datasets scaling parameters alone may yield modest improvements without better data or methods</cite>.
- Efficiency and deployment: <cite id="fd65cfe6-3">Larger models can be faster and smaller than RoBERTa in some finance settings, but general transformer models still outperform lightweight lexicon methods on accuracy</cite>. <cite id="34412564-2">Compute–size–quality trade-offs imply that scaling parameters without steps or data can saturate or degrade returns, especially for fine-grained or noisy sentiment</cite>.

# Representative Papers and Findings (by theme)

- General scaling laws for language modeling:
  - <cite id="34412564-2">Scaling of neural network performance with model size and training steps; Kaplan 2020 power-law behavior and Hoffmann 2022 Chinchilla compute–size–quality scaling</cite>.
  - <cite id="34412564-3">Scaling laws for learning with real and surrogate data show monotonic improvements in a sentiment setup as model size and data proportions vary</cite>.

- Sentiment ablations and architecture swaps:
  - <cite id="eff7a1ec-0">Strong SST-2/IMDB baselines from larger pretrained encoders (BERT/Transformers) under standard fine-tuning</cite>.
  - <cite id="eff7a1ec-3">Replacing BERT with Longformer on longer documents for sentiment tasks</cite>.
  - <cite id="9fa1d57e-4">SENRILLAMA probing across 1B–8B LLaMA-derived models shows increasing base size improves SST-2 and IMDB accuracy; parameter-efficient variants retain competitiveness</cite>.

- Finance sentiment and domain adaptation:
  - <cite id="fd65cfe6-0">FinBERT: BERT-based, financial-domain fine-tuned model for multi-class sentiment on financial text</cite>.
  - <cite id="fd65cfe6-1">FinBERT-FOMC: 17.4% absolute accuracy gain via fine-tuning on complex FOMC-minute sentences</cite>.
  - <cite id="fd65cfe6-4">FinBERT achieves SOTA on Financial PhraseBank, supporting domain-specific scaling benefits</cite>.
  - <cite id="fd65cfe6-3">Runtime and size comparisons: FinBERT smaller than RoBERTa with faster GPU inference; lexicon-based models are orders of magnitude smaller but less accurate</cite>.

- Multimodal and long-context sentiment:
  - <cite id="34412564-4">WisdoM: multimodal sentiment gains increase with larger LVLMs; performance more pronounced at larger scales</cite>.
  - <cite id="eff7a1ec-3">Longformer-based sentiment fine-tuning on long reviews demonstrates context-length benefits with larger architectures</cite>.

- Data sensitivity and compute efficiency:
  - <cite id="9fa1d57e-0">Noise-injective experiments on IMDB/SST-2 show larger models can overfit noisy labels unless training/data are robust</cite>.
  - <cite id="34412564-2">Compute scaling analyses (Chinchilla) inform parameter–FLOPs–data co-ordination to avoid diminishing returns on sentiment</cite>.

# Practical Guidance

- If you need strong zero-shot baselines on movie/IMDB/SST-2, start with larger pretrained encoders (e.g., BERT-large/Transformers) and fine-tune on curated data; expect substantial gains over base models. <cite id="eff7a1ec-0">Larger encoders already achieve mid-80%+ accuracy on IMDB and ~81% on SST-2 under typical setups</cite>.
- For finance/complex text, consider domain-adapted larger models and targeted fine-tuning; headroom can be large on ambiguous financial sentiment. <cite id="fd65cfe6-1">Fine-tuning base FinBERT can yield ~17% absolute accuracy gains on difficult FOMC subsets</cite>.
- Balance size with data quality and compute: scale parameters, data, and steps together; add noise-robust training or data cleaning when using larger models on noisy labels. <cite id="34412564-2">Chinchilla-style scaling ties parameter increases to compute/data to avoid inefficiency</cite>. <cite id="9fa1d57e-0">Larger models amplify both signal and noise in sentiment data</cite>.
- Consider efficiency and interpretability trade-offs; lightweight lexicon methods can be orders of magnitude smaller but typically underperform transformers on nuanced sentiment. <cite id="fd65cfe6-3">Lexicon-based models are ~three orders of magnitude smaller than RoBERTa but lag in accuracy; FinBERT offers a smaller yet faster alternative to RoBERTa in some settings</cite>.

# Open Questions and Suggested Experiments

- Diminishing returns by dataset: Quantify marginal gains of adding parameters on SST-5 vs. SST-2 vs. Twitter and IMDB, including noisy vs. clean splits. <cite id="9fa1d57e-0">Noise sensitivity suggests nontrivial diminishing or harmful effects if not mitigated</cite>.
- Compute-size efficiency frontiers: For a fixed budget, compare parameter scaling vs. data scaling for sentiment; report accuracy–latency–cost surfaces across base, large, and MoE models. <cite id="34412564-2">Chinchilla provides a reference for compute efficiency</cite>.
- Domain-specific scaling: Systematically compare FinBERT-base vs. FinBERT-large vs. DeBERTa/Longformer on FinSent/CAPS and FOMC minutes with ablations on number of layers/attention heads and training steps. <cite id="fd65cfe6-1">There is clear headroom on complex financial text</cite>.
- Multimodal scaling: Measure how much additional parameter count in LVLMs is required to reach saturation on multimodal sentiment across languages. <cite id="34412564-4">Larger LVLMs yield larger gains from world-knowledge fusion</cite>.

In summary, across diverse settings, larger models generally improve sentiment analysis accuracy, especially on complex or long-context text and specialized domains like finance, but the benefits depend critically on data quality, training compute, and deployment constraints, and can exhibit diminishing marginal gains without coordinated scaling and robust training. <cite id="34412564-2">Scaling-law insights and finance/multimodal case studies together explain why model size is a first-order lever for sentiment performance</cite>.
</answer>

Title: Sentiment Gradient - Improving Sentiment Analysis with Entropy Increase
Snippet: In this study, we wanted to define the best sizing of the gradient scale. In order to do this, we varied the algorithm of sentiment series construction from 1 (maximum compacting) to 50 (max number of sentences in the set). Also, we marked as -1 the traditional sentiment analysis. 

That given, we constructed a function of repeated k fold experiment sequence to test which would be the best sequencing size. The repetition is executed 10 times each for a kfold of 5 for each sequencing size then compared to know which sizing gave the best metric output for a set of algorithms used in literature. The used metric to evaluate the ideal sizing was the F1-Measure Micro. 

Sent. Sampling: [1,50] Sent. Sampling: [1,25] Sent. Sampling: [26, The chosen algorithms for this experiment were the KNN, Logistic Regression, Gaussian Naive Bayes, Decision Tree, and Random Forest. Each algorithm was configured with its best parameters through hyperparameter tuning tests, given the following configurations for each: Dec.Tree -max depth = 15, criterion=Entropy GNB -var smoothing = 0.8 KNN -k = 5 LNR -solver = sag, penalty = l2 R.For. -max depth = 10, n estimators = 300, criterion = Gini First, we ran the experiment for the entire dataset. However, we noticed that the model's metrics were affected by the number of sentence paddings chosen. So, we decided to organize our experiment in three scenarios: all (i.e., for all registries), less than 25 (i.e., a dataset with registries that had less than 25 sentences per text), and more than 25 and less than 50 (i.e., registries whose text had sentences in between that interval). 

After this experiment, we have obtained the results shown in Table 5. There is a benefit in using the approach rather than the traditional sentiment analysis, but the method is sensitive to the sentiment gradient sizing, i.e., we obtain different values for max compacting (1) or other expansions of the formula. 

We also analyzed the precision, recall, and accuracy of the best-performing algorithm (Table 6).
