Title: LLaVA-UHD v2: an MLLM Integrating High-Resolution Semantic Pyramid via Hierarchical Window Transformer
Snippet: Vision transformers (ViTs) are widely employed in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) for visual encoding. However, they exhibit inferior performance on tasks regarding fine-grained visual perception. We attribute this to the limitations of ViTs in capturing diverse multi-modal visual levels, such as low-level details. To address this issue, we present LLaVA-UHD v2, an MLLM with advanced perception abilities by introducing a well-designed vision-language projector, the Hierarchical window (Hiwin) transformer. Hiwin transformer enhances MLLM's ability to capture diverse multi-modal visual granularities, by incorporating our constructed high-resolution semantic pyramid. Specifically, Hiwin transformer comprises two key modules: (i) a visual detail injection module, which progressively injects low-level visual details into high-level language-aligned semantics features, thereby forming an inverse semantic pyramid (ISP), and (ii) a hierarchical window attention module, which leverages cross-scale windows to condense multi-level semantics from the ISP. Extensive experiments show that LLaVA-UHD v2 outperforms compared MLLMs on a wide range of benchmarks. Notably, our design achieves an average boost of 3.7% across 14 benchmarks compared with the baseline method, 9.3% on DocVQA for instance. All the data and code will be publicly available to facilitate future research.

Title: InternLM-XComposer2-4KHD: A Pioneering Large Vision-Language Model Handling Resolutions from 336 Pixels to 4K HD
Snippet: In this work, we introduce InternLM-XComposer2-4KHD, a pioneering model that for the first time expands the resolution capabilities of Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) to 4K HD and even higher, thereby setting a new standard in high-resolution vision-language understanding.Designed to handle a broad range of resolutions, InternLM-XComposer2-4KHD supports images with any aspect ratio from 336 pixels up to 4K HD, facilitating its deployment in real-world contexts.

InternLM-XComposer2-4KHD follows patch division [46,50] paradigm and enhances it by incorporating an innovative extension: dynamic resolution with automatic patch configuration.To be specific, scaling the resolution of Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) to 4K HD and even higher standard is far beyond merely increasing the number of patches.It involves a nuanced approach to overcoming specific challenges: (1) Dynamic Resolution and Automatic Patch Configuration: Addressing the scarcity of high-resolution training data, our framework introduces a strategy that dynamically adjusts resolution alongside an automatic layout configuration.During training, it maintains the original aspect ratios of images while adaptively altering patch (336 × 336) layouts and counts.This results in a training resolution that exceeds the original image resolutions, reaching up to 4KHD, addressing the shortfall of high-resolution data.(2) Handling Variability in Patch Configurations: Despite the apparent simplicity of dynamic resolution training, the variability in patch configurations can heavily confuse LVLMs.To mitigate this, we introduce a newline token after each row of patch tokens to clearly delineate patch layouts, reducing training ambiguity and significantly boosting performance.(3) Inference Beyond 4K Resolution: Our observations reveal that, even when trained on images up to 4K resolution, the model can achieve additional performance improvements during inference by processing images at higher resolutions.

Furthermore, scaling the training resolution up to 4K standard results in a consistent improvement in performance, highlighting the potential for training even beyond 4K resolution.This underscores the capacity for further enhancing model capabilities and suggests a promising trajectory for advancing the frontiers of high-resolution image processing within the domain of large vision-language models.

documents.title: InternLM-XComposer2-4KHD: A Pioneering Large Vision-Language Model Handling Resolutions from 336 Pixels to 4K HD
documents.snippet: The Large Vision-Language Model (LVLM) field has seen significant advancements, yet its progression has been hindered by challenges in comprehending fine-grained visual content due to limited resolution. Recent efforts have aimed to enhance the high-resolution understanding capabilities of LVLMs, yet they remain capped at approximately 1500 x 1500 pixels and constrained to a relatively narrow resolution range. This paper represents InternLM-XComposer2-4KHD, a groundbreaking exploration into elevating LVLM resolution capabilities up to 4K HD (3840 x 1600) and beyond. Concurrently, considering the ultra-high resolution may not be necessary in all scenarios, it supports a wide range of diverse resolutions from 336 pixels to 4K standard, significantly broadening its scope of applicability. Specifically, this research advances the patch division paradigm by introducing a novel extension: dynamic resolution with automatic patch configuration. It maintains the training image aspect ratios while automatically varying patch counts and configuring layouts based on a pre-trained Vision Transformer (ViT) (336 x 336), leading to dynamic training resolution from 336 pixels to 4K standard. Our research demonstrates that scaling training resolution up to 4K HD leads to consistent performance enhancements without hitting the ceiling of potential improvements. InternLM-XComposer2-4KHD shows superb capability that matches or even surpasses GPT-4V and Gemini Pro in 10 of the 16 benchmarks. The InternLM-XComposer2-4KHD model series with 7B parameters are publicly available at https://github.com/InternLM/InternLM-XComposer.

documents.snippet:
In recent years, the progress in Large Language Models (LLMs) [10,21,29,39,73,78,[91][92][93] has provoked the development of Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs).These models have demonstrated proficiency in tasks such as image captioning [14,17] and visual-question-answering (VQA) [31,33,57,107].Nevertheless, due to their limited resolution, they struggle with processing images containing fine details, such as charts [68], tables [87], documents [70], and infographics [69].This limitation constrains their prac-tical applicability in real-world scenarios.

Recent advancements have aimed at enhancing the resolution of Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs).Some approaches [36,48,66,97] involve adapting highresolution vision encoders directly.However, the Vision Transformer (ViT) architecture falls short when dealing with images of varying resolutions and aspect ratios, thereby restricting its ability to handle diverse inputs effectively.Alternatively, some methods [37,46,50,51,55,59,99] maintain the vision encoder's resolution, segmenting high-resolution images into multiple low-resolution patches.Yet, these methods are constrained by an inadequate resolution, typically around 1500 × 1500, which does not satisfy the demands of daily content, e.g., website screenshots [85], document pages [70], and blueprints [69].Furthermore, they are confined to either a few predefined high-resolution settings [36,46,48,50,51,55,59,66,97] or a limited range of resolutions [37,99], thereby restricting their utility across a variety of applications.

In this work, we introduce InternLM-XComposer2-4KHD, a pioneering model that for the first time expands the resolution capabilities of Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) to 4K HD and even higher, thereby setting a new standard in high-resolution vision-language understanding.

documents.title: LLaVA-UHD v2: an MLLM Integrating High-Resolution Semantic Pyramid via Hierarchical Window Transformer
documents.snippet: Vision transformers (ViTs) are widely employed in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) for visual encoding. However, they exhibit inferior performance on tasks regarding fine-grained visual perception. We attribute this to the limitations of ViTs in capturing diverse multi-modal visual levels, such as low-level details. To address this issue, we present LLaVA-UHD v2, an MLLM with advanced perception abilities by introducing a well-designed vision-language projector, the Hierarchical window (Hiwin) transformer. Hiwin transformer enhances MLLM's ability to capture diverse multi-modal visual granularities, by incorporating our constructed high-resolution semantic pyramid. Specifically, Hiwin transformer comprises two key modules: (i) a visual detail injection module, which progressively injects low-level visual details into high-level language-aligned semantics features, thereby forming an inverse semantic pyramid (ISP), and (ii) a hierarchical window attention module, which leverages cross-scale windows to condense multi-level semantics from the ISP. Extensive experiments show that LLaVA-UHD v2 outperforms compared MLLMs on a wide range of benchmarks. Notably, our design achieves an average boost of 3.7% across 14 benchmarks compared with the baseline method, 9.3% on DocVQA for instance. All the data and code will be publicly available to facilitate future research.

Title: SmartTrim: Adaptive Tokens and Attention Pruning for Efficient Vision-Language Models
Snippet: The Transformer-based vision-language model (VLM) has emerged as a dominant architecture for various vision-language tasks (Radford et al., 2021;Kim et al., 2021;Li et al., 2021;Bao et al., 2022;Wang et al., 2022b;Yu et al., 2022;Zeng et al., 2022;Xu et al., 2023;Li et al., 2023). Although they achieve satisfactory performance, the extensive amount of parameters inflicts an extravagant computational burden, impeding their scalability and application in the production environment. 4 The resolution of input images is 288 2 .

Title: Degenerate Swin to Win: Plain Window-based Transformer without Sophisticated Operations
Snippet: Recently, the triumph achieved by Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) in natural language processing, some works attempt to deploy Transformer in computer vision applications and built Vision Transformers (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021;Touvron et al., 2021a;Han et al.). Compared with convolutional neural networks (Krizhevsky et al., 2012;He et al., 2016), a Vision Transformer has a larger receptive field, effectively capturing the long-range relations between pixels. Meanwhile, different from convolution layer processing images by a static convolution kernel, the self-attention operations in Vision Transformer are dynamic, which effectively model the relations in the image adaptively. Nevertheless, the powerful representing capacity of the self-attention operations in Vision Transformers is accompanied by the potential efficiency issue. To be specific, the computational complexity of a self-attention operation is proportional to the square of the number of tokens. Thus, only a limited number of tokens can be allowed in the self-attention operation to achieve satisfactory efficiency. The pioneering works, ViT (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021) and DeiT (Touvron et al., 2021a), considering the efficiency, have to partition an image into a low-resolution feature map consisting of only 16 × 16 patches/tokens. Nevertheless, the coarsely partitioned low-resolution feature map limits Vision Transformers' capability in visual understanding, especially for dense prediction tasks such as segmentation. 

For effective dense prediction and acceptable efficiency, Pyramid Vision Transformer (PVT) (Wang et al., 2021), Pooling-based Vision Transformer (PiT) (Heo et al., 2021) and Hierarchical Visual Transformer (HVT) (Pan et al., 2021) design a high-resolution feature map in the initial layer and reduces the resolution in deep layers with a progressive shrinking pyramid structure. In parallel to the pyramid structure, window-based local attention is another widely used manner for improving efficiency. Swin Transformer (Liu et al., 2021) crops an image into non-overlapping windows, and the self-attention is exploited within each window.

Title: Vision-RWKV: Efficient and Scalable Visual Perception with RWKV-Like Architectures
Snippet: Transformers have revolutionized computer vision and natural language processing, but their high computational complexity limits their application in high-resolution image processing and long-context analysis. This paper introduces Vision-RWKV (VRWKV), a model adapted from the RWKV model used in the NLP field with necessary modifications for vision tasks. Similar to the Vision Transformer (ViT), our model is designed to efficiently handle sparse inputs and demonstrate robust global processing capabilities, while also scaling up effectively, accommodating both large-scale parameters and extensive datasets. Its distinctive advantage lies in its reduced spatial aggregation complexity, which renders it exceptionally adept at processing high-resolution images seamlessly, eliminating the necessity for windowing operations. Our evaluations demonstrate that VRWKV surpasses ViT's performance in image classification and has significantly faster speeds and lower memory usage processing high-resolution inputs. In dense prediction tasks, it outperforms window-based models, maintaining comparable speeds. These results highlight VRWKV's potential as a more efficient alternative for visual perception tasks. Code is released at https://github.com/OpenGVLab/Vision-RWKV.

Title: SwinCheX: Multi-label classification on chest X-ray images with transformers
Snippet: ViT showed promising performance, but there are still some challenges regarding transferring the exceptional performance of transformers in the language domain to the computer vision. These challenges can be demonstrated by the existing distinction between these two modalities. Unlike the tokens that work as essential language processing components, different visual elements can vary significantly in scale, a crucial problem in some vision tasks such as object detection. In previous transformerbased models, we have seen that the tokens are all of a fixed size, a property that is problematic for these vision tasks. Another critical difference between language and vision is the high resolution of pixels in images. Numerous computer vision tasks such as semantic segmentation need a pixel-level dense prediction. The computational complexity in existing transformer models is quadratic in the image size, and hence it is impossible to use them in such architectural forms. Swin transformers were proposed to deal with the mentioned challenges, and operate as a general-purpose backbone for various vision tasks 17 .

Title: Discrete Cosine Transform Based Decorrelated Attention for Vision Transformers
Snippet: Transformer architectures have merged as a dominant standard for natural language processing (NLP) tasks [1], [15]. Vision Transformer (ViT) [16] built a bridge between language and vision. It shows that pure transformers can also be applied directly to sequences of image patches for classification tasks. In other words, it partitions images into patches and treats them as word sequences. Then, a shifted windowing scheme was proposed in Swin Transformer [17] to obtain greater efficiency. This limits self-attention computation to non-overlapping local windows while allowing for crosswindow connection. Later, to overcome the limitations of the heavyweights in ViTs, MobileViT [18] combined the strengths of MobileNets [19] and ViTs. It is a lightweight and lowlatency network for mobile vision tasks. Moreover, gSwin [20] combined MLP-based architecture with Swin Transformer and attains superior accuracy with a smaller model size. Vision transformers are now supreme in various computer vision tasks such as super resolution [21], [22], compressive sensing [23], [24], image segmentation [25]- [27], and human mesh reconstruction [28].

Title: How far are we to GPT-4V? Closing the gap to commercial multimodal models with open-source suites
Snippet: As illustrated in Figure 3, InternVL 1.5 employs an architecture akin to widely-used open-source MLLMs, specifically the "ViT-MLP-LLM" configuration referenced in various existing studies [18, 23, 62-64, 71, 142].Our implementation of this architecture integrates a pre-trained InternViT-6B [18] with a pre-trained InternLM2-20B [11] using a randomly initialized MLP projector.

During training, we implemented a dynamic resolution strategy, dividing images into tiles of 448×448 pixels in sizes ranging from 1 to 12, based on the aspect ratio and resolution of the input images.During testing, this can be zero-shot scaled up to 40 tiles (i.e., 4K resolution).To enhance scalability for high resolution, we simply employed a pixel shuffle operation to reduce the number of visual tokens to one-quarter of the original.Therefore, in our model, a 448×448 image is represented by 256 visual tokens.

Title: Expanding Performance Boundaries of Open-Source Multimodal Models with Model, Data, and Test-Time Scaling
Snippet: As shown in Figure 2 and Table 2, InternVL 2.5 retains the same model architecture as its predecessors, InternVL 1.5 [35] and InternVL 2.0, following the "ViT-MLP-LLM" paradigm widely adopted in various MLLM studies [150,151,36,316,162,246,124,256]. 

In this new version, our implementation of this architecture integrates a newly incrementally pre-trained InternViT-6B or InternViT-300M with various pre-trained LLMs of different sizes and types, including InternLM 2.5 [19] and Qwen 2.5 [229], using a randomly initialized 2-layer MLP projector. As in the previous version, to enhance scalability for high-resolution processing, we simply applied a pixel unshuffle operation, reducing the number of visual tokens to one-quarter of the original. Consequently, in our model, a 448×448 image tile is represented by 256 visual tokens. 

In terms of input data preprocessing, we adopted a similar dynamic resolution strategy as InternVL 1.5, dividing images into tiles of 448×448 pixels based on the aspect ratio and resolution of the input images. The key difference, starting from InternVL 2.0, is that we additionally introduced support for multi-image and video data, as shown in Figure 2(b). Different data types correspond to different preprocessing configurations, which we will detail in Section 3.1.

Title: High-resolution Iterative Feedback Network for Camouflaged Object Detection
Snippet: Currently, many of the vision transformers are GPU memory exhaustive and our HR features will further exaggerate the problem. To alleviate this issue, we choose the Pyramid Vision Transformer (PVT) (Wang et al. 2021b) as our feature extraction module, which can extract multi-scale features, and handle relatively higher resolution feature maps with less memory costs by its progressive shrinking strategy and spatial reduction attention mechanism. Multi-scale Feature Extraction. PVT consists of four stages, and each stage includes a patch embedding and an encoder structure. The input features to each stage (F i ) are first divided into patches with size of P i . After that, these features are fed into Transformer encoder structure to get the output features X i for the i-th. Then, we get the multiscale features (X 1 , X 2 , X 3 , X 4 ) with (512,320,128,64) number of channels and with ( 1 32 , 1 16 , 1 8 , 1 4 ) resolution of input images for further processing.

Title: UniViTAR: Unified Vision Transformer with Native Resolution
Snippet: In the era of rapid advancements of multimodal large models, Vision Transformer (ViT) [25], characterized by its simplicity and scalability, has emerged as a foundational architecture for visual representation learning. Drawing inspiration from transformer-based large language models, conventional ViT usually uniformly converts raw visual data into square aspect ratio and standardized resolution to reduce modeling complexity and simplify the training workflow. While this paradigm simplifies feature extraction and aligns with existing engineering practices, it inherently imposes artificial constraints on real-world visual data by disregarding the inherent variability of natural images. Real-world visual content exists across diverse resolutions and aspect ratios, with native shape often preserving finer spatial details and contextual information. 

Recent studies have early explored the vision backbone under the native resolution paradigm. FlexViT [6] introduces a flexible ViT architecture featuring dynamical patch size selection in the patch embedding layer, which facilitates smooth variation of token sequence length through parametric scaling. In contrast, NaViT [22] maintains fixed patch size while directly processing native resolution images with varying aspect ratios, where the token sequence length of different images changes dynamically. This approach demonstrates the feasibility and benefits of adopting natural language processing style packing strategies for vision foundational model. Qwen-VL's [2,86] vision encoder inherits NaViT's core configuration while specifically investigating native resolution impacts from a multimodal large model perspective. While the aforementioned approaches have attracted initial research attention, the field still lacks a comprehensive series of architecture-homologous vision backbones that can simultaneously support native-and fixed-resolution processing, achieve high-fidelity feature extraction for both images and videos. 

To address this gap, we present the Unified Vision Transformer with NAtive Resolution, termed as UniViTAR, a family of vision foundational backbones designed to uniformly process visual modalities (image or video) with native resolution and dynamic aspect ratio. Building upon insights from large language model recent practices and architectural innovations in visual transformers, our approach firstly conduct systematic architectural upgrades to the vanilla ViT paradigm by integrating multiple advanced components: 2D Rotary Position Embedding, SwiGLU activation function, RMSNorm layer, QK-Norm mechanism, and LayerScale module.

Title: Sparrow: Data-Efficient Video-LLM with Text-to-Image Augmentation
Snippet: During our exploration, we mainly utilize two image-LLMs, including Mini-InternVL-Chat-4B-V1.5 [12] (termed as InternVL hereafter), MiniCPM-Llama3-8B-V2.5 [1] (termed as MiniCPM-8B hereafter). These instruction-tuned models are trained with massive image data and equipped with strong foundational capabilities. To support higherresolution vision input, these models adopt the patchifying technique [44][45][46] with a dynamic resolution scheme, where an image can be cropped into multiple sub-images according to different aspect ratios. Specifically, InternVL supports up to 13 sub-images, each of which is converted into 256 visual tokens; MiniCPM-8B slices images into a maximum of 10 patches, where each is represented by 96 visual tokens. 

During training and evaluation, we switch off the patchifying option for higher efficiency.

snippet.text:
As shown in Figure 2 and Table 2, InternVL 2.5 retains the same model architecture as its predecessors, InternVL 1.5 [35] and InternVL 2.0, following the "ViT-MLP-LLM" paradigm widely adopted in various MLLM studies [150,151,36,316,162,246,124,256]. 

In this new version, our implementation of this architecture integrates a newly incrementally pre-trained InternViT-6B or InternViT-300M with various pre-trained LLMs of different sizes and types, including InternLM 2.5 [19] and Qwen 2.5 [229], using a randomly initialized 2-layer MLP projector. As in the previous version, to enhance scalability for high-resolution processing, we simply applied a pixel unshuffle operation, reducing the number of visual tokens to one-quarter of the original. Consequently, in our model, a 448×448 image tile is represented by 256 visual tokens. 

In terms of input data preprocessing, we adopted a similar dynamic resolution strategy as InternVL 1.5, dividing images into tiles of 448×448 pixels based on the aspect ratio and resolution of the input images. The key difference, starting from InternVL 2.0, is that we additionally introduced support for multi-image and video data, as shown in Figure 2(b). Different data types correspond to different preprocessing configurations, which we will detail in Section 3.1.

problem: I need a literature review that examines the intersection of blockchain technology and social networks, focusing on decentralized social protocols, multilayer network structures, and fraud detection mechanisms. We analyze the evolution of blockchain applications beyond decentralized finance, particularly in social networking contexts, and evaluate current approaches to crypto fraud detection using deep neural networks (DNN).
final_response:
# Overview and Scope

Blockchain’s influence in social networking extends far beyond financial applications, with research and practice exploring decentralized governance, tokenized incentives, identity, content moderation, and cross-chain interoperation in social platforms.<cite id="3bf4f583-0,3bf4f583-2">Surveys of blockchain-enabled social media highlight applications in smart contract-based content moderation, user incentives via token economics, DAO-based governance, identity and tokenization, and cross-chain connections, while also noting open issues such as scalability and regulatory compliance</cite>.<cite id="3bf4f583-4">These works argue that existing literature has under-explored blockchain’s role in secure communication, privacy protection, decentralized decision-making, and content management within social media, motivating systematic reviews of implementations and challenges</cite>.<cite id="3bf4f583-3">At the same time, socio-technical analyses caution that decentralization in practice can embed new forms of power and governance concentration, and that decentralized social media protocols vary in how they operationalize “decentralization,” affecting user agency and safety</cite>.

# Decentralized Social Protocols: Concepts, Mechanisms, and Case Studies

Decentralized social protocols leverage smart contracts, token economics, and on-chain reputation to reconfigure who governs, moderates, and benefits in social platforms.<cite id="7129febb-0">Taxonomies of blockchain-enabled social media enumerate social tokens and cryptoeconomics, decentralized social networks, content moderation, peer-to-peer social platforms, and NFT-based content ecosystems, along with constraints and contributions of representative systems</cite>.<cite id="7129febb-1">DAOs exemplify this shift by encoding organizational rules on-chain, enabling self-governance but also facing unresolved security, privacy, and legal status challenges; smart contracts can manage identities, roles, and reputation scores to support governance and moderation</cite>.<cite id="7129febb-2">Tokenized incentive mechanisms can align user behavior (e.g., content creation and curation) with economic rewards, offering potential new business models while raising concerns about scalability and content management</cite>.

Several concrete platforms illustrate these ideas. Steemit (2016) rewards users with tokens for content generation and curation, demonstrating token-follow dynamics and content monetization at scale.<cite id="7129febb-4">Following Steemit, Minds and Mirror adopted similar models for content creation and monetization, while newer Web3 social apps like Friend.tech and Farcaster integrate token incentives and decentralized social graphs</cite>.<cite id="7129febb-4">Farcaster, built on Ethereum, minimizes on-chain operations for performance while relying on smart contracts and a P2P hub architecture to maintain security and consistency off-chain</cite>.<cite id="3bf4f583-3">Community-driven dApps can use tokens to incentivize truth-seeking (e.g., crowdsourced credibility scoring), and projects like Solid and the Content Blockchain Project emphasize user-controlled data, privacy, and standards (e.g., ISCC) for media distribution</cite>.<cite id="7129febb-1">At the same time, reputation systems can be encoded in DLTs to register, update, and revoke publisher identities and reputation scores, aiding content provenance and moderation</cite>.

# Multilayer Network Structures: On-Chain/Off-Chain, Messaging, and Interoperability

Blockchain and social systems increasingly adopt multilayer architectures that separate computation, storage, and communication, while also integrating social graphs, reputation, and cross-chain connectivity.<cite id="f2fc7924-1">A canonical blockchain stack comprises control, consensus, data, and network layers; applications invoke smart contracts to trigger transactions, with on-chain and off-chain processing models at the control layer and diverse consensus mechanisms in public vs. private networks</cite>.<cite id="f2fc7924-2">Off-chain techniques such as state channels (e.g., Bitcoin’s Lightning Network) create long-lived, private channels for many transactions, contacting the main chain only at channel opening/closure or dispute, which offloads workloads, improves resource efficiency, and scales throughput</cite>.<cite id="f2fc7924-2">Interoperability layers (side-chains, cross-chains, child-chains) aim to link multiple blockchains, originally to enable low-risk experiments and later to support general applications, with designs that allow complex smart contracts and promising performance and security properties</cite>.

In social platforms, hybrid on-/off-chain designs become necessary for scalability and usability. Existing blockchain social networks employ off-chain storage for bulk social data (profiles, posts, comments) while keeping access control, authentication, and verification logic on-chain via smart contracts.<cite id="f2fc7924-3">Examples include systems that store user footprints off-chain to assess trust for offline interactions, privacy-first platforms like Minds and Farcaster that minimize on-chain operations, and content-sharing apps (e.g., APPICS) that use token-based rewards and transparent feeds</cite>.<cite id="f2fc7924-4">A representative architecture comprises three layers—an off-chain storage layer (cloud or IPFS), an application layer for user interfaces and real-time features, and a blockchain layer hosting smart contracts for identity, verification, and access control—explicitly designed to manage scalability while preserving integrity</cite>.<cite id="f2fc7924-0">Modeling blockchain social networks as multilayer graphs G = (V(c), E), where nodes have tokens and reputation, and edges reflect social relationships and dissemination decisions, shows how economic incentives and reputation influence information spread and trust in decentralized social graphs</cite>.

# Fraud and Abuse in Decentralized Social Ecosystems

Decentralized social and financial ecosystems are vulnerable to manipulation and abuse, including pump-and-dump schemes, wash trading, Sybil/bot activity, money laundering, and NFT marketplace fraud. Research is emerging to detect these using data-driven methods tailored to blockchain’s graph- and time-series-rich data.

## Pump-and-Dump, Market Manipulation, and DeFi Fraud

Deep neural networks have shown promise for detecting rapid, coordinated price manipulation in crypto markets. Empirical work demonstrates that sequence-based neural models outperform classical machine learning for pump-and-dump detection in cryptocurrencies, addressing the domain’s volatility and the lack of labeled data in prior studies.<cite id="e8a79d38-0">A study introducing two neural network architectures for pump-and-dump detection reports significant performance gains over statistical and classical ML baselines in crypto, highlighting the suitability of deep learning for time-varying market signals</cite>.<cite id="e8a79d38-1">A DeFi fraud detection survey finds that temporal transaction data and sequence models (e.g., RNNs/Transformers) are increasingly adopted as the ecosystem evolves, and that graph-based methods (node/graph embeddings and GNNs) are widely used when sufficient data exist, including heterogeneous graphs that incorporate wallets and smart contracts</cite>.<cite id="e8a79d38-1">However, rapid market changes and high transaction volumes complicate subgraph selection and scalability, indicating a need for efficient, scalable graph processing tailored to dynamic DeFi environments</cite>.

## Ethereum-Specific DL Approaches and GNN Limitations

Ethereum has become a focal point for fraud detection research due to rich on-chain traces and diverse attack surfaces (phishing, Ponzi schemes, ICO scams, money laundering, bot arbitrage).<cite id="e8a79d38-3">A pre-trained Transformer model (BERT4ETH) targets multiple Ethereum fraud tasks, motivated by limitations of purely graph-based methods: they may discard sequential information in transactions, struggle with noise on highly skewed account degree distributions, and optimize for single tasks rather than shared representations</cite>.<cite id="e8a79d38-3">BERT4ETH integrates Transformer sequential modeling with BERT pretraining to support diverse fraud detection tasks with minimal task-specific adaptation, addressing de-anonymization and behavior characterization beyond static graphs</cite>.

## Broader Financial Fraud Detection Trends

Broader reviews of deep learning for fraud detection show sustained growth in sequence models (notably LSTM), steady adoption of MLP/CNN, and rising use of NLP (e.g., BERT) for text-based fraud, with specialized methods like GNNs and GANs gaining traction in blockchain and related domains.<cite id="e8a79d38-2">A systematic review reports that LSTM, MLP, CNN, and RNN dominate, with BERT used for text, and that GNNs/GANs are increasingly applied to specialized fraud problems such as those on blockchains, aided by techniques for handling imbalanced datasets and generating synthetic data</cite>.

## NFT Marketplaces and Cross-Media Fraud

Fraud in NFT ecosystems includes wash trading, pump-and-dump campaigns, and marketplace scams. ML-based anomaly detection is being applied to transactional and collection-level signals to flag suspicious activity.<cite id="e8a79d38-4">A survey on AI for blockchain security notes NFT-specific fraud detection using time-series classification to label collections as whitelisted or blacklisted, with K-means and multiple CNNs evaluated on marketplace transaction data from OpenSea and AtomicHub</cite>.<cite id="e8a79d38-4">Empirical comparisons in adjacent blockchain fraud detection show classical classifiers like AdaBoost, SVM, and Random Forest can achieve high accuracies (around 97%) for transaction fraud, while integrated ML+blockchain systems have been tested against double-spending and Sybil attacks with robust performance</cite>.

# Comparative Analysis: DNN-Based Detection Approaches

- Temporal/Sequence Models: RNNs/LSTMs/Transformers capture temporal dependencies in trades, order books, and on-chain event sequences, improving detection of coordinated manipulation and temporal fraud patterns in DeFi and markets.<cite id="e8a79d38-0">Deep neural detectors outperform classical ML for pump-and-dump detection in crypto, indicating sensitivity to temporal dynamics</cite>.<cite id="e8a79d38-1">Surveys emphasize the rising use of sequence models in DeFi due to evolving temporal fraud patterns and high-volume, time-series data</cite>.
- Graph Neural Networks: GNNs exploit transaction and interaction graphs for wallet/smart contract clustering, anomaly detection, and reputation propagation; heterogeneous GNNs incorporate diverse nodes (accounts, contracts, events).<cite id="e8a79d38-1">Graph-based methods are widely used for DeFi fraud when data is abundant</cite>.<cite id="e8a79d38-3">However, pure graph representations can lose sequential information and face noise on skewed Ethereum account-degree distributions, motivating hybrid designs</cite>.
- Pretraining and Transfer: Pretrained language-style models (e.g., BERT4ETH) provide shared representations across multiple fraud tasks and can better model sequential behavior and de-anonymization features than task-agnostic GNNs.<cite id="e8a79d38-3">BERT4ETH combines Transformer sequential modeling with BERT-style pretraining to generalize across Ethereum fraud tasks</cite>.
- NFT and Cross-Media Detection: Time-series CNNs and clustering detect NFT collection-level manipulation; broader blockchain fraud detection uses classical and deep models to counter double-spending and Sybil attacks, indicating complementary toolkits across media (transactions, collections, contracts).<cite id="e8a79d38-4">NFT fraud detection leverages transactional time-series with CNNs and clustering to identify wash trading and pump-and-dump at the collection level</cite>.<cite id="e8a79d38-4">Classical classifiers and integrated ML+blockchain pipelines show strong results against double-spending and Sybil threats</cite>.

# Architectural and Governance Trade-offs

Decentralized social protocols face trade-offs between openness, scalability, and safety. Tokenized systems can motivate participation and monetization but may also incentivize manipulation if governance and reputation are poorly designed.<cite id="7129febb-3">Tokenized monetization can sustain contributions, yet the field remains early and questions remain about long-term viability</cite>.<cite id="3bf4f583-3">Governance and power distribution vary across protocols (e.g., Mastodon instances, Bluesky), with recurring concerns about re-concentration of power and policy heterogeneity</cite>.<cite id="3bf4f583-0">Scalability and regulatory compliance are persistent challenges for blockchain-enabled social media, affecting content moderation, privacy, and institutional acceptance</cite>.

Multilayer architectures help, but introduce complexity and new failure modes. Off-chain storage and state channels improve scalability and reduce on-chain load, yet require careful trust boundary management and conflict resolution; interoperability layers expand functionality but increase operational and security surface area.<cite id="f2fc7924-2">State channels and off-chain designs offload most workloads and improve application-layer efficiency by contacting the chain only on channel lifecycle events or disputes</cite>.<cite id="f2fc7924-4">Hybrid architectures with distinct off-chain storage, application, and blockchain layers aim to scale social content while keeping verification and access control on-chain, but must optimize storage and notifications to avoid single points of failure</cite>.

# Open Challenges and Future Directions

- Cross-Chain and Interoperable Fraud Detection: Most DNN-based detection targets single chains with rich labels; scalable cross-chain methods for identity, wallet linkage, and graph unification remain underexplored, especially for smaller DeFi components and NFTs.<cite id="e8a79d38-1">Surveys note limited detection techniques for components beyond major chains and call for scalable graph processing to handle dynamic, complex transaction graphs</cite>.
- Data Imbalance, Concept Drift, and Labeling: Fraud patterns evolve quickly; imbalanced datasets and scarce ground truth hinder model training and transfer, suggesting needs for synthetic data (GANs), continual learning, and federated detection across networks.<cite id="e8a79d38-2">Systematic reviews highlight imbalanced data and growing use of GANs/VAEs to generate synthetic fraud samples</cite>.<cite id="e8a79d38-1">Temporal evolution and high transaction volumes complicate method selection and subgraph extraction in DeFi</cite>.
- Privacy-Preserving and On-Chain-Off-Chain Integration: Combining encrypted identifiers, zero-knowledge proofs, and hybrid architectures while retaining effective detection is challenging; research is needed on privacy-preserving features, cross-layer reputation, and auditability without sacrificing user sovereignty.<cite id="f2fc7924-4">Hybrid storage and smart contract-based access control balance usability and integrity, but notification systems and storage choices affect scalability and trust</cite>.
- Governance and Social Ecosystem Health: Empirical, longitudinal studies of decentralized social protocols’ governance and safety are scarce; socio-technical frameworks are needed to measure re-concentration of power, moderation efficacy, and user agency across protocol heterogeneity.<cite id="3bf4f583-3">Analyses emphasize that protocol politics and governance challenges vary, and that understanding these differences is crucial to avoid overgeneralization about user behavior</cite>.

# Conclusion

Title: Seeing the Politics of Decentralized Social Media Protocols
Snippet: The landscape of social media has been dominated by centralized platforms that control the flow of information, user data, and governance structures [26,42,72]. These platforms-such as Facebook, Instagram, and X (formerly Twitter)-have collectively shaped digital experiences for billions of people, but have also raised concerns about privacy, power imbalances, and algorithmic biases [15,30,31,68,73]. In response, new decentralized social media protocols have surged in popularity [18,52,79]. These protocols aim to disseminate power to users, reduce reliance on centralized entities, and empower a rich ecosystem of interoperable social media services [38,58,71]. 

As decentralized social media protocols gain traction, researchers have turned their attention to understanding the user experience in these emerging ecosystems: tracking user behavior following moments of mass migration [18,47,52,79] and identifying potential privacy or safety concerns [25,61]. Underpinning this work is whether decentralized social media protocols can fulfill their promise of user agency and control [32]. Prior studies have examined the policies and agreements formed by user communities on decentralized social media platforms like mastodon.social and Bluesky [40,77,98], as well as documented governance challenges faced by users in administrative roles [4,46,103], with recurring concerns around re-concentration of power [49,88] at key points of decision-making [55]. Crucially, the protocols-which define rules governing the exchange of data across communication channels-undergirding decentralized social media serve as the foundation for practices in these systems. They can vary in ways that reflect protocol developers' goals and values, operationalizing and envisioning "decentralization" in distinct ways. As such, concerns about power in decentralized social media must also be examined in relation to the politics embedded in each protocol. In the absence of such context, researchers risk overgeneralizing user behavior and misattributing the sources and significance of key challenges in decentralized social media. Despite this, there has been a relative lack of scholarly attention to protocols themselves. 

We aim to offer a lens through which social computing scholars and developers can see the politics of decentralized social media protocols.
</snippet>

Title: A Survey on Network Optimization Techniques for Blockchain Systems
Snippet: This section briefly introduces blockchain technology, its architecture and discusses the layers it comprises. The section then discusses blockchain's P2P structure and the gossip dissemination protocol. 

Blockchain is a peer-to-peer distributed ledger that stores transactions in a chain of blocks. It was initially developed as the technology powering the Bitcoin cryptocurrency [53]. It aims to remove the need for a trusted third party who will validate transactions [57,58]. Therefore, transactions are timestamped and verified by all participating nodes and then added as a block in the main chain using cryptographic tools. As shown in Figure 3, the blockchain architecture consists of the control, consensus, data and network layers. 

1. Control Layer: The control layer serves as an interface between applications and the ledger. These applications include finance, data storage, voting, securing IoT, logistics and supply chain tracking [10,51]. They interact with the ledger by invoking smart contracts to trigger transactions. Smart contracts are programmable scripts that interact with the ledger by reading or writing data to the ledger when invoked. 

On-chain and off-chain are the primary processing models at the control layer. 2. Consensus Layer: The algorithms blockchain peers use to agree on the validity of blocks and transactions exists at the consensus layer. Peers in public blockchains use Proof of X (X => Work, Stake and many more) algorithms to reach a consensus [53]. All peers in public blockchains are eligible to participate in the consensus process. However, in private blockchains, validating blocks and transactions are performed mainly by different peers with specific roles. In Hyperledger Fabric (HLF), these roles include orderers, endorsers, validators and leaders [31]. New transactions are first sent to peers who can endorse transactions by executing smart contracts. After endorsement, the transaction is sent to the leader node and maintains a connection to the ordering nodes. Next, ordering nodes add the transactions to a block and send them back to the leader node to be broadcasted in the network. Finally, every peer will have to validate the block before committing it to its local ledger.
</snippet>

Title: Effective scaling of blockchain beyond consensus innovations and Moore's law
Snippet: Offloading workloads. Off-chain is a classic technique which enhances network concurrency by constructing channels [69]. In traditional on-chain topologies, myriad transaction confirmations concentrate on the blockchain network with limited capacity. Off-chain networks, in contrast, build independent and long-lived channels over which an arbitrary amount of transactions can be processed locally between individuals. The blockchain is contacted only when peers initialize and close channels, or the involved parties encounter conflicts, in which case the preset contracts will handle fair settlement. This topology therefore effectively offloads the vast majority of blockchain network's workloads, accommodating more channels and peers. Simultaneously, both sides of channels are free of synchronizing network-wide message or participating in consensus, so the resource efficiency and performance at the application layer are significantly improved. Viewed from blockchain network, however, the resource efficiency keeps unchanged because of no architecture innovations.

The well-known Bitcoin Lightning network [70] and duplex micropayment channel [71] first explored off-chain to overcome the scalability bottleneck. Furthermore, Dziembowski et al. [72] presented the concept of virtual payment channel, which introduced smart contracts to bypass undependable intermediaries when processing cross-channel payments. In order to support general applications rather than cryptocurrencies, they further polished their proposal by building channels recursively and successfully constructed the state channel allowing arbitrarily complex smart contracts to execute [73]. All these designs achieved promising performance and a potential far higher than consensus-based scaling. Moreover, the security of off-chain technology has been elaborated in detail [74], [75]. Title: BERT4ETH: A Pre-trained Transformer for Ethereum Fraud Detection
Snippet: As a decentralized computing platform, Ethereum empowers its developers to create a variety of decentralized applications (DApps). Despite the substantial engagement garnered within the cryptocurrency sphere, Ethereum has also become a hub for a wide range of fraudulent activities, such as phishing scams [31], pump-and-dump schemes [15], Ponzi schemes [6], ICO scams [3], money laundering [30], and bot arbitrage [9], etc. 

Many recent studies [2,4,[20][21][22]31] employ graph representation learning techniques for fraud detection on Ethereum. Although it is intuitive to represent the interactions between accounts as a graph, it is argued that they have the following limitations: 

(i) Graph is not appropriate for capturing the sequential pattern inherent in transactions. Ethereum transactions are high repetitive, indicating the presence of multi-edges between nodes. Current graph-learning methods [24,25,31] integrate multi-edges to a single edge to facilitate graph computations. However, the discarded sequential information is essential for characterizing user behaviors for tasks such as de-anonymization. 

(ii) Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), especially on the highly skew-distributed Ethereum data [19], can suffer from noise when the number of convolution hops increases [14], given that Ethereum accounts are often connected to highly popular accounts. However, limiting the number of convolution hops can restrict the capabilities of GNNs, as the number of hops is typically equivalent to the depth of layers in conventional GNNs [11,17,20,29]. 

(iii) Existing studies primarily target on individual fraud detection tasks in an end-to-end training manner. In light of the successes of Transformer pre-training techniques in NLP [10,28], we believe that a pre-trained Transformer can support various fraud detection tasks with minimal adaptations needed. 

To address the limitations discussed above, we introduce a pretrained model that offers a universal solution for various fraud detection tasks on Ethereum. BERT4ETH features the superior sequential modeling capability of Transformer [28] and the pretraining paradigm of BERT [10].
</snippet>

# Overview and Scope

Blockchain’s influence in social networking extends far beyond financial applications, with research and practice exploring decentralized governance, tokenized incentives, identity, content moderation, and cross-chain interoperation in social platforms.<cite id="3bf4f583-0,3bf4f583-2">Surveys of blockchain-enabled social media highlight applications in smart contract-based content moderation, user incentives via token economics, DAO-based governance, identity and tokenization, and cross-chain connections, while also noting open issues such as scalability and regulatory compliance</cite>.<cite id="3bf4f583-4">These works argue that existing literature has under-explored blockchain’s role in secure communication, privacy protection, decentralized decision-making, and content management within social media, motivating systematic reviews of implementations and challenges</cite>.<cite id="3bf4f583-3">At the same time, socio-technical analyses caution that decentralization in practice can embed new forms of power and governance concentration, and that decentralized social media protocols vary in how they operationalize “decentralization,” affecting user agency and safety</cite>.

# Decentralized Social Protocols: Concepts, Mechanisms, and Case Studies

Decentralized social protocols leverage smart contracts, token economics, and on-chain reputation to reconfigure who governs, moderates, and benefits in social platforms.<cite id="7129febb-0">Taxonomies of blockchain-enabled social media enumerate social tokens and cryptoeconomics, decentralized social networks, content moderation, peer-to-peer social platforms, and NFT-based content ecosystems, along with constraints and contributions of representative systems</cite>.<cite id="7129febb-1">DAOs exemplify this shift by encoding organizational rules on-chain, enabling self-governance but also facing unresolved security, privacy, and legal status challenges; smart contracts can manage identities, roles, and reputation scores to support governance and moderation</cite>.<cite id="7129febb-2">Tokenized incentive mechanisms can align user behavior (e.g., content creation and curation) with economic rewards, offering potential new business models while raising concerns about scalability and content management</cite>.

Several concrete platforms illustrate these ideas. Steemit (2016) rewards users with tokens for content generation and curation, demonstrating token-follow dynamics and content monetization at scale.<cite id="7129febb-4">Following Steemit, Minds and Mirror adopted similar models for content creation and monetization, while newer Web3 social apps like Friend.tech and Farcaster integrate token incentives and decentralized social graphs</cite>.<cite id="7129febb-4">Farcaster, built on Ethereum, minimizes on-chain operations for performance while relying on smart contracts and a P2P hub architecture to maintain security and consistency off-chain</cite>.<cite id="3bf4f583-3">Community-driven dApps can use tokens to incentivize truth-seeking (e.g., crowdsourced credibility scoring), and projects like Solid and the Content Blockchain Project emphasize user-controlled data, privacy, and standards (e.g., ISCC) for media distribution</cite>.<cite id="7129febb-1">At the same time, reputation systems can be encoded in DLTs to register, update, and revoke publisher identities and reputation scores, aiding content provenance and moderation</cite>.

# Multilayer Network Structures: On-Chain/Off-Chain, Messaging, and Interoperability

Blockchain and social systems increasingly adopt multilayer architectures that separate computation, storage, and communication, while also integrating social graphs, reputation, and cross-chain connectivity.<cite id="f2fc7924-1">A canonical blockchain stack comprises control, consensus, data, and network layers; applications invoke smart contracts to trigger transactions, with on-chain and off-chain processing models at the control layer and diverse consensus mechanisms in public vs. private networks</cite>.<cite id="f2fc7924-2">Off-chain techniques such as state channels (e.g., Bitcoin’s Lightning Network) create long-lived, private channels for many transactions, contacting the main chain only at channel opening/closure or dispute, which offloads workloads, improves resource efficiency, and scales throughput</cite>.<cite id="f2fc7924-2">Interoperability layers (side-chains, cross-chains, child-chains) aim to link multiple blockchains, originally to enable low-risk experiments and later to support general applications, with designs that allow complex smart contracts and promising performance and security properties</cite>.

In social platforms, hybrid on-/off-chain designs become necessary for scalability and usability. Existing blockchain social networks employ off-chain storage for bulk social data (profiles, posts, comments) while keeping access control, authentication, and verification logic on-chain via smart contracts.<cite id="f2fc7924-3">Examples include systems that store user footprints off-chain to assess trust for offline interactions, privacy-first platforms like Minds and Farcaster that minimize on-chain operations, and content-sharing apps (e.g., APPICS) that use token-based rewards and transparent feeds</cite>.<cite id="f2fc7924-4">A representative architecture comprises three layers—an off-chain storage layer (cloud or IPFS), an application layer for user interfaces and real-time features, and a blockchain layer hosting smart contracts for identity, verification, and access control—explicitly designed to manage scalability while preserving integrity</cite>.<cite id="f2fc7924-0">Modeling blockchain social networks as multilayer graphs G = (V(c), E), where nodes have tokens and reputation, and edges reflect social relationships and dissemination decisions, shows how economic incentives and reputation influence information spread and trust in decentralized social graphs</cite>.

# Fraud and Abuse in Decentralized Social Ecosystems

Decentralized social and financial ecosystems are vulnerable to manipulation and abuse, including pump-and-dump schemes, wash trading, Sybil/bot activity, money laundering, and NFT marketplace fraud. Research is emerging to detect these using data-driven methods tailored to blockchain’s graph- and time-series-rich data.

## Pump-and-Dump, Market Manipulation, and DeFi Fraud

Deep neural networks have shown promise for detecting rapid, coordinated price manipulation in crypto markets. Empirical work demonstrates that sequence-based neural models outperform classical machine learning for pump-and-dump detection in cryptocurrencies, addressing the domain’s volatility and the lack of labeled data in prior studies.<cite id="e8a79d38-0">A study introducing two neural network architectures for pump-and-dump detection reports significant performance gains over statistical and classical ML baselines in crypto, highlighting the suitability of deep learning for time-varying market signals</cite>.<cite id="e8a79d38-1">A DeFi fraud detection survey finds that temporal transaction data and sequence models (e.g., RNNs/Transformers) are increasingly adopted as the ecosystem evolves, and that graph-based methods (node/graph embeddings and GNNs) are widely used when sufficient data exist, including heterogeneous graphs that incorporate wallets and smart contracts</cite>.<cite id="e8a79d38-1">However, rapid market changes and high transaction volumes complicate subgraph selection and scalability, indicating a need for efficient, scalable graph processing tailored to dynamic DeFi environments</cite>.

## Ethereum-Specific DL Approaches and GNN Limitations

Ethereum has become a focal point for fraud detection research due to rich on-chain traces and diverse attack surfaces (phishing, Ponzi schemes, ICO scams, money laundering, bot arbitrage).<cite id="e8a79d38-3">A pre-trained Transformer model (BERT4ETH) targets multiple Ethereum fraud tasks, motivated by limitations of purely graph-based methods: they may discard sequential information in transactions, struggle with noise on highly skewed account degree distributions, and optimize for single tasks rather than shared representations</cite>.<cite id="e8a79d38-3">BERT4ETH integrates Transformer sequential modeling with BERT pretraining to support diverse fraud detection tasks with minimal task-specific adaptation, addressing de-anonymization and behavior characterization beyond static graphs</cite>.

## Broader Financial Fraud Detection Trends

Broader reviews of deep learning for fraud detection show sustained growth in sequence models (notably LSTM), steady adoption of MLP/CNN, and rising use of NLP (e.g., BERT) for text-based fraud, with specialized methods like GNNs and GANs gaining traction in blockchain and related domains.<cite id="e8a79d38-2">A systematic review reports that LSTM, MLP, CNN, and RNN dominate, with BERT used for text, and that GNNs/GANs are increasingly applied to specialized fraud problems such as those on blockchains, aided by techniques for handling imbalanced datasets and generating synthetic data</cite>.

## NFT Marketplaces and Cross-Media Fraud

Fraud in NFT ecosystems includes wash trading, pump-and-dump campaigns, and marketplace scams. ML-based anomaly detection is being applied to transactional and collection-level signals to flag suspicious activity.<cite id="e8a79d38-4">A survey on AI for blockchain security notes NFT-specific fraud detection using time-series classification to label collections as whitelisted or blacklisted, with K-means and multiple CNNs evaluated on marketplace transaction data from OpenSea and AtomicHub</cite>.<cite id="e8a79d38-4">Empirical comparisons in adjacent blockchain fraud detection show classical classifiers like AdaBoost, SVM, and Random Forest can achieve high accuracies (around 97%) for transaction fraud, while integrated ML+blockchain systems have been tested against double-spending and Sybil attacks with robust performance</cite>.

# Comparative Analysis: DNN-Based Detection Approaches

- Temporal/Sequence Models: RNNs/LSTMs/Transformers capture temporal dependencies in trades, order books, and on-chain event sequences, improving detection of coordinated manipulation and temporal fraud patterns in DeFi and markets.<cite id="e8a79d38-0">Deep neural detectors outperform classical ML for pump-and-dump detection in crypto, indicating sensitivity to temporal dynamics</cite>.<cite id="e8a79d38-1">Surveys emphasize the rising use of sequence models in DeFi due to evolving temporal fraud patterns and high-volume, time-series data</cite>.
- Graph Neural Networks: GNNs exploit transaction and interaction graphs for wallet/smart contract clustering, anomaly detection, and reputation propagation; heterogeneous GNNs incorporate diverse nodes (accounts, contracts, events).<cite id="e8a79d38-1">Graph-based methods are widely used for DeFi fraud when data is abundant</cite>.<cite id="e8a79d38-3">However, pure graph representations can lose sequential information and face noise on skewed Ethereum account-degree distributions, motivating hybrid designs</cite>.
- Pretraining and Transfer: Pretrained language-style models (e.g., BERT4ETH) provide shared representations across multiple fraud tasks and can better model sequential behavior and de-anonymization features than task-agnostic GNNs.<cite id="e8a79d38-3">BERT4ETH combines Transformer sequential modeling with BERT-style pretraining to generalize across Ethereum fraud tasks</cite>.
- NFT and Cross-Media Detection: Time-series CNNs and clustering detect NFT collection-level manipulation; broader blockchain fraud detection uses classical and deep models to counter double-spending and Sybil attacks, indicating complementary toolkits across media (transactions, collections, contracts).<cite id="e8a79d38-4">NFT fraud detection leverages transactional time-series with CNNs and clustering to identify wash trading and pump-and-dump at the collection level</cite>.<cite id="e8a79d38-4">Classical classifiers and integrated ML+blockchain pipelines show strong results against double-spending and Sybil threats</cite>.

# Architectural and Governance Trade-offs

Decentralized social protocols face trade-offs between openness, scalability, and safety. Tokenized systems can motivate participation and monetization but may also incentivize manipulation if governance and reputation are poorly designed.<cite id="7129febb-3">Tokenized monetization can sustain contributions, yet the field remains early and questions remain about long-term viability</cite>.<cite id="3bf4f583-3">Governance and power distribution vary across protocols (e.g., Mastodon instances, Bluesky), with recurring concerns about re-concentration of power and policy heterogeneity</cite>.<cite id="3bf4f583-0">Scalability and regulatory compliance are persistent challenges for blockchain-enabled social media, affecting content moderation, privacy, and institutional acceptance</cite>.

Multilayer architectures help, but introduce complexity and new failure modes. Off-chain storage and state channels improve scalability and reduce on-chain load, yet require careful trust boundary management and conflict resolution; interoperability layers expand functionality but increase operational and security surface area.<cite id="f2fc7924-2">State channels and off-chain designs offload most workloads and improve application-layer efficiency by contacting the chain only on channel lifecycle events or disputes</cite>.<cite id="f2fc7924-4">Hybrid architectures with distinct off-chain storage, application, and blockchain layers aim to scale social content while keeping verification and access control on-chain, but must optimize storage and notifications to avoid single points of failure</cite>.

# Open Challenges and Future Directions

- Cross-Chain and Interoperable Fraud Detection: Most DNN-based detection targets single chains with rich labels; scalable cross-chain methods for identity, wallet linkage, and graph unification remain underexplored, especially for smaller DeFi components and NFTs.<cite id="e8a79d38-1">Surveys note limited detection techniques for components beyond major chains and call for scalable graph processing to handle dynamic, complex transaction graphs</cite>.
- Data Imbalance, Concept Drift, and Labeling: Fraud patterns evolve quickly; imbalanced datasets and scarce ground truth hinder model training and transfer, suggesting needs for synthetic data (GANs), continual learning, and federated detection across networks.<cite id="e8a79d38-2">Systematic reviews highlight imbalanced data and growing use of GANs/VAEs to generate synthetic fraud samples</cite>.<cite id="e8a79d38-1">Temporal evolution and high transaction volumes complicate method selection and subgraph extraction in DeFi</cite>.
- Privacy-Preserving and On-Chain-Off-Chain Integration: Combining encrypted identifiers, zero-knowledge proofs, and hybrid architectures while retaining effective detection is challenging; research is needed on privacy-preserving features, cross-layer reputation, and auditability without sacrificing user sovereignty.<cite id="f2fc7924-4">Hybrid storage and smart contract-based access control balance usability and integrity, but notification systems and storage choices affect scalability and trust</cite>.
- Governance and Social Ecosystem Health: Empirical, longitudinal studies of decentralized social protocols’ governance and safety are scarce; socio-technical frameworks are needed to measure re-concentration of power, moderation efficacy, and user agency across protocol heterogeneity.<cite id="3bf4f583-3">Analyses emphasize that protocol politics and governance challenges vary, and that understanding these differences is crucial to avoid overgeneralization about user behavior</cite>.

# Conclusion

The literature indicates a clear trajectory: blockchain is enabling decentralized social protocols through tokenized incentives, DAO governance, and on-chain identity/reputation, often supported by multilayer architectures that separate scalable off-chain computation and storage from integrity-preserving on-chain logic.<cite id="3bf4f583-0,7129febb-0">Surveys and taxonomies map these applications, including social tokens, DAOs, content moderation, and cross-chain interconnections</cite>.<cite id="f2fc7924-1,f2fc7924-2">On-chain/off-chain layers and state channels, alongside interoperability designs, underpin scalable social systems</cite>.<cite id="7129febb-4">Concrete platforms (e.g., Steemit, Minds, Farcaster, Friend.tech) demonstrate token-follow economies and decentralized social graphs in practice</cite>. For fraud detection, deep neural networks—especially sequence models, graph-based methods, and pretrained Transformers—show strong performance on crypto and DeFi manipulation and abuse, with emerging applications to NFT marketplaces; however, challenges remain in cross-chain generalization, data imbalance, and governance integration.<cite id="e8a79d38-0,e8a79d38-1,e8a79d38-3,e8a79d38-2,e8a79d38-4">Empirical studies report DNN outperformance for pump-and-dump, rising adoption of GNNs and sequence models in DeFi, Ethereum-specific pretraining for fraud, and CNN-based detection of NFT marketplace fraud</cite>. Future work should prioritize interoperable detection frameworks, privacy-preserving analytics, and socio-technical evaluations to ensure decentralized social protocols deliver on user agency while mitigating abuse at scale. </answer>

Title: From Centralization to Decentralization: Blockchain’s Role in Transforming Social Media Platforms
Snippet: Blockchain is influencing the social media platforms by promising to solve the biggest issues of today, such as privacy concerns and content moderation, and the ability to provide a decentralized system for the management of social media platforms through cryptographic techniques and distributed structures. Conventionally, social media systems are based on central architectures that may indirectly solve the problems of data privacy and platform responsibility since there are increased threats, including identity theft and fake news spread across such systems. Blockchain has stepped up as an anti-centralized platform that allows multiple numbers of users to transact securely and authentically through P2P channels without a middleman. Here in this survey, we introduce a brief overview of the latest trends of the blockchain protocols and the interactions with the social media platforms, as well as present a systematic review of the related area. Specifically, the use case we consider and elaborate on is how blockchain can be applied to various types of social media services: smart contract-based content moderation platforms, user incentives using token economics, social media governance through decentralized autonomous organizations, and cross-chain connections. We then go further and offer a comprehensive literature review of blockchain incorporating main social media applications that cutting across them include identity, tokenization, and self-governance. The key points that can be derived from this review of the blockchain-enabled social media services and applications are also underlined here. We conclude this survey by listing the existing issues in the field, including scalability and compliance with the existing regulations, and suggesting the possible areas of research in this ever-evolving field.

Title: Seeing the Politics of Decentralized Social Media Protocols
Snippet: The landscape of social media has been dominated by centralized platforms that control the flow of information, user data, and governance structures [26,42,72]. These platforms-such as Facebook, Instagram, and X (formerly Twitter)-have collectively shaped digital experiences for billions of people, but have also raised concerns about privacy, power imbalances, and algorithmic biases [15,30,31,68,73]. In response, new decentralized social media protocols have surged in popularity [18,52,79]. These protocols aim to disseminate power to users, reduce reliance on centralized entities, and empower a rich ecosystem of interoperable social media services [38,58,71]. 

As decentralized social media protocols gain traction, researchers have turned their attention to understanding the user experience in these emerging ecosystems: tracking user behavior following moments of mass migration [18,47,52,79] and identifying potential privacy or safety concerns [25,61]. Underpinning this work is whether decentralized social media protocols can fulfill their promise of user agency and control [32]. Prior studies have examined the policies and agreements formed by user communities on decentralized social media platforms like mastodon.social and Bluesky [40,77,98], as well as documented governance challenges faced by users in administrative roles [4,46,103], with recurring concerns around re-concentration of power [49,88] at key points of decision-making [55]. Crucially, the protocols-which define rules governing the exchange of data across communication channels-undergirding decentralized social media serve as the foundation for practices in these systems. They can vary in ways that reflect protocol developers' goals and values, operationalizing and envisioning "decentralization" in distinct ways. As such, concerns about power in decentralized social media must also be examined in relation to the politics embedded in each protocol. In the absence of such context, researchers risk overgeneralizing user behavior and misattributing the sources and significance of key challenges in decentralized social media. Despite this, there has been a relative lack of scholarly attention to protocols themselves. 

We aim to offer a lens through which social computing scholars and developers can see the politics of decentralized social media protocols.

Title: From Centralization to Decentralization: Blockchain’s Role in Transforming Social Media Platforms
Snippet: Even though there is a vast, developed literature on the topic of blockchain technology, no scholarly study specifically examines the uses of blockchain technology in social media networks. As for the further development trends of blockchain, it is acknowledged that the application potential of blockchain in many aspects, including secure communication, privacy protection, decentralized decisionmaking, and content management, has been overlooked in existing literature [11], [12], [13], [14], [15], [16], [17], [18], [9]. In addition, an extensive comparison of different blockchain implementations for addressing concerns such as misinformation, rumors, and user shift has not been conducted in the current publication [19], [21], [22], [23], [24], [25]. This gap further encourages us to embark on a comprehensive analysis of the application of blockchain in social media. The novelty of this paper lies in the systematic review of the state of the art of blockchain along with its novel advances at the theoretical and practical level. To this end, the key contributions of this article are highlighted as follows: 

1) We present a cutting-edge review of blockchain applications in social media, beginning with an explanation of the fundamental blockchain technology and how they can revolutionize social media sites. 2) We go over the potential blockchain brings to different social media platforms, such as user-controlled data monetization, community governance, decentralized content production, data privacy and security, and misinformation management. 3) We offer a methodical examination of blockchain technologies and their uses, encompassing the integration of technologies like Ethereum and Hyperledger on various social media networks. 4) To improve the integration of blockchain in social media, we emphasize significant research challenges and recommend future research concepts.

snippet.text:
The landscape of social media has been dominated by centralized platforms that control the flow of information, user data, and governance structures [26,42,72]. These platforms-such as Facebook, Instagram, and X (formerly Twitter)-have collectively shaped digital experiences for billions of people, but have also raised concerns about privacy, power imbalances, and algorithmic biases [15,30,31,68,73]. In response, new decentralized social media protocols have surged in popularity [18,52,79]. These protocols aim to disseminate power to users, reduce reliance on centralized entities, and empower a rich ecosystem of interoperable social media services [38,58,71]. 

As decentralized social media protocols gain traction, researchers have turned their attention to understanding the user experience in these emerging ecosystems: tracking user behavior following moments of mass migration [18,47,52,79] and identifying potential privacy or safety concerns [25,61]. Underpinning this work is whether decentralized social media protocols can fulfill their promise of user agency and control [32]. Prior studies have examined the policies and agreements formed by user communities on decentralized social media platforms like mastodon.social and Bluesky [40,77,98], as well as documented governance challenges faced by users in administrative roles [4,46,103], with recurring concerns around re-concentration of power [49,88] at key points of decision-making [55]. Crucially, the protocols-which define rules governing the exchange of data across communication channels-undergirding decentralized social media serve as the foundation for practices in these systems. They can vary in ways that reflect protocol developers' goals and values, operationalizing and envisioning "decentralization" in distinct ways. As such, concerns about power in decentralized social media must also be examined in relation to the politics embedded in each protocol. In the absence of such context, researchers risk overgeneralizing user behavior and misattributing the sources and significance of key challenges in decentralized social media. Despite this, there has been a relative lack of scholarly attention to protocols themselves. 

We aim to offer a lens through which social computing scholars and developers can see the politics of decentralized social media protocols.

snippet.text:
Even though there is a vast, developed literature on the topic of blockchain technology, no scholarly study specifically examines the uses of blockchain technology in social media networks. As for the further development trends of blockchain, it is acknowledged that the application potential of blockchain in many aspects, including secure communication, privacy protection, decentralized decisionmaking, and content management, has been overlooked in existing literature [11], [12], [13], [14], [15], [16], [17], [18], [9]. In addition, an extensive comparison of different blockchain implementations for addressing concerns such as misinformation, rumors, and user shift has not been conducted in the current publication [19], [21], [22], [23], [24], [25]. This gap further encourages us to embark on a comprehensive analysis of the application of blockchain in social media. The novelty of this paper lies in the systematic review of the state of the art of blockchain along with its novel advances at the theoretical and practical level. To this end, the key contributions of this article are highlighted as follows: 

1) We present a cutting-edge review of blockchain applications in social media, beginning with an explanation of the fundamental blockchain technology and how they can revolutionize social media sites. 2) We go over the potential blockchain brings to different social media platforms, such as user-controlled data monetization, community governance, decentralized content production, data privacy and security, and misinformation management. 3) We offer a methodical examination of blockchain technologies and their uses, encompassing the integration of technologies like Ethereum and Hyperledger on various social media networks. 4) To improve the integration of blockchain in social media, we emphasize significant research challenges and recommend future research concepts.

documents.title: From Centralization to Decentralization: Blockchain’s Role in Transforming Social Media Platforms
documents.snippet: Blockchain is influencing the social media platforms by promising to solve the biggest issues of today, such as privacy concerns and content moderation, and the ability to provide a decentralized system for the management of social media platforms through cryptographic techniques and distributed structures. Conventionally, social media systems are based on central architectures that may indirectly solve the problems of data privacy and platform responsibility since there are increased threats, including identity theft and fake news spread across such systems. Blockchain has stepped up as an anti-centralized platform that allows multiple numbers of users to transact securely and authentically through P2P channels without a middleman. Here in this survey, we introduce a brief overview of the latest trends of the blockchain protocols and the interactions with the social media platforms, as well as present a systematic review of the related area. Specifically, the use case we consider and elaborate on is how blockchain can be applied to various types of social media services: smart contract-based content moderation platforms, user incentives using token economics, social media governance through decentralized autonomous organizations, and cross-chain connections. We then go further and offer a comprehensive literature review of blockchain incorporating main social media applications that cutting across them include identity, tokenization, and self-governance. The key points that can be derived from this review of the blockchain-enabled social media services and applications are also underlined here. We conclude this survey by listing the existing issues in the field, including scalability and compliance with the existing regulations, and suggesting the possible areas of research in this ever-evolving field.
