Over the past decade, social media platforms have played a crucial role in reshaping social interactions, becoming an integral component of daily life.Since the inception of pioneers like MySpace [25] and Facebook [45], these platforms have revolutionized communication experiences and have opened up numerous opportunities for businesses to engage with consumers.However, with the rise of Web3-an iteration of the Internet that incorporates concepts such as decentralization, blockchain technologies, and token-based economics-established social media platforms are now compelled to reassess and adapt their operational models to remain relevant in an increasingly dynamic and rapidly evolving digital landscape.Web3 emphasizes user sovereignty and data privacy.It typically relies on blockchain's distributed data storage and state consensus to ensure users can control their own data, rendering transactions and interactions transparent and trustworthy.The token of Web3 serves as a powerful incentive, rewarding users and contributors for their participation and investment in the ecosystem.

The foundational concept of a Web3 social network lies in establishing a decentralized, verifiable social graph, targeting the prevalent issues of platform fragmentation and monopolization of user data seen in existing social frameworks.Web3 ushers in a user-focused decentralized social graph protocol, facilitating the generation, modification, acquisition, and confirmation of social graph data.Concurrently, Web3 cultivates a distinctive feedback , , Bin Wang, Tianjian Liu, Wenqi Wang, Yuan Weng, Chao Li, Guangquan Xu, Meng Shen, Sencun Zhu, and Wei Wang* loop within the data network, granting users control over their own data.

With the significant influx of users into the Web3, a variety of demands have arisen, leading to the creation of numerous social applications including Steemit, TOMO, Friend3, Cipher.rip,Post.Tech, and friend.tech.In response to the Web3 community's call for unrestricted social interaction, Steemit, a blockchain-powered Web3 blog and social media platform, was launched in 2016.This platform rewards users for generating and curating content through token compensation.Following Steemit, platforms like Minds and Mirror have emerged, enabling users to produce content and monetize their contributions.

Title: A Survey on Network Optimization Techniques for Blockchain Systems
Snippet: This section briefly introduces blockchain technology, its architecture and discusses the layers it comprises. The section then discusses blockchain's P2P structure and the gossip dissemination protocol. 

Blockchain is a peer-to-peer distributed ledger that stores transactions in a chain of blocks. It was initially developed as the technology powering the Bitcoin cryptocurrency [53]. It aims to remove the need for a trusted third party who will validate transactions [57,58]. Therefore, transactions are timestamped and verified by all participating nodes and then added as a block in the main chain using cryptographic tools. As shown in Figure 3, the blockchain architecture consists of the control, consensus, data and network layers. 

1. Control Layer: The control layer serves as an interface between applications and the ledger. These applications include finance, data storage, voting, securing IoT, logistics and supply chain tracking [10,51]. They interact with the ledger by invoking smart contracts to trigger transactions. Smart contracts are programmable scripts that interact with the ledger by reading or writing data to the ledger when invoked. 

On-chain and off-chain are the primary processing models at the control layer. 2. Consensus Layer: The algorithms blockchain peers use to agree on the validity of blocks and transactions exists at the consensus layer. Peers in public blockchains use Proof of X (X => Work, Stake and many more) algorithms to reach a consensus [53]. All peers in public blockchains are eligible to participate in the consensus process. However, in private blockchains, validating blocks and transactions are performed mainly by different peers with specific roles. In Hyperledger Fabric (HLF), these roles include orderers, endorsers, validators and leaders [31]. New transactions are first sent to peers who can endorse transactions by executing smart contracts. After endorsement, the transaction is sent to the leader node and maintains a connection to the ordering nodes. Next, ordering nodes add the transactions to a block and send them back to the leader node to be broadcasted in the network. Finally, every peer will have to validate the block before committing it to its local ledger.

Title: Effective scaling of blockchain beyond consensus innovations and Moore's law
Snippet: Offloading workloads. Off-chain is a classic technique which enhances network concurrency by constructing channels [69]. In traditional on-chain topologies, myriad transaction confirmations concentrate on the blockchain network with limited capacity. Off-chain networks, in contrast, build independent and long-lived channels over which an arbitrary amount of transactions can be processed locally between individuals. The blockchain is contacted only when peers initialize and close channels, or the involved parties encounter conflicts, in which case the preset contracts will handle fair settlement. This topology therefore effectively offloads the vast majority of blockchain network's workloads, accommodating more channels and peers. Simultaneously, both sides of channels are free of synchronizing network-wide message or participating in consensus, so the resource efficiency and performance at the application layer are significantly improved. Viewed from blockchain network, however, the resource efficiency keeps unchanged because of no architecture innovations.

The well-known Bitcoin Lightning network [70] and duplex micropayment channel [71] first explored off-chain to overcome the scalability bottleneck. Furthermore, Dziembowski et al. [72] presented the concept of virtual payment channel, which introduced smart contracts to bypass undependable intermediaries when processing cross-channel payments. In order to support general applications rather than cryptocurrencies, they further polished their proposal by building channels recursively and successfully constructed the state channel allowing arbitrarily complex smart contracts to execute [73]. All these designs achieved promising performance and a potential far higher than consensus-based scaling. Moreover, the security of off-chain technology has been elaborated in detail [74], [75]. Some researchers even claimed that their proposals can sustain dependability when the peers at both sides of one channel are malicious.

Title: Blockchain-Based Scalable and Reliable Social Networking Platform
Snippet: As blockchain technology evolves, a variety of blockchainbased Decentralized Applications (DApps) for social networking services (SNS) have been proposed and launched. Each of these platforms uses both on-chain and offchain storage methods to address the scalability challenges associated with blockchain technology. In bajji [28], where users' footprints are recorded on the blockchain to determine their trustworthiness for offline meetings. This helps establish their trustworthiness, which can be useful for evaluating whether they are reliable for offline meetings. Steemit [29] is an SNS platform that rewards content creators with cryptocurrencies. These rewards are issued on Steemit's own blockchain, providing an incentive for users to create and share content. Minds [30] is a social networking platform that operates on blockchain technology. Its primary focus is on protecting user privacy and ensuring robust security. APPICS [31] is a social media application for image sharing that offers complete transparency through blockchain technology. It returns control over content feeds and rewards to users, with APX tokens used as the platform's reward currency. Farcaster [32] is a decentralized public social network built on Ethereum. To reduce costs and improve performance, on-chain operations are minimized, while security and consistency are maintained through smart contracts. The network uses a P2P system of servers, referred to as ''hubs,'' as an off-chain solution. Unlike the proposed system, existing services primarily use blockchain to focus on rewarding content. 

Table 1 compares the features of the proposed system with those of related studies, highlighting their differences. While previous research has proposed blockchain-based DOSN systems to address OSN security issues, these studies emphasize data security and user privacy but do not address scalability. The proposed system is specifically designed with a storage structure that accounts for blockchain scalability, making it suitable for online social networks. The scalability of our system is improved compared to other platforms that rely solely on IPFS or cloud storage. By optimizing storage management with this hybrid approach, our system can efficiently handle a higher volume of posts and interactions without compromising speed or data security.

Title: Blockchain-Based Scalable and Reliable Social Networking Platform
Snippet: In this section, we provide a detailed explanation of the design of the system, including a description of the key modules and processes. 

Figure 2 demonstrates the hierarchical architecture of the social networking system. The proposed system basically adopts an off-chain storage connection structure to address blockchain scalability. Therefore, it is composed of three layers: the off-chain storage layer, the application layer, and the blockchain layer. The off-chain storage layer serves as the storage component where the actual data associated with the service are stored. The proposed system utilized cloud-based storage platforms, such as Google Cloud Storage, Amazon S3, and Firebase Realtime Database, as the off-chain storage layer. To avoid a single point of centralization inherent in cloud storage systems, a distributed file system such as IPFS can be adopted. As the trustworthiness of the data is verified through the blockchain, the off-chain storage layer focus solely on storing and retrieving data without the need for additional trust considerations. This layer provides efficient and scalable storage for user profiles, posts, comments, and other relevant data. The application layer acts as the interface for users, providing them with access to the platform's functionalities. Users interact with the blockchain through an interface to use social networking services. The blockchain layer is a fundamental component of the proposed system, serving as the backbone for ensuring data integrity and security. This layer hosts smart contracts that are responsible for managing critical functions such as user authentication, content verification, and access control. By leveraging blockchain's inherent immutability, the system guarantees that all transactions and interactions within the platform are secure and tamper-proof. The complexity of the proposed system arises from its architecture and technologies designed to integrate scalability, security, and usability. The system is engineered to manage critical functions such as user management, content integrity, and notification services through smart contracts implemented on the blockchain layer. These contracts are optimized to minimize computational costs by efficiently managing on-chain storage. Additionally, the system includes a decentralized real-time notification system that ensures efficient content management and verification at scale, while preventing single points of failure.

Title: Crypto Pump and Dump Detection via Deep Learning Techniques
Snippet: Despite the fact that cryptocurrencies themselves have experienced an astonishing rate of adoption over the last decade, cryptocurrency fraud detection is a heavily under-researched problem area. Of all fraudulent activity regarding cryptocurrencies, pump and dump schemes are some of the most common. Though some studies have been done on these kinds of scams in the stock market, the lack of labelled stock data and the volatility unique to the cryptocurrency space constrains the applicability of studies on the stock market toward this problem domain. Furthermore, the only work done in this space thus far has been either statistical in nature, or has been concerned with classical machine learning models such as random forest trees. We propose the novel application of two existing neural network architectures to this problem domain and show that deep learning solutions can significantly outperform all other existing pump and dump detection methods for cryptocurrencies.

Title: AI-powered Fraud Detection in Decentralized Finance: A Project Life Cycle Perspective
Snippet: Through the review of fraud detection in the project maturity and decline stage, we have the following findings. 

• Temporal transaction data is now crucial due to the evolving DeFi ecosystem and increased volumes, leading to a dynamic environment and new fraud challenges. To address this, a few sequence-based models have arisen as adopted techniques [78,107,142]. Title: BERT4ETH: A Pre-trained Transformer for Ethereum Fraud Detection
Snippet: As a decentralized computing platform, Ethereum empowers its developers to create a variety of decentralized applications (DApps). Many recent studies [2,4,[20][21][22]31] employ graph representation learning techniques for fraud detection on Ethereum. Although it is intuitive to represent the interactions between accounts as a graph, it is argued that they have the following limitations: 

(i) Graph is not appropriate for capturing the sequential pattern inherent in transactions. Ethereum transactions are high repetitive, indicating the presence of multi-edges between nodes. Current graph-learning methods [24,25,31] integrate multi-edges to a single edge to facilitate graph computations. However, the discarded sequential information is essential for characterizing user behaviors for tasks such as de-anonymization. 

(ii) Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), especially on the highly skew-distributed Ethereum data [19], can suffer from noise when the number of convolution hops increases [14], given that Ethereum accounts are often connected to highly popular accounts. However, limiting the number of convolution hops can restrict the capabilities of GNNs, as the number of hops is typically equivalent to the depth of layers in conventional GNNs [11,17,20,29]. 

(iii) Existing studies primarily target on individual fraud detection tasks in an end-to-end training manner. In light of the successes of Transformer pre-training techniques in NLP [10,28], we believe that a pre-trained Transformer can support various fraud detection tasks with minimal adaptations needed. 

To address the limitations discussed above, we introduce a pretrained model that offers a universal solution for various fraud detection tasks on Ethereum. BERT4ETH features the superior sequential modeling capability of Transformer [28] and the pretraining paradigm of BERT [10].

problem: Advantages  of digital watermarking
final_response:
# Advantages of Digital Watermarking

## Core functional benefits
- Imperceptibility preserves the host media while embedding identifying or control information, so viewers or listeners notice no degradation yet the watermark remains detectable by authorized parties.<cite id="c15fa29c-0">Digital watermarking schemes aim to be imperceptible to the human eye while being detectable by detectors, making them suitable for fingerprinting, copyright protection, and content authentication because the content is inseparable from the watermark.</cite> <cite id="c15fa29c-1">Imperceptibility requires the watermarked image to look identical to the original, ensuring that embedded information is not visible to the naked eye.</cite> <cite id="c15fa29c-3">Imperceptibility is typically measured by metrics like PSNR and ensures the watermarked image remains visually acceptable.</cite>
- Robustness to common manipulations and transmission impairments enables reliable ownership verification and tamper detection after attacks such as compression, filtering, noise addition, scaling, rotation, and cropping.<cite id="c15fa29c-0">Robustness ensures detectability after typical signal-processing operations, a key property for effective watermarking schemes.</cite> <cite id="c15fa29c-1">Robustness is the ability to detect the watermark after manipulations (attacks), with strong performance desired for copyright protection.</cite> <cite id="c15fa29c-2">Robust watermarking resists geometric attacks such as filtering, scaling, noise addition, translation, rotation, and cropping, while fragile/semi-fragile variants support integrity checking and tamper localization.</cite>
- Capacity allows embedding meaningful amounts of data (e.g., identifiers, metadata, messages) without exceeding perceptual thresholds, balancing how much information can be hidden against quality constraints.<cite id="c15fa29c-1">Capacity is the maximum number of bits embedded without degrading quality, and high-capacity methods must maintain image quality while embedding large payloads.</cite> <cite id="c15fa29c-2">Watermarking capacity refers to how much data can be embedded while maintaining host similarity and robustness.</cite> <cite id="c15fa29c-4">Watermark capacity defines the maximum information embeddable without compromising invisibility and durability, highlighting the trade-off with robustness and quality.</cite>
- Security and tamper resistance protect watermarks from removal or alteration by adversaries and enable copy control and traceability strategies.<cite id="c15fa29c-0">Security is a fundamental requirement alongside imperceptibility, robustness, and capacity for secure watermarking schemes.</cite> <cite id="c15fa29c-2">Security implies protection against malicious attacks, complementing robustness and imperceptibility in secure watermarking designs.</cite> <cite id="c15fa29c-3">Balancing capacity, robustness, and security is a central challenge in watermarking system design.</cite>

## Ownership verification, copyright, and control
- Watermarking provides proof of authorship and ownership, enabling content owners to assert rights and deter unauthorized use by making infringement detectable.<cite id="c15fa29c-0">Digital watermarking embeds information to ensure authenticity and protect copyright holders from unauthorized data alteration, supporting ownership verification.</cite> <cite id="c15fa29c-2">Watermarking proves the authenticated owner of media by embedding extractable identifying information.</cite>
- Copy control and broadcast monitoring use watermarking to indicate protected content and verify transmissions, supporting compliance and audit trails.<cite id="c15fa29c-1">For copy protection, watermarks indicate whether content is copyrighted and can be removed only with severe degradation, aligning with standards like CPTWG for DVD copy protection.</cite> <cite id="87fb516c-0">Broadcast monitoring embeds watermarks in advertisements so automated systems can detect and log broadcasts to verify timing and location, aiding royalty tracking and transmission verification.</cite> <cite id="87fb516c-1">In broadcast monitoring, owners embed watermarks prior to transmission; monitoring sites extract them for verification, IPR surveillance, and related applications.</cite>
- Fingerprinting uniquely identifies authorized recipients or copies to trace leakage, supporting accountability and legal action against distributors.<cite id="c15fa29c-0">Watermarking supports fingerprinting for unique identification of media copies, useful for tracking distribution.</cite> <cite id="87fb516c-0">Fingerprinting embeds different watermarks per recipient so that if data is disseminated illicitly, the owner can identify the recipient by extracting the embedded watermark.</cite> <cite id="87fb516c-2">Fingerprinting methods embed unique watermarks to identify and track illicit copies of video content.</cite>

## Integrity, tamper detection, and localization
- Fragile and semi-fragile watermarks enable integrity checking: any alteration renders the watermark invalid, and semi-fragile designs can localize and even reconstruct tampered regions while tolerating benign processing.<cite id="8b0426b8-0">Semi-fragile watermarking detects, localizes, and recovers from tamper attacks; changes in the watermark reflect tampering, while robustness to normal processing distinguishes benign edits from malicious tampering.</cite> <cite id="8b0426b8-1">Semi-fragile watermarks detect tamper locations and manipulations and are robust enough to tolerate normal content changes, supporting content authentication with tamper localization.</cite> <cite id="8b0426b8-2">Fragile watermarks indicate whether data has been altered and can recover tampered regions, while semi-fragile watermarks are robust to some modifications and fragile to intentional attacks, enabling detection and localization of altered regions.</cite>
- These authentication capabilities support forensics and evidence integrity in sensitive domains like surveillance, healthcare, and legal contexts.<cite id="87fb516c-2">Video authentication addresses integrity of surveillance and other critical applications where verifying that content has not been altered is essential.</cite> <cite id="87fb516c-3">Watermarking supports applications such as e-health, forensics, and e-voting where provenance and integrity are crucial.</cite>

## Data hiding and covert communication
- Watermarking provides a covert channel for secret messaging, embedding messages imperceptibly and extracting them only by intended receivers, with lower risk of detection compared to overt signaling.<cite id="c15fa29c-0">Digital watermarking embeds information imperceptibly so that only detectors can reveal it, enabling data hiding for authentication and related purposes.</cite> <cite id="87fb516c-0">Digital watermarking can serve covert communication by embedding secret messages imperceptibly in images or video for communication while minimizing interception by unintended receivers.</cite> <cite id="87fb516c-4">Watermarking supports data authentication and covert communication by embedding hidden messages that are imperceptible to casual observers.</cite>

## Media-specific robustness and quality properties
- Transform-domain watermarking (e.g., DCT/DWT/SVD) typically offers better imperceptibility and robustness than spatial-domain methods, enabling practical deployment across images, audio, and video.<cite id="c15fa29c-2">Transform-domain methods (DWT, DCT, SVD) provide good imperceptibility and robustness, whereas spatial-domain techniques are less robust to geometric attacks but offer higher data hiding capacity.</cite> <cite id="c15fa29c-4">Transform-domain approaches generally demonstrate greater resilience than spatial-domain methods, though both must balance imperceptibility, robustness, and capacity.</cite>
- In audio, robust watermarking is designed to withstand typical processing and compression while remaining inaudible, supporting applications like broadcast monitoring and rights management without perceptual artifacts.<cite id="c15fa29c-3">Audio watermarking systems emphasize robustness to processing and compression and imperceptibility (inaudibility) to maintain quality while enabling verification and tracking.</cite> <cite id="87fb516c-1">Audio and video watermarking leverage robustness and perceptibility to support applications such as broadcast monitoring and copy control across multimedia content.</cite>
- Video watermarking supports copy control, broadcast monitoring, ownership verification, and authentication across large, dynamic media with motion and compression, aligning with real-world workflows in media distribution and archiving.<cite id="87fb516c-2">Video watermarking supports fingerprinting, copy control via protected indications, broadcast monitoring for verification, and authentication for integrity assurance.</cite> <cite id="87fb516c-3">Video watermarking is used for ownership identity, copyright protection, and broadcast monitoring in diverse applications including archiving and digital cinema, emphasizing robustness, perceptibility, capacity, and security.</cite>

## Synergy with related data-hiding techniques
- Compared to steganography, watermarking is more resilient to attacks and better suited for rights management and accountability, while still enabling covert communication when designed for low detectability.<cite id="c15fa29c-3">Steganography can suffer from significant overhead to hide small amounts of data, whereas watermarking provides integrity and robustness; cryptography alone does not prevent illegal copying once decoded.</cite> <cite id="c15fa29c-0">Watermarking is a form of data hiding used for authentication and ownership, distinct from general steganography but sharing the goal of imperceptible embedding.</cite> <cite id="87fb516c-4">Watermarking and steganography both support data authentication and covert communication, with watermarking emphasizing ownership and control (e.g., fingerprinting) and steganography focusing on secrecy of communication.</cite>

- Workflow integration: watermarking can be embedded at creation or distribution time and verified by automated systems, supporting scalable monitoring, auditing, and compliance across networks and broadcast channels.<cite id="87fb516c-0">Embedding watermarks in advertisements enables automated broadcast monitoring systems to identify and time-stamp transmissions for verification and tracking.</cite> <cite id="87fb516c-1">Monitoring sites extract embedded watermarks from transmitted content, feeding data to central databases for verification and IPR surveillance.</cite> <cite id="87fb516c-2">Fingerprinting and copy control provide systematic ways to track and restrict reproduction, aligning with industry-standardized copy protection approaches.</cite>

- Digital watermarking’s core advantages—imperceptibility, robustness, capacity, and security—enable copyright protection, ownership verification, tamper detection/localization, broadcast monitoring and fingerprinting, copy control, and covert communication across images, audio, and video.<cite id="c15fa29c-0">The ideal characteristics of watermarking include imperceptibility, robustness, capacity, and security, supporting applications in fingerprinting, copyright protection, and authentication.</cite> <cite id="8b0426b8-0">Semi-fragile watermarking distinguishes benign processing from tampering and detects/locates alterations, enabling robust content authentication.</cite> <cite id="87fb516c-0">Broadcast monitoring and fingerprinting leverage embedded watermarks to verify transmissions and trace unauthorized distribution, respectively.</cite> <cite id="87fb516c-1">Video watermarking supports fingerprinting, copy control, broadcast monitoring, and authentication in real-world media workflows.</cite> <cite id="87fb516c-4">Watermarking also facilitates data authentication and covert communication by embedding imperceptible information for verification and messaging.</cite>

Snippet: The growth of digital information technologies makes their distribution and duplication much easier. Digital image watermarking has been found to be an effective solution for copyright protection of images [1]. Its basic procedure is to embed imperceptible information, termed watermark, in the original image. Thus, the copyright of the image can be provided by extracting the embedded secret watermark. 

Three main properties are required in image watermarking systems [2]: imperceptibility, capacity, and robustness. Imperceptibility refers to the fact that the watermarked image should look identical to the original one. Capacity represents the maximum number of bits embedded in the original image. It is the primary constraint that should be ensured after imperceptibility [3] in high-capacity methods. Indeed, in this category of techniques, a considerable quantity of information should be embedded without losing image quality. In the copyright protection methods, this constraint is less critical, but it can influence the results in terms of robustness of imperceptibility, especially when the watermark size is too big. Robustness refers to the ability to detect the watermark even if the watermarked image suffered from several manipulations called attacks. A good watermarking scheme should ensure the best trade-off between these three properties. Indeed, generally, with the increase of capacity, the robustness of the image decreases while simultaneously decreasing its imperceptibility and vice versa. The main objective of the proposed method is copyright protection. Therefore, capacity is not a primal issue. Indeed, the main requirements for copyright protection applications are imperceptibility and robustness. 

Watermarking schemes can be categorized according to embedding domain, extracting technique, watermark robustness. The embedding domain can be spatial or a transform domain. Spatial methods [4] embed the watermark by directly altering the pixels, while the transform domain methods embed the watermark after performing a transformation, such as DFT [5,6], DCT [7], DWT [8]. The extraction method can be a non-blind, or semi-blind, or a blind technique.

Digital watermarking is simply the process of embedding some information into a multimedia element, such as image, video or audio that can be extracted later on to prove the authenticated owner of the media. Watermarking may be fragile, semi-fragile, or robust, non-blind, semi-blind or blind, visible or invisible etc. Imperceptibility, robustness, capacity, and security are the basic necessities for a secure watermarking scheme. Watermarking algorithms can be grouped in two categories: spatial domain, and frequency (or transform) domain [1,3]. - Robustness to common manipulations and transmission impairments enables reliable ownership verification and tamper detection after attacks such as compression, filtering, noise addition, scaling, rotation, and cropping.<cite id="c15fa29c-0">Robustness ensures detectability after typical signal-processing operations, a key property for effective watermarking schemes.</cite> <cite id="c15fa29c-1">Robustness is the ability to detect the watermark after manipulations (attacks), with strong performance desired for copyright protection.</cite> <cite id="c15fa29c-2">Robust watermarking resists geometric attacks such as filtering, scaling, noise addition, translation, rotation, and cropping, while fragile/semi-fragile variants support integrity checking and tamper localization.</cite>
- Capacity allows embedding meaningful amounts of data (e.g., identifiers, metadata, messages) without exceeding perceptual thresholds, balancing how much information can be hidden against quality constraints.<cite id="c15fa29c-1">Capacity is the maximum number of bits embedded without degrading quality, and high-capacity methods must maintain image quality while embedding large payloads.</cite> <cite id="c15fa29c-2">Watermarking capacity refers to how much data can be embedded while maintaining host similarity and robustness.</cite> <cite id="c15fa29c-4">Watermark capacity defines the maximum information embeddable without compromising invisibility and durability, highlighting the trade-off with robustness and quality.</cite>
- Security and tamper resistance protect watermarks from removal or alteration by adversaries and enable copy control and traceability strategies.<cite id="c15fa29c-0">Security is a fundamental requirement alongside imperceptibility, robustness, and capacity for secure watermarking schemes.</cite> <cite id="c15fa29c-2">Security implies protection against malicious attacks, complementing robustness and imperceptibility in secure watermarking designs.</cite> <cite id="c15fa29c-3">Balancing capacity, robustness, and security is a central challenge in watermarking system design.</cite>

## Ownership verification, copyright, and control
- Watermarking provides proof of authorship and ownership, enabling content owners to assert rights and deter unauthorized use by making infringement detectable.<cite id="c15fa29c-0">Digital watermarking embeds information to ensure authenticity and protect copyright holders from unauthorized data alteration, supporting ownership verification.</cite> <cite id="c15fa29c-2">Watermarking proves the authenticated owner of media by embedding extractable identifying information.</cite>
- Copy control and broadcast monitoring use watermarking to indicate protected content and verify transmissions, supporting compliance and audit trails.<cite id="c15fa29c-1">For copy protection, watermarks indicate whether content is copyrighted and can be removed only with severe degradation, aligning with standards like CPTWG for DVD copy protection.</cite> <cite id="87fb516c-0">Broadcast monitoring embeds watermarks in advertisements so automated systems can detect and log broadcasts to verify timing and location, aiding royalty tracking and transmission verification.</cite> <cite id="87fb516c-1">In broadcast monitoring, owners embed watermarks prior to transmission; monitoring sites extract them for verification, IPR surveillance, and related applications.</cite>
- Fingerprinting uniquely identifies authorized recipients or copies to trace leakage, supporting accountability and legal action against distributors.<cite id="c15fa29c-0">Watermarking supports fingerprinting for unique identification of media copies, useful for tracking distribution.</cite> <cite id="87fb516c-0">Fingerprinting embeds different watermarks per recipient so that if data is disseminated illicitly, the owner can identify the recipient by extracting the embedded watermark.</cite> <cite id="87fb516c-2">Fingerprinting methods embed unique watermarks to identify and track illicit copies of video content.</cite>

## Integrity, tamper detection, and localization
- Fragile and semi-fragile watermarks enable integrity checking: any alteration renders the watermark invalid, and semi-fragile designs can localize and even reconstruct tampered regions while tolerating benign processing.<cite id="8b0426b8-0">Semi-fragile watermarking detects, localizes, and recovers from tamper attacks; changes in the watermark reflect tampering, while robustness to normal processing distinguishes benign edits from malicious tampering.</cite> <cite id="8b0426b8-1">Semi-fragile watermarks detect tamper locations and manipulations and are robust enough to tolerate normal content changes, supporting content authentication with tamper localization.</cite> <cite id="8b0426b8-2">Fragile watermarks indicate whether data has been altered and can recover tampered regions, while semi-fragile watermarks are robust to some modifications and fragile to intentional attacks, enabling detection and localization of altered regions.</cite>
- These authentication capabilities support forensics and evidence integrity in sensitive domains like surveillance, healthcare, and legal contexts.<cite id="87fb516c-2">Video authentication addresses integrity of surveillance and other critical applications where verifying that content has not been altered is essential.</cite> <cite id="87fb516c-3">Watermarking supports applications such as e-health, forensics, and e-voting where provenance and integrity are crucial.</cite>

## Data hiding and covert communication
- Watermarking provides a covert channel for secret messaging, embedding messages imperceptibly and extracting them only by intended receivers, with lower risk of detection compared to overt signaling.<cite id="c15fa29c-0">Digital watermarking embeds information imperceptibly so that only detectors can reveal it, enabling data hiding for authentication and related purposes.</cite> <cite id="87fb516c-0">Digital watermarking can serve covert communication by embedding secret messages imperceptibly in images or video for communication while minimizing interception by unintended receivers.</cite> <cite id="87fb516c-4">Watermarking supports data authentication and covert communication by embedding hidden messages that are imperceptible to casual observers.</cite>

## Media-specific robustness and quality properties
- Transform-domain watermarking (e.g., DCT/DWT/SVD) typically offers better imperceptibility and robustness than spatial-domain methods, enabling practical deployment across images, audio, and video.<cite id="c15fa29c-2">Transform-domain methods (DWT, DCT, SVD) provide good imperceptibility and robustness, whereas spatial-domain techniques are less robust to geometric attacks but offer higher data hiding capacity.</cite> <cite id="c15fa29c-4">Transform-domain approaches generally demonstrate greater resilience than spatial-domain methods, though both must balance imperceptibility, robustness, and capacity.</cite>
- In audio, robust watermarking is designed to withstand typical processing and compression while remaining inaudible, supporting applications like broadcast monitoring and rights management without perceptual artifacts.<cite id="c15fa29c-3">Audio watermarking systems emphasize robustness to processing and compression and imperceptibility (inaudibility) to maintain quality while enabling verification and tracking.</cite> <cite id="87fb516c-1">Audio and video watermarking leverage robustness and perceptibility to support applications such as broadcast monitoring and copy control across multimedia content.</cite>
- Video watermarking supports copy control, broadcast monitoring, ownership verification, and authentication across large, dynamic media with motion and compression, aligning with real-world workflows in media distribution and archiving.<cite id="87fb516c-2">Video watermarking supports fingerprinting, copy control via protected indications, broadcast monitoring for verification, and authentication for integrity assurance.</cite> <cite id="87fb516c-3">Video watermarking is used for ownership identity, copyright protection, and broadcast monitoring in diverse applications including archiving and digital cinema, emphasizing robustness, perceptibility, capacity, and security.</cite>

## Synergy with related data-hiding techniques
- Compared to steganography, watermarking is more resilient to attacks and better suited for rights management and accountability, while still enabling covert communication when designed for low detectability.<cite id="c15fa29c-3">Steganography can suffer from significant overhead to hide small amounts of data, whereas watermarking provides integrity and robustness; cryptography alone does not prevent illegal copying once decoded.</cite> <cite id="c15fa29c-0">Watermarking is a form of data hiding used for authentication and ownership, distinct from general steganography but sharing the goal of imperceptible embedding.</cite> <cite id="87fb516c-4">Watermarking and steganography both support data authentication and covert communication, with watermarking emphasizing ownership and control (e.g., fingerprinting) and steganography focusing on secrecy of communication.</cite>

## Practical deployment benefits
- Workflow integration: watermarking can be embedded at creation or distribution time and verified by automated systems, supporting scalable monitoring, auditing, and compliance across networks and broadcast channels.<cite id="87fb516c-0">Embedding watermarks in advertisements enables automated broadcast monitoring systems to identify and time-stamp transmissions for verification and tracking.</cite> <cite id="87fb516c-1">Monitoring sites extract embedded watermarks from transmitted content, feeding data to central databases for verification and IPR surveillance.</cite> <cite id="87fb516c-2">Fingerprinting and copy control provide systematic ways to track and restrict reproduction, aligning with industry-standardized copy protection approaches.</cite>
- Trade-offs and adaptability: designers can tune watermark strength and payload to application needs (e.g., high robustness for copy control vs. high capacity for metadata), and modern approaches (including deep learning) aim to improve the balance among imperceptibility, robustness, and capacity.<cite id="c15fa29c-1">There is an inherent trade-off among capacity, robustness, and imperceptibility; applications like copyright protection prioritize imperceptibility and robustness, while high-capacity methods must limit payload to avoid quality loss.</cite> <cite id="c15fa29c-4">Deep learning-based watermarking is proposed to overcome limitations of conventional methods, carefully balancing imperceptibility, robustness, and capacity given their inherent trade-offs.</cite>

## Summary
- Digital watermarking’s core advantages—imperceptibility, robustness, capacity, and security—enable copyright protection, ownership verification, tamper detection/localization, broadcast monitoring and fingerprinting, copy control, and covert communication across images, audio, and video.<cite id="c15fa29c-0">The ideal characteristics of watermarking include imperceptibility, robustness, capacity, and security, supporting applications in fingerprinting, copyright protection, and authentication.</cite> <cite id="8b0426b8-0">Semi-fragile watermarking distinguishes benign processing from tampering and detects/locates alterations, enabling robust content authentication.</cite> <cite id="87fb516c-0">Broadcast monitoring and fingerprinting leverage embedded watermarks to verify transmissions and trace unauthorized distribution, respectively.</cite> <cite id="87fb516c-1">Video watermarking supports fingerprinting, copy control, broadcast monitoring, and authentication in real-world media workflows.</cite> <cite id="87fb516c-4">Watermarking also facilitates data authentication and covert communication by embedding imperceptible information for verification and messaging.</cite>
</answer>

Title: Efficient hybrid digital image watermarking
Snippet: Today, the Internet is the most important and easiest way to connect people all over the world. It allows users to communicate and share multimedia content, such as text, images, audio, and video, with low cost and high quality. However, the most important problem that arises is how to protect critical data during transmission from illegal use [1,2]. Protecting confidential information is a moral and legal requirement. Data hiding is a method for protecting information by hiding it in a multimedia object for the authentication purpose. This process is carried out in such a way that the embedded data is not visible to the naked eye, but it is easily detected by a detector. Data hiding has two main types: digital watermarking and steganography [3,4]. The insertion of a part of information into the multimedia content, where it is not visible to the human eye but can be detected with a detector, is called digital watermarking. Figure 1 introduces the watermarking framework, which consists of the embedding and detection processes. It is suitable for several applications such as fingerprinting, copyright protection, and content authentication, because it has a very important feature that the content is inseparable from the watermark [5,6]. 

Digital watermarking techniques include embedding of a watermark in a multimedia content to ensure authenticity and protect copyright holders from unauthorized data alteration [7]. Consequently, it is vital to specify the prerequisites or properties of a watermarking scheme. The specifications for watermarking schemes are shown in Fig. 2. 

These requirements guarantee the effectiveness of watermarking schemes. The ideal characteristics of digital watermarking include imperceptibility, robustness, capacity, and security [8,9]. 

1. Imperceptibility: Imperceptibility is crucial, when assessing the watermarking scheme effectiveness. It is reflected in faithfulness and invisibility. The watermarked image in this instance needs to look exactly like the original image [10]. 2. Robustness: Robustness is the property that a watermark must have to be detectable after various typical signalprocessing operations used in digital image watermarking systems have been applied.

Title: A Hybrid Robust Image Watermarking Method Based on DWT-DCT and SIFT for Copyright Protection
Snippet: The growth of digital information technologies makes their distribution and duplication much easier. Therefore, the necessity to design secure techniques has increased in the last few decades. Digital image watermarking has been found to be an effective solution for copyright protection of images [1]. Its basic procedure is to embed imperceptible information, termed watermark, in the original image. Thus, the copyright of the image can be provided by extracting the embedded secret watermark. 

Three main properties are required in image watermarking systems [2]: imperceptibility, capacity, and robustness. Imperceptibility refers to the fact that the watermarked image should look identical to the original one. Capacity represents the maximum number of bits embedded in the original image. It is the primary constraint that should be ensured after imperceptibility [3] in high-capacity methods. Indeed, in this category of techniques, a considerable quantity of information should be embedded without losing image quality. In the copyright protection methods, this constraint is less critical, but it can influence the results in terms of robustness of imperceptibility, especially when the watermark size is too big. Robustness refers to the ability to detect the watermark even if the watermarked image suffered from several manipulations called attacks. A good watermarking scheme should ensure the best trade-off between these three properties. Indeed, generally, with the increase of capacity, the robustness of the image decreases while simultaneously decreasing its imperceptibility and vice versa. The main objective of the proposed method is copyright protection. Therefore, capacity is not a primal issue. Indeed, the main requirements for copyright protection applications are imperceptibility and robustness. 

Watermarking schemes can be categorized according to embedding domain, extracting technique, watermark robustness. The embedding domain can be spatial or a transform domain. Spatial methods [4] embed the watermark by directly altering the pixels, while the transform domain methods embed the watermark after performing a transformation, such as DFT [5,6], DCT [7], DWT [8]. The extraction method can be a non-blind, or semi-blind, or a blind technique.

Title: A Hybrid Watermarking Scheme for Increasing Watermark Capacity and Security
Snippet: Since that moment when technology and wireless networks have begun to grow widely around the world a question seemed to arise about how to secure multimedia digital content such as ownership identification, content authentication, copyright protection and tamper detection. From all data hiding techniques (cryptography, watermarking, and steganography), watermarking is the best solution to deal with these tasks. Digital watermarking is simply the process of embedding some information into a multimedia element, such as image, video or audio that can be extracted later on to prove the authenticated owner of the media. Watermarking may be fragile, semi-fragile, or robust, non-blind, semi-blind or blind, visible or invisible etc. Imperceptibility, robustness, capacity, and security are the basic necessities for a secure watermarking scheme. Imperceptible means cover image and watermarked image should be the same. Robustness means that the watermark algorithm should be resistant to geometric attacks (e.g., filtering, scaling, noise addition, translation, rotation, cropping). Security implies protection against noxious attacks [1,2], and capacity simply refers to how much data can be embedded in the original image. 

Watermarking algorithms can be grouped in two categories: spatial domain, and frequency (or transform) domain [1,3]. Transform domain methods (e.g., DWT, DCT, SVD) have good imperceptibility and more robust. Spatial domain techniques are less robust against various geometric attacks, but high data hiding capacity [2]. 

In literature, a tremendous number of research work in watermarking field has been investigated. For example, El-Assy et al. [1] presented a hybrid digital watermarking technique using advantages of four algorithms BEMD, DWT, DCT, and SVD. In their framework, the watermark is embedded into the 2nd IMF and the SVD is applied on the mid frequency band of the DCT block.

Title: Linear Discriminate Analysis based Robust Watermarking in DWT and LWT Domain with PCA based Statistical Feature Reduction
Snippet: With the advancement in technology, digital data is enormously growing in various dimensions.The extensive usage of digital data has now raised the challenge of protecting the integrity and security of data over the internet.With the advancement in technology, altering or updating digital data has become exceedingly more accessible and more straightforward.In order to provide copyright protection and protect the integrity of digital data, there is a requirement of methods or techniques that can assure the integrity of digital data in a sophisticated manner.Various techniques have been suggested for copyright protection and preventing illegal data modification in the literature.Digital image watermarking is one of the oldest and most trusted ways of protecting digital data in a simplified manner [1].Some other techniques are also mentioned in the literature to protect digital content's integrity, like Steganography and cryptography.However, Steganography suffers from the problem of significant overhead to hiding a very tiny amount of information [2].Cryptography is lacking because once a secret message is decoded, it can be copied illegally any number of times without any overhead [1].Keeping the above things in mind, the image watermarking technique has become one of the possible solutions for securing the integrity of digital content.

One of the significant challenges for a watermarking system is to maintain an adequate balance (trade-off) between the image qualities, capacity, and security of the watermarked image [3].The basic requirements for a watermarking system are capacity, robustness, security, and imperceptibility.Capacity is the number of bits embedded using the watermarking process; robustness means exhibiting good performance against most image attacks, and imperceptibility means satisfying watermarked images.Robustness is measured and calculated using normalized coefficient (NC) and bit error rate (BER).On the other hand, imperceptibility is also a standard measure and is calculated in terms of the peak signal to noise ratio (PSNR).On the basis of robustness, a watermarking system can be categorized as robust watermarking, fragile watermarking, and semi-fragile watermarking [3].This technique presents a robust and blind watermarking technique.The embedding and extraction of a watermark can be done using the spatial and frequency transformation of the image.

Title: Deep Learning-Based Image Watermarking Using Catalan Transform and Non-Negative Matrix Factorization
Snippet: The creation, distribution, and consumption of digital content have been transformed by the accelerated advancements in internet and multimedia technologies. However, these developments have also introduced significant challenges in protecting intellectual property rights and ensuring the authenticity of digital media [2], [3], [4]. Digital 

The associate editor coordinating the review of this manuscript and approving it for publication was Olarik Surinta . 

watermarking has become an essential method for embedding identifying information inside digital output, maintaining its quality and usability. Despite extensive research in this domain, conventional watermarking techniques face several limitations, including low robustness against attacks, limited application scope, and trade-offs between imperceptibility, robustness, and watermark capacity [5], [6], [9]. A comprehensive classification of watermarking techniques is presented in Fig. 1, organized into five main categories: visibility, document type, extraction method, attack resistance, and processing domain. This classification highlights the diverse strategies used in watermarking technology, reflecting its complexity and versatility. Conventional watermarking methods, summarized in Fig. 2, include copyright markers by altering either the pixel values or transform coefficients of the host image. Although transform domain methods demonstrate greater resilience compared to spatial domain techniques, they still suffer from limitations such as lower resistance to attacks and restricted application scenarios [8]. The evaluation of watermarking techniques requires a careful analysis of three key factors: imperceptibility, robustness, and watermark capacity. Imperceptibility denotes the degree to which the watermarking procedure influences the visual quality of the source image. Robustness evaluates the watermark's capacity to endure diverse purposeful and inadvertent assaults, like compression, scaling, or noise introduction. The watermark capacity defines the maximum amount of information that can be embedded without compromising invisibility and durability. Fig. 3 illustrates the inherent trade-offs among these factors, highlighting the challenge of balancing them effectively. For example, improving robustness may increase watermark visibility, while increasing the data payload could degrade the host image quality. Deep learning-based watermarking methods have recently gained attention as a promising alternative, offering solutions to some of these challenges [7], [10].

Today, the Internet is the most important and easiest way to connect people all over the world. It allows users to communicate and share multimedia content, such as text, images, audio, and video, with low cost and high quality. However, the most important problem that arises is how to protect critical data during transmission from illegal use [1,2]. Protecting confidential information is a moral and legal requirement. Data hiding is a method for protecting information by hiding it in a multimedia object for the authentication purpose. This process is carried out in such a way that the embedded data is not visible to the naked eye, but it is easily detected by a detector. Data hiding has two main types: digital watermarking and steganography [3,4]. The insertion of a part of information into the multimedia content, where it is not visible to the human eye but can be detected with a detector, is called digital watermarking. Figure 1 introduces the watermarking framework, which consists of the embedding and detection processes. It is suitable for several applications such as fingerprinting, copyright protection, and content authentication, because it has a very important feature that the content is inseparable from the watermark [5,6]. 

Digital watermarking techniques include embedding of a watermark in a multimedia content to ensure authenticity and protect copyright holders from unauthorized data alteration [7]. Consequently, it is vital to specify the prerequisites or properties of a watermarking scheme. The specifications for watermarking schemes are shown in Fig. 2. 

These requirements guarantee the effectiveness of watermarking schemes. The ideal characteristics of digital watermarking include imperceptibility, robustness, capacity, and security [8,9]. 

1. Imperceptibility: Imperceptibility is crucial, when assessing the watermarking scheme effectiveness. It is reflected in faithfulness and invisibility. The watermarked image in this instance needs to look exactly like the original image [10]. 2. Robustness: Robustness is the property that a watermark must have to be detectable after various typical signalprocessing operations used in digital image watermarking systems have been applied.

documents.title: A Hybrid Robust Image Watermarking Method Based on DWT-DCT and SIFT for Copyright Protection
documents.snippet:
The growth of digital information technologies makes their distribution and duplication much easier. Therefore, the necessity to design secure techniques has increased in the last few decades. Digital image watermarking has been found to be an effective solution for copyright protection of images [1]. Its basic procedure is to embed imperceptible information, termed watermark, in the original image. Thus, the copyright of the image can be provided by extracting the embedded secret watermark. 

Three main properties are required in image watermarking systems [2]: imperceptibility, capacity, and robustness. Imperceptibility refers to the fact that the watermarked image should look identical to the original one. Capacity represents the maximum number of bits embedded in the original image. It is the primary constraint that should be ensured after imperceptibility [3] in high-capacity methods. Indeed, in this category of techniques, a considerable quantity of information should be embedded without losing image quality. In the copyright protection methods, this constraint is less critical, but it can influence the results in terms of robustness of imperceptibility, especially when the watermark size is too big. Robustness refers to the ability to detect the watermark even if the watermarked image suffered from several manipulations called attacks. A good watermarking scheme should ensure the best trade-off between these three properties. Indeed, generally, with the increase of capacity, the robustness of the image decreases while simultaneously decreasing its imperceptibility and vice versa. The main objective of the proposed method is copyright protection. Therefore, capacity is not a primal issue. Indeed, the main requirements for copyright protection applications are imperceptibility and robustness. 

Watermarking schemes can be categorized according to embedding domain, extracting technique, watermark robustness. The embedding domain can be spatial or a transform domain. Spatial methods [4] embed the watermark by directly altering the pixels, while the transform domain methods embed the watermark after performing a transformation, such as DFT [5,6], DCT [7], DWT [8]. The extraction method can be a non-blind, or semi-blind, or a blind technique.

documents.title: A Hybrid Watermarking Scheme for Increasing Watermark Capacity and Security
documents.snippet:
Since that moment when technology and wireless networks have begun to grow widely around the world a question seemed to arise about how to secure multimedia digital content such as ownership identification, content authentication, copyright protection and tamper detection. From all data hiding techniques (cryptography, watermarking, and steganography), watermarking is the best solution to deal with these tasks. Digital watermarking is simply the process of embedding some information into a multimedia element, such as image, video or audio that can be extracted later on to prove the authenticated owner of the media. Watermarking may be fragile, semi-fragile, or robust, non-blind, semi-blind or blind, visible or invisible etc. Imperceptibility, robustness, capacity, and security are the basic necessities for a secure watermarking scheme. Imperceptible means cover image and watermarked image should be the same. Robustness means that the watermark algorithm should be resistant to geometric attacks (e.g., filtering, scaling, noise addition, translation, rotation, cropping). Security implies protection against noxious attacks [1,2], and capacity simply refers to how much data can be embedded in the original image. 

Watermarking algorithms can be grouped in two categories: spatial domain, and frequency (or transform) domain [1,3]. Transform domain methods (e.g., DWT, DCT, SVD) have good imperceptibility and more robust. Spatial domain techniques are less robust against various geometric attacks, but high data hiding capacity [2]. 

In literature, a tremendous number of research work in watermarking field has been investigated. For example, El-Assy et al. [1] presented a hybrid digital watermarking technique using advantages of four algorithms BEMD, DWT, DCT, and SVD. In their framework, the watermark is embedded into the 2nd IMF and the SVD is applied on the mid frequency band of the DCT block.

With the advancement in technology, digital data is enormously growing in various dimensions.The extensive usage of digital data has now raised the challenge of protecting the integrity and security of data over the internet.With the advancement in technology, altering or updating digital data has become exceedingly more accessible and more straightforward.In order to provide copyright protection and protect the integrity of digital data, there is a requirement of methods or techniques that can assure the integrity of digital data in a sophisticated manner.Various techniques have been suggested for copyright protection and preventing illegal data modification in the literature.Digital image watermarking is one of the oldest and most trusted ways of protecting digital data in a simplified manner [1].Some other techniques are also mentioned in the literature to protect digital content's integrity, like Steganography and cryptography.However, Steganography suffers from the problem of significant overhead to hiding a very tiny amount of information [2].Cryptography is lacking because once a secret message is decoded, it can be copied illegally any number of times without any overhead [1].Keeping the above things in mind, the image watermarking technique has become one of the possible solutions for securing the integrity of digital content.

One of the significant challenges for a watermarking system is to maintain an adequate balance (trade-off) between the image qualities, capacity, and security of the watermarked image [3].The basic requirements for a watermarking system are capacity, robustness, security, and imperceptibility.Capacity is the number of bits embedded using the watermarking process; robustness means exhibiting good performance against most image attacks, and imperceptibility means satisfying watermarked images.Robustness is measured and calculated using normalized coefficient (NC) and bit error rate (BER).On the other hand, imperceptibility is also a standard measure and is calculated in terms of the peak signal to noise ratio (PSNR).On the basis of robustness, a watermarking system can be categorized as robust watermarking, fragile watermarking, and semi-fragile watermarking [3].This technique presents a robust and blind watermarking technique.The embedding and extraction of a watermark can be done using the spatial and frequency transformation of the image.

documents.snippet:
The creation, distribution, and consumption of digital content have been transformed by the accelerated advancements in internet and multimedia technologies. However, these developments have also introduced significant challenges in protecting intellectual property rights and ensuring the authenticity of digital media [2], [3], [4]. Digital 

The associate editor coordinating the review of this manuscript and approving it for publication was Olarik Surinta . 

watermarking has become an essential method for embedding identifying information inside digital output, maintaining its quality and usability. Despite extensive research in this domain, conventional watermarking techniques face several limitations, including low robustness against attacks, limited application scope, and trade-offs between imperceptibility, robustness, and watermark capacity [5], [6], [9]. A comprehensive classification of watermarking techniques is presented in Fig. 1, organized into five main categories: visibility, document type, extraction method, attack resistance, and processing domain. This classification highlights the diverse strategies used in watermarking technology, reflecting its complexity and versatility. Conventional watermarking methods, summarized in Fig. 2, include copyright markers by altering either the pixel values or transform coefficients of the host image. Although transform domain methods demonstrate greater resilience compared to spatial domain techniques, they still suffer from limitations such as lower resistance to attacks and restricted application scenarios [8]. The evaluation of watermarking techniques requires a careful analysis of three key factors: imperceptibility, robustness, and watermark capacity. Imperceptibility denotes the degree to which the watermarking procedure influences the visual quality of the source image. Robustness evaluates the watermark's capacity to endure diverse purposeful and inadvertent assaults, like compression, scaling, or noise introduction. The watermark capacity defines the maximum amount of information that can be embedded without compromising invisibility and durability. Fig. 3 illustrates the inherent trade-offs among these factors, highlighting the challenge of balancing them effectively. For example, improving robustness may increase watermark visibility, while increasing the data payload could degrade the host image quality. Deep learning-based watermarking methods have recently gained attention as a promising alternative, offering solutions to some of these challenges [7], [10].

Snippet: Semi-fragile watermarking algorithms for image authentication focus on the ability of detection, location and recovery from tamper attacks carried out on images. Because the semi-fragile watermark has a certain degree of fragility, the algorithm can realize the image authentication according to whether the watermarking data is tampered with. When the host image suffers attacks, the watermarking information will make a corresponding change as well. However, for normal image-processing operations, the semi-fragile watermark also has a certain degree of robustness, so that the normal image processing operations and malicious tampering operations can be distinguished. The framework of the semi-fragile watermarking authentication system contains the watermark embedding process and the watermark detection process. In the embedding process, the watermark can be the information that is determined by the contents of the original image, or the information that is irrelevant to the original image. 

In the detection process, the watermarking information in the tested image is extracted and compared with the original watermark. If the two are consistent, we consider that the image has not been tampered with; if the two are inconsistent, we consider that the image has been tampered with. Then the algorithm enters the tamper detection and recovery process. In addition, when the watermarking information is generated using image content features, in the authentication process, there is no need to provide the original watermarking information. Only the comparison between the extracted watermarking information and image content features is needed.

Snippet: Widespread and affordable access to the Internet, smartphones, and other digital devices allow individuals to acquire and share images with millions of people at the click of a button. People are now able to make unlimited copies of digital information [1]. Therefore, image copyright infringement is exceedingly likely. As a security mechanism, digital watermarking may be used to prevent this infringement [2,3]. 

Digital watermarking refers to a process whereby data are embedded into a digital signal such as images, audio clips, or video sequences [2]. The covert marker, inserted in the signal is known as a digital watermark and usually contains signal-related information [4]. 

Based on the robustness, watermarking methods are divided into three categories: (1) robust, (2) fragile, and (3) semi-fragile [5]. In the first group, embedded watermark is robust against any distorting operation and remains extractable and usable. Contrarily, fragile methods are extremely sensitive to signal modification and are typically used to protect signal integrity [5]. Some fragile methods are capable of recovering the tampered regions [6,7,8]. Semi-fragile methods can withstand certain modifications [5]: they are robust against attacks which maintain signal content while being fragile against attacks that aim to modify the meaning of the signal. Semi-fragile methods can detect intentional attacks and identify or even reconstruct the tampered regions [9]. 

Watermarking methods have received considerable research attention; however, attacks on these methods remain to be investigated in greater depth [10]. In general, an attack is a process which interferes with watermark detection or the information communicated by the watermark in the carrier signal. Attacks are either intentional or unintentional [11]. 

As in cryptography, different levels of attacks can be carried out against watermarking methods, depending on the information available to the adversary [12].

Title: A DFT-DWT Domain Invisible Blind Watermarking Techniques for Copyright Protection of Digital Images
Snippet: Although the main motivation behind the digital watermarking is the copyright protection, its applications are not that restricted. There is a wide application area of digital watermarking, including broadcast monitoring, fingerprinting, authentication and covet communication [7,8,9,10]. 

By embedding watermarks into commercial advertisements, the advertisements can be monitored whether the advertisements are broadcasted at the correct instants by means of an automated system [7,8]. The system receives the broadcast and searches these watermarks identifying where and when the advertisement is broadcasted. The same process can also be used for video and sound clips. Musicians and actors may request to ensure that they receive accurate royalties for broadcasts of their performances. 

Fingerprinting is a novel approach to trace the source of illegal copies [7,8]. The owner of the digital data may embed different watermarks in the copies of digital content customized for each recipient. In this manner, the owner can identify the customer by extracting the watermark in the case the data is supplied to third parties. The digital watermarking can also be used for authentication [7,8]. The authentication is the detection of whether the content of the digital content has changed.
