problem: I need a detailed introduction about the principle of Topological Autoencoder. Please give me the most information as you can.
final_response:
# Overview and Motivation

Topological Autoencoders (TAEs) are neural autoencoder models augmented with a topological regularization term that constrains the latent representation to preserve salient topological features of the input data, such as connected components, loops, or higher-dimensional holes, measured via persistent homology (PH). The central idea is to align the multi-scale topological structure of the high-dimensional inputs with that of the low-dimensional latents, so that the learned embeddings are not only faithful to data geometry but also interpretable at the level of topological structure, while maintaining competitive reconstruction quality.<cite id="d4a60e9c-1">Topological Autoencoders aim to preserve topological features of the input in low-dimensional representations by regularizing the similarity of persistence diagrams between the latent and input spaces, treating mini-batches as point clouds and computing PH via Vietoris–Rips complexes</cite><cite id="f91f2402-0">Topological autoencoders preserve persistent homology information of the input space in latent representations, with theoretical justification for combining PH computations with backpropagation and mini-batch approximations</cite><cite id="f91f2402-3">A topological loss based on persistent homology aligns the topology of input and latent spaces so the encoder learns to retain multi-scale connectivity information</cite>.

This direction addresses a gap in standard autoencoders: while they often learn meaningful structures, they do not explicitly guarantee that topological features such as loops or multiple manifolds are preserved. Early works showed that enforcing a preferred topology in the latent space can improve one-class learning and downstream tasks, motivating TAEs as a generic constraint for dimensionality reduction and representation learning.<cite id="d4a60e9c-1">A prior differentiable loss enforcing a preferred topological “scale” in the latent space improved one-class learning, suggesting that constraining latent topology can be beneficial for learning</cite>.

# Core Principle: Preserving Topology via Persistent Homology

Persistent homology provides a multiscale description of topological features (e.g., 0th homology tracks connected components, 1st homology tracks loops, etc.) computed over filtered complexes (e.g., Vietoris–Rips) and summarized as barcodes or diagrams. TAEs leverage PH to define a topology-aware objective: make the PH of the latent space similar to that of the input space, thereby encouraging the encoder to preserve topological structures across scales.<cite id="d4a60e9c-1">The TAE regularization compares persistence diagrams for the input and latent spaces derived from Vietoris–Rips filtrations, treating mini-batches as point clouds and using PH to capture creation/destruction of topological features</cite><cite id="f91f2402-0">Under weak assumptions, PH computations can be combined with backpropagation, and approximating PH on mini-batches is theoretically justified</cite>.

In practice, the method operates on mini-batches as point clouds, computes PH of both the input batch and the encoded latent batch, and aligns corresponding topological signatures. This alignment can be phrased as a distance-based comparison: for simplices that are critical for creating or destroying PH classes (k-critical edges), the model matches selected inter-point distances in the input with those in the latent space, promoting topological similarity across scales.<cite id="d4a60e9c-1">The regularization compares “selected” distances in the data space with the corresponding distances in the latent space for relevant simplices that create or kill PH k classes, and is differentiable when the persistence diagram is discrete</cite>.

# How the Topological Loss Is Defined

A key technical contribution of TAEs is making the PH-based constraint differentiable so it can be integrated into end-to-end training. The loss can be constructed by focusing on k-critical edges in the Vietoris–Rips filtration—edges whose appearance or disappearance creates or destroys a PH_k class—then aligning the associated distances in the input and latent spaces. In the 0th homology case (connected components), this reduces to working with minimum spanning trees (MSTs): critical edges correspond to tree edges whose removal increases the number of connected components, and the loss compares selected tree-edge distances between input and latent encodings.<cite id="d4a60e9c-2">The topological regularization term compares topological abstractions of input and latent representations; for PH0 it uses MST(X) and MST(Z), with k-critical edges corresponding to those that create or kill PH_k classes</cite>.

More generally, the loss compares PH-derived “selected distances” from the full distance matrix in the input to analogous distances in the latent space. When the PH signatures are discrete (no coincident points in the diagram), this comparison is differentiable, enabling standard SGD-based training with automatic gradient computation.<cite id="d4a60e9c-1">By consistently mapping simplices to a given edge in the Vietoris–Rips complex and comparing selected distances between spaces, the regularization is differentiable under the discreteness assumption of persistence diagrams, allowing end-to-end training</cite>.

# Training Objectives and Differentiability

TAEs extend standard autoencoders by adding a topological loss L_t to the reconstruction term (e.g., MSE). The combined objective trains the encoder to compress data while preserving PH-inferred structures, without sacrificing reconstruction fidelity. The differentiability of PH-based terms hinges on discrete diagrams and batch-level approximations: computing PH on mini-batches yields suitable approximations of the full-space PH, and the approach provides theoretical stability for these mini-batch estimates.<cite id="f91f2402-1">A topological loss term harmonizes the data-space and latent-space topology and is shown to be stable on mini-batches, justifying PH approximations for training</cite><cite id="f91f2402-0">The method shows how persistent homology calculations can be combined with backpropagation and proves mini-batch PH approximations are theoretically justified</cite>.

Empirically, the topological loss can be incorporated into various architectures, including variational setups, and can be adapted beyond autoencoders (e.g., a “TopoPCA”), illustrating the generality of the constraint. However, computational complexity grows with the dimension of PH features and batch size, limiting practical use for high-dimensional features without approximations.<cite id="f91f2402-0">The loss is highly generalizable across architectures, including VAEs and PCA variants, but higher-dimensional PH computations scale poorly with batch size</cite>.

# What Is Preserved: From 0th to Higher Homology

- 0th Homology (Connectivity): By aligning MST edge distances between input and latent encodings, the loss encourages the preservation of connected components and global clustering structure in the latent space.<cite id="d4a60e9c-2">For PH0, k-critical edges correspond to MST edges, and the regularization compares selected distances in input and latent spaces</cite>.

- 1st Homology (Loops and Cycles): The same framework generalizes to 1st homology by identifying 1-critical edges in the Vietoris–Rips filtration (edges that create or kill 1D holes) and aligning their associated distances. Implementations often begin with PH0 and extend to higher features as compute allows.<cite id="d4a60e9c-2">The formulation considers k-critical edges for 0 ≤ k ≤ d and discusses PH0/PH1; in practice the method was documented for PH0 using MSTs, with PH1 relying on critical cycles</cite>.

- Higher-Order Features and Limitations: As the target feature dimension increases, computing and matching higher-dimensional critical simplices becomes more expensive, and stability/accuracy of mini-batch PH approximations and differentiability assumptions become more challenging, motivating scalability-focused variants and parameterizations.<cite id="f91f2402-0">Computing the topological loss for higher-dimensional features suffers from growing complexity and scaling issues with batch size</cite>.

# Variants and Extensions

- Topological Autoencoders++ (TopoAE++): Builds on the original TAE by refining how topological information is extracted and matched. It formalizes the alignment of k-critical edges and distances, and focuses on PH0 via MSTs in initial reports, providing a concrete and scalable loss recipe for practical implementations.<cite id="d4a60e9c-2">TopoAE++ summarizes the TAE approach, defines k-critical edges, and specializes the loss for PH0 using MSTs, enabling practical, fast training</cite>.

- Cycle-Aware and Graph-Structured Constraints: By emphasizing cycles and critical structures (edges creating or destroying holes), variants make the loss target specific topological phenomena beyond mere separation of clusters, aligning latent geometry with cyclic features present in the data.<cite id="d4a60e9c-2">The loss targets k-critical edges that create or kill PH classes, focusing the encoder on preserving such topological events</cite>.

- Topology-Aware Parameterizations (Circular Coordinates): Complementary to TAEs, some methods parameterize latent variables or model outputs with circular (angle) coordinates induced by persistent cohomology, providing direct circle-valued functions that reflect 1D homology. This can be useful when data exhibit periodic or annular/toroidal structure and complements PH-based losses by shaping the latent geometry to match homotopy classes of maps to the circle.<cite id="02c44193-0">Circular coordinates leverage H^1(B; Z) ≅ [B, S^1] to turn 1D (persistent) cohomology classes into circle-valued functions on data, enabling topology-aware parameterizations</cite><cite id="02c44193-2">Circular coordinates provide a natural procedure to construct nonlinear, circle-valued parameterizations from persistent topology</cite>.

# Relation to Mapper and Broader TDA+DL

Mapper, a TDA pipeline, builds a compressed representation of data by filtering, covering, and clustering, often revealing global topological structure and networks of loops/handles. While not an autoencoder, Mapper shares the TAE goal of preserving topology for interpretability; indeed, TDA-informed objectives like PH loss can be used to guide dimensionality reduction or segmentation so that resulting embeddings reflect the same topological graphs or manifolds revealed by Mapper.<cite id="02c44193-4">Topological data analysis connects PH and local/global geometry, with methods like persistence landscapes/images vectorizing topology for machine learning and emphasizing that short bars (local features) can be as important as long ones</cite><cite id="02c44193-0">Localization, homological coordinatization, and circular coordinates provide ways to map PH insights into concrete realizations or parameterizations of data structure</cite>.

More broadly, PH-based objectives have diffused across deep learning: they appear both as supervised losses to shape decision boundary topology and as priors in autoencoders to enforce latent topology. TAEs exemplify the latter, integrating PH into unsupervised representation learning, while related works apply PH or Morse-theoretic tools to segmentation and uncertainty quantification.<cite id="02c44193-3">PH objectives have been integrated into deep learning both to shape decision boundaries and to impose topological priors on latent spaces in autoencoders; PH and discrete Morse theory have also been applied to image segmentation and uncertainty quantification</cite>.

# Empirical Behavior and Applications

On synthetic and real-world datasets, TAEs produce latent representations that preserve multi-scale connectivity and spatially arrange classes into entangled structures reflecting underlying manifolds, rather than merely separating them into disjoint clusters. This often improves interpretability and can yield benefits on downstream metrics that depend on proximity on manifolds or density preservation, without significantly increasing reconstruction error.<cite id="f91f2402-0">Experiments show TAEs capture spatial relationships between nested high-dimensional spheres and produce interpretable, manifold-respecting embeddings; competitive performance on multiple quality metrics is observed without harming reconstruction</cite><cite id="f91f2402-3">The approach yields favorable latent representations on synthetic manifolds and image datasets while maintaining low reconstruction error</cite>.

TAE-style losses have also been deployed in segmentation to improve topology-sensitive metrics and in adversarial defenses (e.g., TopoReformer), where a TAE purifies inputs by aligning their latent topology to a desired structure, thereby mitigating adversarial perturbations in OCR tasks. These applications highlight how topology-aware latents can improve robustness and functional alignment with the data’s intrinsic structure.<cite id="f91f2402-2">A persistent-homology-driven topological loss improved segmentation performance on topological-relevant metrics and is generic across architectures</cite><cite id="d4a60e9c-4">TopoReformer uses the TAE methodology, detailing PH, persistence diagrams, and the associated topological loss, and applies it to mitigate adversarial attacks in OCR models</cite>.

# Practical Considerations and Trade-offs

- Choice of PH Features and Scale: Selecting which homology dimensions to regularize (e.g., PH0 vs PH1) and at which filtration scales affects what structure is preserved; focusing on 0th homology aligns clustering via MSTs, while higher homology targets loops and handles but at greater computational cost.<cite id="d4a60e9c-2">PH0 corresponds to MST-based critical edges, while PH1 involves cycle-based criticalities with increased complexity</cite>.

- Differentiability and Stability: The PH-based loss requires discrete diagrams for straightforward differentiability; in practice, mini-batch approximations and discrete sampling are used, with theoretical stability results supporting their use, though higher-dimensional features scale poorly with batch size and resolution.<cite id="d4a60e9c-1">Differentiability follows under discreteness of persistence diagrams and mini-batch approximations</cite><cite id="f91f2402-0">Mini-batch PH approximations are theoretically justified, but higher-dimensional PH computations scale worse with batch size</cite>.

- Architectural Flexibility and Objectives: TAE-style regularization can be added to standard autoencoders or adapted to other dimensionality reduction frameworks (e.g., TopoPCA) and variational setups, but practitioners must balance topological fidelity against reconstruction and training speed.<cite id="f91f2402-0">The topological loss is general and can be integrated into VAEs and PCA variants, though computational costs grow with feature dimension and batch size</cite>.

- Interpretation and Downstream Tasks: TAEs aim for interpretable, topology-respecting embeddings; empirical observations show improved density preservation and meaningful spatial arrangements, though gains are task-dependent and may not universally outperform purely reconstruction-based training on all metrics.<cite id="f91f2402-0">TAEs produce entangled, manifold-respecting structures and perform competitively on multiple quality metrics without degrading reconstruction</cite>.

# Summary

Topological Autoencoders operationalize the principle of preserving the essential shape of data in latent representations by aligning persistent homology between inputs and latents through differentiable, distance-based losses. By constraining k-critical structures (edges creating/destroying PH features) and leveraging mini-batch PH approximations, TAEs provide a theoretically grounded and flexible mechanism to enforce topology in autoencoders, improving interpretability and, in practice, downstream performance on tasks ranging from manifold learning and segmentation to robustness against adversarial attacks. As research continues, extensions such as cycle-aware losses and circular-coordinate parameterizations complement PH regularization, and broader TDA tools like Mapper and vectorization methods (persistence landscapes/images) offer additional pathways to integrate topology into deep learning pipelines.<cite id="d4a60e9c-1">TAEs align persistence diagrams of input and latent spaces via differentiable regularization on mini-batches, extending prior topology-control losses and treating each batch as a point cloud</cite><cite id="d4a60e9c-2">TopoAE++ formalizes k-critical-edge-based losses, specializing to MSTs for PH0 and focusing on computationally tractable cycle-aware constraints</cite><cite id="f91f2402-0">Theoretical results justify combining PH with backpropagation and mini-batch approximations, with empirical evidence of improved interpretability and competitive metrics</cite><cite id="02c44193-0">Circular coordinates and related homological methods provide concrete realizations and parameterizations that complement PH-based regularization</cite><cite id="02c44193-3">PH objectives have been widely adopted across deep learning, both to shape decision boundaries and to impose topology priors in autoencoders</cite><cite id="d4a60e9c-4">Applications such as TopoReformer demonstrate practical efficacy of TAE-style topology purification for robustness</cite>.

Title: A Survey of Topological Machine Learning Methods
Snippet: As a recent example, Moor et al. (2020) propose a topological autoencoder, which aims to preserve topological features of the input data in low-dimensional representations. This is achieved via a regularisation term that incentivises the persistence diagrams of both the latent and input space to be topologically similar. This method acts on the level of mini-batches, treating each of them as a point cloud. Persistence diagrams are obtained from the Vietoris-Rips complex of each space. By tracking the simplices that are relevant for the creation and destruction of topological features, and by consistently mapping simplices to a given edge in the Vietoris-Rips complex, each filtration can be interpreted as a selection of distances from the full distance matrix of the point cloud. The proposed regularisation term then compares the "selected" distances in the data space with the corresponding distances in the latent space (and vice versa). Finally, this regularisation is differentiable under the assumption that the persistence diagram is discrete (i.e., for each of its points, there is an infinitesimal neighbourhood containing no other points). The scheme can thus be directly integrated into the end-to-end training of an autoencoder, making it aware of the topology in the data space. This work can also be considered as an extension of previous work by Hofer C. et al. (2019), who introduced a differentiable loss term for one-class learning that controls the topology of the latent space; in effect, their loss term enforces a preferred "scale" for topological features in the latent space. It does not have to harmonise topological features across different spaces. It turns out that an autoencoder trained with this loss term on unlabelled data can be used on other data sets for one-class learning. This hints at the fact that enforcing a certain topological structure can be beneficial for learning tasks; we will later see that such empirical observations can also be furnished with a theoretical underpinning. 

An approach by Chen et al. (2019) takes a different perspective. The authors develop a measure of the topological complexity (in terms of connected components) of the classification boundary of a given classifier.

Title: Topological Autoencoders
Snippet: We presented topological autoencoders, a novel method for preserving topological information, measured in terms of persistent homology, of the input space when learning latent representations with deep neural networks. Under weak theoretical assumptions, we showed how our persistent homology calculations can be combined with backpropagation; moreover, we proved that approximating persistent homology on the level of mini-batches is theoretically justified. In our experiments, we observed that our method is uniquely able to capture spatial relationships between nested highdimensional spheres. This is relevant, as the ability to cope with several manifolds in the domain of manifold learning still remains a challenging task. On real-world data sets, we observed that our topological loss leads to competitive performance in terms of numerous quality metrics (such as a density preservation metric), while not adversely affecting the reconstruction error. In both synthetic and real-world data sets, we obtain interesting and interpretable representations, as our method does not merely pull apart different classes, but tries to spatially arrange them meaningfully. Thus, we do not observe mere distinct "clouds", but rather entangled structures, which we consider to constitute a more meaningful representation of the underlying manifolds (an auxiliary analysis in Supplementary Section A.10 confirms that our method influences topological features, measured using PH, in a beneficial manner). 

Future work Our topological loss formulation is highly generalisable; it only requires the existence of a distance matrix between individual samples (either globally, or on the level of batches). As a consequence, our topological loss term can be directly integrated into a variety of different architectures and is not limited to standard autoencoders. For instance, we can also apply our constraint to variational setups (see Figure A.3 for a sketch) or create a topology-aware variant of principal component analysis (dubbed "TopoPCA"; see Table A.2 for more details, as well as Figures A.6, A.7, and A.8 for the corresponding latent space representations). Employing our loss term to more involved architectures will be an exciting route for future work. One issue with the calculation is that, given the computational complexity of calculating R (•), for higherdimensional features, we would scale progressively worse with increasing batch size.
</snippet>
<snippet id=f91f2402-1>
Title: Topological Autoencoders
Snippet: While topological features, in particular multi-scale features derived from persistent homology, have seen increasing use in the machine learning community (Carrière et al., 2019, Guss & Salakhutdinov, 2018, Hofer et al., 2017, 2019a,b, Ramamurthy et al., 2019, Reininghaus et al., 2015, Rieck et al., 2019a,b), employing topology directly as a constraint for modern deep learning methods remains a challenge. This is due to the inherently discrete nature of these computations, making backpropagation through the computation of topological signatures immensely difficult or only possible in certain special circumstances (Chen et al., 2019, Hofer et al., 2019a, Poulenard et al., 2018). This work presents a novel approach that permits obtaining gradients during the computation of topological signatures. This makes it possible to employ topological constraints while training deep neural networks, as well as building topology-preserving autoencoders. Title: Topological Autoencoders
Snippet: We propose a novel approach for preserving topological structures of the input space in latent representations of autoencoders. Using persistent homology, a technique from topological data analysis, we calculate topological signatures of both the input and latent space to derive a topological loss term. Under weak theoretical assumptions, we construct this loss in a differentiable manner, such that the encoding learns to retain multi-scale connectivity information. Persistent (co)homology is one avenue to address the topology inference problem [38,12]; it provides a multiscale description of topological features, and satisfies several inference theorems [30,8,10]. Going from a persistent homology computation to actionable knowledge about the initial data set, is in general highly nontrivial. One would like to determine: how are the persistent homology features reflected on the data? if the homology suggests a candidate underlying space X, what is a concrete realization (e.g., via equations or as a quotient)? how does the data fit on/around the realization? At least three approaches have been proposed in the literature to address these questions: localization, homological coordinatization and circular coordinates.

For a relevant homology class, the idea behind localization is to find an appropriate representative cycle. This strategy is successful in low dimensions [15,16], but in general even reasonable heuristics lead to NP-hard problems which are NP-hard to approximate [9]. Homological coordinatization [36] attempts to map a simplicial complex on the data to a simplicial complex with prescribed homology -a model suggested by a persistent homology computation. The map is selected by examining the set of chain homotopy classes of chain maps between the complex on the data and the model. Selecting an appropriate representative chain map, however, involves combinatorial optimizations which are difficult to solve in practice. Circular coordinates [13] leverages the following fact: there is a bijection H 1 (B; Z) ∼ = B, S 1 between the 1-dimensional Z-cohomology of a topological space B, and the set of homotopy classes of maps from B to the circle S 1 . When B is a simplicial complex with the data as vertex set, this observation is used to turn 1-dimensional (persistent) Z/p-cohomology classes for appropriate primes p, into circle-valued functions on the data.

The circular coordinates approach has been used successfully -for instance to parameterize periodic dynamics [14] -and is part of a bigger picture

Title: A Quotient Homology Theory of Representation in Neural Networks
Snippet: Persistent homology is an essential tool for computing homology groups of data from different domains of science (Carlsson (2009); Wasserman (2018)), including machine learning (Papamarkou et al. (2024)). For better or worse, it is not a purely topological method as it also tracks geometric features of the underlying point cloud (Bubenik et al. (2020); Turkes et al. (2022)). Plus, it is highly sensitive to the sampling density and the chosen metric. While sometimes there are ways to overcome these problems, it is likely that geometric properties are sneaking into our discussion of topology. 

To show the effectiveness of our method, we generated datasets of highly non-linear curves by the equation f (θ) = [cos(aθ) cos(bθ), cos(aθ) sin(bθ)] T . The parameters a, b were randomly sampled from a uniform distribution on the interval [−1, 1]. We sampled 500 equally spaced points θ ∈ [−π, π]. Afterwards, we used a MSE loss to optimize a neural network with three layers, each with a width of 50 neurons, to predict these functions given the input points (θ, 0). The parameters for all simulations are described in detail in Appendix C. Following training we compute the first homology groups H 1 of the output of the final network layer. We do this in two ways: standard persistent homology with the Euclidean metric and quotient homology using the metric as described in Appendix A.5.1. 

In Figure 1 we show two examples of learned curves and their associated homology groups given by the barcodes below. One can see that in the first example, standard persistent homology identifies a circular feature as the ends of the interval are close in the output despite the fact that the network does not map them onto each other. This error is avoided when using quotient homology, as seen by the lack of bars in the barcode plot. In the second example, we see that both persistent homology as well as quotient homology generate two persistent features.

Snippet: In a physical setting, circular coordinates occur naturally as angular and phase variables. Spaces like the annulus and the torus are well described by a combination of real and circular coordinates. (The 2-sphere is not so lucky, and must await its day.) 

The goal of this paper is to describe a natural procedure for constructing circular coordinates on a nonlinear data set using techniques from classical algebraic topology and its 21st-century grandchild, persistent topology. We direct the reader to [9] as a general reference for algebraic topology, and to [17] for a streamlined account of persistent homology.

Title: Topology Applied to Machine Learning: From Global to Local
Snippet: Through the use of examples, we explain one way in which applied topology has evolved since the birth of persistent homology in the early 2000s. The first applications of topology to data emphasized the global shape of a dataset, such as the three-circle model for 3 × 3 pixel patches from natural images, or the configuration space of the cyclo-octane molecule, which is a sphere with a Klein bottle attached via two circles of singularity. In these studies of global shape, short persistent homology bars are disregarded as sampling noise. More recently, however, persistent homology has been used to address questions about the local geometry of data. For instance, how can local geometry be vectorized for use in machine learning problems? Persistent homology and its vectorization methods, including persistence landscapes and persistence images, provide popular techniques for incorporating both local geometry and global topology into machine learning. Our meta-hypothesis is that the short bars are as important as the long bars for many machine learning tasks. In defense of this claim, we survey applications of persistent homology to shape recognition, agent-based modeling, materials science, archaeology, and biology. Additionally, we survey work connecting persistent homology to geometric features of spaces, including curvature and fractal dimension, and various methods that have been used to incorporate persistent homology into machine learning.
</snippet></tool_output>

# Overview and Motivation

Topological Autoencoders (TAEs) are neural autoencoder models augmented with a topological regularization term that constrains the latent representation to preserve salient topological features of the input data, such as connected components, loops, or higher-dimensional holes, measured via persistent homology (PH). The central idea is to align the multi-scale topological structure of the high-dimensional inputs with that of the low-dimensional latents, so that the learned embeddings are not only faithful to data geometry but also interpretable at the level of topological structure, while maintaining competitive reconstruction quality.<cite id="d4a60e9c-1">Topological Autoencoders aim to preserve topological features of the input in low-dimensional representations by regularizing the similarity of persistence diagrams between the latent and input spaces, treating mini-batches as point clouds and computing PH via Vietoris–Rips complexes</cite><cite id="f91f2402-0">Topological autoencoders preserve persistent homology information of the input space in latent representations, with theoretical justification for combining PH computations with backpropagation and mini-batch approximations</cite><cite id="f91f2402-3">A topological loss based on persistent homology aligns the topology of input and latent spaces so the encoder learns to retain multi-scale connectivity information</cite>.

This direction addresses a gap in standard autoencoders: while they often learn meaningful structures, they do not explicitly guarantee that topological features such as loops or multiple manifolds are preserved. Early works showed that enforcing a preferred topology in the latent space can improve one-class learning and downstream tasks, motivating TAEs as a generic constraint for dimensionality reduction and representation learning.<cite id="d4a60e9c-1">A prior differentiable loss enforcing a preferred topological “scale” in the latent space improved one-class learning, suggesting that constraining latent topology can be beneficial for learning</cite>.

# Core Principle: Preserving Topology via Persistent Homology

Persistent homology provides a multiscale description of topological features (e.g., 0th homology tracks connected components, 1st homology tracks loops, etc.) computed over filtered complexes (e.g., Vietoris–Rips) and summarized as barcodes or diagrams. TAEs leverage PH to define a topology-aware objective: make the PH of the latent space similar to that of the input space, thereby encouraging the encoder to preserve topological structures across scales.<cite id="d4a60e9c-1">The TAE regularization compares persistence diagrams for the input and latent spaces derived from Vietoris–Rips filtrations, treating mini-batches as point clouds and using PH to capture creation/destruction of topological features</cite><cite id="f91f2402-0">Under weak assumptions, PH computations can be combined with backpropagation, and approximating PH on mini-batches is theoretically justified</cite>.

In practice, the method operates on mini-batches as point clouds, computes PH of both the input batch and the encoded latent batch, and aligns corresponding topological signatures. This alignment can be phrased as a distance-based comparison: for simplices that are critical for creating or destroying PH classes (k-critical edges), the model matches selected inter-point distances in the input with those in the latent space, promoting topological similarity across scales.<cite id="d4a60e9c-1">The regularization compares “selected” distances in the data space with the corresponding distances in the latent space for relevant simplices that create or kill PH k classes, and is differentiable when the persistence diagram is discrete</cite>.

# How the Topological Loss Is Defined

A key technical contribution of TAEs is making the PH-based constraint differentiable so it can be integrated into end-to-end training. The loss can be constructed by focusing on k-critical edges in the Vietoris–Rips filtration—edges whose appearance or disappearance creates or destroys a PH_k class—then aligning the associated distances in the input and latent spaces. In the 0th homology case (connected components), this reduces to working with minimum spanning trees (MSTs): critical edges correspond to tree edges whose removal increases the number of connected components, and the loss compares selected tree-edge distances between input and latent encodings.<cite id="d4a60e9c-2">The topological regularization term compares topological abstractions of input and latent representations; for PH0 it uses MST(X) and MST(Z), with k-critical edges corresponding to those that create or kill PH_k classes</cite>.

More generally, the loss compares PH-derived “selected distances” from the full distance matrix in the input to analogous distances in the latent space. When the PH signatures are discrete (no coincident points in the diagram), this comparison is differentiable, enabling standard SGD-based training with automatic gradient computation.<cite id="d4a60e9c-1">By consistently mapping simplices to a given edge in the Vietoris–Rips complex and comparing selected distances between spaces, the regularization is differentiable under the discreteness assumption of persistence diagrams, allowing end-to-end training</cite>.

# Training Objectives and Differentiability

TAEs extend standard autoencoders by adding a topological loss L_t to the reconstruction term (e.g., MSE). The combined objective trains the encoder to compress data while preserving PH-inferred structures, without sacrificing reconstruction fidelity. The differentiability of PH-based terms hinges on discrete diagrams and batch-level approximations: computing PH on mini-batches yields suitable approximations of the full-space PH, and the approach provides theoretical stability for these mini-batch estimates.<cite id="f91f2402-1">A topological loss term harmonizes the data-space and latent-space topology and is shown to be stable on mini-batches, justifying PH approximations for training</cite><cite id="f91f2402-0">The method shows how persistent homology calculations can be combined with backpropagation and proves mini-batch PH approximations are theoretically justified</cite>.

Empirically, the topological loss can be incorporated into various architectures, including variational setups, and can be adapted beyond autoencoders (e.g., a “TopoPCA”), illustrating the generality of the constraint. However, computational complexity grows with the dimension of PH features and batch size, limiting practical use for high-dimensional features without approximations.<cite id="f91f2402-0">The loss is highly generalizable across architectures, including VAEs and PCA variants, but higher-dimensional PH computations scale poorly with batch size</cite>.

# What Is Preserved: From 0th to Higher Homology

- 0th Homology (Connectivity): By aligning MST edge distances between input and latent encodings, the loss encourages the preservation of connected components and global clustering structure in the latent space.<cite id="d4a60e9c-2">For PH0, k-critical edges correspond to MST edges, and the regularization compares selected distances in input and latent spaces</cite>.

- 1st Homology (Loops and Cycles): The same framework generalizes to 1st homology by identifying 1-critical edges in the Vietoris–Rips filtration (edges that create or kill 1D holes) and aligning their associated distances. Implementations often begin with PH0 and extend to higher features as compute allows.<cite id="d4a60e9c-2">The formulation considers k-critical edges for 0 ≤ k ≤ d and discusses PH0/PH1; in practice the method was documented for PH0 using MSTs, with PH1 relying on critical cycles</cite>.

- Higher-Order Features and Limitations: As the target feature dimension increases, computing and matching higher-dimensional critical simplices becomes more expensive, and stability/accuracy of mini-batch PH approximations and differentiability assumptions become more challenging, motivating scalability-focused variants and parameterizations.<cite id="f91f2402-0">Computing the topological loss for higher-dimensional features suffers from growing complexity and scaling issues with batch size</cite>.

# Variants and Extensions

- Topological Autoencoders++ (TopoAE++): Builds on the original TAE by refining how topological information is extracted and matched. It formalizes the alignment of k-critical edges and distances, and focuses on PH0 via MSTs in initial reports, providing a concrete and scalable loss recipe for practical implementations.<cite id="d4a60e9c-2">TopoAE++ summarizes the TAE approach, defines k-critical edges, and specializes the loss for PH0 using MSTs, enabling practical, fast training</cite>.

- Cycle-Aware and Graph-Structured Constraints: By emphasizing cycles and critical structures (edges creating or destroying holes), variants make the loss target specific topological phenomena beyond mere separation of clusters, aligning latent geometry with cyclic features present in the data.<cite id="d4a60e9c-2">The loss targets k-critical edges that create or kill PH classes, focusing the encoder on preserving such topological events</cite>.

- Topology-Aware Parameterizations (Circular Coordinates): Complementary to TAEs, some methods parameterize latent variables or model outputs with circular (angle) coordinates induced by persistent cohomology, providing direct circle-valued functions that reflect 1D homology. This can be useful when data exhibit periodic or annular/toroidal structure and complements PH-based losses by shaping the latent geometry to match homotopy classes of maps to the circle.<cite id="02c44193-0">Circular coordinates leverage H^1(B; Z) ≅ [B, S^1] to turn 1D (persistent) cohomology classes into circle-valued functions on data, enabling topology-aware parameterizations</cite><cite id="02c44193-2">Circular coordinates provide a natural procedure to construct nonlinear, circle-valued parameterizations from persistent topology</cite>.

# Relation to Mapper and Broader TDA+DL

Mapper, a TDA pipeline, builds a compressed representation of data by filtering, covering, and clustering, often revealing global topological structure and networks of loops/handles. While not an autoencoder, Mapper shares the TAE goal of preserving topology for interpretability; indeed, TDA-informed objectives like PH loss can be used to guide dimensionality reduction or segmentation so that resulting embeddings reflect the same topological graphs or manifolds revealed by Mapper.<cite id="02c44193-4">Topological data analysis connects PH and local/global geometry, with methods like persistence landscapes/images vectorizing topology for machine learning and emphasizing that short bars (local features) can be as important as long ones</cite><cite id="02c44193-0">Localization, homological coordinatization, and circular coordinates provide ways to map PH insights into concrete realizations or parameterizations of data structure</cite>.

More broadly, PH-based objectives have diffused across deep learning: they appear both as supervised losses to shape decision boundary topology and as priors in autoencoders to enforce latent topology. TAEs exemplify the latter, integrating PH into unsupervised representation learning, while related works apply PH or Morse-theoretic tools to segmentation and uncertainty quantification.<cite id="02c44193-3">PH objectives have been integrated into deep learning both to shape decision boundaries and to impose topological priors on latent spaces in autoencoders; PH and discrete Morse theory have also been applied to image segmentation and uncertainty quantification</cite>.

# Empirical Behavior and Applications

On synthetic and real-world datasets, TAEs produce latent representations that preserve multi-scale connectivity and spatially arrange classes into entangled structures reflecting underlying manifolds, rather than merely separating them into disjoint clusters. This often improves interpretability and can yield benefits on downstream metrics that depend on proximity on manifolds or density preservation, without significantly increasing reconstruction error.<cite id="f91f2402-0">Experiments show TAEs capture spatial relationships between nested high-dimensional spheres and produce interpretable, manifold-respecting embeddings; competitive performance on multiple quality metrics is observed without harming reconstruction</cite><cite id="f91f2402-3">The approach yields favorable latent representations on synthetic manifolds and image datasets while maintaining low reconstruction error</cite>.

TAE-style losses have also been deployed in segmentation to improve topology-sensitive metrics and in adversarial defenses (e.g., TopoReformer), where a TAE purifies inputs by aligning their latent topology to a desired structure, thereby mitigating adversarial perturbations in OCR tasks. These applications highlight how topology-aware latents can improve robustness and functional alignment with the data’s intrinsic structure.<cite id="f91f2402-2">A persistent-homology-driven topological loss improved segmentation performance on topological-relevant metrics and is generic across architectures</cite><cite id="d4a60e9c-4">TopoReformer uses the TAE methodology, detailing PH, persistence diagrams, and the associated topological loss, and applies it to mitigate adversarial attacks in OCR models</cite>.

# Practical Considerations and Trade-offs

- Choice of PH Features and Scale: Selecting which homology dimensions to regularize (e.g., PH0 vs PH1) and at which filtration scales affects what structure is preserved; focusing on 0th homology aligns clustering via MSTs, while higher homology targets loops and handles but at greater computational cost.<cite id="d4a60e9c-2">PH0 corresponds to MST-based critical edges, while PH1 involves cycle-based criticalities with increased complexity</cite>.

- Differentiability and Stability: The PH-based loss requires discrete diagrams for straightforward differentiability; in practice, mini-batch approximations and discrete sampling are used, with theoretical stability results supporting their use, though higher-dimensional features scale poorly with batch size and resolution.<cite id="d4a60e9c-1">Differentiability follows under discreteness of persistence diagrams and mini-batch approximations</cite><cite id="f91f2402-0">Mini-batch PH approximations are theoretically justified, but higher-dimensional PH computations scale worse with batch size</cite>.

- Architectural Flexibility and Objectives: TAE-style regularization can be added to standard autoencoders or adapted to other dimensionality reduction frameworks (e.g., TopoPCA) and variational setups, but practitioners must balance topological fidelity against reconstruction and training speed.<cite id="f91f2402-0">The topological loss is general and can be integrated into VAEs and PCA variants, though computational costs grow with feature dimension and batch size</cite>.

- Interpretation and Downstream Tasks: TAEs aim for interpretable, topology-respecting embeddings; empirical observations show improved density preservation and meaningful spatial arrangements, though gains are task-dependent and may not universally outperform purely reconstruction-based training on all metrics.<cite id="f91f2402-0">TAEs produce entangled, manifold-respecting structures and perform competitively on multiple quality metrics without degrading reconstruction</cite>.

# Summary

Topological Autoencoders operationalize the principle of preserving the essential shape of data in latent representations by aligning persistent homology between inputs and latents through differentiable, distance-based losses. By constraining k-critical structures (edges creating/destroying PH features) and leveraging mini-batch PH approximations, TAEs provide a theoretically grounded and flexible mechanism to enforce topology in autoencoders, improving interpretability and, in practice, downstream performance on tasks ranging from manifold learning and segmentation to robustness against adversarial attacks. As research continues, extensions such as cycle-aware losses and circular-coordinate parameterizations complement PH regularization, and broader TDA tools like Mapper and vectorization methods (persistence landscapes/images) offer additional pathways to integrate topology into deep learning pipelines.<cite id="d4a60e9c-1">TAEs align persistence diagrams of input and latent spaces via differentiable regularization on mini-batches, extending prior topology-control losses and treating each batch as a point cloud</cite><cite id="d4a60e9c-2">TopoAE++ formalizes k-critical-edge-based losses, specializing to MSTs for PH0 and focusing on computationally tractable cycle-aware constraints</cite><cite id="f91f2402-0">Theoretical results justify combining PH with backpropagation and mini-batch approximations, with empirical evidence of improved interpretability and competitive metrics</cite><cite id="02c44193-0">Circular coordinates and related homological methods provide concrete realizations and parameterizations that complement PH-based regularization</cite><cite id="02c44193-3">PH objectives have been widely adopted across deep learning, both to shape decision boundaries and to impose topology priors in autoencoders</cite><cite id="d4a60e9c-4">Applications such as TopoReformer demonstrate practical efficacy of TAE-style topology purification for robustness</cite>.

Title: A Survey of Topological Machine Learning Methods
Snippet: As a recent example, Moor et al. (2020) propose a topological autoencoder, which aims to preserve topological features of the input data in low-dimensional representations. This is achieved via a regularisation term that incentivises the persistence diagrams of both the latent and input space to be topologically similar. This method acts on the level of mini-batches, treating each of them as a point cloud. Persistence diagrams are obtained from the Vietoris-Rips complex of each space. By tracking the simplices that are relevant for the creation and destruction of topological features, and by consistently mapping simplices to a given edge in the Vietoris-Rips complex, each filtration can be interpreted as a selection of distances from the full distance matrix of the point cloud. The proposed regularisation term then compares the "selected" distances in the data space with the corresponding distances in the latent space (and vice versa). Finally, this regularisation is differentiable under the assumption that the persistence diagram is discrete (i.e., for each of its points, there is an infinitesimal neighbourhood containing no other points). The scheme can thus be directly integrated into the end-to-end training of an autoencoder, making it aware of the topology in the data space. This work can also be considered as an extension of previous work by Hofer C. et al. (2019), who introduced a differentiable loss term for one-class learning that controls the topology of the latent space; in effect, their loss term enforces a preferred "scale" for topological features in the latent space. It does not have to harmonise topological features across different spaces. It turns out that an autoencoder trained with this loss term on unlabelled data can be used on other data sets for one-class learning. This hints at the fact that enforcing a certain topological structure can be beneficial for learning tasks; we will later see that such empirical observations can also be furnished with a theoretical underpinning. 

An approach by Chen et al. (2019) takes a different perspective. The authors develop a measure of the topological complexity (in terms of connected components) of the classification boundary of a given classifier.

documents.snippet:
As a recent example, Moor et al. (2020) propose a topological autoencoder, which aims to preserve topological features of the input data in low-dimensional representations. This is achieved via a regularisation term that incentivises the persistence diagrams of both the latent and input space to be topologically similar. This method acts on the level of mini-batches, treating each of them as a point cloud. Persistence diagrams are obtained from the Vietoris-Rips complex of each space. By tracking the simplices that are relevant for the creation and destruction of topological features, and by consistently mapping simplices to a given edge in the Vietoris-Rips complex, each filtration can be interpreted as a selection of distances from the full distance matrix of the point cloud. The proposed regularisation term then compares the "selected" distances in the data space with the corresponding distances in the latent space (and vice versa). Finally, this regularisation is differentiable under the assumption that the persistence diagram is discrete (i.e., for each of its points, there is an infinitesimal neighbourhood containing no other points). The scheme can thus be directly integrated into the end-to-end training of an autoencoder, making it aware of the topology in the data space. (2019), who introduced a differentiable loss term for one-class learning that controls the topology of the latent space; in effect, their loss term enforces a preferred "scale" for topological features in the latent space. Title: Topological Autoencoders
Snippet: We presented topological autoencoders, a novel method for preserving topological information, measured in terms of persistent homology, of the input space when learning latent representations with deep neural networks. Under weak theoretical assumptions, we showed how our persistent homology calculations can be combined with backpropagation; moreover, we proved that approximating persistent homology on the level of mini-batches is theoretically justified. In our experiments, we observed that our method is uniquely able to capture spatial relationships between nested highdimensional spheres. This is relevant, as the ability to cope with several manifolds in the domain of manifold learning still remains a challenging task. On real-world data sets, we observed that our topological loss leads to competitive performance in terms of numerous quality metrics (such as a density preservation metric), while not adversely affecting the reconstruction error. In both synthetic and real-world data sets, we obtain interesting and interpretable representations, as our method does not merely pull apart different classes, but tries to spatially arrange them meaningfully. Thus, we do not observe mere distinct "clouds", but rather entangled structures, which we consider to constitute a more meaningful representation of the underlying manifolds (an auxiliary analysis in Supplementary Section A.10 confirms that our method influences topological features, measured using PH, in a beneficial manner). 

Future work Our topological loss formulation is highly generalisable; it only requires the existence of a distance matrix between individual samples (either globally, or on the level of batches). As a consequence, our topological loss term can be directly integrated into a variety of different architectures and is not limited to standard autoencoders. For instance, we can also apply our constraint to variational setups (see Figure A.3 for a sketch) or create a topology-aware variant of principal component analysis (dubbed "TopoPCA"; see Table A.2 for more details, as well as Figures A.6, A.7, and A.8 for the corresponding latent space representations). Employing our loss term to more involved architectures will be an exciting route for future work. One issue with the calculation is that, given the computational complexity of calculating R (•), for higherdimensional features, we would scale progressively worse with increasing batch size.

Title: Topological Autoencoders
Snippet: While topological features, in particular multi-scale features derived from persistent homology, have seen increasing use in the machine learning community (Carrière et al., 2019, Guss & Salakhutdinov, 2018, Hofer et al., 2017, 2019a,b, Ramamurthy et al., 2019, Reininghaus et al., 2015, Rieck et al., 2019a,b), employing topology directly as a constraint for modern deep learning methods remains a challenge. This is due to the inherently discrete nature of these computations, making backpropagation through the computation of topological signatures immensely difficult or only possible in certain special circumstances (Chen et al., 2019, Hofer et al., 2019a, Poulenard et al., 2018). This work presents a novel approach that permits obtaining gradients during the computation of topological signatures. This makes it possible to employ topological constraints while training deep neural networks, as well as building topology-preserving autoencoders. Our method are particularly suitable for fine structure image segmentation. Quantitative and qualitative results show that the proposed topological loss term helps to achieve better performance in terms of topological-relevant metrics. Our proposed topological loss term is generic and can be incorporated into different architectures.

Title: Topological Autoencoders
Snippet: We propose a novel approach for preserving topological structures of the input space in latent representations of autoencoders. Using persistent homology, a technique from topological data analysis, we calculate topological signatures of both the input and latent space to derive a topological loss term. Under weak theoretical assumptions, we construct this loss in a differentiable manner, such that the encoding learns to retain multi-scale connectivity information. We show that our approach is theoretically well-founded and that it exhibits favourable latent representations on a synthetic manifold as well as on real-world image data sets, while preserving low reconstruction errors.

Persistent (co)homology is one avenue to address the topology inference problem [38,12]; it provides a multiscale description of topological features, and satisfies several inference theorems [30,8,10]. Going from a persistent homology computation to actionable knowledge about the initial data set, is in general highly nontrivial. One would like to determine: how are the persistent homology features reflected on the data? if the homology suggests a candidate underlying space X, what is a concrete realization (e.g., via equations or as a quotient)? how does the data fit on/around the realization? At least three approaches have been proposed in the literature to address these questions: localization, homological coordinatization and circular coordinates.

For a relevant homology class, the idea behind localization is to find an appropriate representative cycle. This strategy is successful in low dimensions [15,16], but in general even reasonable heuristics lead to NP-hard problems which are NP-hard to approximate [9]. Homological coordinatization [36] attempts to map a simplicial complex on the data to a simplicial complex with prescribed homology -a model suggested by a persistent homology computation. The map is selected by examining the set of chain homotopy classes of chain maps between the complex on the data and the model. Selecting an appropriate representative chain map, however, involves combinatorial optimizations which are difficult to solve in practice. Circular coordinates [13] leverages the following fact: there is a bijection H 1 (B; Z) ∼ = B, S 1 between the 1-dimensional Z-cohomology of a topological space B, and the set of homotopy classes of maps from B to the circle S 1 . When B is a simplicial complex with the data as vertex set, this observation is used to turn 1-dimensional (persistent) Z/p-cohomology classes for appropriate primes p, into circle-valued functions on the data.

The circular coordinates approach has been used successfully -for instance to parameterize periodic dynamics [14] -and is part of a bigger picture

Title: A Quotient Homology Theory of Representation in Neural Networks
Snippet: Persistent homology is an essential tool for computing homology groups of data from different domains of science (Carlsson (2009); Wasserman (2018)), including machine learning (Papamarkou et al. (2024)). For better or worse, it is not a purely topological method as it also tracks geometric features of the underlying point cloud (Bubenik et al. (2020); Turkes et al. (2022)). Plus, it is highly sensitive to the sampling density and the chosen metric. While sometimes there are ways to overcome these problems, it is likely that geometric properties are sneaking into our discussion of topology. 

To show the effectiveness of our method, we generated datasets of highly non-linear curves by the equation f (θ) = [cos(aθ) cos(bθ), cos(aθ) sin(bθ)] T . The parameters a, b were randomly sampled from a uniform distribution on the interval [−1, 1]. We sampled 500 equally spaced points θ ∈ [−π, π]. Afterwards, we used a MSE loss to optimize a neural network with three layers, each with a width of 50 neurons, to predict these functions given the input points (θ, 0). The parameters for all simulations are described in detail in Appendix C. Following training we compute the first homology groups H 1 of the output of the final network layer. We do this in two ways: standard persistent homology with the Euclidean metric and quotient homology using the metric as described in Appendix A.5.1. 

In Figure 1 we show two examples of learned curves and their associated homology groups given by the barcodes below. One can see that in the first example, standard persistent homology identifies a circular feature as the ends of the interval are close in the output despite the fact that the network does not map them onto each other. This error is avoided when using quotient homology, as seen by the lack of bars in the barcode plot. In the second example, we see that both persistent homology as well as quotient homology generate two persistent features.

Title: Persistent Cohomology and Circular Coordinates
Snippet: In a physical setting, circular coordinates occur naturally as angular and phase variables. Spaces like the annulus and the torus are well described by a combination of real and circular coordinates. (The 2-sphere is not so lucky, and must await its day.) 

The goal of this paper is to describe a natural procedure for constructing circular coordinates on a nonlinear data set using techniques from classical algebraic topology and its 21st-century grandchild, persistent topology. We direct the reader to [9] as a general reference for algebraic topology, and to [17] for a streamlined account of persistent homology.

Title: Scale-Free Image Keypoints Using Differentiable Persistent Homology
Snippet: Recently, differentiable topological objectives have been integrated into deep learning, serving as regularization tools for shaping the topology of decision boundaries in classification tasks (Chen et al., 2019) and as priors for the latent space in autoencoders (Moor et al., 2020).In supervised learning contexts, persistent homology, along with discrete Morse theory, has been applied to image segmentation tasks to enhance the loss function (Hu et al., 2023;2021;Clough et al., 2020), often complemented by the binary cross-entropy loss, and to quantify uncertainty (Gupta et al., 2024).

Our work represents a first attempt at introducing completely unsupervised objectives based on persistent homology within the context of deep learning for data-intensive applications.

Title: Topology Applied to Machine Learning: From Global to Local
Snippet: Through the use of examples, we explain one way in which applied topology has evolved since the birth of persistent homology in the early 2000s. The first applications of topology to data emphasized the global shape of a dataset, such as the three-circle model for 3 × 3 pixel patches from natural images, or the configuration space of the cyclo-octane molecule, which is a sphere with a Klein bottle attached via two circles of singularity. In these studies of global shape, short persistent homology bars are disregarded as sampling noise. More recently, however, persistent homology has been used to address questions about the local geometry of data. For instance, how can local geometry be vectorized for use in machine learning problems? Persistent homology and its vectorization methods, including persistence landscapes and persistence images, provide popular techniques for incorporating both local geometry and global topology into machine learning. Our meta-hypothesis is that the short bars are as important as the long bars for many machine learning tasks. In defense of this claim, we survey applications of persistent homology to shape recognition, agent-based modeling, materials science, archaeology, and biology. Additionally, we survey work connecting persistent homology to geometric features of spaces, including curvature and fractal dimension, and various methods that have been used to incorporate persistent homology into machine learning.

At least three approaches have been proposed in the literature to address these questions: localization, homological coordinatization and circular coordinates.

Selecting an appropriate representative chain map, however, involves combinatorial optimizations which are difficult to solve in practice. When B is a simplicial complex with the data as vertex set, this observation is used to turn 1-dimensional (persistent) Z/p-cohomology classes for appropriate primes p, into circle-valued functions on the data.

Persistent homology is an essential tool for computing homology groups of data from different domains of science (Carlsson (2009); Wasserman (2018)), including machine learning (Papamarkou et al. (2024)). For better or worse, it is not a purely topological method as it also tracks geometric features of the underlying point cloud (Bubenik et al. (2020); Turkes et al. (2022)). Plus, it is highly sensitive to the sampling density and the chosen metric. While sometimes there are ways to overcome these problems, it is likely that geometric properties are sneaking into our discussion of topology. 

To show the effectiveness of our method, we generated datasets of highly non-linear curves by the equation f (θ) = [cos(aθ) cos(bθ), cos(aθ) sin(bθ)] T . The parameters a, b were randomly sampled from a uniform distribution on the interval [−1, 1]. We sampled 500 equally spaced points θ ∈ [−π, π]. Afterwards, we used a MSE loss to optimize a neural network with three layers, each with a width of 50 neurons, to predict these functions given the input points (θ, 0). The parameters for all simulations are described in detail in Appendix C. Following training we compute the first homology groups H 1 of the output of the final network layer. We do this in two ways: standard persistent homology with the Euclidean metric and quotient homology using the metric as described in Appendix A.5.1. 

In Figure 1 we show two examples of learned curves and their associated homology groups given by the barcodes below. One can see that in the first example, standard persistent homology identifies a circular feature as the ends of the interval are close in the output despite the fact that the network does not map them onto each other. This error is avoided when using quotient homology, as seen by the lack of bars in the barcode plot. In the second example, we see that both persistent homology as well as quotient homology generate two persistent features.

snippet.text: Through the use of examples, we explain one way in which applied topology has evolved since the birth of persistent homology in the early 2000s. The first applications of topology to data emphasized the global shape of a dataset, such as the three-circle model for 3 × 3 pixel patches from natural images, or the configuration space of the cyclo-octane molecule, which is a sphere with a Klein bottle attached via two circles of singularity. In these studies of global shape, short persistent homology bars are disregarded as sampling noise. More recently, however, persistent homology has been used to address questions about the local geometry of data. For instance, how can local geometry be vectorized for use in machine learning problems? Persistent homology and its vectorization methods, including persistence landscapes and persistence images, provide popular techniques for incorporating both local geometry and global topology into machine learning. Our meta-hypothesis is that the short bars are as important as the long bars for many machine learning tasks. In defense of this claim, we survey applications of persistent homology to shape recognition, agent-based modeling, materials science, archaeology, and biology. Additionally, we survey work connecting persistent homology to geometric features of spaces, including curvature and fractal dimension, and various methods that have been used to incorporate persistent homology into machine learning.
