final_response:
# Overview

Ray tracing with NURBS targets high-quality rendering and simulation when scenes or objects are represented by NURBS curves and surfaces, which are standard in CAD and graphics due to compactness, local control, and exact geometric properties.<cite id="6dd9447c-0">NURBS surface representation is common for most 3D modeling tools because of its compactness and useful geometric properties, and direct ray tracing of NURBS surfaces can yield higher-quality rendered images compared to indirect approaches</cite> Many modern systems tessellate parametric surfaces to triangles for speed, but this trades robustness and detail for performance, motivating direct NURBS intersection and rendering research.<cite id="f99e9550-1">Most ray tracing applications tessellate parametric surfaces, which increases speed but can produce wrong images if tessellation is not sufficient and requires extra memory; thus, fast and robust ray–parametric (NURBS) surface algorithms remain an open issue</cite>

# Algorithmic Approaches for Ray–NURBS Intersection

A classic taxonomy distinguishes four algorithm families for ray–parametric surface intersections, including NURBS: subdivision, numerical (Newton-type), algebraic, and Bézier clipping; efficient algorithms exist in each class and have been adapted from graphics rendering to boundary representation and simulation contexts.<cite id="f99e9550-0">Algorithms for ray–parametric surface intersection can be classified into subdivision, numerical, algebraic, and Bézier clipping; efficient algorithms for ray–NURBS intersections exist and many were developed for graphics rendering but apply to boundaries described by NURBS</cite> Subdivision methods leverage convex hull and bounding properties, recursively partitioning surfaces until a threshold guarantees an approximate solution; numerical methods (e.g., Newton) offer quadratic convergence when well-initialized; algebraic methods solve implicit equations (e.g., Kajiya’s formulation) but can lead to high-degree systems; Bézier clipping provides robust root-finding for parametric patches via recursive subdivision and line clipping concepts.<cite id="f99e9550-0">Subdivision methods use convex hull properties and repeated subdivision until a threshold; numerical (Newton) methods converge quadratically with good initial guesses; algebraic methods (e.g., Kajiya) solve root-finding for parametric surfaces; Bézier clipping provides robust intersection via subdivision and clipping, with many authors using bounding boxes to initialize Newton and limit tests</cite>

Hybrid and specialized NURBS strategies combine methods for robustness and speed. For example, some works transform NURBS into equivalent rational Bézier sets and apply Bézier clipping, with modifications to improve performance; others interleave Bézier clipping with Newton iteration to handle coherence across pixels and avoid divergence in difficult cases.<cite id="f99e9550-4">NURBS surfaces can be mapped to equivalent rational Bézier sets and then clipped with Bézier cutting; modifications improve activity and effectiveness of Bézier cutting; hybrid schemes combine Bézier cutting for the first intersection with Newton iteration for subsequent rays in a coherence row to avoid divergence</cite> Historical references include reverse NURBS visualization methods using hierarchical node-vector structures and bisection for finding intersection points, alongside early Newton-based approaches by Toth and later work by Martin and others that shaped modern NURBS ray-tracing pipelines.<cite id="f99e9550-4">Reverse NURBS surface visualization in ray tracing used hierarchic structures to reduce tree depth; Toth used Newton’s method for ray–parametric intersections; Martin proposed hierarchical node-vector processing; bisection was used to find intersection points but increases calculation count in some cases</cite>

# Robustness and Border/Cropping Issues

Direct NURBS ray tracing must handle edge cases like trimming boundaries, cropped regions, and surface singularities; many practical systems either avoid these via tessellation or add specialized tests and parameter-space clipping.<cite id="6dd9447c-0">Direct NURBS ray tracing is motivated by better image quality but prior approaches had various limitations; border stability and special-case handling are active concerns</cite> Some methods replace problematic parametric steps with bisection or trimming-based decompositions, but these can be slower or require careful parameter estimation; researchers have proposed Newton/Cramer-based combinations to stabilize solutions and reduce artifacts in difficult surface regions.<cite id="6dd9447c-3">A Newton/Cramer combination approach for ray–NURBS intersection is proposed to improve robustness and efficiency compared to prior methods such as Martin et al.; implementation results are reported</cite><cite id="f99e9550-1">Bisection-based intersection is used in some NURBS ray-tracing approaches but increases computation; border and cropping problems persist in many parametric-surface algorithms, motivating robust methods</cite>

# CAD, Trimmed Surfaces, and B-rep Context

NURBS are the standard freeform representation in CAD; trimming enables complex shapes but introduces gaps and topological complications when stitching trimmed patches, complicating ray intersection and visualization.<cite id="f99e9550-3">NURBS are standard in CAD; trimming creates complex shapes but causes gaps when stitching trimmed NURBS patches and leaves visual trims without altering rectangular topology, complicating operations and requiring re-evaluation of trimming curves</cite> Converting trimmed NURBS to subdivision surfaces (e.g., Catmull–Clark) can eliminate gaps and provide exact boundaries via shared curves, and has been explored as a path to robust ray tracing of trimmed NURBS by represting them as subdivision surfaces.<cite id="f99e9550-3">Subdivision offers arbitrary topology and exact boundary sharing; conversion from Catmull–Clark subdivision to NURBS exists by treating base mesh faces as NURBS patches, while the reverse is nontrivial; this motivates conversion strategies to handle trimmed NURBS</cite> Subdivision-surface ray tracers with adaptive refinement and hierarchical bounding volumes can then be applied to these converted representations, achieving high-quality intersections with controllable error and robustness.<cite id="f99e9550-2">A stackless, massively parallel ray tracer for Catmull–Clark subdivision surfaces uses adaptive subdivision, conservative bounds, and a patch hierarchy; ray–patch intersection proceeds via alternating u/v subdivision, bounding volumes derived for Bézier and Gregory patches, and on-demand refinement, enabling accurate and efficient traversal and intersection</cite>

# Physics-Based Ray Tracing with NURBS

Beyond rendering, NURBS are used for physics-based ray tracing in optics and electromagnetics, where surfaces are described by NURBS and specialized algorithms solve ray reflection/refraction and geodesic paths.<cite id="6dd9447c-2">A NURBS-capable optical design library implements differential ray tracing and ray-aiming to optimize systems with NURBS surfaces and to model structural deformation effects, leveraging NURBS as a standard CAD representation</cite> In high-frequency electromagnetic analysis, NURBS enable precise modeling with fewer patches; geodesic paths on NURBS can be computed by solving geodesic differential equations, with numerical schemes ranging from Euler (efficient but low precision) to Runge–Kutta (more accurate but costly).<cite id="f99e9550-4">NURBS provide high-precision modeling with few patches in electromagnetic analysis; geodesic paths on NURBS are obtained by solving geodesic differential equations using schemes like Euler (first-order, efficient but low precision) or fourth-order Runge–Kutta (accurate but time-consuming)</cite> Newer work proposes adaptive variable-step Euler methods that adjust step sizes using shape factors to balance accuracy and efficiency for creeping rays on arbitrary NURBS surfaces.<cite id="f99e9550-4">An adaptive variable-step Euler method for creeping rays on arbitrary NURBS surfaces adjusts discrete steps via a shape factor, improving accuracy over fixed-step Euler while retaining efficiency compared to Runge–Kutta</cite>

# Practical Systems and Libraries

Industrial and research systems demonstrate end-to-end NURBS ray tracing workflows. The FORMIDABLE library integrates NURBS surfaces, differential ray tracing, and ray-aiming for freeform optical design, enabling optimization under manufacturing constraints.<cite id="6dd9447c-2">FORMIDABLE implements differential ray tracing and ray-aiming for NURBS-based optical systems and simulates performance impacts of structural deformation, reflecting NURBS’ prevalence in CAD</cite> In rendering contexts, CPU-based ray kernels such as Embree can be preferable when complex parametric primitives are involved, as rasterization pipelines may lack the necessary access patterns and NURBS ray tracing is better handled by specialized traversal kernels.<cite id="be63b7be-2">A ray-tracing pipeline on the CPU (e.g., Embree) better supports NURBS-based algorithms than rasterization-based GPU pipelines, which lack required pixel-by-pixel access; commercial GPU products often do not expose the needed accessibility</cite> More broadly, GPU photorealistic systems commonly support acceleration structures (e.g., BVH) and advanced algorithms (e.g., photon mapping), providing a foundation to which complex NURBS intersection strategies can be added or ported.<cite id="be63b7be-4">GPU-based photorealistic rendering systems support BVH and stochastic progressive photon mapping, and can be extended to complex ray tracing algorithms beyond spheres and implicit surfaces using GLSL shaders</cite>

# Notable Papers and Contributions (curated)

- Direct NURBS Ray Tracing and Border Stability: Methods targeting robust intersection and visualization on NURBS, including Newton/Cramer formulations and border-stable approaches, with comparisons to prior NURBS ray tracing by Martin and others.<cite id="6dd9447c-0">Direct NURBS ray tracing is motivated by compact, high-quality representations and better rendered images than triangle-only pipelines</cite><cite id="6dd9447c-3">A Newton/Cramer-based approach is proposed for ray–NURBS intersection and compared to Martin et al.’s method, with implementation results</cite>

- Algorithm Families and Historical Foundations: Surveys and overviews classifying subdivision, Newton, algebraic, and Bézier-clipping approaches for ray–parametric surfaces, with historical milestones (Toth, Kajiya) and practical bounding strategies to initialize Newton iteration.<cite id="f99e9550-0">A classification of ray–parametric surface intersection algorithms (subdivision, numerical/Newton, algebraic, Bézier clipping) and references to efficient methods and bounding boxes to initialize Newton and limit tests</cite><cite id="f99e9550-1">Discussion of why most systems tessellate parametric surfaces and the ongoing need for fast and robust NURBS ray intersection methods</cite><cite id="f99e9550-4">Historical methods include reverse NURBS visualization with hierarchical node-vector structures, Bézier cutting combined with Newton iteration for coherence, and mapping NURBS to rational Bézier sets for clipping</cite>

- Bézier Clipping and Rational Geometry: Transforming NURBS to rational Bézier sets and applying Bézier clipping with modifications to improve robustness and efficiency for ray–NURBS intersections.<cite id="f99e9550-4">NURBS-to-rational-Bézier conversion followed by Bézier cutting, with modifications enhancing activity and effectiveness</cite>

- Subdivision and Trim Handling: Conversion of trimmed NURBS to Catmull–Clark subdivision surfaces to eliminate gaps and provide exact boundaries; robust traversal and intersection for subdivision surfaces via adaptive refinement and hierarchical BVH-like structures.<cite id="f99e9550-3">Trimming introduces gaps and topological issues; conversion to Catmull–Clark subdivision surfaces preserves exact boundaries and simplifies operations</cite><cite id="f99e9550-2">Adaptive subdivision, conservative bounds, and hierarchical traversal yield accurate and efficient ray–patch intersection for subdivision surfaces</cite>

- Physics and Electromagnetics on NURBS: Geodesic/creeping ray tracing on NURBS via GDE solvers and adaptive stepping; NURBS-enabled optical design with differential ray tracing and ray-aiming in a production library.<cite id="f99e9550-4">Geodesic differential equations on NURBS solved by Euler or Runge–Kutta; adaptive variable-step Euler improves accuracy-efficiency for creeping rays</cite><cite id="6dd9447c-2">Differential ray tracing and ray-aiming for NURBS-based optical systems, including deformation effects on performance</cite>

# Practical Trade-offs and Design Choices

Tessellating NURBS for ray tracing trades robustness and detail for speed and ease of implementation, but can misrender features or consume extra memory; direct NURBS methods avoid these costs at the expense of algorithmic complexity and border-case handling.<cite id="f99e9550-1">Tessellation accelerates ray tracing but can produce wrong images if not sufficiently fine and requires extra memory, motivating direct NURBS intersection</cite> Subdivision-based pipelines offer robust, adaptive error control with hierarchical pruning and conservative bounds; Bézier/convex-hull properties enable efficient rejection and early exit, while Newton-type methods provide rapid convergence when well-initialized.<cite id="f99e9550-0">Subdivision and bounding strategies prune work early; Newton-type methods converge quickly with good initial guesses; algebraic and Bézier-clipping approaches provide alternative robustness</cite> For specialized domains like optics and electromagnetics, NURBS-based ray tracing must also handle trimming, geodesics, and specialized sampling strategies to balance accuracy and runtime.<cite id="f99e9550-4">Geodesic path computation on NURBS requires careful numerical schemes; adaptive stepping balances accuracy and efficiency</cite><cite id="6dd9447c-2">Optical systems with NURBS surfaces benefit from differential ray tracing and ray-aiming to optimize performance and alignment</cite>

# Pointers for Further Reading and Recent Directions

Recent GPU and CPU ray-tracing ecosystems provide acceleration structures and traversal patterns that can be paired with NURBS intersection kernels or with converted subdivision representations of trimmed NURBS.<cite id="be63b7be-2">CPU ray kernels (e.g., Embree) better expose the necessary primitives for complex parametric ray tracing than rasterization pipelines</cite><cite id="be63b7be-4">GPU photorealistic systems commonly support BVH and advanced algorithms, offering a base to integrate complex NURBS intersection strategies</cite> In CAD and manufacturing, trendlines include preserving NURBS where possible while handling trims via conversion or clipping, and integrating robust border/cropping logic into B-rep kernels for ray tracing workflows.<cite id="f99e9550-3">CAD workflows face trimming-induced gaps and topology issues; conversion to subdivision surfaces and exact boundary handling are attractive for robust ray tracing</cite> Researchers continue to propose hybrid NURBS methods that combine subdivision/convex-hull pruning, Bézier clipping, and Newton iteration to improve robustness and speed for challenging surface configurations and special-case geometries.<cite id="f99e9550-4">Hybrid Bézier clipping plus Newton iteration and rational-Bézier decomposition are used to improve robustness and efficiency of NURBS ray intersection, with coherence handling across pixels</cite>

Snippet: Moreover, due to the advantages of high precision in modeling with low number of patches and great flexibility in simulation algorithms, NURBS has been introduced into the area of high-frequency electromagnetic analysis [8,9]. When object is described by NURBS surfaces, geodesic path can be obtained by solving the geodesic differential equation [10]. Hence, some numerical schemes were employed to handle the GDE. Title: Conversion of trimmed NURBS surfaces to Catmull-Clark subdivision surfaces
Snippet: Non-Uniform Rational B-Splines (NURBS) are the standard freeform surface representation in Computer-Aided Design (CAD) applications. Due to their limitation of a strict rectangular topology, trimming is an important operation to create complex objects. However, it introduces unavoidable gaps when stitching two trimmed NURBS patches together (Sederberg et al., 2008). Moreover, as the trimmed NURBS are only visually trimmed by skipping the evaluation of the trimmed part in parameter space (Fig. 1(a)), the rectangular NURBS topology is not altered although the geometric shape has changed. As a consequence, many operations on trimmed shapes may require a time-consuming re-evaluation process of the trimming curves (Farin, 2001), e.g., editing and deformation. 

Instead, subdivision, because of its ability to handle arbitrary topology and ease of use, has become an attractive alternative to NURBS, especially for modelling in high-end animation productions (Pixar, DeRose et al., 1998;Stam, 1998). The subdivision representations have the great advantage that if two subdivision surfaces share a boundary edge in base meshes, they both contain exactly that piece of boundary curve. This makes it possible to apply exactly the same trimming curves on two intersecting surfaces and thus provide gap-free models. Although there has been great progress in NURBS-compatible subdivision schemes (Sederberg et al., 1998(Sederberg et al., , 2003;;Müller et al., 2006Müller et al., , 2010;;Cashman et al., 2009aCashman et al., , 2009bCashman et al., , 2009c)), there is little work addressing the conversion algorithms between trimmed NURBS surfaces and subdivision surfaces. The conversion from Catmull-Clark subdivision surfaces to NURBS surfaces can be achieved by viewing each quadrilateral face of the base mesh as a NURBS patch (Loop and Schaefer, 2008). However, conversion in the other direction is nontrivial.

# Overview

Ray tracing with NURBS targets high-quality rendering and simulation when scenes or objects are represented by NURBS curves and surfaces, which are standard in CAD and graphics due to compactness, local control, and exact geometric properties.<cite id="6dd9447c-0">NURBS surface representation is common for most 3D modeling tools because of its compactness and useful geometric properties, and direct ray tracing of NURBS surfaces can yield higher-quality rendered images compared to indirect approaches</cite> Many modern systems tessellate parametric surfaces to triangles for speed, but this trades robustness and detail for performance, motivating direct NURBS intersection and rendering research.<cite id="f99e9550-1">Most ray tracing applications tessellate parametric surfaces, which increases speed but can produce wrong images if tessellation is not sufficient and requires extra memory; thus, fast and robust ray–parametric (NURBS) surface algorithms remain an open issue</cite>

# Algorithmic Approaches for Ray–NURBS Intersection

A classic taxonomy distinguishes four algorithm families for ray–parametric surface intersections, including NURBS: subdivision, numerical (Newton-type), algebraic, and Bézier clipping; efficient algorithms exist in each class and have been adapted from graphics rendering to boundary representation and simulation contexts.<cite id="f99e9550-0">Algorithms for ray–parametric surface intersection can be classified into subdivision, numerical, algebraic, and Bézier clipping; efficient algorithms for ray–NURBS intersections exist and many were developed for graphics rendering but apply to boundaries described by NURBS</cite> Subdivision methods leverage convex hull and bounding properties, recursively partitioning surfaces until a threshold guarantees an approximate solution; numerical methods (e.g., Newton) offer quadratic convergence when well-initialized; algebraic methods solve implicit equations (e.g., Kajiya’s formulation) but can lead to high-degree systems; Bézier clipping provides robust root-finding for parametric patches via recursive subdivision and line clipping concepts.<cite id="f99e9550-0">Subdivision methods use convex hull properties and repeated subdivision until a threshold; numerical (Newton) methods converge quadratically with good initial guesses; algebraic methods (e.g., Kajiya) solve root-finding for parametric surfaces; Bézier clipping provides robust intersection via subdivision and clipping, with many authors using bounding boxes to initialize Newton and limit tests</cite>

Hybrid and specialized NURBS strategies combine methods for robustness and speed. For example, some works transform NURBS into equivalent rational Bézier sets and apply Bézier clipping, with modifications to improve performance; others interleave Bézier clipping with Newton iteration to handle coherence across pixels and avoid divergence in difficult cases.<cite id="f99e9550-4">NURBS surfaces can be mapped to equivalent rational Bézier sets and then clipped with Bézier cutting; modifications improve activity and effectiveness of Bézier cutting; hybrid schemes combine Bézier cutting for the first intersection with Newton iteration for subsequent rays in a coherence row to avoid divergence</cite> Historical references include reverse NURBS visualization methods using hierarchical node-vector structures and bisection for finding intersection points, alongside early Newton-based approaches by Toth and later work by Martin and others that shaped modern NURBS ray-tracing pipelines.<cite id="f99e9550-4">Reverse NURBS surface visualization in ray tracing used hierarchic structures to reduce tree depth; Toth used Newton’s method for ray–parametric intersections; Martin proposed hierarchical node-vector processing; bisection was used to find intersection points but increases calculation count in some cases</cite>

# Robustness and Border/Cropping Issues

Direct NURBS ray tracing must handle edge cases like trimming boundaries, cropped regions, and surface singularities; many practical systems either avoid these via tessellation or add specialized tests and parameter-space clipping.<cite id="6dd9447c-0">Direct NURBS ray tracing is motivated by better image quality but prior approaches had various limitations; border stability and special-case handling are active concerns</cite> Some methods replace problematic parametric steps with bisection or trimming-based decompositions, but these can be slower or require careful parameter estimation; researchers have proposed Newton/Cramer-based combinations to stabilize solutions and reduce artifacts in difficult surface regions.<cite id="6dd9447c-3">A Newton/Cramer combination approach for ray–NURBS intersection is proposed to improve robustness and efficiency compared to prior methods such as Martin et al.; implementation results are reported</cite><cite id="f99e9550-1">Bisection-based intersection is used in some NURBS ray-tracing approaches but increases computation; border and cropping problems persist in many parametric-surface algorithms, motivating robust methods</cite>

# CAD, Trimmed Surfaces, and B-rep Context

NURBS are the standard freeform representation in CAD; trimming enables complex shapes but introduces gaps and topological complications when stitching trimmed patches, complicating ray intersection and visualization.<cite id="f99e9550-3">NURBS are standard in CAD; trimming creates complex shapes but causes gaps when stitching trimmed NURBS patches and leaves visual trims without altering rectangular topology, complicating operations and requiring re-evaluation of trimming curves</cite> Converting trimmed NURBS to subdivision surfaces (e.g., Catmull–Clark) can eliminate gaps and provide exact boundaries via shared curves, and has been explored as a path to robust ray tracing of trimmed NURBS by represting them as subdivision surfaces.<cite id="f99e9550-3">Subdivision offers arbitrary topology and exact boundary sharing; conversion from Catmull–Clark subdivision to NURBS exists by treating base mesh faces as NURBS patches, while the reverse is nontrivial; this motivates conversion strategies to handle trimmed NURBS</cite> Subdivision-surface ray tracers with adaptive refinement and hierarchical bounding volumes can then be applied to these converted representations, achieving high-quality intersections with controllable error and robustness.<cite id="f99e9550-2">A stackless, massively parallel ray tracer for Catmull–Clark subdivision surfaces uses adaptive subdivision, conservative bounds, and a patch hierarchy; ray–patch intersection proceeds via alternating u/v subdivision, bounding volumes derived for Bézier and Gregory patches, and on-demand refinement, enabling accurate and efficient traversal and intersection</cite>

# Physics-Based Ray Tracing with NURBS

Beyond rendering, NURBS are used for physics-based ray tracing in optics and electromagnetics, where surfaces are described by NURBS and specialized algorithms solve ray reflection/refraction and geodesic paths.<cite id="6dd9447c-2">A NURBS-capable optical design library implements differential ray tracing and ray-aiming to optimize systems with NURBS surfaces and to model structural deformation effects, leveraging NURBS as a standard CAD representation</cite> In high-frequency electromagnetic analysis, NURBS enable precise modeling with fewer patches; geodesic paths on NURBS can be computed by solving geodesic differential equations, with numerical schemes ranging from Euler (efficient but low precision) to Runge–Kutta (more accurate but costly).<cite id="f99e9550-4">NURBS provide high-precision modeling with few patches in electromagnetic analysis; geodesic paths on NURBS are obtained by solving geodesic differential equations using schemes like Euler (first-order, efficient but low precision) or fourth-order Runge–Kutta (accurate but time-consuming)</cite> Newer work proposes adaptive variable-step Euler methods that adjust step sizes using shape factors to balance accuracy and efficiency for creeping rays on arbitrary NURBS surfaces.<cite id="f99e9550-4">An adaptive variable-step Euler method for creeping rays on arbitrary NURBS surfaces adjusts discrete steps via a shape factor, improving accuracy over fixed-step Euler while retaining efficiency compared to Runge–Kutta</cite>

# Practical Systems and Libraries

Industrial and research systems demonstrate end-to-end NURBS ray tracing workflows. The FORMIDABLE library integrates NURBS surfaces, differential ray tracing, and ray-aiming for freeform optical design, enabling optimization under manufacturing constraints.<cite id="6dd9447c-2">FORMIDABLE implements differential ray tracing and ray-aiming for NURBS-based optical systems and simulates performance impacts of structural deformation, reflecting NURBS’ prevalence in CAD</cite> In rendering contexts, CPU-based ray kernels such as Embree can be preferable when complex parametric primitives are involved, as rasterization pipelines may lack the necessary access patterns and NURBS ray tracing is better handled by specialized traversal kernels.<cite id="be63b7be-2">A ray-tracing pipeline on the CPU (e.g., Embree) better supports NURBS-based algorithms than rasterization-based GPU pipelines, which lack required pixel-by-pixel access; commercial GPU products often do not expose the needed accessibility</cite> More broadly, GPU photorealistic systems commonly support acceleration structures (e.g., BVH) and advanced algorithms (e.g., photon mapping), providing a foundation to which complex NURBS intersection strategies can be added or ported.<cite id="be63b7be-4">GPU-based photorealistic rendering systems support BVH and stochastic progressive photon mapping, and can be extended to complex ray tracing algorithms beyond spheres and implicit surfaces using GLSL shaders</cite>

# Notable Papers and Contributions (curated)

- Direct NURBS Ray Tracing and Border Stability: Methods targeting robust intersection and visualization on NURBS, including Newton/Cramer formulations and border-stable approaches, with comparisons to prior NURBS ray tracing by Martin and others.<cite id="6dd9447c-0">Direct NURBS ray tracing is motivated by compact, high-quality representations and better rendered images than triangle-only pipelines</cite><cite id="6dd9447c-3">A Newton/Cramer-based approach is proposed for ray–NURBS intersection and compared to Martin et al.’s method, with implementation results</cite>

- Algorithm Families and Historical Foundations: Surveys and overviews classifying subdivision, Newton, algebraic, and Bézier-clipping approaches for ray–parametric surfaces, with historical milestones (Toth, Kajiya) and practical bounding strategies to initialize Newton iteration.<cite id="f99e9550-0">A classification of ray–parametric surface intersection algorithms (subdivision, numerical/Newton, algebraic, Bézier clipping) and references to efficient methods and bounding boxes to initialize Newton and limit tests</cite><cite id="f99e9550-1">Discussion of why most systems tessellate parametric surfaces and the ongoing need for fast and robust NURBS ray intersection methods</cite><cite id="f99e9550-4">Historical methods include reverse NURBS visualization with hierarchical node-vector structures, Bézier cutting combined with Newton iteration for coherence, and mapping NURBS to rational Bézier sets for clipping</cite>

- Bézier Clipping and Rational Geometry: Transforming NURBS to rational Bézier sets and applying Bézier clipping with modifications to improve robustness and efficiency for ray–NURBS intersections.<cite id="f99e9550-4">NURBS-to-rational-Bézier conversion followed by Bézier cutting, with modifications enhancing activity and effectiveness</cite>

- Subdivision and Trim Handling: Conversion of trimmed NURBS to Catmull–Clark subdivision surfaces to eliminate gaps and provide exact boundaries; robust traversal and intersection for subdivision surfaces via adaptive refinement and hierarchical BVH-like structures.<cite id="f99e9550-3">Trimming introduces gaps and topological issues; conversion to Catmull–Clark subdivision surfaces preserves exact boundaries and simplifies operations</cite><cite id="f99e9550-2">Adaptive subdivision, conservative bounds, and hierarchical traversal yield accurate and efficient ray–patch intersection for subdivision surfaces</cite>

- Physics and Electromagnetics on NURBS: Geodesic/creeping ray tracing on NURBS via GDE solvers and adaptive stepping; NURBS-enabled optical design with differential ray tracing and ray-aiming in a production library.<cite id="f99e9550-4">Geodesic differential equations on NURBS solved by Euler or Runge–Kutta; adaptive variable-step Euler improves accuracy-efficiency for creeping rays</cite><cite id="6dd9447c-2">Differential ray tracing and ray-aiming for NURBS-based optical systems, including deformation effects on performance</cite>

# Practical Trade-offs and Design Choices

Tessellating NURBS for ray tracing trades robustness and detail for speed and ease of implementation, but can misrender features or consume extra memory; direct NURBS methods avoid these costs at the expense of algorithmic complexity and border-case handling.<cite id="f99e9550-1">Tessellation accelerates ray tracing but can produce wrong images if not sufficiently fine and requires extra memory, motivating direct NURBS intersection</cite> Subdivision-based pipelines offer robust, adaptive error control with hierarchical pruning and conservative bounds; Bézier/convex-hull properties enable efficient rejection and early exit, while Newton-type methods provide rapid convergence when well-initialized.<cite id="f99e9550-0">Subdivision and bounding strategies prune work early; Newton-type methods converge quickly with good initial guesses; algebraic and Bézier-clipping approaches provide alternative robustness</cite> For specialized domains like optics and electromagnetics, NURBS-based ray tracing must also handle trimming, geodesics, and specialized sampling strategies to balance accuracy and runtime.<cite id="f99e9550-4">Geodesic path computation on NURBS requires careful numerical schemes; adaptive stepping balances accuracy and efficiency</cite><cite id="6dd9447c-2">Optical systems with NURBS surfaces benefit from differential ray tracing and ray-aiming to optimize performance and alignment</cite>

# Pointers for Further Reading and Recent Directions

Recent GPU and CPU ray-tracing ecosystems provide acceleration structures and traversal patterns that can be paired with NURBS intersection kernels or with converted subdivision representations of trimmed NURBS.<cite id="be63b7be-2">CPU ray kernels (e.g., Embree) better expose the necessary primitives for complex parametric ray tracing than rasterization pipelines</cite><cite id="be63b7be-4">GPU photorealistic systems commonly support BVH and advanced algorithms, offering a base to integrate complex NURBS intersection strategies</cite> In CAD and manufacturing, trendlines include preserving NURBS where possible while handling trims via conversion or clipping, and integrating robust border/cropping logic into B-rep kernels for ray tracing workflows.<cite id="f99e9550-3">CAD workflows face trimming-induced gaps and topology issues; conversion to subdivision surfaces and exact boundary handling are attractive for robust ray tracing</cite> Researchers continue to propose hybrid NURBS methods that combine subdivision/convex-hull pruning, Bézier clipping, and Newton iteration to improve robustness and speed for challenging surface configurations and special-case geometries.<cite id="f99e9550-4">Hybrid Bézier clipping plus Newton iteration and rational-Bézier decomposition are used to improve robustness and efficiency of NURBS ray intersection, with coherence handling across pixels</cite>

Snippet: Ray tracing has become a popular method for generating high quality images. Most of the modern ray tracing based applications only deals with triangles as basic primitives. NURBS surface representation is common for most of 3D modelling tools because of its compactness and the useful geometric properties of NURBS surfaces. Title: Implementation of FORMIDABLE: a generalized differential optical design library with NURBS capabilities
Snippet: In the following article we describe our code FORMIDABLE that also allows design of optical surfaces described as NURBS in optical systems. Compared to FANO, FORMIDABLE also implements the following functionalities: differential ray tracing [5] which greatly speeds up optimisation of problems with large number of degrees of freedom, and ray-aiming, which allows to optimise system with a physical pupil defined on one of the intermediate surfaces. 

In the case of ray-aiming, it is unclear to us if FANO implements it, one example [6] does have the physical stop defined on surface 2, which would require ray-aiming though most of the examples have the physical stop on the first surface. 

Another objective of FORMIDABLE was to use its NURBS capabilities to simulate the impact of structural deformation on optical performance, as NURBS are a standard widely used in mechanical Computed-aided software (CAD) software hence the acronym (Freeform Optics Raytracer with Manufacturable Imaging Design cApaBiLitiEs). 

In the following sections we will first introduce the concept of differential ray tracing and its implementation. We will then describe the challenges FORMIDABLE overcome in order to optimise a NURBS based system in the context of a case-study. Finally we will describe the architecture of FORMIDABLE.

Title: Creeping Ray Tracing Algorithm for Arbitrary NURBS Surfaces Based on Adaptive Variable Step Euler Method
Snippet: Moreover, due to the advantages of high precision in modeling with low number of patches and great flexibility in simulation algorithms, NURBS has been introduced into the area of high-frequency electromagnetic analysis [8,9]. When object is described by NURBS surfaces, geodesic path can be obtained by solving the geodesic differential equation [10]. Hence, some numerical schemes were employed to handle the GDE. In [11], to obtain the tracks of creeping rays on NURBS surfaces, the geodesic differential equations are solved by Euler method which is the first-order scheme for differential equations. And in [12], the Runge-Kutta method of order 4 was applied to solving the GDE for determining the tracing on NURBS surfaces. Euler method is highly efficient but with low precision. On the contrary, the Runge-Kutta method is of high precision but time-consuming in the process of creeping ray tracing. 

In this paper, aiming at improving the accuracy and efficiency of creeping ray tracing on arbitrarily shaped NURBS surface, we present a creeping ray tracing algorithm based on a novel adaptive variable step Euler method. Since the adaptive variable step Euler method is based on the conventional Euler method, the efficiency is ensured. And in the process of numerically iteratively solving the GDE, due to the introduction of shape factor , the discrete step sizes are adaptively corrected timely. Hence, compared with the conventional Euler method, the proposed method can easily ensure the accuracy of creeping ray tracing on arbitrarily shaped NURBS surface. Namely, it is more suitable for engineering applications. The efficiency and accuracy of the proposed method will be analyzed and verified by comparing the results of different methods.

According to Pabst [16], the algorithms for finding ray-parametric surface intersection can be classified as follows: subdivision, numerical, algebraic, and Bézier clipping.

Subdivision-based algorithms make use of convex hull property of parametric surfaces [17,18]. The surface is tested for the intersection with ray and in case of success it is subdivided. The process is repeated until no hit is reported or the surface is smaller than the prescribed threshold and therefore is assumed to adequately approximate the real intersection point.

Title: Massively Parallel Stackless Ray Tracing of Catmull-Clark Subdivision Surfaces
Snippet: In a pre-process OpenSubdiv performs feature adaptive subdivision on the input mesh to isolate irregular patches and output patch data. Note that we do not need to differentiate between regular and transition patches since we do not need to take special care at boundaries between subdivision levels. After determining conservative spatial bounds of the patches, a hierarchy referencing the patches is built. A ray is then intersected with the mesh by first traversing this hierarchy, pruning patches that cannot be intersected by the ray, and identifying patches potentially intersected by the ray. 

In order to determine the first intersection of a ray and a bicubic patch, we partition the parametric unit square recursively, alternating u and v direction. Restricting the bicubic patches to the resulting subdomains allows one to determine bounding volumes as derived for Bézier patches in Section 3.1 and Gregory patches in Section 3.2. 

Refining the subdomains on demand results in a sequence of nested axis-aligned bounding boxes and in fact intersecting only bounding boxes is sufficient to compute intersections up to almost floating point precision. Section 3.3 details Algorithm 3 that only uses bit trails instead of a stack and recomputes control points for backtracking. The numerical properties of the algorithm are discussed in Section 3.4, and its efficient parallelization is explained in Section 3.5.

Title: Conversion of trimmed NURBS surfaces to Catmull-Clark subdivision surfaces
Snippet: Non-Uniform Rational B-Splines (NURBS) are the standard freeform surface representation in Computer-Aided Design (CAD) applications. Due to their limitation of a strict rectangular topology, trimming is an important operation to create complex objects. However, it introduces unavoidable gaps when stitching two trimmed NURBS patches together (Sederberg et al., 2008). Moreover, as the trimmed NURBS are only visually trimmed by skipping the evaluation of the trimmed part in parameter space (Fig. 1(a)), the rectangular NURBS topology is not altered although the geometric shape has changed. As a consequence, many operations on trimmed shapes may require a time-consuming re-evaluation process of the trimming curves (Farin, 2001), e.g., editing and deformation. 

Instead, subdivision, because of its ability to handle arbitrary topology and ease of use, has become an attractive alternative to NURBS, especially for modelling in high-end animation productions (Pixar, DeRose et al., 1998;Stam, 1998). The subdivision representations have the great advantage that if two subdivision surfaces share a boundary edge in base meshes, they both contain exactly that piece of boundary curve. This makes it possible to apply exactly the same trimming curves on two intersecting surfaces and thus provide gap-free models. Although there has been great progress in NURBS-compatible subdivision schemes (Sederberg et al., 1998(Sederberg et al., , 2003;;Müller et al., 2006Müller et al., , 2010;;Cashman et al., 2009aCashman et al., , 2009bCashman et al., , 2009c)), there is little work addressing the conversion algorithms between trimmed NURBS surfaces and subdivision surfaces. The conversion from Catmull-Clark subdivision surfaces to NURBS surfaces can be achieved by viewing each quadrilateral face of the base mesh as a NURBS patch (Loop and Schaefer, 2008). However, conversion in the other direction is nontrivial.

All following intersection points in the same pixel row are calculated using Newton iterative algorithm. The last calculated intersection point is used as previous result for the following intersection point. The device for barrier detection is used to check-up whether the intersection point that is calculated using Newton iterative algorithm is the last point. snippet.text:
Non-Uniform Rational B-Splines (NURBS) are the standard freeform surface representation in Computer-Aided Design (CAD) applications. Due to their limitation of a strict rectangular topology, trimming is an important operation to create complex objects. However, it introduces unavoidable gaps when stitching two trimmed NURBS patches together (Sederberg et al., 2008). Moreover, as the trimmed NURBS are only visually trimmed by skipping the evaluation of the trimmed part in parameter space (Fig. 1(a)), the rectangular NURBS topology is not altered although the geometric shape has changed. As a consequence, many operations on trimmed shapes may require a time-consuming re-evaluation process of the trimming curves (Farin, 2001), e.g., editing and deformation. 

Instead, subdivision, because of its ability to handle arbitrary topology and ease of use, has become an attractive alternative to NURBS, especially for modelling in high-end animation productions (Pixar, DeRose et al., 1998;Stam, 1998). The subdivision representations have the great advantage that if two subdivision surfaces share a boundary edge in base meshes, they both contain exactly that piece of boundary curve. This makes it possible to apply exactly the same trimming curves on two intersecting surfaces and thus provide gap-free models. Although there has been great progress in NURBS-compatible subdivision schemes (Sederberg et al., 1998(Sederberg et al., , 2003;;Müller et al., 2006Müller et al., , 2010;;Cashman et al., 2009aCashman et al., , 2009bCashman et al., , 2009c)), there is little work addressing the conversion algorithms between trimmed NURBS surfaces and subdivision surfaces. The conversion from Catmull-Clark subdivision surfaces to NURBS surfaces can be achieved by viewing each quadrilateral face of the base mesh as a NURBS patch (Loop and Schaefer, 2008). However, conversion in the other direction is nontrivial.

In order to specify the boundaries of the enclosure, parametric NURBS surfaces were chosen due to a few reasons. NURBS surfaces are able to describe shapes of high complexity, use little of computer memory and are widely used in CAD programs and computer graphics [14,15]. Moreover, there exist efficient algorithms for finding ray-NURBS surface intersection.

Most of these algorithms were developed for the purposes of surfaces visualization and rendering in computer graphics.

According to Pabst [16], the algorithms for finding ray-parametric surface intersection can be classified as follows: subdivision, numerical, algebraic, and Bézier clipping.

Subdivision-based algorithms make use of convex hull property of parametric surfaces [17,18]. The surface is tested for the intersection with ray and in case of success it is subdivided. The process is repeated until no hit is reported or the surface is smaller than the prescribed threshold and therefore is assumed to adequately approximate the real intersection point.

The core of numerical algorithms is the iterative Newton's method characterized by a quadratic convergence rate, provided it has a good initial guess. The algorithm was first used in the context of finding rayparametric surface intersection by Toth [19]. The initial guesses for Newton's method were obtained from the interval analysis of the surface. Other authors [16,[20][21][22] used hierarchies of axis aligned bounding boxes to properly initialize Newton's method and to limit the number of ray-surface intersection tests, but they implemented different algorithms for bounding the box creation.

Title: An Border-Stable Approach to NURBS Surface Rendering for Ray Tracing
Snippet: Ray tracing has become a popular method for generating high quality images. Most of the modern ray tracing based applications only deals with triangles as basic primitives. NURBS surface representation is common for most of 3D modelling tools because of its compactness and the useful geometric properties of NURBS surfaces. Using the direct ray tracing of NURBS surfaces, one can achieve better quality of rendered images [1]. There are many approaches to solving this problem.

Title: Creeping Ray Tracing Algorithm for Arbitrary NURBS Surfaces Based on Adaptive Variable Step Euler Method

Title: Creeping Ray Tracing Algorithm for Arbitrary NURBS Surfaces Based on Adaptive Variable Step Euler Method
Snippet: Moreover, due to the advantages of high precision in modeling with low number of patches and great flexibility in simulation algorithms, NURBS has been introduced into the area of high-frequency electromagnetic analysis [8,9]. When object is described by NURBS surfaces, geodesic path can be obtained by solving the geodesic differential equation [10]. Hence, some numerical schemes were employed to handle the GDE. In [11], to obtain the tracks of creeping rays on NURBS surfaces, the geodesic differential equations are solved by Euler method which is the first-order scheme for differential equations. And in [12], the Runge-Kutta method of order 4 was applied to solving the GDE for determining the tracing on NURBS surfaces. Euler method is highly efficient but with low precision. On the contrary, the Runge-Kutta method is of high precision but time-consuming in the process of creeping ray tracing. 

In this paper, aiming at improving the accuracy and efficiency of creeping ray tracing on arbitrarily shaped NURBS surface, we present a creeping ray tracing algorithm based on a novel adaptive variable step Euler method. Since the adaptive variable step Euler method is based on the conventional Euler method, the efficiency is ensured. And in the process of numerically iteratively solving the GDE, due to the introduction of shape factor , the discrete step sizes are adaptively corrected timely. Hence, compared with the conventional Euler method, the proposed method can easily ensure the accuracy of creeping ray tracing on arbitrarily shaped NURBS surface. Namely, it is more suitable for engineering applications. The efficiency and accuracy of the proposed method will be analyzed and verified by comparing the results of different methods.

Title: Implementation of FORMIDABLE: a generalized differential optical design library with NURBS capabilities
Snippet: In the following article we describe our code FORMIDABLE that also allows design of optical surfaces described as NURBS in optical systems. Compared to FANO, FORMIDABLE also implements the following functionalities: differential ray tracing [5] which greatly speeds up optimisation of problems with large number of degrees of freedom, and ray-aiming, which allows to optimise system with a physical pupil defined on one of the intermediate surfaces. 

In the case of ray-aiming, it is unclear to us if FANO implements it, one example [6] does have the physical stop defined on surface 2, which would require ray-aiming though most of the examples have the physical stop on the first surface. 

Another objective of FORMIDABLE was to use its NURBS capabilities to simulate the impact of structural deformation on optical performance, as NURBS are a standard widely used in mechanical Computed-aided software (CAD) software hence the acronym (Freeform Optics Raytracer with Manufacturable Imaging Design cApaBiLitiEs). 

In the following sections we will first introduce the concept of differential ray tracing and its implementation. We will then describe the challenges FORMIDABLE overcome in order to optimise a NURBS based system in the context of a case-study. Finally we will describe the architecture of FORMIDABLE.

Title: Implementing a Photorealistic Rendering System using GLSL
Snippet: Ray tracing on GPUs is becoming quite common these days. There are many publicly available documents on how to implement basic ray tracing on GPUs for spheres and implicit surfaces. We even have some general frameworks for ray tracing on GPUs. We however hardly find details on how to implement more complex ray tracing algorithms themselves that are commonly used for photorealistic rendering. This paper explains an implementation of a stand-alone rendering system on GPUs which supports the bounding volume hierarchy and stochastic progressive photon mapping. The key characteristic of the system is that it uses only GLSL shaders without relying on any platform dependent feature. The system can thus run on many platforms that support OpenGL, making photorealistic rendering on GPUs widely accessible. This paper also sketches practical ideas for stackless traversal and pseudorandom number generation which both fit well with the limited system configuration.

In the following article we describe our code FORMIDABLE that also allows design of optical surfaces described as NURBS in optical systems. Compared to FANO, FORMIDABLE also implements the following functionalities: differential ray tracing [5] which greatly speeds up optimisation of problems with large number of degrees of freedom, and ray-aiming, which allows to optimise system with a physical pupil defined on one of the intermediate surfaces. 

In the case of ray-aiming, it is unclear to us if FANO implements it, one example [6] does have the physical stop defined on surface 2, which would require ray-aiming though most of the examples have the physical stop on the first surface. 

Another objective of FORMIDABLE was to use its NURBS capabilities to simulate the impact of structural deformation on optical performance, as NURBS are a standard widely used in mechanical Computed-aided software (CAD) software hence the acronym (Freeform Optics Raytracer with Manufacturable Imaging Design cApaBiLitiEs). 

In the following sections we will first introduce the concept of differential ray tracing and its implementation. We will then describe the challenges FORMIDABLE overcome in order to optimise a NURBS based system in the context of a case-study. Finally we will describe the architecture of FORMIDABLE.

snippet.text: Ray tracing on GPUs is becoming quite common these days. There are many publicly available documents on how to implement basic ray tracing on GPUs for spheres and implicit surfaces. We even have some general frameworks for ray tracing on GPUs. We however hardly find details on how to implement more complex ray tracing algorithms themselves that are commonly used for photorealistic rendering. This paper explains an implementation of a stand-alone rendering system on GPUs which supports the bounding volume hierarchy and stochastic progressive photon mapping. The key characteristic of the system is that it uses only GLSL shaders without relying on any platform dependent feature. The system can thus run on many platforms that support OpenGL, making photorealistic rendering on GPUs widely accessible. This paper also sketches practical ideas for stackless traversal and pseudorandom number generation which both fit well with the limited system configuration.

problem: Find papers on the topic that generative artificial intelligence trends towards the most average response.
final_response:
# Interpreting “average response” in generative AI

In generative AI, “average” can mean several things: (a) the model concentrates probability mass around the dominant modes of the data (mode-seeking), (b) outputs are steered toward the base model’s distribution via KL constraints (averaging/centralization relative to a prior), (c) ensembles or multiple samples are aggregated to a central tendency (mean/centroid) in representation or output space, or (d) controllable objectives optimize toward a user-specified target that sits in the middle of a feasible range. The papers below cover these facets and show how training objectives, control signals, and evaluation practices can trend toward average-like behavior. <cite id="1ea488e5-0">In generative modeling, KL-based objectives are a primary mechanism shaping whether models cover many modes or concentrate around dominant ones</cite><cite id="1ea488e5-3">Reverse KL tends to produce mode-seeking behavior that focuses on the largest modes of the data distribution</cite><cite id="1dd65550-3">KL-regularized control in diffusion and LLM text generation regularizes outputs toward a base model or target distribution</cite><cite id="06731774-0">Centroid and consensus computations are used to summarize multiple model outputs or annotations toward a central tendency</cite><cite id="705c0347-2">Empirically, LLM-as-judge evaluations often concentrate around mid-range scores rather than extreme values</cite>.

# Mechanisms that push toward dominant modes or base-like distributions

A core mechanism is the choice of divergence objective. Under forward KL (data to model), models can spread mass over multiple modes; under reverse KL (model to data), optimization tends to “mode collapse,” concentrating on a single dominant mode—i.e., a form of average-like centralization within the model’s distribution. <cite id="1ea488e5-0">Minimizing DKL(data || model) tends to cover multiple modes, while minimizing DKL(model || data) causes the model to concentrate on a single mode (mode-seeking), often called mode collapse</cite><cite id="1ea488e5-1">Alternative formulations and priors (e.g., reverse KL with mixture or diversity priors) can mitigate or exploit mode-seeking behavior</cite>. In LLM knowledge distillation, aligning a student to a teacher via reverse KL concentrates the student’s output distribution on the teacher’s dominant modes, effectively steering toward “average” teacher behavior. <cite id="1ea488e5-3">Minimizing reverse KLD in LLM distillation causes the student to place high probability on the teacher’s large modes and ignore small ones; forward KLD can push into low-quality regions, whereas reverse KLD focuses on preserving major modes for correctness and faithfulness</cite>.

In diffusion and score-based generation, classifier-free (base-model) guidance and KL-regularized objectives explicitly pull generations toward the base model’s distribution, counteracting overfitting to specific reward objectives and reducing mode collapse. <cite id="1dd65550-3">Classifier-free guidance and RL fine-tuning have been widely used, but can lead to mode collapse and overfitting; KL-constrained optimization regularizes generation back to the base model, though with scheduling or initial-noise caveats</cite>. These methods formalize “averaging” in latent or token space: the generated distribution remains close to the base (average) model’s prior, with control signals modulating deviations. <cite id="1dd65550-3">KL-regularized RL in LLM text generation can be framed via no-regret learning, and related token-level guidance methods target KL-regularized control</cite>.

# Controllable generation toward average-like attributes

Latent and embedding-space steering provide inference-time control that can be tuned to move outputs toward central or preferred attributes (e.g., sentiment, style, safety), often by modifying output embeddings or hidden states. <cite id="1dd65550-1">Latent space manipulation (LSM) alters word/hidden embeddings via a steering matrix to adjust behavior at inference time</cite><cite id="1dd65550-2">Prior steering perturbations include mean difference vectors and PCA directions that identify semantically meaningful latent axes for controlled shifts</cite><cite id="1dd65550-0">On-the-fly controllability can be achieved via external discriminators or in-context demonstrations, with contrastive decoding modulating steering influence through prediction probability shifts</cite>. In diffusion, classifier guidance and classifier-free guidance inject user objectives into the generation process while constraining deviations via KL regularization to maintain base-model-like sampling. <cite id="1dd65550-3">Classifier and classifier-free guidance provide controllable generation when an objective is available, and KL-constrained approaches regularize outputs to the base model to avoid bias and mode collapse</cite>.

Alignment and internal-representation losses also encourage models to behave like a reference (teacher) system—again, a form of averaging toward a central target. <cite id="06731774-2">Knowledge-distilled parametric RAG combines generative losses with alignment losses between teacher and student hidden states at each layer, averaging across layers with weights proportional to depth</cite>. These techniques show that with appropriate regularization and control, models can be steered to produce outputs closer to population/teacher/central behavior rather than exploring fringe modes.

# Evidence of central-tendency behavior in LLM evaluations and aggregation

Several works quantify or leverage central tendency in LLM outputs or judgments. LLM-as-judge evaluations often exhibit “averageness” in scoring: they avoid extreme ratings and cluster in the mid-range, consistent with central tendency and optimism calibration. <cite id="705c0347-2">Across ICLR and NeurIPS papers, LLM ratings concentrate in the mid-range rather than extreme values, with less inflation for high human ratings and stronger inflation for mid-to-low human ratings</cite>. Beyond scoring, methods explicitly compute consensus and centroids to summarize multiple LLM outputs or annotations toward a central tendency, reinforcing the role of averaging in evaluation and decision-making workflows. <cite id="06731774-0">Consensus metrics weight observed LLM ratings by frequency and compute a weighted average; semantic motivations are summarized via centroid computation of cosine similarities</cite><cite id="06731774-1">Theoretical analysis of LLM-as-a-judge shows optimal behavior aligns with majority voting or predicting the mean annotation, formalizing “average” decision rules</cite>.

# Related theoretical and methodological ingredients

Beyond direct central-tendency objectives, several ingredients support average-like behavior: consensus modeling, uniformity/repulsion in representation learning, and hierarchical priors that encode central tendencies and group variation. <cite id="06731774-4">Hierarchical Bayesian models for cultural consensus and respondent bias estimate item consensus locations via learned embeddings and normal population-level priors, capturing central tendency across items and groups</cite><cite id="06731774-3">Kernel-based contrastive learning introduces centroid (average over multiple views) objectives and integrates priors via kernel embeddings to better estimate central representations</cite>. These ideas complement KL-based and steering methods by providing structured ways to pull distributions or representations toward central, consensus-aligned regions.

# Representative papers and what they show

- Generative modeling and KL objectives: <cite id="1ea488e5-0">Forward vs. reverse KL divergence yields contrasting behaviors—multi-mode coverage vs. mode-seeking concentration—highlighting how optimization can push models toward dominant modes</cite><cite id="1ea488e5-1">Alternative KL formulations and mixture/priors can mitigate or modulate mode-seeking (mode collapse), offering control over the balance between diversity and centralization</cite>.
- LLM knowledge distillation: <cite id="1ea488e5-3">Reverse KLD in LLM distillation concentrates student outputs on teacher’s dominant modes, ignoring small ones, supporting a mechanism toward average-like teacher behavior; forward KLD risks low-quality outputs</cite>.
- Diffusion/LLM controllability with KL constraints: <cite id="1dd65550-3">Classifier and classifier-free guidance enable controllable generation; KL-regularized objectives counteract mode collapse and overfitting by regularizing to the base model, with practical considerations on noise schedulers and initial distributions</cite>.
- Latent/activation steering: <cite id="1dd65550-1">Latent space manipulation (LM-Steer) linearly transforms output embeddings to steer style/sentiment while monitoring performance trade-offs</cite><cite id="1dd65550-2">Sparse activation steering constructs perturbations (e.g., mean differences, PCA directions) to move along meaningful latent axes</cite><cite id="1dd65550-0">Dynamic activation composition and contrastive decoding provide on-the-fly steering by modulating prediction probabilities via steering vectors</cite>.
- Empirical central tendency in LLM-as-judge: <cite id="705c0347-2">LLM reviewers’ ratings cluster in the mid-range and avoid extremes, showing an inflation pattern stronger for mid-to-low human scores</cite>.
- Aggregation and consensus: <cite id="06731774-0">Consensus and centroid computations summarize multiple model annotations and outputs toward central tendencies</cite><cite id="06731774-1">Optimal LLM-as-a-judge strategies can be defined via majority vote or mean prediction, formalizing average decision rules</cite>.
- Alignment via internal representation losses: <cite id="06731774-2">Layer-wise cosine alignment losses with weighted averaging across layers align student reasoning processes to a teacher, pulling internal states toward central (teacher-like) representations</cite>.
- Hierarchical/representation-level central tendency: <cite id="06731774-3">Uniformity between image centroids and prior knowledge in kernel contrastive learning provides a route to average-centered representations</cite><cite id="06731774-4">Bayesian hierarchical models estimate item consensus and central tendencies with population-level priors for items and groups</cite>.

# Implications, limitations, and open questions

Taken together, these works show that generative AI can trend toward “average” responses through objective choices (reverse KL, KL regularization), controllable guidance (latent/space steering, classifier guidance), and evaluation/aggregation practices (mean/centroid, majority vote). <cite id="1ea488e5-3">Reverse KL and KL-regularized training concentrate probability on dominant modes or base-like distributions</cite><cite id="1dd65555-3">KL-constrained guidance in diffusion/LLMs steers outputs back to the base model to avoid overfitting and mode collapse</cite><cite id="705c0347-2">LLM-as-judge scoring exhibits mid-range concentration</cite><cite id="06731774-0">Consensus/centroid aggregation formalizes averaging across multiple outputs or annotations</cite>. However, “averageness” is not inherently neutral: it can reduce diversity, introduce bias toward teacher/base behavior, or reflect systemic evaluation trends (e.g., LLM reviewer inflation). <cite id="1ea488e5-0">Reverse KL’s mode-seeking can ignore minority modes and lead to mode collapse</cite><cite id="1dd65555-3">KL-regularized control requires careful scheduling and initialization to avoid bias and maintain diversity</cite><cite id="705c0347-2">LLM-as-judge ratings are systematically higher and mid-range concentrated, indicating potential optimism bias</cite>.

Open questions include: (1) quantifying large-scale homogenization across models and time (e.g., stylistic convergence), (2) principled trade-offs between diversity and central tendency in aligned systems, and (3) robust evaluation of “averageness” against minority or long-tail creative modes. Additional evidence would come from longitudinal analyses of model outputs, audits of style/creativity distributions over time, and benchmarks that explicitly reward both centrality and diversity under different objectives. <cite id="1ea488e5-0">Understanding how objective choices map to mode coverage vs. concentration remains foundational</cite><cite id="1dd65550-3">KL-regularized guidance offers a promising axis for quantifying average-like behavior but needs careful design to balance bias and diversity</cite>.

# Takeaways for research and practice

- If your goal is averageness (e.g., faithful, safe, typical responses), consider reverse KL/distillation objectives, KL-regularized guidance, and centroid/mean targets in latent or token space. <cite id="1ea488e5-3">Reverse KLD focuses on dominant modes for correctness and faithfulness</cite><cite id="1dd65550-3">KL-constrained control regularizes to base distributions to avoid mode collapse and overfitting</cite><cite id="1dd65550-1">Latent steering can nudge outputs toward desired central attributes</cite>.
- If you need diversity, add mixture priors, diversity bonuses, or repulsion terms, and evaluate minority-mode coverage explicitly. <cite id="1ea488e5-1">Mixture generators and alternative divergences can mitigate mode collapse and preserve diversity</cite><cite id="06731774-3">Uniformity constraints at the centroid level can counteract over-concentration</cite>.
- For evaluation, report central tendency (means/medians) and dispersion (variance, tail coverage) of outputs and judge behaviors, and consider both LLM-as-judge and human baselines. <cite id="705c0347-2">LLM-as-judge ratings cluster in mid-range and differ systematically from humans</cite><cite id="06731774-0">Consensus and centroid metrics summarize multiple runs/annotations toward central tendencies</cite>.

Snippet: Generative models are a subarea of research that has been rapidly growing in recent years, and successfully applied in a wide range of modern real-world applications (e.g., see chapter 20 in [9]). Their common approach is to address the density estimation problem where one aims to learn a model distribution p model that approximates the true, but unknown, data distribution p data . Methods in this approach deal with two fundamental problems. First, the learning behaviors and performance of generative models depend on the choice of objective functions to train them [28,13]. The most widely-used objective, considered the de-facto standard one, is to follow the principle of maximum likelihood estimate that seeks model parameters to maximize the likelihood of training data. This is equivalent to minimizing the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between data and model distributions: D KL (p data p model ). It has been observed that this minimization tends to result in p model that covers multiple modes of p data , but may produce completely unseen and potentially undesirable samples [28]. By contrast, another approach is to swap the arguments and instead, minimize: D KL (p model p data ), which is usually referred to as the reverse KL divergence [20,11,13,28]. It is observed that optimization towards the reverse KL divergence criteria mimics the mode-seeking process where p model concentrates on a single mode of p data while ignoring other modes, known as the problem of mode collapse. These behaviors are well-studied in [28,13,11].

The modified representation h ′ (x) is then fed into the subsequent layers of the language model, thereby influencing the final output generation. 

Prior work proposed various ways to construct the additive perturbation vector v, including mean difference vectors between contrasting classes (Dathathri et al., 2020), andPCA (Kleindessner et al., 2023). Title: Efficient Controllable Diffusion via Optimal Classifier Guidance
Snippet: There has been significant interest in controllable generation of diffusion models, starting from Dhariwal & Nichol (2021) which introduced classifier guidance, to then Ho & Salimans (2022) which introduced classifier-free guidance. These methods paved the way for further interest in controllable generation, in particular when there is an objective function to optimize. First demonstrated by Black et al. (2024); Fan et al. (2023), RL fine-tuning of diffusion models has grown in popularity with works such as Clark et al. (2024); Prabhudesai et al. (2023) which use direct backpropagation to optimize the reward function. However, these methods can lead to mode collapse of the generations and overfitting. Further works then focused on maximizing the KL-constrained optimization problem which regularizes the generation process to the base model (Uehara et al., 2024b) but suffer either from needing special memoryless noise schedulers (Domingo-Enrich et al., 2025) or needing to control the initial distribution of the diffusion process (Uehara et al., 2024a) to avoid a bias problem. Our approach does not need to do any of these modification. Li et al. (2024) proposed a method to augment the decoding process and avoid training the underlying base model, but yield an increase in compute time. Their practical approach also does not guarantee to learn the optimal distribution. More broadly, Mudgal et al. (2023);Zhou et al. (2025) investigate token-level classifier guidance for KLregularized controllable generation of large language models. Zhou et al. ( 2025) also demonstrated that to optimize a KL-regularized RL objective in the context of LLM text generation, one just needs to perform no-regret learning. While our approach is motivated by the Q# approach from Zhou et al. ( 2025), we tackle score-based guidance for diffusion models in a continuous latent space and continue time, where the space of actions form an infinite set-making algorithm design and analysis substantially more difficult than the setting of discrete token and discrete-time in prior LLM work.
