# Interpreting “average response” in generative AI

In generative AI, “average” can mean several things: (a) the model concentrates probability mass around the dominant modes of the data (mode-seeking), (b) outputs are steered toward the base model’s distribution via KL constraints (averaging/centralization relative to a prior), (c) ensembles or multiple samples are aggregated to a central tendency (mean/centroid) in representation or output space, or (d) controllable objectives optimize toward a user-specified target that sits in the middle of a feasible range. The papers below cover these facets and show how training objectives, control signals, and evaluation practices can trend toward average-like behavior. <cite id="1ea488e5-0">In generative modeling, KL-based objectives are a primary mechanism shaping whether models cover many modes or concentrate around dominant ones</cite><cite id="1ea488e5-3">Reverse KL tends to produce mode-seeking behavior that focuses on the largest modes of the data distribution</cite><cite id="1dd65550-3">KL-regularized control in diffusion and LLM text generation regularizes outputs toward a base model or target distribution</cite><cite id="06731774-0">Centroid and consensus computations are used to summarize multiple model outputs or annotations toward a central tendency</cite><cite id="705c0347-2">Empirically, LLM-as-judge evaluations often concentrate around mid-range scores rather than extreme values</cite>.

# Mechanisms that push toward dominant modes or base-like distributions

A core mechanism is the choice of divergence objective. Under forward KL (data to model), models can spread mass over multiple modes; under reverse KL (model to data), optimization tends to “mode collapse,” concentrating on a single dominant mode—i.e., a form of average-like centralization within the model’s distribution. <cite id="1ea488e5-0">Minimizing DKL(data || model) tends to cover multiple modes, while minimizing DKL(model || data) causes the model to concentrate on a single mode (mode-seeking), often called mode collapse</cite><cite id="1ea488e5-1">Alternative formulations and priors (e.g., reverse KL with mixture or diversity priors) can mitigate or exploit mode-seeking behavior</cite>. In LLM knowledge distillation, aligning a student to a teacher via reverse KL concentrates the student’s output distribution on the teacher’s dominant modes, effectively steering toward “average” teacher behavior. <cite id="1ea488e5-3">Minimizing reverse KLD in LLM distillation causes the student to place high probability on the teacher’s large modes and ignore small ones; forward KLD can push into low-quality regions, whereas reverse KLD focuses on preserving major modes for correctness and faithfulness</cite>.

In diffusion and score-based generation, classifier-free (base-model) guidance and KL-regularized objectives explicitly pull generations toward the base model’s distribution, counteracting overfitting to specific reward objectives and reducing mode collapse. <cite id="1dd65550-3">Classifier-free guidance and RL fine-tuning have been widely used, but can lead to mode collapse and overfitting; KL-constrained optimization regularizes generation back to the base model, though with scheduling or initial-noise caveats</cite>. These methods formalize “averaging” in latent or token space: the generated distribution remains close to the base (average) model’s prior, with control signals modulating deviations. <cite id="1dd65550-3">KL-regularized RL in LLM text generation can be framed via no-regret learning, and related token-level guidance methods target KL-regularized control</cite>.

# Controllable generation toward average-like attributes

Latent and embedding-space steering provide inference-time control that can be tuned to move outputs toward central or preferred attributes (e.g., sentiment, style, safety), often by modifying output embeddings or hidden states. <cite id="1dd65550-1">Latent space manipulation (LSM) alters word/hidden embeddings via a steering matrix to adjust behavior at inference time</cite><cite id="1dd65550-2">Prior steering perturbations include mean difference vectors and PCA directions that identify semantically meaningful latent axes for controlled shifts</cite><cite id="1dd65550-0">On-the-fly controllability can be achieved via external discriminators or in-context demonstrations, with contrastive decoding modulating steering influence through prediction probability shifts</cite>. In diffusion, classifier guidance and classifier-free guidance inject user objectives into the generation process while constraining deviations via KL regularization to maintain base-model-like sampling. <cite id="1dd65550-3">Classifier and classifier-free guidance provide controllable generation when an objective is available, and KL-constrained approaches regularize outputs to the base model to avoid bias and mode collapse</cite>.

Alignment and internal-representation losses also encourage models to behave like a reference (teacher) system—again, a form of averaging toward a central target. <cite id="06731774-2">Knowledge-distilled parametric RAG combines generative losses with alignment losses between teacher and student hidden states at each layer, averaging across layers with weights proportional to depth</cite>. These techniques show that with appropriate regularization and control, models can be steered to produce outputs closer to population/teacher/central behavior rather than exploring fringe modes.

# Evidence of central-tendency behavior in LLM evaluations and aggregation

Several works quantify or leverage central tendency in LLM outputs or judgments. LLM-as-judge evaluations often exhibit “averageness” in scoring: they avoid extreme ratings and cluster in the mid-range, consistent with central tendency and optimism calibration. <cite id="705c0347-2">Across ICLR and NeurIPS papers, LLM ratings concentrate in the mid-range rather than extreme values, with less inflation for high human ratings and stronger inflation for mid-to-low human ratings</cite>. Beyond scoring, methods explicitly compute consensus and centroids to summarize multiple LLM outputs or annotations toward a central tendency, reinforcing the role of averaging in evaluation and decision-making workflows. <cite id="06731774-0">Consensus metrics weight observed LLM ratings by frequency and compute a weighted average; semantic motivations are summarized via centroid computation of cosine similarities</cite><cite id="06731774-1">Theoretical analysis of LLM-as-a-judge shows optimal behavior aligns with majority voting or predicting the mean annotation, formalizing “average” decision rules</cite>.

# Related theoretical and methodological ingredients

Beyond direct central-tendency objectives, several ingredients support average-like behavior: consensus modeling, uniformity/repulsion in representation learning, and hierarchical priors that encode central tendencies and group variation. <cite id="06731774-4">Hierarchical Bayesian models for cultural consensus and respondent bias estimate item consensus locations via learned embeddings and normal population-level priors, capturing central tendency across items and groups</cite><cite id="06731774-3">Kernel-based contrastive learning introduces centroid (average over multiple views) objectives and integrates priors via kernel embeddings to better estimate central representations</cite>. These ideas complement KL-based and steering methods by providing structured ways to pull distributions or representations toward central, consensus-aligned regions.

# Representative papers and what they show

- Generative modeling and KL objectives: <cite id="1ea488e5-0">Forward vs. reverse KL divergence yields contrasting behaviors—multi-mode coverage vs. mode-seeking concentration—highlighting how optimization can push models toward dominant modes</cite><cite id="1ea488e5-1">Alternative KL formulations and mixture/priors can mitigate or modulate mode-seeking (mode collapse), offering control over the balance between diversity and centralization</cite>.
- LLM knowledge distillation: <cite id="1ea488e5-3">Reverse KLD in LLM distillation concentrates student outputs on teacher’s dominant modes, ignoring small ones, supporting a mechanism toward average-like teacher behavior; forward KLD risks low-quality outputs</cite>.
- Diffusion/LLM controllability with KL constraints: <cite id="1dd65550-3">Classifier and classifier-free guidance enable controllable generation; KL-regularized objectives counteract mode collapse and overfitting by regularizing to the base model, with practical considerations on noise schedulers and initial distributions</cite>.
- Latent/activation steering: <cite id="1dd65550-1">Latent space manipulation (LM-Steer) linearly transforms output embeddings to steer style/sentiment while monitoring performance trade-offs</cite><cite id="1dd65550-2">Sparse activation steering constructs perturbations (e.g., mean differences, PCA directions) to move along meaningful latent axes</cite><cite id="1dd65550-0">Dynamic activation composition and contrastive decoding provide on-the-fly steering by modulating prediction probabilities via steering vectors</cite>.
- Empirical central tendency in LLM-as-judge: <cite id="705c0347-2">LLM reviewers’ ratings cluster in the mid-range and avoid extremes, showing an inflation pattern stronger for mid-to-low human scores</cite>.
- Aggregation and consensus: <cite id="06731774-0">Consensus and centroid computations summarize multiple model annotations and outputs toward central tendencies</cite><cite id="06731774-1">Optimal LLM-as-a-judge strategies can be defined via majority vote or mean prediction, formalizing average decision rules</cite>.
- Alignment via internal representation losses: <cite id="06731774-2">Layer-wise cosine alignment losses with weighted averaging across layers align student reasoning processes to a teacher, pulling internal states toward central (teacher-like) representations</cite>.
- Hierarchical/representation-level central tendency: <cite id="06731774-3">Uniformity between image centroids and prior knowledge in kernel contrastive learning provides a route to average-centered representations</cite><cite id="06731774-4">Bayesian hierarchical models estimate item consensus and central tendencies with population-level priors for items and groups</cite>.

# Implications, limitations, and open questions

Taken together, these works show that generative AI can trend toward “average” responses through objective choices (reverse KL, KL regularization), controllable guidance (latent/space steering, classifier guidance), and evaluation/aggregation practices (mean/centroid, majority vote). <cite id="1ea488e5-3">Reverse KL and KL-regularized training concentrate probability on dominant modes or base-like distributions</cite><cite id="1dd65555-3">KL-constrained guidance in diffusion/LLMs steers outputs back to the base model to avoid overfitting and mode collapse</cite><cite id="705c0347-2">LLM-as-judge scoring exhibits mid-range concentration</cite><cite id="06731774-0">Consensus/centroid aggregation formalizes averaging across multiple outputs or annotations</cite>. However, “averageness” is not inherently neutral: it can reduce diversity, introduce bias toward teacher/base behavior, or reflect systemic evaluation trends (e.g., LLM reviewer inflation). <cite id="1ea488e5-0">Reverse KL’s mode-seeking can ignore minority modes and lead to mode collapse</cite><cite id="1dd65555-3">KL-regularized control requires careful scheduling and initialization to avoid bias and maintain diversity</cite><cite id="705c0347-2">LLM-as-judge ratings are systematically higher and mid-range concentrated, indicating potential optimism bias</cite>.

Open questions include: (1) quantifying large-scale homogenization across models and time (e.g., stylistic convergence), (2) principled trade-offs between diversity and central tendency in aligned systems, and (3) robust evaluation of “averageness” against minority or long-tail creative modes. Additional evidence would come from longitudinal analyses of model outputs, audits of style/creativity distributions over time, and benchmarks that explicitly reward both centrality and diversity under different objectives. <cite id="1ea488e5-0">Understanding how objective choices map to mode coverage vs. concentration remains foundational</cite><cite id="1dd65550-3">KL-regularized guidance offers a promising axis for quantifying average-like behavior but needs careful design to balance bias and diversity</cite>.

# Takeaways for research and practice

- If your goal is averageness (e.g., faithful, safe, typical responses), consider reverse KL/distillation objectives, KL-regularized guidance, and centroid/mean targets in latent or token space. <cite id="1ea488e5-3">Reverse KLD focuses on dominant modes for correctness and faithfulness</cite><cite id="1dd65550-3">KL-constrained control regularizes to base distributions to avoid mode collapse and overfitting</cite><cite id="1dd65550-1">Latent steering can nudge outputs toward desired central attributes</cite>.
- If you need diversity, add mixture priors, diversity bonuses, or repulsion terms, and evaluate minority-mode coverage explicitly. <cite id="1ea488e5-1">Mixture generators and alternative divergences can mitigate mode collapse and preserve diversity</cite><cite id="06731774-3">Uniformity constraints at the centroid level can counteract over-concentration</cite>.
- For evaluation, report central tendency (means/medians) and dispersion (variance, tail coverage) of outputs and judge behaviors, and consider both LLM-as-judge and human baselines. <cite id="705c0347-2">LLM-as-judge ratings cluster in mid-range and differ systematically from humans</cite><cite id="06731774-0">Consensus and centroid metrics summarize multiple runs/annotations toward central tendencies</cite>.

Minimizing reverse KLD has been shown to cause the mode-seeking behavior in generative modeling [Hus15, NCT16, CDP + 18, LPSK23], where q θ assigns high probabilities to p's large modes and ignore the small ones (illustrated in a toy experiment in Figure 2). In this work, we first study this property for KD of LLMs in text generation. Minimizing forward KLD causes q θ to place large probability masses on the zero-probability regions of p, corresponding to the generation of lowquality text in practice, while reverse KLD focuses on p's major modes, which is crucial to ensure the correctness and faithfulness of text generation. Instead, it encourages the student to generate samples preferred by the teacher within its own capacities, which is more possible to achieve. Interestingly, we also find another perspective of understanding MINILLM motivated by Inverse Reinforcement Learning [ZMB + 08]. We present the related derivation in Appendix A.1.

Title: Multi-property Steering of Large Language Models with Dynamic Activation Composition
Snippet: ontrollable Text Generation While controllable generation traditionally requires ad-hoc training to update LLMs behavior (Ziegler et al., 2019;Keskar et al., 2019;Li and Liang, 2021), several works showed that on-the-fly controllability can be achieved by using an external discriminator module for steering the generation style or topic (Dathathri et al., 2020;Carbone and Sarti, 2020;Krause et al., 2021;Yang and Klein, 2021).Recent advances in LLMs' in-context learning capabilities further simplified generation controllability, enabling style conditioning via in-context demonstrations (Suzgun et al., 2022;Reif et al., 2022;Sarti et al., 2023).Our proposed steering method is akin to contrastive decoding (Liu et al., 2021;Li et al., 2023b), using the shift in prediction probabilities produced by steering vectors' addition to modulate their influence over the upcoming generation step.

Title: Automating Steering for Safe Multimodal Large Language Models
Snippet: Model Steering, also referred to as controllable text generation (CTG) (Liang et al., 2024), aims to guide large language models (LLMs) to produce outputs that exhibit desired attributes such as sentiment, style, or safety. Among various techniques, Latent Space Manipulation (LSM) has emerged as a flexible and model-agnostic approach. Rather than modifying model parameters or architecture, LSM operates directly on the model's internal representations, typically word embeddings or hidden states, at inference time. A notable example is LM-Steer (Han et al., 2024), which introduces a simple but effective mechanism to steer generation, by linearly transforming the output embeddings of a frozen language model (LM). This yields a new probability distribution: By modifying the geometry of the output space in a controlled and interpretable way, LM-Steer enables efficient adjustment of model behavior. Title: SAE-SSV: Supervised Steering in Sparse Representation Spaces for Reliable Control of Language Models
Snippet: Steering is a technique for controlling the output of LLMs via small interventions in their internal representations. Let x be an input sequence in LLM and h(x) ∈ R d denote the activation of x at a chosen layer (e.g., the residual stream). Steering can modify h(x) with an additive perturbation v ∈ R d (λ ∈ R is a scaling coefficient) like Equation 1: 

The modified representation h ′ (x) is then fed into the subsequent layers of the language model, thereby influencing the final output generation. 

Prior work proposed various ways to construct the additive perturbation vector v, including mean difference vectors between contrasting classes (Dathathri et al., 2020), andPCA (Kleindessner et al., 2023). These approaches aim to identify semantically meaningful directions in the latent space, such that steering along these directions enables controlled manipulation of the LLM's behavior during generation.

Title: Efficient Controllable Diffusion via Optimal Classifier Guidance
Snippet: There has been significant interest in controllable generation of diffusion models, starting from Dhariwal & Nichol (2021) which introduced classifier guidance, to then Ho & Salimans (2022) which introduced classifier-free guidance. These methods paved the way for further interest in controllable generation, in particular when there is an objective function to optimize. First demonstrated by Black et al. (2024); Fan et al. (2023), RL fine-tuning of diffusion models has grown in popularity with works such as Clark et al. (2024); Prabhudesai et al. (2023) which use direct backpropagation to optimize the reward function. However, these methods can lead to mode collapse of the generations and overfitting. Further works then focused on maximizing the KL-constrained optimization problem which regularizes the generation process to the base model (Uehara et al., 2024b) but suffer either from needing special memoryless noise schedulers (Domingo-Enrich et al., 2025) or needing to control the initial distribution of the diffusion process (Uehara et al., 2024a) to avoid a bias problem. Our approach does not need to do any of these modification. Li et al. (2024) proposed a method to augment the decoding process and avoid training the underlying base model, but yield an increase in compute time. Their practical approach also does not guarantee to learn the optimal distribution. More broadly, Mudgal et al. (2023);Zhou et al. (2025) investigate token-level classifier guidance for KLregularized controllable generation of large language models. Zhou et al. ( 2025) also demonstrated that to optimize a KL-regularized RL objective in the context of LLM text generation, one just needs to perform no-regret learning. While our approach is motivated by the Q# approach from Zhou et al. ( 2025), we tackle score-based guidance for diffusion models in a continuous latent space and continue time, where the space of actions form an infinite set-making algorithm design and analysis substantially more difficult than the setting of discrete token and discrete-time in prior LLM work.

Title: Identifying and Mitigating the Influence of the Prior Distribution in Large Language Models
Snippet: The ability of the user to control LLM text generation in general has been extensively researched. In this paper, we take inspiration from prompt engineering, finetuning, probing, and steering. Prompting has been shown to be able to control text generation through personas (Hu & Collier, 2024), chain-of-thought reasoning (Wei et al., 2022;Yao et al., 2023), refinement, and more esoteric techniques (Salinas & Morstatter, 2024). Other approaches focus on parameter updates including full finetuning (Bommasani et al., 2021) and parameter efficent finetuning (PEFT) techniques such as like LoRA or ReFT (Hu et al., 2021;Wu et al., 2024b). Another line of work controls the model through steering techniques such as dictionary learning (Cunningham et al., 2023), contrastive activation addition (Rimsky et al., 2023), and distributed alignment search (Geiger et al., 2023;Minder et al., 2025).

snippet.text: There has been significant interest in controllable generation of diffusion models, starting from Dhariwal & Nichol (2021) which introduced classifier guidance, to then Ho & Salimans (2022) which introduced classifier-free guidance. These methods paved the way for further interest in controllable generation, in particular when there is an objective function to optimize. First demonstrated by Black et al. (2024); Fan et al. (2023), RL fine-tuning of diffusion models has grown in popularity with works such as Clark et al. (2024); Prabhudesai et al. (2023) which use direct backpropagation to optimize the reward function. However, these methods can lead to mode collapse of the generations and overfitting. Further works then focused on maximizing the KL-constrained optimization problem which regularizes the generation process to the base model (Uehara et al., 2024b) but suffer either from needing special memoryless noise schedulers (Domingo-Enrich et al., 2025) or needing to control the initial distribution of the diffusion process (Uehara et al., 2024a) to avoid a bias problem. Our approach does not need to do any of these modification. Li et al. (2024) proposed a method to augment the decoding process and avoid training the underlying base model, but yield an increase in compute time. Their practical approach also does not guarantee to learn the optimal distribution. More broadly, Mudgal et al. (2023);Zhou et al. (2025) investigate token-level classifier guidance for KLregularized controllable generation of large language models. Zhou et al. ( 2025) also demonstrated that to optimize a KL-regularized RL objective in the context of LLM text generation, one just needs to perform no-regret learning. While our approach is motivated by the Q# approach from Zhou et al. ( 2025), we tackle score-based guidance for diffusion models in a continuous latent space and continue time, where the space of actions form an infinite set-making algorithm design and analysis substantially more difficult than the setting of discrete token and discrete-time in prior LLM work.

snippet.text: The ability of the user to control LLM text generation in general has been extensively researched. In this paper, we take inspiration from prompt engineering, finetuning, probing, and steering. Prompting has been shown to be able to control text generation through personas (Hu & Collier, 2024), chain-of-thought reasoning (Wei et al., 2022;Yao et al., 2023), refinement, and more esoteric techniques (Salinas & Morstatter, 2024). Other approaches focus on parameter updates including full finetuning (Bommasani et al., 2021) and parameter efficent finetuning (PEFT) techniques such as like LoRA or ReFT (Hu et al., 2021;Wu et al., 2024b). Another line of work controls the model through steering techniques such as dictionary learning (Cunningham et al., 2023), contrastive activation addition (Rimsky et al., 2023), and distributed alignment search (Geiger et al., 2023;Minder et al., 2025).

Title: When Your Reviewer is an LLM: Biases, Divergence, and Prompt Injection Risks in Peer Review
Snippet: We first compare the overall ratings assigned by LLMs against those of human reviewers. Across the combined ICLR and NeurIPS datasets (1,441 papers), the average human rating is 5.70, while the average LLM rating is 6.86, which demonstrates an average difference of 1.16 points. This confirms that LLMs generally provide more positive feedback on the research papers than human reviewers, which reflects an inflationary tendency in their evaluations. 

In Figure 2, we visualize the distribution of LLM ratings relative to human ratings. Since ICLR and NeurIPS adopt different scoring standards-ICLR restricts reviewers to a discrete set of ratings 1, 3, 5, 6, 8, 10, whereas NeurIPS allows the full 1-10 scale-we present the two venues separately. On the x-axis, each point corresponds to the average of all human reviewers' scores for a paper, rounded to the nearest 0.5 to facilitate comparison across rating bins. The y-axis represents the number of papers that fall into each bin of human average rating and corresponding LLM-assigned ratings. For instance, in the ICLR 2023 dataset, 168 papers receive an average human rating of 6.0; among these, LLMs assign a rating of 3 to 2 papers, 5 to 24 papers, 6 to 47 papers, and 8 to 95 papers. Figure 2 shows a consistent trend in LLM ratings: LLMs tend to concentrate their scores around the middle range (e.g., [5][6][7][8], rather than assigning extremely low or high values such as 1, 2, or 10. For example, when human reviewers give a paper an average rating of 2.5 or less, LLMs do not mirror these low ratings, instead assigning at least a score of 3. 

A more detailed inspection reveals that alignment between LLM and human ratings improves for papers rated high by human reviewers. As illustrated in Figure 2, when human reviewers rate a paper in a higher range (e.g., 7 or above), LLM ratings show less inflation than mid-range or low-rated papers. In contrast, when human ratings are modest Manuscript submitted to ACM (around 4-6), LLMs frequently increase their assessments to 6-8.

Title: What do Large Language Models Say About Animals? Investigating Risks of Animal Harm in Generated Text
Snippet: Out of the total public sample of 3045 questions we selected a stratified sample of 100 question-answer pairs (10 answers generated per each of the assessed LLMs), and asked human judges to assess them. Overall, 6 human judges completed the survey. The (Pearson) correlation coefficient between scores of five of the six humans ranged from 0.423 to 0.621, with one outlier that correlated 0.05 to 0.20 with the scores of the other five. The (Pearson) correlation between average human score and average LLM-as-judge score was 0.545 (0.574 with the human outlier removed), which suggests a moderate agreement. Notably, humans tended to score the responses more favorably: scores of 0.259 on average (0.304 with the human outlier removed), compared to -0.037 assigned by the LLMs-as-judges on the selected set of question-answer pairs.

In this section, we provide a hierarchical specification of the generative model that underpins Infinite Deep Latent Construct (iDLC-CCT), where population distributions are specified for the parameters using hyperparameters [70]. These hyperparameters are estimated from their own distributions and can represent the central tendency across items or respondents, which may be unique to each dataset. The hierarchical structure of the generative model is as follows: 

Coefficient weights 

Respondent shifting bias 

Group sparsity 

The item consensus T vk is derived by applying Bayesian Ridge Regression to the pretrained embeddings. The location of the item consensus is calculated by taking the dot product of the relevant two row matrices. The other model parameters, E i , λ i , and a i , which are each located on the positive half-line, are log-transformed to the real line and also assumed to be sampled from a normal population-level distribution. The shift bias, b i , is located on the real line, paramaterized with a mean and precision (inverse variance). Note that the respondents' competence parameter remains singly indexed by i, through an indexing technique in which their distribution is specified by their group membership Ω i . Culture assignments are derived via a stick-breaking prior, and this allows for varying probabilities of being in any of V groups; note that V is unknown priori and needs to be estimated from observed data. The sparsity of cultures, β, is sampled from a beta distribution. The variables Ω i and π are removed for the single-truth variant of our model.

problem: sampling methods for reasoning language models
final_response:
# Overview

Sampling methods for reasoning language models (LMs) span two complementary goals: exploring diverse reasoning trajectories at inference time to improve correctness and confidence, and using structured search or training-time distillation to better learn and transfer reasoning behaviors. Sampling-based decoding (e.g., top-k, top-p, temperature, and “sample-and-marginalize” strategies) contrasts with search-based decoding (beam/MCTS) and with training-time techniques (distillation from diverse or self-generated reasoning paths). Together, these methods trade off diversity, coherence, and compute for better reasoning performance on tasks like arithmetic (GSM8K), multi-step strategy, and commonsense reasoning. <cite id="339929da-0">A central idea is to replace greedy decoding with multi-sample exploration and aggregation (e.g., self-consistency) to avoid local optima in a single path</cite> <cite id="339929da-3">and to leverage diversity to surface more reliable final answers</cite> <cite id="3b6eda7a-0">with standard controls like top-k/top-p/temperature governing the exploration-stability balance</cite>.

# Core Sampling Distributions and Multi-Sample Decoding

Temperature, top-k, and nucleus (top-p) sampling modulate the mass spread over tokens, directly affecting diversity and stability. <cite id="3b6eda7a-0">Top-k samples from the highest k probabilities (renormalized), top-p (nucleus) samples from tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds a threshold p, and temperature scaling flattens or sharpens the distribution</cite>. <cite id="3b6eda7a-0">Lower temperatures (≈0.2–0.5) increase precision on math reasoning by concentrating mass, while higher temperatures (≈1.0–1.5) promote diversity but can reduce coherence</cite>. Multi-sample strategies explicitly generate several candidates and aggregate them.

Chain-of-thought (CoT) decoding demonstrates that exposing alternative top-k first-step choices can surface latent reasoning chains, increasing final answer confidence and improving accuracy without changing model architecture or training. <cite id="3b6eda7a-3">On GSM8K, CoT decoding improved PaLM-2 Large accuracy from 34.8% to 63.2% and correlated reasoning paths with higher semantic consistency</cite>. Self-consistency formalizes this by sampling multiple full reasoning paths and selecting the most consistent final answer via majority voting or marginalization. <cite id="339929da-0">It replaces greedy decoding with a “sample-and-marginalize” procedure and acts as a self-ensemble on a single model</cite> <cite id="339929da-2">with strong gains on GSM8K (+17.9%), SVAMP (+11.0%), AQuA (+12.2%), StrategyQA (+6.4%), and ARC-challenge (+3.9%)</cite> <cite id="339929da-4">and by exploring multiple reasoning paths before committing</cite>.

Beyond these, quasi-random and arithmetic sampling generate inherently diverse, parallelizable sequences, enabling multi-sample reasoning and selection schemes (e.g., self-consistency, MBR-style selection) with guaranteed diversity. <cite id="3b6eda7a-4">Arithmetic sampling interprets decoding as sampling code points from a unit interval, yielding embarrassingly parallel samples with diversity by construction</cite> <cite id="3b6eda7a-4">and applying such sampling to CoT with self-consistency and to machine translation with MBR decoding led to accuracy improvements on GSM8K and Commonsense QA, as well as higher COMET scores</cite>. Diversity-oriented token filters like min-p sampling further bias toward higher-probability tokens within a floor threshold. <cite id="3b6eda7a-0">Min-p sampling retains only tokens above a minimum probability and samples from that set</cite>.

# Diversity Controls and Semantic Uncertainty

Diversity controls can be used diagnostically to reveal reasoning uncertainty. <cite id="3b6eda7a-3">Exploring alternative top-k tokens in CoT exposes latent reasoning chains, and the presence of such chains aligns with higher model confidence in the final answer, offering a lens on semantic uncertainty</cite>. This suggests using moderate diversity (e.g., small top-k or calibrated temperature) to surface consistent CoT paths as a proxy for reliability, while avoiding excessive diversity that harms coherence.

# Structured Search at Inference Time

Search-based methods treat reasoning as exploration over a space of partial solutions, trading compute for reliability and controllability. Beam search maintains a fixed number of top candidates (“beam width”) and prunes lower-likelihood branches, enabling parallel exploration of multiple reasoning chains without committing early. <cite id="81dd9858-0">Tree-based decoding explicitly explores a search tree over intermediate states, with beam search as a classic instance used to guide LLM inference paths</cite> <cite id="81dd9858-3">by keeping top-N partial sequences at each step and expanding them, it systematically explores multiple reasoning chains and can improve problem-solving accuracy over greedy decoding</cite>. Dynamic beam variants for reasoning iteratively sample expansions and prune using verifiers. <cite id="81dd9858-1">A beam-based loop starts from sampled candidate thoughts, scores them with a verifier, retains top-B chains, expands each by sampling new thoughts, and repeats until finished states, selecting the highest-scoring final answer</cite>.

Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) iteratively selects, expands, simulates (rollouts), and backpropagates values to focus exploration on promising branches. <cite id="81dd9858-1">MCTS operates through selection, expansion, evaluation, and backpropagation phases to explore most promising reasoning paths</cite> <cite id="81dd9858-2">and has emerged as a powerful approach for LLM reasoning, though rollouts and value estimation can be costly and trajectory scoring remains challenging</cite>. High-level frameworks like Tree-of-Thoughts and Language Agent Tree Search use such trees with lookahead and backtracking, or couple an LLM world model with MCTS, to navigate structured reasoning spaces. <cite id="81dd9858-0">Tree-of-Thoughts organizes reasoning steps into a tree and uses breadth/depth-first search, while reasoning via planning couples an LLM “world model” with MCTS; LATS unifies reasoning and tool use via MCTS</cite> <cite id="81dd9858-3">Beam search is commonly plugged into such trees to maintain promising states at each reasoning step</cite>.

These methods can be combined with sampling. For example, tree-based decoding schemes first sample candidates, then search over them. <cite id="81dd9858-0">Tree-based decoding expands inference beyond a single left-to-right trajectory by explicitly exploring a search tree over intermediate states, trading added test-time compute for higher reliability and controllability</cite>.

# Training-Time Sampling and Distillation for Reasoning

Reasoning-capable models benefit from training on diverse, high-quality reasoning paths generated via sampling. <cite id="8b5c5363-0">One pipeline first uses CoT prompting to generate reference reasoning paths and applies temperature sampling with verification to retain correct paths, forming a synthetic dataset for training</cite>. Chain-of-thought distillation trains students to emulate teacher-generated rationales, improving downstream reasoning ability. <cite id="8b5c5363-1">Chain-of-thought distillation maximizes the likelihood of student models on pairs of rationales and answers from demonstrations</cite>.

Self-enhancement methods use the model itself as a teacher and data generator. <cite id="8b5c5363-1">Self-augmentation first generates diverse data and then trains on it, while self-distillation iteratively uses the model’s own “dark knowledge” to improve performance; self-consistency complements this by sampling multiple candidates and voting on the final answer</cite>. Distillation and preference/verifiable reward training can further boost math reasoning in small models. <cite id="8b5c5363-2">A systematic recipe combining mid-training on diverse long-CoT data, supervised fine-tuning on high-quality CoT, rollout DPO, and RL with verifiable reward improved a 3.8B Phi-4-Mini to outperform much larger distilled reasoning models on Math-500</cite>. Representational analyses examine how distillation changes models’ reasoning representations. <cite id="8b5c5363-3">Recent work studies how distilled models develop distinctive features related to reasoning capabilities, motivated by empirical success of RL- and distillation-based reasoning models like o1 and Deepseek-R1</cite>. Practical distillation also emphasizes constructing teacher reasoning data via structured prompts and transferring reasoning paths. <cite id="8b5c5363-4">Teacher models generate comprehensive reasoning chains (R_i) with explicit step-by-step structure, and small models are fine-tuned on these paths via sequence-level knowledge distillation to transfer reasoning content and patterns</cite>.

# Efficiency, Diversity, and Parallelization

Different decoding strategies have distinct efficiency and diversity properties. <cite id="3b6eda7a-4">Sampling-based ancestral or quasi-random methods can be parallelized but may not guarantee diversity; arithmetic sampling provides guaranteed, by-construction diversity and embarrassingly parallel sampling</cite>. Search-based methods improve reliability but reduce parallelism and increase compute. <cite id="339929da-3">Earlier self-consistency work notes that methods like random beam search or deductive beam search can improve task accuracy but incur additional time costs and model calls, making them less efficient in practice</cite> <cite id="81dd9858-3">Beam search prunes the exponential space but aims for a near-optimal sequence by keeping a fixed number of beams, trading compute for higher-quality reasoning</cite>. Tree/structured search methods can scale inference-time compute, but careful design is needed to manage cost. <cite id="81dd9858-2">MCTS rollouts and backpropagation improve focus on promising branches but incur substantial computational overhead and require reliable scoring to select correct trajectories</cite>.

Empirically, increasing multi-sample counts often improves accuracy for CoT-based reasoning and selection (e.g., self-consistency and MBR-style selection), with diminishing returns and higher latency. <cite id="3b6eda7a-4">Applying arithmetic sampling to CoT with self-consistency and to MBR decoding led to accuracy gains on GSM8K and Commonsense QA, with improvements scaling as the number of sampled sequences increases</cite>. For math-heavy tasks, lower temperatures and constrained sampling can stabilize generation, while moderate diversity helps expose consistent reasoning. <cite id="3b6eda7a-0">Temperature and top-k/top-p settings influence diversity and coherence; lower temperatures improve precision on mathematical reasoning, while higher temperatures increase diversity at the risk of reduced logical consistency</cite> <cite id="3b6eda7a-3">and CoT decoding shows higher confidence when diverse reasoning paths are present</cite>.

# Practical Guidelines and When to Use What

- If you need a simple drop-in improvement: use multi-sample decoding with top-k/top-p (and optionally min-p) and temperature tuning, then aggregate with self-consistency on CoT outputs. <cite id="339929da-2">Self-consistency yields substantial gains on arithmetic and commonsense benchmarks by sampling multiple paths and selecting the most consistent answer</cite> <cite id="3b6eda7a-0">and top-k/top-p/temperature provide fine control over diversity-stability trade-offs</cite> <cite id="3b6eda7a-3">with evidence that moderate diversity exposes reliable reasoning chains</cite>.

- If you can afford more compute and want higher reliability: use beam search with a verifier to explore multiple partial solutions in parallel, or tree-based methods (Tree-of-Thoughts, planning with MCTS, LATS-style agents). <cite id="81dd9858-1">Dynamic beam search maintains and prunes a pool of reasoning chains with per-step expansions and verifier scoring</cite> <cite id="81dd9858-0">Tree-based decoding structures exploration over intermediate states, trading test-time compute for controllability and reliability</cite> <cite id="81dd9858-2">MCTS focuses exploration via rollouts and value backpropagation but adds computational cost and scoring challenges</cite>.

- If you are training or fine-tuning a reasoning model: generate synthetic CoT data via temperature sampling with verification and distill it; consider self-augmentation/self-distillation or RL with verifiable rewards for further gains. <cite id="8b5c5363-0">Temperature-sampled CoT paths verified for correctness can seed a training set of diverse reasoning traces</cite> <cite id="8b5c5363-1">Chain-of-thought distillation and self-enhancement (self-augmentation and self-distillation) leverage the model’s own knowledge to improve reasoning</cite> <cite id="8b5c5363-2">Systematic pipelines combining diverse long-CoT mid-training, SFT, DPO, and RL with verifiable reward substantially boost math reasoning in small models</cite>.

- If you need parallelizable, diverse samples for multi-sample selection or MBR-style decoding: consider arithmetic/quasi-random sampling to guarantee diversity and ease parallelization. <cite id="3b6eda7a-4">Arithmetic sampling yields parallel, diverse sequences and has been shown to improve accuracy when paired with self-consistency or MBR selection on reasoning benchmarks</cite>.

# Summary

Title: Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models
Snippet: Chain-of-thought prompting combined with pre-trained large language models has achieved encouraging results on complex reasoning tasks. In this paper, we propose a new decoding strategy, self-consistency, to replace the naive greedy decoding used in chain-of-thought prompting. It first samples a diverse set of reasoning paths instead of only taking the greedy one, and then selects the most consistent answer by marginalizing out the sampled reasoning paths. Self-consistency leverages the intuition that a complex reasoning problem typically admits multiple different ways of thinking leading to its unique correct answer. Our extensive empirical evaluation shows that self-consistency boosts the performance of chain-of-thought prompting with a striking margin on a range of popular arithmetic and commonsense reasoning benchmarks, including GSM8K (+17.9%), SVAMP (+11.0%), AQuA (+12.2%), StrategyQA (+6.4%) and ARC-challenge (+3.9%).

The authors show that when these CoT paths are present, models demonstrate increased confidence in their final answers, providing a mechanism to identify more semantically consistent outputs. Snippet: Beam search was first introduced in the context of speech recognition [233]. It gained prominence as a decoding strategy for sequence models and was later adopted in neural machine translation and speech systems [234]. With the popularity of LLMs, this algorithm has been used for approximate search in many text generation tasks. 

The concept of Beam search is similar to pruned breadthfirst search, where top N highest-probability partial sequences (the 'beam') are kept at each step, discarding lower-probability paths. By limiting the beam width (N), it manages the exponential search space while aiming to find a near-optimal sequence. These beams are expanded at each decoding step to find multiple probable paths. In reasoning LLMs, such paths allow us to systematically explore multiple reasoning chains in parallel, focusing on the most promising ones. This ensures that high-likelihood reasoning steps are considered, which can improve the chances of finding a correct and coherent solution compared to greedy decoding. It has traditionally been used in tasks such as translation, summarization, and code generation, where the goal is a highly probable correct sequence [93]. 

While modern LLMs often favor stochastic sampling (e.g., temperature sampling) to promote diversity in generated text, beam search is still a valuable technique for structured reasoning problems. For example, the Tree-of-Thoughts framework [84] allows plugging in different search algorithms to explore a tree of possible 'thoughts' or reasoning steps; usually a beam search (with beam width b) is used to maintain the b most promising states at each reasoning step. Here, beam search is used to systematically explore solution steps for tasks like mathematical puzzles and planning problems, pruning less promising reasoning branches and thus improving the model's problem-solving accuracy. Beam search remains a strong baseline for test-time reasoning when one wants the model to output the single most likely reasoning path or answer under the model's learned distribution.

The resulting Phi-4-Mini-Reasoning model exceeds, on math reasoning tasks, much larger reasoning models, e.g., outperforming DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B by 3.2 points and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B by 7.7 points on Math-500. Our results validate that a carefully designed training recipe, with large-scale high-quality CoT data, is effective to unlock strong reasoning capabilities even in resource-constrained small models.

Title: Towards Understanding Distilled Reasoning Models: A Representational Approach
Snippet: The field of natural language processing has witnessed a rapid development of large language models (LLMs) over the past decade. Early breakthroughs like the Transformer architecture (Vaswani et al., 2017) revolutionized sequence modeling by utilizing self-attention mechanisms (Cheng et al., 2016). This enabled training on unprecedented scales, leading to the era of foundation models (Kaplan et al., 2020;Hoffmann et al., 2022). OpenAI's GPT series (Achiam et al., 2023) further scaled model sizes and datasets, showing that performance follows predictable power-law scaling laws in model size and data. These scaling efforts often yielded emergent abilities -qualitative leaps in capability not seen in smaller models. Another key breakthrough that has further enhanced the potential of these models is the incorporation of chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning (Wei et al., 2022). By encouraging models to articulate intermediate reasoning steps, chain-of-thought methods have not only improved task performance but have also enabled more complex, multi-step problem solving. 

While most LLM improvements have come from scale and supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning (RL) has recently emerged as a promising avenue to instill better reasoning abilities. These approaches have culminated in the development of highly competent reasoning models, such as o1 (Jaech et al., 2024) and Deepseek-R1 (Guo et al., 2025), which exhibit exceptional performance on tasks that demand rigorous logical inference. Through RL fine-tuning, these models learned how to refine its reasoning strategies -recognizing mistakes, breaking down complex problems, and trying alternative approaches. Moreover, the output from these reasoning models has also been used to empower smaller models, the process known as model distillation (Polino et al., 2018). 

Despite the empirical success of model distillation, a critical gap remains in our understanding of how distillation modifies the model. Therefore, we take the first modest step toward understanding how distillation changes the model. Specifically, we aim to address the following three questions: 

Q1: What distinctive features do distilled models develop, and how do these features relate to the models' reasoning capabilities?
</snippet>

Title: Self-Enhanced Reasoning Training: Activating Latent Reasoning in Small Models for Enhanced Reasoning Distillation
Snippet: In the final stage, we apply reasoning distillation, where the activated small model learns from the reasoning paths generated by a larger teacher model. 

1) Construction of Teacher Reasoning Data: Following [17], reasoning chains are generated from the large model using a zero-shot chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting technique [6]. Answer: Let's think step by step. R i So the answer is a i .

# Overview

Sampling methods for reasoning language models (LMs) span two complementary goals: exploring diverse reasoning trajectories at inference time to improve correctness and confidence, and using structured search or training-time distillation to better learn and transfer reasoning behaviors. Sampling-based decoding (e.g., top-k, top-p, temperature, and “sample-and-marginalize” strategies) contrasts with search-based decoding (beam/MCTS) and with training-time techniques (distillation from diverse or self-generated reasoning paths). Together, these methods trade off diversity, coherence, and compute for better reasoning performance on tasks like arithmetic (GSM8K), multi-step strategy, and commonsense reasoning. <cite id="339929da-0">A central idea is to replace greedy decoding with multi-sample exploration and aggregation (e.g., self-consistency) to avoid local optima in a single path</cite> <cite id="339929da-3">and to leverage diversity to surface more reliable final answers</cite> <cite id="3b6eda7a-0">with standard controls like top-k/top-p/temperature governing the exploration-stability balance</cite>.

# Core Sampling Distributions and Multi-Sample Decoding

Temperature, top-k, and nucleus (top-p) sampling modulate the mass spread over tokens, directly affecting diversity and stability. <cite id="3b6eda7a-0">Top-k samples from the highest k probabilities (renormalized), top-p (nucleus) samples from tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds a threshold p, and temperature scaling flattens or sharpens the distribution</cite>. <cite id="3b6eda7a-0">Lower temperatures (≈0.2–0.5) increase precision on math reasoning by concentrating mass, while higher temperatures (≈1.0–1.5) promote diversity but can reduce coherence</cite>. Multi-sample strategies explicitly generate several candidates and aggregate them.

Chain-of-thought (CoT) decoding demonstrates that exposing alternative top-k first-step choices can surface latent reasoning chains, increasing final answer confidence and improving accuracy without changing model architecture or training. <cite id="3b6eda7a-3">On GSM8K, CoT decoding improved PaLM-2 Large accuracy from 34.8% to 63.2% and correlated reasoning paths with higher semantic consistency</cite>. Self-consistency formalizes this by sampling multiple full reasoning paths and selecting the most consistent final answer via majority voting or marginalization. <cite id="339929da-0">It replaces greedy decoding with a “sample-and-marginalize” procedure and acts as a self-ensemble on a single model</cite> <cite id="339929da-2">with strong gains on GSM8K (+17.9%), SVAMP (+11.0%), AQuA (+12.2%), StrategyQA (+6.4%), and ARC-challenge (+3.9%)</cite> <cite id="339929da-4">and by exploring multiple reasoning paths before committing</cite>.

Beyond these, quasi-random and arithmetic sampling generate inherently diverse, parallelizable sequences, enabling multi-sample reasoning and selection schemes (e.g., self-consistency, MBR-style selection) with guaranteed diversity. <cite id="3b6eda7a-4">Arithmetic sampling interprets decoding as sampling code points from a unit interval, yielding embarrassingly parallel samples with diversity by construction</cite> <cite id="3b6eda7a-4">and applying such sampling to CoT with self-consistency and to machine translation with MBR decoding led to accuracy improvements on GSM8K and Commonsense QA, as well as higher COMET scores</cite>. Diversity-oriented token filters like min-p sampling further bias toward higher-probability tokens within a floor threshold. <cite id="3b6eda7a-0">Min-p sampling retains only tokens above a minimum probability and samples from that set</cite>.

# Diversity Controls and Semantic Uncertainty

Diversity controls can be used diagnostically to reveal reasoning uncertainty. <cite id="3b6eda7a-3">Exploring alternative top-k tokens in CoT exposes latent reasoning chains, and the presence of such chains aligns with higher model confidence in the final answer, offering a lens on semantic uncertainty</cite>. This suggests using moderate diversity (e.g., small top-k or calibrated temperature) to surface consistent CoT paths as a proxy for reliability, while avoiding excessive diversity that harms coherence.

# Structured Search at Inference Time

Search-based methods treat reasoning as exploration over a space of partial solutions, trading compute for reliability and controllability. Beam search maintains a fixed number of top candidates (“beam width”) and prunes lower-likelihood branches, enabling parallel exploration of multiple reasoning chains without committing early. <cite id="81dd9858-0">Tree-based decoding explicitly explores a search tree over intermediate states, with beam search as a classic instance used to guide LLM inference paths</cite> <cite id="81dd9858-3">by keeping top-N partial sequences at each step and expanding them, it systematically explores multiple reasoning chains and can improve problem-solving accuracy over greedy decoding</cite>. Dynamic beam variants for reasoning iteratively sample expansions and prune using verifiers. <cite id="81dd9858-1">A beam-based loop starts from sampled candidate thoughts, scores them with a verifier, retains top-B chains, expands each by sampling new thoughts, and repeats until finished states, selecting the highest-scoring final answer</cite>.

Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) iteratively selects, expands, simulates (rollouts), and backpropagates values to focus exploration on promising branches. <cite id="81dd9858-1">MCTS operates through selection, expansion, evaluation, and backpropagation phases to explore most promising reasoning paths</cite> <cite id="81dd9858-2">and has emerged as a powerful approach for LLM reasoning, though rollouts and value estimation can be costly and trajectory scoring remains challenging</cite>. High-level frameworks like Tree-of-Thoughts and Language Agent Tree Search use such trees with lookahead and backtracking, or couple an LLM world model with MCTS, to navigate structured reasoning spaces. <cite id="81dd9858-0">Tree-of-Thoughts organizes reasoning steps into a tree and uses breadth/depth-first search, while reasoning via planning couples an LLM “world model” with MCTS; LATS unifies reasoning and tool use via MCTS</cite> <cite id="81dd9858-3">Beam search is commonly plugged into such trees to maintain promising states at each reasoning step</cite>.

These methods can be combined with sampling. For example, tree-based decoding schemes first sample candidates, then search over them. <cite id="81dd9858-0">Tree-based decoding expands inference beyond a single left-to-right trajectory by explicitly exploring a search tree over intermediate states, trading added test-time compute for higher reliability and controllability</cite>.

# Training-Time Sampling and Distillation for Reasoning

Reasoning-capable models benefit from training on diverse, high-quality reasoning paths generated via sampling. <cite id="8b5c5363-0">One pipeline first uses CoT prompting to generate reference reasoning paths and applies temperature sampling with verification to retain correct paths, forming a synthetic dataset for training</cite>. Chain-of-thought distillation trains students to emulate teacher-generated rationales, improving downstream reasoning ability. <cite id="8b5c5363-1">Chain-of-thought distillation maximizes the likelihood of student models on pairs of rationales and answers from demonstrations</cite>.

Self-enhancement methods use the model itself as a teacher and data generator. <cite id="8b5c5363-1">Self-augmentation first generates diverse data and then trains on it, while self-distillation iteratively uses the model’s own “dark knowledge” to improve performance; self-consistency complements this by sampling multiple candidates and voting on the final answer</cite>. Distillation and preference/verifiable reward training can further boost math reasoning in small models. <cite id="8b5c5363-2">A systematic recipe combining mid-training on diverse long-CoT data, supervised fine-tuning on high-quality CoT, rollout DPO, and RL with verifiable reward improved a 3.8B Phi-4-Mini to outperform much larger distilled reasoning models on Math-500</cite>. Representational analyses examine how distillation changes models’ reasoning representations. <cite id="8b5c5363-3">Recent work studies how distilled models develop distinctive features related to reasoning capabilities, motivated by empirical success of RL- and distillation-based reasoning models like o1 and Deepseek-R1</cite>. Practical distillation also emphasizes constructing teacher reasoning data via structured prompts and transferring reasoning paths. <cite id="8b5c5363-4">Teacher models generate comprehensive reasoning chains (R_i) with explicit step-by-step structure, and small models are fine-tuned on these paths via sequence-level knowledge distillation to transfer reasoning content and patterns</cite>.

# Efficiency, Diversity, and Parallelization

Different decoding strategies have distinct efficiency and diversity properties. <cite id="3b6eda7a-4">Sampling-based ancestral or quasi-random methods can be parallelized but may not guarantee diversity; arithmetic sampling provides guaranteed, by-construction diversity and embarrassingly parallel sampling</cite>. Search-based methods improve reliability but reduce parallelism and increase compute. <cite id="339929da-3">Earlier self-consistency work notes that methods like random beam search or deductive beam search can improve task accuracy but incur additional time costs and model calls, making them less efficient in practice</cite> <cite id="81dd9858-3">Beam search prunes the exponential space but aims for a near-optimal sequence by keeping a fixed number of beams, trading compute for higher-quality reasoning</cite>. Tree/structured search methods can scale inference-time compute, but careful design is needed to manage cost. <cite id="81dd9858-2">MCTS rollouts and backpropagation improve focus on promising branches but incur substantial computational overhead and require reliable scoring to select correct trajectories</cite>.

Empirically, increasing multi-sample counts often improves accuracy for CoT-based reasoning and selection (e.g., self-consistency and MBR-style selection), with diminishing returns and higher latency. <cite id="3b6eda7a-4">Applying arithmetic sampling to CoT with self-consistency and to MBR decoding led to accuracy gains on GSM8K and Commonsense QA, with improvements scaling as the number of sampled sequences increases</cite>. For math-heavy tasks, lower temperatures and constrained sampling can stabilize generation, while moderate diversity helps expose consistent reasoning. <cite id="3b6eda7a-0">Temperature and top-k/top-p settings influence diversity and coherence; lower temperatures improve precision on mathematical reasoning, while higher temperatures increase diversity at the risk of reduced logical consistency</cite> <cite id="3b6eda7a-3">and CoT decoding shows higher confidence when diverse reasoning paths are present</cite>.

# Practical Guidelines and When to Use What

- If you need a simple drop-in improvement: use multi-sample decoding with top-k/top-p (and optionally min-p) and temperature tuning, then aggregate with self-consistency on CoT outputs. <cite id="339929da-2">Self-consistency yields substantial gains on arithmetic and commonsense benchmarks by sampling multiple paths and selecting the most consistent answer</cite> <cite id="3b6eda7a-0">and top-k/top-p/temperature provide fine control over diversity-stability trade-offs</cite> <cite id="3b6eda7a-3">with evidence that moderate diversity exposes reliable reasoning chains</cite>.

- If you can afford more compute and want higher reliability: use beam search with a verifier to explore multiple partial solutions in parallel, or tree-based methods (Tree-of-Thoughts, planning with MCTS, LATS-style agents). <cite id="81dd9858-1">Dynamic beam search maintains and prunes a pool of reasoning chains with per-step expansions and verifier scoring</cite> <cite id="81dd9858-0">Tree-based decoding structures exploration over intermediate states, trading test-time compute for controllability and reliability</cite> <cite id="81dd9858-2">MCTS focuses exploration via rollouts and value backpropagation but adds computational cost and scoring challenges</cite>.

- If you are training or fine-tuning a reasoning model: generate synthetic CoT data via temperature sampling with verification and distill it; consider self-augmentation/self-distillation or RL with verifiable rewards for further gains. <cite id="8b5c5363-0">Temperature-sampled CoT paths verified for correctness can seed a training set of diverse reasoning traces</cite> <cite id="8b5c5363-1">Chain-of-thought distillation and self-enhancement (self-augmentation and self-distillation) leverage the model’s own knowledge to improve reasoning</cite> <cite id="8b5c5363-2">Systematic pipelines combining diverse long-CoT mid-training, SFT, DPO, and RL with verifiable reward substantially boost math reasoning in small models</cite>.

- If you need parallelizable, diverse samples for multi-sample selection or MBR-style decoding: consider arithmetic/quasi-random sampling to guarantee diversity and ease parallelization. <cite id="3b6eda7a-4">Arithmetic sampling yields parallel, diverse sequences and has been shown to improve accuracy when paired with self-consistency or MBR selection on reasoning benchmarks</cite>.

# Summary

In practice, the most effective reasoning setups combine calibrated sampling (top-k/top-p/min-p, temperature) with multi-sample aggregation (e.g., self-consistency) for fast, strong gains, while heavier structured search (beam/MCTS) is reserved for higher-stakes decisions where compute can be invested. <cite id="339929da-2">Self-consistency provides large improvements by sampling multiple CoT paths and choosing the most consistent answer</cite> <cite id="3b6eda7a-3">and diversity-aware decoding can increase both accuracy and confidence</cite> <cite id="81dd9858-0">Tree-based search methods further enhance reliability by exploring structured reasoning spaces but at higher compute cost</cite>. Training-time sampling and self-enhancement generate diverse, high-quality reasoning traces to distill into smaller or more efficient models. <cite id="8b5c5363-0">Temperature-sampled verified CoT paths can seed synthetic datasets</cite> <cite id="8b5c5363-1">and self-distillation/self-augmentation leverage the model’s own reasoning to improve performance</cite> <cite id="8b5c5363-2">with RL and preference learning further boosting reasoning in small models</cite>. Together, these sampling methods form the core toolkit for improving and scaling reasoning in language models. </answer>

Title: Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models
Snippet: We first prompt the language model with chain-of-thought prompting, then instead of greedily decoding the optimal reasoning path, we propose a "sample-and-marginalize" decoding procedure: we first sample from the language model's decoder to generate a diverse set of reasoning paths; each reasoning path might lead to a different final answer, so we determine the optimal answer by marginalizing out the sampled reasoning paths to find the most consistent answer in the final answer set. Such an approach is analogous to the human experience that if multiple different ways of thinking lead to the same answer, one has greater confidence that the final answer is correct. Compared to other decoding methods, self-consistency avoids the repetitiveness and local-optimality that plague greedy decoding, while mitigating the stochasticity of a single sampled generation. 

Figure 1: The self-consistency method contains three steps: (1) prompt a language model using chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting; (2) replace the "greedy decode" in CoT prompting by sampling from the language model's decoder to generate a diverse set of reasoning paths; and (3) marginalize out the reasoning paths and aggregate by choosing the most consistent answer in the final answer set. 

Self-consistency is far simpler than prior approaches that either train an additional verifier (Cobbe et al., 2021) or train a re-ranker given additional human annotations to improve generation quality (Thoppilan et al., 2022). Instead, self-consistency is entirely unsupervised, works off-the-shelf with pre-trained language models, requires no additional human annotation, and avoids any additional training, auxiliary models or fine-tuning. Self-consistency also differs from a typical ensemble approach where multiple models are trained and the outputs from each model are aggregated, it acts more like a "self-ensemble" that works on top of a single language model.

Title: Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models
Snippet: Chain-of-thought prompting combined with pre-trained large language models has achieved encouraging results on complex reasoning tasks. In this paper, we propose a new decoding strategy, self-consistency, to replace the naive greedy decoding used in chain-of-thought prompting. It first samples a diverse set of reasoning paths instead of only taking the greedy one, and then selects the most consistent answer by marginalizing out the sampled reasoning paths. Self-consistency leverages the intuition that a complex reasoning problem typically admits multiple different ways of thinking leading to its unique correct answer. Our extensive empirical evaluation shows that self-consistency boosts the performance of chain-of-thought prompting with a striking margin on a range of popular arithmetic and commonsense reasoning benchmarks, including GSM8K (+17.9%), SVAMP (+11.0%), AQuA (+12.2%), StrategyQA (+6.4%) and ARC-challenge (+3.9%).

Title: Path-Consistency with Prefix Enhancement for Efficient Inference in LLMs
Snippet: 2.1 REASONING WITH SELF-CONSISTENCY Self-consistency Wang et al. (2023) is a sampling strategy distinct from greedy decoding Vaswani et al. (2017), significantly enhancing the reasoning performance of language models. This approach generates multiple reasoning paths and aggregates the final output through majority voting. 

Earlier research primarily focused on optimizing reasoning for individual tasks  Paul et al. (2024). For example, self-evaluation guided by random beam search Xie et al. (2024) leverages additional language models to search for the optimal inference path. Other methods, such as Deductive Beam Search Zhu et al. (2024), optimize inference by emphasizing the relationships between each reasoning step. However, these approaches often require increased computational resources and sometimes involve extensive model calls to improve task accuracy in LLMs. This results in additional time costs, always making them inefficient in practical applications and contrary to our original intention.

Title: Exploring the intersection of Generative AI and Software Development
Snippet: Self-consistency is a decoding technique that aims to improve how pre-trained language models reason. Instead of the model taking the first, most obvious reasoning path, this technique explores various reasoning paths. Then, it picks the answer that shows up most consistently across these paths (see Figure 10. This approach helps in situations where there are many ways to come to a correct answer, like in common reasoning tasks or arithmetic. Here is how it works: First, the model is given a question or task. Instead of taking the most common path, which might be incorrect, it explores different reasoning paths using the Chain of Thoughts (CoT) technique. This results in a series of sentences that show how the model is thinking. 

After this, the Self-Consistency method picks the answer that is most consistent across these reasoning paths. This answer is taken as the final response of the model, as illustrated in Figure 11.

2.1 REASONING WITH SELF-CONSISTENCY Self-consistency Wang et al. (2023) is a sampling strategy distinct from greedy decoding Vaswani et al. (2017), significantly enhancing the reasoning performance of language models. This approach generates multiple reasoning paths and aggregates the final output through majority voting. 

Earlier research primarily focused on optimizing reasoning for individual tasks  Paul et al. (2024). For example, self-evaluation guided by random beam search Xie et al. (2024) leverages additional language models to search for the optimal inference path. Other methods, such as Deductive Beam Search Zhu et al. (2024), optimize inference by emphasizing the relationships between each reasoning step. However, these approaches often require increased computational resources and sometimes involve extensive model calls to improve task accuracy in LLMs. This results in additional time costs, always making them inefficient in practical applications and contrary to our original intention.

documents.snippet:
Self-consistency is a decoding technique that aims to improve how pre-trained language models reason. Instead of the model taking the first, most obvious reasoning path, this technique explores various reasoning paths. Then, it picks the answer that shows up most consistently across these paths (see Figure 10. This approach helps in situations where there are many ways to come to a correct answer, like in common reasoning tasks or arithmetic. Here is how it works: First, the model is given a question or task. Instead of taking the most common path, which might be incorrect, it explores different reasoning paths using the Chain of Thoughts (CoT) technique. This results in a series of sentences that show how the model is thinking. 

After this, the Self-Consistency method picks the answer that is most consistent across these reasoning paths. This answer is taken as the final response of the model, as illustrated in Figure 11.

Snippet: We experiment with the following different decoding strategies: 

• Top-k Sampling: Samples from the top k most probable tokens, renormalizing probabilities across this set (Fan et al., 2018). 

• Top-p Sampling: Also known as nucleus sampling, it selects tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds a threshold p (Holtzman et al.). 

• Min-p Sampling: Filters out tokens below a minimum probability threshold p min , sampling is done from the remaining set (Nguyen et al., 2024). 

Temperature scaling adjusts the sharpness of probability distributions, balancing diversity and coherence in language model decoding (Ackley et al., 1985). Lower temperatures (0.2-0.5) concentrate probability mass on high-likelihood tokens, enhancing precision for tasks like mathematical reasoning. In contrast, higher temperatures (1.0-1.5) flatten the distribution, promoting diversity but potentially reducing coherence and logical consistency.

Title: Efficient Reasoning Models: A Survey
Snippet: In the following, we introduce efficient reasoning methods based on three key categories: shortening long chains of thought, as discussed in Section 3.1; developing small language models with strong reasoning capabilities, details of which can be found in Section 3.2; and improving decoding efficiency, which is elaborated in Section 3.3. We present the performance of various efficient reasoning methods on the challenging AIME 24 dataset in Table 1 and further provide a latency-based summary of representative methods across categories on the GSM8K dataset in Table 5.

Title: Semantic uncertainty in advanced decoding methods for LLM generation
Snippet: Recent work by Wang and Zhou (2024) introduced chain-of-thought (CoT) decoding, a novel approach that reveals large language models' inherent reasoning capabilities without relying on prompting techniques. While traditional methods focus on eliciting reasoning through explicit prompts, CoT decoding demonstrates that reasoning paths naturally exist within models' decoding space but are often obscured by conventional greedy decoding approaches. 

The key insight behind CoT decoding is that by exploring alternative top-k tokens during the first decoding step, rather than following only the highest probability path, natural reasoning chains emerge that lead to more reliable outputs. The authors show that when these CoT paths are present, models demonstrate increased confidence in their final answers, providing a mechanism to identify more semantically consistent outputs. This correlation between reasoning paths and output confidence offers a new lens for examining semantic uncertainty in language model outputs. 

Figure 2: Pre-trained LLMs are capable of inherent reasoning without prompting by considering alternative top-k tokens, rather than solely relying on the top-1 greedy decoding path. Moreover, these models tend to display higher confidence in decoding the final answer (indicated by a darker shaded color) when a CoT reasoning path is present. 

On standard reasoning benchmarks, CoT decoding achieves significant improvements over greedy decoding without any modification to model architecture or training. For instance, on the GSM8K mathematical reasoning benchmark, CoT decoding improves accuracy from 34.8% to 63.2% for PaLM-2 Large. More importantly for our investigation of semantic uncertainty, the presence of these natural reasoning paths appears to correlate with higher semantic consistency and reliability in model outputs even though the diversity of possible outputs increases. This approach stands in contrast to previous methods that rely on explicit prompting to elicit reasoning, such as zero-shot or few-shot chain-of-thought prompting techniques (Wei et al. (2023); Kojima et al. (2023)), which can introduce human biases and make it difficult to assess models' intrinsic capabilities. By revealing reasoning paths that exist naturally within models' decoding space, CoT decoding provides a more transparent window into how these models process and generate text, helping us better understand and quantify semantic uncertainty in their outputs.

Title: Quasi-random Multi-Sample Inference for Large Language Models
Snippet: There have been enormous efforts in improving the performance and efficiency of inference with large language models (Ippolito et al., 2019;Su & Collier, 2023;Grubisic et al., 2024;Zhou et al., 2024;Ding et al., 2024) based on system, data, and model level enhancements. In this paper, we consider that any decoding routine can be broadly assessed by its sample diversity (A.1) and parallelizability. Search-based techniques like beam search can approximate maximum a posteriori (MAP) decoding, mitigating duplicate samples at the expense of not being embarrassingly parallel. Sampling-based methods grounded in ancestral sampling techniques are parallel but don't explicitly guarantee diverse sequences. The recently proposed arithmetic sampling Vilnis et al. (2023) technique enables parallel inference with diverse samples -by interpreting the inference as sampling from code points from a unit interval, given code points generating sequences becomes embarrassingly parallel and the sample diversity is guaranteed by construction. 

Decoding from pre-trained LLMs requires varying strategies for different downstream tasks. For complex reasoning and question-answering tasks, chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting Wei et al. (2022) is established for improving inference by instructing the model to generate intermediate reasoning paths. Wang et al. (2023) propose self-consistency as an additional improvement over chain-ofthought reasoning with multi-sample inference, attributable to diverse reasoning paths enhancing the confidence of the majority answer. For machine translation, minimum Bayes risk (MBR) decoding Kumar & Byrne (2004) is a classical approach for selecting the optimal translation from candidate translations generated by an LLM, requiring diversity to ensure performance. Thus, the inherent diversity of sequences generated via arithmetic sampling offers significant potential for enhancing decoding strategies that rely on multi-sample inference. Recognizing the importance of exploring this approach, we apply arithmetic sampling to both reasoning and translation tasks. For CoT reasoning with self-consistency and machine translation with MBR decoding, we observe accuracy improvements on the GSM8K and Commonsense QA datasets, along with substantial COMET score gains as the number of sampled sequences increases.
