problem: what is grokking in the neural network field?
final_response:
# What “grokking” means in neural networks

Grokking refers to a sudden, qualitative change in how a neural network learns, often described as a delayed transition from memorizing examples to generalizing the underlying rule after prolonged training or increased regularization, even when loss decreases slowly during an earlier phase.<cite id="863efcfb-4">Grokking is often described as a delayed transition from memorization to generalization after extended training, though in deep networks this simple narrative is incomplete</cite> <cite id="cb9d0bb0-4">Although multiple factors may contribute to grokking, a key prerequisite is a sharp shift in learning dynamics phase</cite>. Empirically, it manifests as abrupt jumps in accuracy or representational statistics, sometimes after an extended plateau, and can be captured by statistical-physics notions of phase transitions with discontinuous changes and hysteresis.<cite id="863efcfb-0">Ziyin and Ueda showed phase-transition-like behavior in regularized networks, later work linked grokking to first-order transitions in DNNs, and additional transitions appear as data complexity increases</cite> <cite id="863efcfb-2">A teacher–student model with two minima (memorization vs generalization) exhibits a discontinuous jump as minima exchange stability, with hysteresis and mixed phases</cite>.

# Evidence from phase-transition models

Statistical-physics analyses model grokking as a competition between a memorization state and a generalization state, where changing hyperparameters (e.g., regularization) or training time swaps the stability of minima, producing a first-order transition with a discontinuous order parameter.<cite id="863efcfb-2">An effective potential with two competing minima leads to a discontinuous jump in an order parameter as minima exchange stability, with hysteresis and mixed phases characteristic of first-order transitions</cite> <cite id="cb9d0bb0-2">This mapping provides a rigorous justification for treating discontinuities in neural training as genuine phase transitions</cite>. Earlier “onset-of-learning” work showed that increasing L2 regularization can trigger phase-like changes: shallow networks exhibit second-order transitions while deeper networks show first-order behavior, and further transitions emerge as data complexity increases.<cite id="863efcfb-0">Entering an over-regularized phase corresponds to a second-order transition for one-hidden-layer networks and a first-order transition for DNNs; more transitions appear with increased data complexity</cite> <cite id="35adca54-0">Ziyin and Ueda’s results are reproduced and extended, with geometric interpretations and additional transitions for complex datasets</cite>.

# Mechanisms and what triggers grokking

Several mechanisms can precipitate the transition. Regularization (e.g., weight decay) and data-dependent shifts can nudge models away from high-norm memorization solutions toward simpler generalizing solutions, controlling when the transition occurs.<cite id="f014523c-1">Weight decay, dropout, and batch normalization facilitate grokking by pushing the solution from high-norm, memorizing to simpler generalizing regimes, and can mitigate or eliminate double descent</cite>. Geometry and loss-surface structure also matter: information-geometric analyses identify “change-points” in error surfaces and transitions to under-parameterized regimes as plausible drivers of grokking and related phase points during training.<cite id="863efcfb-0">A unified geometric and regularization view reproduces and extends phase transitions, including transitions to under-parameterized phases with measurable geometric change-points</cite> <cite id="35adca54-4">Depth affects transition order: depth-0 has no transition, depth-1 shows second-order, depth-D (D>1) shows first-order, and infinite depth approaches zeroth-order, consistent with Ehrenfest classification</cite>.

Batch normalization (BN) can be a specific trigger when a phase transition occurs: BN’s running statistics computed in a prior phase can mismatch current test-time statistics in a new phase, shifting representations until training settles into a stable regime, at which point test samples move into training-sample “attraction basins” and grokking appears; applying training-mode BN at test time can suppress the effect.<cite id="863efcfb-3">Under BN, historical mean/variance estimates can diverge from current true statistics during a phase transition, biasing inference so test samples fall outside training basins; as training proceeds, the discrepancy diminishes and test samples enter training basins (grokking). Applying training-mode BN at test time eliminates grokking</cite> <cite id="863efcfb-1">Grokking requires a transition in learning dynamics; BN-induced distributional shifts only cause grokking when a phase transition occurs</cite>. Complementary analyses use representation and gradient diagnostics (e.g., RPD, two-dimensional projections) to visualize how attraction basins and population dynamics change at the transition.<cite id="863efcfb-3">Two-dimensional projections of hidden representations show test samples shifting from outside to inside training-sample attraction basins at grokking, tied to changes in RPD gradient distributions during a phase transition</cite>.

# Relation to broader learning phenomena

Grokking connects to double descent: techniques that alter effective model complexity or noise (e.g., regularization, certain BN settings) can change the timing and even suppress the classic U-shaped validation error curve by steering dynamics toward earlier generalization phases.<cite id="f014523c-1">Regularization can mitigate or eliminate double descent via effects on learning dynamics</cite> <cite id="f014523c-3">Double descent has been widely observed and studied across models; recent work reviews theory and links to neural networks, with extensions to epoch count, sparsity, and transfer learning</cite>. Exact-phase-transition theory shows that depth, regularization, and the interplay of simplicity and accuracy produce first-, second-, and even zeroth-order transitions, clarifying when changes are continuous versus abrupt and supporting grokking as a first-order phenomenon in sufficiently deep models.<cite id="35adca54-4">Depth- and regularization-dependent phase transitions range from no transition (depth 0) to second-order (depth 1) to first-order (depth >1), with infinite depth approaching zeroth-order</cite> <cite id="35adca54-1">Regularization reduces parameter correlations in a manner akin to an entropic force, yielding phase transitions from under- to overparametrization with implications for learning phases</cite>.

# When and where grokking is observed

Empirically, grokking can appear as a jump from near-zero to appreciable generalization on algorithmic or synthetic tasks, and as representational reorganization in embedding spaces, especially under increasing regularization or data complexity.<cite id="863efcfb-2">In a two-layer modular addition setup, increasing regularization or time flips stability between memorization and generalization minima, producing a discontinuous jump</cite> <cite id="863efcfb-0">Additional transitions emerge as data complexity increases, with geometric substructures corresponding to learned features</cite>. In practical deep models with BN, grokking often requires a phase transition in the internal population dynamics; without such a transition (e.g., same-phase data distributions), grokking is not observed.<cite id="863efcfb-1">No phase transition implies no notable grokking; BN’s distributional shifts only induce grokking across phases</cite> <cite id="863efcfb-3">Phase transitions in gradient distributions cause mismatched BN statistics at inference, producing basin shifts that underlie grokking</cite>. In small transformers, grokking-like discontinuities in word usage statistics have been interpreted as crossovers between competing representational minima, consistent with the phase-transition view.<cite id="863efcfb-2">Dispersions of word usage flip from near-Poisson to sub-Poisson and vice versa as the network crosses a threshold where generalization overtakes memorization</cite>.

# Open questions and alternative views

While a phase-transition framework explains many observations, open questions remain: general principles governing when transitions are first- vs second-order across architectures and tasks, the full role of stochastic gradient dynamics and criticality, and whether BN-specific effects are necessary or just a common pathway to phase transitions.<cite id="863efcfb-0">A general explanation for phase transitions in DNN training dynamics is still lacking, despite progress in geometry and regularization perspectives</cite> <cite id="863efcfb-4">Alternative narratives beyond “memorization-to-generalization” are needed for deep networks, where grokking arises from phase transitions in dynamics</cite>. Some work emphasizes that regularization and training schedules control timing and severity of grokking and double descent, suggesting practical levers (e.g., weight decay schedules, BN mode) to induce or suppress transitions.<cite id="f014523c-1">Regularization can control timing of grokking and mitigate double descent by steering dynamics toward simpler solutions</cite> <cite id="863efcfb-3">Training-mode vs evaluation-mode BN affects whether grokking manifests, highlighting implementation-dependent dynamics</cite>. Finally, solvable models and tensor-network connections indicate that locality of the teacher and representational structure govern grokking probabilities and critical exponents, pointing to task- and architecture-dependent universality classes.<cite id="cb9d0bb0-4">Two solvable grokking models derive exact expressions for critical exponents, grokking probability, and time distributions, and connect to perceptron/statistical learning theory via tensor networks</cite>.

# Bottom line

In modern neural networks, grokking is a delayed, qualitative reorganization of learning, typically a sudden shift from memorization to generalization that can be modeled as a first- (or, in shallow cases, second-) order phase transition in the model’s macroscopic state, driven by regularization, data complexity, and internal dynamics; it is visible as discontinuous changes in accuracy, hysteresis, and representational basins, and can be triggered or mitigated by training choices like weight decay schedules and batch normalization settings.<cite id="863efcfb-0">Ziyin–Ueda and follow-up work connect phase transitions to grokking across shallow and deep networks, with additional transitions as data complexity increases</cite> <cite id="863efcfb-2">Teacher–student analyses show minima-exchange transitions and hysteresis identifying grokking as a first-order phase transition</cite> <cite id="f014523c-1">Regularization and BN shape dynamics and can mitigate double descent</cite> <cite id="863efcfb-3">BN-induced statistical mismatches across phases and changes in attraction basins provide a concrete mechanism for grokking</cite> <cite id="35adca54-4">Depth and regularization determine transition order, supporting grokking as first-order in sufficiently deep models</cite>.

Title: Phase Transitions between Accuracy Regimes in L2 regularized Deep Neural Networks
Snippet: Introduction-L2 regularization is a common method used to avoid overfitting in different optimization tasks from simple linear regression [16] to regression and classification in artificial Deep Neural Networks (DNNs, i.e. Neural Networks with two or more hidden layers) [15]. There is a rich phenomenology associated with L2 regularization, including phase transitions, non-trivial geometry of the loss landscape, and training dynamics that go well beyond the classical notion of overfitting control [5,6]. For example, Ziyin and Ueda [4] show that NNs entering an over-regularized phase is equivalent to a second-order phase transition in the accuracy for onehidden-layer Neural Networks and to a first-order phase transition for DNNs. Rubin, Seroussi and Ringel [7] have linked the phenomenon of grokking to first order phase transitions using kernel methods. A general explanation for the observation of phase transitions in the training dynamics of DNNs, however, is lacking. In this Letter, we, first provide an explanation of the onsetof-learning phase transition, as observed by Ziyin and Ueda [4], in terms of the geometry of the NNs' error and loss surfaces. Second, we predict and confirm the existence of further phase transitions during regularization, beyond the onset-of-learning, i.e. when the data complexity is increased. And third, we provide an explanation for the phenomenon of grokking, which is a substantial obstacle for fast convergence in the training of large DNNs [8,9]. Our work unifies an information geometric and a regularization perspective, offering a framework for understanding the dynamics of DNN training. Specifically, our contributions include the reproduction and extension of Ziyin et al.'s [4] results, focusing on DNNs, providing a geometric interpretation of the phase transitions they observed and the identification of transitions to under-parameterized phases corresponding to measurable geometric change-points in the error surface. We then observe additional transitions for more complex datasets, indicating the emergence of geometric substructures that represent learned features. We predict the existence of transitions beyond the onset-oflearning when the data complexity is increased.

Meanwhile, regularization effectively prevents the overfitting of the model by reducing the correlation between model parameters in a manner similar to the effect of an entropic force in physics. One thus expects a phase transition in the model behavior from the regime where the regularization is negligible to the regime where it is dominant. In the long history of statistical physics of learning [10,23,18,2], a series of works studied the under-tooverparametrization (UO) phase transition in the context of linear regression [12,13,23,9]. Recently, this type of phase transition has seen a resurgence of interest [8,16]. One recent work by [15] deals with the UO transition in a deep linear model. However, the UO phase transition is not unique to deep learning because it appears in both shallow and deep models and also in non-neural-network models [3]. To understand deep learning, we need to identify what is unique about deep neural networks.

We also show that these phase transitions are unique to machine learning and deep learning. They are unique to machine learning because they are caused by the competition between the need to make predictions more accurate and the need to make the model simpler. Title: Phase Transitions between Accuracy Regimes in L2 regularized Deep Neural Networks
Snippet: Introduction-L2 regularization is a common method used to avoid overfitting in different optimization tasks from simple linear regression [16] to regression and classification in artificial Deep Neural Networks (DNNs, i.e. Neural Networks with two or more hidden layers) [15]. There is a rich phenomenology associated with L2 regularization, including phase transitions, non-trivial geometry of the loss landscape, and training dynamics that go well beyond the classical notion of overfitting control [5,6]. For example, Ziyin and Ueda [4] show that NNs entering an over-regularized phase is equivalent to a second-order phase transition in the accuracy for onehidden-layer Neural Networks and to a first-order phase transition for DNNs. Rubin, Seroussi and Ringel [7] have linked the phenomenon of grokking to first order phase transitions using kernel methods. A general explanation for the observation of phase transitions in the training dynamics of DNNs, however, is lacking. In this Letter, we, first provide an explanation of the onsetof-learning phase transition, as observed by Ziyin and Ueda [4], in terms of the geometry of the NNs' error and loss surfaces. Second, we predict and confirm the existence of further phase transitions during regularization, beyond the onset-of-learning, i.e. when the data complexity is increased. And third, we provide an explanation for the phenomenon of grokking, which is a substantial obstacle for fast convergence in the training of large DNNs [8,9]. Our work unifies an information geometric and a regularization perspective, offering a framework for understanding the dynamics of DNN training. Specifically, our contributions include the reproduction and extension of Ziyin et al.'s [4] results, focusing on DNNs, providing a geometric interpretation of the phase transitions they observed and the identification of transitions to under-parameterized phases corresponding to measurable geometric change-points in the error surface. We then observe additional transitions for more complex datasets, indicating the emergence of geometric substructures that represent learned features. We predict the existence of transitions beyond the onset-oflearning when the data complexity is increased.

# What “grokking” means in neural networks

Grokking refers to a sudden, qualitative change in how a neural network learns, often described as a delayed transition from memorizing examples to generalizing the underlying rule after prolonged training or increased regularization, even when loss decreases slowly during an earlier phase.<cite id="863efcfb-4">Grokking is often described as a delayed transition from memorization to generalization after extended training, though in deep networks this simple narrative is incomplete</cite> <cite id="cb9d0bb0-4">Although multiple factors may contribute to grokking, a key prerequisite is a sharp shift in learning dynamics phase</cite>. Empirically, it manifests as abrupt jumps in accuracy or representational statistics, sometimes after an extended plateau, and can be captured by statistical-physics notions of phase transitions with discontinuous changes and hysteresis.<cite id="863efcfb-0">Ziyin and Ueda showed phase-transition-like behavior in regularized networks, later work linked grokking to first-order transitions in DNNs, and additional transitions appear as data complexity increases</cite> <cite id="863efcfb-2">A teacher–student model with two minima (memorization vs generalization) exhibits a discontinuous jump as minima exchange stability, with hysteresis and mixed phases</cite>.

# Evidence from phase-transition models

Statistical-physics analyses model grokking as a competition between a memorization state and a generalization state, where changing hyperparameters (e.g., regularization) or training time swaps the stability of minima, producing a first-order transition with a discontinuous order parameter.<cite id="863efcfb-2">An effective potential with two competing minima leads to a discontinuous jump in an order parameter as minima exchange stability, with hysteresis and mixed phases characteristic of first-order transitions</cite> <cite id="cb9d0bb0-2">This mapping provides a rigorous justification for treating discontinuities in neural training as genuine phase transitions</cite>. Earlier “onset-of-learning” work showed that increasing L2 regularization can trigger phase-like changes: shallow networks exhibit second-order transitions while deeper networks show first-order behavior, and further transitions emerge as data complexity increases.<cite id="863efcfb-0">Entering an over-regularized phase corresponds to a second-order transition for one-hidden-layer networks and a first-order transition for DNNs; more transitions appear with increased data complexity</cite> <cite id="35adca54-0">Ziyin and Ueda’s results are reproduced and extended, with geometric interpretations and additional transitions for complex datasets</cite>.

# Mechanisms and what triggers grokking

Several mechanisms can precipitate the transition. Regularization (e.g., weight decay) and data-dependent shifts can nudge models away from high-norm memorization solutions toward simpler generalizing solutions, controlling when the transition occurs.<cite id="f014523c-1">Weight decay, dropout, and batch normalization facilitate grokking by pushing the solution from high-norm, memorizing to simpler generalizing regimes, and can mitigate or eliminate double descent</cite>. Geometry and loss-surface structure also matter: information-geometric analyses identify “change-points” in error surfaces and transitions to under-parameterized regimes as plausible drivers of grokking and related phase points during training.<cite id="863efcfb-0">A unified geometric and regularization view reproduces and extends phase transitions, including transitions to under-parameterized phases with measurable geometric change-points</cite> <cite id="35adca54-4">Depth affects transition order: depth-0 has no transition, depth-1 shows second-order, depth-D (D>1) shows first-order, and infinite depth approaches zeroth-order, consistent with Ehrenfest classification</cite>.

Batch normalization (BN) can be a specific trigger when a phase transition occurs: BN’s running statistics computed in a prior phase can mismatch current test-time statistics in a new phase, shifting representations until training settles into a stable regime, at which point test samples move into training-sample “attraction basins” and grokking appears; applying training-mode BN at test time can suppress the effect.<cite id="863efcfb-3">Under BN, historical mean/variance estimates can diverge from current true statistics during a phase transition, biasing inference so test samples fall outside training basins; as training proceeds, the discrepancy diminishes and test samples enter training basins (grokking). Applying training-mode BN at test time eliminates grokking</cite> <cite id="863efcfb-1">Grokking requires a transition in learning dynamics; BN-induced distributional shifts only cause grokking when a phase transition occurs</cite>. Complementary analyses use representation and gradient diagnostics (e.g., RPD, two-dimensional projections) to visualize how attraction basins and population dynamics change at the transition.<cite id="863efcfb-3">Two-dimensional projections of hidden representations show test samples shifting from outside to inside training-sample attraction basins at grokking, tied to changes in RPD gradient distributions during a phase transition</cite>.

# Relation to broader learning phenomena

Grokking connects to double descent: techniques that alter effective model complexity or noise (e.g., regularization, certain BN settings) can change the timing and even suppress the classic U-shaped validation error curve by steering dynamics toward earlier generalization phases.<cite id="f014523c-1">Regularization can mitigate or eliminate double descent via effects on learning dynamics</cite> <cite id="f014523c-3">Double descent has been widely observed and studied across models; recent work reviews theory and links to neural networks, with extensions to epoch count, sparsity, and transfer learning</cite>. Exact-phase-transition theory shows that depth, regularization, and the interplay of simplicity and accuracy produce first-, second-, and even zeroth-order transitions, clarifying when changes are continuous versus abrupt and supporting grokking as a first-order phenomenon in sufficiently deep models.<cite id="35adca54-4">Depth- and regularization-dependent phase transitions range from no transition (depth 0) to second-order (depth 1) to first-order (depth >1), with infinite depth approaching zeroth-order</cite> <cite id="35adca54-1">Regularization reduces parameter correlations in a manner akin to an entropic force, yielding phase transitions from under- to overparametrization with implications for learning phases</cite>.

# When and where grokking is observed

Empirically, grokking can appear as a jump from near-zero to appreciable generalization on algorithmic or synthetic tasks, and as representational reorganization in embedding spaces, especially under increasing regularization or data complexity.<cite id="863efcfb-2">In a two-layer modular addition setup, increasing regularization or time flips stability between memorization and generalization minima, producing a discontinuous jump</cite> <cite id="863efcfb-0">Additional transitions emerge as data complexity increases, with geometric substructures corresponding to learned features</cite>. In practical deep models with BN, grokking often requires a phase transition in the internal population dynamics; without such a transition (e.g., same-phase data distributions), grokking is not observed.<cite id="863efcfb-1">No phase transition implies no notable grokking; BN’s distributional shifts only induce grokking across phases</cite> <cite id="863efcfb-3">Phase transitions in gradient distributions cause mismatched BN statistics at inference, producing basin shifts that underlie grokking</cite>. In small transformers, grokking-like discontinuities in word usage statistics have been interpreted as crossovers between competing representational minima, consistent with the phase-transition view.<cite id="863efcfb-2">Dispersions of word usage flip from near-Poisson to sub-Poisson and vice versa as the network crosses a threshold where generalization overtakes memorization</cite>.

# Open questions and alternative views

While a phase-transition framework explains many observations, open questions remain: general principles governing when transitions are first- vs second-order across architectures and tasks, the full role of stochastic gradient dynamics and criticality, and whether BN-specific effects are necessary or just a common pathway to phase transitions.<cite id="863efcfb-0">A general explanation for phase transitions in DNN training dynamics is still lacking, despite progress in geometry and regularization perspectives</cite> <cite id="863efcfb-4">Alternative narratives beyond “memorization-to-generalization” are needed for deep networks, where grokking arises from phase transitions in dynamics</cite>. Some work emphasizes that regularization and training schedules control timing and severity of grokking and double descent, suggesting practical levers (e.g., weight decay schedules, BN mode) to induce or suppress transitions.<cite id="f014523c-1">Regularization can control timing of grokking and mitigate double descent by steering dynamics toward simpler solutions</cite> <cite id="863efcfb-3">Training-mode vs evaluation-mode BN affects whether grokking manifests, highlighting implementation-dependent dynamics</cite>. Finally, solvable models and tensor-network connections indicate that locality of the teacher and representational structure govern grokking probabilities and critical exponents, pointing to task- and architecture-dependent universality classes.<cite id="cb9d0bb0-4">Two solvable grokking models derive exact expressions for critical exponents, grokking probability, and time distributions, and connect to perceptron/statistical learning theory via tensor networks</cite>.

# Bottom line

In modern neural networks, grokking is a delayed, qualitative reorganization of learning, typically a sudden shift from memorization to generalization that can be modeled as a first- (or, in shallow cases, second-) order phase transition in the model’s macroscopic state, driven by regularization, data complexity, and internal dynamics; it is visible as discontinuous changes in accuracy, hysteresis, and representational basins, and can be triggered or mitigated by training choices like weight decay schedules and batch normalization settings.<cite id="863efcfb-0">Ziyin–Ueda and follow-up work connect phase transitions to grokking across shallow and deep networks, with additional transitions as data complexity increases</cite> <cite id="863efcfb-2">Teacher–student analyses show minima-exchange transitions and hysteresis identifying grokking as a first-order phase transition</cite> <cite id="f014523c-1">Regularization and BN shape dynamics and can mitigate double descent</cite> <cite id="863efcfb-3">BN-induced statistical mismatches across phases and changes in attraction basins provide a concrete mechanism for grokking</cite> <cite id="35adca54-4">Depth and regularization determine transition order, supporting grokking as first-order in sufficiently deep models</cite>.</answer>

Rubin, Seroussi, and Ringel provided the first formal statistical-physics model of grokking, directly linking training dynamics to phase transitions [19]. They studied a twolayer teacher-student network trained on modular addition and derived an effective potential describing the system's macroscopic state. The potential exhibits two competing minima: one corresponding to memorization (fitting training data without generalization) and another to generalization (capturing the underlying rule). As regularization strength or training time increases, the minima exchange stability, producing a discontinuous jump in the order parameteridentifying grokking as a first-order phase transition. Rubin et al. supported this mapping through analytical mean-field approximations and numerical simulations, demonstrating hysteresis and mixed phases characteristic of first-order transitions. They also identified intermediate regimes with Gaussian mixture features, matching empirical embedding structures seen in earlier grokking studies. 

This theoretical work establishes the strongest justification for describing discontinuities in neural training as genuine phase transitions. Rubin et al. demonstrate rigorously that smooth local updates-gradient descent steps-can yield abrupt, global changes in representational order once competing learning modes exchange stability. Although their model applies to simplified two-layer networks and algorithmic tasks, the conceptual framework extends naturally to our setting. The dispersion flip we observe-correct words transitioning from near-Poisson to sub-Poisson while incorrect words move from sub-Poisson to Poisson-likecan be interpreted as the system crossing a critical threshold where the "generalization minimum" (coherent word usage) overtakes the "memorization minimum" (fragmentary output). In this view, our Poisson-centered diagnostics serve as order parameters tracking which representational mode dominates as training progresses.

We demonstrate that the grokking effect observed in DNNs is triggered by the phase transition in conjunction with the training strategy involving BN (see Eq. ( 3)). To visualize this effect, we project the sample representations from the hidden layer adjacent to the output layer into two dimensions. Specifically, we insert a bottleneck layer with two neurons before the output layer [47]. Rather than retraining the model, we perform singular value decomposition on the weight matrix of the original final layer and extract the two leading right-singular vectors as principal directions. These directions are then used to construct the weights of the bottleneck layer. The resulting local fields h 1 and h 2 of the two bottleneck neurons are used as the coordinates in the two-dimensional representation. 

For the 23-layer DNN, we visualize the 2D projections of training and test samples before and after grokking (Figs. 6(a This grokking scenario-where test sample projections collectively shift from outside into the attraction basins of training samples-can be attributed to the perturbation introduced by BN in evaluation mode, under the condition of phase transition in RPD gradient distribution. Phase transitions in learning dynamics (see Fig. 3(g)) can significantly cause these historical estimates to diverge from the current true statistics, introducing a systematic bias in the inference of test samples. As training continues and the network settles into a stable learning phase, this discrepancy gradually diminishes. Consequently, test samples increasingly fall within the attraction basins of training samples, giving rise to the grokking phenomenon. 

Indeed, when the training mode is applied at test time-by setting α = 1 in Eq. ( 3)-the grokking effect disappears. Under this setting, the projected regions of test samples (Fig. 6(e)) already overlap with those of the training samples (Fig. 6(a)) before grokking occurs. Although double descent only gained popular attention since [BHMM19]'s influential paper on the topic, the phenomenon itself had previously been observed: [LVM + 20] provide a historical note highlighting that [VCR89] may have been the first to demonstrate double descent in min-norm linear regression; [BHMM19] themselves note that double descent-like phase transitions in neural networks had previously been observed in [BO96, ASS20, NMB + 18, SGd + 18]. Title: Grokking phase transitions in learning local rules with gradient descent
Snippet: We discuss two solvable grokking (generalisation beyond overfitting) models in a rule learning scenario. We show that grokking is a phase transition and find exact analytic expressions for the critical exponents, grokking probability, and grokking time distribution. Further, we introduce a tensor-network map that connects the proposed grokking setup with the standard (perceptron) statistical learning theory and show that grokking is a consequence of the locality of the teacher model. As an example, we analyse the cellular automata learning task, numerically determine the critical exponent and the grokking time distributions and compare them with the prediction of the proposed grokking model. Finally, we numerically analyse the connection between structure formation and grokking.

Title: Exact Phase Transitions in Deep Learning
Snippet: Understanding neural networks is a fundamental problem in both theoretical deep learning and neuroscience. In deep learning, learning proceeds as the parameters of different layers become correlated so that the model responds to an input in a meaningful way. This is reminiscent of an ordered phase in physics, where the microscopic degrees of freedom behave collectively and coherently. Meanwhile, regularization effectively prevents the overfitting of the model by reducing the correlation between model parameters in a manner similar to the effect of an entropic force in physics. One thus expects a phase transition in the model behavior from the regime where the regularization is negligible to the regime where it is dominant. In the long history of statistical physics of learning [10,23,18,2], a series of works studied the under-tooverparametrization (UO) phase transition in the context of linear regression [12,13,23,9]. Recently, this type of phase transition has seen a resurgence of interest [8,16]. One recent work by [15] deals with the UO transition in a deep linear model. However, the UO phase transition is not unique to deep learning because it appears in both shallow and deep models and also in non-neural-network models [3]. To understand deep learning, we need to identify what is unique about deep neural networks. 

In this work, we address the fundamental problem of the loss landscape of a deep neural network and prove that there exist phase transitions in deep learning that can be described precisely as the first-and second-order phase transitions with a striking similarity to physics. We argue that these phase transitions can have profound implications for deep learning, such as the importance of symmetry breaking for learning and the qualitative difference between shallow and deep architectures. We also show that these phase transitions are unique to machine learning and deep learning. They are unique to machine learning because they are caused by the competition between the need to make predictions more accurate and the need to make the model simpler. These phase transitions are also deep-learning unique because they only appear in "deeper" models.

For a multilayer linear net with stochastic neurons and trained with L 2 regularization, 1. we identify an order parameter and effective landscape that describe the phase transition between a trivial phase and a feature learning phase as the L 2 regularization hyperparameter is changed (Theorem 3); 

2. we show that finite-depth networks cannot have the zeroth-order phase transition (Theorem 2);

snippet.text: Introduction-L2 regularization is a common method used to avoid overfitting in different optimization tasks from simple linear regression [16] to regression and classification in artificial Deep Neural Networks (DNNs, i.e. Neural Networks with two or more hidden layers) [15]. There is a rich phenomenology associated with L2 regularization, including phase transitions, non-trivial geometry of the loss landscape, and training dynamics that go well beyond the classical notion of overfitting control [5,6]. For example, Ziyin and Ueda [4] show that NNs entering an over-regularized phase is equivalent to a second-order phase transition in the accuracy for onehidden-layer Neural Networks and to a first-order phase transition for DNNs. Rubin, Seroussi and Ringel [7] have linked the phenomenon of grokking to first order phase transitions using kernel methods. A general explanation for the observation of phase transitions in the training dynamics of DNNs, however, is lacking. In this Letter, we, first provide an explanation of the onsetof-learning phase transition, as observed by Ziyin and Ueda [4], in terms of the geometry of the NNs' error and loss surfaces. Second, we predict and confirm the existence of further phase transitions during regularization, beyond the onset-of-learning, i.e. when the data complexity is increased. And third, we provide an explanation for the phenomenon of grokking, which is a substantial obstacle for fast convergence in the training of large DNNs [8,9]. Our work unifies an information geometric and a regularization perspective, offering a framework for understanding the dynamics of DNN training. Specifically, our contributions include the reproduction and extension of Ziyin et al.'s [4] results, focusing on DNNs, providing a geometric interpretation of the phase transitions they observed and the identification of transitions to under-parameterized phases corresponding to measurable geometric change-points in the error surface. We then observe additional transitions for more complex datasets, indicating the emergence of geometric substructures that represent learned features. We predict the existence of transitions beyond the onset-oflearning when the data complexity is increased.

snippet.text:
Understanding neural networks is a fundamental problem in both theoretical deep learning and neuroscience. In deep learning, learning proceeds as the parameters of different layers become correlated so that the model responds to an input in a meaningful way. This is reminiscent of an ordered phase in physics, where the microscopic degrees of freedom behave collectively and coherently. Meanwhile, regularization effectively prevents the overfitting of the model by reducing the correlation between model parameters in a manner similar to the effect of an entropic force in physics. One thus expects a phase transition in the model behavior from the regime where the regularization is negligible to the regime where it is dominant. In the long history of statistical physics of learning [10,23,18,2], a series of works studied the under-tooverparametrization (UO) phase transition in the context of linear regression [12,13,23,9]. Recently, this type of phase transition has seen a resurgence of interest [8,16]. One recent work by [15] deals with the UO transition in a deep linear model. However, the UO phase transition is not unique to deep learning because it appears in both shallow and deep models and also in non-neural-network models [3]. To understand deep learning, we need to identify what is unique about deep neural networks. 

In this work, we address the fundamental problem of the loss landscape of a deep neural network and prove that there exist phase transitions in deep learning that can be described precisely as the first-and second-order phase transitions with a striking similarity to physics. We argue that these phase transitions can have profound implications for deep learning, such as the importance of symmetry breaking for learning and the qualitative difference between shallow and deep architectures. We also show that these phase transitions are unique to machine learning and deep learning. They are unique to machine learning because they are caused by the competition between the need to make predictions more accurate and the need to make the model simpler. These phase transitions are also deep-learning unique because they only appear in "deeper" models.

In this case, maintaining consistent attraction basins for both test and training samples eliminates the conditions necessary for grokking to emerge.

Title: Evidence of Phase Transitions in Small Transformer-Based Language Models
Snippet: Rubin, Seroussi, and Ringel provided the first formal statistical-physics model of grokking, directly linking training dynamics to phase transitions [19]. They studied a twolayer teacher-student network trained on modular addition and derived an effective potential describing the system's macroscopic state. The potential exhibits two competing minima: one corresponding to memorization (fitting training data without generalization) and another to generalization (capturing the underlying rule). As regularization strength or training time increases, the minima exchange stability, producing a discontinuous jump in the order parameteridentifying grokking as a first-order phase transition. Rubin et al. supported this mapping through analytical mean-field approximations and numerical simulations, demonstrating hysteresis and mixed phases characteristic of first-order transitions. They also identified intermediate regimes with Gaussian mixture features, matching empirical embedding structures seen in earlier grokking studies. 

This theoretical work establishes the strongest justification for describing discontinuities in neural training as genuine phase transitions. Rubin et al. demonstrate rigorously that smooth local updates-gradient descent steps-can yield abrupt, global changes in representational order once competing learning modes exchange stability. Although their model applies to simplified two-layer networks and algorithmic tasks, the conceptual framework extends naturally to our setting. The dispersion flip we observe-correct words transitioning from near-Poisson to sub-Poisson while incorrect words move from sub-Poisson to Poisson-likecan be interpreted as the system crossing a critical threshold where the "generalization minimum" (coherent word usage) overtakes the "memorization minimum" (fragmentary output). In this view, our Poisson-centered diagnostics serve as order parameters tracking which representational mode dominates as training progresses.

Title: Network Dynamics-Based Framework for Understanding Deep Neural Networks
Snippet: We demonstrate that the grokking effect observed in DNNs is triggered by the phase transition in conjunction with the training strategy involving BN (see Eq. ( 3)). To visualize this effect, we project the sample representations from the hidden layer adjacent to the output layer into two dimensions. Specifically, we insert a bottleneck layer with two neurons before the output layer [47]. Rather than retraining the model, we perform singular value decomposition on the weight matrix of the original final layer and extract the two leading right-singular vectors as principal directions. These directions are then used to construct the weights of the bottleneck layer. The resulting local fields h 1 and h 2 of the two bottleneck neurons are used as the coordinates in the two-dimensional representation. 

For the 23-layer DNN, we visualize the 2D projections of training and test samples before and after grokking (Figs. 6(a This grokking scenario-where test sample projections collectively shift from outside into the attraction basins of training samples-can be attributed to the perturbation introduced by BN in evaluation mode, under the condition of phase transition in RPD gradient distribution. As described by Eq. ( 3), BN relies on running estimates of mean and variance accumulated during earlier training stages. Phase transitions in learning dynamics (see Fig. 3(g)) can significantly cause these historical estimates to diverge from the current true statistics, introducing a systematic bias in the inference of test samples. As training continues and the network settles into a stable learning phase, this discrepancy gradually diminishes. Consequently, test samples increasingly fall within the attraction basins of training samples, giving rise to the grokking phenomenon. 

Indeed, when the training mode is applied at test time-by setting α = 1 in Eq. ( 3)-the grokking effect disappears. Under this setting, the projected regions of test samples (Fig. 6(e)) already overlap with those of the training samples (Fig. 6(a)) before grokking occurs. After grokking, the test sample projections (Fig. 6(f)) remain similar to those in Fig. 6(d) and coincide with the training sample projections (Fig. 6(b)).

Title: Network Dynamics-Based Framework for Understanding Deep Neural Networks
Snippet: RPD and attraction basin analyses provide a systematic framework for understanding neural network behavior, offering insights into the underlying learning dynamics. In this section, we investigate the mechanisms behind the well-known grokking phenomenon. Grokking is often described as a delayed transition from memorization to generalization after extended training [31]. While this interpretation captures the behavior in shallow networks, we show that it does not accurately explain the dynamics in DNNs. Although multiple factors may contribute to grokking, a key prerequisite is a sharp shift in learning dynamics phase.

Indeed, when the training mode is applied at test time-by setting α = 1 in Eq. ( 3)-the grokking effect disappears. Under this setting, the projected regions of test samples (Fig. 6(e)) already overlap with those of the training samples (Fig. 6(a)) before grokking occurs. After grokking, the test sample projections (Fig. 6(f)) remain similar to those in Fig. 6(d) and coincide with the training sample projections (Fig. 6(b)).

documents.title: Network Dynamics-Based Framework for Understanding Deep Neural Networks
documents.snippet: RPD and attraction basin analyses provide a systematic framework for understanding neural network behavior, offering insights into the underlying learning dynamics. In this section, we investigate the mechanisms behind the well-known grokking phenomenon. Grokking is often described as a delayed transition from memorization to generalization after extended training [31]. While this interpretation captures the behavior in shallow networks, we show that it does not accurately explain the dynamics in DNNs. Although multiple factors may contribute to grokking, a key prerequisite is a sharp shift in learning dynamics phase.

problem: What are the latest deep learning techniques and models being used in computer vision for corrosion (rust) detection, classification and segmentation
final_response:
# Overview

Recent work in corrosion (rust) detection in computer vision spans three core tasks—detection, classification, and segmentation—and leverages a range of deep learning techniques from CNNs and classical detectors to transformer-based models and 3D perception, often in UAV/robotic inspection settings with challenging appearance variability and scale/multiview issues.<cite id="47ab002c-1,47ab002c-4">Corrosion varies widely in shape, color, and texture and often requires pixel-level analysis rather than bounding boxes, driving the use of semantic segmentation alongside detection and classification</cite> <cite id="47ab002c-2">UAV imagery is commonly used to capture multi-angle views, and stitched-view segmentation has been proposed to cover larger bridge surfaces while retaining resolution</cite>.

# Detection (Object Detection)

State-of-the-art detection for corrosion employs two-stage and one-stage architectures tailored for speed, accuracy, and deployment:

- Two-stage detectors: Faster R-CNN with strong backbones (e.g., ResNet-101) has achieved high accuracy for rust on transmission line fittings (>97%) and metal corrosion recognition, but suffers from complexity and latency unsuitable for embedded platforms.<cite id="30175470-0">Faster R-CNN with ResNet-101 achieved >97% detection accuracy for rust on transmission line fittings, while a Faster R-CNN with color-feature support achieved high accuracy and recall on metal corrosion; however, two-stage detectors have poor real-time performance and high hardware demands</cite>

- One-stage detectors: Optimized SSD and YOLO variants are favored for real-time inspection. Examples include enhanced SSD-Mobilenet for aircraft corrosion and YOLO-based pipelines for aircraft surface defect detection, with reports of effective detection of corrosion and cracks.<cite id="30175470-0">Optimized single-stage detectors (SSD, YOLO) reduce redundant computation and improve speed; enhanced SSD-Mobilenet detected aircraft defects caused by corrosion and cracks, and YOLO-based models have been used to identify corrosion on aircraft surfaces</cite> <cite id="30175470-2">Prior CNN-based detectors (e.g., Faster R-CNN, YOLO) achieved satisfying results but are unsuitable for MAV on-board platforms due to large model sizes from standard convolutions</cite>

- Transformer-based detectors and hybrids: End-to-end transformer detectors (DETR and its variants) with efficient attention and strong backbones (Swin/PVT) are being adopted for infrastructure inspection and related anomaly detection, showing improved accuracy and especially small-object performance. Deformable DETR and DETR+X backbones have been reported to outperform Faster R-CNN, YOLO, and baseline DETR, with applications to power transformer state recognition and detection on heterogeneous data.<cite id="388a35b8-0">A DETR+X framework with Swin2SR/GAN data augmentation, PVT backbone, and deformable attention outperformed Faster R-CNN, RetinaNet, YOLOv8, and Deformable DETR in mAP50, with notable gains in small-object detection, and achieved 100% accuracy on DGA feature maps for transformer maintenance</cite> <cite id="388a35b8-2">Deformable DETR improves DETR by focusing attention on key sampling points, addressing slow convergence and achieving strong COCO results; Swin Transformer’s shifted window design efficiently handles high-resolution imagery and achieves excellent detection on COCO</cite> 

- Instance segmentation: Mask R-CNN provides pixel-accurate masks over Faster R-CNN proposals and is used when precise corrosion area measurement is required, with strategies to reduce computation (adaptive grids) and to fuse semantic masks with contour segmentation for higher confidence at boundaries.<cite id="30175470-1">Mask R-CNN achieves high-accuracy instance segmentation by refining object proposals from Faster R-CNN for corrosion areas; boundary accuracy can be improved by adaptive subdivision and grid-based prediction</cite> <cite id="30175470-3">A fusion of deep semantic segmentation (FCN/UNet/Mask R-CNN) with color-based contour segmentation yields high-confidence corroded pixels for pixel-level analysis</cite>

# Classification (Recognition and Grading)

Classification ranges from coarse presence/absence to fine-grained stage/level labeling, often trained with transfer learning and data augmentation:

- CNN-based classification and multi-level grading: Fine-tuned CNNs with sliding window or multi-parallel branches have been used for corrosion level classification; studies also train CNNs with data augmentation and side-output layers to distinguish multiple corrosion levels and report improved performance over PSPNet, DeepLab, and SegNet in cross-validation.<cite id="30175470-2">A fine-tuned CNN with sliding window classified corrosion presence and position; a two-parallel CNN was proposed for corrosion level classification</cite> <cite id="47ab002c-4">U-Net and DeepLab variants have been widely used in corrosion segmentation with attention to backbone design and multiscale feature integration</cite> <cite id="47ab002c-4">A study trained a segmentation network based on SegFormer and compared against U-Net and DeepLabV3+, highlighting backbone choices and attention mechanisms</cite> <cite id="47ab002c-0">A multilevel classification framework segmented and classified rust regions into good, fair, poor, and severe states</cite> <cite id="47ab002c-4">A deep CNN with batch normalization, side-output layers, and loss engineering distinguished four corrosion levels and outperformed PSPNet, DeepLab, and SegNet under cross-validation</cite>

- Practical constraints for deployment: Real-time onboard classification/detection on MAVs requires lightweight backbones (e.g., MobileNet/Swish) and reduced convolution counts to manage model size and latency, as heavier two-stage or standard CNN pipelines are impractical for embedded platforms.<cite id="30175470-2">Standard convolution-heavy networks yield large models unsuitable for MAVs; lightweight CNNs and optimized pipelines are needed for onboard real-time inspection</cite>

# Segmentation (Semantic and Instance)

Transformer-based and CNN-based encoders are both prevalent, with clear trends and trade-offs:

- CNN-based segmentation: U-Net and DeepLab families remain strong baselines for corrosion segmentation, with U-Net variants effective at small-area detection but limited for multiscale patterns; DeepLab’s atrous convolutions expand receptive fields while maintaining resolution.<cite id="47ab002c-1">U-Net variants effectively identify small-scale corroded areas but struggle with multiscale tasks; DeepLab uses atrous spatial pyramid pooling and atrous convolutions to maintain resolution and large receptive fields</cite> <cite id="47ab002c-2">U-Net’s contracting/expanding path captures context and precise locations, while DeepLabv3+ performs well in corrosion segmentation via multiscale feature concatenation</cite>

- Transformer-based segmentation: Vision transformers and lightweight transformer backbones (e.g., SegFormer, PVT) have surpassed CNN baselines on corrosion segmentation in recent reports, with active research on efficiency and high-resolution handling. SegFormer and related transformer segmenters improved mIoU over U-Net/DeepLab while offering lower parameter counts than heavier alternatives, though computational complexity can be higher than compact CNNs.<cite id="47ab002c-0">Transformer-based methods have surpassed U-Net/DeepLab for corrosion segmentation in recent work</cite> <cite id="47ab002c-4">SegFormer was adopted for corrosion segmentation and compared to U-Net and DeepLabV3+, motivated by transformer advances and attention mechanisms</cite> <cite id="47ab002c-3">On a metal corrosion dataset, a SegFormer-based variant achieved 67.69% mIoU, 1.49% higher than baseline SegFormer and 3–7.51% higher than UPerNet, SETR, and Segmenter, but heavier CNNs (UPerNet, SETR, Segmenter) had tens to hundreds of times more parameters with higher computational/memory costs; the proposed SegFormer variant balanced performance and efficiency for practical deployment</cite>

- Self-/weakly-supervised and label-free segmentation: To address the scarcity of pixel-labeled datasets, RustSEG proposes a two-stage label-free approach that first classifies corrosion presence and then explains the decision at the pixel level to produce masks, demonstrating per-pixel segmentation on unseen images without per-pixel supervision; limitations include sensitivity to shadows and the need for standardized benchmarks.<cite id="2bfd42ba-2">RustSEG performs corrosion presence classification, then attributes contributions to image pixels and refines into pixel-level masks without per-pixel training labels, enabling automated corrosion detection</cite> <cite id="2bfd42ba-4">RustSEG generated per-pixel masks from unseen images without per-pixel training data but was impacted by shadows and image defects; lack of open corrosion segmentation datasets hinders broad evaluation</cite> <cite id="2bfd42ba-0">RustSEG highlights the need for a standard small-scale comparison benchmark for corrosion segmentation to enable like-for-like evaluation</cite>

- Multi-level and condition-based segmentation: Segmenters are increasingly trained to output multiple condition states (e.g., good, fair, poor, severe) to support grading and prioritization in bridge and infrastructure inspections, often combined with image stitching for larger view coverage without sacrificing resolution.<cite id="47ab002c-1">A multilevel classification and segmentation pipeline evaluated corrosion into multiple condition states and used image stitching to segment larger bridge views while maintaining resolution</cite> <cite id="47ab002c-2">Accurate identification in larger views aids engineers in locating corrosion, and image stitching reduces the need for wide-view recording equipment</cite>

# 3D Perception, Multi-view, and Thermal Imagery

Corrosion monitoring is increasingly integrated with 3D sensing and multi-view fusion:

- 3D/point-cloud and BEV detection: Transformer backbones for point clouds (e.g., Pointformer) and BEV fusion methods (e.g., LSS-based and transformer-based multi-view pipelines) are being adapted from autonomous driving to infrastructure inspection, improving robustness to occlusion and scale by leveraging 3D context and attention mechanisms.<cite id="388a35b8-2">A Pointformer backbone for 3D point clouds effectively learns features and improves detection performance</cite> <cite id="388a35b8-4">LSS-based and transformer-based multi-view 3D detectors convert multi-view images to BEV features for 3D object detection; DETR variants (Deformable DETR, DINO) have been improved for efficiency and matching</cite>

- Thermal-based detection: While not specific to corrosion, thermal object detection pipelines using transformer detectors (e.g., RT-DETR) and YOLO variants show strong performance on thermal anomaly detection in related industrial settings, suggesting applicability to thermal signatures of corrosion and defects where visible light is insufficient.<cite id="388a35b8-1">YOLOv8 achieved 96.0% mAP, 90.8% precision, and 89.9% recall on thermal liquid leak detection; RT-DETR provided slightly lower metrics but leveraged transformer attention to capture subtle thermal variations</cite>

# Training Paradigms and Datasets

- Data scarcity and augmentation: High-quality pixel-labeled datasets are scarce; researchers augment corrosion datasets with scaling, flipping, blurring, rotation, and color distortion to improve generalization and reduce overfitting, and propose pipelines that work with limited labels (e.g., semi-supervised/label-explaining transformers).<cite id="2bfd42ba-0">A standard benchmark for corrosion segmentation is lacking despite the promise of transformer-based methods</cite> <cite id="2bfd42ba-3">Augmentations including random scaling/cropping, flipping, Gaussian blur, rotation, and color distortion improved pipeline generalization and reduced overfitting for pipe corrosion segmentation</cite>

- Efficient and lightweight design: Studies emphasize balancing accuracy with parameter count and inference speed to enable deployment on drones/robots; compact backbones (e.g., PVT/MobileNet-like) and efficient attention (e.g., deformable attention) are favored to keep models practical for embedded platforms.<cite id="388a35b8-0">A DETR+X model with PVT and deformable attention improved transformer-based detection efficiency for infrastructure monitoring</cite> <cite id="30175470-2">Standard convolution-heavy networks are unsuitable for MAVs; optimized lightweight CNNs and reduced convolutions are needed for on-board platforms</cite>

# Application Contexts and Practical Workflows

- Bridge and civil infrastructure: Large-scale inspection often requires stitching multi-image mosaics to cover span lengths while preserving resolution, with segmentation models trained on UAV imagery and evaluated for multilevel grading to support maintenance prioritization.<cite id="47ab002c-1">Image stitching with SegFormer-based segmentation enabled multilevel corrosion classification (good, fair, poor, severe) over larger bridge views without specialized wide-angle equipment</cite> <cite id="47ab002c-2">UAV-acquired images are central for corrosion monitoring, and pixel-level segmentation is needed to measure corrosion area and size accurately</cite>

- Power infrastructure and transformers: Transformer-focused pipelines combine vision transformers, digital twins, and DGA (degassing) analytics with attention mechanisms for state recognition and anomaly detection, showing that DETR-like detectors with strong backbones outperform traditional detectors on small features relevant to internal degradation indicators.<cite id="388a35b8-0">DETR+X achieved 100% accuracy on DGA feature maps and surpassed YOLOv8/Deformable DETR in mAP50 with improved small-object detection for transformer state recognition</cite>

- Aerospace and industrial components: Embedded detection/classification for aircraft and power lines uses optimized one-stage detectors and Faster R-CNN with specialized backbones; these systems must meet real-time constraints and robustness to varied corrosion morphologies.<cite id="30175470-0">Faster R-CNN with ResNet-101 achieved high accuracy for rust on transmission fittings, while YOLO variants have been used for aircraft surface corrosion detection</cite> <cite id="30175470-2">Prior CNN-based pipelines for aircraft corrosion detection highlight the need for lightweight architectures for onboard platforms</cite>

# Emerging Directions and Open Challenges

- Multimodal fusion and explainability: Hybrid pipelines combine semantic segmentation masks with color/contour segmentations to improve boundary accuracy and confidence of corroded pixels, reflecting a trend toward multi-hypothesis fusion for robust pixel-level grading.<cite id="30175470-3">Fusing deep semantic masks (FCN/UNet/Mask R-CNN) with color-based contour segmentation produced high-confidence corroded pixels for structural analysis</cite>

- Standardization and benchmarks: Despite advances, there is a call for standardized small-scale benchmark datasets to enable fair comparison across segmentation methods, as current evaluation is often limited to ad hoc datasets and qualitative analyses.<cite id="2bfd42ba-0">Standard high-performing segmentation methods lack comparable public benchmarks for corrosion; a small (~50–100 image) test set would aid evaluation</cite> <cite id="2bfd42ba-4">RustSEG’s label-free approach was evaluated qualitatively due to dataset scarcity and sensitivity to shadows, underscoring benchmark gaps</cite>

- Efficiency and scalability: Transformer-based models improve accuracy but increase compute and memory demands; recent work emphasizes efficient backbones (Swin/PVT), deformable attention, and model compression to maintain real-time performance for UAV/MAV and embedded systems.<cite id="47ab002c-3">Heavier transformer/segmentation variants (UPerNet, SETR) offer higher accuracy but with much higher parameter counts and computational/memory costs; efficient SegFormer variants balance performance and practicality</cite> <cite id="388a35b8-2">Deformable DETR and Swin Transformer address efficiency and slow convergence while maintaining strong detection performance</cite>

# Summary of Techniques and Models in Use

- CNN-based segmentation/backbones (U-Net, DeepLab, FCN, SegNet) remain strong baselines for corrosion maps and defect regions, with attention to multiscale context and boundary handling.<cite id="47ab002c-1">U-Net and DeepLab series dominate corrosion segmentation; U-Net excels at small-scale detection but struggles with multiscale patterns; DeepLab’s atrous convolutions maintain resolution and field-of-view</cite> <cite id="47ab002c-2">U-Net/DeepLab series are mainstream and widely evaluated for corrosion segmentation with encoder–decoder fusion and atrous pyramid pooling</cite>

- Transformer-based models (SegFormer, RustSEG, DETR/Deformable DETR, PVT/Swin) improve segmentation and detection accuracy, including small-object detection, by leveraging attention and stronger feature pyramids, with active work on efficiency for deployment.<cite id="47ab002c-0">Transformer-based segmentation surpasses U-Net/DeepLab for rust region detection and multi-level classification</cite> <cite id="47ab002c-3">SegFormer-based methods can outperform baselines in mIoU while managing parameter/compute trade-offs</cite> <cite id="388a35b8-0">DETR+X with PVT and deformable attention outperforms Faster R-CNN/YOLO variants in transformer-based detection tasks</cite> <cite id="388a35b8-2">Deformable DETR and Swin Transformer improve efficiency and accuracy for detection tasks</cite>

- Object detectors for corrosion include optimized one-stage (YOLO/SSD) for real-time, two-stage (Faster R-CNN) for high accuracy, and instance segmenters (Mask R-CNN) for precise masks, with trends toward transformer detectors (DETR variants) and efficient backbones for small features.<cite id="30175470-0">YOLO/SSD and Faster R-CNN variants are used for corrosion detection, with two-stage models offering high accuracy but poor real-time performance</cite> <cite id="30175470-1">Mask R-CNN provides pixel-accurate instance masks over Faster R-CNN proposals for corrosion area measurement</cite> <cite id="388a35b8-0">Transformer-based detectors with deformable attention and strong backbones improve small-object detection and overall mAP50</cite>

- Self-/weakly-supervised and label-explaining pipelines (e.g., RustSEG) address labeling scarcity by deriving masks from classification decisions, while data augmentation strategies bolster generalization in limited-label regimes.<cite id="2bfd42ba-2">RustSEG performs label-free pixel-level segmentation by explaining the corrosion presence decision with a mask</cite> <cite id="2bfd42ba-3">Data augmentation (scaling, flipping, blur, rotation, color distortion) reduces overfitting and increases diversity for pipe corrosion segmentation</cite>

- 3D/BEV and multi-view fusion, along with thermal imaging, are emerging modalities for robust corrosion detection, drawing on transformer-based point cloud and image fusion backbones to handle occlusion, scale, and complex geometry.<cite id="388a35b8-4">Transformer-based and LSS-based multi-view BEV detectors convert multi-view images to 3D BEV features for robust detection</cite> <cite id="388a35b8-1">Transformer-based and YOLO-based detectors achieved high mAP and precision/recall on thermal anomaly detection, suggesting potential for thermal corrosion monitoring</cite>

# Practical Recommendations

- For pixel-level grading on large structures, adopt transformer segmentation (SegFormer/PVT variants) with image stitching to cover wide spans, and add contour/color fusion to sharpen boundaries for measurement-grade masks.<cite id="47ab002c-1">SegFormer-based segmentation with image stitching supports multilevel grading over large bridge surfaces</cite> <cite id="30175470-3">Fusing semantic masks with contour segmentation improves boundary confidence and structural analysis readiness</cite>

- For real-time onboard inspection, use optimized one-stage detectors or lightweight transformer detectors with efficient backbones and attention (e.g., Deformable DETR/Swin/PVT) to balance latency and accuracy for UAV/MAV platforms.<cite id="30175470-2">Heavier convolution-heavy models are impractical for MAVs; optimized lightweight architectures are required</cite> <cite id="388a35b8-0">DETR+X with PVT and deformable attention improves detection efficiency for infrastructure monitoring</cite>

- Address data scarcity via semi-supervised/label-explaining transformers (e.g., RustSEG) and comprehensive augmentation; advocate for community benchmarks to enable fair, quantitative comparisons across methods and hardware.<cite id="2bfd42ba-0">A standardized corrosion segmentation benchmark would enable like-for-like comparisons and broader evaluation</cite> <cite id="2bfd42ba-4">RustSEG’s label-free segmentation highlights both promise and sensitivity to shadows, emphasizing the need for robust datasets</cite>

Snippet: In recent years, many deep learning-based semantic segmentation methods have been proposed for detecting steel corrosion. Title: A multilevel bridge corrosion detection method by transformer-based segmentation in a stitched view
Snippet: Deep learning models have been widely used in semantic segmentation tasks for corrosion detection. However, these models have limitations, such as accuracy when dealing with complex corrosion patterns, and fixed receptive field for global contextual information. The performance of different U-Net variants in the steel structure corrosion detection task has been evaluated, demonstrating the effectiveness of the CNN-based model in identifying small-scale corroded areas, but pointing out its limitations in dealing with multiscale tasks [47]. A Transformer-based segmentation model, RustSeg, was proposed for multi-level rust region detection and classification, but there are still challenges in computational efficiency and high-resolution image processing [48]. 

Obtaining images on the surface of large structures is difficult, and the monitoring performance needs to be improved [49]. The constraints of single-image inspections were addressed, and UAVs have been used to capture images from different angles [50][51][52]. Section segmentation has been used in marine defect detection, which shows better performance in larger view [53]. However, after successfully building a dataset and training model, little previous research has considered how to expand the segmentation view for corrosion detection on bridge surfaces. Image capturing is a balance of distance and view size. The image view is always fixed when the distance and recording equipment do not change substantially [54][55][56]. Accurate identification in a larger view helps engineers detect and locate corrosion. In this research, image stitching was utilized for segmentation to determine the corrosion location and evaluate it from a larger view while maintaining the resolution of the input. This image processing method reduces the need for expensive wide-view recording equipment, thereby lowering monitoring costs. 

This study proposes a corrosion localization and evaluation architecture for a larger view based on semantic segmentation and image stitching, which gives multilevel classification and segmentation of corrosion into multiple condition states, such as good, fair, poor, and severe. The method includes a) training a semantic segmentation network based on SegFormer and b) feature point matching, calculating the transformation matrix and image stitching.
</snippet>
<snippet id=47ab002c-2>
Title: A multilevel bridge corrosion detection method by transformer-based segmentation in a stitched view
Snippet: However, corrosion detection is challenging because it has variable color and texture properties and does not have uniform characteristics as do cracks [24]. Due to the randomness of its shape and size, it is not sufficient to label corrosion in bounding boxes, as in the YOLO series [25]. The detection task should be performed not only on regions but also on every image pixel. Semantic segmentation, discussed in the following paragraph, is a better method for classifying and grading corrosion pixel by pixel. 

Semantic segmentation subdivides a digital image into image subregions, simplifies the representation, and makes it easier to understand every image pixel [26]. Semantic segmentation has attracted increased attention in image processing. Some classic and mainstream deep learning-based methods have shown potential and become basic segmentation ideas. For example, the fully convolutional network (FCN) changes the output layer of a traditional CNN from fully connected layers to convolutional layers and uses them as a pixel-level output to classify each pixel [27]. Unlike FCNs, U-Nets are classical U-shaped fully convolutional neural networks containing a contracting path to capture context information and a symmetric expanding path to obtain precise locations. Another mainstream method is DeepLabv3 + , which uses atrous convolution to decrease the downsampling rate while maintaining the receptive field size. Through the encoder-decoder structure, the U-Net series of networks performs data fusion of multiscale dimensions and shows good results in the corrosion segmentation process [28]. The DeepLab series of networks concatenates multiscale features by atrous spatial pyramid pooling (ASSP) and can also perform well in corrosion segmentation [29]. Many variations in CNN-series networks have shown practicality in object segmentation in previous academic research [30,31]. 

Deep learning methods are used for model training and dataset building in corrosion segmentation. Among various models, it is generally accepted that better models and larger datasets contribute to a more accurate system with better generalizability. For example, two FCN models were compared to obtain a model with better bridge corrosion location performance. The model was tested on images taken by a UAV [32].
</snippet>
<snippet id=47ab002c-3>
Title: Research on the performance of the SegFormer model with fusion of edge feature extraction for metal corrosion detection
Snippet: To further explore the performance of the proposed model, this paper replicates the segmentation results of four semantic  segmentation models based on the Transformer on the metal surface corrosion dataset and compares them with the proposed model. Table 6 shows that the proposed model is 67.69% mIoU, which is 1.49% higher than that of the baseline SegFormer model and 7.51%, 3.25%, and 2.63% higher than that of UPerNet, SETR, and Segmenter, respectively. FCN and U-Net lose more detail and local information during downsampling and upsampling. Downsampling results in a reduction in image size and spatial resolution, thus ignoring some subtle corrosion features. In the process of upsampling, the lack of detailed information makes the edge and small structure unable to recover, resulting in a decline in the accuracy of the image segmentation results. The feature extraction ability of HRNet model is insufficient, and it is difficult to capture rich details and texture features in the corrosion image, so the segmentation effect is poor. DeepLabv3+ uses hollow convolution to expand the receptive field. However, due to the discontinuity of the receptive field of the hollow convolution, the details and texture features of the corroded region cannot be accurately captured, which limits the improvement of the model accuracy. The UPerNet, SETR, and Segmenter had better segmentation performance than the CNN model, but their number of parameters was tens to hundreds of times higher than that of the proposed model. This increase in the number of parameters leads to a significant increase in computational complexity, as well as a significant increase in memory and computational power requirements for training and reasoning. Nevertheless, the proposed model strikes a balance between performance and efficiency, and can maintain high segmentation accuracy while while maintaining a lightweight architecture, which is suitable for practical application scenarios with limited computing resources. This high efficiency makes the proposed method more practical in resource-constrained environments. 

The inference speed of the above models was evaluated on a single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060 GPU, and the segmentation accuracy and speed of each model on the metal surface corrosion dataset are presented in Table 6.
</snippet>

Title: A multilevel bridge corrosion detection method by transformer-based segmentation in a stitched view
Snippet: The model was tested on images taken by a UAV [32]. U-Net, as a more accurate model, was utilized in corrosion defect inspection with different backbones [33][34][35][36][37]. 

However, backbone design has been an active area in semantic segmentation development, similar to image classification. Many segmentation frameworks are variants of popular architectures for image classification on ImageNet because segmentation is related to classification, which predicts image categories of images [38]. Optimized single-stage detection methods integrate the two steps of feature extraction and object detection, effectively reducing redundant computations and significantly improving the speed of detection. Title: Deep learning-based corrosion inspection of long-span bridges with BIM integration
Snippet: In this study, we construct a method for automatic corrosion damage detection using Semantic segmentation. Semantic segmentation is a technique to extract object regions at a pixel level from an image, and due to recent advancements in deep learning technology, it is now possible to extract regions with high accuracy. One of the early semantic segmentation methods using deep learning is the Fully Convolutional Network (FCN) [12], based on the image analysis method, Convolutional Neural Network (CNN). CNN is generally used as a classification model, in which case a fully connected layer is provided in the final layer. However, in semantic segmentation, the feature map extracted from the input image by convolution is output without using a fully connected layer in the final layer. This feature map becomes an image that indicates the probability of classification classes at each pixel. Furthermore, FCN integrates the feature maps output in the intermediate layers at the final layer, and it can output not only the feature map of the final layer but also more detailed region extraction results. As a more accurate segmentation method, Mask R-CNN [13], based on Faster R-CNN [14], has been proposed. Faster R-CNN detects object regions from the input image using CNN and classifies those objects. While it is generally possible to detect corrosion using such an object detection algorithm, pixel-level segmentation along the shape of corrosion is necessary to accurately identify the area of corrosion and evaluate its size. Mask R-CNN achieves high-accuracy segmentation by extracting regions from parts of the object regions detected by Faster R-CNN. In this study, we perform extraction of corrosion areas based on Mask R-CNN. However, segmentation methods using CNN tend to have low extraction accuracy at the Fig. 2.
