Title: Pixel-level Corrosion Detection on Metal Constructions by Fusion of Deep Learning Semantic and Contour Segmentation
Snippet: Corrosion detection on metal constructions is a major challenge in civil engineering for quick, safe and effective inspection. Existing image analysis approaches tend to place bounding boxes around the defected region which is not adequate both for structural analysis and pre-fabrication, an innovative construction concept which reduces maintenance cost, time and improves safety. In this paper, we apply three semantic segmentation-oriented deep learning models (FCN, U-Net and Mask R-CNN) for corrosion detection, which perform better in terms of accuracy and time and require a smaller number of annotated samples compared to other deep models, e.g. CNN. However, the final images derived are still not sufficiently accurate for structural analysis and pre-fabrication. Thus, we adopt a novel data projection scheme that fuses the results of color segmentation, yielding accurate but over-segmented contours of a region, with a processed area of the deep masks, resulting in high-confidence corroded pixels.
</snippet>

Title: RustSEG - Automated segmentation of corrosion using deep learning
Snippet: The inspection of infrastructure for corrosion remains a task that is typically performed manually by qualified engineers or inspectors. This task of inspection is laborious, slow, and often requires complex access. Recently, deep learning based algorithms have revealed promise and performance in the automatic detection of corrosion. However, to date, research regarding the segmentation of images for automated corrosion detection has been limited, due to the lack of availability of per-pixel labelled data sets which are required for model training. Herein, a novel deep learning approach (termed RustSEG) is presented, that can accurately segment images for automated corrosion detection, without the requirement of per-pixel labelled data sets for training. The RustSEG method will first, using deep learning techniques, determine if corrosion is present in an image (i.e. a classification task), and then if corrosion is present, the model will examine what pixels in the original image contributed to that classification decision. Finally, the method can refine its predictions into a pixel-level segmentation mask. In ideal cases, the method is able to generate precise masks of corrosion in images, demonstrating that the automated segmentation of corrosion without per-pixel training data is possible, addressing a significant hurdle in automated infrastructure inspection.
</snippet>

Title: A novel method for intelligent operation and maintenance of transformers using deep visual large model DETR + X and digital twin
Snippet: To achieve real-time monitoring and intelligent maintenance of transformers, a framework based on deep vision and digital twin has been developed. An enhanced visual detection model, DETR + X, is proposed, implementing multidimensional sample data augmentation through Swin2SR and GAN networks. This model converts one-dimensional DGA data into three-dimensional feature images based on Gram angle fields, facilitating the transformation and fusion of heterogeneous modal information. The Pyramid Vision Transformer (PVT) is innovatively adopted as the backbone for image feature extraction, replacing the traditional ResNet structure. A Deformable Attention mechanism is employed to handle the complex spatial structure of multi-scale features. Testing results indicate that the improved DETR + X model performs well in transformer state recognition tasks, achieving a classification accuracy of 100% for DGA feature maps. In object detection tasks, it surpasses advanced models such as Faster R-CNN, RetinaNet, YOLOv8, and Deformable DETR in terms of overall mAP50 scores, particularly demonstrating significant enhancements in small object detection. Furthermore, the Llava-7b model, fine-tuned based on domain expertise, serves as an expert decision-making tool for transformer maintenance, providing accurate operational recommendations based on visual detection results. Finally, based on digital twin and inference models, a comprehensive platform has been developed to achieve real-time monitoring and intelligent maintenance of transformers.
</snippet>

# Overview

Recent work in corrosion (rust) detection in computer vision spans three core tasks—detection, classification, and segmentation—and leverages a range of deep learning techniques from CNNs and classical detectors to transformer-based models and 3D perception, often in UAV/robotic inspection settings with challenging appearance variability and scale/multiview issues.<cite id="47ab002c-1,47ab002c-4">Corrosion varies widely in shape, color, and texture and often requires pixel-level analysis rather than bounding boxes, driving the use of semantic segmentation alongside detection and classification</cite> <cite id="47ab002c-2">UAV imagery is commonly used to capture multi-angle views, and stitched-view segmentation has been proposed to cover larger bridge surfaces while retaining resolution</cite>.

# Detection (Object Detection)

State-of-the-art detection for corrosion employs two-stage and one-stage architectures tailored for speed, accuracy, and deployment:

- Two-stage detectors: Faster R-CNN with strong backbones (e.g., ResNet-101) has achieved high accuracy for rust on transmission line fittings (>97%) and metal corrosion recognition, but suffers from complexity and latency unsuitable for embedded platforms.<cite id="30175470-0">Faster R-CNN with ResNet-101 achieved >97% detection accuracy for rust on transmission line fittings, while a Faster R-CNN with color-feature support achieved high accuracy and recall on metal corrosion; however, two-stage detectors have poor real-time performance and high hardware demands</cite>

- One-stage detectors: Optimized SSD and YOLO variants are favored for real-time inspection. Examples include enhanced SSD-Mobilenet for aircraft corrosion and YOLO-based pipelines for aircraft surface defect detection, with reports of effective detection of corrosion and cracks.<cite id="30175470-0">Optimized single-stage detectors (SSD, YOLO) reduce redundant computation and improve speed; enhanced SSD-Mobilenet detected aircraft defects caused by corrosion and cracks, and YOLO-based models have been used to identify corrosion on aircraft surfaces</cite> <cite id="30175470-2">Prior CNN-based detectors (e.g., Faster R-CNN, YOLO) achieved satisfying results but are unsuitable for MAV on-board platforms due to large model sizes from standard convolutions</cite>

- Transformer-based detectors and hybrids: End-to-end transformer detectors (DETR and its variants) with efficient attention and strong backbones (Swin/PVT) are being adopted for infrastructure inspection and related anomaly detection, showing improved accuracy and especially small-object performance. Deformable DETR and DETR+X backbones have been reported to outperform Faster R-CNN, YOLO, and baseline DETR, with applications to power transformer state recognition and detection on heterogeneous data.<cite id="388a35b8-0">A DETR+X framework with Swin2SR/GAN data augmentation, PVT backbone, and deformable attention outperformed Faster R-CNN, RetinaNet, YOLOv8, and Deformable DETR in mAP50, with notable gains in small-object detection, and achieved 100% accuracy on DGA feature maps for transformer maintenance</cite> <cite id="388a35b8-2">Deformable DETR improves DETR by focusing attention on key sampling points, addressing slow convergence and achieving strong COCO results; Swin Transformer’s shifted window design efficiently handles high-resolution imagery and achieves excellent detection on COCO</cite> 

- Instance segmentation: Mask R-CNN provides pixel-accurate masks over Faster R-CNN proposals and is used when precise corrosion area measurement is required, with strategies to reduce computation (adaptive grids) and to fuse semantic masks with contour segmentation for higher confidence at boundaries.<cite id="30175470-1">Mask R-CNN achieves high-accuracy instance segmentation by refining object proposals from Faster R-CNN for corrosion areas; boundary accuracy can be improved by adaptive subdivision and grid-based prediction</cite> <cite id="30175470-3">A fusion of deep semantic segmentation (FCN/UNet/Mask R-CNN) with color-based contour segmentation yields high-confidence corroded pixels for pixel-level analysis</cite>

# Classification (Recognition and Grading)

Classification ranges from coarse presence/absence to fine-grained stage/level labeling, often trained with transfer learning and data augmentation:

- CNN-based classification and multi-level grading: Fine-tuned CNNs with sliding window or multi-parallel branches have been used for corrosion level classification; studies also train CNNs with data augmentation and side-output layers to distinguish multiple corrosion levels and report improved performance over PSPNet, DeepLab, and SegNet in cross-validation.<cite id="30175470-2">A fine-tuned CNN with sliding window classified corrosion presence and position; a two-parallel CNN was proposed for corrosion level classification</cite> <cite id="47ab002c-4">U-Net and DeepLab variants have been widely used in corrosion segmentation with attention to backbone design and multiscale feature integration</cite> <cite id="47ab002c-4">A study trained a segmentation network based on SegFormer and compared against U-Net and DeepLabV3+, highlighting backbone choices and attention mechanisms</cite> <cite id="47ab002c-0">A multilevel classification framework segmented and classified rust regions into good, fair, poor, and severe states</cite> <cite id="47ab002c-4">A deep CNN with batch normalization, side-output layers, and loss engineering distinguished four corrosion levels and outperformed PSPNet, DeepLab, and SegNet under cross-validation</cite>

- Practical constraints for deployment: Real-time onboard classification/detection on MAVs requires lightweight backbones (e.g., MobileNet/Swish) and reduced convolution counts to manage model size and latency, as heavier two-stage or standard CNN pipelines are impractical for embedded platforms.<cite id="30175470-2">Standard convolution-heavy networks yield large models unsuitable for MAVs; lightweight CNNs and optimized pipelines are needed for onboard real-time inspection</cite>

# Segmentation (Semantic and Instance)

Transformer-based and CNN-based encoders are both prevalent, with clear trends and trade-offs:

- CNN-based segmentation: U-Net and DeepLab families remain strong baselines for corrosion segmentation, with U-Net variants effective at small-area detection but limited for multiscale patterns; DeepLab’s atrous convolutions expand receptive fields while maintaining resolution.<cite id="47ab002c-1">U-Net variants effectively identify small-scale corroded areas but struggle with multiscale tasks; DeepLab uses atrous spatial pyramid pooling and atrous convolutions to maintain resolution and large receptive fields</cite> <cite id="47ab002c-2">U-Net’s contracting/expanding path captures context and precise locations, while DeepLabv3+ performs well in corrosion segmentation via multiscale feature concatenation</cite>

- Transformer-based segmentation: Vision transformers and lightweight transformer backbones (e.g., SegFormer, PVT) have surpassed CNN baselines on corrosion segmentation in recent reports, with active research on efficiency and high-resolution handling. SegFormer and related transformer segmenters improved mIoU over U-Net/DeepLab while offering lower parameter counts than heavier alternatives, though computational complexity can be higher than compact CNNs.<cite id="47ab002c-0">Transformer-based methods have surpassed U-Net/DeepLab for corrosion segmentation in recent work</cite> <cite id="47ab002c-4">SegFormer was adopted for corrosion segmentation and compared to U-Net and DeepLabV3+, motivated by transformer advances and attention mechanisms</cite> <cite id="47ab002c-3">On a metal corrosion dataset, a SegFormer-based variant achieved 67.69% mIoU, 1.49% higher than baseline SegFormer and 3–7.51% higher than UPerNet, SETR, and Segmenter, but heavier CNNs (UPerNet, SETR, Segmenter) had tens to hundreds of times more parameters with higher computational/memory costs; the proposed SegFormer variant balanced performance and efficiency for practical deployment</cite>

- Self-/weakly-supervised and label-free segmentation: To address the scarcity of pixel-labeled datasets, RustSEG proposes a two-stage label-free approach that first classifies corrosion presence and then explains the decision at the pixel level to produce masks, demonstrating per-pixel segmentation on unseen images without per-pixel supervision; limitations include sensitivity to shadows and the need for standardized benchmarks.<cite id="2bfd42ba-2">RustSEG performs corrosion presence classification, then attributes contributions to image pixels and refines into pixel-level masks without per-pixel training labels, enabling automated corrosion detection</cite> <cite id="2bfd42ba-4">RustSEG generated per-pixel masks from unseen images without per-pixel training data but was impacted by shadows and image defects; lack of open corrosion segmentation datasets hinders broad evaluation</cite> <cite id="2bfd42ba-0">RustSEG highlights the need for a standard small-scale comparison benchmark for corrosion segmentation to enable like-for-like evaluation</cite>

- Multi-level and condition-based segmentation: Segmenters are increasingly trained to output multiple condition states (e.g., good, fair, poor, severe) to support grading and prioritization in bridge and infrastructure inspections, often combined with image stitching for larger view coverage without sacrificing resolution.<cite id="47ab002c-1">A multilevel classification and segmentation pipeline evaluated corrosion into multiple condition states and used image stitching to segment larger bridge views while maintaining resolution</cite> <cite id="47ab002c-2">Accurate identification in larger views aids engineers in locating corrosion, and image stitching reduces the need for wide-view recording equipment</cite>

# 3D Perception, Multi-view, and Thermal Imagery

Corrosion monitoring is increasingly integrated with 3D sensing and multi-view fusion:

- 3D/point-cloud and BEV detection: Transformer backbones for point clouds (e.g., Pointformer) and BEV fusion methods (e.g., LSS-based and transformer-based multi-view pipelines) are being adapted from autonomous driving to infrastructure inspection, improving robustness to occlusion and scale by leveraging 3D context and attention mechanisms.<cite id="388a35b8-2">A Pointformer backbone for 3D point clouds effectively learns features and improves detection performance</cite> <cite id="388a35b8-4">LSS-based and transformer-based multi-view 3D detectors convert multi-view images to BEV features for 3D object detection; DETR variants (Deformable DETR, DINO) have been improved for efficiency and matching</cite>

- Thermal-based detection: While not specific to corrosion, thermal object detection pipelines using transformer detectors (e.g., RT-DETR) and YOLO variants show strong performance on thermal anomaly detection in related industrial settings, suggesting applicability to thermal signatures of corrosion and defects where visible light is insufficient.<cite id="388a35b8-1">YOLOv8 achieved 96.0% mAP, 90.8% precision, and 89.9% recall on thermal liquid leak detection; RT-DETR provided slightly lower metrics but leveraged transformer attention to capture subtle thermal variations</cite>

# Training Paradigms and Datasets

- Data scarcity and augmentation: High-quality pixel-labeled datasets are scarce; researchers augment corrosion datasets with scaling, flipping, blurring, rotation, and color distortion to improve generalization and reduce overfitting, and propose pipelines that work with limited labels (e.g., semi-supervised/label-explaining transformers).<cite id="2bfd42ba-0">A standard benchmark for corrosion segmentation is lacking despite the promise of transformer-based methods</cite> <cite id="2bfd42ba-3">Augmentations including random scaling/cropping, flipping, Gaussian blur, rotation, and color distortion improved pipeline generalization and reduced overfitting for pipe corrosion segmentation</cite>

- Efficient and lightweight design: Studies emphasize balancing accuracy with parameter count and inference speed to enable deployment on drones/robots; compact backbones (e.g., PVT/MobileNet-like) and efficient attention (e.g., deformable attention) are favored to keep models practical for embedded platforms.<cite id="388a35b8-0">A DETR+X model with PVT and deformable attention improved transformer-based detection efficiency for infrastructure monitoring</cite> <cite id="30175470-2">Standard convolution-heavy networks are unsuitable for MAVs; optimized lightweight CNNs and reduced convolutions are needed for on-board platforms</cite>

# Application Contexts and Practical Workflows

- Bridge and civil infrastructure: Large-scale inspection often requires stitching multi-image mosaics to cover span lengths while preserving resolution, with segmentation models trained on UAV imagery and evaluated for multilevel grading to support maintenance prioritization.<cite id="47ab002c-1">Image stitching with SegFormer-based segmentation enabled multilevel corrosion classification (good, fair, poor, severe) over larger bridge views without specialized wide-angle equipment</cite> <cite id="47ab002c-2">UAV-acquired images are central for corrosion monitoring, and pixel-level segmentation is needed to measure corrosion area and size accurately</cite>

- Power infrastructure and transformers: Transformer-focused pipelines combine vision transformers, digital twins, and DGA (degassing) analytics with attention mechanisms for state recognition and anomaly detection, showing that DETR-like detectors with strong backbones outperform traditional detectors on small features relevant to internal degradation indicators.<cite id="388a35b8-0">DETR+X achieved 100% accuracy on DGA feature maps and surpassed YOLOv8/Deformable DETR in mAP50 with improved small-object detection for transformer state recognition</cite>

- Aerospace and industrial components: Embedded detection/classification for aircraft and power lines uses optimized one-stage detectors and Faster R-CNN with specialized backbones; these systems must meet real-time constraints and robustness to varied corrosion morphologies.<cite id="30175470-0">Faster R-CNN with ResNet-101 achieved high accuracy for rust on transmission fittings, while YOLO variants have been used for aircraft surface corrosion detection</cite> <cite id="30175470-2">Prior CNN-based pipelines for aircraft corrosion detection highlight the need for lightweight architectures for onboard platforms</cite>

# Emerging Directions and Open Challenges

- Multimodal fusion and explainability: Hybrid pipelines combine semantic segmentation masks with color/contour segmentations to improve boundary accuracy and confidence of corroded pixels, reflecting a trend toward multi-hypothesis fusion for robust pixel-level grading.<cite id="30175470-3">Fusing deep semantic masks (FCN/UNet/Mask R-CNN) with color-based contour segmentation produced high-confidence corroded pixels for structural analysis</cite>

- Standardization and benchmarks: Despite advances, there is a call for standardized small-scale benchmark datasets to enable fair comparison across segmentation methods, as current evaluation is often limited to ad hoc datasets and qualitative analyses.<cite id="2bfd42ba-0">Standard high-performing segmentation methods lack comparable public benchmarks for corrosion; a small (~50–100 image) test set would aid evaluation</cite> <cite id="2bfd42ba-4">RustSEG’s label-free approach was evaluated qualitatively due to dataset scarcity and sensitivity to shadows, underscoring benchmark gaps</cite>

- Efficiency and scalability: Transformer-based models improve accuracy but increase compute and memory demands; recent work emphasizes efficient backbones (Swin/PVT), deformable attention, and model compression to maintain real-time performance for UAV/MAV and embedded systems.<cite id="47ab002c-3">Heavier transformer/segmentation variants (UPerNet, SETR) offer higher accuracy but with much higher parameter counts and computational/memory costs; efficient SegFormer variants balance performance and practicality</cite> <cite id="388a35b8-2">Deformable DETR and Swin Transformer address efficiency and slow convergence while maintaining strong detection performance</cite>

# Summary of Techniques and Models in Use

- CNN-based segmentation/backbones (U-Net, DeepLab, FCN, SegNet) remain strong baselines for corrosion maps and defect regions, with attention to multiscale context and boundary handling.<cite id="47ab002c-1">U-Net and DeepLab series dominate corrosion segmentation; U-Net excels at small-scale detection but struggles with multiscale patterns; DeepLab’s atrous convolutions maintain resolution and field-of-view</cite> <cite id="47ab002c-2">U-Net/DeepLab series are mainstream and widely evaluated for corrosion segmentation with encoder–decoder fusion and atrous pyramid pooling</cite>

- Transformer-based models (SegFormer, RustSEG, DETR/Deformable DETR, PVT/Swin) improve segmentation and detection accuracy, including small-object detection, by leveraging attention and stronger feature pyramids, with active work on efficiency for deployment.<cite id="47ab002c-0">Transformer-based segmentation surpasses U-Net/DeepLab for rust region detection and multi-level classification</cite> <cite id="47ab002c-3">SegFormer-based methods can outperform baselines in mIoU while managing parameter/compute trade-offs</cite> <cite id="388a35b8-0">DETR+X with PVT and deformable attention outperforms Faster R-CNN/YOLO variants in transformer-based detection tasks</cite> <cite id="388a35b8-2">Deformable DETR and Swin Transformer improve efficiency and accuracy for detection tasks</cite>

- Object detectors for corrosion include optimized one-stage (YOLO/SSD) for real-time, two-stage (Faster R-CNN) for high accuracy, and instance segmenters (Mask R-CNN) for precise masks, with trends toward transformer detectors (DETR variants) and efficient backbones for small features.<cite id="30175470-0">YOLO/SSD and Faster R-CNN variants are used for corrosion detection, with two-stage models offering high accuracy but poor real-time performance</cite> <cite id="30175470-1">Mask R-CNN provides pixel-accurate instance masks over Faster R-CNN proposals for corrosion area measurement</cite> <cite id="388a35b8-0">Transformer-based detectors with deformable attention and strong backbones improve small-object detection and overall mAP50</cite>

- Self-/weakly-supervised and label-explaining pipelines (e.g., RustSEG) address labeling scarcity by deriving masks from classification decisions, while data augmentation strategies bolster generalization in limited-label regimes.<cite id="2bfd42ba-2">RustSEG performs label-free pixel-level segmentation by explaining the corrosion presence decision with a mask</cite> <cite id="2bfd42ba-3">Data augmentation (scaling, flipping, blur, rotation, color distortion) reduces overfitting and increases diversity for pipe corrosion segmentation</cite>

- 3D/BEV and multi-view fusion, along with thermal imaging, are emerging modalities for robust corrosion detection, drawing on transformer-based point cloud and image fusion backbones to handle occlusion, scale, and complex geometry.<cite id="388a35b8-4">Transformer-based and LSS-based multi-view BEV detectors convert multi-view images to 3D BEV features for robust detection</cite> <cite id="388a35b8-1">Transformer-based and YOLO-based detectors achieved high mAP and precision/recall on thermal anomaly detection, suggesting potential for thermal corrosion monitoring</cite>

# Practical Recommendations

- For pixel-level grading on large structures, adopt transformer segmentation (SegFormer/PVT variants) with image stitching to cover wide spans, and add contour/color fusion to sharpen boundaries for measurement-grade masks.<cite id="47ab002c-1">SegFormer-based segmentation with image stitching supports multilevel grading over large bridge surfaces</cite> <cite id="30175470-3">Fusing semantic masks with contour segmentation improves boundary confidence and structural analysis readiness</cite>

- For real-time onboard inspection, use optimized one-stage detectors or lightweight transformer detectors with efficient backbones and attention (e.g., Deformable DETR/Swin/PVT) to balance latency and accuracy for UAV/MAV platforms.<cite id="30175470-2">Heavier convolution-heavy models are impractical for MAVs; optimized lightweight architectures are required</cite> <cite id="388a35b8-0">DETR+X with PVT and deformable attention improves detection efficiency for infrastructure monitoring</cite>

- Address data scarcity via semi-supervised/label-explaining transformers (e.g., RustSEG) and comprehensive augmentation; advocate for community benchmarks to enable fair, quantitative comparisons across methods and hardware.<cite id="2bfd42ba-0">A standardized corrosion segmentation benchmark would enable like-for-like comparisons and broader evaluation</cite> <cite id="2bfd42ba-4">RustSEG’s label-free segmentation highlights both promise and sensitivity to shadows, emphasizing the need for robust datasets</cite>

Title: A multilevel bridge corrosion detection method by transformer-based segmentation in a stitched view
Snippet: In recent years, many deep learning-based semantic segmentation methods have been proposed for detecting steel corrosion. Among those methods, the U-Net and DeepLab series are dominant in the corrosion segmentation field. However, the transformer-based method has been shown to surpass them in performance [38]. The architectures of the segmentation network are described in the following sections, and the training details are introduced. The evaluation metrics used in the experiment are presented.

Title: A multilevel bridge corrosion detection method by transformer-based segmentation in a stitched view
Snippet: Deep learning models have been widely used in semantic segmentation tasks for corrosion detection. However, these models have limitations, such as accuracy when dealing with complex corrosion patterns, and fixed receptive field for global contextual information. The performance of different U-Net variants in the steel structure corrosion detection task has been evaluated, demonstrating the effectiveness of the CNN-based model in identifying small-scale corroded areas, but pointing out its limitations in dealing with multiscale tasks [47]. A Transformer-based segmentation model, RustSeg, was proposed for multi-level rust region detection and classification, but there are still challenges in computational efficiency and high-resolution image processing [48]. 

Obtaining images on the surface of large structures is difficult, and the monitoring performance needs to be improved [49]. The constraints of single-image inspections were addressed, and UAVs have been used to capture images from different angles [50][51][52]. Section segmentation has been used in marine defect detection, which shows better performance in larger view [53]. However, after successfully building a dataset and training model, little previous research has considered how to expand the segmentation view for corrosion detection on bridge surfaces. Image capturing is a balance of distance and view size. The image view is always fixed when the distance and recording equipment do not change substantially [54][55][56]. Accurate identification in a larger view helps engineers detect and locate corrosion. In this research, image stitching was utilized for segmentation to determine the corrosion location and evaluate it from a larger view while maintaining the resolution of the input. This image processing method reduces the need for expensive wide-view recording equipment, thereby lowering monitoring costs. 

This study proposes a corrosion localization and evaluation architecture for a larger view based on semantic segmentation and image stitching, which gives multilevel classification and segmentation of corrosion into multiple condition states, such as good, fair, poor, and severe. The method includes a) training a semantic segmentation network based on SegFormer and b) feature point matching, calculating the transformation matrix and image stitching.

Title: A multilevel bridge corrosion detection method by transformer-based segmentation in a stitched view
Snippet: However, corrosion detection is challenging because it has variable color and texture properties and does not have uniform characteristics as do cracks [24]. Due to the randomness of its shape and size, it is not sufficient to label corrosion in bounding boxes, as in the YOLO series [25]. The detection task should be performed not only on regions but also on every image pixel. Semantic segmentation, discussed in the following paragraph, is a better method for classifying and grading corrosion pixel by pixel. 

Semantic segmentation subdivides a digital image into image subregions, simplifies the representation, and makes it easier to understand every image pixel [26]. Semantic segmentation has attracted increased attention in image processing. Some classic and mainstream deep learning-based methods have shown potential and become basic segmentation ideas. For example, the fully convolutional network (FCN) changes the output layer of a traditional CNN from fully connected layers to convolutional layers and uses them as a pixel-level output to classify each pixel [27]. Unlike FCNs, U-Nets are classical U-shaped fully convolutional neural networks containing a contracting path to capture context information and a symmetric expanding path to obtain precise locations. Another mainstream method is DeepLabv3 + , which uses atrous convolution to decrease the downsampling rate while maintaining the receptive field size. Through the encoder-decoder structure, the U-Net series of networks performs data fusion of multiscale dimensions and shows good results in the corrosion segmentation process [28]. The DeepLab series of networks concatenates multiscale features by atrous spatial pyramid pooling (ASSP) and can also perform well in corrosion segmentation [29]. Many variations in CNN-series networks have shown practicality in object segmentation in previous academic research [30,31]. 

Deep learning methods are used for model training and dataset building in corrosion segmentation. Among various models, it is generally accepted that better models and larger datasets contribute to a more accurate system with better generalizability. For example, two FCN models were compared to obtain a model with better bridge corrosion location performance. The model was tested on images taken by a UAV [32].

Title: Research on the performance of the SegFormer model with fusion of edge feature extraction for metal corrosion detection
Snippet: To further explore the performance of the proposed model, this paper replicates the segmentation results of four semantic  segmentation models based on the Transformer on the metal surface corrosion dataset and compares them with the proposed model. Table 6 shows that the proposed model is 67.69% mIoU, which is 1.49% higher than that of the baseline SegFormer model and 7.51%, 3.25%, and 2.63% higher than that of UPerNet, SETR, and Segmenter, respectively. FCN and U-Net lose more detail and local information during downsampling and upsampling. Downsampling results in a reduction in image size and spatial resolution, thus ignoring some subtle corrosion features. In the process of upsampling, the lack of detailed information makes the edge and small structure unable to recover, resulting in a decline in the accuracy of the image segmentation results. The feature extraction ability of HRNet model is insufficient, and it is difficult to capture rich details and texture features in the corrosion image, so the segmentation effect is poor. DeepLabv3+ uses hollow convolution to expand the receptive field. However, due to the discontinuity of the receptive field of the hollow convolution, the details and texture features of the corroded region cannot be accurately captured, which limits the improvement of the model accuracy. The UPerNet, SETR, and Segmenter had better segmentation performance than the CNN model, but their number of parameters was tens to hundreds of times higher than that of the proposed model. This increase in the number of parameters leads to a significant increase in computational complexity, as well as a significant increase in memory and computational power requirements for training and reasoning. Nevertheless, the proposed model strikes a balance between performance and efficiency, and can maintain high segmentation accuracy while while maintaining a lightweight architecture, which is suitable for practical application scenarios with limited computing resources. This high efficiency makes the proposed method more practical in resource-constrained environments. 

The inference speed of the above models was evaluated on a single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060 GPU, and the segmentation accuracy and speed of each model on the metal surface corrosion dataset are presented in Table 6.

Title: A multilevel bridge corrosion detection method by transformer-based segmentation in a stitched view
Snippet: The model was tested on images taken by a UAV [32]. U-Net, as a more accurate model, was utilized in corrosion defect inspection with different backbones [33][34][35][36][37]. 

However, backbone design has been an active area in semantic segmentation development, similar to image classification. Many segmentation frameworks are variants of popular architectures for image classification on ImageNet because segmentation is related to classification, which predicts image categories of images [38]. The backbone has been developed and chosen from VGG [39], ResNet [40], 

and other new backbones [41][42][43]. Regarding semantic segmentation, designing modules and operators is another key issue in developing a better model for capturing contextual information. 

Transformers, the mainstream natural language processing (NLP) method, have shown excellent performance in the CV field. After Google proposed the vision transformer for image classification, it achieved powerful scalable performance [44]. Transformer-based algorithms comprehensively outperform CNN-series networks and occupy the top place in the CV ranking [45]. In the previous section, it was highlighted that previous work in image segmentation has predominantly focused on improving the backbone architecture, such as using deeper convolutional neural networks (CNNs) or more advanced architectures such as ResNet [40], VGG [39], or EfficientNet [46]. Backbone networks play a vital role in feature extraction but represent only a portion of the segmentation process. The framework components, such as attention mechanisms, positional encodings, and multiscale feature integration, are equally crucial, especially within transformer-based models. These elements collectively enhance the model performance, highlighting the complexity and interdependence of the segmentation pipeline components. These components play a significant role in improving the overall segmentation performance. In this research, inspired by transformer-based segmentation algorithms, we intend to use SegFormer [38] for corrosion segmentation and compare it with the mainstream segmentation networks U-Net [28] and DeepLabV3+ [29]. 

Deep learning models have been widely used in semantic segmentation tasks for corrosion detection.

Section segmentation has been used in marine defect detection, which shows better performance in larger view [53]. However, after successfully building a dataset and training model, little previous research has considered how to expand the segmentation view for corrosion detection on bridge surfaces. Image capturing is a balance of distance and view size. The image view is always fixed when the distance and recording equipment do not change substantially [54][55][56]. Accurate identification in a larger view helps engineers detect and locate corrosion. In this research, image stitching was utilized for segmentation to determine the corrosion location and evaluate it from a larger view while maintaining the resolution of the input. This image processing method reduces the need for expensive wide-view recording equipment, thereby lowering monitoring costs. 

This study proposes a corrosion localization and evaluation architecture for a larger view based on semantic segmentation and image stitching, which gives multilevel classification and segmentation of corrosion into multiple condition states, such as good, fair, poor, and severe. The method includes a) training a semantic segmentation network based on SegFormer and b) feature point matching, calculating the transformation matrix and image stitching.

documents.snippet:
However, corrosion detection is challenging because it has variable color and texture properties and does not have uniform characteristics as do cracks [24]. Due to the randomness of its shape and size, it is not sufficient to label corrosion in bounding boxes, as in the YOLO series [25]. The detection task should be performed not only on regions but also on every image pixel. Semantic segmentation, discussed in the following paragraph, is a better method for classifying and grading corrosion pixel by pixel. 

Semantic segmentation subdivides a digital image into image subregions, simplifies the representation, and makes it easier to understand every image pixel [26]. Semantic segmentation has attracted increased attention in image processing. Some classic and mainstream deep learning-based methods have shown potential and become basic segmentation ideas. For example, the fully convolutional network (FCN) changes the output layer of a traditional CNN from fully connected layers to convolutional layers and uses them as a pixel-level output to classify each pixel [27]. Unlike FCNs, U-Nets are classical U-shaped fully convolutional neural networks containing a contracting path to capture context information and a symmetric expanding path to obtain precise locations. Another mainstream method is DeepLabv3 + , which uses atrous convolution to decrease the downsampling rate while maintaining the receptive field size. Through the encoder-decoder structure, the U-Net series of networks performs data fusion of multiscale dimensions and shows good results in the corrosion segmentation process [28]. The DeepLab series of networks concatenates multiscale features by atrous spatial pyramid pooling (ASSP) and can also perform well in corrosion segmentation [29]. Many variations in CNN-series networks have shown practicality in object segmentation in previous academic research [30,31]. 

Deep learning methods are used for model training and dataset building in corrosion segmentation. Among various models, it is generally accepted that better models and larger datasets contribute to a more accurate system with better generalizability. For example, two FCN models were compared to obtain a model with better bridge corrosion location performance. The model was tested on images taken by a UAV [32].

documents.snippet:
To further explore the performance of the proposed model, this paper replicates the segmentation results of four semantic  segmentation models based on the Transformer on the metal surface corrosion dataset and compares them with the proposed model. Table 6 shows that the proposed model is 67.69% mIoU, which is 1.49% higher than that of the baseline SegFormer model and 7.51%, 3.25%, and 2.63% higher than that of UPerNet, SETR, and Segmenter, respectively. FCN and U-Net lose more detail and local information during downsampling and upsampling. Downsampling results in a reduction in image size and spatial resolution, thus ignoring some subtle corrosion features. In the process of upsampling, the lack of detailed information makes the edge and small structure unable to recover, resulting in a decline in the accuracy of the image segmentation results. The feature extraction ability of HRNet model is insufficient, and it is difficult to capture rich details and texture features in the corrosion image, so the segmentation effect is poor. DeepLabv3+ uses hollow convolution to expand the receptive field. However, due to the discontinuity of the receptive field of the hollow convolution, the details and texture features of the corroded region cannot be accurately captured, which limits the improvement of the model accuracy. The UPerNet, SETR, and Segmenter had better segmentation performance than the CNN model, but their number of parameters was tens to hundreds of times higher than that of the proposed model. This increase in the number of parameters leads to a significant increase in computational complexity, as well as a significant increase in memory and computational power requirements for training and reasoning. Nevertheless, the proposed model strikes a balance between performance and efficiency, and can maintain high segmentation accuracy while while maintaining a lightweight architecture, which is suitable for practical application scenarios with limited computing resources. This high efficiency makes the proposed method more practical in resource-constrained environments. 

The inference speed of the above models was evaluated on a single NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060 GPU, and the segmentation accuracy and speed of each model on the metal surface corrosion dataset are presented in Table 6.

The model was tested on images taken by a UAV [32]. U-Net, as a more accurate model, was utilized in corrosion defect inspection with different backbones [33][34][35][36][37]. 

However, backbone design has been an active area in semantic segmentation development, similar to image classification. Many segmentation frameworks are variants of popular architectures for image classification on ImageNet because segmentation is related to classification, which predicts image categories of images [38]. The backbone has been developed and chosen from VGG [39], ResNet [40], 

and other new backbones [41][42][43]. Regarding semantic segmentation, designing modules and operators is another key issue in developing a better model for capturing contextual information. 

Transformers, the mainstream natural language processing (NLP) method, have shown excellent performance in the CV field. After Google proposed the vision transformer for image classification, it achieved powerful scalable performance [44]. Transformer-based algorithms comprehensively outperform CNN-series networks and occupy the top place in the CV ranking [45]. In the previous section, it was highlighted that previous work in image segmentation has predominantly focused on improving the backbone architecture, such as using deeper convolutional neural networks (CNNs) or more advanced architectures such as ResNet [40], VGG [39], or EfficientNet [46]. Backbone networks play a vital role in feature extraction but represent only a portion of the segmentation process. The framework components, such as attention mechanisms, positional encodings, and multiscale feature integration, are equally crucial, especially within transformer-based models. These elements collectively enhance the model performance, highlighting the complexity and interdependence of the segmentation pipeline components. These components play a significant role in improving the overall segmentation performance. In this research, inspired by transformer-based segmentation algorithms, we intend to use SegFormer [38] for corrosion segmentation and compare it with the mainstream segmentation networks U-Net [28] and DeepLabV3+ [29]. 

Deep learning models have been widely used in semantic segmentation tasks for corrosion detection.

Title: Detection and recognition of metal surface corrosion based on CBG-YOLOv5s
Snippet: Two-stage algorithms divide feature extraction and object detection into two steps, mainly represented by Regionbased Convolutional Neural Network (R-CNN) [16], Faster R-CNN [17] and Fast R-CNN [18]. For example, Guo et al [19] proposed a Faster R-CNN model with a feature enhancement mechanism. This model used the ResNet-101 residual network as the backbone network and implemented a feature enhancement mechanism after the Region of Interest (ROI) pooling layer to achieve the goal of detecting rust on transmission line fittings, achieving a detection accuracy of more than 97%. Additionally, Tian et al [20] proposed a metal corrosion recognition algorithm based on Faster R-CNN and rust HIS colour features. This algorithm converted the corrosion image into a HIS colour model to determine and annotate the corrosion pixels. The Faster R-CNN model was then used to locate and detect the annotated corrosion areas, achieving high accuracy and recall rates. However, due to the complex network structure of the two-stage object detection models, poor real time performance and the size of the models with high hardware demands, these models are not suitable for subsequent deployment on embedded development platforms. 

Optimized single-stage detection methods integrate the two steps of feature extraction and object detection, effectively reducing redundant computations and significantly improving the speed of detection. SSD [21] and the YOLO series are the most representative methods in this field. For example, Ramalingam et al. [22] proposed an enhanced SSD MobileNet framework, which includes a periodic pattern detection filter based on self-filtering, used to detect surface defects on aircraft caused by corrosion and cracks. Mukhiddinov et al. [23] proposed a multiclass fruit and vegetable classification system based on an improved YOLOv4 model, which divided the recognised fruit types into fresh or rotten categories. Deyin et al. [24] proposed an aircraft surface defect detection model based on the YOLO network, used to automatically identify corrosion and various defects on the aircraft surface. Matthaiou et al. [25] achieved good results by training SSD using transfer learning technology to detect corrosion objects.

Snippet: In this study, we construct a method for automatic corrosion damage detection using Semantic segmentation. Semantic segmentation is a technique to extract object regions at a pixel level from an image, and due to recent advancements in deep learning technology, it is now possible to extract regions with high accuracy. One of the early semantic segmentation methods using deep learning is the Fully Convolutional Network (FCN) [12], based on the image analysis method, Convolutional Neural Network (CNN). CNN is generally used as a classification model, in which case a fully connected layer is provided in the final layer. However, in semantic segmentation, the feature map extracted from the input image by convolution is output without using a fully connected layer in the final layer. This feature map becomes an image that indicates the probability of classification classes at each pixel. Furthermore, FCN integrates the feature maps output in the intermediate layers at the final layer, and it can output not only the feature map of the final layer but also more detailed region extraction results. As a more accurate segmentation method, Mask R-CNN [13], based on Faster R-CNN [14], has been proposed. Faster R-CNN detects object regions from the input image using CNN and classifies those objects. While it is generally possible to detect corrosion using such an object detection algorithm, pixel-level segmentation along the shape of corrosion is necessary to accurately identify the area of corrosion and evaluate its size. Mask R-CNN achieves high-accuracy segmentation by extracting regions from parts of the object regions detected by Faster R-CNN. Title: AMCD: an accurate deep learning-based metallic corrosion detector for MAV-based real-time visual inspection
Snippet: For CNN-based approaches, it is simple to determine the features autonomously, which is able to avoid the requirement of prior information. Several studies on high-accuracy corrosion detection with CNNs have already been proposed recently. Atha and Jahanshahi (2018) finetuned a CNN network to classify and identify the corrosion position through the sliding window technique. Based on corrosion levels, Du et al. (2018) proposed a two parallel CNN architecture to classify corrosions. Apart from aforementioned approaches, there are also some other works that adopted CNN-based object detection approaches to locate corrosions. Faster RCNN was trained by 1737 images to detect the steel corrosion and bolt corrosion in Cha et al. (2018). Li et al. (2018) modified the You Only Look Once (Yolo) architecture to all convolutional layers to detect corrosions of flat steel. These works achieved satisfying corrosion classification or detection results in their scenarios. However, they only focus on image processing without consideration of MAVbased applications. Title: Pixel-level Corrosion Detection on Metal Constructions by Fusion of Deep Learning Semantic and Contour Segmentation
Snippet: Corrosion detection on metal constructions is a major challenge in civil engineering for quick, safe and effective inspection. Existing image analysis approaches tend to place bounding boxes around the defected region which is not adequate both for structural analysis and pre-fabrication, an innovative construction concept which reduces maintenance cost, time and improves safety. In this paper, we apply three semantic segmentation-oriented deep learning models (FCN, U-Net and Mask R-CNN) for corrosion detection, which perform better in terms of accuracy and time and require a smaller number of annotated samples compared to other deep models, e.g. CNN. However, the final images derived are still not sufficiently accurate for structural analysis and pre-fabrication. Thus, we adopt a novel data projection scheme that fuses the results of color segmentation, yielding accurate but over-segmented contours of a region, with a processed area of the deep masks, resulting in high-confidence corroded pixels.

Snippet: For the proposed CNN framework, the total corrosion pixels included in the training and test sets were further distributed into significant and weak corrosion pixels, respectively (Figure 11). It was evident that the extended method displayed superior performance compared to all other models, as shown by the performance evaluation metrics presented in Table 3. The performance of models was assessed using parameters such as GC, CAC, Mean IOU, P, R, and F-score. In addition, cross-validation was performed on each architecture, and the prediction for each method was assessed using the described evaluation metrics.

Title: RustSEG - Automated segmentation of corrosion using deep learning
Snippet: The inspection of infrastructure for corrosion remains a task that is typically performed manually by qualified engineers or inspectors. This task of inspection is laborious, slow, and often requires complex access. Recently, deep learning based algorithms have revealed promise and performance in the automatic detection of corrosion. Title: A novel method for intelligent operation and maintenance of transformers using deep visual large model DETR + X and digital twin
Snippet: To achieve real-time monitoring and intelligent maintenance of transformers, a framework based on deep vision and digital twin has been developed. An enhanced visual detection model, DETR + X, is proposed, implementing multidimensional sample data augmentation through Swin2SR and GAN networks. This model converts one-dimensional DGA data into three-dimensional feature images based on Gram angle fields, facilitating the transformation and fusion of heterogeneous modal information. The Pyramid Vision Transformer (PVT) is innovatively adopted as the backbone for image feature extraction, replacing the traditional ResNet structure. A Deformable Attention mechanism is employed to handle the complex spatial structure of multi-scale features. Testing results indicate that the improved DETR + X model performs well in transformer state recognition tasks, achieving a classification accuracy of 100% for DGA feature maps. In object detection tasks, it surpasses advanced models such as Faster R-CNN, RetinaNet, YOLOv8, and Deformable DETR in terms of overall mAP50 scores, particularly demonstrating significant enhancements in small object detection. Furthermore, the Llava-7b model, fine-tuned based on domain expertise, serves as an expert decision-making tool for transformer maintenance, providing accurate operational recommendations based on visual detection results. Finally, based on digital twin and inference models, a comprehensive platform has been developed to achieve real-time monitoring and intelligent maintenance of transformers.

Title: Liquid Leak Detection Using Thermal Images
Snippet: In conclusion, the results from our experiment of YOLOv8 on thermal liquid leak detection confirmed its suitability and effectiveness. With an mAP of 96.0%, a precision of 90.8%, and a recall of 89.9%, YOLOv8 stands out as a robust solution for detecting thermal liquid leaks, proving its potential in both theoretical and practical scenarios. The Real-Time Detection Transformer (RT DETR) model in our liquid leak detection system played a pivotal role in enhancing the efficacy of identifying leaks, particularly in scenarios involving thermal datasets. RT DETR, optimized for image classification tasks, excels in capturing intricate spatial information crucial for detecting anomalous patterns associated with liquid leaks on the ground as well as the walls in some pictures. Leveraging its transformer-based architecture, RT DETR demonstrated an exceptional ability to analyze thermal data and discern nuanced features indicative of multiple potential leaks in an image [2]. The model's attention mechanisms facilitated the identification of subtle temperature variations and thermal anomalies, contributing to the overall accuracy of early leak detection. By harnessing the strengths of RT DETR, our system not only provided an increased sensitivity to thermal signatures associated with liquid leaks but also demonstrated its adaptability to diverse environmental, lighting conditions, and camera angles, making it a valuable asset in mitigating environmental risks and ensuring the integrity of oil operations. When evaluating the fluid leak detection system, we used two leading object detection models, YOLOv8 and RT-DETR, to evaluate their performance using key metrics such as precision, recall, and mean precision (mAP). YOLOv8 performed well in all metrics, with 90.8% precision, 89.9% recall, and 96.0% mAP. On the other hand, RT-DETR showed slightly lower statistics with 88.1% precision, 85% recall, and 91.7% mAP. The comparison results show that YOLOv8 outperforms RT-DETR in accurately detecting and locating fluid leaks in the system. Several factors contribute to the observed performance differences. The success of YOLOv8 is due to its efficient anchor-free approach, which can perform object detection tasks with high precision and recall.

Title: OPEN: Object-wise Position Embedding for Multi-view 3D Object Detection
Snippet: 2D Object Detection with DETR.DETR [2] is the pioneering work that achieves end-to-end object detection by transformer [34].DETR takes learnable object queries as the query and image features as the key and value for the transformer.To achieve end-to-end detection, DETR utilizes Hungarian Matching for ground-truth label assignment.Many works [4,12,20,24,37,43,47] follow the successful architecture of DETR and further improve the performance.For example, Deformable DETR [47] proposed deformable attention, which greatly alleviates the problem of slow convergence of DETR.DINO [43] utilized denoising training to reduce the learning difficulty of Hungarian Matching.

LiDAR-based 3D Object Detection.According to the point cloud processing method, LiDAR-based 3D object detectors can be divided into point-based and voxel-based.Point-based 3D object detectors [5,6,28,32,41,42,44] usually randomly sample point clouds and directly consume sampled point clouds for extracting 3D features by a PointNet-like [29] backbone.For voxel-based 3D object detectors [3,11,30,31,39,45], these methods first quantify point clouds into regular grids and then utilize a 3D sparse convolution backbone to extract 3D features.

Multi-view 3D Object Detection.Multi-view 3D object detectors consume multi-view images from surrounding camera sensors and detect 3D objects in the 3D space.According to the view transformation paradigm, multi-view 3D object detectors can be divided into LSS-based and transformer-based.For LSS-based multi-view 3D object detectors [9,14,15], these methods utilize Lift-Splat-Shot (LSS) operation [27] to convert multi-view image features to bird's-eye view (BEV) feature and BEV-based 3D detection head to detect objects on the BEV feature.For transformer-based methods [16,21,35,38], these methods utilize the transformer to convert multi-view image features to 3D features.

problem: Recent advancements in software defined radio
final_response:
# What “Software-Defined Radio” (SDR) Means Today
<cite id="858fb026-0">Software-defined radio places core radio functions into the digital domain so that waveforms and protocols can be reconfigured by software, exemplified by commercial transceivers such as the NI USRP 2920 operating from 50 MHz to 2.2 GHz with up to 20 MHz bandwidth and 31 dB gain</cite>. <cite id="98edf0f2-0">SDR is typically multiband and supports multiple air interfaces and protocols through reconfigurable DSP or general-purpose processors, while cognitive radio builds on SDR to be context-aware and adapt its parameters and behaviors autonomously</cite>. <cite id="98edf0f2-1">Standards bodies have codified relationships among SDR, cognitive radio, policy-based control, and dynamic spectrum access, providing normative definitions and informative annexes that clarify how these technologies interrelate</cite>. <cite id="858fb026-2">At the ecosystem level, both radio- and network-level functions are moving onto software-reconfigurable platforms (SDR and SDN), with the O-RAN movement aiming to revolutionize wireless implementations; this flexibility brings new security challenges that must be addressed alongside performance metrics like spectral efficiency and latency</cite>.

# Open-Source Platforms and Hardware Ecosystems
<cite id="3c634a25-0">Modern SDR work commonly combines open-source software and commodity hardware; representative stacks include GNU Radio, Gr-OsmoSDR, SDR#, HDSDR, and Gqrx on receivers such as HackRF One, BladeRF, USRP B200/B210, and RTL-SDR dongles</cite>. <cite id="3c634a25-1">Open platforms like HackRF One provide full-duplex transceiver capability from roughly 1 MHz to 6 GHz at up to 20 MHz bandwidth and include Linux distributions tailored for GNU Radio-based experimentation</cite>. <cite id="3c634a25-2">USRP boards offer high baseband sampling but often rely on host CPUs for baseband processing; mapping GNU Radio blocks to FPGA co-processors can reduce processing time and even enable standalone USRP platforms via frameworks like RF Network-on-Chip (RFNoC)</cite>. <cite id="3c634a25-2">Standalone embedded options such as the USRP E310 integrate a baseband processor and a Zynq SoC, and lower-cost ZC702 boards provide the FPGA fabric needed for accelerated baseband functions</cite>.

# Hardware-Software Codesign and Performance
<cite id="3c634a25-2">Case studies (e.g., IEEE 802.11p) show that accelerating GNU Radio blocks—such as FIR filters—on Zynq can increase throughput several-fold versus software-only implementations, motivating hardware-software co-design to meet latency and power targets</cite>. <cite id="3c634a25-4">In 3GPP physical-layer prototyping, end-to-end flowgraphs can be split between GNU Radio on the host and custom RFNoC hardware IPs on the USRP FPGA; measured execution time differences for PHY blocks (e.g., cell search) demonstrate the benefits of offloading to FPGA for parallel processing and tight host–FPGA interfaces</cite>. <cite id="3c634a25-3">These studies typically combine GNU Radio with USRP B210, Zynq SoC, and open embedded toolchains to demonstrate practical, reconfigurable testbeds for 802.11p and similar PHYs</cite>.

# AI/ML-Native SDR: PHY Learning and Control
<cite id="b7fb75c5-0">AI methods are being applied across 5G case studies including modulation classification, channel coding, massive MIMO, caching, energy efficiency, and cybersecurity, with the conclusion that AI can add intelligence and flexibility but needs to address complexity for real-time, low-power deployment and more realistic testbeds</cite>. <cite id="b7fb75c5-2">Surveys categorize AI/ML for 5G by supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning, with deep learning highlighted for its promise in handling 5G’s high complexity across physical-layer tasks and network functions</cite>. <cite id="b7fb75c5-3">At the physical layer, deep learning has been used for channel estimation, symbol detection, and autoencoder-based signal reconstruction through impaired channels, and there is potential to improve 5G LDPC encoding/decoding via ML to reduce bit error rates</cite>. <cite id="b7fb75c5-4">For 5G mmWave systems, ML-based channel-learning schemes can enhance beam and blockage prediction and accelerate initial access; end-to-end demonstrations implement cell and beam index search “softwarized” on off-the-shelf SDRs, showing practical gains in beam index detection under heterogeneous channel conditions</cite>.

# Dynamic Spectrum Access and Cognitive Radio
<cite id="98edf0f2-0">Cognitive radio extends SDR by sensing the environment and autonomously adapting waveforms, transmission parameters, and networking functions to improve spectrum usage beyond simple, preprogrammed air interfaces</cite>. <cite id="98edf0f2-1">Dynamic spectrum access standards and frameworks define how radios coordinate spectrum use, manage interference, and share spectrum across technologies, situating SDR as the substrate for cognitive behavior and policy-driven control</cite>. <cite id="98edf0f2-3">By integrating radio and networking functions, cognitive radios aim to increase spectrum efficiency via secondary users exploiting spectrum holes while adapting to operating conditions, aligning with broader 5G goals of high data rates and QoS</cite>.

# 5G/6G Prototyping and O-RAN
<cite id="858fb026-2">The convergence of SDR, SDN, and O-RAN is reshaping wireless architectures, pushing functions like RAN intelligence and control into software on flexible platforms</cite>. <cite id="858fb026-2">Security is a first-order concern for beyond-5G systems, as performance-focused research has historically underweighted security constraints at the physical and radio-control layers, motivating co-design of secure, low-latency SDR/O-RAN stacks</cite>. <cite id="b7fb75c5-4">Practical 5G prototyping increasingly leverages SDR-based cell search and beam management with ML, demonstrating end-to-end workflows from signal capture to detection and beam selection on commercial platforms</cite>. <cite id="b7fb75c5-3">Looking ahead to 6G, AI coupling is expected across sub-6 GHz, mmWave, and THz, with IoT, energy-efficient control, and federated learning as enablers for automated, multi-band, context-aware operation</cite>.

# High-Frequency and Emerging Bands
<cite id="b7fb75c5-4">At mmWave (e.g., 5G), ML-based schemes enhance blind beam index detection and initial access by learning channel conditions and blockage patterns, which is critical given high path loss and directional propagation</cite>. <cite id="b7fb75c5-3">Surveys anticipate broad investigation of sub-6 GHz, mmWave, and THz to achieve higher data rates in 6G, with AI/ML aiding automation and management across these bands</cite>. <cite id="b7fb75c5-0">Even as most hobbyist and academic SDRs operate below 6 GHz, the trend toward multi-band, multi-protocol platforms is preparing the way for experimentation in higher bands relevant to 5G/6G</cite>.

# Security and Safety Considerations
<cite id="858fb026-2">The expansion of reconfigurable radio and network software introduces security challenges at the physical layer and beyond, as traditional analyses often optimize only spectral efficiency, latency, and network metrics without enforcing security constraints</cite>. <cite id="3c634a25-1">Open SDR hardware and GNU Radio-based toolchains have been used in security studies and attacks on wireless ecosystems (e.g., smart homes), underscoring the need for secure-by-default designs and hardened protocol stacks on SDR platforms</cite>. <cite id="98edf0f2-1">Standards like IEEE 1900.1 clarify terminology and interrelationships (SDR, cognitive/policy-based radios), offering a foundation for secure, policy-coordinated dynamic spectrum access and coexistence across technologies</cite>.

# Open Challenges and Outlook
<cite id="3c634a25-2">Hardware-software partitioning remains a key design question: while host CPUs provide flexibility, FPGAs can deliver the latency and throughput needed for real-time PHY processing, especially as waveforms grow more complex</cite>. <cite id="b7fb75c5-0">AI/ML integration is promising but must reduce model and inference complexity to fit time-sensitive networks and low-power devices, and be validated in realistic, SDR-based testbeds rather than only simulations</cite>. <cite id="b7fb75c5-4">For 5G/6G, learning-based beam management and initial access on SDR are advancing, but robustness to mobility, blockage, and interference demands continued co-design of algorithms and radio architectures</cite>. <cite id="858fb026-2">Finally, as SDR/O-RAN ecosystems mature, end-to-end security and compliance—spanning PHY to control plane—must be addressed alongside performance and flexibility to ensure safe, trustworthy deployment</cite>.

# Practical Ecosystem Snapshot
- Software: GNU Radio and its ecosystem (Gr-OsmoSDR, RFNoC, block accelerators) are central for rapid prototyping and FPGA co-processing, enabling flexible PHY development and hardware acceleration where needed. <cite id="3c634a25-0">GNU Radio, Gr-OsmoSDR, and SDR# are commonly used with devices like USRP B200/B210, HackRF One, and BladeRF</cite> <cite id="3c634a25-4">RFNoC provides a path to accelerate PHY blocks on USRP FPGAs and integrate them with GNU Radio via Ethernet and AXI interfaces</cite>.
- Hardware: Ettus/NI USRP families, embedded Zynq platforms, and open hardware like HackRF/bladeRF provide a spectrum from high-performance front-ends to low-cost FPGA-rich boards for codesign. <cite id="3c634a25-2">USRP boards offload RF and high baseband sampling to host systems or standalone SoCs, with Zynq-based E310 and ZC702 boards enabling FPGA acceleration for baseband functions</cite> <cite id="3c634a25-1">HackRF One offers 1 MHz–6 GHz TX/RX with 20 MHz bandwidth and Linux distributions tailored for GNU Radio experimentation</cite>.
- Cognitive/DSA: SDR remains the foundation for implementing sensing, policy-driven RAT selection, and DSA coordination per emerging standards and frameworks. <cite id="98edf0f2-0">Cognitive radios use SDR to sense and adapt, with DSA enabling improved spectrum use across technologies</cite> <cite id="98edf0f2-1">Standards clarify definitions and interrelationships to support coordinated spectrum access and multi-technology coexistence</cite>.

In sum, recent advancements center on three pillars: (1) open, flexible SDR platforms and codesign methods that push real-time functions onto FPGAs while retaining software agility; (2) AI/ML-native PHYs that learn and adapt beamforming, detection, and control to heterogeneous and high-mobility environments; and (3) cognitive/dynamic spectrum access and O-RAN-style architectures that make radios and networks policy-aware and reconfigurable, with growing emphasis on security and safety. <cite id="3c634a25-2">These trends are visible in FPGA-accelerated GNU Radio flows, RFNoC integrations, and 5G PHY prototypes</cite> <cite id="b7fb75c5-4">as well as ML-enhanced cell/beam search on SDR</cite> <cite id="98edf0f2-1">and the maturing standards landscape for DSA and cognitive radio</cite>.

Since GNU Radio blocks exhibit parallelism, it is possible to map them totally or partially on an FPGA co-processor architecture. The benefits behind this mapping is mainly to improve the processing time of some blocks exploiting the parallel processing power of FPGAs. In addition, SDR designer can rid of host computer using only USRP boards as standalone SDR platform. RFNoc -RF Network-on-Chip [7] is a new open source framework similar to GNU Radio, but for developing applications which run on the FPGA. The USRP E310 is the embedded standalone SDR platform designed by Ettus Research [8]. The cost of such a board is expensive for hobbyists and users of free open source solutions. ZC702 [9] board contains a similar FPGA as USRP E310 but without a front end radio. Title: Design and Performance Analysis of Hardware Realization of 3GPP Physical Layer for 5G Cell Search
Snippet: In academia as well as industry, GNU Radio is widely used for prototyping wireless systems and integration with the radio front-end of the USRP platform for demonstration in a real-radio environment. Since the GNU Radio tool is deployed on the host processor, the performance of signal processing algorithms is limited due to its sequential nature. To address this issue, Ettus Research developed the RFNoC tool that enables the acceleration of GNU Radio algorithms on hardware such as USRP FPGA [22], [23]. It offers a seamless tight interface between GNU Radio software and FPGA for data transfer thus enabling hardware-software codesign between a host processor and FPGA. Like GNU Radio, RFNoC is free and open-source software. 

In this work, we design complete software realization of the CS transmitter and receiver PHY using GNU Radio. Next, we have modified the AXI-Stream compatible hardware IPs discussed in Sections III and IV for different building blocks of the CS transmitter and receiver PHY, respectively, into the custom RFNoC hardware IPs. Then, we have verified the functional correctness of these IPs using custom test benches and an out-of-tree module-based approach which allows integration and verification of RFNoC blocks in GNU Radio. For instance, one of the configurations with CS transmitter PHY in GNU Radio and CS receiver PHY on USRP FPGA is shown in Fig. 15. As per the requirement of the RFNoC framework, the proposed receiver PHY hardware IP with AXI-stream interface is integrated with the AXI wrapper and network-on-chip (NoC) shell. This integrated IP is capable of transmitting and receiving data packets from GNU Radio over an Ethernet interface using the RFNoC framework. The received packets from the transmitter are decoded by the NoC shell to extract the data samples which are then forwarded to receiver PHY along with appropriate control signals via the settings bus. The processed data is then sent back to GNU Radio via another packet using the NoC shell. In the same fashion, multiple blocks in GNU Radio can be moved to USRP FPGA to improve the execution time via parallel processing on the FPGA.
