# What “Software-Defined Radio” (SDR) Means Today
<cite id="858fb026-0">Software-defined radio places core radio functions into the digital domain so that waveforms and protocols can be reconfigured by software, exemplified by commercial transceivers such as the NI USRP 2920 operating from 50 MHz to 2.2 GHz with up to 20 MHz bandwidth and 31 dB gain</cite>. <cite id="98edf0f2-0">SDR is typically multiband and supports multiple air interfaces and protocols through reconfigurable DSP or general-purpose processors, while cognitive radio builds on SDR to be context-aware and adapt its parameters and behaviors autonomously</cite>. <cite id="98edf0f2-1">Standards bodies have codified relationships among SDR, cognitive radio, policy-based control, and dynamic spectrum access, providing normative definitions and informative annexes that clarify how these technologies interrelate</cite>. <cite id="858fb026-2">At the ecosystem level, both radio- and network-level functions are moving onto software-reconfigurable platforms (SDR and SDN), with the O-RAN movement aiming to revolutionize wireless implementations; this flexibility brings new security challenges that must be addressed alongside performance metrics like spectral efficiency and latency</cite>.

# Open-Source Platforms and Hardware Ecosystems
<cite id="3c634a25-0">Modern SDR work commonly combines open-source software and commodity hardware; representative stacks include GNU Radio, Gr-OsmoSDR, SDR#, HDSDR, and Gqrx on receivers such as HackRF One, BladeRF, USRP B200/B210, and RTL-SDR dongles</cite>. <cite id="3c634a25-1">Open platforms like HackRF One provide full-duplex transceiver capability from roughly 1 MHz to 6 GHz at up to 20 MHz bandwidth and include Linux distributions tailored for GNU Radio-based experimentation</cite>. <cite id="3c634a25-2">USRP boards offer high baseband sampling but often rely on host CPUs for baseband processing; mapping GNU Radio blocks to FPGA co-processors can reduce processing time and even enable standalone USRP platforms via frameworks like RF Network-on-Chip (RFNoC)</cite>. <cite id="3c634a25-2">Standalone embedded options such as the USRP E310 integrate a baseband processor and a Zynq SoC, and lower-cost ZC702 boards provide the FPGA fabric needed for accelerated baseband functions</cite>.

# Hardware-Software Codesign and Performance
<cite id="3c634a25-2">Case studies (e.g., IEEE 802.11p) show that accelerating GNU Radio blocks—such as FIR filters—on Zynq can increase throughput several-fold versus software-only implementations, motivating hardware-software co-design to meet latency and power targets</cite>. <cite id="3c634a25-4">In 3GPP physical-layer prototyping, end-to-end flowgraphs can be split between GNU Radio on the host and custom RFNoC hardware IPs on the USRP FPGA; measured execution time differences for PHY blocks (e.g., cell search) demonstrate the benefits of offloading to FPGA for parallel processing and tight host–FPGA interfaces</cite>. <cite id="3c634a25-3">These studies typically combine GNU Radio with USRP B210, Zynq SoC, and open embedded toolchains to demonstrate practical, reconfigurable testbeds for 802.11p and similar PHYs</cite>.

# AI/ML-Native SDR: PHY Learning and Control
<cite id="b7fb75c5-0">AI methods are being applied across 5G case studies including modulation classification, channel coding, massive MIMO, caching, energy efficiency, and cybersecurity, with the conclusion that AI can add intelligence and flexibility but needs to address complexity for real-time, low-power deployment and more realistic testbeds</cite>. <cite id="b7fb75c5-2">Surveys categorize AI/ML for 5G by supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning, with deep learning highlighted for its promise in handling 5G’s high complexity across physical-layer tasks and network functions</cite>. <cite id="b7fb75c5-3">At the physical layer, deep learning has been used for channel estimation, symbol detection, and autoencoder-based signal reconstruction through impaired channels, and there is potential to improve 5G LDPC encoding/decoding via ML to reduce bit error rates</cite>. <cite id="b7fb75c5-4">For 5G mmWave systems, ML-based channel-learning schemes can enhance beam and blockage prediction and accelerate initial access; end-to-end demonstrations implement cell and beam index search “softwarized” on off-the-shelf SDRs, showing practical gains in beam index detection under heterogeneous channel conditions</cite>.

# Dynamic Spectrum Access and Cognitive Radio
<cite id="98edf0f2-0">Cognitive radio extends SDR by sensing the environment and autonomously adapting waveforms, transmission parameters, and networking functions to improve spectrum usage beyond simple, preprogrammed air interfaces</cite>. <cite id="98edf0f2-1">Dynamic spectrum access standards and frameworks define how radios coordinate spectrum use, manage interference, and share spectrum across technologies, situating SDR as the substrate for cognitive behavior and policy-driven control</cite>. <cite id="98edf0f2-3">By integrating radio and networking functions, cognitive radios aim to increase spectrum efficiency via secondary users exploiting spectrum holes while adapting to operating conditions, aligning with broader 5G goals of high data rates and QoS</cite>.

# 5G/6G Prototyping and O-RAN
<cite id="858fb026-2">The convergence of SDR, SDN, and O-RAN is reshaping wireless architectures, pushing functions like RAN intelligence and control into software on flexible platforms</cite>. <cite id="858fb026-2">Security is a first-order concern for beyond-5G systems, as performance-focused research has historically underweighted security constraints at the physical and radio-control layers, motivating co-design of secure, low-latency SDR/O-RAN stacks</cite>. <cite id="b7fb75c5-4">Practical 5G prototyping increasingly leverages SDR-based cell search and beam management with ML, demonstrating end-to-end workflows from signal capture to detection and beam selection on commercial platforms</cite>. <cite id="b7fb75c5-3">Looking ahead to 6G, AI coupling is expected across sub-6 GHz, mmWave, and THz, with IoT, energy-efficient control, and federated learning as enablers for automated, multi-band, context-aware operation</cite>.

# High-Frequency and Emerging Bands
<cite id="b7fb75c5-4">At mmWave (e.g., 5G), ML-based schemes enhance blind beam index detection and initial access by learning channel conditions and blockage patterns, which is critical given high path loss and directional propagation</cite>. <cite id="b7fb75c5-3">Surveys anticipate broad investigation of sub-6 GHz, mmWave, and THz to achieve higher data rates in 6G, with AI/ML aiding automation and management across these bands</cite>. <cite id="b7fb75c5-0">Even as most hobbyist and academic SDRs operate below 6 GHz, the trend toward multi-band, multi-protocol platforms is preparing the way for experimentation in higher bands relevant to 5G/6G</cite>.

# Security and Safety Considerations
<cite id="858fb026-2">The expansion of reconfigurable radio and network software introduces security challenges at the physical layer and beyond, as traditional analyses often optimize only spectral efficiency, latency, and network metrics without enforcing security constraints</cite>. <cite id="3c634a25-1">Open SDR hardware and GNU Radio-based toolchains have been used in security studies and attacks on wireless ecosystems (e.g., smart homes), underscoring the need for secure-by-default designs and hardened protocol stacks on SDR platforms</cite>. <cite id="98edf0f2-1">Standards like IEEE 1900.1 clarify terminology and interrelationships (SDR, cognitive/policy-based radios), offering a foundation for secure, policy-coordinated dynamic spectrum access and coexistence across technologies</cite>.

# Open Challenges and Outlook
<cite id="3c634a25-2">Hardware-software partitioning remains a key design question: while host CPUs provide flexibility, FPGAs can deliver the latency and throughput needed for real-time PHY processing, especially as waveforms grow more complex</cite>. <cite id="b7fb75c5-0">AI/ML integration is promising but must reduce model and inference complexity to fit time-sensitive networks and low-power devices, and be validated in realistic, SDR-based testbeds rather than only simulations</cite>. <cite id="b7fb75c5-4">For 5G/6G, learning-based beam management and initial access on SDR are advancing, but robustness to mobility, blockage, and interference demands continued co-design of algorithms and radio architectures</cite>. <cite id="858fb026-2">Finally, as SDR/O-RAN ecosystems mature, end-to-end security and compliance—spanning PHY to control plane—must be addressed alongside performance and flexibility to ensure safe, trustworthy deployment</cite>.

# Practical Ecosystem Snapshot
- Software: GNU Radio and its ecosystem (Gr-OsmoSDR, RFNoC, block accelerators) are central for rapid prototyping and FPGA co-processing, enabling flexible PHY development and hardware acceleration where needed. <cite id="3c634a25-0">GNU Radio, Gr-OsmoSDR, and SDR# are commonly used with devices like USRP B200/B210, HackRF One, and BladeRF</cite> <cite id="3c634a25-4">RFNoC provides a path to accelerate PHY blocks on USRP FPGAs and integrate them with GNU Radio via Ethernet and AXI interfaces</cite>.
- Hardware: Ettus/NI USRP families, embedded Zynq platforms, and open hardware like HackRF/bladeRF provide a spectrum from high-performance front-ends to low-cost FPGA-rich boards for codesign. <cite id="3c634a25-2">USRP boards offload RF and high baseband sampling to host systems or standalone SoCs, with Zynq-based E310 and ZC702 boards enabling FPGA acceleration for baseband functions</cite> <cite id="3c634a25-1">HackRF One offers 1 MHz–6 GHz TX/RX with 20 MHz bandwidth and Linux distributions tailored for GNU Radio experimentation</cite>.
- Cognitive/DSA: SDR remains the foundation for implementing sensing, policy-driven RAT selection, and DSA coordination per emerging standards and frameworks. <cite id="98edf0f2-0">Cognitive radios use SDR to sense and adapt, with DSA enabling improved spectrum use across technologies</cite> <cite id="98edf0f2-1">Standards clarify definitions and interrelationships to support coordinated spectrum access and multi-technology coexistence</cite>.

In sum, recent advancements center on three pillars: (1) open, flexible SDR platforms and codesign methods that push real-time functions onto FPGAs while retaining software agility; (2) AI/ML-native PHYs that learn and adapt beamforming, detection, and control to heterogeneous and high-mobility environments; and (3) cognitive/dynamic spectrum access and O-RAN-style architectures that make radios and networks policy-aware and reconfigurable, with growing emphasis on security and safety. <cite id="3c634a25-2">These trends are visible in FPGA-accelerated GNU Radio flows, RFNoC integrations, and 5G PHY prototypes</cite> <cite id="b7fb75c5-4">as well as ML-enhanced cell/beam search on SDR</cite> <cite id="98edf0f2-1">and the maturing standards landscape for DSA and cognitive radio</cite>. </answer>

Title: Challenges and Opportunities for Beyond-5G Wireless Security
Snippet: Software-Defined Radios and Networks: Both radio-level and network-level functionality are moving to platforms that can be readily reconfigured through software. The capabilities of software-defined radios (SDRs) continue to improve, and they are widely available commercially-off-the-shelf throughout the world. Software-defined networks (SDNs) are also in widespread use due to their offered flexibility in network reconfiguration. There is also the emerging open-radio access network (O-RAN) movement that may soon revolutionize how wireless networks are implemented and commercialized. 

These technology areas have led to many vibrant research directions in communications and networking. At the same time, these areas have generated unforeseen security challenges that will greatly impact radio and network operation moving forward. The vast majority of research at the physical layer has focused on optimizing performance metrics such as spectral efficiency (bits/second/Hz), network efficiency (bits/second/Hz/area), and latency (seconds), while often ignoring any security constraints that arise. 

Wireless communication and networking researchers can no longer afford to conduct research that does not consider security challenges. In this paper, we discuss the emerging security challenges of beyond-5G wireless systems, and explore research directions aimed at addressing these challenges.

snippet.text:
Software-Defined Radios and Networks: Both radio-level and network-level functionality are moving to platforms that can be readily reconfigured through software. The capabilities of software-defined radios (SDRs) continue to improve, and they are widely available commercially-off-the-shelf throughout the world. Software-defined networks (SDNs) are also in widespread use due to their offered flexibility in network reconfiguration. There is also the emerging open-radio access network (O-RAN) movement that may soon revolutionize how wireless networks are implemented and commercialized. 

These technology areas have led to many vibrant research directions in communications and networking. At the same time, these areas have generated unforeseen security challenges that will greatly impact radio and network operation moving forward. The vast majority of research at the physical layer has focused on optimizing performance metrics such as spectral efficiency (bits/second/Hz), network efficiency (bits/second/Hz/area), and latency (seconds), while often ignoring any security constraints that arise. 

Wireless communication and networking researchers can no longer afford to conduct research that does not consider security challenges. In this paper, we discuss the emerging security challenges of beyond-5G wireless systems, and explore research directions aimed at addressing these challenges.

Title: Dynamic Spectrum Access: Signal Processing, Networking, and Regulatory Policy
Snippet: Software-Defined Radio and cognitive radio were coined by Mitola in 1991 and 1998, respectively. Software-defined radio, sometimes shortened to software radio, is generally a multiband radio that supports multiple air interfaces and protocols and is reconfigurable through software run on DSP or general-purpose microprocessers [15]. Cognitive radio, built upon a software radio platform, is a context-aware intelligent radio capable of autonomous reconfiguration by learning and adapting to the communication environment [16]. While dynamic spectrum access is certainly an important application of cognitive radio, cognitive radio represents a much broader paradigm where many aspects of communication systems can be improved via cognition.

Title: A Roadmap to International Standards Development for Cognitive Radio Systems and Dynamic Spectrum Access
Snippet: The DySPAN (Dynamic Spectrum Access) standards committee had its beginning in early 2005 jointly under CSSB and EMC. It was initially known as the 1900 Committee and later as the Standards Coordinating Committee 41 (SCC41). The scope of the DySPAN-SC includes the following: 

 dynamic spectrum access radio systems and networks with the focus on improved use of spectrum,  new techniques and methods of dynamic spectrum access including the management of radio transmission interference, and  coordination of wireless technologies including network management and information sharing amongst networks deploying different wireless technologies. 

Additional information on DySPAN-SC may be found at www.dyspan-sc.org. The IEEE 1900.1 WG is responsible for DSA definitions and concepts and published its first standard in 2008. This standard provides definitions and explanations of key concepts in the fields of spectrum management, cognitive radio, policy-defined radio, adaptive radio, software-defined radio (SDR), and related technologies. The standard goes beyond simple, short definitions by providing amplifying text that explains these terms in the context of the technologies that use them. The document also describes how these technologies interrelate and create new capabilities while at the same time providing mechanisms supportive of new spectrum management paradigms such as CRS and DSA. (IEEE 2008a). 

The body of this standard is "normative" meaning that the material is a required part of the standard. Because of the complexity of the technology, the 1900.1 Standard provides amplifying material in "informative" annexes. Although these "informative" annexes are not a required part of the standard, these annexes are helpful to users of the standard in fully understanding the meaning of the "normative" definitions. A key annex is the annex that describes the relationship of terms such cognitive radio, software defined radio, software-controlled radio, intelligent radio, policy-based radio, and reconfigurable radio. 

The IEEE 1900.1 Standard TM defines "cognitive radio" (CR) and "cognitive radio network" but does not define "cognitive radio system" which is a term defined by the ITU-R and the US National Telecommunications and Information Administration and provided earlier in this chapter. (ITU 2009 andNTIA 2011).

Title: Manipulating Users' Trust on Amazon Echo: Compromising Smart Home from Outside
Snippet: Software Defined Radio (SDR) technology is to use modern software tools to control and manipulate the traditional "pure hardware circuit" wireless communication. The key idea of SDR is keeping the Analog-to-Digital and Digital-to-Analog converter as close to the antenna as possible, and letting software implements as many radio functions as possible. GNU Radio software is a free software development toolkit which provides several wireless communication blocks to implement SDR. It can be used to attack smart home systems, vehicles, and launch side channel attacks to crack encryption algorithms. Various hardware can be utilized to build SDR platform, e.g, HackRF One, bladeRF, ASR-2300. In particular, HackRF One is an open source hardware platform that provides both reception and transmission functionalities, capable of transmitting or receiving radio signals from 1 MHz to 6 GHz, with the maximum bandwidth of 20 MHz. A special Linux distribution, Pentoo, with full support for GNU Radio can be installed on HackRF one. In this paper, we use HackRF One and its default antenna ANT500 to broadcast radio and TV signals.

Title: Hardware-Software Codesign for Software Defined Radio: IEEE 802.11p receiver case study
Snippet: USRP boards from Ettus Research [4] is a good candidate to perform a Front End (FE) radio offering high baseband sampling. Although the USRP holds a Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA), it needs a host computer to perform baseband processing using high level programming (i.e. C++ and Python). Since GNU Radio blocks exhibit parallelism, it is possible to map them totally or partially on an FPGA co-processor architecture. The benefits behind this mapping is mainly to improve the processing time of some blocks exploiting the parallel processing power of FPGAs. In addition, SDR designer can rid of host computer using only USRP boards as standalone SDR platform. RFNoc -RF Network-on-Chip [7] is a new open source framework similar to GNU Radio, but for developing applications which run on the FPGA. The USRP E310 is the embedded standalone SDR platform designed by Ettus Research [8]. It contains a baseband processor, Xilinx Zynq ZC702 SoC (System on Chip) combined with a dual core ARM CPU, both into a single chip. The cost of such a board is expensive for hobbyists and users of free open source solutions. ZC702 [9] board contains a similar FPGA as USRP E310 but without a front end radio. It is affordable and it costs not more than 900 $. Our objective is to deploy GNU Radio platform on this board. Then we would test and analyze the performances of GNU Radio flow graphs chains. 

Many works have been published to make use of GNU Radio on FPGA based embedded plateform. Obviously, the subject is not purely scientific but its technical benefit allows researchers to have specific information in order to prototype efficiently proof of concepts. In [10], J. Pendlum has presented a first thought and implementation of GNU Radio block to support FPGA co-processing with Xilinx's Zynq SoC. Finite Impulse Response (FIR) filter has been accelerated. Obtained results showed that the FPGA FIR filter processes samples five times quicker than FIR filter for the same number of taps. However, software and hardware setups are out of date or obsolete as announced in [11].

Title: Hardware-Software Codesign for Software Defined Radio: IEEE 802.11p receiver case study
Snippet: This section gives a background about our Software Defined Radio, embedded systems and hardware acceleration method. GNU Radio, USRP B210, Zynq SoC and OpenEmbedded are our hardware and software tools.

Title: Design and Performance Analysis of Hardware Realization of 3GPP Physical Layer for 5G Cell Search
Snippet: In academia as well as industry, GNU Radio is widely used for prototyping wireless systems and integration with the radio front-end of the USRP platform for demonstration in a real-radio environment. Since the GNU Radio tool is deployed on the host processor, the performance of signal processing algorithms is limited due to its sequential nature. To address this issue, Ettus Research developed the RFNoC tool that enables the acceleration of GNU Radio algorithms on hardware such as USRP FPGA [22], [23]. It offers a seamless tight interface between GNU Radio software and FPGA for data transfer thus enabling hardware-software codesign between a host processor and FPGA. Like GNU Radio, RFNoC is free and open-source software. 

In this work, we design complete software realization of the CS transmitter and receiver PHY using GNU Radio. Next, we have modified the AXI-Stream compatible hardware IPs discussed in Sections III and IV for different building blocks of the CS transmitter and receiver PHY, respectively, into the custom RFNoC hardware IPs. Then, we have verified the functional correctness of these IPs using custom test benches and an out-of-tree module-based approach which allows integration and verification of RFNoC blocks in GNU Radio. For instance, one of the configurations with CS transmitter PHY in GNU Radio and CS receiver PHY on USRP FPGA is shown in Fig. 15. As per the requirement of the RFNoC framework, the proposed receiver PHY hardware IP with AXI-stream interface is integrated with the AXI wrapper and network-on-chip (NoC) shell. This integrated IP is capable of transmitting and receiving data packets from GNU Radio over an Ethernet interface using the RFNoC framework. The received packets from the transmitter are decoded by the NoC shell to extract the data samples which are then forwarded to receiver PHY along with appropriate control signals via the settings bus. The processed data is then sent back to GNU Radio via another packet using the NoC shell. In the same fashion, multiple blocks in GNU Radio can be moved to USRP FPGA to improve the execution time via parallel processing on the FPGA. 

In Table IV, we compare the execution time of the PSS search block on GNU Radio and RFNoC platforms.

GNU Radio software is a free software development toolkit which provides several wireless communication blocks to implement SDR. It can be used to attack smart home systems, vehicles, and launch side channel attacks to crack encryption algorithms. Various hardware can be utilized to build SDR platform, e.g, HackRF One, bladeRF, ASR-2300. In particular, HackRF One is an open source hardware platform that provides both reception and transmission functionalities, capable of transmitting or receiving radio signals from 1 MHz to 6 GHz, with the maximum bandwidth of 20 MHz. A special Linux distribution, Pentoo, with full support for GNU Radio can be installed on HackRF one. In this paper, we use HackRF One and its default antenna ANT500 to broadcast radio and TV signals.

snippet.text:
USRP boards from Ettus Research [4] is a good candidate to perform a Front End (FE) radio offering high baseband sampling. Although the USRP holds a Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA), it needs a host computer to perform baseband processing using high level programming (i.e. C++ and Python). Since GNU Radio blocks exhibit parallelism, it is possible to map them totally or partially on an FPGA co-processor architecture. The benefits behind this mapping is mainly to improve the processing time of some blocks exploiting the parallel processing power of FPGAs. In addition, SDR designer can rid of host computer using only USRP boards as standalone SDR platform. RFNoc -RF Network-on-Chip [7] is a new open source framework similar to GNU Radio, but for developing applications which run on the FPGA. The USRP E310 is the embedded standalone SDR platform designed by Ettus Research [8]. It contains a baseband processor, Xilinx Zynq ZC702 SoC (System on Chip) combined with a dual core ARM CPU, both into a single chip. The cost of such a board is expensive for hobbyists and users of free open source solutions. ZC702 [9] board contains a similar FPGA as USRP E310 but without a front end radio. It is affordable and it costs not more than 900 $. Our objective is to deploy GNU Radio platform on this board. Then we would test and analyze the performances of GNU Radio flow graphs chains. 

Many works have been published to make use of GNU Radio on FPGA based embedded plateform. Obviously, the subject is not purely scientific but its technical benefit allows researchers to have specific information in order to prototype efficiently proof of concepts. In [10], J. Pendlum has presented a first thought and implementation of GNU Radio block to support FPGA co-processing with Xilinx's Zynq SoC. Finite Impulse Response (FIR) filter has been accelerated. Obtained results showed that the FPGA FIR filter processes samples five times quicker than FIR filter for the same number of taps. However, software and hardware setups are out of date or obsolete as announced in [11].

snippet.text:
In academia as well as industry, GNU Radio is widely used for prototyping wireless systems and integration with the radio front-end of the USRP platform for demonstration in a real-radio environment. Since the GNU Radio tool is deployed on the host processor, the performance of signal processing algorithms is limited due to its sequential nature. To address this issue, Ettus Research developed the RFNoC tool that enables the acceleration of GNU Radio algorithms on hardware such as USRP FPGA [22], [23]. It offers a seamless tight interface between GNU Radio software and FPGA for data transfer thus enabling hardware-software codesign between a host processor and FPGA. Like GNU Radio, RFNoC is free and open-source software. 

In this work, we design complete software realization of the CS transmitter and receiver PHY using GNU Radio. Next, we have modified the AXI-Stream compatible hardware IPs discussed in Sections III and IV for different building blocks of the CS transmitter and receiver PHY, respectively, into the custom RFNoC hardware IPs. Then, we have verified the functional correctness of these IPs using custom test benches and an out-of-tree module-based approach which allows integration and verification of RFNoC blocks in GNU Radio. For instance, one of the configurations with CS transmitter PHY in GNU Radio and CS receiver PHY on USRP FPGA is shown in Fig. 15. As per the requirement of the RFNoC framework, the proposed receiver PHY hardware IP with AXI-stream interface is integrated with the AXI wrapper and network-on-chip (NoC) shell. This integrated IP is capable of transmitting and receiving data packets from GNU Radio over an Ethernet interface using the RFNoC framework. The received packets from the transmitter are decoded by the NoC shell to extract the data samples which are then forwarded to receiver PHY along with appropriate control signals via the settings bus. The processed data is then sent back to GNU Radio via another packet using the NoC shell. In the same fashion, multiple blocks in GNU Radio can be moved to USRP FPGA to improve the execution time via parallel processing on the FPGA. 

In Table IV, we compare the execution time of the PSS search block on GNU Radio and RFNoC platforms.

Title: Artificial Intelligence for 5G Wireless Systems: Opportunities, Challenges, and Future Research Direction
Snippet: In this paper, we presented AI for 5G wireless communication systems. We studied several case studies including modulation classification, channel coding, massive MIMO, caching, energy efficiency, and cybersecurity. As a conclusion of this in-depth study, AI enabled 5G wireless communication and networking is a promising solution that can provide wireless networks with the intelligence, efficiency, and flexibility required to manage the scare radio resource well and deliver high quality of service to the users. However, some efforts are still needed to reduce the complexity of deep learning so it can be implemented in time-sensitive networks and low power devices and test the models in more realistic scenarios.

Title: Automatic Modulation Classification Based on Deep Learning for Software-Defined Radio
Snippet: No content available

Title: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning in 5G and beyond: A Survey and Perspectives
Snippet: With the increasing advances and advantages of ML in the wireless communications, each research community has tried to evaluate the impact of ML on 5G in its discipline. As result, we have several publication for ML impact on physical layer, security aspects, radio resource managements, etc. This makes it very difficult to give short overview on the utilization and the impact of AI/ML in 5G. Therefore, we can summarize the works applying ML to 5G according to two principles: a "general ML categorization", where we consider all possible ML approaches from the literature, and a "Deep Learning-based Categorization", which focuses only the deep learning, because several leading publications consider deep learning as the most promising approach of ML for the high complexity of 5G.

A general ML categorization in case of 5G follows the general structure of ML as seen in the first sections, which uses three classes of ML: supervised learning, unsupervised learning and reinforcement learning. Table 2 shows an example of such classification giving the used learning approaches from each class and a concrete example of application in 5G, [17]. In the next section, some 5G use cases will be described and solution for AI/ML integration in mobile network operators will be proposed.

Some research works focus only on the deep learning, because it is considered as most powerful learning approach of AI/ML. This gives a very large spectrum of applications in 5G and its different aspects, as detailed in the most recent surveys from examples [10,18]. Figure 8 shows just a small part of possible applications in Latency reduction by clustering fog nodes to automatically decide which low power node (LPN) is upgraded to a high power node (HPN) in heterogeneous cellular networks.

Title: A Review on Machine Learning for Channel Coding
Snippet: Reinforcement learning for routing protocol design in underwater sensor networks was studied in [23] to achieve an energy-efficient scheme.Numerous studies have been conducted on AI for the wireless network layer, including those on traffic flow prediction [24], and traffic congestion control [25] utilising autoencoders and K-means clustering, respectively.

In the physical layer, deep learning for channel estimation and symbol detection has been conducted in [26].Authors in [27] also show that using deep learning for symbol detection can achieve good performance with low complexity in the design.Other deep learning application also includes channel estimation accuracy in [28] and the development of autoencoders in [29], which are able to reconstruct the signals from an impaired channel.

Current 5G standards in the case of eMBB employed Low-Density Parity-Check codes as standard.High throughput is required by 5G deployment scenarios, particularly the eMBB case.To manage this, the encoding and decoding of 5G channel codes specifically for data has to be created.5G low-density parity check (LDPC) codes use a quasicyclic (QC) LDPC coding structure [30].However, there is a potential to improve the channel coding aspect of wireless communication using ML.This remaining problem in wireless communication needs to be addressed as it will improve the bit error rate (BER) for any transmitted signal through an efficient channel coding scheme.

One of the challenges of 5G includes achieving a short packet with high-reliability and low-latency service [31].6G wireless communication networks will need significant paradigm changes to address these shortcomings of 5G [32].All spectra, including the sub-6 GHz, mmWave, THz, and optical frequency bands, will be thoroughly investigated in order to provide a better data rate [33].AI technologies will effectively be coupled with 6G wireless communication networks to provide comprehensive applications for enhanced network automation and management [34].The development of 6G wireless communication networks will be significantly aided by Internet of Things (IoT), energy-efficient wireless network control, and federated learning systems.

Table 1 is a compilation of existing research and surveys on AI for wireless communication systems.

Title: Exploitation of Channel-Learning for Enhancing 5G Blind Beam Index Detection
Snippet: The ML techniques can infer and provide appropriate parameters by considering channel environments in an efficient way. In [12], the state-of-art ML-based techniques are discussed to deal with the issues of heterogeneous networks (HetNets), such as self-configuration, self-healing, and self-optimization. [13] - [15] also deal with emerging 5G challenges that can be overcome by the ML technologies. In addition, there are a number of research works that propose applicable MLbased schemes in cellular systems. For instance, an MLbased context-aware algorithm for initial access is proposed in a 5G mmWave system [16]. [17] proposes a deep learningbased pilot assignment scheme for a massive multiple-input multiple-output system that supports multiple users. [18] proposes mapping functions and applies them to a deep learning model to enhance prediction of mmWave beam and blockage. Also, a deep learning solution was proposed in [19] for faster and more precise initial access in 5G mmWave networks. 

In this paper, we describe all the technical aspects that compose the 5G cell search, and show the practical details including its implementation and experimental results. We first start with comprehensible explanations of the cell and beam index search procedure in 5G standards. We then investigate how the blind detection of a beam index can be improved by channel-learning schemes through mathematical formulations. Then we present an in-depth description of the practical implementation for the 5G cell and beam index search which is softwarized in full scale through the off-theshelf Software Defined Radio (SDR) platforms. Lastly, we evaluate the performance at a system level through extensive experiments, and discuss to deduce insight and applicability of the channel-learning schemes.

final_response:
# Purpose of “Dialogue” in Dialogue Systems and NLP: Definitions and Framings

Dialogues in both dialogue systems and NLP are typically framed as cooperative, goal-directed exchanges where participants use language to exchange information, coordinate actions, and manage shared understanding to achieve individual or joint objectives. Different research communities emphasize different facets of “purpose”: whether the exchange targets the completion of a concrete task (task-oriented systems), the fulfillment of communicative functions (dialogue acts), or broader social aims (open-domain/chat/proactive interaction). These perspectives are complementary and inform both system design and evaluation criteria. <cite id="b9c72e1e-0">A common definition in dialogue system work is that a dialogue system is a computer system that interacts with a human to achieve a task using dialogue, requiring the system to interpret user inputs via dialogue acts that capture semantics relevant to the dialogue process and underlying task</cite> <cite id="b9c72e1e-2">Dialogues are often modeled as goal-directed, cooperative turn-taking among agents, with task-oriented spoken dialogues distinguished when the interaction is dedicated to realizing a particular task</cite>.

## Foundational Definitions and Purposes (1990s–2000s)

Early dialogue research formalized dialogue purpose by decomposing goals into two levels: substantive (S-goals) and communicative (C-goals). <cite id="5feedce1-2">At the transaction level, dialogues are functional units for effecting high-level goals; these goals can be substantive (e.g., seek information, make a train journey, make a reservation) and are realized through exchanges that are “topic-bearing elements” of the dialogue</cite>. This framing treats dialogue as a means to advance participants’ objectives while coordinating how content is conveyed, anticipating modern distinctions between “what” vs. “how” in communicative planning. <cite id="5feedce1-2">Communicative goals determine “how to say it” and may include rhetorical choices (direct vs. indirect strategies) conditioned by social context</cite>.

In parallel, NLP/psycholinguistic traditions defined dialogue purpose in terms of communicative functions and speech-act-inspired dimensions. <cite id="5feedce1-3">Dialogues are often understood as exchanges of symbols among co-present participants, coordinated and mutually interdependent activities; temporal sequencing and perlocutionary effects (e.g., persuading) are also central to purpose</cite>. <cite id="5feedce1-4">Dynamic Interpretation Theory (DIT) models utterances as combinations of dialogue acts whose semantic content and communicative functions change the interlocutors’ information state, organizing functions across multiple dimensions (e.g., task, feedback, interaction and social obligation management)</cite>. <cite id="5feedce1-0">More broadly, dialogue acts are defined as combinations of communicative function and semantic content, capturing the intended action and purpose of an utterance (e.g., inform, request, offer) and enabling multi-dimensional functions within a single utterance</cite>.

## Task-Oriented Systems: Purpose as Goal Completion and Coordination

Contemporary task-oriented dialogue systems operationalize purpose through goal-directed architectures and evaluation centered on achieving user goals. <cite id="b9c72e1e-0">A task-oriented dialogue system is one that interacts with a user to achieve a task, requiring interpretation of user turns via dialogue acts that capture semantics for both the dialogue process and the task</cite>. <cite id="b9c72e1e-4">These systems are characterized by an underlying goal (e.g., scheduling, restaurant booking) and employ modules for tracking (belief state) and planning/policy to select actions that move the conversation toward goal completion</cite>. <cite id="a07bdd27-1">In modular pipelines, a Dialogue State Tracker (DST) estimates beliefs about user goals and slot values; a policy module then selects actions based on these states, and a generator produces responses, making purpose explicit as incremental progress toward joint goals</cite>. <cite id="a07bdd27-4">Benchmark corpora like DSTC explicitly instantiate goals (e.g., restaurant reservations) and annotate user/system actions at the dialogue-act level to evaluate whether systems model goal constraints and progress</cite>.

Success and evaluation criteria in task-oriented dialogue thus align with goal attainment and information-state change. <cite id="a07bdd27-4">Dialogue acts (inform, request, etc.) and slot-goal annotations make explicit which constraints are satisfied and how goal achievement is measured</cite>. <cite id="a07bdd27-4">Evaluation metrics track precision/recall/F1 over dialogue-act predictions and goal-constraint satisfaction, tying purpose to whether the system can elicit, confirm, and act on necessary information</cite>. <cite id="b9c72e1e-0">Dialogues are also sequences of turns where each utterance’s dialogue acts advance the task and manage process (e.g., eliciting missing slots), reinforcing the dual purpose of task completion and process coordination</cite>.

## Dialogue Acts as Units of Purpose and Process

A central NLP framing treats purpose as realized through dialogue acts—labeled communicative functions with semantic content that orchestrate information exchange and control. <cite id="5feedce1-1">Dialogue-act classification labels utterances with types such as greeting or information-elicitation and guides system strategies (e.g., responding to suggestion-elicitation with a suggestion), capturing the intended action and communicative purpose</cite>. <cite id="5feedce1-1">Acts can be multi-functional (e.g., informing while declining an invitation) and are annotated across communication-oriented dimensions (illocutionary function, backward-facing relations) and domain-oriented content</cite>. <cite id="5feedce1-3">Taxonomies such as DAMSL and DIT++ organize acts into representative, directive, commissive, expressive, and declarative categories, and add layers for turn management and social obligations, reflecting multiple simultaneous communicative purposes</cite>. <cite id="5feedce1-4">DIT further formalizes that each utterance may perform several acts across dimensions, with feedback, interaction, and social-obligation management interacting with the task dimension to model how purpose is negotiated in real time</cite>.

This act-based view provides a shared linguistic interface between NLP and dialogue management. <cite id="5feedce1-4">Dialogues can be modeled as sequences of acts whose semantic content and functions update the shared information state, offering a formal lens on “purpose” as information-state change and social coordination</cite>. <cite id="a07bdd27-4">Modern benchmarks integrate act labels and goal constraints to assess whether systems both manage conversation (e.g., request, confirm) and move goals forward (e.g., slot fulfillment), aligning evaluation with purposeful behavior</cite>.

## Open-Domain/Chat and Proactive Dialogue: Beyond Fixed Tasks

In contrast to task-oriented systems, open-domain and chat dialogue emphasize social interaction, exploration, and sustained engagement without a fixed endpoint. <cite id="b9c72e1e-3">Modern systems are often classified into task-oriented and open-domain categories, with the latter lacking a pre-specified task</cite>. <cite id="b9c72e1e-2">Even in goal-directed models, dialogues can be cooperative and multi-dimensional, with social conventions shaping rhetorical choices and strategies beyond mere task completion</cite>. Proactive dialogue extends this by treating purpose as goal acquisition and strategy selection itself. <cite id="a07bdd27-2">When user goals are ambiguous or conflicting, systems may proactively chat to clarify or pursue their own goals, unifying negotiation and topic management under a broader purpose of complex goal attainment and planning</cite>. <cite id="a07bdd27-2">Frameworks inspired by Belief–Desire–Intention (BDI) model agents with beliefs, desires (goals), and intentions, explicitly representing degree of goal achievement and selecting actions accordingly, which aligns with viewing dialogue as goal-directed behavior in open-ended settings</cite>.

Open-domain/chat work also emphasizes communicative purpose as social and informational exchange. <cite id="5feedce1-1">Acts like greeting, inform, and respond are central to maintaining interactional flow and fulfilling social functions, not just domain tasks</cite>. <cite id="5feedce1-3">Perlocutionary effects (e.g., maintaining engagement, building rapport) are part of dialogue’s purpose, aligning with broader aims such as mutual enjoyment or relationship building</cite>. <cite id="5feedce1-0">Multi-dimensional dialogue-act taxonomies capture both content and social/rhetorical purposes, supporting systems that manage turn-taking, obligations, and adjacency pairs to sustain natural, goal-pursuing conversation</cite>.

## Synthesis: Defining the Purpose of “Dialogue” Across Paradigms

- Task-oriented dialogue systems: Purpose is to achieve specified user goals through cooperative information exchange and action coordination. <cite id="b9c72e1e-0">Dialogues are defined to achieve a task, with dialogue acts encoding both process and content relevant to the task</cite> <cite id="b9c72e1e-2">Interactions are goal-directed and cooperative turn-taking</cite> <cite id="b9c72e1e-4">Architectures separate tracking of belief state and planning toward goal completion, with evaluation tied to goal constraints and satisfaction</cite>.

- Dialogue acts and information state: Purpose is realized as communicative functions that change shared information and manage interaction. <cite id="5feedce1-4">Acts have semantic content and communicative functions that update information state across multiple dimensions</cite> <cite id="5feedce1-0">Acts are defined by communicative function plus content and can be multi-dimensional within a single utterance</cite> <cite id="5feedce1-3">Speech-act and perlocutionary perspectives tie purpose to intended effects and social coordination</cite>.

- Open-domain/chat and proactive dialogue: Purpose extends beyond fixed tasks to social connection, exploratory information seeking, and goal clarification. <cite id="b9c72e1e-3">Open-domain systems lack a pre-defined task, contrasting with task-oriented ones</cite> <cite id="a07bdd27-2">Proactive systems may initiate chatting to clarify or pursue goals, modeled via BDI-style desires and intentions</cite> <cite id="5feedce1-1">Acts like greeting and information-elicitation maintain social and informational flows without a single endpoint</cite>.

In practice, these perspectives are not mutually exclusive. <cite id="5feedce1-2">Even task-oriented dialogues can be analyzed at multiple levels of goal abstraction, from high-level transactions to local communicative choices</cite>, while <cite id="a07bdd27-1">modem modular systems instantiate both process (e.g., request, confirm) and content (e.g., slot-filling) goals through dialogue-act-aware components</cite>. Together, they define dialogue’s purpose as a multi-level, cooperative endeavor: exchanging and coordinating information to achieve individual or joint goals, while managing interactional processes and social commitments in context. <cite id="5feedce1-4">This aligns with formalizations where dialogue acts operate on information state and success is measured by progress toward goals and adherence to communicative obligations</cite> <cite id="b9c72e1e-0">and with system definitions that center task accomplishment via dialogue acts and turn semantics</cite>.

There are different planes and dimensions for communicative functions in the utterances [19]. Title: A Wizard of Oz Study Simulating API Usage Dialogues With a Virtual Assistant
Snippet: A dialogue act is a spoken or written utterance that accomplishes a specific purpose in a conversation. Dialogue act classification refers to the task of labeling utterances with descriptive dialogue act types, such as "greeting" or "information-elicitation" [30]. 

To create a dialogue system, both language and dialogue act types must be known for utterances in example conversations [13]. A virtual assistant must learn to mimic good strategies in terms of dialogue act flow (e.g., it must recognize that it should respond to a suggestion-elicitation with a suggestion). Once it knows that it should respond with a particular dialogue act type (e.g., a restaurantsuggestion), it must then collect the information to portray in an utterance (e.g., a restaurant to recommend) and then convert the information into an understandable utterance in natural language. As Serban et. al [10] point out in a recent survey, several datasets, especially involving Wizard of Oz experiments, have been created for a variety of domains to serve as starting points for training virtual assistants. 

It is important to note that a single dialogue act can serve multiple functions simultaneously; for instance, the utterance "I have to work tonight" in response to an invitation serves as an informative act as well as a rejection of the previous utterance. To account for these independent functions, annotators often label dialogue acts across several different dimensions [31]. 

Dialogue act dimensions can be broadly characterized as either communication-oriented or domain-oriented. Communication-oriented dimensions relate solely to the communicative role of an utterance in a conversation, rather than the content of the utterance. For instance, a communication-oriented dimension may capture the illocutionary function of an utterance (i.e. the speaker's intention in producing an utterance) using dialogue act types such as "inform", "suggest", or "offer" [19], [31]. A different communication-oriented dimension may describe the backward-facing function of an utterance (i.e. how an utterance relates to a previous utterance in the conversation) with dialogue act types like "accept", "repeat", or "answer" [32].
</snippet>

Title: A Two-Level Dialogue Representation
Snippet: The following two assumptions form the basis for a pairing of a dialogue planning mechanism with elexents of the clialogue description system: dialogue participants always have two cooperating types of goals, substantive real life goals (Sgoals), which determine "what to say", and linguistic/communicative goals (C-goals), which determine "how to say it". 

No relation of necessity seems to hold between them. In fact, in most cases there are many different ways of expressing the same goal. it is possible to identify hierarchical relations between goals and subgoals both for substantive and communicative goals. However, in the high level dialogue description system units S-goals see/~1 to be more important, while at the low levels C-goal seem to prevail. 

The highest level of the discourse structure is the transaction. Given that the dialogue as a whole is a means of effecting the high-level goals of one or other of the participants, we can functionally define transaction as the unit of dialogue concerned with effecting these high-level goals. 

At the highest lewi.~l of the dialogue's goal structure the dominant goals motivating the transaction are those concerned with the substance of the dialogue, not the means by which the substance is conveyed. 

As we move down this hierarchy it is possible to discern a bifurcation of goals into one group concerned with the substance of the dialogue, and the other concerned with communication of this substance. 

These are the Sgoals and C-goals (or more properly, S and C subgoals) mentioned above. 

A transaction is always motivatedby a general goal such as seek information, make a train journey (Allen, 1982), make a reservation. 

The social context, for example the relation between speaker and hearer or simply a social convention, can suggest rhetorical choices. 

Among these might be the direct stating of the general goal, the indirect revelation ofthe general goal by several related questions, the questioning of a system's general capabilities before asking, and so on. 

Essentially, exchanges can be thought of as the topic-bearing elements of the dialogue.

Title: Dialogue processes in online information seeking and sharing: a study of an asynchronous discussion group
Snippet: The term dialogue stems from the Greek διάλογος (dialogos, conversation); its roots are dia (across; through) and logos (speech, reason) (Lewinski and Blair, 2011, p. 4). As a fundamental constituent of human interaction, dialogue is an old subject of research; to which leading ancient thinkers such as Plato made important contributions (Walton, 2000). There is no generally accepted definition of the concept of dialogue. According to Booth (1989, p. 46), dialogue may be understood as 'the exchange of symbols between two or more parties, as well as being the meanings that the participants in the communicative process assign to these symbols'. Markova and Linell (1996, p. 353) provide a more detailed definition by characterizing human dialogue as 'an interaction between two or more co-present participants using a system of signs,' while dialogical interactions are 'such discursive processes and their products that are conceptualised as joint, coordinated and mutually interdependent activities of both (all) participants'. 

Researchers have also devoted attention to the temporal qualities of dialogue processes. For example, Grant and associates (2004, p. 4) define dialogue as 'chronologically sequenced discursive acts between discussants and the ideas they use'. 

Pioneering contributions to research on dialogue include Austin's (1962) speech act theory. It proposes that in human communication, meaning is constructed in a relation among linguistic conventions correlated with words or sentences, the situation where the speaker actually says something to the hearer, and associated intentions of the speaker. Austin identified three types of speech acts. Locutionary act refers to the actual performance of an utterance and its ostensible meaning, while illocutionary act denotes the pragmatic force of the utterance. Finally, perlocutionary act refers to an utterance's actual effect, such as persuading someone to do something. Searle (1976) elaborated Austin's theory by dividing illocutionary acts into five basic types. Assertives refer to speech acts that commit a speaker to the truth of the expressed proposition, while directives are speech acts that are to cause the hearer to take a particular action, for example, advice.
</snippet>

Title: Evaluating Combinations of Dialogue Acts for Generation
Snippet: In Dynamic Interpretation Theory (DIT) (Bunt, 2000), utterances in a dialogue are modelled in terms of combinations of dialogue acts that operate on the information state of the dialogue participants. A dialogue act has a semantic content, expressing what the act is about, and a communicative function specifying how the semantic content is to be taken to change the information state of the addressee. Communicative functions are organised in a 10-dimensional taxonomy, in which the dimensions reflect different aspects of communication that speakers may address simultaneously in their dialogue behaviour. In each utterance, several dialogue acts can be performed, each dialogue act from a different dimension. The overview below shows a layered structure in which the dimensions are given in boldface italic. So, besides the Task dimension, the taxonomy provides for several Dialogue Control dimensions, organised into the layers of Feedback, Interaction Management (IM) and Social Obligations Management (SOM). 

• Task/domain: acts that concern the specific underlying task and/or domain; In keeping track of the participants' processing states in the cognitive context, four levels of understanding are distinguished: 1) perception: the system was able to hear the utterance (successful speech recognition), 2) interpretation: the system understood what was meant by the utterance (successful dialogue act recognition), 3) evaluation: the information presented in the utterance did not conflict with the system's context (successful consistency checking), and 4) execution: the system could act upon, do something with, the utterance (for example, answering a question, adopting the information given, carrying out a request, etcetera). 

These levels of understanding are also used in distinguishing different types of auto-and allofeedback dialogue acts, each for signalling processing problems on a specific level.
</snippet></tool_output><think>

Title: Scalable and Accurate Dialogue State Tracking via Hierarchical Sequence Generation
Snippet: A Dialogue State Tracker (DST) is a core component of a modular task-oriented dialogue system (Young et al., 2013). For each dialogue turn, a DST module takes a user utterance and the dialogue history as input, and outputs a belief estimate of the dialogue state. Then a machine action is decided based on the dialogue state according to a dialogue policy module, after which a machine response is generated.

Title: Proactive User Information Acquisition via Chats on User-Favored Topics
Snippet: Task-oriented dialogue systems are designed to talk with users to achieve specific goals, typically assuming the user's goals are clearly defined (Chen et al., 2017). However, in some cases, they may be ambiguous, or the systems themselves have their goals conflicting with the user's. In such situations, the systems need to chat proactively to clarify goals or achieve their own goals. Such dialogues are called proactive dialogues and have been studied as tasks requiring advanced strategies (Deng et al., 2023a). While they have been treated in specific contexts like negotiation (Samad et al., 2022;Li et al., 2020), we extend this framework to a versatile, domain-independent task, which could result in unifying and enhancing techniques across various fields of dialogue system research to handle complex goals and strategies. One existing framework for studying open-domain proactive dialogues is the target-guided dialogue task, which aims to guide topic transitions during chats with users (Tang et al., 2019;Wu et al., 2019;Yang et al., 2022). With the advent of LLMs, achieving natural topic transitions has become feasible (Deng et al., 2023b). We tackle a more challenging task involving acquiring information while deepening a single topic, which includes complementary actions to such topic transition. 

Due to limitations in LLMs' planning abilities, 

1 Our dataset will be released. 

they struggle with proactive dialogue tasks that require complex planning (Deng et al., 2023b). Systems based on the Belief-Desire-Intention (BDI) model have proven effective in tasks involving planning (Ichida and Meneguzzi, 2023;Frering et al., 2025). The BDI model is a framework in artificial intelligence and cognitive science that describes rational agents based on their Beliefs (information about the world), Desires (objectives or goals), and Intentions (current plans or commitments to actions) (Bratman, 1987;Rao and Georgeff, 1991). 

The BDI-model-based systems explicitly consider their goals and current situations-including the degree of goal achievement-and select suitable actions. In this study, we developed and evaluated a simple BDI-model-based system that incorporated the findings obtained from our dataset analysis.

Title: Flexible and Scalable State Tracking Framework for Goal-Oriented Dialogue Systems
Snippet: Goal-oriented dialogue systems typically rely on components specifically developed for a single task or domain. This limits such systems in two different ways: If there is an update in the task domain, the dialogue system usually needs to be updated or completely re-trained. It is also harder to extend such dialogue systems to different and multiple domains. The dialogue state tracker in conventional dialogue systems is one such component - it is usually designed to fit a well-defined application domain. For example, it is common for a state variable to be a categorical distribution over a manually-predefined set of entities (Henderson et al., 2013), resulting in an inflexible and hard-to-extend dialogue system. In this paper, we propose a new approach for dialogue state tracking that can generalize well over multiple domains without incorporating any domain-specific knowledge. Under this framework, discrete dialogue state variables are learned independently and the information of a predefined set of possible values for dialogue state variables is not required. Furthermore, it enables adding arbitrary dialogue context as features and allows for multiple values to be associated with a single state variable. These characteristics make it much easier to expand the dialogue state space. We evaluate our framework using the widely used dialogue state tracking challenge data set (DSTC2) and show that our framework yields competitive results with other state-of-the-art results despite incorporating little domain knowledge. We also show that this framework can benefit from widely available external resources such as pre-trained word embeddings.
</snippet>

Snippet: A dialogue act is "a combination of a communicative function and a semantic content" [18]. It refers to the intended action and communicative purpose of an utterance. For instance, when asking for help to open a door, various utterances can fulfill the same dialogue act. This analysis is crucial for social AI systems in natural language understanding, intent detection, and contextual awareness. 

There are different planes and dimensions for communicative functions in the utterances [19]. Some dimensions stem from speakers' mental states [20], [21] and taxonomize dialogue acts into Representatives (assertion, conclusion, etc.), Directives (request, question, suggestion, etc.), Commissives (promise, threat, offer, etc.), Expressives (thanks, apologize, welcome, congratulation, etc.) and Declarations (christening, firing from employment, excommunication, declaration of war, etc.). Different dialogue acts can also be categorized based on conversation management [22], [23], with categorization such as take turn, maintain turn, give turn, and let others maintain the turn. Moreover, dialogue acts can be defined with rhetorical roles and relations [24], [25] (e.g., purpose, condition, contrast etc.) or the notion of "face" [26] (face saving and face threatening). In addition, some work recognizes functions of pared utterances and introduce types for such adjacency pairs [27], [28] like assess → agree/disagree, question → answer, thank → welcome, offer → accept/refuse and so on.

Title: A Wizard of Oz Study Simulating API Usage Dialogues With a Virtual Assistant
Snippet: A dialogue act is a spoken or written utterance that accomplishes a specific purpose in a conversation. Dialogue act classification refers to the task of labeling utterances with descriptive dialogue act types, such as "greeting" or "information-elicitation" [30]. 

To create a dialogue system, both language and dialogue act types must be known for utterances in example conversations [13]. A virtual assistant must learn to mimic good strategies in terms of dialogue act flow (e.g., it must recognize that it should respond to a suggestion-elicitation with a suggestion). Once it knows that it should respond with a particular dialogue act type (e.g., a restaurantsuggestion), it must then collect the information to portray in an utterance (e.g., a restaurant to recommend) and then convert the information into an understandable utterance in natural language. As Serban et. al [10] point out in a recent survey, several datasets, especially involving Wizard of Oz experiments, have been created for a variety of domains to serve as starting points for training virtual assistants. 

It is important to note that a single dialogue act can serve multiple functions simultaneously; for instance, the utterance "I have to work tonight" in response to an invitation serves as an informative act as well as a rejection of the previous utterance. To account for these independent functions, annotators often label dialogue acts across several different dimensions [31]. 

Dialogue act dimensions can be broadly characterized as either communication-oriented or domain-oriented. Communication-oriented dimensions relate solely to the communicative role of an utterance in a conversation, rather than the content of the utterance. For instance, a communication-oriented dimension may capture the illocutionary function of an utterance (i.e. the speaker's intention in producing an utterance) using dialogue act types such as "inform", "suggest", or "offer" [19], [31]. A different communication-oriented dimension may describe the backward-facing function of an utterance (i.e. how an utterance relates to a previous utterance in the conversation) with dialogue act types like "accept", "repeat", or "answer" [32].
</snippet>

Title: Inter-annotator Agreement Using the Conversation Analysis Modelling Schema, for Dialogue
Snippet: Though it was philosophers such as Austin (1962) and Searle (1969), who reconceptualized speech as "actions," the term dialogue act was introduced by Bunt (1978). Bunt (2000), argued that a notion of communicative functions is required, which establish semantic definitions in terms of dialogue context changes, and further that, communication has many "dimensions" that a speaker can address simultaneously. For instance, "Yes, but what is it?", indicates both an understanding of what was previously said, and a request for more information. From this example we can define DA in terms of two components: i) its communicative function, what the speaker is trying to achieve, and ii) the semantic content, which describes the information that is being addressed -the entities, their properties, and relations that are referred to. Thus, while DA labels are intended for single utterances of dialogue, they can be both multidimensional (have more than one function), and be prospective, or reactive, to surrounding utterances; a property that is particularly advantageous when viewed in conjunction with the broader structural descriptions provided by AP. 

As previously discussed, DA are commonly used for NLP purposes. However, historically there has been quite a range of different labeling schemes developed. Most notably, the Discourse Annotation and Mark-up System of labeling (DAMSL) (Allen & Core, 1997), which was used to annotate the Switchboard Dialogue Act dataset (Jurafsky et al., 1997), and a slight variation was used to label the Meeting Recorder Dialogue Act (MRDA) corpus (Shriberg et al., 2004). Also, corpora created for the development of dialogue systems, such as the Dialogue State Tracking Challenge (DSTC) (Williams et al., 2016), and FRAMES (Asri et al., 2017), typically define their own bespoke set of DA labels. While there is some commonality between them, the net result is a collection of different DA labeling schemes that are, to some degree, incompatible. In a move to address this problem the Dialogue Act Mark-up Language (DiAML) was developed and forms part of ISO 24617 (British Standards Institution, 2012).

# Purpose of “Dialogue” in Dialogue Systems and NLP: Definitions and Framings

Dialogues in both dialogue systems and NLP are typically framed as cooperative, goal-directed exchanges where participants use language to exchange information, coordinate actions, and manage shared understanding to achieve individual or joint objectives. Different research communities emphasize different facets of “purpose”: whether the exchange targets the completion of a concrete task (task-oriented systems), the fulfillment of communicative functions (dialogue acts), or broader social aims (open-domain/chat/proactive interaction). These perspectives are complementary and inform both system design and evaluation criteria. <cite id="b9c72e1e-0">A common definition in dialogue system work is that a dialogue system is a computer system that interacts with a human to achieve a task using dialogue, requiring the system to interpret user inputs via dialogue acts that capture semantics relevant to the dialogue process and underlying task</cite> <cite id="b9c72e1e-2">Dialogues are often modeled as goal-directed, cooperative turn-taking among agents, with task-oriented spoken dialogues distinguished when the interaction is dedicated to realizing a particular task</cite>.

## Foundational Definitions and Purposes (1990s–2000s)

Early dialogue research formalized dialogue purpose by decomposing goals into two levels: substantive (S-goals) and communicative (C-goals). <cite id="5feedce1-2">At the transaction level, dialogues are functional units for effecting high-level goals; these goals can be substantive (e.g., seek information, make a train journey, make a reservation) and are realized through exchanges that are “topic-bearing elements” of the dialogue</cite>. This framing treats dialogue as a means to advance participants’ objectives while coordinating how content is conveyed, anticipating modern distinctions between “what” vs. “how” in communicative planning. <cite id="5feedce1-2">Communicative goals determine “how to say it” and may include rhetorical choices (direct vs. indirect strategies) conditioned by social context</cite>.

In parallel, NLP/psycholinguistic traditions defined dialogue purpose in terms of communicative functions and speech-act-inspired dimensions. <cite id="5feedce1-3">Dialogues are often understood as exchanges of symbols among co-present participants, coordinated and mutually interdependent activities; temporal sequencing and perlocutionary effects (e.g., persuading) are also central to purpose</cite>. <cite id="5feedce1-4">Dynamic Interpretation Theory (DIT) models utterances as combinations of dialogue acts whose semantic content and communicative functions change the interlocutors’ information state, organizing functions across multiple dimensions (e.g., task, feedback, interaction and social obligation management)</cite>. <cite id="5feedce1-0">More broadly, dialogue acts are defined as combinations of communicative function and semantic content, capturing the intended action and purpose of an utterance (e.g., inform, request, offer) and enabling multi-dimensional functions within a single utterance</cite>.

## Task-Oriented Systems: Purpose as Goal Completion and Coordination

Contemporary task-oriented dialogue systems operationalize purpose through goal-directed architectures and evaluation centered on achieving user goals. <cite id="b9c72e1e-0">A task-oriented dialogue system is one that interacts with a user to achieve a task, requiring interpretation of user turns via dialogue acts that capture semantics for both the dialogue process and the task</cite>. <cite id="b9c72e1e-4">These systems are characterized by an underlying goal (e.g., scheduling, restaurant booking) and employ modules for tracking (belief state) and planning/policy to select actions that move the conversation toward goal completion</cite>. <cite id="a07bdd27-1">In modular pipelines, a Dialogue State Tracker (DST) estimates beliefs about user goals and slot values; a policy module then selects actions based on these states, and a generator produces responses, making purpose explicit as incremental progress toward joint goals</cite>. <cite id="a07bdd27-4">Benchmark corpora like DSTC explicitly instantiate goals (e.g., restaurant reservations) and annotate user/system actions at the dialogue-act level to evaluate whether systems model goal constraints and progress</cite>.

Success and evaluation criteria in task-oriented dialogue thus align with goal attainment and information-state change. <cite id="a07bdd27-4">Dialogue acts (inform, request, etc.) and slot-goal annotations make explicit which constraints are satisfied and how goal achievement is measured</cite>. <cite id="a07bdd27-4">Evaluation metrics track precision/recall/F1 over dialogue-act predictions and goal-constraint satisfaction, tying purpose to whether the system can elicit, confirm, and act on necessary information</cite>. <cite id="b9c72e1e-0">Dialogues are also sequences of turns where each utterance’s dialogue acts advance the task and manage process (e.g., eliciting missing slots), reinforcing the dual purpose of task completion and process coordination</cite>.

## Dialogue Acts as Units of Purpose and Process

A central NLP framing treats purpose as realized through dialogue acts—labeled communicative functions with semantic content that orchestrate information exchange and control. <cite id="5feedce1-1">Dialogue-act classification labels utterances with types such as greeting or information-elicitation and guides system strategies (e.g., responding to suggestion-elicitation with a suggestion), capturing the intended action and communicative purpose</cite>. <cite id="5feedce1-1">Acts can be multi-functional (e.g., informing while declining an invitation) and are annotated across communication-oriented dimensions (illocutionary function, backward-facing relations) and domain-oriented content</cite>. <cite id="5feedce1-3">Taxonomies such as DAMSL and DIT++ organize acts into representative, directive, commissive, expressive, and declarative categories, and add layers for turn management and social obligations, reflecting multiple simultaneous communicative purposes</cite>. <cite id="5feedce1-4">DIT further formalizes that each utterance may perform several acts across dimensions, with feedback, interaction, and social-obligation management interacting with the task dimension to model how purpose is negotiated in real time</cite>.

This act-based view provides a shared linguistic interface between NLP and dialogue management. <cite id="5feedce1-4">Dialogues can be modeled as sequences of acts whose semantic content and functions update the shared information state, offering a formal lens on “purpose” as information-state change and social coordination</cite>. <cite id="a07bdd27-4">Modern benchmarks integrate act labels and goal constraints to assess whether systems both manage conversation (e.g., request, confirm) and move goals forward (e.g., slot fulfillment), aligning evaluation with purposeful behavior</cite>.

## Open-Domain/Chat and Proactive Dialogue: Beyond Fixed Tasks

In contrast to task-oriented systems, open-domain and chat dialogue emphasize social interaction, exploration, and sustained engagement without a fixed endpoint. <cite id="b9c72e1e-3">Modern systems are often classified into task-oriented and open-domain categories, with the latter lacking a pre-specified task</cite>. <cite id="b9c72e1e-2">Even in goal-directed models, dialogues can be cooperative and multi-dimensional, with social conventions shaping rhetorical choices and strategies beyond mere task completion</cite>. Proactive dialogue extends this by treating purpose as goal acquisition and strategy selection itself. <cite id="a07bdd27-2">When user goals are ambiguous or conflicting, systems may proactively chat to clarify or pursue their own goals, unifying negotiation and topic management under a broader purpose of complex goal attainment and planning</cite>. <cite id="a07bdd27-2">Frameworks inspired by Belief–Desire–Intention (BDI) model agents with beliefs, desires (goals), and intentions, explicitly representing degree of goal achievement and selecting actions accordingly, which aligns with viewing dialogue as goal-directed behavior in open-ended settings</cite>.

Open-domain/chat work also emphasizes communicative purpose as social and informational exchange. <cite id="5feedce1-1">Acts like greeting, inform, and respond are central to maintaining interactional flow and fulfilling social functions, not just domain tasks</cite>. <cite id="5feedce1-3">Perlocutionary effects (e.g., maintaining engagement, building rapport) are part of dialogue’s purpose, aligning with broader aims such as mutual enjoyment or relationship building</cite>. <cite id="5feedce1-0">Multi-dimensional dialogue-act taxonomies capture both content and social/rhetorical purposes, supporting systems that manage turn-taking, obligations, and adjacency pairs to sustain natural, goal-pursuing conversation</cite>.

## Synthesis: Defining the Purpose of “Dialogue” Across Paradigms

- Task-oriented dialogue systems: Purpose is to achieve specified user goals through cooperative information exchange and action coordination. <cite id="b9c72e1e-0">Dialogues are defined to achieve a task, with dialogue acts encoding both process and content relevant to the task</cite> <cite id="b9c72e1e-2">Interactions are goal-directed and cooperative turn-taking</cite> <cite id="b9c72e1e-4">Architectures separate tracking of belief state and planning toward goal completion, with evaluation tied to goal constraints and satisfaction</cite>.

- Dialogue acts and information state: Purpose is realized as communicative functions that change shared information and manage interaction. <cite id="5feedce1-4">Acts have semantic content and communicative functions that update information state across multiple dimensions</cite> <cite id="5feedce1-0">Acts are defined by communicative function plus content and can be multi-dimensional within a single utterance</cite> <cite id="5feedce1-3">Speech-act and perlocutionary perspectives tie purpose to intended effects and social coordination</cite>.

- Open-domain/chat and proactive dialogue: Purpose extends beyond fixed tasks to social connection, exploratory information seeking, and goal clarification. <cite id="b9c72e1e-3">Open-domain systems lack a pre-defined task, contrasting with task-oriented ones</cite> <cite id="a07bdd27-2">Proactive systems may initiate chatting to clarify or pursue goals, modeled via BDI-style desires and intentions</cite> <cite id="5feedce1-1">Acts like greeting and information-elicitation maintain social and informational flows without a single endpoint</cite>.

In practice, these perspectives are not mutually exclusive. <cite id="5feedce1-2">Even task-oriented dialogues can be analyzed at multiple levels of goal abstraction, from high-level transactions to local communicative choices</cite>, while <cite id="a07bdd27-1">modem modular systems instantiate both process (e.g., request, confirm) and content (e.g., slot-filling) goals through dialogue-act-aware components</cite>. Together, they define dialogue’s purpose as a multi-level, cooperative endeavor: exchanging and coordinating information to achieve individual or joint goals, while managing interactional processes and social commitments in context. <cite id="5feedce1-4">This aligns with formalizations where dialogue acts operate on information state and success is measured by progress toward goals and adherence to communicative obligations</cite> <cite id="b9c72e1e-0">and with system definitions that center task accomplishment via dialogue acts and turn semantics</cite>.</answer>
