# What “action chunking with transformers with goal condition” means

Action chunking refers to predicting sequences of several actions at once (a “chunk”) rather than single-step actions, which reduces the effective horizon and can mitigate error compounding in imitation learning and planning for long-horizon tasks.<cite id="8aa21fbb-0">Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) predicts action sequences (chunks) to reduce the effective horizon of long-horizon tasks and alleviate compounding errors in behavior cloning when learning from human demonstrations</cite><cite id="8aa21fbb-1">Given an observation, the model outputs the next K actions to be executed sequentially, with a fixed chunk size K</cite>. 

Goal conditioning means the model’s policy or planning procedure is conditioned on a desired goal state or task specification (e.g., a target image, language instruction, or future observation), so that both the choice of sub-goals and the action distribution are directed toward achieving that goal.<cite id="8aa21fbb-0">By casting these actions as goal states for the manipulator to reach, a temporal aggregation method can be used to combine predicted actions from multiple previous time steps</cite><cite id="8aa21fbb-3">The CVAE encoder includes a transformer encoder that processes camera pose changes and a sequence of target control commands, outputting a style variable z that captures high-level features or style of the observations and action sequences</cite><cite id="aa0c1f0f-4">Recent works show that conditioning for goal states can significantly improve planning; some integrate goal information as a semantic anchor in both observation synthesis and action refinement</cite>. 

# Core architectures

## Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT)
ACT combines a Conditional Variational Autoencoder (CVAE) with a Transformer to predict multi-step action sequences from multimodal inputs, enabling behavior cloning with chunked actions and improved robustness to out-of-distribution states through temporal aggregation.<cite id="8aa21fbb-0">ACT uses a CVAE to model diverse scenes and a transformer to predict action sequences (chunks) given multimodal input; by casting actions as goal states, temporal aggregation across overlapping predictions moderates compounding errors</cite><cite id="8aa21fbb-1">The CVAE uses a BERT-like transformer encoder/decoder; the encoder takes current joint position and target action sequence to predict a style latent z for multi-modal demonstrations, while temporal ensembling smooths output actions</cite><cite id="8aa21fbb-3">ACT’s CVAE encoder/decoder both leverage transformer architectures, enabling multi-modal inputs and long-term dependency capture to generate coherent, diverse actions; the final output action is derived using temporal ensemble smoothing</cite>. 

Goal conditioning in ACT is introduced by providing goal-related signals to the CVAE’s encoder and/or using the latent variable to model “style” across goals; at inference, temporal smoothing blends overlapping chunk predictions to produce stable actions.<cite id="8aa21fbb-1">The CVAE encoder takes current joint position and target action sequence to predict mean/variance of a style variable z that helps handle multi-modal demonstrations; z is used during training and discarded at test by zeroing it out</cite><cite id="8aa21fbb-0">By combining multiple predictions via weighted averaging, the approach mitigates compounding errors and out-of-distribution responses</cite><cite id="8aa21fbb-1">Temporal ensembling applies an exponential weighted scheme across overlapping predictions to obtain a weighted average of actions at each timestep</cite>. 

ACT has been adapted to diffusion-based policies and language-conditioned multi-task settings, showing how the chunking idea generalizes beyond behavior cloning and into generative and multimodal control.<cite id="4aa21fbb-3">Prior work notes predicting action sequences benefits imitation learning; ACT instantiates this with transformers and a conditional VAE; separately, a goal-conditioned reinforcement learning method (CRL) parameterizes value functions as log-linear representations</cite><cite id="8aa21fbb-4">Multi-Task ACT augments the framework to handle multiple tasks with a FiLM network for language-conditioned learning, aligning tasks with language instructions to dynamically adapt to varying task demands</cite><cite id="8aa21fbb-1">A diffusion policy variant replaces the CVAE/DETR decoder with a diffusion process to generate diverse and adaptable action sequences</cite>. 

## Decision Transformers and multi-goal conditioning
Decision Transformer (DT) casts reinforcement learning as conditional sequence modeling with a Transformer, and has been extended to handle multi-goal settings by enriching the input with goal objectives and sparse rewards.<cite id="aa0c1f0f-0">Decision Transformer uses state, action, and returns-to-go as tokens in a Transformer model and has achieved strong performance on robotics tasks</cite><cite id="aa0c1f0f-2">A modified Decision Transformer enriched with the capability to interpret desired goals in an offline robotic setting outperforms online RL methods on an open-ended, sparse-reward multi-task dataset</cite>. In robotics, multi-goal conditioning improves planning and decision-making by making the policy explicitly optimize trajectories toward specified goals.<cite id="aa0c1f0f-4">Extending decision transformers with goal interpretation enables multi-goal learning in robotics and shows improved performance over online RL</cite>. 

## Goal-conditioned diffusion and generative policies
Diffusion-based policies model the visuomotor policy as a conditional denoising diffusion process, generating diverse and adaptable action sequences; goal-conditioned variants integrate goals as part of the conditioning, enabling exploration of multi-modal actions consistent with a target.<cite id="8aa21fbb-1">Diffusion Policy models robot behavior through a conditional denoising diffusion process, leveraging stochasticity to generate diverse and adaptable action sequences</cite><cite id="8aa21fbb-4">The Multi-Task ACT re-implementation integrates a FiLM network to align language-conditioned tasks, enabling dynamic adaptation to varying task demands</cite><cite id="8aa21fbb-3">BridgeData V2 evaluates a goal-conditioned reinforcement learning method (CRL) alongside ACT-style sequence generation, modifying GCBC to represent the policy via a diffusion process trained with the DDPM objective</cite>. 

## Language- and LLM-conditioned Transformers for goals
Multimodal Transformer policies encode linguistic goals alongside visual inputs to align semantics and support language-conditioned control over 6-DOF manipulation and broader task categories, enabling precise goal understanding and execution.<cite id="aa0c1f0f-1">PerAct encodes linguistic goals with a Transformer together with RGB-D voxel observations and integrates voxelized 3D action spaces to learn 6-DOF manipulation; HULC and Σagent use multimodal Transformers for language-conditioned policies, and RT1/RT2/FP2AT integrate Transformers with contrastive learning to improve task performance</cite>. These approaches demonstrate that goal conditioning can come from language rather than pixels alone, and that Transformers excel at cross-modal alignment for robust goal interpretation.<cite id="aa0c1f0f-1">Transformers align linguistic and visual features via multimodal fusion, and contrastive learning strengthens cross-modal connections to improve task execution accuracy and efficiency</cite>. 

## Goal-driven hierarchical and perceptual-action integration
Beyond sequence models, goal-driven frameworks explicitly treat the goal as a semantic anchor that guides both perception (what to look for) and action refinement (how to adjust actions to close the gap to the goal), improving planning and task decomposition for long-horizon tasks.<cite id="aa0c1f0f-4">H-GAR introduces a goal observation as a semantic anchor and integrates it into both observation synthesis and action refinement, contrasting with methods that treat goals as mere constraints or inputs</cite>. Related robotics works learn dynamics conditioned on latent goals and perform backward planning from goal states to improve manipulation, while instruction-following systems combine language instructions with value grounding to guide behavior.<cite id="aa0c1f0f-4">LBP learns dynamics conditioned by latent goals and plans backward from the goal; SayCan combines language instructions with value grounding to guide robotic behavior; PEG encourages goal-driven exploration; hierarchical policies decompose long-horizon tasks into goal-conditioned subtasks</cite>. 

# How to implement goal conditioning with Transformers

- Input encoding: Provide the current observation alongside a goal representation (e.g., target image, language instruction, future imagined scene, or latent goal embedding). Transformers’ self-attention then jointly model observation–goal interactions over time.<cite id="8aa21fbb-1">Images and proprioception are encoded (e.g., ResNet-18), and the CVAE encoder takes current joint position and target action sequence to predict a style latent z for multi-modal demonstrations</cite><cite id="8aa21fbb-3">The CVAE encoder includes a transformer encoder that processes camera pose changes and a sequence of target control commands, outputting a style latent z</cite><cite id="aa0c1f0f-1">PerAct encodes linguistic goals and RGB-D voxel observations with a Transformer to align language and vision for goal-conditioned control</cite>. 

- Latent conditioning with CVAE: Use a Transformer-based CVAE where the encoder conditions on goal-related signals (e.g., target actions or latent goal z) to learn multi-modal action styles, while the decoder generates action chunks; at test time, z is omitted and temporal smoothing replaces aggressive chunk resets.<cite id="8aa21fbb-1">The CVAE encoder predicts mean/variance of a style variable z conditioned on current state and target action sequence; z aids multi-modal demonstration handling and is discarded at test, where temporal ensembling averages overlapping predictions</cite><cite id="8aa21fbb-0">By casting actions as goal states and aggregating across multiple predictions, the approach mitigates compounding errors and out-of-distribution responses</cite>. 

- Decision Transformer with goals: In a DT, augment the state-action-returns-to-go sequence with goal embeddings or future goals as tokens. Train with next-state and reward supervision to learn a conditional policy over trajectories that reach the goal; inference uses autoregressive decoding or beam search conditioned on the goal.<cite id="aa0c1f0f-0">Decision Transformer casts RL as conditional sequence modeling with a Transformer, achieving strong performance on robotics tasks</cite><cite id="aa0c1f0f-2">A multi-goal Decision Transformer enriched with goal objectives and sparse rewards outperforms online RL on an offline multi-task dataset</cite>. 

- Diffusion policies with goals: Model the policy as a conditional diffusion denoiser pθ(a|s,g) where s is the state and g is the goal; training maximizes log-likelihood under a DDPM objective, and sampling explores diverse action chunks consistent with the goal and current context.<cite id="8aa21fbb-1">Diffusion Policy characterizes the visuomotor policy as a conditional denoising diffusion process and leverages stochasticity to generate diverse and adaptable action sequences</cite><cite id="8aa21fbb-3">BridgeData V2 evaluates a diffusion-based GCBC with the DDPM objective alongside ACT-style baselines and a goal-conditioned contrastive RL method</cite>. 

- Temporal smoothing and inference: Regardless of the exact model, apply temporal ensembling/aggregation across overlapping chunk predictions to stabilize execution and reduce jitter, especially when goals or contexts change gradually.<cite id="8aa21fbb-1">ACT uses temporal ensembling with exponential weights over overlapping predictions to obtain a weighted average of actions at each timestep</cite><cite id="8aa21fbb-3">The final output action is derived using temporal ensemble smoothing over predicted action sequences</cite>. 

# Practical techniques and benefits

- Reducing error compounding: By planning several actions at once and smoothing over time, chunking reduces sensitivity to single-step errors and improves long-horizon task performance compared to stepwise policies.<cite id="8aa21fbb-0">Predicting action chunks reduces the effective horizon and mitigates compounding errors; temporal aggregation moderates erroneous single-step choices</cite><cite id="8aa21fbb-3">ACT transforms a stepwise policy π(a_t | o_t) into a chunk policy π(a_t: a_{t+k} | o_t), with the final action derived via temporal ensemble</cite>. 

- Multi-modal and language conditioning: Transformers align visual and linguistic goals, enabling robust goal understanding from sparse or ambiguous observations and supporting zero-shot generalization to new tasks via language instructions.<cite id="aa0c1f0f-1">Transformers align linguistic and visual features through multimodal fusion; contrastive learning strengthens cross-modal connections; language-conditioned policies (PerAct, HULC, Σagent) demonstrate improved execution accuracy and generalization</cite>. 

- Multi-task and hierarchical policies: Language-conditioned FiLM layers and hierarchical goal decomposition allow a single model to adapt to many tasks and plan at multiple abstraction levels, with low-level execution powered by chunked action policies.<cite id="8aa21fbb-4">Multi-Task ACT uses a FiLM network to align language commands with the ACT policy, enabling concurrent manipulation tasks conditioned by language instructions</cite><cite id="aa0c1f0f-4">Hierarchical policies decompose long-horizon tasks into goal-conditioned subtasks using hierarchical policies; goal-conditioned planning improves manipulation performance</cite>. 

- Robustness to out-of-distribution scenes: CVAE latent style and temporal smoothing help maintain reasonable behavior when demonstrations do not cover the exact current scene, by drawing on learned styles and averaging across overlapping predictions.<cite id="8aa21fbb-0">By combining multiple predictions, the approach mitigates unpredictable responses to out-of-distribution states; correct previously predicted actions moderate final choices</cite><cite id="8aa21fbb-1">The style latent z helps deal with multi-modal demonstrations and is used to condition the action decoder during training (discarded at test, where temporal smoothing replaces z)</cite>. 

# Datasets, benchmarks, and reported outcomes

- Robotic manipulation benchmarks commonly evaluate chunked Transformer policies on pick-and-place, bin-picking, and household tasks. ACT and its variants report improved robustness and performance over traditional behavior cloning by reducing error compounding and leveraging multi-modal inputs and temporal smoothing.<cite id="8aa21fbb-2">ACT is designed for complex manipulation (e.g., pick-and-place), using a Transformer backbone to learn long-range dependencies and chunk action sequences for efficient, robust execution</cite><cite id="8aa21fbb-3">In view-planning for harvesting, ACT behavior cloning addresses compounding error and reduces effective decision-making span; the CVAE with Transformer encoder/decoder generates coherent, diverse actions with temporal ensemble at inference</cite>. 

- Datasets like BridgeData V2 and multi-task bimanual household datasets incorporate goal-conditioned baselines (ACT, diffusion, goal-conditioned RL) and multi-goal setups, enabling evaluation of goal-conditioned policies across many tasks and embodiments.<cite id="8aa21fbb-3">BridgeData V2 evaluates ACT-style sequence generation and a goal-conditioned RL method (CRL), with diffusion-based GCBC trained with DDPM</cite><cite id="8aa21fbb-4">A bimanual-mobile manipulation dataset for household tasks discusses ACT, Diffusion Policy, and a language-conditioned MT-ACT variant using FiLM to align language instructions with policy learning</cite>. 

- Decision Transformer evaluations in offline multi-goal robotics show improved performance over online RL with sparse rewards, demonstrating the value of goal-conditioned conditional sequence models for data-efficient planning.<cite id="aa0c1f0f-2">A modified Decision Transformer trained offline with multi-goal objectives and sparse rewards performs better than online RL methods in an open-ended robotic environment</cite>. 

# Design choices and trade-offs

- Chunk size and temporal smoothing: Choose K (chunk length) to balance planning benefit against responsiveness; temporal ensembling/aggregation should weight recent observations heavily while stabilizing long-horizon execution.<cite id="8aa21fbb-1">ACT fixes chunk size K and uses exponential-weighted temporal ensembling across overlapping predictions to obtain a weighted average of actions at each timestep</cite>. 

- Conditioning signals: Pixel-based goals, language instructions, or latent goals each have pros/cons. Pixel-only goals can be noisy; language goals require strong cross-modal alignment; latent goals can compactly encode abstract targets but require generative models (e.g., VAEs, diffusion) to map goals to actions.<cite id="8aa21fbb-1">The CVAE style latent z captures high-level features or styles of observations and action sequences in multi-modal demonstrations</cite><cite id="aa0c1f0f-1">Transformers align linguistic and visual features, and contrastive learning strengthens cross-modal connections for robust goal-conditioned control</cite>. 

- Model class: Transformers offer long-range dependency modeling and natural multi-modal input handling; diffusion models support multi-modal action generation and exploration; Decision Transformers provide a decision-theoretic framing with strong sample efficiency in offline settings.<cite id="8aa21fbb-1">Transformer encoder/decoder CVAE supports multi-modal inputs and temporal dependencies for chunk generation</cite><cite id="8aa21fbb-1">Diffusion policies generate diverse and adaptable action sequences via conditional denoising</cite><cite id="aa0c1f0f-0">Decision Transformer uses a Transformer over state/action/returns-to-go tokens and achieves strong performance on robotics tasks</cite>. 

- Robustness and generalization: CVAE latent style and temporal smoothing improve robustness to OOD scenes; language conditioning and cross-modal contrastive learning improve generalization to unseen tasks; hierarchical goal decomposition supports compositional skills.<cite id="8aa21fbb-0">Temporal aggregation across predictions moderates erroneous actions and improves robustness to OOD states</cite><cite id="aa0c1f0f-1">Contrastive learning and multimodal alignment strengthen cross-modal connections, improving execution accuracy and efficiency across tasks</cite><cite id="aa0c1f0f-4">Hierarchical, goal-conditioned subtask decomposition and goal-driven observation–action refinement improve planning and manipulation</cite>. 

# When to use which approach

- Use ACT-style CVAE+Transformer chunkers when you have demonstrations and want data-efficient behavior cloning with multi-modal inputs and explicit goal-conditioning via latent styles and temporal smoothing.<cite id="8aa21fbb-0">ACT predicts action chunks with a CVAE+Transformer and uses temporal aggregation to mitigate compounding errors and OOD responses</cite><cite id="8aa21fbb-1">The CVAE encoder predicts a style latent conditioned on target action sequences, with z discarded at test and replaced by temporal ensembling</cite>. 

- Use Decision Transformer variants when you can frame control as conditional sequence modeling with returns-to-go and have goal annotations or language instructions; offline RL settings benefit from sparse rewards and goal-conditioned planning.<cite id="aa0c1f0f-0">Decision Transformer models trajectories with a Transformer and achieves strong performance in robotics</cite><cite id="aa0c1f0f-2">Goal-conditioned Decision Transformers trained offline with sparse rewards outperform online RL on multi-goal tasks</cite>. 

- Use diffusion-based policies when you need multi-modal, diverse action exploration consistent with a goal under uncertainty or sparse feedback, especially with long horizons and multiple sub-goals.<cite id="8aa21fbb-1">Diffusion policies model policies as conditional denoising processes to generate diverse and adaptable action sequences</cite><cite id="8aa21fbb-3">Diffusion-based GCBC with DDPM objective is evaluated alongside ACT and goal-conditioned RL on large-scale robotic datasets</cite>. 

- Use language-conditioned Transformers/LLM-integrated agents when goals are specified naturally; these systems leverage cross-modal alignment and pretraining to achieve robust goal interpretation and broad task coverage.<cite id="aa0c1f0f-1">PerAct and related systems encode language goals with Transformers to align with visual inputs for 6-DOF manipulation and broader task categories, supported by contrastive learning for stronger cross-modal ties</cite>. 

# Summary

In goal-conditioned action chunking with Transformers, the policy predicts multi-step actions conditioned on the current observation and a goal (pixel, language, or latent), often via a Transformer-based CVAE or Decision Transformer, and applies temporal smoothing to stabilize execution. This family of methods—exemplified by ACT, goal-conditioned Decision Transformers, diffusion-based policies, and language-conditioned Transformers—consistently reduces error compounding, improves robustness to OOD scenes, and enables efficient long-horizon manipulation across diverse tasks and embodiments.<cite id="8aa21fbb-0">By casting actions as goal states and aggregating across overlapping predictions, ACT mitigates compounding errors and OOD responses</cite><cite id="8aa21fbb-1">Transformer-based CVAE with temporal ensembling predicts action chunks from multi-modal inputs and discards style latent at test, relying on smoothing</cite><cite id="aa0c1f0f-2">Goal-conditioned Decision Transformers in offline settings outperform online RL with sparse rewards on multi-goal robotic tasks</cite><cite id="8aa21fbb-1">Diffusion policies generate diverse and adaptable action sequences conditioned on state and goal</cite><cite id="aa0c1f0f-1">Language- and vision-aligned Transformer policies support robust, instruction-conditioned manipulation across tasks</cite>. </answer>

Snippet: Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) is a behavior cloning algorithm that uses a Conditional Variational Autoencoder (CVAE) to model diverse scenes, combined with a transformer to be able to predict action sequences (chunks) given a multimodal input [17]. By combining multiple predictions, this approach mitigates the problems of compounding errors and unpredictable responses to out-of-distribution states. Although erroneous actions may still be chosen by the model, correct actions, predicted during previous time steps, will provide a moderating influence on the final action. Additionally, the transformer network structure [31] allows for a wide range of multi-model inputs, such as text prompts, further improving the robustness of the ACT framework [32].

Title: Generative Image as Action Models
Snippet: Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) [23] predicts action chunks (or sequences) to reduce the effective horizon of long-horizon tasks. This helps alleviate compounding errors in behaviorcloning when learning from human demonstrations. The chunk size is fixed at length K. Architecture. Images are encoded with a pre-trained ResNet-18 [47]. The vision features from each camera and proprioceptive features are then fed into a conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE). 

The CVAE consists of a BERT-like [95] transformer encoder and decoder. The encoder takes in the current joint position and target action sequence to predict the mean and variance of a style variable z. This style variable z helps in dealing with multi-modal demonstrations. It is only used to condition the action decoder during training and is discarded at test time by zeroing it out. The action decoder is based on DETR [34], and is trained to maximize the log-likelihood of action chunks from human demonstrations using two losses: an action reconstruction loss and a KL regularization term to encourage a Gaussian prior for z.

documents.title: One ACT Play: Single Demonstration Behavior Cloning with Action Chunking Transformers
documents.snippet: Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) is a behavior cloning algorithm that uses a Conditional Variational Autoencoder (CVAE) to model diverse scenes, combined with a transformer to be able to predict action sequences (chunks) given a multimodal input [17]. By casting these actions as goal states for the manipulator to reach, a temporal aggregation method can be used to combine predicted actions from multiple previous time steps through a weighted average. By combining multiple predictions, this approach mitigates the problems of compounding errors and unpredictable responses to out-of-distribution states. Although erroneous actions may still be chosen by the model, correct actions, predicted during previous time steps, will provide a moderating influence on the final action. Additionally, the transformer network structure [31] allows for a wide range of multi-model inputs, such as text prompts, further improving the robustness of the ACT framework [32].

documents.title: Generative Image as Action Models
documents.snippet:
Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) [23] predicts action chunks (or sequences) to reduce the effective horizon of long-horizon tasks. This helps alleviate compounding errors in behaviorcloning when learning from human demonstrations. The chunk size is fixed at length K. Given an observation, the model outputs the next K actions to be executed sequentially. 

Architecture. Images are encoded with a pre-trained ResNet-18 [47]. The vision features from each camera and proprioceptive features are then fed into a conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE). 

The CVAE consists of a BERT-like [95] transformer encoder and decoder. The encoder takes in the current joint position and target action sequence to predict the mean and variance of a style variable z. This style variable z helps in dealing with multi-modal demonstrations. It is only used to condition the action decoder during training and is discarded at test time by zeroing it out. The action decoder is based on DETR [34], and is trained to maximize the log-likelihood of action chunks from human demonstrations using two losses: an action reconstruction loss and a KL regularization term to encourage a Gaussian prior for z. 

Temporal Smoothing. To avoid jerky robot motions, ACT [23] uses temporal ensembling at each timestep. An exponential weighted scheme w i = exp(−m * i) is applied to obtain a weighted average of actions from overlapping predictions across timesteps, where w 0 is the coefficient for the oldest action and m controls the speed for incorporating new observations. 

Our modifications to ACT. We made several modifications to ACT [23] in our implementation to improve data-efficiency and robustness: 

• Data augmentation: we use random-crops [36], color jitters, elastic transforms and Gaussian noise from Torchvision6 . The original ACT [23] does not use any data augmentation. 

• Sliding window sampling: we apply a sliding window along each demonstration trajectory to obtain action chunks. The original ACT [23] samples action chunks sparsely from each trajectory. The sliding-window ensures full data-coverage every epoch. 

• Discrete gripper loss: we use cross entropy loss for gripper open and close actions instead of an L1-loss.

Title: Multi-embodiment Legged Robot Control as a Sequence Modeling Problem
Snippet: Learning-based methods, such as reinforcement learning (RL), have proven effective at solving an increasing number of real-world locomotion tasks [26], [27], [28]. Chen et al. [29] formulate the policy as a function of the current state and the hardware property encoding. However, it either requires the full kinematics information of the robot, or implicitly learns the hardware representation, in which case it is challenging for zero-shot transfer to unseen robots. Schaff et al. [30] maintain a distribution over designs and use RL to maximize expected rewards over the design distribution. Since the policy optimization is still embedded in a controlmorphology co-optimization pipeline, it would be inefficient to update the morphology in the real world. Regarding the morphology as a graph structure, preliminary works also explore this problem through graph neural networks for morphology generalization [31], [32], [33], but none of which is validated in the real world. Concurrently with our work, Feng et al. [34] propose an RL-based general-purpose locomotion controller, GenLoco, using morphology randomization. They validate their controller on three commerciallyavailable robots in the real world. 

Note there are recent works formulating RL as a sequence arXiv:2212.09078v1 [cs.RO] 18 Dec 2022 

modeling problem [35], [36]. Decision Transformer [37], [38], [39] uses state, action, and returns-to-go (sum of future rewards) as tokens in a Transformer model. Trajectory Transformer [40] uses a Transformer model to predict the dynamics of a robot and uses beam search [41] for planning. These Transformer-based approaches have achieved similar or better performances in benchmark tasks compared with classic RL algorithms thanks to the model capacity and the self-attention mechanism. 

In this work, we also take advantage of Transformer models to design a controller for robots with changing morphology. In particular, we present Embodiment-aware Transformer (EAT), an architecture that casts this control problem as conditional sequence modeling.

Title: GPA-RAM: Grasp-Pretraining Augmented Robotic Attention Mamba for Spatial Task Learning
Snippet: The development of Transformer models has evidently enhanced end-to-end methods, particularly in handling multimodal inputs. Relying solely on visual input often falls short in specifying complex task requirements, prompting researchers to integrate language and vision as complementary inputs. Transformers excel at aligning linguistic and visual features, enabling a more comprehensive understanding of tasks through multimodal fusion. Additionally, contrastive learning further enhances performance by strengthening cross-modal connections, improving task execution accuracy and efficiency. This synergy between visual and linguistic information highlights the potential of Transformers in tackling multimodal tasks. 

For instance, PerAct [12] employed a Transformer to encode linguistic goals and RGB-D voxel observations, integrating voxelized 3D action spaces for efficient learning of 6-DOF manipulation tasks. However, the large size of the voxel data slows training. BC-Z [35] addressed the challenge of generalization by enabling robots to adapt to new tasks based on user-provided language or video commands, though its adaptability remains limited. HULC [36] adopted a multimodal Transformer to learn language-conditioned policies from unstructured data. Meanwhile, RVT and RVT2 [15], [16] mitigated the high computational cost of traditional 3D explicit representations (e.g., point clouds) by employing crossview aggregation and virtual re-rendering but failed to focus on fine-grained task manipulation. ARP + [17] integrated an autoregressive architecture for robotic manipulation. The Σagent [37] integrated an MVQ-Former to aggregate language information, enhancing robots' understanding and execution of natural language instructions across multi-task scenarios. Combining Transformers with contrastive learning has become a mainstream approach, as seen in RT1 [38], RT2 [39], and FP2AT [40], further improving task performance. 

However, existing vision-based robot learning methods primarily focus on the overall process of robot manipulation, failing to achieve precise manipulation and grasping. Transformer methods face challenges like quadratic complexity. In contrast, this paper addresses these limitations by adopting a two-tier skill-learning framework and leveraging the strengths of Mamba. This approach enhances the robot's ability to comprehend task skills and generalize more to novel scenarios.

Title: Solving Multi-Goal Robotic Tasks with Decision Transformer
Snippet: The recent advancements in transformer neural network architectures have significantly impacted the reinforcement learning field, including the robotics domain [15], [16]. One of the most recent advancements, the decision transformer, casts the problem of RL as conditional sequence modeling, leveraging modern neural network mechanisms such as attention to provide high-quality decision-making capabilities [17], [18]. The decision transformer proved to work efficiently in domains such as robotics, games, task planning, prompting, [15], [16], [19], [20], [21], [22]. 

However, while all three aspects mentioned-offline reinforcement learning, multi-goal learning, and transformer architecture-are present in robotic research, they have never been coupled together. To fill this gap, we explore the possibility of adopting a transformer for multi-goal problems in robotics domain and offline settings. To achieve this purpose, we first create a dataset for offline reinforcement learning leveraging a Franka Emika Panda robotic environment with multiple tasks. Then, we modify a decision transformer, enriching it with the capability to receive and interpret information about the desired goal. Moreover, we leverage a sparse reward system instead of dense to ensure a high-quality definition of rewards. Finally, we conduct an exhaustive experimental study showcasing that our modified decision transformer can perform better than online reinforcement learning methods. 

The contributions of these paper can be summarized as follows: 

• Extending a decision transformer architecture with the capability to interpret the goal objectives, effectively creating a multi-goal decision transformer able to learn in an offline setting. 

• Devising and publishing a new robotic dataset for offline reinforcement learning. 

• Conducting an extensive experimental evaluation that shows that our approach provides an efficient and robust solution to the problem.

Title: Advances in Transformers for Robotic Applications: A Review
Snippet: Their adaptability and scalability have made them powerful tools in various applications. Initially designed for NLP [144], transformers have been introduced in robotics [165] [163] [147], Signal Processing [145][47] [16], Medical Imaging [5][73] [126][41] [155][40] [56], and many other areas. Transformers have consistently outperformed RNNs and CNNs in various sequence modeling tasks [129]. Since then, innovations such as Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding(BERT) [26], Generative Pre-trained Transformer(GPT) [113] , and Vision Transformers [29] have extended their applicability to robotics. This paper explores the role of transformers in advancing robotic perception, control, and decision making [108]. In robotics, Transformers are being adopted in three major ways: (1) as pre-trained foundation models facilitating Human-Robot Interaction and generalization [98][163] [11][12] [62]. (2) as transformer variants integrated with Deep Reinforcement Learning enhancing long-horizon planning (3) To enhance perception, planning, and control systems. Recent models like Decision Transformer [17] and Trajectory Transformer [52] highlight how Transformers can be applied in robotics, enabling complex task planning and autonomous control in dynamic scenarios [3] [77]. There have been many survey papers covering the use of Transformers as pre-trained foundation models in robotics [163][147] [54][32][45] [63][59] [155]. Some survey papers have covered integration of transformers in RL covering all applications [3][77] [44] , while some have exclusively focused on application in Robotics [90] [160].Our paper gives a broad overview of all the different ways Transformers have been used in Robotics. At the same time, the scope of our paper is narrower than surveys covering various advances in Transformers [137][48] [158][80], in this paper we wish to exclusively focus on applications in robotics. Some Transformer architectures have been tailored for robotic perception, planning, and control, other areas of usage include pre-trained foundation models to specialized variants used in DRL.

Title: H-GAR: A Hierarchical Interaction Framework via Goal-Driven Observation-Action Refinement for Robotic Manipulation
Snippet: Goal-Conditioned Planning for Robotics. Recent works have shown that conditioning for goal states can significantly improve planning (Luo and Du 2024;Bae, Park, and Lee 2024;Gong et al. 2024;Rens 2025;Li et al. 2024cLi et al. , 2025d;;Zhang et al. 2025b;Lyu et al. 2025;Shao et al. 2019;Shen et al. 2024;Chen et al. 2025). LBP (Liu et al. 2025) learns the dynamics conditioned by latent goals and performs backward planning from the goal, improving the manipulation in the simulation. In the real world, SayCan (Brohan et al. 2023) combines language instructions with value grounding to guide robotic behavior, demonstrating strong performance in instruction-following tasks. Hu et al. (Hu et al. 2023) propose Planning Exploratory Goals (PEG) to encourage intrinsic goal-driven exploration, while Li et al. (Li et al. 2022) decompose long-horizon tasks into goalconditioned subtasks using hierarchical policies. Although these approaches leverage goal conditioning to improve efficiency or task decomposition, they often treat goal information as a constraint or policy input, without explicitly incorporating it into the perception-action generation process. 

In contrast, our method introduces a goal observation as a semantic anchor and explicitly integrates it into both observation synthesis and action refinement. 

Future Observation Prediction for Robotic Manipulation. Anticipating future visual observations has proven to be a powerful mechanism for enhancing policy learning in robotics (Hu et al. 2024;Lu et al. 2025;Huang et al. 2025;Zhao et al. 2024;Xu, Qiu, and She 2025;Zhu et al. 2025a;Shao, Wu, and Liu 2023). UWM (Zhu et al. 2025a) integrates action and video diffusion within a unified transformer, enhancing robustness and generalization in imitation learning. UVA (Li et al. 2025a) introduces the unified video action model, which jointly optimizes video and action predictions to achieve high accuracy.

In the real world, SayCan (Brohan et al. 2023) combines language instructions with value grounding to guide robotic behavior, demonstrating strong performance in instruction-following tasks. Hu et al. (Hu et al. 2023) propose Planning Exploratory Goals (PEG) to encourage intrinsic goal-driven exploration, while Li et al. (Li et al. 2022) decompose long-horizon tasks into goalconditioned subtasks using hierarchical policies. Although these approaches leverage goal conditioning to improve efficiency or task decomposition, they often treat goal information as a constraint or policy input, without explicitly incorporating it into the perception-action generation process. 

In contrast, our method introduces a goal observation as a semantic anchor and explicitly integrates it into both observation synthesis and action refinement. 

Future Observation Prediction for Robotic Manipulation. Anticipating future visual observations has proven to be a powerful mechanism for enhancing policy learning in robotics (Hu et al. 2024;Lu et al. 2025;Huang et al. 2025;Zhao et al. 2024;Xu, Qiu, and She 2025;Zhu et al. 2025a;Shao, Wu, and Liu 2023). UWM (Zhu et al. 2025a) integrates action and video diffusion within a unified transformer, enhancing robustness and generalization in imitation learning. UVA (Li et al. 2025a) introduces the unified video action model, which jointly optimizes video and action predictions to achieve high accuracy.

documents.title: Multi-embodiment Legged Robot Control as a Sequence Modeling Problem
documents.snippet:
Learning-based methods, such as reinforcement learning (RL), have proven effective at solving an increasing number of real-world locomotion tasks [26], [27], [28]. Chen et al. [29] formulate the policy as a function of the current state and the hardware property encoding. However, it either requires the full kinematics information of the robot, or implicitly learns the hardware representation, in which case it is challenging for zero-shot transfer to unseen robots. Schaff et al. [30] maintain a distribution over designs and use RL to maximize expected rewards over the design distribution. Since the policy optimization is still embedded in a controlmorphology co-optimization pipeline, it would be inefficient to update the morphology in the real world. Regarding the morphology as a graph structure, preliminary works also explore this problem through graph neural networks for morphology generalization [31], [32], [33], but none of which is validated in the real world. Concurrently with our work, Feng et al. [34] propose an RL-based general-purpose locomotion controller, GenLoco, using morphology randomization. They validate their controller on three commerciallyavailable robots in the real world. 

Note there are recent works formulating RL as a sequence arXiv:2212.09078v1 [cs.RO] 18 Dec 2022 

modeling problem [35], [36]. Decision Transformer [37], [38], [39] uses state, action, and returns-to-go (sum of future rewards) as tokens in a Transformer model. Trajectory Transformer [40] uses a Transformer model to predict the dynamics of a robot and uses beam search [41] for planning. These Transformer-based approaches have achieved similar or better performances in benchmark tasks compared with classic RL algorithms thanks to the model capacity and the self-attention mechanism. 

In this work, we also take advantage of Transformer models to design a controller for robots with changing morphology. In particular, we present Embodiment-aware Transformer (EAT), an architecture that casts this control problem as conditional sequence modeling.

documents.title: GPA-RAM: Grasp-Pretraining Augmented Robotic Attention Mamba for Spatial Task Learning
documents.snippet:
The development of Transformer models has evidently enhanced end-to-end methods, particularly in handling multimodal inputs. Relying solely on visual input often falls short in specifying complex task requirements, prompting researchers to integrate language and vision as complementary inputs. Transformers excel at aligning linguistic and visual features, enabling a more comprehensive understanding of tasks through multimodal fusion. Additionally, contrastive learning further enhances performance by strengthening cross-modal connections, improving task execution accuracy and efficiency. This synergy between visual and linguistic information highlights the potential of Transformers in tackling multimodal tasks. 

For instance, PerAct [12] employed a Transformer to encode linguistic goals and RGB-D voxel observations, integrating voxelized 3D action spaces for efficient learning of 6-DOF manipulation tasks. However, the large size of the voxel data slows training. BC-Z [35] addressed the challenge of generalization by enabling robots to adapt to new tasks based on user-provided language or video commands, though its adaptability remains limited. HULC [36] adopted a multimodal Transformer to learn language-conditioned policies from unstructured data. Meanwhile, RVT and RVT2 [15], [16] mitigated the high computational cost of traditional 3D explicit representations (e.g., point clouds) by employing crossview aggregation and virtual re-rendering but failed to focus on fine-grained task manipulation. ARP + [17] integrated an autoregressive architecture for robotic manipulation. The Σagent [37] integrated an MVQ-Former to aggregate language information, enhancing robots' understanding and execution of natural language instructions across multi-task scenarios. Combining Transformers with contrastive learning has become a mainstream approach, as seen in RT1 [38], RT2 [39], and FP2AT [40], further improving task performance. 

However, existing vision-based robot learning methods primarily focus on the overall process of robot manipulation, failing to achieve precise manipulation and grasping. Transformer methods face challenges like quadratic complexity. In contrast, this paper addresses these limitations by adopting a two-tier skill-learning framework and leveraging the strengths of Mamba. This approach enhances the robot's ability to comprehend task skills and generalize more to novel scenarios.

documents.title: Solving Multi-Goal Robotic Tasks with Decision Transformer
documents.snippet:
The recent advancements in transformer neural network architectures have significantly impacted the reinforcement learning field, including the robotics domain [15], [16]. One of the most recent advancements, the decision transformer, casts the problem of RL as conditional sequence modeling, leveraging modern neural network mechanisms such as attention to provide high-quality decision-making capabilities [17], [18]. The decision transformer proved to work efficiently in domains such as robotics, games, task planning, prompting, [15], [16], [19], [20], [21], [22]. 

However, while all three aspects mentioned-offline reinforcement learning, multi-goal learning, and transformer architecture-are present in robotic research, they have never been coupled together. To fill this gap, we explore the possibility of adopting a transformer for multi-goal problems in robotics domain and offline settings. To achieve this purpose, we first create a dataset for offline reinforcement learning leveraging a Franka Emika Panda robotic environment with multiple tasks. Then, we modify a decision transformer, enriching it with the capability to receive and interpret information about the desired goal. Moreover, we leverage a sparse reward system instead of dense to ensure a high-quality definition of rewards. Finally, we conduct an exhaustive experimental study showcasing that our modified decision transformer can perform better than online reinforcement learning methods. 

The contributions of these paper can be summarized as follows: 

• Extending a decision transformer architecture with the capability to interpret the goal objectives, effectively creating a multi-goal decision transformer able to learn in an offline setting. 

• Devising and publishing a new robotic dataset for offline reinforcement learning. 

• Conducting an extensive experimental evaluation that shows that our approach provides an efficient and robust solution to the problem.

documents.title: Advances in Transformers for Robotic Applications: A Review
documents.snippet: Their adaptability and scalability have made them powerful tools in various applications. Initially designed for NLP [144], transformers have been introduced in robotics [165] [163] [147], Signal Processing [145][47] [16], Medical Imaging [5][73] [126][41] [155][40] [56], and many other areas. Transformers have consistently outperformed RNNs and CNNs in various sequence modeling tasks [129]. Since then, innovations such as Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding(BERT) [26], Generative Pre-trained Transformer(GPT) [113] , and Vision Transformers [29] have extended their applicability to robotics. This paper explores the role of transformers in advancing robotic perception, control, and decision making [108]. In robotics, Transformers are being adopted in three major ways: (1) as pre-trained foundation models facilitating Human-Robot Interaction and generalization [98][163] [11][12] [62]. (2) as transformer variants integrated with Deep Reinforcement Learning enhancing long-horizon planning (3) To enhance perception, planning, and control systems. Recent models like Decision Transformer [17] and Trajectory Transformer [52] highlight how Transformers can be applied in robotics, enabling complex task planning and autonomous control in dynamic scenarios [3] [77]. There have been many survey papers covering the use of Transformers as pre-trained foundation models in robotics [163][147] [54][32][45] [63][59] [155]. Some survey papers have covered integration of transformers in RL covering all applications [3][77] [44] , while some have exclusively focused on application in Robotics [90] [160].Our paper gives a broad overview of all the different ways Transformers have been used in Robotics. At the same time, the scope of our paper is narrower than surveys covering various advances in Transformers [137][48] [158][80], in this paper we wish to exclusively focus on applications in robotics. Some Transformer architectures have been tailored for robotic perception, planning, and control, other areas of usage include pre-trained foundation models to specialized variants used in DRL.

problem: How do people in the field of NLP assess the organization of generated documents?
final_response:
# What “organization” means and why it matters

In NLP, assessing the organization of generated documents typically means evaluating how well a text is structured (e.g., introduction, sections, claims with evidence, transitions, and conclusion), how coherent ideas flow across sentences and sections, and how effectively long-range dependencies and references are maintained across thousands of words.<cite id="62c1bd73-4">Academic manuscripts require sustained coherence across thousands of words, and methods that decompose writing into hierarchical stages (outlining → elaboration → verification) are used to preserve logical connections across sections and maintain factual stability</cite>.<cite id="62c1bd73-0">Recent benchmarks note that many existing evaluations focus on isolated aspects like factuality or citation but do not assess the synthesized information as a whole, limiting their ability to evaluate long-form outputs such as full research reports</cite>.

# Automatic metrics used to assess organization

## Limits of lexical/semantic overlap for organization

Classic overlap-based metrics like BLEU and ROUGE measure lexical n-gram match and soft semantic overlap, but they do not reliably capture discourse coherence or long-range document structure; BERT-based sentence-level metrics correlate with quality but degrade for longer texts and inter-sentence dependencies.<cite id="76e5baaa-0">BLEU/ROUGE and BERT-based metrics fail to properly judge text coherence and are weak at recognizing inter-sentence coherence in long texts; averaging sentence-level scores does not capture document-level dependencies</cite>.<cite id="76e5baaa-1">Automatic metrics like ROUGE and BERTScore often fail to penalize coherence errors in long summaries, motivating better automatic and human evaluation tools</cite>.<cite id="76e5baaa-2">ROUGE remains widely used in summarization but is limited by exact token matching and neglect of semantic relations; quality should be multi-dimensional (relevance, factual consistency, conciseness, semantic coherence)</cite>.

## Discourse- and structure-aware metrics

Document- and discourse-structure metrics explicitly model rhetorical relations and hierarchical organization to better reflect coherence and alignment with reference structure. DiscoTK-based discourse-tree kernels and discourse-aware extensions to MT metrics improved correlation with human judgments by comparing discourse parses and integrating cohesion with rhetorical structure.<cite id="0d9db182-3">Discourse-based evaluation that compares RST discourse trees with subtree kernels improved correlation with human judgments and can be combined with cohesion metrics; discourse similarity has been shown to improve existing evaluation metrics and outperform prior lexical cohesion-only approaches</cite>.

Positional Discourse Divergence (PDD) evaluates how discourse structures align across position bins in long articles, improving agreement with human and GPT-4 coherence judgments across domains (news, long QA, recipes).<cite id="0d9db182-0">PDD partitions sentences into position bins and measures divergence in discourse structure, showing the highest agreement with human evaluations on News Discourse, Long-Form QA, and Recipe1M+, and better alignment with GPT-4 coherence evaluations than existing methods</cite>.<cite id="0d9db182-1">PDD targets long-form generation by capturing discourse divergence; BLEU, ROUGE, and BERTScore cannot effectively capture discourse coherence, and PDD outperforms existing evaluation methods on multiple datasets</cite>. FFCD provides a fast-and-frugal coherence detection approach validated on peer-reviewed manuscript corpora using criteria like clarity to discriminate global discourse quality.<cite id="0d9db182-4">FFCD analyzes long documents (e.g., ACL2017 peer reviews) to assess whether its global coherence measure discriminates discourse quality across clarity-labeled documents</cite>.

## Hierarchical and retrieval-grounded structure metrics for long documents

Beyond reference-based metrics, long-document QA and summarization often assess organization via discourse-aware retrieval and structure-guided evidence selection. Discourse trees and hierarchical retrieval methods evaluate how evidence is organized and retrieved according to semantic groupings, with performance measured by standard QA/retrieval metrics under fixed-length context constraints.<cite id="76e5baaa-4">In long-document QA, hierarchical retrieval constructs semantic trees (e.g., RST-based) and compares methods under F1/Recall or accuracy, with metrics including BLEU, ROUGE, and METEOR under fixed total retrieved length to ensure fairness</cite>.<cite id="76e5baaa-4">Flattening chunking versus discourse-tree structures provides baselines where hierarchical organization of evidence is explicitly compared, and results show benefits of discourse-aware tree structures for retrieval</cite>.

## Document-level structure and outline fidelity

For outline-to-document generation, automatic outline evaluation can capture heading consistency, section boundary alignment, and heading–section coherence. The outline-generation task formalizes three-level coherence (paragraph-to-paragraph, heading–section, and heading-to-heading) and uses hierarchical structured prediction with mechanisms like paragraph dependency, section-aware attention, and heading dependency to improve consistency and reduce duplication, with large-scale datasets for evaluation.<cite id="c55fdad4-0">Outline Generation treats document organization as inherent structure to be recovered by identifying sections and headings, formalizing three-level coherence and using hierarchical structured prediction (HiStGen) with mechanisms for paragraph, heading–section, and heading dependencies on a dataset with 1.75M document–outline pairs</cite>.<cite id="c55fdad4-0">The model improves consistency and eliminates duplication via heading dependencies, reflecting explicit evaluation of organizational structure</cite>.

# Human evaluation protocols for organization

Human protocols often assess coherence, flow, and structure with Likert scales and structured rubrics, but consensus can be hard to reach for longer narratives and multi-dimensional quality. Summarization work shows that 5-point coherence ratings can have low agreement for 500+ word summaries, indicating the need for richer rubrics and multi-aspect scoring.<cite id="76e5baaa-1">A 5-point overall coherence annotation for longer narrative summaries shows much lower agreement than news summaries, highlighting difficulty in consensus on a single scalar for long texts</cite>.<cite id="76e5baaa-2">Quality should be measured multi-dimensionally—relevance, factual consistency, conciseness, and semantic coherence—guiding rubric design for structured evaluations</cite>.

Outline-centric pipelines employ expert or LLM-as-judge rubrics to score organization aspects like instruction following, depth, breadth, balance, support, and insightfulness across iterative outline rounds, demonstrating steady gains that validate the importance of structured outlines.<cite id="c55fdad4-2">Iterative outline optimization increases outline quality scores (e.g., 81.9 → 92.3 on DeepResearch Bench; 77.2 → 88.2 on DeepResearchGym) using LLM-as-a-judge across dimensions like instruction following, depth, breadth, support, and insight</cite>.<cite id="c55fdad4-2">End-to-end ablations show that better-structured outlines drive gains in comprehensiveness, breadth, and support, indicating stronger scaffolding for tightly linking claims to evidence</cite>.

Report-style generation tasks increasingly use structured human rubrics aligned to research-writing criteria (e.g., clarity, evidence support, organization), paired with tool-assisted moderation and multi-speaker perspective balancing to improve coverage and fairness via organized outlines.<cite id="c55fdad4-1">In outline creation for document summarization over multiple speakers, structured outlines improve organization and lead to better coverage and fairness; ablations show that tailored outlines and speaker moderation enhance outline quality</cite>.<cite id="c55fdad4-4">Survey-writing systems explicitly generate structured outlines to ensure comprehensive coverage and logical structuring, then refine sections to maintain a seamless narrative and coherence</cite>.

# Task-based assessments that stress organization

## Long-document QA, summarization, and report-like generation

Benchmarks like LongBench and its variants explicitly evaluate multi-document QA, long-form summarization, and long-context reasoning, which require selecting, structuring, and synthesizing evidence spread across many sources. LongBench-v2 spans multi-file code repositories and multi-document QA, with evaluation under compute-matched budgets showing gains on settings where evidence is diffuse, reflecting the importance of organization for retrieval and integration.<cite id="62c1bd73-1">LongBench-v2 includes multi-file code and multi-document QA, where models must synthesize spans across sources; improvements (e.g., 40.0 → 46.0 on Multi-Document QA) indicate better handling of diffuse evidence and varied context types</cite>.<cite id="62c1bd73-2">Detailed LongBench results show improvements in single/multi-document QA and summarization for methods that emphasize long-context capabilities, underscoring the role of organization in these tasks</cite>. LongCite extends LongBench to long-context citation tasks, requiring long-form responses with fine-grained citations across QA datasets and summarization, which directly tests organized evidence integration and attribution.<cite id="62c1bd73-3">LongBench-Cite curates long-context datasets (e.g., multi-field QA, HotpotQA, DuReader, GovReport) and requires LLMs to generate long-form responses with citations, assessing organization and evidence grounding</cite>.

Report-oriented benchmarks and agents assess organization by simulating research workflows where outlining, section planning, and verification are integral; multi-stage frameworks mirror human progressive drafting to preserve logical flow and cross-section consistency, with academic checklists used for verification.<cite id="62c1bd73-4">A three-phase hierarchical documentation process—structural outlining, template-guided elaboration, and hierarchical verification—addresses LLM limitations in cross-reference consistency and factual stability over long outputs</cite>.<cite id="62c1bd73-0">ReportBench-style evaluations highlight that existing benchmarks miss holistic assessment of synthesized long-form reports, motivating integrated measures beyond factuality and citation</cite>.

## Long-context reasoning and discourse-aware evaluation

Long-context studies evaluate organization by measuring how well models locate and compose evidence across long documents, and by using discourse-aware retrieval and evaluation protocols. Work on long-context reasoning shows consistent gains on multi-hop QA and comprehension when using discourse-aware strategies, indicating better organization of retrieved evidence and passage-level coherence.<cite id="62c1bd73-1">ZeroScrolls groups tasks into multi-hop reasoning, long-form summarization, and long-passage comprehension, with consistent gains from test-time training across these settings</cite>.<cite id="76e5baaa-4">Discourse-tree-based retrieval evaluates how evidence is organized and retrieved, comparing hierarchical vs. flattened chunking and reporting standard QA and summarization metrics under fixed-length context constraints</cite>.

# Practical evaluation workflows in NLP

- Use lexical/overlap metrics (ROUGE variants) for surface coverage and reference alignment, but supplement them with discourse/structure metrics for coherence and organization (e.g., PDD, FFCD, discourse-tree kernels) and with human rubrics for multi-dimensional quality (relevance, factual consistency, conciseness, coherence).<cite id="76e5baaa-2">ROUGE is standard but limited; quality should be multi-dimensional including semantic coherence</cite>.<cite id="0d9db182-0">PDD aligns better with human coherence judgments across long-document domains and captures positional discourse structure</cite>.<cite id="0d9db182-3">Discourse-tree comparisons improve correlation with human judgments, integrating cohesion and rhetorical structure</cite>.

- For outline-guided generation, evaluate outline quality and heading consistency (three-level coherence) and track how improvements in outlines translate to better section-level writing and overall document coherence; LLM-as-judge rubrics and domain expert annotations can operationalize organization dimensions like breadth, depth, balance, and support.<cite id="c55fdad4-0">Outline Generation formalizes and measures heading–section and heading–heading coherence, improving consistency and reducing duplication</cite>.<cite id="c55fdad4-2">Iterative outline optimization increases LLM-judged outline quality and yields end-to-end gains in comprehensiveness, breadth, and support, validating structured scaffolding</cite>.

- In long-document QA and summarization, assess organization via discourse-aware retrieval and structure-guided evidence selection, measuring how well evidence is grouped, ranked, and presented under constraints; compare hierarchical vs. flat chunking baselines to isolate gains from discourse organization of evidence.<cite id="76e5baaa-4">Hierarchical discourse-aware retrieval constructs semantic trees and compares methods with standard QA and summarization metrics under fixed-length context, showing benefits of structured evidence organization</cite>.<cite id="76e5baaa-4">Flattening strategies versus discourse trees provide clear baselines for organizational effectiveness</cite>.

- For report-like generation, incorporate structured planning and verification (outlines, checklists), and use domain rubrics and citation-grounded evaluation (e.g., LongCite) to ensure claims are well-supported and organized around clear sectioning and argumentation.<cite id="62c1bd73-3">LongCite requires long-form responses with fine-grained citations across multi-document QA and summarization datasets, testing organized evidence integration</cite>.<cite id="62c1bd73-4">Multi-stage outlining and verification help preserve logical connections across sections and maintain factual integrity in long-form documents</cite>.

# Open challenges and trade-offs

Researchers consistently note that automatic metrics still struggle with long-range coherence and alignment to abstract organizational schemas, and human annotation is time-consuming and can have lower agreement for long narratives; thus, hybrid pipelines combining structured planning, discourse-aware retrieval, and multi-rater rubrics are emerging as best practice.<cite id="76e5baaa-0">BERT-based and other sentence-level metrics are weak for document-level coherence; averaging or concatenation approaches miss inter-sentence dependencies</cite>.<cite id="76e5baaa-1">Coherence Likert annotations for long narratives show low agreement, suggesting limits of single-number judgments and the need for richer evaluation</cite>.<cite id="76e5baaa-2">Summarization quality requires multi-dimensional assessment beyond lexical overlap to capture coherence and support</cite>.<cite id="c55fdad4-2">Iterative outline optimization and LLM-as-judge rubrics provide structured, incremental assessment of organization and support, but require additional compute and human-in-the-loop steps</cite>.

# Summary

In practice, NLP researchers assess document organization with a layered toolkit: (1) task-based evaluations that require structured integration of evidence (LongBench family, LongCite, multi-hop QA and long-form summarization), (2) automatic discourse and structure metrics that go beyond lexical overlap (discourse-tree kernels, PDD, FFCD, hierarchical retrieval coherence), and (3) human-centered protocols and structured rubrics (coherence Likert scales, multi-dimensional rubrics, LLM-as-judge outline scoring) to capture coherence, coverage, balance, and support across sections and claims.<cite id="62c1bd73-1">LongBench-v2 and related long-context suites evaluate multi-document QA and long-form synthesis where organization is central</cite>.<cite id="62c1bd73-3">LongCite adds citation-grounded long-form evaluation that stresses organized evidence integration</cite>.<cite id="0d9db182-0">PDD and related structure metrics better align with human coherence judgments in long documents</cite>.<cite id="76e5baaa-1">Human coherence annotation remains challenging for long texts, motivating richer rubrics and hybrid evaluation</cite>.<cite id="c55fdad4-0">Outline-centric methods formalize and measure heading and section coherence as part of document organization</cite>.<cite id="62c1bd73-4">Structured, multi-stage writing pipelines with verification aim to preserve logical flow and cross-section consistency in long-form generation</cite>.

Title: AI-Researcher: Autonomous Scientific Innovation
Snippet: Overcoming Document-Scale Coherence Challenges. Academic manuscripts require sustained coherence across thousands of words-a significant challenge for LLMs that typically struggle with cross-reference consistency and factual stability over extended outputs. Analyzing how researchers draft papers progressively from outlines to full texts and inspired by [17], we developed a multi-stage generation framework that mirrors this hierarchical approach. This methodology systematically overcomes LLM limitations by decomposing the complex writing task into manageable components while preserving logical connections across sections and maintaining factual integrity throughout the document. 

Three-Phase Hierarchical Documentation. Our writing approach employs a systematic three-stage process: (1) Synthesizing Research Artifacts: structural outlining based on domain-appropriate templates that establish section hierarchies and logical flow; (2) Template-Guided Structure: methodical content elaboration that develops explanations maintaining cross-document consistency; and (3) Hierarchical Documentation Process: systematic verification using specialized academic checklists that identify and remediate inaccuracies or omissions. This "one more step" review process enhances factual integrity and completeness, ensuring manuscripts meet publication standards without the hallucinations and inconsistencies that typically plague LLM-generated long-form content.

Snippet: Evaluation Metrics. Traditional metrics such as BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002) and ROUGE (Lin, 2004) measure lexical n-gram overlap between a hypothesis and a human reference. As they fail to measure semantic similarity in the absence of lexical overlap, several metrics have been proposed to overcome this issue, which carry out soft lexical matching with static word embeddings (Ng and Abrecht, 2015) and synonym matching (Lavie and Agarwal, 2007). However, none of those metrics can properly judge text coherence (Kryscinski et al., 2019;Zhu and Bhat, 2020).

Recently, a class of novel metrics based on BERT (Devlin et al., 2019) has received a surge of attention, as they correlate strongly with human judgment of text quality in both reference-based and reference-free scenarios (Zhao et al., 2019;Zhang et al., 2020;Sellam et al., 2020;Rei et al., 2020;Gao et al., 2020;Thompson and Post, 2020;Zhao et al., 2020;Pu et al., 2021;Chen et al., 2021). While strong at sentence-level, these metrics are weak in recognizing coherence in inter-sentence contexts (just like BLEU and ROUGE), as BERT and the majority of BERT variants 2 that these metrics build on only capture discourse phenomena to a certain extent (Koto et al., 2021;Laban et al., 2021;Beyer et al., 2021). Thus, they are not suitable for evaluating long texts as in document-level MT evaluation. Works that either (i) average sentencelevel evaluation scores as document score or (ii) assign a score to the concatenation of sentences within a document (Xiong et al., 2019;Liu et al., 2020;Saunders et al., 2020) do not factor interdependence between sentences into a document score, e.g., do not explicitly punish incoherent elements, thus are also inadequate.

Title: Outline Generation: Understanding the Inherent Content Structure of Documents
Snippet: In this paper, we introduce and tackle the Outline Generation (OG) task, which aims to unveil the inherent content structure of a multi-paragraph document by identifying its potential sections and generating the corresponding section headings. Without loss of generality, the OG task can be viewed as a novel structured summarization task. To generate a sound outline, an ideal OG model should be able to capture three levels of coherence, namely the coherence between context paragraphs, that between a section and its heading, and that between context headings. The first one is the foundation for section identification, while the latter two are critical for consistent heading generation. In this work, we formulate the OG task as a hierarchical structured prediction problem, i.e., to first predict a sequence of section boundaries and then a sequence of section headings accordingly. We propose a novel hierarchical structured neural generation model, named HiStGen, for the task. Our model attempts to capture the three-level coherence via the following ways. First, we introduce a Markov paragraph dependency mechanism between context paragraphs for section identification. Second, we employ a section-aware attention mechanism to ensure the semantic coherence between a section and its heading. Finally, we leverage a Markov heading dependency mechanism and a review mechanism between context headings to improve the consistency and eliminate duplication between section headings. Besides, we build a novel Wriptsize IKI OG dataset, a public collection which consists of over 1.75 million document-outline pairs for research on the OG task. Experimental results on our benchmark dataset demonstrate that our model can significantly outperform several state-of-the-art sequential generation models for the OG task.
