# What “organization” means and why it matters

In NLP, assessing the organization of generated documents typically means evaluating how well a text is structured (e.g., introduction, sections, claims with evidence, transitions, and conclusion), how coherent ideas flow across sentences and sections, and how effectively long-range dependencies and references are maintained across thousands of words.<cite id="62c1bd73-4">Academic manuscripts require sustained coherence across thousands of words, and methods that decompose writing into hierarchical stages (outlining → elaboration → verification) are used to preserve logical connections across sections and maintain factual stability</cite>.<cite id="62c1bd73-0">Recent benchmarks note that many existing evaluations focus on isolated aspects like factuality or citation but do not assess the synthesized information as a whole, limiting their ability to evaluate long-form outputs such as full research reports</cite>.

# Automatic metrics used to assess organization

## Limits of lexical/semantic overlap for organization

Classic overlap-based metrics like BLEU and ROUGE measure lexical n-gram match and soft semantic overlap, but they do not reliably capture discourse coherence or long-range document structure; BERT-based sentence-level metrics correlate with quality but degrade for longer texts and inter-sentence dependencies.<cite id="76e5baaa-0">BLEU/ROUGE and BERT-based metrics fail to properly judge text coherence and are weak at recognizing inter-sentence coherence in long texts; averaging sentence-level scores does not capture document-level dependencies</cite>.<cite id="76e5baaa-1">Automatic metrics like ROUGE and BERTScore often fail to penalize coherence errors in long summaries, motivating better automatic and human evaluation tools</cite>.<cite id="76e5baaa-2">ROUGE remains widely used in summarization but is limited by exact token matching and neglect of semantic relations; quality should be multi-dimensional (relevance, factual consistency, conciseness, semantic coherence)</cite>.

## Discourse- and structure-aware metrics

Document- and discourse-structure metrics explicitly model rhetorical relations and hierarchical organization to better reflect coherence and alignment with reference structure. DiscoTK-based discourse-tree kernels and discourse-aware extensions to MT metrics improved correlation with human judgments by comparing discourse parses and integrating cohesion with rhetorical structure.<cite id="0d9db182-3">Discourse-based evaluation that compares RST discourse trees with subtree kernels improved correlation with human judgments and can be combined with cohesion metrics; discourse similarity has been shown to improve existing evaluation metrics and outperform prior lexical cohesion-only approaches</cite>.

Positional Discourse Divergence (PDD) evaluates how discourse structures align across position bins in long articles, improving agreement with human and GPT-4 coherence judgments across domains (news, long QA, recipes).<cite id="0d9db182-0">PDD partitions sentences into position bins and measures divergence in discourse structure, showing the highest agreement with human evaluations on News Discourse, Long-Form QA, and Recipe1M+, and better alignment with GPT-4 coherence evaluations than existing methods</cite>.<cite id="0d9db182-1">PDD targets long-form generation by capturing discourse divergence; BLEU, ROUGE, and BERTScore cannot effectively capture discourse coherence, and PDD outperforms existing evaluation methods on multiple datasets</cite>. FFCD provides a fast-and-frugal coherence detection approach validated on peer-reviewed manuscript corpora using criteria like clarity to discriminate global discourse quality.<cite id="0d9db182-4">FFCD analyzes long documents (e.g., ACL2017 peer reviews) to assess whether its global coherence measure discriminates discourse quality across clarity-labeled documents</cite>.

## Hierarchical and retrieval-grounded structure metrics for long documents

Beyond reference-based metrics, long-document QA and summarization often assess organization via discourse-aware retrieval and structure-guided evidence selection. Discourse trees and hierarchical retrieval methods evaluate how evidence is organized and retrieved according to semantic groupings, with performance measured by standard QA/retrieval metrics under fixed-length context constraints.<cite id="76e5baaa-4">In long-document QA, hierarchical retrieval constructs semantic trees (e.g., RST-based) and compares methods under F1/Recall or accuracy, with metrics including BLEU, ROUGE, and METEOR under fixed total retrieved length to ensure fairness</cite>.<cite id="76e5baaa-4">Flattening chunking versus discourse-tree structures provides baselines where hierarchical organization of evidence is explicitly compared, and results show benefits of discourse-aware tree structures for retrieval</cite>.

## Document-level structure and outline fidelity

For outline-to-document generation, automatic outline evaluation can capture heading consistency, section boundary alignment, and heading–section coherence. The outline-generation task formalizes three-level coherence (paragraph-to-paragraph, heading–section, and heading-to-heading) and uses hierarchical structured prediction with mechanisms like paragraph dependency, section-aware attention, and heading dependency to improve consistency and reduce duplication, with large-scale datasets for evaluation.<cite id="c55fdad4-0">Outline Generation treats document organization as inherent structure to be recovered by identifying sections and headings, formalizing three-level coherence and using hierarchical structured prediction (HiStGen) with mechanisms for paragraph, heading–section, and heading dependencies on a dataset with 1.75M document–outline pairs</cite>.<cite id="c55fdad4-0">The model improves consistency and eliminates duplication via heading dependencies, reflecting explicit evaluation of organizational structure</cite>.

# Human evaluation protocols for organization

Human protocols often assess coherence, flow, and structure with Likert scales and structured rubrics, but consensus can be hard to reach for longer narratives and multi-dimensional quality. Summarization work shows that 5-point coherence ratings can have low agreement for 500+ word summaries, indicating the need for richer rubrics and multi-aspect scoring.<cite id="76e5baaa-1">A 5-point overall coherence annotation for longer narrative summaries shows much lower agreement than news summaries, highlighting difficulty in consensus on a single scalar for long texts</cite>.<cite id="76e5baaa-2">Quality should be measured multi-dimensionally—relevance, factual consistency, conciseness, and semantic coherence—guiding rubric design for structured evaluations</cite>.

Outline-centric pipelines employ expert or LLM-as-judge rubrics to score organization aspects like instruction following, depth, breadth, balance, support, and insightfulness across iterative outline rounds, demonstrating steady gains that validate the importance of structured outlines.<cite id="c55fdad4-2">Iterative outline optimization increases outline quality scores (e.g., 81.9 → 92.3 on DeepResearch Bench; 77.2 → 88.2 on DeepResearchGym) using LLM-as-a-judge across dimensions like instruction following, depth, breadth, support, and insight</cite>.<cite id="c55fdad4-2">End-to-end ablations show that better-structured outlines drive gains in comprehensiveness, breadth, and support, indicating stronger scaffolding for tightly linking claims to evidence</cite>.

Report-style generation tasks increasingly use structured human rubrics aligned to research-writing criteria (e.g., clarity, evidence support, organization), paired with tool-assisted moderation and multi-speaker perspective balancing to improve coverage and fairness via organized outlines.<cite id="c55fdad4-1">In outline creation for document summarization over multiple speakers, structured outlines improve organization and lead to better coverage and fairness; ablations show that tailored outlines and speaker moderation enhance outline quality</cite>.<cite id="c55fdad4-4">Survey-writing systems explicitly generate structured outlines to ensure comprehensive coverage and logical structuring, then refine sections to maintain a seamless narrative and coherence</cite>.

# Task-based assessments that stress organization

## Long-document QA, summarization, and report-like generation

Benchmarks like LongBench and its variants explicitly evaluate multi-document QA, long-form summarization, and long-context reasoning, which require selecting, structuring, and synthesizing evidence spread across many sources. LongBench-v2 spans multi-file code repositories and multi-document QA, with evaluation under compute-matched budgets showing gains on settings where evidence is diffuse, reflecting the importance of organization for retrieval and integration.<cite id="62c1bd73-1">LongBench-v2 includes multi-file code and multi-document QA, where models must synthesize spans across sources; improvements (e.g., 40.0 → 46.0 on Multi-Document QA) indicate better handling of diffuse evidence and varied context types</cite>.<cite id="62c1bd73-2">Detailed LongBench results show improvements in single/multi-document QA and summarization for methods that emphasize long-context capabilities, underscoring the role of organization in these tasks</cite>. LongCite extends LongBench to long-context citation tasks, requiring long-form responses with fine-grained citations across QA datasets and summarization, which directly tests organized evidence integration and attribution.<cite id="62c1bd73-3">LongBench-Cite curates long-context datasets (e.g., multi-field QA, HotpotQA, DuReader, GovReport) and requires LLMs to generate long-form responses with citations, assessing organization and evidence grounding</cite>.

Report-oriented benchmarks and agents assess organization by simulating research workflows where outlining, section planning, and verification are integral; multi-stage frameworks mirror human progressive drafting to preserve logical flow and cross-section consistency, with academic checklists used for verification.<cite id="62c1bd73-4">A three-phase hierarchical documentation process—structural outlining, template-guided elaboration, and hierarchical verification—addresses LLM limitations in cross-reference consistency and factual stability over long outputs</cite>.<cite id="62c1bd73-0">ReportBench-style evaluations highlight that existing benchmarks miss holistic assessment of synthesized long-form reports, motivating integrated measures beyond factuality and citation</cite>.

## Long-context reasoning and discourse-aware evaluation

Long-context studies evaluate organization by measuring how well models locate and compose evidence across long documents, and by using discourse-aware retrieval and evaluation protocols. Work on long-context reasoning shows consistent gains on multi-hop QA and comprehension when using discourse-aware strategies, indicating better organization of retrieved evidence and passage-level coherence.<cite id="62c1bd73-1">ZeroScrolls groups tasks into multi-hop reasoning, long-form summarization, and long-passage comprehension, with consistent gains from test-time training across these settings</cite>.<cite id="76e5baaa-4">Discourse-tree-based retrieval evaluates how evidence is organized and retrieved, comparing hierarchical vs. flattened chunking and reporting standard QA and summarization metrics under fixed-length context constraints</cite>.

# Practical evaluation workflows in NLP

- Use lexical/overlap metrics (ROUGE variants) for surface coverage and reference alignment, but supplement them with discourse/structure metrics for coherence and organization (e.g., PDD, FFCD, discourse-tree kernels) and with human rubrics for multi-dimensional quality (relevance, factual consistency, conciseness, coherence).<cite id="76e5baaa-2">ROUGE is standard but limited; quality should be multi-dimensional including semantic coherence</cite>.<cite id="0d9db182-0">PDD aligns better with human coherence judgments across long-document domains and captures positional discourse structure</cite>.<cite id="0d9db182-3">Discourse-tree comparisons improve correlation with human judgments, integrating cohesion and rhetorical structure</cite>.

- For outline-guided generation, evaluate outline quality and heading consistency (three-level coherence) and track how improvements in outlines translate to better section-level writing and overall document coherence; LLM-as-judge rubrics and domain expert annotations can operationalize organization dimensions like breadth, depth, balance, and support.<cite id="c55fdad4-0">Outline Generation formalizes and measures heading–section and heading–heading coherence, improving consistency and reducing duplication</cite>.<cite id="c55fdad4-2">Iterative outline optimization increases LLM-judged outline quality and yields end-to-end gains in comprehensiveness, breadth, and support, validating structured scaffolding</cite>.

- In long-document QA and summarization, assess organization via discourse-aware retrieval and structure-guided evidence selection, measuring how well evidence is grouped, ranked, and presented under constraints; compare hierarchical vs. flat chunking baselines to isolate gains from discourse organization of evidence.<cite id="76e5baaa-4">Hierarchical discourse-aware retrieval constructs semantic trees and compares methods with standard QA and summarization metrics under fixed-length context, showing benefits of structured evidence organization</cite>.<cite id="76e5baaa-4">Flattening strategies versus discourse trees provide clear baselines for organizational effectiveness</cite>.

- For report-like generation, incorporate structured planning and verification (outlines, checklists), and use domain rubrics and citation-grounded evaluation (e.g., LongCite) to ensure claims are well-supported and organized around clear sectioning and argumentation.<cite id="62c1bd73-3">LongCite requires long-form responses with fine-grained citations across multi-document QA and summarization datasets, testing organized evidence integration</cite>.<cite id="62c1bd73-4">Multi-stage outlining and verification help preserve logical connections across sections and maintain factual integrity in long-form documents</cite>.

# Open challenges and trade-offs

Researchers consistently note that automatic metrics still struggle with long-range coherence and alignment to abstract organizational schemas, and human annotation is time-consuming and can have lower agreement for long narratives; thus, hybrid pipelines combining structured planning, discourse-aware retrieval, and multi-rater rubrics are emerging as best practice.<cite id="76e5baaa-0">BERT-based and other sentence-level metrics are weak for document-level coherence; averaging or concatenation approaches miss inter-sentence dependencies</cite>.<cite id="76e5baaa-1">Coherence Likert annotations for long narratives show low agreement, suggesting limits of single-number judgments and the need for richer evaluation</cite>.<cite id="76e5baaa-2">Summarization quality requires multi-dimensional assessment beyond lexical overlap to capture coherence and support</cite>.<cite id="c55fdad4-2">Iterative outline optimization and LLM-as-judge rubrics provide structured, incremental assessment of organization and support, but require additional compute and human-in-the-loop steps</cite>.

# Summary

In practice, NLP researchers assess document organization with a layered toolkit: (1) task-based evaluations that require structured integration of evidence (LongBench family, LongCite, multi-hop QA and long-form summarization), (2) automatic discourse and structure metrics that go beyond lexical overlap (discourse-tree kernels, PDD, FFCD, hierarchical retrieval coherence), and (3) human-centered protocols and structured rubrics (coherence Likert scales, multi-dimensional rubrics, LLM-as-judge outline scoring) to capture coherence, coverage, balance, and support across sections and claims.<cite id="62c1bd73-1">LongBench-v2 and related long-context suites evaluate multi-document QA and long-form synthesis where organization is central</cite>.<cite id="62c1bd73-3">LongCite adds citation-grounded long-form evaluation that stresses organized evidence integration</cite>.<cite id="0d9db182-0">PDD and related structure metrics better align with human coherence judgments in long documents</cite>.<cite id="76e5baaa-1">Human coherence annotation remains challenging for long texts, motivating richer rubrics and hybrid evaluation</cite>.<cite id="c55fdad4-0">Outline-centric methods formalize and measure heading and section coherence as part of document organization</cite>.<cite id="62c1bd73-4">Structured, multi-stage writing pipelines with verification aim to preserve logical flow and cross-section consistency in long-form generation</cite>.

With the rapid advancement of information synthesis research, the evaluation of long-form reports has become increasingly important. Existing evaluation benchmarks focus primarily on individual aspects such as fact checking, citation judgment, or overall writing quality. Although these benchmarks can assess the quality of the report to some extent, several limitations remain unaddressed. 

Fact Checking Evaluation Driven by efforts from both academia and industry, automated fact checking has evolved into a well-established multistage pipeline, which has become the dominant research paradigm in the field Eldifrawi et al. (2024). Claim detection aims to identify factual statements worth verifying from large volumes of text Guo et al. ( 2022); Panchendrarajan & Zubiaga (2024), while evidence retrieval focuses on retrieving relevant documents or textual snippets that support or refute a given claim Eldifrawi et al. (2024); Nanhekhan et al. (2025). Building on this pipeline, several benchmarks have been proposed to evaluate the performance of fact checking in both the general domain Thorne et al. (2018); Ma et al. (2024) and the scientific domain Wadden et al. (2020;2022); Ho et al. (2025). However, these benchmarks focus solely on fact-checking components, rather than Preprint evaluating the synthesized information as a whole, limiting their ability to assess recent long-form output from large language models (LLMs), such as full research reports.

Title: Let's (not) just put things in Context: Test-Time Training for Long-Context LLMs
Snippet: LongBench-v2. LongBench-v2 (Bai et al., 2023b)   questions across a variety of context types: given multi-file project trees in the Code Repositories setting, to resolve arguments of a particular function; and given the context as a set of related documents in the Multi-Document QA setting, synthesize spans across sources to answer a question. This allows us to assess the applicability of qTTT across forms of input contexts. 

Figure 4 shows that, under compute-matched budgets, qTTT delivers consistent and often substantial gains across model sizes. On Long Dialogue History and Multi-Document QA, where evidence is most diffuse, qTTT outperforms standard in-context and thinking by wide margins (e.g., for Qwen3-4B: 30.8 → 43.6 on Long Dialogue History; 40.0 → 46.0 on Multi-Document QA). In Code Repositories, qTTT scales especially well with model size (for Qwen3-8B: 30.0 → 44.0 → 52.0). Overall, the LongBench-v2 results indicate that qTTT fares well across markedly different context types. 

ZeroScrolls. ZeroScrolls (Shaham et al., 2023) evaluates long-context reasoning across diverse tasks. We group the datasets into three categories: (i) Multi-hop reasoning (MuSiQue, QASPER, NarrativeQA), which require locating and composing evidence spread across long documents; (ii) Long-form summarization (GovReport, QMSum, SQuALITY), which emphasize distilling lengthy inputs; and (iii) Long-passage comprehension (QAuLITY), which measures multiple-choice accuracy over extended contexts. In contrast to LongBench-v2, this suite of tests evaluates the ability to utilize some long context to solve a variety of different tasks. 

Figure 9 shows that qTTT consistently outperforms vanilla thinking on multi-hop QA and comprehension tasks, with gains that strengthen with model size.

Title: LongCite: Enabling LLMs to Generate Fine-grained Citations in Long-context QA
Snippet: To evaluate LLMs' performance on LQAC task, we curate a new benchmark LongBench-Cite by collecting data from existing bilingual long-context benchmarks LongBench (Bai et al., 2023) and LongBench-Chat (Bai et al., 2024), covering multiple key user-intensive tasks in both English and Chinese. Specifically, LongBench is a comprehensive benchmark with an average length of 7k words (English) and 13k characters (Chinese), and we select two single-doc QA datasets MultiFieldQA-en/zh (Bai et al., 2023), two multi-doc QA datasets HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018) and DuReader (He et al., 2018), and one summarization dataset GovReport (Huang et al., 2021) from it. LongBench-Chat comprises 50 real-world queries with long contexts ranging from 10k to 100k in length, covering various scenarios such as document QA, summarization, and coding, and we adopt all the queries. The detailed data statistics are listed in Table 1. For all datasets, we require LLMs to generate long-form responses with citations.

Title: AI-Researcher: Autonomous Scientific Innovation
Snippet: Overcoming Document-Scale Coherence Challenges. Academic manuscripts require sustained coherence across thousands of words-a significant challenge for LLMs that typically struggle with cross-reference consistency and factual stability over extended outputs. Analyzing how researchers draft papers progressively from outlines to full texts and inspired by [17], we developed a multi-stage generation framework that mirrors this hierarchical approach. This methodology systematically overcomes LLM limitations by decomposing the complex writing task into manageable components while preserving logical connections across sections and maintaining factual integrity throughout the document. 

Three-Phase Hierarchical Documentation. Our writing approach employs a systematic three-stage process: (1) Synthesizing Research Artifacts: structural outlining based on domain-appropriate templates that establish section hierarchies and logical flow; (2) Template-Guided Structure: methodical content elaboration that develops explanations maintaining cross-document consistency; and (3) Hierarchical Documentation Process: systematic verification using specialized academic checklists that identify and remediate inaccuracies or omissions. This "one more step" review process enhances factual integrity and completeness, ensuring manuscripts meet publication standards without the hallucinations and inconsistencies that typically plague LLM-generated long-form content.

documents.title: AI-Researcher: Autonomous Scientific Innovation
documents.snippet:
Overcoming Document-Scale Coherence Challenges. Academic manuscripts require sustained coherence across thousands of words-a significant challenge for LLMs that typically struggle with cross-reference consistency and factual stability over extended outputs. Analyzing how researchers draft papers progressively from outlines to full texts and inspired by [17], we developed a multi-stage generation framework that mirrors this hierarchical approach. This methodology systematically overcomes LLM limitations by decomposing the complex writing task into manageable components while preserving logical connections across sections and maintaining factual integrity throughout the document. 

Three-Phase Hierarchical Documentation. Our writing approach employs a systematic three-stage process: (1) Synthesizing Research Artifacts: structural outlining based on domain-appropriate templates that establish section hierarchies and logical flow; (2) Template-Guided Structure: methodical content elaboration that develops explanations maintaining cross-document consistency; and (3) Hierarchical Documentation Process: systematic verification using specialized academic checklists that identify and remediate inaccuracies or omissions. This "one more step" review process enhances factual integrity and completeness, ensuring manuscripts meet publication standards without the hallucinations and inconsistencies that typically plague LLM-generated long-form content.

Title: SNaC: Coherence Error Detection for Narrative Summarization
Snippet: Summary-level Likert scale annotations are the most commonly used setup for collecting coherence in single-document news summarization research (Fabbri et al., 2021). Here, we run an analogous study for our longer narrative summaries. We ask 3 Mechanical Turk workers with prior experience in annotation for NLP tasks, specifically discourse analysis and text simplification, to rate the overall coherence of 100 generated summaries on a 5-point scale. Table 1 reports the observed agreement, measured by Kripendorff's α. Compared to newswire summaries collected under a similar setup (Fabbri et al., 2021), annotations for longer narratives have a much lower agreement. This shows the difficulty in obtaining a consensus on coherence for a 500+ word summary through a single value on a 5-point scale. 

In Appendix B, we further show that automatic metrics like ROUGE and BERTScore (Zhang et al., 2019) that are primarily used for evaluating long document summarization fail to penalize coherence errors in summaries. Better tools for both automatic and human evaluation are needed.

Title: An Empirical Survey on Long Document Summarization: Datasets, Models, and Metrics
Snippet: As evaluating generated summary outputs using manual efforts are costly and impractical, the efficient ROUGE metric [70] has long been the standard way of comparing summarization model performance. It measures the lexical overlap between reference and candidate summary and the common n-gram measures are unigram (ROUGE-1), bigram (ROUGE-2) and longest common sub-sequence (ROUGE-L). However, as it is based on exact token matches and overlap between synonymous tokens or phrases will be ignored, the limitation of ROUGE score metrics have been widely explored [3,11,44,61] and many have also attempted to propose more comprehensive content overlap metrics using soft semantic overlap [33,130]. Further, while content overlap is the fundamental objective of summarization, the quality of a summary, as Gehrmann et al. [36] and Peyrard [92] suggested, should be measured in a multi-dimensional way including relevance, factual consistency, conciseness and semantic coherence. Relevance refers to whether the candidate summary contains the main ideas. Factual consistency metric measures whether a candidate summary is factually consistent with the source document. Conciseness measure whether important information is encapsulated in a short and brief manner. Semantic coherence relates to the collective quality and fluency of summary sentences. Based on these quality aspects, the following discusses the research efforts in the wider summarization domain with a focus on the long document summarization research settings at the end of this section.

Snippet: Datasets and Evaluation Metrics. We evaluate our approach on three challenging long document QA datasets: QASPER (Dasigi et al., 2021) for research paper understanding (averaging 4170 words), QuALITY (Pang et al., 2022) for long-form reading comprehension (averaging 5022 words), and NarrativeQA (Kočiský et al., 2018) for QA over exceptionally long narrative documents (averaging 51,372 words). For QASPER, we use F1-Match for QA performance and token-level Algorithm 1: Structure-Guided Evidence Retrieval Input: Query q, discourse tree T , evidence limit K, subtree selection size k Output: Evidence set E / * Compute node similarities and rank * / eq ← Encoder(q) ; scores[v] ← cosine(eq, ev) for all v ∈ T ; Vranked ← sort(scores, descending) ; 

F1/Recall for retrieval evaluation. For QuALITY, we report accuracy as the primary metric. And for NarrativeQA, we measure performance using BLEU(B-1), ROUGE(R-L) and METEOR(M) metrics. To ensure fair comparison, we fix the total length of retrieved context across all methods. 

Baselines. We evaluate our approach against several strong retrieval baselines: 

• Flatten-chunk splits articles into chunks of maximum 100 words while preserving sentence boundaries for semantic coherence. 

• Flatten-sentence adopts sentence-level splitting and direct retrieval, providing a direct comparison baseline for our hierarchical approach. 

• RAPTOR constructs a semantic tree through recursive embedding, clustering, and summarization, with retrieval performed on a collapsed tree structure following Sarthi et al. (2024).

Title: Outline Generation: Understanding the Inherent Content Structure of Documents
Snippet: In this paper, we introduce and tackle the Outline Generation (OG) task, which aims to unveil the inherent content structure of a multi-paragraph document by identifying its potential sections and generating the corresponding section headings. Without loss of generality, the OG task can be viewed as a novel structured summarization task. To generate a sound outline, an ideal OG model should be able to capture three levels of coherence, namely the coherence between context paragraphs, that between a section and its heading, and that between context headings. The first one is the foundation for section identification, while the latter two are critical for consistent heading generation. In this work, we formulate the OG task as a hierarchical structured prediction problem, i.e., to first predict a sequence of section boundaries and then a sequence of section headings accordingly. We propose a novel hierarchical structured neural generation model, named HiStGen, for the task. Our model attempts to capture the three-level coherence via the following ways. First, we introduce a Markov paragraph dependency mechanism between context paragraphs for section identification. Second, we employ a section-aware attention mechanism to ensure the semantic coherence between a section and its heading. Finally, we leverage a Markov heading dependency mechanism and a review mechanism between context headings to improve the consistency and eliminate duplication between section headings. Besides, we build a novel Wriptsize IKI OG dataset, a public collection which consists of over 1.75 million document-outline pairs for research on the OG task. Experimental results on our benchmark dataset demonstrate that our model can significantly outperform several state-of-the-art sequential generation models for the OG task.

Title: MODS: Moderating a Mixture of Document Speakers to Summarize Debatable Queries in Document Collections
Snippet: We ensure all parts of MODS are useful by ablating our outline creation and summarization steps. 

In outline creation, having individual speakers respond versus combining all speaker biographies in a prompt (No Speak), tailoring queries (No Tailor), and picking speakers via CoT (No CoT) all improve outlines (Table 5). No Speak has the worst outlines, confirming the strength of equally treating document speakers for DQFS. We also test our moderator's abilities by having all speakers respond (No Mod) instead of selecting speakers. No Mod has higher DC as all speakers respond, but fewer perspectives per document, meaning our moderator adeptly selects speakers with relevant perspectives. 

To see how outline O alters summaries, we compare MODS (with no moderator) updating an outline to updating free-form paragraphs (-O). Using O greatly improves coverage and fairness (Table 6,top), showing structured outlines are better intermediate outputs than free-form text in multi-LLM systems. Further, extra organization in O (stances, tailored queries) aids summarization (Table 6, bot-tom), so richer outlines yield better summaries.

Title: WebWeaver: Structuring Web-Scale Evidence with Dynamic Outlines for Open-Ended Deep Research
Snippet: To isolate and quantify the benefits of outline optimization, as reported in Fig. 6, 7, we conducted an ablation study by evaluating the end-to-end benchmark  performance. We collect the samples with three-round outline optimization from DeepResearch Bench and DeepResearchGym, adopting the same writing strategy for them. 

The benefits of this iterative refinement are evident across both benchmarks. On DeepResearch Bench, the overall score steadily climbs, driven primarily by significant gains in comprehensiveness (48.85 → 50.82) and insight (46.33 → 48.35). This directly validates our hypothesis that each optimization round allows the planner to build a more detailed and logically structured outline. This enhanced structure is further reflected in DeepResearchGym's metrics, where later rounds achieve near-perfect scores in depth (100) and breadth (99.58), indicating a more exhaustive topic coverage. Crucially, this is not just about adding more content; the steady rise in support (95.91 → 98.33) demonstrates that a more refined outline creates a better-scaffolded structure, enabling the writer to more tightly link claims to evidence. In summary, this analysis empirically demonstrates that iterative outline optimization is not a redundant step but a critical mechanism for elevating a report from a simple summary to a deep, insightful, and well-supported piece of research. LLM judgement for varying rounds of outlines. To directly evaluate whether our optimization truly improves outline quality, we utilized an LLM-as-a-judge (Zheng et al., 2023) to assess the outlines from each of the three optimization rounds using gpt-4.1-mini-2025-04-14 in terms of instruction following, depth, balance, breadth, support, and insightfulness. The judgment prompt is provided in Appendix A. 

The results in Fig. 8, 9 provide a resounding confirmation of our iterative approach. On both benchmarks, the overall score for the outline quality shows a significant, monotonic increase, jumping from 81.9 to 92.3 on DeepResearch Bench and from 77.2 to 88.2 on DeepResearchGym.

Title: ConvergeWriter: Data-Driven Bottom-Up Article Construction
Snippet: To accurately evaluate ConvergeWriter's performance, we rigorously follow the incremental comparison principle, selecting representative Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) baselines for comparison: 

• Direct RAG (Lewis et al. 2020): The foundational paradigm retrieves relevant documents once based on the topic and directly inputs them to the LLM for single-step generation of the complete article. • Two-Stage RAG: A two-stage approach: First, it generates a retrieval-augmented outline; then, it expands content section by section based on the outline (retrieving topic-relevant documents again for each section); finally, it concatenates the sections into a full article. outline. The article is subsequently written section by section according to this outline. • OmniThink (Xi et al. 2025): It extends knowledge breadth via an "information tree," deepens cognitive associations through a "concept pool," and dynamically broadens knowledge boundaries to accomplish concept abstraction, outline generation, and citation-aware paragraph writing. These baselines span from basic retrieval augmentation (Direct RAG (Lewis et al. 2020)) and structured staged augmentation (Two-Stage RAG) to state-of-theart complex knowledge planning and integration methods (STORM (Shao et al. 2024), OmniThink (Xi et al. 2025)), aiming to isolate and assess the impact of diverse knowledge utilization strategies and content organization structures on long-text generation.

Title: AutoSurvey: Large Language Models Can Automatically Write Surveys

snippet.text: In this paper, we introduce and tackle the Outline Generation (OG) task, which aims to unveil the inherent content structure of a multi-paragraph document by identifying its potential sections and generating the corresponding section headings. Without loss of generality, the OG task can be viewed as a novel structured summarization task. To generate a sound outline, an ideal OG model should be able to capture three levels of coherence, namely the coherence between context paragraphs, that between a section and its heading, and that between context headings. The first one is the foundation for section identification, while the latter two are critical for consistent heading generation. In this work, we formulate the OG task as a hierarchical structured prediction problem, i.e., to first predict a sequence of section boundaries and then a sequence of section headings accordingly. We propose a novel hierarchical structured neural generation model, named HiStGen, for the task. Our model attempts to capture the three-level coherence via the following ways. First, we introduce a Markov paragraph dependency mechanism between context paragraphs for section identification. Second, we employ a section-aware attention mechanism to ensure the semantic coherence between a section and its heading. Finally, we leverage a Markov heading dependency mechanism and a review mechanism between context headings to improve the consistency and eliminate duplication between section headings. Besides, we build a novel Wriptsize IKI OG dataset, a public collection which consists of over 1.75 million document-outline pairs for research on the OG task. Experimental results on our benchmark dataset demonstrate that our model can significantly outperform several state-of-the-art sequential generation models for the OG task.

To isolate and quantify the benefits of outline optimization, as reported in Fig. 6, 7, we conducted an ablation study by evaluating the end-to-end benchmark  performance. We collect the samples with three-round outline optimization from DeepResearch Bench and DeepResearchGym, adopting the same writing strategy for them. 

The benefits of this iterative refinement are evident across both benchmarks. On DeepResearch Bench, the overall score steadily climbs, driven primarily by significant gains in comprehensiveness (48.85 → 50.82) and insight (46.33 → 48.35). This directly validates our hypothesis that each optimization round allows the planner to build a more detailed and logically structured outline. This enhanced structure is further reflected in DeepResearchGym's metrics, where later rounds achieve near-perfect scores in depth (100) and breadth (99.58), indicating a more exhaustive topic coverage. Crucially, this is not just about adding more content; the steady rise in support (95.91 → 98.33) demonstrates that a more refined outline creates a better-scaffolded structure, enabling the writer to more tightly link claims to evidence. In summary, this analysis empirically demonstrates that iterative outline optimization is not a redundant step but a critical mechanism for elevating a report from a simple summary to a deep, insightful, and well-supported piece of research. LLM judgement for varying rounds of outlines. The judgment prompt is provided in Appendix A. 

The results in Fig. 8, 9 provide a resounding confirmation of our iterative approach. On both benchmarks, the overall score for the outline quality shows a significant, monotonic increase, jumping from 81.9 to 92.3 on DeepResearch Bench and from 77.2 to 88.2 on DeepResearchGym.

snippet.text:
To accurately evaluate ConvergeWriter's performance, we rigorously follow the incremental comparison principle, selecting representative Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) baselines for comparison: 

• Direct RAG (Lewis et al. 2020): The foundational paradigm retrieves relevant documents once based on the topic and directly inputs them to the LLM for single-step generation of the complete article. • Two-Stage RAG: A two-stage approach: First, it generates a retrieval-augmented outline; then, it expands content section by section based on the outline (retrieving topic-relevant documents again for each section); finally, it concatenates the sections into a full article. outline. The article is subsequently written section by section according to this outline. • OmniThink (Xi et al. 2025): It extends knowledge breadth via an "information tree," deepens cognitive associations through a "concept pool," and dynamically broadens knowledge boundaries to accomplish concept abstraction, outline generation, and citation-aware paragraph writing. These baselines span from basic retrieval augmentation (Direct RAG (Lewis et al. 2020)) and structured staged augmentation (Two-Stage RAG) to state-of-theart complex knowledge planning and integration methods (STORM (Shao et al. 2024), OmniThink (Xi et al. 2025)), aiming to isolate and assess the impact of diverse knowledge utilization strategies and content organization structures on long-text generation.

Title: Unlocking Structure Measuring: Introducing PDD, an Automatic Metric for Positional Discourse Coherence
Snippet: A common baseline metric for measuring functional discourse structure is the exact match, which compares structure elements one-to-one at each exact position. However, this metric is notably sensitive to local variations and differences in the lengths of articles. 

To address this gap, we propose a novel automatic model-free metric, Positional Discourse Divergence (PDD), specifically designed to evaluate the underlying discourse structure of articles in comparison to references. PDD partitions the sentences of an article into multiple position bins and calculates the divergence in discourse structures within each bin. This approach renders PDD re-silient to various challenges encountered in longform text generation, such as accommodating local variations and handling misaligned numbers of sentences. 

To validate the effectiveness and generalizability of the PDD, we evaluate the inter-agreement with human evaluations and GPT-4 coherence evaluations on three representative datasets with different discourse schema: News Discourse (Choubey et al., 2020), Long-Form Question Answering (Xu et al., 2022a) and Recipe1M+ (Liu et al., 2022). Across all three domains, PDD demonstrates the highest agreement with human judgements on coherence.

Title: Discourse Structure in Machine Translation Evaluation
Snippet: However, they could not improve correlation with human judgments as evaluated on the MetricsMATR dataset, which consists of 249 manually-assessed segments. Compared to that previous work, here (i) we used a different discourse representation (RST), (ii) we compared discourse parses using allsubtree kernels (Collins and Duffy 2001), (iii) we evaluated on much larger datasets, for several language pairs and for multiple metrics, and (iv) we did demonstrate better correlation with human judgments. 

Recently, other discourse-related extensions of MT metrics (such as BLEU, TER and METEOR) were proposed (Wong et al. 2011;Wong and Kit 2012), which use document-level lexical cohesion (Halliday and Hasan 1976). In that work, lexical cohesion is achieved using word repetitions and semantically similar words such as synonyms, hypernyms, and hyponyms. For BLEU and TER, they observed improved correlation with human judgments on the MTC4 dataset (900 segments) when linearly interpolating these metrics with their lexical cohesion score. However, they ignored a key property of discourse, i.e., the coherence structure, which we have effectively exploited in both tuning and no-tuning scenarios. Furthermore, we have shown that the similarity in discourse trees can yield improvements in a larger number of existing MT evaluation metrics. Finally, unlike their work, which measured lexical cohesion at the document-level, here we are concerned with coherence (rhetorical) structure, primarily at the sentence-level. 

Finally, we should note our own previous work, on which this journal paper is based. In (Guzmán et al. 2014b), we showed that using discourse can improve a number of pre-existing evaluation metrics, while in (Joty et al. 2014) we presented our DiscoTK family of discourse-based metrics. In particular, the DISCOTK party metric (discussed in Section 4.3) combined several variants of a discourse tree representation with other metrics from the ASIYA MT evaluation toolkit, and yielded the best-performing metric in the WMT14 Metrics shared task.

This approach renders PDD re-silient to various challenges encountered in longform text generation, such as accommodating local variations and handling misaligned numbers of sentences. 

To validate the effectiveness and generalizability of the PDD, we evaluate the inter-agreement with human evaluations and GPT-4 coherence evaluations on three representative datasets with different discourse schema: News Discourse (Choubey et al., 2020), Long-Form Question Answering (Xu et al., 2022a) and Recipe1M+ (Liu et al., 2022). Across all three domains, PDD demonstrates the highest agreement with human judgements on coherence.

However, they could not improve correlation with human judgments as evaluated on the MetricsMATR dataset, which consists of 249 manually-assessed segments. Compared to that previous work, here (i) we used a different discourse representation (RST), (ii) we compared discourse parses using allsubtree kernels (Collins and Duffy 2001), (iii) we evaluated on much larger datasets, for several language pairs and for multiple metrics, and (iv) we did demonstrate better correlation with human judgments. 

Recently, other discourse-related extensions of MT metrics (such as BLEU, TER and METEOR) were proposed (Wong et al. 2011;Wong and Kit 2012), which use document-level lexical cohesion (Halliday and Hasan 1976). In that work, lexical cohesion is achieved using word repetitions and semantically similar words such as synonyms, hypernyms, and hyponyms. For BLEU and TER, they observed improved correlation with human judgments on the MTC4 dataset (900 segments) when linearly interpolating these metrics with their lexical cohesion score. However, they ignored a key property of discourse, i.e., the coherence structure, which we have effectively exploited in both tuning and no-tuning scenarios. Furthermore, we have shown that the similarity in discourse trees can yield improvements in a larger number of existing MT evaluation metrics. Finally, unlike their work, which measured lexical cohesion at the document-level, here we are concerned with coherence (rhetorical) structure, primarily at the sentence-level. 

Finally, we should note our own previous work, on which this journal paper is based. In (Guzmán et al. 2014b), we showed that using discourse can improve a number of pre-existing evaluation metrics, while in (Joty et al. 2014) we presented our DiscoTK family of discourse-based metrics. In particular, the DISCOTK party metric (discussed in Section 4.3) combined several variants of a discourse tree representation with other metrics from the ASIYA MT evaluation toolkit, and yielded the best-performing metric in the WMT14 Metrics shared task.

# Overview: Models and Simulation for MRAM and Related Materials

Magnetoresistive Random Access Memory (MRAM) research relies on multi-scale modeling spanning materials physics (spin–orbit and magnetic interactions in free/fixed layers and barriers), mesoscopic device physics (micromagnetics, stochastic switching), and circuit/system co-simulation (write/verify paths, retention, and architecture-level performance). Spin–transfer torque (STT) and spin–orbit torque (SOT) variants each have distinct modeling emphases: STT focuses on current density profiles, thermal stability, and read–write path co-design, while SOT emphasizes interfacial spin–orbit physics (spin Hall, Rashba, spin–momentum locking) and torque efficiencies that drive voltage-controlled, potentially lower-power operation. <cite id="635edb24-2">STT-MRAM uses in-device current directly for writing, whereas SOT-MRAM leverages bulk and interfacial spin–orbit effects to generate torques, offering improved energy efficiency and versatility</cite> <cite id="635edb24-0">SOTs arise from bulk spin Hall, interfacial Rashba effects, and spin–momentum locking, enabling magnetization switching, domain wall motion, and high-frequency dynamics relevant to MRAM</cite>.

# Device and Circuit-Level Simulation Tools and Workflows

Micromagnetic and finite-element solvers are widely used to simulate magnetization dynamics and spin accumulation in MRAM cells, often coupled with device geometries and realistic biasing. <cite id="635edb24-3">A finite-element solver based on the Landau–Lifshitz–Gilbert (LLG) equation and drift–diffusion spin accumulation has been developed to simulate spin torques in heavy metal/ferromagnet bilayers, enabling realistic device geometry modeling and SOT/STT torques</cite>. <cite id="07369896-0">OOMMF-based micromagnetics with rare-event enhancement is used to evaluate write current–time–error trade-offs for SOT- and STT-MRAM devices at the device level</cite>. At the circuit level, compact models are integrated into industry EDA flows for co-simulation. <cite id="07369896-1">Cadence Virtuoso has been used to simulate logic with SOT/STT/Vg-SOT MRAM models, leveraging provided Verilog-A MRAM models and 45 nm PDKs</cite> <cite id="07369896-2">A circuit-level SOT-MRAM Verilog-A model has been used in Cadence Virtuoso with NCSU FreePDK 45 nm to simulate in-memory computing circuits and verify memory behavior</cite>. Comparative device studies also explore design knobs that translate materials choices into performance, such as barrier thickness and oxide engineering for SOT devices. <cite id="07369896-3">SOT-MRAM device designs achieved 45% lower write energy and significantly reduced read energy and higher read-disturb margin by optimizing oxide thickness and resistance, illustrating how materials stack choices affect device-level metrics</cite>.

# STT-MRAM: Modeling Variability, Reliability, and System-Level Impacts

STT devices exhibit stochastic write processes governed by thermal fluctuations and process variations, motivating analytical and stochastic models beyond brute-force Monte Carlo. <cite id="0ca6a0e8-2">The write error rate (WER) in STT-MRAM is inherently stochastic; binomial sampling with large run counts is computationally heavy, motivating reduced-order approaches</cite> <cite id="0ca6a0e8-3">A Fokker–Planck-based modeling framework reproduces experimental WER and enables efficient yield analysis for STT-MRAM and RRAM by directly modeling state distributions during write</cite>. Reliability must be assessed across error modes—write failure, read disturbance, and retention—under process variations and workloads. <cite id="0ca6a0e8-0">System-level formulations show how parameters like thermal stability factor Δ, critical switching current, free-layer moment, and spin polarization, which are influenced by process variations, exponentially impact write failure and retention/read-disturb rates</cite> <cite id="0ca6a0e8-4">Workload-dependent access patterns and data content interact with PVs to determine cache error rates; integrating write, read-disturb, and retention vulnerabilities at system level is necessary for reliable design</cite>. Application-driven targets for retention vs. write performance further shape materials and device choices. <cite id="0ca6a0e8-1">SCM applications demand Δ≈80 and long retention, while cache applications allow trading retention for better write performance, with specialized retention tests required due to stochastic, temperature- and perturbation-sensitive retention faults</cite>.

# SOT-MRAM: Device Simulation and Materials-Driven Torque Engineering

SOT devices benefit from compact models and circuit co-simulation while enabling materials-focused optimization of torque generation and efficiency. <cite id="635edb24-1">Physical modeling of two-terminal SOT-MRAM shows that in-plane-only SOT materials offer little improvement over STT, whereas out-of-plane torques with efficiencies as low as 0.1 can significantly reduce write energy at nanoscale device dimensions; device geometry and SOT efficiency directly impact write energy and path design</cite>. <cite id="635edb24-4">Materials platforms that support strong spin–orbit coupling—such as heavy-metal/ferromagnet interfaces, Rashba 2DEGs, and 2D Rashba ferromagnetic electron gases—provide routes to large SOTs, with SOT magnitude often proportional to current density and linked to band-structure-derived transport properties</cite>. Device- and circuit-level evaluations increasingly use compact models to integrate SOT physics into logic and memory arrays, with voltage control and potential energy savings. <cite id="07369896-1">Circuit simulations of SOT/STT/Vg-SOT MRAM models in Cadence Virtuoso demonstrate feasibility of using compact models for logic and memory integration</cite> <cite id="07369896-3">Stack engineering (e.g., thicker MgO-like oxides in SOT devices) can improve read energy and disturb margin at the expense of higher resistance, illustrating materials–device co-optimization</cite>.

# Materials Modeling for MRAM Stacks and Torques

Materials-level modeling connects interfacial and bulk spin–orbit phenomena to device-level torque efficiency and stability. <cite id="635edb24-0">SOTs in HM/FM stacks originate from spin Hall effects in heavy metals, interfacial Rashba spin–orbit coupling at interfaces, and spin–momentum locking in topological materials, all of which are materials parameters that determine device torque efficiency</cite>. <cite id="635edb24-4">At interfaces, two-dimensional Rashba ferromagnetic electron gases emerge as ideal platforms to study SOT, with the SOT magnitude tied to current density and band-structure characteristics, and with no single universal relation to conductivity</cite>. Device simulators increasingly incorporate these physics via spin accumulation and torque modules to predict magnetization dynamics and switching in realistic geometries. <cite id="635edb24-3">Finite-element LLG solvers coupled with drift–diffusion spin accumulation can simulate spin Hall-driven torques and provide spin accumulation distributions and torque components in HM/FM bilayers, enabling direct linkage from materials parameters to device switching</cite>.

# Thermal, Stochastic, and Micromagnetic Modeling

Thermal fluctuations and rare events govern write reliability and speed, and require specialized acceleration and modeling techniques. <cite id="07369896-0">OOMMF-based micromagnetics augmented with rare-event enhancement is used to explore write current–time–error trade-offs, addressing the scarcity of switching events in thermal simulations</cite> <cite id="0ca6a0e8-2">Fokker–Planck approaches provide a reduced-order stochastic description of write processes, capturing binomial sampling challenges and enabling faster WER estimation for yield analysis</cite>. Device- and system-level evaluations further connect materials parameters (e.g., thermal stability Δ, spin polarization) to reliability under variations and workloads. <cite id="0ca6a0e8-0">Process variations that increase Δ, critical switching current, free-layer moment, or spin polarization increase write failure probability, while decreasing thermal stability factors reduce it, highlighting the sensitivity of reliability to materials and device parameters</cite> <cite id="0ca6a0e8-4">Retaining the inter-correlation among retention, read disturbance, and write failure rates is essential for accurate system-level reliability exploration under PVs and workload dependence</cite>.

# Selected Papers and Resources (by Topic)

- Spin–orbit torque materials physics and device prospects:
  - <cite id="635edb24-0">Benchmarking of Spin–Orbit Torque Switching Efficiency in Pt Alloys: reviews SOT mechanisms (spin Hall, interfacial Rashba, spin–momentum locking) and positions SOT-MRAM as energy-efficient and fast</cite>.
  - <cite id="635edb24-4">2D Rashba Ferromagnetic Electron Gas Transport and SOT: discusses SOT origins at interfaces and links to band structure, with implications for materials selection and device physics</cite>.
  - <cite id="635edb24-2">Roadmap of Spin–Orbit Torques: contrasts STT vs SOT MRAM, outlines key device metrics (TMR, BEOL compatibility, write efficiency), and identifies research and integration challenges</cite>.

- Device and circuit compact models and co-simulation:
  - <cite id="635edb24-3">Finite Element Modeling of Spin–Orbit Torques: LLG + drift–diffusion solver for HM/FM bilayers with SOT/STT simulation and realistic geometries</cite>.
  - <cite id="07369896-0">Impact of Technology Scaling and BEOL on MRAM: OOMMF-based micromagnetics with rare-event enhancement to quantify write current–time–error trade-offs for SOT/STT/ME devices</cite>.
  - <cite id="07369896-1">Comparative Vg-SOT/STT/SOT logic simulations in Cadence Virtuoso using Verilog-A MRAM models and 45 nm PDKs</cite>.
  - <cite id="07369896-2">Circuit-level SOT-MRAM Verilog-A model integrated with NCSU FreePDK 45 nm for in-memory computing architectures</cite>.
  - <cite id="07369896-3">SOT-MRAM Array/Device Optimization: oxide-thickness and resistance engineering leading to lower write and read energies and improved disturb margin</cite>.

- STT-MRAM variability, reliability, and system-level modeling:
  - <cite id="0ca6a0e8-2">Fokker–Planck Approach for Modeling Stochastic Phenomena in STT/RRAM: reduced-order WER modeling that reproduces experiments and accelerates yield analysis</cite>.
  - <cite id="0ca6a0e8-0">System-Level Reliability Formulation for STT-MRAM Caches: error-rate dependencies on Δ, critical current, free-layer moment, and spin polarization under PVs and workloads</cite>.
  - <cite id="0ca6a0e8-1">Survey on STT-MRAM Testing: retention fault characteristics, trade-offs between retention (Δ≈80 for SCM) and performance (cache applications), and specialized retention tests</cite>.
  - <cite id="0ca6a0e8-4">Workload- and PV-Dependent Cache Vulnerability: integrated formulation of retention, read disturbance, and write failure rates for early system-level exploration</cite>.

# Practical Modeling Workflow and Considerations

- Materials-to-device linkage: Use materials parameters (spin Hall angle, spin diffusion, interfacial Rashba parameters, damping, anisotropy) in device simulators to compute torque magnitudes and directions, then propagate to switching fields/currents and energy. <cite id="635edb24-0">SOT efficiency and origin (bulk vs interfacial) determine device write schemes and energy scaling</cite> <cite id="635edb24-3">Finite-element LLG+spin-accumulation solvers map materials-level spin transport to device geometry and torque profiles</cite>.
- Device/circuit co-simulation: Employ compact models (Verilog-A) within SPICE flows for logic and array simulations, while using micromagnetics for write dynamics and rare-event statistics. <cite id="07369896-1">Industry PDKs and Verilog-A models enable co-simulation of SOT/STT devices with digital circuits</cite> <cite id="07369896-0">OOMMF with rare-event acceleration supports device-level write-error characterization</cite>.
- Reliability and variability: Combine analytical models (Fokker–Planck) with system-level formulations to capture WER, retention, and read-disturb interplay under process variations and workloads. <cite id="0ca6a0e8-2">Fokker–Planck WER modeling reduces simulation costs while preserving accuracy</cite> <cite id="0ca6a0e8-4">System-level error integration is needed due to conflicting dependencies across error modes</cite>.

# Notes on Open-Source and Commercial Ecosystems

Open-source and commercial environments increasingly support MRAM simulation, though access to vendor-validated compact models and technology parameters can be critical for accurate co-simulation. <cite id="07369896-1">Cadence Virtuoso has been used with SOT/STT/Vg-SOT Verilog-A models at 45 nm</cite> <cite id="07369896-2">NCSU FreePDK 45 nm enables SPICE-level exploration of SOT-MRAM circuits</cite>. Micromagnetic toolchains such as OOMMF (or its modern counterparts) remain standard for device-level analysis with thermal noise and rare-event acceleration. <cite id="07369896-0">OOMMF-based simulations with rare-event enhancement quantify write errors and trade-offs in SOT/STT devices</cite>.

# Takeaways

- Materials choices that enhance SOT (e.g., HM/FM interfaces with spin Hall and Rashba effects) directly improve device-level write efficiency and enable voltage-driven schemes, while STT relies on current-driven torques with distinct scaling and reliability challenges. <cite id="635edb24-0">SOTs from spin Hall/interfacial effects and momentum locking enable efficient switching</cite> <cite id="635edb24-2">STT uses direct current-induced torques; SOT offers alternative energy/latency trade-offs</cite>.
- Robust evaluation requires multi-scale simulation: LLG/drift–diffusion for spin dynamics, micromagnetics with noise/rare-event handling for write reliability, and compact models within SPICE for circuit/system performance and verification. <cite id="635edb24-3">Finite-element LLG+spin-accumulation solvers for realistic geometries</cite> <cite id="07369896-0">OOMMF-based rare-event micromagnetics for write characterization</cite> <cite id="07369896-1">Verilog-A MRAM models in Cadence Virtuoso for logic/array co-simulation</cite>.
- Reliability under process variations and workloads must be assessed across WER, retention, and read-disturb, often via reduced-order stochastic models and system-level formulations. <cite id="0ca6a0e8-2">Fokker–Planck WER modeling accelerates yield analysis</cite> <cite id="0ca6a0e8-4">Integrating error modes under PVs and workloads is essential for dependable MRAM design</cite>.

Title: Finite Element Modeling of Spin-Orbit Torques
Snippet: Spin-orbit torques (SOTs) allow for efficient manipulation of magnetization in emerging spintronic devices such as nano-oscillators and nonvolatile magnetoresistive random access memories (MRAM). 

To facilitate the research and development of such devices, it is important to have software capable of simulating the spin and magnetization dynamics involved in their operation. To be able to simulate realistic devices the flexibility of the software with regards to geometry is critical. To address these needs, a solver has been developed with the capabilities to model spin-transfer torques (STT) in STT-MRAM cells. The solver uses the finite element method to model magnetization and spin dynamics on a mesh by solving the Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation (LLG) and a drift-diffusion model for spin accumulation [1], respectively. The capabilities of this solver have been extended to include the spin Hall effect (SHE), the main driving force behind SOT. In this work we present simulation results for the spin accumulation and spin torques in a heavy metal/ferromagnet (HM/FM) bilayer.
</snippet>

Title: Transport Property and Spin–Orbit Torque in 2D Rashba Ferromagnetic Electron Gas
Snippet: In recent years, spin-orbit torque has become one of the most attractive topics in the field of spintronics because of its great application prospects in magnetic information storage technology [1][2][3]. spin-orbit torque (SOT) is based on spin-orbit interaction (SOI), which uses the non-equilibrium spin accumulation induced by charge flow to generate a torque on a local magnetic moment [4,5], thus achieving the purpose of regulating magnetic storage units. SOT-based magnetic random access memory (SOT-MRAM) overcomes the disadvantages of STT-MRAM, especially the fact that it separates the read and write paths, so it has a higher read and write speed and lower power consumption than STT-MRAM [6,7]. Relevant studies show that SOT-MRAM can achieve ultra-fast information writing, which is reduced from the tens of nanoseconds required by the original STT-MRAM to less than 10 ns, while the power consumption of the device is further reduced [8,9]. 

The essence of spin-orbit torque is that the directional movement of electrons produces a non-equilibrium spin accumulation in the spin-orbit coupling system, by means of the s-d interaction, the spin accumulation of conducting electrons applies a torque on the local magnetic moment [10,11]. Meanwhile, this directional movement of electrons also generates a charge current in general. Thus, the current and spin-orbit torque are both manifestations of the non-equilibrium transport properties of the SOC system, there must be some relations between them. Literature have showed that the magnitude of spin-orbit torque is often proportional to the current density [12][13][14][15]. Because the spin accumulation and charge current are proportional to the external electric field under linear transport conditions, the ratio depends on the band structure of the system [4,5]. There is no clear conclusion about the underlying relationship between spin-orbit torque and conductivity. 

Two-dimensional Rashba ferromagnetic electron gas is an ideal platform for investigating spin-orbit torque [16,17], and the latter is often realized at heavy metal/ferromagnetic interfaces [18,19].

Title: A Detailed Study of SOT-MRAM as an Alternative to DRAM Primary Memory in Multi-Core Environment
Snippet: Reliable evaluation of SOT-MRAM-based main memory is challenging due to the public unavailability of parameters related to timing and current. The significant advantage of MRAM devices is scalability, and they do not require any refresh, reducing static power consumption. STT-MRAM has been explored as the main memory in recent research [1], [7] providing promising results. The average speedups of Open and Close Page Techniques with a 1.2x configuration, as mentioned in [1], are 2.4% and 2.7%, respectively. Additionally, there was 4.6 times more power consumption than DRAM. One setback for STT-MRAM is its write latency, write energy and reliability [7]. SOT-MRAM provides better read/write latency, retention time, reliability and endurance than STT-MRAM [5], [8]. 

SOT-MRAM has not yet been evaluated as the primary memory for multi-core systems using full system simulators and benchmark programs, such as PARSEC [9]. Given its attractive features, SOT-MRAM has the potential to serve as the main memory. This research seeks to propose and explore its behaviour in a multi-core environment when handling shared memory workloads. We have derived SOT-MRAM main memory's timing and current parameters using the approach in [1]. The authors in [10] and [1] have validated the method and the parameters from industry estimation. Figure 1 depicts the different memory architectures used in our study. 

The contributions of this work are: 

• The first (best of our knowledge) to integrate SOT-MRAM into multi-core systems extending its application scope and three memory structures. 

• To address the challenge of parameter absence, the study estimates and scales parameters, ensuring a robust analysis of three memory structures. 

• A comprehensive survey and micro-architectural exploration reveal SOT-MRAM's superior circuit-level metrics. 

• Thorough system-level simulations provide a holistic evaluation, covering power consumption, bandwidth utilization, EDP, and total latency. 

The subsequent sections of the work are presented as follows: In Section II, we provide an introduction to MRAM memory.

Title: Survey on STT-MRAM Testing: Failure Mechanisms, Fault Models, and Tests
Snippet: In Section IV-B(2), we have discussed the characteristics, causes, and influencing factors of retention fault in STT-MRAMs. Yet, the requirement of retention time for STT-MRAMs ranges from a few seconds to ten years, depending on the specific application. For the storage-class memory (SCM) application, 10+ years of retention time is desired as most of the data is rarely revisited. This requires a thermal stability (∆) as high as 80, which is experimentally achievable at the expense of high write energy and latency. In contrast, for the last-level-cache application which is seen as one of the most important markets for applying STT-MRAM technology in the short term, the average revival time of cache blocks is below 1 s [5]. This allows us to trade the retention time of STT-MRAMs for better write performance, which has been extensively studied [127][128][129]. 

Regardless of the different requirements of retention time of STT-MRAMs for different applications, testing retention time of STT-MRAMs is very important. However, characterizing STT-MRAM retention time is very challenging, since retention fault is essentially a transient and stochastic fault which depends on temperature, process variations, magnetic perturbation, and disturb current. Thus, March tests are not suitable to test it, and traditional retention tests for DRAMs cannot be directly applied to STT-MRAMs. This calls for special test techniques. Next, we will introduce three test approaches dedicated to testing STT-MRAM retention time.
</snippet>

Title: A Fokker–Planck Approach for Modeling the Stochastic Phenomena in Magnetic and Resistive Random Access Memory Devices
Snippet: Due to increasing demand for memory-intensive applications such as hardware accelerators for AI, embedded non-volatile memory (eNVM) technologies such as resistive random access memory (RRAM) [1] and spin-transfer torque magnetic random access memory (STT MRAM) [2] have been widely explored for these applications [3]- [8] due to their comparative advantage (such as non-volatility, near-zero standby leakage power, small cell size and scalability [9]- [17]) over other memory technologies. However, the programming mechanisms in RRAM [18] and STT MRAM [19] are inherently stochastic, which introduce write errors that may drastically impact the robustness and reliability of the memory and thus, pose a significant challenge to their widespread adoption. Moreover, the impact of the write error rate (WER) needs to be investigated alongside process variations during yield analysis, which may significantly increase the complexity of conventional methods based on the Monte Carlo approach. Consider the simulation of WER in STT MRAM for example. The WER is estimated by counting the number of failures out of N simulation runs and the probability of obtaining each observation follows a binomial distribution. The number of simulation runs needed to estimate the WER and the accuracy of the estimation are graphed in Figure 1. Thus, a significant amount of computing resources may be required to perform yield analysis in RRAM and STT MRAM. 

Alternatively, it was shown that the WER of STT MRAM can be estimated using an approach based on the Fokker-Planck (FP) equation [20], [21]. In this approach, the distribution of memory cell states during the write process is modeled directly, which significantly reduces the computation effort for estimating the WER. In this paper, we propose a generalized approach for estimating the WER in STT MRAM and steady state analysis

Title: A Fokker–Planck Approach for Modeling the Stochastic Phenomena in Magnetic and Resistive Random Access Memory Devices
Snippet: Embedded nonvolatile memory technologies, such as resistive random access memory (RRAM) and spin-transfer torque magnetic RAM (STT MRAM), are increasingly being researched for application in neuromorphic computing and hardware accelerators for artificial intelligence (AI). However, the stochastic write processes in these memory technologies affect their yield and need to be studied alongside process variations, which drastically increase the complexity of yield analysis using the Monte Carlo approach. Therefore, we propose an approach based on the Fokker–Planck equation for modeling the stochastic write processes in STT MRAM and RRAM devices. Moreover, we show that our proposed approach can reproduce the experimental results for both STT-MRAM and RRAM devices.
</snippet>

Title: A System-Level Framework for Analytical and Empirical Reliability Exploration of STT-MRAM Caches
Snippet: Although the error rate of a single STT-MRAM cell can be estimated using its physical parameters, the vulnerability estimation of the entire STT-MRAM cache requires systemlevel analysis considering the workloads behaviors as well as PV effects. A recent study has reported only the rate of write failure and read disturbance in STT-MRAM cache and shown that these rates are strongly workload-dependent [20], [28]. To the best of our knowledge, none of the previous studies neither have addressed the workloads-and PVs-dependent vulnerability of STT-MRAM caches considering all types of errors, nor reported the cache reliability considering the conflicting sources of errors. Therefore, to achieve an acceptable level of reliability in STT-MRAM cache with affordable costs, it is necessary to a) estimate the vulnerability of the cache to each error type as well as the total cache vulnerability considering the conflicting dependencies of error types to different factors and b) utilize effective mitigation techniques for each error type according to its contribution in the total cache vulnerability. 

In this paper, we propose a system-level framework for early exploration of STT-MRAM cache reliability, which considers a) workload-dependent cache access patterns and data content, b) PV affected STT-MRAM cell vulnerability to errors, and c) inter-correlation between the rate of threementioned errors, i.e., retention failure, read disturbance, and write failure, for reliability exploration. To this end, we first formulate the vulnerability of STT-MRAM caches to each error type by extrapolating the error probability of PV affected cache blocks from nominal error probability of a single STT-MRAM cell. Then, we deduce the error probability of a PV affected STT-MRAM cache from the blocks error probability. Our formulation is then extended to integrate probabilities of the three differently-originated and exclusively-occurred error types into a single cache vulnerability equation.
