# Overview: Models and Simulation for MRAM and Related Materials

Magnetoresistive Random Access Memory (MRAM) research relies on multi-scale modeling spanning materials physics (spin–orbit and magnetic interactions in free/fixed layers and barriers), mesoscopic device physics (micromagnetics, stochastic switching), and circuit/system co-simulation (write/verify paths, retention, and architecture-level performance). Spin–transfer torque (STT) and spin–orbit torque (SOT) variants each have distinct modeling emphases: STT focuses on current density profiles, thermal stability, and read–write path co-design, while SOT emphasizes interfacial spin–orbit physics (spin Hall, Rashba, spin–momentum locking) and torque efficiencies that drive voltage-controlled, potentially lower-power operation. <cite id="635edb24-2">STT-MRAM uses in-device current directly for writing, whereas SOT-MRAM leverages bulk and interfacial spin–orbit effects to generate torques, offering improved energy efficiency and versatility</cite> <cite id="635edb24-0">SOTs arise from bulk spin Hall, interfacial Rashba effects, and spin–momentum locking, enabling magnetization switching, domain wall motion, and high-frequency dynamics relevant to MRAM</cite>.

# Device and Circuit-Level Simulation Tools and Workflows

Micromagnetic and finite-element solvers are widely used to simulate magnetization dynamics and spin accumulation in MRAM cells, often coupled with device geometries and realistic biasing. <cite id="635edb24-3">A finite-element solver based on the Landau–Lifshitz–Gilbert (LLG) equation and drift–diffusion spin accumulation has been developed to simulate spin torques in heavy metal/ferromagnet bilayers, enabling realistic device geometry modeling and SOT/STT torques</cite>. <cite id="07369896-0">OOMMF-based micromagnetics with rare-event enhancement is used to evaluate write current–time–error trade-offs for SOT- and STT-MRAM devices at the device level</cite>. At the circuit level, compact models are integrated into industry EDA flows for co-simulation. <cite id="07369896-1">Cadence Virtuoso has been used to simulate logic with SOT/STT/Vg-SOT MRAM models, leveraging provided Verilog-A MRAM models and 45 nm PDKs</cite> <cite id="07369896-2">A circuit-level SOT-MRAM Verilog-A model has been used in Cadence Virtuoso with NCSU FreePDK 45 nm to simulate in-memory computing circuits and verify memory behavior</cite>. Comparative device studies also explore design knobs that translate materials choices into performance, such as barrier thickness and oxide engineering for SOT devices. <cite id="07369896-3">SOT-MRAM device designs achieved 45% lower write energy and significantly reduced read energy and higher read-disturb margin by optimizing oxide thickness and resistance, illustrating how materials stack choices affect device-level metrics</cite>.

# STT-MRAM: Modeling Variability, Reliability, and System-Level Impacts

STT devices exhibit stochastic write processes governed by thermal fluctuations and process variations, motivating analytical and stochastic models beyond brute-force Monte Carlo. <cite id="0ca6a0e8-2">The write error rate (WER) in STT-MRAM is inherently stochastic; binomial sampling with large run counts is computationally heavy, motivating reduced-order approaches</cite> <cite id="0ca6a0e8-3">A Fokker–Planck-based modeling framework reproduces experimental WER and enables efficient yield analysis for STT-MRAM and RRAM by directly modeling state distributions during write</cite>. Reliability must be assessed across error modes—write failure, read disturbance, and retention—under process variations and workloads. <cite id="0ca6a0e8-0">System-level formulations show how parameters like thermal stability factor Δ, critical switching current, free-layer moment, and spin polarization, which are influenced by process variations, exponentially impact write failure and retention/read-disturb rates</cite> <cite id="0ca6a0e8-4">Workload-dependent access patterns and data content interact with PVs to determine cache error rates; integrating write, read-disturb, and retention vulnerabilities at system level is necessary for reliable design</cite>. Application-driven targets for retention vs. write performance further shape materials and device choices. <cite id="0ca6a0e8-1">SCM applications demand Δ≈80 and long retention, while cache applications allow trading retention for better write performance, with specialized retention tests required due to stochastic, temperature- and perturbation-sensitive retention faults</cite>.

# SOT-MRAM: Device Simulation and Materials-Driven Torque Engineering

SOT devices benefit from compact models and circuit co-simulation while enabling materials-focused optimization of torque generation and efficiency. <cite id="635edb24-1">Physical modeling of two-terminal SOT-MRAM shows that in-plane-only SOT materials offer little improvement over STT, whereas out-of-plane torques with efficiencies as low as 0.1 can significantly reduce write energy at nanoscale device dimensions; device geometry and SOT efficiency directly impact write energy and path design</cite>. <cite id="635edb24-4">Materials platforms that support strong spin–orbit coupling—such as heavy-metal/ferromagnet interfaces, Rashba 2DEGs, and 2D Rashba ferromagnetic electron gases—provide routes to large SOTs, with SOT magnitude often proportional to current density and linked to band-structure-derived transport properties</cite>. Device- and circuit-level evaluations increasingly use compact models to integrate SOT physics into logic and memory arrays, with voltage control and potential energy savings. <cite id="07369896-1">Circuit simulations of SOT/STT/Vg-SOT MRAM models in Cadence Virtuoso demonstrate feasibility of using compact models for logic and memory integration</cite> <cite id="07369896-3">Stack engineering (e.g., thicker MgO-like oxides in SOT devices) can improve read energy and disturb margin at the expense of higher resistance, illustrating materials–device co-optimization</cite>.

# Materials Modeling for MRAM Stacks and Torques

Materials-level modeling connects interfacial and bulk spin–orbit phenomena to device-level torque efficiency and stability. <cite id="635edb24-0">SOTs in HM/FM stacks originate from spin Hall effects in heavy metals, interfacial Rashba spin–orbit coupling at interfaces, and spin–momentum locking in topological materials, all of which are materials parameters that determine device torque efficiency</cite>. <cite id="635edb24-4">At interfaces, two-dimensional Rashba ferromagnetic electron gases emerge as ideal platforms to study SOT, with the SOT magnitude tied to current density and band-structure characteristics, and with no single universal relation to conductivity</cite>. Device simulators increasingly incorporate these physics via spin accumulation and torque modules to predict magnetization dynamics and switching in realistic geometries. <cite id="635edb24-3">Finite-element LLG solvers coupled with drift–diffusion spin accumulation can simulate spin Hall-driven torques and provide spin accumulation distributions and torque components in HM/FM bilayers, enabling direct linkage from materials parameters to device switching</cite>.

# Thermal, Stochastic, and Micromagnetic Modeling

Thermal fluctuations and rare events govern write reliability and speed, and require specialized acceleration and modeling techniques. <cite id="07369896-0">OOMMF-based micromagnetics augmented with rare-event enhancement is used to explore write current–time–error trade-offs, addressing the scarcity of switching events in thermal simulations</cite> <cite id="0ca6a0e8-2">Fokker–Planck approaches provide a reduced-order stochastic description of write processes, capturing binomial sampling challenges and enabling faster WER estimation for yield analysis</cite>. Device- and system-level evaluations further connect materials parameters (e.g., thermal stability Δ, spin polarization) to reliability under variations and workloads. <cite id="0ca6a0e8-0">Process variations that increase Δ, critical switching current, free-layer moment, or spin polarization increase write failure probability, while decreasing thermal stability factors reduce it, highlighting the sensitivity of reliability to materials and device parameters</cite> <cite id="0ca6a0e8-4">Retaining the inter-correlation among retention, read disturbance, and write failure rates is essential for accurate system-level reliability exploration under PVs and workload dependence</cite>.

# Selected Papers and Resources (by Topic)

- Spin–orbit torque materials physics and device prospects:
  - <cite id="635edb24-0">Benchmarking of Spin–Orbit Torque Switching Efficiency in Pt Alloys: reviews SOT mechanisms (spin Hall, interfacial Rashba, spin–momentum locking) and positions SOT-MRAM as energy-efficient and fast</cite>.
  - <cite id="635edb24-4">2D Rashba Ferromagnetic Electron Gas Transport and SOT: discusses SOT origins at interfaces and links to band structure, with implications for materials selection and device physics</cite>.
  - <cite id="635edb24-2">Roadmap of Spin–Orbit Torques: contrasts STT vs SOT MRAM, outlines key device metrics (TMR, BEOL compatibility, write efficiency), and identifies research and integration challenges</cite>.

- Device and circuit compact models and co-simulation:
  - <cite id="635edb24-3">Finite Element Modeling of Spin–Orbit Torques: LLG + drift–diffusion solver for HM/FM bilayers with SOT/STT simulation and realistic geometries</cite>.
  - <cite id="07369896-0">Impact of Technology Scaling and BEOL on MRAM: OOMMF-based micromagnetics with rare-event enhancement to quantify write current–time–error trade-offs for SOT/STT/ME devices</cite>.
  - <cite id="07369896-1">Comparative Vg-SOT/STT/SOT logic simulations in Cadence Virtuoso using Verilog-A MRAM models and 45 nm PDKs</cite>.
  - <cite id="07369896-2">Circuit-level SOT-MRAM Verilog-A model integrated with NCSU FreePDK 45 nm for in-memory computing architectures</cite>.
  - <cite id="07369896-3">SOT-MRAM Array/Device Optimization: oxide-thickness and resistance engineering leading to lower write and read energies and improved disturb margin</cite>.

- STT-MRAM variability, reliability, and system-level modeling:
  - <cite id="0ca6a0e8-2">Fokker–Planck Approach for Modeling Stochastic Phenomena in STT/RRAM: reduced-order WER modeling that reproduces experiments and accelerates yield analysis</cite>.
  - <cite id="0ca6a0e8-0">System-Level Reliability Formulation for STT-MRAM Caches: error-rate dependencies on Δ, critical current, free-layer moment, and spin polarization under PVs and workloads</cite>.
  - <cite id="0ca6a0e8-1">Survey on STT-MRAM Testing: retention fault characteristics, trade-offs between retention (Δ≈80 for SCM) and performance (cache applications), and specialized retention tests</cite>.
  - <cite id="0ca6a0e8-4">Workload- and PV-Dependent Cache Vulnerability: integrated formulation of retention, read disturbance, and write failure rates for early system-level exploration</cite>.

# Practical Modeling Workflow and Considerations

- Materials-to-device linkage: Use materials parameters (spin Hall angle, spin diffusion, interfacial Rashba parameters, damping, anisotropy) in device simulators to compute torque magnitudes and directions, then propagate to switching fields/currents and energy. <cite id="635edb24-0">SOT efficiency and origin (bulk vs interfacial) determine device write schemes and energy scaling</cite> <cite id="635edb24-3">Finite-element LLG+spin-accumulation solvers map materials-level spin transport to device geometry and torque profiles</cite>.
- Device/circuit co-simulation: Employ compact models (Verilog-A) within SPICE flows for logic and array simulations, while using micromagnetics for write dynamics and rare-event statistics. <cite id="07369896-1">Industry PDKs and Verilog-A models enable co-simulation of SOT/STT devices with digital circuits</cite> <cite id="07369896-0">OOMMF with rare-event acceleration supports device-level write-error characterization</cite>.
- Reliability and variability: Combine analytical models (Fokker–Planck) with system-level formulations to capture WER, retention, and read-disturb interplay under process variations and workloads. <cite id="0ca6a0e8-2">Fokker–Planck WER modeling reduces simulation costs while preserving accuracy</cite> <cite id="0ca6a0e8-4">System-level error integration is needed due to conflicting dependencies across error modes</cite>.

# Notes on Open-Source and Commercial Ecosystems

Open-source and commercial environments increasingly support MRAM simulation, though access to vendor-validated compact models and technology parameters can be critical for accurate co-simulation. <cite id="07369896-1">Cadence Virtuoso has been used with SOT/STT/Vg-SOT Verilog-A models at 45 nm</cite> <cite id="07369896-2">NCSU FreePDK 45 nm enables SPICE-level exploration of SOT-MRAM circuits</cite>. Micromagnetic toolchains such as OOMMF (or its modern counterparts) remain standard for device-level analysis with thermal noise and rare-event acceleration. <cite id="07369896-0">OOMMF-based simulations with rare-event enhancement quantify write errors and trade-offs in SOT/STT devices</cite>.

# Takeaways

- Materials choices that enhance SOT (e.g., HM/FM interfaces with spin Hall and Rashba effects) directly improve device-level write efficiency and enable voltage-driven schemes, while STT relies on current-driven torques with distinct scaling and reliability challenges. <cite id="635edb24-0">SOTs from spin Hall/interfacial effects and momentum locking enable efficient switching</cite> <cite id="635edb24-2">STT uses direct current-induced torques; SOT offers alternative energy/latency trade-offs</cite>.
- Robust evaluation requires multi-scale simulation: LLG/drift–diffusion for spin dynamics, micromagnetics with noise/rare-event handling for write reliability, and compact models within SPICE for circuit/system performance and verification. <cite id="635edb24-3">Finite-element LLG+spin-accumulation solvers for realistic geometries</cite> <cite id="07369896-0">OOMMF-based rare-event micromagnetics for write characterization</cite> <cite id="07369896-1">Verilog-A MRAM models in Cadence Virtuoso for logic/array co-simulation</cite>.
- Reliability under process variations and workloads must be assessed across WER, retention, and read-disturb, often via reduced-order stochastic models and system-level formulations. <cite id="0ca6a0e8-2">Fokker–Planck WER modeling accelerates yield analysis</cite> <cite id="0ca6a0e8-4">Integrating error modes under PVs and workloads is essential for dependable MRAM design</cite>.
</answer>

Title: Modeling and Optimization of Two-Terminal Spin-Orbit-Torque MRAM
Snippet: This paper presents physical modeling and benchmarking for two-terminal spin-orbit torque magnetic random-access memory (2T-SOT-MRAM). The results indicate that the common SOT materials that provide only in-plane torque can provide little to no improvement over spin-transfer-torque (STT) MRAM in terms of write energy. However, emerging SOT materials that provide out-of-plane torques with efficiencies as small as 0.1 can result in significant improvements in the write energy for such 2-terminal devices, especially when the magnet lateral dimensions are scaled down to 30 or 20 nm. Additionally, a novel 2T-SOT MRAM device is proposed that can increase the path electrons pass through the SOT layer; hence, increasing the generated spin current and the energy efficiency of the device. Our benchmarking results indicate that an out-of-plane SOT efficiency of 0.051 for 20nm wide devices can result in write energies approaching SRAM at the 7nm technology node.

Title: Finite Element Modeling of Spin-Orbit Torques
Snippet: Spin-orbit torques (SOTs) allow for efficient manipulation of magnetization in emerging spintronic devices such as nano-oscillators and nonvolatile magnetoresistive random access memories (MRAM). 

To facilitate the research and development of such devices, it is important to have software capable of simulating the spin and magnetization dynamics involved in their operation. To be able to simulate realistic devices the flexibility of the software with regards to geometry is critical. To address these needs, a solver has been developed with the capabilities to model spin-transfer torques (STT) in STT-MRAM cells. The solver uses the finite element method to model magnetization and spin dynamics on a mesh by solving the Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation (LLG) and a drift-diffusion model for spin accumulation [1], respectively. The capabilities of this solver have been extended to include the spin Hall effect (SHE), the main driving force behind SOT. In this work we present simulation results for the spin accumulation and spin torques in a heavy metal/ferromagnet (HM/FM) bilayer.

Title: Transport Property and Spin–Orbit Torque in 2D Rashba Ferromagnetic Electron Gas
Snippet: In recent years, spin-orbit torque has become one of the most attractive topics in the field of spintronics because of its great application prospects in magnetic information storage technology [1][2][3]. spin-orbit torque (SOT) is based on spin-orbit interaction (SOI), which uses the non-equilibrium spin accumulation induced by charge flow to generate a torque on a local magnetic moment [4,5], thus achieving the purpose of regulating magnetic storage units. SOT-based magnetic random access memory (SOT-MRAM) overcomes the disadvantages of STT-MRAM, especially the fact that it separates the read and write paths, so it has a higher read and write speed and lower power consumption than STT-MRAM [6,7]. Relevant studies show that SOT-MRAM can achieve ultra-fast information writing, which is reduced from the tens of nanoseconds required by the original STT-MRAM to less than 10 ns, while the power consumption of the device is further reduced [8,9]. 

The essence of spin-orbit torque is that the directional movement of electrons produces a non-equilibrium spin accumulation in the spin-orbit coupling system, by means of the s-d interaction, the spin accumulation of conducting electrons applies a torque on the local magnetic moment [10,11]. Meanwhile, this directional movement of electrons also generates a charge current in general. Thus, the current and spin-orbit torque are both manifestations of the non-equilibrium transport properties of the SOC system, there must be some relations between them. Literature have showed that the magnitude of spin-orbit torque is often proportional to the current density [12][13][14][15]. Because the spin accumulation and charge current are proportional to the external electric field under linear transport conditions, the ratio depends on the band structure of the system [4,5]. There is no clear conclusion about the underlying relationship between spin-orbit torque and conductivity. 

Two-dimensional Rashba ferromagnetic electron gas is an ideal platform for investigating spin-orbit torque [16,17], and the latter is often realized at heavy metal/ferromagnetic interfaces [18,19].

snippet.text: This paper presents physical modeling and benchmarking for two-terminal spin-orbit torque magnetic random-access memory (2T-SOT-MRAM). The results indicate that the common SOT materials that provide only in-plane torque can provide little to no improvement over spin-transfer-torque (STT) MRAM in terms of write energy. However, emerging SOT materials that provide out-of-plane torques with efficiencies as small as 0.1 can result in significant improvements in the write energy for such 2-terminal devices, especially when the magnet lateral dimensions are scaled down to 30 or 20 nm. Additionally, a novel 2T-SOT MRAM device is proposed that can increase the path electrons pass through the SOT layer; hence, increasing the generated spin current and the energy efficiency of the device. Our benchmarking results indicate that an out-of-plane SOT efficiency of 0.051 for 20nm wide devices can result in write energies approaching SRAM at the 7nm technology node.

Title: Impact of Technology Scaling and Back-End-of-the-Line Technology Solutions on Magnetic Random-Access Memories
Snippet: Fig. 1 shows the schematics and layouts for SOT-, STT-, and ME-MRAM cells based on earlier works [9], [10]. SOT-and ME-MRAM cells use two separate transistors for read and write operations, while STT-MRAM uses a single transistor for both operations. In terms of device operation, SOT-and STT-MRAM are current-controlled, while ME-MRAM is voltage-controlled. To evaluate various trade-offs among the write current, time, and error rate for SOT-and STT-MRAM devices, we perform object oriented micromagnetic framework (OOMMF)-based [11] micromagnetic simulations, which are augmented with rare event enhancement [12].

Title: Comparative performance evaluation of voltage gate-spin orbit torque MTJ-based digital logic circuits with 45 nm CMOS technology
Snippet: The CADENCE VIRTUOSO software was utilized to simulate the Full Adder and logic gates based on VgSOT technology. The simulations were conducted on a 45 nm technology node with a VDD (supply voltage) of 1.2 V. The Verilog model of VgSOT MRAM [35], STT MRAM [38,39], and SOT MRAM [40] have been employed. Table 1 presents the device parameters used for the model simulation of VgSOT, SOT, and STT technologies.

Title: In-Memory Computing Architecture for a Convolutional Neural Network Based on Spin Orbit Torque MRAM
Snippet: The SOT-MRAM model is built at the circuit level. The MRAM model used in our research is the same as that presented in [17]. That study's authors provided the SOT-MRAM Verilog-A model file that is used to facilitate simulations and verifications of the real-world performance of MRAM memory. Figure 11 presents the simulation results of MRAM Verilog-A in Cadence Virtuoso. We used NCSU FreePDK 45 nm [16] to simulate the SA circuit architecture and the digital circuit synthesis in Hspice. In addition, we chose StrongARM Latch [18], which consumes zero static power and has low latency. Thus, it is suitable for edge computing in the CIM architecture presented as Figure 12.

Title: Area Optimization Techniques for High-Density Spin-Orbit Torque MRAMs
Snippet: F-SOT-MRAM and R-SOT-MRAM achieve 45% lower write energy compared to STT-MRAM. Additionally, unlike STT-MRAM, in which the oxide thickness (tMgO) is determined by the tradeoff between read stability and write-ability, two proposed designs can optimize tMgO for a read operation only. In our work, tMgO for F-SOT-MRAM and R-SOT-MRAM was 1.30 nm, as opposed to 1.05 nm for STT-MRAM, as in Table 1. The thicker tMgO translates into the higher MTJ resistance, in turn, the smaller current required to develop the identical BL voltage during a read operation. Table 2 shows that F-SOT-MRAM and R-SOT-MRAM achieved 84% lower read energy and 2.3 x higher read-disturb margin in comparison to STT-MRAM.

Title: A Detailed Study of SOT-MRAM as an Alternative to DRAM Primary Memory in Multi-Core Environment
Snippet: Reliable evaluation of SOT-MRAM-based main memory is challenging due to the public unavailability of parameters related to timing and current. The significant advantage of MRAM devices is scalability, and they do not require any refresh, reducing static power consumption. STT-MRAM has been explored as the main memory in recent research [1], [7] providing promising results. The average speedups of Open and Close Page Techniques with a 1.2x configuration, as mentioned in [1], are 2.4% and 2.7%, respectively. Additionally, there was 4.6 times more power consumption than DRAM. One setback for STT-MRAM is its write latency, write energy and reliability [7]. SOT-MRAM provides better read/write latency, retention time, reliability and endurance than STT-MRAM [5], [8]. 

SOT-MRAM has not yet been evaluated as the primary memory for multi-core systems using full system simulators and benchmark programs, such as PARSEC [9]. Given its attractive features, SOT-MRAM has the potential to serve as the main memory. This research seeks to propose and explore its behaviour in a multi-core environment when handling shared memory workloads. We have derived SOT-MRAM main memory's timing and current parameters using the approach in [1]. The authors in [10] and [1] have validated the method and the parameters from industry estimation. Figure 1 depicts the different memory architectures used in our study. 

The contributions of this work are: 

• The first (best of our knowledge) to integrate SOT-MRAM into multi-core systems extending its application scope and three memory structures. 

• To address the challenge of parameter absence, the study estimates and scales parameters, ensuring a robust analysis of three memory structures. 

• A comprehensive survey and micro-architectural exploration reveal SOT-MRAM's superior circuit-level metrics. 

• Thorough system-level simulations provide a holistic evaluation, covering power consumption, bandwidth utilization, EDP, and total latency. 

The subsequent sections of the work are presented as follows: In Section II, we provide an introduction to MRAM memory.

documents.title: A Detailed Study of SOT-MRAM as an Alternative to DRAM Primary Memory in Multi-Core Environment
documents.snippet:
Reliable evaluation of SOT-MRAM-based main memory is challenging due to the public unavailability of parameters related to timing and current. The significant advantage of MRAM devices is scalability, and they do not require any refresh, reducing static power consumption. STT-MRAM has been explored as the main memory in recent research [1], [7] providing promising results. The average speedups of Open and Close Page Techniques with a 1.2x configuration, as mentioned in [1], are 2.4% and 2.7%, respectively. Additionally, there was 4.6 times more power consumption than DRAM. One setback for STT-MRAM is its write latency, write energy and reliability [7]. SOT-MRAM provides better read/write latency, retention time, reliability and endurance than STT-MRAM [5], [8]. 

SOT-MRAM has not yet been evaluated as the primary memory for multi-core systems using full system simulators and benchmark programs, such as PARSEC [9]. Given its attractive features, SOT-MRAM has the potential to serve as the main memory. This research seeks to propose and explore its behaviour in a multi-core environment when handling shared memory workloads. We have derived SOT-MRAM main memory's timing and current parameters using the approach in [1]. The authors in [10] and [1] have validated the method and the parameters from industry estimation. Figure 1 depicts the different memory architectures used in our study. 

The contributions of this work are: 

• The first (best of our knowledge) to integrate SOT-MRAM into multi-core systems extending its application scope and three memory structures. 

• To address the challenge of parameter absence, the study estimates and scales parameters, ensuring a robust analysis of three memory structures. 

• A comprehensive survey and micro-architectural exploration reveal SOT-MRAM's superior circuit-level metrics. 

• Thorough system-level simulations provide a holistic evaluation, covering power consumption, bandwidth utilization, EDP, and total latency. 

The subsequent sections of the work are presented as follows: In Section II, we provide an introduction to MRAM memory.

Title: Survey on STT-MRAM Testing: Failure Mechanisms, Fault Models, and Tests
Snippet: In Section IV-B(2), we have discussed the characteristics, causes, and influencing factors of retention fault in STT-MRAMs. Yet, the requirement of retention time for STT-MRAMs ranges from a few seconds to ten years, depending on the specific application. For the storage-class memory (SCM) application, 10+ years of retention time is desired as most of the data is rarely revisited. This requires a thermal stability (∆) as high as 80, which is experimentally achievable at the expense of high write energy and latency. In contrast, for the last-level-cache application which is seen as one of the most important markets for applying STT-MRAM technology in the short term, the average revival time of cache blocks is below 1 s [5]. This allows us to trade the retention time of STT-MRAMs for better write performance, which has been extensively studied [127][128][129]. 

Regardless of the different requirements of retention time of STT-MRAMs for different applications, testing retention time of STT-MRAMs is very important. However, characterizing STT-MRAM retention time is very challenging, since retention fault is essentially a transient and stochastic fault which depends on temperature, process variations, magnetic perturbation, and disturb current. Thus, March tests are not suitable to test it, and traditional retention tests for DRAMs cannot be directly applied to STT-MRAMs. This calls for special test techniques. Next, we will introduce three test approaches dedicated to testing STT-MRAM retention time.

Title: A Fokker–Planck Approach for Modeling the Stochastic Phenomena in Magnetic and Resistive Random Access Memory Devices
Snippet: Due to increasing demand for memory-intensive applications such as hardware accelerators for AI, embedded non-volatile memory (eNVM) technologies such as resistive random access memory (RRAM) [1] and spin-transfer torque magnetic random access memory (STT MRAM) [2] have been widely explored for these applications [3]- [8] due to their comparative advantage (such as non-volatility, near-zero standby leakage power, small cell size and scalability [9]- [17]) over other memory technologies. However, the programming mechanisms in RRAM [18] and STT MRAM [19] are inherently stochastic, which introduce write errors that may drastically impact the robustness and reliability of the memory and thus, pose a significant challenge to their widespread adoption. Moreover, the impact of the write error rate (WER) needs to be investigated alongside process variations during yield analysis, which may significantly increase the complexity of conventional methods based on the Monte Carlo approach. Consider the simulation of WER in STT MRAM for example. The WER is estimated by counting the number of failures out of N simulation runs and the probability of obtaining each observation follows a binomial distribution. The number of simulation runs needed to estimate the WER and the accuracy of the estimation are graphed in Figure 1. Thus, a significant amount of computing resources may be required to perform yield analysis in RRAM and STT MRAM. 

Alternatively, it was shown that the WER of STT MRAM can be estimated using an approach based on the Fokker-Planck (FP) equation [20], [21]. In this approach, the distribution of memory cell states during the write process is modeled directly, which significantly reduces the computation effort for estimating the WER. In this paper, we propose a generalized approach for estimating the WER in STT MRAM and steady state analysis

of RRAM devices, based on the Fokker-Planck equation.

Title: A Fokker–Planck Approach for Modeling the Stochastic Phenomena in Magnetic and Resistive Random Access Memory Devices
Snippet: Embedded nonvolatile memory technologies, such as resistive random access memory (RRAM) and spin-transfer torque magnetic RAM (STT MRAM), are increasingly being researched for application in neuromorphic computing and hardware accelerators for artificial intelligence (AI). However, the stochastic write processes in these memory technologies affect their yield and need to be studied alongside process variations, which drastically increase the complexity of yield analysis using the Monte Carlo approach. Therefore, we propose an approach based on the Fokker–Planck equation for modeling the stochastic write processes in STT MRAM and RRAM devices. Moreover, we show that our proposed approach can reproduce the experimental results for both STT-MRAM and RRAM devices.

Title: A System-Level Framework for Analytical and Empirical Reliability Exploration of STT-MRAM Caches
Snippet: Although the error rate of a single STT-MRAM cell can be estimated using its physical parameters, the vulnerability estimation of the entire STT-MRAM cache requires systemlevel analysis considering the workloads behaviors as well as PV effects. A recent study has reported only the rate of write failure and read disturbance in STT-MRAM cache and shown that these rates are strongly workload-dependent [20], [28]. To the best of our knowledge, none of the previous studies neither have addressed the workloads-and PVs-dependent vulnerability of STT-MRAM caches considering all types of errors, nor reported the cache reliability considering the conflicting sources of errors. Therefore, to achieve an acceptable level of reliability in STT-MRAM cache with affordable costs, it is necessary to a) estimate the vulnerability of the cache to each error type as well as the total cache vulnerability considering the conflicting dependencies of error types to different factors and b) utilize effective mitigation techniques for each error type according to its contribution in the total cache vulnerability. 

In this paper, we propose a system-level framework for early exploration of STT-MRAM cache reliability, which considers a) workload-dependent cache access patterns and data content, b) PV affected STT-MRAM cell vulnerability to errors, and c) inter-correlation between the rate of threementioned errors, i.e., retention failure, read disturbance, and write failure, for reliability exploration. To this end, we first formulate the vulnerability of STT-MRAM caches to each error type by extrapolating the error probability of PV affected cache blocks from nominal error probability of a single STT-MRAM cell. Then, we deduce the error probability of a PV affected STT-MRAM cache from the blocks error probability. Our formulation is then extended to integrate probabilities of the three differently-originated and exclusively-occurred error types into a single cache vulnerability equation.

snippet.text:
Although the error rate of a single STT-MRAM cell can be estimated using its physical parameters, the vulnerability estimation of the entire STT-MRAM cache requires systemlevel analysis considering the workloads behaviors as well as PV effects. A recent study has reported only the rate of write failure and read disturbance in STT-MRAM cache and shown that these rates are strongly workload-dependent [20], [28]. To the best of our knowledge, none of the previous studies neither have addressed the workloads-and PVs-dependent vulnerability of STT-MRAM caches considering all types of errors, nor reported the cache reliability considering the conflicting sources of errors. Therefore, to achieve an acceptable level of reliability in STT-MRAM cache with affordable costs, it is necessary to a) estimate the vulnerability of the cache to each error type as well as the total cache vulnerability considering the conflicting dependencies of error types to different factors and b) utilize effective mitigation techniques for each error type according to its contribution in the total cache vulnerability. 

In this paper, we propose a system-level framework for early exploration of STT-MRAM cache reliability, which considers a) workload-dependent cache access patterns and data content, b) PV affected STT-MRAM cell vulnerability to errors, and c) inter-correlation between the rate of threementioned errors, i.e., retention failure, read disturbance, and write failure, for reliability exploration. To this end, we first formulate the vulnerability of STT-MRAM caches to each error type by extrapolating the error probability of PV affected cache blocks from nominal error probability of a single STT-MRAM cell. Then, we deduce the error probability of a PV affected STT-MRAM cache from the blocks error probability. Our formulation is then extended to integrate probabilities of the three differently-originated and exclusively-occurred error types into a single cache vulnerability equation.

problem: what are faceted plots
final_response:
# What are faceted plots?

Faceted plots, also called trellis displays or small multiples, show the same plot type repeated in multiple panels, each displaying a subset of the data determined by one or more variables, so the viewer can compare patterns across groups while keeping the visual encoding consistent across panels.<cite id="5bb4264d-0">In the Grammar of Graphics, facets are defined as displaying subsets of a data set in panels of the same graphic</cite><cite id="5bb4264d-2">Trellis displays, also known as small multiples or faceted plots, arrange multiple plots of the same type but for different subsets of data in a structured manner</cite><cite id="77b40137-0">Trellis displays, also known as small multiples or faceted plots, are a widely used and effective method in data visualization</cite>.

In practice, faceting conditions the display on categorical (or discretized) variables to partition the data and repeat the plot template for each partition, typically in a grid of rows and columns, with shared axes and labels to support comparison.<cite id="5bb4264d-0">In ggplot2, facets coordinate the scales and labels for each panel</cite><cite id="5bb4264d-2">Typically, trellis displays are configured in a rectangular layout with each panel having the same rectangular dimensions, and a high-level specification defines rows, columns, or mapping of subsets to panels</cite><cite id="11551ee0-0">There are two faceting functions: facet_wrap() and facet_grid(), which repeat a plot for subgroups and use a formula to determine the layout</cite>.

# How faceted plots work (mechanics)

Most systems implement faceting by binding a variable (or variables) to a “facet” layer that generates panels and assigns data points to panels according to the factor levels or bins, while keeping the core plot encoding (scales, geoms, stats, coordinates) the same across panels.<cite id="5bb4264d-2">ggplot2 composes plots from modular objects and uses Facet objects to layout panels according to their aspect ratios, margins, and dimensions</cite><cite id="11551ee0-0">Both facet_grid() and facet_wrap() take formulas to define panel rows and columns and share a common scales argument</cite><cite id="5bb4264d-1">The grammar defines how components like data, aesthetics, geoms, scales, stats, and coordinates are organized and coordinated, which faceting leverages to repeat a plot template under different subsets</cite>.

- Grid faceting: Two-variable conditioning often arranges panels in a 2D grid. For example, in ggplot2, facet_grid(~ group) lays out panels by group in columns, facet_grid(group ~ .) lays out panels by group in rows, and facet_grid(group ~ sex) makes a 2D grid by both group and sex.<cite id="11551ee0-0">facet_grid(.~ group) generates multipanel plots per level of a factor by column; facet_grid(group ~ .) by row; facet_grid(group ~ sex) makes a 2D grid</cite><cite id="11551ee0-3">Note that facet_grid(GEN~.) creates a panel plot by row, whereas facet_grid(.~ GEN) creates a panel plot by column</cite>.

- Wrap faceting: One-dimensional panel sequences can be “wrapped” into a compact 2D layout. facet_wrap() reshapes a “ribbon” of panels into a grid and lets you control the number of columns/rows and ordering (table-like or inverted).<cite id="11551ee0-0">facet_wrap() reshapes a 1D ribbon into a 2D arrangement and can wrap into a square-like layout, with options for column count and ordering</cite>.

- Scale behavior and layout controls: Faceting often shares axes across panels for direct comparison, but options like “free” scales per dimension, adjusted spacing, and custom panel order/rotation exist to handle long labels or uneven group sizes.<cite id="5bb4264d-0">ggplot2 facets coordinate scales and labels; for long labels, rotation and layout adjustments are recommended</cite><cite id="5bb4264d-2">Panels are typically rectangular and laid out via a high-level specification of rows/columns and ordering</cite><cite id="5bb4264d-0">For relative abundance facets, values should have the same visual weight across panels (space = free_x or free_y) and labels may need rotation to remain legible</cite>.

# Common uses and examples

Faceted plots are useful for exploring and comparing distributions, time series, or relationships across discrete groups, especially when a single composite plot would obscure patterns or overplot data.<cite id="5bb4264d-4">Facets repeat a plot for several to many subgroups and are a great way to inspect longitudinal data by distributing them along one dimension while keeping axes and other aesthetics consistent</cite><cite id="11551ee0-0">You can choose aesthetic mappings to distinguish subgroups within a single region or use faceting to separate group-wise behavior into subpanels</cite>.

- Longitudinal or time-series inspection: Distribute time or category levels along one axis and keep scales consistent to reveal level-specific trends and variation.<cite id="5bb4264d-4">They are a great way of inspecting longitudinal data by distributing them along one dimension while keeping axes consistent</cite>.

- Comparative grouping: Show the same relationship (e.g., scatter, line, bar) per category or treatment to compare effects across factors, including nested or crossed designs via 1D or 2D grids.<cite id="11551ee0-0">Facet_grid() can produce 1D and 2D grids, and facet_wrap() reshapes panel arrangements, aiding visualization of complex clinical data with multiple dose levels or drugs</cite>.

- Domain-specific workflows: In fields like paleoenvironmental science, specialized facets enforce best-practice scaling and labeling for multi-parameter or relative-abundance displays, and packages provide tailored facet types and labellers.<cite id="5bb4264d-0">Plotting multiple parameters using facets is natural for one-row-per-measurement data; facets coordinate scales and labels</cite><cite id="5bb4264d-3">Relative abundance facets wrap facet_grid() with rules for equal visual weight and tailored labellers; packages like tidypaleo provide facet_geochem_* wrappers and discuss alignment with patchwork for mixed data types</cite>.

# Variants and controls

Most modern systems provide a small set of faceting recipes and fine-grained controls:

- Base faceting functions: 1D wrap vs 2D grid; column-wise vs row-wise layouts; control of panel count, ordering, and “as.table”-like orientation.<cite id="11551ee0-0">facet_grid() vs facet_wrap(); column vs row; 2D grids via crossed variables; facet_wrap() panel ribbon and layout control via ncol/nrow and as.table-like behavior</cite>.

- Scale sharing and freedom: Choose shared (synchronized) scales across panels or “free” scales per dimension to avoid compressing or stretching variation; this is especially useful when groups have different ranges or long labels require extra spacing.<cite id="5bb4264d-0">Relative abundance facets recommend space = free_x or free_y so that percent values have equal visual weight across panels</cite><cite id="5bb4264d-2">High-level layout control includes panel dimensions and margins to accommodate consistent scaling across small multiples</cite>.

- Interactive/dynamic facets: Allow users to vary conditioning variables on the fly or toggle subsets, which helps with high-dimensional data and large datasets that don’t fit in a static page.<cite id="5bb4264d-4">Interactive and dynamic plots can let readers select facets on the fly and inspect multidimensional data; these are often used online as supplements</cite>.

- Facet composition and programmatic use: Some workflows combine facets with other composites (e.g., patchwork) or build programmatic stacks; limitations exist when deeply customizing aesthetics per panel inside a single faceted ggplot2 object, which can push users to restructure data or use additional tools.<cite id="5bb4264d-3">The patchwork package can align multiple ggplot2 plots for mixed data types, grouping same-type panels and sharing scales</cite><cite id="11551ee0-4">ggplot2’s faceting supports multiple subplots but limits aesthetic customization per facet; complex designs may require data restructuring or alternative plotting strategies</cite>.

# Best practices and pitfalls

Faceted plots are powerful for comparison, but they can also clutter a figure or mislead if scales or layout are not handled carefully.

- Clutter and empty panels: Many combinations can produce sparse or empty panels; choose variables with moderate numbers of levels and collapse or summarize where appropriate, and allow some panel omission or clear spacing to avoid confusion.<cite id="77b40137-0">Constructing trellis displays requires arranging plots according to aspect ratios, margins, and panel dimensions; a high-level specification is often used to define rows/columns and mapping of subsets to panels</cite><cite id="5bb4264d-2">Panel dimensions and margins are critical to maintain legibility in rectangular layouts</cite>.

- Scale choices: Use consistent scales to support direct comparison; use “free” scales when group ranges differ widely or when text labels require extra panel spacing; avoid synchronized axes that obscure group-specific variation when that is the intent.<cite id="5bb4264d-0">Facets coordinate scales and labels; for relative abundance, equal visual weight across panels is recommended via free spacing and appropriate scales</cite><cite id="5bb4264d-4">Keeping axes consistent is a key benefit of faceting for inspecting longitudinal data</cite>.

- Labels and legends: Rotate long labels to fit, control panel ordering, and ensure legends and axes remain readable across all panels; avoid overloading panel headers with too much text.<cite id="5bb4264d-0">Facet labels can be long and need rotation to be legible; layout controls and clipping adjustments are often necessary</cite>.

- Don’t overuse or encode too much per panel: If each panel already encodes many variables, faceting can explode the total cognitive load. Consider simplifying per-panel encodings and using complementary faceting or alternative encodings (line type, color, shape) within a single plot, or combine small multiples with mosaic-style composites when appropriate.<cite id="11551ee0-4">ggplot2 faceting has limits for per-panel aesthetic customization; restructuring data and using alternative plotting approaches may be required for complex composites</cite><cite id="5bb4264d-3">For mixed data types, aligning grouped plots with patchwork and assigning common scales can improve readability compared to complex single-faceted plots</cite>.

- Choose the right number of dimensions to facet: Faceting two variables in a 2D grid is natural; adding more than two or too many levels can defeat the purpose. For more than three dimensions, consider combining small multiples with other designs (e.g., color mapping, mosaics) to keep the display comprehensible.<cite id="77b40137-3">Small multiples facilitate comparison across panels, but with more than three axes the interpretability drops; alternative forms like stacked bar or mosaic charts may be better for higher-dimensional comparisons</cite>.

- Use faceting to avoid overplotting and to expose data: Show all raw points within each facet and keep consistent transparency or jitter to reveal distributional details; this is especially helpful in time series and grouped scatter plots.<cite id="5bb4264d-4">Plotting all raw data points is useful for inspecting variation and distributional information in longitudinal settings when using facets</cite>.

# When to use faceted plots vs alternatives

Faceted plots are particularly effective when:
- You need to compare the same relationship or distribution across discrete groups or time points while preserving consistent mappings for direct comparison.<cite id="5bb4264d-4">Facets repeat a plot for subgroups and keep axes consistent, aiding inspection of longitudinal and grouped data</cite><cite id="11551ee0-0">Faceting separates group-wise behavior into subpanels for complex clinical or experimental data</cite>.
- Your dataset is naturally partitioned (e.g., by subject, site, condition) and the within-group pattern is the primary interest, while between-group differences are secondary.<cite id="11551ee0-0">Facet_grid and facet_wrap support multiple subgroups and complex designs like multiple dose levels or drugs</cite>.

Consider alternatives when:
- The number of groups is large or combinations explode; then use color, shape, or line type to encode group membership within a single panel and/or use interactive faceting to filter groups on demand.<cite id="11551ee0-4">ggplot2 faceting limits per-panel aesthetic customization and can become unwieldy; programmatic or alternative approaches may be needed</cite><cite id="5bb4264d-4">Interactive facets let readers select subsets on the fly for high-dimensional data</cite>.
- You need to emphasize joint relationships among many variables; then combine small multiples with other encodings (parallel coordinates, mosaics) rather than forcing all dimensions into panel axes.<cite id="77b40137-3">With more than three axes, hive plots and other forms degrade in interpretability; small multiples can be combined with other encodings to manage dimensionality</cite>.

# Summary

In short, faceted plots are small multiples that repeat a consistent plot template for data subsets defined by one or more variables, arranged in a grid to support comparative reasoning and exploratory analysis.<cite id="5bb4264d-0">Facets display subsets of a dataset in panels of the same graphic</cite><cite id="5bb4264d-2">Trellis displays arrange multiple plots of the same type for different subsets in a structured, rectangular layout</cite><cite id="11551ee0-0">Facet_grid() and facet_wrap() implement 2D grids and ribbon wraps to partition data and repeat the plot</cite>. They are powerful when used judiciously with appropriate scales, spacing, and panel ordering, and with awareness of their limits for high-dimensional or highly granular groupings; when these limits arise, combine faceting with other encodings or interactive features to maintain clarity.<cite id="5bb4264d-0">Facets coordinate scales and labels, with options for free spacing and label rotation to maintain legibility</cite><cite id="5bb4264d-4">Interactive and dynamic facets can handle larger, multidimensional data by enabling on-the-fly selection</cite><cite id="11551ee0-4">Complex composites can push against ggplot2 faceting limits, suggesting data restructuring or alternative plotting strategies</cite>.

package provides facet types for two common cases: relative abundance data and geochemical data.

When plotted, relative abundance values on each panel should have the same weight (i.e., 5% on one panel should take up the same amount of space as 5% on another panel; space = "free_x" or space = "free_y"). Title: Application of ggplot2 to Pharmacometric Graphics
Snippet: The ggplot2 package, authored by Hadley Wickham, 1 is an implementation of the theory described in "The Grammar of Graphics" by Leland Wilkinson. 2 In a nutshell, the grammar defines a set of rules by which components of a statistical graphic are organized, coordinated, and rendered. The package is programmed entirely in the R statistical programming environment 3 using the grid graphics system, 4 extending Wilkinson's theory to a "layered" grammar of graphics. 5 he grammar implemented in ggplot2 provides an infrastructure for composing a graphic from multiple elements: 

• An input data object, usually an R data frame. 

• Aesthetics (abbreviated "aes"), which refer to visual attributes that affect how data are displayed in a graphic, e.g., color, point size, or line type. • Geometric objects ("geoms" for short), such as points, lines, polygons, box plots, error bars, etc. • Scale transformations, which map aesthetics to unique values of variables, in addition to mathematical transformations to produce positional axes (e.g., logarithms). This process entails a conversion from "data units" to "graphical units." The inverse mapping of a scale transformation is rendered in the graphic as a guide, either a positional scale or a legend, in the original data units. • Statistical transformations ("stats"), which refer to some type of data summarization such as a five-number summary for a box plot (stat_boxplot) or counts of observations by bin (stat_bin). The objective of statistical transformation is to supply the inputs necessary to produce a geom; for example, stat_bin sets up the data structure necessary for geom_bar and geom_histogram. Many stat_functions can be invoked directly to generate ggplot layers. • Coordinate transformations ("coord"), which specify how a coordinate system is specified in a graphic. The default is the Cartesian coordinate system, but several others are built in, such as polar coordinates (coord_ polar) or flips of the x and y coordinates (coord_flip).
</snippet>

Title: Examining the Interface Design of Tidyverse
Snippet: Trellis displays, also known as small multiples or faceted plots, are a widely used and effective method in data visualization. These displays involve arranging multiple plots, each representing the same plot type but with different subsets of data, in a structured manner (Becker, Cleveland, and Shyu 1996). Constructing trellis displays requires a mechanism for arranging the plots according to their aspect ratios, margins, and panel dimensions (Murrell 1999). Typically, trellis displays are configured in a rectangular layout, with each plot panel having the same rectangular dimensions. Consequently, a high-level specification is often employed to define the display layout, such as the number of rows and columns or the mapping of plots or data subsets to individual panels. 

The layouts in ggplot2 (Wickham 2010) are primarily controlled by Facet objects. More specifically, ggplot2 composes plots based on assembling modular objects (data, aesthetic mapping, layer, geometric objects, statistics, coordinate system, theme, facet, scales, and guides). These modular objects are primarily defined though an object oriented system called ggproto, inspired by the grammar of graphics by Wilkinson (2005). A new plot in ggplot2 is made by substituting these modular objects. 

Code 2.2 demonstrates a ggplot2 syntax for constructing a trellis display using the penguins data. Lines 2-3 specifies the primary data and the aesthetic mapping of data to graphical elements. Line 4 specifies the plot type (with default statistics calculated from frequency of bin width of 1 and bars outlined in black). Line 5 details the layout of the trellis display (referred to as facet in ggplot2), indicating that the panel data is separated by species, organized into one column, with the row order adjusted so that the first factor level appears at the bottom and the last factor level appears at the top. 

Code 2.2 (Tidyverse approach): data visualisation 1 library(ggplot2) 2 ggplot(penguins) + Base R (through the graphics package) specifies the layout of plots using par(), after which users print each individual plot to the graphics output sequentially. Code 2.3 shows a near equivalent output to Code 2.2 using a Base R approach.

Snippet: Hive plots adapt parallel coordinate plots (Inselberg, 2009;Wegman, 1990) to a radial arrangement, compacting the layout and making the connections easier to follow. Hive plots typically rely on a three-axis model, with the total circle area being uniformly divided between all segments (the areas between two axes). An illustrative adapted stacked hive plot, like the ones used throughout this study is presented in Figure S1 in Supporting Information S1. As demonstrated in this study, the three axes we utilize reflect three dynamic properties of the SOWs generated. More than three dimensions can be used, but by having only three axes, hive plots accommodate connections (lines) between each axis pair, without having to cross the axes themselves. With more than three axes this can only be achieved if connections are only drawn between neighboring axes, or if axes are duplicated at multiple positions. This negatively impacts the interpretability of the figure, which defies the aim of creating meaningful and salient narratives, central to our framework. The originators of the figure indeed discourage its use with more than three axes (Krzywinski et al., 2012), and most common applications in network science (e.g., Engle & Whalen, 2012) and gene sequencing (e.g., Yang et al., 2017) also only use three axes. Furthermore, the compactness of this figure allows us to generate multiple panels reflecting alternative dynamic properties or robustness performance measures, in a "small multiples" visualization (Tufte, 1990). Combining many small visualizations simultaneously allows the reader to compare the separate panels and look for patterns or outliers in the matrix of visuals, and facilitates presentation and storytelling of large amounts of data in a single figure (van den Elzen & van Wijk, 2013). In situations where more than three pairs of dynamic properties need to be used, alternative graphical forms (e.g., stacked bar charts or Marimekko (mosaic) charts (Friendly, 2002)) are also suited to FRNSIC scenario discovery, but they have their own strengths and weaknesses (presented in Figure S1 in Supporting Information S1).

Title: Application of ggplot2 to Pharmacometric Graphics
Snippet: The concept of conditioning plots by the levels of one or more factors is called faceting in ggplot2. There are two faceting functions: facet_wrap() and facet_grid(). Both use a formula to determine the layout, and both share a common argument scales =, but otherwise, they are separate entities. facet_grid() is capable of generating a 2D grid of graphics panels-by column and/or by row. For example, facet_grid(.~ group) generates multipanel plots per level of a factor group by column, but facet_grid(group ~.) will generate plots by row. The dot (.) indicates that no variable is specified for that side of the formula. By specifying both sides, such as facet_grid(group ~ sex), a 2D grid of multipanel plots by group and by sex will be produced. In contrast, facet_wrap() reshapes a 1D ribbon of plots into a 2D arrangement. Instead of a 2D grid of panels associated with the level combinations of two variables, facet_wrap() creates a string of panels and "wraps" them into the graphics region like a ribbon, patterned on how the lattice behaves. You can specify ncol and/or nrow to control the arrangement of panels. You could write facet_wrap(~ group, ncol=4)to create a graph with four panels per row. The default (if you do not specify ncol or nrow) action is to attempt to lay out the panels as close to a square as possible. The default action is to start in the top left corner, moving left to right and then down, starting each new row from the left. The argument as.table = TRUE controls this ordering. Setting it to FALSE initiates wrapping from the bottom left corner of the graphics region and upward (see Supplementary Material online for the example code for facet_wrap()). 

Here is an illustration to visualize complex clinical data (e.g., multiple dose levels, different drugs, etc.). You can choose aesthetic mappings to distinguish behavior among subgroups in a single graphics region or use faceting to separate group-wise behavior into multiple subpanels.
</snippet>

Snippet: Trellis displays, also known as small multiples or faceted plots, are a widely used and effective method in data visualization. These displays involve arranging multiple plots, each representing the same plot type but with different subsets of data, in a structured manner (Becker, Cleveland, and Shyu 1996). Constructing trellis displays requires a mechanism for arranging the plots according to their aspect ratios, margins, and panel dimensions (Murrell 1999). Typically, trellis displays are configured in a rectangular layout, with each plot panel having the same rectangular dimensions. Consequently, a high-level specification is often employed to define the display layout, such as the number of rows and columns or the mapping of plots or data subsets to individual panels. 

The layouts in ggplot2 (Wickham 2010) are primarily controlled by Facet objects. More specifically, ggplot2 composes plots based on assembling modular objects (data, aesthetic mapping, layer, geometric objects, statistics, coordinate system, theme, facet, scales, and guides). These modular objects are primarily defined though an object oriented system called ggproto, inspired by the grammar of graphics by Wilkinson (2005). A new plot in ggplot2 is made by substituting these modular objects. 

Code 2.2 demonstrates a ggplot2 syntax for constructing a trellis display using the penguins data. Lines 2-3 specifies the primary data and the aesthetic mapping of data to graphical elements. Line 4 specifies the plot type (with default statistics calculated from frequency of bin width of 1 and bars outlined in black). Line 5 details the layout of the trellis display (referred to as facet in ggplot2), indicating that the panel data is separated by species, organized into one column, with the row order adjusted so that the first factor level appears at the bottom and the last factor level appears at the top. 

Code 2.2 (Tidyverse approach): data visualisation 1 library(ggplot2) 2 ggplot(penguins) + Base R (through the graphics package) specifies the layout of plots using par(), after which users print each individual plot to the graphics output sequentially. Code 2.3 shows a near equivalent output to Code 2.2 using a Base R approach.

package provides facet types for two common cases: relative abundance data and geochemical data. 

Facets for relative abundance data (facet_abundance() and facet_abundanceh()) wrap ggplot2::facet_grid(), applying best-practice rules for the relationship between abundance scales. When plotted, relative abundance values on each panel should have the same weight (i.e., 5% on one panel should take up the same amount of space as 5% on another panel; space = "free_x" or space = "free_y"). Facet labels must have species names italicized for publication in most journals, but modifiers (e.g., strain III) must not be italicized. This constraint can be accommodated by setting the default labeller to a function that understands the form of most species input (label_species()). Finally, facet labels are typically too long to fit horizontally above each panel and must be rotated to be legible. While rotating a facet label is possible using ggplot2 theme modifications, eliminating the horizontal clip is not. Panels representing different geochemical parameters do not require space = "free_x" or space = "free_y", and thus can wrap either facet_wrap() or facet_grid(). # What are faceted plots?

Faceted plots, also called trellis displays or small multiples, show the same plot type repeated in multiple panels, each displaying a subset of the data determined by one or more variables, so the viewer can compare patterns across groups while keeping the visual encoding consistent across panels.<cite id="5bb4264d-0">In the Grammar of Graphics, facets are defined as displaying subsets of a data set in panels of the same graphic</cite><cite id="5bb4264d-2">Trellis displays, also known as small multiples or faceted plots, arrange multiple plots of the same type but for different subsets of data in a structured manner</cite><cite id="77b40137-0">Trellis displays, also known as small multiples or faceted plots, are a widely used and effective method in data visualization</cite>.

In practice, faceting conditions the display on categorical (or discretized) variables to partition the data and repeat the plot template for each partition, typically in a grid of rows and columns, with shared axes and labels to support comparison.<cite id="5bb4264d-0">In ggplot2, facets coordinate the scales and labels for each panel</cite><cite id="5bb4264d-2">Typically, trellis displays are configured in a rectangular layout with each panel having the same rectangular dimensions, and a high-level specification defines rows, columns, or mapping of subsets to panels</cite><cite id="11551ee0-0">There are two faceting functions: facet_wrap() and facet_grid(), which repeat a plot for subgroups and use a formula to determine the layout</cite>.

# How faceted plots work (mechanics)

Most systems implement faceting by binding a variable (or variables) to a “facet” layer that generates panels and assigns data points to panels according to the factor levels or bins, while keeping the core plot encoding (scales, geoms, stats, coordinates) the same across panels.<cite id="5bb4264d-2">ggplot2 composes plots from modular objects and uses Facet objects to layout panels according to their aspect ratios, margins, and dimensions</cite><cite id="11551ee0-0">Both facet_grid() and facet_wrap() take formulas to define panel rows and columns and share a common scales argument</cite><cite id="5bb4264d-1">The grammar defines how components like data, aesthetics, geoms, scales, stats, and coordinates are organized and coordinated, which faceting leverages to repeat a plot template under different subsets</cite>.

- Grid faceting: Two-variable conditioning often arranges panels in a 2D grid. For example, in ggplot2, facet_grid(~ group) lays out panels by group in columns, facet_grid(group ~ .) lays out panels by group in rows, and facet_grid(group ~ sex) makes a 2D grid by both group and sex.<cite id="11551ee0-0">facet_grid(.~ group) generates multipanel plots per level of a factor by column; facet_grid(group ~ .) by row; facet_grid(group ~ sex) makes a 2D grid</cite><cite id="11551ee0-3">Note that facet_grid(GEN~.) creates a panel plot by row, whereas facet_grid(.~ GEN) creates a panel plot by column</cite>.

- Wrap faceting: One-dimensional panel sequences can be “wrapped” into a compact 2D layout. facet_wrap() reshapes a “ribbon” of panels into a grid and lets you control the number of columns/rows and ordering (table-like or inverted).<cite id="11551ee0-0">facet_wrap() reshapes a 1D ribbon into a 2D arrangement and can wrap into a square-like layout, with options for column count and ordering</cite>.

- Scale behavior and layout controls: Faceting often shares axes across panels for direct comparison, but options like “free” scales per dimension, adjusted spacing, and custom panel order/rotation exist to handle long labels or uneven group sizes.<cite id="5bb4264d-0">ggplot2 facets coordinate scales and labels; for long labels, rotation and layout adjustments are recommended</cite><cite id="5bb4264d-2">Panels are typically rectangular and laid out via a high-level specification of rows/columns and ordering</cite><cite id="5bb4264d-0">For relative abundance facets, values should have the same visual weight across panels (space = free_x or free_y) and labels may need rotation to remain legible</cite>.

# Common uses and examples

Faceted plots are useful for exploring and comparing distributions, time series, or relationships across discrete groups, especially when a single composite plot would obscure patterns or overplot data.<cite id="5bb4264d-4">Facets repeat a plot for several to many subgroups and are a great way to inspect longitudinal data by distributing them along one dimension while keeping axes and other aesthetics consistent</cite><cite id="11551ee0-0">You can choose aesthetic mappings to distinguish subgroups within a single region or use faceting to separate group-wise behavior into subpanels</cite>.

- Longitudinal or time-series inspection: Distribute time or category levels along one axis and keep scales consistent to reveal level-specific trends and variation.<cite id="5bb4264d-4">They are a great way of inspecting longitudinal data by distributing them along one dimension while keeping axes consistent</cite>.

- Comparative grouping: Show the same relationship (e.g., scatter, line, bar) per category or treatment to compare effects across factors, including nested or crossed designs via 1D or 2D grids.<cite id="11551ee0-0">Facet_grid() can produce 1D and 2D grids, and facet_wrap() reshapes panel arrangements, aiding visualization of complex clinical data with multiple dose levels or drugs</cite>.

- Domain-specific workflows: In fields like paleoenvironmental science, specialized facets enforce best-practice scaling and labeling for multi-parameter or relative-abundance displays, and packages provide tailored facet types and labellers.<cite id="5bb4264d-0">Plotting multiple parameters using facets is natural for one-row-per-measurement data; facets coordinate scales and labels</cite><cite id="5bb4264d-3">Relative abundance facets wrap facet_grid() with rules for equal visual weight and tailored labellers; packages like tidypaleo provide facet_geochem_* wrappers and discuss alignment with patchwork for mixed data types</cite>.

# Variants and controls

Most modern systems provide a small set of faceting recipes and fine-grained controls:

- Base faceting functions: 1D wrap vs 2D grid; column-wise vs row-wise layouts; control of panel count, ordering, and “as.table”-like orientation.<cite id="11551ee0-0">facet_grid() vs facet_wrap(); column vs row; 2D grids via crossed variables; facet_wrap() panel ribbon and layout control via ncol/nrow and as.table-like behavior</cite>.

- Scale sharing and freedom: Choose shared (synchronized) scales across panels or “free” scales per dimension to avoid compressing or stretching variation; this is especially useful when groups have different ranges or long labels require extra spacing.<cite id="5bb4264d-0">Relative abundance facets recommend space = free_x or free_y so that percent values have equal visual weight across panels</cite><cite id="5bb4264d-2">High-level layout control includes panel dimensions and margins to accommodate consistent scaling across small multiples</cite>.

- Interactive/dynamic facets: Allow users to vary conditioning variables on the fly or toggle subsets, which helps with high-dimensional data and large datasets that don’t fit in a static page.<cite id="5bb4264d-4">Interactive and dynamic plots can let readers select facets on the fly and inspect multidimensional data; these are often used online as supplements</cite>.

- Facet composition and programmatic use: Some workflows combine facets with other composites (e.g., patchwork) or build programmatic stacks; limitations exist when deeply customizing aesthetics per panel inside a single faceted ggplot2 object, which can push users to restructure data or use additional tools.<cite id="5bb4264d-3">The patchwork package can align multiple ggplot2 plots for mixed data types, grouping same-type panels and sharing scales</cite><cite id="11551ee0-4">ggplot2’s faceting supports multiple subplots but limits aesthetic customization per facet; complex designs may require data restructuring or alternative plotting strategies</cite>.

# Best practices and pitfalls

Faceted plots are powerful for comparison, but they can also clutter a figure or mislead if scales or layout are not handled carefully.

- Clutter and empty panels: Many combinations can produce sparse or empty panels; choose variables with moderate numbers of levels and collapse or summarize where appropriate, and allow some panel omission or clear spacing to avoid confusion.<cite id="77b40137-0">Constructing trellis displays requires arranging plots according to aspect ratios, margins, and panel dimensions; a high-level specification is often used to define rows/columns and mapping of subsets to panels</cite><cite id="5bb4264d-2">Panel dimensions and margins are critical to maintain legibility in rectangular layouts</cite>.

- Scale choices: Use consistent scales to support direct comparison; use “free” scales when group ranges differ widely or when text labels require extra panel spacing; avoid synchronized axes that obscure group-specific variation when that is the intent.<cite id="5bb4264d-0">Facets coordinate scales and labels; for relative abundance, equal visual weight across panels is recommended via free spacing and appropriate scales</cite><cite id="5bb4264d-4">Keeping axes consistent is a key benefit of faceting for inspecting longitudinal data</cite>.

- Labels and legends: Rotate long labels to fit, control panel ordering, and ensure legends and axes remain readable across all panels; avoid overloading panel headers with too much text.<cite id="5bb4264d-0">Facet labels can be long and need rotation to be legible; layout controls and clipping adjustments are often necessary</cite>.

- Don’t overuse or encode too much per panel: If each panel already encodes many variables, faceting can explode the total cognitive load. Consider simplifying per-panel encodings and using complementary faceting or alternative encodings (line type, color, shape) within a single plot, or combine small multiples with mosaic-style composites when appropriate.<cite id="11551ee0-4">ggplot2 faceting has limits for per-panel aesthetic customization; restructuring data and using alternative plotting approaches may be required for complex composites</cite><cite id="5bb4264d-3">For mixed data types, aligning grouped plots with patchwork and assigning common scales can improve readability compared to complex single-faceted plots</cite>.

- Choose the right number of dimensions to facet: Faceting two variables in a 2D grid is natural; adding more than two or too many levels can defeat the purpose. For more than three dimensions, consider combining small multiples with other designs (e.g., color mapping, mosaics) to keep the display comprehensible.<cite id="77b40137-3">Small multiples facilitate comparison across panels, but with more than three axes the interpretability drops; alternative forms like stacked bar or mosaic charts may be better for higher-dimensional comparisons</cite>.

- Use faceting to avoid overplotting and to expose data: Show all raw points within each facet and keep consistent transparency or jitter to reveal distributional details; this is especially helpful in time series and grouped scatter plots.<cite id="5bb4264d-4">Plotting all raw data points is useful for inspecting variation and distributional information in longitudinal settings when using facets</cite>.

# When to use faceted plots vs alternatives

Faceted plots are particularly effective when:
- You need to compare the same relationship or distribution across discrete groups or time points while preserving consistent mappings for direct comparison.<cite id="5bb4264d-4">Facets repeat a plot for subgroups and keep axes consistent, aiding inspection of longitudinal and grouped data</cite><cite id="11551ee0-0">Faceting separates group-wise behavior into subpanels for complex clinical or experimental data</cite>.
- Your dataset is naturally partitioned (e.g., by subject, site, condition) and the within-group pattern is the primary interest, while between-group differences are secondary.<cite id="11551ee0-0">Facet_grid and facet_wrap support multiple subgroups and complex designs like multiple dose levels or drugs</cite>.

Consider alternatives when:
- The number of groups is large or combinations explode; then use color, shape, or line type to encode group membership within a single panel and/or use interactive faceting to filter groups on demand.<cite id="11551ee0-4">ggplot2 faceting limits per-panel aesthetic customization and can become unwieldy; programmatic or alternative approaches may be needed</cite><cite id="5bb4264d-4">Interactive facets let readers select subsets on the fly for high-dimensional data</cite>.
- You need to emphasize joint relationships among many variables; then combine small multiples with other encodings (parallel coordinates, mosaics) rather than forcing all dimensions into panel axes.<cite id="77b40137-3">With more than three axes, hive plots and other forms degrade in interpretability; small multiples can be combined with other encodings to manage dimensionality</cite>.

# Summary

In short, faceted plots are small multiples that repeat a consistent plot template for data subsets defined by one or more variables, arranged in a grid to support comparative reasoning and exploratory analysis.<cite id="5bb4264d-0">Facets display subsets of a dataset in panels of the same graphic</cite><cite id="5bb4264d-2">Trellis displays arrange multiple plots of the same type for different subsets in a structured, rectangular layout</cite><cite id="11551ee0-0">Facet_grid() and facet_wrap() implement 2D grids and ribbon wraps to partition data and repeat the plot</cite>. They are powerful when used judiciously with appropriate scales, spacing, and panel ordering, and with awareness of their limits for high-dimensional or highly granular groupings; when these limits arise, combine faceting with other encodings or interactive features to maintain clarity.<cite id="5bb4264d-0">Facets coordinate scales and labels, with options for free spacing and label rotation to maintain legibility</cite><cite id="5bb4264d-4">Interactive and dynamic facets can handle larger, multidimensional data by enabling on-the-fly selection</cite><cite id="11551ee0-4">Complex composites can push against ggplot2 faceting limits, suggesting data restructuring or alternative plotting strategies</cite>.
</answer>

Title: Application of ggplot2 to Pharmacometric Graphics
Snippet: The ggplot2 package, authored by Hadley Wickham, 1 is an implementation of the theory described in "The Grammar of Graphics" by Leland Wilkinson. 2 In a nutshell, the grammar defines a set of rules by which components of a statistical graphic are organized, coordinated, and rendered. The package is programmed entirely in the R statistical programming environment 3 using the grid graphics system, 4 extending Wilkinson's theory to a "layered" grammar of graphics. 5 he grammar implemented in ggplot2 provides an infrastructure for composing a graphic from multiple elements: 

• An input data object, usually an R data frame. 

• Aesthetics (abbreviated "aes"), which refer to visual attributes that affect how data are displayed in a graphic, e.g., color, point size, or line type. • Geometric objects ("geoms" for short), such as points, lines, polygons, box plots, error bars, etc. • Scale transformations, which map aesthetics to unique values of variables, in addition to mathematical transformations to produce positional axes (e.g., logarithms). This process entails a conversion from "data units" to "graphical units." The inverse mapping of a scale transformation is rendered in the graphic as a guide, either a positional scale or a legend, in the original data units. • Statistical transformations ("stats"), which refer to some type of data summarization such as a five-number summary for a box plot (stat_boxplot) or counts of observations by bin (stat_bin). The objective of statistical transformation is to supply the inputs necessary to produce a geom; for example, stat_bin sets up the data structure necessary for geom_bar and geom_histogram. Many stat_functions can be invoked directly to generate ggplot layers. • Coordinate transformations ("coord"), which specify how a coordinate system is specified in a graphic. The default is the Cartesian coordinate system, but several others are built in, such as polar coordinates (coord_ polar) or flips of the x and y coordinates (coord_flip).
