In the Grammar of Graphics, facets are defined as displaying subsets of a data set in panels of the same graphic (Wilkinson 2005). Using a data structure with one row per measurement, plotting multiple parameters on same plot using facets is a natural way to represent these data. In ggplot2, facets also coordinate the scales and labels for each panel. Figure 7: Adding units to multi-parameter plots using the geochemistry labeller. 

package provides facet types for two common cases: relative abundance data and geochemical data. 

Facets for relative abundance data (facet_abundance() and facet_abundanceh()) wrap ggplot2::facet_grid(), applying best-practice rules for the relationship between abundance scales. When plotted, relative abundance values on each panel should have the same weight (i.e., 5% on one panel should take up the same amount of space as 5% on another panel; space = "free_x" or space = "free_y"). Facet labels must have species names italicized for publication in most journals, but modifiers (e.g., strain III) must not be italicized. This constraint can be accommodated by setting the default labeller to a function that understands the form of most species input (label_species()). Finally, facet labels are typically too long to fit horizontally above each panel and must be rotated to be legible. While rotating a facet label is possible using ggplot2 theme modifications, eliminating the horizontal clip is not. Control over the clip parameter of the strip text is likely in a future ggplot2 version, however packaging both as part of the facet is a way make this implementation detail transparent to the user. 

Panels representing different geochemical parameters do not require space = "free_x" or space = "free_y", and thus can wrap either facet_wrap() or facet_grid(). The tidypaleo package provides facet_geochem_wrap(), facet_geochem_grid(), facet_geochem_wraph(), and facet_geochem_gridh() for geochemical measurements (Figure 1).

The ggplot2 package, authored by Hadley Wickham, 1 is an implementation of the theory described in "The Grammar of Graphics" by Leland Wilkinson. 2 In a nutshell, the grammar defines a set of rules by which components of a statistical graphic are organized, coordinated, and rendered. The package is programmed entirely in the R statistical programming environment 3 using the grid graphics system, 4 extending Wilkinson's theory to a "layered" grammar of graphics. 5 he grammar implemented in ggplot2 provides an infrastructure for composing a graphic from multiple elements: 

• An input data object, usually an R data frame. 

• Aesthetics (abbreviated "aes"), which refer to visual attributes that affect how data are displayed in a graphic, e.g., color, point size, or line type. • Geometric objects ("geoms" for short), such as points, lines, polygons, box plots, error bars, etc. • Scale transformations, which map aesthetics to unique values of variables, in addition to mathematical transformations to produce positional axes (e.g., logarithms). This process entails a conversion from "data units" to "graphical units." The inverse mapping of a scale transformation is rendered in the graphic as a guide, either a positional scale or a legend, in the original data units. • Statistical transformations ("stats"), which refer to some type of data summarization such as a five-number summary for a box plot (stat_boxplot) or counts of observations by bin (stat_bin). The objective of statistical transformation is to supply the inputs necessary to produce a geom; for example, stat_bin sets up the data structure necessary for geom_bar and geom_histogram. Many stat_functions can be invoked directly to generate ggplot layers. • Coordinate transformations ("coord"), which specify how a coordinate system is specified in a graphic. The default is the Cartesian coordinate system, but several others are built in, such as polar coordinates (coord_ polar) or flips of the x and y coordinates (coord_flip).

Trellis displays, also known as small multiples or faceted plots, are a widely used and effective method in data visualization. These displays involve arranging multiple plots, each representing the same plot type but with different subsets of data, in a structured manner (Becker, Cleveland, and Shyu 1996). Constructing trellis displays requires a mechanism for arranging the plots according to their aspect ratios, margins, and panel dimensions (Murrell 1999). Typically, trellis displays are configured in a rectangular layout, with each plot panel having the same rectangular dimensions. Consequently, a high-level specification is often employed to define the display layout, such as the number of rows and columns or the mapping of plots or data subsets to individual panels. 

The layouts in ggplot2 (Wickham 2010) are primarily controlled by Facet objects. More specifically, ggplot2 composes plots based on assembling modular objects (data, aesthetic mapping, layer, geometric objects, statistics, coordinate system, theme, facet, scales, and guides). These modular objects are primarily defined though an object oriented system called ggproto, inspired by the grammar of graphics by Wilkinson (2005). A new plot in ggplot2 is made by substituting these modular objects.

Title: Scenario Storyline Discovery for Planning in Multi‐Actor Human‐Natural Systems Confronting Change
Snippet: Hive plots adapt parallel coordinate plots (Inselberg, 2009;Wegman, 1990) to a radial arrangement, compacting the layout and making the connections easier to follow. Hive plots typically rely on a three-axis model, with the total circle area being uniformly divided between all segments (the areas between two axes). An illustrative adapted stacked hive plot, like the ones used throughout this study is presented in Figure S1 in Supporting Information S1. As demonstrated in this study, the three axes we utilize reflect three dynamic properties of the SOWs generated. More than three dimensions can be used, but by having only three axes, hive plots accommodate connections (lines) between each axis pair, without having to cross the axes themselves. With more than three axes this can only be achieved if connections are only drawn between neighboring axes, or if axes are duplicated at multiple positions. This negatively impacts the interpretability of the figure, which defies the aim of creating meaningful and salient narratives, central to our framework. The originators of the figure indeed discourage its use with more than three axes (Krzywinski et al., 2012), and most common applications in network science (e.g., Engle & Whalen, 2012) and gene sequencing (e.g., Yang et al., 2017) also only use three axes. Furthermore, the compactness of this figure allows us to generate multiple panels reflecting alternative dynamic properties or robustness performance measures, in a "small multiples" visualization (Tufte, 1990). Combining many small visualizations simultaneously allows the reader to compare the separate panels and look for patterns or outliers in the matrix of visuals, and facilitates presentation and storytelling of large amounts of data in a single figure (van den Elzen & van Wijk, 2013). In situations where more than three pairs of dynamic properties need to be used, alternative graphical forms (e.g., stacked bar charts or Marimekko (mosaic) charts (Friendly, 2002)) are also suited to FRNSIC scenario discovery, but they have their own strengths and weaknesses (presented in Figure S1 in Supporting Information S1).

snippet.text:
Hive plots adapt parallel coordinate plots (Inselberg, 2009;Wegman, 1990) to a radial arrangement, compacting the layout and making the connections easier to follow. Hive plots typically rely on a three-axis model, with the total circle area being uniformly divided between all segments (the areas between two axes). An illustrative adapted stacked hive plot, like the ones used throughout this study is presented in Figure S1 in Supporting Information S1. As demonstrated in this study, the three axes we utilize reflect three dynamic properties of the SOWs generated. More than three dimensions can be used, but by having only three axes, hive plots accommodate connections (lines) between each axis pair, without having to cross the axes themselves. With more than three axes this can only be achieved if connections are only drawn between neighboring axes, or if axes are duplicated at multiple positions. This negatively impacts the interpretability of the figure, which defies the aim of creating meaningful and salient narratives, central to our framework. The originators of the figure indeed discourage its use with more than three axes (Krzywinski et al., 2012), and most common applications in network science (e.g., Engle & Whalen, 2012) and gene sequencing (e.g., Yang et al., 2017) also only use three axes. Furthermore, the compactness of this figure allows us to generate multiple panels reflecting alternative dynamic properties or robustness performance measures, in a "small multiples" visualization (Tufte, 1990). Combining many small visualizations simultaneously allows the reader to compare the separate panels and look for patterns or outliers in the matrix of visuals, and facilitates presentation and storytelling of large amounts of data in a single figure (van den Elzen & van Wijk, 2013). In situations where more than three pairs of dynamic properties need to be used, alternative graphical forms (e.g., stacked bar charts or Marimekko (mosaic) charts (Friendly, 2002)) are also suited to FRNSIC scenario discovery, but they have their own strengths and weaknesses (presented in Figure S1 in Supporting Information S1).

documents.snippet:
Trellis displays, also known as small multiples or faceted plots, are a widely used and effective method in data visualization. These displays involve arranging multiple plots, each representing the same plot type but with different subsets of data, in a structured manner (Becker, Cleveland, and Shyu 1996). Constructing trellis displays requires a mechanism for arranging the plots according to their aspect ratios, margins, and panel dimensions (Murrell 1999). Typically, trellis displays are configured in a rectangular layout, with each plot panel having the same rectangular dimensions. Consequently, a high-level specification is often employed to define the display layout, such as the number of rows and columns or the mapping of plots or data subsets to individual panels. 

The layouts in ggplot2 (Wickham 2010) are primarily controlled by Facet objects. More specifically, ggplot2 composes plots based on assembling modular objects (data, aesthetic mapping, layer, geometric objects, statistics, coordinate system, theme, facet, scales, and guides). These modular objects are primarily defined though an object oriented system called ggproto, inspired by the grammar of graphics by Wilkinson (2005). A new plot in ggplot2 is made by substituting these modular objects. 

Code 2.2 demonstrates a ggplot2 syntax for constructing a trellis display using the penguins data. Lines 2-3 specifies the primary data and the aesthetic mapping of data to graphical elements. Line 4 specifies the plot type (with default statistics calculated from frequency of bin width of 1 and bars outlined in black). Line 5 details the layout of the trellis display (referred to as facet in ggplot2), indicating that the panel data is separated by species, organized into one column, with the row order adjusted so that the first factor level appears at the bottom and the last factor level appears at the top. 

Code 2.2 (Tidyverse approach): data visualisation 1 library(ggplot2) 2 ggplot(penguins) + Base R (through the graphics package) specifies the layout of plots using par(), after which users print each individual plot to the graphics output sequentially. Code 2.3 shows a near equivalent output to Code 2.2 using a Base R approach.

Title: Application of ggplot2 to Pharmacometric Graphics
Snippet: The concept of conditioning plots by the levels of one or more factors is called faceting in ggplot2. There are two faceting functions: facet_wrap() and facet_grid(). Both use a formula to determine the layout, and both share a common argument scales =, but otherwise, they are separate entities. facet_grid() is capable of generating a 2D grid of graphics panels-by column and/or by row. For example, facet_grid(.~ group) generates multipanel plots per level of a factor group by column, but facet_grid(group ~.) will generate plots by row. The dot (.) indicates that no variable is specified for that side of the formula. By specifying both sides, such as facet_grid(group ~ sex), a 2D grid of multipanel plots by group and by sex will be produced. In contrast, facet_wrap() reshapes a 1D ribbon of plots into a 2D arrangement. Instead of a 2D grid of panels associated with the level combinations of two variables, facet_wrap() creates a string of panels and "wraps" them into the graphics region like a ribbon, patterned on how the lattice behaves. You can specify ncol and/or nrow to control the arrangement of panels. You could write facet_wrap(~ group, ncol=4)to create a graph with four panels per row. The default (if you do not specify ncol or nrow) action is to attempt to lay out the panels as close to a square as possible. The default action is to start in the top left corner, moving left to right and then down, starting each new row from the left. The argument as.table = TRUE controls this ordering. Setting it to FALSE initiates wrapping from the bottom left corner of the graphics region and upward (see Supplementary Material online for the example code for facet_wrap()). 

Here is an illustration to visualize complex clinical data (e.g., multiple dose levels, different drugs, etc.). You can choose aesthetic mappings to distinguish behavior among subgroups in a single graphics region or use faceting to separate group-wise behavior into multiple subpanels.

Title: tidypaleo: Visualizing Paleoenvironmental Archives Using ggplot2
Snippet: In the Grammar of Graphics, facets are defined as displaying subsets of a data set in panels of the same graphic (Wilkinson 2005). Using a data structure with one row per measurement, plotting multiple parameters on same plot using facets is a natural way to represent these data. In ggplot2, facets also coordinate the scales and labels for each panel. Figure 7: Adding units to multi-parameter plots using the geochemistry labeller. 

package provides facet types for two common cases: relative abundance data and geochemical data. 

Facets for relative abundance data (facet_abundance() and facet_abundanceh()) wrap ggplot2::facet_grid(), applying best-practice rules for the relationship between abundance scales. When plotted, relative abundance values on each panel should have the same weight (i.e., 5% on one panel should take up the same amount of space as 5% on another panel; space = "free_x" or space = "free_y"). Facet labels must have species names italicized for publication in most journals, but modifiers (e.g., strain III) must not be italicized. This constraint can be accommodated by setting the default labeller to a function that understands the form of most species input (label_species()). Finally, facet labels are typically too long to fit horizontally above each panel and must be rotated to be legible. While rotating a facet label is possible using ggplot2 theme modifications, eliminating the horizontal clip is not. Control over the clip parameter of the strip text is likely in a future ggplot2 version, however packaging both as part of the facet is a way make this implementation detail transparent to the user. 

Panels representing different geochemical parameters do not require space = "free_x" or space = "free_y", and thus can wrap either facet_wrap() or facet_grid(). The tidypaleo package provides facet_geochem_wrap(), facet_geochem_grid(), facet_geochem_wraph(), and facet_geochem_gridh() for geochemical measurements (Figure 1).

Title: Visualization of Composite Plots in R Using a Programmatic Approach and smplot2
Snippet: In psychology and human neuroscience, the practice of creating multiple subplots and combining them into one composite plot is common (Kubilius, 2014). This method of data visualization is known as "subplotting." In the last few decades, it has become more widespread as research has become increasingly sophisticated, as demonstrated by the recent trend of including more variables and conditions in experiments, conducting collaborations with other laboratories if possible, and implementing multiple methodologies for data collection and analysis (Lin & Lu, 2023). These, in turn, create data sets with complicated structures, thereby requiring complex forms of data visualizations. However, as a high-level plotting librarywhich does not require users to plot each detail of the plot separately-ggplot2 has some built-in restrictions that are most noticeable when one creates a composite plot. 

Currently, creating a composite plot in ggplot2 is complex for several reasons. First, although ggplot2 allows for flexible customization of individual plots with concise codes, it is not compatible with the most wellknown programmatic approach-iteration using a for loop-unless unorthodox methods are used. Consequently, users unfamiliar with proper methods may struggle with applying iterations in ggplot2. 

Second, ggplot2 provides limited options for subplotting. A typical ggplot2 operation returns a single plot object that can be easily manipulated or stored. Although facet_wrap() and facet_grid() support data allocation into multiple subplots (facets) within a single plot object, ggplot2 limits aesthetic customization of these subplots within a faceted plot. For example, assigning subsets of data to different subplots using multiple or hierarchical variables or applying dynamic color schemes for each variable level is challenging. To circumvent this, users might need to restructure their data frames to visualize data as intended, but this affects only components that map data variables to aesthetics, not elements such as axis limits, background themes, or coordinate systems. 

For plotting unique visual elements that have no relation to the given data across panels, a third method has been used.

To get individual lines for each panel of Figure 1b, it is necessary for the input data frame to contain a GEN variable so that ggplot2 knows which vertical line to associate with each panel. Without this information, the default action would be to plot both lines in each panel. 

In Figure 1c, the x variable GEN is a factor and the y variable WT is numeric. geom_boxplot() produces separate box plots of WT for both females and males. The remaining code is used to customize the plot by adding a title, changing the axis labels, etc. 

Next, let us use Theoph (data from an experiment on the pharmacokinetics of theophylline) from the nlme package to illustrate another feature of ggplot2. We often want to be able to plot lines for different groups of data without mapping a variable to an aesthetic. The group = aesthetic in ggplot2 allows you to do this easily. We consider two   This produces separate lines for each level of Subject without having to define an aesthetic. 

For case (ii), consider the problem of adding a line that connects the means of each group (note: for this case, we need a nominal time postdose (ntpd) to calculate mean values, and the R-code to calculate "ntpd" is provided in the Supplementary Material online). The default behavior in ggplot2 is to ignore a call to geom_line() when the x variable is a factor; to get around this, we use the group = 1 aesthetic, which is used to plot an overall "average" line across the levels of the factor.

snippet.text:
In psychology and human neuroscience, the practice of creating multiple subplots and combining them into one composite plot is common (Kubilius, 2014). This method of data visualization is known as "subplotting." In the last few decades, it has become more widespread as research has become increasingly sophisticated, as demonstrated by the recent trend of including more variables and conditions in experiments, conducting collaborations with other laboratories if possible, and implementing multiple methodologies for data collection and analysis (Lin & Lu, 2023). These, in turn, create data sets with complicated structures, thereby requiring complex forms of data visualizations. However, as a high-level plotting librarywhich does not require users to plot each detail of the plot separately-ggplot2 has some built-in restrictions that are most noticeable when one creates a composite plot. 

Currently, creating a composite plot in ggplot2 is complex for several reasons. First, although ggplot2 allows for flexible customization of individual plots with concise codes, it is not compatible with the most wellknown programmatic approach-iteration using a for loop-unless unorthodox methods are used. Consequently, users unfamiliar with proper methods may struggle with applying iterations in ggplot2. 

Second, ggplot2 provides limited options for subplotting. A typical ggplot2 operation returns a single plot object that can be easily manipulated or stored. Although facet_wrap() and facet_grid() support data allocation into multiple subplots (facets) within a single plot object, ggplot2 limits aesthetic customization of these subplots within a faceted plot. For example, assigning subsets of data to different subplots using multiple or hierarchical variables or applying dynamic color schemes for each variable level is challenging. To circumvent this, users might need to restructure their data frames to visualize data as intended, but this affects only components that map data variables to aesthetics, not elements such as axis limits, background themes, or coordinate systems. 

For plotting unique visual elements that have no relation to the given data across panels, a third method has been used.

documents.title: Application of ggplot2 to Pharmacometric Graphics
documents.snippet:
The concept of conditioning plots by the levels of one or more factors is called faceting in ggplot2. There are two faceting functions: facet_wrap() and facet_grid(). Both use a formula to determine the layout, and both share a common argument scales =, but otherwise, they are separate entities. facet_grid() is capable of generating a 2D grid of graphics panels-by column and/or by row. For example, facet_grid(.~ group) generates multipanel plots per level of a factor group by column, but facet_grid(group ~.) will generate plots by row. The dot (.) indicates that no variable is specified for that side of the formula. By specifying both sides, such as facet_grid(group ~ sex), a 2D grid of multipanel plots by group and by sex will be produced. In contrast, facet_wrap() reshapes a 1D ribbon of plots into a 2D arrangement. Instead of a 2D grid of panels associated with the level combinations of two variables, facet_wrap() creates a string of panels and "wraps" them into the graphics region like a ribbon, patterned on how the lattice behaves. You can specify ncol and/or nrow to control the arrangement of panels. You could write facet_wrap(~ group, ncol=4)to create a graph with four panels per row. The default (if you do not specify ncol or nrow) action is to attempt to lay out the panels as close to a square as possible. The default action is to start in the top left corner, moving left to right and then down, starting each new row from the left. The argument as.table = TRUE controls this ordering. Setting it to FALSE initiates wrapping from the bottom left corner of the graphics region and upward (see Supplementary Material online for the example code for facet_wrap()). 

Here is an illustration to visualize complex clinical data (e.g., multiple dose levels, different drugs, etc.). You can choose aesthetic mappings to distinguish behavior among subgroups in a single graphics region or use faceting to separate group-wise behavior into multiple subpanels.

documents.title: Examining the Interface Design of Tidyverse
documents.snippet:
Trellis displays, also known as small multiples or faceted plots, are a widely used and effective method in data visualization. These displays involve arranging multiple plots, each representing the same plot type but with different subsets of data, in a structured manner (Becker, Cleveland, and Shyu 1996). Constructing trellis displays requires a mechanism for arranging the plots according to their aspect ratios, margins, and panel dimensions (Murrell 1999). Typically, trellis displays are configured in a rectangular layout, with each plot panel having the same rectangular dimensions. Consequently, a high-level specification is often employed to define the display layout, such as the number of rows and columns or the mapping of plots or data subsets to individual panels. 

The layouts in ggplot2 (Wickham 2010) are primarily controlled by Facet objects. More specifically, ggplot2 composes plots based on assembling modular objects (data, aesthetic mapping, layer, geometric objects, statistics, coordinate system, theme, facet, scales, and guides). These modular objects are primarily defined though an object oriented system called ggproto, inspired by the grammar of graphics by Wilkinson (2005). A new plot in ggplot2 is made by substituting these modular objects. 

Code 2.2 demonstrates a ggplot2 syntax for constructing a trellis display using the penguins data. Lines 2-3 specifies the primary data and the aesthetic mapping of data to graphical elements. Line 4 specifies the plot type (with default statistics calculated from frequency of bin width of 1 and bars outlined in black). Line 5 details the layout of the trellis display (referred to as facet in ggplot2), indicating that the panel data is separated by species, organized into one column, with the row order adjusted so that the first factor level appears at the bottom and the last factor level appears at the top. 

Code 2.2 (Tidyverse approach): data visualisation 1 library(ggplot2) 2 ggplot(penguins) + Base R (through the graphics package) specifies the layout of plots using par(), after which users print each individual plot to the graphics output sequentially. Code 2.3 shows a near equivalent output to Code 2.2 using a Base R approach.

documents.title: tidypaleo: Visualizing Paleoenvironmental Archives Using ggplot2
documents.snippet:
In the Grammar of Graphics, facets are defined as displaying subsets of a data set in panels of the same graphic (Wilkinson 2005). Using a data structure with one row per measurement, plotting multiple parameters on same plot using facets is a natural way to represent these data. In ggplot2, facets also coordinate the scales and labels for each panel. Figure 7: Adding units to multi-parameter plots using the geochemistry labeller. 

package provides facet types for two common cases: relative abundance data and geochemical data. 

Facets for relative abundance data (facet_abundance() and facet_abundanceh()) wrap ggplot2::facet_grid(), applying best-practice rules for the relationship between abundance scales. When plotted, relative abundance values on each panel should have the same weight (i.e., 5% on one panel should take up the same amount of space as 5% on another panel; space = "free_x" or space = "free_y"). Facet labels must have species names italicized for publication in most journals, but modifiers (e.g., strain III) must not be italicized. This constraint can be accommodated by setting the default labeller to a function that understands the form of most species input (label_species()). Finally, facet labels are typically too long to fit horizontally above each panel and must be rotated to be legible. While rotating a facet label is possible using ggplot2 theme modifications, eliminating the horizontal clip is not. Control over the clip parameter of the strip text is likely in a future ggplot2 version, however packaging both as part of the facet is a way make this implementation detail transparent to the user. 

Panels representing different geochemical parameters do not require space = "free_x" or space = "free_y", and thus can wrap either facet_wrap() or facet_grid(). The tidypaleo package provides facet_geochem_wrap(), facet_geochem_grid(), facet_geochem_wraph(), and facet_geochem_gridh() for geochemical measurements (Figure 1).

problem: literature review on synthetic tabular data generation
final_response:
# Introduction and Motivation

Synthetic tabular data generation (STDG) aims to produce statistically plausible, privacy-preserving surrogates of real relational datasets for training, testing, and analytics under constraints such as privacy, compliance, or data scarcity.<cite id="f53c5626-0">A comprehensive survey highlights that modern STDG spans end-to-end pipelines, diverse generative families, and application-driven evaluations, and organizes methods via a new taxonomy tailored to tabular data</cite>.<cite id="f53c5626-3">Common benchmark datasets are drawn from UCI, OpenML, and Kaggle, with many studies focusing on mixed-type data and missingness (e.g., Adult, California Housing, Beijing)</cite>.<cite id="f53c5626-4">The literature emphasizes both usefulness for model training and risks of leakage, motivating rigorous evaluation protocols across utility and privacy dimensions</cite>.

# Taxonomy of Methods and Representative Techniques

Modern STDG methods can be organized by generative family and by how they handle mixed data types (numerical, categorical, and missing values), with distinct trade-offs in stability, fidelity, and scalability.<cite id="f53c5626-0">A recent survey proposes a taxonomy that groups techniques by architecture (e.g., GANs/VAEs/flows/diffusions/structured models), by conditioning/controllability, and by post-processing for calibration and missingness</cite>.

- Generative adversarial networks (GANs)
  - Conditional Tabular GAN (CTGAN) and successors: CTGAN is a GAN designed for tabular data that jointly models discrete and continuous features, uses conditional generation to steer output distributions, and applies mode-specific normalization to handle multi-modal continuous columns via variational mixture models, mitigating mode collapse and class imbalance during training.<cite id="e3909a75-0">CTGAN supports discrete and continuous features, conditional generators, and sampling strategies to avoid mode collapse and imbalance</cite>.<cite id="e3909a75-1">CTGAN augments training with mode-specific normalization (variational Gaussian mixtures per column) and conditional generation with training-by-sampling to ensure even exploration of discrete categories</cite>.<cite id="edaf7cc2-4">CTGAN introduced a mode-specific encoding for real features, Gumbel-softmax for categorical sampling, and masking to counter mode collapse, with later work improving conditioning for mixed columns</cite>.
  - Early tabular GANs and variants: TableGAN adapted DCGAN ideas to tabular data but introduced spatial inductive bias; MedGAN handled only categorical features; subsequent work (e.g., CTAB-GAN) improved conditioning and mixed-column handling.<cite id="edaf7cc2-4">TableGAN first applied DCGAN to tabular data but added spatial bias; MedGAN generated medical records but only for categorical data; CTAB-GAN improved conditioning and mixed-column handling</cite>.
  - Healthcare-focused GANs and distributed/privacy-aware variants: Conditional and distributed GANs have been used to generate EHRs, including federated and differentially private versions; DP-CTGAN and federated GANs target medical tabular data with comparative utility analyses under OCL constraints.<cite id="e3909a75-1">CTGAN builds on VeeGAN, TableGAN, and MedGAN, modeling multi-modal continuous columns and conditional distributions for many dimensions</cite>.<cite id="e3909a75-3">FDP-CTGAN extends CTGAN with differential privacy and has a federated variant; federated GANs for EHRs combine local models to generate synthetic patients across hospitals; DP-CTGAN and CTGAN often outperform federated baselines in utility metrics</cite>.

- Variational autoencoders (VAEs) and latent models
  - TVAE and hybrids: TVAE provides an autoregressive alternative to GANs for mixed tabular data; VAEs learn latent representations and can capture complex distributions but may assume simple latent forms, risking under-fitting to complex dependencies.<cite id="edaf7cc2-3">TVAE is proposed alongside CTGAN as a state-of-the-art tabular generator; VAEs learn latent representations but can assume simple latent forms, limiting capture of complex distributions</cite>.<cite id="edaf7cc2-0">VAEs have been adapted to tabular synthesis; a limitation is the simple parametric latent space, which can hinder capturing complex distributions</cite>.
  - Limitations and stability: Early GAN/VAE tabular models can struggle with mixed types and imbalanced data; conditionalization and improved architectures (e.g., CTGAN, TVAE) improve convergence and fidelity for categorical-continuous mixes.<cite id="edaf7cc2-3">Vanilla GAN-based approaches struggled with mixed data types and imbalanced datasets; conditional GANs like CTGAN and VAE-based TVAE improved performance</cite>.

- Flow-based and invertible models
  - Normalizing flows and copulas: Invertible neural networks (including copula flows and neural ODE variants) support exact likelihoods and flexible densities for tabular data, enabling private generation via mechanism compatibility; however, they often require extensive hyperparameter tuning and may make simplifying distributional assumptions.<cite id="edaf7cc2-0">Invertible neural networks (neural ODEs, copula flows, normalizing flows) have been proposed for private tabular data generation, but hyperparameter tuning is extensive and distributional assumptions can be restrictive</cite>.<cite id="edaf7cc2-4">Copulas and Bayesian networks are classical approaches; invertible flows (e.g., KAD21) and learned causal models (e.g., WCY+22) have also been proposed</cite>.

- Diffusion models
  - TabDDPM and conditionals: TabDDPM is a DDPM tailored to mixed numerical and categorical features using Gaussian diffusion for continuous variables and multinomial diffusion for categorical ones, trained with an objective combining MSE and per-column KL terms; conditional variants extend to task-specific conditioning for tabular workflows in energy modeling and education analytics.<cite id="c76d3f1e-0">TabDDPM introduced diffusion models to tabular data by modeling numerical columns via Gaussian diffusion and categorical via multinomial diffusion with an MLP, combining losses to maintain coherence across data types</cite>.<cite id="c76d3f1e-4">TabDDPM defines a forward-noise and reverse-denoising process; Gaussian diffusion handles continuous features with MSE losses, while multinomial diffusion handles categorical features with class-wise KL terms; conditional variants extend to domain workflows</cite>.<cite id="c76d3f1e-2">TabDDPM’s reverse process uses an MLP; losses include simple-t MSE for Gaussian columns and KL divergences per categorical column, with normalization across categorical features</cite>.
  - Strengths and critiques: Diffusion models can produce high-fidelity samples and diverse tabular data; however, one-hot encoding for categorical variables can induce sparsity and limit relational expressivity, especially at small sample sizes.<cite id="c76d3f1e-3">TabDDPM generates high-quality samples on benchmarks but relies on one-hot encoding, which can cause sparsity and fail to capture relationships between feature types for small samples</cite>.<cite id="c76d3f1e-1">TabDDPM is a recent diffusion-based alternative for generating tabular datasets in mixed-type settings</cite>.

- Tree/Bayesian and structured causal models
  - Bayesian networks and tree-based methods: Bayesian networks approximate conditional distributions and can encode causal structure, but often rely on simplifying assumptions; tree-based and adversarial random forest approaches offer practical synthesis with mixed privacy-utility trade-offs needing further study.<cite id="edaf7cc2-0">Bayesian networks can generate synthetic records by approximating CPDs but often rely on simplifying assumptions; tree-based methods and adversarial random forests have shown competitive synthetic quality, with privacy-utility trade-offs under-explored</cite>.<cite id="edaf7cc2-4">Learned structured causal models (e.g., WCY+22) are part of the modern tabular synthesis landscape alongside flows and GANs</cite>.

# Handling Mixed Data Types, Missingness, and Imbalanced Classes

Robust tabular synthesis must address heterogeneous feature types, missing values, and class imbalance through careful modeling choices and conditioning strategies.<cite id="e3909a75-1">CTGAN treats each continuous column with a variational mixture model to estimate and normalize multiple modes, and uses conditional vectors and training-by-sampling to ensure representation of minority discrete categories</cite>.<cite id="e3909a75-0">CTGAN’s design explicitly targets discrete/continuous support, conditional sampling, and mode collapse mitigation for imbalanced data</cite>.<cite id="edaf7cc2-3">Tabular data often contain missing values, outliers, and heterogeneous correlations; preprocessing for DNNs can cause information loss, motivating models that respect sparsity and mixed types</cite>.<cite id="edaf7cc2-4">CTAB-GAN improves conditioning for mixed columns, addressing challenges in tabular heterogeneity</cite>.<cite id="edaf7cc2-0">Invertible flow approaches for private tabular generation and Bayesian networks with causal structure offer complementary mechanisms for handling complex dependencies and missingness under distributional assumptions</cite>.

# Data Quality, Stability, and Failure Modes

Generative tabular models face distinct failure modes: mode collapse, unstable training with mixed types, under-fitting complex dependencies, and fidelity gaps under privacy constraints.<cite id="edaf7cc2-0">VAEs may oversimplify latent structure, limiting capture of complex data distributions</cite>.<cite id="edaf7cc2-4">CTGAN introduced techniques to counter mode collapse (masking, Gumbel-softmax, mode-specific encoding), reflecting a common failure mode in tabular GANs</cite>.<cite id="edaf7cc2-3">Early GANs struggled with mixed-type and imbalanced data; conditionalization and specialized architectures (CTGAN, TVAE) improved convergence and sample quality</cite>.<cite id="c76d3f1e-3">Diffusion-based TabDDPM achieves strong sample quality but can suffer from sparsity and limited relational capture due to one-hot encoding of categorical features</cite>.<cite id="edaf7cc2-0">Invertible flow approaches often require extensive hyperparameter tuning to achieve satisfactory utility, indicating sensitivity to model configuration</cite>.

# Evaluation: Utility, Statistical Similarity, Coverage, and Privacy

Evaluating synthetic data requires multi-criteria assessment spanning downstream utility, internal statistical similarity, coverage of rare categories, and privacy leakage risks.<cite id="edaf7cc2-1">A universal metric framework evaluates synthesized tabular data using statistical similarity (e.g., basic statistics, correlation scores) and coverage (support-coverage), along with ML efficacy; for example, TVAE-based synthesis shows increasing S_basic, S_corr, S_cr, and S_ml with training, while certain metrics like S_pMSE may increase after overfitting</cite>.<cite id="e3909a75-1">Utility is commonly measured by training classifiers/regressors on synthetic data and evaluating accuracy/F1 (classification) or R^2 (regression) on held-out real data</cite>.<cite id="f53c5626-0">Surveys emphasize thorough evaluation protocols that include both predictive utility and statistical fidelity, alongside application-specific criteria and privacy assessments</cite>.

- Downstream utility: Transfer learning metrics on held-out tasks (classification/regression) quantify whether models trained on synthetic data generalize to real-world tasks.<cite id="e3909a75-1">Machine learning efficacy is evaluated by training on generated data and testing on holdout real data using accuracy, F1, and R^2</cite>.
- Statistical similarity and coverage: Scores capture distributional fidelity and rare-category support to avoid bias against underrepresented groups or events.<cite id="edaf7cc2-1">Evaluation includes S_basic (basic statistics), S_corr (correlation structure), S_cr (support-coverage), and S_ml (ML efficacy), with observed trends across training epochs</cite>.
- Record linkage and privacy leakage: Linkage rates and membership inference tests probe whether synthetic releases can be linked back to individuals; surveys and domain studies call for explicit leakage metrics alongside utility.<cite id="f53c5626-4">The usefulness/leakage tension motivates end-to-end evaluation that includes leakage risks as well as utility</cite>.
- Domain-specific metrics: In healthcare and finance, clinical calibration, interpretability, and domain constraints (e.g., risk score behavior) complement statistical tests and utility checks.<cite id="e3909a75-3">Federated and DP-CTGAN studies compare AUC, PR-AUC, and F1 for synthetic EHRs under privacy constraints, illustrating domain metrics in privacy-aware evaluation</cite>.

# Privacy-Preserving and Federated Directions

Privacy requirements often necessitate differential privacy (DP), local differential privacy, or federated training to prevent leakage from synthetic releases and to allow multi-institutional data collaboration.<cite id="e3909a75-3">DP-CTGAN integrates differential privacy into tabular GANs for medical data; federated versions may underperform non-federated CTGAN/DP-CTGAN on some utility metrics, highlighting trade-offs between privacy strength and predictive performance</cite>.<cite id="edaf7cc2-0">Invertible-flow-based generators have been explored for private tabular data, leveraging exact likelihoods and flexible densities compatible with privacy mechanisms</cite>.<cite id="e3909a75-3">Alternatives like SGDE train local VAE generators under DP and combine outputs client-side, showing improved accuracy over non-federated local baselines but without cross-client aggregation; federated GANs for EHRs combine local parameters to train a central generator across hospitals</cite>.

# Benchmarks and Datasets

Evaluation commonly uses UCI, OpenML, and Kaggle datasets, with emphasis on mixed-type and missing-value settings and domain-specific repositories for EHRs and finance.<cite id="f53c5626-3">Surveys summarize 20 widely used tabular datasets across tasks, drawing from UCI, OpenML, and Kaggle, and highlight missing-value-focused datasets like Beijing, Adult, and California Housing</cite>.<cite id="edaf7cc2-1">Studies using TVAE report training dynamics and metric trends (S_basic, S_corr, S_cr, S_ml, S_pMSE) across datasets such as Concrete and Electrical Power Plant</cite>.<cite id="c76d3f1e-1">Diffusion-based tabular generation has been applied to finance-related tabular data, with CTGAN and TVAE as baselines and standard evaluation protocols for synthetic data</cite>.

# Domain Applications

- Healthcare (EHRs): GANs and VAEs generate synthetic patient records for research and analytics; privacy-preserving and federated variants support multi-institutional collaboration while tracking utility trade-offs under DP and linkage risks.<cite id="e3909a75-3">CTGAN and DP-CTGAN synthesize tabular medical data, with federated GAN variants evaluated across hospitals; DP-CTGAN often matches or exceeds federated baselines on AUC and F1</cite>.<cite id="e3909a75-0">CTGAN’s handling of discrete/continuous features and conditional generation is well-suited to EHRs with mixed types and class imbalance</cite>.
- Finance: Synthetic financial tabular data (e.g., firm-level records) are generated with CTGAN and TVAE to address data scarcity and enable robust modeling under privacy constraints; diffusion-based methods have been proposed to capture complex financial dependencies.<cite id="c76d3f1e-1">FinDiff highlights diffusion models for financial tabular generation alongside CTGAN/TabDDPM as strong baselines</cite>.<cite id="edaf7cc2-2">A case study on Polish limited liability companies uses CTGAN and TVAE with established evaluation procedures for synthetic financial data</cite>.
- Education and operational analytics: Conditional diffusion models and tabular generators have been integrated into workflows for knowledge tracing and energy modeling, demonstrating sample quality and downstream utility improvements when augmenting real data.<cite id="c76d3f1e-2">Conditional diffusion over tabular education data improved downstream DKT model training and evaluation</cite>.<cite id="c76d3f1e-4">Conditional TabDDPM adapts diffusion to tabular workflows in building energy modeling, combining Gaussian and multinomial diffusion components</cite>.

# Limitations and Open Problems

Despite progress, several limitations persist: handling categorical sparsity, mode collapse and instability in deep generative training, heavy hyperparameter dependence in flows, and under-specified privacy leakage metrics that may miss linkage mechanisms in relational settings.<cite id="edaf7cc2-0">Invertible flow-based generators require extensive tuning and rely on distributional assumptions, limiting generality</cite>.<cite id="edaf7cc2-3">CTGAN can struggle to converge on continuous-only data without careful conditioning, and broader evaluation of privacy-utility trade-offs for tree-based density estimators remains insufficient</cite>.<cite id="c76d3f1e-3">Diffusion-based generators like TabDDPM can suffer from one-hot-induced sparsity and limited relational structure capture for categorical features</cite>.<cite id="f53c5626-4">Surveys emphasize the need for standardized leakage evaluations and end-to-end protocols that jointly assess utility and privacy risks</cite>.

# Practical Guidance and Takeaways

# Introduction and Motivation

Synthetic tabular data generation (STDG) aims to produce statistically plausible, privacy-preserving surrogates of real relational datasets for training, testing, and analytics under constraints such as privacy, compliance, or data scarcity.<cite id="f53c5626-0">A comprehensive survey highlights that modern STDG spans end-to-end pipelines, diverse generative families, and application-driven evaluations, and organizes methods via a new taxonomy tailored to tabular data</cite>.<cite id="f53c5626-3">Common benchmark datasets are drawn from UCI, OpenML, and Kaggle, with many studies focusing on mixed-type data and missingness (e.g., Adult, California Housing, Beijing)</cite>.<cite id="f53c5626-4">The literature emphasizes both usefulness for model training and risks of leakage, motivating rigorous evaluation protocols across utility and privacy dimensions</cite>.

# Taxonomy of Methods and Representative Techniques

Modern STDG methods can be organized by generative family and by how they handle mixed data types (numerical, categorical, and missing values), with distinct trade-offs in stability, fidelity, and scalability.<cite id="f53c5626-0">A recent survey proposes a taxonomy that groups techniques by architecture (e.g., GANs/VAEs/flows/diffusions/structured models), by conditioning/controllability, and by post-processing for calibration and missingness</cite>.

- Generative adversarial networks (GANs)
  - Conditional Tabular GAN (CTGAN) and successors: CTGAN is a GAN designed for tabular data that jointly models discrete and continuous features, uses conditional generation to steer output distributions, and applies mode-specific normalization to handle multi-modal continuous columns via variational mixture models, mitigating mode collapse and class imbalance during training.<cite id="e3909a75-0">CTGAN supports discrete and continuous features, conditional generators, and sampling strategies to avoid mode collapse and imbalance</cite>.<cite id="e3909a75-1">CTGAN augments training with mode-specific normalization (variational Gaussian mixtures per column) and conditional generation with training-by-sampling to ensure even exploration of discrete categories</cite>.<cite id="edaf7cc2-4">CTGAN introduced a mode-specific encoding for real features, Gumbel-softmax for categorical sampling, and masking to counter mode collapse, with later work improving conditioning for mixed columns</cite>.
  - Early tabular GANs and variants: TableGAN adapted DCGAN ideas to tabular data but introduced spatial inductive bias; MedGAN handled only categorical features; subsequent work (e.g., CTAB-GAN) improved conditioning and mixed-column handling.<cite id="edaf7cc2-4">TableGAN first applied DCGAN to tabular data but added spatial bias; MedGAN generated medical records but only for categorical data; CTAB-GAN improved conditioning and mixed-column handling</cite>.
  - Healthcare-focused GANs and distributed/privacy-aware variants: Conditional and distributed GANs have been used to generate EHRs, including federated and differentially private versions; DP-CTGAN and federated GANs target medical tabular data with comparative utility analyses under OCL constraints.<cite id="e3909a75-1">CTGAN builds on VeeGAN, TableGAN, and MedGAN, modeling multi-modal continuous columns and conditional distributions for many dimensions</cite>.<cite id="e3909a75-3">FDP-CTGAN extends CTGAN with differential privacy and has a federated variant; federated GANs for EHRs combine local models to generate synthetic patients across hospitals; DP-CTGAN and CTGAN often outperform federated baselines in utility metrics</cite>.

- Variational autoencoders (VAEs) and latent models
  - TVAE and hybrids: TVAE provides an autoregressive alternative to GANs for mixed tabular data; VAEs learn latent representations and can capture complex distributions but may assume simple latent forms, risking under-fitting to complex dependencies.<cite id="edaf7cc2-3">TVAE is proposed alongside CTGAN as a state-of-the-art tabular generator; VAEs learn latent representations but can assume simple latent forms, limiting capture of complex distributions</cite>.<cite id="edaf7cc2-0">VAEs have been adapted to tabular synthesis; a limitation is the simple parametric latent space, which can hinder capturing complex distributions</cite>.
  - Limitations and stability: Early GAN/VAE tabular models can struggle with mixed types and imbalanced data; conditionalization and improved architectures (e.g., CTGAN, TVAE) improve convergence and fidelity for categorical-continuous mixes.<cite id="edaf7cc2-3">Vanilla GAN-based approaches struggled with mixed data types and imbalanced datasets; conditional GANs like CTGAN and VAE-based TVAE improved performance</cite>.

- Flow-based and invertible models
  - Normalizing flows and copulas: Invertible neural networks (including copula flows and neural ODE variants) support exact likelihoods and flexible densities for tabular data, enabling private generation via mechanism compatibility; however, they often require extensive hyperparameter tuning and may make simplifying distributional assumptions.<cite id="edaf7cc2-0">Invertible neural networks (neural ODEs, copula flows, normalizing flows) have been proposed for private tabular data generation, but hyperparameter tuning is extensive and distributional assumptions can be restrictive</cite>.<cite id="edaf7cc2-4">Copulas and Bayesian networks are classical approaches; invertible flows (e.g., KAD21) and learned causal models (e.g., WCY+22) have also been proposed</cite>.

- Diffusion models
  - TabDDPM and conditionals: TabDDPM is a DDPM tailored to mixed numerical and categorical features using Gaussian diffusion for continuous variables and multinomial diffusion for categorical ones, trained with an objective combining MSE and per-column KL terms; conditional variants extend to task-specific conditioning for tabular workflows in energy modeling and education analytics.<cite id="c76d3f1e-0">TabDDPM introduced diffusion models to tabular data by modeling numerical columns via Gaussian diffusion and categorical via multinomial diffusion with an MLP, combining losses to maintain coherence across data types</cite>.<cite id="c76d3f1e-4">TabDDPM defines a forward-noise and reverse-denoising process; Gaussian diffusion handles continuous features with MSE losses, while multinomial diffusion handles categorical features with class-wise KL terms; conditional variants extend to domain workflows</cite>.<cite id="c76d3f1e-2">TabDDPM’s reverse process uses an MLP; losses include simple-t MSE for Gaussian columns and KL divergences per categorical column, with normalization across categorical features</cite>.
  - Strengths and critiques: Diffusion models can produce high-fidelity samples and diverse tabular data; however, one-hot encoding for categorical variables can induce sparsity and limit relational expressivity, especially at small sample sizes.<cite id="c76d3f1e-3">TabDDPM generates high-quality samples on benchmarks but relies on one-hot encoding, which can cause sparsity and fail to capture relationships between feature types for small samples</cite>.<cite id="c76d3f1e-1">TabDDPM is a recent diffusion-based alternative for generating tabular datasets in mixed-type settings</cite>.

- Tree/Bayesian and structured causal models
  - Bayesian networks and tree-based methods: Bayesian networks approximate conditional distributions and can encode causal structure, but often rely on simplifying assumptions; tree-based and adversarial random forest approaches offer practical synthesis with mixed privacy-utility trade-offs needing further study.<cite id="edaf7cc2-0">Bayesian networks can generate synthetic records by approximating CPDs but often rely on simplifying assumptions; tree-based methods and adversarial random forests have shown competitive synthetic quality, with privacy-utility trade-offs under-explored</cite>.<cite id="edaf7cc2-4">Learned structured causal models (e.g., WCY+22) are part of the modern tabular synthesis landscape alongside flows and GANs</cite>.

# Handling Mixed Data Types, Missingness, and Imbalanced Classes

Robust tabular synthesis must address heterogeneous feature types, missing values, and class imbalance through careful modeling choices and conditioning strategies.<cite id="e3909a75-1">CTGAN treats each continuous column with a variational mixture model to estimate and normalize multiple modes, and uses conditional vectors and training-by-sampling to ensure representation of minority discrete categories</cite>.<cite id="e3909a75-0">CTGAN’s design explicitly targets discrete/continuous support, conditional sampling, and mode collapse mitigation for imbalanced data</cite>.<cite id="edaf7cc2-3">Tabular data often contain missing values, outliers, and heterogeneous correlations; preprocessing for DNNs can cause information loss, motivating models that respect sparsity and mixed types</cite>.<cite id="edaf7cc2-4">CTAB-GAN improves conditioning for mixed columns, addressing challenges in tabular heterogeneity</cite>.<cite id="edaf7cc2-0">Invertible flow approaches for private tabular generation and Bayesian networks with causal structure offer complementary mechanisms for handling complex dependencies and missingness under distributional assumptions</cite>.

# Data Quality, Stability, and Failure Modes

Generative tabular models face distinct failure modes: mode collapse, unstable training with mixed types, under-fitting complex dependencies, and fidelity gaps under privacy constraints.<cite id="edaf7cc2-0">VAEs may oversimplify latent structure, limiting capture of complex data distributions</cite>.<cite id="edaf7cc2-4">CTGAN introduced techniques to counter mode collapse (masking, Gumbel-softmax, mode-specific encoding), reflecting a common failure mode in tabular GANs</cite>.<cite id="edaf7cc2-3">Early GANs struggled with mixed-type and imbalanced data; conditionalization and specialized architectures (CTGAN, TVAE) improved convergence and sample quality</cite>.<cite id="c76d3f1e-3">Diffusion-based TabDDPM achieves strong sample quality but can suffer from sparsity and limited relational capture due to one-hot encoding of categorical features</cite>.<cite id="edaf7cc2-0">Invertible flow approaches often require extensive hyperparameter tuning to achieve satisfactory utility, indicating sensitivity to model configuration</cite>.

# Evaluation: Utility, Statistical Similarity, Coverage, and Privacy

Evaluating synthetic data requires multi-criteria assessment spanning downstream utility, internal statistical similarity, coverage of rare categories, and privacy leakage risks.<cite id="edaf7cc2-1">A universal metric framework evaluates synthesized tabular data using statistical similarity (e.g., basic statistics, correlation scores) and coverage (support-coverage), along with ML efficacy; for example, TVAE-based synthesis shows increasing S_basic, S_corr, S_cr, and S_ml with training, while certain metrics like S_pMSE may increase after overfitting</cite>.<cite id="e3909a75-1">Utility is commonly measured by training classifiers/regressors on synthetic data and evaluating accuracy/F1 (classification) or R^2 (regression) on held-out real data</cite>.<cite id="f53c5626-0">Surveys emphasize thorough evaluation protocols that include both predictive utility and statistical fidelity, alongside application-specific criteria and privacy assessments</cite>.

- Downstream utility: Transfer learning metrics on held-out tasks (classification/regression) quantify whether models trained on synthetic data generalize to real-world tasks.<cite id="e3909a75-1">Machine learning efficacy is evaluated by training on generated data and testing on holdout real data using accuracy, F1, and R^2</cite>.
- Statistical similarity and coverage: Scores capture distributional fidelity and rare-category support to avoid bias against underrepresented groups or events.<cite id="edaf7cc2-1">Evaluation includes S_basic (basic statistics), S_corr (correlation structure), S_cr (support-coverage), and S_ml (ML efficacy), with observed trends across training epochs</cite>.
- Record linkage and privacy leakage: Linkage rates and membership inference tests probe whether synthetic releases can be linked back to individuals; surveys and domain studies call for explicit leakage metrics alongside utility.<cite id="f53c5626-4">The usefulness/leakage tension motivates end-to-end evaluation that includes leakage risks as well as utility</cite>.
- Domain-specific metrics: In healthcare and finance, clinical calibration, interpretability, and domain constraints (e.g., risk score behavior) complement statistical tests and utility checks.<cite id="e3909a75-3">Federated and DP-CTGAN studies compare AUC, PR-AUC, and F1 for synthetic EHRs under privacy constraints, illustrating domain metrics in privacy-aware evaluation</cite>.

# Privacy-Preserving and Federated Directions

Privacy requirements often necessitate differential privacy (DP), local differential privacy, or federated training to prevent leakage from synthetic releases and to allow multi-institutional data collaboration.<cite id="e3909a75-3">DP-CTGAN integrates differential privacy into tabular GANs for medical data; federated versions may underperform non-federated CTGAN/DP-CTGAN on some utility metrics, highlighting trade-offs between privacy strength and predictive performance</cite>.<cite id="edaf7cc2-0">Invertible-flow-based generators have been explored for private tabular data, leveraging exact likelihoods and flexible densities compatible with privacy mechanisms</cite>.<cite id="e3909a75-3">Alternatives like SGDE train local VAE generators under DP and combine outputs client-side, showing improved accuracy over non-federated local baselines but without cross-client aggregation; federated GANs for EHRs combine local parameters to train a central generator across hospitals</cite>.

# Benchmarks and Datasets

Evaluation commonly uses UCI, OpenML, and Kaggle datasets, with emphasis on mixed-type and missing-value settings and domain-specific repositories for EHRs and finance.<cite id="f53c5626-3">Surveys summarize 20 widely used tabular datasets across tasks, drawing from UCI, OpenML, and Kaggle, and highlight missing-value-focused datasets like Beijing, Adult, and California Housing</cite>.<cite id="edaf7cc2-1">Studies using TVAE report training dynamics and metric trends (S_basic, S_corr, S_cr, S_ml, S_pMSE) across datasets such as Concrete and Electrical Power Plant</cite>.<cite id="c76d3f1e-1">Diffusion-based tabular generation has been applied to finance-related tabular data, with CTGAN and TVAE as baselines and standard evaluation protocols for synthetic data</cite>.

# Domain Applications

- Healthcare (EHRs): GANs and VAEs generate synthetic patient records for research and analytics; privacy-preserving and federated variants support multi-institutional collaboration while tracking utility trade-offs under DP and linkage risks.<cite id="e3909a75-3">CTGAN and DP-CTGAN synthesize tabular medical data, with federated GAN variants evaluated across hospitals; DP-CTGAN often matches or exceeds federated baselines on AUC and F1</cite>.<cite id="e3909a75-0">CTGAN’s handling of discrete/continuous features and conditional generation is well-suited to EHRs with mixed types and class imbalance</cite>.
- Finance: Synthetic financial tabular data (e.g., firm-level records) are generated with CTGAN and TVAE to address data scarcity and enable robust modeling under privacy constraints; diffusion-based methods have been proposed to capture complex financial dependencies.<cite id="c76d3f1e-1">FinDiff highlights diffusion models for financial tabular generation alongside CTGAN/TabDDPM as strong baselines</cite>.<cite id="edaf7cc2-2">A case study on Polish limited liability companies uses CTGAN and TVAE with established evaluation procedures for synthetic financial data</cite>.
- Education and operational analytics: Conditional diffusion models and tabular generators have been integrated into workflows for knowledge tracing and energy modeling, demonstrating sample quality and downstream utility improvements when augmenting real data.<cite id="c76d3f1e-2">Conditional diffusion over tabular education data improved downstream DKT model training and evaluation</cite>.<cite id="c76d3f1e-4">Conditional TabDDPM adapts diffusion to tabular workflows in building energy modeling, combining Gaussian and multinomial diffusion components</cite>.

# Limitations and Open Problems

Despite progress, several limitations persist: handling categorical sparsity, mode collapse and instability in deep generative training, heavy hyperparameter dependence in flows, and under-specified privacy leakage metrics that may miss linkage mechanisms in relational settings.<cite id="edaf7cc2-0">Invertible flow-based generators require extensive tuning and rely on distributional assumptions, limiting generality</cite>.<cite id="edaf7cc2-3">CTGAN can struggle to converge on continuous-only data without careful conditioning, and broader evaluation of privacy-utility trade-offs for tree-based density estimators remains insufficient</cite>.<cite id="c76d3f1e-3">Diffusion-based generators like TabDDPM can suffer from one-hot-induced sparsity and limited relational structure capture for categorical features</cite>.<cite id="f53c5626-4">Surveys emphasize the need for standardized leakage evaluations and end-to-end protocols that jointly assess utility and privacy risks</cite>.

# Practical Guidance and Takeaways

- Choose architectures to match data structure and constraints: use CTGAN/TVAE for mixed-type and missing data with conditional generation; consider flows for exact likelihoods and privacy-compatible training when feasible; adopt diffusion models when high-fidelity samples and diversity are priorities, while mitigating categorical sparsity (e.g., via ResBit or alternative encodings).<cite id="e3909a75-1">CTGAN’s conditional generation and mode-specific normalization help with multi-modal continuous columns and class imbalance</cite>.<cite id="edaf7cc2-3">TVAE and CTGAN are state-of-the-art baselines for tabular synthesis, with VAEs capturing complex dependencies but sensitive to latent assumptions</cite>.<cite id="c76d3f1e-0">TabDDPM combines Gaussian and multinomial diffusion to model mixed types with an MLP-based reverse process</cite>.<cite id="c76d3f1e-3">ResBit and bit diffusion preprocessing address discrete representation to enable continuous diffusion modeling without one-hot encodings</cite>.
- Evaluate with multi-criteria protocols: track downstream utility on held-out tasks, statistical similarity and rare-category coverage, and leakage risks; in regulated domains, include DP settings and federated training evaluations to quantify privacy-utility trade-offs.<cite id="edaf7cc2-1">Universal metric frameworks quantify basic statistics, correlation, support-coverage, ML efficacy, and prediction error for synthetic data</cite>.<cite id="e3909a75-3">DP-CTGAN and federated comparisons show how privacy strength affects AUC, F1, and ROC/PR performance in EHR settings</cite>.
- Leverage domain knowledge: encode causal or structural priors where appropriate (Bayesian networks/structured causal models) to improve fidelity of constrained domains like healthcare and finance, especially when data have conditional dependencies and policy constraints.<cite id="edaf7cc2-0">Bayesian networks and causal models can encode domain structure but may rely on simplifying assumptions; they remain complementary to deep generative models</cite>.

# Conclusion

Synthetic tabular data generation has advanced from early GANs and VAEs to richer families including flows, diffusion, and structured models that better handle mixed types, missingness, and conditional generation, with growing emphasis on privacy and federated settings.<cite id="edaf7cc2-4">The landscape includes GANs (CTGAN, CTAB-GAN), VAEs (TVAE), invertible flows and copulas, and learned causal models, each with distinct strengths and assumptions</cite>.<cite id="c76d3f1e-0">Diffusion models (TabDDPM) offer a promising alternative for high-fidelity, diverse tabular synthesis across numerical and categorical features</cite>.<cite id="f53c5626-0">Surveys emphasize the need for comprehensive evaluation protocols and practical guidance, spanning utility, statistical fidelity, and privacy, to support adoption in enterprise and research contexts</cite>. Continued progress will hinge on robust leakage evaluation, principled handling of categorical sparsity and missingness, and standardized benchmarks that reflect real-world utility and privacy constraints.<cite id="f53c5626-4">Balancing usefulness and leakage remains central, motivating end-to-end evaluations and standardized protocols</cite>.
</answer>

Title: A Comprehensive Survey of Synthetic Tabular Data Generation
Snippet: In this work, we present a comprehensive survey of synthetic tabular data generation, covering the end-to-end generation process and introducing a novel taxonomy to categorize existing generation methods. Our goal is to provide practical guidance for enterprises and organizations seeking to adopt synthetic tabular data generation techniques. At the same time, we offer insights into the key challenges and opportunities within the field, along with a thorough summary of evaluation protocols and real-world applications. Furthermore, we highlight promising directions for future research. We hope that this work will contribute to advancing the development of synthetic tabular data generation and inspire further exploration in this rapidly evolving area.

Commonly used tabular datasets for synthetic data generation are primarily sourced from three major repositories: UCI Machine Learning Repository, OpenML, and Kaggle. Most existing studies on tabular data generation rely on datasets from these platforms. In this survey, we summarize 20 widely used datasets across various tasks, including regression, binary classification, and multi-class classification. Among them, datasets such as Beijing, Adult, and California Housing are frequently used in studies focusing on synthetic tabular data generation with missing values, as shown in Table IV.

Title: Synthetic Tabular Data Based on Generative Adversarial Networks in Health Care: Generation and Validation Using the Divide-and-Conquer Strategy
Snippet: The CTGAN is specifically designed for generating synthetic data from tabular data. The CTGAN exhibits several unique features, including the ability to handle discrete and continuous features, the use of conditional generators, and sampling-specific training to avoid mode collapse and data imbalance problems.

Title: Distributed Conditional GAN (discGAN) For Synthetic Healthcare Data Generation
Snippet: A. CTGAN: Modeling Conditional Tabular Data from Synthetic Data Vault [4] From MIT, CTGAN is the SOTA tabular data generator with the ability to generate discrete and continuous values, model non-Gaussian multi-model data, and learn conditional distributions for many dimensions. [5] builds on previous tabular GAN implementations such as VeeGAN [6], TableGAN [7], and MedGAN [8]. CTGAN's contributions include "augmenting the training procedure with mode-specific normalization" to address multi-modal continuous columns. For each continuous column a variational Gaussian mixture model estimates the number of modes, then for each record in the column the probability of the value coming from each mode is calculated, then the sampled mode from the probability density is used for normalization of the value. Ultimately, the column value is represented as a scalar and a one-hot vector indicating which mode the value is from. 

Additionally, CTGAN adds a conditional generator and training-by-sampling to address a lack of samples from minor categories during training, i.e. unbalanced data. CTGAN samples in a way "that all the categories from discrete attributes are sampled evenly (though not necessarily uniformly)" during training. CTGAN learns a conditional vector indicating which condition should be sampled. During training the generator is penalized for generating data that does not match an indicated conditional vector. CTGAN's training-by-sampling approach ensures that the model "evenly explore[s] all possible values in discrete columns", even minor categories.For benchmark datasets of real data, machine learning efficacy was used to evaluate performance. A set of test data was held out during training, and classification and regression models were trained on generated data, then tested on the holdout data. Classification tasks used accuracy and F1 metrics, and regression tasks used R 2 .

Title: Prior-informed optimization of treatment recommendation via bandit algorithms trained on large language model-processed historical records
Snippet: After successfully structuring the clinical notes, we tackled the issue of limited data availability by generating synthetic data using a Conditional Tabular Generative Adversarial Network (CTGAN). This section outlines the outcomes of our synthetic data generation approach and the validation methods that followed.

Title: Federated learning for generating synthetic data: a scoping review
Snippet: • FDP-CTGAN [66] -it should be noted this paper concentrates on presenting a version of CTGAN [17] (which is a GAN specifically designed to generate tabular data) with the addition of DP (DP-CTGAN), and a federated version is only briefly described. FDP-CTGAN synthesises tabular medical data, and its performance in terms of utility (predictive performance of a model trained on synthetic data but tested on real data) is compared to other (non-FL) methods; the federated version is outperformed (in terms of, the Area Under Receiver Operating Curve and Area Under the Precision-Recall curve metrics) in all but one case by CTGAN and DP-CTGAN. 

• SGDE [45] presents a different way to generate synthetic data by having each client train a data generator locally (VAE are used) using DP; each client sends their generator to the server, but they are not aggregated or combined (as is typical in FL). In the final phase each client can access the set of generators stored on the Figure 5: The different GAN (Generative Adversarial Network) configurations used on the server and client devices, for federated synthesis server and use some/all of these to generate synthetic data locally. This method is not compared to others, but to a local and federated version, with the synthetic data version outperforming those overall, in terms of prediction accuracy, AUC and F1 score. 

• Weldon et al. [74] generate synthetic electronic health records (EHR) using federated GANs and tested their method by constructing the scenario of multiple hospitals, each with unique data silos, training a GAN locally and combining their parameters into one central GAN, which generated the synthetic patient data.

Title: An improved CTGAN for data processing method of imbalanced disk failure
Snippet: Conditional Tabular Generative Adversarial Networks(CTGAN) [20] is a GAN-based method to model tabular data distribution and sample rows from the distribution. In CTGAN, they invented the mode-specific normalization to overcome the non-Gaussian and multimodal distribution. They designed a conditional generator and training-by-sampling to deal with the imbalanced discrete columns. CTGAN model used continuous data and adds the conditional loss to discrete data to synthesize high quality data. CTGAN models continuous data and adds the conditional loss to discrete data to synthesize high quality data. 

Inspired by CTGAN, improveds CTGAN is proposed to generate disk failure data. 

The contributions of this paper are summarized as follows: 

1. The artificial neural network of the discriminator in CTGAN is replaced with a residual network to enhance the stability of the neural network when generating adversarial networks for adversarial training. 

2. Add a classifier based on the CTGAN framework. The classifier further improves the ability of the model to synthesize data by distinguishing fault samples, normal samples and generated samples. 

3. The classifier loss and the discriminator loss are combined into a total loss of discriminating the true and false samples to against the generator loss. 

The experimental results show that the RCTGAN algorithm can generate synthetic data with the same distribution as the original data. 

The remaining article is structured as follows: "Related work" discusses the related work to solve the imbalance of disk failure data. "Proposed method" provides the details of the proposed approach. "Experiments" discusses the datasets and neural network structure. "Results and Discussion" provides insight into performance evaluation and its comparison with CTGAN approaches. Finally, in "Conclusion", the research is concluded with some future recommendations.

Title: CasTGAN: Cascaded Generative Adversarial Network for Realistic Tabular Data Synthesis
Snippet: Tabular data is broadly used in regression and classification tasks, which facilitates a growing interest in tabular data synthesis for machine learning applications, especially in domains with limited training data. Bayesian networks can be used for generating synthetic records by approximating the conditional probability distribution from the data [21]. While the Bayesian networks can in practice be additionally used for exploring causal relationships between the independent variables, estimating the distributions is often built on simplifying assumptions on the data [22]. Meanwhile, tree-based methods were first utilised for generating partial synthetic data in [23], and has further explored in [24] where adversarial random forest has demonstrated comparable performance to deep learning techniques in terms of synthetic data quality. However, the privacy-utility trade-offs for synthetic data generation using tree-based density estimators is not sufficiently explored. 

Deep neural networks have been widely studied for synthetic data generation, thanks to their capabilities for handling and approximating the distributions of large datasets. Variational auto-encoders (VAEs) [25] estimate the probabilistic distribution of by finding a lower-dimensional latent representation of the data. The application of VAEs has been extended to image data generation [26], oversampling of anomaly event data [27] and tabular data synthesis [28]. An underlying limitation with variational autoencoders is the assumption of the a simple parametric form of the latent space, which leads to a difficulty in capturing complex data distributions [29]. Invertible neural networks have also been proposed for tabular data synthesis through variants based on neural ordinary differential equations [30], copula flows [31] and normalizing flows for private tabular data generation [32]. A drawback of the invertible neural network based synthesis is that extensive hyperparameter tuning is needed to achieve satisfactory classification and regression performance. 

Within deep learning based generative models, GANs are favourable due to their ability to generate complex synthetic data in an adversarial and unsupervised setting [37]. table-GAN [33] is one of the earliest generative models for producing tabular synthetic output based on adversarial training.
