# Why “ranking accuracy” alone is insufficient for evaluating reward models

Recent work emphasizes that a reward model’s ability to predict human preferences accurately is necessary but not sufficient; quality RMs must also provide informative gradients, sufficient variance, and good calibration to drive effective and safe alignment. <cite id="7471b74b-3">Even when a reward model is “accurate” at predicting preferences, if it fails to capture nuanced criteria or lacks sufficient reward variance, it will not enable effective policy improvement, underscoring the need for evaluation beyond raw accuracy</cite>. <cite id="7471b74b-4">Systematic evaluations have further revealed that many widely used reward models are unreliable for both optimization and evaluation, motivating rigorous, multi-dimensional assessments rather than reliance on a single accuracy metric</cite>.

Concurrently, broader RM evaluation efforts highlight that accuracy-focused leaderboards (e.g., RewardBench) do not translate into reliable alignment outcomes or human-aligned rankings. <cite id="87c184d7-0">Analyses of RM quality argue that leaderboards alone are insufficient to choose models that yield good alignment, since the relationship between RM accuracy and downstream alignment performance is not resolved by ranking accuracy alone</cite>. <cite id="329132b4-4">Moreover, difficult reasoning tasks reveal that even top reward models achieve relatively modest pairwise accuracy (e.g., 64% on JudgeBench), indicating substantial headroom and the need for metrics beyond simple win rates</cite>.

# Evidence of failures revealed when relying only on pairwise accuracy

High pairwise accuracy can coexist with structural biases and poor generalization, which are not captured by ranking accuracy alone. <cite id="96d656e1-1">For instance, RLHF pipelines commonly evaluate RM “accuracy” using RewardBench pairwise setups, treating an RM as correct if it ranks the preferred response higher, but this hides issues like miscalibration and preference biases that affect safety and efficacy</cite>. <cite id="96d656e1-4">Empirical studies on length bias show that standard RM training and evaluation can induce or fail to correct strong length preferences; calibration methods and analyses are required to detect and mitigate these biases, which pairwise accuracy does not by itself diagnose</cite>.

Robustness analyses further demonstrate that pairwise accuracy can be misleading. <cite id="329132b4-2">By examining how RM outputs change with KL divergence (a stress test for overoptimization), researchers find that models with high RewardBench scores can still rapidly over-optimize and exhibit reward “collapse” at certain divergences; performance on RewardBench does not reliably predict robustness, and tailored benchmarks like REWARD-MATH better expose these failures</cite>. <cite id="329132b4-2">In contrast, REWARD-MATH shows clearer trends: stronger models on this benchmark are better at avoiding overoptimization, directly linking evaluation outcomes to robustness rather than just pairwise win rate</cite>. <cite id="329132b4-3">Similarly, information-theoretic debiasing shows a trade-off—overcorrecting bias can substantially drop RewardBench accuracy while reducing spurious correlations, illustrating that optimizing pairwise accuracy can damage the very preference learning the RM is meant to encode</cite>.

# Calibration, bias, and alignment with human preferences

Because pairwise accuracy treats all misrankings equally, it cannot capture confidence miscalibration, selection biases, or misalignment with broader human judgments. <cite id="96d656e1-0">Work on reward calibration introduces methods (e.g., PPO-M and PPO-C) to improve how RMs express and learn confidence, motivated by the observation that standard pairwise training does not enforce calibrated confidence and can produce over- or under-confident scores</cite>. <cite id="96d656e1-4">Length-bias case studies quantify and mitigate spurious length preferences through calibration and principled bias modeling, again pointing to limitations of accuracy-only evaluation</cite>.

Alignment with human preferences requires more than correctly ordered pairs; it requires that RMs’ learned preferences generalize and reflect nuanced human choices. <cite id="96d656e1-3">Calibrating RMs using Chatbot Arena human preference data and comparing RM-inferred win rates to human Elo shows that calibration can improve agreement with human judgments, indicating that raw pairwise accuracy without calibration may not reflect true human-aligned preferences</cite>. <cite id="87c184d7-1">Benchmarking that reports both instance-level pairwise accuracy and ranking correlation (e.g., Kendall’s Tau) illustrates why a single accuracy number is incomplete: models can have high accuracy but suboptimal global ranking correlation, and vice versa</cite>. <cite id="96d656e1-2">Further, studies show that judgment granularity and inference-time considerations (e.g., Likert scale choice, use of chain-of-thought) materially affect both accuracy and calibration, reinforcing that pairwise accuracy alone is not a faithful proxy for human-aligned evaluation</cite>.

# Benchmarking and evaluation frameworks beyond pairwise accuracy

Several recent efforts explicitly critique and extend RM evaluation beyond pairwise accuracy, proposing multi-metric and stress-test oriented frameworks. <cite id="7471b74b-1">The “Elephant in the Room” analysis curates cleaner preference datasets and systematically studies how RM accuracy relates to alignment performance across reward-utilization paradigms, arguing that current RM leaderboards fail to connect accuracy to downstream alignment outcomes</cite>. <cite id="329132b4-0">Complementary work on robustness explores how to structure benchmarks (e.g., RewardBench and REWARD-MATH) and how to detect overoptimization, highlighting that robustness requires metrics and settings that pairwise accuracy alone cannot capture</cite>. <cite id="329132b4-4">At the same time, harder reasoning-oriented evaluations like JudgeBench reveal that top RM scores can still struggle, motivating inclusion of challenging, nuanced tasks in evaluation suites</cite>.

These developments reinforce that a comprehensive RM evaluation should include:
- Calibration metrics (e.g., expected calibration error for RMs; calibration of model confidence and RM outputs). <cite id="96d656e1-1">ECE-style measures and calibrated reward modeling are explicitly proposed alongside accuracy to assess confidence alignment</cite>.
- Bias and spurious attribute metrics (e.g., length preference, harmfulness/helpfulness confounds; bias-aware stress tests). <cite id="96d656e1-4">Length-bias analyses provide concrete procedures to quantify and mitigate spurious preferences that accuracy alone misses</cite>.
- Robustness/overoptimization tests (e.g., KL-divergence sweeps; pass@1/oracle reward trends). <cite id="329132b4-2">Divergence-based sweeps and REWARD-MATH show how to detect reward collapse and connect benchmark scores to robustness</cite>.
- Human alignment beyond pairwise accuracy (e.g., correlation with human Elo; arena-based validation). <cite id="96d656e1-3">Arena-based calibration demonstrates improved alignment of RM rankings with human preferences, beyond instance-level accuracy</cite>.
- Domain/task-specific stress tests and coverage (e.g., reasoning, multimodal, long-tail). <cite id="87c184d7-1">Multimodal evaluation shows the need for multiple correlation and accuracy measures to capture nuanced ranking behavior</cite>; <cite id="329132b4-4">JudgeBench complements RewardBench for reasoning tasks where pairwise accuracy alone is insufficient</cite>.

# Representative works and what they show

- RewardAnything (general RM quality): <cite id="7471b74b-3">Argues that “accuracy in predicting preferences is key but not the sole determinant,” emphasizing sufficient reward variance and calibration for effective alignment</cite>.
- Elephant in the Room (evaluation reliability): <cite id="7471b74b-4">Shows that many widely used RMs are unreliable for optimization/evaluation and calls for rigorous, RM-centric evaluation tied to alignment outcomes rather than accuracy-only leaderboards</cite>.
- Post-hoc reward calibration and length bias: <cite id="96d656e1-1">Introduces calibration-aware evaluation and training modifications alongside RM accuracy to address confidence and preference learning issues</cite>; <cite id="96d656e1-4">Demonstrates that strong length preferences can persist and that calibration methods outperform ensembling for bias reduction, revealing limitations of accuracy-centric evaluation</cite>.
- Overoptimization and robustness: <cite id="329132b4-2">Shows high RewardBench scores can coexist with rapid reward collapse under KL divergence increases and that REWARD-MATH better tracks robustness than RewardBench</cite>; <cite id="329132b4-3">Highlights a calibration-vs-preference trade-off: overcorrecting bias can drop RewardBench accuracy, underscoring that pairwise accuracy does not capture bias trade-offs</cite>.
- Human-aligned ranking and arena validation: <cite id="96d656e1-3">Uses Chatbot Arena to align RM win rates with human Elo, showing that calibration improves human alignment beyond raw pairwise accuracy</cite>; <cite id="87c184d7-1">Reports both accuracy and Kendall’s Tau to capture global ranking quality, illustrating why single-metric evaluations are incomplete</cite>.
- Benchmarking frameworks and limits: <cite id="87c184d7-0">Analyzes why RM leaderboards (e.g., RewardBench) do not directly translate to alignment performance and calls for evaluation that connects RM quality to downstream outcomes</cite>; <cite id="329132b4-4">JudgeBench demonstrates that even top models struggle on reasoning tasks, arguing for broader, harder evaluations</cite>.

# Practical recommendations for evaluating reward models

- Include multi-metric evaluation: <cite id="96d656e1-1">Pair pairwise ranking accuracy with calibration metrics (e.g., ECE for confidence alignment) and bias metrics (e.g., length or attribute preferences)</cite>. <cite id="96d656e1-4">Use bias quantification (Spearman correlation with bias attributes; length preference margins) and targeted penalties/penalties to detect and mitigate spurious preferences</cite>.
- Stress-test robustness: <cite id="329132b4-2">Perform KL-divergence or dataset perturbation sweeps to detect overoptimization and reward collapse; prefer benchmarks like REWARD-MATH that reveal robustness trends linked to downstream behavior</cite>.
- Anchor to human preferences and rankings: <cite id="96d656e1-3">Validate RM rankings against human preference data (e.g., Arena Elo) and measure alignment (e.g., correlation, calibrated judgments) rather than relying on accuracy alone</cite>. <cite id="87c184d7-1">Report both instance-level accuracy and global ranking correlation (e.g., Kendall’s Tau) to capture different aspects of alignment with human preferences</cite>.
- Connect RM evaluation to alignment outcomes: <cite id="7471b74b-4">Use ablations to trace how RM accuracy, variance, and calibration affect downstream policy performance and safety, not just RM ranking accuracy on static leaderboards</cite>.

# Takeaway

Multiple strands of recent work converge on a single conclusion: pairwise or ranking accuracy is necessary but not sufficient for evaluating reward models. <cite id="7471b74b-3">RM quality requires informative variance and calibration</cite>, <cite id="96d656e1-1">bias control</cite>, <cite id="329132b4-2">robustness to distribution shift and overoptimization</cite>, and <cite id="96d656e1-3">alignment with human preferences beyond static accuracy</cite>. <cite id="87c184d7-0">Leaderboards and single-metric evaluations risk selecting models that look good on pairwise accuracy yet fail in real alignment tasks, calling for comprehensive, multi-dimensional evaluation frameworks</cite>.
</answer>

Title: Reward Difference Optimization For Sample Reweighting In Offline RLHF
Snippet: In LLMs alignment, a reward model assesses a response to a given query, generating a score representing its quality (Stiennon et al., 2020;Ouyang et al., 2022). This score serves as a guide for the alignment process and can be used for two main purposes: 1) During alignment, the score acts as a training signal for online RLHF (Ouyang et al., 2022); 2) It helps gather human preferences for response selection (Yuan et al., 2023). Typically, training reward models employed the Bradley-Terry (BT) model (Bradley and Terry), which estimates the likelihood of one response being better than another based on their individual scores. However, this method often falls short of capturing true human preferences. 

Several recent studies have tackled the limitations of conventional reward models by exploring diverse solutions. Touvron et al. (2023) and Bai et al. (2023) propose to train fine-grained reward models that evaluate the response from different aspects, e.g. helpfulness, and harmlessness. Other studies consider taking uncertainty in the learned functions into account (Liang et al., 2023;Yue et al., 2023). These methods, however, focus on "pointwise" reward models which independently predict a reward score for each response. Recently, SLiC-HF (Zhao et al., 2023) is introduced to utilize a rank model that takes a query and two response candidates as input, ultimately indicating the chosen response via a token identifier (e.g., A/B). While bearing similarities with our difference model, SLiC-HF's ranking model outputs a categorical token, not a quantitative score reflecting the difference between responses. 

Offline RLHF methods usually omit the process of reward modeling. However, it has been shown in recent studies (Xu et al., 2024;Azar et al., 2023) that the reward model plays an important role in LLM alignment. We verify this finding and provide a simple yet effective way to enhance multiple offline RLHF methods.

Title: Elephant in the Room: Unveiling the Impact of Reward Model Quality in Alignment
Snippet: In this work, we conduct systematic experiments on the first two types of alignment methods that rely on reward models for alignment signals, analyzing the relationship between reward model accuracy and alignment performance. For DPO-like methods that do not rely on reward models, we experimentally explore the relationship between data quality and alignment performance. Recently, several works have begun to focus on reward models. REWARDBENCH [Lambert et al., 2024] is a concurrent work, which uses existing datasets and evaluate existing open-source reward models. However, they only establish a leaderboard for reward models, and fail to unveil the relationship between alignment performance and the quality of reward models. In this situation, even with a leaderboard clearly reflecting the performance of various reward models, it remains uncertain which reward model should be chosen to achieve good alignment. In another work research about reward models, [Wang et al., 2024a] mainly analyzes the impact of data quality on reward model performance, and also proposes to use contrastive learning to enhance the abilities of reward models. Nevertheless, this work also fails to analyze the impact of data or reward model on alignment, which is a key gap we aim to fill in this work. 

3 Are Reward Models Reliable in Current Alignment Works? 

Alignment is an important step to ensure the reliability of LLMs. Existing alignment works rely on reward models for alignment optimization or evaluation. But are these reward models reliable?To address this question, we begin by analyzing the noise present in the widely utilized HH-RLHF dataset [Bai et al., 2022] and curate a cleaned version to serve as a reliable testbed for subsequent evaluations of reward models. We then evaluate the performance of different reward models to have a clear understanding of their quality.

Title: Systematic Evaluation of LLM-as-a-Judge in LLM Alignment Tasks: Explainable Metrics and Diverse Prompt Templates
Snippet: In this section, we discuss the limitations in this study and outline the directions for future research. 

First, our current studies focus on commercial LLMs (e.g.,  rather than open-source LLMs. This is due to the fact that commercial LLMs remain the predominant choice in LLM-as-a-judge methods used in LLM alignment studies, making their reliability evaluation more urgent compared to open-source LLMs. 

Second, our evaluation studies concentrate on LLM-as-a-Judge methods, although open-source reward models (RMs) also hold the potential to serve as judges on LLM alignment tasks (Wang et al., 2024b). Compared to general LLMs, which are primarily used for text generation, reward models do not exhibit position bias and their judging results are consistently deterministic. Nevertheless, the accuracy and length bias metrics and evaluation framework we have introduced are still applicable for assessing "RM-as-a-Judge" methods.

snippet.text:
In LLMs alignment, a reward model assesses a response to a given query, generating a score representing its quality (Stiennon et al., 2020;Ouyang et al., 2022). This score serves as a guide for the alignment process and can be used for two main purposes: 1) During alignment, the score acts as a training signal for online RLHF (Ouyang et al., 2022); 2) It helps gather human preferences for response selection (Yuan et al., 2023). Typically, training reward models employed the Bradley-Terry (BT) model (Bradley and Terry), which estimates the likelihood of one response being better than another based on their individual scores. However, this method often falls short of capturing true human preferences. 

Several recent studies have tackled the limitations of conventional reward models by exploring diverse solutions. Touvron et al. (2023) and Bai et al. (2023) propose to train fine-grained reward models that evaluate the response from different aspects, e.g. helpfulness, and harmlessness. Other studies consider taking uncertainty in the learned functions into account (Liang et al., 2023;Yue et al., 2023). These methods, however, focus on "pointwise" reward models which independently predict a reward score for each response. Recently, SLiC-HF (Zhao et al., 2023) is introduced to utilize a rank model that takes a query and two response candidates as input, ultimately indicating the chosen response via a token identifier (e.g., A/B). While bearing similarities with our difference model, SLiC-HF's ranking model outputs a categorical token, not a quantitative score reflecting the difference between responses. 

Offline RLHF methods usually omit the process of reward modeling. However, it has been shown in recent studies (Xu et al., 2024;Azar et al., 2023) that the reward model plays an important role in LLM alignment. We verify this finding and provide a simple yet effective way to enhance multiple offline RLHF methods.

In this work, we conduct systematic experiments on the first two types of alignment methods that rely on reward models for alignment signals, analyzing the relationship between reward model accuracy and alignment performance. For DPO-like methods that do not rely on reward models, we experimentally explore the relationship between data quality and alignment performance. Recently, several works have begun to focus on reward models. REWARDBENCH [Lambert et al., 2024] is a concurrent work, which uses existing datasets and evaluate existing open-source reward models. However, they only establish a leaderboard for reward models, and fail to unveil the relationship between alignment performance and the quality of reward models. In this situation, even with a leaderboard clearly reflecting the performance of various reward models, it remains uncertain which reward model should be chosen to achieve good alignment. In another work research about reward models, [Wang et al., 2024a] mainly analyzes the impact of data quality on reward model performance, and also proposes to use contrastive learning to enhance the abilities of reward models. Nevertheless, this work also fails to analyze the impact of data or reward model on alignment, which is a key gap we aim to fill in this work. 

3 Are Reward Models Reliable in Current Alignment Works? 

Alignment is an important step to ensure the reliability of LLMs. Existing alignment works rely on reward models for alignment optimization or evaluation. But are these reward models reliable?To address this question, we begin by analyzing the noise present in the widely utilized HH-RLHF dataset [Bai et al., 2022] and curate a cleaned version to serve as a reliable testbed for subsequent evaluations of reward models. We then evaluate the performance of different reward models to have a clear understanding of their quality.

Snippet: To assess the consistency between LLaVA-Critic and human evaluators in pairwise ranking, we use the battle data from WildVision Arena [28], which comprises 11k human-annotated preference relations among LMM response pairs. Each relation includes a question-image pair and two responses generated by different models, accompanied by a human-annotated preference (including ties). Experimental results are reported in Table 3. While existing open-source LMMs exhibit initial pairwise ranking ability, there is a notable performance gap compared to GPT-4V/4o. After training with critic data, LLaVA-Critic achieves significant improvements. Title: Aligning with Human Judgement: The Role of Pairwise Preference in Large Language Model Evaluators
Snippet: To mitigate biased predictions from LLMs, calibration techniques have been developed to ensure less biased outcomes (Liu et al., 2023b;Li et al., 2023a;Zhou et al., 2023a). Motivated by this line of work, we first conduct a systematic analysis of the effectiveness of calibration techniques in aligning LLM evaluators with human judgements. We find that existing calibration methods are insufficient for aligning LLM evaluators, even provided with  supervised data. We discover that misalignment in evaluation is not primarily due to biased priors over evaluation scores, but rather from misaligned evaluation standards, i.e., the likelihood of LLM evaluators. Therefore, we are motivated to explore a new evaluation paradigm with LLMs to facilitate a more aligned judgement. 

Inspired by how LLMs are aligned through a reward model with preference data in RLHF, we argue that LLM evaluators can produce more aligned evaluations by leveraging their pairwise ranking abilities. Recent work has started exploring this intrinsic property by prompting LLMs with a pair of candidates (Wang et al., 2023b;Chen et al., 2023;Qin et al., 2023;Li et al., 2024). However, the complexity and scalability of evaluating with pairwise preference have been largely overlooked. To produce a preference ranking for evaluation, existing methods require exhaustive pairwise comparisons, as they ignore the transitivity assumption1 (Qin et al., 2023). This makes the evaluation procedure intractable as the number of comparisons grows quadratically (Zheng et al., 2024b;Liusie et al., 2024). 

In this work, we investigate the full potential of pairwise preference in LLM evaluators and its alignment with human judgements. We propose Pairwise-preference Search (PAIRS), an uncertainty-guided searching method that efficiently estimates the Maximum Likelihood Estimate (MLE) of preference rankings by searching through an uncertainty-pruned pairwise comparison space. PAIRS is more effective and query-efficient than existing pairwise baselines while significantly outperforming traditional direct scoring evaluations.

snippet.text: The demand for regulating potentially risky behaviors of large language models (LLMs) has ignited research on alignment methods. Since LLM alignment heavily relies on reward models for optimization or evaluation, neglecting the quality of reward models may cause unreliable results or even misalignment. Despite the vital role reward models play in alignment, previous works have consistently overlooked their performance and used off-the-shelf reward models arbitrarily without verification, rendering the reward model ``\emph{an elephant in the room}''. To this end, this work first investigates the quality of the widely-used preference dataset, HH-RLHF, and curates a clean version, CHH-RLHF. Based on CHH-RLHF, we benchmark the accuracy of a broad range of reward models used in previous alignment works, unveiling the unreliability of using them both for optimization and evaluation. Furthermore, we systematically study the impact of reward model quality on alignment performance in three reward utilization paradigms. Extensive experiments reveal that better reward models perform as better human preference proxies. This work aims to awaken people to notice this huge elephant in alignment research. We call attention to the following issues: (1) The reward model needs to be rigorously evaluated, whether for alignment optimization or evaluation. (2) Considering the role of reward models, research efforts should not only concentrate on alignment algorithm, but also on developing more reliable human proxy.

documents.title: Elephant in the Room: Unveiling the Impact of Reward Model Quality in Alignment
documents.snippet:
In this work, we conduct systematic experiments on the first two types of alignment methods that rely on reward models for alignment signals, analyzing the relationship between reward model accuracy and alignment performance. For DPO-like methods that do not rely on reward models, we experimentally explore the relationship between data quality and alignment performance. Recently, several works have begun to focus on reward models. REWARDBENCH [Lambert et al., 2024] is a concurrent work, which uses existing datasets and evaluate existing open-source reward models. However, they only establish a leaderboard for reward models, and fail to unveil the relationship between alignment performance and the quality of reward models. In this situation, even with a leaderboard clearly reflecting the performance of various reward models, it remains uncertain which reward model should be chosen to achieve good alignment. In another work research about reward models, [Wang et al., 2024a] mainly analyzes the impact of data quality on reward model performance, and also proposes to use contrastive learning to enhance the abilities of reward models. Nevertheless, this work also fails to analyze the impact of data or reward model on alignment, which is a key gap we aim to fill in this work. 

3 Are Reward Models Reliable in Current Alignment Works? 

Alignment is an important step to ensure the reliability of LLMs. Existing alignment works rely on reward models for alignment optimization or evaluation. But are these reward models reliable?To address this question, we begin by analyzing the noise present in the widely utilized HH-RLHF dataset [Bai et al., 2022] and curate a cleaned version to serve as a reliable testbed for subsequent evaluations of reward models. We then evaluate the performance of different reward models to have a clear understanding of their quality.

To assess the consistency between LLaVA-Critic and human evaluators in pairwise ranking, we use the battle data from WildVision Arena [28], which comprises 11k human-annotated preference relations among LMM response pairs. Each relation includes a question-image pair and two responses generated by different models, accompanied by a human-annotated preference (including ties). From this dataset, we randomly sample  MMHal-Bench 8 2k response pairs and assign them to evaluation prompts from the pairwise ranking prompt template set mentioned in Section 3.2, creating the in-domain evaluation dataset. We report average accuracy, with and without ties, to assess alignment with human evaluators at the instance level. 

For model-level consistency, we calculate the Elo rating for each response LMM and report Kendall's Tau to measure the overall ranking correlation with human preferences. 

Experimental results are reported in Table 3. While existing open-source LMMs exhibit initial pairwise ranking ability, there is a notable performance gap compared to GPT-4V/4o. After training with critic data, LLaVA-Critic achieves significant improvements. Specifically, LLaVA-Critic-72B achieves an average accuracy of 73.6% in pairwise comparisons without tie, outperforming both GPT-4o and GPT-4V. For pairwise accuracy with tie and model-level ranking (Kendall's Tau), LLaVA-Critic-72B shows only a marginal gap compared to GPT-4V/4o, with an accuracy of 60.5% and a score of 0.779, respectively. Notably, despite a substantial reduction in the number of parameters, LLaVA-Critic-7B still achieves an average accuracy of 59.6% in pairwise ranking with ties and 72.2% without ties, alongside a Kendall's tau of 0.763. These results underscore the strong alignment between LLaVA-Critic and human evaluators in pairwise ranking LMM responses.

Snippet: In summary, the baseline Length Penalty is already strong when RMs exhibit strong length bias. However, both reward scales and length margins should be considered to adjust the penalty weight, impairing its practicability. In contrast, the proposed method RC-LWR is robust to different hyper-parameter choices, yielding stable improvements in different settings. Reward models with more substantial bias are improved more. Furthermore, we argue that the optimal α is challenging to search for the following reasons: 

(1) both the reward distribution of the model and the length distribution of the task affect α, asking users to search different α per reward model and tasks repeatedly; (2) the method is very sensitive to the value of α, for some values the model may even collapse. On the contrary, our proposed method could robustly adapt to different reward models and tasks. 

Reward calibration v.s. Reward Ensemble As discussed in our related work section, previous works can utilise ensemble techniques to mitigate the potential bias. The last row is the calibrated performance of models. We find that the calibration outperforms most ensemble results except for ensembles with a much stronger model. Title: Evaluating Robustness of Reward Models for Mathematical Reasoning
Snippet: Evaluating the robustness of reward models via reward overoptimization. Typically, a robust proxy reward model trained to capture human preferences should exhibit increasing gold rewards as KL divergence increases. Conversely, a collapse in gold rewards at certain point during an increase in KL divergence indicates a lack of robustness in the proxy reward model. Figure 5 illustrates how dataset size impacts the behavior of reward model within a synthetic setup. We find that proxy reward models trained on smaller datasets reach peak rewards at lower KL divergences, indicating faster overoptimization. This finding suggests that larger datasets can help mitigate reward overoptimization, aligning with findings from Gao et al. (2023). Furthermore, we confirm that reward overoptimization can also be observed through oracle rewards (i.e. pass@1) in tasks with welldefined human preferences, such as mathematics. REWARDMATH serves as a reliable metric for evaluating the reward models. We have confirmed that larger dataset sizes generally improve the robustness of RMs. This trend is evident in Table 3, where the performance on RE-WARDMATH consistently improves as the dataset size increases. However, no such improvement is observed in RewardBench, indicating a lack of reliability in its evaluation results for reward models. Additionally, Figure 6 illustrates how gold and oracle rewards change with increasing KL divergence based on benchmark performance. Notably, some models with high scores on RewardBench also exhibit overoptimizaton, and there is no clear relationship between performance on RewardBench and overoptimization. For example, Oasst-rm-2.1-pythia-1.4b (i.e. 'J' in Figure 6a), which is one of the top-ranked models on RewardBench, exhibits a rapid overoptimization. However, the results from REWARDMATH exhibit a clear trend: the higher the performance (i.e. the darker the line color in Figure 6), the less reward collapse occurs. This underscores the reliability of RE-WARDMATH-models with strong performance on REWARDMATH are more effective at avoiding overoptimization, thereby providing more accurate rewards.

Title: Eliminating Inductive Bias in Reward Models with Information-Theoretic Guidance
Snippet: As shown in the figure, when  is too small (e.g., 0.1), the debiasing signal is insufficient. The model behaves similarly to a standard BT model, exhibiting a high bias metric (e.g., high Pearson correlation with a bias attribute) while achieving good performance on RewardBench. Conversely, when  is too large (e.g., 10), the debiasing objective dominates the training. The resulting "over-correction" successfully minimizes the bias metric but severely compromises the reward model's ability to learn true preference signals, leading to a significant drop in RewardBench accuracy. Moreover, we observe that  = 1 strikes an optimal balance. At  = 1, the bias metric is substantially reduced, while the preference learning performance on RewardBench is maximized. The behavior demonstrates that the proposed method can effectively neutralize spurious correlations without damaging-and in fact while enhancing-the reward model's core capabilities. Therefore, all main experiments in this paper use  = 1.

Background: Reward Modeling. Typical reward model training uses pairwise human preference data with binary ranking labels (chosen and rejected). Let D = {(x i , y i c , y i r )} n i=1 be the training dataset for the reward model, where x i is the prompt, and y i c is the chosen response preferred over the rejected response y i r . A binary preference ranking loss (Ouyang et al., 2022) is applied to enforce that the chosen responses receive a higher score than the rejected one, as illustrated in equation 1. 

where the reward model R θ is typically initialized from the SFT model. The LM head on top of the last layer is replaced with a linear layer to yield a single scalar reward prediction R θ (x, y) for a given prompt x and response y. Here, y c and y r denote the chosen and rejected responses respectively. 

PPO-M: PPO with Calibrated Reward Modeling. Existing reward model training datasets generally lack prompts explicitly requesting verbalized confidence scores or responses that include explicit confidence levels. To address this gap, we propose a straightforward modification to the existing binary pairwise ranking datasets by incorporating a confidence-query system prompt (shown in Fig. 4) and appending randomly generated confidence scores to model responses, consistent with the format in our preliminary experiments. This approach results in a modified training dataset for the reward model, denoted as 

, where xi represents the prompt with confidence-query system prompt prepended, h and l denote randomly assigned high and low confidence scores, respectively. We propose the following calibrated reward modeling loss: (yc,hc),(yc,lc),(yr,hr),(yr,lr))

Title: Post-Training Large Language Models via Reinforcement Learning from Self-Feedback
Snippet: We report three evaluation metrics to quantify model and reward model performance: 

Answer Accuracy measures the percentage of model responses that exactly match the correct answers in the dataset. This metric applies to both arithmetic (via numeric equivalence) and multiplechoice questions. 

Expected Calibration Error (ECE) assesses the alignment between token-level confidence estimates and actual correctness, indicating the degree of over-or under-confidence in the model's predictions. Note that this is calculated on the answer tokens for the arithmetic task and the choice token in the multiple-choice questions. 

Reward Model Accuracy is evaluated using the RewardBench mathematical reasoning subset. Each instance contains two model responses to the same question and a human-provided preference label. The reward model produces a scalar score for each response, and a prediction is considered correct if it assigns a higher score to the preferred response. Overall accuracy reflects the proportion of correctly ranked response pairs.

Tables 11 (K = 9) and 14 (K = 99) show pointwise results over methods (expanded versions of Tables 4 and 6). Tables 12 and 13 show expanded tie analyses on RewardBench (simplified in Table 5) and MT-Bench.

Title: CHARM: Calibrating Reward Models With Chatbot Arena Scores
Snippet: In this section, we aim to address the following questions through experiments to validate the effectiveness of our calibration method: 

Question 1. Does calibration enhance the reward model's judging capability, leading to more accurate and reliable evaluations? How does the mismatch degree influence calibration effectiveness, and is there a measurable correlation? 

• We evaluate calibrated reward models on benchmarks such as RM-Bench and Reward-Bench, which consist of diverse instructions paired with two candidate responses. The reward model must assess and select the better response, providing a robust framework to measure its judging capability. We analyze the impact of MD on calibration performance by selecting model pairs with varying MD values as over-valued and reference models. By examining how calibration affects performance across these pairs, we explore the correlation between initial misalignment and calibration effectiveness. 

Question 2. Does calibration successfully reduce preference bias, improving alignment with human preferences? 

• We construct a battlefield using responses from various LLMs on 805 prompts from AlpacaEval. Each response is scored by the reward models, allowing us to compute pairwise win rates between models. We then compare these RM-derived win rates against Elo-based win rates obtained from Chatbot Arena, which reflect human preferences. By analyzing their alignment, we assess whether the calibration process effectively reduces bias and produces rankings that more accurately reflect human judgments.

Title: Post-hoc Reward Calibration: A Case Study on Length Bias
Snippet: In summary, the baseline Length Penalty is already strong when RMs exhibit strong length bias. However, both reward scales and length margins should be considered to adjust the penalty weight, impairing its practicability. In contrast, the proposed method RC-LWR is robust to different hyper-parameter choices, yielding stable improvements in different settings. Reward models with more substantial bias are improved more. Results in Fig. 4 motivate us to investigate how calibration gains vary for RMs with different length bias. Therefore, we selected Chat Hard, the most challenging subset of RewardBench, for our investigation. Results are shown in Fig. 10. We use the Spearman correlation to represent the RMs' length preference on the x-axis; we then plot the RM's performance and RC-LWR improvements, different points in Fig. 10  method. Furthermore, we argue that the optimal α is challenging to search for the following reasons: 

(1) both the reward distribution of the model and the length distribution of the task affect α, asking users to search different α per reward model and tasks repeatedly; (2) the method is very sensitive to the value of α, for some values the model may even collapse. On the contrary, our proposed method could robustly adapt to different reward models and tasks. 

Reward calibration v.s. Reward Ensemble As discussed in our related work section, previous works can utilise ensemble techniques to mitigate the potential bias. We thus try to compare our proposed RC-LWR with the ensemble. Specifically, we use normalize-then-average to aggregate rewards from different reward models. We first select the top nine models from the RewardBench Leaderboard as of Aug and then aggregate them. The results are shown in the Fig. 16. In Fig. 16, the number in the cell [i, j] denotes the ensemble performance of model i and model j where i and j are the model's rank on the RewardBench leaderboard. The last row is the calibrated performance of models. We find that the calibration outperforms most ensemble results except for ensembles with a much stronger model. And intuitively, ensemble-based methods may not address common bias across models. For example, if these models overly prefer lengthy outputs, their ensemble model will also prefer lengthy output.

problem: Predictive models in Computer-based health information services Usage
final_response:
# Scope: What “Computer-based health information services” encompasses

Computer-based health information services include electronic health records (EHRs), patient portals for consumer access to records and messaging, telehealth and remote monitoring platforms, and health information exchange (HIE) systems that enable interoperability across providers and organizations.<cite id="0818ab68-4">Electronic Health Records (EHRs) constitute evidence of online health information management and underpin health information exchange in modern health systems</cite> Predictive models in these domains aim to forecast adoption and ongoing use, identify high-need or high-risk users, and guide personalized or population-level interventions.

# Predictive modeling approaches used in practice

Modern predictive work spans statistical and machine learning models tailored to binary adoption, longitudinal usage, and risk stratification. Studies have applied multivariate logistic regression and tree-based methods to predict patient portal adoption and utilization, while broader reviews catalog ML for risk prediction, triage, decision support, EHR-integrated analytics, and telemedicine services.<cite id="c33f4efd-1">Machine learning models identified privacy and data protection concerns as negative predictors and proactive portal access offers as positive predictors of portal use</cite> <cite id="c33f4efd-3">A cross-validated random forest plus logistic regression and evolved decision trees predicted portal access from survey features, finding privacy concerns, portal knowledge, and provider patient conversations as predictors</cite> <cite id="0818ab68-1">Machine learning in telehealth spans risk prediction, triage, personalized treatment planning, clinical decision support, and predictive analytics integrated with EHRs and remote monitoring</cite> Predictive modeling also leverages rich longitudinal EHR/HIE data to produce risk scores for social or clinical needs and to inform downstream interventions via clinical decision support in acute settings.<cite id="0818ab68-0">Predictive modeling can capitalize on EHR and health information exchange data to generate longitudinal risk scores that feed clinical decision support, but clinicians prefer explainable models over highly opaque systems</cite>

# Determinants of usage: intention models and user factors

Usage intention is shaped by perceived benefits, barriers, trust, and facilitating conditions. Health Belief Model constructs (perceived susceptibility, severity, benefits, barriers, cues to action, self-efficacy) and Technology Acceptance Model constructs (perceived usefulness, ease of use) explain telehealth adoption intentions and behaviors, with evidence that telehealth use can be treated as a preventive health behavior when supported by services and workforce integration.<cite id="0818ab68-2">Telehealth usage intention aligns with Health Belief Model constructs, with barriers and self-efficacy influencing intention; integrating specialist and nurse support is critical since successful telehealth is both an information system and a health service</cite> In e-healthcare more broadly, performance and effort expectancies, social influence, perceived value, and facilitating conditions predict intention and actual use, while perceived risk often plays a smaller role.<cite id="d79d181a-4">Performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, and perceived product value significantly influence intention, and facilitating conditions influence both intention and actual usage; perceived risk had an insignificant negative effect in a UTAUT-extended model</cite> For portals and EHRs, demographics, health burden, and prior interactions matter, and multivariate logistic regression is commonly used to model binary adoption/utilization outcomes at scale.<cite id="c33f4efd-4">A multivariate logistic regression modeled whether patients accessed a portal over three years using demographics, health characteristics, and portal utilization data from 1.1 million records</cite>

# Predictive models for specific services and measured effects

- Patient portals and consumer portals:
  - ML models outperform standard regression in cross-cycle generalization and reveal key levers. Decision trees and random forests identified privacy concerns and provider-proactive portal access offers as top predictors; clustering revealed consistent non-use groups by privacy concerns and heavy users focused on refill and messaging.<cite id="c33f4efd-1">Tree models produced more consistent accuracy across cycles; privacy concerns and proactive portal access offers were most significant determinants, with clusters of non-users due to privacy concerns and frequent refills/messaging among users</cite> <cite id="c33f4efd-3">Random forest feature selection plus logistic and tree models confirmed privacy, portal knowledge, and provider conversations as predictors of portal access</cite> These findings directly inform personalized onboarding and engagement strategies during registration and messaging.<cite id="c33f4efd-1">The authors recommend asking about privacy concerns and proactively offering online access or alternatives (e.g., text, calls) based on patient responses</cite>

- Telehealth and remote care:
  - Predictive models support risk prediction, triage, and engagement measurement. Reviews document trials in disease-specific telehealth and predictive analytics across diagnosis, anomaly detection, and risk stratification, leveraging EHRs and RPM data.<cite id="0818ab68-1">Clinical trials span pain prediction, telemedicine services, and telehealth systems; models support risk prediction, triage, and decision support with data from EHRs and remote monitoring</cite> ML-based engagement estimators using multimodal signals (affective/cognitive features) achieved notable accuracy gains and correlated with psychotherapists’ alliance measures, suggesting utility for monitoring participation in tele-mental health.<cite id="24b41906-3">A multimodal ML engagement estimator improved RMSE by 40% over prior methods and showed positive correlations with psychotherapists’ Working Alliance Inventory scores in real-world tests</cite> Supervised ML can also predict whether patients follow physician advice for visit support, informing targeted outreach and care management.<cite id="24b41906-2">A random forest model (AUC 0.677) predicted follow-up hospital visit behavior from chief complaint, medical advice, and user characteristics, indicating that telehealth advice influenced subsequent visits</cite>

- Health information exchange (HIE) and EHR-driven services:
  - At the organizational level, determinants of HIE breadth and depth include hospital size, ownership, system affiliation, physician–hospital integration, revenue models, and market structure; market-level variables like competition and urbanness do not moderate hospital-level effects, guiding policy to focus on intra-organizational levers.<cite id="d79d181a-0">There is a gap between health IT adoption and actual information exchange; outcomes improve where EHRs are actively used rather than merely adopted</cite> <cite id="d79d181a-1">Hospital-level variables (size, ownership, system affiliation, physician–hospital arrangements, revenue model) affect information exchange; market variables (concentration, urbanness, income) do not moderate these relationships</cite> <cite id="d79d181a-3">The study frames determinants of HIE as broader than prior adoption-only work and examines breadth and depth of exchange, with physician–hospital integration as a key hospital-level factor</cite> EHR-integrated decision support can translate predictive analytics into action, with “active choice” prompts increasing influenza vaccination and screening orders.<cite id="0818ab68-3">EHR “active choice” nudges significantly increased influenza vaccination rates and ordering of colonoscopy and mammography screening</cite>

- EHR adoption and national trends:
  - Forecasting models can simulate adoption trajectories under different policy or accountability scenarios. An interrupted time series model on OECD EHR data incorporated assumptions about information accountability technologies to project adoption trends and evaluate potential interventions at the country level.<cite id="0818ab68-4">An interrupted time series model of OECD EHR data simulated the impact of information accountability on adoption, enabling projections of adoption trajectories</cite>

# From prediction to action: interventions informed by models

Predictive models feed interventions through clinical decision support, proactive outreach, and service design. Risk scores derived from EHR/HIE can trigger referrals to social services in emergency departments, while portal-use predictions can personalize registration workflows and communication channels to address privacy concerns and support refill/messaging behaviors.<cite id="0818ab68-0">Risk scores from predictive modeling can be inputs to clinical decision support that refer patients to needed services, though clinician preference for explainable models must be addressed</cite> <cite id="c33f4efd-1">Predictors of portal use (privacy concerns, proactive access offers) suggest personalized onboarding and alternative communication modalities to increase engagement</cite> EHR-integrated nudges demonstrate that predictive or rule-based prompts can increase preventive service utilization, illustrating how analytics can be operationalized at point-of-care.<cite id="0818ab68-3">EHR “active choice” prompts increased vaccination rates and preventive screening orders</cite> In telehealth, ML-based engagement monitoring and advice-follow-through prediction enable targeted coaching and resource allocation to improve adherence and appropriate service use.<cite id="24b41906-3">ML engagement estimation correlates with alliance measures, suggesting a basis for targeted support during teletherapy sessions</cite> <cite id="24b41906-2">Predicting follow-up behavior from advice and user factors allows tailoring of outreach and care navigation</cite>

# Implementation, trust, and ethics shaping adoption and usage

Clinician and patient acceptance of predictive systems depends on transparency, usability, and alignment with workflow. Emergency department stakeholders favored explainable predictive models for social risk screening over opaque alternatives, underscoring the need for interpretable algorithms and stakeholder engagement in deployment.<cite id="0818ab68-0">Physicians and administrators prefer explainable predictive models; mixed reactions can arise when introducing advanced prediction in ED settings</cite> Privacy and data protection concerns consistently suppress portal adoption and must be addressed through clear governance, consent, and secure architectures, especially when integrating EHR/HIE data for risk modeling.<cite id="c33f4efd-1">Privacy and data protection concerns were the strongest negative predictors of portal use in ML models</cite> <cite id="0818ab68-4">EHR adoption has lagged due to privacy and security concerns, highlighting the need for accountability and trust-enhancing measures</cite> Facilitating conditions—training, infrastructure, and supportive policies—are critical bridges from intention to actual use across e-healthcare services.<cite id="d79d181a-4">Facilitating conditions significantly influenced intention and actual usage of e-healthcare services in UTAUT-extended modeling</cite>

# Practical deployment considerations

- Data sources and interoperability: Models benefit from EHRs, HIE, and non-clinical social determinants, but require interoperable, longitudinal data with attention to privacy and security to build trust and utility.<cite id="0818ab68-0">EHR and HIE data provide longitudinal, cross-organizational views enabling comprehensive risk prediction for clinical decision support</cite> <cite id="0818ab68-4">EHRs underpin modern health information exchange, yet adoption lags due to privacy/security concerns</cite>
- Model selection and governance: Tree-based and logistic models are common for adoption/usage prediction due to interpretability and feature importance; more complex models may be used for engagement or risk tasks when labeled data are scarce, with semi-supervised approaches and multimodal sensing in telehealth.<cite id="c33f4efd-3">Random forest feature selection plus logistic/decision trees captured portal access predictors across cycles</cite> <cite id="24b41906-3">A semi-supervised multimodal ML approach improved engagement estimation accuracy for teletherapy</cite>
- Stakeholder alignment: Clinician preference for explainability and workflow fit must be balanced with predictive performance; patient-facing models should reduce perceived risks and simplify onboarding through proactive, personalized offers.<cite id="0818ab68-0">Clinicians favor explainable models over opaque predictive systems when implementing risk screening in ED encounters</cite> <cite id="c33f4efd-1">Proactive portal access offers and addressing privacy concerns can directly increase portal use</cite>
- Policy and organizational levers: At scale, HIE breadth/depth depend more on hospital-level strategy and integration than market competition, guiding investments in system affiliation, revenue models, and physician–hospital integration to realize predictive analytics benefits across providers.<cite id="d79d181a-1">Hospital-level determinants drive information exchange; market-level variables like concentration and income do not moderate these effects</cite> <cite id="d79d181a-3">Physician–hospital integration and revenue model are key levers for enhancing information exchange</cite>

# Limitations and future directions

Evidence shows predictive models can forecast adoption and usage and support targeted interventions in portals, telehealth, and EHR-driven services, but high-quality causal evaluations of sustained behavior change remain limited. Telehealth ML studies often use observational data and retrospective cohorts, and portal/usage models are typically cross-sectional; more randomized or quasi-experimental evaluations of personalized reminders, tailored onboarding, and decision-support nudges are needed to quantify long-term impact on engagement and health outcomes.<cite id="24b41906-2">Machine learning predicted follow-up behavior in a historical cohort, demonstrating influence on visit behavior but not providing causal randomized evidence</cite> <cite id="c33f4efd-1">Predictive modeling identified determinants and clusters for portal use, suggesting actionable levers but calling for prospective validation of personalized engagement strategies</cite> Finally, ethical deployment requires ongoing work on privacy-preserving analytics, transparent explanations, and equitable access to ensure that predictive-driven interventions do not widen digital divides.<cite id="0818ab68-4">Privacy and security concerns impede EHR adoption, emphasizing the need for accountability and trust</cite> <cite id="0818ab68-0">Stakeholder acceptability hinges on explainability and alignment with clinical workflows when implementing predictive screening and CDS</cite>

# Takeaways for health systems and vendors

Title: Using a Machine Learning Algorithm to Predict Online Patient Portal Utilization: A Patient Engagement Study.
Snippet: Objective
There is a low rate of online patient portal utilization in the U.S. This study aimed to utilize a machine learning approach to predict access to online medical records through a patient portal.


Methods
This is a cross-sectional predictive machine learning algorithm-based study of Health Information National Trends datasets (Cycles 1 and 2; 2017-2018 samples). Survey respondents were U.S. adults (≥18 years old). The primary outcome was a binary variable indicating that the patient had or had not accessed online medical records in the previous 12 months. We analyzed a subset of independent variables using k-means clustering with replicate samples. A cross-validated random forest-based algorithm was utilized to select features for a Cycle 1 split training sample. A logistic regression and an evolved decision tree were trained on the rest of the Cycle 1 training sample. The Cycle 1 test sample and Cycle 2 data were used to benchmark algorithm performance.


Results
Lack of access to online systems was less of a barrier to online medical records in 2018 (14%) compared to 2017 (26%). Patients accessed medical records to refill medicines and message primary care providers more frequently in 2018 (45%) than in 2017 (25%).


Discussion
Privacy concerns, portal knowledge, and conversations between primary care providers and patients predict portal access.


Conclusion
Methods described here may be employed to personalize methods of patient engagement during new patient registration.
</snippet>

Title: Do Market Characteristics Matter? Factors Associated with Health Information Exchange
Snippet: Many economically developed countries have put great effort into implementing health information technology (IT) to reduce healthcare costs and improve quality of care [1,2]. Examples include the Health Information Technology for Economic and Clinical Health (HITECH) Act passed in the U.S., which provided USD 27 billion in incentive payments to encourage adoption of electronic health records over a 10-year period [1], and the U.K. government's 2018 announcement of an approximately USD 540 million investment in hospital information technology [2]. Although the U.S. Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology (2018) reported 96% of all non-federal acute care hospitals to possess a certified health IT system as of 2017 [3]; however, there exists a gap between health IT adoption and use, specifically with regard to information exchange among healthcare providers. Despite a high rate of health IT adoption, 32% of patients who visited a healthcare provider within the past 12 months reported having to repeat a procedure, provide their medical history again, or bring a test result to an appointment because of the unavailability of prior data [4]. The implication is that there exists many hospitals that have adopted health IT and do not successfully share electronic information among providers. 

Scholars, taking note of the importance of information exchange, have begun to focus on how information is incorporated and shared in healthcare settings [5]. A study comparing length of stay and readmission rates between instances of assimilation of electronic health records, measured as achievement of meaningful use and mere adoption, found patient outcomes to improve only in the former case [6]. Another study found that electronic mobilization of healthcare information across organizations could save as much as USD 1.9 million in emergency department settings annually [7]. These results commonly support the idea that it is the actual use of health IT, not mere adoption, that determines the extent of benefits, which a hospital gains from IT investment [8]. 

Increasing interest notwithstanding, little is known about what affects information exchange in the healthcare setting. Determinants of adoption have been widely studied [9][10][11][12][13], but information exchange has not. Exceptions, such as studies examining determinants of meaningful use [14,15], have been based on early stage of meaningful use that has not involved robust electronic health information exchange.
</snippet>
<snippet id=d79d181a-1>
Title: Do Market Characteristics Matter? Factors Associated with Health Information Exchange
Snippet: We analyzed multiple years of national data to inform understanding of the use of health IT, specifically, information exchange, beyond mere adoption. Aided by detailed datasets rarely used previously, our study examines the relationship between select unexamined variables and breadth and depth of information exchange in healthcare settings. We found that hospital-level variables such as size, ownership type, system affiliation, physician-hospital arrangement, and revenue model affect information exchange, and that market-level variables such as concentration ratio, urbanness, and median household income, although they directly affect information exchange, do not moderate the relationship between hospital-level variables and information exchange. 

This paper enhances understanding of factors associated with information exchange via health IT and its implications for the sustainability of the healthcare system. Efforts in many countries to increase information exchange using health IT effectively have gained added importance during the present pandemic. Among the insights related to theory and policy yielded by our results is that hospital administrators and policymakers who seek to increase health IT-driven information exchange should focus on hospital-level determinants and not differentially formulate strategies according to market-level characteristics.
</snippet>
<snippet id=d79d181a-2>
Title: Do Market Characteristics Matter? Factors Associated with Health Information Exchange
Snippet: Exceptions, such as studies examining determinants of meaningful use [14,15], have been based on early stage of meaningful use that has not involved robust electronic health information exchange. That only the final stage of meaningful use (termed "promoting interoperability" in fall 2018) includes electronic information exchange as a major requirement, and its reporting years are ongoing (2019-2021) [16], suggests that prior studies provide limited understanding of what affects the exchange of health information. Recently, scholars have started examining the factors associated with health information exchange, but they have either focused on a few individual relevant factors such as system membership or incentives [17][18][19] or on one aspect of information shared electronically, e.g., volume [20]. 

With the goal of providing a more comprehensive picture of drivers of health information exchange, the present study examines specific factors that affect information exchange among health IT systems. We investigate, based on findings reported in the prior literature about their effect on "mere adoption" of health IT [9][10][11][12], whether factors such as size, concentration, system affiliation, ownership type, teaching status, urbanness, etc. affect information exchange similarly or differently. Responding to the increasing importance of information exchange among healthcare providers, as detailed above, our study focuses on configuration strategies found to affect hospital performance [21], specifically, what affects the breadth (i.e., the extent to which patient health information is shared electronically among stakeholders) and depth (i.e., the level of detail at which patient health information is shared electronically) of information exchange among stakeholders. 

Using data sets from the American Hospital Association's (AHA's) annual and IT surveys, and the Census Bureau's small-area income and poverty estimates for the 2014-2016 period, we estimate the association of key factors with breadth and depth of information exchange and derive important policy implications from evaluations of previously studied determinants of health IT adoption. The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we describe our data and ex-ante predictions. Results are discussed in Section 3. We present our conclusions in Section 4.
</snippet>
<snippet id=d79d181a-3>
Title: Do Market Characteristics Matter? Factors Associated with Health Information Exchange
Snippet: Our study makes a number of contributions. First, to the best of our knowledge, the current study is the first to investigate determinants of information exchange in the healthcare setting. Previous research has focused mostly on determinants of adoption, and in such studies of meaningful use as existing information exchange has only recently been added as a requirement [17][18][19][20]. Understanding of the determinants of information exchange has thus been limited. The results of our study should contribute to the realization of many of the benefits of health IT, including those associated with enhanced information exchange. 

Second, our study helps to provide a more comprehensive picture of drivers of health information exchange. Rather than merely focusing on the percentage of information shared electronically, the current study focused on the relevant factors associated with the breadth and depth of information shared. Moreover, our study examines one of the key hospital-level factors not previously studied: physician-hospital integration. Even among hospital-level variables, it is relatively easier to change physician-hospital arrangements than to change, for example, ownership type. Those interested in enhancing information exchange should continue to search for other unexamined factors that might increase cross-party sharing of detailed information. 

Last but not least, our analysis elucidates the effect of specific market-level determinants on information exchange. The finding of our sub-sample analysis that market-level variables such as concentration, urbanness, and median household income do not moderate the relation between hospital-level variables and information exchange is particularly important, as hospital-level determinists are more amenable and hospital administrators and policymakers thus do not need to pursue different strategies to promote the widespread use of health IT using the results of our study. The government with limited resources should thus revisit policies of increasing health information exchange and focus more on hospital-level determinants, such as revenue model or system affiliation. 

Few limitations of our paper could shed light on noble opportunities for future research. In examining the determinants of information exchange, the current study only looks at two dimensions: the breadth (extent) and depth (level of detail). Recent studies suggests that four dimensions, including volume, diversity, breadth, and depth are important [17,19].
</snippet>
<snippet id=d79d181a-4>
Title: Ageing well with tech: Exploring the determinants of e-healthcare services adoption in an emerging economy
Snippet: The adoption of e-healthcare services is critical for improving healthcare accessibility and efficiency, particularly in regions with diverse populations, such as Malaysia. Although e-healthcare services offer numerous advantages, their adoption is considerably low and requires a thorough understanding of the key factors that influence their use. This study investigated the determinants and dynamics of e-healthcare adoption among adults over 40 years by extending the unified theory of acceptance and use of technology. We employed a quantitative research approach, specifically a cross-sectional design. Data were collected from 393 Malaysian respondents through a structured survey questionnaire, using convenience sampling. They were analyzed using partial least-squares-structural equation modeling. The findings revealed that performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, and perceived product value significantly influenced individuals’ intentions to use e-healthcare services. Meanwhile, perceived risk had an insignificant negative effect. Facilitating conditions significantly influenced individuals’ intentions and actual usage of e-healthcare services. Furthermore, individuals’ intentions to use e-healthcare services significantly affected their actual use of these services. Additionally, the intention to use e-healthcare services mediated the relationship between the factors and usage of e-healthcare services, except for perceived risk. Surprisingly, perceived service accuracy had no significant moderating effect on the relationship between individuals’ intention to use and their actual use of e-healthcare services. This study offers valuable insights for educators, practitioners, and policymakers, enriching the scholarly discourse in this field. For education, integrating e-healthcare topics into curricula can enhance digital health literacy. In practice, healthcare providers should focus on improving user experience and addressing barriers to technology adoption. For policy making, developing supportive policies, and infrastructure to facilitate e-healthcare adoption is crucial to enhancing public health outcomes.
</snippet></tool_output><think>

Title: A telehealth application for adequate hospital visit advice by physicians affected users’ subsequent hospital visit behavior: a historical cohort study with machine learning
Snippet: The effectiveness of telehealth strategies toward support for adequate hospital visits is vital. We examined whether individuals who received advice from a physician via an online application subsequently visited hospitals. Further, we examined the background factors associated with their hospital visit behavior.We used machine learning to examine whether chief complaint, medical advice, and user background characteristics could be used to predict their subsequent hospital visit.Among 7,152 participants, those in their 30s were the most frequent users. The proportion of each medical advice was significantly different between the group that did and the one that did not follow physicians’ advice. We further performed supervised machine learning using random forest modeling to categorize those who (1) followed physicians’ advice or (2) did not follow physicians’ advice. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.677. Consequently, the aforementioned model soundly categorized whether users followed physicians’ advice. Chief complaint and medical advice were the most important variables to predict whether users followed the advice.The telehealth system to provide support for adequate hospital visits influenced patients’ subsequent hospital visit behavior. Patients’ chief complaint was the most important variable in discriminating whether users followed physicians’ advice.

Title: Developing a Machine Learning–Based Automated Patient Engagement Estimator for Telehealth: Algorithm Development and Validation Study
Snippet: Background Patient engagement is a critical but challenging public health priority in behavioral health care. During telehealth sessions, health care providers need to rely predominantly on verbal strategies rather than typical nonverbal cues to effectively engage patients. Hence, the typical patient engagement behaviors are now different, and health care provider training on telehealth patient engagement is unavailable or quite limited. Therefore, we explore the application of machine learning for estimating patient engagement. This can assist psychotherapists in the development of a therapeutic relationship with the patient and enhance patient engagement in the treatment of mental health conditions during tele–mental health sessions. Objective This study aimed to examine the ability of machine learning models to estimate patient engagement levels during a tele–mental health session and understand whether the machine learning approach could support therapeutic engagement between the client and psychotherapist. Methods We proposed a multimodal learning-based approach. We uniquely leveraged latent vectors corresponding to affective and cognitive features frequently used in psychology literature to understand a person’s level of engagement. Given the labeled data constraints that exist in health care, we explored a semisupervised learning solution. To support the development of similar technologies for telehealth, we also plan to release a dataset called Multimodal Engagement Detection in Clinical Analysis (MEDICA). This dataset includes 1229 video clips, each lasting 3 seconds. In addition, we present experiments conducted on this dataset, along with real-world tests that demonstrate the effectiveness of our method. Results Our algorithm reports a 40% improvement in root mean square error over state-of-the-art methods for engagement estimation.
