# Scope: What “Computer-based health information services” encompasses

Computer-based health information services include electronic health records (EHRs), patient portals for consumer access to records and messaging, telehealth and remote monitoring platforms, and health information exchange (HIE) systems that enable interoperability across providers and organizations.<cite id="0818ab68-4">Electronic Health Records (EHRs) constitute evidence of online health information management and underpin health information exchange in modern health systems</cite> Predictive models in these domains aim to forecast adoption and ongoing use, identify high-need or high-risk users, and guide personalized or population-level interventions.

# Predictive modeling approaches used in practice

Modern predictive work spans statistical and machine learning models tailored to binary adoption, longitudinal usage, and risk stratification. Studies have applied multivariate logistic regression and tree-based methods to predict patient portal adoption and utilization, while broader reviews catalog ML for risk prediction, triage, decision support, EHR-integrated analytics, and telemedicine services.<cite id="c33f4efd-1">Machine learning models identified privacy and data protection concerns as negative predictors and proactive portal access offers as positive predictors of portal use</cite> <cite id="c33f4efd-3">A cross-validated random forest plus logistic regression and evolved decision trees predicted portal access from survey features, finding privacy concerns, portal knowledge, and provider patient conversations as predictors</cite> <cite id="0818ab68-1">Machine learning in telehealth spans risk prediction, triage, personalized treatment planning, clinical decision support, and predictive analytics integrated with EHRs and remote monitoring</cite> Predictive modeling also leverages rich longitudinal EHR/HIE data to produce risk scores for social or clinical needs and to inform downstream interventions via clinical decision support in acute settings.<cite id="0818ab68-0">Predictive modeling can capitalize on EHR and health information exchange data to generate longitudinal risk scores that feed clinical decision support, but clinicians prefer explainable models over highly opaque systems</cite>

# Determinants of usage: intention models and user factors

Usage intention is shaped by perceived benefits, barriers, trust, and facilitating conditions. Health Belief Model constructs (perceived susceptibility, severity, benefits, barriers, cues to action, self-efficacy) and Technology Acceptance Model constructs (perceived usefulness, ease of use) explain telehealth adoption intentions and behaviors, with evidence that telehealth use can be treated as a preventive health behavior when supported by services and workforce integration.<cite id="0818ab68-2">Telehealth usage intention aligns with Health Belief Model constructs, with barriers and self-efficacy influencing intention; integrating specialist and nurse support is critical since successful telehealth is both an information system and a health service</cite> In e-healthcare more broadly, performance and effort expectancies, social influence, perceived value, and facilitating conditions predict intention and actual use, while perceived risk often plays a smaller role.<cite id="d79d181a-4">Performance expectancy, effort expectancy, social influence, and perceived product value significantly influence intention, and facilitating conditions influence both intention and actual usage; perceived risk had an insignificant negative effect in a UTAUT-extended model</cite> For portals and EHRs, demographics, health burden, and prior interactions matter, and multivariate logistic regression is commonly used to model binary adoption/utilization outcomes at scale.<cite id="c33f4efd-4">A multivariate logistic regression modeled whether patients accessed a portal over three years using demographics, health characteristics, and portal utilization data from 1.1 million records</cite>

# Predictive models for specific services and measured effects

- Patient portals and consumer portals:
  - ML models outperform standard regression in cross-cycle generalization and reveal key levers. Decision trees and random forests identified privacy concerns and provider-proactive portal access offers as top predictors; clustering revealed consistent non-use groups by privacy concerns and heavy users focused on refill and messaging.<cite id="c33f4efd-1">Tree models produced more consistent accuracy across cycles; privacy concerns and proactive portal access offers were most significant determinants, with clusters of non-users due to privacy concerns and frequent refills/messaging among users</cite> <cite id="c33f4efd-3">Random forest feature selection plus logistic and tree models confirmed privacy, portal knowledge, and provider conversations as predictors of portal access</cite> These findings directly inform personalized onboarding and engagement strategies during registration and messaging.<cite id="c33f4efd-1">The authors recommend asking about privacy concerns and proactively offering online access or alternatives (e.g., text, calls) based on patient responses</cite>

- Telehealth and remote care:
  - Predictive models support risk prediction, triage, and engagement measurement. Reviews document trials in disease-specific telehealth and predictive analytics across diagnosis, anomaly detection, and risk stratification, leveraging EHRs and RPM data.<cite id="0818ab68-1">Clinical trials span pain prediction, telemedicine services, and telehealth systems; models support risk prediction, triage, and decision support with data from EHRs and remote monitoring</cite> ML-based engagement estimators using multimodal signals (affective/cognitive features) achieved notable accuracy gains and correlated with psychotherapists’ alliance measures, suggesting utility for monitoring participation in tele-mental health.<cite id="24b41906-3">A multimodal ML engagement estimator improved RMSE by 40% over prior methods and showed positive correlations with psychotherapists’ Working Alliance Inventory scores in real-world tests</cite> Supervised ML can also predict whether patients follow physician advice for visit support, informing targeted outreach and care management.<cite id="24b41906-2">A random forest model (AUC 0.677) predicted follow-up hospital visit behavior from chief complaint, medical advice, and user characteristics, indicating that telehealth advice influenced subsequent visits</cite>

- Health information exchange (HIE) and EHR-driven services:
  - At the organizational level, determinants of HIE breadth and depth include hospital size, ownership, system affiliation, physician–hospital integration, revenue models, and market structure; market-level variables like competition and urbanness do not moderate hospital-level effects, guiding policy to focus on intra-organizational levers.<cite id="d79d181a-0">There is a gap between health IT adoption and actual information exchange; outcomes improve where EHRs are actively used rather than merely adopted</cite> <cite id="d79d181a-1">Hospital-level variables (size, ownership, system affiliation, physician–hospital arrangements, revenue model) affect information exchange; market variables (concentration, urbanness, income) do not moderate these relationships</cite> <cite id="d79d181a-3">The study frames determinants of HIE as broader than prior adoption-only work and examines breadth and depth of exchange, with physician–hospital integration as a key hospital-level factor</cite> EHR-integrated decision support can translate predictive analytics into action, with “active choice” prompts increasing influenza vaccination and screening orders.<cite id="0818ab68-3">EHR “active choice” nudges significantly increased influenza vaccination rates and ordering of colonoscopy and mammography screening</cite>

- EHR adoption and national trends:
  - Forecasting models can simulate adoption trajectories under different policy or accountability scenarios. An interrupted time series model on OECD EHR data incorporated assumptions about information accountability technologies to project adoption trends and evaluate potential interventions at the country level.<cite id="0818ab68-4">An interrupted time series model of OECD EHR data simulated the impact of information accountability on adoption, enabling projections of adoption trajectories</cite>

# From prediction to action: interventions informed by models

Predictive models feed interventions through clinical decision support, proactive outreach, and service design. Risk scores derived from EHR/HIE can trigger referrals to social services in emergency departments, while portal-use predictions can personalize registration workflows and communication channels to address privacy concerns and support refill/messaging behaviors.<cite id="0818ab68-0">Risk scores from predictive modeling can be inputs to clinical decision support that refer patients to needed services, though clinician preference for explainable models must be addressed</cite> <cite id="c33f4efd-1">Predictors of portal use (privacy concerns, proactive access offers) suggest personalized onboarding and alternative communication modalities to increase engagement</cite> EHR-integrated nudges demonstrate that predictive or rule-based prompts can increase preventive service utilization, illustrating how analytics can be operationalized at point-of-care.<cite id="0818ab68-3">EHR “active choice” prompts increased vaccination rates and preventive screening orders</cite> In telehealth, ML-based engagement monitoring and advice-follow-through prediction enable targeted coaching and resource allocation to improve adherence and appropriate service use.<cite id="24b41906-3">ML engagement estimation correlates with alliance measures, suggesting a basis for targeted support during teletherapy sessions</cite> <cite id="24b41906-2">Predicting follow-up behavior from advice and user factors allows tailoring of outreach and care navigation</cite>

# Implementation, trust, and ethics shaping adoption and usage

Clinician and patient acceptance of predictive systems depends on transparency, usability, and alignment with workflow. Emergency department stakeholders favored explainable predictive models for social risk screening over opaque alternatives, underscoring the need for interpretable algorithms and stakeholder engagement in deployment.<cite id="0818ab68-0">Physicians and administrators prefer explainable predictive models; mixed reactions can arise when introducing advanced prediction in ED settings</cite> Privacy and data protection concerns consistently suppress portal adoption and must be addressed through clear governance, consent, and secure architectures, especially when integrating EHR/HIE data for risk modeling.<cite id="c33f4efd-1">Privacy and data protection concerns were the strongest negative predictors of portal use in ML models</cite> <cite id="0818ab68-4">EHR adoption has lagged due to privacy and security concerns, highlighting the need for accountability and trust-enhancing measures</cite> Facilitating conditions—training, infrastructure, and supportive policies—are critical bridges from intention to actual use across e-healthcare services.<cite id="d79d181a-4">Facilitating conditions significantly influenced intention and actual usage of e-healthcare services in UTAUT-extended modeling</cite>

# Practical deployment considerations

- Data sources and interoperability: Models benefit from EHRs, HIE, and non-clinical social determinants, but require interoperable, longitudinal data with attention to privacy and security to build trust and utility.<cite id="0818ab68-0">EHR and HIE data provide longitudinal, cross-organizational views enabling comprehensive risk prediction for clinical decision support</cite> <cite id="0818ab68-4">EHRs underpin modern health information exchange, yet adoption lags due to privacy/security concerns</cite>
- Model selection and governance: Tree-based and logistic models are common for adoption/usage prediction due to interpretability and feature importance; more complex models may be used for engagement or risk tasks when labeled data are scarce, with semi-supervised approaches and multimodal sensing in telehealth.<cite id="c33f4efd-3">Random forest feature selection plus logistic/decision trees captured portal access predictors across cycles</cite> <cite id="24b41906-3">A semi-supervised multimodal ML approach improved engagement estimation accuracy for teletherapy</cite>
- Stakeholder alignment: Clinician preference for explainability and workflow fit must be balanced with predictive performance; patient-facing models should reduce perceived risks and simplify onboarding through proactive, personalized offers.<cite id="0818ab68-0">Clinicians favor explainable models over opaque predictive systems when implementing risk screening in ED encounters</cite> <cite id="c33f4efd-1">Proactive portal access offers and addressing privacy concerns can directly increase portal use</cite>
- Policy and organizational levers: At scale, HIE breadth/depth depend more on hospital-level strategy and integration than market competition, guiding investments in system affiliation, revenue models, and physician–hospital integration to realize predictive analytics benefits across providers.<cite id="d79d181a-1">Hospital-level determinants drive information exchange; market-level variables like concentration and income do not moderate these effects</cite> <cite id="d79d181a-3">Physician–hospital integration and revenue model are key levers for enhancing information exchange</cite>

# Limitations and future directions

Evidence shows predictive models can forecast adoption and usage and support targeted interventions in portals, telehealth, and EHR-driven services, but high-quality causal evaluations of sustained behavior change remain limited. Telehealth ML studies often use observational data and retrospective cohorts, and portal/usage models are typically cross-sectional; more randomized or quasi-experimental evaluations of personalized reminders, tailored onboarding, and decision-support nudges are needed to quantify long-term impact on engagement and health outcomes.<cite id="24b41906-2">Machine learning predicted follow-up behavior in a historical cohort, demonstrating influence on visit behavior but not providing causal randomized evidence</cite> <cite id="c33f4efd-1">Predictive modeling identified determinants and clusters for portal use, suggesting actionable levers but calling for prospective validation of personalized engagement strategies</cite> Finally, ethical deployment requires ongoing work on privacy-preserving analytics, transparent explanations, and equitable access to ensure that predictive-driven interventions do not widen digital divides.<cite id="0818ab68-4">Privacy and security concerns impede EHR adoption, emphasizing the need for accountability and trust</cite> <cite id="0818ab68-0">Stakeholder acceptability hinges on explainability and alignment with clinical workflows when implementing predictive screening and CDS</cite>

# Takeaways for health systems and vendors

- Build adoption- and usage-aware predictive pipelines: Combine EHR/HIE and social risk data for risk stratification; deploy explainable models and dashboards for clinicians; implement privacy-first architectures and transparent consent for patients.<cite id="0818ab68-0">Predictive risk scores integrated into CDS can refer patients to services, but clinician preference for explainability must be addressed</cite> <cite id="c33f4efd-1">Privacy concerns dominate non-use; proactive access offers and tailored communication improve portal uptake</cite>
- Personalize engagement at point of care: Use model-derived segments to guide registration and messaging (e.g., offer portals or alternatives), and embed nudges in EHRs to increase preventive services and follow-up care.<cite id="0818ab68-3">EHR “active choice” nudges increased vaccination and preventive screening</cite> <cite id="c33f4efd-1">Personalized registration strategies based on privacy concerns and usage patterns can improve engagement</cite>
- Invest in organizational readiness for HIE: Prioritize hospital-level levers (system affiliation, revenue models, physician integration, workflows) to unlock the full benefits of predictive analytics across providers.<cite id="d79d181a-1">Hospital-level variables significantly affect information exchange; market-level factors do not moderate these effects</cite> <cite id="d79d181a-3">Physician–hospital integration and revenue model are actionable levers for promoting HIE and realizing analytics benefits</cite>
</answer>

Title: Machine Learning Models and Technologies for Evidence-Based Telehealth and Smart Care: A Review
Snippet: The contribution of this review article is to study and analyze ML models and technologies that support telehealth and smart care in the health sector. It focuses on evidence-based models and their application in various health domains and tasks. The article provides detailed findings and classifications of studies based on the health domain, product/service they support, and the type of ML they use. Specifically, ML models and technologies can be applied in telehealth and SC in various ways. These include risk prediction, remote monitoring, personalized treatment plans, decision support systems, telemedicine triage, patient demographics, clinical measurements, EHRs, remote patient monitoring, and NLP. 

Summarizing the investigation for RQ1, as it is stated that in this review, 17 relevant clinical trials concerning the development of pain prediction models, telemedicine services, and telehealth systems for various diseases were identified. In detail, two trials were identified in the health domain of neoplasms, two trials in the health domain of respiratory tract diseases, five trials in nervous system diseases, three trials in cardiovascular diseases, three trials in nutritional and metabolic diseases, one trial in pathological conditions, signs, and symptoms and one more trial was identified in autism spectrum disorder. 

In relation to the RQ2, the answers given are summarized as follows: 

In the Health Conditions category based on the ICD-11 Standard, four healthcare sectors were identified: disease diagnosis (five trials), clustering and subtyping (five trials in six studies), and anomaly detection (one trial). 

In the Classification of Digital Health Interventions category based on the DHIS Standard the following sectors were identified: electronic health records (EHR) (two trials), telemedicine (six trials), image analysis (one trial), patient risk stratification (two trials), natural language processing (NLP) (two trials), clinical decision support (one trial), healthcare resource allocation (one trial), and predictive analytics (one trial). 

In the ICHI category, the following sectors were identified: interventions into drug discovery (one trial), personalized medicine (four trials), and genomics and precision medicine (one trial), using machine learning for drug efficacy, safety, and optimal treatment.

Title: An Empirical Study to Explore the Adoption of Telehealth: Health Belief Model Perspective
Snippet: Based on the Health Belief Model, this study proposed a research model to better understand the older residents' usage intention of telehealth system. The model considered the relationships among perceived susceptibility, perceived severity, perceived benefits, perceived barriers, cues to action, self efficacy and intention to use. Using Structural Equation Modeling (SEM), the hypotheses are proposed to validate the fit of empirical data and model. 

This empirical study has highlighted how rural residents are reported to have benefited from the telehealth system. The findings have also reported that the Health Belief Model is a suitable model to explain and predict the usage compliance of telehealth. That is, the routine usage behavior of telehealth could be treated as a preventive health behavior. Based on information system adoption perspective, many telehealth researches have utilized TAM (Technology Acceptance Model) to demonstrate that the constructs of perceived ease of use and usefulness of telehealth equipment are primary factors in technology user acceptance and usage. However, the major purpose of telehealth is to provide increased access to medical care for rural residents. Successful deployment of this innovation requires much more than the installation of the equipment. The role of specialists and community nurses is important, since it is already used to underpin services for residents [8]. Therefore, a successful telehealth system is not only an information system but also a health service provider to the residents. We believe that more integrated model (e.g., integrative perspective of HBM and TAM) applied in future studies should provide more valuable and informative contributions toward development of successful telehealth. ______________________________

First, one national level research reported the adoption level of EHR as it was higher in rural practices than urban counterparts, reversing the earlier trends. 72 Another similar research also reported the necessity of considering the patient's behavioral aspects while using the tool during patient rendering procedures so as to increase patient's engagement level. 73 These issues may call for behavioral scientists to address this particular patient concern.

Title: Patient-Empowered Electronic Health Records
Snippet: Electronic Health Records (EHRs) constitute evidence of online health information management. Critical healthcare information technology (HIT) infrastructure facilitates health information exchange of 'modern' health systems. The growth and implementation of EHRs are progressing in many countries while the adoption rate is lagging and lacking momentum amidst privacy and security concerns. This paper uses an interrupted time series (ITS) analysis of OECD data related to EHRs from many countries to make predictions about EHR adoption. The ITS model can be used to explore the impact of various HIT on adoption. Assumptions about the impact of Information Accountability are entered into the model to generate projections if information accountability technologies are developed. In this way, the OECD data and ITS analysis can be used to perform simulations for improving EHR adoption.

The findings have also reported that the Health Belief Model is a suitable model to explain and predict the usage compliance of telehealth. That is, the routine usage behavior of telehealth could be treated as a preventive health behavior. Based on information system adoption perspective, many telehealth researches have utilized TAM (Technology Acceptance Model) to demonstrate that the constructs of perceived ease of use and usefulness of telehealth equipment are primary factors in technology user acceptance and usage. These include risk prediction, remote monitoring, personalized treatment plans, decision support systems, telemedicine triage, patient demographics, clinical measurements, EHRs, remote patient monitoring, and NLP. 

Summarizing the investigation for RQ1, as it is stated that in this review, 17 relevant clinical trials concerning the development of pain prediction models, telemedicine services, and telehealth systems for various diseases were identified. In detail, two trials were identified in the health domain of neoplasms, two trials in the health domain of respiratory tract diseases, five trials in nervous system diseases, three trials in cardiovascular diseases, three trials in nutritional and metabolic diseases, one trial in pathological conditions, signs, and symptoms and one more trial was identified in autism spectrum disorder.

In the Health Conditions category based on the ICD-11 Standard, four healthcare sectors were identified: disease diagnosis (five trials), clustering and subtyping (five trials in six studies), and anomaly detection (one trial).

Title: Using a Machine Learning Algorithm to Predict Online Patient Portal Utilization: A Patient Engagement Study.
Snippet: Objective
There is a low rate of online patient portal utilization in the U.S. This study aimed to utilize a machine learning approach to predict access to online medical records through a patient portal.


Methods
This is a cross-sectional predictive machine learning algorithm-based study of Health Information National Trends datasets (Cycles 1 and 2; 2017-2018 samples). Survey respondents were U.S. adults (≥18 years old). The primary outcome was a binary variable indicating that the patient had or had not accessed online medical records in the previous 12 months. We analyzed a subset of independent variables using k-means clustering with replicate samples. A cross-validated random forest-based algorithm was utilized to select features for a Cycle 1 split training sample. A logistic regression and an evolved decision tree were trained on the rest of the Cycle 1 training sample. The Cycle 1 test sample and Cycle 2 data were used to benchmark algorithm performance.


Results
Lack of access to online systems was less of a barrier to online medical records in 2018 (14%) compared to 2017 (26%). Patients accessed medical records to refill medicines and message primary care providers more frequently in 2018 (45%) than in 2017 (25%).


Discussion
Privacy concerns, portal knowledge, and conversations between primary care providers and patients predict portal access.


Conclusion
Methods described here may be employed to personalize methods of patient engagement during new patient registration.

Title: Do Market Characteristics Matter? Factors Associated with Health Information Exchange
Snippet: Many economically developed countries have put great effort into implementing health information technology (IT) to reduce healthcare costs and improve quality of care [1,2]. Examples include the Health Information Technology for Economic and Clinical Health (HITECH) Act passed in the U.S., which provided USD 27 billion in incentive payments to encourage adoption of electronic health records over a 10-year period [1], and the U.K. government's 2018 announcement of an approximately USD 540 million investment in hospital information technology [2]. Although the U.S. Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology (2018) reported 96% of all non-federal acute care hospitals to possess a certified health IT system as of 2017 [3]; however, there exists a gap between health IT adoption and use, specifically with regard to information exchange among healthcare providers. Despite a high rate of health IT adoption, 32% of patients who visited a healthcare provider within the past 12 months reported having to repeat a procedure, provide their medical history again, or bring a test result to an appointment because of the unavailability of prior data [4]. The implication is that there exists many hospitals that have adopted health IT and do not successfully share electronic information among providers. 

Scholars, taking note of the importance of information exchange, have begun to focus on how information is incorporated and shared in healthcare settings [5]. A study comparing length of stay and readmission rates between instances of assimilation of electronic health records, measured as achievement of meaningful use and mere adoption, found patient outcomes to improve only in the former case [6]. Another study found that electronic mobilization of healthcare information across organizations could save as much as USD 1.9 million in emergency department settings annually [7]. These results commonly support the idea that it is the actual use of health IT, not mere adoption, that determines the extent of benefits, which a hospital gains from IT investment [8]. 

Increasing interest notwithstanding, little is known about what affects information exchange in the healthcare setting. Determinants of adoption have been widely studied [9][10][11][12][13], but information exchange has not. Exceptions, such as studies examining determinants of meaningful use [14,15], have been based on early stage of meaningful use that has not involved robust electronic health information exchange.

Title: Do Market Characteristics Matter? Factors Associated with Health Information Exchange
Snippet: We analyzed multiple years of national data to inform understanding of the use of health IT, specifically, information exchange, beyond mere adoption. Aided by detailed datasets rarely used previously, our study examines the relationship between select unexamined variables and breadth and depth of information exchange in healthcare settings. We found that hospital-level variables such as size, ownership type, system affiliation, physician-hospital arrangement, and revenue model affect information exchange, and that market-level variables such as concentration ratio, urbanness, and median household income, although they directly affect information exchange, do not moderate the relationship between hospital-level variables and information exchange. 

This paper enhances understanding of factors associated with information exchange via health IT and its implications for the sustainability of the healthcare system. Efforts in many countries to increase information exchange using health IT effectively have gained added importance during the present pandemic. Among the insights related to theory and policy yielded by our results is that hospital administrators and policymakers who seek to increase health IT-driven information exchange should focus on hospital-level determinants and not differentially formulate strategies according to market-level characteristics.

Title: Do Market Characteristics Matter? Factors Associated with Health Information Exchange
Snippet: Exceptions, such as studies examining determinants of meaningful use [14,15], have been based on early stage of meaningful use that has not involved robust electronic health information exchange. That only the final stage of meaningful use (termed "promoting interoperability" in fall 2018) includes electronic information exchange as a major requirement, and its reporting years are ongoing (2019-2021) [16], suggests that prior studies provide limited understanding of what affects the exchange of health information. Recently, scholars have started examining the factors associated with health information exchange, but they have either focused on a few individual relevant factors such as system membership or incentives [17][18][19] or on one aspect of information shared electronically, e.g., volume [20]. 

With the goal of providing a more comprehensive picture of drivers of health information exchange, the present study examines specific factors that affect information exchange among health IT systems. We investigate, based on findings reported in the prior literature about their effect on "mere adoption" of health IT [9][10][11][12], whether factors such as size, concentration, system affiliation, ownership type, teaching status, urbanness, etc. affect information exchange similarly or differently. Responding to the increasing importance of information exchange among healthcare providers, as detailed above, our study focuses on configuration strategies found to affect hospital performance [21], specifically, what affects the breadth (i.e., the extent to which patient health information is shared electronically among stakeholders) and depth (i.e., the level of detail at which patient health information is shared electronically) of information exchange among stakeholders. 

Using data sets from the American Hospital Association's (AHA's) annual and IT surveys, and the Census Bureau's small-area income and poverty estimates for the 2014-2016 period, we estimate the association of key factors with breadth and depth of information exchange and derive important policy implications from evaluations of previously studied determinants of health IT adoption. The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we describe our data and ex-ante predictions. Results are discussed in Section 3. We present our conclusions in Section 4.

Title: Do Market Characteristics Matter? Factors Associated with Health Information Exchange
Snippet: Our study makes a number of contributions. First, to the best of our knowledge, the current study is the first to investigate determinants of information exchange in the healthcare setting. Previous research has focused mostly on determinants of adoption, and in such studies of meaningful use as existing information exchange has only recently been added as a requirement [17][18][19][20]. Understanding of the determinants of information exchange has thus been limited. The results of our study should contribute to the realization of many of the benefits of health IT, including those associated with enhanced information exchange. 

Second, our study helps to provide a more comprehensive picture of drivers of health information exchange. Rather than merely focusing on the percentage of information shared electronically, the current study focused on the relevant factors associated with the breadth and depth of information shared. Moreover, our study examines one of the key hospital-level factors not previously studied: physician-hospital integration. Title: A telehealth application for adequate hospital visit advice by physicians affected users’ subsequent hospital visit behavior: a historical cohort study with machine learning
Snippet: The effectiveness of telehealth strategies toward support for adequate hospital visits is vital. We examined whether individuals who received advice from a physician via an online application subsequently visited hospitals. Further, we examined the background factors associated with their hospital visit behavior.We used machine learning to examine whether chief complaint, medical advice, and user background characteristics could be used to predict their subsequent hospital visit.Among 7,152 participants, those in their 30s were the most frequent users. The proportion of each medical advice was significantly different between the group that did and the one that did not follow physicians’ advice. We further performed supervised machine learning using random forest modeling to categorize those who (1) followed physicians’ advice or (2) did not follow physicians’ advice. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.677. Consequently, the aforementioned model soundly categorized whether users followed physicians’ advice. Chief complaint and medical advice were the most important variables to predict whether users followed the advice.The telehealth system to provide support for adequate hospital visits influenced patients’ subsequent hospital visit behavior. Patients’ chief complaint was the most important variable in discriminating whether users followed physicians’ advice.

Title: Developing a Machine Learning–Based Automated Patient Engagement Estimator for Telehealth: Algorithm Development and Validation Study
Snippet: Background Patient engagement is a critical but challenging public health priority in behavioral health care. During telehealth sessions, health care providers need to rely predominantly on verbal strategies rather than typical nonverbal cues to effectively engage patients. Hence, the typical patient engagement behaviors are now different, and health care provider training on telehealth patient engagement is unavailable or quite limited. Therefore, we explore the application of machine learning for estimating patient engagement. This can assist psychotherapists in the development of a therapeutic relationship with the patient and enhance patient engagement in the treatment of mental health conditions during tele–mental health sessions. Objective This study aimed to examine the ability of machine learning models to estimate patient engagement levels during a tele–mental health session and understand whether the machine learning approach could support therapeutic engagement between the client and psychotherapist. Methods We proposed a multimodal learning-based approach. We uniquely leveraged latent vectors corresponding to affective and cognitive features frequently used in psychology literature to understand a person’s level of engagement. Given the labeled data constraints that exist in health care, we explored a semisupervised learning solution. To support the development of similar technologies for telehealth, we also plan to release a dataset called Multimodal Engagement Detection in Clinical Analysis (MEDICA). This dataset includes 1229 video clips, each lasting 3 seconds. In addition, we present experiments conducted on this dataset, along with real-world tests that demonstrate the effectiveness of our method. Results Our algorithm reports a 40% improvement in root mean square error over state-of-the-art methods for engagement estimation. In our real-world tests on 438 video clips from psychotherapy sessions with 20 patients, in comparison to prior methods, positive correlations were observed between psychotherapists’ Working Alliance Inventory scores and our mean and median engagement level estimates. This indicates the potential of the proposed model to present patient engagement estimations that align well with the engagement measures used by psychotherapists. Conclusions Patient engagement has been identified as being important to improve therapeutic alliance. However, limited research has been conducted to measure this in a telehealth setting, where the therapist lacks conventional cues to make a confident assessment. The algorithm developed is an attempt to model person-oriented engagement modeling theories within machine learning frameworks to estimate the level

documents.snippet: The effectiveness of telehealth strategies toward support for adequate hospital visits is vital. We examined whether individuals who received advice from a physician via an online application subsequently visited hospitals. Further, we examined the background factors associated with their hospital visit behavior.We used machine learning to examine whether chief complaint, medical advice, and user background characteristics could be used to predict their subsequent hospital visit.Among 7,152 participants, those in their 30s were the most frequent users. The proportion of each medical advice was significantly different between the group that did and the one that did not follow physicians’ advice. We further performed supervised machine learning using random forest modeling to categorize those who (1) followed physicians’ advice or (2) did not follow physicians’ advice. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.677. Consequently, the aforementioned model soundly categorized whether users followed physicians’ advice. Chief complaint and medical advice were the most important variables to predict whether users followed the advice.The telehealth system to provide support for adequate hospital visits influenced patients’ subsequent hospital visit behavior. Patients’ chief complaint was the most important variable in discriminating whether users followed physicians’ advice.

documents.snippet: Background Patient engagement is a critical but challenging public health priority in behavioral health care. During telehealth sessions, health care providers need to rely predominantly on verbal strategies rather than typical nonverbal cues to effectively engage patients. Hence, the typical patient engagement behaviors are now different, and health care provider training on telehealth patient engagement is unavailable or quite limited. Therefore, we explore the application of machine learning for estimating patient engagement. This can assist psychotherapists in the development of a therapeutic relationship with the patient and enhance patient engagement in the treatment of mental health conditions during tele–mental health sessions. Objective This study aimed to examine the ability of machine learning models to estimate patient engagement levels during a tele–mental health session and understand whether the machine learning approach could support therapeutic engagement between the client and psychotherapist. Methods We proposed a multimodal learning-based approach. We uniquely leveraged latent vectors corresponding to affective and cognitive features frequently used in psychology literature to understand a person’s level of engagement. Given the labeled data constraints that exist in health care, we explored a semisupervised learning solution. To support the development of similar technologies for telehealth, we also plan to release a dataset called Multimodal Engagement Detection in Clinical Analysis (MEDICA). This dataset includes 1229 video clips, each lasting 3 seconds. In addition, we present experiments conducted on this dataset, along with real-world tests that demonstrate the effectiveness of our method. problem: what is mutual information and condition mutual information
final_response:
# Overview

Mutual information (MI) quantifies the amount of information that one random variable contains about another, or equivalently the reduction in uncertainty of one variable given knowledge of the other.<cite id="6d7c2dfe-1">Mutual information measures the amount of information one random variable contains about another.</cite> In continuous settings, MI can be defined via a Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence between the joint distribution and the product of marginals, or equivalently through entropies and conditional entropies.<cite id="c896a596-1">Mutual information between X and Y is the KL divergence between the joint distribution p(x,y) and the product p(x)p(y).</cite><cite id="c896a596-2">Mutual information can be written as H(X) − H(X|Y) = H(Y) − H(Y|X), and conditional mutual information as H(X|Z) − H(X|YZ).</cite> Conditional mutual information (CMI) extends this to the average information between two variables given a third, and is central to multivariate information theory and causal analysis.<cite id="23e122e0-0">Conditional mutual information is the average information in one variable about another given knowledge of a third and is used to compute transfer entropy and interaction information.</cite>

# Formal definitions

- Mutual information MI(X;Y): The KL divergence between the joint distribution and the product of marginals, with equivalent entropy expressions:
  - I(X;Y) = D_KL(P_{X,Y} || P_X ⊗ P_Y).<cite id="c896a596-1">Mutual information is the KL divergence between the joint and product distributions.</cite>
  - I(X;Y) = H(X) + H(Y) − H(X,Y) = H(X) − H(X|Y) = H(Y) − H(Y|X).<cite id="c896a596-2">Mutual information equals the difference of entropy and conditional entropy.</cite>

- Conditional mutual information CMI(X;Y|Z): The average additional information Y provides about X given Z, with equivalent forms:
  - I(X;Y|Z) = D_KL(P_{X,Y|Z} || P_{X|Z} ⊗ P_{Y|Z}).<cite id="c896a596-2">Conditional mutual information quantifies H(A|C) − H(A|BC) via conditional entropies and can be expressed as a KL between conditional distributions.</cite>
  - I(X;Y|Z) = H(X|Z) − H(X|Y,Z) = H(Y|Z) − H(Y|X,Z) = H(X) + H(Y|Z) − H(X,Y|Z).<cite id="c896a596-2">Conditional MI has symmetric entropy representations.</cite>

# Key properties and inequalities

- Nonnegativity and independence: I(X;Y) ≥ 0 with equality if and only if X and Y are independent; the same characterization holds for CMI: I(X;Y|Z)=0 iff X and Y are conditionally independent given Z.<cite id="6d7c2dfe-1">Non-negativity of mutual information with equality iff variables are independent.</cite><cite id="6d7c2dfe-3">Conditional mutual information is symmetric and non-negative, with definitions in terms of conditional entropies.</cite>

- Symmetry: MI is symmetric, I(X;Y)=I(Y;X).<cite id="6d7c2dfe-1">Symmetry of mutual information follows from the symmetric joint and marginals.</cite><cite id="6d7c2dfe-4">Mutual information is symmetric and non-negative.</cite>

- Chain rule and factorization: MI admits a chain rule that extends to multiple variables and underpins decompositions and proofs in information theory.<cite id="6d7c2dfe-1">Chain rule: I(X;Y|Z)=H(X|Z)−H(X|Y,Z) and generalizes to multiple variables.</cite><cite id="6d7c2dfe-4">Chain rule decomposes mutual information among multiple variables.</cite>

- Data processing inequality: If X → Y → Z form a Markov chain (X independent of Z given Y), then I(X;Z) ≤ I(X;Y), so no post-processing of Y can reveal more information about X than Y itself contains.<cite id="6d7c2dfe-1">Data processing inequality: for a Markov chain X→Y→Z, I(X;Z) ≤ I(X;Y).</cite><cite id="6d7c2dfe-2">The data processing inequality follows from nonnegativity and chain rule.</cite><cite id="6d7c2dfe-3">Data-processing inequality ensures post-processing does not increase information about X.</cite>

# Estimation in practice

Discrete variables:
- In low dimensions, MI/CMI can be estimated by direct histogramming of P_{X,Y}, P_X, P_Y and plugging into entropy/mutual information formulas; unbiasedness requires careful binning and large samples.<cite id="c896a596-3">Mutual information can be related to KL divergence and bounded via Pinsker’s inequality, which underpins estimation strategies and error control.</cite>

Continuous variables and high dimensions:
- Nonparametric k-nearest-neighbor (k-NN) estimators (KSG/Kraskov) avoid explicit discretization by using local volume estimates from neighbor distances. For MI, the KSG estimator computes a data-dependent k and counts neighbors within a joint-space radius to derive an entropy-based MI estimate; the same idea extends to CMI by conditioning on Z via joint and marginal k-NN counts.<cite id="fb0cb8e1-0">The KSG mutual information estimator uses neighbor counts and digamma terms; conditional mutual information can be computed by applying the KSG estimator to (X,[Y,Z]) and (X,Z).</cite><cite id="fb0cb8e1-2">Kraskov’s estimator counts points within a k-th neighbor-determined radius along joint and marginal axes to estimate MI directly from point clouds without binning.</cite>

Properties and caveats of k-NN estimators:
- KSG is widely used for continuous MI, combining entropy estimation with a data-driven k; it can be written in terms of the Kozachenko–Leonenko (KL) entropy estimator, but has noted biases in certain regimes (e.g., strong dependence and boundary bias) and only weak asymptotic consistency under strong conditions.<cite id="fb0cb8e1-3">The KSG estimator expands MI into a sum estimated via the KL entropy estimator with a data-dependent k; despite widespread use, there are negative results for strongly dependent variables and boundary bias, with only limited asymptotic guarantees.</cite><cite id="23e122e0-1">KSG-based estimators depend only on distances and mitigate the curse of dimensionality, with analytically characterized bias and empirical success in simulations.</cite>

Conditional MI estimation:
- Conditional MI I(X;Y|Z) can be estimated by adapting k-NN to conditional distributions (e.g., counting neighbors in joint (X,Y) and (X,Z) while conditioning on Z) or by sampling “negative” conditionals to form a tractable contrastive estimator.<cite id="23e122e0-0">Conditional MI can be estimated using Kozachenko–Leonenko–based nearest-neighbor methods, with extensions to transfer entropy and interaction information.</cite><cite id="23e122e0-4">A conditional-noise-contrastive estimation (CNCE) functional provides a tractable estimator for I(X;Y|Z) by sampling from P(X|Z) and P(X,Y|Z), with theoretical properties including convergence as the number of negative samples grows.</cite>

# Applications and uses

- Independence testing and model selection: MI vanishes if and only if variables are independent; CMI vanishes if and only if two variables are conditionally independent given a third, enabling conditional independence tests used in graphical model inference and causal discovery workflows.<cite id="6d7c2dfe-1">Mutual information is nonnegative with equality iff variables are independent, enabling independence tests.</cite><cite id="23e122e0-0">Conditional mutual information underlies transfer entropy and interaction information, enabling causality and multivariate dependence analysis.</cite><cite id="23e122e0-2">CMI is a primitive in conditional independence testing, graphical model inference, causal strength estimation, and time-series problems, with k-NN-based estimators and importance sampling provided.</cite>

- Causality and directed interactions: Transfer entropy T(Y→X) = I(X;Y|父母集) measures the directed information from Y to X using conditional MI, offering a model-free causal measure complementary to Granger causality.<cite id="23e122e0-0">Transfer entropy is built from conditional mutual information to measure causality in time series in a model-free way.</cite>

- Multivariate information and redundancy/unique/shared information: CMI and generalized k-NN estimators support higher-order decompositions such as partial information decomposition and related measures (total correlation, O-information) without discretization.<cite id="23e122e0-2">K-NN estimators for CMI and variants enable multivariate information measures and dynamical system inference.</cite><cite id="fb0cb8e1-2">Kraskov-style estimators support generalizations like total correlation and O-information directly from point clouds.</cite>

- Out-of-distribution detection and representation evaluation: MI/CMI are used to assess dependence and redundancy between representations and labels or between domains, with practical implementations for conditional MI like CNCE.<cite id="23e122e0-4">Conditional mutual information appears in representation learning, with CNCE-based estimators providing tractable approximations and convergence guarantees as negative samples grow.</cite><cite id="6d7c2dfe-0">Expansions of MI via chain rule and conditional independence arguments underpin data processing and independence-based analyses in domain adaptation contexts.</cite>

# Practical guidance and limitations

- Scale and normalization: MI is unbounded and depends on variable scales and supports; normalized variants are often used for comparability across datasets or tasks.<cite id="6d7c2dfe-1">Mutual information is unbounded and scale-dependent, motivating normalized mutual information for comparisons.</cite>

- Dimensionality and sample complexity: Model-free estimation of MI/CMI suffers from the curse of dimensionality; k-NN methods alleviate this by relying on distances and nearest-neighbor structure, but require large samples for accuracy and exhibit bias depending on bandwidth k and distribution tails.<cite id="23e122e0-1">Kozachenko–Leonenko–based nearest-neighbor estimators depend only on distances and mitigate dimensionality, with analytically characterized bias and demonstrated performance on simulated data.</cite><cite id="fb0cb8e1-3">Theoretical analysis highlights limitations and biases of the KSG estimator for certain distributions and dependencies, despite its practical success.</cite>

- Choosing estimators: For discrete data in low dimensions, histogram-based entropy estimates are feasible; for continuous or high-dimensional data, prefer k-NN (KSG) or conditional-neighbor methods; for conditional settings, adapt joint/marginal neighbor counts or use contrastive sampling schemes like CNCE.<cite id="fb0cb8e1-0">KSG provides a practical formula via neighbor counts and digamma terms, with conditional MI obtained by applying the estimator to (X,[Y,Z]) and (X,Z).</cite><cite id="23e122e0-4">CNCE provides a tractable conditional MI estimator via positive/negative sampling with convergence properties as negative samples grow.</cite>

# Intuition and interpretation

- MI as shared information: MI equals the reduction in uncertainty of X upon observing Y (or vice versa), and can be interpreted as the “shared information” between variables beyond their individual entropies.<cite id="c896a596-2">Mutual information H(X) − H(X|Y) quantifies the reduction in uncertainty of X given Y.</cite><cite id="6d7c2dfe-1">Equivalently, MI is the amount of information Y contains about X, with nonnegativity and zero iff independence.</cite>

- CMI as conditional dependence: CMI measures how much X and Y still convey about each other after conditioning out Z, and is central to decomposing mechanisms in multivariate systems and to directed measures like transfer entropy.<cite id="c896a596-2">Conditional mutual information H(X|Z) − H(X|YZ) quantifies dependence after conditioning on Z.</cite><cite id="23e122e0-0">CMI is used to compute transfer entropy, a model-free causal measure, and interaction information for higher-order dependence.</cite>

# Summary

- Mutual information I(X;Y) = D_KL(P_{X,Y} || P_X P_Y) = H(X) − H(X|Y) quantifies shared information and equals zero iff X and Y are independent; it is symmetric and nonnegative, obeys a chain rule, and satisfies the data processing inequality.<cite id="c896a596-1">Mutual information is defined as KL between joint and product marginals.</cite><cite id="6d7c2dfe-1">MI is nonnegative with equality iff independent, is symmetric, obeys chain rule and data processing inequality.</cite>

- Conditional mutual information I(X;Y|Z) = D_KL(P_{X,Y|Z} || P_{X|Z} P_{Y|Z}) = H(X|Z) − H(X|YZ) quantifies dependence after conditioning and vanishes iff X and Y are conditionally independent given Z; it supports directed and multivariate analyses via transfer entropy and interaction information.<cite id="c896a596-2">Conditional MI has entropy and KL forms and reduces to zero under conditional independence.</cite><cite id="23e122e0-0">CMI underlies transfer entropy and interaction information for causality and higher-order interactions.</cite>

- Estimation: Discrete MI/CMI by entropy difference; continuous MI/CMI via k-NN (KSG) or contrastive sampling for conditioning; k-NN methods are widely used but can exhibit bias and require careful choice of k and sufficient samples.<cite id="fb0cb8e1-0">KSG uses neighbor counts and a data-driven k to estimate MI and can be adapted to conditional MI.</cite><cite id="fb0cb8e1-3">KSG is practical but has known biases and limited asymptotic guarantees in certain regimes.</cite><cite id="23e122e0-4">CNCE provides a tractable conditional MI estimator with theoretical properties and practical scalability.</cite>

Title: Nearest-Neighbours Estimators for Conditional Mutual Information
Snippet: The mutual information is a fundamental and common approach to assessing the relationship between random variables. It calculates the amount of information the value of one random variable contains, on average, about the value of another. The conditional mutual information is a natural extension of this, it is the average information in one variable about another, given knowledge of a third. 

The conditional mutual information has many applications. In particular it is used to calculate the transfer entropy [1,2]; the transfer entropy is a powerful approach to measuring causality which extends in a model-free manner the insight provided by the autoregressive formulation of commonly-used Granger causality [3]. Conditional mutual information is also used to calculate the interaction information, the natural generalization of mutual information to more than two random variables [4,5]. 

Mutual information is often difficult to calculate in a model-free way: there is typically a huge data requirement when estimating it and it suffers from the curse of dimensionality, with the data required increasing rapidly as the dimension increases. This often renders conditional mutual information and transfer entropy impractical for problems involving the sort of multidimensional variables typically encountered in scientific applications and in data science and machine learning. In [6,7] a Kozachenko-Leonenko (KL) [8,9] estimator is presented, this gives a metric-based method for estimating mutual information. Since it uses only the distance between data points it wards off the curse of dimensionality. Here, this metricspace KL approach is extended to estimating conditional mutual information. 

This gives a formula for mutual information similar in spirit to the one derived in [9]. They are both nearest neighbour formulae derived using the KL estimator. The estimator described in [9] has been adapted to conditional mutual information [10,11] and transfer entropy [12]; here these are referred to as the 'KSG' estimators. The novel estimator that is introduced here is referred to as the 'new' estimator. 

There are two significant differences between the KSG and new estimators; the first is that the derivation of the new estimator relies only on metric space properties of the data.
</snippet>
<snippet id=23e122e0-1>
Title: Nearest-Neighbours Estimators for Conditional Mutual Information
Snippet: The conditional mutual information quantifies the conditional dependence of two random variables. It has numerous applications; it forms, for example, part of the definition of transfer entropy, a common measure of the causal relationship between time series. It does, however, require a lot of data to estimate accurately and suffers the curse of dimensionality, limiting its application in machine learning and data science. However, the Kozachenko-Leonenko approach can address this problem: it is possible, in this approach to define a nearest-neighbour estimator which depends only on the distance between data points and not on the dimension of the data. Furthermore, the bias can be calculated analytically for this estimator. Here this estimator is described and is tested on simulated data.
</snippet>
<snippet id=23e122e0-2>
Title: Potential conditional mutual information: Estimators and properties
Snippet: The conditional mutual information I(X;Y|Z) measures the average information that X and Y contain about each other given Z. This is an important primitive in many learning problems including conditional independence testing, graphical model inference, causal strength estimation and time-series problems. In several applications, it is desirable to have a functional purely of the conditional distribution p_{Y|X,Z} rather than of the joint distribution p_{X,Y,Z}. We define the potential conditional mutual information as the conditional mutual information calculated with a modified joint distribution p_{Y|X,Z} q_{X,Z}, where q_{X,Z} is a potential distribution, fixed airport. We develop K nearest neighbor based estimators for this functional, employing importance sampling, and a coupling trick, and prove the finite k consistency of such an estimator. We demonstrate that the estimator has excellent practical performance and show an application in dynamical system inference.
</snippet>

Snippet: Typically, information-theoretic measures are computed on discrete probability distributions, where variables can take on a finite number of mutually-exclusive states. For continuous random variables, Shannon defined the differential entropy: 

and from this, continuous analogs of all previously introduced measures can be constructed. 

Unlike discrete probability distributions, however, the problem of estimating P(x) from data is more involved. If one can assume that the data is multivariate-normal, Gaussian estimators exist and are popular in neuroscience, particularly when using fMRI signals (e.g. [9,37]). However, for continuous, real-valued data that doesn't satisfy parametric assumptions, a comparatively novel class of estimators based on K-nearest neighbors graphs have been developed. 

A detailed formal treatment is beyond the scope of this manuscript, but the fundamental intuitions are reasonably straightforward. Imagine sampling points from some (potentially highdimensional) probability manifold with non-trivial structure. Sampled points will, necessarily, cluster more in the high-probability regions, while points in low-probability regions will be more isolated. The distance from a given point to its k th nearest neighbor can then be used to estimate probabilities. The longer the distance, the lower the local probability in that region. This forms the basis of the Kozachenko-Leonenko non-parametric entropy estimator [38,39], and subsequent

For each point, a diameter is defined by the distance from that point to it's fourth nearest neighbor. The estimator then counts the number of points within the diameter projected down to the constituent axes, and from that computes the local (pointwise) mutual information [36]. The expected value over all the pointwise values gives the estimated mutual information.

Snippet: KSG mutual information estimator, which is based on the distances of each sample to its k-th nearest neighbor, is widely used to estimate mutual information between two continuous random variables. Existing work has analyzed the convergence speed of this estimator for random variables with bounded support. In practice, however, KSG estimator also performs well for a much broader class of distributions, including not only those with bounded support but also those with long tail distributions. In this paper, we analyze the convergence speed of the error of KSG estimator for smooth distributions, whose support can be both bounded and unbounded. As KSG mutual information estimator can be viewed as an adaptive combination of KL entropy estimators, in our analysis, we also provide convergence analysis of KL entropy estimator for a broad class of distributions.

Snippet: In general contexts, only weak consistency of the KL estimator is known (Kozachenko & Leonenko, 1987). Biau & Devroye (2015) recently reviewed finite-sample results known for the KL estimator, including bounds on the bias and variance, under very restrictive conditions (i.e., β-Hölder continuous (β ∈ (0, 1]) densities bounded away from 0 on the interval [0, 1]). Our results generalize these results substantially, weakening the boundedness assumptions to tail conditions, and considering the multidimensional case and more smoothness classes. 

The KL estimator is also important for its role in the mutual information estimator proposed by Kraskov et al. (2004), which we refer to as the KSG estimator. The KSG estimator expands the mutual information as a sum of entropies, which it estimates via the KL estimator with a particular random (i.e., data-dependent) choice of the nearestneighbor parameter k. The KSG estimator is perhaps the most widely used estimator for the mutual information between continuous random variables, despite the fact that it currently appears to have no theoretical guarantees, even asymptotically. In fact, one of the few theoretical results, due to Gao et al. (2015b), concerning the KSG estimator is a negative result: when estimating the mutual information between strongly dependent variables, the KSG estimator tends to systematically underestimate mutual information, due to increased boundary bias. 3 Nevertheless, the widespread use of the KSG estimator motivates study of its behavior. We hope that our analysis of the KL estimator, in terms of which the KSG estimator can be written, will lead to a better understanding of the latter.

# Overview

Mutual information (MI) quantifies the amount of information that one random variable contains about another, or equivalently the reduction in uncertainty of one variable given knowledge of the other.<cite id="6d7c2dfe-1">Mutual information measures the amount of information one random variable contains about another.</cite> In continuous settings, MI can be defined via a Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence between the joint distribution and the product of marginals, or equivalently through entropies and conditional entropies.<cite id="c896a596-1">Mutual information between X and Y is the KL divergence between the joint distribution p(x,y) and the product p(x)p(y).</cite><cite id="c896a596-2">Mutual information can be written as H(X) − H(X|Y) = H(Y) − H(Y|X), and conditional mutual information as H(X|Z) − H(X|YZ).</cite> Conditional mutual information (CMI) extends this to the average information between two variables given a third, and is central to multivariate information theory and causal analysis.<cite id="23e122e0-0">Conditional mutual information is the average information in one variable about another given knowledge of a third and is used to compute transfer entropy and interaction information.</cite>

# Formal definitions

- Mutual information MI(X;Y): The KL divergence between the joint distribution and the product of marginals, with equivalent entropy expressions:
  - I(X;Y) = D_KL(P_{X,Y} || P_X ⊗ P_Y).<cite id="c896a596-1">Mutual information is the KL divergence between the joint and product distributions.</cite>
  - I(X;Y) = H(X) + H(Y) − H(X,Y) = H(X) − H(X|Y) = H(Y) − H(Y|X).<cite id="c896a596-2">Mutual information equals the difference of entropy and conditional entropy.</cite>

- Conditional mutual information CMI(X;Y|Z): The average additional information Y provides about X given Z, with equivalent forms:
  - I(X;Y|Z) = D_KL(P_{X,Y|Z} || P_{X|Z} ⊗ P_{Y|Z}).<cite id="c896a596-2">Conditional mutual information quantifies H(A|C) − H(A|BC) via conditional entropies and can be expressed as a KL between conditional distributions.</cite>
  - I(X;Y|Z) = H(X|Z) − H(X|Y,Z) = H(Y|Z) − H(Y|X,Z) = H(X) + H(Y|Z) − H(X,Y|Z).<cite id="c896a596-2">Conditional MI has symmetric entropy representations.</cite>

# Key properties and inequalities

- Nonnegativity and independence: I(X;Y) ≥ 0 with equality if and only if X and Y are independent; the same characterization holds for CMI: I(X;Y|Z)=0 iff X and Y are conditionally independent given Z.<cite id="6d7c2dfe-1">Non-negativity of mutual information with equality iff variables are independent.</cite><cite id="6d7c2dfe-3">Conditional mutual information is symmetric and non-negative, with definitions in terms of conditional entropies.</cite>

- Symmetry: MI is symmetric, I(X;Y)=I(Y;X).<cite id="6d7c2dfe-1">Symmetry of mutual information follows from the symmetric joint and marginals.</cite><cite id="6d7c2dfe-4">Mutual information is symmetric and non-negative.</cite>

- Chain rule and factorization: MI admits a chain rule that extends to multiple variables and underpins decompositions and proofs in information theory.<cite id="6d7c2dfe-1">Chain rule: I(X;Y|Z)=H(X|Z)−H(X|Y,Z) and generalizes to multiple variables.</cite><cite id="6d7c2dfe-4">Chain rule decomposes mutual information among multiple variables.</cite>

- Data processing inequality: If X → Y → Z form a Markov chain (X independent of Z given Y), then I(X;Z) ≤ I(X;Y), so no post-processing of Y can reveal more information about X than Y itself contains.<cite id="6d7c2dfe-1">Data processing inequality: for a Markov chain X→Y→Z, I(X;Z) ≤ I(X;Y).</cite><cite id="6d7c2dfe-2">The data processing inequality follows from nonnegativity and chain rule.</cite><cite id="6d7c2dfe-3">Data-processing inequality ensures post-processing does not increase information about X.</cite>

# Estimation in practice

Discrete variables:
- In low dimensions, MI/CMI can be estimated by direct histogramming of P_{X,Y}, P_X, P_Y and plugging into entropy/mutual information formulas; unbiasedness requires careful binning and large samples.<cite id="c896a596-3">Mutual information can be related to KL divergence and bounded via Pinsker’s inequality, which underpins estimation strategies and error control.</cite>

Continuous variables and high dimensions:
- Nonparametric k-nearest-neighbor (k-NN) estimators (KSG/Kraskov) avoid explicit discretization by using local volume estimates from neighbor distances. For MI, the KSG estimator computes a data-dependent k and counts neighbors within a joint-space radius to derive an entropy-based MI estimate; the same idea extends to CMI by conditioning on Z via joint and marginal k-NN counts.<cite id="fb0cb8e1-0">The KSG mutual information estimator uses neighbor counts and digamma terms; conditional mutual information can be computed by applying the KSG estimator to (X,[Y,Z]) and (X,Z).</cite><cite id="fb0cb8e1-2">Kraskov’s estimator counts points within a k-th neighbor-determined radius along joint and marginal axes to estimate MI directly from point clouds without binning.</cite>

Properties and caveats of k-NN estimators:
- KSG is widely used for continuous MI, combining entropy estimation with a data-driven k; it can be written in terms of the Kozachenko–Leonenko (KL) entropy estimator, but has noted biases in certain regimes (e.g., strong dependence and boundary bias) and only weak asymptotic consistency under strong conditions.<cite id="fb0cb8e1-3">The KSG estimator expands MI into a sum estimated via the KL entropy estimator with a data-dependent k; despite widespread use, there are negative results for strongly dependent variables and boundary bias, with only limited asymptotic guarantees.</cite><cite id="23e122e0-1">KSG-based estimators depend only on distances and mitigate the curse of dimensionality, with analytically characterized bias and empirical success in simulations.</cite>

Conditional MI estimation:
- Conditional MI I(X;Y|Z) can be estimated by adapting k-NN to conditional distributions (e.g., counting neighbors in joint (X,Y) and (X,Z) while conditioning on Z) or by sampling “negative” conditionals to form a tractable contrastive estimator.<cite id="23e122e0-0">Conditional MI can be estimated using Kozachenko–Leonenko–based nearest-neighbor methods, with extensions to transfer entropy and interaction information.</cite><cite id="23e122e0-4">A conditional-noise-contrastive estimation (CNCE) functional provides a tractable estimator for I(X;Y|Z) by sampling from P(X|Z) and P(X,Y|Z), with theoretical properties including convergence as the number of negative samples grows.</cite>

# Applications and uses

- Independence testing and model selection: MI vanishes if and only if variables are independent; CMI vanishes if and only if two variables are conditionally independent given a third, enabling conditional independence tests used in graphical model inference and causal discovery workflows.<cite id="6d7c2dfe-1">Mutual information is nonnegative with equality iff variables are independent, enabling independence tests.</cite><cite id="23e122e0-0">Conditional mutual information underlies transfer entropy and interaction information, enabling causality and multivariate dependence analysis.</cite><cite id="23e122e0-2">CMI is a primitive in conditional independence testing, graphical model inference, causal strength estimation, and time-series problems, with k-NN-based estimators and importance sampling provided.</cite>

- Causality and directed interactions: Transfer entropy T(Y→X) = I(X;Y|父母集) measures the directed information from Y to X using conditional MI, offering a model-free causal measure complementary to Granger causality.<cite id="23e122e0-0">Transfer entropy is built from conditional mutual information to measure causality in time series in a model-free way.</cite>

- Multivariate information and redundancy/unique/shared information: CMI and generalized k-NN estimators support higher-order decompositions such as partial information decomposition and related measures (total correlation, O-information) without discretization.<cite id="23e122e0-2">K-NN estimators for CMI and variants enable multivariate information measures and dynamical system inference.</cite><cite id="fb0cb8e1-2">Kraskov-style estimators support generalizations like total correlation and O-information directly from point clouds.</cite>

- Out-of-distribution detection and representation evaluation: MI/CMI are used to assess dependence and redundancy between representations and labels or between domains, with practical implementations for conditional MI like CNCE.<cite id="23e122e0-4">Conditional mutual information appears in representation learning, with CNCE-based estimators providing tractable approximations and convergence guarantees as negative samples grow.</cite><cite id="6d7c2dfe-0">Expansions of MI via chain rule and conditional independence arguments underpin data processing and independence-based analyses in domain adaptation contexts.</cite>

# Practical guidance and limitations

- Scale and normalization: MI is unbounded and depends on variable scales and supports; normalized variants are often used for comparability across datasets or tasks.<cite id="6d7c2dfe-1">Mutual information is unbounded and scale-dependent, motivating normalized mutual information for comparisons.</cite>

- Dimensionality and sample complexity: Model-free estimation of MI/CMI suffers from the curse of dimensionality; k-NN methods alleviate this by relying on distances and nearest-neighbor structure, but require large samples for accuracy and exhibit bias depending on bandwidth k and distribution tails.<cite id="23e122e0-1">Kozachenko–Leonenko–based nearest-neighbor estimators depend only on distances and mitigate dimensionality, with analytically characterized bias and demonstrated performance on simulated data.</cite><cite id="fb0cb8e1-3">Theoretical analysis highlights limitations and biases of the KSG estimator for certain distributions and dependencies, despite its practical success.</cite>

- Choosing estimators: For discrete data in low dimensions, histogram-based entropy estimates are feasible; for continuous or high-dimensional data, prefer k-NN (KSG) or conditional-neighbor methods; for conditional settings, adapt joint/marginal neighbor counts or use contrastive sampling schemes like CNCE.<cite id="fb0cb8e1-0">KSG provides a practical formula via neighbor counts and digamma terms, with conditional MI obtained by applying the estimator to (X,[Y,Z]) and (X,Z).</cite><cite id="23e122e0-4">CNCE provides a tractable conditional MI estimator via positive/negative sampling with convergence properties as negative samples grow.</cite>

# Intuition and interpretation

- MI as shared information: MI equals the reduction in uncertainty of X upon observing Y (or vice versa), and can be interpreted as the “shared information” between variables beyond their individual entropies.<cite id="c896a596-2">Mutual information H(X) − H(X|Y) quantifies the reduction in uncertainty of X given Y.</cite><cite id="6d7c2dfe-1">Equivalently, MI is the amount of information Y contains about X, with nonnegativity and zero iff independence.</cite>

- CMI as conditional dependence: CMI measures how much X and Y still convey about each other after conditioning out Z, and is central to decomposing mechanisms in multivariate systems and to directed measures like transfer entropy.<cite id="c896a596-2">Conditional mutual information H(X|Z) − H(X|YZ) quantifies dependence after conditioning on Z.</cite><cite id="23e122e0-0">CMI is used to compute transfer entropy, a model-free causal measure, and interaction information for higher-order dependence.</cite>

# Summary

- Mutual information I(X;Y) = D_KL(P_{X,Y} || P_X P_Y) = H(X) − H(X|Y) quantifies shared information and equals zero iff X and Y are independent; it is symmetric and nonnegative, obeys a chain rule, and satisfies the data processing inequality.<cite id="c896a596-1">Mutual information is defined as KL between joint and product marginals.</cite><cite id="6d7c2dfe-1">MI is nonnegative with equality iff independent, is symmetric, obeys chain rule and data processing inequality.</cite>

- Conditional mutual information I(X;Y|Z) = D_KL(P_{X,Y|Z} || P_{X|Z} P_{Y|Z}) = H(X|Z) − H(X|YZ) quantifies dependence after conditioning and vanishes iff X and Y are conditionally independent given Z; it supports directed and multivariate analyses via transfer entropy and interaction information.<cite id="c896a596-2">Conditional MI has entropy and KL forms and reduces to zero under conditional independence.</cite><cite id="23e122e0-0">CMI underlies transfer entropy and interaction information for causality and higher-order interactions.</cite>

- Estimation: Discrete MI/CMI by entropy difference; continuous MI/CMI via k-NN (KSG) or contrastive sampling for conditioning; k-NN methods are widely used but can exhibit bias and require careful choice of k and sufficient samples.<cite id="fb0cb8e1-0">KSG uses neighbor counts and a data-driven k to estimate MI and can be adapted to conditional MI.</cite><cite id="fb0cb8e1-3">KSG is practical but has known biases and limited asymptotic guarantees in certain regimes.</cite><cite id="23e122e0-4">CNCE provides a tractable conditional MI estimator with theoretical properties and practical scalability.</cite>
