Title: Nearest-Neighbours Estimators for Conditional Mutual Information
Snippet: The mutual information is a fundamental and common approach to assessing the relationship between random variables. It calculates the amount of information the value of one random variable contains, on average, about the value of another. The conditional mutual information is a natural extension of this, it is the average information in one variable about another, given knowledge of a third. 

The conditional mutual information has many applications. In particular it is used to calculate the transfer entropy [1,2]; the transfer entropy is a powerful approach to measuring causality which extends in a model-free manner the insight provided by the autoregressive formulation of commonly-used Granger causality [3]. Conditional mutual information is also used to calculate the interaction information, the natural generalization of mutual information to more than two random variables [4,5]. 

Mutual information is often difficult to calculate in a model-free way: there is typically a huge data requirement when estimating it and it suffers from the curse of dimensionality, with the data required increasing rapidly as the dimension increases. This often renders conditional mutual information and transfer entropy impractical for problems involving the sort of multidimensional variables typically encountered in scientific applications and in data science and machine learning. In [6,7] a Kozachenko-Leonenko (KL) [8,9] estimator is presented, this gives a metric-based method for estimating mutual information. Since it uses only the distance between data points it wards off the curse of dimensionality. Here, this metricspace KL approach is extended to estimating conditional mutual information. 

This gives a formula for mutual information similar in spirit to the one derived in [9]. They are both nearest neighbour formulae derived using the KL estimator. The estimator described in [9] has been adapted to conditional mutual information [10,11] and transfer entropy [12]; here these are referred to as the 'KSG' estimators. The novel estimator that is introduced here is referred to as the 'new' estimator. 

There are two significant differences between the KSG and new estimators; the first is that the derivation of the new estimator relies only on metric space properties of the data.

Title: Nearest-Neighbours Estimators for Conditional Mutual Information
Snippet: The conditional mutual information quantifies the conditional dependence of two random variables. It has numerous applications; it forms, for example, part of the definition of transfer entropy, a common measure of the causal relationship between time series. It does, however, require a lot of data to estimate accurately and suffers the curse of dimensionality, limiting its application in machine learning and data science. However, the Kozachenko-Leonenko approach can address this problem: it is possible, in this approach to define a nearest-neighbour estimator which depends only on the distance between data points and not on the dimension of the data. Furthermore, the bias can be calculated analytically for this estimator. Here this estimator is described and is tested on simulated data.

Title: Potential conditional mutual information: Estimators and properties
Snippet: The conditional mutual information I(X;Y|Z) measures the average information that X and Y contain about each other given Z. This is an important primitive in many learning problems including conditional independence testing, graphical model inference, causal strength estimation and time-series problems. In several applications, it is desirable to have a functional purely of the conditional distribution p_{Y|X,Z} rather than of the joint distribution p_{X,Y,Z}. We define the potential conditional mutual information as the conditional mutual information calculated with a modified joint distribution p_{Y|X,Z} q_{X,Z}, where q_{X,Z} is a potential distribution, fixed airport. We develop K nearest neighbor based estimators for this functional, employing importance sampling, and a coupling trick, and prove the finite k consistency of such an estimator. We demonstrate that the estimator has excellent practical performance and show an application in dynamical system inference.

Title: The topology of synergy: Linking topological and information-theoretic approaches to higher-order interactions in complex systems

Unlike discrete probability distributions, however, the problem of estimating P(x) from data is more involved. If one can assume that the data is multivariate-normal, Gaussian estimators exist and are popular in neuroscience, particularly when using fMRI signals (e.g. [9,37]). However, for continuous, real-valued data that doesn't satisfy parametric assumptions, a comparatively novel class of estimators based on K-nearest neighbors graphs have been developed.

documents.title: Nearest-Neighbours Estimators for Conditional Mutual Information
documents.snippet:
The mutual information is a fundamental and common approach to assessing the relationship between random variables. It calculates the amount of information the value of one random variable contains, on average, about the value of another. The conditional mutual information is a natural extension of this, it is the average information in one variable about another, given knowledge of a third. 

The conditional mutual information has many applications. In particular it is used to calculate the transfer entropy [1,2]; the transfer entropy is a powerful approach to measuring causality which extends in a model-free manner the insight provided by the autoregressive formulation of commonly-used Granger causality [3]. Conditional mutual information is also used to calculate the interaction information, the natural generalization of mutual information to more than two random variables [4,5]. 

Mutual information is often difficult to calculate in a model-free way: there is typically a huge data requirement when estimating it and it suffers from the curse of dimensionality, with the data required increasing rapidly as the dimension increases. This often renders conditional mutual information and transfer entropy impractical for problems involving the sort of multidimensional variables typically encountered in scientific applications and in data science and machine learning. In [6,7] a Kozachenko-Leonenko (KL) [8,9] estimator is presented, this gives a metric-based method for estimating mutual information. Since it uses only the distance between data points it wards off the curse of dimensionality. Here, this metricspace KL approach is extended to estimating conditional mutual information. 

This gives a formula for mutual information similar in spirit to the one derived in [9]. They are both nearest neighbour formulae derived using the KL estimator. The estimator described in [9] has been adapted to conditional mutual information [10,11] and transfer entropy [12]; here these are referred to as the 'KSG' estimators. The novel estimator that is introduced here is referred to as the 'new' estimator. 

There are two significant differences between the KSG and new estimators; the first is that the derivation of the new estimator relies only on metric space properties of the data.

documents.title: Nearest-Neighbours Estimators for Conditional Mutual Information
documents.snippet: The conditional mutual information quantifies the conditional dependence of two random variables. It has numerous applications; it forms, for example, part of the definition of transfer entropy, a common measure of the causal relationship between time series. It does, however, require a lot of data to estimate accurately and suffers the curse of dimensionality, limiting its application in machine learning and data science. However, the Kozachenko-Leonenko approach can address this problem: it is possible, in this approach to define a nearest-neighbour estimator which depends only on the distance between data points and not on the dimension of the data. Furthermore, the bias can be calculated analytically for this estimator. Here this estimator is described and is tested on simulated data.

documents.title: Potential conditional mutual information: Estimators and properties
documents.snippet: The conditional mutual information I(X;Y|Z) measures the average information that X and Y contain about each other given Z. This is an important primitive in many learning problems including conditional independence testing, graphical model inference, causal strength estimation and time-series problems. In several applications, it is desirable to have a functional purely of the conditional distribution p_{Y|X,Z} rather than of the joint distribution p_{X,Y,Z}. We define the potential conditional mutual information as the conditional mutual information calculated with a modified joint distribution p_{Y|X,Z} q_{X,Z}, where q_{X,Z} is a potential distribution, fixed airport. We develop K nearest neighbor based estimators for this functional, employing importance sampling, and a coupling trick, and prove the finite k consistency of such an estimator. We demonstrate that the estimator has excellent practical performance and show an application in dynamical system inference.

documents.title: The topology of synergy: Linking topological and information-theoretic approaches to higher-order interactions in complex systems
documents.snippet:
Typically, information-theoretic measures are computed on discrete probability distributions, where variables can take on a finite number of mutually-exclusive states. For continuous random variables, Shannon defined the differential entropy: 

and from this, continuous analogs of all previously introduced measures can be constructed. 

Unlike discrete probability distributions, however, the problem of estimating P(x) from data is more involved. If one can assume that the data is multivariate-normal, Gaussian estimators exist and are popular in neuroscience, particularly when using fMRI signals (e.g. [9,37]). However, for continuous, real-valued data that doesn't satisfy parametric assumptions, a comparatively novel class of estimators based on K-nearest neighbors graphs have been developed. 

A detailed formal treatment is beyond the scope of this manuscript, but the fundamental intuitions are reasonably straightforward. Imagine sampling points from some (potentially highdimensional) probability manifold with non-trivial structure. Sampled points will, necessarily, cluster more in the high-probability regions, while points in low-probability regions will be more isolated. The distance from a given point to its k th nearest neighbor can then be used to estimate probabilities. The longer the distance, the lower the local probability in that region. This forms the basis of the Kozachenko-Leonenko non-parametric entropy estimator [38,39], and subsequent 

Figure 2: Kraskov mutual information estimator. A brief cartoon detailing the basic logic of the Kraskov mutual information estimator [35]. For each point, a diameter is defined by the distance from that point to it's fourth nearest neighbor. The estimator then counts the number of points within the diameter projected down to the constituent axes, and from that computes the local (pointwise) mutual information [36]. The expected value over all the pointwise values gives the estimated mutual information. 

derivatives. For a visualization, see Figure 1. 

The original estimators, developed by Kozachenko and Leonenko [38], have since been generalized and refined. The most well-known of these is the Kraskov (or KSG) mutual information estimator [35], which provides a non-parametric estimator of the coupling between two variables.

Existing work has analyzed the convergence speed of this estimator for random variables with bounded support. In practice, however, KSG estimator also performs well for a much broader class of distributions, including not only those with bounded support but also those with long tail distributions. In this paper, we analyze the convergence speed of the error of KSG estimator for smooth distributions, whose support can be both bounded and unbounded. Title: The topology of synergy: Linking topological and information-theoretic approaches to higher-order interactions in complex systems
Snippet: The most well-known of these is the Kraskov (or KSG) mutual information estimator [35], which provides a non-parametric estimator of the coupling between two variables. 

Visualized in Figure 2, for two variables X and Y , for each data point, the Kraskov estimator counts the number of points along the marginal X and Y axes that fall between the point and its k th -nearest neighbor. This adaptive approach allows estimates of mutual information, and subsequently, generalizations such as the total correlation, dual total correlation, O-information, and S-information directly from point clouds without the need for discretizing the data or imposing parametric assumptions. For formal details of the non-parametric O-information estimator, see Sec. 4.1. All measures reported here are implemented in the JIDT package [36]. Title: Analysis of k-Nearest Neighbor Distances with Application to Entropy Estimation
Snippet: In general contexts, only weak consistency of the KL estimator is known (Kozachenko & Leonenko, 1987). Biau & Devroye (2015) recently reviewed finite-sample results known for the KL estimator, including bounds on the bias and variance, under very restrictive conditions (i.e., β-Hölder continuous (β ∈ (0, 1]) densities bounded away from 0 on the interval [0, 1]). Our results generalize these results substantially, weakening the boundedness assumptions to tail conditions, and considering the multidimensional case and more smoothness classes. 

The KL estimator is also important for its role in the mutual information estimator proposed by Kraskov et al. (2004), which we refer to as the KSG estimator. The KSG estimator expands the mutual information as a sum of entropies, which it estimates via the KL estimator with a particular random (i.e., data-dependent) choice of the nearestneighbor parameter k. The KSG estimator is perhaps the most widely used estimator for the mutual information between continuous random variables, despite the fact that it currently appears to have no theoretical guarantees, even asymptotically. In fact, one of the few theoretical results, due to Gao et al. (2015b), concerning the KSG estimator is a negative result: when estimating the mutual information between strongly dependent variables, the KSG estimator tends to systematically underestimate mutual information, due to increased boundary bias. 3 Nevertheless, the widespread use of the KSG estimator motivates study of its behavior. We hope that our analysis of the KL estimator, in terms of which the KSG estimator can be written, will lead to a better understanding of the latter.

Clearly, the estimated density as well as the information quantity assessed via the density estimation will depend on k. However, Kraskov et al. [35] have empirically studied the influence of k, or more exactly a fixed k N on the estimation result and concluded that in the limit of infinitely many sample points the exact choice of k does not matter as all choices will converge. 

D. Generalizing the KSG estimator for I sx a. Adapting local probability density estimation for redundant information To understand how to estimate the continuous redundancy I sx ∩ using an approach similar to Kraskov et al. [35]'s, first consider the case of estimating the mutual information I(T : S) between a single target random variable T and two joint source variables S = (S 1 , S 2 ) using the KSG estimator. In the first step, the radius ϵ i is determined as the smallest radius in the joint space for which the k-th neighbor of the point x i = (t i , s 1,i , s 2,i ) lies within the Ball B ϵi (x i ). Using the maximum norm, this ball in the joint space is equal to the product of the ϵ-balls in the marginal spaces, i.e., B ϵi (t i )×B ϵi (s 1,i )×B ϵi (s 2,i ) (square region in Figure 4.A). In the second step, neighbours are counted within the marginal space of S, where only those points are counted which lie within less than the distance ϵ i to x i in both dimensions S 1 and S 2 simultaneously.

problem: potential methodologies for small dataset problems with classification
final_response:
# Potential Methodologies for Small-Dataset Classification

Small datasets pose challenges for classifier calibration, variance control, and generalization. A robust approach combines data-centric improvements, careful model selection, label-efficient learning, and rigorous evaluation. Below are evidence-backed methodologies and trade-offs for classification with limited data.

## 1) Data-centric strategies: collection, cleaning, and augmentation

- Augmentation and oversampling for imbalance. Synthetic oversampling methods such as SMOTE create minority-class examples by interpolating between existing samples to balance the distribution; variants like Borderline-SMOTE, ADASYN, WK-SMOTE, and MC-SMOTE aim to mitigate SMOTE’s risk of generating redundant/noisy samples by targeting difficult regions or leveraging model guidance (e.g., SVM, clustering) <cite id="955adf6e-0">Data-level solutions include resampling and augmentation to adjust imbalance ratios; oversampling is often applied only to the training set to avoid overfitting</cite> <cite id="955adf6e-0">SMOTE generates minority samples via interpolation, but can create redundant/noisy samples; Borderline-SMOTE, ADASYN, WK-SMOTE, and MC-SMOTE address specific limitations</cite>. 

- When labels are scarce, combining augmentation with active learning can sharply reduce the labeled fraction needed to reach high accuracy; for example, in a text classification study, SMOTE reduced the training share from 100% (passive) to 31.9% (active) to reach ~99% accuracy, and further to 17.8% when using SMOTE within an active loop <cite id="955adf6e-2">SMOTE significantly reduced the number of training samples needed for active learning (17.8% vs 31.9% vs 100%), enabling ~99% accuracy at substantially lower annotation cost</cite>.

- Caveats: Undersampling the majority class in very small datasets risks losing signal; oversampling should typically be local to the training fold to prevent leakage and overfitting <cite id="955adf6e-0">Undersampling can discard valuable majority-class information; oversampling is usually applied only to the training set to avoid overly optimistic performance estimates</cite>. For tabular or high-dimensional data, augmentation can still improve diversity, but poorly chosen transforms waste compute on non-informative samples <cite id="955adf6e-0">Data augmentation enhances diversity and can generate high-quality samples, but application and tuning are key to avoid inefficiency</cite>.

## 2) Model and training strategies tailored to small data

- Prefer simple, regularized models and conservative priors. With few examples, high-capacity models are prone to overfitting; regularization, early stopping, and simpler baselines can stabilize learning and improve generalization, especially when labeled data is limited <cite id="5281882b-0">Active learning and uncertainty-based selection aim to maximize model performance with minimal labels by querying informative samples, reflecting the broader principle of focusing resources where the model is uncertain</cite>. 

- Cost-sensitive and resampling-aware objectives. For class-imbalanced small datasets, cost-sensitive losses and resampling-aware training can improve minority-class recall without overfitting. Ensemble approaches with resampling (e.g., SMOTE-boosted trees) have been effective in practice for tabular domains with scarce labels <cite id="955adf6e-1">SMOTE and its variants generate synthetic minority examples and have been widely applied across domains; weighted/geometry-aware SMOTE adapt generation to local density and class difficulty</cite> <cite id="955adf6e-1">Alterations such as geometric and weighted SMOTE extend the basic approach to better handle imbalanced tabular data</cite>.

- Ensemble methods and diversity. Ensembles can reduce variance and improve calibration on small datasets; diversity-promoting selection (e.g., in query strategies) helps avoid overcommitting to a single model’s uncertainties <cite id="5281882b-3">Diversity sampling complements uncertainty sampling by ensuring the labeled subset covers representative regions, mitigating bias from a single model’s predictions</cite>.

## 3) Label-efficient supervision: active learning and uncertainty sampling

- Core idea. Active learning iteratively selects the most informative unlabeled examples for labeling, reducing annotation cost while improving accuracy with small labels budgets. Common acquisition functions include least confidence (max predicted probability), margin (difference between top two scores), and entropy over classes <cite id="5281882b-0">Uncertainty sampling selects the most uncertain samples via least confidence, margin, or entropy; BALD and DBAL formalize information gain for Bayesian active learning</cite> <cite id="5281882b-0">DBAL achieved 5% test error with 295 labeled samples (vs 835 for random), demonstrating substantial label efficiency gains</cite>.

- Practical guidance and theory. Uncertainty-based strategies are simple and fast but can be biased toward boundary regions; diversity and disagreement-based strategies (e.g., query-by-committee) provide alternative coverage and can alleviate mode collapse. Recent work analyzes convergence and bias-variance trade-offs for uncertainty sampling <cite id="5281882b-3">Uncertainty sampling is widely used due to simplicity and speed, while diversity and query-by-committee address representativeness and disagreement; theoretical work studies convergence of uncertainty sampling</cite>.

- Multi-class considerations. In multi-class problems, entropy and margin criteria can outperform single-pair margins; empirical comparisons show entropy often yields better gains than best-versus-second-best in batch selection <cite id="5281882b-2">In multi-class active learning, entropy outperformed best-versus-second-best margin in SVM-based settings, motivating entropy-based batch selection</cite>.

- Implementation tips. Start with a small seed set, use a calibrated classifier to score uncertainty, and maintain a pool of unlabeled examples; retrain incrementally and re-score until budget exhaustion or satisfactory performance <cite id="5281882b-0">Active learning proceeds by iteratively querying samples that maximize mutual information or reduce predictive uncertainty (e.g., BALD)</cite>.

## 4) Semi- and self-supervised learning with pseudo-labeling

- Framework. Combine a small labeled set with a large unlabeled set via a joint loss: a supervised term on labeled data plus an unsupervised term (e.g., consistency regularization or generative reconstruction) on unlabeled data <cite id="eca520e5-1">Semi-supervised learning trains with both labeled and unlabeled data via L_SemiSL = L_cls + L_unsup, where L_unsup encourages learning meaningful structures from unlabeled data</cite>.

- Pseudo-labeling wrapper. Train on the small labeled set; predict high-confidence pseudo-labels on the unlabeled set; retrain on the augmented set. Iterating this self-training can expand the effective dataset while avoiding full relabeling <cite id="eca520e5-0">Pseudo-labeling assigns temporary labels to unlabeled data based on a model’s predictions and augments the labeled set, improving generalization in text classification with limited labels</cite> <cite id="eca520e5-1">Pseudo-labeling typically selects the class with highest softmax probability; self-training and self-supervised pretraining are common self-training strategies</cite>.

- Consistency regularization. For images, augment the same input multiple ways and penalize inconsistent predictions, which improves robustness with few labels; this is complementary to pseudo-labeling <cite id="eca520e5-3">Consistency regularization assumes a model should produce consistent predictions across perturbations of the same input, added to the supervised loss to leverage unlabeled data</cite>.

- Caveats. Pseudo-labels can propagate errors; screening pseudo-labels by confidence and validating error rates is important, especially for noisy or ambiguous data <cite id="eca520e5-2">Pseudo-labeling can introduce errors if the model mislabels; quality control and validation of pseudo-labels are crucial before retraining</cite>.

## 5) Few-shot and meta-learning for extremely small N

- Prototypical Networks (ProtoNets). Learn an embedding space where each class is represented by a prototype (mean embedding); classify new samples by distance to prototypes. This metric-based approach is simple and effective in low-data regimes <cite id="525d22ae-1">ProtoNets compute class prototypes as mean embeddings and classify via distance (e.g., squared Euclidean), often with a softmax over distances</cite> <cite id="525d22ae-4">ProtoNets achieve excellent few-shot results by learning a metric space where classification is via distances to class prototypes</cite>.

- Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML). Meta-trains an initialization so that a small number of gradient steps on new tasks quickly adapt to new classes; works with various models and can improve generalization from very few examples <cite id="525d22ae-2">MAML learns parameter initializations that enable rapid adaptation with few samples per class, benefiting from transfer across tasks</cite> <cite id="525d22ae-4">MAML aims to find a good initialization that adapts quickly with limited labeled samples, contrasting with ProtoNets’ metric-space approach</cite>.

- Hybrid and advanced meta-learning. Hybrids like Proto-MAML combine linear-layer initialization from ProtoNets with MAML adaptation, improving optimization and performance in few-shot settings <cite id="525d22ae-1">Proto-MAML integrates ProtoNets’ linear classification with MAML adaptation, yielding significant improvements over either alone</cite>. Evaluations also reveal limitations and complementary strengths: ProtoNets favor simple metric inductive biases, while MAML excels at parameter initialization; task similarity matters for avoiding negative transfer <cite id="525d22ae-4">MAML and ProtoNets have complementary strengths; meta-learning can suffer negative transfer if tasks are dissimilar, emphasizing the importance of task distribution</cite>.

- Practical caution. Benchmarks like Meta-Dataset show that popular methods can be exposed; careful evaluation on diverse, realistic datasets is essential to avoid overestimating few-shot gains <cite id="525d22ae-0">Meta-Dataset evaluates meta-learners and exposes weaknesses in Prototypical Networks and MAML, proposing hybrids that achieve SOTA within that environment</cite>.

## 6) Domain adaptation and transfer learning

- Transfer learning. When labeled target data is scarce, pretrain models on related source domains and fine-tune on the small target dataset. This leverages shared features and can improve performance despite limited labels; semi-supervised losses (e.g., consistency) often complement transfer by stabilizing fine-tuning on noisy pseudo-labels <cite id="eca520e5-3">Combining labeled and unlabeled data with consistency regularization and augmentation supports efficient fine-tuning, aligning with transfer-learning strategies on limited target labels</cite>.

- Domain adaptation. Methods that align distributions between source and target (e.g., adversarial alignment or domain confusion) can further reduce domain shift when labels are only available in the target domain; these are especially useful for out-of-distribution small datasets and can be combined with pseudo-labeling to expand labeled target data <cite id="eca520e5-4">Semi-supervised approaches like distribution alignment and augmentation anchoring improve pseudo-labeling in weakly annotated data, illustrating domain-adaptation ideas that pair with few labels</cite>.

## 7) Synthetic data generation (GANs/Deepfakes) and tabular analogs

- Data synthesis. For image or sequential data, generative models (GANs, diffusion) can produce realistic augmentations that expand the effective dataset; in vision tasks, active learning with uncertainty and synthetic augmentation can jointly expand and prioritize data <cite id="5281882b-0">Bayesian active learning (DBAL) with deep models shows that carefully selected augmentations and queries can reach low errors with hundreds rather than thousands of labeled samples</cite>. For tabular or text classification with small N, SMOTE-like methods and learned embeddings can approximate synthetic neighbors; wrapper semi-supervised methods then integrate generated samples into training pipelines <cite id="eca520e5-1">Self-training and pseudo-labeling can be combined with synthetic data to expand the labeled set; semi-supervised objectives blend supervised and unsupervised terms</cite>.

- Caveat. Synthetic data must reflect underlying distributions and decision boundaries; methods like Borderline-SMOTE or density-aware variants help avoid mode collapse and redundant samples in tabular domains <cite id="955adf6e-0">Advanced SMOTE variants (Borderline-SMOTE, ADASYN, WK-SMOTE, MC-SMOTE) target complex class manifolds and reduce noise from synthetic samples</cite>.

## 8) Evaluation and statistical rigor for small datasets

- Cross-validation and resampling. K-fold cross-validation remains essential on small datasets; careful fold construction and repeated CV reduce variance and improve reliability of error estimates <cite id="09d8e499-4">k-fold cross-validation is a benchmark for small datasets; repeated CV and careful fold design yield robust error estimates</cite>.

- Permutation and bootstrap tests for significance. With limited samples, permutation tests assess whether observed accuracy significantly exceeds chance by relabeling and re-evaluating; bootstrap quantifies confidence intervals and p-values when the empirical distribution is discrete, controlling for bias in small N <cite id="09d8e499-0">Permutation tests reassign labels and evaluate classifier generalization under the null to determine statistical significance</cite> <cite id="09d8e499-1">Permutation tests with corrections for discrete distributions address p-value bias in small datasets; significance and chance-level comparisons are reported with appropriate adjustments</cite> <cite id="09d8e499-2">Bootstrap resampling provides 95% confidence intervals and p-values for accuracy over chance, trading computational cost for statistical precision</cite> <cite id="09d8e499-3">Permutation testing can be framed as comparing the real generalization rate against 95% of rates from relabeled data to establish reliability</cite>.

- Baseline comparisons under identical protocols. Ensure both labeled-augmentation and active/semi-supervised methods are evaluated under the same data splits and computational budgets to isolate the effect of label scarcity; report not just accuracy but also error rates relative to chance and robustness across folds <cite id="09d8e499-2">Statistical evaluation compares model accuracy to chance using binomial or permutation methods and bootstrap to quantify uncertainty across small-sample predictions</cite>.

## 9) Putting it together: a practical recipe

## 10) Trade-offs and limitations

- Over-smoothing and redundancy: oversampling and augmentation can create synthetic samples that collapse into low-variance modes, harming generalization; density-aware and boundary-focused methods mitigate this but require careful tuning <cite id="955adf6e-0">SMOTE can generate redundant/noisy samples; Borderline-SMOTE, ADASYN, WK-SMOTE, and MC-SMOTE target difficult regions and distributions</cite>.

Although the unlabelled data is often available in abundance, it is usually under-utilized because of the budget involved in labelling. One of the promising methodologies that addresses this problem is Active Learning (AL), which is a sub-field of machine learning [38]. AL generally employs an incremental or an iterative training strategy. The main aim of AL is to select (or query) those data points from an unlabelled set for labelling at every iteration such that it maximizes the model performance. Thus, for a given budget, AL aims to achieve the best model performance using as few labelled instances as possible by employing an acquisition function for querying.

Snippet: Intrinsically, semi-supervised approaches are designed to incorporate both labelled and unlabelled data during the learning process [35], [36], [37]. These methods leverage a combination of labelled and unlabelled loss terms to optimize the model performance. By jointly considering labelled and unlabelled data, the model can learn better representations and improve generalization. Techniques such as entropy minimization [38], consistency regularization [39], and generative models [40] are commonly used to effectively exploit unlabelled data. Intrinsically semi-supervised methods have proven effective in text classification scenarios with limited labelled data [41], [42]. 

Wrapper methods in semi-supervised learning involve a sequential process where a subset of labelled data is used for initial model training, followed by performance evaluation on a separate validation set. Subsequently, the trained model is employed to generate predictions on the unlabelled data, and a subset of instances with high prediction confidence or low uncertainty scores is selected to augment the labelled set. This combined labelled data, comprising the original labelled data along with the newly selected instances, is then utilized to retrain the model [43]. 

Pseudo-labeling is one of the most commonly used wrapper methods for semi-supervised learning [44], [45]. Pseudolabeling involves assigning temporary labels to the unlabelled data based on the predictions made by a pre-trained model. These pseudo-labels are then processed as additional labelled data and combined with the original labelled data for model training. The pre-trained model is often trained using only the labelled data and is used to make predictions on the unlabelled instances. Pseudo-labeling has emerged as a prominent technique for enhancing the performance of text classification tasks, particularly in scenarios with limited datasets [10], [54], [55], [56]. 

The existing semi-supervised approaches have their own advantages and drawbacks. While graph-based approaches for semi-supervised learning do offer advantages by utilizing the relationships between data points, they do come with certain limitations. These methods can become computationally intensive, which can become an obstacle when working with large datasets. Moreover, they demand careful consideration in terms of selecting appropriate similarity measures and constructing graphs [57].
</snippet>

Snippet: Semi-supervised learning is a type of learning that involves training a model using both labeled and unlabeled data. It becomes beneficial when it is difficult or expensive to obtain a large amount of labeled data, and only a few labeled samples are available with a large amount of unlabeled data. Specifically, given a small labeled dataset D L with a larger unlabeled dataset D U , the goal is to train a model f that leverages the unlabeled data D U alongside D L to enhance learning. The learning objective often combines a supervised classification loss L cls (f (x i ), y i ) on D L with an unsupervised loss L unsup (f (x j )) on D U , where L unsup encourages the model to learn meaningful structures from D U . As illustrated in Fig. 4, the overall objective becomes L SemiSL = L cls + L unsup , where both losses are added together during training. However, one challenge in semi-supervised learning still achieving the best balance of learning from both labeled and unlabeled samples. 

In this survey, we categorize semi-supervised learning approaches into self-training-based methods and generic regularization-based methods. 

1) Self-training Methods: Self-training involves assigning labels to the unlabeled data to train the model. It can be implemented either by pseudo-labeling or self-supervised pretraining. 

a) Pseudo-Labeling: Pseudo labeling leverages a small set of labeled data to initially train a model, which is then used to generate pseudo labels for the unlabeled data, based on the assumption that these labels are likely accurate. The typical method for producing pseudo labels involves applying the softmax function to the model's predictions. Specifically, if a model predicts the output probabilities p i for a data point, the pseudo label is assigned by selecting the class with the highest probability after applying softmax, which is mathematically represented as: pseudo-label = arg max(softmax(p i )). 

For example, Wang et al. [55] generate pseudo labels from the model predictions to the unlabeled data and use leastsquare regression to learn both shapelets and classification boundaries.

Title: An Overview of Deep Learning Architectures in Few-Shot Learning Domain
Snippet: Semi-supervised learning [15] is a machine learning technique that involves training a model on both labeled and unlabeled data. In traditional supervised learning, models are trained only on labeled data, which is expensive and timeconsuming to obtain. However, with semi-supervised learning, models can leverage the vast amount of unlabeled data available to improve performance on labeled data. 

Suppose we have 10,000 data points, out of which only 20,000 are labeled, and the rest 80,000 are unlabeled. In such cases, we can take the help of semi-supervised learning to train a more accurate model. Semi-supervised learning [15] goes through a pseudo-labeling technique to increase the training set. In this technique, we train a model using the 20,000 labeled dataset and use it on an equally sized test dataset to create pseudo-labels for the unlabeled data points. After obtaining pseudo-labels, we concatenate the real labels with the pseudo-labels and real features with the pseudo-features. We then train a new model on the concatenated dataset, which has been shown to be more accurate than the initial model. We repeat this process until optimal accuracy is achieved. 

Semi-supervised learning works well in scenarios where labeled data is scarce, and there is a vast amount of unlabeled data available. By leveraging the unlabeled data, models can gain a better understanding of the population structure in general, leading to improved performance on the labeled data. Semi-supervised learning has been applied in various fields such as computer vision, natural language processing, and speech recognition. 

However, it is important to note that semi-supervised learning is not a panacea, and it may not always lead to improved performance. The success of semi-supervised learning depends on various factors such as the quality of the unlabeled data, the complexity of the task, and the type of model used. Additionally, the pseudo-labeling technique may introduce errors if the model makes incorrect predictions on the unlabeled data. Therefore, it is crucial to validate the accuracy of the pseudolabels before using them to train the model.
</snippet>

Title: FMSA: a meta-learning framework-based fast model stealing attack technique against intelligent network intrusion detection systems
Snippet: While performing well on multiple tasks, machine learning and deep learning cannot adapt to new tasks as quickly as humans can based on a minimal amount of prior knowledge. Inspired by the fast learning ability of humans, researchers want machine learning models to learn quickly with only a limited number of samples for new classes after learning a vast amount of tasks and data, hence the proposal of meta-learning (Tian et al. 2022), or learning to learn. The benefit of employing meta-learning lies in its ability to dynamically adjust to different tasks and datasets by utilizing learning algorithms. This adaptation enhances the efficiency and accuracy of the learning process. In the area of supervised learning, few-shot learning (Wang et al. 2020) is a metalearning application. It tackles intricate classification and regression problems using a limited number of training samples, addressing challenges commonly encountered in traditional machine learning and deep learning, such as overfitting issues. 

In our scenario, we set the meta-stealer to go through several different scenarios of stealing tasks and finally apply it to the target model. Model-agnostic meta-learning (MAML) (Finn et al. 2017) and prototypical networks (Snell et al. 2017) are two more representative few-shot learning algorithms. MAML is designed to teach models how to initialize parameters for a specific task so that they can converge quickly after only a few samples of training, and the underlying assumption of the prototypical network is that there exists a low-latitude embedding space in which the sample distributions of all categories are far from each other. Both methods have advantages in facilitating knowledge transfer across diverse tasks and datasets, as they enhance the adaptability and generalization capability of the learning process. In our study, we adopt the MAML algorithm to guide the training of our meta-learners and incorporate the concept of prototypical networks to extract features from limited auxiliary information, promoting the generation of more representative query samples.

Here a classifier must generalize to new classes not seen in the training set, given only a small number of examples of each new class. Prototypical networks learn a metric space in which classification can be performed by computing distances to prototype representations of each class. Compared to recent approaches for few-shot learning, they reflect a simpler inductive bias that is beneficial in this limited-data regime, and achieve excellent results. 

It's well established that meta-learning algorithms generalize well for tasks with low-data. However, one of the biggest limitations to meta learning is the problem of negative transfer. Meta learning only works if the meta-training tasks are similar enough for the training to be relevant. If the meta training is too far off the mark, the model may actually perform worse than if it had never been trained at all. Hence, it is imperative to study the task distribution and if possible, augment the data with external sources of information. 

In this project, we aim to inform the task distribution of meta-train and meta-test tasks through an external source of information -namely the WordNet hierarchy. # Potential Methodologies for Small-Dataset Classification

Small datasets pose challenges for classifier calibration, variance control, and generalization. A robust approach combines data-centric improvements, careful model selection, label-efficient learning, and rigorous evaluation. Below are evidence-backed methodologies and trade-offs for classification with limited data.

## 1) Data-centric strategies: collection, cleaning, and augmentation

- Augmentation and oversampling for imbalance. Synthetic oversampling methods such as SMOTE create minority-class examples by interpolating between existing samples to balance the distribution; variants like Borderline-SMOTE, ADASYN, WK-SMOTE, and MC-SMOTE aim to mitigate SMOTE’s risk of generating redundant/noisy samples by targeting difficult regions or leveraging model guidance (e.g., SVM, clustering) <cite id="955adf6e-0">Data-level solutions include resampling and augmentation to adjust imbalance ratios; oversampling is often applied only to the training set to avoid overfitting</cite> <cite id="955adf6e-0">SMOTE generates minority samples via interpolation, but can create redundant/noisy samples; Borderline-SMOTE, ADASYN, WK-SMOTE, and MC-SMOTE address specific limitations</cite>. 

- When labels are scarce, combining augmentation with active learning can sharply reduce the labeled fraction needed to reach high accuracy; for example, in a text classification study, SMOTE reduced the training share from 100% (passive) to 31.9% (active) to reach ~99% accuracy, and further to 17.8% when using SMOTE within an active loop <cite id="955adf6e-2">SMOTE significantly reduced the number of training samples needed for active learning (17.8% vs 31.9% vs 100%), enabling ~99% accuracy at substantially lower annotation cost</cite>.

- Caveats: Undersampling the majority class in very small datasets risks losing signal; oversampling should typically be local to the training fold to prevent leakage and overfitting <cite id="955adf6e-0">Undersampling can discard valuable majority-class information; oversampling is usually applied only to the training set to avoid overly optimistic performance estimates</cite>. For tabular or high-dimensional data, augmentation can still improve diversity, but poorly chosen transforms waste compute on non-informative samples <cite id="955adf6e-0">Data augmentation enhances diversity and can generate high-quality samples, but application and tuning are key to avoid inefficiency</cite>.

## 2) Model and training strategies tailored to small data

- Prefer simple, regularized models and conservative priors. With few examples, high-capacity models are prone to overfitting; regularization, early stopping, and simpler baselines can stabilize learning and improve generalization, especially when labeled data is limited <cite id="5281882b-0">Active learning and uncertainty-based selection aim to maximize model performance with minimal labels by querying informative samples, reflecting the broader principle of focusing resources where the model is uncertain</cite>. 

- Cost-sensitive and resampling-aware objectives. For class-imbalanced small datasets, cost-sensitive losses and resampling-aware training can improve minority-class recall without overfitting. Ensemble approaches with resampling (e.g., SMOTE-boosted trees) have been effective in practice for tabular domains with scarce labels <cite id="955adf6e-1">SMOTE and its variants generate synthetic minority examples and have been widely applied across domains; weighted/geometry-aware SMOTE adapt generation to local density and class difficulty</cite> <cite id="955adf6e-1">Alterations such as geometric and weighted SMOTE extend the basic approach to better handle imbalanced tabular data</cite>.

- Ensemble methods and diversity. Ensembles can reduce variance and improve calibration on small datasets; diversity-promoting selection (e.g., in query strategies) helps avoid overcommitting to a single model’s uncertainties <cite id="5281882b-3">Diversity sampling complements uncertainty sampling by ensuring the labeled subset covers representative regions, mitigating bias from a single model’s predictions</cite>.

## 3) Label-efficient supervision: active learning and uncertainty sampling

- Core idea. Active learning iteratively selects the most informative unlabeled examples for labeling, reducing annotation cost while improving accuracy with small labels budgets. Common acquisition functions include least confidence (max predicted probability), margin (difference between top two scores), and entropy over classes <cite id="5281882b-0">Uncertainty sampling selects the most uncertain samples via least confidence, margin, or entropy; BALD and DBAL formalize information gain for Bayesian active learning</cite> <cite id="5281882b-0">DBAL achieved 5% test error with 295 labeled samples (vs 835 for random), demonstrating substantial label efficiency gains</cite>.

- Practical guidance and theory. Uncertainty-based strategies are simple and fast but can be biased toward boundary regions; diversity and disagreement-based strategies (e.g., query-by-committee) provide alternative coverage and can alleviate mode collapse. Recent work analyzes convergence and bias-variance trade-offs for uncertainty sampling <cite id="5281882b-3">Uncertainty sampling is widely used due to simplicity and speed, while diversity and query-by-committee address representativeness and disagreement; theoretical work studies convergence of uncertainty sampling</cite>.

- Multi-class considerations. In multi-class problems, entropy and margin criteria can outperform single-pair margins; empirical comparisons show entropy often yields better gains than best-versus-second-best in batch selection <cite id="5281882b-2">In multi-class active learning, entropy outperformed best-versus-second-best margin in SVM-based settings, motivating entropy-based batch selection</cite>.

- Implementation tips. Start with a small seed set, use a calibrated classifier to score uncertainty, and maintain a pool of unlabeled examples; retrain incrementally and re-score until budget exhaustion or satisfactory performance <cite id="5281882b-0">Active learning proceeds by iteratively querying samples that maximize mutual information or reduce predictive uncertainty (e.g., BALD)</cite>.

## 4) Semi- and self-supervised learning with pseudo-labeling

- Framework. Combine a small labeled set with a large unlabeled set via a joint loss: a supervised term on labeled data plus an unsupervised term (e.g., consistency regularization or generative reconstruction) on unlabeled data <cite id="eca520e5-1">Semi-supervised learning trains with both labeled and unlabeled data via L_SemiSL = L_cls + L_unsup, where L_unsup encourages learning meaningful structures from unlabeled data</cite>.

- Pseudo-labeling wrapper. Train on the small labeled set; predict high-confidence pseudo-labels on the unlabeled set; retrain on the augmented set. Iterating this self-training can expand the effective dataset while avoiding full relabeling <cite id="eca520e5-0">Pseudo-labeling assigns temporary labels to unlabeled data based on a model’s predictions and augments the labeled set, improving generalization in text classification with limited labels</cite> <cite id="eca520e5-1">Pseudo-labeling typically selects the class with highest softmax probability; self-training and self-supervised pretraining are common self-training strategies</cite>.

- Consistency regularization. For images, augment the same input multiple ways and penalize inconsistent predictions, which improves robustness with few labels; this is complementary to pseudo-labeling <cite id="eca520e5-3">Consistency regularization assumes a model should produce consistent predictions across perturbations of the same input, added to the supervised loss to leverage unlabeled data</cite>.

- Caveats. Pseudo-labels can propagate errors; screening pseudo-labels by confidence and validating error rates is important, especially for noisy or ambiguous data <cite id="eca520e5-2">Pseudo-labeling can introduce errors if the model mislabels; quality control and validation of pseudo-labels are crucial before retraining</cite>.

## 5) Few-shot and meta-learning for extremely small N

- Prototypical Networks (ProtoNets). Learn an embedding space where each class is represented by a prototype (mean embedding); classify new samples by distance to prototypes. This metric-based approach is simple and effective in low-data regimes <cite id="525d22ae-1">ProtoNets compute class prototypes as mean embeddings and classify via distance (e.g., squared Euclidean), often with a softmax over distances</cite> <cite id="525d22ae-4">ProtoNets achieve excellent few-shot results by learning a metric space where classification is via distances to class prototypes</cite>.

- Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML). Meta-trains an initialization so that a small number of gradient steps on new tasks quickly adapt to new classes; works with various models and can improve generalization from very few examples <cite id="525d22ae-2">MAML learns parameter initializations that enable rapid adaptation with few samples per class, benefiting from transfer across tasks</cite> <cite id="525d22ae-4">MAML aims to find a good initialization that adapts quickly with limited labeled samples, contrasting with ProtoNets’ metric-space approach</cite>.

- Hybrid and advanced meta-learning. Hybrids like Proto-MAML combine linear-layer initialization from ProtoNets with MAML adaptation, improving optimization and performance in few-shot settings <cite id="525d22ae-1">Proto-MAML integrates ProtoNets’ linear classification with MAML adaptation, yielding significant improvements over either alone</cite>. Evaluations also reveal limitations and complementary strengths: ProtoNets favor simple metric inductive biases, while MAML excels at parameter initialization; task similarity matters for avoiding negative transfer <cite id="525d22ae-4">MAML and ProtoNets have complementary strengths; meta-learning can suffer negative transfer if tasks are dissimilar, emphasizing the importance of task distribution</cite>.

- Practical caution. Benchmarks like Meta-Dataset show that popular methods can be exposed; careful evaluation on diverse, realistic datasets is essential to avoid overestimating few-shot gains <cite id="525d22ae-0">Meta-Dataset evaluates meta-learners and exposes weaknesses in Prototypical Networks and MAML, proposing hybrids that achieve SOTA within that environment</cite>.

## 6) Domain adaptation and transfer learning

- Transfer learning. When labeled target data is scarce, pretrain models on related source domains and fine-tune on the small target dataset. This leverages shared features and can improve performance despite limited labels; semi-supervised losses (e.g., consistency) often complement transfer by stabilizing fine-tuning on noisy pseudo-labels <cite id="eca520e5-3">Combining labeled and unlabeled data with consistency regularization and augmentation supports efficient fine-tuning, aligning with transfer-learning strategies on limited target labels</cite>.

- Domain adaptation. Methods that align distributions between source and target (e.g., adversarial alignment or domain confusion) can further reduce domain shift when labels are only available in the target domain; these are especially useful for out-of-distribution small datasets and can be combined with pseudo-labeling to expand labeled target data <cite id="eca520e5-4">Semi-supervised approaches like distribution alignment and augmentation anchoring improve pseudo-labeling in weakly annotated data, illustrating domain-adaptation ideas that pair with few labels</cite>.

## 7) Synthetic data generation (GANs/Deepfakes) and tabular analogs

- Data synthesis. For image or sequential data, generative models (GANs, diffusion) can produce realistic augmentations that expand the effective dataset; in vision tasks, active learning with uncertainty and synthetic augmentation can jointly expand and prioritize data <cite id="5281882b-0">Bayesian active learning (DBAL) with deep models shows that carefully selected augmentations and queries can reach low errors with hundreds rather than thousands of labeled samples</cite>. For tabular or text classification with small N, SMOTE-like methods and learned embeddings can approximate synthetic neighbors; wrapper semi-supervised methods then integrate generated samples into training pipelines <cite id="eca520e5-1">Self-training and pseudo-labeling can be combined with synthetic data to expand the labeled set; semi-supervised objectives blend supervised and unsupervised terms</cite>.

- Caveat. Synthetic data must reflect underlying distributions and decision boundaries; methods like Borderline-SMOTE or density-aware variants help avoid mode collapse and redundant samples in tabular domains <cite id="955adf6e-0">Advanced SMOTE variants (Borderline-SMOTE, ADASYN, WK-SMOTE, MC-SMOTE) target complex class manifolds and reduce noise from synthetic samples</cite>.

## 8) Evaluation and statistical rigor for small datasets

- Cross-validation and resampling. K-fold cross-validation remains essential on small datasets; careful fold construction and repeated CV reduce variance and improve reliability of error estimates <cite id="09d8e499-4">k-fold cross-validation is a benchmark for small datasets; repeated CV and careful fold design yield robust error estimates</cite>.

- Permutation and bootstrap tests for significance. With limited samples, permutation tests assess whether observed accuracy significantly exceeds chance by relabeling and re-evaluating; bootstrap quantifies confidence intervals and p-values when the empirical distribution is discrete, controlling for bias in small N <cite id="09d8e499-0">Permutation tests reassign labels and evaluate classifier generalization under the null to determine statistical significance</cite> <cite id="09d8e499-1">Permutation tests with corrections for discrete distributions address p-value bias in small datasets; significance and chance-level comparisons are reported with appropriate adjustments</cite> <cite id="09d8e499-2">Bootstrap resampling provides 95% confidence intervals and p-values for accuracy over chance, trading computational cost for statistical precision</cite> <cite id="09d8e499-3">Permutation testing can be framed as comparing the real generalization rate against 95% of rates from relabeled data to establish reliability</cite>.

- Baseline comparisons under identical protocols. Ensure both labeled-augmentation and active/semi-supervised methods are evaluated under the same data splits and computational budgets to isolate the effect of label scarcity; report not just accuracy but also error rates relative to chance and robustness across folds <cite id="09d8e499-2">Statistical evaluation compares model accuracy to chance using binomial or permutation methods and bootstrap to quantify uncertainty across small-sample predictions</cite>.

## 9) Putting it together: a practical recipe

- Diagnose data: quantify class imbalance, feature coverage, and noise; consider domain shift from training to deployment <cite id="955adf6e-0">Resampling and augmentation must be tuned to class distribution complexity to avoid redundancy and overfitting</cite>.

- Start simple: train regularized baselines (e.g., SVMs, boosted trees, simple neural networks) with stratified CV and significance tests; establish a reference error floor <cite id="09d8e499-4">Cross-validation is essential for small datasets to estimate generalization with fewer samples</cite> <cite id="09d8e499-1">Permutation tests assess dependence between labels and data when samples are limited</cite>.

- Augment and balance thoughtfully: apply SMOTE-like oversampling to the training fold only, with density-aware variants for hard decision boundaries; add domain-informed augmentations to increase diversity without noise <cite id="955adf6e-0">Oversampling only the training set and using advanced SMOTE variants can improve minority-class learning while mitigating overfitting</cite>.

- Add label efficiency: run active learning on unlabeled pools using uncertainty (entropy/margin/least confidence) plus diversity to cover the feature space; screen pseudo-labels by confidence and validate periodic accuracy to avoid error propagation <cite id="5281882b-0">Uncertainty-based active learning (and BALD/DBAL) reduces labels needed substantially relative to random selection</cite> <cite id="5281882b-2">Entropy-based multi-class selection can outperform margin criteria in batch AL</cite> <cite id="eca520e5-2">Validate pseudo-label quality before retraining to prevent error amplification</cite>.

- Exploit semi-/self-supervision: for image/sequence/tabular data with structure, add consistency regularization or reconstruction losses on unlabeled data; iterate self-training with pseudo-labeling on increasingly confident predictions to expand the labeled set <cite id="eca520e5-3">Consistency regularization leverages unlabeled data by penalizing prediction changes under augmentation</cite> <cite id="eca520e5-1">Self-training via pseudo-labeling expands labeled data with a combined supervised+unsupervised objective</cite>.

- Consider few-shot/meta-learning if N per class is extremely small (<5–10): use ProtoNets or MAML (or hybrids) with diverse, representative support examples and broad meta-training tasks; verify generalization on new classes/tasks and guard against negative transfer from dissimilar tasks <cite id="525d22ae-4">ProtoNets and MAML have complementary strengths in few-shot learning, with task similarity critical to avoid negative transfer</cite> <cite id="525d22ae-1">Hybrid Proto-MAML improves adaptation by initializing linear layers with prototype information</cite>.

- Transfer and adapt: fine-tune models pretrained on related domains, and when possible, align domains using adaptation techniques; combine with pseudo-labeling to generate additional target-domain examples <cite id="eca520e5-4">Distribution alignment and augmentation anchoring improve semi-supervised learning on weakly annotated data, supporting domain adaptation with few labels</cite>.

- Synthesize and test: generate synthetic data (GANs/tabular SMOTE) to cover missing manifolds; evaluate under identical protocols with permutation/bootstrapped significance; compare against active and semi-supervised variants with the same computational budget; iterate selection and synthesis to improve coverage without overwhelming the model with noise <cite id="955adf6e-0">Synthetic data can enhance diversity, but must avoid redundancy and leakage; oversampling should be local to training folds</cite> <cite id="09d8e499-0">Permutation testing provides a principled way to assess significance with limited samples</cite>.

## 10) Trade-offs and limitations

- Over-smoothing and redundancy: oversampling and augmentation can create synthetic samples that collapse into low-variance modes, harming generalization; density-aware and boundary-focused methods mitigate this but require careful tuning <cite id="955adf6e-0">SMOTE can generate redundant/noisy samples; Borderline-SMOTE, ADASYN, WK-SMOTE, and MC-SMOTE target difficult regions and distributions</cite>.

- Active learning pitfalls: uncertainty-only strategies can get stuck near decision boundaries or duplicate similar high-uncertainty regions; diversity and disagreement signals help, and confidence thresholds prevent error amplification in pseudo-labels <cite id="5281882b-3">Diversity sampling and query-by-committee address representativeness and disagreement, complementing uncertainty-based selection</cite> <cite id="eca520e5-2">Screen pseudo-labels by confidence to avoid propagating model errors</cite>.

- Meta-learning limits: performance gains depend on task similarity; dissimilar meta-training tasks can cause negative transfer; few-shot methods may underperform naive baselines on small, noisy datasets without careful regularization and broad task coverage <cite id="525d22ae-4">Meta-learning’s effectiveness hinges on task distribution; negative transfer is a major risk when tasks are too different</cite>.

- Computational cost: bootstrap and permutation tests are necessary for significance but can be expensive on very small datasets; choose conservative thresholds and report effect sizes alongside p-values to contextualize gains <cite id="09d8e499-2">Bootstrap and permutation tests provide robust uncertainty estimates but increase computation on small datasets</cite>.

By combining data augmentation and cleaning, label-efficient querying, semi-/self-supervised learning, few-shot/meta-learning when appropriate, and rigorous statistical evaluation, practitioners can substantially improve classification performance and reliability even when labeled data is scarce. Start with a minimal seed, measure uncertainty and diversity, and iteratively expand and refine the training set while controlling for overfitting and variance through validated cross-validation and significance testing <cite id="955adf6e-0">Resampling and augmentation should be applied to training folds only and tuned to class complexity to avoid overfitting</cite> <cite id="5281882b-0">Active learning reduces annotation budgets by selecting informative samples, improving accuracy per labeled example</cite> <cite id="09d8e499-1">Permutation tests with discrete-p value corrections provide valid inference for small datasets</cite>.

Title: A Survey on Small Sample Imbalance Problem: Metrics, Feature Analysis, and Solutions
Snippet: This section method focuses on addressing small-sample and imbalance issues, with less emphasis on analyzing interclass and intra-class difficulty factors. However, data augmentation remains an effective strategy for S&I datasets, as it enhances diversity and generates high-quality samples. Therefore, these methods do not imply an inability to handle complex datasets. The key lies in how they are applied. 

1) Data-level solutions Table V summarizes data-level solutions. These methods balance class distributions by modifying or augmenting data to adjust imbalance ratios while maintaining majority class recognition performance [73]. Resampling: Undersampling is less commonly applied to S&I datasets because it balances data by reducing majorityclass samples. When data is limited, this can lead to the loss of valuable information and negatively impact classification performance. In practice, oversampling is applied only to the training set, rather than the entire dataset, to avoid overly optimistic performance estimates [34]. 

The Synthetic Minority Over-Sampling Technique (SMOTE) [74] is a widely adopted resampling technique. It generates new minority samples by interpolating in the feature space to balance the dataset. However, it has limitations, including neglecting class distribution complexity and producing redundant or noisy samples. To address these issues, several extensions have been developed. Borderline-SMOTE [75] enhances classification by generating samples near decision boundaries, improving robustness in critical regions. Adaptive Synthetic Sampling (ADASYN) [76] further refines sample generation by prioritizing hard-to-classify instances, better aligning with the data distribution. The Weighted Kernel-based SMOTE (WK-SMOTE) algorithm [77] improves SMOTE by performing oversampling in the feature space of a Support Vector Machine (SVM). This approach effectively addresses SMOTE limitations in nonlinear problems. Minority Clustering SMOTE (MC-SMOTE) [78] applies K-means clustering to minority-class samples and generates new samples between neighboring clusters. It balances data distribution and enhances classification performance. However, these do not explicitly address uncertainty issues.

Title: A review of ensemble learning and data augmentation models for class imbalanced problems: combination, implementation and evaluation
Snippet: The focus of this paper is the CI problem and the combination of data augmentation and ensemble learning for tabular datasets. The most prominent approach in using data augmentation for CI datasets is generating examples in the minority class using synthetic minority oversampling technique (SMOTE) [208] that uses the k-nearest neighbour (KNN) model [209]. SMOTE generates synthetic examples in a less applicationspecific manner, by operating in "feature space" rather than "data space." We can increase the minority class by taking each minority class sample and introducing synthetic examples along the line segments joining any or all of the nearest neighbours of the minority class. We can choose neighbours for KNN depending on the amount of oversampling required. Although SMOTE was developed for classification problems, it can also be extended to regression problems [210]. SMOTE has made an impact in various domains over the decade with a diverse set of applications [211]. 

Furthermore, a number of alterations of SMOTE, such as geometric SMOTE [212] and weighted SMOTE [213] exist. In our study, we implement some of the prominent SMOTE-based methods discussed hereafter for implementing a computational review.

Title: A comprehensive survey on Arabic text augmentation: approaches, challenges, and applications
Snippet: While data augmentation can waste computational resources by randomly generating non-informative samples, [6] suggested using active learning to save computational resources and time by selecting the most informative unlabeled training data subset. The number of training samples required for both active and passive learning was greatly decreased [7] by SMOTE augmentation. Prior to SMOTE, 100% of training samples were needed for passive learning to reach the same accuracy as active learning, which only needed 31.9% of training samples to reach 99% accuracy. SMOTE significantly reduced the number of training samples needed for active learning, which was able to achieve 99% accuracy with just 17.8% of training samples and 86.6% for passive learning.

Title: Comparative analysis of the spatial distribution of brain metastases across several primary cancers using machine learning and deep learning models
Snippet: SMOTE is a data augmentation method used to address a class imbalance in supervised machine learning problems. Class imbalance occurs when one class of a classification problem has significantly fewer samples than the other classes, which can lead to poor performance of the classifier on the minority class. SMOTE creates synthetic samples of the minority class by interpolating between existing minority class samples. The method selects a minority class sample and identifies its k nearest neighbors in the feature space. SMOTE then creates a new sample by randomly selecting one of the "k" nearest neighbors and creating a synthetic sample between the original sample and each of its neighbors that is a linear combination of the original and selected neighbors. The process repeats until the desired balance between the classes is achieved. The synthetic samples created by SMOTE increase the size of the minority class, making it more representative and improving the classifier's ability to learn the patterns in the minority class [14].

Snippet: As the number of normal records are more compared to suspected and pathological, this leads to class imbalance and hence decreases the model performance. to address this class imbalance issue we have implemented SMOTE data augmentation technique. SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique) is a technique used to address class imbalance in classification tasks. SMOTE works by generating synthetic samples for the minority class based on the existing minority samples. It creates synthetic samples by interpolating between existing minority samples in the feature space.

Snippet: We used a permutation test approach [54,55] to evaluate the statistical significance of the classification's results. In this procedure, labels are assigned randomly to the example trials, then the classifier is trained on the task with the permuted condition labels and finally the generalization performance is tested with a ''leave-one-out'' cross-validation strategy.

Title: An Efficient Data Partitioning to Improve Classification Performance While Keeping Parameters Interpretable
Snippet: In addition to reporting general classification accuracy for each of the datasets, we also report the proportion of results that were found to indicate accuracies significantly above chance. In the context of classification, statistical significance indicates whether a statistical dependence between labels and data can be assumed. A statistically significant results would reject the null hypothesis that the association of data and labels comes about by chance, and the p-value would indicate the probability of false rejection of the null hypothesis. Statistical significance was evaluated with a permutation test (number of permutations was fixed to 1,000 and statistical significance level to 0.05) [15]. 

It is worth noting that our datasets are sometimes very small and we have to repeat the permutation test many times. For that reason, it becomes important to correct the p-value for the bias introduced by the discrete nature of classification results as described in [16]. If in one permutation test the resulting p-value was in between two possible p-values around the significance level a probabilistic approach was used to determine if the given run was significant or not. Otherwise the nominal alpha level could never be approximated. The implementation of it can be found from the code in S1 Public Repository. The effect of the correction was small and did not change the results.

Title: Where do I go? Decoding temporal neural dynamics of scene processing and visuospatial memory interactions using convolutional neural networks
Snippet: After training the model on 80% of the full pooled dataset (i.e., containing data from all the subjects) with early stopping, performance was evaluated on the 20% remaining dataset using five-fold cross-validation for each individual subject. Classification accuracy was then compared with chance levels using a binomial cumulative distribution approach. For each analysis, a binomial distribution was computed using MATLAB's binoinv function, taking into account the predefined significance level (α = 0.05), the number of predictions (the average number of classifications made per participant), and the number of classes (2 for task predictions, 7 for affordances, and 8 for wall color). The binomial method was used to determine statistical significance, as it is comparable in reliability to permutation testing for datasets with more than 100 trials, but does not have the extensive computational requirements of permutation testing (Combrisson & Jerbi, 2015;Vahid, Mückschel, Stober, Stock, & Beste, 2020). We then used 100,000 iterations of bootstrap resampling to calculate the mean difference between model accuracy and a random sample drawn from the generated binomial distribution. From the bootstrap distribution of the mean differences between accuracy of the model and chance, we derived a 95% confidence interval and a p value, which are presented in the Results.

Title: Discriminative Analysis of Parkinson’s Disease Based on Whole-Brain Functional Connectivity
Snippet: In this study, we used a non-parametric permutation test to assess the statistical significance of the classification accuracy [25,26]. In permutation testing, we randomly permuted the class labels of the training data and performed the above cross-validation procedure 1,000 times. It was assumed that a classifier could reliably learn the relationship between the data and the labels when the generalization rate GR 0 obtained by the classifier that was trained on the real class labels exceeded 95% of the generalization rate obtained using randomly relabeled class labels.

Title: High Accurate and a Variant of k-fold Cross Validation Technique for Predicting the Decision Tree Classifier Accuracy
Snippet: The k-fold cross validation is a bench mark technique for evaluating the performances of classification algorithms. Cross validation is a technique that is used for finding the optimal complexity of the model. It is one among the many techniques useful to fine-tune model complexity. When the data set is very large it is divided into k-distinct groups such that each group is again divided into one training set and one validation set. All the k-folds are trained and validated separately. When the dataset is small then the same dataset is spilt into different ways for getting k-groups of training and validation sets. Repeatedly dividing the same small data set into k-groups such that each group consists of well separated training dataset and validation dataset pair is called cross validation. Cross validation is a machine learning technique used for evaluating machine learning model when the data set size is small. The bootstrap method is a basic building block for developing advanced machine learning algorithms such as Ada-Boost and XGBoost. Bootstrap technique is a data re-sampling technique using random sampling with tuple replacement. Bootstrap aggregating is frequently used in ensemble based machine learning techniques. 

If the sample dataset is very big then there is a possibility of getting a number of training/validation set pairs for k-fold cross validation and the typical value of k is generally 10 or 30. In k-fold cross validation given input dataset is divided randomly into k-partitions and again each partition is randomly divided into two equal parts such that one part is used for training and another part is used for validation. The k-fold cross validation is particularly useful when the dataset is small. It is a well known fact that repeatedly dividing the same small dataset into different pairs such that within the pair non overlapping is applied and there is a overlapping between the pairs such that each pair consists of one training set and validation set is called cross validation. In order to obtain robust error estimated training and validation sets dataset size must be large enough with minimum overlap between different k-fold groups. 

Given dataset is generally divided into pairs of training and validation sets for exclusively testing purpose. After completion of all the tests finally the entire single dataset is used only once for training and once for testing.
